summary: First end-to-end version of the ingest worker works locally: it takes a JSON batch over HTTP/2, validates it, and writes the events to Postgres in one transaction.
body:
Started the day with an empty Go module and ended with a worker that accepts a batch of events on the ingest endpoint and stores it. The HTTP/2 server is the standard library one with h2c disabled, since the load balancer will terminate TLS later. The handler reads the body with a size cap of 5 MB and rejects anything larger with 413.

The event schema is still small: an event id, a tenant id, an event type, a timestamp, and a free form properties object. I wrote it as a Go struct and a JSON schema file side by side so the two can be compared in a test. The validator is hand written for now. It checks required fields, that the timestamp parses as RFC 3339, and that the type is one of the known types.

Writes go through pgx. Each batch opens one transaction and runs a multi-row INSERT with a conflict clause on the event id, so a client that sends the same batch twice does not create duplicates. I checked this by posting the same file three times and counting rows, which stayed at 500.

A first rough measurement on my laptop with a local Postgres gave about 4000 events per second with batches of 500. CPU was mostly in JSON decoding and in the validator, not in the database. I did not tune anything yet because the numbers on a laptop mean little.

Error handling is the part I am least happy with. A batch with one bad event currently fails as a whole with 400 and a message naming the first bad index. Customers will probably want partial acceptance, so I wrote that down as an open question for the next days.

I also added a plain /healthz endpoint that returns 200 without touching the database. It is enough for the load balancer for now, but it does not say anything about whether writes work, and that needs a proper look later.

Tests cover the handler with valid batches, an empty batch, malformed JSON, an oversized body and a duplicate batch. They run against a Postgres in Docker started by a Makefile target. Everything passes in about 6 seconds.

Next steps are metrics on accepted and rejected batches, a graceful shutdown so a restart does not lose in-flight work, and a real load test on a machine that is not my laptop.

summary: Added Prometheus counters for accepted, rejected and failed batches in the ingest worker, with labels for the rejection reason.
body:
Added three counters to the ingest worker: ingest_batches_accepted_total, ingest_batches_rejected_total and ingest_batches_failed_total. The rejected counter has a reason label with the values schema, size and backpressure. A histogram for the write time of a batch was added too, with buckets from 5 ms to 5 s.

The /metrics endpoint runs on a separate port, 9102, so it does not sit behind the public listener. Checked with curl that the numbers move when I send a bad batch and a good one. Still open: a Grafana board for these, which Tobias wants to build once the worker runs on ECS.

summary: Graceful shutdown for the ingest worker now drains in-flight batches on SIGTERM, so a deploy no longer loses events.
body:
The worker used to exit at once on SIGTERM. In a test with a steady load of 50 batches per second and a kill in the middle, 11 batches that had been acknowledged were gone. That is the thing the shutdown work had to fix.

The new flow: on SIGTERM the listener stops accepting new connections, the handlers finish their current request, then the channel to the writer is closed and the main function waits on a WaitGroup for the writer to flush. A hard limit of 25 seconds applies, because ECS sends SIGKILL after 30 by default and I wanted some margin.

Repeated the kill test ten times. No acknowledged batch was lost in any run. In two runs the drain took about 4 seconds, in the rest under one second. I also added a log line with the number of batches flushed during shutdown, so we can see in production whether the limit is ever near.

One thing to watch: the load balancer keeps sending requests for a few seconds after the deregistration starts. The handlers that arrive after the listener closed get a connection reset, and the client has to retry. Tobias will set the deregistration delay on the target group to cover this, noted for the Terraform work.

summary: Added graceful drain on SIGTERM tests and a deploy check, confirming that in-flight batches finish before the ingest worker exits.
body:
Wrote a test that sends a slow batch, then signals the worker with SIGTERM while the batch is still being written. The worker stops accepting new connections, finishes the batch and exits with code 0, and the client gets its 200. Without the drain the same test fails with a connection reset, which is how I made sure the test checks the right thing.

The shutdown timeout is 25 seconds. ECS sends SIGKILL after its stop timeout, so I set the task definition stop timeout to 30 to leave some room. A batch that takes longer than 25 seconds is cancelled and the client sees a 503, which it can retry safely because of the conflict clause on the event id.

I also noticed the readiness path kept answering 200 during the drain. It now returns 503 as soon as the signal arrives, so the load balancer stops sending new requests. Next is to try this on staging with a real deploy under a steady stream of test traffic.

summary: Replaced the hand written schema validation in the ingest worker with a table driven validator, cutting its share of CPU from about 40 to 9 percent.
body:
The profile from last week showed that the validation switch was the biggest cost in the worker. I replaced it with a validator built once at startup from the schema definition: each field gets a small function for its type, and the events are checked by looping over a precompiled slice instead of reflecting over a map.

A benchmark in internal/schema with 10000 mixed events shows 41 microseconds per event before and 7 after. In the full worker profile the validation went from about 40 percent to 9 percent of the CPU.

The rules are the same as before, and I checked that with a test that feeds both validators 5000 generated events, including broken ones, and compares the error messages. Two messages differed: the old one said 'bad type' where the new one names the field. The new text is better and I kept it, and updated the two tests that matched the old string.

The timestamp question from earlier is not solved yet. The validator accepts both formats and normalizes them. I will write down in the docs that RFC 3339 is the recommended one.

Next: a load test on staging with a real Postgres size instance, to see where the writer limits us.

summary: The first load test on staging showed the Postgres writer as the limit at about 9000 events per second, caused by one index too many on the events table.
body:
Ran the first real load test against staging: 8 parallel clients, batches of 500 events, for ten minutes. The worker accepted about 9000 events per second and then the 503s started with the reason backpressure.

The write time histogram showed batches taking 300 to 400 ms. In Postgres, the events table had four indexes, one of them on (customer_id, received_at, type) that nobody queries yet, left over from an early idea. Dropping it raised the rate to about 13000 events per second at the same batch size.

The remaining cost is mostly the index on the event id and the WAL writes. Moving to COPY instead of multi-row INSERT looks like the next gain; I will try it tomorrow and compare. Also noted that the table is not partitioned, which will matter once the data grows, but that is a topic for later.

summary: Switched the ingest writer from multi-row INSERT to COPY, which raised throughput to about 21000 events per second, and fixed a duplicate event bug found on the way.
body:
Today's work was the writer. The multi-row INSERT built a statement with up to 500 times 9 parameters, which Postgres has to parse every time. I switched to the COPY protocol through pgx's CopyFrom, into the same table.

First result on staging with the same load as last time: about 21000 events per second before the first 503, against 13000. The write time per batch of 500 events dropped from about 300 ms to 60 ms. CPU on the database instance is now lower than on the worker tasks, so the worker is the next limit.

COPY brought one problem. The INSERT had an ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING clause that made client retries safe. COPY has no such clause, so a retried batch gave a unique violation and the entire batch failed, even though most events were new. I found that when a test client resent a batch after a timeout.

The fix: copy into a temporary table per transaction and then run INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into the real table. It costs some of the gain. The measured rate with the temp table approach is about 17500 events per second, still better than before by a good margin.

I wrote a test that sends the same batch three times and checks that the table has exactly one copy of each event. It passes. A second test sends a batch with half known and half new ids and checks the counts as well.

Open points: the temp table is created and dropped for each batch, and ON COMMIT DROP is used, which adds catalog churn. If it shows up in the vacuum stats later, a long living staging table could replace it. For now I leave it and will watch pg_stat_user_tables over the next days.

Next step is the worker CPU. The JSON decoding looks like the main part, and I will profile it tomorrow.

summary: Profiled the ingest worker: JSON decoding is 35 percent of the CPU, and swapping encoding/json for a faster decoder looks worth a try.
body:
A CPU profile under load shows encoding/json decode at about 35 percent, followed by the validator at 9 and GC at 12. Most allocation comes from decoding each event into map[string]interface{} before validation.

I sketched a decoder that reads into the typed struct for the known fields and keeps only the free-form payload as raw bytes. A quick benchmark of this on 10000 events gives 2.8 times fewer allocations and about half the time. The validator needs a small change to work on the struct. I will do that tomorrow and compare the full-worker numbers.

summary: Typed decoding of events in the ingest worker halved decode time, but a customer-style payload with nested arrays exposed a mismatch with the old validator that is now covered by tests.
body:
Implemented the typed decoding plan from this morning. The event struct has the fixed fields (event_id, customer_id, type, timestamp) and a json.RawMessage for the payload. The payload is only checked for being valid JSON and for size, up to 64 KB.

The benchmark on 10000 mixed events: 38 microseconds per event before, 17 after, and allocations per event went from 61 to 22. Under the staging load the worker CPU dropped by about a third, and the rate before the first 503 went from 17500 to about 24000 events per second, now limited by Postgres again.

While testing with a sample file that Sam took from a prospect's staging export, I found a difference. The old validator rejected events whose payload contained a nested array of objects deeper than 8 levels, by accident, because of a recursion limit in my own code. The typed version accepts them. I looked at the schema notes and nothing says that depth must be limited, but a limit protects the later search and the analytics queries from absurd input.

I added an explicit depth check with a limit of 16, implemented with a json.Decoder token walk over the payload bytes. It costs about 3 microseconds per event on the typical small payload and more on large ones.

Tests added:
- depth 16 passes, depth 17 is rejected with the reason schema
- a payload of exactly 64 KB passes, one byte more is rejected with reason size
- invalid JSON in the payload is rejected, and the rest of the batch is reported per event

The per event error report is a change in the response too. Before, a bad event failed the whole batch. Now the response lists the indexes of rejected events and the good ones are written. I discussed this with myself in the code comments: partial acceptance is friendlier for the customers, and with the idempotent write from yesterday a client can safely resend the whole batch.

The API doc draft needs this change. I left a note in docs/ingest.md for Sam, who starts on the docs later.

Still open: the temp table churn from yesterday. I looked at pg_stat_user_tables after the load tests and the catalog tables show a lot of dead tuples, so the plan to move to a long living staging table is likely needed.

summary: Replaced the per-batch temporary table in the writer with a long living staging table, which removed the catalog bloat seen after the load tests.
body:
After the load tests, pg_class and pg_attribute in staging had tens of thousands of dead tuples, because each batch created and dropped a temp table. Autovacuum kept up, but it is silly work for a hot path.

The new design: one unlogged table events_staging with the same columns plus a batch_id uuid. Each batch is copied into it with its own batch_id, and then one statement inserts from it into events with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and deletes the rows of that batch. All of it is one transaction.

First version had a problem. Under 8 parallel writers the DELETE by batch_id did a sequential scan of the staging table, as the table is mostly empty but has bloat from the churn, and that led to lock waits. I added an index on batch_id. Then the scan disappeared, but the index itself became hot and grew. Tried a different approach: partition the staging table by hash of batch_id into 8 partitions, one per writer slot. Too complicated for the gain, so I dropped that idea after an hour.

Final choice is the plain unlogged table with the batch_id index, and a TRUNCATE in a maintenance step at startup of the worker when no other worker is running is not safe, so no truncate; instead autovacuum settings for this table are tightened: scale factor 0.01 and cost delay 2 ms.

Measured on staging with the usual load: about 23000 events per second, close to the 24000 of the temp table-free ideal from the morning, and the dead tuples in the catalog tables stay flat. The unlogged table loses its content on a crash, which is fine because acknowledged batches are in events after the commit and the staging rows are only valid inside a transaction.

I wrote a test for the crash case with a kill -9 of Postgres in a docker container in the middle of a load. After the restart the events table had no partial batches and no duplicates after the clients resent.

The migration for the new table is in migrations/0007_staging.sql. Next topic is the CSV importer for bigger customer files.

summary: Started the batch importer for CSV and NDJSON files: a streaming reader maps rows to events and sends them through the same writer as the API, tested on a 2 GB file.
body:
Began the batch importer today. The goal is that a customer can hand us a big CSV or NDJSON file with historical events, and we load it with the same validation and write path as the API, without loading the file into memory.

The structure is a command, cmd/importer, with three parts. A reader streams the file line by line, with a bufio.Reader of 1 MB so long lines are fine. A mapper turns a CSV row into an event using a column mapping from a small YAML file, or passes the NDJSON line to the typed decoder from the ingest worker. A sender collects events into batches of 1000 and calls the shared writer package.

The writer was inside the worker package until now. I moved it to internal/writer so both programs use it. The move changed import paths in 14 files and the tests passed without other edits, which is a good sign for the boundaries.

First test: a generated 2 GB NDJSON file with about 9 million events. The importer ran for 7 minutes 20 seconds, about 20000 events per second, with a memory use under 90 MB. That matches the writer limits we measured, so the reader and mapper are not the bottleneck.

CSV is harder. Quoted fields with line breaks inside broke the line based reader. I switched the CSV path to encoding/csv with LazyQuotes off and ReuseRecord on. A test file with embedded newlines and escaped quotes now parses correctly. Wrong rows are written to a rejects file next to the input, with the line number and the reason, and the run continues.

The timestamp issue from the first week comes back here: CSV files have all kinds of date formats. For now the mapping file takes a layout string for the timestamp column, in Go's reference time format, and the default is RFC 3339. Sam will probably get questions about this later, so I wrote an example into the importer README.

What is missing:
- resume after a crash; at the moment a failed run starts from the beginning, and the idempotent write makes that safe but slow
- progress output; only a line every 100000 events
- a limit on parallel importers so that they do not starve the live API

The last point worries me most. A second importer run at the same time as the load test cut the API rate by half. A simple token bucket in the sender, with a configured events per second, comes next. Then the resume feature through an offset file.

summary: Added a rate limit to the importer sender and an offset file for resuming, so a crashed import continues where it stopped and does not starve the live API.
body:
Two features for the importer, both from the list this morning.

The rate limit uses golang.org/x/time/rate with a flag --max-eps, default 5000. The sender waits on the limiter before it writes a batch of 1000. With a second importer and the live load test running at once, the API rate stayed within 4 percent of the baseline at 5000 events per second.

For the resume, the sender writes an offset file after each committed batch, with the byte offset of the last line in that batch and the number of events so far. The write is to a temp file and a rename, so it is never half written. At startup the importer reads the file, seeks to the offset and continues. For gzip input a seek is not possible, so the importer reads and discards up to the offset; slow but correct.

Tested with kill -9 at random points, 15 runs on a 500 MB file. Every run finished with exactly the expected event count and no duplicates. In 3 runs the last batch was written twice, which the idempotent write absorbed.

One detail to remember: the offset must be taken after the commit, not before. I first had it the wrong way round and a kill between them lost a batch. The test with the final count caught it, and I fixed the order.

Progress output now prints events per second and an estimate of the time left, based on the file size and the offset.

summary: Wired the importer to the staging database and found that long files stall because a single transaction held the whole import; it now commits every chunk.
body:
Ran the batch importer on staging with a 6 GB NDJSON file late in the evening. After about 20 minutes the throughput dropped to almost nothing and the database showed one transaction open for the whole run, with autovacuum unable to clean anything behind it.

The cause was my own change from the day before. The importer opened one transaction per file to make a failed import all or nothing. For large files this is the wrong choice, because it blocks vacuum and grows the table without bound while it runs.

I changed it to commit every 50,000 events, and the offset of the last commit is stored next to the data. A crashed import now keeps the finished chunks, and the next run continues from the stored offset. Since the writer already ignores duplicate event ids, a chunk that is repeated after a crash does no harm.

The same 6 GB file then ran through in 31 minutes at a steady rate, and the oldest open transaction stayed under a few seconds. Memory of the importer stayed flat at around 120 MB, which confirms the streaming reader does its job.

One leftover is that the progress log prints a line per chunk, which is too noisy for files with hundreds of chunks. I will move it to one line per minute. I also want a summary at the end with counts of read, written and rejected rows, since support will ask for exactly that after the first customer import.

summary: Moved ingest worker config and secrets out of plain environment variables into AWS Secrets Manager, with the task role reading them at startup.
body:
The staging service still took the database password and the API signing key from plain environment variables in the task definition, which means they show up in the console. Today I moved them to Secrets Manager.

In Terraform, each secret is an aws_secretsmanager_secret with the value set outside of the state through a manual put, so the secret does not land in the state file. The task definition uses the secrets block with valueFrom, and ECS injects the value into the container at start. The execution role got a policy limited to those secret ARNs.

The first apply failed with an access denied on the KMS key, because the secrets use a customer managed key. I added kms:Decrypt for the execution role on that key, and then the tasks started.

A side effect to know: ECS reads the secret at task start only. Changing a secret needs a new deployment of the service. I added a short section about that to the runbook, with the command to force a new deployment.

Tobias and I looked at rotation. The database password could be rotated by the managed Lambda, but the worker keeps a pool of connections opened with the old password, and new connections only after the restart. For now no automatic rotation, a manual one with a rolling restart.

Checked after the deploy:
- the task definition shows only the secret ARNs, no values
- the service reached steady state with 2 tasks
- a test batch through the load balancer arrived in the events table

I also removed the old plain variables from the staging definition and rebuilt the production definition draft in the same way, not yet applied. Production comes with the first customer deploy, which is a few days away.

The next point is the deploy pipeline, a build that pushes the image and updates the service without manual steps.

summary: First version of the deploy pipeline builds the worker image, pushes it to ECR and updates the staging ECS service after the tests pass.
body:
Set up the pipeline in the CI system today. The stages are: run go vet and go test, build the Docker image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, tag it with the commit sha, push to ECR and then update the ECS service with a new task definition revision.

The final image is based on distroless static and is 19 MB. The build takes about 3 minutes, most of it the module download, so I added a cache for the Go module directory, which brought the build to about 90 seconds.

The deploy step uses a small script that renders the task definition with the new image tag, registers it and calls update-service, then waits for the service to be stable. If it is not stable after 10 minutes the script fails and prints the last events of the service.

A first run failed on that wait: the new task did not pass its health check since I had forgotten that the staging table migration must run before the worker starts. I added a migration step before the deploy, using the same image with the migrate command, as a one-off ECS task.

The second run went through. Rollback is manual for now: re-register the previous revision. I wrote the command in the runbook. A proper automatic rollback on failed health checks is something the circuit breaker setting of ECS can do, and I will look at it next.

summary: Enabled the ECS deployment circuit breaker and tracked down a startup crash loop to the worker reading a secret before its database was reachable.
body:
I turned on the deployment circuit breaker with rollback in the Terraform for the service, as planned. To test it, I deployed a build on purpose that exits with an error at startup. ECS tried the new task three times, marked the deployment failed and went back to the previous revision after about 6 minutes. That works as hoped.

While testing I hit a real problem. A deployment of a good build crash-looped about once in five tries. The log said 'dial tcp: i/o timeout' to the database at startup, and the worker exited at once, because the startup code does one connection attempt and fails hard.

The reason is the order of events in staging: when Postgres is restarted for maintenance, or when security group changes are still applying, the first attempt can time out. With the circuit breaker, a crash loop then leads to a rollback of a good build, which is confusing.

Change in the worker: the startup connection now tries up to 10 times with a growing wait, starting at 500 ms and doubling to a cap of 8 seconds, and logs each attempt with the error. After that it exits. The health check grace period of 60 seconds covers the longest series of waits, which is about 45 seconds in total.

I tested this by blocking the database port with a security group rule for 20 seconds during a deploy. The worker logged 4 failed attempts, connected on the fifth and passed the health check. Before the change the same test ended in a rollback.

Smaller things done in the same session:
- the health endpoint now reports 503 until the pool has one working connection, so the load balancer does not send traffic early
- the log line format at startup includes the image tag, which helps when looking at the rollback events
- removed a duplicated environment block in the Terraform module

Open: the circuit breaker only watches the task start. If a build starts fine and then fails on a code path that the health check does not touch, ECS will not notice. A deeper health check that writes a test event is possible, but it would add a write on every check, so I want to talk to Tobias before doing it.

Next: the first production environment, with the same module and a larger database instance.

summary: Decided against a write-probing health check for the ingest worker and added a cheap readiness check on the writer queue depth instead.
body:
Talked it over with Tobias, and we agreed that a health check that writes an event every few seconds is not worth it. It adds load, it adds fake events that need to be filtered everywhere, and it can make a healthy worker look sick when the database is merely slow.

Instead the readiness endpoint now checks three cheap things: the pool has a working connection, the writer goroutine is alive (it updates a timestamp every second), and the queue to the writer is not full for more than 10 seconds in a row. If any of them fails the endpoint returns 503.

The writer liveness is the part that was missing. I once saw in a test that the writer goroutine had died from a panic in the COPY code while the HTTP handlers still ran, and the worker went on accepting batches that were never written. A recover with a log line and a process exit now handles the panic, so ECS replaces the task.

Tests:
- a unit test that blocks the writer and checks that the readiness turns to 503 after the limit
- a unit test that panics in the writer and checks that the exit function is called

I ran both on the staging service as well. Blocking the writer with a lock on the events table made the readiness turn to 503 after about 12 seconds, and the load balancer stopped sending traffic to that task. After releasing the lock it came back after one more check.

The load balancer health check interval is 10 seconds with 2 failures to unhealthy, so the full time from fault to removal is about 30 seconds, which I find acceptable for now. I wrote the numbers in the runbook.

summary: Created the production environment with the same Terraform module, a larger Postgres instance and a first customer API key, and ran a smoke test against it.
body:
Applied the Terraform module for production today with its own variables: 4 worker tasks, a db.r6g.xlarge Postgres instance with 500 GB of storage and backups on, and the load balancer with a real certificate from ACM for the ingest domain.

The certificate validation by DNS took about 20 minutes and delayed the listener. Everything else applied in one go after I fixed a naming clash with a staging security group by adding the environment name as a prefix.

The secrets were put in by hand as with staging, and the migration task ran before the first deploy. After that I created the first customer account and an API key through the SQL script in tools/, since the admin console does not exist yet.

Smoke test: a script sent 100 batches of 500 events with the new key. All 50000 events were in the table, the metrics showed 100 accepted and none rejected, and the p99 write time was 45 ms. A second run with a wrong key returned 401 as it should.

Notes for later: no alarms exist yet on production, only the dashboards in Grafana that Tobias copied from staging. Alerts are the next piece, then the onboarding of the first customer, which is planned for the coming days.

summary: Added the first alerts for production ingest: error rate of the API, writer queue depth and database connections close to the limit.
body:
Wrote three alert rules in Prometheus for the production ingest service, wired to PagerDuty through Alertmanager.

The first fires when the share of 5xx answers is above 2 percent for 5 minutes. The second fires when the writer queue is above 80 percent full for 3 minutes, which is the early sign of backpressure. The third fires when the database connections are above 85 percent of max_connections.

I tested the first two in staging by stopping the database for a minute and by throttling the writer. Both alerts fired and the PagerDuty test incident came to my phone. The thresholds are guesses and I will tune them once there is real traffic. The rules are in the monitoring directory of the repository so they are reviewed like code.

summary: First customer onboarding went through: their NDJSON history of 14 million events was imported at a limited rate, and two schema surprises led to fixes in the mapper.
body:
The first customer sent an NDJSON export of about 14 million events, and I ran the importer against production with --max-eps 6000 so the live traffic of the other test accounts was not disturbed. The run took about 40 minutes.

The first attempt failed after 3 minutes with many rejects. The reason in the rejects file was 'timestamp' for about 30 percent of the lines. Looking at the lines, the customer's export mixes epoch seconds and epoch milliseconds in the same field, depending on which of their services wrote the event. The worker took everything as milliseconds, and the seconds values were rejected as too old.

I first thought of a heuristic: values below 10 to the power of 11 are seconds. That is the kind of guess that goes wrong silently one day, so instead I added an explicit option to the mapping, timestamp_unit with the values s, ms and auto. Auto applies the heuristic, but it logs a warning with a count when it triggers, and it is off by default. For this customer we use auto, after checking a sample of 200 lines by hand, where all seconds values were from the right year range.

The second surprise: some events had a customer_id field inside the payload that differed from the account of the API key. The writer overwrites the customer id from the key, which is correct, but the customer wondered why their own ids disappeared. The original value stays in the payload, so nothing is lost, and I explained that in the reply that Sam helped draft.

Second run went through with 14012330 events written, 118 rejected for broken JSON, and the rejects file was sent back to the customer. The idempotent write meant that rerunning the first 3 minutes did not duplicate anything, and I checked the count with a query grouped by event_id that returned no duplicates.

Metrics during the import: the writer queue stayed under 30 percent, the live API p99 stayed at 50 ms, and the database CPU peaked at 55 percent. The rate limit worked as designed.

What I want to improve:
- the importer should print the reject count by reason at the end
- a dry run mode that only validates and counts, so we can check a file before the real run
- Postgres storage grew by about 9 GB for this customer, which is more than I had estimated, so I should look at the table and index sizes soon

The dry run mode is the next small task.

summary: Added a dry run mode and a reject summary by reason to the importer, so a customer file can be checked before the real import.
body:
Both improvements from the onboarding are in. With --dry-run the importer reads and maps the file and runs the full validation, but the sender does not call the writer. The output is the number of events that would be written, the number that would be rejected and a table of reject reasons with counts and the first example line for each reason.

The summary is printed at the end of every run now, dry or real. For the customer file it shows 118 rejects, all with the reason json, which matches what we saw.

I ran the dry run on the same 14 million event file and it took 6 minutes, since no database is involved, about 39000 events per second on my laptop. That makes it practical to check big files in advance.

One bug showed up: the dry run still wrote the offset file, so a following real run would have skipped everything. Fixed by not writing offsets in dry run mode, and I added a test that runs a dry run and then a real run on a small file and checks the count.

Docs are updated in the importer README with the new flag, the timestamp_unit option and an example output of the summary.

Also looked at the storage question. The events table is 21 GB for roughly 20 million events, about 1 KB per event, and the payload JSON is stored as jsonb. The index on event_id is 1.4 GB. Nothing alarming yet, but it is a number to track.

summary: Looked at table and index sizes of the events table in Postgres and decided to partition it by month before more customers arrive.
body:
After the onboarding I wanted a plan for growth. With 20 million events at 21 GB and about 40 customers expected over the coming months, some of them sending much more than the first one, the table will reach hundreds of gigabytes. A single table of that size makes vacuum, index maintenance and deletes slow.

I wrote a design note, docs/design/events-partitioning.md. The proposal is declarative range partitioning on received_at by month, with the unique constraint on event_id becoming (event_id, received_at), because Postgres requires the partition key in a unique index. That changes the idempotency of the write: the same event_id sent in two different months would no longer collide. I think that is acceptable, since a retry arrives within minutes, not weeks, but it must be said in the docs.

I tested this on a copy of staging with 20 million generated events. The partitioned version had inserts at the same speed as before, 22000 events per second, and a query for one customer and one day touched only one partition and ran in 40 ms instead of 180 ms.

A migration of the live table is the hard part. The plan is to create the partitioned table next to the old one, switch the writer to the new table, and move old rows in batches by a background job. During the move reads must look at both tables, through a view with UNION ALL.

Questions left for the next days:
- who creates the next month's partition; a job in the worker at startup is fragile, so a scheduled task is better
- what to do with events with a wrong timestamp far in the future, which would need a default partition
- how the importer behaves with old events, which land in old partitions and need them to exist

I will start with the scheduled task for creating partitions, since the other steps depend on it.

summary: Built the partition maintenance job for the events table with a default partition for odd timestamps, and tested the importer against old months.
body:
First step of the partitioning plan: the maintenance job. It is a small Go command, cmd/partitions, that runs as a scheduled ECS task once a day. It makes sure that partitions exist for the current month and the next three, and it creates missing ones with CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF, using IF NOT EXISTS so a rerun does nothing.

A default partition, events_default, catches everything that has no matching month. The job also counts the rows in the default partition and exposes the number as a metric, with an alert rule at more than 1000 rows. A growing default partition means either broken client clocks or old data without a partition, and both want a human to look.

For the importer, historic files will have events from many months. I added a pre-scan option --ensure-partitions: the importer does a quick pass over the file, takes the min and max timestamps and calls the same partition code for that range. The dry run reports the range as well. Tested with a file spanning 26 months, and the 26 partitions were created before the first write.

One problem: creating a partition takes a lock on the parent table, which blocks inserts for the moment it takes. In staging under load, the creation took 30 to 80 ms and the writers waited that long, no failures. Since the job runs daily and creates only a few partitions, it is fine. For the importer pre-scan with many partitions I serialize creation, one at a time with a short pause, so the live writers are not blocked for longer stretches.

A test for the job runs against a real Postgres in docker:
- first run creates 4 partitions, second run creates none
- an event with a timestamp ten years ahead lands in the default partition and the metric shows 1
- a missing middle partition is filled in without touching the others

The next steps are the writer switch to the new table and the view for reads. I will write the migration script for moving old rows tomorrow, in batches of 50000 with a pause between them so vacuum can keep up.

summary: Partition maintenance now runs from a scheduled ECS task, and a month boundary test showed that rows landing exactly at midnight go to the right partition.
body:
The maintenance job from the morning was still only a binary I ran by hand. I wrapped it in a scheduled ECS task that runs once a day and creates partitions for the next three months.

The main worry was the month boundary. I wrote a test that inserts events with timestamps at 23:59:59.999 and 00:00:00.000 around a month change, in UTC and with offsets from customer payloads. All of them ended up in the expected partitions.

One case failed at first. Events with a timezone offset were converted by the writer after routing, so a few rows near midnight went to the neighbouring month. The writer now normalizes the timestamp to UTC before it builds the COPY batch.

The default partition catches anything older than the first partition or far in the future. I added a Prometheus gauge for its row count. If the gauge is above zero, something odd arrived and I want to look at it.

I also checked that the unique index on the event id still works across partitions. It does, because the partition key is part of the index, but this means duplicate detection is now per month. The duplicate fix from last week only needs the id and the timestamp, so it is not affected.

Still to do: drop old partitions by policy, which needs a decision with the customers about retention. The task has a dry run flag that prints what it would create. Next I will run it against staging for a few days and watch the gauge.

summary: Load tested the partitioned events table on staging: write throughput held at about 20000 events per second, and queries with a time filter prune partitions as expected.
body:
After partitioning the events table by month I wanted proof that nothing got worse. I ran the same load test as before the change, with the staging worker and a synthetic stream of 30 million events spread over six months.

Write throughput was about 20000 events per second, against 21000 before. The small drop comes from routing rows to partitions in COPY. I think it is acceptable, and I did not try to fix it.

For reads, I ran the five slowest queries from the support list with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Four of them have a time range, and the plans show only the relevant partitions scanned. The count by customer for the last 30 days went from 4.1 seconds to 0.9 seconds on the test data.

The fifth query has no time filter and scans every partition. It is the 'all events of one customer' export. It is slower than before by about 15 percent because of the extra plan nodes. I noted it, since the export is rare.

Autovacuum behaves better. Each month is a small table and the old months stop changing, so vacuum has nothing to do for them. The big table had bloat after the importer runs.

One surprise was planning time. With 24 partitions it is still low, about 2 ms, but it grows with the partition count. I checked the Postgres docs and the limit is far away for us.

I also tested a backup restore of a single partition into a scratch database. It works and takes a few minutes.

Open points: the index set per partition is created by the maintenance job, so I need a check that the indexes of new partitions match the old ones. I will write that check next.

The results table is in the repo notes folder, under the partitioning file, with the exact queries so I can repeat the test after the next schema change.

summary: Wrote a check that compares the indexes of every events partition with the template and found that two older partitions miss the customer index.
body:
The partition job creates indexes on each new partition, so a typo in the job would silently produce partitions without them. I wrote a small check that reads pg_indexes for all partitions and compares them with the definition on the template table.

The first run on staging reported two partitions without the customer and time index. They were the two created by hand during the first test of the migration, before the job existed. I created the indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and the check passed.

The check compares index definitions after stripping the partition name, so it compares the columns and the method. It does not compare storage parameters. I thought about that and decided it was not worth the complexity.

I added the check as a mode of the maintenance binary. It exits non-zero and prints the partition and the missing index. The scheduled task runs it after the creation step.

A failing check should alert. I added a Prometheus counter for failed checks and a rule that fires if it is above zero for ten minutes. The alert text says which partition and which index.

I tested the failure path by dropping an index on a staging partition. The alert fired after about eleven minutes, as expected, and the job output named the right index.

One more thing I found: the default partition has no customer index at all, on purpose. If it ever has rows, queries on it are slow. The gauge for its row count already covers this.

Next is production. The plan is to run the migration of the existing events table in a quiet window, with the importer paused. I will write the runbook first.

summary: Drafted the runbook for moving the production events table to monthly partitions, with a rollback point after each step.
body:
The runbook has six steps: pause the importer, create the partitioned table, copy by month, verify counts, swap the names in one transaction, and resume. Each step lists the command and what to check.

The copy runs month by month with INSERT SELECT, so a failure leaves earlier months done. The rollback up to the swap is to drop the new table. After the swap, the old table stays for a week under a different name.

I estimated the copy time from staging at about 40 minutes for the current size. I asked nobody to review yet. I will read it once more tomorrow and then ask Tobias to check the Terraform side, since the database instance needs spare disk for the copy.

summary: Tobias confirmed the production database has enough disk for the partition copy, and I added a free space check to the first step of the runbook.
body:
Tobias looked at the production Postgres volume. It is at 48 percent, and the copy needs about the size of the events table once more, so there is room. He still wanted a safety margin.

I added a first step to the runbook: check free disk, and stop if it is below 40 percent. I also added a note to watch the WAL size during the copy, since the replica could lag.

Tobias suggested raising the volume size anyway before the window, because resizing later takes time. He did it in Terraform and applied it to production. No downtime was involved. The runbook is ready for the window.

summary: Ran the production partition migration in a quiet window: 61 million events copied in 38 minutes, counts matched, and the swap took under a second.
body:
I started at about 16:00 after pausing the importer. The disk check passed at 46 percent free after Tobias's resize.

The copy ran month by month, as planned. Total time was 38 minutes for 61 million rows. The replica lag peaked at about 40 seconds during the largest month and went back to zero a few minutes after.

For verification I compared the row count per month in the old and new tables, and also a checksum over the event ids per month. All twelve months matched. I did not trust the counts alone, because the duplicate bug from earlier could have left rows that differ only in id.

The swap was a single transaction with two renames and a lock on both tables. The live API kept accepting batches in the writer queue during that second, and the queue depth rose briefly but drained.

After the swap I ran the index check on the new partitions, and it passed. I resumed the importer and watched the ingest dashboard for half an hour. Error rate stayed at zero, and the writer latency was about the same as before.

One problem appeared. A reporting query used by support referred to the table with a hard coded index hint in a view, and the view broke after the rename. I recreated the view against the new table. It was my miss, I had only grepped the code, not the database objects.

I added a step to the runbook for listing dependent views before a swap. I also wrote a note for Sam, in case he sees stale numbers in his saved queries.

The old table stays as events_old for a week. After that I will drop it. Disk use is about the same as before, as expected.

What remains is the retention policy for old partitions. I do not want to drop anything until the customers have been told.

summary: Switched the events table partition job to the new monthly layout in the importer and API writers, and a test with out-of-order timestamps showed the default partition catches only truly odd rows.
body:
Slot 7 sits between the partition maintenance job and the production runbook, so this session was about making the writers agree with the layout. The ingest writer and the batch importer both insert through the same function, and I checked that neither one sets the partition by hand; Postgres routes each row by its timestamp, which is what we want.

I wrote a test that sends a batch with timestamps spread over six months, shuffled, plus a handful of rows far in the future and a few with a zero timestamp. The six months landed in their own partitions. The future and zero rows went to the default partition, as designed, and nothing else did.

One surprise: the COPY into the long living staging table and then INSERT SELECT into the events table was fine, but the old importer path that wrote chunks directly with COPY into the parent table was about 8 percent slower. The cause was the routing cost for batches that mix many months. Sorting each chunk by timestamp before writing removed most of that gap, so the importer sorts chunks now.

I also looked at what the default partition would hold after a large historical import. With the dry run mode, the reject summary now lists how many rows would go to the default partition, so a customer file with odd dates is visible before the real import. This is a small addition in the dry run report, with a test.

Remaining: the check that compares the indexes of all partitions with the template, and the runbook for the production move. Next I will write the index check, since a missing index on one partition would show up only under load.

summary: Built the first Fastify search endpoint with API key authentication, a query string parameter and a time range, returning hits and a total count.
body:
I created the search service as a small Fastify app with one route, GET /v1/search. It takes a query string q, from and to timestamps, and a limit with a maximum of 100.

Authentication reads the API key from a header and looks it up in Postgres. The result is cached in memory for 60 seconds, so the key lookup does not hit the database on each request. The customer id from the key is always added as a filter to the OpenSearch query. I wrote a test that tries to search with another customer's id in the query string, and it must be ignored.

The query is a bool query with the customer filter and the time range as filters, so they are cacheable, and a simple query string for the text. I disabled the lenient wildcards on leading characters, since a leading wildcard scans the whole index.

The response has the hits with id, time, type and a short message, plus a total. Total hits are capped at 10000 in OpenSearch by default. I kept that cap and return a flag when the number is a lower bound, because exact counts are expensive.

Pagination is by search_after on time and id, not by offset. Deep offsets are slow, and the console only needs next page.

Schema validation of the query parameters uses the Fastify JSON schema support. Wrong input gives a 400 with a clear message. I added tests for empty q, a time range in the wrong order and a limit of zero.

I ran a quick load test with 50 concurrent clients. The median latency was 45 ms, the 99th percentile about 300 ms, mostly from the phrase queries.

It is not deployed yet. The next steps are the deploy to staging, the metrics and an error format that matches the ingest API.

summary: Deployed the search API to staging on ECS and added request metrics and a shared error format, after a startup crash from a missing OpenSearch credential.
body:
I added the search service to the Terraform module as another ECS service behind its own target group. It reuses the pattern of the ingest worker: config from Secrets Manager, readiness check, circuit breaker on deploy.

The first deploy failed. The task started, then crashed, and the circuit breaker rolled it back. The log showed that the OpenSearch password was read from a secret that did not exist in staging. I had created it only in my local setup. I created the secret and added it to the Terraform for both environments, so production will not have the same surprise.

After that the service came up. I called the endpoint with a staging key and got results from the 5 million events.

For metrics, I used prom-client with a histogram of request durations, labelled by route and status code. The buckets go from 10 ms to 5 s. I also count OpenSearch errors separately from client errors.

The error format is the same as in the ingest API: a JSON object with a code and a message, and a request id. The request id is also logged. Support will be able to ask a customer for the id.

I added a readiness check that runs a trivial query against OpenSearch with a one second timeout. If OpenSearch is down, the service reports not ready and the load balancer stops sending traffic.

One decision: timeouts. The search request has a 5 second timeout on the OpenSearch side, set in the query. A runaway query should not hold a thread for a long time. The API returns 504 with a code for it.

I will watch the staging metrics for two days. Next, the rate limiter, which Redis will hold. Without a limit a customer script could take the whole search cluster.

summary: First version of the Redis rate limiter for the search API: a fixed window counter per API key, tested with a burst script, with the window key naming chosen.
body:
The limiter lives in the search service as a Fastify hook. For each request it increments a counter in Redis and sets a TTL on the first increment. If the count is above the limit, the request gets 429 with a Retry-After header.

Key naming: rl:search:{apiKeyId}:{windowStart}, where windowStart is the current time divided by the window length. The prefix lets me find and count the keys in a monitor session. The TTL is the window length plus a few seconds, so old windows go away.

I used a Lua script for increment plus expire, so both are atomic. An earlier version did INCR and then EXPIRE as two calls, and a crash between them could leave a key with no TTL. I found this in a test where I killed the process at the wrong moment on purpose.

The default limit is 600 requests per minute per key. It is stored in the settings table in Postgres, with an override per customer. The service reads the settings with a cache of a minute.

I ran a burst script with 20 parallel clients using one key. The limit worked: exactly 600 requests passed in the window and the rest got 429. At the window edge a client can send up to twice the limit within a short time, which is the known weakness of fixed windows. For now this is fine.

Redis latency for the limiter call was about 0.4 ms from the ECS task in staging. The connection uses a small pool of 10 connections per task.

What happens if Redis is down? I decided to fail open: the request passes, and an error counter in Prometheus is incremented. A broken limiter should not become a search outage. I added a test for this with the client pointed to a closed port.

Next: expose the limit in response headers, and think about a sliding window.

summary: Added rate limit headers to the search responses and tried a sliding window counter, which was dropped because the extra Redis calls were not worth the smoother limit.
body:
First the simple part. Every search response now has X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset. The Lua script returns the count, and the hook computes the rest from it and the window start. A 429 response also has the Retry-After in seconds.

Then I tried the sliding window. The idea is to keep the count of the current and the previous window and weigh the previous one by how much of it still overlaps. It removes the edge burst of the fixed window.

I implemented it in a second Lua script with two keys and ran the same burst test. The numbers were better at the window edge: a client could send about 10 percent over the limit, not 100 percent.

The cost was visible. Each request now reads two keys, and the script is more complex. The Redis time per call went from 0.4 to 0.6 ms in staging, and the code needed a lot more test cases around the weighting and rounding. There were also off by one results in the tests, where a client got a 429 one request early.

I asked myself what the limit protects. It protects the search cluster from a runaway script, and a burst of twice the limit for a few seconds does not hurt it. So the smoother limit does not buy us anything real. I removed the sliding window script and kept the fixed window. The branch commit is gone, only a note in the docs file stays about why.

I also wrote a test for the headers, including the reset time near the window edge.

Sam asked what customers will see in the docs, so I wrote a short paragraph: the limits, the headers and the advice to back off on 429 with the Retry-After value. He will fit it into the public API docs later.

Next: look at the admin console, where customers should see their usage.

summary: Wrote the first admin console API for customers: account settings, API key list with create and revoke, and a usage endpoint fed from the rate limiter counters.
body:
Lena starts on the React part of the admin console next week, so I built the backend endpoints she needs first. They are in the same Fastify codebase, under /admin, with session authentication.

The session store is Redis. A session is a random id in a cookie, httpOnly and secure, and a hash in Redis with the user id and the customer id. The TTL is 8 hours and gets refreshed on use. Logout deletes the key.

Endpoints: GET and PATCH for account settings, GET for the list of API keys, POST to create a key and DELETE to revoke one. A new key is shown once in the response, and only a hash is stored in Postgres. The list shows a prefix of the key, the name, the creation time and the last used time.

Revoking a key has to take effect quickly. The search service caches key lookups for 60 seconds, so a revoked key could work for another minute. I added a small Redis set of revoked key ids that the lookup checks before the cache, so the effect is immediate.

The usage endpoint reads the daily counts of requests per key. The limiter counters are short lived, so I added a job that adds them to a Postgres table every five minutes by scanning the current window keys. It works, but scanning keys by pattern is something I do not like on a bigger Redis. I noted it, and a better way is to increment a second daily counter in the same Lua script. I did that, and the scan job is not needed anymore.

Tests cover the authorization: a user of one customer cannot read or revoke the keys of another customer. I wrote ten cases for this, and found that the revoke endpoint checked only the key id. It now also checks the customer id.

I wrote an OpenAPI description of the admin endpoints for Lena. Next is the audit of who changed what, which compliance will want.

summary: Slow dashboard queries for the largest customer hit 30 seconds on the Postgres events table, and EXPLAIN showed a sequential scan from a stale statistics problem on the new partitions.
body:
Support forwarded a complaint: the dashboard of our largest customer times out. I looked at the query first. It counts events by type per hour for the last seven days.

On production it took about 30 seconds. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on the two newest partitions, with an estimate of a few hundred rows against 9 million real ones. So the planner chose a bad plan because of the missing statistics.

The cause is the way partitions are created: a new partition is empty, gets filled by the writer fast, and autovacuum analyze runs only after 10 percent of the rows have changed plus a threshold. On a fast growing table that came late. Also, the parent table has no statistics of its own unless analyze runs on it directly, and autovacuum does not do that for partitioned tables.

I ran ANALYZE on the two partitions by hand, and the query went to 2.3 seconds with an index scan. That is still not good, but it is the actual query cost.

For a lasting fix I changed the maintenance job. After the creation step it sets lower autovacuum analyze scale factors on the current month partitions, 0.01, and it runs ANALYZE on the previous month on the first day of a month. I tested it on staging with a synthetic load.

I also looked at the 2.3 seconds. The query groups by hour on a timestamp column, and a covering index with customer, time and type would allow an index only scan. I tried the index on one partition. The time dropped to 0.8 seconds, but the index is 2 GB. I held back, since the real answer is probably a pre-aggregated table, and the dashboards are the reason for that.

I wrote a summary for the team, with the numbers. The timeouts of the dashboards for large customers are going to be a recurring problem in this design. I plan to think about a rollup table next.

summary: Built an hourly rollup table in Postgres for dashboard counts, filled by a job, which brought the largest customer's weekly dashboard query from 2.3 seconds to about 40 ms.
body:
The dashboards mostly need counts by event type and hour. Those can be computed once per hour and stored. I created a table events_hourly with customer id, hour, event type and count, with a primary key on those three columns.

The job runs every five minutes. It recomputes the current and the previous hour from the events partitions with an INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. The previous hour is included because late events arrive, and some customers send batches with timestamps up to half an hour old.

Late events older than two hours are a problem. A customer who imports history, with the importer, writes into months back. For those, the job would not see the change. I added a dirty marker: the writer records the touched customer and hour pairs in a small table when the event time is older than two hours, and the job recomputes those hours and clears the markers.

I first tried to do this with a trigger on the events table. It slowed the COPY a lot, down to about 14000 events per second in the test. So I dropped the trigger and did the marker in the writer, once per batch and distinct pair, which cost almost nothing.

The backfill of the existing data took 25 minutes on production, one month at a time, run at low priority at a quiet moment. I compared the sums against the raw counts for a sample of 20 customer weeks, and all matched.

The dashboard query now reads the rollup. For the largest customer and a week, the time went from 2.3 seconds to about 40 ms. A month view takes about 120 ms.

Limitations: only counts by type. Anything with attribute filters still goes to the raw table. Lena wants a filter by one attribute in the dashboards, and this is going to need more thought.

I added a gauge for the age of the newest rolled up hour and an alert if it is more than 30 minutes behind.

summary: Wired the admin console dashboard endpoint to the hourly rollup and kept a fallback to the raw table for attribute filters, with a visible limit on the time range.
body:
The dashboard endpoint now chooses its source. Without an attribute filter it reads events_hourly. With a filter, it reads the raw partitions, and the time range is limited to 7 days so a query cannot scan the whole history.

The limit is returned as an error with a clear code, and Lena can show it as a message in the console. I tested both paths with the staging data and compared the counts for the same range without a filter. They matched.

I also added the response time to the logs for both sources. The raw path takes about one second for a week of the large customer, which is acceptable for filtered views for now.

summary: Started the audit log in Postgres: an append only table with actor, action, target and a JSON detail, written from the admin API in the same transaction as the change.
body:
Compliance questions are coming from two customers, and the admin console already lets users change settings and keys. I started on an audit log for those changes.

The table audit_log has an id, the time, the customer id, the actor (user id or system), an action name like api_key.revoke, a target type and id, the source IP and a JSONB detail field. It is partitioned by month, like the events, with the same maintenance job creating the partitions.

The important design point is that the audit entry is written in the same transaction as the change. If the change is rolled back, the entry is gone. If the entry cannot be written, the change fails. I wrote a small helper, withAudit, that takes the transaction handle and the entry. I considered a queue and an asynchronous writer, but then a crash could lose an entry, and for an audit log that is the wrong way around.

Append only: I revoked UPDATE and DELETE on the table for the application role, and a trigger raises an error on those operations as a second line. The maintenance role can drop whole old partitions later, once there is a retention rule.

For the detail field I store the old and the new value of a changed setting. Secrets are never stored. For API keys only the key id and prefix are written. I wrote a test that creates a key, revokes it, and checks that no part of the key appears in any audit row.

I added entries for these actions so far: login, logout, settings change, key create and key revoke. Login failures are also logged, with the IP, but with a rate cap so that an attacker cannot fill the table.

The read side is a paginated endpoint with filters on actor, action and time range. The index is on customer id and time. I checked the plan on a table with 2 million generated rows, and a one week filter took 6 ms.

Next: look at what the auditors want in an export, and write the docs for Sam.

summary: Went through the audit log with Sam against the questions two customers sent, and found three missing actions and a missing field for the user agent.
body:
Sam collected the questionnaires from the two customers and we compared them with what the audit log records. Most of the questions are about who can see and change data, and how long we keep records.

Missing actions: changing the member roles of an account, inviting a user, and changing the data retention setting of a customer. The first two do not exist yet in the console, but Lena will build them, so I wrote the action names down for her. The retention setting exists and I added the audit call.

One customer also asks for the user agent of the session. I added a user_agent field to the table as a nullable column, and the helper fills it from the request. A migration with a default null on a partitioned table is cheap, and it ran in under a second on production.

The retention question is open. At the moment audit entries are kept forever, simply because nothing deletes them. Sam will propose a period in the docs, and I told him a year is easy for us, and longer is also fine because the table is small, about 400 rows per customer per month at the moment.

We also talked about showing the audit log to customers in the console. A read endpoint exists, so Lena can add a page. Only admin users of a customer should see it, and I wrote the check for the role.

Sam is writing a short security page for the docs. I gave him the facts: append only, written in the same transaction, no secrets stored, partitioned by month. I read his draft and fixed two details about when a failed login is logged.

The next step on my side is the monthly review of the first alerts. After that, the importer needs a look, because two customers have files over 10 GB.

summary: The importer handled a 12 GB NDJSON file in 51 minutes, but memory crept up to 3 GB from a growing reject list, so rejects now stream to a file.
body:
A customer announced files of about 12 GB, so I tested the importer with a generated file of that size, with realistic nested events and about 0.5 percent invalid lines.

The import finished in 51 minutes at the rate limit I set earlier to protect the live API. Throughput was not the issue. The memory was. The process grew slowly to 3 GB, and the ECS task for imports has 4 GB, so it would have been killed with a bigger file.

I took a heap profile with pprof at the 30 minute mark. Most of the memory was the list of rejected lines with their reasons, which the importer kept to print the reject summary at the end. With 0.5 percent of 40 million lines, that is 200 thousand entries, each with the raw line.

The fix: rejects are written to a file next to the offset file, one line per reject with the line number and the reason. In memory the importer keeps only a count per reason. The summary at the end reads from the counters, and the file is available for the customer to fix their data. I wrote the file to a path that the dry run mode also uses.

I ran the test again. Memory stayed flat at about 400 MB for the whole run. The reject file was 38 MB.

Another thing I noticed: the offset file is written after each chunk commit, with a plain write. If the process is killed during the write, the file could be half written. I changed it to write a temporary file and rename it, which is atomic on the same filesystem. I tested by killing the process in a loop 50 times, and every time the resume worked.

I also checked what happens when the file has a very long line. The scanner buffer had a limit of 1 MB, and a line over it stopped the import with an error. Now such a line is counted as a reject with the reason line_too_long, and the import goes on.

Next: the same test in the production environment with a smaller file, to be sure about the task memory settings.

summary: Production import of a 6 GB customer file ran overnight without trouble, but the reject file showed 2 percent bad timestamps that need a mapping rule for a second date format.
body:
The customer sent the first big file, 6 GB with about 19 million events. I ran the dry run in the afternoon, and it reported a reject rate of 2 percent, so I did not start the real import until the cause was clear.

The reject file showed that almost all of them were the reason bad_timestamp. The values looked like 2 digit day first strings, with a slash separator, in about 2 percent of the lines. The rest used ISO format. It seems that two of their systems write the events. I asked the customer by mail, through Sam, and they confirmed that the second system uses local time of their data center.

I added an optional mapping rule per customer: a list of accepted timestamp layouts with a time zone for each. The importer tries the ISO format first and then the layouts in order. I did not add this as a global fallback, because day first and month first formats are ambiguous, and a wrong guess would put events in the wrong month without any error.

The tests cover three layouts, a daylight saving change where a local time exists twice, and a string that fits no layout. For the repeated hour I take the first occurrence and write a note into the summary count.

I started the real import at about 20:00. It ran at the limit rate, and the task memory stayed at about 450 MB. The live ingest metrics showed no change in latency, and the writer queue depth stayed low.

It finished in the early hours with 18.97 million events accepted and about 3 thousand rejects, from lines cut off at the end of some of their chunks. I sent the reject file to Sam to pass on.

The partitions for the older months were all present, since the importer test with old months from a while ago paid off, and the default partition has no rows. The hourly rollup picked up the history through the dirty markers within about 40 minutes.

I wrote down the customer layout in the config and in the onboarding notes. Next I want to check that the dashboard for this customer shows the right counts.

summary: Checked the new customer's dashboard against raw counts and found an off by one hour shift in the rollup for events in the repeated daylight saving hour.
body:
After the big import I compared the dashboard of the new customer with counts straight from the events partitions. For most days the numbers match exactly. For one day in the autumn clock change, the rollup showed one hour with double the count and another hour with none.

The cause is the way the hourly job computes the hour. It used date_trunc on a timestamp in the session time zone of the database connection, and that zone was not UTC for the importer's connection. In the repeated local hour, two different hours of UTC collapsed into one bucket.

I checked the database setting: the server default is UTC, but the importer's connection string set a zone from the environment of the ECS task, a leftover from the first customer onboarding. The rollup job itself used the server default and was fine, but the dirty marker path in the writer computed the hour in the connection zone, then the job recomputed the wrong hour for the history.

The fix is in two places. The writer now computes the hour in Go with UTC explicitly, and the SQL uses date_trunc on a timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'. I also removed the zone from the importer's connection string and added a startup check that fails if SHOW timezone is not UTC.

Then I recomputed the affected hours for this customer and for the first customer, whose import was also done with that setting. The first customer had the same problem in two months. After the recompute, the sums matched the raw counts for all 30 sample weeks I use.

I added a regression test with events around a clock change in a zone that has the repeated hour, and it checks both buckets. The test failed on the old code and passes now.

It makes me want a periodic consistency check: compare the sum of the rollup against the raw count for a sample of customer days, and alert on a difference. I wrote it down as a task, and I will do it after the next two items.

summary: Added a nightly consistency check that compares rollup sums with raw event counts for a sample of customer days, and it passed on its first production run.
body:
The check picks 30 random customer days from the last two weeks and compares the sum in events_hourly with a count on the raw partitions. It runs as a scheduled task at night, when the load is low, and takes about two minutes.

For each mismatch it logs the customer, the day and both numbers. A Prometheus gauge holds the number of mismatches of the last run, and an alert fires if it is above zero. I allowed a difference for the current day, since the job is always some minutes behind.

I tested it by changing a row in the rollup on staging, and the alert fired after the run. The first run on production reported zero mismatches. I will look at the gauge for a week before I trust it.

summary: Looked into why staging deploys got slower and found that the image build no longer used its layer cache after a dependency change, cutting the pipeline from 11 to 4 minutes once fixed.
body:
Tobias mentioned that the deploy pipeline for staging had become slow, about 11 minutes from push to running service. I looked at the build log to see where the time went.

The test stage takes about two minutes and the ECS update about one and a half. The image build took more than six, and it downloaded all Go modules every time. The layer cache was not used.

The Dockerfile copied the whole source tree before running go mod download, so any change in any file invalidated the module layer. That had been fine when the project was small, but the module download is the slow part. I changed the order: copy go.mod and go.sum first, download modules, then copy the source and build. The same change was made for the TypeScript services with package files and the install step.

That alone was not enough, because the CI runners are fresh each time and have no local cache. I changed the build to pull the previous image from ECR and use it as a cache source, with the inline cache option set when pushing. After this, the module layer comes from the registry when go.sum has not changed.

The result: the image build dropped to about 50 seconds when only code changes, and the whole pipeline to about 4 minutes. When go.sum changes, it is still slow, as expected, but that is rare.

One side effect I checked: the image size stayed the same, at about 24 MB for the Go worker, since the final stage is still a minimal image with only the binary.

I also pinned the base image versions by digest in the Dockerfile after seeing that the build had picked up a new patch release without anyone noticing. Tobias wants the digests updated by a monthly job, and I wrote a short note in the repo.

I have not touched production deploys. They use the same pipeline after a manual approval, so they get the faster build as well. I will watch the next two production deploys.

Next task is the first customer-facing documentation for the search API, together with Sam.

summary: Found that the ingest worker's flush interval left small batches sitting in memory for up to 10 seconds, so it now flushes at 2 seconds or 500 events.
body:
A customer asked why a test event took so long to show up in search. I traced it to the writer in the ingest worker, which flushed on a fixed 10 second timer or at 5000 events, and the test sent only one event.

I changed the flush rule to 2 seconds or 500 events, whichever comes first. A local run with a trickle of 5 events per second now shows each event written within about 2 seconds.

The load test on staging showed no drop in throughput, since busy tenants still fill the 500 event batches quickly. The number of insert statements per second went up by about 15 percent at low load, which is fine for the database.

I added the two values as environment settings so Tobias can tune them in Terraform without a rebuild. Next I want a metric for the age of the oldest unflushed event.

summary: Built the first version of the public API docs with an OpenAPI file for ingest and search, checked against the real handlers by a contract test in CI.
body:
The docs had been a wiki page that drifted from the code, and two customers hit wrong field names last week. I started an OpenAPI 3.1 file in the repo for the ingest endpoint and the search endpoint.

The ingest part describes the batch body, the limit of 1000 events per request and the error format. I wrote the schemas by hand from the Go structs because the generators I tried produced names that did not match the event schema.

The search part covers the query string parameter, the time range and the pagination. The rate limit headers are listed in every response.

To keep the file honest I wrote a contract test in CI. It starts the search API against a stub OpenSearch, sends the examples from the spec and validates each response against its schema. It failed immediately on two things: the total count was returned as a string in one error path, and the error body lacked the request id that the spec promised.

I fixed both in the handlers instead of weakening the spec. The same test for the ingest API runs against a local worker with a throwaway Postgres, and it caught that a 413 for oversized bodies came back as plain text.

The rendered docs use a static page built in the pipeline, published to a staging address for now. Sam read the first render and asked for a short getting started section with a curl example and a note on how to read the 429 headers.

I wrote the curl example and tested it with a staging key. Still open are the examples for the importer and a page on the error codes. I will do those when Sam has the wording for the error explanations.

summary: Added the missing error code table to the API docs after Sam rewrote the explanations in plain words, and every code is now covered by a test.
body:
Sam sent the wording for the error codes this afternoon. I put them into the OpenAPI file as a table of codes, with the cause and what the client should do for each.

I wrote a small script that collects every error code the handlers can return and compares the list with the table. It found two codes in the code that Sam had not seen, one for an unknown event type and one for a disabled key.

Sam wrote text for both and the script passes in CI now. The docs build also fails if a code is added without an explanation, which should stop the next drift.

Open is the importer page, planned for the next days.

summary: Wrote the docs page for the batch importer and found that the dry run flag was missing from the CLI help, which is fixed.
body:
The importer page describes the file formats, CSV and NDJSON, the mapping of columns to event fields and the reject file. I took the examples from the real customer imports and removed anything that identified a customer.
