While writing the section on the dry run mode I ran the CLI help and saw that the flag was not listed. The flag worked, but the help text was never updated when I added it. I fixed the help and added a test that every flag in the parser appears in the help output.

The page also explains the reject summary by reason. I generated a sample from a deliberately broken file with bad timestamps, an unknown field type and a missing customer id, so the numbers in the docs match what the tool prints.

Sam read it and found that the explanation of the rate limit option was unclear. I rewrote it with a worked example: 20000 events per second against a database that should not exceed 5000 gives the value to use.

Open question from Sam: whether customers may run the importer themselves. For now it stays with us, and the page says to contact support.

summary: Replaced the hand written duplicate check in the ingest worker with a batch lookup on event id, cutting duplicate handling cost by about 70 percent.
body:
Customers resend batches after timeouts, so the worker must drop duplicates by event id. The old code did one SELECT per event against the partition for the event time, which showed up as the top query in the slow log.

I first tried an in-memory set of recent ids per worker. That worked for a single worker, but with several workers behind the load balancer a resent batch often lands on another one, so I dropped the idea after a test showed 40 percent of duplicates getting through.

The second version collects all ids of a batch, and runs one query with ANY on an array, restricted to the time range of the batch. The index on event id per partition makes this a cheap lookup.

Benchmark on staging with a stream that has 10 percent duplicates:
- old: 18 ms per batch of 500 for the check
- new: 5.4 ms per batch of 500

I also found that the time range restriction mattered. Without it the query touched every partition, which took 60 ms. The batch range usually covers one or two months, so only those partitions are read.

Edge case: a batch contains the same id twice. The new code removes it in memory before the query, and I added a test for that. Another case is a duplicate that arrives with a different timestamp, which the range check misses if it falls in an older month. I decided this is acceptable and wrote it in the code comment, because the customers' clients generate the timestamp once at the source.

After the change the worker CPU at the same load dropped by about 8 percent. I deployed to staging and will watch the slow log for two days before production.

The unit tests cover empty batches, all duplicates and a mix. The integration test uses a real Postgres in a container and passes.

summary: Checked the duplicate change on staging with a replay of a day of production traffic: no lost events and no slow queries, so it is ready for production.
body:
To check the new duplicate lookup, I replayed a recorded day of ingest traffic from the largest customer against staging. The recording has about 9 million events and roughly 8 percent resent batches.

The count of stored events matched the count of unique ids in the recording exactly. I compared the id sets with a query on both sides, and the difference was zero.

The slow query log showed nothing above 50 ms for the duplicate check. The p99 of the check was 11 ms.

One detail came up: when a replay hit the month boundary, the batch range covered two partitions and the planner picked a sequential scan on the older one for two batches. I ran ANALYZE on that partition and the plan went back to the index. The maintenance job from the partition work should run ANALYZE after creating a partition, so I added that call.

I also checked memory of the worker. It stayed flat at about 220 MB through the replay.

Tobias looked at the deploy plan and agreed to roll it out after the evening peak. I wrote the rollback as one command to redeploy the previous image, since there is no schema change.

I will watch the error rate and the writer queue depth after the deploy.

summary: Deployed the batch duplicate lookup to production after the evening peak, and the writer queue depth and error rate stayed flat.
body:
I rolled out the new image in two steps, first one worker task and then the rest. The circuit breaker stayed quiet.

After 20 minutes I compared the database CPU with the same hour of last week. It was about 6 percent lower, which fits the staging result.

The queue depth peaked at 1200 messages during the evening burst and drained within a minute. That is the same shape as before.

The duplicate rate seen in the logs, about 7 percent, matches what the replay showed.

I left a log line with the duplicate count per batch at info level for a few days. If it is too noisy I will turn it to debug.

Nothing else to do except check the slow query log tomorrow morning. Tobias asked whether we can lower the database instance size later. I said not yet, because the dashboard queries are the heavier load and are not part of this change.

summary: Investigated why the admin console login felt slow, and found the session lookup in Redis was repeated three times per request, now cached for the request.
body:
Lena reported that the admin console took more than a second for the first page after login. In the browser the API calls were fast, but each one waited about 80 ms before the handler ran.

I added timing around the Fastify hooks and found that three hooks each loaded the session from Redis: the auth hook, the account settings hook and the audit actor hook. Each was one round trip, and on the staging network that was about 25 ms each, more under load.

The fix attaches the session to the request object on the first load, and the other hooks read it from there. This was a small change in one file, plus a test that counts Redis calls per request, which is now one.

I also looked at the key naming. The session keys are session:{id}, and the account settings cache uses a different prefix. I left that alone for now.

Result on staging: the wait before the handler dropped from about 80 ms to 28 ms, and the first page of the console loads in 400 ms instead of 1.2 seconds. Lena confirmed it feels right in the browser.

A second finding: the session TTL was refreshed on every request with an extra EXPIRE call. I changed that to refresh only when more than half the TTL has passed. This removes one more write per request. The test for the sliding session still passes, and I added a case for a session just before half its life.

In production the Redis command rate from the console should fall by about two thirds. I will check the Grafana panel after the deploy tomorrow morning.

Not done: the usage endpoint does its own lookup of counters and is still a bit slow, but that is a separate topic.

summary: Deployed the session lookup change to production, and Redis commands from the console dropped from about 900 to 300 per second at the same traffic.
body:
The deploy went out this afternoon and I watched the Redis panel in Grafana. Before the change the console generated about 900 commands per second at working hours. After the change it was about 300.

The session tests ran green in CI and a manual login on production worked. I also tested a logout from one tab while another was open, and the second tab was asked to log in again on its next request, as it should.

There was one surprise. The audit actor hook had assumed the session was loaded a second time to get the user agent. Now it reads it from the request session, and the user agent was still present in the audit entries I checked.

Sam asked whether the audit log still shows the right actor for key revocations. I made a revocation with a test account and the entry had the right actor and user agent.

I noted the numbers in the docs for the console. No more work planned on this topic except the usage endpoint, which I will look at when I have time.

summary: Looked at the usage endpoint of the admin console and moved the counter reads into one pipelined Redis call, from 14 round trips to one.
body:
The usage endpoint shows the request counts of the last 24 hours per API key. It read one counter per hour and key in separate calls, so a customer with 10 keys made 240 calls.

I changed it to build all key names first and send them in one pipeline. For a customer with 10 keys the call count fell from 240 to 1, and the response time on staging from 310 ms to 35 ms.

For the rate limiter window counters I did not change anything, because those are on the hot path of the search API and already use a single call.

A test with 50 keys passes and takes 60 ms. I also made the endpoint return zero for missing counters instead of null, as the console chart expected, which removes a workaround in Lena's code.

Lena will remove the workaround on her side this week.

summary: Wrote a script that checks the OpenSearch mapping against the event schema, and it found that two fields were mapped as text instead of keyword.
body:
Searches filtered on the event type field sometimes returned nothing for types with a dash in the name. I compared the live mapping with the event schema in the repo.

The script reads the schema, builds the expected mapping and diffs it with the output of the mapping API. It found two fields, event_type and source, mapped as text with the standard analyzer, so a value like page-view was split into two tokens.

The cause was dynamic mapping in the first index, created before the schema was fixed. Newer fields use an explicit template.

I cannot change a mapping in place, so the fix needs a new index and a reindex. I wrote the template change and will use the nightly reindex job to produce the new index, then switch the alias.

In the meantime I told Sam that filters on those two fields should use the match query on the full value. I added the diff script to CI so a new field cannot slip in unmapped.

summary: Switched the search index to the explicit template with keyword fields through the nightly reindex, and dash filters on event type now return the right hits.
body:
The nightly reindex built the new index with the explicit template, and this afternoon I checked it before moving the alias. The mapping diff script reported no differences.

I compared document counts between the old and new index: 41.2 million each. A sample of 200 random ids matched on all fields.

Then I ran the filter that had failed, event type page-view for the large customer, against both indexes. The old one returned zero hits, the new one 318000, which equals the count in Postgres for that day.

I switched the alias with the atomic alias action and watched the search API error rate and latency. Nothing changed in the latency, p95 stayed at about 120 ms.

The old index stays for three days as a fallback and then I delete it. I told Sam the filter works now and that the workaround note can be removed from the support answers.

summary: Tried a Go library for faster JSON parsing in the ingest worker and dropped it, because the gain was small and it failed on one edge case with escaped Unicode.
body:
The worker spends about 22 percent of its CPU in JSON decoding, so I tried a drop-in faster parser from the Go ecosystem on a branch of the main checkout.

A microbenchmark with real batches of 500 events showed a gain of about 30 percent in decode time. That sounded good, but in a worker profile the total CPU saving was only about 5 percent, because the rest of the decode cost is in the mapping to our structs.

Then the test suite found a difference: an event with an escaped surrogate pair in a string was decoded to a replacement character, while the standard library produced the correct emoji. A customer sends such text in page titles, so this would be a silent data change.

I looked at the issue tracker of the library and the problem is known, with no fix. I considered a fallback to the standard parser on error, but the library does not report an error in that case.

I also thought about writing a custom decoder for our event schema. A rough estimate says it would take days and add a lot of code to maintain for 5 percent.

Decision: drop the library, keep the standard one. I kept the benchmark file and the Unicode test in the repo, because the test is useful anyway.

If CPU becomes a problem later, the better lever is the batch size and the number of workers, not the parser.

The branch is deleted. I wrote a short note in the journal of decisions for the repo so the next person does not try it again without knowing.

summary: Built the first version of the search query parser for field filters like status:error and quoted phrases, with tests for 40 query forms and no changes to the API yet.
body:
The search API passes the query string almost directly to OpenSearch as a simple query string. Customers asked for field filters, so I started a small parser in TypeScript.

The grammar supports terms, quoted phrases, field:value filters, a minus for exclusion and uppercase AND and OR. I wrote a tokenizer first, then a recursive descent parser that produces a small tree.

The tree is converted to a bool query. Terms go to must clauses on the message field, filters go to the filter context so they are cached and not scored, and exclusions go to must_not.

I wrote tests for 40 query forms, such as:
- status:error
- "connection refused" host:web-1
- -status:ok timeout
- status:(error OR warn)

The last one needed grouping, which I added to the grammar. Nested groups work to any depth, and I limited the depth to 5 to avoid abuse.

Error handling was the tricky part. An unclosed quote or a dangling operator should return a clear message with the position, and not a 500. The parser throws a typed error with the offset, and the handler maps it to a 400 in the shared error format.

Field names are checked against the list of known fields from the schema. An unknown field returns a 400 with the list of valid names, which should help customers.

I did not touch the live endpoint. The parser sits in its own module and the endpoint will call it behind a flag, so we can compare results with the old behavior.

A quick performance check parsed 100000 random queries in 1.4 seconds, so the parser is not a concern.

Next step is the flag and a comparison run of real queries from the logs, to see where results differ. The work runs on the search-v2 branch from the next entry on.

summary: Added a flag to run the new query parser next to the old path and compared 5000 real queries: 4.1 percent returned different hit counts, mostly from phrase handling.
body:
The search endpoint now has a flag that runs the new parser in shadow mode. It builds both queries, sends the old one to OpenSearch for the answer and the new one for a comparison, and logs the hit counts of both.

I took 5000 real queries from the staging logs, which came from the test traffic of two customers and our own use, and replayed them through a script. The results: 95.9 percent had the same total count.

The 4.1 percent that differed fell into three groups.

The first and biggest group was phrases. The old simple query string handled a quoted phrase with the default operator, and in a few cases split on punctuation. The new parser makes a match_phrase query, which is stricter and correct, so fewer hits.

The second group was queries with a minus inside a word, like web-1. The old path treated the minus as exclusion in some cases. The new tokenizer keeps a dash inside a word as part of the term. I think the new way is right, but it changes the results for customers who typed a dash on purpose to exclude.

The third group was a bug of mine: a field filter with a colon inside the value, like time:12:30, was cut at the first colon. I changed the tokenizer to split only at the first colon of a token and added a test.

After the fix the difference dropped to 3.6 percent.

I went through the remaining differences with Sam, who knows what customers type. Sam said exclusion with a leading minus is used, but a dash inside a word is not meant as exclusion. That matches the new behavior.

The change in phrase handling needs a note in the docs. Sam will write a short paragraph about it.

No performance difference was visible in the shadow run: the p95 of the new query was 118 ms against 121 ms.

Before the flag goes on for customers I want to test queries with special characters and very long input. I wrote a fuzz test that sends random strings to the parser and checks that it either returns a tree or a typed error, never an exception. It ran 200000 cases without a crash.

Next: enable the flag for our own test account and watch for a few days.

summary: Enabled the new parser for our own test account and found that long OR chains made OpenSearch reject the query, so the parser now limits clauses to 64.
body:
I turned the flag on for the internal test account this morning and used search through the admin console for most of the day.

The filters worked well. In the afternoon I pasted a list of 300 host names joined by OR into the search box, as a customer might do, and got a 500 from the search API. OpenSearch returned too_many_clauses for the bool query.

The old path had passed the string to the simple query string, which handles long input in a different way, so this problem is new with the parser.

I considered two options. One is raising the limit in OpenSearch, which is a cluster setting and affects memory use of every query. The other is to turn a long OR of values for one field into a terms query, which has a separate and much higher limit.

I implemented the second: when the tree has an OR of three or more values for the same field, the converter emits a terms query. The 300 hosts query now runs in 40 ms.

For OR chains over different fields or over free terms, the parser counts the clauses and returns a 400 with a clear message if there are more than 64. That is a reasonable limit, and the message says how to narrow the query.

I wrote tests for both paths, one with 300 values for a field and one with 100 mixed terms.

A second finding from the day: the highlight of the matched terms in the console still used the old query string. With a field filter the highlight showed nothing. I changed the highlight to use the terms from the tree that belong to the message field. Lena checked the console and the highlight is right now.

The test account has no complaints so far. The next step is to enable the flag for one friendly customer, and I will ask Sam who could be asked. Before that the docs paragraph about phrases and dashes has to be live, and Sam has a draft.

I also noted that the parser module is now about 600 lines with tests. I split the tokenizer and the converter into two files for readability.

summary: Postgres autovacuum was falling behind on the audit log table, so I set per-table thresholds, and the dead tuple count fell from 2 million to under 50000.
body:
A Grafana panel for dead tuples showed the audit log table at 2 million, which surprised me because the table is append only. The cause was the updates that set a processed flag in the export preparation, a small job I added earlier.

The default autovacuum scale factor of 20 percent is far too lazy for a table with tens of millions of rows. I set the scale factor to 0.01 and a fixed threshold of 5000 for this table with ALTER TABLE.

After the next autovacuum run the dead tuples dropped to under 50000 and the table size stopped growing. The vacuum took 4 minutes and the IO impact on the instance was not visible in the dashboard.

I also thought about removing the flag update by moving the flag to a separate small table. That is cleaner but a bigger change, so it goes on the list.

I added a panel with dead tuples per table to the Postgres dashboard, so Tobias and I can see the next one early.

summary: Moved the processed flag of the audit log out of the big table into a small state table, so the audit log is truly append only again.
body:
After the vacuum tuning I did the cleaner fix. The export preparation job had updated a processed flag on each audit row, which made the table write-heavy and left dead tuples.

The new design is a one-row-per-job state table that stores the highest audit id processed. The job reads rows with an id above that value in batches of 5000, and updates the state row in the same transaction as its work.

I wrote the migration in three steps so that nothing breaks:
- create the state table and fill it from the current maximum processed id
- deploy the job that uses it
- drop the flag column in a later migration

The first two steps are done. A test with 100000 rows ran the job twice in a row and the second run processed nothing, as expected. Another test killed the job in the middle of a batch, and the next run continued without a gap or a repeat.

On staging the vacuum has nothing to do for the audit table now. The dead tuples are zero.

I will drop the old column after a week, so the previous job version could still be rolled back if needed. I noted the date as a reminder in the migration file comment, in relative words: one week after the deploy.

Sam asked if the audit export for customers is affected. It is not, but the new state approach should help when that export becomes a real feature.

summary: Reviewed the Terraform for the ingest service with Tobias and found three security group rules that were wider than needed, now narrowed to the load balancer.
body:
Tobias asked for a review of the Terraform module before more customers come in. I read through the ECS service, the load balancer and the security groups.

Three rules were wider than needed. The ingest worker security group allowed the port from the whole VPC range, and the Postgres group allowed the port from the same range. The Redis group did the same.

I changed each to allow traffic only from the security group of the callers: the load balancer for the workers, the workers and the search API for Postgres, and the workers, search API and console for Redis.

The plan showed six rule changes and no replacement of resources. Tobias applied it to staging first. I ran the smoke test, a batch ingest and a search, and both worked.

One problem came up: the partition maintenance task runs in its own security group that I had forgotten, and it could not reach Postgres. The log said connection timed out. I added the group to the Postgres rule and the task ran fine.

We also noticed that the load balancer access logs are not enabled for production. Tobias will add that, with an S3 bucket and a 30 day expiry.

Production apply is planned in the quiet window tonight, with the same smoke test.

summary: Applied the narrowed security groups to production in the quiet window, and one forgotten caller, the nightly consistency check task, was fixed within minutes.
body:
Tobias and I applied the Terraform change to production this evening. The plan was the same six rule changes as on staging, with no replacements.

After the apply I ran the smoke test: an ingest batch with a customer key, a search for the batch, and a console login. All three passed.

I then went through the list of everything that connects to Postgres and Redis, to find callers I had missed after the partition task on staging. The list had the importer, the rollup job, the partition maintenance and the consistency check.

The consistency check task was not in the Postgres rule. Its next run is at night, so nothing had failed yet. I added its security group to the rule and applied again, which took two minutes. Then I started the task by hand and it passed.

To avoid this in the future I made a small change in the module: every scheduled task takes its security group from one shared variable that is already allowed in the database rule. A new task now gets access without a separate rule.

The ingest error rate stayed at its normal level of 0.02 percent during the work. The writer queue depth did not change.

I also checked that the alerts on database connections still work. The connection count stayed at 140 of 400.

Tobias enabled the load balancer access logs in the same session. The first log files arrived in the bucket after a few minutes, and I looked at a sample to see that the client IP and the response times are there.

There are no open items from this change. A follow up for later: move the rule definitions to a module input list, so the review of who may connect is one place in the code.

I wrote a short summary of the rule changes in the runbook for infrastructure.

summary: Wrote a runbook page for on-call with the five most likely ingest problems and the first command to run for each, after reviewing it with Tobias.
body:
The alerts exist, but the on-call person has no list of what to do. I wrote a page in the runbook for the five problems we have seen or can foresee.

The five are: a high API error rate, a growing writer queue, database connections near the limit, a stuck partition maintenance task and a failing deploy.

For each I wrote what the alert means, the first dashboard to open, the first command and when to escalate. For the growing queue, for example, the first step is to look at the writer task count and the database CPU, because a slow database is the usual cause.

Tobias read it and added the commands for scaling the number of tasks by hand in Terraform and in the console of the service, in case Terraform is too slow in an emergency.

He also said the page should state who is called when the first person does not answer. I added the escalation order: the on-call person, then Tobias, then me.

Sam will read it as a first time reader, because the docs and support side may need to understand the alerts when customers ask. I will fix the unclear parts after that.

summary: Added a per-customer limit on the importer's database write rate, after a large import slowed dashboards for others, and tested with two imports in parallel.
body:
This morning a customer ran a 9 GB NDJSON import and the dashboards of other customers got slow for about 30 minutes. The importer had a rate limit option, but it was per process and a second import doubled the load.

The database CPU rose from 35 to 85 percent during the two imports. The slow query log showed ordinary dashboard queries waiting on IO, not a bad plan.

I changed the importer so the write rate comes from a shared token bucket in Redis. All importer processes take tokens from the same bucket, with a total rate of 8000 events per second by default.

Each process asks for tokens in chunks of one batch, which means one Redis call per 500 events, so the cost is small. If Redis is not reachable, the importer falls back to its own local limit and logs a warning, so an import does not stop because of a cache problem.

The bucket key is import:rate and has no TTL, since it only stores the last refill time and the token count. I tested key naming with a prefix per environment so that staging cannot touch production.

Test: two imports in parallel against staging, each with a 2 million event file. Before the change the combined write rate reached 15000 events per second. After it, the combined rate stayed at 8000 and the two imports finished in similar times, 4.5 and 4.7 minutes.

I also tested a kill of one import in the middle. The other import took the whole rate within a second, since the tokens are not reserved per process.

There is still an open point: the limit is global, so one large customer import delays the import of another. A fairer split per customer is possible but I do not think it is needed with 40 customers.

Tobias will check the database CPU during the next large import. I set an alert at 80 percent CPU for 10 minutes, which would have fired this morning.

I updated the importer page of the docs with the shared limit and Sam read the change. The change is deployed to the staging environment, and production follows tomorrow.

summary: Deployed the shared import rate limit to production and ran a small test import to check that tokens are taken and the fallback does not trigger.
body:
The change went out to production this morning after the staging test. I ran a small import of 500000 events for our own test account.

The Redis key import:rate showed up with a changing token count, and the import ran at the configured 8000 events per second, as the throughput panel showed.

I then blocked Redis from the importer task for one minute with a security group change on staging only, to see the fallback. The importer logged the warning once and continued with its local limit of 5000. When Redis came back it switched to the shared bucket again.

The database CPU stayed under 40 percent during the production test.

Nothing else is open for this topic. I will look at the alert for high database CPU after the next real customer import.

summary: Ran a load test of the shared import rate limit with four parallel imports and found the fallback path was too eager, so the token refill now uses a smoother window.
body:
After this morning's deploy of the shared import limit I wanted to see it under harder conditions than the two-import test. I started four imports of 2 GB NDJSON files against staging, each for a different customer, and watched the writer queue and the dashboard latency.

The limit held the total database write rate where it should be, but the fallback to the local limiter triggered about 30 times in ten minutes. The cause was the Redis token bucket refilling in whole seconds: at the start of each second all four importers grabbed tokens at once and then waited. The result was a sawtooth in the write rate.

I changed the refill to a finer window of 100 ms with proportional tokens, in importer/limiter.go. The Lua script that takes tokens stayed the same except for the time unit. I added a unit test with a fake clock that checks the refill is linear.

On the second run the fallback did not trigger at all, and the write rate curve was flat within about 5 percent. Total import time for the four files grew from 22 to 27 minutes, which is the price of the limit and is acceptable.

I also checked Redis itself. The limiter adds about 40 commands per second per importer, which is nothing next to the console traffic. Key names follow the existing pattern imp:rl:{customer}, with a TTL of 60 seconds so abandoned buckets disappear.

Open points: the limit per customer is still a constant in config, and Sam asked whether support can raise it for a customer that has a deadline. I will add an override in the settings table next. The new window is not deployed yet. I will ship it tomorrow after the morning peak and watch the fallback counter in Grafana for a day.

summary: Ingest worker memory grew slowly over long runs, and a pooled buffer that was never reset after large batches turned out to be the cause, now fixed.
body:
Tobias noticed in Grafana that the resident memory of the ingest workers climbed from about 300 MB to 1.2 GB over a day and only dropped on deploys. I took a heap profile from one worker on staging after a replay of production traffic. Most of the retained memory sat in byte buffers from a sync.Pool used for batch decoding.

The pool handed out buffers that had grown for a few very large batches, and they were put back without being trimmed. Over time every pooled buffer had the size of the largest batch seen. I added a size cap, so buffers above 1 MB are dropped instead of returned to the pool.

I also reset the slice length on return, which the old code skipped in one error path. After the change I ran the replay for six hours. Memory stayed flat at about 350 MB and the allocation rate fell by roughly 15 percent.

The unit test for the pool helper now covers the oversize case. Throughput in the replay was unchanged. I opened the pull request for Mara to review, and the production deploy is planned for the quiet window tomorrow. I will watch the memory graph for two days after it.

summary: Built the first version of the per-customer usage export for finance, a CSV of daily event counts and storage, and found that two customers had gaps from a rollup bug.
body:
Sam asked for a monthly usage export so that billing no longer depends on someone copying numbers from the admin console. I started with a small command in the admin API that writes a CSV with customer id, day, event count and stored bytes. The counts come from the nightly rollup table, and the stored bytes come from a per-customer size table.

While checking the first output against the console I found that two customers had missing days. Both had no events on those days, but the rollup job skipped empty days instead of writing a zero row. The console hid this because it fills gaps on the client side. For billing this is wrong, since a missing row cannot be told apart from a failed job.

I changed the rollup job to write explicit zero rows for every active customer. A one-off backfill script then filled the gaps for the last 90 days. I ran it in a transaction first and compared the row counts with the expected number of customer days, and they matched.

The export itself got a few details. Days are in UTC and the header says so. The file is sorted by customer and day. Large customers produce about 30 rows per month, so size is not a concern.

I added tests for an empty day, a customer created mid-month and a customer with a deleted account. The last case showed that deleted accounts were dropped from the export, so I made it include them with a flag column. Sam read the output and asked for a column with the plan name, which I added from the settings table.

What is left is a scheduled run on the first of the month that stores the file in the finance bucket. I will do that next, with a check that the row count is plausible before the file is published.

summary: Scheduled the monthly usage export and added a plausibility check that stops publishing when the row count or totals look wrong, after a dry run on staging.
body:
I continued with the usage export from two days ago and made it run on a schedule. The job runs as a small ECS task on the first of the month at 03:00 UTC and writes the CSV to the finance bucket. Tobias added the task role and the bucket policy in Terraform, limited to write access for this prefix.

Before the file is published, the job runs a plausibility check. It compares the number of rows with active customers times days in the month, and it compares total events with the sum of the raw daily rollups. If either differs by more than one percent, the job stops and sends an alert to the team channel instead of publishing.

I tested the check with a staging copy where I deleted a few rollup rows on purpose. The job stopped with a clear message that named the missing customer days. With the data restored, it published the file and the totals matched.

A question came up about late events that arrive after the month ends. The rollup of a day can still change for a short time, so the export would then disagree with the console. I settled on running the job on the third day of the month rather than the first, which leaves a margin. I updated the schedule and the docs note.

Sam will read the first real file and compare it with two invoices. If that goes well, the finance team can take the file as the source for billing. I also added the job to the on-call runbook with the command to rerun it manually.

summary: Looked into slow Postgres queries on the settings tables and found a missing index on the API key lookup that made every ingest auth check scan about 40000 rows.
body:
Tobias pointed out that the Postgres CPU had a steady baseline that grew with the number of API keys. I turned on pg_stat_statements for the day and sorted by total time.

The top query was the API key lookup for the ingest auth check. It filters on the hash of the key and a revoked flag. The existing index was only on the customer id, so Postgres scanned all keys of the customer, and for the largest customers that is about 40000 rows. The ingest workers cache the result for a minute, but with many workers and many keys the misses add up: about 300 calls per second at peak, each around 6 ms.

I wrote a migration with a partial index on key_hash where revoked is false. I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so there was no lock on the table. On staging with a copy of production data, the query went from 6 ms to 0.1 ms.

I ran the migration on production in the evening. The index build took 11 seconds. Afterwards the CPU baseline of the database dropped from about 28 percent to 17 percent, and the auth check no longer appears in the top ten queries.

Second finding: the audit log has a query by actor that is slow for the large customers, but it runs only from the admin console and only a few times a day. I left it and noted it as a candidate.

I also checked the bloat of the settings tables. It is small, so nothing to do there. Next I want to look at the third query in the list, a count on the events table used by the usage page.

summary: Traced the usage page count on the events table, which took 4 seconds for large customers, and replaced it with the nightly rollup plus a small live delta.
body:
The usage page of the admin console shows how many events a customer sent this month. Behind it was a count(*) on the events table with a time filter. For the largest customers this took about 4 seconds and showed up in the Postgres statistics as the third most expensive query.

The nightly rollup job already stores daily counts per customer. I changed the query to sum the rollups for the finished days and add a live count only for today, which touches a few hundred thousand rows at most. The result is the same number, and I checked it against the old query for 20 customers over three months: identical for 19, and off by 12 events for one customer, whose rollup was computed just before a late batch arrived.

That difference is expected, because the consistency check tolerates late events up to a point. I decided to leave the rollup as it is and show the usage as approximately current, with the exact number in the monthly report.

The new query takes 15 ms for the largest customer. I added a test for the sum of rollups plus today and one for a customer without rollups, which must fall back to the live count.

The change is merged and deployed to staging. I will deploy it to production tomorrow.

summary: Deployed the rollup based usage query to production and confirmed that the usage page now answers in under 50 ms for all customers.
body:
The usage page change went to production in the late evening. I deployed it and then opened the page for the five largest customers by hand.

Response times were between 12 and 40 ms. Before, the slowest was 4.2 seconds. The Postgres statistics showed that the count query was gone from the top list, and the CPU baseline dropped by a further 3 percent.

I checked the numbers of two customers against what Sam had in a support ticket from last week, and they matched.

One small thing: the page cached its answer in Redis for 5 minutes, and the key name still contained the old query version. I renamed the key to include the new version so that old and new values do not mix during the rollout. Old keys expire on their own through their TTL.

Nothing else is open for this topic.

summary: Reviewed Mara's change to the ingest worker error responses and asked for the retry hint header to be sent only for 429 and 503, not for validation errors.
body:
Mara's pull request changes the error bodies of the ingest API so that every error has a code, a message and a request id. That matches the error code table in the docs, and the contract test passed.

My one real objection was the Retry-After header, which the change added to every error. A client that gets a 400 for a bad event should not retry at all, and a header telling it to wait two seconds invites a loop. I asked her to send the header only with 429 and 503.

Smaller points: a log line printed the full event on validation errors, which could put customer data into the logs, so it should print only the event id. A test name was misleading. She agreed to all of it, and I approved once the changes were in.

summary: Upgraded the Redis minor version on staging and ran the console and limiter tests against it, with no behavior change found.
body:
Tobias had prepared the Terraform change for a newer minor release of Redis, and I took the staging part of it. The change only bumps the engine version of the cache cluster and keeps the parameter group.

After the apply, staging restarted the node in about 90 seconds. The admin console reconnected by itself, and the pool in the search API needed no action either.

I ran the integration tests for the session store, the rate limiter Lua scripts and the query cache. All of them passed. I also ran the importer limiter test with four parallel imports, because it uses a script with time arithmetic, and the result was the same as before.

I compared the INFO output before and after for memory use and connected clients. Both were within a few percent. The command statistics showed the same mix.

One thing I noticed: the client library in the search API logs a deprecation warning at startup for an old option that is unrelated to the upgrade. I made a ticket for it.

The plan is to run staging for two days and then do production in the quiet window.

summary: Fixed the deprecation warning in the search API's Redis client setup by removing an old option, and confirmed that the connection settings are otherwise unchanged.
body:
The warning noticed during the staging upgrade came from a client option that was renamed two releases ago. The old name was still accepted but ignored, so it did nothing.

I replaced it with the new name in the shared Redis config of the search API and checked what the value was supposed to do: it sets the delay between reconnect attempts. With the old name, the client had used its default of 50 ms increasing, which is fine, so I kept the default and just removed the option.

I added a startup test that fails if the client logs any warning on connect, so such drift is noticed earlier. It uses a fake logger.

The change was small. Tests passed and it is merged. It goes out with the next regular deploy.

summary: Wrote a script that lists Redis key prefixes with counts and sampled TTLs, and found two prefixes without any TTL that came from an old feature.
body:
While looking at the Redis memory graph on staging I wanted to know which parts of the application own the keys. I wrote a small script, tools/redis-prefixes.ts, that scans with SCAN in small steps, groups keys by the part before the first colon or the second, and prints the count and the sampled TTL for each group.

The script is careful: it uses a count of 200 per step, sleeps 10 ms between steps and refuses to run against the production host unless a flag is given. On staging it ran in 20 seconds.

The result had the expected groups: sess for sessions, rl for the rate limiter, qc for the query cache, imp for the import limiter and usage for the usage page. Two groups were a surprise. A prefix called digest: had 8000 keys and no TTL, and a prefix called tmpexp: had 1200 keys and no TTL either.

I searched the code history. The digest keys came from a daily email digest feature that was removed over a year ago, and the tmpexp keys from a one-off export. Nobody reads them.

I checked production with the flag, in the quiet hour: digest had 61000 keys and tmpexp 9000. Together they are about 40 MB, which is small, but they would live forever.

I deleted them in steps with UNLINK, 500 at a time, and checked that no code path reads those prefixes. The memory graph dropped slightly.

I added the script to the runbook for Redis problems. Next step is to add a rule to the code review checklist: every new key prefix needs a TTL or a written reason.

summary: Built the first part of the schema registry: a table of event schemas with versions, a compatibility check on registration, and API endpoints to register and fetch a schema.
body:
The event schema so far lives in one Go file and a copy in the docs. Customers have started to send events with new optional fields, and the ingest worker needs to know which version applies. I started the schema registry on its own branch.

The data model is two tables in Postgres: schemas, with a name and an owner, and schema_versions, with the version number, the JSON schema document, a hash and the creation time. Versions are append only, like the audit log, and a version can be marked deprecated but never changed.

The compatibility check runs when a new version is registered. For now it knows three rules: a field may be added if it is optional, a field may not change its type, and a required field may not be removed. I wrote the checker as a pure function over two parsed documents so it is easy to test. There are 34 test cases, including nested objects, arrays of objects and enums where a new value is added, which is allowed, and where a value is removed, which is not.

The API has two endpoints so far: POST /schemas/{name}/versions, which runs the check and returns the list of violations as errors, and GET /schemas/{name}/versions/{n}. Authentication is the same as for the admin API, and each registration writes an audit log entry in the same transaction.

I hit one problem with the hash. Two documents with the same content but different key order got different hashes. I fixed it by canonicalizing the document before hashing, with sorted keys and no whitespace, and added a test.

I ran the checker on the real history of the event schema, six versions from the Git log. It accepted five and flagged one, where a field had changed from integer to string. That change was in fact made on purpose back then with a data fix, so the flag is right, and I will document it as a known exception for the import of history.

Next: loading the six historical versions as the first data, and a read path for the ingest worker with a local cache.

summary: Imported the six historical event schema versions into the registry and added a cached read path for the ingest worker, with a fallback to the compiled in schema.
body:
The registry now holds real data. I wrote a one-off command that reads the six versions from the repository history and registers them in order. For the version with the integer to string change, the command takes a flag that records an exception reason in the version row, so the history stays honest.

For the read path, the ingest worker asks the registry for the active version of a schema when it starts and then every 30 seconds. The answer is cached in memory with the hash, and a changed hash triggers a reload. If the registry is not reachable, the worker keeps the last known schema, and on a cold start without any it uses the schema compiled into the binary. I chose this order because an unreachable registry must never stop ingest.

I added a metric for the active schema version per worker, so that Grafana shows if workers disagree. After a registration, all workers should converge within about 30 seconds.

Tests: a worker test with a fake registry that changes its answer, one that times out, and one that returns a broken document. In the broken case the worker must keep the old schema and log an error. All three pass.

Then I ran a local ingest with the replay of an hour of staging traffic against the new path. Validation results were the same as with the compiled schema for all 410000 events. The extra cost per event is not measurable, because the schema is compiled once per version.

What is left: the active version flag, so that a registered version is not used until someone activates it, and a page in the admin console. I will ask Lena about the page after the API is stable.

summary: Added the active version flag to the registry so a registered schema version does nothing until it is activated, and activation writes an audit entry.
body:
Until now the newest registered version was also the one the workers used. That is too risky, since a mistaken registration would change validation at once.

I added an active column on the schema row that points to a version. A new endpoint, POST /schemas/{name}/activate, sets it, checks that the version is not deprecated and writes an audit log entry with the old and the new version. Registering a version no longer changes the active one.

The workers read the active version, so the cache logic did not change. I updated the tests, and one test now checks that a freshly registered version is ignored by a worker until activation.

I activated version six on staging and saw all workers report it within 30 seconds.

summary: Investigated a slow search for one customer and found that the new query parser produced hundreds of prefix clauses for a wildcard heavy query, which is now capped.
body:
Sam forwarded a ticket from a customer whose searches took 8 to 15 seconds, while the typical search takes about 200 ms. I got the query from the logs: a long filter with six terms, each ending in a wildcard, such as err* timeout* conn*.

I ran it against staging with the explain output of OpenSearch. The new parser expanded each wildcard term into a prefix query over every text field of the mapping, 23 fields. With six terms that is 138 clauses, and the prefix expansion on the large customer index is expensive.

The old path did not do this, because it searched only the default field. The parser expands to all fields when no field is named, which is what the tests asked for, but nobody had tested wildcards at that size.

I made three changes in the parser. First, a wildcard term without a field only searches the message and the title fields, which are the ones users mean. Second, a term needs at least 3 characters before the wildcard, otherwise the parser returns a validation error with a clear message. Third, the number of wildcard terms per query is limited to 4, besides the existing limit of 64 clauses.

The parser tests got 12 new cases for these limits. I also ran the comparison against 5000 real queries again. The share with different hit counts is 3.8 percent, a little below the 4.1 percent from before, since the narrower fields removed some false hits.

On staging the customer's query now takes 340 ms. I asked Sam to tell the customer that very short wildcards are limited now, with an example of the error text.

One more finding: the parser did not escape a backslash correctly at the end of a quoted phrase, which gave a syntax error from OpenSearch. I fixed it and added a test.

The change is on the search-v2 branch and merged to main behind the parser flag. I will turn the flag on for more accounts next week, after checking the error rate for the test accounts.

summary: Enabled the new query parser for five more customer accounts and watched the error rate and latency for two hours, with no increase compared to the old path.
body:
After the wildcard fix I turned on the parser flag for five accounts that agreed to test: two small ones and three medium ones. I picked them with Sam, partly because they use field filters a lot.

I set up a Grafana panel that splits search latency and error rate by parser version, so that the two groups can be compared side by side. During the first two hours the new path had a p50 of 190 ms and a p95 of 620 ms, the old path 210 and 650 ms. The error rate for both was around 0.4 percent, mostly from bad syntax typed by users.

I looked at the rejected queries of the new parser one by one, 31 of them. Most were the new validation errors: a wildcard that was too short, or too many clauses. Two were real bugs. One was a query with a colon inside a quoted phrase, which the parser mistook for a field filter. The other was a field name with a dash, such as user-agent, which the tokenizer split.

I fixed both in the tokenizer and added tests. The dash case needed a decision: field names may contain dashes and underscores, and the parser checks the name against the mapping before it treats the colon as a field filter. If the name is not in the mapping, the term is a plain word.

I redeployed to the same five accounts. In the next 30 minutes there were no new parser errors apart from legitimate ones.

I left the flag at five accounts over the weekend plan. The next step is a broader group, and per-field boosts after that.

summary: Started per-field boosts for search v2 with a config table for title, message and tags, and tested the ranking on 50 saved queries from support.
body:
Per-field boosts are the next part of search v2. The goal is that a hit in the title ranks higher than a hit in a long message body.

I started with a boost config as a JSON object per customer, with a default for all customers: title 3, tags 2, message 1. It is stored in the settings table and loaded with the query cache, so changes need no deploy. The query builder turns the boosts into the fields list of a multi_match query with the caret syntax.

To see if the ranking is better, I took 50 queries that Sam collected from support tickets, each with the document the customer expected near the top. I ran them with the old ranking and with the default boosts. With the old ranking the expected document was in the top 3 for 31 of 50 queries. With the boosts it was 39 of 50.

For seven queries the boost made it worse, because a very common word in a title pushed less relevant documents above the real match. A lower title boost of 2 gave 37 of 50 with only three worse cases, so the numbers will need a closer look and probably a per-customer value.

I did not set the final defaults. For now the code uses title 2 and I wrote the results into a notebook file in the repo so that Mara can see them.

Next: a small tool to run the 50 queries against any index, so every change to the boosts can be measured the same way.

summary: Wrote the ranking check tool that runs the 50 saved support queries against an index and prints how many expected documents land in the top 3 and top 10.
body:
Instead of redoing the measurement by hand each time, I put it in a script: tools/rank-check.ts. It reads a YAML file with the query, the customer and the id of the expected document, runs each query through the real search API path with the given boost config, and prints the rank of the expected document.

The summary at the end gives the share in the top 3 and top 10, and a list of the queries that got worse compared to a stored baseline run. The baseline file is committed, so a pull request that changes boosts can show the difference.

With title 2, tags 2, message 1 the result is 37 of 50 in the top 3 and 46 of 50 in the top 10, which equals the earlier measurement. I confirmed that the script gives the same result on two runs, since OpenSearch scoring can differ a little between shards, and it did.

One caveat I wrote into the readme: the scoring depends on the shard layout, so numbers from staging and production are not comparable. That matters later when the index layout changes.

The tool is merged. Tomorrow I will try boosts per customer type.

summary: Built the first version of the loader retry logic for large files: failed chunks are retried with backoff and a state file records finished chunks so a restart skips them.
body:
Large files fail halfway too often. A customer file of 8 GB lost its connection to the object store after 70 percent, and the loader started from the beginning. I started the loader-retry branch for this.

The design has two parts. First, the loader reads a file in chunks of about 64 MB aligned to line ends, and each chunk is an independent unit of work. A chunk that fails with a transient error, such as a timeout, a connection reset or a 5xx from the store, is retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff starting at 500 ms and a random jitter of up to 20 percent. Errors that are not transient, like a parse error rate over the threshold, fail the chunk at once.

Second, a state file next to the import job records the chunk number, the byte range and a checksum of each finished chunk. On restart, the loader reads the state file and skips finished chunks. The state is written after the events of the chunk are committed, using write to a temp file and rename, so a crash cannot leave a half written state.

The tricky part was duplicates. If a chunk is committed but the process dies before the state is written, the chunk is loaded again. The batch duplicate lookup on event id in the ingest path takes care of that, but the importer writes directly, so I added the same lookup to the importer for chunks that have no state record but whose first event id already exists.

Tests: a fake object store that fails on request, with cases for one failure, five failures, a permanent failure, and a kill of the process in between commit and state write. All pass. In the kill case the second run loads zero extra events.

I tried it on staging with a 3 GB file and an artificially unstable store with 10 percent failure per request. The import finished in 31 minutes instead of 19 and loaded the exact event count.

Open: metrics for retries per chunk, a maximum total time per file, and the question of what happens to the state file when the file in the store changes. I will use the etag for that, in the next step.

summary: Added the object etag to the loader state file, so a changed source file invalidates the saved progress instead of mixing chunks of two versions.
body:
A state file is only valid for the file it was made from. If a customer replaces the file under the same name, the saved chunk ranges point into different content.

The loader now stores the etag and the size of the source object in the header of the state file. On start it compares both with the current object. If they differ, the loader refuses to resume, logs the old and new etag and asks for a flag to start over, which also removes the old state.

I added tests for same etag, changed etag and missing etag, which some stores do not send. In the last case the loader falls back to size plus last modified time. All pass.

summary: Added retry metrics to the loader and a total time limit per file, so a stuck import stops after two hours with a clear error instead of retrying for ever.
body:
The loader now exports three metrics: chunks retried, retries per chunk as a histogram, and chunks failed for good. They go to the same Prometheus endpoint as the rest of the importer, and I added a small panel to the importer dashboard.

I also added a limit on total time per file, two hours by default and configurable per job. When it is reached, the loader stops after the current chunk, writes the state and exits with a specific code and the message that progress is saved and the job can be resumed.

I tested with a fake store that always times out. Each chunk used its five retries, the job stopped at the limit and a second run with a working store continued from the saved state.

One detail: the backoff sleeps count toward the limit, which I checked in a test with a fake clock. The metrics showed the expected numbers.

summary: Deployed the retrying loader to production and finished a 14 GB customer file that had failed twice before, with 9 chunk retries and no duplicate events.
body:
The loader-retry branch was merged and I deployed the new importer image in the quiet window. The first real job was a 14 GB file of a customer whose two earlier attempts died when the connection to the object store dropped.

I started the import at midday and watched the new panel. The loader split the file into 224 chunks. During the run there were 9 chunk retries, all of them transient timeouts from the store, and each succeeded on the first or second retry. No chunk failed for good. The total time was 71 minutes.

After the import I checked the result in three ways. The count of loaded events plus rejected lines matched the line count of the file. The consistency check of the rollups, which I ran for the affected days, passed. And a query for duplicate event ids over the imported range returned nothing.

I also tested the resume path on production with a small file. I started a job, killed the importer task by hand after a few chunks and started it again. It continued from the state file, skipped the finished chunks and finished correctly. The source etag check passed.

The import limiter from last week worked together with the retries. While the large import ran, the dashboards of other customers stayed at their normal latency, with p95 around 400 ms.

A small thing I noticed: the log level for retries was error, which would page nobody but made the logs noisy. I changed it to warning for the first four retries and error for the last.

I wrote a short note for Sam on how to resume a failed import with the command and what the error messages mean. The docs page for the importer will get a section on it next.

summary: Wrote the importer docs section on resuming failed imports with Sam, who reworded the error messages so that support can act on them without asking engineering.
body:
Sam and I went through the loader error messages one by one. Of eleven messages, four were written for developers, for example a message about a state file etag mismatch with no hint of what to do.

We reworded them. The etag message now says that the file in the store changed since the import started, and that the choices are to start over with the flag or to restore the old file. The time limit message says that progress is saved and the same command resumes the job. Each message now has a short code, so support can look it up in the docs table.

I then wrote the new section of the importer page: how a chunked import works in two paragraphs, what resuming does, when it refuses to resume, and the commands. Sam added a table of the codes with the cause and the action, and a note on when to call engineering: only if a chunk fails for good three times in a row.

To keep the table honest, I added a test that goes through all codes in the loader source and fails if one is missing from the docs file, the same way it works for the API error codes.

Sam also asked for a way to see the progress of a running import without logs. I proposed a progress line in the job status in the admin console, with chunks done and retries. Lena can add it to the console, and the loader already writes those numbers to the state file, so the backend part is small.

The docs are merged. The progress item is in the backlog.

summary: Added an endpoint for import job progress that reads the loader state file, so the admin console can show chunks done and retries for a running import.
body:
For Sam's request I added GET /admin/imports/{id}/progress. It reads the state file of the job from the object store and returns the chunks done, the chunks total, the number of retries so far and the time of the last finished chunk.

The response is cached for 5 seconds in Redis under a short key, so a console page that polls does not hit the store each time. For finished jobs it returns the final numbers from the job row in Postgres instead.

I wrote tests for a running job, a finished one, an unknown id and a job of another customer, which must return 404. The access check uses the same helper as the other import endpoints.

I showed Lena the response format. She will add a progress bar and a retry counter to the job page. Nothing is deployed to production yet, since the console part is missing.

summary: Reviewed the planned changes for the schema registry admin page with Lena and settled on a read-only first version with a version diff, because activation needs more safeguards.
body:
Lena asked what the admin console page for the schema registry should do. We went through the API together and talked about what an operator really needs.

The first version will be read-only: the list of schemas, the versions of each with the creation time and the deprecated flag, which one is active, and a diff between two versions. The diff is the useful part. It shows added fields and their types, and the compatibility result that was computed at registration.

We decided against putting the activate button in the first version. Activation changes validation in every worker within 30 seconds, and a click in a browser has no review step. I want at least a confirmation that shows the diff to the active version, the number of events per second that would be affected, and an audit entry with a reason text. That needs a small change in the API, a required reason field, so I will do that first.

I also changed the diff output of the API itself. It returned a flat list of paths, which is hard to show in a tree, so it now returns the paths with the kind of change: added, removed, type changed, enum extended. Lena checked the shape against her component and asked for the parent path as a separate field, which I added.

Tests for the new diff format were added, with nested objects and arrays. They pass.

Lena will build the read-only page this week against the staging registry, and I will do the reason field and the impact numbers for activation.

summary: Built the read-only schema registry admin page with a version list and a side-by-side diff, after the review with Lena settled the scope.
body:
Started the admin page for the schema registry with Lena's component structure. The page lists schemas by event type and shows each version with its active flag and the author of the registration.

The diff view compares two versions field by field and marks added, removed and type-changed fields. I reused the compatibility check from the registry API so the page can show why a pair of versions is incompatible.

There is no activate button on purpose. Activation writes an audit entry and needs safeguards that are not designed yet.

The endpoint for the list returned all versions with the full schema body, which made the page slow for the event type with six versions. I added a summary mode that returns only the metadata, and the full body loads when a version is opened. Lena checked the layout in the console and asked for monospace in the diff, which is done. Left for next time: empty state for event types without a schema and tests for the diff of nested fields.

summary: Added tests for the schema diff on nested fields and the empty state, and found that arrays of objects were diffed by position, which gave noisy results.
body:
Wrote the missing tests for the registry admin page. The empty state for an event type without schema now shows a short text instead of an empty table.

The nested field tests showed a real problem. The diff walked arrays of objects by index, so inserting one field in the middle of a list marked every following entry as changed. For event schemas the arrays are mostly lists of property definitions, so this happened often.

I changed the diff to match array items by their name key when they have one and to fall back to the index otherwise. The test case from the checkout event, which had 14 changed lines before, now shows one added field.

I also fixed a crash when a version had a null description. Lena will review the page tomorrow. The remaining work is a link from the audit log entry to the diff of the activated version.

summary: Looked at Redis memory growth on staging and found a session prefix with no TTL left over from an old console feature, now cleaned and given a 30 day TTL.
body:
The memory graph for the staging Redis had been climbing slowly for two weeks, so I used the prefix listing script from earlier this week to see where it came from. Two prefixes without TTL made up about 70 percent of the keys. One was the old console preview feature, which no code writes any more.

The second prefix belongs to the session store. Sessions were written with a TTL, but a refresh path used SET without the expiry argument and so removed the TTL on every refresh. That explains why active users left keys that never expired.

I fixed the refresh path to keep the TTL, added a unit test that reads the TTL after a refresh, and deleted the old preview keys on staging with a scan and a batch delete. Memory fell from 1.9 GB to 600 MB.

On production the same bug exists, so I prepared the deploy and a one-off script that sets a 30 day TTL on session keys without one. I will run it tomorrow in daytime and watch the login rate. Mara asked for key naming rules in the docs, which I added to the list for Sam.

summary: Deployed the session TTL fix to production, set a TTL on 212000 old session keys in batches, and saw no change in login errors while memory dropped by half.
body:
Deployed the session refresh fix first and checked that new refreshes keep their TTL. A sampled key showed about 29 days left a minute after a refresh, as expected.

Then I ran the one-off script that sets a 30 day TTL on session keys without one. It scans with a count of 500, sets the expiry in pipelines of 200 and sleeps 20 ms between batches so the limiter counters on the same instance are not slowed. I did a dry run first that only counted: 212000 keys without TTL, of which 9000 belonged to sessions active in the last day.

The real run took 26 minutes. During it the p99 of Redis commands stayed under 3 ms and the login error rate did not move from its usual 0.2 percent.

The old preview prefix was deleted in the same way, 61000 keys. Used memory went from 4.1 GB to 2.2 GB over the hour.

I added a Prometheus gauge for the number of keys without TTL per prefix, filled from the same scan once an hour at low rate. Tobias suggested an alert if any prefix other than the known two exceeds 1000 keys, which I wrote as a rule in the alert repo. The key naming rules went to Sam as a short list: prefix per feature, TTL required, no user data in the key itself. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Wrote the first part of the audit export: a streaming query over the audit log that writes NDJSON pages with a stable cursor, tested on 3 million rows.
body:
Started the audit export for compliance customers. They want the full audit log of their account as a file, including old entries.

The query reads the audit table in pages ordered by id, using the last id as cursor instead of offset, so a page costs the same at the beginning and at the end. The writer streams each page to NDJSON and does not hold more than one page in memory.

On a copy of production with 3 million audit rows for one large customer the export took 41 seconds and used about 80 MB. An offset based first try took over 6 minutes, so I dropped it.

Open points: the file format for the second step, signing the file so the customer can show it was not changed, and where the files are stored. I will ask Mara about the storage.

summary: Mara and I agreed that audit export files go to a private bucket with a 7 day lifetime and a signed link, so no file lives in the database or on the API host.
body:
Talked through storage for the audit export with Mara. Keeping files on the API host does not work with several tasks, and keeping them in Postgres would bloat the database.

We chose a private bucket with a prefix per customer, a 7 day lifecycle rule and a signed download link that is valid for one hour. The link is created when the customer asks for it, not when the export finishes.

The export runs as a job with a status row: queued, running, done, failed. The console will poll it. Tobias will add the bucket and the lifecycle rule in Terraform.

summary: Built the export job runner and the status endpoints for the audit export, with a checksum file next to the data so customers can verify the download.
body:
Implemented the job table and the runner for audit exports. A POST creates a job, a worker picks it up, runs the streaming query from last week and uploads the pages as one gzip file to the bucket.

The upload uses multipart so a large export does not need a local copy. I tested it against the staging bucket with a 2 GB export and it finished in about four minutes.

Next to the data file the job writes a small checksum file with the SHA-256 of the data and the row count. That is the first form of integrity proof. Signing with a key comes later if the compliance customers ask for more.

A GET on the job returns status, row count and, when done, a signed link. A failed job keeps the error text, and the runner marks a job as failed if it has not sent a heartbeat for ten minutes, which covers a crashed worker.

I found one bug in testing: two workers could pick up the same queued job. I changed the claim to an UPDATE with a condition on the status and check the affected row count. A test with eight parallel workers now shows exactly one winner.

Still to do: a limit of one running export per customer, the console button with Lena, and the audit entry that records who requested an export. That entry is important, because the export of the audit log should itself appear in the audit log.

summary: Added the one running export per customer limit and the audit entry for each export request, and tested a double click in the API.
body:
Two small but necessary pieces for the audit export. A second request while a job is queued or running for the same customer now returns 409 with the id of the existing job, so a double click does not start two exports.

Every request writes an audit entry with the user, the time range asked for and the job id. When the download link is created, another entry records that too. I checked that these entries appear in the next export of the same customer.

I wrote tests for the 409 path and for the race of two simultaneous requests. The race is covered by a unique partial index on active jobs, so the database decides and not the application code. Lena can now build the console button against these endpoints.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console page for audit exports and asked for polling backoff and a clear message for expired links, then fixed a timezone bug in the range filter.
body:
Reviewed Lena's pull request for the export page in the admin console. The structure is good: a form with a date range, a list of past exports and a download button.

Three comments. The page polled the job status every second, which for a four minute export is 240 calls, so I asked for a backoff from 2 to 15 seconds. A link older than one hour returned an error page, and it should instead request a fresh link. And the table showed a job that failed with the raw error string, which Sam will not be able to explain to a customer, so we agreed on a short message plus a code.

While testing her page I found a bug on my side. The range filter treated the end date as midnight at the start of that day in the server timezone, so entries of the last chosen day were missing. The API now takes the end as exclusive and the console sends the next day at 00:00 UTC. I added a test with an entry at 23:59.

Lena fixed her points the same afternoon. I tried the whole flow on staging with a customer that has 3 million entries: request, wait, download, verify the checksum. It worked. Sam will write the help text for the page next week.

summary: Prepared the audit export for a pilot with two customers: checked the bucket rule with Tobias, ran a large export on staging and read the database load.
body:
Prepared the audit export for a pilot with two customers who asked for it, one of them the largest on the platform. Nothing is enabled in production yet. Before anything goes out, Tobias confirmed that the bucket and the lifecycle rule exist in the production account, and I checked the rule by reading its configuration.

I ran a large export on staging with a copy of 5.4 million audit rows, the size of the big customer's table. It took 78 seconds and produced a 410 MB gzip file. I watched the Postgres graphs during the run: CPU rose by about 4 percent and no dashboard query slowed down. The cursor query reads in id order and does not sort, which is why the load stayed small.

The checksum matched when I downloaded the file and ran sha256sum. The row count in the checksum file matched a count query on the staging table. A second test exported a single month of 12000 rows and finished in two seconds.

One problem showed up. The signed link used the internal bucket host name, which customers cannot reach from outside. The link was valid but useless. I started changing the signing to use the public endpoint. The change is written and works on staging, and it still needs a review from Mara.

I also checked what happens when a worker is stopped in the middle of a job. I killed one task during an export on staging, the heartbeat check marked the job failed after ten minutes, and the customer could start a new one.

Next steps: get the signing fix reviewed, add the feature flag for the two pilot accounts, and agree the rollout time with both customers. Sam will write the help page before the pilot starts.

summary: Pilot feedback on the audit export asked for a CSV option and a filter by user, and I decided to add the user filter now and leave CSV for later.
body:
One pilot customer replied to the export. They like the file, but their compliance team opens it in a spreadsheet, so they asked for CSV, and they want to filter by the user who did an action.

The user filter is cheap, because the audit table already has an index on account and user. I added it as an optional parameter and tested that the cursor still works with it. An export for one user among 5 million rows took 3 seconds.

CSV is harder than it looks. Audit entries carry a JSON detail field with different shapes per action, so there is no fixed column set. I would have to either flatten it or put the JSON in one column. I wrote that down for the customer and suggested the one column version, and they accepted it for now. I will build it later if more customers ask.

summary: Checked the Postgres autovacuum stats on the audit table and found it was fine, so no change was made to its settings.
body: After the export pilot I looked at whether the audit table needed different vacuum settings, since it only gets inserts. The pg_stat_user_tables numbers showed few dead tuples and an autovacuum run every few hours. Insert only tables get vacuumed for freezing, and the last run was recent. Table size is 14 GB and growing by about 200 MB a week. I left the settings as they are and wrote the numbers in the ops notes for later comparison.

summary: Tried to speed up the ingest worker with a sync.Pool for decoded event structs and rolled it back, because it saved little and caused a data race in one path.
body:
Looked for easy allocation savings in the ingest worker, starting from a CPU and allocation profile of a 10 minute run at production-like load. Event decoding was the top allocator, with about 22 percent of allocated bytes.

I tried a sync.Pool of event structs that are reset after a batch is written. In the benchmark the allocation count per batch fell by a third, but the time per batch changed by less than 2 percent, which is within the noise of the machine. The garbage collector is not the bottleneck at this load.

Worse, the race detector found a problem in the error path. When a batch failed validation, the struct went back to the pool while the error report still held a pointer to its fields. That could have shown wrong data in a rejection message.

I could fix it by copying the fields for the report, but then most of the saved allocations would be gone again. With almost no speed gain and a new class of bugs, the change is not worth it.
