I reverted the branch and kept the benchmark file, because it is useful for later work. I also wrote the profile numbers in the notes so nobody repeats the experiment without a new reason.

The better lead from the profile is the database write per batch, which is where batching helps. That will be the next topic, and I will talk to Mara about how large a batch can be before the latency for the customer gets visible.

summary: Wrote the design for batch writes in the ingest worker with Mara: group events by event type, flush at 500 events or 200 ms, and acknowledge only after the write.
body:
Sat down with Mara and wrote the design for batching in the ingest worker. Today the worker writes each queue message with its own insert round trip, which is the main cost in the profile.

The plan is to collect messages per event type and flush when a group reaches 500 events or when 200 ms have passed since the first message in the group. One multi-row insert replaces many small ones.

The important rule is that the offset on the queue is committed only after the insert succeeded. If the worker crashes in the middle, the messages come again and the dedup key on the event id removes the duplicates. Mara checked that the unique index covers this.

We discussed the flush delay. 200 ms adds to the time until an event is searchable, but the search index is updated seconds later anyway, so customers will not see it. We set both numbers as config so they can be changed without a deploy.

Failure handling needs care. If one event in a batch violates a constraint, the whole insert fails. The design falls back to single inserts for that batch and sends the bad event to the dead letter topic.

I will start with the buffer and the flush loop, with tests using a fake store.

summary: Implemented the batch buffer and flush loop in the ingest worker with a fake store, including the single insert fallback and the dead letter path.
body:
Built the first working version of the batching from the design. A buffer per event type collects events, a timer per group triggers the flush after 200 ms, and a size check flushes at 500.

The flush calls the store with one multi-row insert and returns the offsets that can be committed. I kept the store behind an interface, so the tests use a fake that can fail on request.

Tests cover: flush by size, flush by time, a failing batch that falls back to single inserts, one bad event that goes to the dead letter topic while the other 499 are stored, and a shutdown that flushes what is in the buffers before exiting. The shutdown test caught a bug at once, because the timer goroutine was still running and wrote after the final flush. I fixed it by stopping the timers inside the same lock.

One decision: the buffer has a hard maximum of 5000 events across all groups. When it is full the worker stops reading from the queue until a flush frees space, so memory cannot grow without limit.

Not done yet: the real Postgres store with the multi-row insert, metrics for batch size and flush reason, and a load test. I expect the insert code to be short but want to check how many parameters a statement can take, since Postgres allows 65535 and wide events with many columns could hit that at 500 rows.

summary: Added the Postgres multi-row insert for batching with a parameter limit check, and a load test on staging showed about 3.1 times more events per second per worker.
body:
Wrote the real store for the batching branch. It builds one INSERT with many value tuples for the events of a flush, using ON CONFLICT on the event id to skip duplicates.

The parameter limit was a real concern. The events table insert uses 14 columns, so 500 rows need 7000 parameters, far below 65535. I still added a guard that splits a batch if rows times columns would exceed 60000, with a unit test, so a later schema change cannot break it silently.

I added three metrics: batch size as a histogram, flush reason as a counter with the values size, time and shutdown, and the insert duration. Mara looked at the names and asked for a worker label, which I added.

Then the load test on staging, with the replayed stream of a busy customer. Before the change one worker handled about 4200 events per second at full CPU. With batching it handled 13000 per second, so 3.1 times more, and CPU was at 70 percent at that rate.

The median batch size at the production rate was 310, and most flushes were by time. At low traffic the batches are small, which is as intended, because the delay is bounded.

I checked duplicates by replaying the same 200000 events twice. The table count did not change in the second run.

A second check was the crash case. I killed the worker with SIGKILL during a run and restarted it. The messages after the last committed offset came again, and the final count matched the input exactly.

Open: the p99 of the time from ingest to stored, which I want to measure, and a gradual production rollout with a flag per worker group.

summary: Measured end to end latency of batched ingest on staging: median 90 ms, p99 260 ms, and set the flush time to 150 ms because the tail was dominated by the timer.
body:
To decide the flush delay I measured the time from the HTTP response of the ingest API until the event is in the table, using a marker event every second during a load run.

With the 200 ms flush the median was 110 ms and the p99 was 310 ms. The tail was mostly the timer, since quiet event types wait the full delay. With 100 ms the median was 60 ms and the p99 190 ms, but batch size at low load fell to about 40 and the insert rate went up by a third.

I chose 150 ms as the compromise. Results: median 90 ms, p99 260 ms, and at the production rate the batch median stayed over 250. Mara agreed, since nothing downstream needs the event faster than a second.

The tail also showed one outlier pattern: every few minutes a batch took over 800 ms. It matched Postgres checkpoints on the staging instance. Production has more IO headroom, so I expect less, but I will watch the insert duration histogram there.

I updated the config default and the design notes. The rollout flag is ready, with the first step on one of the three worker groups.

summary: Rolled out batching to one ingest worker group in production and compared it with the other two groups for two hours, with lower CPU and no change in errors.
body:
Turned on the batching flag for one of three worker groups and left the other two on the old path as a comparison.

After two hours the batched group used about 38 percent CPU against 71 percent for the others at the same share of traffic. The queue lag was the same in all groups, under one second. The error rate and the dead letter count were unchanged, with zero new messages in the dead letter topic.

Insert duration p99 was 45 ms on the batched group, and database CPU went down slightly because there were fewer statements. The Postgres connection count also fell, since fewer round trips hold a connection.

I checked a sample of 1000 events from the batched group against the source in the queue, and all were stored once. Tomorrow I will enable the second group if the night stays quiet. Tobias knows about the rollout and the flag name for the on-call.

summary: Enabled batching on the remaining ingest worker groups and lowered the worker task count from 12 to 8, which Tobias applied in Terraform.
body:
The first group ran through the night without problems, so I enabled batching on the second group in the morning and on the third after lunch. Each step was followed by an hour of watching queue lag, errors and the insert histogram.

With all groups batched, CPU at the daily peak was around 40 percent. Tobias and I agreed that 12 tasks were too many for this. He changed the count to 8 in Terraform and applied it in the quiet window, keeping headroom of about 60 percent for a traffic spike.

The saving is about a third of the ingest compute cost. I added the numbers to the cost notes.

One small issue remained. The metric for flush reason showed many shutdown flushes during the task replacement, which is normal, but it made a dashboard panel look odd. I excluded that reason from the panel. The branch can be merged after Mara's final review.

summary: Looked at Redis connection counts from the search API after a complaint about slow first requests and found the client created a new connection pool per Fastify plugin instance.
body:
Sam passed on a customer report that the first search after some idle minutes was slow, about 400 ms more than usual. I looked at the search API and its Redis connections first, since the cache lookup is the first step of each request.

The connection count graph showed 4 connections per API task at idle and then a rise under load, with many connects per minute. The cause was in the setup code. A plugin created its own client for the cache and another for the rate limiter, and the plugin was registered in two scopes, so there were four pools per task instead of one.

The idle connections closed after the client timeout, so a request after a quiet time had to open a new connection with the TLS handshake, which explained the extra 400 ms.

I moved the client creation to one shared decorator that both users read, and set the keepalive so the connection stays open during quiet times. A small test checks that only one client is created per process.

On staging the connect rate dropped from about 30 per minute to nearly zero, and the first request after ten idle minutes took the normal 35 ms.

I also looked at the total connections to Redis. With 8 search tasks and the change, they fall from about 120 to 40 at peak. That leaves more room under the server limit, which matters since the ingest side also uses connections.

Deployed to production in the afternoon and checked the same graphs. The connects per minute fell to the same low level, and Sam confirmed with the reporting customer that the slow first request was gone. I will keep the keepalive value in the notes, because it must be shorter than any idle timeout of the load balancer in between.

summary: Added a Grafana panel for Redis connections per service and a note in the runbook on how to read it, after the pool fix in the search API.
body:
Built a panel that shows Redis connections per service, split by the client name that each service sets. Before this the graph only showed the total, which hid that one service had four pools.

The search API, the ingest workers and the console now set distinct client names. I added the panel to the Redis dashboard with a line for the server limit.

In the on-call runbook I wrote a paragraph on how to read it: normal values per service, what a sawtooth means (connections opened and closed by idle timeouts) and the first check to make. Tobias reviewed the runbook text and corrected the server limit I had written.

summary: Reworked the key naming of the rate limiter counters in Redis so every key carries a customer prefix and a window suffix, and migrated live counters without letting any customer's limit reset.
body:
The rate limiter counters had grown into three naming styles over the last months: some keys were just the API key, some had a limiter: prefix, and the newest ones had the window length in the middle. That made the prefix listing script from the other week hard to read and made it impossible to tell whose counter a key was without a lookup. I decided to move all of them to one scheme: rl:{customer_id}:{key_id}:{window}.

The change was in the limiter module of the search API and in the ingest auth path. Both now build keys through one helper in a shared package, and a unit test checks that no other code builds a key by string concatenation. I also added a test that the helper escapes a colon in a key id, because one old test key had one in it.

The risky part was the switch. If the new code read only new keys, every customer would start with an empty counter and could briefly exceed their limit. So the first deploy read the new key and, when it was missing, fell back to the old key and copied its value over with the remaining TTL. It wrote only the new key. After one full window length, almost all active counters had moved.

I deployed this to staging first and ran the limiter tests plus a small script that sent requests across a window boundary. The counts matched before and after the switch. In production I deployed at midday, when traffic is steady, and watched the 429 rate in Grafana for an hour. It stayed flat, and the fallback path was hit about 4000 times in the first ten minutes and then dropped to nearly zero.

The old keys were left to expire on their own TTLs, which are short, so no cleanup job was needed. The prefix listing script showed the old prefixes down to a few dozen keys by the end of the afternoon. Left to do: remove the fallback read in a later release once the old prefixes are gone, and add the new key scheme to the Redis section of the runbook.

summary: Added the rate limit headers and the 429 response body, with the retry hint only on 429 as agreed in the earlier review.
body:
Added the headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset to every response that passes through the per key limiter. The reset value is the number of seconds until the oldest bucket in the window leaves.

The 429 response has a JSON body with a code, the limit and the key id, and a Retry-After header. As Mara asked in the earlier review of error responses, the retry hint is sent only for 429 and 503, not for validation errors.

Tests check the header values at the start, in the middle and at the limit. I also tested that a key without a row uses the customer default.

summary: Wrote the admin endpoints to read and set the limit per API key, with validation and an audit entry for each change, and shared the contract with Lena.
body:
Implemented GET and PUT for the limit of one key and a list endpoint for all keys of a customer, with the current usage in the last minute next to the limit.

Validation: the limit must be between 10 and 100000 per minute and may not exceed the customer's plan maximum. A request over the maximum returns 422 with the plan value, so the console can show it.

Every change writes an audit entry with the old and new value and the user. This ties in with the audit export, so limit changes will show up in the files compliance customers download.

The usage number is read from the Redis buckets with one pipeline for all keys of a customer. For a customer with 60 keys that took 4 ms on staging.

I wrote the contract as an OpenAPI snippet and sent it to Lena. She will build a table with an inline edit field. One open question is whether a limit change should also clear the current counter. I decided no, because it would let someone reset a throttle by editing, and wrote that in the endpoint docs.

summary: Reviewed Lena's rate limit page in the console and found it sent the limit as a string, which the API now rejects clearly, and tested the flow on staging with a throttled key.
body:
Looked at Lena's first version of the limits page. It shows the keys of a customer with usage and the limit, and an inline edit.

The first save failed with 422. The page sent the number as a string from the input field. The API had accepted it quietly at first because of loose parsing, and I had made the validation stricter, with a message naming the field. Lena converted the value before sending.

I tested the flow on staging: I set a limit of 20 per minute for a test key, ran a script that sent 50 requests, saw 30 get 429, and watched the usage column on the page follow. The headers matched what the page showed.

Two more points for her: show the plan maximum as a hint next to the field, and disable the save button while a request is running. She will fix both. After that I want to run the new limiter next to the old one in shadow mode for a few days, comparing decisions before switching customers over.

summary: Added a per-key limit override cache in Redis with a 60 second TTL, so the limiter stops reading Postgres on every request, and checked that changes show up within a minute.
body:
After yesterday's review of Lena's page, the next step was the limiter lookup. Each request read the key's limit from Postgres, which was fine at low volume but showed up in the slow query list on staging. I added a Redis cache under the key name rl:limit:<customer>:<key> with a 60 second TTL.

The admin endpoint that sets a limit now deletes the cached entry, so a change is visible at once on the node that handled it and within a minute on the others. I tested this with a throttled key on staging: set to 5 per second, saw 429 responses, raised to 50, and the 429s stopped after the next request. Postgres reads from the limiter dropped to nearly zero in the staging graph. Still to do: a test for the case where Redis is down, which should fall back to the default limit.

summary: Made the rate limiter fall back to the stored limit when Redis is unreachable and tested it by blocking the Redis port on staging; requests kept flowing with a warning metric.
body:
The open point from yesterday was what the limiter does when Redis is down. Before the change, a connection error turned into a 500 for the caller, which is the wrong trade for a protective feature.

The limiter now catches connection errors and timeouts, lets the request pass, and increments a counter named ratelimit_redis_bypass_total. It logs one warning per 10 seconds, not one per request. I blocked the Redis port on a staging task for three minutes and sent traffic at 200 requests per second; no errors reached the client and the counter rose as expected. After the port opened, counting resumed with no restart.

I also added a Grafana alert if the bypass counter stays above zero for 5 minutes. Mara read the diff and asked for a test of the timeout value; it is 50 ms and I added that to the test file. Next is documenting the limits in the public API docs.

summary: Wrote the public docs page for rate limits with header descriptions, the 429 body and client backoff examples in curl and TypeScript, and checked each example against staging.
body:
Today's work was the docs for the rate limit feature. The page covers the three headers, the 429 response body, and what a client should do when it hits the limit.

I ran every example against staging before putting it in the page. The curl example prints the headers with -i and shows a real 429. The TypeScript example reads the reset header and waits until then, with a little random jitter so many clients do not all return at the same second.

One example was wrong at first: I had written that the reset header is a timestamp, but it is the number of seconds until the window ends. I fixed the text and the example together. I also added a table with the default limits per plan and a note that large customers can ask support for a higher limit.

The page says that limits count per API key, not per customer. That matches the code, but I checked it with a test that used two keys of the same customer; each had its own counter.

I sent the draft to Sam for review of wording. He will check that support can answer the usual question, why a key gets 429 while the dashboard shows low traffic. I expect his notes tomorrow. The remaining item is a short changelog entry once the page is live. I did not touch code today beyond a typo in a header name in the OpenAPI file.

summary: Applied Sam's review of the rate limit docs, added a troubleshooting section for unexpected 429s, and fixed an OpenAPI mismatch that listed the wrong header name.
body:
Sam sent his notes in the afternoon and most were about wording. He asked for plain language where I had used the term window, so the page now says the period in which requests are counted, and the term window is explained once.

He also pointed out that support gets the same question again and again: a key gets 429 while the customer thinks it sends little. I wrote a troubleshooting section with four checks. First, look at whether several services share one key. Second, look at bursts inside a single second. Third, look at the limit set for the key in the console. Fourth, look at the headers of the last 429.

While checking the OpenAPI file I found it still listed X-RateLimit-Limits with an s, while the API sends X-RateLimit-Limit. The generated client docs showed the wrong name. I fixed the spec and added a small test that compares the header names in the spec with those in the code constants.

I rebuilt the docs site locally and clicked through the page. Links to the API reference work. The changelog entry is written and waits for the deploy of the docs tomorrow morning. Lena asked whether the console could link to this page from the rate limit screen; I said yes and gave her the final address.

summary: Published the rate limit docs page and changelog entry, and Lena added the link from the console limit screen; the page loads and all examples still match staging.
body:
I deployed the docs site first thing. After the build I opened the page on production and checked the links and the code blocks. The curl examples point at the staging host in the draft, and I replaced them with the public host before the build, which I verified once more now.

Lena merged the link from the console rate limit screen. It opens the page in a new tab at the anchor for the headers section.

I wrote the changelog entry in two sentences and listed the new headers. Nothing else changed in code today.

summary: Looked at the slow query list in Postgres and found the audit log listing sorting without a matching index; added a composite index on customer and created time, built concurrently.
body:
The weekly slow query report showed the audit log listing in the admin console at about 900 ms for the larger customers. The explain output showed a sort over many rows after a filter by customer id.

I added a composite index on (customer_id, created_at desc) and built it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on staging first. It took 4 minutes on a copy of the table and the listing dropped to about 25 ms.

On production the build ran during the quiet hours of the afternoon and took 7 minutes, with no lock waits. The old single column index on customer id is now mostly redundant, but I left it for a week to watch the plans before dropping it.

summary: Reviewed the first full day of the batching and limiter changes in Grafana, found one worker group with a higher dead letter count, and traced it to a malformed event type from one customer.
body:
I started with the dashboards of the ingest workers, since batching has run everywhere for a while. Most numbers were calm: CPU per task, flush sizes and acknowledge latency all matched the staging tests.

One worker group had a dead letter count above the others, about 40 events in a day against single digits elsewhere. I pulled the dead letter records and saw the same error in all of them: the event type field held an empty string.

The batch buffer groups events by type, and the empty type went to a group that the store insert rejected, so the single insert fallback ran for the whole group and then each event went to the dead letter path. The fallback worked as designed, but the log did not say why. I looked at the source of the events. They came from one customer using an old SDK version that sends the type in a different field when a batch holds mixed events.

The fix in the worker was small. Events with an empty type now get rejected at the validation step with a clear error message, before they enter a batch, and the response to the client names the event index. I added a test with a mixed batch where one event is invalid and the others are written.

I told Sam about the customer and the SDK version, so support can contact them. I did not change the dead letter format. I deployed the validation to one group and will compare the counts tomorrow before rolling out to the rest.

summary: Rolled the event type validation out to all ingest worker groups; the dead letter count is down to zero from that customer and the 400 responses name the bad event index.
body:
The group with the new validation had no dead letters from the empty type problem over the weekend, so I rolled it out to the other groups this afternoon. The customer with the old SDK now gets a 400 with the index of the bad event, and Sam heard back that they will update the SDK next week.

I watched the error rate for an hour after the rollout. It stayed flat apart from the expected 400s from that one customer. The valid events in the same batches were written normally.

summary: Checked rate limiter behavior at the window boundary on staging with a burst test, found a double-count of one request at the rollover, and fixed it in the Lua script.
body:
After the override cache and the Redis fallback were in, I wanted to see how the limiter behaves exactly at the edge of a window. I wrote a small Go script that sends bursts of 100 requests per second with one throttled key, and ran it against staging for ten minutes.

Most windows were exact. In about 1 of 40 rollovers the key was allowed 101 requests instead of 100 within a window, and in a few cases a request at the boundary was counted in both windows. The cause was in the Lua script that increments the counter. It computed the window suffix from the client clock of the API host, while the TTL was set by Redis. Two hosts with a clock difference of about 80 ms disagreed about which window a request belonged to.

The fix was to take the time from Redis with the TIME command inside the script and build the window suffix from that value. The script now sets the expiry only when the key is created, so a late request does not extend an old window. I kept the customer prefix and the window suffix from the key naming change, so no live counters needed migration.

I reran the burst test with three API hosts at once. Over 60 rollovers there was no window with more than 100 requests and no double count. The extra call to TIME added less than 0.1 ms per request in the Redis latency panel in Grafana.

I added a test for the script that sets two fake host clocks apart and checks that the count stays exact. The change is deployed to staging only. Next step is to watch it for a day and then roll it out to production with Mara reviewing the script. I also noted in the runbook why the script must not use the host clock.

summary: Settled with Mara that the registry blocks breaking schema changes but allows an override with a reason, and added enum handling where a removed value breaks and an added value only warns.
body:
We met in the morning about what the compatibility check should do with a failure. Mara argued that blocking everything would push people to work around the registry, and I argued that warnings alone would be ignored. We agreed on blocking by default, with an override flag that needs a written reason, and the reason goes into the audit log.

For enums I implemented this: removing a value is breaking, because old events with that value become invalid. Adding a value is a warning, since consumers that switch on the value may not know it. The result of the check now has two lists, errors and warnings, and only errors block.

The register endpoint returns 409 with the list of errors when the check fails. With override=true and a reason field of at least 10 characters, the version is stored and the audit entry holds the errors that were overridden. A request with override but no reason returns 422.

I wrote tests for six cases: clean change, warning only, error blocked, error overridden with a reason, override without a reason, and the first version of a new schema which has nothing to compare with. All pass.

One detail took time. The audit entry first held the full schema text, which was large for some schemas. I changed it to hold the schema id, the version numbers and the list of errors only.

I ran the endpoint on staging with the real pairs from yesterday and the results matched. I have not yet told Lena about the new 409 body, and the admin page does not show it. That is the next item, together with the docs for the people who register schemas.

summary: Shared the 409 and 422 response contracts of the registry with Lena and made the registry docs describe the override flow and the reason field.
body:
I wrote down the response bodies for the registry endpoint. A 409 holds an errors array with path, rule and a short message, plus a warnings array. A 422 holds a single message about the missing reason.

I sent this to Lena with an example for each case. She asked whether the path uses dots or slashes. It uses dots for objects and [] for array items, like items[].id, and I added that to the contract.

In the docs I added a section on registering a new version. It explains the two outcomes, what counts as breaking, and how to override. I put a warning there that an override is recorded in the audit log with the name of the user.

Sam read the section and suggested an example that fails on purpose, so I added one that adds a required field. I checked the example on staging and the output matches the text.

summary: Looked into Redis memory use on production after an alert at 80 percent, found a cache key family for dashboard queries with TTLs set far too long, and shortened them with a staged change.
body:
The memory alert for Redis fired in the evening and I looked at it before the on-call had to. Used memory was at 80 percent of the instance limit and had grown for about two weeks.

I sampled keys with SCAN and the memory usage command, in batches, not with KEYS. The biggest family by far was the dashboard query cache, with names like dq:<customer>:<hash>. They made up about 60 percent of the memory.

The TTL of these keys was 24 hours, which came from the first version of the dashboards, when the data was refreshed once per day. Now the data is much fresher, and the cache hit rate showed that most hits happen within 10 minutes of the first request. I checked the hit rate in Grafana by key age: more than 95 percent of the hits were younger than 15 minutes.

I changed the TTL to 30 minutes in the search API config. I did not delete anything by hand. The old keys expire on their own within a day, and the memory graph should come down by tomorrow.

I deployed to one task first and checked that new keys got the 30 minute TTL with the TTL command. Then I deployed to the rest.

Two cautions. A shorter TTL means more cold queries for the large customers, so I will watch the p95 of the dashboard endpoint tomorrow. And the memory alert threshold itself is fine, but the alert text did not say which key family is the biggest, so I added a line in the runbook on how to sample keys by prefix.

I also noted that the sampling script is slow on a big keyspace, so I limited it to 5000 keys per run.

summary: Memory in Redis dropped from 80 to 46 percent after the shorter dashboard cache TTL, and the dashboard p95 rose only slightly, from 310 ms to 340 ms.
body:
I checked the graphs this afternoon, a day after the TTL change. Redis memory went from 80 percent down to 46 percent as the old long-lived keys expired, and it is now flat.

The cache hit rate of the dashboard queries fell from 91 to 88 percent. The p95 of the dashboard endpoint rose from 310 ms to 340 ms, which I think is acceptable. The large customers show the biggest change, but none is above 600 ms at p95.

I looked at the slowest 20 requests and they were all cold queries on the largest customer, so the longer TTL was never what kept them fast.

I added the numbers to the runbook next to the sampling note. No further change is planned for this topic, except to look at the numbers again after a week.

summary: Went through the ingest dead letter queue by hand after batching and sorted the 140 messages into three causes; two were customer data problems and one was a timeout in the multi-row insert.
body:
After the first week of batching I wanted to know what is really in the dead letter queue, because the count never reached zero. I exported the 140 messages from the last seven days and grouped them by the error text and the customer.

The first group, 61 messages, came from the malformed event type of one customer that we already fixed with validation. They were old and I removed them after saving a copy. The second group, 52 messages, had timestamps far in the future, up to three years ahead, from a customer device with a wrong clock. The schema accepts them, but the insert into a partitioned table failed because no partition existed. That is a customer data problem, and I will ask Sam to write to the customer.

The third group, 27 messages, was the interesting one. The error was a statement timeout in the multi-row insert, and all of them were batches of 500 events with large payloads. The single insert fallback then handled the events one by one and some also timed out, so they ended in the dead letter path. The timeout is 5 seconds, and a batch of 500 large events can take longer when the table is busy with vacuum.

I changed the flush rule so a batch is also limited by total payload size, 2 MB for now, and not only by 500 events or 150 ms. A test with the large payloads from that customer gave no timeouts in 20 minutes. I will watch the dead letter count for three days before I touch the timeout itself.

summary: Ran the checksum-verifying loader on a 9 GB customer file, saw 6 retries and no mismatches, and documented the new log lines for support.
body:
Sam had a customer with a 9 GB NDJSON file waiting for an import, which was a good test for the verification from this afternoon. I ran the loader in production at a quiet time, with Sam watching the progress in the console.

The import took 52 minutes. The loader recorded 6 chunk retries, all from timeouts on the store side, and after each one the hash check passed, so no chunk had to be redone because of a mismatch. The final event count was 18.4 million, which matched the number of lines in the file, and I checked that there were no duplicate event ids with a count query.

I also looked at the new cost of hashing. CPU on the loader task was about 4 percent higher than before, and the throughput was within 2 percent of the previous run on a file of similar size. That is not a problem.

Then I wrote the docs. The new log lines are: chunk verified, chunk hash mismatch and reprocessing, and state file without hashes so verification skipped. For each I wrote what it means and whether support has to do anything. Only the second one deserves attention if it appears often, because it means the file changed during the import.

Sam read the draft and asked what to do if the customer replaces the file while a job is paused. I added a paragraph: a resume with a changed file will reprocess from the first chunk that differs, and the customer should start a new import if the file is different in a big way.

I also fixed a small thing in the progress endpoint, which now returns the number of verified chunks next to the chunks done. Lena will show it in the console later if she wants.

Next I want to look at the total time limit once more, since a long verified resume could take longer than the two hours that were set for a stuck job. I will look at it tomorrow.

summary: Changed the loader time limit to count only time without progress, so a long healthy import is no longer stopped after two hours, while a stuck one still ends after 20 minutes.
body:
The two hour limit per file made sense when imports were small. With verification and 9 GB files, a healthy import can come near it. I changed the limit to measure time without progress: the timer resets whenever a chunk finishes.

The default is 20 minutes without a finished chunk, and the job ends with the same clear error message as before, which now says that no chunk finished for 20 minutes. I kept a hard upper limit of 12 hours as a safety net.

Tests cover a slow but steady run, a stuck chunk, and the hard limit with a fake clock.

summary: Planned the search API latency work: profiled the slowest query shapes, found that wildcard prefix queries on the message field dominate the p99, and listed three options without choosing yet.
body:
The p99 of the search API has been creeping up for several weeks, so I spent the evening on measuring, not on changing code. I took one day of request logs, grouped them by query shape and computed the percentiles for each group.

The overall p50 is 120 ms and the p99 is 1.4 seconds. The groups tell a clearer story. Plain term queries have a p99 of 300 ms. Filters by time range and event type are at 250 ms. Wildcard prefix queries on the message field, like err*, have a p99 of 3.8 seconds, and they are only 4 percent of the requests but 70 percent of the slow ones.

I checked what the console sends. Lena's search box adds a trailing wildcard to each term as the user types, so the prefix queries are partly the result of that choice.

I also looked at the OpenSearch side. The slow queries touch many shards because the index is split by customer, and a customer with a large index has to scan a lot for a prefix. This ties into the plan for a new shard layout, but that is a bigger step and I do not want to depend on it.

Three options came out of this:
- Make the console send the wildcard only after a pause and only for terms of at least 3 characters, which cuts the count of the expensive queries.
- Index the message field with edge n-grams for prefix search, which makes those queries fast but makes the index bigger and needs a reindex.
- Cache the results of wildcard queries for 60 seconds in Redis, which helps repeated queries only.

I estimated the first as one day of work with Lena, the second as about a week including the reindex, and the third as a day with an unclear gain since most prefix queries differ.

I did not decide. I wrote the numbers and the options in the planning doc and I will bring it to the team meeting. My own guess is that the first option will take away most of the pain, and the second can wait for the new shard layout.

summary: Asked Lena to add a debounce and a minimum term length of 3 to the console search box, and sent her the query shape numbers that justify it.
body:
After the meeting the team agreed to try the cheap option first. I wrote to Lena with the numbers: wildcard prefix queries are 4 percent of requests but 70 percent of the slow ones.

I proposed a debounce of 300 ms and a minimum term length of 3 characters before a wildcard is added. She agreed and will do it tomorrow. I will compare the p99 on the following day.

summary: Found that the ingest client library retried on 400 responses and flooded the API for one customer, and changed it to retry only on 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff and jitter.
body:
Support forwarded a complaint from a customer whose traffic to the ingest API was five times larger than usual for a few hours, with almost all of it failing. I looked at the access logs and saw the same batches sent again and again, each answered with 400.

The cause was in our own client library for Node, which the customer uses. Its retry logic treated every non-2xx response as retryable, up to 8 attempts. A 400 means the batch is invalid and sending it again changes nothing, but it multiplies the load by 8.

I changed the library so that it retries only on 429, 502, 503, 504 and on network errors. For 429 it honors the reset header. The delay grows exponentially from 200 ms to a cap of 10 seconds, with full jitter, and the attempts are capped at 5.

I wrote tests with a mock server for each status code, and for a connection reset. A 400 now throws at once with the error body, so the caller sees what was wrong.

I also checked the Go and Python clients. The Go client already had the right rule. The Python client had the same problem as Node, so I made the same change there, with a test for each status.

Because 400 responses now include the index of the bad event, which came from the validation change last week, the thrown error includes the index too.

I released the patch versions of both libraries and wrote the changelog entry. Sam will tell the customer to upgrade. On our side I added a Grafana panel for 400 responses per customer, so a flood like this shows up earlier than a complaint.

summary: The search box debounce is live and the p99 of the search API dropped from 1.4 seconds to 820 ms, with wildcard queries down to about a third of their earlier count.
body:
Lena shipped the debounce and the minimum term length yesterday evening, and I looked at the numbers this morning with a full night of traffic, which is a small sample but a useful one.

The share of wildcard prefix queries fell from 4 percent to 1.3 percent of the requests. The overall p99 went from 1.4 seconds to 820 ms, and the p50 stayed at 120 ms. The p99 of the wildcard group itself did not change, still near 3.8 seconds, which is expected since the queries are as expensive as before and there are just fewer.

I went through the remaining wildcard queries in the logs. Most come from the API and not from the console, from customers who built their own search boxes. That means a client change cannot help with those.

So the second option from the plan stays on the list, the edge n-grams for the message field. I wrote down in the planning doc that it fits best with the reindex that comes with the new shard layout, so that the data is rebuilt only once.

I wrote a short note for Sam as well, so that support can explain to customers who ask that prefix search is slower than term search, and that a minimum of 3 characters helps.

Nothing else changed today, and I will check the numbers again after a week with the normal weekday mix of traffic.

summary: Added a registry check that rejects a schema with a field name used twice at different nesting levels with a different type, and wrote tests for it after a confusing case in the dry run.
body:
A user of the dry run endpoint sent me a schema that passed the check but made the query side confused. A field called id was a string at the top level and a number inside a nested object. Both are legal on their own, but the search mapping merges field names by their last part in some views, so the types clashed there.

I discussed it with Mara and we decided not to block it hard. The registry now returns a warning for the same field name with different types at different levels, and a block only if the field is part of the search mapping. The override with a reason still works for the block case.

The code walks the schema once and keeps a map from the field name to the type and the path. I wrote tests for five cases: the same type in two places, different types in two places, a nested array of objects, a field outside the mapping and a field inside it. The array case needed a fix, because the walker skipped array items and so missed the clash.

The dry run response lists both paths in the warning, so the user can see where the clash is. I updated the registry docs with one example and asked Lena to show warnings in yellow on the admin page. The next step is to check the existing schemas for such clashes before the rule goes live.

summary: Wrote the registry enum docs, then added a dry run endpoint so users can check a schema against the current version without registering it, and tested it with the admin page.
body:
I started with the docs I had put off. The enum section now says that removing a value is an error and adding a value is a warning, with the reason for each, and an example of the 409 body that a removal produces.

While writing the examples I noticed that a user can only find out about a failed check by trying to register, which creates noise in the audit log when the override is used by mistake. A dry run would help. I added POST /schemas/:name/check, which runs the same compatibility function and returns the same errors and warnings, but stores nothing and writes no audit entry.

The handler shares the code with the register endpoint. I split the register handler into a function that does the check and one that stores the version, so that both paths use the same check and cannot drift apart. I wrote tests that call both endpoints with the same inputs and compare the results.

The response of the dry run has a field compatible that is true when there are no errors, and the lists of errors and warnings. It does not accept the override flag, and returns 400 if it is sent, because the flag has no meaning there.

I told Lena about the endpoint. She wants a Check button on the admin page, next to Register. For now the page is read-only for the versions and that is still the plan, so we agreed that the button goes into a later version together with the activation step.

I ran the dry run against the 30 real pairs once more as a regression check, and all gave the same result as the register endpoint did before.

One more thing I found: the check treated a change from required to optional as safe, which is correct for readers. But a producer that relied on the field now may omit it, and consumers may break. I decided to report this as a warning and added a test. I updated the docs list to include that case.

The docs are built and I read the page once, and the examples match staging output.

summary: Dropped the old single column audit log index after a week of watching the plans, and checked that the listing and the export query still use the composite index.
body:
A week ago I added the composite index on customer and created time for the audit log listing. Today I checked whether anything still used the old index on customer id alone.

The statistics view showed zero scans on the old index since the new one went live. I also ran explain on the three queries that touch the table: the console listing, the audit export cursor query and the retention job. The listing and the retention job use the composite index. The export query uses the id cursor on the primary key, as before, and never used either.

I dropped the old index with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY during the afternoon. It freed about 1.8 GB on the table, and the write path got a little cheaper, since there is one index less to update.

I watched the slow query list for an hour afterwards and saw nothing new for this table. I wrote the size and the reason in the migration note, in case someone wonders why the index is gone.

summary: Added the CSV option for audit export that pilot customers asked for, using the same cursor and writing a header from a fixed column list, with proper quoting tested on nasty values.
body:
The pilot feedback from a while ago asked for CSV, and after the user filter went in I had left it for later. Today I did it, since the export code was fresh in my mind from the index work.

The export job gets a format parameter, ndjson by default or csv. The query and the cursor are the same, so only the writer differs. For CSV the columns come from a fixed list, with a header line, and the details field is written as a JSON string in one column.

Quoting was the part that needed care. I wrote tests with values that contain commas, quotes, newlines and a leading equals sign, since spreadsheet programs may run a cell that starts with that. Those cells are prefixed with a single quote, which is a common precaution. The checksum file works as before, over the bytes of the file.

I exported 3 million rows in CSV on staging and the job took about as long as the NDJSON one. The file was 18 percent smaller. Lena will add a format choice to the console page, and I sent her the parameter name.

summary: Deployed the CSV audit export to production and had Sam run one with a pilot customer, who opened the file in a spreadsheet without problems and confirmed the checksum matched.
body:
I deployed the CSV format this morning and kept the default as NDJSON, so existing automation is not affected. The status endpoint now reports the format of each job.

Sam ran an export for one of the two pilot customers on a call. The file opened in their spreadsheet program with the columns in the expected order, and the text with commas stayed in one cell. They verified the download with the checksum file and it matched.

One remark from the customer was that the timestamps are in UTC with a Z suffix, and they would like a local time column. I did not decide on that. It goes on the list for the pilot feedback, with the question of whether it should be a time zone parameter. The database read load during the export stayed small, as with the NDJSON ones.

summary: Wrote the first draft of the search-v2 query parser grammar for field filters, quoted phrases and boolean operators, and parsed 40 real customer queries with it.
body:
Started the new query parser for search v2 today. The old parser split on spaces and guessed at field names, which is why queries like status:error AND "timeout after" returned odd results. The new grammar handles field:value filters, quoted phrases, AND, OR, NOT and parentheses.

I wrote it as a small recursive descent parser in TypeScript in src/search/parser.ts instead of pulling in a parser generator. The grammar is short enough that a generator would add a build step for no gain. Precedence is NOT over AND over OR, as in the docs.

To test it I took 40 real queries from the search log, with customer names removed, and ran them through both parsers. 34 gave the same structure. Of the 6 that differed, 5 were cases where the old parser was simply wrong, for example treating the word AND inside a quoted phrase as an operator. The sixth was a query with an unclosed quote, which the new parser rejects with an error that gives the position.

I still have to decide what an unclosed quote should do in the console: reject or auto-close. I left it as a rejection for now. Next step is the translation from the parse tree to OpenSearch bool queries, and then the per-field boosts.

summary: Translated the parser's tree into OpenSearch bool queries and found that NOT inside OR needs a must_not wrapper, which the first version silently dropped.
body:
Continued on the search-v2 branch with the step after the parser: turning the parse tree into an OpenSearch query body. Each AND node becomes a bool with must clauses, each OR becomes a bool with should and minimum_should_match 1, and a phrase becomes match_phrase on the message field.

The first version had a bug. A NOT directly under an OR, as in level:error OR NOT host:web-1, produced a should clause that contained a bare must_not, and OpenSearch treats a bool that has only must_not inside should as matching nothing useful. The result was that the second branch of the OR never matched. The fix is to wrap a negation under OR in a bool with must_not plus a match_all in must, so it means everything except those hits.

I wrote 31 unit tests for the translator, one for each shape in the grammar and several for nesting. I also added a snapshot test that checks the generated JSON for 10 of the real queries from yesterday, so later changes to boosts show up as a visible diff.

I ran the translated queries against the staging index and compared hit counts with the old parser on the queries where both agreed in structure. Counts matched on all 34. The 5 queries where the old parser was wrong now return fewer, more correct hits.

The unclosed quote case: I decided to reject, and the API returns 400 with the character position. I asked Lena to show that message under the search box. Per-field boosts come next, probably tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why a customer saw different hit counts for the same query before and after the parser change, with two concrete causes.
body:
Sam asked this morning why a customer reported that a search for error AND timeout gave 1,900 hits last week and 1,240 today. I checked the search log and ran the query through the old and new parser on staging.

There were two causes. The old parser treated the unquoted AND inside a longer phrase as a word, so it matched events containing the literal text. The new parser applies it as an operator, so events must contain both terms. The second cause was that the customer's query also contained a stray trailing quote, which the old parser dropped and the new one rejects. The customer had probably retyped it without the quote.

I wrote a short answer for Sam to send, with a before and after example, and added a line to the search docs draft about operators needing to be written in capitals. Nothing is broken; the new numbers are the correct ones.

summary: Added per-field boosts to search v2, with message at 1.0, service at 2.0 and event type at 3.0, and checked the ranking on 25 saved queries with Mara.
body:
Today's work on the search-v2 branch was the per-field boosts. Until now every field counted the same, so a hit in the free text message ranked like a hit in the event type, which made short exact matches sink below long noisy ones.

I made the boosts a config map in src/search/boosts.ts rather than hardcoding them in the translator. The default is message 1.0, service 2.0, event type 3.0 and host 1.5. Customers cannot change them yet; I kept the map keyed by field so a per-customer override can come later without changing the query code.

To judge the result I took 25 saved queries that Sam had collected from support tickets where people complained about ordering. For each one I marked by hand which hit should be first. With the old equal weights, the right hit was in the top 3 for 14 of 25. With the new boosts it was 21 of 25. I tried event type at 5.0 as well, and that pushed too many low value hits to the top for queries that were really text searches, so I stayed at 3.0.

Mara reviewed the change in the afternoon. She pointed out that the boost applies to match clauses but not to phrases, and the phrase clauses were still on message only. I fixed that by building the phrase as a multi_match of type phrase over the boosted fields. This changed the ranking of 2 queries, both for the better.

The 4 queries that still rank wrongly are all ones where the right answer depends on recency. I noted that as a follow-up for a time decay, but I have not decided whether it is worth the complexity. The reindex job needs no change for this, because boosts are applied at query time.

summary: Ran the search v2 parser against a week of real customer queries, found three classes of parse failure, and fixed two of them in the grammar while leaving one on the fallback path.
body:
Today's session was the first large replay of the search v2 parser against real traffic. I exported the query strings of the last seven days from the search API logs, removed duplicates and got about 18,400 distinct queries. I ran every one through the new parser in a script, without sending anything to OpenSearch, and counted parse errors.

412 queries failed to parse, which is about 2.2 percent. I sorted them by hand into three classes. The first and largest class, 251 queries, had an unbalanced quote, usually a stray apostrophe inside a message text such as don't. The grammar treated it as the start of a phrase. I changed the lexer so that a quote only opens a phrase at the start of a term or after a colon, and an apostrophe inside a word is plain text. That fixed all 251.

The second class, 118 queries, used a field name with a dot, like request.path:/login. The first draft only allowed letters and underscores in field names. I widened the field name rule to allow dots and checked that it still does not swallow a URL such as http://host, which has a colon inside a term. Two odd cases remained and I added them as tests.

The third class, 43 queries, mixed a leading minus with parentheses, for example -(error timeout). The old parser ignored this silently and the new grammar does not define it. I did not fix it today, since the meaning is not obvious. These queries go to the fallback to the old parser, which is already in the plan, and I added a counter metric for the fallback so we can see how often it happens.

After the two grammar fixes the failure rate is 43 of 18,400, or 0.23 percent. I added 30 of the failing strings as regression tests in the parser test suite. Next I will ask Mara whether negated groups should be supported at all, and I will check if the 43 come from a few customers only.

summary: Built the reindex job change for search v2 so it writes to a new index alias and swaps only after document counts match, then tested it on a copy of 2 million events.
body:
The nightly reindex job so far rewrote the live index in place, which meant a failure halfway left a half built index. For search v2 the new parser and boosts need field mappings that differ slightly, so I changed the job to build a fresh index and switch an alias at the end.

The steps are: create events-v2-<run id> with the new mapping, stream documents from Postgres in batches of 2,000 with the bulk API, compare the document count with the source count, then move the alias atomically and keep the previous index for one day. If the counts differ by more than 0.1 percent the job stops, leaves the alias alone and logs the difference.

I tested on staging with a copy of 2 million events. The first run took 11 minutes, and the count check passed. I then killed the job after the first million to simulate a crash. The alias stayed on the old index, the half built one was left behind, and the next run deleted it as stale. That cleanup of leftovers was something I had not planned and added after seeing the leftover in the index list.

One thing that went wrong: the bulk batches of 5,000 that I tried first caused 429 responses from OpenSearch on the small staging node, so I went back to 2,000. For production I will need to check the numbers with Tobias before the first real run, since the cluster there is bigger but also busier at night.

The remaining work is the alias use in the search API, which still uses the concrete index name in two places, and a Grafana panel for job duration.

summary: Replaced the two hardcoded index names in the search API with the alias and confirmed with a staging reindex that queries kept working during the swap.
body:
Followed up on yesterday's reindex change. The search API had the concrete index name in the suggest endpoint and in the export helper, so after an alias swap they would have kept reading the old index. I replaced both with the alias name from the shared config.

To check it, I ran a reindex on staging while a loop sent 10 queries a second to the search API. During the swap there were no errors and no gap in results; the hit counts changed only once, from the old to the new index. I also confirmed that the suggest endpoint now returns terms from the new index.

summary: Reviewed Mara's batching change for the ingest worker and asked for a limit on batch bytes, since 500 large events could exceed the Postgres statement size.
body:
Mara asked for a review of the first version of batch writes in the ingest worker. The idea is to collect events and write them with one multi-row insert instead of one insert each. It looked sound, and the benchmark she attached showed the insert time per event falling from 1.9 ms to 0.4 ms.

My main concern was that the batch is limited only by count, 500 events. Most customers send small events, but one large customer sends events of up to 200 KB. 500 of those would make a statement of 100 MB, which is far over what we want to send in one go, and it would hold a connection for a long time.

I asked for a second limit on total bytes, I suggested 4 MB, so that the batch is flushed when either limit is reached. I also asked that the flush on a timer stays at 200 ms so low traffic does not wait.

Two smaller points: the error path should split a failed batch into single inserts so one bad event does not drop the whole batch, and the metric for batch size should be a histogram, not a gauge. Mara agreed with all of them and will push the changes tomorrow. I will run the load test on staging after that.

summary: Wrote the load test for batched ingest on staging with a mix of small and 200 KB events, to check the byte limit and the timer flush.
body:
To prepare for Mara's updated batching change I built a load test script in tools/loadtest that replays a mix modeled on production: 95 percent events of about 1 KB and 5 percent of around 200 KB. It sends batches over HTTP/2 at a configurable rate, and I can set the number of connections.

The script prints the rate of accepted events, the 99th percentile of latency and the count of non-2xx responses. It also checks the row count in Postgres at the end against the number of events sent, so lost events show up as a number rather than a feeling.

I ran it against the current staging build, which still has single inserts, to get a baseline: 1,800 events a second at saturation, p99 of 410 ms, no losses. That number is what the batched build has to beat.

I also wrote a second profile with only slow trickle traffic, 5 events a second, to verify that the timer flush works. With the old build, latency there is simply the insert time, and with the batched build it should be near 200 ms at worst, which I will check once the change is pushed.

One annoyance was that the first runs filled the staging disk with test events. I added a cleanup option that deletes rows tagged with the test customer id, and I documented it in the README of the tool.

summary: Ran the batching load test against Mara's updated build: 4,100 events a second at saturation, p99 of 190 ms, no lost rows, and the trickle profile flushes in under 210 ms.
body:
Mara pushed the byte limit, the split on error and the histogram metric, and I deployed the build to staging this evening and ran both load profiles.

The mixed profile reached 4,100 events a second, compared with the baseline of 1,800, and p99 latency fell from 410 ms to 190 ms. The row count in Postgres matched the number of events sent exactly, with zero losses over three runs of 10 minutes.

The trickle profile showed a worst flush latency of 207 ms, which fits the 200 ms timer. The batch size histogram showed that large events flush at about 20 per batch because of the 4 MB limit, as intended.

I also injected one malformed event in every 1,000. The affected batch split into single inserts, the bad event went to the dead letter queue and the other events were stored. I wrote the results into the pull request and recommended a rollout to one worker group first.

summary: Looked into why the batched ingest worker used more memory on staging after Mara's change, and found the batch buffer was sized per partition instead of per worker, so it is capped per worker now.
body:
Mara noticed that the ingest workers on staging used about 40 percent more memory after the batching change, and asked me to find out why before the load test goes further. I started with a heap profile of one worker under the mixed load of small and 200 KB events. Most of the extra memory sat in the batch buffers, not in the Postgres driver.

The cause was in the buffer setup. Each partition the worker reads got its own buffer with the full byte limit, so a worker with eight partitions could hold eight times the intended maximum. The limit was meant to apply to the worker as a whole. With large events that was the difference between about 16 MB and about 128 MB per worker.

I changed the code so the byte limit is shared across the partitions of a worker. A flush of the fullest buffer happens when the total goes over the limit, in addition to the timer flush. I also added a gauge for buffered bytes per worker so we can watch it in Grafana.

I repeated the load test on staging with the same mix. Memory per worker is back to within 5 percent of the old numbers, throughput is unchanged at about 4,100 events a second, and the p99 moved from 190 ms to 195 ms. The trickle profile still flushes by the timer in under 210 ms. Mara reviewed the diff and will merge it, and I will keep the gauge on the dashboard for the next week.

summary: Added the field-level highlighting to the search v2 response, after trying a fragment size of 100 characters that cut JSON values in half and settling on 250.
body:
The console shows hit snippets, and until now they came from a client side substring around the first match. With the new parser I wanted the API to return highlights from OpenSearch itself, so the result matches what actually matched, including phrases and field filters.

I added a highlight section to the generated query for the message, service and event type fields, with pre and post tags as plain markers, which the console turns into elements. Using plain markers instead of HTML keeps the API from returning markup that could carry injected content from events.

The first setting was fragment_size 100 with 2 fragments. Many events carry a JSON text in the message, and 100 characters cut values in the middle, so the snippet showed things like "user_id": 48 with the rest missing. I raised the size to 250 and set number_of_fragments to 1 for the message field. Snippets got longer but readable, and the payload of a result page grew by about 18 percent, which I judged acceptable.

I also found that highlighting on the large 200 KB events made the query slow, since OpenSearch has to analyze the whole field. I set max_analyzed_offset to 100000 so very long messages are only highlighted in their first part. The p95 of a highlighted query on staging went from 640 ms to 210 ms with that limit.

The unit tests now cover three highlight cases: a single term, a phrase, and a field filter, where only the filtered field should be marked. All of them pass. Lena has the new response shape and will adapt the console tomorrow. The old snippet field stays in the response for one release so nothing breaks while she does.

Open question: boosts and highlights both depend on the field map, and I want to keep those in one place. I will fold the highlight fields into the config map next time I touch it.

summary: Investigated a cache hit rate drop of the search API from 71 to 52 percent and found the new parser produced different cache keys for equivalent queries.
body:
The cache hit rate for search results in Redis fell from 71 to 52 percent after the staging build with the new parser went to the canary group. I looked for the cause because the latency was starting to rise for those customers.

The cache key was built from the raw query string. With the old parser that was fine, since users mostly typed the same strings. The new parser accepts more forms, so status:error and status:"error" and STATUS:error gave three different keys for the same result.

I changed the key to a hash of the normalized parse tree: field names lowercased, operands sorted inside AND and OR, redundant quotes dropped. The key keeps the existing customer prefix, so the naming scheme from before stays valid. A test compares 12 equivalent spellings of one query and expects one key.

On the canary group the hit rate recovered to 69 percent within an hour of the fix, and p95 returned to its earlier level. The TTL of these keys did not change.

One thing to keep in mind: sorting operands is only right for AND and OR, not for anything where order matters, and the grammar has none of that today. I left a comment at the normalizer so that anyone adding such an operator sees it.

summary: Dropped the idea of a time decay for ranking after a test on 25 saved queries showed it helped 2 and hurt 5, and wrote down why.
body:
I tried the time decay that I noted after the boost work, using a gauss function on the event timestamp with a scale of 7 days. The idea was to fix the 4 queries where recency decides the right answer.

On the 25 saved queries from support, it fixed 2 of those 4, but it pushed the right hit out of the top 3 for 5 queries that had been right before, mostly lookups of old incidents where a customer searches for a past event by exact text. Making the scale longer reduced the damage and also the benefit, so no setting gave a clear win.

I removed the code and wrote the result in the search-v2 notes. The console already lets users sort by time, which covers the recency case without hidden ranking changes.

summary: Planned the rollout of search v2 in three steps, canary customers, half the customers, then all, with the criteria for going on and the way back.
body:
Search v2 has the parser, boosts, highlights and the alias based reindex on the branch, so I wrote down the rollout. I discussed it with Mara and Tobias in the afternoon.

Step one is the canary group of 3 customers who already agreed, for a week. Step two is half of the customers, chosen by id parity, for another week. Step three is everybody. A flag per customer in the settings table in Postgres decides which parser is used, and the search API reads it with the same override cache as the rate limits, so a change takes effect within a minute.

The criteria for going on: p95 of the search API not more than 10 percent above the old level, cache hit rate above 65 percent, and no more than 2 support tickets about wrong results in the week. If any of them fails, we switch the flag back, which needs no deploy.

Tobias asked about the reindex during the rollout. Both mappings are served from separate aliases, so old and new can live side by side for the time of the rollout, at the price of extra disk, about 30 percent more. He will check that the cluster has room.

Sam will prepare a short note for customers about the operators and the quoted phrases. I will start the canary step once his note is ready.

summary: Wrote the per-customer flag for search v2 and the fallback to the old parser on a parse error, then tested both on staging with a flag flipped during live traffic.
body:
Today I built the switch that the rollout plan needs. A new column search_version in the customer settings table in Postgres holds 1 or 2, and the default stays 1. The migration added the column with a default in one fast statement, and I checked on a copy that it took under a second.

The search API reads the value through the existing override cache in Redis, with a 60 second TTL, and chooses the parser accordingly. The cache key follows the customer prefix scheme, with a new family name for this setting so it is easy to find and clear.

I added a fallback that was not in the plan. If the new parser throws on a query, the API logs the query shape and the error, increments a counter, and answers with the old parser for that one request. The reason is that a bug in the grammar should not turn into an error page for a customer in the canary group. The exception is the unclosed quote, which is still an intended 400.

For testing, I ran a loop of queries against staging for a customer with the flag at 1 and changed it to 2 through the admin endpoint. The responses changed their shape within 58 seconds, with no errors in between. I flipped it back and saw the same delay.

I also ran 3,000 queries from the search log in flag 2 mode to look for exceptions. 4 queries raised an error in the parser: all of them contained a backslash before a colon, which the grammar did not handle. I added escape handling for backslash followed by any character and wrote tests for those four. A rerun showed zero exceptions.

The counter of fallbacks has a Grafana panel and an alert rule at more than 5 per hour. Next is the note from Sam and then the canary customers.

summary: Started search v2 for the canary customers and found one customer's saved dashboards used the old operator spelling, which broke 6 of their saved searches until a compatibility rule was added.
body:
The canary step began this morning, with the flag set to 2 for the three agreed customers at about 10:00. I watched the dashboards for the first hours: p95 stayed within 4 percent of the earlier level, the cache hit rate was 68 percent, and the fallback counter showed 0.

Around noon Sam forwarded a message from one of the canary customers. Six of their saved searches in the console returned nothing or an error. I looked at them: they used a form like status=error and the word and in lowercase between terms, which the old parser had accepted by accident.

I considered rejecting the old forms and asking the customer to edit the saved searches, but six searches across a team is a poor experience for a change they did not ask for. Instead I added a compatibility rule only for saved searches: when a saved search is loaded under parser 2, a small rewrite maps field=value to field:value and lowercase and, or, not between terms to the capital forms. Searches typed freshly in the box are not rewritten, so the docs stay simple.

The rewrite has 14 tests including the cases where the word and sits inside a quoted phrase, which must stay unchanged. I checked all 6 saved searches of this customer on staging with copies, and each returned the same hit count as under the old parser, within 1 percent.

I deployed the rule at 14:30. The customer confirmed in the afternoon that the searches worked again. I also scanned the saved searches of the other two canary customers and of all customers for the old forms; 31 saved searches in total use them, so the rule will matter in later steps of the rollout.

It is a good sign that the first real problem was about old habits and not about the grammar. I will keep the canary for the remaining days and then look at the half step. A note for the docs is still open, covering the rewrite for saved searches.

summary: Bumped the Redis client library to the latest minor version after reading the changelog, and rolled it to staging without any change in connection counts.
body:
The Redis client library in the TypeScript services was three minor versions behind, and the changelog mentioned a fix for reconnect handling that matters for us after the earlier connection alerts. I read the notes of the three versions and found no breaking changes for the commands we use.

I updated the search API and the console on staging, ran the integration tests, which all passed, and watched the connection count panel for an hour. Counts stayed the same as before, 8 for the console and 24 for the search API, and a manual restart of the staging Redis was followed by a clean reconnect in about 2 seconds.

I will roll it to production with the next normal deploy. The ingest limiter is in Go and uses a different library, so it is not affected.

summary: Wrote the docs page for search v2 operators, quoted phrases, field filters and escapes, with examples checked against staging, and sent it to Sam for review.
body:
Sam's customer note needed a docs page to link to, so I wrote the one for the new query syntax. It covers field filters like level:error, quoted phrases, the capital operators AND, OR and NOT, parentheses, and escaping a colon with a backslash.

Every example in the page is a real query that I ran on staging against the demo customer data. For each I put the number of hits next to it in my notes, so a later change to the parser shows up as a mismatch in the docs check. The page also explains the 400 for an unclosed quote and what the position in the error means.

I added a short section on saved searches, which says that older spellings in saved searches keep working while new queries should use the documented forms. I left out the field boosts on purpose, since the weights can change and customers cannot tune them.

Sam will review it this afternoon, mostly for wording and for the questions that support gets most often.

summary: Applied Sam's review of the search syntax page, added a section for the most common mistakes, and published it with a link in the console search box help.
body:
Sam's review had five comments. The most important was that people do not read the page from the top, so the common mistakes should come first. I moved a section called "Why do I get no results?" to the top of the page with the four causes that Sam sees most: lowercase operators in a new query, a space after the colon, an unescaped colon in a value, and a quote that is not closed.

Sam also asked for an example with an IP address as a value, since the colons of an IPv6 address are an escape case. I added one and verified it on staging. Two wording fixes and a corrected anchor link made up the rest.

I published the page and Lena added the help link next to the search box. The page loads and the examples still return the hit counts I noted. The canary has been running for a few days, so this lands at the right time before the half step.

summary: Moved the search v2 rollout to half of the customers, then handled a latency rise for two large customers by capping the phrase highlight to the first 50 KB of a message.
body:
After a clean week the canary met all three criteria: p95 within 4 percent, cache hit rate between 66 and 69 percent, and one support ticket. Today I moved the flag to 2 for customers with an even id, 19 customers in all. The change went out at 09:30 using the admin endpoint, in two groups of ten minutes apart so I could watch the effect.

The first group showed no change. After the second group, which contained two of the large customers, the p95 of the search API rose from 520 ms to 780 ms in the early afternoon, which is above the 10 percent limit. The fallback counter was still 0, so it was not a parser problem.

I looked at the slow queries in the search log. They were all queries with highlighting on events with long messages from those two customers, where the average message is much larger than for others. The limit of 100000 characters from the earlier work still meant a lot of analysis per hit, and ten hits per page multiplied it.

I reduced max_analyzed_offset from 100000 to 50000 for all customers, which is a config value and needs no deploy of the parser. I tested on staging with the large events: p95 for a highlighted query on those went from 700 ms to 330 ms. Snippets from the first 50 KB still cover nearly all real matches, since the messages of these customers carry the interesting part at the start.

I set the new value live at 16:20. The p95 for the half group came back to 540 ms within 30 minutes, which is 4 percent above the earlier level and inside the criteria. I will keep watching tomorrow, in particular the evening peak.

A few other observations from the day:
- the fallback counter stayed at 0 for all 19 customers
- the saved search rewrite was used 22 times, with no complaints
- the cache hit rate in the half group was 67 percent

If tomorrow stays calm, the last step to all customers can be scheduled for next week. I told Mara about the highlight limit, since it changes what the API promises.

summary: Checked the evening peak for search v2 on half of the customers, saw p95 at 560 ms and no fallbacks, and scheduled the rollout to everybody for the following week.
body:
I reviewed the dashboards for the peak between 17:00 and 20:00 yesterday and this morning's traffic. The p95 of the search API in the half group was 560 ms at the highest point, against 520 ms for the old parser group in the same hours, which is 8 percent more and within the limit of 10 percent. The cache hit rate was 66 percent.

The fallback counter showed 0 again, and the support queue had no new tickets about wrong results. I also compared the number of 400 responses: they rose from 0.3 to 0.9 percent of queries in the half group, which are the unclosed quotes.
