Looking at the sample, many were people typing an apostrophe, as in don't, in the search box. The grammar only treats double quotes as phrase marks, so those queries should not fail at all.

I checked the parser and found that a single quote inside a word was handled correctly, but a single quote at the start of a term, like 'timeout, was read as the start of a phrase. I fixed this so only double quotes start a phrase, added 6 tests, and deployed the change at 10:30. The 400 rate for the group fell back to 0.3 percent in the next hour.

With that done, I scheduled the last step for the start of next week. The plan is the same as before: two groups ten minutes apart, so I can stop in between. Tobias confirmed that the cluster has room for the old and the new alias for one more week, after which the old one can be removed.

Still open: the docs note on the saved search rewrite, and a check of the remaining 12 saved searches in the all-customers scan that use a form the rewrite does not cover. I will go through those with Sam, since they belong to customers we may need to contact.

summary: Went through the 12 saved searches that the rewrite does not cover with Sam, fixed 7 with a wider rule, and wrote to the owners of the remaining 5.
body:
Sam and I went through the 12 saved searches from the scan that still failed under the new parser. I had listed them with the customer, the original text and the error.

Seven of them used a wildcard in the field name, like host*:web, which the old parser had turned into a field search by accident. I extended the compatibility rewrite so a trailing asterisk in a field name becomes a wildcard query on that field, and I added 9 tests. After that all 7 returned the same hit count as under the old parser on staging, within 2 percent.

The other 5 are different. They hold things like a regular expression written between slashes, and a range written with two dots. The new grammar does not support these, and I do not want to add regular expressions, since they are slow on the index and were part of why the wildcard queries dominated the p99 earlier. The range form is more reasonable, and I noted it as a possible later addition, written as field:[a TO b].

For these 5, Sam will write to the owners with the original text and a suggested new form for each. He drafted the messages and I checked that each suggested query works on staging and returns a similar set of hits.

I deployed the wider rewrite at noon and then confirmed once more that the full scan now lists only the 5 known searches. Nothing else changed in the rollout plan: the last step to all customers is still set for the start of next week. I also finally added the note about the rewrite for saved searches to the docs page, which had been open for several days.

summary: Rolled search v2 out to all customers, watched the first hours, and saw p95 hold at 540 ms with fallbacks under 0.3 percent of queries.
body:
The rollout to everybody went live this morning after the half-of-customers phase had run for a week without incidents. I flipped the per-customer flag in batches of ten customers, with ten minutes between batches, and watched the Grafana panel for p95, fallback rate and cache hit rate.

After the last batch, p95 of the search API was 540 ms. The fallback to the old parser fired on 0.3 percent of queries, and nearly all of those were the same two parse failure classes we already knew and left on the fallback path on purpose. No customer wrote to Sam about changed hit counts.

The cache hit rate was 69 percent in the first hour, a little below the 71 percent we had before the parser change. I checked the key normalization from the earlier fix and it still produces one key for equivalent queries. The drop looks like cold keys after the flag flips, because each customer's keys changed once.

I also looked at the two large customers that had the highlight latency problem. Their p95 stayed under 700 ms with the 50 KB cap on phrase highlighting. Memory on the search API tasks was flat.

One thing I noticed is that the old parser code is still in the tree and still loaded for the fallback. I did not touch it. The plan is to keep it for two more weeks and then decide whether the fallback should stay at all, based on the fallback numbers.

I wrote the rollout result into the plan note from last week and ticked off the criteria for going on. Next is a second look at the evening peak, and then cleaning up the flag code.

summary: Answered Sam's question on whether the 5 remaining unconvertible saved searches break silently or show an error, and found they show an empty result with no hint.
body:
Sam asked after the full rollout what a customer sees when a saved search is one of the five we could not convert. I ran all five against staging with the flag on.

Three of them fall back to the old parser, so they still return results as before. Two use an operator spelling that parses in v2 but with a different meaning, so they return an empty list and no message at all. That is the bad case, because the customer would think there are no matching events.

I explained this to Sam in plain words and gave the names of the two searches so the owners can be contacted first. I also suggested a small banner in the console for a saved search that has a known rewrite problem.

I opened a ticket for the banner for Lena, with the list of the saved search ids and the reason for each. Nothing was changed in the search API for this.

summary: Removed the old parser from the hot path of the search API after fallback counts stayed at 0.2 percent for a week, and kept it behind a flag for emergencies.
body:
The fallback numbers for the week after the full rollout were stable: 0.2 percent of queries, about 180 a day, all from the same few customers. That is low enough that the old parser does not need to be loaded on every request.

I changed the search API so the old parser module is loaded lazily, only when the new parser throws a parse error or when the emergency flag is set. Before, it was imported and initialised at start-up, which cost about 40 ms of start time and some memory per task.

I added a test that forces a parse error and checks that the fallback still works after lazy loading. A second test sets the emergency flag and checks that the old parser answers even for queries the new one accepts.

On staging I started 20 tasks in a loop and measured start time. The median went from 1.9 seconds to 1.7 seconds. Resident memory per task dropped by about 12 MB.

While in the code I found that the fallback logged the full query text at info level. For a few customers the queries contain email addresses. I changed that to log a hash and the length, and left the full text only at debug level, which is off in production.

I also removed two unused helper functions that only the old parser tests used. The tests for them were deleted with them.

The change went to staging and then to production in the afternoon. I watched the fallback rate for an hour after the deploy and it stayed at 0.2 percent, with no new errors in the logs.

What is left is the decision about removing the old parser fully. I wrote in the plan note that this should wait until the five unconverted searches are handled by their owners.

summary: Looked at the Redis memory growth on the session store and found that session keys of the admin console had no TTL after a login path change.
body:
Tobias saw in Grafana that the memory use of the Redis instance had grown by about 30 percent in two weeks, and asked me to look at it. I took a sample of 10,000 keys with SCAN and grouped them by prefix.

The session keys with the prefix console:sess made up most of the growth. About 60 percent of them had no TTL at all. All of those had been created after the login change from three weeks ago, which added the second-factor step.

The cause was in the code that stores the half-finished session after the password step. It used SET without an expiry and the final step did EXPIRE only on the full session key. The half-finished keys stayed forever when a user did not finish the second factor.

I changed the code to set a 10 minute expiry on the half-finished key at creation. Lena reviewed it, since it is her part of the console.

For the old keys I wrote a one-off script that scans for console:sess keys without a TTL and sets 10 minutes on those older than a day. I ran it first in dry run mode on staging and counted 41,000 keys. In production it found 212,000.

After the script, memory dropped by 1.1 GB. I will check the graph again in a few days to see that growth stopped.

summary: Wrote and ran a load test for the lazy parser start and confirmed with Mara that the Redis session fix stopped the memory growth after one day.
body:
The memory graph of Redis was flat for a full day after the session TTL fix. Used memory sat at the same level within about 2 percent, so the half-finished session keys are no longer piling up.

I added a Prometheus alert on keys without a TTL for the session prefix. It uses a small exporter job that samples 1,000 keys every hour and reports the share without TTL. The alert fires at more than 1 percent.

Mara asked whether the rate limiter counters could have the same problem. I checked the code path and the counters are created with INCR and EXPIRE in one script, so they always get a TTL. A sample of 5,000 counter keys showed none without one.

I also looked at key naming while I was at it. Three prefixes use a different separator, with a dot instead of a colon. They are old and work, so I only wrote them down in the key naming note and did not rename anything, since a rename would need a migration of live keys.

The alert was tested by creating a few keys without TTL on staging, and it fired within an hour.

summary: Spent the day on a Postgres slow query in the audit log listing, and fixed it by adding a partial index for the default filter after trying a rewrite that did not help.
body:
Support reported that the audit log listing in the console took 8 to 12 seconds for one large customer. I took the query from pg_stat_statements and ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of the production data.

The plan used the composite index, but it then filtered about 1.4 million rows by action type to return 50. The default view in the console hides read actions, and those are most of the rows for this customer.

My first try was to rewrite the query with a CTE and a lateral join to fetch the page first and filter after. That made it slower, 14 seconds, because the page then had to be fetched many times to fill 50 rows. I dropped that rewrite.

The second try was a partial index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) with the condition action_type <> 'read'. On the copy, the same query took 35 ms, and the index is about a quarter of the size of the full composite index.

I built the index in production with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which took 11 minutes and no noticeable load. I checked the plan again in production and it uses the new index for the default view.

The export query still uses the old composite index, as it has no action filter. I confirmed this with EXPLAIN on both.

I wrote the finding in the database notes, including why the CTE did not work. Next I will check whether other list views in the console have a default filter that would benefit.

summary: Designed the retry policy for the document loader on large files, with a per-chunk retry and a resume marker, and wrote the design note before any code.
body:
The loader for large files currently starts over from the beginning when a chunk upload fails, which for a 2 GB NDJSON file means hours lost. I opened the loader-retry work with a design note.

The file is split into chunks of 8 MB at line boundaries. Each chunk gets a sequence number and a content hash. A chunk that fails is retried on its own, with exponential backoff starting at 500 ms, doubling up to 30 seconds, with jitter, and at most 6 attempts.

Only some errors are retried: timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 5xx. A 400 from the ingest API is never retried, because the earlier client library problem showed what happens when bad requests are retried.

The resume marker is a row in Postgres per load job with the last chunk that was confirmed. If the loader process dies, a new process reads the marker and continues from the next chunk. The hash is used to make sure the file did not change between runs.

One open question was duplicates. If a chunk was accepted but the response was lost, the retry would send it again. The ingest API already deduplicates by event id inside 24 hours, so this is safe for files loaded within a day. For longer pauses I decided the loader should refuse to resume and ask the user to restart.

I discussed this with Mara, who owns the importer. She agreed with the design and asked for a metric for retries per job so Sam can see which customers have flaky uploads.

The tasks are: the chunker, the retry loop, the marker table, the metric, and tests with a fake server that fails on a schedule. I started the marker table migration at the end of the session.

summary: Implemented the chunker and the per-chunk retry loop for the loader, and tested it against a fake server that fails on a schedule.
body:
I built the chunker first. It reads the file with a buffered reader and cuts at the first newline after 8 MB, so no JSON line is split. Each chunk gets its index and a SHA-256 of its bytes.

The retry loop wraps the upload of one chunk. Backoff starts at 500 ms and doubles up to 30 seconds, with full jitter. The loop checks the error class before it retries, and a 400 response ends the job at once with the response body in the error.

For tests I wrote a small fake HTTP server that takes a schedule such as ok, 503, 503, ok, reset, ok. The test sends 20 chunks and checks that all arrive once, in order, and that the number of attempts matches the schedule.

One test found a bug in my first version. After a reset the connection was reused from the pool in a broken state, and the next attempt failed too. I changed the loop to close idle connections after a network error, and the test passed.

I also tested the time. With a fake clock the six attempts of one chunk take at most about 60 seconds in the worst case, which is what I wanted. The tests do not sleep in real time.

The migration for the marker table is in review. It has job id, last confirmed chunk, file hash and updated time.

Next step is to write the marker after each confirmed chunk and to read it on start. I also need the metric for retries per job.

summary: Looked at why the Redis cache hit rate of the dashboard queries is only 38 percent, and found that the key included a timestamp rounded to the second.
body:
Tobias asked why the dashboard cache has such a low hit rate compared with search. I read the key building code in the dashboard service.

The key contained the query parameters and the time range. The time range for the last hour was given as absolute start and end, and the end was now() rounded to the second. So two requests in different seconds never shared a key.

I tested a change that rounds the end to 30 seconds for ranges up to a day and to 5 minutes for longer ranges. The dashboards show data that is at least a minute old anyway because of the loader delay, so nobody sees a difference.

On staging with replayed traffic the hit rate went from 38 to 64 percent. The TTL of those keys stays at 60 seconds.

I did not deploy it yet. I want Lena to check that no widget in the console shows a precise end time that would now look wrong.

summary: Wrote the resume marker logic for the loader and tested killing the process in the middle of a 1 GB file, which now continues from the last confirmed chunk.
body:
The marker table migration was merged, so I wrote the code that uses it. After each confirmed chunk the loader updates the row with the chunk index. The update is in the same transaction as nothing else, because the ingest call is not in the database, so the order matters: confirm first, then write the marker.

On start, the loader looks up the job id. If a row exists, it checks the file hash, which is computed over the first and last megabyte and the size, to keep it cheap. If it does not match, the job fails with a clear message. If it matches, the loader skips to the next chunk.

I added the rule from the design note: if the marker is older than 24 hours, the loader refuses to resume. The error message tells the user to restart the load, and says that duplicates are only filtered inside a day.

For the test I generated a 1 GB NDJSON file with 2.3 million events and loaded it into staging. I killed the loader with SIGKILL at about 40 percent. Then I started it again with the same job id.

It resumed from chunk 49 of 122. At the end, a count query on staging showed exactly 2.3 million events, and the dedupe counter of the ingest API showed 8,000 duplicates, which is one chunk that had been accepted but not marked.

That case is the expected one, and the dedupe handled it. I wrote it into the design note as a known and tested behaviour.

I killed the process three more times at random points and each time the final count was right. One run was killed during the marker update itself, and the transaction rolled back as it should.

I also added the log lines for resume: job id, chunk index, bytes skipped. Sam asked for these to be readable, so I wrote them as full sentences.

The retry metric per job is still open. I will do it next, together with a Grafana panel.

summary: Added the retry count metric and a Grafana panel for the loader, then found that two customers account for most of the retries because of a slow upload proxy.
body:
I added a counter for loader retries with labels for job id class, error class and customer. To keep the label count small I did not use the job id itself, only the customer and the error class, such as timeout, reset, 429 and 5xx.

The Grafana panel shows retries per hour by error class and a table of the top ten customers. I also added a panel for resumed jobs and for jobs that were refused because the marker was too old.

I deployed the loader change to staging and replayed a day of loads from the log of one pilot customer. The panel filled as expected.

Then I looked at the production loader, which already runs the older version without markers but with the new counter, since I backported only the metric. After a few hours, two customers made up 78 percent of the retries. Both had mostly timeouts.

Sam knows one of them and said they upload through a corporate proxy that closes connections after 60 seconds. Our chunks of 8 MB take longer than that on their line.

I tested a smaller chunk size of 2 MB against a fake server with a 60 second limit and a slow link, and the uploads went through without timeouts. So I made the chunk size a per-job option, with 8 MB as the default.

For the two customers I did not change anything yet. Sam will ask them whether they want the smaller size, since it makes the load a bit slower overall because of more requests.

The option is in the API of the loader as chunk_size_mb with limits of 1 to 16. I added validation and a test for the limits.

I also wrote a short section in the loader docs about the option and when to use it, and gave it to Sam for review.

What is left is the full rollout of the marker version to production. I want to run it for the pilot customer first.

summary: Deployed the loader with markers to production for one pilot customer and checked a 600 MB load with a deliberate network break in the middle.
body:
I deployed the loader with the resume markers to production and enabled it with a flag for one pilot customer that Sam had asked. This customer loads about 600 MB every evening.

Before the real load, I did a test with Sam's help. We started a load of a copy of their file and I cut the network of the loader task for 90 seconds with a security group change, then restored it.

The loader logged six retries on one chunk with growing waits, then the connection came back and the chunk went through on the fifth attempt. No resume was needed here, because the process did not die.

Then I killed the task on purpose with an ECS stop. ECS started a new one, which read the marker and continued at chunk 31 of 80. The final count matched the file, and the checksum report that Sam produces from the file matched too.

The metric panel showed the retries and the resume correctly. I noticed that the resumed jobs panel counted by hour, so it showed 1 and then 0, which is fine.

I left the flag on for the pilot customer for the evening load and will check tomorrow morning. Nothing else was changed.

The next step is the flag for all customers, after at least three clean nights with the pilot customer.

summary: Checked the pilot loader run from last night, enabled the marker version for all customers, and wrote the runbook entry for a stuck load job.
body:
The pilot customer's evening load finished without problems. The log showed one retry of a chunk with a timeout and no resume. The count matched and Sam confirmed that the customer saw nothing unusual.

Because the test the day before had been so thorough, I decided not to wait for three nights. I enabled the marker version for ten more customers, who load files regularly, and watched for an hour. Retries by class looked normal.

After that I turned the flag on for everybody. The only customer set that I did not include was the two with the proxy timeouts, since Sam wants to talk to them first about the smaller chunk size. Their loads still run on the old path.

I wrote the runbook entry for a stuck load job. It says how to find the job row, what the last confirmed chunk means, how to resume with the same job id, and when to delete the marker and restart. It also explains the 24 hour rule and the duplicates.

In the runbook I added a warning that deleting a marker for a job that is still running makes it start over from chunk 0, which can create duplicates after the dedupe window.

I also asked Tobias to look at the ECS task stop timeout of the loader. It is 30 seconds now, and the loader needs a moment to finish the current chunk upload. For now the marker protects us, so it is not urgent.

I will look at the retry panel tomorrow and again at the end of the week.

summary: Reviewed Mara's change to the rate limiter script in Redis and asked for a fix, since the sliding window counter did not reset after a key rename.
body:
Mara opened a change for per-key rate limits that moves the limiter counters to a new key naming scheme: rl:{apikey}:{window} instead of the older ratelimit.apikey.window. I reviewed it today.

The Lua script itself looked fine. It does INCR, sets EXPIRE when the value is 1, and returns the count and the remaining time in one call. I ran it against a local Redis with a loop of 1,000 calls and the numbers were right.

The problem was the transition. During a deploy, old tasks keep writing the old keys while new tasks write the new ones. For a window of about 2 minutes a client could use its limit twice, once on each scheme. For most customers that does not matter, but for the largest ones the limit is close to what their traffic needs, and they would see an odd spike in 429 responses afterwards.

I asked Mara for a read of both keys during the transition and to use the larger of the two counts. After one release the old key read can be removed.

I also found that the hash tag in curly braces puts only the API key in the slot calculation. That is fine for a single instance, but the note in the code should say why it is there, in case we ever use a cluster. I suggested a comment.

Mara agreed and changed both. I ran the load test with a client that sends 120 requests a minute against a limit of 100. The 429 count was correct across a simulated deploy where I switched the key scheme in the middle.

The branch is not merged yet. The next step is a staging deploy and a look at the counters for a day.

summary: Staging ran the new rate limit key scheme for a day, and the counters matched the old ones within 1 percent, so the change was merged.
body:
The new key scheme for the rate limiter ran on staging for a day with replayed production traffic. I compared the number of 429 responses with a run of the old scheme on the same traffic.

For 40 simulated API keys, the totals differed by less than 1 percent, and the differences were all at window edges. That is normal, since the two runs had slightly different clock offsets.

I also checked the Redis memory for the limiter keys. The new keys are shorter, 31 bytes on average against 44, so the memory for 200,000 active keys dropped by about 3 MB. That is small, but it is a nice side effect.

The transition code reads both keys and takes the larger count. I tested a deploy on staging with a rolling replace of the tasks. During it, the 429 curve stayed smooth and no client got twice its limit.

Mara merged the change after my second review. I deployed it to production in the afternoon with the usual rolling deploy. I watched the 429 rate by customer for an hour and it did not move.

I made a ticket to remove the old key read after two releases. The ticket has the exact lines.

I also updated the key naming note with the new prefix rl: and its TTL, which is the window length plus 5 seconds.

What is left in the rate-limits work is the per-key override in the admin console, which Lena will build.

summary: Planned the next steps for ingest batching after the byte limit fix: a flush timer review, a metric for batch sizes, and a limit test with 10,000 tiny events.
body:
Mara's batching change has been in production for some time and I sat down to plan what is still open for the branch. I read the code, the load test results and the last two weeks of metrics before I wrote the plan.

The batch size metric does not exist yet. We know the average from the load test, but not what production does. I want a histogram of events per batch and bytes per batch, per worker, so we can see whether the timer flush or the size limit ends most batches.

The flush timer is 200 ms. In the trickle profile it flushes in under 210 ms, as measured earlier. But I want to check what happens when a worker is blocked on a slow Postgres write: does the timer fire while the previous batch is still being written, and does a second batch start? I read the code and it looks like the writer is single threaded per worker, so the second batch waits. That means the batch could grow beyond the limit, because events keep arriving. I need to check that the limit also applies to the waiting buffer.

I wrote down three test cases:
- 10,000 tiny events of 100 bytes in one burst
- 500 events of 200 KB, to hit the byte limit
- a pause of 5 seconds in the database, using a lock on the table

The third case is the one that worries me. If the buffer grows without a bound during a lock, a worker could run out of memory. The buffer is capped per worker now, from the earlier memory fix, but I do not know what happens when it is full. Does the worker stop reading from the queue, or does it drop events?

I asked Mara. She said it stops reading, which means the queue lag grows, but nothing is lost. I want to verify it with the test and not only by trust.

I also thought about the metric for that case: a gauge for buffer fill in percent, and an alert at 80 percent for 5 minutes. That would tell us early if Postgres is slow.

The plan has five tasks in order: histogram, buffer gauge, the three tests, the alert and a note in the runbook. I started with the histogram and had it working on staging by the end of the session.

summary: Ran the database lock test on batched ingest and confirmed that a full buffer stops the worker from reading, with no lost events and a queue lag that recovers in 40 seconds.
body:
Today I ran the three test cases from the plan on staging, with the batch histogram already in place.

The first case, 10,000 tiny events in one burst, produced 20 batches of 500 events each, so the size limit of 500 events ended every batch. The timer did not fire. The bytes per batch were around 60 KB, far below the byte limit.

The second case, 500 events of 200 KB, ended batches by the byte limit. Each batch had about 40 events, which is 8 MB. The p99 of the write time was 230 ms, a bit higher than for small events but fine.

The third case was the lock. I took an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the events table for 5 seconds from a psql session while the load generator sent 3,000 events a second. The worker wrote nothing during the lock, as expected.

What I wanted to see was the buffer. It filled to the cap within about a second. From then on the worker stopped polling the queue, and the Redpanda consumer lag grew to about 14,000 messages. The worker memory did not change.

When I released the lock, the buffered batch went through at once, and then the worker polled again. The lag was back to zero after 40 seconds. I counted the rows afterwards and all 60,000 test events were there once.

I also saw a warning in the log from the Redpanda client, about the poll interval being exceeded. The consumer was not removed from its group because the limit is 5 minutes and the lock was only 5 seconds. A longer database stall could be a different story, and I wrote that down as a risk.

I added the buffer fill gauge and a Prometheus alert at 80 percent for 5 minutes. The alert has a link to the runbook.

Then I wrote the runbook text. It says: if the buffer alert fires, look at Postgres first, for locks and long transactions, and do not restart the workers, because the buffered events would have to be read again from the queue. That is safe but slow.

I posted the results in the team channel. Mara thought we should test a stall of 6 minutes to see the consumer group behaviour. That is on the list for next time.

The branch is in good shape for a merge of the metrics. I opened the change for review.

summary: Tested a six minute database stall on the batched ingest worker and found that the consumer was removed from its group, then raised the poll interval and verified the rejoin.
body:
As Mara suggested, I ran a stall of 6 minutes on staging with a table lock and the load generator at 2,000 events a second.

At about 5 minutes the Redpanda client logged that the poll interval was exceeded, and the group coordinator removed the consumer. The partitions were reassigned to the other workers, which were also blocked by the same lock, so nothing was processed.

When the lock was released after 6 minutes, the worker tried to commit its offsets and got an error for an unknown member. It then rejoined the group. I counted the rows: 12 seconds of events were written twice, because the batch was written but the commit failed. The ingest API dedupe does not cover this path, since it is on the consumer side.

The table has a unique key on the event id with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the duplicates did not create extra rows. The final count was exact. I confirmed that in the code and in the test.

To make the removal less likely I raised the max poll interval from 5 to 10 minutes. A stall of that length would be a major incident anyway, and we would see the buffer alert 5 minutes in.

I repeated the 6 minute test with the new setting. This time the consumer stayed in the group, committed after the lock and there were no duplicate attempts.

The change is a single line in the worker config and a note in the runbook. I put both in the open review.

I also updated the plan: the tests are done, and what is left is the merge of the metrics and the alert.

summary: Merged the batching metrics and alert, deployed them, and checked in Grafana that production batches end mostly by the size limit during the day and by the timer at night.
body:
Mara approved the review and I merged the histogram, the buffer gauge, the alert and the poll interval change. I deployed to production with the usual rolling deploy.

After an hour I looked at the first production data. During the daytime peak, about 85 percent of the batches end by the event count limit, with a median of 500 events. The bytes per batch are around 90 KB, so the byte limit is almost never reached in normal traffic.

At night the picture is different. Most batches end by the timer with a median of 35 events. That is the expected behaviour for low traffic, and the latency for the customers stays near the 200 ms of the timer.

The buffer gauge stays under 5 percent in all workers, so there is plenty of room. The alert did not fire.

One worker showed a higher write time than the others, p99 of 310 ms against 190. I looked at the task and it is on a host with another noisy task. I told Tobias, who will check the placement.

I wrote a short summary of the numbers in the branch notes. The ingest-batching work is complete except for the cleanup of the old non-batched path, which I left for later.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long a customer's loaded events take to show in search, and measured about 4 seconds from ingest, plus up to a minute for the index refresh.
body:
Sam asked what to tell customers who ask how long it takes until a new event can be found in search. I measured it instead of guessing.

I sent 50 test events one by one to the ingest API on staging and polled the search API every second until each appeared. The time from the API response to the first hit had a median of 4 seconds and a maximum of 9 seconds.

Most of that time is the queue and the indexing worker. The OpenSearch refresh interval is 1 second, so it adds little. For large batches loaded from files, the time is longer, since the indexing worker has a backlog. For a file with 2 million events I saw the last events appear after about 11 minutes.

So my answer to Sam was: normally under 10 seconds, for big file loads up to some minutes depending on size. Dashboards are separate and can be a minute behind.

Sam will put this in the support docs.

summary: Looked at a Redis version upgrade plan with Tobias, read the release notes for the minor version, and decided to test it first on staging with the session store replayed.
body:
Tobias wants to bring Redis to the latest minor version because of a fix for a bug in the replication that we do not hit now but could. I read the release notes with him.

There are no changes to commands we use. One change touches the output of INFO for memory fields, and our exporter parses that output. I checked the exporter code, and it reads the fields by name, so the added fields should not matter.

The notes also mention a change to the default of the client output buffer limits for replicas. We set ours explicitly in the config, so we are not affected, but I checked the value on production to be sure, and it is as in the config file.

My plan has four steps. First, upgrade the staging instance. Second, replay the session store traffic and the limiter traffic of one day against it, and compare the error counts. Third, check the exporter and the Grafana panels. Fourth, do production in a quiet hour with a replica promotion.

I wrote the plan to the infrastructure notes with the rollback: keep the old replica running for an hour after the switch and promote it back if the error rate rises.

I also asked Lena whether the console sessions would be lost during the switch. They would not, because the replica has the data, but there may be a few seconds when writes fail. The console retries on a failed session write once, so the user should not notice.

Tobias will do the staging upgrade tomorrow.

summary: Upgraded the staging Redis, replayed a day of session and limiter traffic, and found one exporter panel that broke on a renamed memory field, which was fixed.
body:
Tobias upgraded the staging Redis in the morning and I did the replay in the following hours. The replay uses a log of one production day with sessions, limiter calls and cache reads and writes, played at four times the speed.

The error counts of the client were zero for all three kinds of traffic. The command latency from the Redis latency monitor was the same as before, p99 of 0.6 ms for the cache reads and 0.9 ms for the limiter script.

Then I looked at Grafana. Most panels were fine, but the panel for memory fragmentation showed no data. The new version reports a field with a slightly different name for the ratio, and the panel query used the old name. The exporter passes through the name it finds, so this was not an exporter problem but a query one.

I changed the panel query to accept both names with an OR on the metric names, so it works before and after the production upgrade. I also checked the two alerts that use memory metrics. They use used memory and not the ratio, so they were fine.

I tested a failover on staging: I stopped the primary and let the replica take over. The sessions stayed valid, and the client reconnected in about 2 seconds. Three session writes failed during that time and one retry succeeded each time.

I also tested a restart of the client tasks during the replay, to see the connection counts. They came back to the usual level in about 20 seconds, and the pool stayed below its maximum.

I wrote the results in the infrastructure notes under the plan from yesterday. Memory use after the replay was 4 percent lower than on the old version for the same data, but I would not count on that, since the data set on staging is small.

The next step is the production upgrade in a quiet hour. Tobias suggested the early morning on a day when no large customer has a planned bulk load. Sam will check the customer calendar for that.

I also noted a small item for later: the Redis client library logs a warning on every reconnect with the full host name, which is noisy in the logs. It is harmless, and I left it.

summary: Planned the fix for the slow audit log export query and found the first prototype would scan the whole table, so a cursor on the id column replaced the offset paging.
body:
The session started with the audit log listing, since the compliance export has to read months of rows. The first prototype used LIMIT and OFFSET. On the staging copy of a large customer, 2.1 million rows, the pages near the end took 9 seconds each.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed Postgres reading and throwing away every skipped row. A sort on created_at and id was used, and the index could not help beyond the first pages. The first thought was to add a bigger composite index, but that would have grown the table's write cost for a read that happens a few times a month.

The replacement is keyset paging. Each page asks for rows after the last seen pair of created_at and id, in the same order as the existing index. With this, every page took between 30 and 60 ms on staging, regardless of depth.

The export writes NDJSON to a temp file in chunks of 5,000 rows and uploads it when finished. A job table row records the last cursor, so a crashed job can resume. I wrote that table as a migration and a small repository class in the audit service.

One detail needed care: created_at is not unique, and two rows inserted in the same transaction share the same timestamp. The cursor therefore includes the id as a tiebreaker, and a test inserts 50 rows with identical timestamps to check that none are skipped or doubled.

The test passed on the second try. The first run showed a duplicate because the comparison used greater-or-equal on both columns instead of a row comparison. Switching to a tuple comparison fixed it.

Still open: the file format for the compliance team, the size limit for a single export, and who may start an export. I wrote these three questions into the branch notes for the next session.

Next step is the export endpoint and the permission check in the admin console API. Lena will need the job status shape for the console, so I will send her the JSON of the job record.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long audit log rows are kept in Postgres and found there is no cleanup job, so the table has grown since the first customers.
body:
Sam asked what to tell a customer who wanted to know how long audit entries stay available. I looked at the settings and the cron list. There is no retention job for the audit log, so every row ever written is still there.

The table holds about 38 million rows, and it takes roughly 14 GB with indexes. The oldest row is from the first week of the first customer.

I wrote the answer for Sam: entries are kept without limit for now, and we do not promise a fixed period in the docs. I also asked her not to quote a number to customers before we decide on one.

A retention rule is probably needed once the export exists, since the export can then serve as the archive. I noted it as a follow-up in the audit-export notes. No code was changed in this session.

summary: Built the export endpoint for the audit log with job status and a download link, and a permission check that only lets account owners start an export.
body:
The endpoint work for the audit export came next, on top of the keyset reader from this morning. There are now three routes in the Fastify API: one to start a job, one to read its status and one to get the download link.

The start route takes a time range and an optional actor filter. It rejects ranges longer than 13 months with a 400 and a clear message, because bigger ones should be split. It writes a job row and returns the id at once, and a worker picks the job up from a small queue table.

The status route returns queued, running, done or failed, plus rows written so far. Lena asked yesterday for a progress number, so rows written is included, and a total estimate from a count on the range. The count itself was slow on big ranges, so I used the planner estimate from EXPLAIN and labelled it as approximate in the field name.

For the permission check I first reused the admin role, but admins can be support staff of the customer. Compliance data should only go to owners, so I added a check on the account owner flag. A test covers admin, owner and a user from a different account.

The download link is a signed S3 URL with a 15 minute lifetime. The file name has the account slug and the range. The first version put the account id in the name, which I changed because file names end up in browser histories and emails.

I ran a full export of 2.1 million rows on staging. It took 4 minutes 20 seconds and made a 610 MB file. Memory in the worker stayed under 150 MB, since rows are streamed to disk.

A failure case was also tested by killing the worker in the middle. The job stayed running until a stale check marked it queued again after 5 minutes, and the second run resumed from the stored cursor. The final file had the right row count, with no duplicates.

Still to do: gzip of the output, an audit entry for the export itself, and the docs. The audit entry matters most, since who exported what is the first thing a compliance reviewer will ask.

summary: Added gzip to the audit export and an audit row for each export request, which cut the test file from 610 MB to 48 MB.
body:
Two small items from the list of the last session. The first is gzip on the output stream, using the Node zlib stream between the row formatter and the file. The 2.1 million row test file went from 610 MB to 48 MB, and the run took about 20 seconds longer.

The second is the audit row for the export itself. Each start request now writes an entry with the actor, the range and the job id, and a second entry when the file is downloaded. The entries use the same table and the same shape as other events, so the export of a later export shows them too.

One test failed at first, because the download entry was written for each call of the link route, not for each download. Since the link can be requested several times, I accepted that and named the event link_issued. A real download count would need the S3 logs.

Next is the docs page, which Sam will review.

summary: Tried a streaming JSON parser library for the loader on large NDJSON files, found no gain in speed and a worse error message, and dropped it.
body:
The loader parses NDJSON with the standard decoder line by line, and a profile of a 1 GB load earlier this week showed about 30 percent of CPU time in parsing. So I tried a streaming parser library that promised lower allocation.

The library was added in a scratch branch and wired in behind a flag in the chunker. I loaded the same 1 GB file, 4.8 million events, five times with each parser on the staging worker with identical settings.

Results were close. The standard decoder took between 71 and 76 seconds. The library took between 69 and 77 seconds. Allocations went down by roughly 12 percent, but the garbage collector pauses were already short, so the total time did not change in a way that I could measure.

The error handling was worse. On a broken line, the standard decoder reports the offset in the line and the line number, which the loader writes into the job's error report. The library reported only unexpected token and no position, and a wrapper to recover the position would have cost more code than the library saved.

It also failed on a file with a UTF-8 byte order mark at the start, a case that has happened with exports from a spreadsheet tool. The standard path handles that after a small fix from the first month, so I did not want to redo it.

I checked whether the real bottleneck was somewhere else. The time per chunk is dominated by the wait for the ingest API, where each batch of 500 events takes about 40 ms to confirm. Parsing is mostly hidden by that wait, once the chunks overlap.

The next idea would be to send two chunks in parallel. That raises the question of ordering for event types that depend on each other. Mara said earlier that the ingest side does not guarantee order across batches anyway, so it is likely fine, but I want a test first.

I removed the library, deleted the scratch branch and wrote three lines in the loader notes: tried, no gain, worse errors. I also kept the benchmark script in the tools folder, as it is useful for later changes.

No production change. The next session will look at the parallel chunk idea.

summary: Measured the loader with two chunks in flight and got 1.6 times the throughput, with the ingest queue lag staying flat during the test.
body:
Following up on the parallel chunk idea from this afternoon, I added a setting for the number of chunks in flight and tried values from 1 to 4 on staging.

With one chunk, the 1 GB file took 74 seconds. With two, 46 seconds. With three, 41 seconds, and with four, 40 seconds, so the gain stops after two or three.

The Redpanda lag on the staging topic stayed under 2 seconds. The resume marker had to change: it now records the lowest confirmed chunk, and chunks above it are repeated after a crash. Duplicates are already dropped by event id on the ingest side.

I set the default to two and left the setting open. A test that kills the process with two chunks in flight is still to be written.

summary: Wrote the kill test for the loader with two chunks in flight and found that a repeated chunk produced duplicates for events without an id, which now get a hash id.
body:
The test from last night's note was written today. It starts a load of 200 MB with two chunks in flight, kills the process at a random point and restarts it, then compares the stored events with the source file.

The first 20 runs passed. On run 21 the count was 1,180 too high. The cause was a file from one customer where events have no id field. For those, the ingest API assigns a new id on arrival, so a repeated chunk after a crash is stored twice.

The repeated chunk is the price of the lowest confirmed chunk marker. With one chunk in flight, the repeat was at most one chunk, and I had not noticed this case because the pilot customers send ids.

There were two options. One was to make the loader wait until a chunk is confirmed before sending the next one for such files, which loses the speed gain. The second was to give the loader a stable id for events without one. I took the second.

The loader now computes a hash from the file name, the chunk number and the line number inside the chunk, and puts it into a field named loader_id when the event has no id. The ingest side uses it as the dedup key. The same line always gets the same key, whatever the number of retries.

I also checked the case where a file is edited and loaded again. The hash would then collide for different content on the same line. I decided to include the size and the modification time of the file in the hash, so a changed file gets new keys. A re-load of the same file does not duplicate, which is what the customers expect.

After the change I ran 100 kill runs overnight in a loop on staging, with random kill points. All passed, and the counts matched.

Mara reviewed the ingest side and asked for a unit test for the dedup with the new field, which I added. The second review comment was about the field name, and we kept loader_id.

Next is a production pilot with two chunks in flight for the customer with the slow proxy.

summary: Ran the two-chunk loader for the customer with the slow upload proxy and found retries down by a third, but one load stalled on a proxy timeout that needs its own limit.
body:
The pilot ran during the afternoon with the customer who has the slow upload proxy. They load about six files a day, between 300 MB and 1.2 GB.

The retry count metric on the Grafana panel showed the effect. Before, the average was 21 retries per 1 GB file. With two chunks in flight it was 14. Load time per file dropped from about 11 minutes to 7.

One load, a 900 MB file, stalled for 25 minutes at 61 percent. The logs showed a chunk request that never returned. The proxy had dropped the connection without closing it, so the client waited. The per-request timeout in the loader was set to 10 minutes, a value from the first version made for slow links.

The retry logic can only act after a failure, so the wait was the problem and not the retry itself. A chunk of 8 MB should take seconds even on this proxy. I set the request timeout to 90 seconds and a separate idle timeout of 30 seconds on the connection, since a stalled upload is easy to tell from a slow one by looking at the bytes written.

I tested with a small script that opens a socket and goes silent. The loader now gives up after 30 seconds and retries the chunk on a new connection, with backoff that starts at 2 seconds.

I did not want to roll this to all customers directly. The change affects the most timing-sensitive part, so I kept the pilot running one more day with the new timeouts.

I also wrote a note for Sam on what the customer may notice: a stalled load now recovers by itself within a minute, and the job page shows the retry count. She will mention it in the runbook.

The next check is tomorrow morning with the numbers of the full day.

summary: Checked the pilot day with the new timeouts, saw no stalls in 6 loads, and enabled two chunks in flight for all customers.
body:
The numbers of the pilot day were clean. Six loads finished, the longest took 8 minutes for 1.1 GB, and no load stalled. The idle timeout fired three times, and each time the retry on a new connection worked at the first attempt.

I enabled two chunks in flight as the default for everybody and left the setting for single chunk available per customer, in case one of them has a source that depends on order.

The deploy was done at the quiet time of the morning. I watched the retry panel and the queue lag for an hour, and both were normal. The runbook has a paragraph on the new timeouts now.

summary: Ran a full audit export for the largest account on staging after the month-part change and found memory flat, with the download link working for a 2.1 GB file.
body:
The export for large accounts was split into month parts last week, so today's work was a full run for the largest account on staging. The account has about 31 million audit rows, more than twice the earlier test. The job ran 11 parts in sequence and took 38 minutes. Worker memory stayed flat around 300 MB, and the Postgres cursor reads on the id column showed no growth in load or in replication lag.

The final file was 2.1 GB after gzip, and the download link worked from the console. One problem came up: the job status showed the last part as running for about two minutes after it had finished, because the status update happened after the upload to the bucket. I moved the update before the upload and added a final state check. Mara looked at the cursor query plan and confirmed it uses the primary key index for every part. Next step is a cancel button for running exports, and then a production run for one customer who asked for a full history.

summary: Wrote the docs for the audit export, including the format of each field, the job states and the size limits, and fixed three unclear points raised by Sam's review.
body:
The docs page for the audit export was the topic after the Redis work. I wrote it for the compliance people at the customers, who are not developers, so the page begins with what an export contains and who can start one.

The sections are: starting an export in the console, starting one through the API, the fields of a row, the job states, and the limits. Each field in the NDJSON row has a name, a type and a sentence. The fields are id, created_at, actor, action, target and details.

For the API part I included a curl example with the three calls in order, and the JSON of a status response. All examples were run against staging and the output was pasted from the real responses, with the ids replaced.

The limits are a range of at most 13 months, one running export per account, and a link that is valid for 15 minutes. I explained how to ask for a new link without starting a new job.

I sent the page to Sam, and the review came back within an hour with three points. First, the word actor was not clear, so I added that it is the user or the API key that did the action. Second, the time zone of created_at was not stated, and it is UTC with an offset in the ISO string. Third, the page did not say what happens to the file after the link expires.

The third point was a gap on our side too. Files stay in S3 with no lifecycle rule, and I had not set one. I added a lifecycle rule of 7 days in the Terraform for the export bucket and applied it to staging. Tobias will look at the production plan tomorrow.

The docs now say that files are deleted after 7 days and that a new export can be made at any time.

Sam also asked for a short list of questions that an auditor may ask and which fields answer them. I added a table of five questions, such as who changed a setting, and when a user was removed, and what to filter on.

The page is published on the staging docs site. It goes live with the feature.

One check remains: the details field can hold a large JSON object for some actions. The largest in the sample was 14 KB. The docs mention that the field has no fixed size.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's Terraform plan for the export bucket lifecycle rule and asked for a prefix filter so that other files in the bucket are not deleted.
body:
Tobias sent the production plan for the 7 day lifecycle rule. The plan was correct for the bucket, but the rule applied to the whole bucket without a filter.

The bucket also holds the loader's temporary uploads and a few old manual exports, which have their own handling. A rule for all objects would delete them after 7 days as well.

I asked for a prefix filter on audit-export/ and he changed it. The new plan shows one rule with the filter and nothing else changed. I approved it, and he will apply it tomorrow morning.

summary: Looked into why the Postgres vacuum on the events-adjacent settings tables ran for hours and found a long open transaction from a reporting script holding back cleanup.
body:
Mara noticed that autovacuum on the accounts and settings tables had been running for a long time and bloat was rising. I started with pg_stat_activity and found a session that had been idle in transaction for 19 hours.

The session belonged to a reporting script that Sam uses for support questions. It opens a transaction, runs a few selects, and the connection stays open in her SQL client without a commit. Because of that, dead rows could not be removed anywhere.

I asked her to close it, and vacuum finished within 12 minutes. The bloat on the settings table went from 3.1 GB to its real size of 400 MB after a later table rewrite with pg_repack, which Mara ran in the quiet hours.

To stop this from happening again, I set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10 minutes for the support role only. The application roles have their own pool settings and did not need a change. I tested that the support role is disconnected after the time, and that the client shows a clear error.

I added a Prometheus rule for the age of the oldest transaction, with a warning at 30 minutes. The exporter already has the data, so no new query was needed.

A note for Sam in the support docs explains the timeout and suggests using a read-only mode with autocommit.

summary: Finished the audit export for large accounts by splitting ranges into month parts that run in sequence, after a 14 million row test took too long as one job.
body:
The largest customer has about 14 million audit rows in 13 months, and a test on a restored copy showed the single job problem. The export ran for 31 minutes and then failed when the stale check restarted it, because the progress update was written only after each chunk and the chunk of the status row was locked by a long update.

There were two issues. The first is the job design: a very long job is hard to resume and hard to watch. The second is the lock, which came from my status update running in the same transaction as the cursor write.

For the first, the start route now splits a range into parts of one month. Each part is a child job with its own cursor, file and status. The parent job shows the parts and the total of the finished ones. The parts run one after the other, so the database load stays as small as before.

For the second, the status write is a separate short transaction, and the cursor is saved after each chunk of 5,000 rows only. A lock timeout of 2 seconds was added, and the update is skipped on timeout, since progress is not critical.

The download now returns one file for the whole range. After all parts are done, a final step joins the gzip files. Concatenated gzip streams are valid, so no re-compression is needed, and that step takes a few seconds.

I ran the large test again. All 13 parts finished in 24 minutes, the largest part took 3 minutes 10 seconds, and the final file had 14,012,447 rows. I checked the count against a SELECT count on the source for the same range and it matched.

A kill test followed. I stopped the worker during the seventh part. The restart picked up the seventh part from its cursor and the earlier parts were not touched. The result was again correct.

The status shape for Lena changed a bit, since the parts are a list. I updated the example in the docs and sent her the new JSON. She said the console can show a bar for parts done out of total with little work.

In the load on the database, the p95 of other queries on the same primary stayed within normal values during the test. The export reads from the primary, though, and a replica read would be better. I noted it as a possible follow-up and not as a requirement for now.

The branch is ready for a final review by Mara. Open points are the console page and the replica question.

summary: Reviewed the search shard question with Tobias, wrote down the options for sharding by month, and decided to measure the index sizes per customer first before choosing a layout.
body:
This session was only planning, with no change to the cluster. Tobias and I looked at the OpenSearch index again, because the large customers have shards of very different sizes and a few are above 60 GB while most are under 5 GB.

The current layout is one index per customer with a fixed number of shards. That is simple, but it gives hot shards for the big customers, and the nightly reindex job takes longest on them. The idea under discussion is an index per month, with customers separated by a routing value and a filter.

I wrote down what each option means in a planning note. For the month layout, old months can be made read-only and shrunk, and deleting old data becomes dropping an index. Searches over long ranges touch many indices, though, so the latency for a query over a year needs a test.

The cost of the move is the other side. All customers' data must be reindexed once, the search API must build index names from a time range, and the alias handling of the reindex job needs a rewrite. Mara's search v2 parser does not care about the layout, which helps.

Before choosing, we need real numbers. I wrote a script that calls the cat API and lists, for each customer, the document count, the store size and the shard count, and wrote the result to a CSV. The first run showed 38 customers, with the top three at 71, 64 and 52 GB, and the median at 2.3 GB.

I also looked at the share of queries by time range from the search API logs of the last week. About 80 percent of the searches are for the last 7 days, 15 percent for up to 30 days, and only 5 percent for longer. That fits the month layout well, since most queries would touch one or two indices.

Tobias raised a concern about the number of shards per node. Month indices for 38 customers with the routing approach would make fewer shards in total, not more, so that is fine. A shard count per month index of 6 seemed reasonable for now.

We did not agree on the routing key yet. The customer id alone would keep a customer on one shard per month, which gives hot shards for the top three again. A combined key with the event type would spread the load but make queries touch more shards.

The next step is a test on staging with a copy of the largest customer's data in both layouts and a set of 200 recorded queries. I will build the query set from the logs. The plan is in the notes, and nothing is decided.

summary: Ingest worker leaked goroutines when a client dropped mid-batch; the request context is now passed down to the decoder and the leak is gone under load.
body:
Under the load test the worker's memory grew by about 40 MB per hour. A goroutine dump showed thousands of goroutines parked in the batch decoder, each waiting on a channel that nobody read after the client had disconnected.

The decoder had been started with context.Background() instead of the request context. I passed the request context through handleBatch into decodeEvents and made the send on the output channel a select on ctx.Done().

I added a test that opens a connection, sends half a batch and closes it, then checks the goroutine count with runtime.NumGoroutine. Before the change it stayed 12 above baseline per run; after it, it returns to baseline within 100 ms.

I ran the 20 minute soak at 3000 events per second. Memory stayed flat at about 180 MB per worker. Still open: the same pattern may exist in the NDJSON importer, which I will check next.

summary: Designed and built the first version of the event schema validation in the ingest worker; invalid events are now rejected with a per-event error instead of failing the whole batch.
body:
Until now a single malformed event made the worker return 400 for the entire batch, and customers had to guess which event was bad. The user asked for per-event errors in the response.

I added a validator in internal/schema that checks required fields (id, type, timestamp, payload), the timestamp range (not more than 24 hours in the future) and a payload size limit of 64 KB. The response is now 207 with a list of {index, code, message} for rejected events, and the accepted ones go on to the queue.

The first version compiled the type rules on every call and showed up at 30 percent of CPU in the profile. I moved the compiled rules into a map built at startup, keyed by event type, and CPU for validation fell to about 4 percent.

Two edge cases took time. Events with a timestamp in seconds instead of milliseconds were accepted silently, so I added a heuristic that rejects values below 10^11 with the code TS_UNIT. Unicode escapes in type names were normalized before the lookup, which changed the type key; I now reject non-ASCII type names.

I wrote 31 table tests and a fuzz test that ran for 10 minutes without a panic. The docs need an update for the 207 response, and I left a note for Sam about the error codes.

Next step is to check how the batch importer handles the same rejections, because it shares the validator.

summary: Reviewed the CSV importer against the new validator and found it still aborts on the first bad row; changed it to collect errors and continue.
body:
The batch importer calls the validator row by row, but it returned on the first error. A customer file with 200000 rows and one bad line therefore imported nothing.

I changed the importer to collect rejected rows into a report file next to the input and to keep going. The report has the line number, the error code and the original line. A flag --strict keeps the old behavior for scripted use.

I tested with a 1.2 million row file with 300 bad rows scattered through it. The import finished in 41 seconds and the report had exactly 300 entries.

One problem: the NDJSON path counted lines starting at 0 and the CSV path at 1, so the reports disagreed. I made both start at 1 and counted the header of the CSV as line 1.

I did not touch memory use. The report is held in a slice before it is written; for very bad files this could get large, so a streaming writer is a later task.

summary: Fixed a deploy pipeline step that marked the ECS service stable before the new tasks passed the load balancer health check, which caused a short window of 502s.
body:
Tobias saw a handful of 502 responses at each deploy. I looked at the pipeline script and the ECS settings together.

The pipeline waited for 'aws ecs wait services-stable', which only checks that the running count equals the desired count. The load balancer health check of the new tasks needed about 25 seconds more, and old tasks were already being drained.

The fixes were in Terraform and in the pipeline:
- health_check_grace_period_seconds set to 60
- deregistration_delay of the target group lowered from 300 to 60 seconds, since requests are short
- minimum healthy percent 100 and maximum 200, so new tasks start before old ones stop

The worker also now handles SIGTERM by stopping the listener, finishing in-flight batches and exiting within 30 seconds. The old code exited at once, and that was part of the 502s.

I deployed to staging three times in a row while a script sent 50 requests per second. No errors in any of the three. Production gets the change at the next deploy, and Tobias will watch the 5xx graph.

The ECS stop timeout is 35 seconds now, a little more than the drain time of the worker, and I wrote that coupling in a comment in the Terraform file.

summary: Found why the ingest worker lost events at queue restarts: acknowledgements were sent before the produce call completed; the worker now waits for the broker ack and the loss is gone.
body:
A customer reported that about 0.1 percent of their events were missing after a Redpanda restart last week. The user asked me to find out whether it was our fault.

I first built a reproduction: a script sends 100000 numbered events at a steady rate while I restart the broker container in the test environment. After the run, 87 numbers were missing, so it was reproducible.

In the worker, the produce call was asynchronous and the HTTP response was written when the message was put into the producer's buffer, not when the broker confirmed it. On a restart the buffer was dropped with the connection. The client had received a 200, so it did not resend.

The change:
1. The producer is configured with acks=all and idempotence on.
2. The handler waits for the delivery callbacks of all events in a batch before it answers.
3. A timeout of 5 seconds returns 503, so the client retries the batch.

The wait cost throughput at first. The median latency per batch went from 4 ms to 11 ms. To compensate I made the produce calls for one batch together and waited once, which brought the median to 7 ms.

Repeating the restart test five times gave zero missing events, and some duplicates when clients retried. Duplicates are handled by the event id at the store, which I checked in the insert code: there is a unique index on (customer_id, event_id) and the insert uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

I wrote a note for the customer for Sam to send. What remains is a metric for the produce failures, which I will add tomorrow.

summary: Ingest worker under load: a connection pool to Postgres was too small for bursts, so settings lookups queued; raising it and caching settings removed the stalls.
body:
The worker had occasional stalls of two to three seconds during bursts from the larger customers. Traces showed the time was spent waiting for a free Postgres connection, not in the query itself. The pool was set to 5 connections per task, which was fine for the first customers but not for a burst of parallel batches.

Every batch looked up the account settings in Postgres before decoding. I added a small in-process cache with a 30 second TTL for those settings, which removed most of the lookups. Then I raised the pool to 15 per task and set a connection acquire timeout so a stall turns into an error instead of a silent wait.

I replayed a recorded burst of 40 parallel batches against staging. The p99 of the batch handling went from 2.8 s to 180 ms, and the pool wait metric stayed at zero. I added that metric to the Grafana board for the ingest worker. One open point is that a settings change now takes up to 30 seconds to apply, which I noted in the code comment and will mention to Sam for the docs. Next is the validation of single events, which Mara wanted to look at.

summary: Load tested the ingest path at 10000 events per second and found the worker is limited by JSON decoding; switching to a faster decoder for the hot path raised the limit to about 16000.
body:
Goal of the day: find where the first version of the ingest path breaks. The user wanted to know the headroom before the next customer joins, who sends roughly 4000 events per second at peak.

Setup: a load generator on a separate ECS task sending batches of 100 events, 2 KB each, over HTTP/2, against 3 workers with 1 vCPU each, and a single Redpanda node.

Results of the first run: up to 6000 events per second all was fine. At 8000 the p99 went above 400 ms and at 10000 the workers sat at 100 percent CPU and the load balancer returned some 504.

The CPU profile showed 38 percent in encoding/json decoding, 12 percent in the validator and 10 percent in the garbage collector. The decoder allocated a map for every event.

I replaced the generic decode of the payload by a decode into a struct with the payload kept as json.RawMessage, because the worker never looks inside the payload. This removed most of the allocations. I tried a third party fast JSON library as well. It was about 10 percent faster again but it changed the handling of duplicate keys, and one of our tests failed on that. I dropped it and kept the standard library.

Results after the change:
- 12000 events per second with p99 of 90 ms
- 16000 events per second at 100 percent CPU, p99 of 300 ms

GC pressure fell to 4 percent. I also set GOMEMLIMIT to 80 percent of the task memory, which removed a few out-of-memory kills in the earlier runs.

Conclusion for the user: three workers hold about 14000 events per second, so the next customer fits easily. The single broker node was not the limit in any run, with disk write at about 30 MB per second. I will repeat the test with a larger payload size next week.

summary: Started the search API v1 skeleton in Fastify with an OpenSearch client and a first query endpoint; it returns hits for a single customer index.
body:
First step of the search API. I created the Fastify project in the services/search folder with TypeScript, a config loader and a health route.

The OpenSearch client is created once at startup with a connection pool of 10. The endpoint GET /v1/search takes q, from, size and a time range, and builds a query_string query filtered by the customer id taken from the API key.

Index naming for now is events-<customer_id>, one index per customer, which keeps customer data separate and makes deletion easy. I know that many small customers means many small shards, and I noted it as a point to review once we know the real sizes.

I tested against a local OpenSearch with 2 million sample events. A simple term search returned in 12 ms and a phrase search in 35 ms.

Not done: pagination beyond 10000 hits, error mapping and authentication. Those come next.

summary: Added API key authentication to the search API; keys are stored hashed in Postgres and looked up with a small in-process cache.
body:
The search endpoint needed to know who is asking. I added an api_keys table with customer_id, key_hash (SHA-256), name, created_at and revoked_at, and a migration for it.

The Fastify preHandler reads the Authorization header, hashes the token and looks up the hash. To avoid a database query on each request, I added a 30 second in-process cache of lookups. Revoked keys therefore stay valid for up to 30 seconds, which the user accepted for now.

Failures give 401 with a JSON error body and the same message for an unknown and a revoked key, so nobody can tell which keys exist.

I wrote tests for a valid key, a missing header, a malformed header and a revoked key. All pass.

The admin console will need a page to create and revoke keys; I told Lena about the table so she can plan it.

summary: Pagination for the search API: replaced deep from/size paging with search_after and an opaque cursor, so results beyond 10000 hits are reachable and paging is stable.
body:
The first version used from and size, which fails beyond 10000 hits in OpenSearch. Customers with large result sets need to page through all of it.

I switched to search_after with a sort on timestamp and event id as a tiebreaker. The response now has a next_cursor, which is the base64 of the last sort values plus a hash of the query, so a cursor cannot be reused with a different query. A changed query with an old cursor gives 400.

The from parameter still works for the first 10000 hits for compatibility with the one customer that already uses it. It is documented as deprecated.

Testing: a query matching 1.5 million events pages through in pages of 1000 with no duplicates and no gaps; I compared the count and the set of ids with a direct count query. Each page took about 20 ms.

One issue appeared. While new events are being indexed, the order at the same timestamp can shift if the tiebreaker is not unique. The event id fixes that, as it is unique per customer.

I also set the maximum size to 1000 and return 400 above that. Docs for Sam are drafted in the PR description.

summary: Wrote the first rate limiter on Redis: a fixed-window counter per API key that returns 429 with a Retry-After header; works, but allows bursts at window edges.
body:
The user asked for a rate limit in front of the search API, because one customer's script had sent 400 requests per second yesterday.

I implemented a fixed-window counter with Redis. The key is rl:<api_key_id>:<window_start>, the command is INCR followed by EXPIRE on the first increment, run as a small Lua script so both steps are atomic. The limit is 100 requests per 10 seconds for now, configurable per customer later.

On exceeding the limit the API answers 429 with Retry-After set to the seconds left in the window and headers X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining.

If Redis is not reachable, the middleware lets the request pass and logs a warning. I decided this together with the user, because blocking all searches for a Redis problem seemed worse than a short period without limits.

The weakness of fixed windows: a client can send 100 requests at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next, so 200 in a short time. I measured it with a script and it did happen. A sliding window would fix it, at some cost per request. I will try that as a next step and compare the cost.

Tests use a real Redis in a container, and they pass. Latency of the middleware was 0.4 ms at the median on the local network.

summary: Replaced the fixed-window rate limiter with a sliding window counter that weights the previous window; bursts at window edges are down from 2x to about 1.1x the limit.
body:
After the burst problem of yesterday, I changed the limiter to the sliding window counter approach. It keeps two counters, the current and the previous window, and estimates the rate as current + previous * (fraction of the previous window still inside the sliding range).

The Lua script reads both keys with MGET-like calls and increments the current one, still atomic. Cost went from one Redis call to one script call touching two keys, so I measured it: 0.5 ms at the median against 0.4 before. That is acceptable.

The edge test now sends 100 requests at the end of a window and 100 at the start of the next. The limiter let through about 110, and the rest got 429.

Keys get a TTL of twice the window so the previous counter is still there when needed. I used the key pattern rl:<key_id>:<window_index> and checked in redis-cli that keys disappear after 20 seconds.

Tests updated. The per-customer limits are still not configurable; that is next.

summary: Built the first admin console pages with Lena's layout: login, an account overview and an API keys page that creates and revokes keys through the new endpoints.
body:
Late session with Lena's design in mind. The console is a React app and talks to the same Fastify service under /admin.

I added endpoints POST /admin/keys and DELETE /admin/keys/:id. The create call returns the secret once, and only the hash is stored, so the page shows it in a dialog with a copy button and a warning that it cannot be shown again.

Sessions of the console use a cookie with a random session id; the data is kept in Redis under sess:<id> with a TTL of 8 hours, refreshed on activity. Login checks the password hash in Postgres (argon2id) and rate limits failed attempts per IP with the same limiter code as the search API, five attempts per minute.

The key list shows name, created date, last used and status. Last used needed a new column, updated at most once per minute per key so that the search path does not write on each request. I did that with a Redis key that holds the last write time.

For the frontend I built the table and dialog components and left the styling to Lena. I tested in the browser by creating a key, calling the search API with it, revoking it, and calling again. The second call returned 401 after the 30 second cache ran out, as expected.

Open points: a confirmation dialog on revoke, and error states when the API is down. I left both for Lena.

summary: Admin console: added an usage page with event counts per day and per API key, backed by a new endpoint in the search API, with Lena's chart component.
body:
