Lena asked for a usage page in the admin console so customers can see how many events they sent. I built the backend part first: a new endpoint that returns event counts per day for the last 30 days, optionally split by API key. The query runs on the Postgres events table and groups by day.

On the largest account the first version took about 6 seconds, which is too slow for a page load. I added an index on account id and received time, which brought it to 1.4 seconds. That is still slow, so I added a Redis cache for the result with a TTL of 5 minutes. The key name includes the account id and the range, so a change of range does not hit stale data.

On the frontend I used Lena's chart component and wrapped it in a page with a range picker. The picker offers 7, 14 and 30 days. The chart showed gaps for days without events, because the endpoint returns only days that have rows. I fixed that in the endpoint by filling the missing days with zero, so the frontend stays simple.

I also checked the permissions. The endpoint takes the account from the session, never from the request, so one customer cannot ask for another account. I wrote a test for that case, and it passes. The loading state and the error state are covered with the shared components.

Lena reviewed the layout and wanted the numbers formatted with thousands separators, which I changed. The page is in staging now. What is left is a table view under the chart and an export to CSV, which can wait. I am also unsure the Postgres query will hold up as the table grows, so I noted it in the plan for the dashboard queries.

summary: Public API docs: wrote the first reference pages for ingest and search, with request examples that were each run against staging to make sure they work.
body:
Sam asked for a first version of the public docs, and I wrote the reference for POST /v1/events and GET /v1/search from the code.

Each example is a curl command with the expected output. I ran all nine against staging and fixed two mistakes: the timestamp example used seconds, which the validator rejects with TS_UNIT, and the search example used the deprecated from parameter.

The docs list the error codes of the 207 response in a table, the rate limit headers and the cursor paging. I also added a short page on batch size: up to 500 events and 1 MB per request.

Sam will review the wording tomorrow. The docs are built with a static generator in the docs folder and deploy with the same pipeline as the rest.

summary: Public docs: wrote the authentication and error codes pages, and found two documented error responses that the API did not actually return, so the code matches the docs now.
body:
I wrote two more pages for the public docs: authentication and error codes. For each error I wanted a real response, so I triggered it against staging and pasted the actual body. That turned up two mismatches. The docs promised a 413 for oversized batches, but the ingest API returned a generic 400. The search API returned 500 instead of 400 for a malformed cursor.

I fixed both in the code rather than the docs, since the documented behavior is the more useful one. The 413 now includes the size limit in the message. The bad cursor case returns 400 with a code field named invalid_cursor.

The authentication page explains the API key header, how to create and revoke keys in the console, and what a 401 means compared to a 403. I added a short note on rate limit responses with the Retry-After header. Sam read the pages and asked for a table of all error codes, so I added one at the end of the error page.

Tests for the two changed responses are in. Next I will add examples for the batch import endpoints, and Sam will check the wording of the whole section.

summary: Small cleanup: the importer now streams its error report to disk instead of holding all rejected rows in memory, after a test file with 5 million bad rows used 3 GB.
body:
This was the follow-up I noted about the importer report. I generated a file where every row was invalid, 5 million rows, and the importer used 3 GB before it finished.

The report writer now uses a buffered writer and flushes every 1000 rows. Memory stayed at about 90 MB for the same file and the time was almost the same, 58 seconds.

I also cap the report at 100000 entries and then write one line with the number of omitted rows. The cap is documented in the importer help text.

summary: Search v1 performance pass: slow phrase queries traced to wildcard prefixes in query_string; added a guard and a cheaper path, taking p95 from 1.9 s to 240 ms on the large index.
body:
Customers started to use the search more, and the p95 for the largest customer index was 1.9 seconds. The user asked me to find out why.

I collected the 200 slowest queries from the search API logs. Most had a leading wildcard such as *error* or a very broad time range with no filter, and OpenSearch had to check a huge number of terms.

Findings:
- Leading wildcards were responsible for about 70 percent of the slow queries.
- Queries without a time range scanned the whole index, with about 600 million documents.
- The default field list was all fields, which matched on large payload text.

Changes made:
1. A leading wildcard is rejected with 400 and a message that points to the prefix search; trailing wildcards still work.
2. If the request has no time range, the API applies the last 30 days and says so in a response field applied_range.
3. The default fields are now message, type and tags, while the payload fields need an explicit field:value.

I also put the time range into the filter context instead of the query context so OpenSearch can cache it. That alone gave a good gain for repeated dashboard-like queries.

Before and after, on a replay of the 200 queries against a copy of the index:
- p50 from 310 ms to 45 ms
- p95 from 1.9 s to 240 ms
- p99 from 6.2 s to 900 ms

The 400 for leading wildcards is a change of behavior. I checked the logs and found two customers using it, so Sam will write to them before the change goes out. I will hold the release until that is done.

Next I want to look at the shard count of the large index, which has 5 primaries and could be too few, but I will measure before changing it.

summary: Added the nightly reindex job for OpenSearch as a scheduled ECS task that builds a fresh index from Postgres and swaps an alias, so mapping changes no longer need manual work.
body:
Until now a mapping change meant that someone had to reindex by hand. The user asked for a repeatable job.

The job is a Go program in cmd/reindex. For each customer it creates events-<customer>-<timestamp>, streams events from Postgres in chunks of 5000 using a keyset on id, bulk indexes them, and then switches the alias events-<customer> to the new index in a single atomic call. The old index is kept for one day and then deleted.

During the run, new events still go to the old index, so I added a catch-up step: after the main pass the job copies events with received_at later than the pass start, and then swaps. A short gap can still exist for events that arrive during the swap, which I handle by indexing with the same ids so a second catch-up is harmless.

On staging, a customer with 8 million events took 11 minutes, and the largest production-like copy with 400 million events would take about 9 hours, which is long. I set the bulk size to 8 MB and 4 parallel workers, and the 8 million case dropped to 6 minutes.

The load on Postgres from the reads is visible. I run the job with a read replica connection string, so the primary does not see it.

Scheduled with an EventBridge rule at 02:00 for now. It also logs a summary with counts per customer, and exits non-zero on any count mismatch between Postgres and the new index, so the alias is not switched in that case.

Not done: resuming after a crash. It starts over.

summary: Reindex job got a resume marker after a crash on staging lost four hours of work; progress is stored per customer in Postgres and a restart skips finished customers.
body:
Last night's staging run died after a deploy replaced the task, and the job had to start from zero. I added a reindex_progress table with customer_id, run_id, last_id and status.

After each chunk the job updates last_id, and a restart with the same run_id continues from there, writing into the same new index. The run_id is the date-based name of the index, so a new night gets a new run.

I tested by killing the task twice in the middle of the largest customer. The final document count matched Postgres exactly, and bulk indexing with the same ids meant no duplicates from re-sent chunks.

One detail: the progress update runs in the same loop as the bulk call, so a crash between them can repeat one chunk. That is fine because of the ids.

I also made the deploy pipeline not stop scheduled tasks that are running, since that was the cause.

summary: Wrote the plan for moving dashboard queries off the Postgres events table, listing the slow queries, their cost and three options; no code yet, the user will decide after reading it.
body:
The partial index of last week only bought time. The user asked me to prepare a plan for the analytics queries, since the dashboards get slower every month.

I collected data first. From the slow query log of the last 30 days, 6 queries make up 91 percent of the total time. They are daily counts, top event types, unique users per day, a funnel query, error rates by hour and the latency percentiles. All of them scan a time range of one customer and aggregate.

Growth: the events table grows by about 60 million rows per month and is at 430 million rows and 380 GB with indexes. The daily counts query for the largest customer was 4 s after the partial index and is already creeping up to 6 s.

Options I wrote down:
1. Keep everything in Postgres and add partitioning by month plus pre-aggregated summary tables, refreshed by a job. Smallest change, but each new dashboard question needs a new summary, and unique counts are hard to pre-aggregate.
2. A separate store built for analytical queries, loaded from the queue next to the Postgres writer. Larger change, new operations burden for Tobias, but the query shapes fit it.
3. Push the load to OpenSearch aggregations. We already run it, but the cluster is sized for search and the aggregations on high cardinality fields are expensive.

For each option I estimated the work in days, the risk and the effect on the current dashboards. Option 1 is about 8 days, option 2 about 25 days including a backfill, option 3 about 12 days.

I recommended not to decide yet and to run a time-boxed benchmark of option 2 with real data, because the cost is hard to guess from documents. I also noted what we need for such a benchmark: a copy of a week of real events, the 6 queries as a query set, and a target of 2 seconds for the largest customer.

The plan is in docs/plans/analytics-store.md. I will talk to the user about it tomorrow, and Tobias should read the operations part.

summary: Fixed the admin console session cookie: it was missing the Secure and SameSite flags, and sessions were not removed from Redis on logout.
body:
A review of the console login by the user found two problems. The session cookie was set without Secure and SameSite, and the logout only cleared the cookie in the browser while the sess:<id> key stayed in Redis until its TTL ended.

I set the cookie to HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax, and the logout handler now deletes the Redis key. I added a test that logs out and then replays the old cookie; it gets 401.

As a related change, a password change now removes all other sessions of that user. For this I keep a set sessions:<user_id> with the session ids, and it gets the same TTL as the sessions.

I checked on staging in the browser dev tools that the flags are present. Lena was told because her local dev setup uses plain http and now needs the flag turned off by an environment variable.

summary: Search API: added highlighting of matched terms and a fields filter to limit the response size, which cut the payload for large result pages by about two thirds.
body:
Customers asked for highlighted matches in search results, and the console team wanted smaller responses. I did both in the search API in one go because they touch the same response builder.

Highlighting uses the OpenSearch highlighter on the message and a few other text fields. I limited it to three fragments of 150 characters per field, since the default returned whole fields and made responses big. Fragments use em tags, and the text is escaped before the tags are added, so event content cannot inject markup into the console. I wrote a test with a message containing a script tag to be sure.

The second part is a fields parameter. A client can list the fields it wants, and the query then uses source filtering so OpenSearch returns only those. Unknown field names return 400 with the list of valid ones. Without the parameter the behavior is unchanged, so existing clients are not affected.

I measured a page of 100 hits on the large index. The response was 410 KB before and 130 KB with fields set to the timestamp, type and message. The latency went from 210 ms to 150 ms at p95, mostly from less serialization and less transfer.

One problem came up with highlighting on wildcard queries, where the guard from the earlier performance pass disables the expensive path. In that case there are no fragments, and the response says so with an empty highlight object. I documented this in the draft for the docs. Left to do: the docs page for both parameters, and a check with Lena that the console handles the empty highlight case.

summary: Built the first version of the search query parser for customer filters, so field:value and quoted phrases are translated into bool queries instead of raw query_string input.
body:
Until now the search API passed the user's text straight into query_string, which caused the wildcard problems we fixed last week and let users write queries that touched fields they should not see. I wrote a small tokenizer in src/search/parse.ts that understands field:value, quoted phrases, a leading minus for exclusion, and AND/OR with parentheses.

The parser produces an AST, and a second step turns it into an OpenSearch bool query. Unknown fields are rejected with a 400 and a message that lists the allowed fields. Every query is also forced into a filter on the customer's index, so the parser cannot widen the scope.

I wrote 64 unit tests, mostly for odd input: unbalanced quotes, empty parentheses, a colon at the end, very long terms. Two bugs came out of them. A minus sign inside a word such as user-id was read as exclusion, and nested parentheses deeper than 20 levels used too much stack. The first is fixed by only treating a minus at the start of a token as exclusion. The second is fixed with a depth limit of 10 and a clear error.

I compared results with the old path on 200 real queries taken from the access log of staging. 187 return the same hit sets. Of the other 13, 9 had used wildcards that the new parser now rejects on purpose, and 4 were queries where the old path matched across all fields and the new one needs a field name. I will ask Sam whether any customer docs use the second form.

The parser is not wired into the production route yet. It sits behind a flag called query_parser_v2 that is off by default. Next I want to add a default-fields setting per customer, so a bare word still searches the usual text fields. Latency was not measured yet; building the query adds well under a millisecond in a quick local run, but that needs a real test.

summary: Wired the new query parser behind a flag on staging and found bare words searched nothing, so a default field list per customer is now read from settings.
body:
I switched on query_parser_v2 on staging this evening and ran the replay of the 200 queries again. Bare words returned zero hits for most queries, because the parser had no field to attach them to.

I added a default_fields setting to the customer settings table in Postgres, with a migration that fills it with message, title and tags for existing customers. The search API reads it through the same small cache that holds the other settings, so there is no extra query per request. The bool query now wraps bare words in a multi_match across those fields.

After that the replay matched the old path on 193 of 200 queries. The seven differences are the wildcard cases the parser rejects on purpose and a few that depend on analyzer behaviour for hyphenated words. I wrote those down in the PR description so they are not a surprise.

One more thing: the 400 error message listed fields in random order because it came from an object. I sorted them, which makes the tests stable and the message easier to read. The flag stays off in production for now. Tomorrow I plan to test it on one internal account and then ask Sam to check the public docs for the query syntax.

summary: Postgres slow query review: the audit log listing used a sequential scan, and a composite index on customer and created time brought it from 1.4 s to 12 ms.
body:
Mara noticed that the audit log page in the admin console took more than a second for the larger customers. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the listing query and saw a sequential scan over about 3 million rows with a sort on top.

The query filters by customer_id and orders by created_at descending. There was only an index on customer_id. I added a composite index on (customer_id, created_at desc) using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes were not blocked.

After the index was built, the plan changed to an index scan with no sort, and the time dropped from 1.4 s to 12 ms on the biggest customer. The index is about 180 MB. I also checked that the insert rate of the audit log did not suffer; it is low enough that this is not a concern.

The old single-column index is now redundant. I left it for a week before dropping it, in case a query I did not see still uses it.

summary: Tobias and I traced a Redis connection warning on the admin console to one pool per request in the session middleware; it now shares one client per process.
body:
The logs of the admin console showed a growing number of Redis connections after each deploy, and one warning about too many clients on staging. I looked at the session middleware and found that it created a new client inside the request handler for the logout path.

I moved the client creation to the process start and passed it in. The logout path and the normal session lookup now use the same client. I also set a connection name so that CLIENT LIST shows which service owns which connection, which helps Tobias read it.

After the change the number of connections stayed flat at 6 per process during a short load test with 500 logins and logouts, where before it climbed past 400. The fix is deployed to staging.

I added a test that counts connections through the INFO command before and after a few hundred requests. Production gets the change with the next regular deploy.

summary: Added per-field boosts to the search query builder and tuned them on real queries, so title matches now rank above message matches without drowning out recall.
body:
The new parser gave us a place to apply boosts, so I started on per-field weights. The goal was that a match in title or tags ranks above the same match in message text, which customers have asked for several times through Sam.

First I made the boost a map in the customer settings, with defaults of title 3, tags 2, message 1. The query builder applies them in the multi_match fields list as title^3 and so on. A field named in a query such as title:error is not boosted, since the user already picked it.

To see if the numbers made sense, I took 50 queries from staging logs and had Sam mark the best three results for each from a customer she knows well. Then I computed how often those three appeared in the top 5 for different weights.

With no boosts the best results were in the top 5 for 61 percent of the queries. With 3/2/1 it was 78 percent. With 5/2/1 it was 80 percent, but a few queries then listed only title matches even where the message was clearly more relevant. I took 3/2/1 as the default and left the settings open for change.

One side effect: scores are no longer comparable between customers with different boosts. The search_after cursor does not depend on absolute scores, so paging is unaffected. I checked this with a test that pages through 300 hits with boosts changed between pages and the order stayed stable.

I also noticed that tie breaking used the internal document id, which changes after a reindex. I added the event timestamp as a second sort key so equal scores come out in a stable and understandable order.

The settings page in the admin console does not show the boosts yet. I will ask Lena if she has room for a small form next week. For now, changes go through a script that Mara and I can run.

summary: Postgres vacuum review: the events table had a long-running idle transaction pinning dead rows, and fixing the stuck job and tuning autovacuum brought bloat down from 38 percent to 6.
body:
Mara noticed that dashboard queries on the events table were slower than the row count explained, so I looked at table health first. pg_stat_user_tables showed about 38 percent dead tuples on events, and autovacuum had been running on it for hours without finishing the work.

The cause was an idle-in-transaction session left open by the CSV importer on staging-like load: it opened a transaction at the start of a file and held it while parsing. That pinned the oldest transaction id, so vacuum could not remove any dead rows newer than it. I found it with pg_stat_activity, sorted by xact_start.

The importer now commits per batch of 5000 rows instead of holding one transaction for the whole file. I also set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10 minutes for the importer role, so a stuck session cannot pin rows again.

For the table itself I lowered autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 on events and raised the cost limit, since the default scale factor waits for far too many dead rows on a table this size. After one full autovacuum pass the dead tuple share fell to 6 percent. I did not run VACUUM FULL, because it would lock the table, and the space will be reused.

The p95 of the usage endpoint went from 2.4 s to 1.7 s. That is a modest gain, and the real fix for the dashboards is still the plan for moving them off this table. Next I will add a Grafana panel for dead tuples and the age of the oldest transaction, with an alert.

summary: Added a Grafana alerting setup for Redis and Postgres basics, after the vacuum problem showed nobody would have noticed bloat or a stuck transaction without a person looking.
body:
After the vacuum finding two days ago, I wanted the numbers that would have shown it earlier on a dashboard, with alerts on the ones that matter. I added a Postgres panel group in Grafana using the postgres exporter we already run: dead tuple ratio per large table, age of the oldest transaction, number of idle-in-transaction sessions, and connection count against the maximum.

The alert rules are conservative. The oldest transaction age pages at 30 minutes and warns at 10. The dead tuple ratio warns above 20 percent for an hour on tables over a million rows. Connection use warns above 80 percent of the maximum. I tested each rule by lowering its threshold on staging and checking that the notification arrived in the right channel.

I added the same kind of group for Redis. It shows connected clients, used memory against the configured maximum, hit rate from keyspace hits and misses, and the number of keys by prefix, taken from a small script that samples the key names. The rate limiter keys and the session keys are the largest groups, as expected.

One attempt did not work out. I first tried to use the exporter's per-query statistics to show the slowest statements in Grafana. The label cardinality exploded because query text varied, and Prometheus memory grew by 1.5 GB in an hour. I removed it and went back to looking at slow queries by hand with pg_stat_statements.

The rules live in the repository next to the other dashboards, not only in the Grafana UI, so they can be reviewed. Tobias checked the PagerDuty routing: warnings go to the team channel and only the transaction age and connection alerts page the on-call.

Still open: a panel for the replication lag once we add the replica, and a runbook page for each alert so that whoever is paged knows the first three things to check. Sam offered to review the runbook wording, which I will send tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the public docs section for the search query syntax with examples, each run against staging, and found the exclusion example returned the wrong hits until the parser bug was fixed.
body:
Sam asked for a page that explains the new query syntax to customers, so I wrote it today. It covers bare words, field:value, quoted phrases, exclusion with a minus, AND/OR with parentheses, and the timestamp ranges that were added yesterday.

Every example in the page was run against staging with a test account that has a known set of 400 events. I put the request and the expected count next to each example in a small script, so the docs can be checked again after changes.

The check found a real bug. The example `error -host:test` returned events from host test as well. The parser put the exclusion in a should clause when it was combined with a bare word, instead of must_not. I fixed the builder so that all exclusions go to must_not no matter where they appear, and added three tests for that case.

The second finding was less serious. The docs said that field names are case-insensitive, but the allowed fields list was compared in a case-sensitive way. I decided to make it match the docs, and lowercased field names in the parser. The error message still shows the lowercase names.

The page now has a short section on limits: query length is cut at 1000 characters, nesting at 10 levels, and a query may have at most 20 terms. Those numbers match the code, and I put them in constants that both the docs script and the parser read.

I asked Lena whether the admin console should have a small help popover for the syntax. She said she can add one if I send the text, so I wrote four lines of help.

Open points: the docs do not yet say what happens with unknown fields in the default list; and the page needs a note on the flag, because customers will not see the new syntax until the flag is on for them. Sam will review the wording tomorrow.

summary: Turned on the new query parser for two internal accounts and one pilot customer, and watched error rates and latency for the afternoon; no regressions, one confusing 400 message fixed.
body:
With the docs reviewed in draft I enabled query_parser_v2 for our own two accounts and for one friendly customer who had asked for better filtering. I watched the dashboards for about three hours.

The error rate of the search endpoint stayed at the usual 0.2 percent. The p50 latency went from 38 ms to 41 ms and the p95 from 210 ms to 190 ms. The p95 drop is probably because wildcard-heavy queries are now refused early, but I did not isolate that.

There were 14 requests with 400 from the new parser. Most were typos in field names. One was a customer query with a trailing colon, written as status: , and the message said unexpected token at position 7, which means nothing to a customer. I changed it to say that a field name needs a value after the colon, with an example.

Another 400 came from a query with a curly quote copied from a document. I now normalize typographic quotes to plain ones before the tokenizer runs. That is cheap, and it removes a class of confusing errors.

I also logged the parsed AST for a sample of 1 percent of requests at debug level, so we can see what customers write without storing the raw text beyond the normal access log. This helps decide on defaults later.

The pilot customer wrote back through Sam that the exclusion filter was what they needed. They also asked for a way to search a time range with relative words such as last 24h. That is a feature for later and goes on the list.

Plan: keep the flag on for these three accounts for a week, then roll it to all customers in two steps.

summary: Upgraded the Redis minor version on staging and checked that the session store, rate limiter Lua script and cache keys all behave the same; production follows after a quiet period.
body:
Tobias prepared a new minor version of Redis for staging, and I used the afternoon to check that nothing in our use breaks. The admin console session store, the rate limiter and the query cache all depend on it.

First the functional checks. Logging in and out of the console worked, and sessions survived a restart of the Redis task because of the snapshot. The rate limiter Lua script loaded and ran with the same results as before, and my test of 1 million key ids gave identical output.

Then a short load test with the same mix as production: 70 percent reads of cache keys, 20 percent limiter calls, 10 percent session reads. At 15000 operations per second the latency at p99 was 1.1 ms, the same as on the old version within noise. Memory use for the same data set was about 2 percent lower.

One difference showed up in the client library log: a deprecation message for a command we use in the cache health check. It still works, but I replaced it with the recommended one so the log stays clean.

I checked the TTLs on session keys, which are 8 hours, and on query cache keys, which range from 30 seconds to 10 minutes. All were kept after the upgrade and after a restart.

The plan is to run it on staging for a week, and then Tobias will upgrade production in a quiet hour with a replica ready for fail-back.

summary: Fixed the admin console usage chart showing a gap for days without events; the endpoint now fills missing days with zero.
body:
Lena reported that the usage chart in the admin console drew a line that skipped days when a customer had no events, which made quiet weekends look like missing data. I looked at the endpoint behind the chart.

The SQL groups events by day, so days without rows are not returned at all. The chart component draws what it gets. I could have fixed it in the frontend, but it is better for every client of the API to receive a complete series.

I changed the query to join against generate_series for the requested range, so each day appears with a count of zero where nothing happened. The range is limited to 92 days, so the series stays small.

The query time stayed about the same, 90 ms for the largest customer. I added tests for a range with no events at all, one event in the middle, and a range that crosses a change of daylight saving time, which produced a duplicate day in the first version. I fixed that by building the series in UTC.

Lena checked the chart on staging and confirmed it looks right now. No change was needed in the React code. The fix is merged and goes out with the next deploy.

summary: Rolled the new query parser out to all customers in two steps and wrote down the cases where the old query_string behaviour differs, so support can answer questions quickly.
body:
After a week with three accounts and no problems, I enabled query_parser_v2 for half of the customers this evening, chosen by a hash of the customer id. The second half follows tomorrow if the numbers stay good.

I watched the error rate and the 400 rate by customer. The 400 rate for the new group was 1.8 percent of requests, compared to 0.1 percent before. That sounds high, but almost all of it came from two customers whose integrations send wildcard queries such as *error*. Those queries were already slow and are now refused with a message that explains the alternative.

I wrote to Sam with the two customer names and the exact query patterns, so she can contact them before their integrations break for the other half. For these two I added an override in the settings so they stay on the old path for another two weeks. That gives them time to change their code, and it is documented in the settings table with an expiry note.

Latency looked fine. P95 stayed at 190 ms for the group on the new path. The cache hit rate for search results went up slightly, because the parser normalizes whitespace and case in the query before it builds the cache key. Two queries that differ only in spacing now share an entry.

I also wrote a short internal page listing the differences between the old and the new behaviour: wildcard prefixes are refused, bare words use the default fields, unknown fields give 400, exclusions apply anywhere, and typographic quotes are normalized. Sam can paste from it into support answers.

There was one scare around 21:00 when the 400 rate jumped for a few minutes. It was a customer test script that sent the same bad query in a loop. The rate limiter handled it and the script stopped by itself.

Tomorrow I will enable the second half. If a customer asks for the old behaviour, the override is available, but only with my approval.

summary: Enabled the new parser for the remaining customers, removed the flag code path for the old default, and left only the temporary override for two customers.
body:
The second half of the customers went to query_parser_v2 today without problems. The numbers at the end of the evening matched the first half: 400 rate around 1.5 percent, mostly from the same two wildcard integrations, p95 at 190 ms.

With everyone on the new path I started removing the flag. The route now always uses the parser, and the old query_string code is only called when the customer has the legacy_query override set. That override applies to two customers and has an expiry date in the settings table two weeks out, after which a small job removes it and the code can go.

I deleted about 140 lines of old guard code that handled wildcard prefixes inside query_string, because they are not reachable for any customer except the two overrides. For those two the guard stays, so I moved it into a separate file called legacy.ts. This makes the later deletion a simple removal.

The tests needed work. Some old tests assumed that unknown input is passed through, and they now expect a 400. I updated 11 tests and wrote 6 new ones for the override path. The whole suite runs in 38 seconds.

I checked the cache keys for search results. They are built from the customer id, the normalized AST and the cursor, and are named search:v2:{customer}:{hash}. Old keys under search:v1 expire after at most 10 minutes, so nothing has to be deleted by hand.

One thing I noticed in the metrics: the number of distinct cache keys fell by about a third, because equal queries now share entries. The hit rate rose from 41 to 47 percent for search results. That is a nice side effect, though the main aim of the work was safety and clearer syntax.

I wrote the summary of the rollout for the team chat. Mara asked whether the parser could be used for the export endpoint, which has its own filter format. I think yes, but only after the audit work, so I put it on the list.

After this the first stage of the search work is done: parser, boosts, docs and rollout. The next steps are range shortcuts like last 24h, and a look at the reindex job, since the field boosts also depend on the mapping.

summary: Added relative time shortcuts such as last 24h and last 7d to the query syntax, parsed into range filters in UTC, with docs and tests.
body:
The pilot customer asked for a simple way to search the last day, so I added relative time words to the query parser. The syntax is timestamp:last 24h in quotes, or the shorter form since:24h, and the units are m, h and d.

I discussed the two forms with Sam. She felt that since:24h reads more naturally for customers, so I made that the documented form and kept timestamp:"last 24h" as an accepted alias that is not in the docs. Fewer forms in the docs means fewer questions.

The parser turns the shortcut into a range filter with gte set to now minus the amount. The tricky part is caching: if now is part of the query, no two requests share a cache key. I round the lower bound down to the minute before it is built into the key, so requests within the same minute are served from one entry. The result can be up to a minute stale at the lower edge, and the docs say that.

Limits matter here. I cap the amount at 90 days, because larger ranges touch many indices for no good reason, and reject zero or negative values with a clear message. Combinations like since:24h and since:7d in one query are refused as ambiguous.

For tests I froze the clock in the builder. I wrote 22 cases: each unit, the rounding at minute edges, a leap of daylight saving time, large values, nonsense units, and mixing with an absolute range. One bug showed up in the third case. A value like 24H in uppercase fell through to the unknown unit error, so I lowercase the unit first, which also matches the rule for field names.

Then I compared results on staging. For 30 queries, since:24h gave the same hit count as an explicit range written by hand, within events arriving during the test. The p95 latency stayed the same, because the filter is a cheap range on an indexed field.

I updated the docs page with the new shortcut, and the script that checks docs examples against staging now covers it, so it will fail if the behaviour changes. Sam read it and asked for one more example with exclusion, which I added.

One open question is time zones. Everything is UTC, and the docs say so, but customers in other zones may expect local days for a shortcut such as today. I did not add that; it needs a per-customer setting and a decision from the user.

The change is merged and enabled for everyone. The pilot customer got a note through Sam and said they would try it tomorrow.

summary: Dropped the redundant single-column audit log index a week after the composite one went in; no query used it and the table lost 90 MB.
body:
Last week I added the composite index on (customer_id, created_at desc) for the audit log listing and left the old customer_id index in place. Today I checked pg_stat_user_indexes to see if anything still reads it.

The scan counter of the old index had not moved since the day the new one was created, so the planner prefers the composite index for every query we run. I also searched the code and the reports scripts for queries that filter by customer_id alone, and found none that would need the old one.

I dropped it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid a lock. The table and index size went down by about 90 MB, and the insert path has one less index to update.

I watched the slow query log for an hour afterwards and saw nothing new for the audit table. The listing still took about 12 ms for the largest customer.

summary: Looked at why the reindex job on staging takes 55 minutes and found most of the time goes to fetching events per customer one row at a time; batching the fetch cuts it to 21 minutes.
body:
The nightly reindex job is slow on staging, even though the data set is only a fraction of production, and I wanted to know why before it becomes a problem with the large customers. I profiled it with timing logs per stage.

The biggest share, about 70 percent, was spent in the loop that reads events from Postgres. The code fetched events per customer in pages, but for each page it also ran a separate query for the customer's mapping settings, so a customer with 400 pages ran 400 settings queries. The settings never change during a run.

I moved the settings read out of the loop, so it happens once per customer. I also raised the page size from 500 to 5000 events, which fits comfortably in memory, and used a server-side cursor instead of offset paging. Offset paging got slower with each page, which was visible in the logs.

With both changes the run on staging took 21 minutes instead of 55. The bulk requests to OpenSearch are now the longest stage, which is the right bottleneck to have. I checked that the resume marker still works by killing the task midway; the restart skipped the finished customers and the final index had the same document count as before.

I have not tested this on the production size. I will ask Tobias for a run on a copy of production data before the change goes live.

summary: Admin console login flow: fixed a redirect loop after session expiry that happened when the return path itself required login, and added a test.
body:
Lena reported a redirect loop in the admin console: after a session expired, opening a bookmarked page sent the browser to login, and after login back to the login page. I reproduced it on staging with a short session TTL.

The login page stored the original path as a return parameter. When the original path was already the login page with its own return parameter, it stored that value again, and the nesting grew until the browser gave up with too many redirects.

I fixed it in two places. The redirect helper now ignores a return path that starts with /login, and it only accepts paths that start with a single slash, which also closes the possibility of an open redirect to an external address. The second part was something I noticed while reading the code, and it deserved a fix on its own.

I wrote tests for six cases: a normal path, a nested login path, a path with two slashes at the start, an absolute URL, an empty value, and a very long value. All behave as expected now.

Lena checked the flow in the browser and confirmed the bookmark case works. The session cookie flags from the earlier fix were not touched. This goes out with the next deploy.

summary: Production-size test of the faster reindex job on a copy of the data: 3 hours 10 minutes down to 1 hour 5 minutes, with one memory problem in the bulk stage that is now bounded.
body:
Tobias restored a copy of production data into a separate Postgres instance so I could test the changes to the reindex job at real size. It has the large customers, and the biggest one has about 90 million events.

The first run used the batched settings and the cursor fetch. It ran for 1 hour 5 minutes, compared to 3 hours 10 minutes for the old code on the same copy. The cursor fetch gave most of the gain on the large customers, because offset paging had become very slow past a few million rows.

The run was not clean. About 40 minutes in, the task's memory use climbed to 3.4 GB and the container was close to its limit. The reason was the bulk stage: pages were read faster than OpenSearch accepted them, and the queue between the stages had no bound, so read pages piled up in memory.

I changed the queue to a bounded channel that holds at most 4 pages. The reader now waits when the writer is behind. Memory stayed under 700 MB for the whole second run, and the run time was almost the same, 1 hour 8 minutes.

I also lowered the bulk size from 10 MB to 5 MB per request after seeing a few 429 responses from OpenSearch with the larger size. The client retries these with a pause, and with 5 MB there were none in the second run.

The resume marker was tested at this size as well. I stopped the task after 25 minutes and restarted it. It skipped the 11 finished customers and carried on with the one that was in progress, which started from its beginning, as designed. The final document counts matched Postgres for every customer I sampled, 20 in all.

One caveat is that the OpenSearch cluster in this test was the staging one and had no other load. In production the nightly job competes with search traffic, though at night that is light.

The branch is search-v2 because the new mapping with boosts also has to be built by this job. I merged the reindex changes into it and wrote the numbers into the PR. The next step is a review by Mara and then a deploy to production with a first run watched by Tobias.

summary: Reviewed Mara's change to the importer for NDJSON files and found it accepted lines longer than the limit by splitting them; it now rejects them with a line number.
body:
Mara asked me to review her pull request that makes the NDJSON importer faster by reading in large chunks. The speed gain was real: a 2 GB test file went from 9 minutes to 4.

While reading the code I looked at how lines are cut. The chunk reader uses a fixed buffer of 1 MB, and when a line did not fit, the remainder was handled as a new line. A very long line, for example an event with a huge payload field, was therefore split into two broken lines, which the validator then reported as two separate invalid events with confusing errors.

I wrote a test file with a 3 MB line between normal lines to confirm it. The importer reported two errors, both parse errors, with the wrong line numbers for the rest of the file, because the count was off by one after the split.

We discussed it in the pull request. Mara first wanted to raise the buffer, but a bigger buffer only moves the limit. The better fix is a hard maximum line length of 2 MB, in line with the documented size limit for one event. Lines above it are rejected as one error that says the line number and the length, and the reader skips to the next newline without keeping the data in memory.

Mara implemented it, and I added tests for a line exactly at the limit, one byte above it, a file that ends without a final newline, and Windows line endings. The last case also showed that a trailing carriage return was kept in the last field of some lines. She strips it now.

I ran the full set of importer tests and a before and after run on the 2 GB file. The time with the fix was 4 minutes 10 seconds, almost the same as without, and the error report for the long line was correct with the right line number for everything after it.

One more remark in the review concerned memory. The error report is streamed to disk since the earlier cleanup, and the new code keeps to that. I checked peak memory on the big file: 140 MB, flat.

Mara merged it after the tests passed. I left a note in the docs task for Sam that the line limit should be named on the importer page.

summary: Added the line length limit and the CSV quoting rules to the importer docs page, with examples that were run against staging.
body:
Following the importer review I wrote the missing parts of the docs page for file imports. Sam had asked for it as well, because support had questions about files that were partly rejected.

The page now says that one event may be at most 2 MB and that a longer line is rejected with its line number while the rest of the file is still processed. It explains that the error report lists each rejected row with a reason, and how to download it from the admin console.

For CSV I described the quoting rules that the importer follows: double quotes around fields with commas or line breaks, and a doubled quote for a quote inside a field. I also wrote down that the first row must be a header, and what happens with unknown columns, which are kept in a payload field.

Each example was run against staging with a small file. One example claimed that empty values become null, but the importer drops the field instead. I changed the text to match the behaviour, since a change in the importer would affect customers' data.

Sam read it and asked for a short table of the error codes. I added it, and linked to the error codes page. She will publish it tomorrow.

summary: Ran the first production reindex with the faster job under Tobias's watch: 1 hour 12 minutes, search stayed healthy, and the alias swap worked.
body:
The reindex changes were reviewed by Mara and merged, and last night's run on production was the first with the new code. Tobias watched it, and I read the logs this morning.

The job took 1 hour 12 minutes. The old job had been taking a little over 3 hours on production data, so it is in line with the test on the copy. The memory of the task peaked at 820 MB, with the bounded queue doing its job.

The search API stayed healthy during the run. P95 latency went from the usual 190 ms to about 230 ms while the bulk writes were running, and returned to normal after the alias swap. No 5xx responses were seen. The OpenSearch cluster showed a few bulk rejections early on, 6 in total, which the client retried with a pause, and none failed in the end.

After the run I compared document counts per customer between Postgres and the new index through a small script. All 38 customers that had events matched. I also ran 100 stored queries against the old and the new index, and the hit counts were equal except for events that had arrived in between.

The old index is kept for two days in case a problem shows up, and then a cleanup step removes it. I checked that the step works by running it for an older index on staging.

The boosts were not part of the mapping in this run, because the search-v2 mapping change is a separate step. I will do that in the next session. The reindex job itself is now fast enough that a mapping change can be rolled out in a normal night.

summary: Small fix: the search API returned 500 instead of 400 for a malformed cursor, so a bad cursor now gives a clear error and is logged at info level.
body:
A customer's script sent an old cursor with a character cut off, and the search API answered with a 500 and a stack trace in the log. The cursor is base64 of a JSON array, and the decode step threw on invalid input without a catch.

I wrapped the decode in a try block and return a 400 with the message that the cursor is invalid or expired. I also check the decoded value: it has to be an array of the expected length, otherwise the same error is returned. This protects against hand-made cursors that would make a strange search_after request.

I wrote three tests: a cut cursor, a valid base64 value that is not JSON, and a JSON value of the wrong shape. All three return 400 now. The log entry is at info level since this is a client error and should not page anyone.

summary: Planned the mapping change for field boosts and the new analyzers, listed what a reindex has to rebuild, and tested the new mapping on a staging index with promising results.
body:
The next step of the search work is the mapping. Boosts at query time are in, but we also wanted a better analyzer for message text and an extra keyword sub-field for tags, so I spent the session on the plan and a first test.

I wrote down the changes. The message field gets a custom analyzer with a lowercase filter, an ASCII folding filter and a word delimiter step that splits on underscores and dots, so a search for timeout finds read_timeout. Tags get a keyword sub-field for exact filters and aggregations. Title stays as it is, except for a shorter max length for the indexed text.

I built a test index on staging with the new mapping through the reindex job, pointing at the test account with 400 events and then at a mid-sized customer with about 2 million. The build for the mid-sized one took 6 minutes. The index was 9 percent larger because of the extra sub-field.

For the evaluation I used the 50 queries that Sam had judged earlier. The share of queries with the best three results in the top 5 went from 78 to 84 percent. Queries with underscored names gained most. Two queries got worse: one with a product code that contains a dot, now split into two terms, so it also matched unrelated codes. I put a note on that and will decide if the delimiter step should keep the dot between digits.

There is a risk in analyzer changes that I want to name: a mapping change means all customers must be reindexed before the new analyzer is used at query time, otherwise indexed and searched terms are analyzed differently. The alias swap handles this, because a query only meets the new analyzer once the new index is live, but the mapping and the query builder must ship together.

I listed the order of work: first fix the dot case, then run the full production-size build on the copy and measure size and time, then ship the mapping and the query builder in one deploy. I also want a rollback plan that keeps the old index for a week this time.

Open questions for the user: whether the 9 percent size growth is acceptable, and whether to rebuild everything in one night or to go customer by customer. I wrote both options with their cost into the PR, and I lean towards one night, since the job now finishes in about an hour.

summary: Rebuilt the staging index with the new analyzers and boosts and compared 200 real queries against the old mapping; ranking improved for 71 of them and got worse for 6.
body:
I loaded the mapping drafted three days ago into a fresh staging index and replayed 200 real customer queries against both indexes. Results were diffed by top-10 order.

Ranking improved for 71 queries, mostly title matches that used to sit behind message matches. Six got worse. Five of the six were short queries where the new stemming analyzer merged two different words, such as 'logging' and 'logs'.

I kept the stemmer but excluded the 'message.raw' subfield from it, which fixed four of the six. The remaining two are acceptable for now and are listed in the planning note.

Next step is a full reindex timing on the production-size copy, then a flag per customer for the new mapping.

summary: Production-size reindex with the new mapping took 1 hour 20 minutes and the index grew 14 percent, mostly from the extra analyzer subfields; one customer's custom field broke the mapping.
body:
Ran the reindex job with the new mapping on the copy of production data, with Tobias watching the ECS task memory. Total time was 1 hour 20 minutes, eight minutes more than the current mapping, which fits the extra analysis work.

The index grew by 14 percent. I checked where it came from: the 'message' field now has three subfields, and two of them hold almost the same tokens. I dropped the one that only served a prefix experiment, which brought growth down to 9 percent.

One customer failed during the bulk stage with 'mapper_parsing_exception'. They send a field named 'meta' as a string in some events and as an object in others. The old dynamic mapping coped by accident, the new strict template did not. I added a rule in the reindex job that stores the string variant under 'meta_text' and logged how many events are affected, 3,412 in total.

I also re-ran the 200 query comparison against the full-size index and the numbers matched staging. The alias swap was tested on the copy and took under a second.

Left to do: a per-customer flag to choose the mapping, and a note for Sam about the 'meta' behaviour, because customers might ask why the field looks different in search.

summary: Fixed the custom field that broke the new mapping in the production-size reindex, by mapping unknown customer fields as plain keyword subfields, and reran the failing customer's index.
body:
The production-size reindex of yesterday failed for one customer whose custom field was named meta_text. It collided with the new meta_text subfield that the analyzers add, and OpenSearch rejected the mapping with a conflict error. I first confirmed it on a staging copy of that customer's data, where the same error showed up within seconds.

The cause was that custom fields were copied into the mapping under their own names, next to the generated fields. Nothing stopped a customer from picking a name that the mapping already uses. The old mapping had no generated subfields, so the problem never came up before.

I moved all custom fields under a custom object, so a customer field can no longer collide with a generated one. The query builder now rewrites field:value filters for custom fields to the new path. The default field lists in settings needed the same rewrite, and I wrote a small script that does it and prints each change before it applies it.

I checked the other customers for the same risk by listing every custom field name against the generated names. Only this one collided, but two others used names close to the reserved ones, so I added a validation to the settings endpoint that rejects reserved names with a clear message. The message names the field and says which names are taken.

The parser tests got four new cases for custom fields with dots and dashes in the name. One of them failed at first, because a dash was read as an exclusion, and the parser now handles it in the field position.

After the fix I reran the reindex for that customer alone on staging. It finished in 6 minutes and the document count matched Postgres exactly. I also compared 50 of their saved queries before and after the move, and the hits were the same for all of them.

The full production reindex with the new mapping is not repeated yet. I want the progress marker question checked first, because a restart in the middle of the new step might skip work. Next I will write that test, then plan a pilot with one customer.

summary: Wrote a reindex test that kills the job mid-run and checks the new mapping step resumes correctly, and found the progress marker skipped customers whose last batch was only half written.
body:
After the custom field fix I wanted proof that a restart in the middle of the reindex is safe with the new mapping. I wrote an integration test that starts the job on a small staging dataset, kills the process at a random point, restarts it and compares the final index with a clean run.

The first runs passed, but with 40 repeated kills one run showed 212 documents missing for a single customer. The cause was the resume marker. It was written when the last bulk request was sent, not when OpenSearch confirmed it, so a crash between the two lost a batch while the customer counted as finished.

I changed the job to write the marker only after the bulk response shows no errors for the whole batch. Partial failures now keep the customer open, and the job retries only the failed documents once before it gives up and logs them. The marker also records the mapping version, so a job started with a new mapping never trusts progress from an old one.

I reran the kill test 100 times and every final index matched the clean run. The test is slow, about 4 minutes, so it runs only in the nightly pipeline and not on every push. Next I will take the full production-size run again and watch memory in the bulk stage.

summary: Wrote a short support note on the new ranking and the meta_text field, so Sam can answer questions before the pilot customer sees any change.
body:
Wrote a one-page note for Sam covering what changes for a customer on mapping version 2. Title matches rank higher, stemming now matches 'logging' with 'logs', and the quoted phrase syntax is untouched.

I listed the two known queries where ranking got slightly worse and gave the exact text, so support can recognise them. I also explained 'meta_text' and how to query it.

Sam read it and asked for an example of how to turn stemming off for one query. There is no such option yet, so I wrote down the workaround of using a quoted phrase, which searches the unstemmed field. I tested that on staging.

Open item: whether to expose a 'exact:' operator in the parser. I will put it on the list rather than build it now.

summary: Looked at index size growth from the analyzer subfields and cut it from 14 to 6 percent by dropping the stemmed subfield on fields nobody searches with it.
body:
The production-size reindex made the index 14 percent bigger, and Tobias asked whether that fits the disk we have before the next growth step. I broke the size down per field with the index disk usage API on the staging copy. Almost all of the growth came from the extra analyzer subfields on the message and title fields.

The stemmed subfield was the largest part. I checked the last two weeks of search logs and found that only the message and title fields are ever hit through stemming, because customers search those with free text. The other twelve text fields got a stemmed subfield but were queried by exact value or phrase.

I limited the stemmed subfield to message and title and kept the ngram-free standard subfield everywhere else. The mapping template now lists the fields explicitly instead of using a dynamic rule. A new field gets only the basic analyzer until someone adds it to the list.

On staging the index went from 14 percent larger to 6 percent larger than the old one. I then reran the 200 real queries from last week against the smaller mapping. The ranking result stayed the same for 69 of the 71 improved queries, and two lost a little. I looked at those two and the loss came from a stemmed match in a field that no longer has the subfield, which is acceptable.

The reindex time also dropped a little, from 1 hour 20 minutes to about 1 hour 12 on the same data. I noted both numbers in the plan document. Lena asked whether the console shows index size anywhere, and it does not, so I added that to the list of small console requests. The next step is a pilot with one customer on the smaller mapping.

summary: Added the api_key_limits table and the admin endpoints to read and set limits per key, with the limiter falling back to the customer default when a key has no row.
body:
Created the migration for 'api_key_limits' with key id, requests per minute, burst and an updated-by column. Primary key is the key id and there is a foreign key to the API keys table.

The admin API got two endpoints: GET returns the effective limit and where it comes from, key or customer default; PUT sets or clears it. Validation rejects a burst smaller than the per-second rate and limits above the customer total.

The limiter looks up the limit through a small in-process cache with a 30-second TTL, so the Postgres table is not hit per request. I measured the lookup path at about 0.1 ms on a warm cache.

Writing the tests, I found that clearing a limit did not invalidate the cache, so a cleared key kept the old limit for up to 30 seconds. That is acceptable, but the response now says so in the documentation text.

Every change writes a row to the audit log with the old and new values. I checked the log listing and the row appears with the right actor.

Still missing: the 429 response headers with remaining quota and reset time, and the Lena's console form. I told Lena the endpoint shape so she can start.

summary: Returned standard rate limit headers on every response and a Retry-After on 429s, and found the limiter counted rejected requests, which made a throttled client stay throttled.
body:
Added 'RateLimit-Limit', 'RateLimit-Remaining' and 'RateLimit-Reset' headers to the search API responses, plus 'Retry-After' on 429. Values come from the Lua script, which now returns the three numbers instead of a bare allow flag.

While testing a client that hammered the API at twice its limit, I saw it never recovered after backing off. The script incremented the counter before deciding, so rejected requests also counted, and the weighted window kept the high count into the next window. A polite client would still be rejected for a full extra window.

I changed the script to increment only when the request is allowed. The test is a loop at double speed for 20 seconds, then a 5 second pause, then a single request. Before the fix it returned 429, after the fix it passes.

There is one cost: a flood of rejected requests is no longer visible in the counters. I added a separate plain counter 'rl:rejected:<key_id>' with a one-minute TTL for the metrics.

Prometheus now exports allowed and rejected per key class, not per key, to keep the label count down. I checked the series count on staging, 14 new series.

Next: docs for the headers, then the console form once Lena has it.

summary: Wrote the docs page for rate limit headers and 429 handling with a client example that honours Retry-After, and ran it against staging.
body:
Added a page to the public docs describing the three rate limit headers, what 429 means and how a client should wait. The example is a short loop in Python that reads 'Retry-After' and sleeps, with jitter added.

I ran the example against staging with a key limited to 60 per minute. It sent 200 requests and finished in 2 minutes 5 seconds with no failures, which matches the limit.

The first draft claimed the reset header is a Unix timestamp. It is seconds until reset, so I corrected the text and added a line of explanation.

Sam will review the wording tomorrow.

summary: Postgres slow query check on the settings table: the per-request lookup scanned a text column, and a unique index on the API key hash removed a 30 ms cost from key authentication.
body:
While measuring limiter lookups I noticed API key authentication in the pg_stat_statements top list. The query looks up a key by its hash and the column had no index, only the primary key on id. With 9,000 keys it was a sequential scan at about 30 ms.

I added a unique index on 'key_hash' with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so no lock. The query dropped to 0.08 ms in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

The unique constraint also found something: two test keys in staging had the same hash because a seed script reused a value. I removed one.

The index added 1.2 MB. A Redis cache for key lookups is possible but not needed now.

summary: Started the pilot for mapping version 2: moved one customer, compared their top queries before and after, and fixed a boost that pushed log-level matches above exact message hits.
body:
The pilot customer agreed through Sam, so I switched their account to mapping version 2 at the start of the evening and pulled their 150 most frequent queries from the search log.

I replayed those against both mappings and compared the top 5 hits. 118 were identical, 24 improved by my reading, and 8 differed in ways that needed a look.

The cause of five of the eight was the boost on the 'level' field. A query like 'error timeout' matched events with level=error above events whose message said 'timeout while calling the payment service', which is what the user wants. I lowered the 'level' boost from 3 to 1.2 and replayed the 8 again.

After the change, six were fine. The other two were ties broken by timestamp, and the old mapping broke them the same way, so I left them.

I watched live traffic for the customer for a while. Error rate was zero and p95 was 190 ms, a bit lower than before because the old query had a wildcard fallback.

One small bug showed up: the highlighter did not mark stemmed matches, since it worked on the unstemmed text. Highlights for 'logs' did not show for 'logging'. I changed the highlighter to request the stemmed subfield too. The fix is in the query builder, a few lines, with a test.

I noted the boost change in the planning note and re-ran the staging comparison to make sure the first 200 queries did not regress; 69 improved now, 5 got worse, so the boost change helped there as well.

Tomorrow I check the pilot customer's dashboards and ask Sam for feedback.

summary: Pilot feedback was positive; moved ten more customers to mapping version 2 and found the reindex progress marker did not cover the new meta_text step after a forced restart.
body:
Sam relayed the pilot customer's reaction: better ordering and the highlights now look right. No complaints in the morning.

I moved ten more customers to version 2 in the settings table, starting with the smaller ones. The search error rate stayed flat and latency was unchanged.

As a precaution I tested the reindex job crashing mid-run on staging by killing the task at about 40 percent. The resume marker skipped the finished customers as designed, but for the customer that was in progress the 'meta_text' rewrite ran twice on the already converted documents. It produced an object under 'meta_text' for 12 events, which the mapping rejected.

The cause is that the rewrite checked for a string at 'meta', and after the first pass the string was already moved. I made the rewrite idempotent: if 'meta_text' already exists it is left alone, and the original is only moved when 'meta' is a string.

I added a test with a document that goes through the rewrite twice. I re-ran the crash scenario and all customers finished with no mapping errors.

The resume marker still works per customer only, which is fine for now.

Remaining in this topic: the rest of the customers, the two with the temporary parser override, and removing the version 1 path after a quiet period.

summary: Moved the remaining customers to mapping version 2 in three batches, and the two with the parser override needed their default field lists extended first.
body:
Switched the rest of the customers over this evening, in three batches of about ten with a check between each one. After every batch I looked at error rate, p95 and the number of zero-result queries.

The two customers with the temporary parser override used a default field list that did not include 'meta_text'. Their searches that relied on the string form of 'meta' returned fewer hits after the switch. I added 'meta_text' to their default fields in settings and the counts came back.

One large customer showed a rise in p95 from 280 ms to 340 ms right after the move. I looked at it for a while: their queries hit the new stemmed fields with a long list of terms. The cause was cold caches after the alias swap, and a half hour later it was back to 270 ms.

The zero-result rate across all customers fell from 6.1 percent to 5.4 percent over the evening.

I did not remove the version 1 code path. It stays for two weeks in case a customer has to go back, and I put a reminder in the planning note.

Next up is the admin console form for the rate limits, which is waiting on Lena's UI.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console form for per-key rate limits and found it allowed a burst below the rate, which the API rejects with an unhelpful message; the form now validates first.
body:
Lena opened her pull request for the per-key limits form in the admin console. I ran it against staging and went through the cases.

Setting and clearing a limit worked, and the effective limit label showed whether it came from the key or the customer default. The audit log row appeared for each change.

If the user entered a burst smaller than the per-second rate, the API returned 422 with a technical message and the form showed only 'Request failed'. I suggested validating in the form with the same rule and showing the API message when it does get through. Lena changed it the same morning.

Two smaller points:
- the number input accepted negative values in the browser
- after saving, the form did not refresh the 'effective' label until a page reload

She fixed both. I tested again and everything behaved.

I also asked that the limits above the customer total be explained in the text under the field, not only on error. She added a line.

Approved and merged into the branch. The rollout to production is planned for tomorrow with the limiter in log-only mode first.

summary: Deployed the per-key limiter in log-only mode and compared what it would have rejected with real traffic: 0.3 percent of requests, almost all from three keys with default limits that were too low.
body:
Deployed the new limiter to production with an 'enforce' flag set to false. It evaluates every request, increments counters and logs the decision, but never returns 429.

After four hours I summed the log. Of about 2.1 million requests, 6,300 would have been rejected, 0.3 percent. Three keys accounted for 5,900 of them.

I looked at those keys with Sam. Two belong to a customer who runs a nightly export that sends bursts of 400 requests. The third is a monitoring script polling every second. The default limit for the first customer was too low for the export, so I wrote per-key limits for their two keys. Sam will talk to the monitoring customer about polling.

The Redis side looked fine. The new limiter keys added about 40 MB at the busiest point, and the command latency stayed under 1 ms. The connection count did not change.

One thing I found in the logs: keys that had been deleted from Postgres still got counters for a few minutes, because the in-process cache returned the old row. This is harmless but I made the cache drop a key on a 401.

I leave the log-only mode on overnight and check the summary again tomorrow before turning enforcement on for a small group of customers.

summary: Turned enforcement on for five small customers after a clean night in log-only mode; the only 429s were two test keys.
body:
The overnight summary showed 1,100 would-be rejections, down from 6,300 per four hours, since the export keys now had higher limits. The monitoring customer reduced polling after Sam's message.

I set 'enforce' for five small customers in the settings and watched for an hour. The only 429s came from two test keys that I used to confirm the headers in production, and they showed the right values.

No support messages arrived. I will extend the group tomorrow.

summary: Enforced limits for all customers and fixed a clock drift problem: workers computing the window from local time disagreed by up to a second, so the script now uses Redis time.
body:
After a calm day with five customers I turned on enforcement for everyone in two steps. The first half went well.

Shortly after the second step I saw an odd pattern in the logs: a few keys got a 429 while the remaining quota header showed a positive number. That is inconsistent, so I traced it. The API workers passed their own clock into the Lua script to select the window, and two ECS tasks were nearly a second apart, so at window boundaries they used different windows for the same key.

The fix is to call TIME inside the script and not accept the timestamp from the caller. The script was run on a Redis replica-free setup, so using TIME inside a script is fine here and I wrote that into a comment. I updated the unit tests that had passed a fake clock; they now set the window through a script argument only in test mode.

After deploying, the inconsistent responses stopped. I counted none in the next 40 minutes of logs.

I also asked Tobias to look at the time sync settings of the tasks, because a second of drift seemed large. He said he will check the NTP configuration of the base image next week.

The branch is complete apart from docs review. I will merge it tomorrow after Sam's read.

summary: Merged the rate-limits branch after Sam's review of the docs page, with two wording fixes about what counts toward the limit.
body:
Sam read the rate limit docs and asked two things: whether rejected requests count toward the limit, and whether limits are per key or shared among keys of a customer. I had answers for both from the work this week, so I wrote them into the page. Rejected requests do not count. Each key has its own limit and the customer total caps them together.

I merged the branch into main after the tests passed and removed the log-only code path. The flag stays as a kill switch.

summary: Started the audit log review for the next topic: listed what the log records today and found that API key changes and login failures are not captured.
body:
Began planning the audit work with a read of what the audit log holds. It records settings changes, user invitations and limit changes, all written from the admin API. It does not record API key creation or deletion, and failed logins appear only in application logs.

I counted the writes in the table over the last month: about 41,000 rows, with 80 percent from settings changes by two automated customers. That means the table grows slowly, but the rows have no structure for filtering by action. The 'action' column is free text and I found 63 distinct values with slight spelling variants like 'key.create' and 'key_created'.

I drafted a list of standard action names and a mapping from the old values. Writing the mapping showed that 11 old values cannot be mapped with certainty. I will keep those as they are and tag them 'legacy'.

For key events, the code that creates keys lives in two places, the admin API and an old support script. Both need the audit write. The script was last used months ago, but Sam still has it, so I will wire it in as well.

No code changed today. The draft of names and the mapping is in the planning note and I will ask Mara to look at the backend side.

summary: Wrote the migration that normalizes audit action names with a legacy tag for the 11 uncertain values, and ran it on a staging copy in 4 seconds.
body:
Mara agreed to the names, with one change: she prefers 'api_key.created' over 'key.create' so that the noun comes first, which sorts better. I changed the list.

The migration adds a column 'action_v2' and fills it from the mapping with a CASE expression, leaving the old column untouched. Rows with the 11 uncertain values get 'legacy.<old value>'. A later step can drop the old column once everything reads the new one.

I ran it on a staging copy with 41,000 rows. It took 4 seconds and no locks that mattered. A second run did nothing, so it is safe to repeat.

I then added an index on customer, action_v2 and created time, since the export will filter by action. I checked a query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and it used the index and returned in 3 ms.

The listing endpoint now accepts an 'action' filter and reads the new column. I wrote tests for the filter and for the legacy rows.

Still to do: the writes for API keys and login failures, then the export itself.

summary: Added audit writes for API key creation and deletion and for failed logins, including the old support script, and limited failed login rows to one per minute per account to avoid flooding.
body:
The key create and delete paths in the admin API now write 'api_key.created' and 'api_key.deleted' with the key id and a prefix of the key, never the key itself. I double checked that by grepping the test output for the full key value.

The old support script uses a different database helper. I made it call the same audit function, and ran it once against staging to see the row appear with the actor set to 'support-script'.

Failed logins were the harder part. A password guessing attempt could write thousands of rows, so I used a Redis key 'audit:loginfail:<account>' with a 60-second TTL and a set-if-absent write. Only the first failure per minute is written, and the row has a count field updated from a second counter. The test fires 30 failures in a row and finds one row with count 30 after the minute passes.

I also noticed the login failure write ran inside the request and added 6 ms. I moved it to a fire-and-forget call after the response, with errors logged and not thrown.

The branch tests pass. Tomorrow I look at the export format with Mara.

summary: Postgres check on the audit log table after the new writes: autovacuum settings are fine, and the table is 220 MB with the new index taking 40 MB of it.
body:
Looked at the audit table on production after a week of the new action column on staging only, to see what the migration will cost there. The table is 220 MB, of which the indexes are 70 MB. The planned composite index would add about 40 MB.

Dead tuples were low, 2 percent, because the table is append-mostly. Autovacuum ran twice in the last day and took under a second each time.

I ran the migration against a restored backup on a scratch instance and checked the time again: 11 seconds for the real row count of 480,000. That is longer than staging but still short. I will run it in a quiet hour.

I also checked that the planner picks the new index for the listing query with realistic customer ids, and it does.

summary: Ran the audit action migration on production in a quiet hour; it took 12 seconds and the listing endpoint works with the new action filter.
body:
