I ran the migration this morning while traffic was low. It took 12 seconds, close to the scratch run, and the index was built concurrently afterwards in about 20 seconds.

After that I deployed the API version that reads the new column. The listing endpoint with an action filter returned in 4 ms for a large customer. I looked at a sample of rows with the legacy tag and they were what I expected.

There were no errors in the logs. The old column stays for now.

summary: Designed the audit export with Mara: streamed NDJSON and CSV through a background job that writes to S3 and sends a signed link, with a size limit and a checksum file.
body:
Met with Mara to settle the export design. Compliance customers want the full audit history for a date range, sometimes millions of rows, so a synchronous download will not work.

The design is a background job. A customer requests an export in the console, a row in an 'audit_exports' table tracks the state, and a worker reads the rows with a keyset cursor on created time and id, writing NDJSON or CSV to a file in S3 through multipart upload. When it ends, the worker writes a checksum file and sets a signed URL valid for 24 hours.

We discussed two points at some length:
- Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET, so the cost does not grow with the page
- A limit of 10 million rows per export, with a message to narrow the range

Mara will write the worker and I will do the table, the request endpoint and the audit entry of the export itself, since an export is a sensitive action. That entry will be called 'audit_export.requested'.

I created the migration for 'audit_exports' with state, range, format, row count, file key and checksum, and wrote the request endpoint with validation of the range and format. It returns 202 with the export id. A test posts a request and reads the row back.

The worker will run as a scheduled ECS task like the reindex job, polling for queued rows. Tobias still needs to add its task definition in Terraform; I opened an issue for him with the memory estimate of 512 MB.

summary: Built the first streaming version of the audit export job: it reads audit rows in pages and writes NDJSON to S3 in parts, with a checksum file at the end.
body:
Started the export job in the audit-export worktree. The job takes a customer id and a time range, reads audit_log rows in pages of 5000 ordered by id, and writes NDJSON parts to S3 through a multipart upload. Keyset pagination on id replaced the offset pages in the first draft, because offset got slower with each page on the 2 million row test customer.

The checksum file is a SHA-256 over the finished object, computed while streaming so the rows are not read twice. Memory stayed flat at about 90 MB on the largest staging customer, which has 2.1 million rows.

The first run took 48 seconds for that customer. Most of the time went into the JSON encoding, not the query. I left that alone for now.

Not done yet: the CSV writer, the size limit, and the signed link mail. Mara will take the mail part. Next step is the CSV writer, which needs the same column order as the listing endpoint so compliance people see the same thing in both places.

One open question for Mara is whether the export should include rows tagged legacy by the action migration. I included them with the tag visible as a column until we decide.

summary: Added the CSV writer to the audit export with the same column order as the listing endpoint, and fixed quoting for details fields that contain newlines.
body:
The CSV writer shares the row mapping with the NDJSON writer, so only the final encoding differs. Columns follow the listing endpoint: id, created_at, actor, action, target, ip, details, legacy_tag.

The details column is JSON text and many rows contain commas and quotes. Some also contain newlines from old support scripts. The first test file broke in a spreadsheet because the newlines were not inside quoted fields. I switched to a proper CSV encoder with always-quote for the details column and added a test with 6 awkward rows.

Timestamps are written in UTC with a Z suffix in both formats. Before, the CSV used the server zone by accident.

Ran the job for the 2.1 million row customer: the CSV came out at 310 MB against 380 MB for NDJSON. Next is the size limit and the failure handling when the S3 upload part fails.

summary: Added a size limit to the audit export and found that a failed S3 part left the multipart upload open, which would have cost storage until cleaned up.
body:
The limit is 5 million rows or 2 GB per export, whichever comes first. A request above it is rejected at creation time with a count and a suggestion to narrow the time range. The count comes from a cheap estimate query, so the check does not scan the table.

While testing failures I killed the S3 connection in the middle of a run with a firewall rule on the staging task. The job reported an error, but the multipart upload stayed open. Open uploads keep their parts and are billed. The job now calls abort on any error path, and a lifecycle rule on the export bucket aborts incomplete uploads after one day as a second safety net. Tobias added the rule in Terraform and I reviewed the plan.

The job status row now moves to failed with the error text, and it retries a failed part up to three times with a short backoff before giving up.

A test for the abort path is in. Left: the signed link and the mail text, and a cleanup of finished exports after 14 days.

summary: Wired the signed link mail for finished audit exports and chose a 24 hour expiry after Mara and I went through who can forward such a link.
body:
Mara had the mail template ready. I connected the job completion to it. The link is a pre-signed S3 URL for the data file and a second one for the checksum file.

We discussed the expiry. A link is a bearer secret, so anyone who gets the mail can download the audit data. We chose 24 hours and put a note in the mail that the export can be requested again from the console. The mail goes only to the address of the admin who requested it, not to a distribution list.

We also decided to write an audit row for each export request and each download request. A download itself is not visible to us once the link is signed, so only the request and the completion are recorded.

Tested on staging: request, job, mail, download, checksum matched. The mail arrived in about 20 seconds after the job ended.

One rough edge: the mail shows the size in bytes. Mara will change it to MB. Next up is the console button, which is Lena's part, and the cleanup job.

summary: Wrote the cleanup job for finished audit exports, which removes files after 14 days, and tested it against a bucket with 300 fake objects.
body:
The cleanup runs daily from the existing cron runner. It lists export records older than 14 days, deletes the data and checksum objects, and marks the row as expired. It does not trust the bucket listing alone, because other tools also write there.

In the first version I deleted the object before updating the row. If the delete failed halfway, the row stayed active with a missing file. The order is now: mark expiring, delete objects, mark expired. A row stuck in expiring is picked up again on the next run.

Tested with 300 fake objects, of which 120 were older than the limit. The job removed 120 and left the rest. A second run did nothing, as expected.

The download endpoint for an expired export now answers 410 with a clear message instead of a raw S3 error. Left for tomorrow: a review pass of the whole branch and a test with a customer-sized export in the production-like environment.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console page for audit exports and asked for a status poll that stops on failure; the page also showed raw action names, which now use the readable labels.
body:
Lena's page has a form with the time range and the format, plus a list of past exports with their status. I read it and tried it on staging.

The poll for status kept running forever after a failed export, once per two seconds. I asked for a stop on failed and expired and a slower interval after the first 30 seconds. She changed it the same day.

The list showed action names like api_key.create as they are stored. Support will read this page, so the labels now come from the same map the listing page uses. Legacy tagged actions show the old name with a small marker.

The empty state and the error for a range above the limit read well. I asked for the limit text to show the actual row count. Approved after those changes.

summary: Ran an audit export of a customer-sized dataset in the production-like environment: 4.8 million rows in 6 minutes, with one slow page query that needed an index.
body:
Used the copy of production data in the staging account. The test customer had 4.8 million audit rows and the export finished in 6 minutes 10 seconds, producing a 640 MB NDJSON file with a matching checksum.

The progress log showed that pages slowed down after about 3 million rows. The query filtered by customer and time range and ordered by id, and the planner chose the time index and then sorted. EXPLAIN showed a sort of 400 thousand rows per page for some ranges. I added an index on (customer_id, id) and the page time went from around 700 ms to 25 ms. The index takes 60 MB on the staging copy.

Peak memory of the worker was 110 MB. The S3 upload used 8 MB parts, which is fine.

The index migration will go out with the branch. I want to run it on production in a quiet hour, as with the earlier audit migration. Next is the final review with Mara.

summary: Created the production index for the audit export in a quiet hour with a concurrent build; it took 40 seconds and added 18 MB.
body:
Ran CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on audit_log (customer_id, id) late in the evening. It took 40 seconds. The table is smaller in production than the staging copy, so the index is 18 MB.

I watched the lock waits and the replication lag while it ran. Neither moved. Afterwards I ran ANALYZE on the table and checked the plan of the export page query: it uses the new index and no sort step.

The branch can now be merged once Mara has looked at the last two commits. I also added the index name to the migration notes in the repo so nobody drops it as unused.

summary: Merged the audit-export branch after Mara's review, then did a first real export for a pilot customer and found the signed link mail landed in spam for one mail provider.
body:
Mara reviewed the last commits and asked for two changes: the failure mail should not include the raw error text, and the cleanup job should log how many objects it removed. Both were small. I merged the branch after the tests passed.

The pilot was a mid-size customer who needs the log for a compliance audit. Their admin requested an export of 11 months, 920 thousand rows, and it finished in 70 seconds. The checksum matched on their side.

Their mail provider put the signed link mail into spam. The mail had a long URL with the signature in it, and the sender domain had no dedicated header for transactional mail. Sam talked to the customer. Meanwhile I shortened the visible link text and added a plain text part to the mail. Tobias checked the SPF and DKIM records for the sending domain and found DKIM was set only for the marketing sender. He added the record for the sending domain.

After that change a test mail to the same provider arrived in the inbox. We did not wait for the customer to confirm; Sam will ask them on the next call.

I also wrote the docs page for the export for Sam to review. It covers the formats, the limit, the link expiry and the checksum, with an example that verifies the file with sha256sum. I ran the example against staging.

Still open: a way to schedule a recurring export. Nobody asked for it yet, so I left it out and noted it in the backlog.

summary: Started the loader-retry work: mapped how the document loader fails on large files today and found it restarts from the beginning after any network error.
body:
The document loader pulls large files from customer-provided URLs or S3 and feeds them to the importer. Support has had three cases this month where a 2 GB file failed near the end and the customer had to start over.

I read the loader code and wrote down the failure modes. A connection reset mid-download aborts the whole job. A 503 from the source on the first request aborts it as well, with no wait. A slow source hits the 60 second read timeout. There is no record of how many bytes were handled.

Plan for the branch: use range requests so a download can resume at the byte offset, store the offset and the batch number in the job row, retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, and give up after a bounded number of attempts with a clear error. Non-transient errors such as 403 and 404 should fail at once.

A hard part is that the importer is not idempotent per batch at the moment. If a batch is applied and the process dies before the offset is saved, a resume would apply it twice. Event ids are unique in the schema, so a duplicate insert is rejected, but the counters in the job summary would be off. I will record the offset in the same transaction as the batch where possible.

I set up a fake source server for tests that can reset connections at a chosen byte and return 503 N times. That was the first commit. It is a small Go test helper and it works already against a 50 MB file.

Next step is the range request support in the download part.

summary: Implemented resumable downloads with range requests in the loader and tested them with the fake source that resets the connection at chosen byte offsets.
body:
The download function now keeps a byte offset and, after a transient error, asks for the rest with a Range header. If the server answers 200 instead of 206, it does not support ranges, so the loader starts over once and marks the job as not resumable.

I also check the ETag on resume. If the object changed between attempts, the loader fails with a message instead of mixing two versions of a file.

Tests with the fake source: a reset at 30 percent, three resets in a row, and a server without range support. All passed. The 50 MB test file arrives intact each time, confirmed by hash. Backoff and the job row offset come next.

summary: Added backoff with jitter and a retry budget to the loader, and made the job row record the offset and batch number in the same transaction as each batch.
body:
The backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles up to 30 seconds and adds up to 25 percent jitter. A job gets 8 attempts across the whole file, not per chunk, so a source that fails every few megabytes cannot keep a job alive forever.

The job row gets two columns, byte_offset and batch_no, written in the same transaction that applies the batch. With that, a crash between applying and saving cannot happen any more. I tested by killing the process at random points in 40 runs; the final counts were right each time.

Error classes: 5xx, resets and timeouts are transient; 4xx other than 408 and 429 fail at once. For 429 the loader honours Retry-After when the source sends it.

The migration for the new columns is in. It is a nullable add, so it is quick on production.

summary: Tested the loader with a real 2 GB customer file from staging storage while injecting failures, and found the progress counters double counted rows after a resume.
body:
I used a 2 GB NDJSON file with about 6 million events, stored in the staging bucket, and a proxy in front of it that resets the connection every 300 MB or so. The job completed after five resumes, which is the goal.

The final row count in the job summary said 6.4 million, while the file has 6.0 million lines. The event table had the right number, so the data was fine, but the counters were wrong. The cause was that the importer counted the lines of a partly read batch before the resume point and then counted them again after resuming. The batch boundary and the byte offset did not match: the offset was saved at the end of the last full batch, but the counter was kept in memory and carried over.

I moved the counters into the job row, saved in the same transaction as the offset. On a resume the loader reads the counters from the row. After that the six-reset run gave exactly 6,000,000 rows and 0 rejected.

I also found that the progress shown in the console used the byte offset divided by Content-Length. With a resume against a server that sent chunked data there was no length, and the bar showed NaN. The console now shows only rows when the length is unknown. Lena has the small change.

Time for the 2 GB file: 11 minutes without failures and 14 minutes with five resets, most of the difference being the backoff waits. That is acceptable.

Tobias asked about memory. The worker peaked at 180 MB for the entire run, so the existing task size is fine.

To do: a test for the case where the source object changes during a resume, and the docs text on what customers will see when a job gives up.

summary: Added the test where the source file changes between attempts; the loader now fails with a clear message and keeps the rows already imported.
body:
The fake source can now change the ETag after a given number of requests. The test starts a job, resets the connection, changes the object and lets the loader resume.

The loader compares the ETag on every ranged request, sees the mismatch and ends the job as failed with the text that the source changed during the import. The rows imported before are kept, and the summary says how many.

I considered restarting from the beginning in that case, but that would silently import part of the old version and then all of the new one. Failing is the honest option. The customer can start a new job.

summary: Looked at Redis memory growth in the staging cluster: the cache keys of the search API had no TTL after a refactor, and 40 percent of the memory held keys nobody read.
body:
Tobias pointed out that Redis used memory on staging rose by about 1 GB per week. I looked at the keys with SCAN and a sampling script, grouped by prefix.

The prefix search:v2: held 40 percent of the memory. About 80 percent of those keys had no TTL. The cause was in the cache helper: after the key naming refactor two weeks ago, the helper took the TTL from an options object, and the search code passed the options under a different property name, so the TTL was undefined and SET went without EX.

I fixed the property name and added a type so the compiler catches it. I also added a test that fails when a cache write has no TTL. For the keys already there, a one-off script sets a TTL of 6 hours on every search:v2: key that has none. On staging it touched 1.9 million keys in about 4 minutes, scanning in batches of 500.

Production has the same code, so I checked it as well. It had 5.4 million keys without a TTL under that prefix, and memory use was at 62 percent of the instance. I ran the same script there at low priority, with a short pause between batches to keep the latency steady. The p99 of Redis commands stayed under 2 ms during the run.

After the script, used memory dropped from 62 to 41 percent within the hour. I put a Grafana panel on the number of keys without a TTL per prefix, based on a small exporter that samples 10 thousand keys, so we see this earlier next time.

I told Mara, since her code introduced the options object. She was not worried and will check the other helpers for the same pattern. Nothing else was found yet in my quick read.

summary: Started ingest-batching: measured the worker writing one row per event to Postgres and found 70 percent of the time went into round trips, not into the inserts.
body:
The branch is about writing events in batches from the ingest worker instead of one by one. First I wanted numbers, so I profiled the worker on a staging load of 20 thousand events per second.

The worker takes a message from the queue, validates it, writes it to Postgres and acknowledges it. With pprof and the database statement stats I saw that about 70 percent of the wall time per event was spent waiting on the network for the insert, and the inserts themselves took around 0.2 ms. The connection pool was saturated at 20 connections while the CPU of the database was at 25 percent.

Design: collect events per worker goroutine until either 500 events or 50 ms have passed, then write them with one multi-row insert using COPY for large batches and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for smaller ones. Acknowledge the queue messages only after the commit.

The tricky part is partial failure. One bad row in a batch of 500 should not drop the others. The plan is to validate before the batch is built, so the database sees only valid rows, and if the insert still fails, fall back to single inserts for that batch to find the bad one and send it to the dead letter topic.

I wrote the batcher as a small type with a flush on size, a flush on timer and a flush on shutdown. The shutdown case matters, since a deploy would otherwise lose up to 50 ms of buffered events. Messages are not acknowledged until flush, so they would be redelivered anyway, but I want a clean exit.

A unit test covers the three flush triggers with a fake clock. Another test checks that a failed flush does not acknowledge anything.

First benchmark with a batch size of 200: throughput went from 20 thousand to 41 thousand events per second per worker in staging with the same pool size. I did not tune further. The next step is the fallback path for bad rows and the dead letter test.

summary: Built the fallback for a failing batch in ingest-batching: single inserts find the bad row, which goes to the dead letter topic, and the rest of the batch is saved.
body:
When a multi-row insert fails with a constraint or data error, the worker now rolls back and retries the same events one at a time inside one transaction per event. Events that fail again are sent to the dead letter topic with the error text. The rest are committed and acknowledged.

I built a test with a batch of 500 where 3 events have a value that is too long for its column. The result: 497 rows saved, 3 in the dead letter topic, nothing acknowledged twice.

There is a cost: the fallback is much slower than the normal path, about 12 times for that batch. If a customer sends mostly bad events, every batch takes the slow path. So I added a counter and a rule: if three batches in a row fall back, the worker validates more strictly against the column limits before building the next batch. In the schema the limits are known, so most of these cases can be caught before the insert anyway.

I did find one case that validation missed: a null byte in a string, which Postgres rejects in text. I added it to the validator and to the test data.

A transient database error, such as a connection reset, is not a data error. The worker must not send those events to the dead letter topic. I separated the error classes by SQLSTATE: class 22 and 23 are data errors, and everything else leads to a retry of the whole batch with backoff. A test with a killed connection confirms that nothing reaches the dead letter topic in that case.

Metrics: batch size histogram, flush reason counter, fallback counter and the time per flush. I added them to the worker dashboard in Grafana as a new row.

Remaining work is a soak test over a few hours at production-like load, and a decision on the default batch size and timer.

summary: Ran a four hour soak test of ingest-batching on staging at production-like load; throughput held, but the 50 ms timer made the p99 of ingest latency worse at low load.
body:
The test replayed a recorded production hour at 1.5 times speed for four hours, with two workers.

Throughput and CPU were fine. Each worker handled the peak of 38 thousand events per second with 40 percent CPU. The database CPU stayed below 35 percent, which is a clear improvement on the one-by-one writer.

The surprise came at low load, in the quiet part of the recorded hour. When only a few events per second arrive, the batch is never full, so every event waits for the 50 ms timer. The end-to-end latency of the ingest acknowledgement for a customer sending single events went from about 8 ms to about 60 ms at the p99. The customers do not wait for the write itself, only for the queue, so this does not hit the API response. It does show in the time until an event becomes searchable.

I made the timer adaptive in a simple way: if the buffer is empty when the first event arrives and there is no backlog in the queue, flush after 5 ms; if there is a backlog, wait up to 50 ms. After this change the low load p99 went back to 14 ms, and the peak throughput did not change.

I looked at the memory of the worker: flat at 140 MB over the four hours, no growth.

One issue came up in the log: two redeliveries of messages after a worker restart in the middle of the test. That is expected with acknowledgement after commit, and the ON CONFLICT clause absorbed them. The row count at the end matched the replay exactly.

Next I will write the rollout plan. I propose a feature flag per worker group, so Tobias can switch one of four groups first.

summary: Wrote the rollout plan for batched writes: one worker group first behind a flag, then compare row counts and latency for a day before the others.
body:
The plan has four steps. First, deploy the code with the flag off in all groups. Second, turn the flag on in group A, which takes about a quarter of the traffic. Third, watch for a day: the dead letter count, the fallback counter, the lag of the queue and the database CPU. Fourth, move the other groups one by one.

To check correctness I proposed a comparison of daily row counts per customer between group A and the older groups, normalised by the share of traffic. Large differences would show lost or duplicated events.

Rollback is the flag. The batcher flushes on shutdown, so switching it off does not lose events. Tobias agreed and will do the deploy tomorrow morning.

summary: Group A ran batched writes for a day: queue lag dropped and database CPU fell by a third, but a customer with very large events hit the batch byte limit and had slower flushes.
body:
The flag went on for group A at 09:00 and I watched the dashboards through the day with Tobias checking in.

Results against the other groups: queue lag at the peak was 1.2 seconds instead of 6 seconds, and the database CPU on the connection serving group A fell by a third. Dead letter count was 11 for the day, the same rate as the older groups. The fallback counter showed 9 fallbacks out of about 400 thousand flushes. All nine were null bytes in strings from one customer's mobile app, and I added a counter on that source so Sam can tell them.

The row counts per customer matched the expected share with differences below 0.1 percent, which is the noise from partition timing.

The problem: one large customer sends events with a big payload field, up to 200 KB each. A batch of 500 of those is 100 MB, which is far too big for one statement and caused flushes of 3 to 4 seconds and a spike in worker memory to 900 MB. I added a byte limit next to the count limit: the batch is flushed when either 500 events or 4 MB are reached. With that, the memory peak for that customer's group fell to 260 MB and the flush times to about 120 ms.

I also noticed that COPY is used above 100 rows and the insert below that. For big payloads the TOAST writes dominate, so the choice makes little difference there.

The byte limit went out in the same afternoon, and I checked it on group A again for two hours with clean results. The other groups follow in the next days. I wrote the figures into the branch notes so that the later comparison has a baseline.

summary: All worker groups now run batched writes; the last group needed a pool size change because the batcher held connections longer than the old writer did.
body:
I moved groups B and C two days ago without trouble and group D today. Group D handles the busiest customers, and within ten minutes the workers logged pool timeouts: could not get a connection in 2 seconds.

The reason is how the batcher uses connections. The old writer held a connection for a fraction of a millisecond per event. The batcher holds one for the entire flush, and with four goroutines per worker and a big batch this ran into the pool limit of 8 for that group. The pool for groups A to C was 20, so they never noticed. Group D had been set lower years ago to keep the database connections in check.

I raised the pool for group D to 16 and reduced the goroutines per worker from four to three, so the total number of database connections is the same as before plus 8. The database max_connections has enough room; I checked the current peak, which is 140 of 300.

After the change the pool timeouts stopped and the queue lag of group D went from 9 seconds to under 2 at the evening peak.

The flag is now on everywhere. I left the flag in the code for another week so the older path is available for an emergency, and I will remove it after that. The branch is ready for merge with one more review from Mara.

Cost side effect: the database instance load dropped enough that Tobias thinks we can go down one size next month. That belongs to the cost work and I added a note for it.

summary: Merged ingest-batching after Mara's review and removed the old per-event write path along with the flag, since all groups ran on batches for a week without incident.
body:
Mara's review had three comments. The flush on shutdown should have a deadline so a stuck database does not block a deploy. A metric label used the customer id, which would make too many series. And the byte limit should be configurable.

The deadline is now 10 seconds, after which the worker exits and the messages are redelivered. The label is gone; the per-customer fallback counts are in the logs. The limit is an environment variable with 4 MB as the default.

I deleted the single-insert writer, except the part used by the fallback, and removed the flag. The diff is minus 380 lines.

After the merge I deployed to staging, ran the test suite and the short load test, and Tobias rolled it to production in the usual way. No change in the dashboards.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why some events appear in search a few seconds later than before; the adaptive batch timer explains it and it stays under 60 ms.
body:
Sam asked whether a customer's report of events showing up slightly later was a bug. I checked the ingest path for that customer, who sends a steady stream of about 300 events per second.

With batching the events wait for a flush, up to 50 ms when there is a backlog. The search indexing adds its own delay of about one second. So the batching adds well under 100 ms and cannot explain seconds.

I measured the end-to-end time for that customer: the median was 1.3 seconds and the p99 2.4 seconds, the same as the week before the change. The customer's report likely referred to a short slow period caused by a reindex of another customer. I told Sam the figures and that the search delay is about one to two seconds by design.

summary: Reviewed the Terraform plan for cost work on the log retention of ECS tasks and found two log groups with no expiry; set 30 days and estimated 90 dollars a month saved.
body:
Tobias is looking at AWS costs and asked me to read through the plan for the CloudWatch changes. The plan itself was fine.

While reading the state I listed all log groups and found two with no retention at all: the old importer tasks and a staging group that was created by hand. Together they held 1.4 TB. The storage cost of that is around 90 dollars a month, and the data was older than a year in large part.

I set retention to 30 days for the importer group, since the logs have no audit value, and 14 days for the staging one. The importer logs are also copied into the job rows for failures, so the useful parts are kept elsewhere.

I checked that nothing reads the old logs: no Grafana panel and no alert rule queries these groups. The Terraform change went through the plan with only the retention attributes changing.

Tobias applied it. Deletion of the old data happened over the next hours. I noted the figure in the cost notes. A remaining item on the list is the ingest log group, which is large but used by the on-call, so it stays at 30 days for now.

summary: Looked into a slow settings query after a Postgres statistics change: the planner chose a sequential scan for the customer lookup, and an ANALYZE fixed it.
body:
An alert for the admin console latency fired in the afternoon. The settings lookup per customer took 180 ms instead of 3 ms.

I ran EXPLAIN on the query. It used a sequential scan on the settings table, which has 40 thousand rows, instead of the index on customer_id. The table had received a bulk update from a migration script that morning, and the statistics were out of date: the planner thought most rows matched.

Autovacuum had not yet run ANALYZE on the table, because the change threshold had not been reached in its view. I ran ANALYZE by hand and the plan went back to the index scan with 3 ms.

To prevent this, I added an ANALYZE step at the end of the migration script template, and lowered the analyze scale factor for this one table to 0.02. Latency returned to normal right after the manual run and stayed there.

summary: Fixed the loader's double counted progress rows after a resume by deriving the counter from the committed batch offset instead of adding per attempt.
body:
The bug from the 2 GB test was that after a resume the job row showed more rows than the file had. The cause was that each attempt kept its own in-memory counter and added it to the stored total when it finished. An attempt that died after committing a batch but before the final add left the two out of step, and the next attempt counted the same batch again.

The counter is now computed from the job row itself. Each batch commit sets rows_done to the previous value plus the batch size inside the same transaction that writes the offset and batch number. A resume reads rows_done and does not keep a total of its own. The final summary reads the row and never sums attempts.

I wrote a test with the fake source that resets the connection at three chosen offsets, one of them right after a commit. It asserts that rows_done equals the file's line count after each resume. The old code failed this with 41 extra rows. The new code passes with the reset at every batch boundary, which is 200 resets over a 100 MB file.

I also checked the progress shown in the console. It reads the same column, so it needed no change. One leftover is that the failure message still includes the attempt count from the old counter, and I renamed that field so it is not mistaken for rows. Next step is a rerun of the real 2 GB file with failures injected, then Mara's review.

summary: Put TTLs back on the search API cache keys in production Redis and let the old keys expire on their own, which should cut memory use by about 40 percent.
body:
The staging finding from a few days ago held for production too. After the refactor the cache helper wrote keys with a plain set and no expiry, so memory grew with every new query shape. I changed the helper so that every write requires a TTL argument, and the type checker now rejects a call without one.

The default is 120 seconds for search results and 10 minutes for the facet counts, which change slowly. Customer settings keep their 1 hour TTL.

I did not delete the old keys by hand. A scan with a pattern over the production keyspace would add load for no gain, so I wrote a small script that samples 5000 keys and reports how many have no TTL. It found 38 percent without one. I set a 24 hour TTL on those in batches of 500 with a pause between, using the sampled prefix list. Memory use fell from 6.1 GB to 3.9 GB over the afternoon.

Cache hit rate did not change, which confirms the dropped keys were never read. I added a Grafana panel for keys without TTL, fed by the same sampling script on a 15 minute schedule. It should stay at zero.

summary: Found why the dashboard for the largest customer times out: the daily counts query scans 190 million event rows in Postgres because the index leads with the wrong column.
body:
Lena passed on a complaint from support that the overview dashboard of our largest customer never loads, and the request log shows the 30 second statement timeout firing. I took the query from the log and ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a replica.

The query counts events per day and per event type for a 90 day window. The plan used the index on (event_type, received_at), but the filter is mainly on the account id and the time window. Postgres therefore read about 190 million rows of the one account and filtered them by time afterwards. The buffers line showed 11 GB read from disk.

The index we have for this is (account_id, received_at), but the planner did not choose it. The table statistics for account_id are skewed, because one account owns about a third of all rows, and the estimate for this account was far too low. I raised the statistics target on account_id to 1000 and ran ANALYZE. The plan then switched to the account index and took 14 seconds instead of timing out.

That is still too slow for a dashboard. A bitmap scan over 60 million rows is the limit of this table design. I wrote up three options: a pre-aggregated daily table, a partitioned events table, or a cache with a longer TTL. I am leaning towards the daily table for the counts, and I will talk to Mara tomorrow about who maintains it.

summary: Designed how the rate limiter counts requests in Redis: a sliding window made of per-second buckets in a hash, chosen over fixed windows because of burst traffic at the boundary.
body:
The current limiter uses a fixed one minute counter per API key. Two customers showed that this allows double the limit in a short burst across the minute boundary, and that was the reason for the redesign.

I looked at three designs. A sorted set with one member per request is exact but costs memory in proportion to the request rate, and our largest keys do 400 requests per second. A sliding window log has the same problem. Per-second buckets in a hash, with 60 fields per key, cost a constant 60 small fields and give an error of at most one second of traffic.

We will use the hash design. A Lua script does the work in one round trip. It increments the field for the current second, deletes fields older than the window, sums the rest and returns the count and the seconds until the oldest bucket expires. The key gets a TTL of the window plus 5 seconds so that idle keys vanish.

The key name is rl:{account}:{keyid}, with the account id in braces so that all keys of one account land on the same node if we ever use cluster mode. I wrote the script and a table of expected results for 12 traffic patterns. Implementation and load testing follow tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question on which headers the API sends when a customer hits the rate limit, and found the docs listed a header the service never sets.
body:
Sam is writing the public docs page about rate limits and asked what a client sees when it goes over the limit. I checked the Fastify hook instead of answering from memory.

The response is a 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds and a JSON body with the code rate_limited. The docs also mention X-RateLimit-Remaining, but the service has never sent it. The old fixed counter did not make it cheap to return, so it was left out.

The new limiter script returns the count, so we can set X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining on every response. I told Sam the docs should describe only Retry-After for now and that the other two headers come with the new limiter in the next days.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console change for the API key list and asked for the key creation date and last used time to be shown, since support needs them when a customer asks about an old key.
body:
Lena's pull request adds a table of API keys to the account page of the admin console, with a button to create and one to revoke. The code is clean and the revoke button asks for confirmation.

I asked for three changes. First, show the creation date and the last used time, because the audit log has these and support asks for them in almost every ticket about keys. Second, the key secret must be shown once at creation and never be fetched again, and the response from the create endpoint was kept in the React query cache. That cache entry has to be cleared when the dialog closes. Third, the revoke call should be optimistic only after the server confirms, since a failed revoke that looks successful is a security problem.

She agreed and will push the update tomorrow. The last used time needs a column that the API does not yet update. I will add a write to it in the auth hook, throttled to once per five minutes per key.

summary: Merged loader-retry after Mara's review and a clean rerun of the 2 GB file with 30 injected failures, then wrote the short guide for support on resumed imports.
body:
The rerun of the real customer file passed. I injected 30 failures: connection resets at random offsets, five timeouts, two truncated responses and one 503 from the storage service. The loader resumed each time, the final row count matched the file's 18.4 million lines, and the counter never exceeded it.

Mara reviewed the branch yesterday and asked for two small things. The first was to cap the backoff at 60 seconds, which was already the case but not in the config docs, so I wrote it there. The second was a metric for resumes per job, which is now loader_resumes_total with a label for the reason.

I squashed the branch into five commits and merged. The deploy went out in the evening to the one worker that runs imports, and I watched a small CSV import and a 400 MB NDJSON import finish. Both ran without a resume, as expected.

For Sam I wrote a half page note. If an import shows as running for longer than usual, look at the offset on the job row, and if it moves, leave it alone. If it has not moved for 10 minutes, the retry budget is probably spent and the job will fail with a message that names the cause. The note also says that a file changed during an import fails on purpose and the customer should upload it again.

The retry budget defaults to 8 attempts per job. After a week of data I want to look at the histogram to see whether that is too tight or too loose.

summary: Built a daily counts table in Postgres for the dashboards, filled by a nightly job, and measured the overview query at 90 ms instead of 14 seconds for the largest customer.
body:
Mara and I agreed that the dashboards should read pre-aggregated counts, so I built the first version of the table. It is called event_daily_counts and has the columns account_id, day, event_type, count and a bytes sum. The primary key is (account_id, day, event_type).

A nightly job fills it. For each day that has changed, it deletes that day's rows and inserts a fresh aggregation in one transaction, so a rerun is always safe. Late events are the catch: some customers send events with timestamps from three days back. The job therefore recomputes the last four days every night, not only the previous one.

I wrote the backfill as a separate script that works account by account and day by day, in chunks that take under a minute each. On the replica it processed 190 million rows of the largest account in 38 minutes with a low CPU load. For the whole database I estimate about 3 hours.

I changed the overview query in the search API to read the table for windows longer than 2 days. The current day still reads the events table directly, and the two results are merged. For the largest customer the 90 day overview now takes 90 ms. The check against the raw events gave identical counts for 200 random account and day pairs.

Open issues: the table is always a day behind for older ranges, which I want to make visible on the dashboard. Also, the time zone handling is by UTC day only, and customers who want local days will need another solution. I wrote both in the ticket.

summary: Analysed the slow search queries on the OpenSearch index and found that wildcard queries on the message field cause most of the p99 latency, not the size of the index.
body:
Support passed on three customers who say search got slower over the last weeks. I looked at the slow log of OpenSearch with the threshold at 1 second and collected a day of entries.

There were 2,300 slow queries. Of these, 71 percent had a leading wildcard on the message field, such as *timeout*, which cannot use the term index and walks all terms of the shard. Another 14 percent were queries over a 12 month range without any other filter. The remaining 15 percent were scattered.

I ran the five worst queries by hand with the profile API. The wildcard queries spent almost all their time in the term enumeration. The index has 18 shards per large customer's data, and each query goes to all of them, which multiplies that cost.

I considered three changes. The first was to index the message field also with an ngram analyzer, which would make infix search fast but would grow the index by roughly 30 percent. The second was to reject leading wildcards for ranges over 30 days. The third was to set a per-query timeout and return partial results with a flag.

I tried the timeout on staging first. With 5 seconds, the worst queries returned partial results and the p99 fell from 9 seconds to 5. That does not fix the cause but it protects the cluster. I will propose it with a message in the console that tells the user the results are partial.

The ngram idea needs a test on a copy of a real customer's index, because the size estimate is a guess. I started a reindex of a mid-size customer into a test index with the new analyzer. It will run overnight, and I will compare sizes and query times in the morning.

I did not touch production settings today.

summary: Implemented the sliding window rate limiter as a Lua script in Redis and covered it with 12 table tests; one off-by-one at the bucket boundary was caught by the tests.
body:
I implemented the design from last week. The script takes the key, the window in seconds, the limit and the current time from the application, so that tests can control the clock.

The first run of the table tests failed on two cases. With a window of 60 seconds, the script kept 61 buckets because the cleanup removed fields older than now minus 60, which includes the bucket exactly 60 seconds back. A request in that second was counted twice in the window sum. I changed the cleanup to remove fields at or below now minus 60. All 12 cases passed after that.

The script returns three values: allowed as 0 or 1, the current count, and the seconds until the oldest bucket drops out. The application sets Retry-After from the third value when the request is denied.

I also wrote a test with 50 parallel clients hitting the same key. Because the script runs atomically in Redis, the count never went above the limit. In a quick benchmark on staging, one call takes 0.4 ms on average on top of the round trip.

summary: Wrote down the Redis key naming convention and renamed the three keys that broke it, so every key now starts with a prefix for its purpose.
body:
With the limiter, the cache and the console sessions in the same Redis, I wanted a rule before more key shapes appear. The convention is purpose, then the account id in braces, then the details: cache:{acct}:search:<hash>, rl:{acct}:<keyid>, sess:<id>.

I scanned a sample of production keys and found three groups that did not follow it. The facet cache used facets_ plus the account, an old import status key had no prefix, and a feature flag cache used a colon in a different place. I changed the code for the first two and gave them a short TTL so the old names vanish on their own.

The flag cache was left alone, because the flag client library builds its own key names. I noted that in the convention file.

The file is in docs/engineering/redis-keys.md and has a short table. I also added a lint test that greps the source for calls to the Redis client with a string literal key not starting with one of the known prefixes.

summary: Dropped the attempt to replace our hand-written query builder with a third-party library, because it could not express the nested boolean filters that customers use.
body:
The search API builds OpenSearch queries from the customer's query string with about 600 lines of hand-written code. I wanted to try a query builder library to cut that code, so I spent the morning on a spike.

The library has a typed API and produces valid query JSON for simple cases. I converted the ten most common query shapes from our tests, and eight worked without change. For two, it gave different output.

The first was a nested boolean with must_not inside should. The library flattened it in a way that changed the meaning, and the test for it caught this. The second case was the per-account field filters that we add as a filter context. The library put them in the scoring context, which changes ranking and makes results slower to cache.

I looked at whether I could fix these with its extension hooks. The hook for the boolean case needs a patched copy of the library, and I do not want to maintain that. I also checked the size: it adds 400 KB to the bundle of the API and has two dependencies that we do not use otherwise.

I decided to stop. The hand-written builder is ugly but it is tested with 140 cases, and it does what customers rely on. I deleted the spike branch and wrote the findings in the ticket so nobody tries it again without reading them.

Instead I spent the last hour on cleaning the builder: I split it into one function per clause type, and I wrote the missing test for the case that failed in the library. The behaviour is unchanged and all 141 tests pass.

summary: Added curl and Node examples to the public API docs for the ingest endpoint and checked each one against staging so that they run as written.
body:
Sam asked for examples on the ingest page because new customers keep sending single events in a loop. I wrote a curl example for a batch of three events and a Node example with fetch, and I put in a note on the maximum batch size.

I ran both against staging with a test key. The first run of the curl example failed, because the docs used a field name, ts, where the schema expects timestamp. That error had been in the page for months. I fixed the field name in all three places on the page.

The batch note says 1000 events or 5 MB per request, whichever comes first. I checked the limits in the ingest API code and they match. The 413 response for a batch that is too large is also shown, with its JSON body.

I also added a short section on the 429 response with Retry-After, in the wording Sam and I agreed on yesterday. Sam will review the text, and I will publish after that. The examples live in docs/examples/, and a script runs them against staging in CI, so they cannot rot.

summary: Fixed an on-call page for slow ingest acknowledgements caused by a worker group that had not picked up the new pool size, and restarted it with the right config.
body:
The page said ingest p99 was above 800 ms for ten minutes. In Grafana, only one of the worker groups was slow, and its database pool metric showed 10 connections where the others had 25.

The cause was that the last pool size change had been applied in Terraform, but the service for that group had not been redeployed, so it still ran on the old task definition. I forced a new deployment and the group picked up the setting. The p99 dropped back to 120 ms within three minutes.

To avoid this, I added a check to the deploy script that compares the running task definition revision of each group with the latest. It prints a warning if they differ.

summary: Wrote the first version of the rate limit settings per API key in Postgres, with a default tier and an override column that support can change without a deploy.
body:
The rate limiter design from the last entries needed a place to keep the limits, so I added a table for per key limits in Postgres. Each row holds the API key id, requests per second, the burst size and an optional note for support. Keys without a row fall back to a default tier read from the account settings.

The migration adds the table and a unique index on the key id. I ran it on a staging copy and it took well under a second, since the table starts empty. The search API now loads the limits for a key on its first request and caches them in Redis under the new rate prefix, with a TTL of 5 minutes so that a changed override reaches all instances without a restart.

I wrote a small admin script for support that sets or clears an override and writes an audit log row with the old and new values. Mara asked in review whether a limit of zero should block a key; I made zero invalid and added a separate blocked flag, because a zero would be too easy to enter by mistake.

Tests cover the default fallback, an override, a cleared override and the cache refresh after the TTL. All pass. Still open: the console page where customers see their own limits, which Lena will pick up, and the rollout order, which is next.

summary: Rolled out per key limits in shadow mode on staging, where the limiter only logged would-be rejections, and found two internal health checks that would have been blocked.
body:
After the settings table was in, I turned on the new limiter in shadow mode on staging. In this mode the Lua script counts every request and logs what it would have rejected, but lets the request through. I let it run for about two hours against replayed traffic from a production sample.

The log showed 312 would-be rejections. Most came from one synthetic load test key with a very low default, which is expected. Two others were not: the internal health checks of the search API and the console both use an API key and send a request every second from several instances. Together they would have hit the default burst limit and been blocked, which would have paged us for nothing.

I gave those keys an explicit high override through the support script and also made the limiter skip keys flagged as internal. The flag is a column on the key table, set only by hand. After the change a second shadow run produced no rejections for internal keys.

I also checked the Redis side. The hash per key with per-second buckets stayed small, about 60 fields at most, and the Lua script took under 1 ms in the slowlog. Memory use of the rate prefix was negligible for the staging key count.

Next step is shadow mode on one production instance for a day, then comparing the logged rejections against the customers with known heavy use before enforcing anything.

summary: Upgraded Postgres to the latest 16 minor release on staging and production in a rolling restart with a short failover, and nothing changed in the query plans we track.
body:
A new 16 minor release came out with security fixes, so I scheduled the update. On staging I updated the replica first, then did a failover and updated the old primary. The whole thing took 25 minutes.

Before it, I saved the plans of our 15 slowest queries with EXPLAIN. After the update I compared them and found no differences. I also ran the test suite of the search API against staging, and it passed.

On production I did the same in a quiet hour. The failover caused 9 seconds of failed writes, which the ingest workers handled by queueing in Redpanda. Queue lag peaked at 4000 messages and cleared in two minutes.

I noted the version and the steps in the runbook.

summary: Set explicit connection pool limits for the search API's Redis client after seeing 140 connections open from 6 instances at idle.
body:
While checking the Redis dashboard I saw 140 client connections at idle load. The search API has six instances, and the client library default creates a pool that grows without a limit under bursts and does not shrink quickly.

I set a maximum of 12 connections per instance and a minimum of 2, with an idle timeout of 30 seconds. A request that cannot get a connection waits at most 200 ms, then fails open for the cache, meaning it queries OpenSearch directly. For the rate limiter, it fails open as well and logs a warning.

On staging, a load test with 300 parallel requests showed 62 connections at peak and the cache hit rate unchanged. I deployed it to production in the afternoon, and the idle count dropped to 25.

summary: Answered Sam on how long console login sessions last and where they are stored, and noted that a Redis restart would log everyone out.
body:
Sam asked for the docs of the admin console what happens to a session. Sessions live in Redis under sess:<id> with a TTL of 8 hours that is renewed on each request, so an active user stays logged in and an idle one is logged out after 8 hours.

Sam also asked what happens during maintenance. If Redis restarts without persistence, all sessions are gone and everyone logs in again. We have snapshotting on, so a normal restart keeps most of them, but a failover can lose the last minutes. I suggested the docs say that users may be asked to log in again after maintenance.

I also pointed out that the password reset invalidates all sessions of that user, using an index set per user. That is worth a sentence in the docs.

summary: Moved the nightly OpenSearch reindex to build into a new index and switch an alias at the end, so searches during the job no longer see half-built data.
body:
Today support got a report that search results for one customer shrank in the early morning and recovered later. It fits the nightly reindex, which deletes documents of an account and writes them again in place. For a big account that takes 50 minutes, and during that window results are incomplete.

I changed the job to write into a new index named with a timestamp, for example events-20240101, and to switch the alias events-read when the build is done. The old index stays for one day and is then deleted, so that a bad build can be undone by switching the alias back.

The job now has these steps: create the index with the current mapping, bulk load from Postgres in chunks of 5000, refresh, compare document counts against Postgres, switch the alias, and delete the index from two days ago. If the count differs by more than 0.1 percent, the job stops before the switch and sends an alert.

While testing on staging, I found that writes from the ingest path during the build went to the old index only, so the new one missed events that arrived in the meantime. I fixed it by recording the start time and doing a second pass for events newer than that before the switch. The second pass usually takes under a minute.

The disk use doubles for a short time during the job. I checked the free space on the production nodes, and it is 55 percent, which is enough. Running it for the first time in production is planned for tonight, and I will look at the log tomorrow morning.

I also wrote the rollback in the runbook: one curl command that points the alias back to the previous index.

summary: The first production run of the alias-based reindex finished in 1 hour 12 minutes with matching counts, but the second-pass step took 9 minutes instead of one.
body:
I checked the reindex log from the night. The build of all accounts took 1 hour 12 minutes, which is a little longer than the old in-place job. The count comparison passed with a maximum difference of 0.02 percent, and the alias switched without errors.

The second pass for events that arrived during the build took 9 minutes, because it used a query on received_at without a suitable index for the large account. I ran EXPLAIN and saw a scan of the account index with a filter. I added the time condition to use (account_id, received_at), which was available, but the query used the older index. A fresh ANALYZE of the table fixed the choice on staging.

I will run ANALYZE as the first step of the job. The search results were complete the whole night, and no customer reported a gap in the morning.

summary: Rolled back a refactor that moved the cache helper into a shared package, because the second service picked up a different Redis client version and broke the TTL argument.
body:
I had started to move the cache helper from the search API into a shared package so the admin console backend could use it too. The change itself was mostly moving files and changing imports, and the search API tests passed.

In the admin console backend, the helper failed at runtime with an error about an invalid argument for the expiry. The console backend pins an older version of the Redis client, where the option for TTL has a different name. The type checker did not catch it because the shared package resolved types from the newer version.

I first tried to make the helper work with both versions by checking the version at start. That worked but made the code ugly, and it hid the real problem, which is that the two services should not differ. Upgrading the console backend's client was another option. I looked at the changelog and found changes to the connection handling that need their own testing, and I did not want to bundle that into this refactor.

So I reverted the change with git revert and kept the helper in the search API. I wrote a ticket to upgrade the client in the console backend first. When both services run on the same version, the move will be a simple change.

The revert went out in the afternoon. The cost of the attempt was half a day, but the finding about the version difference is useful, and the console had been using a client with a known bug on reconnect.

summary: Upgraded the Redis client of the admin console backend and tested reconnect behaviour by killing Redis in staging, which removed a stuck-connection bug.
body:
After the failed refactor, I did the upgrade of the Redis client in the console backend on its own. The jump was two minor versions. The changelog lists a fix for connections that stay in a half-open state after the server drops them, and this explains a report from Lena about the console hanging after a Redis failover.

I reproduced the old behaviour first. On staging, with the old client, I stopped Redis for 20 seconds and started it again. The console requests that needed a session hung for 30 seconds and then failed, even after Redis was back. The new client reconnected within 2 seconds.

The upgrade needed two code changes. The option for the TTL on set was renamed, and the event for connection errors now carries a different object, so our logging line printed undefined. I fixed both and added a test for the logging.

I ran the console end-to-end tests that Lena wrote, 64 in all. Two failed at first because they relied on a key being present after the TTL had expired in a mock clock, and the new client handles that differently. I adjusted the tests to use the mock clock properly.

On staging I repeated the kill test three times, once during a login and once during a page load of the key list. All recovered without a restart. I also checked memory in the process for 30 minutes under load and saw no growth.

I deployed the console backend to production in the evening. The login rate was low, and nothing odd showed in the logs. Both services now use the same client version, so the shared helper can be tried again later this week.

I told Lena about the cause of her hang report, and she will close the ticket after a day without a new one.

summary: Wrote the plan for the next two weeks: finish the new rate limiter rollout, decide on the ngram analyzer for search, and add the daily counts table to the on-call checks.
body:
I went through the open work and the findings of the last week and wrote down a plan with Mara in mind, since she reviews most of it.

First, the rate limiter. The Lua script and its tests are done. What is missing is the rollout. I want to run the new limiter in shadow mode for three days, where it counts and logs what it would deny, but the old one still decides. Then I compare the numbers per account and switch if they make sense. The headers for the remaining requests go out with the switch.

Second, search. The ngram test index of the mid-size customer is built. It is 27 percent larger than the standard index, and infix queries on message fell from 3.8 seconds to 140 ms. That is a good result, but the cost in disk is real for the largest accounts. I propose to enable it only for the message field and only for accounts that ask for infix search, and to measure the disk growth for two accounts first. The partial results timeout goes in independently.

Third, the daily counts table needs a check. If the nightly job fails, the dashboards silently show old data. I will add a Prometheus gauge for the age of the newest complete day, and an alert if it is older than 30 hours.

Fourth, smaller items: the last used column for API keys, the removal of the old fixed counter keys, the second attempt at the shared cache helper, and the clean-up of the events table bloat, for which I need a decision on partitioning.

I do not plan to do the partitioning now. It touches too many things, and the daily table already solved the visible problem. I put it on the list for a later review of the database.

Mara agreed with the order and asked to see the shadow mode comparison before the switch.

summary: Finished the rate limiter rollout to production for the first group of customers, with per key limits enforced and only two false rejections, both traced to a stale settings cache.
body:
The shadow mode on staging had been clean for a week, so today the limiter moved from logging to enforcing for the first ten customers. I picked the smallest and mid-sized ones first, and left the three large customers for the next step.

The enforcement went in behind a flag per customer in Postgres, so support can switch one customer back without a deploy. I watched the Grafana panel for 429 responses for two hours. The rate of 429s stayed near zero for nine customers, which matched what the shadow logs predicted.

Two requests were rejected that should not have been. Both came from one customer whose tier support had raised a few minutes earlier. The search API reads the tier from a cache with a 5 minute TTL, so it still saw the old default limit. This is not a bug in the Lua script. It is the cache doing what it was told.

I added a small step to the support override path: when the override column changes, the settings service deletes the cached key for that API key. I tested it on staging by lowering a limit and raising it again, and the new limit applied on the next request each time.

I also checked the Redis side. The bucket hashes for ten customers use about 30 MB in total, and each hash expires with the window, so memory does not grow. The Lua script takes 0.3 ms on average in the Redis slowlog sample.

Next step is the three large customers. For them I want to talk to Sam first, so the support team knows what the headers look like when a limit is hit. I also noted that the docs page for rate limits has to mention that a changed limit can take effect within seconds, not minutes.

summary: Decided against the ngram analyzer for the message field: it grew the index by 2.4 times and the gain over a simple prefix analyzer was small.
body:
I finished the comparison of the ngram analyzer that the plan from last week asked for. I built a test index with 20 million events from the largest customer, using ngrams of 3 to 5 characters on the message field.

The index grew from 38 GB to 91 GB. That is a lot of disk and it also makes the nightly reindex longer. The wildcard queries that caused the p99 latency got faster, from about 1.8 seconds to 140 ms.

Then I tried the cheaper option, an edge ngram analyzer for prefixes only. The index grew by 20 percent, and the wildcard queries with a leading term became fast. Queries with a wildcard at the start of a word are still slow, but the query logs show that they are under 4 percent of all wildcard queries.

The decision is the prefix analyzer. I wrote the numbers into the search notes so the choice can be checked later. The mapping change needs a reindex, which will happen with the alias-based job, so there is no downtime. I will do it after the rate limiter work is done.

summary: Added the daily counts table to the on-call checks and wrote the runbook step for when the nightly job that fills it fails or runs late.
body:
The daily counts table in Postgres makes the dashboards fast, but it is only correct if the nightly job ran. If it fails, the dashboards show old numbers and nobody notices until a customer writes in. So today it became part of the on-call checks.

I added a Prometheus metric that the job writes at the end: the time of the last success and the number of rows written. An alert fires if the last success is older than 26 hours. A second alert fires if the row count is under half of the average of the last seven runs, which catches the case where the job finishes but reads nothing.

I tested both alerts on staging. For the first I stopped the job for a day, and for the second I pointed the job at an empty source table. Both alerts reached the test channel in PagerDuty within the expected time.

The runbook has a new section with three steps. First, check the job log in ECS. Second, run the job by hand for the missing day with the date argument. Third, check the row count against the events table for one customer. The rerun is safe, because the job replaces the rows of a day in one transaction.

One thing I found while testing: when the job is rerun for a day in the past, it does not update the rows for days after it. That is correct, but I wrote it into the runbook so nobody expects otherwise.

I also asked Tobias to look at the schedule. The job runs at 02:00, close to the reindex window, and both use the database replica. We agreed to move the counts job to 03:00 next week.

summary: Enabled the rate limiter for the three large customers after agreeing the limits with Sam, and saw no rejections in the first day.
body:
Sam talked to the three large customers about their expected peak traffic, and we set the limits at about three times their highest hour of the last month. That gives room for bursts, and still protects the shared ingest path.

I set the tiers in Postgres and turned on enforcement for each customer one at a time, with an hour between them. For each I watched the 429 panel and the p99 latency of the search API.

The Lua script now handles about 900 calls per second at peak. The Redis CPU went from 11 to 14 percent, so there is a lot of room left. The latency of the limiter call at p99 is 1.1 ms.

We saw no rejections for the large customers during the day. One of them has a nightly export job that makes a burst at 03:00, and I will look at that in the morning logs to be sure it does not hit the limit.

The rollout of the rate limiter is done now, apart from that check. I removed the shadow mode code path from the search API, because it was only useful during the rollout.

summary: Traced the slow Postgres vacuum on the audit log table to a long running report transaction and moved the report to the replica.
body:
On-call showed the autovacuum of the audit log table running for over six hours, and the dead tuple count growing. The table is about 80 GB and gets many inserts, but few updates, so this was not normal.

I looked at pg_stat_activity and found a transaction that had been open for nine hours. It came from the monthly compliance report, which a script ran on the primary inside one transaction. While it was open, vacuum could not remove anything newer than its snapshot.

The script read from the audit log with a cursor and did a lot of work between the reads, writing a CSV file. I confirmed this in the code. The simple fix is to run it on the read replica. That has its own problem: long queries on a replica can be cancelled because of conflicts with the replay of changes from the primary.

I set max_standby_streaming_delay on the replica to 15 minutes, which is a compromise. Then I changed the script to read in pages by the primary key and to commit between pages, so no single query is long. I ran it on the replica against the production data, and it finished in 34 minutes without a conflict.

After I killed the old transaction, the vacuum finished within 40 minutes and removed about 12 million dead tuples. The table size did not shrink, as expected, but new inserts reuse the space.

I added an alert on the age of the oldest transaction, at 30 minutes, because this problem was invisible until the vacuum was far behind. I also wrote a note in the audit export plan: the export that is coming must use the same paging approach.

summary: Checked the 03:00 export burst of the large customer and found it stays under its limit, but only by a small margin.
body:
I looked at the logs for the nightly export of the customer with the biggest burst. The job sends about 2,400 requests in the first minute, and the limit for the customer is 3,000 per minute on the sliding window.

So nothing was rejected, but the margin is 20 percent. If the customer grows, the export will start to hit 429s. The export client does not honor the Retry-After header, it retries after a fixed one second.

I wrote to Sam with the numbers, so that he can suggest to the customer a spread of the requests over several minutes, or raise the limit. I prefer the first, but the second is easy for us.

summary: Wrote the first design for the schema registry: versioned event schemas in Postgres, compatibility checks on registration, and a cache in the ingest worker.
body:
The event schemas now live in files in the repo, and a change needs a deploy of the ingest workers. Customers add fields all the time, and every new field costs us a release. The registry is meant to remove that.

The design has three parts. The first is a table in Postgres with the schema name, the version number, the JSON schema document and the time of creation. A version is never changed after it is written. The second is a small API in the admin backend to register a new version. The third is a cache in the ingest worker that loads the active versions on start and refreshes them every minute.

The compatibility check runs when a version is registered. I decided on one rule for now: a new version may add optional fields, and may not remove a field or change its type. A version that breaks the rule is rejected with a message that names the field.

I looked at what happens to events that arrive with a schema version the worker does not know yet. There are two options, reject or accept with the last known version. I chose accept with a counter metric, because a rejected event is lost data, and the cache refresh closes the gap within a minute.

I wrote a test with ten schema changes taken from real customer history. Seven pass the rule. The other three remove a field, which customers did, so we will need a way to mark a field as deprecated instead of deleting it. That goes in the next step.

Open questions for Mara: whether the worker should validate against the schema or only tag the version, and where the validation cost fits into the batch writer. I will measure the validation cost on a sample before I propose anything.

summary: Measured the cost of schema validation in the ingest worker: about 18 microseconds per event, small enough to validate every event.
body:
Mara asked in review whether validating each event against its schema would slow the ingest worker. I wrote a Go benchmark using the compiled schema form and a sample of 100,000 real events.

The result is 18 microseconds per event on one core, with 4 allocations. At the peak of 20,000 events per second per worker group that is about 36 percent of one core, spread across the workers. This is small.

I also tried the library that does not compile schemas ahead of time, and it was about six times slower, so the compiled form is needed. The compiled schemas go in the cache next to the raw documents.

One detail: the batch writer holds events in memory until the flush, and validation before the batch adds latency only to the receive path, not to the flush. The p99 of the receive path went up by 0.2 ms in the staging load test.

I will go with validation of every event, and with a flag to turn it off per schema if some customer sends something strange. I wrote the numbers in the design notes.

summary: Fixed a Redis memory alarm that came from the session store growing, since sessions of a removed test tenant were never deleted.
body:
At the start of the day a warning showed Redis memory at 78 percent, higher than the usual 55. The query cache keys have TTLs since last week, so I did not expect them to be the cause.

I sampled the key space with SCAN and counted by prefix. The session prefix had 410,000 keys, where the real number of active admin console users should be a few hundred. Looking at the sessions, almost all belonged to one tenant that was used for load tests of the console.

The load test script logged in for each simulated user and never logged out, and the session keys were written without a TTL when the sliding refresh was added. I found the line in the console backend: the refresh call used SET instead of keeping the existing expiry, so the TTL was dropped on the first refresh.

I fixed the refresh to use EXPIRE after the write, and added a test that checks the TTL after a refresh. Then I deleted the test tenant's sessions in batches of 1,000 with a pause, so the Redis latency stayed flat. Memory went down to 52 percent.

I also checked that no real user sessions lost their TTL. There were 38 real sessions without TTL, I set 8 hours on them, which is the normal length.

Follow up: the load test script should log out at the end, and I opened a small task for that. I added a Grafana panel with the key count by prefix, which would have shown this earlier.

summary: Added the key count by prefix panel to the Redis dashboard and set a warning when the session prefix goes above 5,000 keys.
body:
A short follow-up to the memory finding. A small exporter script runs SCAN with a count of 500 every ten minutes and writes the number of keys per prefix as Prometheus gauges. It runs against the replica so the primary has no extra load.

The Grafana panel shows the six prefixes from the key naming convention. The alert for the session prefix is set at 5,000 keys. Cache keys can vary a lot, so I only put a trend panel there and no alert.

The exporter takes 4 seconds per pass and the replica showed no change in CPU.

summary: Registered the first real schemas in the registry on staging and found that two customer schemas used a field type the compatibility check could not compare.
body:
The registry API is running on staging, so I loaded the 31 current event schemas from the repo as version 1 each. Then I registered the latest changes from the history, as version 2, to see how the checks behave.

Twenty-eight schemas passed. Two failed in an unexpected way: the checker crashed instead of returning a message. Both used a field with a list of types, for example string or null, which my code did not handle in the type comparison.

I wrote a function that turns a type, or a list of types, into a sorted set. A change is compatible if the new set contains the old set. Adding null to a string field is allowed, and removing it is not. I added eleven test cases for this and they pass.
