The third failure was correct. A customer schema had changed a field from integer to string in the history, and the check rejected it. That change did, in fact, break their dashboards once, so I take it as a sign that the rule is useful.

I also tried the deprecation mark that I wanted. A field can now carry a flag deprecated, which keeps it in the schema but makes it optional, and the check allows this one-way change. Removing a deprecated field in a later version is still rejected, to keep old events valid.

The worker cache refresh was tested with a new version registered while the load test ran. The worker saw it within 60 seconds, and the counter for unknown versions went up and then back to zero.

Next: the admin console needs a page to see the versions, which is for Lena, and I will write the API description for her.

summary: Wrote the API description of the registry for Lena and answered her question about how the console should show a rejected schema.
body:
Lena needs the contract for the registry page in the admin console, so I wrote it down today. There are three endpoints: list the schemas with their active versions, get the versions of one schema, and register a new version.

For the list I decided the response is paged and sorted by name, with the count of events seen in the last day for each. That count comes from a Redis counter that the worker increments, and it has a TTL of two days. It is an approximation, and I wrote that into the description so that the console does not present it as exact.

Lena asked what to show when a registration is rejected. The API returns status 422 with a list of problems, each with the field path, the old type, the new type and a short reason. The console can show them as a table. She also asked whether a dry run exists, and it does not yet. I added a query parameter dry_run that does the check and writes nothing. It was a ten line change.

I tested the dry run on staging with the three failing cases from yesterday, and it returned the right problems each time.

She also asked about permissions. Only the roles admin and schema-editor may register, and everyone in the console can read. The roles are already in the Postgres accounts table, so I did not need a new one.

I noted for later that the registry changes should go in the audit log with the user and the diff. I will do that when the audit log work is touched next. For now the registration writes one audit row with the version number.

summary: Dealt with an on-call page for ingest lag by finding that one worker group had a stuck consumer and restarting it, then added a lag per consumer alert.
body:
The page came at night with the queue lag above the threshold for ten minutes. The total lag was high, but only one partition showed it, the one for a high-volume event type.

In the Redpanda consumer group view, one consumer had held the partition for hours without committing offsets. The worker process was alive and passed its health check, but its batch writer was waiting on a database connection that never came back. The connection had been cut by a network change on the database side, and the pool did not notice.

I restarted the worker group in ECS, and the lag cleared in about 12 minutes, with no lost events, as the offsets were not committed for the stuck batch.

The real fix has two parts. First, the batch writer now uses a context with a 30 second timeout on every database call, so a dead connection fails the batch and the pool removes it. I wrote it and tested it by dropping the connection with a proxy on staging. Second, the health check now reports unhealthy if no batch has been committed in 5 minutes while the queue is not empty.

The alert I added looks at lag per consumer, not only the total, so one stuck consumer pages us sooner. I set it at 3 minutes of growing lag on any single partition.

Mara will review the timeout change tomorrow, I want her opinion on whether 30 seconds is right for the large batches.

summary: Mara's review of the batch timeout change led to a 60 second timeout for large batches after a test with the biggest customer's events showed flushes of 20 seconds.
body:
Mara asked in review why 30 seconds, and I did not have a good answer except that it was round. So I measured.

I replayed one hour of the largest customer's events on staging with the new timeout set very high, and logged the duration of each flush. The median was 80 ms, the p99 was 2.1 seconds, and the maximum was 21 seconds. The maximum came during a vacuum on the staging database, so it can happen in production too.

A 30 second timeout would have been close to that maximum. If a flush fails, the batch is retried, which is safe because the writer uses the event id for deduplication, but a retry of a slow flush while the database is busy adds load at the wrong time.

We agreed on 60 seconds for the flush of a batch, and 10 seconds for the single calls, such as taking a connection from the pool. The timeouts are now settings in the worker config, not constants.

I also added a metric for timeouts per cause, so we can see if the number grows. The first day in staging showed zero.

Mara also asked for a test for the case where the timeout hits in the middle of a transaction. I wrote it with a fake database that sleeps, and it checks that nothing is committed and the offsets are kept.

The change was merged to the main branch and will roll out group by group tomorrow.

summary: Rolled out the batch timeout settings to all worker groups one at a time and saw no timeouts and no change in lag.
body:
The rollout started with the smallest group at 09:40 and went on through the day. After each group I waited 30 minutes and checked the lag, the timeout metric, and the database connection count.

The first two groups showed no timeouts. The third group, which has the large customer's event type, had one timeout at 11:15, during a short database spike. The batch was retried and committed on the second try, the lag went up by 4 seconds and came back.

The health check change did what it should. During the restart of group two, a worker took longer to get started, and the new check waited until the first batch was committed before it reported healthy. This delayed the rolling deployment by about two minutes per task, which is fine.

The database connection count is the same as before, at an average of 62 for the writers, so the timeouts do not leave connections behind.

By 13:00 all groups were done. I wrote a short note in the runbook about the settings and the metric names. One small thing is left: the dashboard panel for the timeouts needs a title that says what the unit is.

summary: Checked the Postgres index bloat on the events table and found two indexes with over 40 percent bloat, to be rebuilt concurrently.
body:
I ran the bloat estimate query on the main tables. Most are fine, but two indexes on the old events table are above 40 percent bloat. They are the index on the customer and time, and the one on the event type.

The table is still used for the raw event lookup in the admin console, so the indexes matter. A rebuild with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY takes longer but does not block writes. I tried it on a staging copy: 14 minutes for the first index, 9 for the second, using extra disk of about the size of the index.

The production disk has enough room. I scheduled the rebuild for a quiet time tonight, with a check that no long transactions are open. I will check the result in the morning.

summary: Built the first version of the audit export for compliance: a paged job that writes the audit log of one customer to a signed NDJSON file in S3.
body:
The compliance customers ask for their audit log as a file, and until now support did it by hand with a SQL query. This is the first version of the job that replaces it.

The job takes a customer id and a time range. It reads the audit log table by the primary key in pages of 5,000 rows and commits between pages, as we decided after the vacuum problem. It runs on the replica. Each page is written to the output as NDJSON, one event per line, in order.

The file goes to an S3 bucket with a key that contains the customer id and the job id. When the job is done, it writes a second small file with the row count, the first and last row id and a SHA-256 of the data file. The checksum is signed with a key from the secrets store, so the customer can verify that we made the file and nobody changed it.

I tested with the biggest audit log, 41 million rows for a customer. The export took 52 minutes and the file is 9.8 GB compressed with gzip. Memory of the job stayed under 200 MB since it streams. The replica showed some replay delay, up to 20 seconds, but no cancelled queries.

I found one problem. The audit rows have a details column in JSON, and 600 rows had invalid UTF-8 from old imports. The export failed on them at first. I now replace the bad bytes and add a field that says the row was repaired, so nothing is hidden.

The job is started by an internal endpoint, for now only by support through a script. A progress row in Postgres shows the pages done, so a failed job can resume from the last committed page. I reused the pattern from the loader for this, and it worked with little change.

What is left is an access check on who may start an export, the retention of the files in S3, which I would set at 14 days, and a test for the signature check. Tomorrow I will write these and ask Mara to review.

summary: Added the access check and the 14 day retention for audit export files and wrote a verify script that customers can run on the checksum signature.
body:
The export endpoint now requires the role compliance-admin in the accounts table, and every start writes an audit row itself, with the user, the customer and the time range. It felt right that the audit export is in the audit log.

For the files in S3, I added a lifecycle rule in Terraform that deletes objects under the export prefix after 14 days. The bucket is not public, and download links are presigned for 24 hours. Tobias looked at the plan and asked for server-side encryption with the account key, which I added.

The verify script is a single small Node file with no dependencies. It reads the data file and the signature file, computes the SHA-256 and checks the signature with a public key that we put in the docs. I tested it with a good file, a file with one byte changed, and a file with a missing last line. The last two failed with different messages, which is what I wanted.

There was one problem with the key. The signing key is stored in the secrets store as a private key in a format that the Node crypto module reads, but the first test used a different encoding for the public key in the docs. I corrected the docs example, and checked it by following the steps as a customer would.

I wrote the short guide for Sam on how to start an export and what to send to the customer. It has the three commands and the usual times: about one minute per million rows.

The branch is ready for the review. I listed what I tested in the pull request.

summary: Reviewed the audit export branch with Mara; she found that a page boundary could split rows with the same timestamp and cause duplicates on resume.
body:
Mara read the pull request this morning and tested the resume by killing the job. She found a bug that my test did not catch.

The job paged by the timestamp of the audit row, not by the primary key as I thought. In the code, the page query used created_at greater than the last value. When several rows have the same timestamp, and the page ends between them, the next page skips some, or after a resume, repeats some. Audit rows written in a batch share a timestamp, so this does happen.

I changed the page query to order by the id, which is a bigserial, and to read where id is greater than the last id. The ids are unique and monotonic, so the pages are exact. The time range filter is still applied, but only as a condition, not as the paging key.

I then wrote a test with 10,000 rows that all share one timestamp and a page size of 700, and killed the job in the middle three times. The output file had exactly 10,000 lines, with no duplicates and no gaps. Before the fix, the same test gave 10,212 lines.

Mara also asked whether the id order matches the time order well enough that customers would not see a strange order in the file. For rows written in one transaction yes, for concurrent writers the order can differ by milliseconds. I wrote this in the docs of the export format.

She approved after the change. I ran the full export of the 41 million rows once more, and the count matched the table.

summary: Merged audit-export and ran the first real export for a compliance customer, 12 million rows in 16 minutes, with the checksum verified on their side.
body:
After the review changes, I merged the branch and deployed the job with the endpoint. Sam had a customer waiting for the file, a request from their auditor.

We ran the export for the last twelve months. It read 12.1 million rows and took 16 minutes. The file was 2.6 GB compressed. I checked the row count against a count query on the replica and they matched.

Sam sent the presigned link and the verify script to the customer. About an hour later they wrote back that the signature check passed on their machine. They asked whether the file could also be in CSV, which I noted as a request but did not promise.

While running, I watched the replica. The replay delay peaked at 9 seconds and nothing was cancelled. The autovacuum on the primary did not slow down, so the paging approach works as planned.

One small thing to fix: the progress row stays in Postgres after the job is done. I added a cleanup that removes progress rows older than 30 days.

summary: Investigated why the search API p95 rose after the Redis client pool change and found evidence that the pool is too small for peak, with a fix still to be tried.
body:
After the pool limits of last week, the p95 of the search API went from 120 ms to 170 ms at the afternoon peak. I suspected the limits first.

I added a metric for the wait time on the pool, in the search API client wrapper, and kept it on a branch for now. At peak, the median wait was 0 ms, but the p99 was 40 ms, and the instances with the highest traffic showed the longest waits. The limit was 10 connections per instance, which I had set from the idle number, not from the peak.

I looked at the peak concurrency from the logs. A single instance has up to 18 Redis calls in flight, because each search request does the cache read, the rate limit call and sometimes a settings read in parallel. With 10 connections, the others wait.

I did the arithmetic for a larger limit. A maximum of 20 per instance with a minimum idle of 4 would give at most 120 connections with 6 instances, which is still below the 140 open at idle before the change. I have not changed anything in production yet. The plan is to try it on one instance first and compare it with the others for an hour, and only then think about the rest.

I also noticed that the pool does not close connections that were idle for a long time. That is fine for now. I wrote the numbers in the notes, together with the idea of sizing by peak concurrency in the guideline for the next services.

summary: Planned the registry rollout to production in four steps, from tagging events with a version to enforcing the compatibility rule, and listed what could go wrong at each step.
body:
The registry works on staging, so today I wrote the plan to bring it into production without a surprise. I split it into four steps, each one independent and reversible.

Step one is to load the existing schemas into the production registry as version 1 and not use them yet. This only fills a table. If something is wrong, nothing is affected. I also compare the loaded documents with the files in the repo by hash.

Step two is to make the ingest workers read the registry and tag each event with the schema version. No validation yet. The risk is the cache refresh: if the registry table is unreachable at start, the worker must fall back to the files in the image. I wrote this fallback and tested it by blocking the database on staging, and the worker started with the built-in schemas and logged a warning.

Step three is validation in warning mode. Every event is checked, and failures only increase a counter per schema and write a sample to a log, at most one per minute per schema. I would run this for a week and look for customers who send events that do not match. From the benchmark the cost is 18 microseconds per event, so we can afford it.

Step four is enforcement per schema, with a flag. Events that fail go to a rejected topic in Redpanda, and the customer gets a count in the console. I did not decide yet whether the ingest API should answer with an error for the whole batch or accept the good events, and I will ask Mara. My own view is to accept the good ones and report the others in the response.

Things that could go wrong: a customer with a schema that is stricter than what they really send, which step three will show; a registry change at the same time as a deploy; and the schema cache using too much memory, though 31 schemas take under 2 MB.

I also listed the tasks for others. Lena has the console page, Sam has to write the customer note about the new response for rejected events, and Tobias has to add the registry table to the backup check.

I will start with step one tomorrow morning and write the result here.

summary: Started rolling out the schema registry to production by tagging every incoming event with a schema version, without any enforcement yet.
body:
This was step one of the four-step plan from yesterday. The ingest worker now looks up the schema version for the event type in its local cache and writes it into a new `schema_version` field on each event. If the registry has no entry for the type, the field is set to 0 and a counter `schema_unknown_total` is incremented.

I deployed to one worker group first. The cache refresh interval is 60 seconds, and the registry reads go to the Postgres replica. Over the first hour the group handled about 2.1 million events and 0.4 percent of them had version 0. These came from two event types that nobody had registered yet.

I registered those two types on production with the schemas Sam had collected from the customer docs. The counter went to zero within two refresh cycles.

I checked the extra field in the queue. The average event grew by 6 bytes, which is not a concern. The per event cost matched the 18 microsecond measurement from before, within noise.

Nothing downstream reads the field yet, so the dashboards were unaffected. I rolled the change to the other worker groups one at a time with 20 minutes between them. Lag stayed flat throughout.

Step two is to report incompatible events in a log-only mode. For that I need to decide how to sample the logs, so they do not fill the disk on the large customers. I put that on the list for tomorrow.

summary: Wrote log-only validation for the registry: events that break their schema are counted and sampled, but still accepted.
body:
Step two of the registry rollout is in the ingest worker. For each event the worker validates against the cached schema and, on failure, increments `schema_violation_total` labelled by event type and customer. It also logs one sample per type per minute with the field path and the reason. The event is accepted either way.

The sampling was the open question from this morning. A per type per minute limit keeps the log under about 300 lines a minute even with all types failing, which I checked with a synthetic run.

I deployed to staging and replayed an hour of production traffic through it. 1.8 percent of events violated their schema, but almost all of those came from one customer that sends `user_id` as a number in some events and a string in others. The registered schema says string.

I do not want to enforce anything against that. I asked Sam to contact the customer and find out whether the number form is intended. If it is, the better move is probably a new schema version that allows both.

I also added a Grafana panel with the violation rate by customer. It shows the problem customer clearly, and everyone else is below 0.05 percent.

Next: production deploy of the log-only mode after Sam has an answer, and a week of watching the numbers before step three.

summary: Long session on Redis memory: key naming was inconsistent across three services, so I wrote a naming convention and migrated the cache keys of the search API.
body:
The Redis memory graph had been creeping up for two weeks. Today I looked at what is in there instead of just reading the total. The key count by prefix panel from the session work showed the usual prefixes, but a scan of a sample of 50,000 keys showed three more naming styles: `search:q:<hash>`, `cache/search/<hash>` and `sq_<hash>`. They were all the same data, written by different versions of the cache helper.

The old styles still had live TTLs, so we were holding the same results two or three times. I estimated the duplicates by counting hash collisions across the prefixes in the sample. About 31 percent of the cache memory was duplicate entries.

I wrote down a convention in the docs folder: `<service>:<purpose>:<version>:<id>`, all lower case, colon separated, with the version bumped when the value format changes. Examples are `search:result:v2:<hash>` and `console:session:v1:<id>`.

Then I changed the search API cache helper to use only the new form. It reads the new key first. On a miss it checks the old key once, copies the value over and sets the new TTL. That avoids a cold cache when we deploy.

I deployed it to staging first. The hit rate stayed at 82 percent through the switch.

On production the hit rate dipped to 74 percent for ten minutes after the deploy. It then recovered to 83 percent as the copy path filled the new keys.

The old keys will expire by their own TTLs, which are at most 6 hours for search results. I will check memory tomorrow morning after they have gone.

The console sessions and the rate limiter counters already follow the convention more or less. I did not touch them in this change, because renaming session keys would log everyone out. I added a note to the convention that sessions stay as they are until we have a planned reason to restart them.

I also wrote a small script, `scripts/redis_prefix_report.ts`, that samples keys and reports the prefix distribution and the share of keys without a TTL. I will run it weekly. The first run found 212 keys without TTL, all from an old debugging tool, and I deleted them.

summary: Memory in Redis fell by about a quarter after the old cache key styles expired, confirming the duplicate keys were the cause of the creep.
body:
I checked the Redis memory graph this morning, after the duplicate key styles from two days ago had time to expire. Used memory went from 6.1 GB to 4.6 GB over about six hours, which is close to the 31 percent duplicate estimate for the cache part.

The weekly prefix report showed only the new `search:result:v2:` prefix for search results. The cache hit rate sits at 84 percent.

I left the copy-from-old-key path in the helper for one more week and then will remove it. Nothing else is left from this work.

summary: Wrote the plan for enforcing the schema rule per customer, with a switch, a warning period and a rollback path for each customer.
body: The log-only phase showed that most violations come from a few SDK versions, so enforcement should go customer by customer. The plan has four parts: a per customer switch, a warning email with sample violations, a seven day grace period, and then enforcement. Rollback is the same switch and takes effect within a minute through the settings cache. I listed the open points for Mara's review: what the API returns for a rejected event, and whether partial acceptance of batches is needed first. I think it is, because one bad event rejecting a batch of 500 would cause support load. Next is the design of the batch response.

summary: Reviewed the union type comparison with Mara and fixed a case where a union with the same members in another order was called incompatible.
body:
Mara read the diff of the union comparison in the compatibility checker and asked three questions. The most useful one was whether `["string","integer"]` and `["integer","string"]` compare as equal. They did not, because I had compared the lists by position.

I changed the comparison to treat the members as a set. I added test cases for reordered members, a widened union, a narrowed union and a union against a plain scalar. The narrowed one is rejected as breaking, which is correct for consumers that expect both types.

Her second point was about error messages. The old text said only `incompatible type`. It now says which field path changed and from what to what, so Lena's console can show it directly. I sent her an example of the new message.

Her third point was that the check should not run on the ingest hot path, and it does not. It runs on registration only. The worker uses the validation code, which has no compatibility logic.

After the fixes all 41 registry tests pass. I registered version 2 of the customer schemas on production with the tool. The registry showed both versions active for the types.

The log-only validation had not been deployed to production yet. I started it on one worker group after the registration. The violation rate for this customer was 0, and the rate for all others was unchanged.

Tomorrow I roll the log-only mode to the other groups and start the week of watching.

summary: Rolled the log-only schema validation to all worker groups; overall violation rate is 0.3 percent, mostly from two small customers.
body:
I rolled the log-only validation to the remaining worker groups with 20 minutes between them. Lag and CPU did not change visibly. The CPU of the workers went up by about 1 percent, as expected from the earlier measurement.

The violation panel shows 0.3 percent overall. Two small customers account for most of it. One sends a timestamp in seconds where the schema says milliseconds, and the other sends an empty string for a required field.

I wrote both to Sam with the sample lines from the log. She will contact them. The watching period of a week starts now.

summary: Implemented the per event error list in the ingest batch response, so clients see which events were rejected and why while the rest are accepted.
body:
The ingest API used to answer a batch with either 200 or 400. For partial acceptance it needs to say which events failed, so I added an errors array with the event index, an error code and a short message. The status is 207-style in meaning but we kept 200 with a field accepted_count, because several SDKs treat any other 2xx oddly. I wrote the change in the handler and in the response type, and added tests for all-valid, all-invalid and mixed batches.

The messages come from the schema checker. At first they included the full path and expected type, which for deep payloads produced long strings, so I cut them to 200 characters. I also capped the errors array at 100 entries and added a truncated flag. Without the cap a batch of 5,000 bad events would make a response of over a megabyte.

Mara reviewed the first draft and asked that the error codes be stable strings and not numbers. We settled on schema_violation, unknown_type and payload_too_large. I updated the docs draft for Sam with examples. Still to do: the metrics for rejected events by code, and a test with the large customer's real batch shapes. Enforcement stays off until both are done.

summary: Tested the monthly index recreation job on staging, and it swapped the partial index without blocking writes; one lock wait showed up and was fixed.
body:
I ran the job that recreates the `api_key_usage` partial index with a new cutoff on staging. It creates the new index concurrently under a temporary name, drops the old one, and renames the new one.

The first run failed. The drop waited for a lock behind a long running query from the reporting tool and the job hit its 30 second statement timeout. The new index was left behind with the temporary name.

I made two changes. The job now sets `lock_timeout` to 5 seconds and retries the drop up to 5 times with a pause of 10 seconds. If all of them fail, it removes the new index and exits with an error, so no stray index stays. I also made the start of the job check for leftovers of an earlier failed run and clean them up.

I repeated the test while a 2 minute query was running on staging. The drop retried twice, then succeeded when the query ended. The queries on the settings page stayed fast during the whole swap, because the old index was in place until the drop.

I checked that the query planner uses the renamed index with a fresh `EXPLAIN`. It does.

The job is scheduled for the first of each month at 04:00 on production. I added an alert on a failed run. The runbook explains how to run it by hand and what the leftover index looks like.

This finishes the settings page problem. The page now loads in about 80 ms in total, according to Lena's check.

summary: Checked the first week of log-only validation: violation rate dropped to 0.08 percent after two customers fixed their SDK calls, so enforcement is next.
body:
The week of watching for step two of the registry rollout is done. The overall violation rate fell from 0.3 to 0.08 percent. The customer with timestamps in seconds fixed it on their side, and the one with an empty required field changed their code too.

What is left is a customer that sends an optional field with null where our schema says string. Strictly this is a violation. Most JSON libraries produce null for missing values, so it will happen again with other customers.

I discussed it with Mara in the chat. We agreed that null for an optional field counts as absent. I changed the validator to treat null the same as a missing field for optional ones. For required fields null stays a violation. After that the violation rate dropped to 0.02 percent.

The remaining violations are spread over four customers, all of them different problems and a few events each. Sam has the list.

Step three in the plan is to enforce the rule for new schema versions only. When a customer registers a version, events that break it are rejected with a 422 and a message that names the field. Events for versions registered before today stay in log-only mode.

I decided to write the rejection path before the production switch. It needs a clear error body, a metric `schema_rejected_total`, and a per customer switch in the settings, so we can turn it off for one customer without a deploy.

I wrote the design notes and the list of what could go wrong. The one I worry about is a batch of 500 events with one bad event. Rejecting the whole batch would be harsh. The plan is to accept the good events and return the bad ones in a `rejected` array in the response, with the index and the reason of each.

summary: Implemented partial acceptance of batches in the ingest API, so one event that fails validation no longer rejects the other events of the batch.
body:
The ingest handler used to treat a batch as all or nothing. For enforcement that is wrong, so I changed it. Events are validated one by one, the valid ones go to the queue, and the response lists the rejected ones.

The response now has `accepted` as a count and `rejected` as an array of `{index, event_type, reason}`. The status code is 200 when all events are accepted. If some are rejected it is 207, and if all are rejected it is 422. I checked this with Sam's docs, which say clients should treat any 2xx as success. A client that ignores the body would then silently lose the rejected events. For that reason the docs need a clear note, and I wrote one for her to review.

The tests cover a clean batch, a batch with one bad event in the middle, a batch with all bad events and an empty batch. The index in the rejection array refers to the position in the original batch, which I checked with a batch where the bad events were first and last.

The queue write order is the same as before for the accepted events. I compared the output of a replay with the old handler on a clean batch, and it is identical.

One more thing is the batch size limit. It is still checked before validation, so a huge batch is rejected up front with a 413 and no work is done.

The per customer switch for enforcement is not built yet. It is the next step, and then I deploy to staging.

summary: Added the per customer enforcement switch to the account settings and the console API, defaulting to off.
body:
The switch is a column `schema_enforcement` on the account settings table with the values `off`, `new_versions` and `all`. The default is `off`, which keeps the log-only behaviour. I wrote the migration and it runs quickly because the column has a default and no rewrite.

The ingest worker reads the setting from the same settings cache as the other limits, with a refresh every 60 seconds. This is the cache that caused the two false rejections of the rate limiter, so I checked how the refresh works. A changed value takes up to 60 seconds to apply, which is acceptable here, and I noted it in the docs for the support team.

The console API got a PATCH endpoint for the setting, restricted to admin users of our own team. Customers cannot switch it themselves yet. I sent Lena the description so she can add it to the internal part of the console.

I added tests for the three modes. In `new_versions` mode an event with an old schema version is only logged, and an event with a newer version is rejected on a violation.

Deploy to staging is done and I switched one test account to `new_versions`. A bad event came back in the rejected array as expected.

summary: Enabled enforcement for new schema versions on production for our own test account and one friendly customer, with no problems in the first hours.
body:
I switched the test account to `new_versions` on production, then the friendly customer that Sam had asked. They agreed to be first and registered a new version of one event type to see it work.

In the first four hours there were 3 rejected events from them, all caused by a field that was newly required in their version and missing in an old app build. The rejection arrived in the response, and their developer saw it in the logs and fixed the field. That is the intended behaviour.

The `schema_rejected_total` metric and the Grafana panel work. Worker CPU and lag are unchanged.

I will wait a few days before enabling it for more customers. Sam will write a short announcement.

summary: Widened schema enforcement to the first five customers and found that one SDK sends timestamps as strings, which the check rejected until we added a coercion rule.
body:
Enforcement went on for five customers this evening, after the grace period mails had gone out a week ago. For the first hour the rejection rate was low, around 0.05 percent. Then one customer showed a spike of rejections, all on the timestamp field.

Their older SDK version sends the timestamp as an ISO string where the schema says integer milliseconds. In log-only mode this had been counted in the 0.08 percent and looked like noise, but it came in bursts from one batch job. I checked the sampled violations and confirmed all had the same shape.

We do not want to reject valid data over a representation issue, so I added a coercion rule in the schema checker. A string that parses as an ISO timestamp is converted before validation, and the event is stored in the normal form. The rule is only active for fields typed as timestamp. I added tests for several formats, including a timezone offset and a bare date, and the bare date is rejected on purpose.

After the deploy the rejections for that customer fell to zero. I told Sam so she can answer the customer if they ask, and noted that the SDK fix is still worth asking for. Tomorrow I will check the other four customers and look at the rejection metrics by code.

summary: Talked with Tobias about the hot partition and agreed to first measure how often it happens before any change to the key.
body:
Tobias and I went through last week's hot partition. He pointed out that a change of the partition key affects ordering guarantees for events of one type, which some customers rely on for session views.

We agreed not to change anything yet. First I will collect the maximum partition lag per day for a month from Prometheus and see if the problem repeats. If it is a once in a quarter event, the new alert and the manual boost of the worker group are enough.

I added a recording rule for the daily maximum. Tobias will look at the CPU headroom of the worker groups in the meantime.

summary: Used the CPU headroom after batch writes to cut the ingest worker task count from 24 to 16 in steps, with lag and latency staying flat at each step.
body:
Since the batch writer rollout the workers sit at about 25 percent CPU, so we pay for tasks that do little. I proposed to remove tasks in steps and watch for a day each. Tobias agreed and changed the desired count in Terraform, with a note in the pull request.

The first step was from 24 to 20 tasks. I watched the consumer lag per partition, the p99 of the write path and the CPU. Lag stayed under 2 seconds and the p99 did not move. CPU rose to about 33 percent.

The second step was from 20 to 16. At the evening peak the CPU reached 48 percent, which is still well below the 70 percent we use as a limit. There was one short lag rise to 6 seconds when a task was replaced during a deploy, which cleared by itself.

I checked the cost view in AWS for the effect. The estimate is a saving of roughly a third of the ingest compute bill, which is the largest single item of that service. I did not go below 16, because a failure of two tasks at the same time must still leave room for the peak.

One caveat: the three large customers send bursts at the top of the hour, and the lag at those times is the number to watch. I added a panel for it to the ingest dashboard. Next I will write the capacity note for the on-call runbook, so the number 16 has a reason next to it.

summary: Wrote the shard questions for the search index: by month or by customer, shard size, reindex cost and what a customer deletion would mean.
body:
Today I collected the open questions about the shard layout of the search index before anyone changes anything. Right now the index has one shard group per customer, which gives uneven sizes. The largest customer has a shard of around 80 GB, while many small ones have shards of a few hundred MB.

The main question is whether to shard by month. Queries mostly cover the last weeks, so month shards would let old data stay cold and be searched less often. But queries over a long range would touch many shards, and I want a number for that. I wrote a script that takes a week of real queries from the search API log and counts how many months each one spans. The first result is that about 85 percent of queries span one or two months.

Second, the shard size. The usual advice is to stay between 10 and 50 GB, and I will compute the monthly sizes from the stats API. The largest months may need more than one shard.

Third, deletions. When a customer leaves we must delete all their data, and with month shards that becomes a delete by query across all shards rather than dropping an index. I noted that this needs a plan and a check for compliance.

Fourth, the reindex job. The full build takes 52 minutes now, and with the new layout it could run per month and only for changed months. That would be a clear gain, but the alias switch logic needs a rewrite.

Fifth, the per customer filter. Customers must never see each other's data, so every query needs the customer filter, and routing by customer might still help speed.

I put all of this in a document and asked Mara and Tobias to add comments. Nothing is decided and no change to the index has been made. Next step is the size computation and a test on staging with a month layout.

summary: Answered Sam on what happens to a customer's events when the schema check rejects them, and where the rejection counts can be seen.
body:
Sam asked what to tell a customer who says events are missing after enforcement was turned on for them. I looked at what the system does and wrote it down so she can reuse the answer.

A rejected event is not stored. It is counted in a metric with the customer and the error code, and a sample of the rejected payloads is kept for seven days in a table in Postgres. The sample holds at most 50 events per customer per hour, so it will not show everything, but it shows the typical reasons.

The client gets the error in the batch response, with the index of the event and the code. If the SDK ignores the errors array, the customer sees nothing on their side, and that is the usual cause of the complaint. I suggested that Sam ask which SDK version they use and compare it with our list of versions that log the errors.

For the numbers, I showed her the Grafana panel for rejections by customer and code. It has a one hour resolution and keeps 30 days. I also wrote the query she can run in the console API to list the samples of one customer.

One gap came up: there is no way yet for a customer to see their own rejections in the console. I told Lena about it and she thinks a simple table is enough for a first version. I will open a ticket for the API side.

summary: Canary of the batch writer ran for three days without errors, so I rolled it out to all worker groups and cut worker CPU by about 60 percent.
body:
The canary group ran through three days including the peak. No lost events, no growth in lag and no change in the error rate. I compared the counts of events in the queue and in the downstream store for the canary window with a count query, and they matched exactly.

The group's CPU stayed at 15 to 20 percent against about 40 percent for the others. The p99 latency of the API was within 1 ms of the old.

I rolled the new path out to the remaining groups, one group at a time with 30 minutes between them, watching lag, 5xx rate and the backpressure metric. The last group was done by the afternoon.

After the rollout the average worker CPU was 16 percent against 40 before. That is a drop of 60 percent. The queue broker CPU also fell, from 55 to 31 percent, because it handles far fewer produce requests.

The backpressure counter stayed at zero through the whole rollout.

The obvious next step is to use the headroom. Tobias and I talked about reducing the number of worker tasks on ECS. He wants to keep the headroom for the hot partition case from last week, which has one consumer and not many tasks, so we will reduce the count of the groups that do not have a hot type. This reduces the AWS bill, and I wrote down the saving as roughly 8 tasks, but I will wait a week before I make the change.

I wrote the notes on the branch, with the benchmark numbers, the failure cases and the rollback flag. The branch is merged to main. The flag stays for one more month, then the old path will be deleted.

One loose end is a doc page in the internal wiki, which still says that each event is a separate produce call. I fixed it.

summary: Answered Sam on whether customers can see which schema version each of their events was stored with, and where that data lives.
body:
Sam asked if a customer can find out which schema version an event had when it was ingested, because one customer's developer wants to see when their events moved to the new version.

The answer is yes with a limit. Since the rollout of step one, each event carries a `schema_version` field, and the analytics store has it as a column. The console search does not show it, and the search index does not have the field, so a full text search cannot filter on it.

For the customer it is possible through the dashboards query API, which can group by `schema_version`. Events from before the registry rollout have version 0, which means unknown.

I gave her an example query for the docs, with a count by day and version for the last 14 days. I ran it for the customer on staging data to check that the result looks reasonable.

Lena could add the version to the event detail view in the console. The data is there already in the event record, so only the display is missing. I told Sam to ask her, and put it on the list of small console tasks.

summary: Removed the copy-from-old-key path from the search cache helper, now that the old Redis key styles have all expired.
body:
A week has passed since the key naming change, so I checked the prefix report. There are no keys with the old `cache/search/` or `sq_` styles left. The longest TTL was 6 hours, so this was expected.

I deleted the fallback that read the old key and copied the value. The helper is shorter by about 30 lines and a read does only one Redis call on a miss now. Tests were updated for that.

The cache hit rate stayed at 84 percent after the deploy. Memory is stable at 4.6 GB.

summary: Measured how often the hot partition happens and found two short periods a day where one partition gets about 40 percent of all events, tied to one event type.
body:
After the talk with Tobias I measured the hot partition before suggesting any change to the partition key. I pulled the per partition message rates from Prometheus for the last 14 days at one minute resolution and computed the share of each partition.

Most of the time the shares are within a factor of 1.5 of each other. There are two periods per day, each about 10 minutes long, where one partition receives around 40 percent of all messages. Both match the scheduled export jobs of one large customer, which send a single event type in a big burst.

Because partitioning is by event type, that burst lands in one partition. The consumer of that partition falls behind, up to 25 seconds of lag, and recovers in a few minutes. Other partitions stay near zero lag during that time.

I checked whether the lag causes any harm. The data arrives in the store late by that amount, and the dashboards for that customer lag a little, but no alarm fires, as the threshold is 60 seconds. So the effect is small today.

I see two ways to fix it: add a secondary key such as the batch id to spread one type over several partitions, or give the burst a separate topic. Both change ordering guarantees, which I need to check with Mara, because some consumers rely on order within a type. I wrote the numbers and both options into the ticket and will not change anything until that check is done.

summary: Confirmed the batched second pass ran in 68 seconds on production, then looked at the first pass, which is the real cost of the reindex at 70 minutes.
body:
The production run of last night finished the second pass in 68 seconds with no failed items. The counts matched, and the alias switch happened as before. That finishes the problem of the second pass.

The first pass, the full build, still takes about 70 minutes. I looked at where the time goes. The job reads the documents from Postgres in pages of 5,000 and sends them to OpenSearch in bulk requests. The log timings show that the Postgres read takes about 35 percent of the time and the indexing the rest.

The read uses OFFSET paging. As the offset grows, each page gets slower, and the last pages take about 4 times as long as the first. A keyset page on the primary key would fix that.

I wrote the keyset version on a scratch branch and tested it on staging. The read part fell from 25 minutes to 9. The total went from 70 to about 54 minutes.

I did not merge it yet because the job also runs for single customers with a filter, and the keyset version needs a stable order for that. I need to check the filter case. For the all customers case the result is the same.

Mara had a suggestion in the chat to run two readers in parallel by splitting the id range. That could save another 10 minutes or so, but it makes the job more complicated and the indexing side may become the limit. I put it down as a later idea.

summary: Merged the keyset paging for the reindex job after checking the per customer filter case, and the full build now takes 52 minutes on production.
body:
I came back to the keyset paging from this afternoon. The open question was the per customer filter. The job for one customer reads `WHERE account_id = $1 ORDER BY id`, and the keyset version needs the same ordering, which the primary key gives. The query is `WHERE account_id = $1 AND id > $2 ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000`.

I checked the plan on the replica. There is an index on `(account_id, id)`, so the plan is an index scan with no sort. Without the filter the plan uses the primary key. Both are fast on every page.

I wrote tests for it. One test builds a small index for two accounts and compares the document ids in the index against the table. Another test covers the page boundary, with exactly 5,000 rows and with 5,001 rows. The boundary tests passed at the first run, which I did not trust, so I broke the `>` into `>=` on purpose and saw them fail.

A subtle point is documents created while the first pass runs. The keyset reader may or may not see them depending on their id. That is fine, because the second pass takes all changes since the start of the job and applies them. So nothing is missed, and the second pass handles the overlaps with the last change per document logic.

I ran the full job on staging and compared the counts and the id checksum with an OFFSET run on the same data. They are equal.

Then I merged it. The production run of tonight will be the first with it. I set a reminder for myself to check the duration.

While I was at it, I updated the runbook for the reindex with the new timings. A normal run is now about 52 minutes for the first pass and about 1 minute for the second, and the page should be investigated if it takes more than 90 minutes. Before it said 2 hours, based on the old runs.

The parallel readers idea stays on the list. With 52 minutes the job is far from a problem, and the benefit does not justify the complexity now.

summary: Wrote the weekly plan: widen schema enforcement to five more customers, use the CPU headroom on ECS, and write down the search index shard questions.
body:
The week was a good one for ingest. The batch writer is out, the registry is at step three for one customer, and the reindex job is faster. This is the plan for the next days, written so I do not have to rebuild it from memory.

Schema registry:
- Enable `new_versions` enforcement for five more customers, chosen with Sam from those with the lowest violation rate. The friendly customer has had no problems for a few days.
- Sam writes the announcement and the docs page on the rejected array in the 207 response. The note for clients that ignore the body is the most important part.
- After two weeks without issues, decide about step four, enforcing the rule for all versions, and probably not before the customers with the remaining violations are fixed.

Ingest and AWS:
- Reduce the number of worker tasks of the groups without a hot type, as Tobias and I discussed. I do it in Terraform in two steps, 8 tasks removed in total, and watch the CPU and lag after each step. The rollback is one variable.
- Look at the daily maximum partition lag from the recording rule after two more weeks. Then decide whether the hot partition needs more than the alert.

Search:
- The shard layout of the search index is a question that keeps coming up. Today the index is sharded by customer, and the large customers have big shards, while the small ones share. I want to write a note with the numbers: shard sizes, documents per shard, and query latency by customer size. No decision and no migration, only the facts to talk about with Tobias.
- The note also needs the reindex duration for each layout, since the job is part of any change.

Redis:
- Run the prefix report weekly. Check the share of keys without TTL, which was 212 keys last time and should be zero.

Small things:
- Ask Lena about showing the schema version in the event detail view.
- Remove the old path flag of the batch writer in a month.

I do not plan more than this, because on-call can eat a day at any time, as the hot partition page showed.

summary: Widened schema enforcement to five more customers after checking their violation counts, and one needed a coercion rule for numeric strings in a price field.
body:
Following the weekly plan, I looked at the log-only counts for the next five customers before switching anything. Four of them were under 0.05 percent violations. The fifth sent a price field as a numeric string from an older mobile SDK, which the check would have rejected.

I added a coercion rule for numeric strings on that field and wrote a test with the exact payload from the sample log. Then I switched enforcement on for the four clean customers first and watched the rejection counter for an hour. It stayed flat.

The fifth customer went on after the coercion rule was deployed. Their rejection count was 11 events in the first hour, all from one app build that sends null for a required field. I wrote to Sam with the build number so support can tell them.

Enforcement now covers ten customers. Next is to read the sampled rejections tomorrow and see whether the null case needs a rule or a customer fix.

summary: Used the idle ECS capacity to test a smaller task size for the ingest workers; 1 vCPU held latency and lag flat, so the change stays on staging for a day.
body:
After the task count cut, the next question was the task size itself. Each worker still has 2 vCPU but now sits at roughly 25 percent CPU at peak. I changed the Terraform variable for the staging service to 1 vCPU and 2 GB and replayed a recorded peak hour.

Consumer lag stayed under 2 seconds and p99 of the batch write did not move. Memory peaked at 1.1 GB, which leaves room. I did not touch production.

One thing I watched for was garbage collection pauses with fewer cores. The Go runtime showed pauses under 4 ms, so that is fine.

Tobias asked whether the load balancer health check timeout needs a change with slower startup. Startup went from 6 to 7 seconds, so no. The plan is to leave staging on the small size for a day and then roll one worker group in production.

summary: Read the sampled schema rejections from the five new customers: all null-field cases came from one app build, so it is a customer fix and not a new rule.
body:
I went through the rejection samples that the log-only and enforcement paths keep. The null required field comes from one build of one customer's app, about 200 events an hour. Adding a rule that accepts null would weaken the schema for everyone.

I wrote the customer a short note with the field name, the build and two example event ids, and gave it to Sam to send. The other four customers show no rejections at all.

I left the enforcement switch on for the customer. Their rejected events come back in the per event error list, so their client can see them. I will check their count in two days.

summary: Started the search index shard design by pulling real document counts and sizes per customer, which show that three customers hold most of the data.
body:
To answer the shard questions written last week, I needed numbers. I queried the OpenSearch cat API for index sizes and joined them with the customer ids from the settings table in Postgres.

The result is lopsided. Three customers hold about 70 percent of all documents, and the largest alone has 38 percent. The median customer has under 200 MB. That makes the current layout by customer awkward: the large ones have shards far beyond the comfortable size and the small ones have many tiny shards.

I also counted shards per node. The cluster has 3 data nodes and about 160 shards, which is a lot for the heap we have. Each tiny shard costs memory for nothing.

I put the numbers in a table in the planning doc:
- total documents and size per customer
- shard count per customer
- documents per month for the last year for the top ten

By month would give about 12 shards for a year, with even sizes, but a query for one customer would hit all of them. I need to measure how many queries span more than a month before deciding. I pulled the query log for a week and started counting the time ranges in the filters.

So far about 60 percent of queries filter to the last 7 days. The rest is unclear because many have no time filter at all, which is the dangerous case for a month layout. I will look at those next.

summary: Finished the query log analysis: 22 percent of search queries have no time filter, so a month layout needs a default time range in the API.
body:
I finished counting the week of search queries. Of the total, 61 percent filter to 7 days or less, 17 percent to 30 days or less, and 22 percent have no time filter. Those 22 percent would touch every monthly shard.

I looked at who sends them. Most are from the admin console search box and from one customer's integration that looks up an event by id. The id lookups could use a routing hint or the id could carry its month. The console box can simply default to the last 30 days, with a visible option for all time.

I wrote this into the planning doc as a requirement: the search API gets a default range, and the all-time case is allowed but slower and rate limited. Lena said the console change is small.

Open question: what a customer deletion costs. With monthly shards it becomes a delete by query over all shards, which is heavier than dropping an index. I will estimate that tomorrow with a test on staging.

summary: Measured delete by query for one customer on a staging copy of monthly shards: 4 minutes for a mid-size customer, which is acceptable for a rare operation.
body:
I built a staging index set in the monthly layout from a snapshot of production, 12 shards for a year, and ran a customer deletion on it.

The test customer has about 9 million documents spread over all months. A delete by query with slices set to auto took 4 minutes 10 seconds and left the cluster calm. Search latency on the staging cluster rose by about 15 percent during it and recovered within a minute after the merge finished.

For the largest customer, with roughly 40 times the data, the extrapolation is over two hours. That is still fine if deletion is a background job, which it already is in the console. But the disk space is only released after merges, so I added a forced merge step as an option in the notes.

I also checked what the audit log needs. A deletion must write an audit row with the count of documents removed. The delete by query response has that count, so it is easy.

An alternative I considered was a hybrid: the three large customers keep their own indexes and everyone else goes into monthly shared indexes. It makes deletions trivial for the large ones, but it needs two code paths in the search API and the reindex job. I do not like the extra complexity, but I wrote it into the doc as option B with the cost.

Summary for Mara, who will review: option A, monthly for all, needs a default time range and a slower deletion; option B costs a second code path. I lean towards A. I asked her to read the doc before we decide.

The numbers for reindex cost are still missing. The keyset paging work made the first pass 52 minutes, and monthly shards might parallelise better. That is the next test.

summary: Checked whether the reindex can build monthly shards in parallel: four workers cut the staging build time from 52 to about 19 minutes.
body:
I changed the reindex job on a scratch branch to take a month as its unit of work and ran four in parallel against staging. With the keyset paging in place each month is an independent range scan, so no coordination is needed.

The full build took 19 minutes against 52 for the serial one. Postgres read load went up, but the replica we read from stayed under 40 percent CPU. With eight workers the time only fell to 15 minutes, because the bulk indexing on OpenSearch became the limit.

So four workers is a good default. I noted that the job must not run together with the backup window, which fits with the nightly time we have. No code is merged yet; this was a test.

summary: Mara reviewed the shard planning doc and agreed on option A, monthly shards for everyone, with two conditions on the id lookup and on the default time range.
body:
Mara read the doc and we talked for about 40 minutes. She agreed with option A mainly because of the second code path in option B, which she would have to maintain in the reindex job.

Her two conditions: first, the id lookup for the one integration must not become a scan over all months. We settled on putting the month in the event id prefix for new events and, for old ones, falling back to a query by id over all shards, which is cheap because it is a term lookup. Second, the default time range must be documented in the public API docs and announced to customers, because it changes results for callers that expect all time.

She also asked about the number of shards per month. One primary per month is enough for most months, but the largest months might exceed 50 GB. We agreed to use a rule: one primary per 30 GB of expected data, decided when a month index is created.

I wrote the decision into the doc. I also made a list of work items:
- default time range in the search API
- month in event id prefix
- month-based index naming and aliases
- reindex job by month
- migration plan with dual reads

Sam will draft the customer note after the API change is specified. Nothing has started in code yet.

summary: Specified the migration plan for the search index with dual reads and a per month switch, but left the start date open until the shard count and aliases are tested.
body:
I wrote the migration plan as a document. The idea is that the old customer indexes stay live while the monthly ones are built beside them, and a read alias decides per month which one answers.

Steps in order:
1. Build the monthly indexes for the oldest month with the parallel reindex job.
2. Compare counts and a sample of 1,000 documents against the old index.
3. Switch the alias for that month, keep the old index for a week.
4. Repeat for the next month, ending with the current month last, which needs a live dual write.

The current month is the hard part. New events must go to both layouts until the switch, otherwise there are gaps. The ingest worker writes to OpenSearch through a small indexer module, so a dual write is a change in one place. I sketched it but did not write it.

Risks I listed: disk space on the data nodes during the overlap, which needs about 60 percent more than now; heap pressure from more shards at the same time; and the rollback, which is just switching the alias back as long as the old indexes exist.

Tobias checked the disk numbers. We have room for the overlap only if we do it in the order oldest first and delete old indexes each week. Otherwise we need one more data node, which he can add with Terraform in about an hour.

I did not set a start date. First I want to test alias switching on staging with a real query load.

summary: Looked at the log-only rejections of the next customer group and found that one customer sends event types in mixed case, which the schema treats as unknown.
body:
Before widening enforcement to the next group, I read their violation counts. Most are near zero. One customer sends event types as both Page_View and page_view, and the registry knows only the lowercase form.

I do not want to normalise case silently for everyone. I added a per customer coercion option that lowercases the event type, off by default, and turned it on for this customer. A test covers the mixed case payload.

The group is now ready for enforcement tomorrow morning.

summary: Redis memory crept up again on the search cache; a scan showed a TTL missing on the suggestion keys, so they never expired.
body:
The Grafana panel for Redis memory showed a slow rise over three days, about 2 percent a day, after the key cleanup that had flattened it before.

I used SCAN with a sample, counting keys by prefix and checking TTL. The prefix suggest: made up 31 percent of the keyspace and every one of those keys had a TTL of -1, meaning none. The code that writes them used SET and then EXPIRE in a separate call, and the second call was skipped on one branch when the suggestion list was empty.

I changed the helper to use SET with EX in one call, which removes that class of bug. I added a unit test that checks that no write path leaves a key without a TTL, by running the helper against a test Redis and scanning.

For the existing keys I wrote a one time script that sets a 6 hour TTL on suggest: keys with no TTL. I ran it in batches of 500 with a small pause to avoid latency spikes. About 410,000 keys were touched in 9 minutes.

Command output from the script, final line: fixed 412,338 keys, skipped 0. I watched p99 of Redis commands during the run and it stayed under 2 ms.

I checked for the same pattern elsewhere with a grep for expire calls. Two more places use the two call form, in the rate limiter and the session helper. The rate limiter one is safe because the key is created by INCR and the expire follows in a pipeline, but I added a comment. The session helper I changed too.

Memory should fall over the next 6 hours as keys expire. I will check the panel tonight and tomorrow.

One more thing for the key naming convention doc: every key must have a TTL, enforced by the helper. I added that line and a note to the review checklist.

summary: Enabled schema enforcement for the next five customers; one raised a ticket within an hour because a test script of theirs started getting partial acceptance responses.
body:
I enabled the switch for the five customers at 14:00 after checking the log-only counts again. Four had no rejections in the first hour.

The fifth, a small customer, opened a ticket with Sam: their integration test script posts a batch and expects an HTTP 200 with an empty error list, and now gets 200 with an error list of two events. The behaviour is correct under the partial acceptance we built, but their script treats any error entry as a failure.

I looked at the events. Both have an extra field name the schema forbids, which their test generator adds. That is a real violation, so I did not loosen anything. I explained it to Sam and suggested they either remove the field or ask us to enable the additional properties option for their schema.

While there, I noticed that the error list in the response does not include the schema version the check used. For a customer debugging this, the version is what matters. I added schema_version to each error object. It is a backwards compatible change because clients ignore unknown fields in the response.

Tests:
- a batch with one forbidden field returns the error with version
- a batch with no errors returns an empty list
- the old response shape in the docs example still validates

I also updated the public API docs example to show an error entry with the version. Sam reviewed the wording.

The ticket was answered within the afternoon: they will remove the field from their generator. Enforcement is now on for fifteen customers. The remaining customers are the large ones, which I want to treat separately, with a longer warning period.

I will write down what the large customers need: a notice two weeks ahead, a per customer report of violations, and a quick rollback via the switch. Mara will help with the report query.

summary: Memory in Redis fell by 12 percent after the suggest key fix, and the rise has stopped; the panel is flat for the first time in a week.
body:
I checked the Redis memory panel after the TTL script and the helper change. The used memory dropped from 7.4 GB to 6.5 GB over about five hours as the 6 hour TTL ran out on the old suggest keys.

Since then the line is flat. The count of keys without TTL, which I now export as a gauge from a small scan job, is zero.

I added an alert on that gauge being above zero for 30 minutes. No further work needed on this topic except keeping the gauge.

summary: Built a per month index naming scheme and read and write aliases on staging; alias switching worked, but dual write of the current month needed a fix for duplicate ids.
body:
I started on the staging test of the alias design. The monthly indexes are named events-YYYY-MM style with one write alias for the current month and a read alias per customer that includes a filter on the customer id. A filtered alias lets the search API stay almost unchanged.

First test: the alias for one old month switched from the customer index to the monthly index while a query load of 50 requests a second was running. No errors and no gap in results. The switch is one atomic call to the alias API, as expected.

Second test: dual write for the current month. I changed the indexer module on a scratch branch to write each document twice, once to the old customer index and once to the monthly write alias, using the event id as the document id. That gave a problem. Retried batches in the worker reuse the event id, which is fine for an index operation, but in the monthly index two of my test documents landed in different months because the id prefix used the ingest time and not the event time. A retry crossing midnight at month end would create a duplicate in two months.

The fix is to take the month from the event time, which is stable across retries. I changed the id builder to do that and added a test with a retry across a month boundary.

Third, I counted documents after a one hour run: 412,880 in the old index and 412,880 in the monthly one for the test customer. A sample of 1,000 documents compared equal on all fields.

Things still open:
- the filtered alias adds a small cost per query, which I want to measure
- the write alias rollover at month end must be done by a job, not by hand
- heap use with all the monthly shards

I wrote these into the plan doc. Tobias will look at the heap numbers on the staging nodes tomorrow.

summary: Measured the cost of filtered aliases on staging: p95 rose from 38 to 41 ms, small enough to accept, and a term filter on customer id is cached well.
body:
The open question from yesterday was the price of the filtered alias. I replayed an hour of real search queries against staging twice: once against the old customer indexes and once against the monthly layout with filtered aliases.

Results for p50 and p95:
- old layout: 14 ms and 38 ms
- monthly with aliases: 15 ms and 41 ms

The increase is small. The filter is a term on the customer id, and the filter cache makes it nearly free after the first hit. Queries without a time filter, replaced by the default 30 day range, were faster than before, not slower.

I also tested the all-time query that remains allowed. It hits all 12 monthly shards plus older ones and took p95 210 ms against 95 ms in the old layout. Rate limiting that case makes sense, and the number goes into the doc.

I checked the heap on the staging nodes with Tobias. With the monthly shards for a year the shard count drops by about two thirds compared with now, so the heap use is lower, not higher. He saw it in the node stats: from 61 percent to 44 percent of heap.

The rollover job for the write alias is what I wrote next. It runs on the first of each month early in the morning, creates the next index with the right shard count and moves the write alias. I made it idempotent, so running it twice does nothing the second time, and added a dry run flag. A test covers the case where the index already exists.

I ran it on staging with the clock set one month ahead. It created the index, set the mapping from the template and moved the alias in under a second.

One caveat: the mapping template must be in code, not copied from an existing index. I put the template into the repo next to the reindex job and made both use it.

Next I want to review the plan against the list of work items and see what can be merged early without changing any behaviour. The id prefix and the default time range are the two candidates.

summary: Implemented the default 30 day time range in the search API behind a flag, with an explicit all-time option and a warning field in the response when it applies.
body:
The default time range is the first piece of the search change that customers will notice, so I made it careful. In the Fastify search route, when a request has no time filter and no explicit all_time flag, the API now adds a range of the last 30 days. It is controlled by a feature flag in settings so we can turn it on per customer.

To make the change visible, the response gets a field default_range_applied with the range used. A caller that did not expect it can see why results are fewer. With the flag off, the response is exactly as before.

The explicit option is all_time=true on the request. I added it to the request schema and the validation, and a test that a request with both a time filter and all_time returns a 400 with a clear message.

For rate limiting the all-time case, I used the existing limiter on Redis with a separate bucket: 10 all-time queries a minute per API key. The key follows the naming convention and has a TTL of two minutes, checked by the helper.

Tests added:
- no filter, flag off: unchanged behaviour
- no filter, flag on: range added, field present
- all_time with flag on: no range, bucket counted
- the eleventh all-time query in a minute returns 429

I ran the whole test suite and the integration tests against staging. One older test failed because it asserted the exact response keys; I updated it to allow the new field.

The console search box is Lena's part. I sent her the API contract and she will add a date picker default and an All time link. She thinks it is half a day.

I did not turn the flag on for anyone yet. The plan is to turn it on for our own account, then for customers in groups, with Sam's note sent two weeks before. I added a line about this to the rollout part of the doc.

summary: Wrote the draft customer note on the new default search range for Sam, with an example request and the all-time option explained in plain words.
body:
Sam asked for text she could send to customers. I wrote a draft with three parts: what changes (searches without a time range cover the last 30 days), why (faster and more stable search), and what to do if you need all time (add all_time=true, limited to 10 a minute).

I included one example request and one response excerpt showing the default_range_applied field. I left out the shard details since customers do not need them. Sam will adapt the tone and add it to the docs changelog. The send date depends on when Lena's console change is merged.

summary: Reviewed the large customer enforcement plan with Mara and built the per customer violation report query, which runs in 6 seconds on a week of data.
body:
For the large customers, I want them to see their own numbers before enforcement is on. Mara and I sat down and agreed the report should list, per schema version and field, the count of violations in the last 7 days, plus three sample event ids.

I wrote the query against the violation log table in Postgres. The first version took 41 seconds for the largest customer because it scanned the whole table. Mara spotted that the filter by customer came after the date range in the index, so I changed the composite index to start with customer id. A partial index was not needed. After that the query took 6 seconds.

Creating the index on the production table was the part to be careful with. I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on staging first and measured about 3 minutes for a copy of the data. On production it will take longer, so I scheduled it for a quiet hour.

The report output is a CSV that Sam can send. I made a small script that takes a customer id and writes the file. I ran it for two large customers on staging data and checked the numbers against the raw counters, which matched.

Looking at the data, one large customer has 1.9 percent violations, almost all from one field with a wrong type. That is much higher than the small customers. Enforcing there would reject a lot, so the two week warning period is justified.

Mara asked whether the sample ids could expose data from other customers. They cannot, since the query always filters by the customer id, and I added a test with two customers in the table to prove it. She also wants the report to say clearly that the counts are from sampled events, not all, because the log only keeps a sample for high volume customers. I added that sentence to the CSV header.

Next, a notice date for the first large customer.

summary: Created the violation log index on production in a quiet hour; it took 11 minutes without lock waits and the report query now runs in 5 seconds.
body:
I ran CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the violation log table at the quiet hour we agreed. It finished in 11 minutes. I watched pg_locks and the write latency of the ingest workers during the run: no waits over 50 ms.

After it, I ran the report for the largest customer and it took 5 seconds. I dropped the old index the next minute after checking with pg_stat_user_indexes that no query used it. The table is a bit smaller for it.

summary: Wrote the enforcement runbook for the large customers: per customer checklist, warning period, rollback switch, and who gets told at each step.
body:
The first ten customers were small enough that we could watch them by hand. The large ones send millions of events a day, so a single bad SDK build can reject a lot of data before anyone notices. I wrote a runbook that treats each large customer as its own small rollout.

Step one is the violation report from last week. I run the per customer query and require the rate to be under 0.1 percent for seven days in a row. If it is higher, Sam contacts the customer with the sampled rejections and we wait. The report runs in about 5 seconds on a week of data, so this check is cheap.

Step two is a warning period of five days. The customer gets a note from Sam with the top three violation types, an example of the partial acceptance response, and the date on which enforcement turns on. During this period the switch stays off and we keep counting violations. If the rate rises in that time, the date moves.

Step three is turning the switch on in the account settings, in a quiet hour for that customer. I picked quiet hours from the ingest volume per hour of the last month. For the three biggest customers there is a window of about two hours where the volume is under a third of the peak. Someone watches the rejection panel and the queue lag for the first hour.

Step four is the rollback. The switch goes back to off in the console API, and that takes effect on the next batch without a deploy. I tested this on our own test account and the change showed up in the worker within a few seconds. The runbook says to roll back if the rejection rate goes above 2 percent in any ten minute window, or if the customer opens a ticket about missing data.

I also added what to tell the customer after a rollback: rejected events are counted and sampled but not stored, so they need to resend them. That is the part Sam asked to have in plain words, so I wrote it as a short paragraph she can paste into a ticket.
