Mara will read the runbook tomorrow. Next I want to pick the first large customer, which should be the one with the lowest violation rate, and set the warning date.

summary: Picked the first large customer for enforcement by violation rate and volume, and sent Sam the warning note details for the five day period.
body:
I ran the per customer violation report for all customers over a million events a day. Four of them qualify, and their rates over the last seven days were 0.02, 0.05, 0.4 and 1.1 percent. The last two need SDK fixes before they can be considered. I chose the customer with 0.02 percent, because their remaining violations are all one optional field sent as an empty string. That field is easy to cover with a coercion rule, so I added the rule on staging and replayed a day of their sampled events, and none were rejected afterwards.

The second customer at 0.05 percent has a mix of causes, so it goes second. I gave Sam the sample counts and the three top violation types for the first customer, so she can fill in the warning note from the template. The warning period starts today and the switch date is five days out, in the quiet window of two hours I found in the volume data. I put the date and the rollback threshold in the runbook, and I will check the report again the day before the switch.

summary: Ran REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on the older violation log indexes in the quiet hour; bloat fell from 25 to 3 percent and no writes were blocked.
body:
I ran the planned REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on the three older indexes of the violation log table, one after another. Each took between 4 and 7 minutes.

I watched write latency of the ingest workers and the lock view. No waits longer than 40 ms. One invalid leftover index showed up from an earlier failed attempt on staging, which I dropped there.

After the run the bloat estimate was 3 percent. The alert for dead tuples stays quiet.

summary: Answered Sam on why a customer saw fewer results after the default range was turned on, and showed her how to read default_range_applied in the console network tab.
body:
Sam relayed a question from the friendly customer: a search that returned 140 results before now returns 96. I checked the request in the logs. It had no time filter, so the 30 day default applied, and the 44 missing results are older.

I explained that the response includes default_range_applied with the range, and showed Sam where to see it in the browser network tab. She will tell the customer to use all_time=true for the old ones, within the limit of 10 a minute. The behaviour is as designed.

summary: Tried a generic Go validation library for the schema check in the ingest worker, but it was 3 times slower than our own checker, so I dropped it.
body:
Mara suggested we might replace our hand-written schema checker with a well-known JSON schema validation library for Go, to reduce code we maintain. I gave it a fair try on a scratch branch.

I wrote an adapter that compiles each registry schema once and validates events against it. The first run on the benchmark set of 200,000 events showed our checker at 1.1 microseconds per event and the library at 3.4. That is a factor of three, and the allocations per event were 12 against 2.

I tried to reduce the cost by reusing compiled schemas across goroutines and avoiding the generic map decoding, which brought the library to 2.6 microseconds. Still more than twice as slow.

It also lacked two things we need. The union type comparison rule we fixed with Mara is specific to our registry, and the coercion rules for strings that are timestamps or numbers would have to run before the validation, which means a second pass over each event. The error messages also differ, and the customers' error lists rely on a stable format. Mapping them would be a layer of code about as big as what we would remove.

At our event volume, 2 microseconds more per event means a couple of percent more CPU on the workers, which we just worked hard to save. It was not worth it.

I wrote up the numbers in the branch description and closed it without merging. I kept the benchmark as a file in the repo under the tools folder, so the next time someone suggests it, there is a quick comparison.

Mara agreed with the decision. She said the maintenance worry is lower than she thought, since the checker is 400 lines and well tested.

What I did take from the exercise: our checker had no fuzz test. I added a short Go fuzz target that generates random JSON against a schema and checks that the checker never panics. It found one panic in the first minute, on a deeply nested array of unions with an empty member list. I fixed it with a guard and added a regression test.

summary: Turned on the default search range for three more customers after Sam's note went out, and wrote the check list for widening it to everyone.
body:
Sam's note on the default 30 day range had gone out two weeks ago for the first group. I checked support tickets mentioning search results: none beyond the one already answered. So I turned the flag on for three more customers, each one a medium size account with normal search use.

I watched the search API for the first hours. Error rates stayed the same. The share of all_time requests was 3 percent, and none hit the limit of 10 a minute. The Redis bucket keys showed the right TTL, which I checked with a scan.

I also compared p95 for these customers before and after. For two of them it fell by about 20 percent, since their no-filter queries no longer scan years of data. The third was unchanged.

Then I wrote the list for widening the flag to all customers:
- no open tickets about missing results from the previous group
- all_time share under 5 percent
- Sam's note sent two weeks before each group
- the large three get a personal message from Sam first
- the docs page with the new parameter is published

I checked the docs page. It had the parameter but not the example response with default_range_applied, so I added it. Sam reviewed it.

One item I could not close: one customer integration uses the search API to look for a single event by id, and I am not sure it sends a time filter. The id prefix work is not done, so with the default range, an id lookup for an old event would return nothing. I checked the logs and found it sends a time range of its own, which is fine. But to be safe I made an exception in the default range code: a query with an exact id term skips the default range. I added a test for it.

Next is the id prefix change, then the reindex job by month on production data.

summary: Widened the default 30 day search range to every customer after the check list passed, with the all-time option and the warning field unchanged.
body:
I went through the check list from this morning item by item before touching the flag. First, the three customers that got the default range earlier showed no rise in support tickets and no change in the share of empty result pages. Second, the share of queries that send an explicit time filter stayed at 78 percent, so the default only applies to the rest.

Then I checked the console. Lena's search page reads default_range_applied from the response and shows a small banner, and it rendered correctly on staging for both a normal query and an all-time query. I also ran the 40 most common queries from the query log against staging with the flag on and compared the hit counts with the old behavior. Thirty-seven were the same, and the three that differed all matched documents older than 30 days, as expected.

After that I turned the flag on for all customers in steps: first the small ones, then the mid-size ones, and last the three large customers. I waited ten minutes between steps and watched p95 of the search API in Grafana. It went down slightly, from 61 to 54 ms, because fewer old documents are scanned.

One issue came up. A customer with a saved dashboard that calls the search API with an empty body got the warning field and fewer results. That is the intended behavior, but the dashboard owner would not know why. I sent Sam the details so she can write to them with the all-time parameter named in the text.

The flag stays in the config for a week as a rollback switch. Next I will remove the flag code once no ticket has come in. The monthly shard plan can now assume the default range is in place for everyone.

summary: Looked into a slow audit log query in Postgres and fixed it with a composite index on account and created time, cutting it from 4.1 seconds to 30 ms.
body:
Mara noticed that the audit log page in the admin console took several seconds to load for the larger customers. I took the query from the Fastify log and ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of production data. It filtered by account_id and ordered by created_at descending with a limit of 50. The planner used the single column index on account_id and then sorted millions of rows.

The table has about 61 million rows now. The biggest account has 9 million of them, so the sort was the cost. A composite index on (account_id, created_at desc) was the obvious fix.

I tested it on the copy first. The query went from 4.1 seconds to 30 ms and the plan became an index scan with no sort. The index is 1.9 GB.

On production I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the quiet hour late in the evening. It took 14 minutes and I saw no lock waits and no rise in replication lag. After the build I ran ANALYZE on the table and checked the query again in the live log: p95 for that endpoint fell from 3.8 seconds to 45 ms.

The old single column index is now redundant for most queries. I did not drop it yet, because the export job Mara is writing uses it for a different filter. I put a note in the ticket to check its usage counts in pg_stat_user_indexes after a week.

One more thing I noticed: the page also asks for a total count, which is a full count per account. That is still slow for the biggest account, about 1.2 seconds. I suggested to Lena to drop the exact total and show 'more than 10,000' instead. She will look at it tomorrow.

summary: Redis client connections from the search API grew after yesterday's deploy, and the cause was a second client created in the suggest helper.
body:
The connection graph in Grafana showed the search API holding 38 connections per task instead of the usual 20 after the deploy. I looked through the helpers and found that the suggest module created its own Redis client instead of using the shared one from the cache module. It was a leftover from a refactor.

I changed it to take the shared client and removed the extra options block. Locally the connection count per process went back to the expected number. I will deploy it to staging this morning and watch the graph for an hour.

summary: Deployed the shared Redis client fix; connections per search API task fell from 38 to 19 and the cache hit rate stayed at 91 percent.
body:
The fix went to staging first and then to production before lunch. I checked three things after the rollout. Connections per task dropped from 38 to 19 within a few minutes, as tasks were replaced.

The cache hit rate of the search cache stayed at 91 percent, so the suggest keys still work through the shared client. Latency of the suggest endpoint did not change, p95 was 22 ms before and after.

I also wrote a small test that counts the clients created when the search API starts. It fails if there is more than one for the cache and session use. That should catch the same mistake in the future.

While looking at the connection code I saw that the pool has no idle timeout set. It is not a problem now, but after a spike the extra connections would stay open. I opened a ticket for it and did not change it today.

Next is a review of the key naming. Some keys still use the old prefix without the customer id, and I want a list of them before anyone renames anything.

summary: Listed all Redis key prefixes in use and found two old prefixes without customer id, both small and safe to leave until their TTLs run out.
body:
I ran a scan with a count limit on a read replica and grouped the keys by prefix. There are 14 prefixes. Twelve follow the current scheme: area, customer id, then the hash.

Two do not. One is rl:tmp, used by an old rate limit path that Mara says no code writes to anymore. It holds about 3,000 keys. The other is dash:q, from the dashboard query cache, with about 11,000 keys.

I checked their TTLs with a sample of 500 keys each. The rl:tmp keys all have a TTL under an hour. The dash:q keys have a TTL of 6 hours. So both will vanish by themselves, and there is nothing to migrate.

I still looked for the code that writes dash:q and found it in the old dashboard handler. It is still called by one report. I changed it to the new key scheme in a small commit, with the customer id first, and added a line to the key naming doc.

Memory by prefix was also interesting. The search cache uses 71 percent of the memory, the sessions 9 percent and the rate limiter 6 percent. Nothing there looks wrong.

I saved the scan script in the tools folder so that Sam or Tobias can run it. It only reads and uses SCAN, never KEYS.

summary: Started a review of the schema registry branch by reading how versions of an event type are stored and found no unique constraint on type and version.
body:
I opened the schema-registry worktree and read the migration and the repository code. Each schema version is a row with the event type, a version number and the JSON schema text. There is no unique constraint on (event_type, version), only an index.

That means two parallel publishes could create the same version twice. The code reads the max version and adds one, without a lock. I wrote a short test that shows it with two concurrent calls.

The fix is a unique constraint and a retry of the insert on conflict. I started on the migration and will finish it this afternoon.

summary: Added the unique constraint on event type and version to the schema registry, with a retrying insert, and the concurrent publish test now passes.
body:
The migration adds a unique index on (event_type, version). Before it could run, I checked the data on staging for duplicates and found none. On production there is no registry data yet, so the migration is safe.

In the repository code, the publish function now reads the next version and inserts it. If Postgres returns a unique violation, it reads again and tries once more, up to three times. After that it returns a conflict error to the caller. This is an ordinary retry of an insert and fits the way the rest of the service handles races.

The concurrent test starts 20 publishes for the same type. Before the fix it produced duplicate versions in 14 of 20 runs. After the fix all runs gave versions 1 to 20 with no gaps and no duplicates.

I also looked at what the API returns on conflict. It was a plain 500. I changed it to 409 with a message saying that another publish won and the client can try again.

One point is still open: compatibility checks run before the insert and read the latest version. Under a race, a check could run against a version that is no longer the latest. I think it is acceptable now, because publishing is a rare admin action, but I wrote it into the branch notes for Mara.

Tomorrow I will go on with the part of the review about deleting a version.

summary: Wrote the plan for deleting schema versions in the registry: soft delete only, blocked while any customer enforcement rule points at the version.
body:
The last open piece of the registry review was what happens when someone deletes a version. Right now the endpoint removes the row. That is dangerous, because the ingest worker caches schemas by version and enforcement rules refer to them by id.

I listed the cases. A version used by an active enforcement rule must not be deletable. A version that only appears in old violation log rows can be hidden, but the log rows must still show its number. A version never used can be removed.

The plan has three parts. First, add a deleted_at column and make all reads skip deleted rows, except the violation report. Second, make the delete endpoint return 409 and list the rules that use the version. Third, add an admin-only purge for versions with no references, which I may leave for later.

I asked Mara to read it. She agreed on the soft delete and said the purge is not needed now, since the table is small. She also asked that the ingest worker log a warning if it is asked for a deleted version, so that a mistake does not go unseen.

I implemented the column and the read filter today, with tests for the filter. The endpoint change and the worker warning are for tomorrow.

summary: Finished the delete endpoint of the schema registry so it refuses versions used by enforcement rules and lists the rules in the 409 response.
body:
The endpoint now looks up enforcement rules that reference the version before it sets deleted_at. If it finds any, it returns 409 with the rule ids and the customer names. The test covers three cases: a used version, an unused version and a version that is already deleted, which returns 404.

I also added the warning in the ingest worker when it is asked for a deleted version. It logs the type, the version and the customer once per minute at most, so it cannot flood the logs. I will open the pull request for Mara after a last run of the full suite.

summary: Mara's review of the registry branch found two issues, a missing index on the rule lookup and a wrong status code, and both are fixed.
body:
Mara reviewed the schema-registry pull request in the afternoon and left six comments. Four were about naming and comments, which I fixed quickly. Two mattered.

The first was that the lookup of enforcement rules by schema version had no index. With few rules it does not matter, but the table will grow when the large customers get rules per event type. I added an index on (schema_version_id) and checked that EXPLAIN uses it.

The second was the status code for deleting an already deleted version. I had used 404, and she pointed out that the delete call should be idempotent for the console, which may send it twice on a double click. I changed it to 204 for a repeat call and kept 404 only for a version that never existed.

I ran the whole test suite after the changes. All 412 tests passed, and I ran the registry tests ten times in a row to check for flakiness. No failures.

Mara also asked whether the ingest worker cache invalidates when a version is deleted. It does not, it uses a 5 minute TTL. For the soft delete that is fine, because rules block deletion of used versions, and unused ones are not requested.

I updated the branch notes and the API docs page for the endpoint. Sam will read the docs text tomorrow.

The branch is ready to merge after one more look from Mara in the morning.

summary: Checked the Redis memory graph and cache hit rates for the week, found them steady, and noted that the planned monthly shards will change the search cache keys.
body:
Looked at the Redis memory graph for the week late in the evening, when traffic is low, and compared it with the cache hit rate. Memory grew by 1.5 percent over seven days, which matches the growth of the customer data. The creeping rise from before is gone.

The hit rate of the search cache was between 89 and 92 percent. The dashboard query cache sits at 74 percent. That is expected, since dashboard queries have many more different filters.

I looked at the dashboard TTL of 6 hours against the access pattern in a sample of queries. Most repeated queries come within 30 minutes, so a longer TTL would not add many hits. I left the TTL as it is.

The number of connections per search API task looked normal. The ticket for the idle timeout is still open, and I moved it to next week.

For the shard plan I noted that the search cache keys include the index name in their hash. When the monthly shards come, the keys will change and the hit rate will drop for a while. I will write that into the migration plan so nobody is surprised by the graph.

summary: Merged the schema registry branch after Mara's last look, then deployed it and checked that publishing, deleting and the worker warning work on production.
body:
Mara approved the pull request first thing in the morning, with one small comment about a log message, which I changed. I merged the branch after the pipeline was green.

The migration ran during the deploy and took under a second, since the tables are small. I then tested on production with a test event type that I created for this purpose. Publishing version 1 and version 2 worked and returned the right numbers.

I tried to delete version 2 while a test enforcement rule pointed at it. The endpoint answered 409 and listed the rule, as planned. After I removed the rule, the delete worked and returned 204. A second delete call also returned 204.

I then asked the ingest worker on staging for the deleted version by sending a batch with that version in the header. It logged the warning once and went on with the latest version. The log line had the type, the version and the customer name.

After the check I deleted the test type through the purge in the database, since the API has no purge. I noted that in the branch notes.

Sam has the docs text for the endpoint. She asked for one more example with the 409 response, and I added it.

What is left: the registry has no console page yet. Lena said she could start next week, and I will write down the API calls she needs.

summary: Set up the benchmark plan for the new analytics store: the event sample, the query set and the success criteria were written down before any load test
body:
Wrote the plan for next week's benchmark of a new store for the analytics events. The dashboards on the Postgres events table time out for the large customers, so the goal is to find a store where the slowest dashboard query finishes in under 3 seconds on real data.

Picked the sample: 90 days of the real event stream, taken from the queue topic and the Postgres table, about 1.8 billion events. Mara checked that the sample includes the three largest customers, because they drive the worst queries.

Listed 14 queries from the dashboards, among them the events per hour by type, the top 20 properties, the unique users per day and the funnel of three steps. Each query gets a name and a fixed time range so runs can be compared.

Criteria written down: disk size for the same 90 days, query time at the median and at the 95th percentile, load speed in events per second, and the effort to keep it running. Tobias asked that we also record the memory use on the node.

Nothing was run yet. Next is the test machine in the staging account and the export script for the sample.

summary: Built the export script for the benchmark sample and wrote the first 200 million events to NDJSON files, with a checksum per file
body:
Wrote scripts/bench/export_sample.go, which reads the events table in Postgres in ranges of event id and writes NDJSON files of 1 million lines each. It runs with 4 parallel readers against the read replica, so the production database is not touched.

The first run was too slow: 9,000 events per second. The reason was a sort on created_at without a usable index for the range. Switching the range to the primary key id raised the speed to 61,000 events per second, and 200 million events were written in about 55 minutes.

Each file gets a SHA-256 checksum in a manifest, so that every candidate loads exactly the same data. A small check script counts lines and compares them to the manifest; all 200 files matched.

Found 3,112 events with a null customer_id in the old data from the first version. They are real events of the early test accounts. Decision: keep them in the sample, since the loaders must handle them anyway.

The files take 74 GB uncompressed, and gzip brings them to 11 GB. They are in the staging bucket now.

The remaining 1.6 billion events are exported overnight by a job that Tobias started with a larger instance. Tomorrow the test machines get set up.

summary: Set up two identical test machines in staging for the benchmark and checked the disk and network baselines
body:
Tobias created two instances of the same type with Terraform, in a separate module that is easy to delete after the week. Both have 16 vCPU, 64 GB of memory and a 1 TB NVMe volume.

Measured the baseline of each machine with fio: about 2.1 GB/s sequential read and 180,000 random read IOPS. The two machines were within 3 percent of each other, so they can be compared fairly.

Copying the sample from the bucket took 14 minutes per machine. The checksums were checked on both after the copy, and all 1,000 files matched the manifest.

Installed the first candidate on machine A with default settings, plus the settings the vendor recommends for the memory limit. Machine B got the second candidate in the same way. No tuning yet; the plan is to run a first pass with defaults and tune only after that.

Wrote the table definitions. Both use the same columns as our event schema: event id, customer id, type, timestamp, a user id and a JSON properties field. The ordering and partition choices are the main difference, and the notes on them are in bench/NOTES.md.

Next is the loader for both, to see how fast 90 days of events go in.

summary: Loaded the first 300 million events into both candidates and noted where the load speed and the disk use differ
body:
Wrote a small loader in Go with a configurable batch size and number of writers. It reads the NDJSON files and inserts them into either candidate, so the code path is the same except for the driver.

First pass with batches of 10,000 rows and 4 writers. Both machines took the 300 million events without errors. The raw numbers are in bench/results-load-1.csv; I do not interpret them yet because the settings are still defaults.

The load speed changed a lot with the batch size. Batches of 1,000 rows were far slower on both machines, and above 50,000 rows there was no further gain. Chose 20,000 as the batch size for all later runs.

One problem: the properties field has about 40 events with invalid UTF-8 from an old client. Machine A rejected the batch with a clear error, B accepted it. Added a cleanup step to the loader that replaces bad bytes, so both get identical data.

Mara asked whether we should also test while writes keep coming in, since production has constant ingest. Agreed. I will add a second phase where a writer keeps inserting 5,000 events per second while the queries run.

Tomorrow: finish the load of the full 90 days and take the disk sizes.

summary: Finished loading 90 days of events on both machines and recorded the disk size after each had settled its background work
body:
The full load of 1.8 billion events finished overnight on both machines without errors. Row counts were checked against the manifest and matched exactly.

Disk size must be taken only after background merges and compaction are done, otherwise the numbers are misleading. Waited until the disk activity was flat for 20 minutes on each machine, then recorded the sizes in bench/results-size.csv. I do not copy the figures here yet, because Mara wants a second measurement with a different ordering of the columns before we trust them.

Ran a first smoke test of three queries on each machine to see that the results are the same. The results match for two queries. The unique users per day differed by 0.4 percent on one machine because one of the engines uses an approximate count by default. Changed that query to use the exact count on both for the fair comparison, and noted the approximate variant as a separate test.

Wrote the runner for the query set: it runs each query 5 times after one warm-up run, clears nothing between runs, and records the time for each run. A second mode clears the OS cache first, to measure cold queries.

The next step is the full run of the 14 queries on both machines.

summary: First full run of the 14 dashboard queries on both machines: results saved, two queries behaved oddly and need a look at the settings
body:
Ran the full set of 14 queries with the runner, warm and cold. Each run was 5 repetitions, and all raw times are in bench/results-queries-1.csv. The runner printed the median and the 95th percentile for each query and machine.

Two queries stood out. The funnel query with three steps took far longer than the others on one machine, and the top 20 properties query had a very high spread between repetitions on the other. Looked at both before drawing any conclusion.

For the funnel query, the plan showed that a join on user id was being done with a hash table that did not fit in the memory limit and spilled to disk. Raising the per-query memory limit from the default to 20 GB made the time drop sharply. This is a settings problem and not a property of the engine, so the result of the first run is not fair, and it will be redone.

For the top properties query, the spread came from a background job running at the same time on the other machine. The job is a statistics refresh that starts at fixed intervals. I did not turn it off, because it also runs in production use; instead I noted when it runs and the runner now records the start time of every repetition so I can see the overlap.

Other findings from the first run:
- 9 of the 14 queries ran in under 2 seconds on both machines when warm.
- Cold runs were slower on both, as expected, by factors between 2 and 8.
- The three queries over a full 90 days of data were the slowest group on both machines.

The settings used in each run are written into a header of the result file so that nobody has to guess later. Wrote this into the runner after noticing that the first run did not have it.

Plan for tomorrow: redo the funnel query with the memory setting fixed, rerun the top properties query with the job times recorded, and then start the test with constant writes. Lena asked whether the dashboards could show approximate counts for unique users; I noted it as a question for the user, since it changes what customers see.

summary: Reran the two odd queries with fixed settings and started the mixed test with constant writes at 5,000 events per second
body:
Redid the funnel query on the machine where it had spilled to disk, with the per-query memory limit at 20 GB. The time became stable across 5 repetitions, with a spread under 6 percent. Wrote the old and the new result side by side in the notes so the change is visible.

The top properties query was rerun with the start times of the background statistics job recorded. The two repetitions that overlapped with the job were 30 to 40 percent slower, and the other three were close to each other. I report the median, which hides the overlap, and the 95th percentile, which shows it.

Then started the mixed test. A writer inserts 5,000 events per second into the table, the same rate as the average load of the busiest day last month. At the same time the query runner executes the set of 14 queries in a loop for one hour.

What I saw in the first 20 minutes:
- Inserts kept up on both machines with no growing lag.
- Query times went up on both when the writes were running, by a different amount for each query.
- One machine showed a short pause in the inserts of about 2 seconds every few minutes; the cause was not clear yet.

To find the cause of the pause, I looked at the logs and the disk graphs in Grafana. The pauses lined up with the writing of larger chunks from memory to disk. I will check if a different batch size changes it.

Tobias noted that production ingest also has bursts of up to 30,000 events per second for a minute, so a burst test should follow. I added it to the list with a clear start and end, so that the burst can be repeated.

The one hour run finished at the end of the session, with the output saved to bench/results-mixed-1.csv. I will read it properly tomorrow when I am fresh, and I will not draw conclusions from the first 20 minutes alone.

summary: Read the mixed test results and found that the insert pauses on one machine depend on the batch size
body:
Looked at the results of the one hour mixed test. Query times under constant writes were higher than in the quiet runs on both machines, and the data is in bench/results-mixed-1.csv.

The insert pauses of 2 seconds on one machine went away when the writer used batches of 50,000 rows instead of 5,000. The cost was a higher delay before an event could be read, about 10 seconds instead of 1. For dashboards that is acceptable.

Saved a plot of the insert latency over the hour for each machine.

Next: the burst test at 30,000 events per second for one minute, then a repeat of everything with the second column ordering that Mara asked for.

summary: Ran the burst test at 30,000 events per second and checked that both machines recovered without losing a single event
body:
Wrote the burst test as a mode of the writer: 5,000 events per second for 5 minutes, then 30,000 per second for one minute, then back to 5,000 for 10 minutes. The query runner kept running during the whole test.

Counted the events at the end by their ids. Both machines had every one of the 1.5 million burst events, so nothing was lost or doubled.

During the burst, the insert call took longer on both machines, with the worst single call at a few seconds. The lag between the writer and the readable data grew for about a minute and then went back to normal within 3 minutes after the burst ended. That is similar to what the real ingest workers can take, as they are behind the queue.

Query times during the burst were the most affected. The slowest queries became much slower for the minute of the burst, and I recorded the numbers per query in bench/results-burst-1.csv.

One issue in my own test: the first try used one connection, which became the limit at about 22,000 events per second. Moved to 4 connections and the limit went away. I mention it because the first numbers in the file marked as try-1 should be ignored.

Mara reviewed the test code and asked me to record the memory use of the machines as well. Added a sampling of memory every 10 seconds to the runner. The burst test is repeated with it this afternoon, and the notes will contain both memory graphs.

Still open are the second column ordering and the test of the approximate count variant. They are both for tomorrow, and the day after the real work of comparing starts.

summary: Repeated the load and the query set with the second column ordering and wrote down how much the ordering changes sizes and times
body:
Mara had asked for a second ordering of the columns because the first choice might favor some queries over others. Created the second table on both machines with the order starting with customer id and then timestamp, instead of type and then timestamp.

Loading the 1.8 billion events again took about 6 hours on each machine, running in the background while I did other things. Row counts matched the manifest on both.

After the background work settled, recorded the disk sizes again. The size changed by a few percent only, so the choice of ordering has a small effect on the size. I put both numbers in bench/results-size.csv in separate rows.

The query times changed more than the size. Queries that filter by customer first became faster, as expected, since most dashboard queries are about one customer. Queries over all customers, which we only run for internal reports, became slower. We run 11 of the 14 queries per customer, so the second ordering fits the real use better.

The approximate count variant for unique users was tested too. It was about 3 to 5 times faster than the exact count on both machines, with an error under 1 percent. I do not think we should show approximate numbers without asking the user, so I wrote it as an option.

Some notes about quality of the test itself:
- All runs use the same query text on both machines, with only the syntax changes that each engine needs.
- The settings of each run are in the header of the result file.
- Runs that were disturbed by background jobs are marked.

Summary of the day: the data for the comparison is nearly complete. What is missing is the check of operations work, like backups, upgrades and what it takes to run it, which Tobias will do in the next days.

summary: Tobias and I tested backup, restore and a node restart on both candidates, and I collected the operations notes for the comparison
body:
The numbers for speed and size are not the only part of the decision, so today was about running the thing. Tobias took the backup and restore part, and I took the restart and upgrade part.

Backup: both candidates have a way to make a consistent copy while writes continue. Tobias made a backup of the 90 days on each machine to the staging bucket and timed it. He then restored it onto a clean instance and ran three of the queries to check the result. Both restores worked, and the times are in bench/NOTES.md. The one thing he noted was that the restore of one candidate needed more steps to get the extension and the settings right before the data could be loaded.

Node restart: I killed the database process on each machine in the middle of the constant write test, to see what happens to data in flight.
- Both came back up without manual repair.
- The recovery time differed; one was ready in under a minute and the other needed a few minutes to replay its log.
- After the restart, I counted the events by id. A few thousand events from the last second before the kill were missing on both, which is expected, because the writer had not yet received the confirmation for them. The writer retried them and the final count was exact.

Upgrade: both have a minor version newer than the one installed. I upgraded one machine of each type in place. One was a simple package update with a restart. The other needed a step to update the extension in each database after the package update, which is easy to forget.

Monitoring: both can expose metrics for Prometheus. One has a built-in endpoint; the other needs an exporter that we would have to run and keep up to date. This is a small cost but it is a cost. I started on the Grafana dashboard for both, with disk, memory, insert rate and query time.

Access control: both support users with read-only roles. I created a role for the search API on each and checked that it cannot write.

The operations notes are now about two pages. Neither candidate has a problem that would stop us. I am still collecting the details and I will not rank them in the notes until all tests are done.

Open questions for tomorrow: how the dashboards queries look in the dialect of each one, and how hard it is to rewrite the 14 queries. Lena will look at the queries in the console code to see how many places call them.

summary: Counted the places in the admin console and search API that run analytics queries, to estimate the rewrite effort for a new store
body:
Lena and I searched the code for every place that builds an analytics query. There are 23 call sites in the search API and the admin console backend, which use 14 distinct query shapes. They match the benchmark query set.

Most queries are built with a small helper that adds the customer filter and the time range, in src/analytics/queryBuilder.ts. That helper is the main place that would have to change, plus the SQL strings in 6 files.

Three queries use window functions and one uses a lateral join, which are the hardest to port. The funnel query is the most complex of all, with 80 lines of SQL.

Rough estimate: about two weeks of work for one person to port and test all queries, not counting the data loader and the backfill of old events.

I added the estimate to the notes. Lena will write a list of dashboard screens and which query each one uses, so that we can test them one by one later.

summary: Ported four of the benchmark queries to the dialect of the second candidate to measure how much work a rewrite really is
body:
To check the estimate of two weeks, I ported 4 of the 14 queries to the SQL dialect of the second candidate. The first was the events per hour by type, the second the top 20 properties, the third the unique users per day and the fourth the funnel.

The simple ones took 10 to 15 minutes each. The differences were mostly in the names of the date functions, the way arrays are handled and the syntax for reading a field out of the JSON properties.

The funnel query took about 2 hours. Its window function needed a different form, and my first version gave wrong counts for users who did two steps on the same second. I compared the output with the Postgres result for one customer and found the mismatch, then fixed the ordering with a tie-break on event id.

I checked the results of all four against Postgres for three customers and a 30-day range, and they were the same after the fix.

How I tested:
- A script runs the Postgres query and the new query for the same customer and range.
- It compares the rows and prints the first difference.
- It also prints both times.

The script is in bench/compare_results.ts and it will be useful again for the real port, whichever store is chosen.

The result for effort: about 3 days for the four queries including tests, which fits the two week estimate for all of them. I wrote it in the notes.

Tomorrow I do the same for the other candidate with the same four queries, so that the effort is compared on equal terms.

summary: Ported the same four queries to the first candidate and compared results with Postgres, finding one wrong count in the funnel query
body:
Did the same exercise as yesterday for the other candidate: the four queries, events per hour by type, top 20 properties, unique users per day and the funnel.

The simple queries were quick, around 10 minutes each, with the usual changes of date functions and JSON field access. The unique users query needed one change to use the exact count instead of the default approximate one, which I already knew from the first test.

The funnel query had a wrong count again, but for a different reason than on the other candidate. Users with two events in the same millisecond were counted twice in step two. With a distinct on user id and the tie-break on event id, the output matched Postgres for the three customers.

The joins are the interesting part. The funnel query in its natural form wants a join between the events and a small table of segments. This candidate handled it, but the join was slow when the right table was large, so I rewrote it with a subquery and a filter. It works, but it is a bit different from how we write SQL now.

The effort is similar to the other one: about 3 days for the four queries including tests. Neither is clearly cheaper to port.

I put both sets of ported queries in bench/queries/ in two folders, with the compare script, so that anyone can rerun them.

The tests are done in this phase. The remaining work is to put all numbers into one table. Tobias will check my ops notes in the morning, and Mara will review the query results.

summary: Collected all benchmark results into one table and checked each number against the raw files before sharing it with the team
body:
Today I made the summary table from all result files. Each row is a test, each column a candidate, and every cell links to the raw CSV where it came from.

Before sharing I checked the numbers one by one against the raw files. This found two mistakes in my own summary script:
- The median for the cold runs used the warm results for one query, because the filter on the mode column was missing.
- The 95th percentile was computed over all queries together instead of per query.

Both were fixed, and I reran the script. The numbers changed in a few cells, so it was worth the check. I added a test for the script with a small fake result file where the right answers are known.

The table has these groups:
- Disk size for the same 90 days, with both column orderings.
- Load speed in events per second.
- Query times: warm, cold, and under constant writes.
- Burst test results and recovery.
- Restart and recovery times.
- Effort of the port of the four queries.
- Operations notes from Tobias and me.

I also wrote down the things that the benchmark does not tell us. It was run on one node each, so it says nothing about clusters. It used 90 days of data and we will grow beyond that. The queries were tested on the current dashboards only, and new dashboards may need new query shapes.

Mara reviewed the test code for the runner and the loader. She found that the loader did not check the row count after each file, only at the end, and asked for it to be added. It makes no difference for the results because all counts matched at the end, but it is better for later use.

Tobias added to the ops notes that he would prefer the candidate with fewer moving parts, as long as the speed is good enough. I wrote that into the notes as his opinion, not as a finding.

The next step is a short meeting where the user looks at the table with all of us. I prepared a one page summary to go with it, with the three or four numbers that matter most for the decision, and a list of questions we cannot answer from the data.

There is nothing left to run, except a last check that the machines are shut down after the decision, to avoid costs. I noted that in the Terraform module so it is not forgotten.

summary: Wrote the one page summary for the decision meeting with the key numbers, the open questions and what the benchmark does not cover
body:
Wrote the one page summary for the meeting. It has the short table with the main numbers, a few lines about operations, and the open questions.

What I put on the page:
- The disk size for 90 days of events for each candidate.
- The median and the 95th percentile of the 14 queries, warm.
- The result under constant writes and in the burst test.
- The port effort for the four queries: about 3 days each way.
- The ops differences that Tobias and I found, in three lines.

What I kept off the page is any recommendation, because the user should decide with the whole team. I added a short list of the things that could change the picture, like growth of the data and the need for joins in future dashboards.

Open questions I listed:
- Do we want approximate unique counts on the dashboards, which makes them much faster?
- How long should raw events be kept, since it changes the disk need a lot?
- Can we do the few joins in the API instead of in the database?
- Who is on call for the new store, and how fast can we all learn it?

Sam read the summary for clarity, since he will need to write the docs for customers if dashboards change. He asked for a glossary of two terms, and I added them at the bottom.

I checked once more that every number on the page matches the summary table, and that the table matches the raw CSV files. They do.

Last, I wrote a small checklist for after the decision: stop the test machines, archive the result files in the bucket, delete the extra copies of the sample and start the plan for the loader and the backfill. The checklist is in bench/NEXT.md.

The meeting is tomorrow morning for the team, and I expect the decision to be written down the same day.

summary: Started the loader for ClickHouse: a Go service that reads the events topic and writes batches into a first table, running against staging only
body:
After yesterday's decision I started the real loader. It is a new Go service in cmd/ch-loader that reads the events topic from Redpanda with a consumer group and writes batches of rows to ClickHouse.

The table is the one from the second ordering of the benchmark, with customer id first and then the timestamp, partitioned by month. I took the column types from the benchmark and changed the properties field to a string column holding JSON, as the queries read it with the JSON functions.

The loader collects rows until it has 50,000 rows or 5 seconds have passed, whichever comes first, and then sends one insert. Only after the insert is confirmed does it commit the offsets to Redpanda. That means a crash can lead to a repeated batch, so the table needs to handle duplicates; I will deal with that in the next step.

In staging I ran it against the live copy of the event stream for 2 hours. It kept up with the staging rate of about 800 events per second and the lag stayed under 3 seconds.

Problems found:
- The first version held rows in a slice that was never reset, and memory grew. Fixed by reusing a buffer.
- A time zone mistake put events one hour in the past in the partition key. Fixed by using UTC everywhere in the loader.

Metrics for Prometheus are in: rows per second, batch size, insert time, and consumer lag. I started a Grafana panel for them.

Tomorrow: duplicates after a crash, and a test where I kill the loader on purpose. The backfill of old events comes after that.

summary: Made the ClickHouse loader safe against repeated batches after a crash and tested it by killing the process during inserts
body:
The loader commits offsets only after a confirmed insert, so a crash between the insert and the commit repeats a batch. Today I made the table tolerate that.

I changed the table to a ReplacingMergeTree keyed on event id, so repeated rows collapse into one after merges. The queries for dashboards cannot wait for merges, though, so the counts could be off until then. For exact counts the queries need a final modifier, which costs speed.

The better fix was to make the batches repeatable. The loader now gives each insert a deduplication token made from the topic, partition and the first and last offset of the batch. When the same batch is sent again, the server ignores it. That keeps the plain table fast and the counts exact in the normal case.

Test: with a script, I killed the loader at random moments while staging events flowed in, 40 times. After each restart I compared the number of rows with the number of events in the topic for the same offset range. All 40 comparisons matched exactly, with no missing and no double events.

One case is not covered: if the loader is restarted with a different batch size, the offsets in a batch differ and the token differs too. I wrote this in the README of the loader and added a check that the batch size is read from a fixed setting.

Mara reviewed the change and asked for a test for the token logic. I added a unit test for the token with 6 cases.

Next is the backfill of the old events from Postgres, which will use a different path because it reads from the table and not from the queue.

summary: Wrote the backfill tool that copies old events from Postgres into ClickHouse in id ranges and tested it on one customer in staging
body:
Wrote cmd/ch-backfill. It reads the Postgres events table by ranges of the primary key, 500,000 rows per range, from the read replica, and writes them in batches into ClickHouse.

Each range gets a row in a small progress table in Postgres with its start id, end id, state and the number of rows. If the tool stops, it starts again with the ranges that are not done. A range is marked done only after the count in ClickHouse for that id range matches the count in Postgres.

The insert uses the same deduplication token idea as the loader, with the range id as the token, so running a range twice does no harm.

Test on the staging data for one mid-size customer, about 40 million events:
- The copy took 11 minutes with 4 parallel ranges.
- The counts matched for all 80 ranges.
- I checked the three dashboard queries for this customer against Postgres and the results were the same.

One problem: the Postgres read took longer for ranges with big properties fields, and the replica showed some lag during the run. I reduced the parallel ranges to 3 and added a pause when the replica lag is above 5 seconds. The tool reads the lag from a Postgres query.

A second finding: some old events have timestamps in the far future from clients with a wrong clock. They go into a partition for that future month. I decided to keep them as they are and note it, because rewriting them would change the data. A decision on how to treat them is for later.

The plan for production is to run the backfill in the night, when the load is low, and to start with the smallest customers. Tobias will check the disk space on the production server before we start.

summary: Looked at the events with future timestamps found by the backfill and decided with Mara to keep them but exclude them from the dashboards
body:
The backfill test showed events with timestamps far in the future. I counted them in the production replica: 18,400 events in total, from 9 customers, with timestamps up to 3 years ahead. The cause is client devices with a wrong clock.

Mara and I talked about three options:
- Fix the timestamp to the time when the event was received. That changes data that customers see in their exports.
- Drop the events. That loses data, which we do not want.
- Keep them as they are and make sure the dashboards do not show them.

We chose the third. Dashboard queries already filter on a time range, so these events would show only if a customer picked a range in the future, which the console does not allow. They stay in their own partitions, which are small.

I checked what happens in ClickHouse with partitions of far future months. There are 31 extra partitions for these events, a small number. I added a check to the loader that logs a warning with the customer id when an event is more than one day in the future. It does not change the event.

The warning counter went into Prometheus as a metric by customer. Sam can use it in support: if a customer asks why their dashboard misses events, he can see that their devices have a wrong clock. I wrote a short note for him in the support docs draft.

Small other work today: I added the received time as a column in the new table. The ingest worker already has the value, and for old events it is null. It lets us compare the event time and the receive time later.

The column needed a change in the loader and in the backfill. I did both and reran the staging test for the one customer; the counts were still the same.

summary: Rewrote the first six dashboard queries for ClickHouse behind a switch in the query builder and checked them against Postgres for five customers
body:
Started the port of the dashboard queries. I added a setting in the query builder, analytics.store, with the values postgres and clickhouse, so that each customer or the whole staging environment can be switched without code changes.

Six queries are done today: events per hour by type, events per day by type, top 20 properties, unique users per day, the count of events by customer and the top event types.

The main changes were:
- Date functions: date_trunc became toStartOfHour and toStartOfDay.
- Reading a property from the JSON string: the Postgres arrow operator became JSONExtractString.
- Counting unique users: uniqExact, because we agreed not to show approximate numbers without asking.
- Parameters: the driver wants typed parameters in the form of {name:Type}, so the helper that builds them had to change.

For each query I ran my compare script on five customers, with ranges of 7, 30 and 90 days, which makes 15 runs per query. Results matched in 88 of the 90 runs. The two that differed were both the top 20 properties query, where two properties had the same count and came in a different order. I added a tie-break on the property name to both versions, and then all 90 runs matched.

Times for the largest customer on 90 days, warm:
- events per hour by type: 41 seconds before on Postgres and 0.9 seconds now.
- unique users per day: 58 seconds and 1.6 seconds.

The others were also much faster. These were measured on staging data with the full copy for that customer, so I expect similar results in production.

One thing to watch is the first call after a long time of no use, which was slower, about 3 times. It is the cold cache of the disk, and it shows in the first dashboard load of the morning. I made a note for later to think about it.

Lena tested the console against staging with the switch on for one test customer, and all six dashboards drew correctly. She found a chart that expected the hour as a string with a time zone, while the new query returns it without one. I changed the query to format it in the same way, and the chart works.

The rest of the queries, with the funnel and the lateral join, come next.

summary: Ported the funnel query to ClickHouse using windowFunnel and compared it with the Postgres result for several customers
body:
Did the funnel query today, the hardest of the 14. In Postgres it is 80 lines with window functions and a self-join. ClickHouse has a function called windowFunnel which does this in one aggregation.

The new query groups by user id and calls windowFunnel with a window in seconds and the three step conditions. It then counts the users by the level they reached. It is about 15 lines.

First results did not match Postgres. The reason was a difference in the meaning: the Postgres version let the steps happen in any order inside the window if the timestamps were increasing, and windowFunnel in default mode wants the steps in order of events. After reading the definition with Mara, we found that the Postgres version was the one with the wrong meaning for customers who did step 3 before step 2. The product description says the steps must happen in order, so the new behavior is the right one.

That means the numbers on the funnel dashboard will change a little for some customers. I measured how much for 8 customers on a 30-day range:
- For 6 customers the difference was under 1 percent.
- For 2 customers it was 3 and 5 percent lower in step three.

I wrote that down for Sam, because a customer may ask why the numbers moved. I also wrote a short sentence for the docs: steps are counted only when they happen in the order given.

To be sure the new query is correct, I wrote a test with a small set of events where the right answer is known by hand, 12 users with different orders of steps. The new query gives the right answer for all of them.

Time for the largest customer, 90 days: 2 minutes 10 seconds before on Postgres, 2.4 seconds now.

Left for tomorrow: the lateral join query and the two queries that use the events together with the account settings, which will need a join in the API.

summary: Ported the remaining dashboard queries to ClickHouse behind the query builder switch; 11 of 14 now match Postgres for the five test customers, three still differ
body:
Continued the query rewrite from the funnel work. Eleven of the 14 dashboard queries now run on ClickHouse and return the same numbers as Postgres for the five test customers.

The three that differ are the retention query, the top-pages query and the unique-users-per-hour query. Retention differs because Postgres counted events with future timestamps and the ClickHouse side excludes them, as decided with Mara last week. That is expected, so I added a filter to the Postgres reference so the comparison is fair.

Top-pages differed by a handful of rows because of a different tie-break in ORDER BY. I added the page path as a second sort key on both sides and the results are identical now.

Unique-users-per-hour is still off by about 0.4 percent. I suspect uniq() is approximate, so tomorrow I will try uniqExact on a small customer and see whether the gap closes. If it does, I will look at what the exact version costs on the large customers before choosing.

summary: Dashboard queries 12 to 14 are in the ClickHouse builder; with the earlier ones, 11 of 14 match Postgres for five test customers, three still differ
body:
Today I ported the remaining dashboard queries to ClickHouse behind the query builder switch. These were the retention panel, the top referrers list and the sessions per hour chart, plus a few variants of the earlier ones. The switch still defaults to Postgres, and I only turned it on in the staging checks.

Then I ran the comparison script against the five test customers that I used for the first six queries. The script runs both paths with the same time range and compares every row, with a tolerance of 0.5 percent for the approximate counts. In the end 11 of the 14 panels match for all five customers.

Three panels still differ. The first is the unique users panel. ClickHouse gives numbers about 1.2 percent lower for the largest of the five customers. I had used uniq there, which is approximate, and the Postgres side counts exactly. Switching to uniqExact brought the numbers into line, but the query got three times slower on the 90 day range. I did not decide yet which one to keep and wrote both variants into the query file.

The second difference is the bounce rate panel. Postgres counts a session with one event as a bounce, while my first port counted sessions with one distinct page. The old SQL had a comment about this, and I had missed it. I will fix the definition tomorrow and rerun it.

The third is the daily panel for one customer, where the totals are off at the day borders. I suspect a timezone problem, because the customer is the one with an odd offset in the settings table. I did not dig into it today and noted it in the list of open points.

The retention panel was the most work. It needed an array join and a different way to build the cohorts, and the first version used 6 GB of memory on the staging node. After I moved the filter on the event type before the grouping, it dropped to 900 MB. The query now takes 0.3 seconds on 90 days of events for the biggest of the five customers.

Next I will fix the bounce definition, decide on the unique users variant with Mara, and look at the timezone case. After that I want to start the rollup design, because several panels read hourly numbers and should not scan raw events.

summary: Designed the first materialized view for hourly rollups per customer and event type, with a sketch of the target table and the columns that need merge states
body:
Started on the materialized views, because the heaviest dashboard panels scan raw events for each load. The first view is the hourly rollup per customer and event type.

The target table uses AggregatingMergeTree. Columns: customer_id, event_type, hour, a count as a plain sum, and unique users as an AggregateFunction(uniq, UInt64) state. Ordering is (customer_id, event_type, hour), which matches how the panels filter.

I wrote the view definition and ran it by hand against one day of staging data. The sums matched a direct count query on the raw table. The state column needs uniqMerge in the read queries, so the query builder needs a small change to emit the merge functions when it reads from a rollup.

One question came up. A materialized view only sees rows inserted after it was created, so existing events need a separate fill. The backfill tool writes through the normal insert path, so the view will fill itself during backfill. I still want to confirm that with a test before relying on it.

I wrote the plan in the working notes and left the view in staging only. Tomorrow I will test the backfill interaction and compare rollup numbers to the raw table for a full week.

summary: Confirmed that the backfill tool fills the hourly rollup view through normal inserts; a week of rollup numbers matches the raw table for three customers
body:
Tested the open question from this morning: does the rollup view fill during a backfill? I ran the backfill tool for one small customer in staging with the view in place, then compared the rollup against a direct query on the raw table.

Counts matched for every hour of the week. The unique user states merged to the same values as uniq() over the raw rows. I repeated it for two more customers of different sizes with the same result.

One case needs care. If the backfill runs twice for the same range, the view would add the rows again, because the dedup in the loader works on batches and not on the rollup. The tool already refuses to rerun a finished id range, but I added a check that prints a clear error when the range was done before.

I also noted that dropping and recreating the view means an empty rollup, so any change to the view needs a refill from the raw table. I wrote that down in the notes for whoever changes it next. Next up is the query builder change to read from the rollup.

summary: Query builder now reads the hourly panels from the rollup table with merge functions; the staging dashboard for the largest customer loads in under a second
body:
Changed the query builder so panels with an hourly or coarser resolution read from the rollup table. It emits countMerge-style sums and uniqMerge for the user counts, and falls back to the raw table for finer resolutions.

I checked three panels on the largest customer in staging. The page-views panel went from 1.4 seconds on raw events to 90 ms. The unique-users panel went from 0.6 seconds to 120 ms. The whole dashboard now loads in under one second.

One test failed at first. The builder produced uniqMerge on a column that was a plain sum for one panel, and ClickHouse answered with an illegal type error. The cause was a wrong column mapping in my lookup table, which I fixed and covered with a test.

The switch for ClickHouse is still off in production. Before enabling it I want a full comparison run for ten customers, which I will start tomorrow.

summary: Ran the full comparison of ClickHouse and Postgres dashboard results for ten customers; all panels agree within the agreed tolerance except one with a timezone offset
body:
Ran the comparison script over ten customers, including the three largest, for all 14 queries and several date ranges each.

Nearly everything agrees. Exact queries match to the row, and approximate ones stay within 0.5 percent. One panel, the daily active users chart, was off for two customers in the evening hours.

The cause was the timezone. The Postgres query groups by day in the customer's configured timezone, and the ClickHouse query grouped by UTC day. I added the customer timezone to the toStartOfDay call in the builder. After that the panel matched, and I reran the two customers to be sure.

The hourly rollup is stored in UTC, which is fine for hours but not for days in timezones with a half hour offset. For those the builder reads the raw table. I noted this as a known limit and will ask Mara whether any customer uses such a timezone.

summary: Enabled the ClickHouse query path for two small customers in production behind the switch and watched the dashboards and error rates for the whole morning
body:
Turned on the ClickHouse switch for two small customers who had agreed to be first. The switch is per customer in the settings table, so turning it off again is one update.

Before the change I wrote down the Postgres panel timings for both customers, so there is something to compare. Then I enabled the first one at about 10:30 and watched Grafana. The p95 of the dashboard API for that customer dropped from 1.1 seconds to 160 ms. No errors showed up in the logs.

I asked Sam to check the console with the first customer's data. She compared three panels with the numbers the customer had sent in a support ticket last month. They matched.

The second customer was enabled at about 11:15. It has a large share of events with odd timestamps, which the dashboards now exclude. I checked the totals before and after. They differ by the count of future-dated events, as expected, and I told Sam so she can explain it if the customer asks.

Things I watched:
- ClickHouse query errors: none
- slow query log: two queries over 1 second, both from my own checks
- memory of the ClickHouse node: stable

The loader was still lagging by about 2 seconds behind the topic, which is within what I expected. I will keep both customers on for a few days before adding more.

summary: Asked Mara about customers with half hour timezones; two customers use them, so their daily panels stay on the raw table for now
body:
The timezone difference in the daily panel from last week turned out to be a real design question, so I asked Mara this morning. She knew the answer at once: customers can set any offset in their account settings, and two of them use half hour offsets. One is in India and the other in Newfoundland.

The hourly rollup table groups by whole hours in UTC. For a customer with a half hour offset, a local day does not start on an hour border of that table. Summing 24 rollup rows therefore gives numbers that are wrong at the edges, which is exactly the mismatch I saw in the comparison for one customer.

We talked through three options. The first was to build a rollup per half hour for everybody, which doubles the rows for a problem that touches two customers. The second was to build special rollups only for those customers, which adds a new thing to maintain. The third was to leave their daily panels on the raw events table.

We chose the third for now. The raw table is fast enough, because the daily panel filters on customer and a date range and the ordering key covers both. I tested it on the staging copy of the customer with the larger volume, and the query took 0.6 seconds for 30 days.

I added a setting in the query builder that lists the customers whose daily panels always use the raw table. At the moment it holds two customer ids and is read from the config file. The comparison for those two customers now agrees with Postgres.

I wrote a note in the open points that this should be revisited if more customers with such offsets come in. Mara will tell Sam so support knows about the limit if somebody asks.

summary: Asked Mara about customers with half hour timezones; two customers use them, so their daily panels stay on the raw table for now
body:
Followed up on the timezone limit of the hourly rollup. Mara queried the settings table and found two customers with a timezone that has a 30 or 45 minute offset.

For those, daily panels cannot be built from UTC hourly rollups without error. The builder already falls back to the raw table in that case. Both customers are mid-sized, so the raw query is still fast, around 400 ms.

I added a test with a fixed timezone offset of 5 hours 30 minutes to make sure the fallback is used. I also logged a note in the migration checklist for those two customers, so I do not forget to check their dashboards by hand when they are enabled.

summary: Wrote the runbook page for the ClickHouse loader: how to restart it, how to read the lag panel, and what to do when a batch is rejected
body:
Wrote a short runbook for the loader because Tobias is on call next week and has not worked with it yet.

The page covers how to restart the service in ECS and what to expect afterwards: the loader resumes from the committed offset and the dedup logic handles the repeated batch. It also explains the three panels in Grafana and which numbers matter.

A section on rejected batches describes the error message ClickHouse returns for a malformed row, where the loader writes the rejected batch, and how to replay it after fixing the cause. I tested that by hand with a broken row in staging.

Tobias read it and asked two questions, which I answered in the text: how to check the offset by hand, and who to wake up. The second answer is me or Mara. The page lives in the docs repo next to the other runbooks.

summary: Enabled ClickHouse for five more customers after two quiet days; the dashboard p95 fell from about 2 seconds to 200 ms across them
body:
The first two customers ran for two days without an error, so I enabled five more this evening, ranging from small to mid-sized.

Before enabling each one I ran the comparison script against its data. All five passed within tolerance. One customer showed a difference in the retention panel, which turned out to be future-dated events again, and not a new problem.

After the change the combined p95 of the dashboard API for these customers fell from about 2 seconds to 200 ms. The loader lag stayed under 3 seconds, and the batch duration tail did not grow.

A support ticket from one of the five customers about a timeout last month is closed by this change. I told Sam so. The large customers are next, but I want to see the load on the ClickHouse node with them first, and Tobias will help plan the sizing.

summary: Sized the ClickHouse node for the large customers with Tobias and found that the current instance has enough disk but too little memory for the biggest queries
body:
Sat down with Tobias to decide whether the staging-sized ClickHouse node can carry the large customers. Disk is fine: the 90 day sample took 38 GB, so even a full year per customer fits with large room to spare.

Memory is the issue. I ran the heaviest queries of the largest customer with the real data volume. Two of them used about 11 GB of RAM at peak, and the node has 16 GB. With several panels running at once, that would hit the memory limit.

We looked at two options. One is a bigger instance, the other is lowering max_memory_usage per query and rewriting the two queries to use less. We decided to do both: move to an instance with 32 GB, and set a per-query limit of 6 GB so one bad query cannot take down the node.

Tobias will write the Terraform change and plan the move for a quiet hour. Because the data is on its own volume, the move is a detach and attach, with the loader paused for a few minutes. Meanwhile I will look at the two heavy queries to see why they use so much memory.

summary: Found why two heavy dashboard queries use 11 GB: a GROUP BY on a high cardinality path column; pre-aggregating by path hash cut the memory to 2 GB
body:
Looked into the two queries that used most of the memory. Both group by the full page path, and the largest customer has tens of millions of distinct paths per month, so the hash table gets very large.

First I tried setting max_bytes_before_external_group_by. It works, but the query became about four times slower because of the spill to disk, so I dropped that idea.

The second idea was better. The panels only show the top 50 paths, so I added a second materialized view that aggregates per customer, day and path, and reads from it with a limit. The path column is stored as is, but the grouping happens in the view, at insert time, in small pieces.

Results for the largest customer in staging, 30 day range:
- top pages: 11 GB and 1.9 s before, 2 GB and 0.3 s after
- top referrers: 9 GB and 1.6 s before, 1.7 GB and 0.25 s after

The new views make the insert path slightly heavier. The loader batch duration went up by about 10 percent, which I accept. I still need to fill the views for old data with the backfill and to compare the top lists with the raw results. Both are on tomorrow's list.

summary: Filled the path and referrer views from the raw table and compared the top 50 lists for all ten migrated customers; they match, apart from ties at the bottom
body:
Filled the two new views for the existing data with an INSERT SELECT from the raw table, in day-sized chunks so memory stayed low. The largest customer took about 25 minutes, and the others a few minutes each.

Then I compared the top 50 paths and top 50 referrers from the views to the same lists computed from the raw table, for all ten migrated customers and three date ranges each. The counts match for every row.

The differences are only at the bottom of the lists. When several paths have the same count at rank 50, the two queries choose different ones. I added the path as a tie-break in the view read, so the order is now stable and the same on both sides.

A second finding: the path column in the view can contain very long values, because some customers send full URLs with query strings of several kilobytes. That makes the view table larger than needed. I looked at the biggest values and found they are mostly tracking parameters. I will ask Mara whether the ingest side should cut paths at a maximum length. For now I did not change any data.

The query builder reads from the new views for the top lists. I ran the whole test suite and it passed. I will enable it for the migrated customers tomorrow, after the node has the new memory.

Open items:
- decision on path length with Mara
- node move by Tobias
- large customers still on Postgres

summary: Asked Mara about cutting long page paths at ingest; she prefers to keep the raw value and cut only in the views at 512 characters
body:
Talked to Mara about the multi-kilobyte paths. She does not want to change the ingest side, since customers may use the full URL in the search later, and the raw value is the source of truth.

We agreed to cut the value only when it is written to the path view, at 512 characters, using substring in the view definition. The raw table keeps the whole string. Top lists show the first 512 characters, which is more than the console can display anyway.

I will change the view definition and refill it, which takes about half an hour in staging. Since a changed view needs a refill, I noted the steps in the migration notes.

summary: Recreated the path view with the 512 character cut and refilled it; the table shrank by 31 percent and the top lists are unchanged
body:
Recreated the path aggregation view with substring(path, 1, 512) and refilled it from the raw table in staging, following the steps from the notes: drop the view, truncate the target, recreate, fill in day chunks.

The target table went from 5.2 GB to 3.6 GB for the 90 day sample, a drop of 31 percent. The merge of parts also got faster, because there are fewer large strings to compare.

I repeated the comparison of the top 50 lists with the raw results, again for the ten customers. Only one customer had a changed list: two paths that were identical in the first 512 characters were now counted together. That is the expected effect of the cut, and the combined count equals the sum of the two raw counts.

I added a test for it with a path of 2,000 characters. The change is merged, and I will apply the same steps in production once the node move is done.

summary: Tobias moved the ClickHouse volume to the 32 GB instance in a quiet hour; the loader was paused for 4 minutes and caught up in under 2 minutes after that
body:
Tobias and I did the node move early this morning. He had the Terraform change reviewed yesterday, and I paused the loader at 08:00 so it would not write during the detach.

The volume was detached, attached to the new instance, and ClickHouse started with the existing data. The total pause of the loader was 4 minutes. After the restart I checked row counts of the raw table and the rollups against the numbers I wrote down before, and they were equal.

The loader resumed from its committed offset. It had about 1,200 events per second waiting and caught up in under 2 minutes. No batch was rejected and no duplicate was found by the check I run on event ids.

We also set max_memory_usage to 6 GB per query in the user profile of the API. I ran the two former heavy queries once more to confirm they stay far below that. They use around 2 GB now.

summary: Applied the path and referrer views in production, filled them for the migrated customers and switched the top list panels to them
body:
With the bigger node in place, I created the path and referrer views in production using the steps from the notes. I filled them in day chunks, one customer at a time, and kept an eye on the node memory in Grafana. It never went above 40 percent.
