After the fill, I ran the comparison script of the top lists for the ten migrated customers against Postgres. All matched except the expected merged paths of one customer, which I recognized from yesterday's test.

Then I switched the panels to read from the views. Timings for the biggest migrated customer:
- top pages 30 days: 1.8 s to 0.28 s
- top referrers 30 days: 1.5 s to 0.22 s

Loader batch duration rose by about 12 percent after the views were added, and lag stayed under 3 seconds. I added the two views to the runbook, including the warning that changing a view means a refill.

I have not yet enabled the large customers. Tomorrow I plan to look at their query load patterns first, so I know which hours are risky.

summary: Looked at the query load pattern of the three largest customers to pick a safe hour for enabling them on ClickHouse
body:
Pulled the dashboard API logs of the last two weeks and counted queries per hour for the three largest customers. Two of them peak between 09:00 and 11:00 UTC, when their teams start the day. The third has an even load with a small peak in the evening.

The quietest window for all three is between 03:00 and 05:00 UTC, with fewer than 20 dashboard queries per hour. I would like to enable them in the late afternoon instead, when load is moderate but I am around to watch, and not at night.

I also counted the longest date ranges that are requested. About 6 percent of queries ask for 12 months, which the raw table handles slower, around 2 seconds for the biggest customer. The rollups cover those queries for hourly or daily panels. I will check that the builder picks the rollup for every 12 month request.

Plan: enable the smallest of the three tomorrow at 16:00, wait a day and then add the others.

summary: Enabled the first large customer on ClickHouse at 16:00 yesterday-style slot plan, then checked the full day; p95 fell from 7 seconds to 0.4 seconds with no errors
body:
Enabled the smallest of the three large customers this morning instead of the afternoon, after the comparison script passed for them over the night. I preferred to watch the morning peak, because that is when the load is highest.

Before the change, the p95 for the customer's dashboard was about 7 seconds, and the old Postgres query timed out a few times per week. After the change, p95 was 0.4 seconds over the morning peak. The slowest single query was the 12 month unique users panel at 1.3 seconds.

I checked the logs for errors and found none. ClickHouse memory peaked at 9 GB on the 32 GB node, and the slow query log had four entries, all above 1 second but below 2.

Sam asked the customer's account contact whether they noticed anything. The answer was that the dashboards simply felt faster. The customer's own scripts that call the API also finished sooner.

I looked at one more thing: the rollup use for 12 month ranges. The builder picked the rollup for all panels except the half hour timezone case, which is not relevant for this customer.

Next steps are the other two large customers, which I plan for the coming days if this one stays quiet.

summary: Wrote down the steps and checks for enabling a customer on ClickHouse so Mara or Tobias can do the remaining ones without me
body:
Turned my own routine into a checklist in the docs repo. Steps: run the comparison script, note Postgres timings, enable the switch, watch Grafana for the first hour, check the loader lag, tell Sam.

I also added how to turn the switch off again and what to say to the customer if numbers differ: future-dated events are excluded, and approximate counts differ by under 0.5 percent.

Mara read it and added a line about customers with half hour timezones. The list of those two customers is in the checklist now.

summary: Enabled the other two large customers; one showed a slow 12 month panel at 3 seconds, which a missing rollup column explained and a small view change fixed
body:
The first large customer stayed quiet for two days, so I enabled the second one in the morning and the third after lunch.

The second customer was fine. The third customer's dashboard had one slow panel, the 12 month event type breakdown, at about 3 seconds. I looked at the query plan: it read the raw table because the hourly rollup did not have the event subtype column that this customer's panel groups by.

Only this customer uses the subtype in a panel, so I did not want to add it to the main rollup, which would increase its size for everybody. I created a separate small view at daily resolution with customer, event type, subtype and a count. Its fill from the raw table took 6 minutes.

After the change the panel took 0.2 seconds. I compared the numbers with the raw query for three date ranges, and they were equal.

Overall results after all three large customers were on:
- dashboard p95: 6 to 8 seconds before, 0.3 to 0.5 seconds after
- ClickHouse node memory peak: 14 GB of 32 GB
- loader lag: under 3 seconds
- errors: none

The remaining customers are small and I plan to enable them in groups of five. I should still tell Tobias the memory peak, to keep the node size under review as more customers and views are added.

summary: Enabled the last 20 small customers in groups of five, including the two with half hour timezones; all dashboards now read from ClickHouse
body:
Went through the remaining customers in four groups using the checklist. Each group passed the comparison script first. Differences were only the known ones: future-dated events, approximate counts and the merged long paths.

The two customers with half hour timezones needed a manual check. The builder used the raw table for their daily panels as designed, and the numbers matched Postgres for three date ranges. Their daily panel p95 is around 400 ms, which is fine.

After the last group, I looked at the node. Memory peaked at 15 GB, loader lag stayed below 3 seconds, and the slow query log had a few entries from the 12 month ranges.

One customer reported that the number in their conversion panel changed by 0.3 percent compared with last week. That is the approximate unique count. I sent Sam a short explanation she could forward, and she did.

All 40 customers read their dashboards from ClickHouse now. The Postgres events table is still being written, and I want to leave it that way for a while as a fallback. Tomorrow I will write down what is left: the removal of the switch code, and a plan for when to stop writing events to Postgres.

summary: Listed what remains after the move of all dashboards to ClickHouse: the switch code, the dual writes to Postgres, the old queries and the backfill of the oldest events
body:
Wrote a list of the remaining work, now that every customer is on ClickHouse. I went through the code and the settings table to find everything that still depends on the old path.

The list:
- the per customer switch in the query builder and the settings column
- the Postgres versions of the 14 queries, which the comparison script still uses
- the dual write of events into the Postgres events table
- the backfill for events older than the first 90 days, which is only done for 60 percent of customers
- the alert rules that still point at Postgres query times

I checked the backfill status for each customer. 24 customers are complete, and 16 have older data that was not copied. Three of those have more than a year of history, which will take a few hours each at the current speed of the tool.

I discussed the order with Mara. She wants the backfill finished first, then a week of waiting, then the end of the dual write, and only after that the removal of the switch code. The comparison script stays until the end, because it is a good safety net.

I started the backfill for the first of the three long-history customers in id ranges overnight, with a limit on the insert rate so the loader is not slowed down. The progress is tracked in the backfill state table.

summary: Checked the overnight backfill of the first long-history customer: 78 percent copied, no errors, and the loader lag stayed under 3 seconds
body:
Looked at the backfill from last night. It copied 78 percent of the id ranges for the first long-history customer, about 410 million events, at the limited rate.

The state table shows no failed range. I spot checked row counts per month for the copied part against Postgres and found them equal. The rollups and the path views filled themselves during the backfill, so the history shows up in the dashboards as it arrives.

Loader lag stayed under 3 seconds during the whole night, so the insert rate limit seems right. Node memory peaked at 17 GB during a large merge, which is higher than during the day. I will keep an eye on it for the next two customers.

The tool will finish the rest of this customer in about two hours. I plan to start the second one right after and to compare the monthly counts again when it is done.

summary: Removed the query builder switch for the dashboards after checking that no customer still reads from the Postgres path, so the builder only emits ClickHouse SQL now
body:
The switch was added in the first week of the migration so each customer could be moved on its own. Since all customers have been on ClickHouse for a few days, it only adds branches that nobody takes. I grepped for every use of the flag and found it in the query builder, in two route handlers and in the settings loader.

I removed the flag from the settings schema and deleted the Postgres variants of the 14 dashboard queries. The builder tests that compared both paths were replaced by tests that check the generated ClickHouse SQL against stored snapshots. The suite went from 212 to 187 tests and still passes.

One thing kept me from deleting everything: the two customers with half hour timezones still use a raw table fallback for the daily panels. That code is separate from the switch, so I left it alone and put a comment on it.

I deployed to staging and clicked through the dashboards of three customers. Panels render the same as before, and the error rate stayed flat for an hour. The production deploy waits until tomorrow morning so Mara can watch the first hours.

The dual writes to Postgres are the next item on the list. They need a separate look, because the backfill still reads from the Postgres events table.

summary: Deployed the removal of the Postgres dashboard path to production and saw no change in error rate or p95 over the afternoon
body:
Mara reviewed the diff from this morning and had one comment: keep a short note in the runbook that the Postgres path no longer exists. I added that and deployed.

I watched the dashboard error rate, the p95 and the ClickHouse query log for three hours. Error rate stayed at 0.1 percent, which is the usual noise from client disconnects. The p95 over all customers was 210 ms, as before.

The query log showed no queries for the old Postgres reports path, which confirms that nothing was calling it. Postgres CPU also dropped a little in the afternoon, from about 38 to 31 percent, since the analytics reads are gone.

The backfill for the long-history customer finished at 17:50 with no errors. I compared row counts per day with Postgres for the full range and they match.

Next is the question of the dual writes. I will look at what the loader does on a Postgres failure before I touch them.

summary: Read through the ingest worker's dual write path and found that a Postgres write failure still blocks the ClickHouse loader from committing its offsets
body:
I wanted to know what happens to the loader if Postgres is slow, since the dual writes are still active. The worker writes the batch to Postgres first, then hands it to the queue consumer for ClickHouse.

In the code, both writes sit in one function and the offset commit comes after both. If Postgres returns an error, the batch is retried as a whole. That means a Postgres problem delays ClickHouse too, even though the dashboards no longer need Postgres for events.

I reproduced this in staging by blocking the Postgres port for 30 seconds. The loader lag grew to 41 seconds and recovered about 20 seconds after the port opened.

This is a good reason to end the dual writes soon. But the events table in Postgres is still the source for the oldest backfill ranges and for the search reindex, so I cannot just switch it off.

I wrote the findings in the migration notes and listed the two readers of the events table that remain. I will ask Mara tomorrow whether the reindex can read from somewhere else.

summary: Asked Mara whether the nightly reindex can stop reading events from Postgres; she says it needs the raw payload, which ClickHouse keeps too
body:
I asked Mara about the two remaining readers of the Postgres events table. The reindex job reads the full event body and a few metadata columns.

She checked the ClickHouse schema and confirmed that the raw payload column holds the same JSON. So the reindex could read from ClickHouse, but the read would be a big scan, and she does not want that to compete with dashboard queries during the day.

We agreed to test it at night first. She will write a reader that pulls ranges by event id and run it on staging this week.

Until then the dual writes stay.

summary: Wrote a ClickHouse reader for the reindex job that pulls events in id ranges and ran it on staging against a copy of one large customer
body:
Mara had started the reader, so I took over the testing part today. The reader replaces the Postgres query in the reindex job and fetches events by id range from ClickHouse, 50,000 rows per request.

The first run on staging was slow: 14 minutes for 9 million events, against 6 minutes from Postgres. The cause was that the table is ordered by customer and time, not by id, so each id range scanned many parts. I changed the reader to page by customer and timestamp instead and carry the last id as a tiebreaker.

With that change the same run took 5 minutes. Memory use of the ClickHouse node stayed under 9 GB during the run.

I then compared the documents that the job produced with the ones from the Postgres run. I hashed the documents and compared per customer. For 9 million events, 14 differed. All 14 had a payload with a unicode escape sequence that Postgres normalizes in jsonb and ClickHouse keeps as it came in.

Those differences are harmless for search, since OpenSearch normalizes the text anyway. I added the case to the comparison script as a known difference.

Left to do: a run for all customers on staging over a night, and a check of how it affects dashboard latency while it runs. I set up the night run for 02:00 staging time.

summary: The night run of the new reindex reader on staging finished in 52 minutes with no dashboard slowdown; Postgres is no longer needed for it
body:
I checked the staging run from last night. The whole reindex took 52 minutes for all staging customers, compared with 47 minutes on the Postgres reader. That is acceptable.

During the run I had a script query the dashboard API every 10 seconds. The p95 stayed at 230 ms, and the highest single request was 640 ms. I saw no memory warnings on the node.

The document counts per customer match the previous night's index exactly. The hash comparison found the same unicode difference as before and nothing else.

I looked at one more risk, which is a batch that fails in the middle. The reader keeps the last customer and timestamp, so a restarted job continues from there. I killed the job twice during the run in a second test and it resumed correctly both times.

Mara will merge the reader tomorrow and switch the production reindex to it for one night, with the Postgres reader still available behind a setting. If that works, the reindex stops reading the events table.

I also noted that the backfill tool is the last user of the Postgres events table after that. It will be done once the oldest customer is copied.

summary: Documented the loader's failure modes in the runbook after replaying three kinds of broken batches in staging
body:
The runbook page for the loader says what to do when a batch is rejected, but not why batches get rejected. I replayed three kinds of broken batches in staging to write that part properly.

The first was an event with a timestamp that did not parse. The loader rejects the row, writes it to the dead letter topic and carries on with the rest. The second was a batch with a column type mismatch, for example a string in a numeric field. The whole batch is rejected, because ClickHouse refuses the insert, and the loader splits it in halves until it finds the bad rows. That took 11 steps for a batch of 2,000 rows with one bad row.

The third was an oversized payload above 1 MB. The loader drops the payload column, keeps the metadata and marks the row as truncated.

For each case I added the log line to look for and the number to expect on the lag panel. The split case makes the lag jump for a short moment, which looked like a stall before I knew about it.

I also added a short list of what not to do. Do not restart the loader while it splits a batch, because it starts again from the full batch. Do not clear the dead letter topic before somebody has looked at the rows.

Sam read the page and asked for a plain description of the lag panel for the support team. I will write that next.

summary: Traced the ingest worker's dual write path again for the Postgres commit order and wrote down which failures can leave ClickHouse and Postgres out of step
body:
I spent the morning reading how the ingest worker writes one batch to both stores, because the plan to end the dual writes depends on knowing exactly what can go wrong in between. The worker writes to Postgres first and then hands the same batch to the ClickHouse loader through the queue. If the Postgres insert fails, the batch is retried, and the loader waits for it. That is the blocking behavior I found last week.

I listed four failure cases and tried each one in staging. A Postgres timeout leaves ClickHouse behind by one batch until the retry succeeds. A worker crash after the Postgres commit but before the offset commit replays the batch, and the loader's batch id check drops the repeat. A rejected ClickHouse batch leaves Postgres ahead, and the lag panel shows it within a few seconds. A full Postgres disk stops everything, which is the worst case and the main reason to end the dual writes.

In staging I blocked the Postgres port for two minutes during a steady stream of 2,000 events per second. The queue lag grew to about 240,000 events and cleared in under four minutes once the port opened again. No events were lost and the counts matched afterwards. The same test with the ClickHouse port blocked behaved better, since the queue simply holds the data.

I wrote the four cases into a short note with the observed lag numbers and the commands I used to block the ports. Mara read it and agreed that the order of writes should change so ClickHouse goes first. She also asked for a side topic for failed Postgres writes instead of blocking, and I added that to the plan. The next step is the worker change itself, with a staging test for each case. I did not touch production code today.

summary: Wrote the plain description of the loader lag panel for support, with three example situations and what each means for customers
body:
Sam asked for a version of the lag panel description that does not need knowledge of the loader. I wrote it as a short page in the support docs.

The panel shows the seconds between an event arriving at the ingest API and its appearance in ClickHouse. Normal is under 5 seconds. Between 5 and 60 seconds, dashboards are a little behind but nothing is lost. Above 60 seconds, customers may see missing recent data and support should tell the on-call.

I added three examples from staging tests. A short pause after a restart gives a brief jump. A bad batch gives a jump that falls again in a minute. A stuck loader gives a line that climbs without stopping.

For each example I wrote what customers may notice and what to say to them. I avoided words like offset and partition. Sam read it and changed two sentences to sound more like the other support pages.

I also linked the page from the runbook so on-call people can find the technical version from it.

summary: Production reindex ran on the ClickHouse reader for three nights with no differences in search results, so the Postgres reader setting is removed
body:
Three nights have passed since the switch. The job took between 55 and 60 minutes each time and the document counts stayed in line with the event volume.

I also ran a set of 40 saved search queries from the support team before and after the switch and compared the results. The top ten hits were identical for 39 queries. The one difference was a tie in scores where the order changed, which has happened before between reindex runs.

I removed the fallback setting and the old Postgres query from the reindex code. Mara approved the change this afternoon.

The backfill tool is now the only reader of the Postgres events table apart from the dual write itself. The oldest customer has 62 percent of its range copied. At the current speed it needs about four more days.

Once that is done I can plan the end of the dual writes.

summary: Checked the backfill of the oldest customer after the night: 71 percent copied, no errors, and the loader lag stayed below 4 seconds
body:
The backfill ran through the night on the oldest customer, which has the most events. It copied about 9 percent of the range, which is a bit slower than the days before.

I looked for the reason and found that the Postgres side was busy with the nightly vacuum from 03:00 to 04:30, which slowed the range reads. The copy speed dropped from 40,000 to 25,000 rows per second in that period.

No errors were logged and the rows per range match between both stores for the first 40 ranges I sampled. The lag panel showed 2 to 4 seconds all night.

I left the speed as it is. Lowering it would only make the backfill take longer.

summary: Asked Tobias whether the Postgres vacuum window can move so it does not overlap the backfill; he says it can shift by an hour, not more
body:
Following the slow hours from last night, I asked Tobias if the vacuum schedule could be moved. The window is set in the maintenance settings of the instance.

He said he can shift it by an hour without trouble, but a bigger shift would collide with the backup. The backup runs at 05:00 and must not overlap with vacuum on the big tables.

Since the gain would only be about 15 minutes per night, I decided not to ask for the change. The backfill will finish in a few days anyway.

I noted the vacuum window in the backfill notes, so that anyone watching the speed knows the cause of the dip.

summary: Wrote a script that compares event counts per customer and day between Postgres and ClickHouse and ran it on all customers that are fully backfilled
body:
Before the dual writes end, I want a check that tells us if the two stores hold the same events. I wrote a script that counts events per customer and day in both stores and prints the differences.

The script reads from a Postgres replica to avoid load on the main database. For ClickHouse it uses the raw table, not the rollups, because the rollups hide duplicates. It runs customers in parallel, four at a time.

I ran it on the 38 customers that are fully copied. For 35 of them the counts match on every day. Three customers show small differences on a total of 9 days.

I looked at the 9 days. On 6 of them, Postgres has more events, with between 1 and 14 rows missing in ClickHouse. These are the events with future timestamps, which the dashboards exclude, and the backfill stores them under their future date. The script had counted them on the wrong day because it cut days by the Postgres session timezone.

On the other 3 days ClickHouse has a few more rows. That fits the double inserts from the crash tests of the loader a few weeks ago, before the batch ids were made safe. Counts were 3, 5 and 2 extra rows.

I fixed the timezone in the script to use UTC on both sides and ran it again. Now only the 3 days with extra rows remain. I will check whether the extra rows are exact duplicates and remove them from ClickHouse if so.

The oldest customer is not in the check yet, since its backfill is still running.

summary: The extra rows on three days in ClickHouse were exact duplicates from the loader crash tests, and I removed them with a targeted delete
body:
I looked at the three days from the count comparison. For each one I grouped the rows by event id and found 10 ids that appeared twice, all inserted within the same second.

The insert times match the days when I killed the loader during inserts to test the batch safety. So these are leftovers from the test, not a new bug.

I deleted the duplicate rows using an ALTER TABLE DELETE with the event id and the insert time of the second copy. The mutation finished in under a minute for each day. I ran the count script again and all 38 customers now match.

The rollup tables had counted those rows twice. I refilled the hourly rollups for the three days and checked the numbers against the raw table.

summary: Planned how to end the dual writes to Postgres in three steps, with a check after each step and a way back until the last one
body:
The backfill is nearly done, so I wrote the plan for ending the dual writes. I discussed it with Mara in the morning and changed two parts after her comments.

Step one: the ingest worker writes to ClickHouse first and to Postgres second, and a Postgres failure no longer blocks the offset commit. Failed Postgres writes go to a side topic. This removes the coupling that I found in the staging test.

Step two: the Postgres write is turned off with a setting, one day for a small customer group, then for all. The count script runs every night to show any difference between the stores. Postgres still holds all the old data, so going back means turning the setting on and copying the gap with the backfill tool.

Step three: after two weeks without problems, the events table in Postgres is dropped from the schema and an archive dump is stored. Mara wants the dump kept for at least a year.

Mara also asked about the size of the table. It is 410 GB and a large part of the Postgres disk. Dropping it will make backups much faster, which Tobias will like.

I added the risks to the plan: the audit log reads some event ids, so I need to check whether it joins on the events table. I will do that next.

summary: Checked every reader of the Postgres events table, found the audit log joins on it in one report, and moved that report to store the needed fields itself
body:
To be sure that nothing else needs the events table, I searched the whole repository and the SQL of the Grafana dashboards for its name. I also checked the Postgres statistics for queries on that table over the last week.

The code search found the ingest worker, the backfill tool, the count script and a few old migrations. The statistics added one more: a weekly report of the audit log that joins audit entries with events by event id to show the event type.

The report is used by Sam and a few customers who ask for activity summaries. It takes about 40 seconds and is run rarely, which is why it had not shown up before.

I looked at what the report needs from the events: only the event type and the customer id. The audit log table stores the event id because of how the first version was made. I added a column for the event type to the audit log table and filled it with one update in batches of 100,000 rows. That took 25 minutes and had no effect on the other queries.

Then I changed the report to read the new column and compared its output with the old one for four weeks of data. The numbers match.

The writer of the audit log now fills the column when it writes a new entry. I tested this in staging with a few hundred entries.

After this change, the events table has no readers other than the dual write and the tools of the migration. I updated the plan with this result.

summary: Changed the ingest worker so ClickHouse is written first and a Postgres failure goes to a side topic, tested with a blocked Postgres port in staging
body:
This is step one of the plan. The worker used to write the batch to Postgres and then to ClickHouse in one function, and the offset was committed only after both.

I changed the order. The batch goes to ClickHouse through the loader path first, then the offset is committed. The Postgres write happens afterwards and, if it fails, the batch is published to a side topic called events-pg-failed with the original batch id.

A small consumer reads that topic and tries the Postgres write again with a pause that grows from 1 to 60 seconds. After 10 failures the batch stays in the topic and an alert is sent. The batch ids make the Postgres insert safe against repeats, as they do on the ClickHouse side.

I tested it in staging with the same method as before. I blocked the Postgres port for 30 seconds while the load generator ran at production speed. This time the loader lag stayed at 2 to 3 seconds. The side topic collected 18 batches, and after the port opened the consumer wrote them all within 40 seconds.

I ran the count script afterwards and the stores match.

One test failed on the first try: the side topic consumer did not start when the topic did not exist yet. I added the topic to the Terraform of staging and production, and Tobias will apply it.

The change goes to production after Tobias has created the topic.

summary: Switched the three largest customers off the Postgres event writes in the quiet hour and confirmed the counts match, so no customer writes events to Postgres any more
body:
I turned off the Postgres event writes for the three largest customers today in the quiet hour, which completes the second step of the plan. Before the change I ran the count script for all three and saved the output, so there was a clean baseline. Tobias was on hand in case the Postgres side needed anything, and the change was one flag per customer, set one at a time.

After each flag I watched the ingest error rate, the loader lag and the Postgres write rate for ten minutes. The loader lag stayed below 3 seconds the whole time, and the error rate did not move. The Postgres write load dropped by another large step, and the primary now shows mostly settings and audit log traffic. The write latency on the accounts tables also became a little steadier.

In the evening I ran the count script again on the full day for all 33 customers. Every customer matched per day between the stores, including the three large ones up to the hour of the switch. The side topic for failed Postgres writes stayed empty, as expected, since nothing writes there now.

The way back still exists: the flag can be turned off again, and the backfill tool can copy a range from ClickHouse to Postgres if needed. That path ends when the table is dropped. Next is step three, the archive dump of the events table and the restore test, which I will do after a few quiet days. I told Mara and Sam that dashboards and search are unaffected.

summary: Turned off the Postgres event writes for four small customers and checked the count script the next morning; all stores still match for them
body:
This is the first part of step two. I picked four small customers and set the new flag that skips the Postgres write for them. The flag lives in the settings table and the worker reads it every minute.

I turned it on at 17:30 yesterday. In the morning I ran the count script for these customers over the last 24 hours. ClickHouse holds all events and Postgres stops at 17:30 as expected.

The dashboards for the four customers worked as always. No customer contacted support and the error rate stayed the same.

The Postgres write rate fell by about 1 percent, which is what four small customers should account for.

I also checked that the side topic received nothing from these customers. It did not. The audit log report from last week works without the events table, so the weekly run of Sam's report had no problem either.

I will extend the flag to the next group of ten customers tomorrow.

summary: Extended the skip flag to ten more customers, then found the backfill tool still reads their newest ranges from Postgres and fixed its end condition
body:
After a quiet day, I turned off the Postgres writes for ten more customers. While I checked their counts, I noticed that the backfill tool log still listed them as having a range up to the current id.

The tool decides the end of the range by the highest id in Postgres at the start of a run. For customers whose Postgres writes stopped, that is the id from the moment of the switch, so the end is right. But for two of them the tool had started its range before the switch and had a later end id than the data in Postgres.

This did no harm, because the tool only reads, and it found no rows in the empty part of the range. But it made the progress numbers look wrong, as if 8 percent of the range was missing.

I changed the tool to take the end of the range from the settings: the time when the flag was set. If the flag is not set, it keeps using the highest id. I added a test for it with a fake settings table.

I ran the tool again for the two customers and the progress now shows 100 percent. The count script confirms that all twelve customers with the flag match.

The oldest customer finished its backfill during the night. Its count check passed on the first run, with no differences.

So all customers are copied now. The next group for the flag is the rest of the small customers.

summary: Turned off the Postgres event writes for all customers except the three largest, and the Postgres write load dropped by about 40 percent
body:
I set the flag for the remaining small and medium customers this afternoon, 33 in total. The three large ones keep their Postgres writes for two more days, because they carry most of the volume and I want one more day of data on the smaller groups first.

After the change, the Postgres write rate fell from about 9,000 to 5,400 rows per second. The CPU of the main instance went from 31 to 24 percent.

The loader lag did not change, and the count script for the 33 customers showed no differences for the period before the change. I will run it again tonight and tomorrow morning for the period after.

Tobias saw the lower write rate on the Postgres dashboard and asked whether the vacuum could be made less frequent. I told him to wait until the table is dropped, as the vacuum work will disappear with it.

The side topic stayed empty during the afternoon.

Tomorrow I will check the numbers and, if they are good, plan the switch for the three large customers.

summary: Count check after the change shows all 33 customers match; I scheduled the three large customers for the switch in the quiet hour tomorrow
body:
I ran the count script this morning for the period since yesterday afternoon. All 33 customers match between ClickHouse and the archive state in Postgres, which means that nothing was missing from ClickHouse and nothing unexpected was written to Postgres.

I also checked the dead letter topic. It holds 212 rejected rows from the whole day, the same normal level as before, mostly from unparsable timestamps.

For the three large customers, I picked the quiet hour at 04:00 with Tobias, who will be awake for the planned database work anyway. I will set the flag then and watch the lag and the write rate for an hour.

If something looks wrong, I can turn the flag off again and copy the gap with the backfill tool. I tested that way back in staging last week and it took 6 minutes for an hour of data.

After the switch, step two is complete and the two week wait of step three begins.

summary: Wrote the notes for step three: the archive dump of the Postgres events table, how to restore it, and what to check before the table is dropped
body:
While the wait for step three starts, I prepared the notes for dropping the table. Mara wants an archive dump that stays for at least a year, so I tested how to make and restore one.

On staging, I dumped the events table with pg_dump in the custom format, in parallel with four jobs. The staging table has 12 GB and the dump took 4 minutes and made a 3 GB file. Scaled up, the production table of 410 GB would take about 2.5 hours and make a file of around 100 GB.

I restored the staging dump into an empty database and compared row counts and a checksum over the id column. Both matched. The restore took 11 minutes.

The notes list the steps in order: make the dump from the replica, not the main instance, copy it to the archive bucket with versioning, verify the checksum from the bucket, restore a sample of one day to a scratch database, and only then drop the table.

I also wrote down who has to agree. Mara signs off on the dump, and Tobias on the bucket setting and the backup change afterwards.

The last item is a reminder to remove the dual write code, the side topic and its consumer after the drop.

summary: Wrote the archive dump script for the Postgres events table and tested a dump and restore on staging with a copy of one large customer; the counts matched after restore.
body:
The notes from this morning described the archive dump, but nothing had run yet, so I wrote scripts/archive_events.sh. It dumps the events table in id ranges with pg_dump in custom format, one file per range, and writes a manifest with row counts and sha256 sums.

On staging I loaded a copy of one large customer, about 41 million rows, and ran the dump. It took 19 minutes and produced 23 files, 11 GB in total. The manifest rows added up to the count in the table.

Then I restored into an empty database with pg_restore using four parallel jobs. That took 26 minutes. I compared per-day counts between the restored table and the original with the count script, and all days matched.

One problem came up. The first restore failed on the second range with a missing sequence owner, because the dump had been taken with the table alone. I added the --no-owner flag to both dump and restore, and the second try passed.

I also checked that the dump does not hold long locks. During the run the ingest path on staging kept writing, and the longest wait on the table was under 200 ms. The dump uses a snapshot, so that is as expected.

What is left: the production dump needs about 3 TB of free space in the archive bucket path, and I have to ask Tobias for the lifecycle rule so the files move to cold storage after a month. The dump itself waits until the last three customers are switched off the Postgres writes tomorrow.

summary: Checked the three large customers before tomorrow's switch: queue lag, Postgres write rate and ClickHouse loader lag are all calm, and I added a rollback line to the plan.
body:
Tomorrow in the quiet hour the three largest customers stop writing events to Postgres. Tonight I went through the checks one more time so that tomorrow is only execution.

First, the Postgres write rate. After the change for the small customers it is about 40 percent lower than a week ago, and the remaining writes come only from these three. The peak is about 2,900 rows per second, well under what the primary handled before.

Second, the loader lag in Grafana. For the last 24 hours it stayed under 3 seconds for all three, with one short bump to 6 seconds at the time of the hourly rollup. That bump is known and harmless.

Third, the side topic for failed Postgres writes. It has 0 messages. I also checked that the consumer for that topic is still running, so a failure would be seen.

The count script ran on all 33 customers a second time and showed no differences for any complete day. Today's partial day is skipped by design.

I added a rollback line to the plan. If counts differ after the switch, the skip flag for the customer is set back to false, and the backfill tool copies the missing range from ClickHouse into Postgres. I tested that command on staging with a gap of two hours, and it filled the gap in 40 seconds.

I told Mara what time the switch happens so she knows why the Postgres write graphs will drop in the morning. She had no objections. Nothing was changed in production tonight.

summary: Switched the three largest customers off the Postgres event writes in the quiet hour; counts matched in two checks and no customer writes events to Postgres now.
body:
The switch ran at 06:00 in the quiet hour. I set the skip flag one customer at a time, with ten minutes between them, and watched the loader lag and the error rate after each one.

The first customer was the one with the highest volume. After the flag the Postgres writes for it stopped within one deploy cycle, and the ClickHouse loader lag stayed at 2 seconds. The second and third showed the same picture.

After the last switch I ran the count script for the three customers on the hour before and the hour after the change. All counts matched, with no duplicates and no gaps. I ran it again two hours later on the full morning and got the same result.

The Postgres write load on the primary fell to almost nothing for the events table. Only a few rows per minute still arrive, which turned out to be test events from the staging health check, since it points at the production table by mistake. I noted that and will move it.

The side topic for failed Postgres writes stayed empty. The dashboards for the three customers loaded normally and the p95 did not change.

What comes now is step three of the plan: the archive dump of the table, and later the drop. Before the dump I want to wait two days with everything reading only from ClickHouse, to be sure no hidden reader exists. I will look at Postgres query statistics for the table during that time.

summary: Looked at pg_stat_statements for the events table after the switch and found two readers still active: a weekly export script and a support query saved in Metabase.
body:
Now that no customer writes events to Postgres, any query that still touches the events table is a risk for the drop. I reset the statistics for that table's queries yesterday evening and looked at them this morning.

There were 14 distinct statements. Most were the vacuum and the autoanalyze, which do not matter. Of the real readers, two were new to me.

The first is a weekly export script in the ops repository that Sam uses to send event counts to a customer who asked for them. It runs a count by day on the events table. It last ran on the weekend, and the numbers it gave would now be stale for recent days. I rewrote it to use the ClickHouse client with the same output format, and ran both versions for the last full week. The output was identical for every day.

The second is a saved question in Metabase called "events by type, last 30 days". Sam uses it for support calls. It had been run 9 times in the last two days. I asked Sam and she agreed to switch it to the ClickHouse connection. I changed the SQL since ClickHouse needs toStartOfDay instead of date_trunc, and checked that the result matched.

I also searched the repositories for the table name once more. Nothing new appeared apart from migration files and the archive script from yesterday.

I will reset the statistics again after these fixes and look in two days. If the list shows only maintenance, the dump can start.

summary: Moved the staging health check off the production events table; it was writing a few test rows per minute to Postgres by mistake.
body:
After the switch of the large customers, a few rows per minute still arrived in the Postgres events table. I traced them to the staging health check, which sends a test event every 15 seconds.

The check config in the staging repository had the production database URL in an old variable, DATABASE_URL_LEGACY, that the check script reads before the new one. That was left over from the first setup, when staging and production shared a host.

I changed the script to read only EVENTS_STORE_URL, which points at the staging ClickHouse. I deleted the legacy variable from the staging environment and from the template file so it cannot come back.

After the deploy I watched the table for twenty minutes. No new rows came in. I then deleted the 2,300 test rows with a delete on the test customer id, after checking with a select that nothing else was in the set.

I also checked that production health checks use the right variable. They do. No other service reads the legacy name according to a search of all repositories.

This was a small thing, but it would have made the final row count of the table look wrong before the archive dump.

summary: Wrote the plan for the final drop of the Postgres events table with checks before each command, and sent it to Tobias and Mara for review.
body:
The archive dump and the drop are the last steps of ending the dual writes, and they cannot be undone cheaply, so I wrote the plan down as a checklist in docs/events-table-retirement.md.

The order is: confirm the reader statistics show only maintenance, take the archive dump, verify the manifest, upload and verify the checksums in the bucket, restore one range on staging as a final test, rename the table to events_retired, wait seven days, then drop it.

The rename is the important part. If something still reads the table, it fails with a clear error and the table can be renamed back in a second. A drop would not allow that without the restore, which takes about 30 minutes per large range.

Each step has a check that has to pass before the next one. For example, before the rename, the row count of the table must equal the sum in the manifest, and the newest row must be older than the switch time of the last customer.

I also listed who to tell: Sam for the support queries, Mara for the reindex job, which no longer reads the table, and Tobias for disk space. After the drop, the Postgres storage should shrink by about 2.8 TB once the vacuum full or a table rewrite has run. I put in a note that the space is only returned to the operating system after the drop, not after the delete.

I sent the document to Tobias and Mara with a request for comments by tomorrow midday. Tobias already answered that the lifecycle rule for the archive bucket needs one day to set up.

summary: Tobias and Mara reviewed the retirement plan; one change added: keep the renamed table for ten days instead of seven, because of the monthly customer report.
body:
Both reviews came back this morning. Mara pointed out that the monthly report for two customers runs on the first of the month, and it could contain a path I missed. Seven days might pass before it runs.

I checked the report code. It reads from ClickHouse already, but one old helper still has a fallback to Postgres when the ClickHouse call fails. I removed the fallback and added a clear error instead.

Still, I changed the waiting time to ten days to cover the next run. Tobias confirmed that the bucket lifecycle rule is in place and that there is enough disk for the dump.

I updated the checklist with both changes. The dump starts after the statistics check tomorrow.

summary: Removed the Postgres fallback from the report helper and tested the failure case in staging, where a stopped ClickHouse node now gives a clear error instead of old data.
body:
Mara's review of the plan made me look at the report helper in the reports service. It had a try/catch around the ClickHouse call that fell back to the old Postgres query on any error.

That fallback was a good idea during the move, but now it is dangerous. The Postgres table has no data after the switch time of each customer, so a fallback would return silently wrong numbers, lower than the real ones, with no error.

I removed the fallback and the old SQL. If the ClickHouse query fails now, the helper throws a ReportSourceError with the query name and the cluster node, and the report job marks the run as failed and posts to the ops channel.

To test it, I stopped one ClickHouse node in staging and ran the report for a test customer. The query went to the second replica and succeeded, as it should. Then I stopped both and ran it again. The job failed with the new error within 8 seconds, the status was set, and the message appeared in the channel.

I also added a unit test for the error path, using a fake client that raises. It runs in under a second.

The change went to production after review by Mara. The report jobs of the afternoon ran fine with it.

summary: Started the archive dump of the Postgres events table in production after the reader statistics showed only maintenance statements; the first 9 of 23 ranges are done.
body:
The statistics check came first. After the export script and the Metabase question were moved, the list of statements on the events table held only vacuum, analyze and the checkpoint related ones over two days. No application reads.

I started scripts/archive_events.sh on the production replica, not the primary, to keep the load away from the write path. The replica lags by under a second, so the data is the final state because no new rows come in.

The dump runs in id ranges of about 130 million rows each. The first nine ranges are finished after 2 hours 10 minutes, each about 25 minutes, with manifest entries written. I checked the sha256 of three of them against the files in the bucket, and they match.

One thing I watched was the replica's disk read rate. It reached 220 MB/s but stayed within what Tobias said is fine, and the query latency of the replica for the admin console did not change.

The job runs in a tmux session on the ops host and writes a log. If the host restarts, the script skips ranges already in the manifest, so it can continue.

I will check the rest tonight and tomorrow morning. After the last range, the verification of the full manifest against the table count comes next.

summary: The archive dump of the events table finished with 23 ranges and a matching row count; one range was re-dumped after a checksum mismatch in the bucket upload.
body:
The dump finished in the late afternoon. Total rows in the manifest: 2,914,306,118. The count on the table, taken on the replica, gave the same number, and the difference is zero.

Then I verified every file in the bucket against the manifest sha256. Twenty-two files matched. The file for range 14 had a different checksum. Its size was also a few megabytes smaller than the local one.

I looked at the upload log and found a connection reset in the middle of the transfer, which the upload tool had retried but with a resumed part that was wrong. I deleted the object, uploaded the local file again with a whole-file checksum option, and compared again. This time it matched.

To be safe, I added a verification step to the script that downloads the checksum from the bucket metadata after each upload and compares it with the local one. A mismatch stops the run. I ran this step over all 23 files, and all passed.

The lifecycle rule from Tobias is active. The files are in standard storage and move to cold storage after 30 days. The bucket has versioning on and deletion protection for 90 days.

I also noted the restore time estimate for the full table: with four parallel jobs about 4 hours for all ranges, and about 20 minutes for a single range. This goes into the runbook.

Next: restore range 1 and range 14 on staging from the bucket files as a final check, then the rename. I did not rename anything today.

summary: Restored two ranges of the archive from the bucket onto staging and compared them with the production replica; both matched, so the table can be renamed.
body:
I ran the restore test from the bucket today, not from local files, since the bucket copy is the one that counts. I chose range 1, the oldest, and range 14, the one that had the upload problem.

The download of range 1 took 6 minutes and the restore with four jobs 22 minutes. For range 14, the download took 7 minutes and the restore 24 minutes. Neither one showed errors in pg_restore.

The comparison was done in three ways. First, the row count of each restored range against the manifest. Second, a checksum over the id column and the created_at column, computed as md5 of the string aggregate per thousand rows on both sides. Third, I took 5,000 random rows from each range and compared the full payload column byte by byte with the replica.

All three agreed for both ranges. The payload comparison found no difference, including for rows with unicode and large payloads over 100 KB.

I also tested what happens with the indexes. The dump has the table data only. The restore script creates the primary key and the index on customer id and day afterward, which took 9 minutes for one range. That is important for the runbook, because without the indexes a restored table is hard to query. I wrote it in.

With this, every condition on the checklist before the rename is true. I told Tobias and Mara and asked them to say if they know of anything else. Mara asked only that the rename happens outside the reindex window, which is now at night, so I picked the early afternoon tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the runbook page for restoring the retired events archive, including the index step and the time estimates measured on staging.
body:
Since the restore test worked, I turned my notes into a proper runbook page in the docs repository, docs/runbooks/restore-events-archive.md. Sam will use the same page if a customer asks for very old raw data that the retention has already removed from ClickHouse.

The page has these parts: where the files are, how to read the manifest, how to download and verify a range, how to restore into a scratch database, how to create the indexes, and how to query by customer and day.

I put in the measured times: about 7 minutes download, 24 minutes restore and 9 minutes for the indexes for one range of 130 million rows. For a single customer, restoring the full range is wasteful, so I added a way to restore a range and then run a select into a CSV for just one customer id. The select with the index takes less than a minute for the largest customer in the range.

I added the warning about the owner flag, because the first restore on staging failed without it. I also wrote down the schema of the table at the time of the dump, so that a restore into a later schema version does not surprise someone.

I asked Sam to read it as if she had never seen the topic. She found two places where I wrote a command without the bucket name and one place with an unclear word, "range", which I now explain with an example of ids.

The page is linked from the retirement plan. I also added a short line to the on-call notes so that the page can be found.

summary: Renamed the Postgres events table to events_retired in the early afternoon window and watched errors for two hours; nothing failed, and the ten day wait has started.
body:
The rename ran at 13:00 as planned. Before it, I went through the checklist line by line: reader statistics clean, manifest count equal to table count, bucket checksums verified, restore test passed, and Tobias and Mara informed.

The command was a single ALTER TABLE events RENAME TO events_retired inside a transaction, together with the renames of its sequence and its indexes so the names stay consistent. It needed an access exclusive lock for a very short moment. The lock was taken in 40 ms, since no queries were waiting on it.

After the rename I watched several signals. The error rate of the ingest API stayed at its normal level. The loader lag stayed under 3 seconds. The side topic for failed Postgres writes stayed empty, which also shows that nothing tries to write to the old name. The Postgres log showed no relation does not exist error for events.

I also tested a few paths on purpose. The dashboards of the three large customers loaded with the usual p95. The admin console event view loaded. The search reindex dry run in staging worked, as did the monthly report in a test run.

A reminder is now in the team calendar and in the retirement document: drop the table in ten days, after the monthly report has run. I wrote the exact drop command with the check of the manifest count beside it.

The write load on Postgres has fallen a lot, but the disk usage is the same until the drop. Tobias knows.

summary: Checked the Postgres error log and the on-call channel after the rename and found nothing about the events table; also confirmed the monitoring queries do not use it.
body:
Early in the morning I looked again at the places where a missing table would show up. The Postgres log for the last 17 hours had no error mentioning events or events_retired apart from my own test select.

The on-call channel had two alerts overnight. One was a disk warning on a staging host and one was a slow query on the audit log, neither related to the rename.

I also searched the Prometheus exporter config for the Postgres exporter. It has custom queries, and I found one that counted rows of the events table for a size graph. It would fail silently and give an empty graph. I changed it to read the size of events_retired from pg_class, so the graph for the table size stays until the drop, and I will remove it afterward.

The Grafana panel "events table size" showed data again after the exporter restarted. I checked that the other custom queries run without errors in the exporter log.

The ten day wait goes on.

summary: Looked at the biggest remaining Postgres tables after the events move: the audit log is now the largest, and its index on actor and time is bloated at 38 percent.
body:
With the events table out of the way, I wanted to see what the primary database looks like now, so I ran a size query and a bloat estimate on all tables above 1 GB.

The largest live table is the audit log at 61 GB, followed by the sessions archive at 9 GB and the settings history at 4 GB. The events_retired table is still 2.8 TB but is not counted as live.

For the audit log I checked the indexes. The index on actor_id and created_at has an estimated bloat of 38 percent, which means about 5 GB of waste. The cause is the cleanup job that deletes rows older than the retention and leaves holes in the index pages. The autovacuum keeps up with the dead rows but does not shrink the index.

I tested REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on a copy in staging. It took 14 minutes on that copy and the index went from 13.1 GB to 8.2 GB. No locks blocked writes, though concurrent reindex uses extra disk and takes longer under write load.

I did not run this in production yet. The audit log is written by every admin action, and I want Tobias to know the time slot first, since the vacuum window moved by an hour for the backfill, and this should not overlap with it. I wrote the proposal in the ops channel with the staging numbers.

I also noticed that the cleanup job deletes in one large statement per night. Splitting it into batches of 50,000 rows would be better for replica lag, which reached 4 seconds last night during the delete. That is a small change in the job, and I added a ticket.

No production change today.

summary: Changed the audit log cleanup job to delete in batches of 50,000 rows, and tested it on staging, where the replica lag during the run stayed under one second.
body:
The cleanup job for the audit log deleted all expired rows with a single DELETE every night. Last night that took 7 minutes and the replica lag rose to 4 seconds, which makes the admin console show stale audit entries for a short time.

I changed the job to delete in a loop. Each round selects 50,000 ids of expired rows with a limit, deletes them by primary key, commits, and sleeps for 200 ms. It stops when a round deletes fewer rows than the batch size.

On staging I filled the audit log with 3 million expired rows and ran the new job. It took 11 minutes in total, longer than the single statement, but the replica lag stayed under 1 second the whole time, and the writes from a parallel test client were not slowed.

I also added a log line per 20 batches with the total deleted so far, and a limit of 4 million rows per night so a mistake in the retention setting cannot delete everything in one go. If the limit is hit, the job logs a warning and continues the next night.

The change was reviewed by Mara and deployed. The first production run is tonight, and I will look at the lag graph tomorrow morning.

summary: Checked the audit log retention after the batch cleanup change: rows older than the policy are gone, the table stopped growing, and one customer's export still needs a longer window.
body:
After the cleanup job moved to batches of 50,000 rows, I looked at how the audit log behaved over its first full run in production. The job removed about 14 million rows older than the retention setting and finished in 47 minutes. Replica lag stayed under one second the whole time, and write latency for new audit entries was the same as before.

I then compared the row counts per customer before and after the run. For 39 of the 40 customers the numbers matched what the retention setting predicts. One customer has a contract that asks for a longer audit history than the default, and the job had deleted rows that this customer is entitled to keep. The retention value is global today, so nothing in the table says which customers need longer.

I restored the missing rows for that customer from last night's snapshot on staging and copied them back in one transaction. I checked the count and the oldest timestamp afterwards, and both match the contract. Then I paused the cleanup job so it cannot repeat the deletion tonight.

I wrote a short proposal for a per-customer retention column with the global value as the default, and sent it to Mara, because the audit log code is mostly hers. The cleanup job would read that column and skip nothing else. Until it is merged the job stays paused, and the table will grow for a few days, which is fine given the space we freed with the index rebuild. Next I will write the migration and a test with two customers that have different retention values.

summary: Ran REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on the audit log actor index in the quiet hour; the index shrank from 13 GB to 8 GB and write latency for audit entries did not change.
body:
The reindex of the index on audit_log (actor_id, created_at) ran in the quiet hour after Tobias confirmed the slot. I checked beforehand that the vacuum was not running on the table and that there was 20 GB of free disk on the primary.

I started REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY and watched pg_stat_progress_create_index. It took 17 minutes, a bit more than the 14 on staging because of the write traffic. The phases were as expected: building the index, then the validation scan, then the swap.

The index size went from 13.0 GB to 8.1 GB, so almost 5 GB came back. The estimated bloat is now 3 percent.

During the run I watched the p95 of the audit write in the admin API. It stayed at 6 ms, as in the normal hours, and the replica lag stayed under a second. No query waited on a lock for more than a few milliseconds.

One detail needs care: a failed concurrent reindex leaves an invalid index with the suffix _ccnew. I checked pg_index for invalid entries after the run, and there were none. I added that query to the runbook for future reindex work.

I also looked at the other indexes of the audit log. The index on resource_id is at 12 percent bloat, not worth a run now. I put a reminder to check the bloat again in two months.

The disk graph of the primary shows the 5 GB freed. Most of the space is still held by events_retired, which will go with the drop in a week.

summary: Answered Sam's question about how far back raw events can be shown to customers now that the Postgres table is archived; the answer is ClickHouse for the whole period.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel what she should say to a customer who wants to see raw events from the first months of their account, now that the old Postgres table is renamed and about to be dropped.

I checked what ClickHouse holds. The backfill finished for all customers, and the oldest event per customer is the same as in the Postgres archive, which I verified with a query for min(created_at) per customer on both sides, using the restored range 1 on staging. For all 33 customers the dates are identical.

So the answer for her is: all raw events are visible in the dashboards and in search exactly as before, and nothing was lost by the move. The archive dump is only a safety copy, and customers do not need it.

I then explained the one case where the archive matters. If a customer asks for an export of events that ClickHouse no longer has, the restore runbook applies, and she should ask me or Mara. I told her this should not happen soon, since the retention of the raw events in ClickHouse covers all the events that exist now.

Sam also asked whether the export from the admin console is slower now. I measured an export of one million events for a mid-size customer: 38 seconds from ClickHouse, compared with about 2 minutes 10 seconds from Postgres last month in the notes of the old export test. She can tell customers that exports are quicker.

I added both answers to the support FAQ in the docs, with the wording kept simple and no database names, because customers do not need them. Sam reviewed the text and changed one sentence to sound friendlier.

Nothing was changed in the systems for this.

summary: Cleaned up the code left over from the dual writes: removed the side topic consumer, the skip flag and two config options, after checking that nothing in production sets them.
body:
With the Postgres events table renamed and every customer on ClickHouse only, a number of pieces in the code have no purpose any more. I went through them one by one and removed those that are safe.

First the skip flag, events_postgres_skip, in the customer settings. All 33 customers have it set to true, so the flag has no effect on behavior. I removed the reads in the ingest worker and left the column in the settings table for now, with a note, since dropping a column on a busy table needs its own plan.

Second, the Postgres write branch in the ingest worker. The code now writes to ClickHouse and nothing else. This removed about 300 lines, including the retry loop for Postgres failures and the logic for the side topic. I kept the commit order test for ClickHouse offsets, because the offset commit after a ClickHouse write still matters.

Third, the consumer for the side topic. It had been running with zero messages. I stopped it in staging first, waited an hour, then in production. The topic itself I left in place for ten days together with the table, in case a rollback is needed.

Fourth, two config options, POSTGRES_EVENTS_DSN and EVENTS_DUAL_WRITE, which are no longer read. I searched the Terraform files and the ECS task definitions. Both were still set in the staging task definition and one production template. I removed them there. Tobias reviewed the Terraform change, and the plan showed only the environment variables changing, with no resource replaced.

I ran the full test suite of the worker, 412 tests, and the integration tests against staging with a loaded stream for 30 minutes. All passed, and the loader lag was at 2 seconds in that test.

The deploy to production went in two steps with a check in between. The ingest error rate stayed at 0.02 percent, the same as before. Memory use of the workers dropped by about 6 percent, probably because the Postgres connection pool is gone.

What remains: the settings column and the topic after the drop, and the Postgres connection permissions for the worker's database role, which Tobias will remove.

summary: Removed the worker's database role permissions on the retired events table with Tobias and updated the retirement checklist; five of the ten waiting days are left.
body:
Tobias and I went through the roles in Postgres. The ingest worker's role still had insert and select rights on events_retired, which makes no sense now that the worker has no Postgres events code.

He revoked all rights for that role on the table, and I made the same change in the Terraform code for the role grants so that the next apply does not give them back. The plan showed one grant removed and nothing else.

To be sure, I tried an insert with the worker's credentials on staging after the same change. It failed with permission denied, as it should. The production ingest error rate did not move after the revoke.

I updated the checklist in docs/events-table-retirement.md. The done steps are marked: dump, bucket checks, restore test, rename, code cleanup, role revoke. The open ones are the drop in five days, the removal of the settings column and the removal of the side topic.

I also wrote down the numbers for the final note to the team: about 2.8 TB to be freed, the Postgres write load down by roughly 40 percent after the first step and almost all of the events part after the last, and the removal of about 300 lines from the worker.

summary: Wrote the day-by-day checklist for the last five waiting days of events_retired and set a reminder to drop it, with the checks that must pass first.
body:
The renamed events_retired table waits five more days before it is dropped. I wrote the checklist as a page in the runbook so that nobody has to remember the details.

Before the drop, the checklist asks for four checks. First, pg_stat_statements must show no statement that reads events_retired since the rename. Second, the archive in the bucket must list all 23 ranges, and the checksums must match the manifest written on the day of the dump. Third, the restore runbook must have been tested by a person who did not write it. Fourth, the monthly customer report must have run once without touching the table.

I asked Sam to do the restore test from the runbook alone on staging, as the third check, because Sam has not seen the dump work and will find the unclear steps. Mara asked whether the drop should wait for the monthly report. It should, and that is why the wait is ten days.

I added the drop command to the page, but commented out, with the table name written in full so that a copy mistake cannot hit another table. The command is meant to be run by two people, Tobias and me, on a call.

There was a small finding. The disk usage graph in Grafana still counts the retired table in the Postgres total, so the number will drop on the day of the drop and look like an incident to somebody. I added a note to the dashboard description. A reminder is set for the morning of the last waiting day.

summary: Sam ran the restore runbook for the events archive on staging alone and got stuck at the index step; I fixed two unclear lines in the page.
body:
Sam followed the restore page for the retired events archive on staging without my help. The restore of one range worked, but Sam stopped at the index step, because the page said to create the indexes after loading without saying which file holds the statements.

I added the file name and the exact psql command. I also fixed a line that told the reader to set a connection setting that does not exist in our staging role.

The second run took 41 minutes for one range, the same as my earlier estimate, so the time table in the page stays. Sam asked what to do if a checksum does not match. I added a short paragraph: download that range again, compare, and only then ask for help. The page is ready for the drop.

summary: Reviewed the Postgres tables and queries left after the events move, found three slow queries on the accounts side, and added one index that cut the worst from 900 ms to 40 ms.
body:
With the events table gone from the hot path, I looked at what Postgres does now. The goal was to see whether the load that remains has any slow spots that were hidden before.

I took the top twenty statements from pg_stat_statements by total time, after resetting the counters yesterday evening. The list is much shorter than before. Three queries stood out.

The first is the lookup of API keys by customer and status in the accounts schema. It did a sequential scan on a table of only 60,000 rows, but it runs thousands of times a minute, so it adds up. The second is the settings read of the admin console, which was fine. The third is a join between sessions and accounts that Lena's admin console runs on every page load of the user list.

For the API key lookup, I tested a partial index on customer_id where status is active on staging with a copy of the data. The plan changed to an index scan and the time went from 900 ms in the worst case to 40 ms. The mean went from 6 ms to under 1 ms.

I created the index in production with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the quiet hour. It took 3 seconds and there were no lock waits. I checked that the index is valid in pg_index afterwards, since a failed concurrent build leaves an invalid one.

For the sessions join, the plan is fine, but the query asks for columns that it never uses. I opened a note for Lena to trim the select list; it is not worth a change by me in her code.

I also looked at the autovacuum statistics. The audit log is the only large table with real churn, and the cleanup job in batches keeps its dead tuples low. The old events_retired table has none because it receives no writes.

What is left: watch the API key lookup for a day to see that the planner keeps the new index, and then look at the total CPU of the Postgres primary, which should be lower after the 40 percent drop in writes. The graph so far shows it about a quarter lower.

summary: Redis memory grew by a third over the last two weeks; the cause is session keys without a TTL from an old admin console release, and I set one on new sessions.
body:
Grafana showed Redis memory rising slowly, from 3.1 GB to 4.2 GB in two weeks, while the cache hit rate stayed flat. That pattern points to keys that are written and never read or expired.

I sampled the keyspace with SCAN and counted by prefix. The prefix sess: holds 38 percent of all keys, and about half of them had no TTL. I checked the admin console code. Sessions written before Lena's release two months ago were set without an expiry, and the refresh path of the new code only sets a TTL when the key is new.

The fix is in the session store module: every write now sets the TTL, also on refresh. Lena reviewed it and agreed. The test checks the TTL after a refresh.

For the old keys, I wrote a one-time script that lists sess: keys with a TTL of -1, and sets 7 days on those that were not used. I ran it on staging first, where it touched 1,200 keys. In production it will touch about 410,000.

I ran it in the quiet hour in batches of 1,000 with a short pause. Memory was at 3.6 GB at the end of the run, and I will look again tomorrow, because Redis does not always give memory back to the system at once.

I also noted that the rate limiter keys and the query cache keys all have TTLs, so they are not the cause.

summary: Redis memory fell to 3.0 GB after the session TTL cleanup, and the hit rate of the query cache did not change, so the cleanup cost nothing.
body:
I checked Redis the day after the session cleanup. Used memory is 3.0 GB, below the level from before the growth. The resident size of the process is a bit higher, about 3.3 GB, because of fragmentation, and it will go down slowly.

The query cache hit rate stayed at 71 percent, the same as before. No user complained about being logged out, and the support channel had no questions from Sam about sessions. The count of sess: keys without a TTL is zero now.

I added a small check to the weekly report script: it counts keys by prefix without a TTL and prints the number. If it is not zero, someone should look. I did not make an alert from it, because one stray key does not need a page.

Next I want to write down the key naming rules, since the sessions problem came partly from each module choosing names and expiry by itself. That will be a short page.

summary: Wrote the Redis key naming page: prefix per module, version in the name, and a TTL required on every write, with a lint check that finds missing TTLs.
body:
After the session keys problem I wrote down how Redis keys are named and expire, so the next module does not repeat it.

The rules are short. Every key starts with the module prefix, such as sess:, rl: for the rate limiter and qc: for the query cache. After the prefix comes a version number when the stored format may change, for example qc:v3:. Customer ids come next, and then the specific part. Every write must set a TTL, and the page lists the usual values: 7 days for sessions, 60 seconds for rate limiter windows, 5 minutes to 1 hour for cache entries.

To help with the rule, I wrote a small wrapper function in the TypeScript shared package. It takes the TTL as a required argument, so a call without one does not compile. The old direct calls to set are still allowed in tests.

I also wrote a lint rule that flags direct set and hset calls outside the wrapper in the search API and the admin console. It found four places. Three were already fine because they used SETEX; the fourth was a debug helper that I removed.

Mara read the page and asked for the version number rule to be mandatory for cache keys, since a format change last year left old entries that broke a reader. I changed the page.

The lint rule is in CI now. It fails on new violations only, so the build stays green.

summary: Planned the upgrade of Redis to the next minor version: read the release notes, tested the client library on staging, and picked a rolling order for the replica and primary.
body:
Redis is on an older minor version and the provider announced the end of support for it in a few months. I started the plan for the upgrade today. Nothing was changed in production.

I read the release notes between our version and the target. The relevant changes for us are small: a change in how the latency of some commands is reported, a fix for a memory leak in replica buffers, and new defaults for a few client output settings. None of the commands we use changed in behavior.

On staging I upgraded the node and ran the full test suite of the search API and of the admin console. All tests passed. I also ran the rate limiter load test, which sends 5,000 requests per second for ten minutes. The p99 of the limiter check was 2.1 ms before and 2.0 ms after, so nothing moved.

The client library, ioredis, is two minor versions behind. I tested the newest one on staging as well. One test failed, because the new version changed how it handles a reconnect when the server closes the connection during a pipeline. The old version returned an error, and the new one retries the commands. That sounds good, but the rate limiter would then count some requests twice. I decided not to upgrade the client in the same step. Only the server goes first.

The production plan has these steps. First, take a snapshot of the primary and check that it restores on staging. Second, upgrade the replica and let it catch up. Third, fail over in the quiet hour so that the upgraded node becomes the primary. Fourth, upgrade the old primary, which is now the replica.

For each step I wrote what to check: replication lag under one second, the count of connected clients, the memory use, and the error rate in the search API. The rollback is to fail back to the old node, which stays at the old version until the end of the plan.

Tobias will do the failover with me, since he owns the infrastructure side and the alerts. I sent the plan to him and Mara.
