Open question: how long the clients take to reconnect after a failover. I measured 8 seconds on staging, but production has more clients, so I will ask Tobias to watch the connection count.

summary: Tobias and I upgraded the Redis replica and failed over in the quiet hour; clients reconnected within 12 seconds and error rates stayed normal.
body:
We did the Redis upgrade as planned. Before starting, I took a snapshot of the primary and restored it on staging; it loaded in 40 seconds and the key count matched.

Step one was the replica. Tobias replaced the node with the new version, and it synced from the primary in about six minutes. Replication lag was under 100 ms afterwards.

Then we did the failover. The search API and the admin console reconnected within 12 seconds, a little more than on staging. In that time the search API served cache misses straight from OpenSearch, so p99 latency rose from 180 ms to 420 ms for those seconds and then went back. The rate limiter failed open as designed, so no customer got a wrong 429.

The connection count came back to the normal 38 within a minute. The error rate in the search API had a small peak of 0.4 percent for the 12 seconds.

The old primary was upgraded after that and is the replica now. Both nodes show the new version. I left the old node image in place for a day in case we want to go back.

To do: upgrade the client library in a separate change after I look at the double-count in the pipeline retry. I also need to write the result to the infrastructure notes.

summary: Wrote up the Redis upgrade in the infrastructure notes with timings and the reconnect gap, and removed the old node image after a quiet day.
body:
One day after the upgrade, Redis is stable. Memory use is about the same, the hit rate of the query cache is 71 percent, and the replica lag stays under 100 ms. Nothing in the on-call channel mentions Redis.

I wrote the upgrade into the infrastructure notes: the versions, the four steps, the timings, and the 12 second gap while the clients reconnected. I added the advice to do the failover in the quiet hour, since the search API goes to OpenSearch for every miss during the gap.

Tobias removed the old node image. I closed the plan page and left a link to it from the notes.

The client library upgrade is the next piece. The double-count issue needs a test that sends a pipeline during a reconnect and checks the limiter counter. I will write that test first and look at the library options, since one option may turn the automatic retry of commands off.

summary: Upgraded the ioredis client after turning off its automatic command retry for the rate limiter, and wrote the pipeline test that showed the double count.
body:
The new ioredis version retries queued commands after a reconnect. For the rate limiter that is a problem, since an increment can be sent twice and the customer gets counted twice. I wrote the test first, to see it fail.

The test starts a local Redis, sends a pipeline of increments for one key, kills the connection in the middle of it, and reads the counter at the end. With the new library and default options, the counter was 14 after 10 sends in four of ten runs. With the old library it was 10 or less. The old behavior is an error for the caller, and the limiter ignores it, which is the safe side.

The library has an option, maxRetriesPerRequest, and one for offline queue behavior. I set maxRetriesPerRequest to 0 for the limiter client only, so commands fail at once on a broken connection. The test passes with that: the counter never went over 10 in 200 runs.

The query cache and session clients are different. A repeated read or a repeated set is harmless there, so they keep the library defaults of a few retries. I made two separate client factories in the shared package, so the choice is visible in the code.

I checked the other places that use pipelines. The search API's cache warm-up uses one, but it only sets keys with fixed values, so a repeat does not matter.

I also reread the changelog of the library for the two versions I skipped. There is a change in how the cluster mode finds nodes, which we do not use, and a fix for a memory leak in the subscriber, which we also do not use.

On staging, I ran the limiter load test again with the new client: 5,000 requests per second for ten minutes. p99 of the check was 2.0 ms, the same as before. Then I killed the Redis node during the test. The limiter failed open for 9 seconds and recovered, and the counter showed no double counts.

Mara reviewed the change and asked for a comment in the code that explains why the limiter has zero retries. I added three lines at the factory.

The change goes to production tomorrow morning together with the regular release. If the error rate of the limiter shows something odd, the way back is to pin the old version in the lockfile.

summary: The ioredis upgrade went out with the release; the limiter error counter and the cache hit rate looked the same as before for the first hours.
body:
The release with the new ioredis version and the two client factories went out in the morning window. I watched the search API and the limiter for the next hours.

The limiter error counter, which counts failed Redis calls, stayed at 0 to 2 per minute, as before. The cache hit rate was 71 percent. The p99 of the search API stayed near 190 ms. The reconnect count of the clients is flat.

I also checked the memory of the Node processes, because the new library keeps a different internal buffer. It grew by about 6 MB per process, which is fine.

I will look again tomorrow, and if nothing changed, I will close the Redis topic. The plan was upgrade, naming, cleanup of the session keys, and the client; all four parts are done.

summary: Started the rate limit counters per API key as a branch plan: wrote the design for the window size and key layout, and tested a sliding window script in Redis on staging.
body:
I began planning rate limits per API key. Today was design and a first test, no production change.

Until now, the limiter counts per customer. Large customers have several apps, each with its own API key, and one noisy app uses the whole allowance of the others. The wish from support, passed on by Sam, is a limit per key with the customer limit as the upper bound.

The key layout I chose is rl:v1:{customer}:{key_id}:{window}. I added the version number as the new naming page asks. The TTL is twice the window, so the last window still exists for the sliding calculation.

For the algorithm I compared two options on paper. A fixed window counter is simple but allows double bursts at the window edge. A sliding window using two counters, the current and the previous window with a weighted sum, is cheap and close enough. I did not want the log version with sorted sets, since it costs memory for every request and our memory use is a concern after the session problem.

I wrote the Lua script for the sliding window. It increments the current counter, reads the previous one, and returns the weighted count and a flag whether the limit is exceeded. It does all of this in one call, so there is no race between the read and the write.

I tested it on staging with a script that sends 2,000 requests per second from 20 keys, of which two send ten times more than their limit. The two noisy keys got 429 for the excess, and the other 18 were not affected. The customer-wide limit also held when I set it low.

The test measured the cost: one Redis call per request, with a mean of 0.4 ms and a p99 of 1.9 ms. That is the same as the old limiter.

The open questions are the defaults for keys that have no limit set, and how the admin console lets customers see and change the limits. For the defaults I propose that a key without a setting gets the customer limit divided by two, so one key can still not take everything. Lena will need an API for the console.

I also wrote the headers we should return: the limit, the remaining count and the reset time, in the style of the public API docs. The docs need a section, which Sam can write.

Next: create the branch worktree, put the script and the middleware in place behind a flag, and write the tests for the edge of the windows.

summary: Wrote the questions for Lena and Sam about the per-key limits: the settings API for the console and the wording of the new 429 headers in the docs.
body:
Before more code, I sent two sets of questions on the rate limit work.

For Lena: the console needs to show a limit per API key and let an admin change it. I proposed a settings endpoint, GET and PUT on /keys/{id}/limit, with a value in requests per minute and a null for the default. I asked whether the table of keys in the console can take one more column and an edit field, and whether she wants a warning when the sum of the key limits is higher than the customer limit.

For Sam: the new response headers are the limit, the remaining count and the reset time. I asked Sam to write the docs section with an example of a 429 and how a client should back off. I gave Sam the exact header names so the text matches the code.

I also asked both of them whether any customer has an agreement with a special limit, because those must keep working at the switch. Sam knows of two customers and will send the list.

The work continues in the branch; I will not turn the flag on in production before the list of special agreements is checked.

summary: Built the per-key limiter middleware behind a flag, with the Lua script, the key layout, and tests for window edges, and the customer cap still applies.
body:
I worked in the rate-limits worktree and put the per-key limiter into the search API and the ingest API middleware layer, off by default.

The middleware reads the API key id from the request context, which the auth step already sets. It loads the limit for the key from a small in-process cache of the settings, with a 30 second refresh from Postgres, so there is no database call per request. If no limit is set for the key, the default is half of the customer limit, as proposed.

The order of the checks is: first the key limit, then the customer limit. If either is over, the request gets a 429. The response carries the headers for the one that is closer to its limit, so a client sees the number that matters.

The Lua script is loaded with SCRIPT LOAD at startup and called with EVALSHA. I added a fallback for the case that Redis lost the script after a failover, since the upgrade last week showed that a node restart clears it. On a NOSCRIPT error, the middleware loads the script again and repeats the call once.

The tests cover these cases:
- a request at the end of one window and one at the start of the next, where the weighted sum must be right
- two keys of one customer, where one is over its limit and the other is not
- the customer cap lower than the sum of the key limits
- Redis down, where the limiter fails open
- NOSCRIPT after a flush

The window edge test needed a clock I can move. I made the limiter take a time function as an argument. The default is the real clock, and tests pass a fake one.

One bug showed up. At the very start of a window, the previous counter does not exist and the script returned nil, which the middleware read as an error and failed open. The script now treats a missing previous counter as zero. A test covers it.

I ran the staging load test again with the flag on. At 2,000 requests per second from 20 keys, the p99 of the limiter was 1.8 ms. The two noisy keys were limited and the rest were fine.

The things that remain are the settings API for Lena, the migration of the two special customers, and the flag rollout in steps by customer. Sam's list of the special agreements has come in: the two customers have limits twice the normal one, set by a manual entry in the settings table.

I also checked what the flag does when the settings cache is empty after a restart. It uses the default and logs a warning, which seems right.

summary: Wrote the first test run of the per-key limiter in staging with load from a script; the window sums matched the expected counts and one edge case showed a key layout gap.
body:
Ran the first load test of the per-key limiter in staging, using a small Go script that sends requests with 20 different API keys at fixed rates. Each key had its own limit between 50 and 2,000 requests per minute, and the customer cap was set above all of them. The window sums in Redis matched the expected counts to within one request for all 20 keys.

One gap showed up in the key layout. Two test keys from the same customer shared a prefix, and my cleanup script with a pattern match deleted the counters of both. The limiter itself was fine, but the layout puts the key id after the customer id, so the scan pattern has to end with a colon. I fixed the script and added a line about it to the key naming page.

I also checked the TTL on the counter keys. Each write sets a TTL of twice the window size, and the keys disappeared on time after the test stopped. The Redis memory use during the test grew by about 4 MB for the 20 keys, which is small, but I want to see the number again with the real key count before the large customers are switched.

The p99 latency of the limiter script was 1.1 ms in staging. Next I want to review the script with Mara and then turn the flag on for our own test customer.

summary: Mara reviewed the limiter script and found that a very large increment argument could overflow the window sum; I added a bound and a test.
body:
Mara read the Lua script of the per-key limiter and the middleware. Most of the comments were about naming, which I fixed.

One comment was real. The script takes an increment argument, which is 1 for normal calls, but the bulk ingest endpoint will later call it with the number of events in a batch. With a large value, the weighted sum of the two windows could grow beyond what the script expects, and the floor operation on the weight gave a result that is too low by one. That would let one request through that should be refused.

I changed the script to compute with integers scaled by 1000 and to cap the increment at the limit plus one. A request that asks for more than the whole limit is refused at once, and it does not write to the counter. I added a test with an increment of 50,000 against a limit of 600.

Mara also asked why the TTL is twice the window. I added a comment that explains it: the previous window must still exist for the whole current window. The review is closed and the branch is ready for the flag step one.

summary: Turned the per-key limiter on for our own test customer and ten small customers; 429 counts stayed the same except one key that now hits its new limit.
body:
The rollout of the per-key limiter started with step one in the morning. The flag was on for our own test customer in production, and I sent traffic from a script at the key limit to see the headers. The 429 responses carried the limit, the remaining count and the reset time, and the values matched the Redis counters.

After two hours without problems, I did step two earlier than planned and enabled ten small customers. For each, I compared the number of 429 responses in the last hour with the same hour a week ago, using the new Grafana panel.

Nine of the ten had zero before and after. One customer, with three keys, had 12 responses with 429 before, all from one key, and 340 after. The difference came from the default of half of the customer limit, which the busy key of this customer now reaches. The customer's total is under the cap, so before this change the key could use the whole allowance.

I looked at the traffic of the key over the last two weeks. It sends bursts of about 900 requests per minute every few minutes, and the customer limit is 1,000. The new default is 500. The right fix is a limit for this key of 900, set through the new endpoint, and the other two keys of the customer stay at the default. The audit entry names the reason.

This points to a weakness of the default. Half of the cap may be too low for customers with one dominant key. I thought about a default of the cap divided by the number of keys with at least one request in the last day, but that is variable and hard to explain in the docs. I prefer a plain rule that the support team can say out loud. For now the default stays at half, and I will make a list of all keys that exceed it in the last 14 days before the large customers are switched.

I wrote the script for that list. It reads the per-minute peak of each key from Prometheus and compares it with the effective limit. It found 11 keys across 8 customers, mostly the large ones. Those keys will get explicit limits before their customers are switched.

Other findings of the day:
- the settings cache refresh of 30 seconds means a changed limit takes up to 30 seconds to apply; the console should say so
- the ingest API logs the 429 at warning level, which will be noisy for the keys over their limit, so I changed it to count only and log one line per key per minute
- the Grafana panel is slow with the key label over 7 days, so I limited the default range to 24 hours

Step three waits until the explicit limits are set and Sam has told the customers' contacts. Sam will send the message tomorrow.

summary: Set explicit limits for the 11 keys that exceed the default and wrote the docs input for Sam, so the large customers can be switched to per-key limits.
body:
I used the list from yesterday to set limits for the 11 keys whose peak traffic is above half of their customer cap. For each key, I set the limit to the peak of the last 14 days plus 20 percent, but never above the customer cap. The endpoint wrote an audit entry for each change, with the reason text.

Three of the keys are from the two customers with special agreements. For them I kept the limits in line with what Sam knows of the agreements, and Sam confirmed the numbers.

Then I ran the comparison script again. With the explicit limits, no key in production would be limited at its current traffic, except test keys that I know send bursts on purpose.

Sam has the docs section for the headers in draft. I read it and corrected two details. The reset time header is in seconds until the window ends, not a timestamp. And the 429 body has a field called retry_after, which I had not mentioned. I sent Sam an example for both.

Sam also asked how a customer can see which limit applies to a key. The answer is the console column that Lena is adding, and for now the GET endpoint through the admin API. Sam will add that to the support notes.

Lena's console change is on staging and works with the endpoint. She found that the PUT returned 200 with an empty body, so she could not show the new value without another request. I changed the response to return the same object as GET.

The plan for the rest of the rollout:
1. tomorrow, the remaining small and mid-sized customers, 20 in all
2. the day after, the five large customers one by one, with a check of 429 counts after an hour for each
3. a week of watching, and then removal of the old customer-only limiter code

I also thought about what happens during a Redis failover. The limiter fails open, as before, and the 12 second gap that we measured is short. I do not see a new risk from the per-key counters.

One more point for later: the bulk ingest endpoint should use the increment for the batch size. That is a separate change, to be done together with the ingest batching work, and I put it on the list. Until then, a batch counts as one request.

summary: Switched the remaining 20 customers to per-key limits in two groups; the only 429 changes came from two test keys that send bursts on purpose.
body:
The flag went on for the next 20 customers in two groups of ten, with an hour between them. Before each group I ran the comparison script, and it showed no key that would be limited at its normal traffic.

After the first group, the 429 counts in the hour were the same as a week ago for nine customers. One customer had a few more, from a test key that sends a burst of 3,000 requests every day at the same time. That key has no explicit limit, so it gets the default. The burst fails for most requests now. I asked Sam to ask the customer whether the burst is a real need. If it is, we set a limit; if it is a load test, the customer should use the staging environment.

The second group showed no change. The p99 of the limiter stayed at 1.8 ms, and Redis memory grew by about 20 MB for the new counters, which is expected for the key layout and the TTL of twice the window.

The settings cache works as designed. I changed one limit through the endpoint and watched the effect arrive in the middleware logs after 24 seconds.

Tomorrow the five large customers follow, one by one. Their explicit limits are already set. I will do each one in the quiet hour and look at the limiter panel for the hour after it.

summary: Ran the per-key limiter for a full day after the last customer switch, checked 429 counts and Redis load, and found one key layout leftover to clean up.
body:
Slot 19 moved the last 20 customers to per-key limits yesterday, so today was the first full day with every customer on the new limiter. I compared the 429 counts per customer with the same day a week earlier, using the limiter counters in Prometheus. Eleven customers showed no change at all, and the others moved by less than two percent, which is within the normal daily spread.

The two test keys that send bursts on purpose hit their limits as expected, and their headers showed the new remaining and reset values. I also checked the Redis side, since the limiter now writes one key per API key and window. Memory for the limiter prefix grew by about 90 MB, which is close to the estimate in the design page. The TTL lint check passed for the Lua script, and a scan of a sample of 2,000 limiter keys found a TTL on every one of them.

Command latency in Redis stayed flat. The p99 of the limiter script was 1.4 ms in the morning peak and 1.1 ms in the evening, and the connection count did not change. I looked at the staging edge case from the first test run, the key layout gap, and confirmed that the fix from last week covers it in production too.

While scanning I found old counter keys of the customer-level limiter that nothing reads any more. They have a TTL, so they expire on their own within a day, but the code that wrote them is still there. I removed that write path behind the existing flag and added a test that the customer cap still applies through the new path. I did not touch the cap itself.

I also wrote a short note for Sam with the numbers, so support can answer questions about 429s from the new dashboard panel. The panel shows rejections per key and per hour and links to the docs page on headers. What is left is to remove the old flag after a quiet week and to ask Lena whether the console should show the current usage per key. I will pick that up with her next week.

summary: Merged the smaller reindex batch size for customers with large documents and left the 8,000 character truncation waiting for the answer from the customer.
body:
I split yesterday's change in two. The batch size part does not change any search result, so I merged it alone. The reindex job now uses 500 documents per bulk request when the average document size of a customer is above 3 KB, and 1,000 otherwise.

I ran the job on staging with the full copy of the data. The thread pool rejections in the log were gone, and the total time dropped by four minutes, because fewer batches had to be repeated.

The truncation part stays in a separate branch of my local work, not merged. Sam has sent the proposal to the customer's contact and will tell me the answer. If the customer says no, we can still reduce the cost in another way, for example with a separate index for this field.

To see the effect in production, I will compare tonight's job time with the 95 minutes of this week. I do not expect a large change, since the batch size mostly removes the rejections.

summary: The customer agreed to the 8,000 character limit for the payload_text search, so I merged the truncation and the nightly reindex fell from 95 to 71 minutes.
body:
Sam came back with the answer: the customer's team only searches for the error name and the first lines of the trace, and they are fine with 8,000 characters. The stored value stays complete and is shown in full in the event detail.

I merged the truncation in the reindex job and the live indexing path together, as planned. The unit test for 20,000 characters is part of it. I also added a test in the search API that a search for a string at position 9,000 of a text finds nothing, and one for position 100 finds the event, so the behavior is written down.

Because live indexing and reindex now work the same, I checked a sample of 500 events of the customer. The indexed text length was at most 8,000 in both paths.

The reindex job ran last night with the batch change from yesterday and ran tonight with the truncation. The time for the large customer went down to 14 minutes, and the whole job needed 71 minutes, below the 95 of last week and a little above the 70 of last month. The extra minute comes from the document growth.

The index size on disk for this customer also dropped by about a quarter after the reindex, which gives us some room on the data nodes.

I added the truncation limit to the docs for the search API, under the field description, and told Sam, so the support team can answer questions about it. The limit is a constant in the config, so it can be changed per customer later if there is a need.

The topic is closed. I will watch the job time for a week, since the growth of other customers can bring it up again, and I noted the 8,000 characters in the notes for the planned new shard layout, because the sizes per shard depend on it.

summary: Wrote a first estimate of index sizes per customer and per month, as input for the plan to move the search index from shards by customer to shards by month.
body:
The search index is sharded by customer today, and the idea is to shard by month instead, since old months rarely change and could be handled differently. This is only a planning step, and nothing in the cluster was changed.

I wanted data before any design. I wrote a script that asks the OpenSearch cat APIs for the size and the document count of each shard, and joins it with the customer and the month from the events' timestamps, which I sampled through aggregations. The output is a table of size per customer per month for the last 24 months.

The main findings are these:
- the total index size is 1.9 TB, with the five largest customers holding 71 percent
- the largest customer alone is 520 GB, in one shard family of three shards, so the shards of this customer are far larger than those of small customers
- a month of data across all customers is about 85 GB for recent months and less before, since the old events are fewer
- 14 small customers together hold less than 2 percent, and each of them has a full primary shard that is nearly empty

The last point is the first argument for the change. Many shards that are almost empty cost heap on the data nodes, and I counted 96 shards that are under 1 GB.

The argument against is that a search of one customer has to ask a shard of every month in the range. For a typical search over 30 days that means one or two shards, but for a search over a year, it means twelve. With routing by customer inside the month shard, that is still fast, but I have to measure it.

For the target I propose 12 shards for the first set, which is what the key entry of the plan assumed, one per month of the retention window of the search index, with the routing key set to the customer id. A month shard of 85 GB is within the usual range.

I also thought about what happens with the nightly reindex. It works per customer today. Under the new layout, it would work per month, and the months before the last two are never changed, so the job could skip them. That could cut the job time a lot, perhaps to a third.

There are risks that I wrote down for the plan. The first is the migration itself, which must be done without a gap in search results. The second is deleted data: retention by month becomes simple with a month shard, but a deletion for a single customer, for example when a customer leaves, needs a delete by query instead of dropping an index. The third is the audit export, which reads the index by customer.

Next I will write the migration plan itself, with the steps and the checks, and send it to Tobias and Mara for comments. The data table is saved in the repository docs folder so that later entries can use it.

summary: Answered Mara's question about why the per-month shards need a routing key: without it, a small customer's search would ask every shard of the range.
body:
Mara read my size estimate and asked why the plan needs a routing key by customer inside the month shards, and whether it adds complexity.

My answer was this. With 12 month shards and no routing, a search for one customer in a one-year range must be sent to all 12 shards, and each shard has to filter by the customer id on its own. With the routing key, a document of a customer lands on one shard of each month, but that is true for every month already, so the routing does not reduce the number of shards for a year-long search.

So Mara's question had a good point: for the months, routing by customer does not help, since the month shard is already chosen by time. What routing could do is spread each month over several shards and let a search for one customer ask only one of them. That would be needed only when a month grows beyond a good shard size, and at 85 GB it does not.

I changed the plan: no routing key in the first version. The customer filter works as a term filter, which the engine caches. I will test the cost of that on a copy before I decide. If the test shows a problem for the largest customer, we can use a split of the month into two shards for that case.

I wrote the changed assumption in the plan page and thanked Mara for the question, since it removed a part that I would have had to build and migrate.

summary: Measured searches by one customer over a year range on a test index shaped like the month layout; the largest customer stays under 300 ms p95 without routing.
body:
To check the no-routing decision from the previous entry, I built a test index on the staging cluster with the month layout: 12 shards, one per month, filled with a copy of real events from the last year. I used the data of the largest customer and of three small ones, about 160 GB in total, as the full copy would not fit on staging.

I ran query sets of 200 searches for each type with the usual mix: a text search, a filter on event type, and a date range. The ranges were 7 days, 30 days and 365 days.

The results for the largest customer were these. For 7 and 30 days, p95 was 120 ms and 190 ms. For the year range, p95 was 280 ms, which is under the 300 ms that I set as the acceptable limit. The current layout has about 210 ms for the same query on staging, so the year range is somewhat slower, as expected.

For the small customers, the numbers were better than today for all ranges, about 40 ms at p95 for a year. The reason is that the small data sets are cached well, and no empty shards must be asked.

The filter cache hit rate for the customer term filter was 94 percent after the warm-up, which supports the decision to skip routing.

I noted two caveats. The staging cluster has less load than production, so absolute numbers will be higher there. And the test did not include writes during the searches, so I plan one more run with live indexing.

For the plan, the decision stands: month shards, no routing, and a check of the year range for the largest customer after the first migrated months. I will write the migration steps next.

summary: Cleaned up the last key layout leftover of the per-key limiter and confirmed that no old customer-wide counters are written any more.
body:
The full day run last week showed one leftover: a set of counter keys under the old layout that the middleware still wrote when a key had no explicit limit. I changed the middleware to use only the new layout and removed the fallback path.

After the deploy I listed the old-layout keys in Redis with a scan on staging and in production. They had a TTL of one hour, as the naming rules require, so they expired by themselves within the hour. No new ones appeared after that.

The customer cap test still passes, and I added a test that fails if the middleware writes a key without the version prefix. 429 counts per customer were the same as the day before. Redis memory fell by about 40 MB, which is small but expected. The branch is ready to merge once Sam's docs text for the 429 headers is in.

summary: Merged the rate-limits branch after Sam's header wording went in; the docs now describe the per-key limits and the Retry-After header.
body:
Sam finished the docs page for the per-key limits and I read it against the code. Two details were wrong: the window size was given as 30 seconds, but it is 60, and the header name for the remaining count was written in a different case from the one the middleware sends. Sam fixed both.

I merged the branch into main and removed the flag from the config. The flag had been on for all customers for a week, so nothing changes in behavior. The worktree of the branch is deleted.

One open point is Lena's settings screen, where an admin can change the limit of a key. The API for it works, but the console form does not show the current usage yet. Lena plans it for next week. I wrote the usage endpoint contract into the ticket so she can start without me.

summary: Started the query parser for search v2 as a small grammar with field filters, phrases and boolean operators, and got the first 40 test queries to parse into the same AST shape.
body:
The old search API builds the OpenSearch query by string handling, which breaks on quotes and on field names with dots. For v2 I wrote a parser in TypeScript with a tokenizer and a recursive descent step, no parser library.

Supported so far: field:value, quoted phrases, AND, OR, NOT, parentheses and a minus prefix. Bare words go to the default fields. Unknown field names produce a parse error with the position, not a silent empty result.

I took 40 real queries from the search log of the last month, with customer ids removed, and wrote them as test cases. 37 parse as expected. The three failures use a wildcard in the middle of a word, which the grammar does not allow yet, and one query with an unmatched quote.

I looked at a parser library first. It parsed the grammar but its error messages gave no position, and it added a dependency of 400 kB for something short, so I dropped it after an hour.

Next step is to turn the AST into OpenSearch bool queries and compare the hits with v1 on the same 40 queries. The wildcard rule needs a decision: allow it only at the end of a term, as v1 effectively does.

summary: The parser now turns the AST into OpenSearch bool queries, and 36 of 40 logged queries return the same top ten as v1; the differences are all explained.
body:
I wrote the translation from AST to the OpenSearch query and ran the 40 logged queries against the staging index with both versions.

Thirty six give the same top ten in the same order. Two differ in order only, because v1 put a phrase match in a should clause that v2 puts in must. One differs because v1 ignored a NOT term when it came after a parenthesis, which was a bug in v1. The last differs because the wildcard in the middle of the word is now an error instead of being cut off.

I decided to allow the wildcard only at the end of a term, and wrote it into the grammar. The three queries that used a middle wildcard return a clear error, and I will tell Sam so the docs can mention it.

The next piece is per-field boosts. I wrote a config shape for it, a map of field to weight, but did not wire it in. Mara asked whether the boosts should be per customer. I think not at first, one global set, and we can add overrides if a customer asks. That keeps the cache keys of the search results simple.

summary: Looked at the Postgres autovacuum log after the events table move and found the accounts tables vacuum fine, with one settings table that needs a lower threshold.
body:
I read the autovacuum log of the last two weeks. Most tables are vacuumed within minutes of crossing the threshold. The exception is the settings table, which has few rows but many updates, and it carried about 60 percent dead tuples at one point.

I set a lower scale factor for that table only, with ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02). I did not change the global settings.

After an hour the table had 3 percent dead tuples. The read latency of the settings query was already fine, so this is mostly housekeeping. I will check the log again in a few days.

summary: Wired per-field boosts into the search v2 query builder and measured the effect on a labeled set of 60 queries; the title field boost of 3 gave the best ranking.
body:
With the parser done I connected the boost map to the query builder. Each field in the default list gets a weight in a multi_match, and a field filter from the user query ignores the boosts.

To choose weights I needed something better than a feeling. Sam had marked up 60 queries from support tickets with the one document the customer wanted. I used the rank of that document as the measure.

Results on the staging index:
- no boosts: the wanted document was in the top three for 31 of 60 queries
- title 2, message 1: 38 of 60
- title 3, message 1, tags 1.5: 44 of 60
- title 5: 41 of 60, worse than 3

I went with title 3, message 1, tags 1.5 and payload_text 0.5. The payload_text field is long and matches too much, so a low weight helps.

Two of the 60 queries got worse than with no boosts. I looked at both. In one, the wanted document had the term only in the message, and a log line with the term in a title ranked above it. That is an inherent trade of boosts, not a bug.

I wrote the weights into the config file, not into the code, and added a test that the builder reads them. The reindex job needs no change, since boosts apply at query time.

The labeled set is in the repo under the test fixtures now, with Sam's agreement, so we can repeat the measure when the weights change. The next step is to put v2 behind a header for the console so Lena can compare the results by eye.

summary: Added a request header that switches a search to the v2 parser, so Lena can compare results in the admin console without a deploy of its own.
body:
The search API now reads x-search-version. With the value 2 it uses the new parser and boosts, with anything else or nothing it uses v1. The default stays v1.

I added the header to the response too, so a trace shows which path ran. The query cache key now includes the version, because otherwise a v2 request could be served a cached v1 answer. I found that by test before it could happen.

I wrote a short note for Lena on how to set the header in the console's search box, behind a developer toggle she already has. She plans to build a side by side view next week.

No customer traffic uses v2 yet.

summary: Tobias and I looked at why the staging Redis hit rate is lower than production and found the staging test jobs use random key suffixes that never repeat.
body:
Staging showed a cache hit rate of 22 percent while production sits near 80. Tobias wondered if the staging Redis was configured differently.

We compared the settings and they match. Then I sampled the keys of the query cache in staging. Many carried a random suffix. A load test script from the rate limit work added a nonce to each query to avoid caching, and it was still running on a schedule every ten minutes.

I turned the schedule off and flushed the cache keys with that prefix. After an hour the hit rate on staging rose to 61 percent, which is what a small staging dataset gives.

I added a line to the key naming page: test scripts must use their own prefix, so they can be cleaned up by pattern. Tobias will add the prefix to the script. Nothing to change in production.

summary: Wrote the plan for how the nightly reindex will build v2 indexes in the background so customers can be moved one at a time.
body:
The reindex job currently rebuilds the whole index at night. For search v2 we want to move customers to the new parser and boosts without a big switch, and the mapping stays the same, so the plan is simple.

Plan in short:
- the job keeps writing one index per customer as now
- an alias per customer points to the live index
- the search API reads through the alias, so a rebuild can swap atomically
- a per-customer setting chooses v1 or v2 parsing

The alias part is new. At the moment the API names the index directly. I checked all places that use the index name and found six, four in the search API and two in the job.

I asked Mara to review the plan, since she wrote the job. She asked what happens if the swap happens during a long scroll. The old index stays until the scroll ends, as the alias swap does not delete it, and the job deletes it only after an hour. I added that to the plan.

summary: Implemented the index alias per customer in the search API and the reindex job, and tested the swap on staging with a running search load.
body:
Following the plan from earlier today I changed the six places that used the index name directly. The search API now resolves customer id to alias name through one function, and the job writes to a dated index and then swaps the alias.

The job steps are now: create the dated index, bulk load, check the document count against the source within 0.5 percent, swap the alias in one request, and delete indexes older than one hour after the swap.

On staging I ran a load script with 20 searches per second against one customer while the job rebuilt the index. During the swap there were no errors and no search returned an empty result. The p95 latency rose from 80 to 95 ms for about ten seconds while the new index warmed up.

One problem showed up. The first run on the old data had an index with the plain customer name, and an alias cannot have the same name as an index. I wrote a one-off migration that reindexes that index to a dated name and then removes it and creates the alias. It ran on staging for all 12 test customers. For production I will do it customer by customer, small ones first.

I also added a check to the job that refuses to swap if the count check fails, and an alert on that case to the alert rules in code.

Tests: 14 new unit tests for the name resolution and two integration tests for the swap. All pass.

Tomorrow Mara reviews the diff, and if she agrees I will run the migration on the five smallest customers in production.

summary: Mara reviewed the alias change and asked for the old index deletion to wait for open scrolls, which I added; then I migrated the five smallest customers.
body:
Mara found one gap in the review: the job deleted old indexes after one hour regardless of open scroll contexts. A long export could still be reading. I changed the delete step to query the stats for open scroll contexts on the index and postpone if any exist.

She also asked for a log line with both index names at the swap, so a bad swap can be traced. Added.

After the fixes I ran the one-off migration for the five smallest customers in production. Each took under a minute. I searched each customer before and after and the hit counts were the same for a set of ten queries.

I left the other customers for tomorrow in case something shows up overnight, since the nightly job will use the alias for these five.

summary: The nightly job ran with aliases for the first five customers without problems, so I migrated the remaining customers in three groups.
body:
The nightly reindex finished for the five migrated customers, with the alias swapped and the count check within 0.1 percent. The old indexes were deleted after the hour.

I migrated the next 15 customers, then the next 14, then the six that remain, among them the largest ones. For the large ones I used the reindex API with slices to speed it up. The largest took 41 minutes, and during it searches kept going to the old index until the alias swap.

Checks after each group: the hit counts for ten queries per customer, the search API error rate and the p95 latency. Nothing moved beyond noise.

One customer had a second alias for a test setup from long ago. The migration script stopped on it, as intended. I looked at the alias, it pointed to nothing in use, and I removed it and ran the script again.

All customers now read through aliases. The v1 and v2 switch per customer is the next step, with a setting in Postgres and a column in the console, which Lena will look at.

I also updated the runbook page about the reindex job so that it describes the alias steps and how to roll back a swap, which is a single alias request to the previous dated index while it still exists.

summary: Added the per-customer search version setting in Postgres and the API read for it, with v1 as the default for all customers.
body:
I added a column search_version to the customer settings table with a default of 1 and a check constraint for values 1 and 2. The migration was a plain ADD COLUMN with a default, which is quick on Postgres 16 and did not lock the table for a noticeable time.

The search API reads the setting with the other customer settings, which are already cached in Redis with a TTL of five minutes under the settings prefix. The header from the earlier work overrides the setting, so a developer can still compare.

Tests cover the default, the setting and the header override. I set it to 2 for our own test customer to see it in the console. Search works as expected there.

Lena can now build the toggle. The settings API returns the field, and I wrote it in the API docs for internal use.

summary: Checked the error log from the night and found only the usual client timeouts; the new alias swap ran for all customers with no failed count checks.
body:
The nightly reindex now swaps aliases for all customers. I looked at the job log this morning. All swaps passed the count check, and the longest build was the large customer at 58 minutes.

The search API error log had the usual client timeouts, about 30 in the night, similar to other nights. Nothing from the alias change.

The job total was 69 minutes, close to the 71 from before the change, so the alias step adds almost nothing.

summary: Put two internal users on search v2 for a trial and collected their notes; the main complaint is that a bare word with a dash is now split into two terms.
body:
Sam and one support colleague used v2 for their daily ticket work for a day. I set search_version to 2 for the test customer account they use.

They found the ranking better, mostly. The main complaint was about a query like order-4471, which the tokenizer treated as order and NOT 4471 because of the minus rule. That is wrong in the middle of a word. I changed the tokenizer so a minus counts as an operator only at the start of a term.

Another note was that an unknown field gives an error, which they liked, but the message should list the known fields. I added that.

I added both cases to the test set. The parser tests are at 58 now and all pass. I will let them use v2 for a few more days before choosing a first customer.

summary: Read the slow query log for the search API Postgres lookups and fixed two N+1 patterns in the settings loading, cutting requests per search from 7 to 2.
body:
While tracing a v2 search I noticed the API made seven Postgres queries per request, which I did not expect. I enabled query logging on staging for ten minutes and grouped by statement.

Two patterns stood out:
- the customer settings were read once per setting group, four reads
- the API key lookup ran twice, once in the auth hook and once in the rate limiter

I changed the settings loader to read the row once and to pass the object along in the request context. I also let the limiter use the key record that the auth hook had loaded.

The result is two queries per search, the key lookup and the settings read, and the settings read is mostly served from Redis anyway. The measured median latency on staging fell from 34 to 27 ms.

One risk is stale data in the context, but it lives only for the request, so that is fine.

I wrote tests that count queries per request with a mock pool and fail if it goes above three. That should catch the pattern if it comes back.

In production I expect little change in latency, since the cache hid most of it, but the load on the Postgres primary should fall a little. I will check the connection count graph tomorrow.

I did not touch the key lookup cache. An idea was to put the whole key record in Redis, but then a revoked key would stay valid until the TTL ends, and for the security side that is not acceptable without extra work.

summary: Postgres connections on the primary fell from about 90 to 70 at peak after the query count change in the search API.
body:
I looked at the connection graph after the release of the settings loader change. At the daily peak the primary held about 90 connections before, and now about 70. The search API is the main user of the pool.

The query rate for the settings table fell by about half. The key lookup rate is unchanged in the auth hook, as expected.

The pool maximum is still at the old value. I will not lower it yet and will watch for a week. Tobias asked whether this lets us keep the smaller database instance size, and I think yes for now, though the current instance has headroom anyway.

summary: Lena showed the first version of the search version toggle in the console; I reviewed the API calls and asked for a confirmation step before a customer is switched.
body:
Lena built the toggle in the customer settings page with a select for v1 and v2. It calls the settings API and shows the saved value.

I reviewed the calls. Two issues. First, the form sent the whole settings object, which could overwrite a change another admin made at the same time. I asked for a PATCH with only the field. Second, a switch changes what a customer sees at once, so a confirmation dialog with the customer name makes sense.

She agreed to both and will change them tomorrow. I added the PATCH route to the API with a test for the partial update and an entry in the audit log for the change, as for the other settings.

summary: Added the audit log entry for search version changes and checked that the actor and old value are stored the way the audit export will need them.
body:
A settings change must be written to the audit log with who did it, the old value and the new value. I wrote the entry in the PATCH route with the action name settings.search_version.changed.

I looked at what other settings entries store in the details column and used the same shape, so old and new are keys of one JSON object. The audit export branch is planned, and the shared shape means it needs no special case.

Test: change the value twice and read two rows with the right actor. It passes.

summary: Switched the first real customer, a small one that asked for better search, to v2 and watched search results, latency and errors for the afternoon.
body:
A small customer had asked support for better ranking, so Sam agreed we start with them. I set the search version to 2 through the new console toggle, after Lena's fixes were merged.

Before the switch I replayed their last 200 logged queries on both versions on staging. 189 returned the same top ten, the rest differed in the order only. Two returned an error with v2: one with a wildcard in the middle of a word and one with an unmatched quote. I told Sam so she could write to the customer if needed.

After the switch I watched for the afternoon:
- search errors for the customer: zero parse errors in the first three hours except one unmatched quote, which gave the message with the position
- p95 latency: 62 ms, before 70 ms
- cache hit rate for their queries stayed about the same

The customer wrote no complaint by the evening. Sam will ask them in a few days how it feels.

I left the next customers for the coming week and wrote the order down: small ones first, the largest last, with a pause of two days between groups so problems show up before the next group.

Open: the docs page for the query syntax is still the v1 text. Sam will update it when the second group is switched.

summary: Switched four more customers to search v2 and fixed a tokenizer problem with emails in queries that one of them hit within an hour.
body:
The first customer had no complaints after two days, so I switched four more small ones.

Within the hour one of them searched for an email address, and the tokenizer split it at the at sign, because I had made the at sign a separator by mistake in the term characters. The result was zero hits where v1 found the address. I added at sign, dot and underscore to the allowed term characters and a test with three email shaped queries.

I deployed the fix and the same query returned the expected hits. I told the customer's contact through Sam, who confirmed it.

After that I replayed the logged queries of the other three customers with the fixed tokenizer on staging and found no more differences from v1 other than order.

I wrote the case into the test fixtures and also added a small fuzz test that makes random strings of allowed characters and checks that the parser never throws anything but its own error type. It ran 10,000 cases without a crash.

The next group waits for two days as planned.

summary: Switched the mid-size customers to search v2 in two groups and measured p95 latency per group; the largest customers stay on v1 until the shard plan is further along.
body:
After two quiet days I switched nine mid-size customers in two groups, with a day between them.

For each group I took p95 search latency and the error count for the day before and the day after. Group one improved from 88 to 79 ms. Group two, which has larger documents, stayed at about 120 ms. Errors were only parse errors that came from wildcards in the middle of words, 14 in total across all customers, and each was shown with the position.

Sam updated the query syntax page and added a short list of what is not allowed.

I decided to keep the three largest customers on v1 for now. Their queries run over many documents and the parser change is not the risk, but I want to see the effect of the boosts on their ranking against labeled data first, and we have none for them. Sam will ask each of them for a few examples of searches that should find a particular document.

There is also the shard layout plan. The estimate of index sizes by month that I did earlier will change how these customers' indexes look, and I prefer not to change the parser and the layout for the biggest customers in the same weeks.

A small cleanup was to remove the v1 query builder tests that no longer ran, a file of 300 lines. The v1 builder itself stays until the last customer has moved.

To do next: the labeled examples from the large customers and a look at the slowest v2 queries from the log.

summary: Looked at the ten slowest v2 queries of the week; seven share a leading NOT clause that forces a scan, and I changed the builder to move it into a filter.
body:
I took the ten slowest v2 queries from the search log. Seven of them began with NOT and a field filter, for example NOT status:ok, and nothing else.

The builder put the must_not in the bool query next to a match_all for the rest, and OpenSearch scored every document. I changed the builder so that must_not clauses go into the filter context with no scoring. On the staging index for the largest customer this query took 410 ms before and 140 ms after.

The other three slow queries were wildcard at the end of a term over payload_text. They are legitimately costly. I did not change those, but I thought about requiring a minimum of three characters before the wildcard, and put the question to Mara.

Tests added: two builder tests for the filter placement, and the hit counts were compared with the old placement on the 60 labeled queries and were the same.

summary: Mara agreed to a minimum of three characters before a trailing wildcard, and I added it to the parser with a clear error message.
body:
Mara answered the question from yesterday: a one or two character prefix matches half the index, so the limit makes sense. She suggested three.

I added the rule to the parser. A term like ab* now gives a parse error that says the prefix must have at least three characters, with the position.

I checked the logged queries of the past month and found 11 with a short prefix, from four customers, all on v1 so far. Sam will mention it in the docs page.

The parser tests are at 63 and pass.

summary: Collected the labeled examples from two of the three large customers and compared v1 and v2 ranking; v2 is better for one and about equal for the other.
body:
Sam got examples of searches with the wanted document from two of the three large customers, 25 queries for the first and 18 for the second. The third has not answered yet.

I ran them on staging with the copied indexes of both customers, with v1 and with v2 and the chosen boosts.

For the first customer, the wanted document was in the top three for 12 of 25 with v1 and 19 of 25 with v2. For the second, 11 of 18 with v1 and 12 of 18 with v2, so about equal.

Looking at the second customer, their documents have no useful title field. Most of the text is in the message, so the title boost gives little. A per-customer boost override would help, but I said earlier we would wait until someone asks. This is such a case, though a small gain, so I will not build it now and will note it in the plan.

The first customer can move to v2 with a clear gain. The second has no loss, so it can move as well. I will switch them after the next nightly reindex, so the aliases are fresh, and one at a time, with a day between.

I wrote the results into the search v2 notes with the numbers per customer, so the third customer can be compared the same way when the examples come.

summary: Wrote down the open points for moving the large customers to search v2 and ordered them by risk, with the shard plan first.
body:
After the label comparison this morning I wrote a short list of what stands between the three large customers and search v2. The first point is index size: the largest customer has an index that takes about 71 minutes of the nightly reindex, and a v2 build runs next to it for a while.

The second point is the dash handling. Two internal trial users complained that a bare word with a dash is split into two terms. I proposed to keep the split for the analyzer but add a phrase fallback when the whole token matches a stored value. Mara has not answered yet.

The third point is the leading NOT change from two days ago. It helps the ten slow queries, but I want to check that the filter placement does not change the ranking for queries with boosts. I ran 20 of the labeled queries with and without the move and the top ten were identical for 19.

The twentieth differs only in position seven and eight, so I counted it as harmless.

The fourth point is disk headroom on the cluster during a double build. Tobias will look at the numbers. I did not touch any customer setting in this session; the list is in the branch notes and it is the base for the next planning talk.

summary: Added a phrase fallback for dashed bare words in the v2 parser, so a query like order-4411 matches the stored value again.
body:
The trial complaint about dashes came from the tokenizer splitting order-4411 into order and 4411, which matches far too many events. I changed the parser so that a bare word with a dash produces a bool should of the split terms and a phrase clause on the whole token, with the phrase boosted.

On the 60 labeled queries nothing moved except the six that contain dashes; for those the wanted event is now in the top three for five and in the top ten for the sixth. Latency did not change in a measurable way.

I added eight parser tests for dashes, including a leading dash, which still means NOT. Mara read the change in the afternoon and had no objection. The two trial users get it with the next deploy.

summary: Looked at Redis memory growth in production and found the per-session keys of the admin console grow with a long TTL, which explains most of it.
body:
Tobias asked why the Redis memory graph climbs about 3 percent a week. I scanned the key space on a replica with a sampled SCAN and grouped the keys by prefix.

The session store of the admin console holds about 41 percent of the memory. Its TTL is 30 days and it is refreshed on every request, so sessions of users who stopped using the console stay for a month. The query cache is about 35 percent and the rate limiter counters are small.

I did not change anything. I wrote the numbers into the ticket and proposed a TTL of 7 days with a sliding refresh, which Lena has to confirm because it logs people out. The key naming of the session prefix is also inconsistent: two versions with and without a colon. I listed both, to be cleaned up later.

summary: Built the first background v2 reindex for the largest customer on staging and learned that the double build needs about 1.8 times the disk of the old index.
body:
The goal of the evening was to see what the largest customer costs when its v2 index is built next to the v1 index. I used the alias mechanism from last month and started the reindex on staging with a copy of the customer's documents, 214 million events.

The build took 2 hours 40 minutes with the current batch size. The nightly window would not hold it together with the other customers, so for this customer the build has to start earlier or run in several nights. I tried a batch size of 4,000 instead of 2,000 and the time fell to 2 hours 5 minutes, but heap use of the data nodes rose and one node logged a long garbage collection pause of 9 seconds.

Disk use is the main finding. During the build the two indexes together used 1.8 times the old index. The swap and the delayed deletion of the old index, which waits for open scrolls, keep both on disk for a while longer.

I looked at the segment count after the build. It was high, so I ran a force merge to one segment per shard on the new index. The index shrank by 11 percent and a test search got faster, from 210 to 170 ms p95.

The force merge needs to be a standard step of the job for the large customers, but it should run before the swap, not after. I added it behind a flag and tested it once.

What is open: the heap pressure at the larger batch size, and the disk headroom on production. Tobias has to say how much room there is. I also want to check whether the shard by month layout changes these numbers, since it would build per month and not per customer. I wrote the figures into the plan document and stopped there. Production was not touched.

summary: Reviewed the first design of the schema registry with Mara and settled on versioned JSON schemas stored in Postgres, with compatibility checked on write.
body:
Mara and I spent the late morning on the schema registry design. The problem is that event schemas live in three places now: the ingest validator, the loader into ClickHouse and the docs. They drift.

We decided on a registry table in Postgres with one row per schema version, a customer or global scope, the JSON schema document and a hash. A schema is immutable once saved. A new version is accepted only if it is backward compatible with the previous one, meaning no removed required field and no changed type.

We discussed whether to use an existing registry product. It would be one more service to run and its compatibility rules do not fit our free-form properties field, so we dropped it.

The compatibility check is the part with real work. I wrote the rules as a list: added optional field is fine, added required field is not, narrowing an enum is not, widening is fine, integer to number is fine, number to integer is not. Mara asked about nested objects. Same rules apply recursively, and arrays are compared by item type.

The ingest validator will read from a cache of the registry, refreshed every minute, so a registry outage does not stop ingest. The cache falls back to the last good copy. Mara wants a metric for the age of that copy and I agreed.

We split the work. I take the table, the check and the write API; Mara takes the validator cache. The first migration is written and applied to my local database, with an index on scope and name.

I also drafted six unit tests for the compatibility rules. Two of them failed at first because my enum rule compared lists by order. Fixed with a set comparison. The open question is how customers see schema errors, which I left for Sam and the docs.

summary: Fixed the enum comparison in the registry compatibility check and added tests for nested arrays and widening.
body:
The enum test failure from the design session had a second cause besides the list order. A schema without an enum was compared with one that had an enum, and my code treated that as narrowing only in one direction.

Now a new enum on a field that had none counts as narrowing and is rejected, and removing an enum counts as widening and is accepted. I added tests for both cases.

Nested arrays of objects were the other gap. The check descended into the item schema for arrays of objects but not for arrays of arrays. I made the descent generic and added a test with three levels. All 14 tests of the compatibility module pass.

summary: Wrote the write API for the schema registry and checked that a rejected schema returns the exact incompatible field path.
body:
The registry write endpoint is in place: POST of a schema for a scope and a name, answer with the new version number or a 409 with a list of problems. Each problem has the JSON path of the field and a short reason such as required_field_added.

I chose 409 over 422 because the document itself is valid; it conflicts with the stored version. Mara agreed when I showed her the first responses.

The endpoint locks the row of the latest version while it checks, so two writes at once cannot both become version 5. I tested it with 20 parallel posts on my machine. One got version 5 and the others either got 6 and following when compatible, or 409. No duplicate numbers.

I also added a dry run flag that only checks. Sam will want that for the docs, because customers can try a schema before they commit it.

What is missing is the read side with caching headers and the audit log entry for a new version. The audit entry uses the same actor and old value format as the search version change, so I can reuse the helper.

summary: Added the audit log entries and the read endpoint with ETags for the schema registry, then hit a deadlock in the test database that came from the lock order.
body:
I did two things in the registry today: the audit entry on every new schema version, and the read endpoint with an ETag based on the schema hash.

The audit entry uses the helper from the search version change. It stores actor, scope, name, the old hash and the new hash. I checked a row in the database and the fields match what the audit export will need.

The read endpoint returns the latest version by default and a given version on request. The ETag is the hash. A conditional request with a matching tag returns 304 with no body. Mara's validator cache can use that to poll cheaply every minute.

The deadlock showed up when I ran the write test with 20 parallel posts again, now with the audit insert inside the transaction. Postgres reported deadlock detected on two sessions. The write took the registry row lock first and then inserted the audit row, but the audit helper also updates a counter row of the actor, and another path took that counter first and then the registry row.

I changed the order so that the actor counter is always touched last. After that I ran the parallel test 50 times and saw no deadlock.

I also looked at whether the counter update is needed inside the transaction at all. It is not strictly needed, but moving it out changes the helper for every user of it, so I left that for another day and noted it.

Some smaller points. The 409 body for a failed dry run is the same as for a real write, which is good for the docs. The scope check rejects a customer scope for a customer the caller does not belong to. I tested that with two keys.

Next is the validator cache by Mara, then a migration of the three existing schemas into the registry.

summary: Imported the three existing event schemas into the registry and found that the loader schema had two fields with a different type than the validator.
body:
I wrote a one-off script that reads the schemas of the ingest validator, the ClickHouse loader and the docs and writes them to the registry as version 1 of the global scope.

The validator and the docs matched except for one description text. The loader schema differed in two fields: duration_ms is an integer in the validator but a float in the loader, and session_id is allowed to be null in the loader only.

I checked the data. In the last week about 0.3 percent of events have a null session_id, and the loader accepts them because the ClickHouse column is nullable. The validator lets them through too, because the field is not required there, so the null is just an absent field that the loader turns into null. That means the loader schema was stricter in documentation only. I used the validator version.

For duration_ms I looked at values from the stream. All were whole numbers, but a customer SDK could send 12.5. The validator rejects it today. I kept integer and noted that the loader schema was wrong.

The import ran on staging first. Version 1 of the three schemas exists, the hashes are stored, and the audit log has three entries with the actor set to the script.

Then I ran the import on production with the dry run flag first and the real run after. Both went through. I did not switch any consumer yet; the validator still reads its own file.

The next step is the switch of the validator to the cache, which Mara has on her branch. We want both versions to run side by side for a day and compare the verdicts on the live stream.

One thing to remember: the docs build should also read from the registry. Sam has to be told when that is ready.

summary: Ran the registry validator in shadow mode against the live stream for two hours and saw no difference in verdicts on 9.1 million events.
body:
Mara's cache of the registry is merged on the branch, so I turned on shadow mode in one ingest worker group. It validates each event with both the old file and the registry copy and only counts the differences.

After two hours the counter showed 9.1 million events checked and zero differences. I also sent 200 hand made bad events, with wrong types and missing fields, through staging. Both validators rejected the same 200.

The cache age metric works. It stays under 60 seconds and rose to 70 once while a deploy restarted the registry service, then fell back. The fallback to the last good copy was used for that period and nothing failed.

CPU of the workers rose by about 2 percent in the shadow group, which is expected as both validators run. I will leave shadow mode on overnight and read the counters in the morning.

Open: the old validator file stays until the switch. I wrote the switch as a flag so it can be undone quickly.

summary: Switched the ingest validators to the schema registry after a clean night of shadow mode, and fixed a startup case where the cache was empty.
body:
The shadow counters from the night showed 61 million events and zero differences, so I switched the validator in all worker groups to read the registry cache. The old schema file stays in the repository for now, behind the flag.

While watching the rollout I found a problem with the startup. A worker that starts while the registry service is down has no last good copy and the cache was empty, so it rejected every event with schema_unknown. It only happened once in staging when I restarted both services together, but it would be bad in production.

The fix is to ship a snapshot of the schemas in the worker image, written at build time from the registry. A starting worker loads the snapshot first and then refreshes. The snapshot is at most a few days old, but schemas are immutable and new versions are rare, so that is fine.

I added the build step in the pipeline and a test that starts a worker with the registry unreachable and sends a valid event. It passes. Before the fix, the same test failed with the error above.

Tobias reviewed the pipeline change and asked that the build fail if the registry is down at build time, instead of baking an empty snapshot. I added the check and a clear message.

After the rollout I looked at the reject rate for an hour. It stayed at 0.8 percent, the same as before the switch. P95 of the ingest API is unchanged at 38 ms.

I also told Sam that the docs build could now read from the registry. He will try it next week and say what he needs for the examples.

Left for later: removing the old file and the flag. I want a week without incidents first. The shared audit counter in the transaction is also still on my list.

summary: Spent the evening on Postgres vacuum for the audit log table, which grew to 38 GB, and set per-table thresholds plus a plan for partitioning it by month.
body:
The audit log table passed 38 GB and a monitoring query showed dead tuples building up in it. The table is append mostly, but the actor counter update and a status column that is changed once after the insert create dead rows.

I looked at pg_stat_user_tables. Autovacuum ran on it only every two to three days because the default scale factor of 0.2 means millions of dead rows before it starts. I set the scale factor to 0.01 and the threshold to 50,000 for this table and ran a manual vacuum once. It took 41 minutes and removed 6.2 million dead tuples.

Bloat estimate after the vacuum is about 9 percent, which is acceptable. A full rewrite would give back the space but needs a lock, so I decided against it.

The longer fix is partitioning the audit log by month. The audit export for compliance will read ranges by time, and old months could be detached and archived. I wrote the plan: a partitioned copy, a backfill in batches of 100,000 rows and a short switch with a rename. It needs the indexes to include the time column, and the primary key changes to id plus created_at.

That key change is the risky part. Two places refer to the audit id from other tables. I searched the code and found only the export prototype and one admin console view. Lena has to adjust the view to pass the time as well.

I also checked the settings table which needed a lower threshold from the autovacuum review last week; it is fine now with the lower value.

I did not start the partition work. I put the plan into the audit-export notes, since the export is the reason for it, and asked Mara for her view on the key change.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why a customer sees schema_unknown in a test and showed that the schema name had a typo in their SDK config.
body:
Sam forwarded a customer ticket: their test events were rejected with schema_unknown. I looked at the rejects in the log for their key. The name in the events was page_viewed and the registry knows page_view.

It is a typo in their SDK config, not a registry problem. I checked that no other customer sends unknown names in a significant number; there were two more, both with tiny volume.

I suggested that the error message lists the closest known names. That is a small change in the validator, and I opened a ticket for it. Sam replied to the customer with the right name.

summary: Added the closest-name hint to the schema_unknown error and tested it with the typo from the customer ticket.
body:
The reject message for an unknown schema name now includes up to three close names, using edit distance on the names visible to that customer. The names of other customers are never part of the candidates; I added a test for that because it would be a leak.

With page_viewed as input the message says: schema_unknown: page_viewed, did you mean page_view. A name with no close match returns the old message.

The cost is small. The distance runs only on a reject, and the list of names is at most a few dozen per customer. I measured 0.02 ms per reject.

One case surprised me: a customer with a name like page_view_v2 and another with page_view_v1 both got each other's suggestion when they were in the same scope. That is correct, since both are in their own scope and visible to them.

Mara reviewed the change and merged it. Sam will add a line about the hint to the docs page on schema errors.

summary: Started the audit export design: a streamed NDJSON download by time range, built on the monthly partitions of the audit log, and wrote the first query.
body:
The compliance customers need an export of the audit log for a time range, signed off by us as complete. I started the design today in the audit-export branch.

The export is an NDJSON stream, one audit entry per line, ordered by created_at and id. A time range selects the monthly partitions, once the partitioning is done, and for now the query uses the index on created_at.

I wrote the first query with keyset pagination: where (created_at, id) is greater than the last pair, limit 5,000. Offset pagination was the first idea but it got slow for deep ranges. In a test over 12 million rows the keyset version took 80 ms per page at any depth, while offset 10 million took 3.4 seconds.

The stream is written through a Fastify reply stream so memory stays flat. I tested a 12 million row export and the process stayed at about 150 MB.

Completeness is the point of the compliance use. I thought about how a customer can verify it. Each file ends with a trailer line that holds the row count, the first and last ids and a SHA-256 over all lines. A customer can recompute it.

What about entries written while the export runs? The query takes a snapshot boundary at the start: the maximum created_at at that moment, and the trailer says so. Entries after it belong to the next export.

I asked Mara whether the clock of the writers can make created_at go backwards between servers. She said the value is set by the database with now(), so one clock only. Good.

Access is limited to the customer's admin keys, and each export writes its own audit entry with the range and the row count. I added that entry in the same way as the other helpers.

To do next: the partitioning of the table, test of the trailer hash against an independent script, and the console button by Lena. Also the question of how long exports are kept if they are stored; for now they are only streamed.

summary: Wrote an independent script that recomputes the export trailer hash and found that my first version hashed lines with and without the newline in different places.
body:
To trust the trailer I wrote a small Python script outside the project that reads an exported file, recomputes the count and the SHA-256, and compares them with the trailer.

The first run failed. The server hashed each line without the newline, while the script hashed the file bytes including newlines.
