I decided that the hash is over the exact bytes of the data lines including newline, since that is what a customer can compute with standard tools like sha256sum on the file minus the last line.

I changed the server and the script agrees now on a 100,000 row export and on a 12 million row export. The count and the first and last id match too.

Two more cases I tested. An empty range gives just the trailer with count 0 and the hash of nothing. A range where one entry has a field with a unicode line separator is escaped by JSON.stringify, so lines are never split inside.

I added both as automated tests. The script goes into docs/ as an example for customers; Sam will check the wording.

Open: the format of timestamps in the lines. They are ISO strings in UTC, which is what I chose, but the compliance customers may want local time. I will ask.

summary: Looked at the cache hit rate of the search API after a key naming change and found that two key formats for the same query halve it for v2 customers.
body:
The hit rate of the search cache in Redis was 58 percent for v2 customers and 81 percent for v1 customers. I suspected the key naming.

The cache key contains the customer, the normalized query and the page. For v1 the normalization lowercases the query and strips extra spaces. For v2 the key is built from the parsed AST, but the AST keeps the original case of phrase text, so Error and error make different keys even though the analyzer treats them the same.

I sampled 2,000 keys of v2 customers and found 640 pairs that differ only in case. That roughly explains the gap.

The fix is to lowercase text nodes when the AST is serialized for the key. It does not change the query that is sent to OpenSearch, only the key. I made the change and wrote a test with three spellings of one query that now give a single key.

I also added the search version to the key. Without it, a customer switched from v1 to v2 could be served an old cached v1 result for up to the TTL of five minutes. That did not hurt yet but it makes comparisons wrong. The prefix now reads search:v2:customer:... and the old keys expire on their own.

After the deploy I watched the hit rate for two hours. It climbed from 58 to 74 percent for v2 customers as the cache refilled, and the v1 customers stayed at 81.

The remaining gap seems to come from the dashboards of v2 customers that use many different filters. I did not chase it.

Memory use of Redis rose a little because of the new prefix for the transition, about 2 percent, and it went down again after the TTL.

I wrote the key layout into the key naming document, which was missing the search keys. Tobias asked for the same for the rate limiter keys, which I will do separately.

summary: Documented the Redis key layout for the rate limiter and the session store, and listed three prefixes that do not follow the naming rule.
body:
Tobias asked for a complete list of Redis key prefixes with owner, TTL and typical size. I went through the code of the rate limiter, the session store and the search cache and wrote the list.

Rate limiter: rl:key:{apikey}:{window} with a TTL of twice the window, small values. Sessions: sess:{id} with 30 days, about 2 KB each. Search cache: search:v2:{customer}:{hash} with 5 minutes. Query cache for dashboards: dash:{customer}:{hash} with 60 seconds.

Three prefixes break the rule of lowercase words separated by colons: one session prefix with a second variant without the colon, a leftover Sessions: with a capital from the old console, and a temporary key tmp_import from the loader.

I counted them. The capital one has 1,100 keys and the colon-less one has 3,900, both from clients that were never updated. They will go away when the TTL ends or I delete them with a scan job. I did not delete anything today.

The document says who owns each prefix and what to do before adding a new one.

summary: Ran the audit export for a full month on staging and found the memory use stays flat at about 120 MB, but the first byte took 9 seconds until I added an index hint.
body:
Today I ran the first full-size test of the audit export on the staging copy of the audit log, using the monthly partitions that went in last week. The test range was one whole month, which is about 4.2 million rows and a 1.6 GB NDJSON file. The export is streamed, and the process memory stayed flat at about 120 MB for the whole run, so the cursor approach works as planned.

The first byte of the download took 9 seconds, which is too long for a client that may time out at 10. EXPLAIN showed that the planner picked a sequential scan on the single partition and then sorted by created_at and id. The partition has an index on created_at alone, so the sort on the pair of columns could not use it. I added a composite index on (created_at, id) per partition in the migration script, and the first byte dropped to 0.4 seconds.

The total time for the month went from 7 minutes 40 seconds to 5 minutes 5 seconds with the same index. Most of the remaining time is JSON serialization of the details column, not the database. I tried a larger fetch size of 5,000 rows instead of 1,000, and it gave only 3 percent, so I left it at 1,000.

I also checked what happens if the client drops the connection in the middle. The server noticed the closed socket within a second, closed the cursor and released the transaction, so no long transaction was left on the primary. That matters because an open transaction there would hold back vacuum on the audit table, which we just fixed.

One open point is the range that spans two partitions. The query reads them in order, and the rows were correct at the boundary, but I only tested it with a synthetic boundary row. Next I want a test with real rows on both sides of midnight at the month end. After that, the trailer hash check goes into the same test run, using the independent script from earlier.

summary: Added a staging test for the audit export that crosses a month boundary and checks row counts and the trailer hash, and it found a duplicated row at the partition edge.
body:
I wrote the boundary test I planned after the full-month run. It creates audit rows at 23:59:59 and 00:00:00 on both sides of a month end, with a few sharing the exact same timestamp, and then exports a range that spans both partitions. The test compares the row count and the ids against a plain query on the parent table, and then runs the independent trailer hash script on the file.

The first run failed. One row appeared twice in the export, and the count was one too high. The cause was the resume condition in the cursor query: I used created_at >= last_seen when moving from the first partition to the second, instead of a strict comparison on the pair (created_at, id). A row at exactly midnight was read once at the end of the old partition range and again at the start of the new one.

I changed the condition to compare the pair (created_at, id) as a tuple, so each row is read exactly once. The test then passed, with the same count as the parent table query and matching ids in the same order. The trailer hash matched too, which shows the newline fix from earlier still holds across partitions.

I added a second case where many rows share one timestamp, 500 of them, because that is what a bulk settings change by an admin produces. They exported in id order without gaps. Total test time is about 40 seconds, so it can run in the normal suite.

Next I will give the export an optional from and to parameter check, so a reversed range returns a clear 400 instead of an empty file. Mara should also look at the tuple comparison, since it is the kind of change that looks harmless and is easy to get wrong.

summary: Planned the monthly partitioning of the audit log, wrote the migration with batched backfill and tested it on a staging copy of 38 GB.
body:
With the vacuum settings in place, I started the partitioning of the audit log that the export needs. Mara had agreed to the primary key change to id plus created_at.

The migration creates audit_log_new as a table partitioned by range on created_at, with one partition per month and a default partition for anything outside. Indexes are created on the parent: created_at plus id, actor and scope.

The backfill copies rows in batches of 100,000 ordered by created_at, committing after each batch. It records the last copied pair in a small progress table, so it can be stopped and continued. On the staging copy it took 3 hours 10 minutes for 38 GB, with the primary busy at about 15 percent more IO.

A trigger on the old table copies new inserts into the new one while the backfill runs. I tested that by inserting 1,000 rows during the copy; all arrived once. One conflict showed up when the trigger and the backfill both wrote the same row at the boundary, and I added on conflict do nothing.

The switch is a transaction that takes a short lock, checks that the counts match, renames the tables and drops the trigger. On staging it held the lock for 300 ms.

Checks after the switch: row counts equal, the max id equal, a sample of 10,000 random rows identical by hash. The export query uses the new indexes and for a one month range it reads one partition; the explain output shows the others pruned.

The admin console view that uses the audit id needs the time as well. Lena has a small change ready for it, and we agreed that it ships before the production switch.

I also wrote a rollback: keep the old table, renamed, for a week, and switch the names back if something is wrong. Disk is enough for that.

A partition creation job is still missing. Without it, new months land in the default partition. I wrote it as a monthly cron that creates the next three months, and added an alert if fewer than two future partitions exist.

summary: Ran the audit log partition switch on production in a quiet window; counts matched and the export query now reads a single partition for a month range.
body:
The backfill on production ran through the afternoon and finished at 3 hours 40 minutes, a bit slower than staging. Primary IO stayed within normal limits and no alert fired.

I did the switch at a quiet time. The lock was held for 420 ms. Row counts matched at 41,882,217 rows, the max id matched, and 10,000 sampled rows had identical hashes.

Lena's console view change was deployed an hour before, so the audit page keeps working; I checked it by hand with two customers.

The old table stays renamed as audit_log_old for a week. The partition cron created the next three months and the alert for missing partitions is quiet.

I ran the export of one month on production for a test customer. It read one partition, took 6 seconds for 700,000 rows and the trailer hash agrees with the script.

summary: Checked disk headroom on the OpenSearch data nodes with Tobias for a double build of the largest customer; there is room for one at a time only.
body:
Tobias pulled the disk numbers of the data nodes. They stand at 61 percent used on average, with the fullest node at 68 percent. The watermark for new shards is at 85 percent.

The v2 index of the largest customer is about 1.8 times the v1 size in the double phase according to my staging test. That is roughly 14 percent of the cluster disk. One customer at a time fits, but two large ones in parallel would push the fullest node near the watermark.

So the nightly job must build large customers one after another and wait for the deletion of the old index, which waits for open scrolls, before it starts the next one. I added that as a rule to the job config, with a limit of one large build at a time.

Tobias suggested adding two data nodes before the shard migration by month, since that layout will need room too. He will make an estimate of the cost.

summary: Made the reindex job build large customers one at a time and wait for the old index deletion, and tested the order on staging with three large copies.
body:
The job config now has a field for the size class of a customer. Customers above 100 million events are large, and the job keeps a queue of them with a concurrency of one. Small and mid-size customers still run in parallel up to four at a time.

The step after the swap waits until the old index has no open scrolls and is deleted before the next large build starts. I put a timeout of 30 minutes on this wait, after which it logs a warning and goes on, because a stuck scroll should not block the night.

I tested it on staging with three copies of the largest customer. The builds ran in sequence and the disk of the fullest node peaked at 74 percent of the smaller staging cluster, below the watermark. Total time was 5 hours 50 minutes with the force merge step before the swap.

That is longer than the nightly window of about 6 hours if the small customers also run. The small ones run in parallel to the large queue, so it still fits, but only barely. I noted that the large customers may need to be spread over two nights in the first weeks.

I also added a log line per customer with build time, size before and after, and the force merge gain. Mara will read it when the first large customer runs. The production switch of the large customers waits for the shard plan and the extra nodes.

summary: Prepared the first v2 reindex of a large customer on production: checked the one-at-a-time order against the disk estimate and wrote down what to measure during the build.
body:
After the staging test of the new build order, I went through the plan for the first v2 reindex of the second largest customer on production. The build has not started yet. Tobias and I looked at the data node disk graphs together and compared them with the staging numbers. The staging runs with three large copies showed a peak of about 1.8 times the size of the old index, and on the busiest production node that would put disk use near 71 percent. That leaves room for one build at a time, and we agreed that is the only safe way to run it.

I wrote down what to measure during the build: peak disk use per node, total duration, indexing throughput and search p95 for that customer on v1. From the staging runs I expect about 2 and a half hours for roughly 212 million documents, but that is a guess, since staging has smaller nodes. I set the alert threshold on the disk graph a bit lower than usual so Tobias gets a warning before the limit matters.

I also thought about the document count comparison after the build. The new mapping skips documents with an empty text field on purpose, so I expect v2 to have a few more than zero fewer documents. I added a line to the reindex notes about this, so the difference can be checked against a count of empty text fields in the old index and not chased as a bug.

The job waits for the old index deletion before the next large customer starts. On staging that wait was short, but the delete is throttled on the cluster, so production may be slower. I left the wait as it is and will look at the real time once a build has run.

Open: the largest customer stays on v1 and needs the shard plan first. Next I want to prepare a table for the disk numbers per customer, so the order of the nightly job can be planned.

summary: Wrote the plan for the large customers' move to search v2: order by size, a rollback switch per customer, and a list of checks before each step, with the first candidate named.
body:
Today I turned the open points from the risk list of a few days ago into a plan that Mara and Tobias can follow without me. The shard layout stays the first blocker, so the plan starts with what can be done on the current customer-based layout and what has to wait for the monthly one. The first reindex of a large customer on production is the template for the rest, and I used its disk and duration numbers as the planning basis.

The customers go in order of size, smallest of the large ones first. For each customer the plan has the same steps: build the v2 index in the background, compare result counts on the last week of real queries, switch a share of the traffic, watch p95 latency and the error rate, then switch the rest. Every step has a number that must hold before the next one starts. For latency the limit is that p95 stays within 20 percent of v1, and for errors it is no rise over the normal level of the customer.

The rollback is a per-customer setting in the admin console that sends searches back to the v1 index. I checked that it works without a deploy and that the v1 index is kept for seven days after the switch. That costs disk, and the disk headroom that Tobias and I checked earlier allows only one double build at a time. So the plan allows one customer per week at most, and never two builds in parallel.

I also listed what we do not know yet. The query cache entries for v2 are larger than for v1, so Redis memory has to be watched during each switch. Two customers use wildcard queries a lot, and the three character minimum may show up as errors in their client code. Sam will send a short note to these two customers before their switch, so the change does not surprise them.

For the checks I wrote a small script that takes a customer id and the last week of queries and prints the count difference between v1 and v2 per query. Differences above 5 percent are listed with the query text, so I can look at them by hand. I ran it on the customer from the first production reindex and found 14 queries with a difference, nearly all of them dashed words that the phrase fallback now handles. That gave me some confidence in the method.

Open questions: whether the largest customer should wait for the monthly shard layout, since its index would be rebuilt again soon after. My view is yes, and I wrote that into the plan as a proposal for Mara to confirm. Next step is the review of the plan with Mara and Tobias, then the second large customer.

summary: Reviewed the large-customer v2 plan with Mara and Tobias; they confirmed the largest customer waits for the monthly shards and asked for a Redis memory check at each switch.
body:
The review of the move plan took about forty minutes and led to three changes. Mara agreed that the largest customer should wait for the monthly shard layout, because two full rebuilds in a short time would cost more disk and more risk than one. The plan now lists that customer as the last step, after the shard migration.

Tobias asked for a Redis memory check at every switch. The v2 query cache entries are about twice the size of the v1 ones, and a large customer sends many distinct queries. We agreed on a simple rule: before each switch I note the used memory and the key count of the query cache prefix, and after an hour I compare them. If memory grows by more than 5 percent of the total, the switch is paused and the TTL of the v2 entries is looked at again.

Mara also wanted the per-customer rollback tested once on a real customer, not only on staging. I did that with a small customer that is already on v2. I switched it back to v1, ran its normal queries for ten minutes, and switched it forward again without errors. The switch took effect in under a minute for new searches, and cached results from before the switch were still served until their TTL ended, which is fine.

I updated the plan document with the three changes and sent it to Sam for the customer notes. The next step is to pick the date of the second large customer and start its background build.

summary: Looked at why the Redis hit rate of the rate limiter keys looked low in Grafana and found the panel counted first requests of every window as misses.
body:
The Grafana panel for the rate limiter showed a hit rate of 38 percent, and I wanted to know if that was a real problem. I read the panel query and the limiter code.

Every new window starts with a key that does not exist yet, so the first request in each window is counted as a miss. With many keys that expire after short windows, this is normal and not a cache failure. The limiter works as designed.

I changed the panel to show the number of limiter decisions per second and the share of rejected requests instead. That is what we actually watch. I left the old panel in a collapsed row with a note that explains the number.

summary: Wrote a small script that checks the audit export trailer hash for any month on staging, so the check can run after every deploy.
body:
The independent hash script from a few days ago was a one-off. Today I turned it into a command that takes a month, calls the export endpoint, recomputes the trailer hash and compares it with the one in the stream.

It exits with code 1 and prints the first differing line number if the hashes differ. I tested it on three months of staging data and it passed. I also edited one byte in a saved copy and it failed at the right line.

I added it to the staging deploy checklist. It takes about 40 seconds for a month, which is fine.

summary: Built the first version of the search v2 query explain tool for support, then dropped the idea of showing raw OpenSearch JSON to customers and kept it internal.
body:
Sam often has to ask me why a query returned a given result, so I started an explain endpoint on the search API. It takes a query and a document id and returns the parsed query tree, the final OpenSearch query and the score breakdown for that document.

The first version returned the raw explain output of OpenSearch. It was 400 lines for a simple query and nobody could read it. I wrote a reducer that keeps only the top contributions per field and prints them as a short list with the boost, the term frequency and the field norm.

I tested it on five real tickets from last month. In four of them the explanation showed the reason at once: a field boost, a stemmed term and two cases of a missing filter. The fifth involved a document that was not in the index at all, so the tool said so with a clear message.

I had planned to offer this to customers in the admin console. After thinking about it I decided against it. The score breakdown exposes field names and the internal mapping, and customers would start to depend on exact numbers that change with every reindex. So the endpoint requires the internal role and is documented only for the team.

I also added a check that the document belongs to the tenant in the request, so support cannot see another customer's data by accident. A test covers it.

I wrote down two limits. The tool does not show highlight logic, and the scores are only valid on the shard set of the moment. Tomorrow I will show it to Sam and watch how Sam uses it, since that decides what else is needed.

summary: Showed Sam the explain tool and fixed two things that confused Sam right away: field names in the parsed tree and a missing hint for stemmed terms.
body:
Sam tried the explain endpoint on a live ticket this morning. The first problem was that the parsed tree used internal field names such as txt_main instead of the names customers know. I added a mapping back to the public names.

The second problem was that a stemmed term showed only the stem. Sam did not see why the word running matched run. I added the original token next to the stem in the output.

Sam solved the ticket in ten minutes with it, which used to take half a day with me. I will leave it as it is for now.

summary: Measured Redis memory per key prefix in production and found the v2 query cache entries are about twice as large as the v1 ones because they store the highlight fragments.
body:
After the key layout work I wanted real numbers per prefix. I used a sampling scan over 200k keys and summed the sizes with MEMORY USAGE, grouped by prefix.

The session keys are still the largest group at 41 percent, which fits the earlier finding. The search cache is second at 33 percent. Within it, v2 entries average 9.4 KB and v1 entries 4.6 KB.

The difference comes from the highlight fragments that v2 stores in the cached response. Most clients of the search API show them only on the first page, so I tested caching the fragments separately. That split made the code more complex and saved only about 12 percent, so I did not keep it.

A simpler change is to compress cached values above 4 KB. I tried it with gzip on a sample and got 3.1 times smaller values, but the CPU cost on the search API went up by 6 percent at peak. That is not a good trade yet.

I wrote the numbers into the Redis notes and put the compression idea on the list for when memory is a real problem. For now the instance sits at 58 percent of memory.

summary: Fixed a flaky audit export test that depended on the order of rows with equal timestamps at the partition edge.
body:
The month boundary test for the audit export failed once on CI. The failing check compared the order of two rows that have the same timestamp to the millisecond.

The export query sorted only by timestamp, so rows with equal timestamps came out in any order. I added the row id as a second sort key in the query. That also makes the export stable between runs, which the trailer hash needs anyway.

I ran the test 200 times and it passed every time. I checked the query plan and the index still serves the sort.

summary: Wrote the first version of per-key rate limits: a limit field on the API key, a lookup cached in Redis, and a check in the limiter before the global limit.
body:
The rate limiter today knows only the limit per customer. Customers asked for separate limits per API key, so I started the work on this branch.

I added a nullable column rate_limit_per_min to the api_keys table in Postgres. The migration is small and runs in a second. If the column is null, the key uses the customer limit as before.

The limiter now reads the key limit through a small lookup. The result is cached in Redis for 60 seconds under the existing limiter prefix, so a change in the admin console takes at most a minute to apply. I kept the key name in line with the naming rule.

The check order matters. The key limit is checked first, then the customer limit, so one noisy key cannot use up the whole customer budget without being stopped. A request that passes the key check still counts against the customer counter.

I wrote tests for four cases: key limit only, customer limit only, both with the key lower, and both with the customer lower. All passed. A load test with 2,000 requests per second across 50 keys showed no extra latency worth mentioning, about 0.2 ms.

Open points: what the error body says when the key limit is hit, and whether the Retry-After header should differ. I will ask Mara tomorrow.

summary: Tried to speed up the cold start of the ingest worker by loading the schema cache in parallel; it saved only 0.4 seconds, so I dropped the change and kept the simple loop.
body:
Last week's schema registry change made the ingest worker load all schemas from Postgres at startup, and Tobias noticed that a fresh task needs a few seconds before it takes traffic. I measured it first: the startup is about 6.2 seconds, and the schema load is 1.1 seconds of that. The rest is the connection setup to Redpanda and the first health check.

I wrote a version that loads the schemas with several goroutines at once, one per schema name. On staging with the real count of schemas it saved 0.4 seconds. It also made the code harder to read, since errors from several goroutines have to be collected and the cache has to be filled in a fixed order for the tests.

Because the gain was so small against the total, I went back to the plain loop and deleted the branch of the change. The bigger part of the startup is the broker connection, and Tobias said he would look at the health check interval on the ECS side, which is his area and needs no code change from me. I added a log line with the time of each startup phase, so the next measurement does not need a debug build. The line printed 1.0, 3.9 and 1.2 seconds on staging for schemas, broker and health check. Nothing else changed in the worker today.

summary: Planned the shard layout for the search index by month with Tobias, listed sizes per customer and found two customers that would give shards far above the size target.
body:
Tobias and I spent the morning on the plan to split the search index by month instead of by customer. I pulled the document counts and store sizes per customer and per month from the cluster.

The target is shards of 20 to 40 GB. With the monthly layout and the current growth, most customers fit one shard per month. Two large customers do not: their busiest months are about 110 GB and 140 GB, so they need three to four shards for those months.

We discussed routing. With monthly indexes, a query over the last 30 days touches one or two indexes, which is good. A query without a time range touches all of them, and for old customers that means about 30 indexes. I measured a test of this on staging with 24 small indexes, and the fan-out cost about 35 ms more at p95.

We decided to default the search API to a time range of the last 90 days when the client sends none, and to document it. Mara still has to agree because it changes behavior for existing clients.

Tobias worried about the number of shards in the cluster. With the plan we would have about 1,100 instead of 400. His estimate is that the data nodes cope with that if the shards are not tiny. We will merge months for small customers into quarterly indexes to keep the count down.

The migration needs the double build again, and the disk limit from last week still holds: one large customer at a time.

I wrote the plan as a document with the numbers and the open decisions. The next step is to build a prototype alias scheme on staging and test queries over it.

summary: Checked Redis memory after the TTL change for admin console sessions and saw the session prefix shrink by about a third in two days, with no complaints about logouts.
body:
A few days ago I shortened the TTL of the per-session keys of the admin console, because they were the main reason for the Redis memory growth. Today I compared the memory per key prefix with the numbers from before the change. The session prefix went down from about 2.1 GB to 1.4 GB, and the total used memory fell by roughly the same amount.

I worried that users would be logged out too early, so I looked at the session logs. The TTL is renewed on every request, and the shorter value only affects people who leave the console idle. There were 3 support messages about it in the shared inbox, and Sam confirmed that none of them was about a logout. Lena checked the login screen for the expired session case, and the message is clear enough.

The curve is still falling slowly, because old keys with the long TTL are expiring by themselves. I expect the final number in about a week. I added the session prefix size to the Grafana memory panel, so the number is visible without running a script. Next I will look at the three prefixes that do not follow the naming rule.

summary: Looked at the slowest Postgres queries of the admin console and added an index on the audit log read path that cut a 1.4 second query to 30 ms.
body:
The pg_stat_statements top list showed one query of the admin console taking 1.4 seconds on average. It lists the latest audit log entries of a customer filtered by user.

After the partitioning, the query used the right partition but a sequential scan inside it, because the existing index started with the timestamp. I added an index on customer_id, user_id and timestamp descending on the partitioned table.

On production, the index build on each partition took between 20 and 90 seconds, and I ran it with CONCURRENTLY. Afterward the same query took 30 ms.

I checked write latency of the audit log for an hour and saw no change. The index adds about 1.2 GB in total. I also removed an older index that the new one makes unnecessary, which gives back 800 MB.

summary: Wrote the retry plan for the document loader with large files: which errors are retried, backoff values, and how a partial upload resumes from a part number.
body:
The loader branch starts today with a plan, written before any code. Large files go in as multipart uploads to S3, and today a failed part means the whole file starts over. For files of several GB that wastes hours.

The plan retries only errors that can pass: timeouts, connection resets, 500 and 503 from S3. It does not retry 403 or 404. Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles per attempt with jitter, and stops after 6 attempts or 2 minutes per part.

For resume, the loader stores the upload id and the list of finished parts with their ETags in Postgres after every part. If the process dies, the next run reads the list and continues from the first missing part. Uploads older than 24 hours are aborted by a cleanup job.

I also wrote what must be tested: a killed process in the middle, a part that fails five times and then works, and a part that never works. Each should end in a clear state, either finished or failed with the part number in the log.

Mara read the plan and asked for a metric on retries per file. I added it to the list. I will start with the state table tomorrow.

summary: Built the part-level state table and resume logic for the document loader and got a killed 6 GB upload to finish from part 212 on staging.
body:
Most of the evening went into the loader resume. I created the table loader_parts with upload id, part number, ETag and status, and a migration for it. The loader writes a row after each completed part, in the same step that records the ETag.

The resume code reads all finished parts of an upload id, skips them and starts at the first gap. The first version had a bug: it trusted the table even when S3 did not know the part anymore after an abort. I added a call to ListParts at the start of a resume and compare it with the table. If they differ, S3 wins and the table is corrected.

I tested with a 6 GB file on staging. I killed the loader process at part 212 of 480 with kill -9. The next run found 211 finished parts, continued from 212 and completed the file. The final object checksum matched the source.

Then I tested a part that fails. I put a proxy in front of S3 that returns 503 for a chosen part four times. The loader retried with the backoff values from the plan and the fifth attempt worked. The log showed each attempt with its delay, 0.6 s, 1.1 s, 2.3 s and 4.4 s.

A part that always fails ended the upload as failed after 6 attempts, with part 77 in the error. The state stays in the table so a person can look at it.

Not done yet: the cleanup job for old uploads and the retry metric. Memory use stayed at about 90 MB during the 6 GB test, which is what I hoped.

summary: Added the retry counter metric and the cleanup job for abandoned multipart uploads in the loader, and checked both on staging.
body:
I added a Prometheus counter loader_part_retries_total with a label for the error class, not for the file, to keep the number of series low. A dashboard panel shows retries per hour.

The cleanup job runs hourly. It finds uploads in the state table that are older than 24 hours and not finished, aborts them on S3 and marks the rows aborted. I tested with three fake old uploads on staging and all three were aborted. S3 showed no leftover parts.

I also set an S3 lifecycle rule as a second guard that aborts incomplete uploads after 3 days, so a bug in the job does not cost storage. Tobias will add the rule to Terraform, and I sent him the block.

The next step is a larger test with a real customer file from the support backlog.

summary: Reviewed the Terraform change from Tobias for the S3 lifecycle rule and asked to scope it to the loader prefix only.
body:
Tobias sent the Terraform diff for the abort rule. It applied to the whole bucket, which also holds exports that use their own multipart uploads with longer times.

I asked him to scope the rule to the loader prefix. He changed it and the plan output now shows one rule for that prefix. I read the plan twice and approved it.

He applied it on staging first. The rule showed up correctly in the console, and production follows tomorrow.

summary: Ran the loader on a real 14 GB customer file in production with a forced failure halfway and confirmed that it resumed and the row counts matched.
body:
A customer from the support backlog had a 14 GB NDJSON file that failed twice with the old loader. With Mara's agreement I used it for the first production test of the new resume logic.

I started the load in a quiet period. At about 50 percent, I stopped the loader task in ECS on purpose, which is a harder stop than a normal deploy. The task restarted within a minute and the loader found 466 finished parts out of 940.

It continued from part 467. The retry counter showed 9 retries in the whole run, all from timeouts of S3 in one short period. The file was complete after 52 minutes in total.

I compared the row count after the import with the line count of the file: 31,882,410 on both sides. The checksum of the stored object matched too.

One thing I noticed is that the progress shown in the admin console jumped back to 0 for a moment after the restart, because it was computed from the current run only. I changed it to count finished parts from the state table. It is a small fix, and I tested it on staging.

The lifecycle rule is now also on production. I told the customer through Sam that the file is in.

summary: Built the prototype alias scheme for monthly indexes on staging and measured query latency over 3, 12 and 30 months, which stayed within the target for ranges up to a year.
body:
With the shard plan agreed, I built the prototype on staging. I took one mid-size customer and created monthly indexes for 30 months, with a write alias that points to the current month and a read alias that covers all of them.

The reindex into the monthly indexes used a script that routes each document by its event time. It took 1 hour 10 minutes for 64 million documents. The documents with a missing event time went into a separate index, and I counted 3,100 of them. We need a rule for those before anything like this goes near production.

Then I ran the standard query set against the prototype. For a range of 3 months, p95 was 74 ms, against 71 ms on the old layout. For 12 months it was 112 ms against 98 ms. For all 30 months it was 205 ms against 130 ms.

The all-time case is the weak point, as expected. It is rare in the logs of the search API: less than 2 percent of queries have no range or a range over a year. So the default range plan helps.

I also tried the can-match phase and a smaller number of shards per index. Going from 3 shards to 1 for small months cut the all-time p95 from 205 to 168 ms. That is a useful lever.

This was only a staging prototype on a copy of one customer. The production index is untouched and no real migration has started. I wrote the numbers to the plan document. Open: the rule for events without an event time, probably the ingest time, and how aliases are switched without a gap at the month change. Tobias will look at the second point since it touches the cron jobs.

summary: Decided with Mara that events without an event time go to the month of their ingest time, and counted how many such events each customer has.
body:
I asked Mara about the 3,100 documents without an event time. We agreed to use the ingest time, because that field is always there and is set by us. The documents also get a flag so we can find them later.

I counted these events in production for all customers. The total is 0.04 percent, and 90 percent of them come from two old SDK versions. One customer has about 70 percent of the missing times, so I will tell Sam to ask that customer to update the SDK.

I updated the routing script and tested it on the staging prototype: the documents now land in the right monthly index and keep the flag.

I put the rule in the plan document and the list of the two SDK versions in the support notes. This closes one of the open points of the plan.

The second point, the alias switch at the month change, is still with Tobias.

summary: Wrote the cron job design for next month's index creation: a script that is safe to run twice, checks the alias, and alerts if the new index is missing.
body:
After the talk with Tobias about the alias switch, I wrote the script that the cron job will call. It creates the index for the next month three days before the month change, with the same settings and mappings as the current one. If the index already exists, it does nothing and exits with success, so a second run is harmless.

The script also checks the aliases. It confirms that the write alias points to the current month and that the read alias covers the months of the default range. On a mismatch it prints what it found and exits with an error, but does not change anything by itself. I tested this on staging by deleting an alias on purpose, and the error text named the missing alias.

For the alert, the job sends a metric with the time of its last successful run, and a Prometheus rule fires if it is older than 36 hours in the last five days before a month change. Tobias will add the cron entry in Terraform tomorrow. I still need a test for the month change itself, which I will do with a faked date on staging next.

summary: Tried a different library for NDJSON parsing in the loader to speed up large files, measured only 4 percent gain and went back to the existing parser.
body:
The loader spends a lot of CPU on parsing, so I tried a faster streaming JSON library for the NDJSON path. I made a branch of the loader code and replaced the parser behind the existing interface.

On the 6 GB staging file, the old parser needed 11 minutes of CPU and the new one 10 minutes 34 seconds, about 4 percent less. The time of the whole upload did not change at all, because the network and the S3 part uploads dominate.

The new library also had a difference in how it handles invalid UTF-8. The old one replaces bad bytes, the new one fails the line. We have customers with such files, and a failure here would change behavior. I could have added a wrapper to fix it, but with so small a gain it was not worth the risk.

I dropped the experiment and deleted the local branch. I wrote a short note in the loader readme: parsing is not the bottleneck, and the part size and the number of parallel parts matter more.

That led to a quick test of parallel parts. With 4 in parallel the 6 GB file took 14 minutes, with 8 in parallel 9 minutes, and with 16 it was 8.5 minutes with more S3 timeouts. I set the default to 8 and made it a setting.

The retry counter showed 3 times more retries at 16 parallel parts, which fits the picture. I left the default at 8 and documented the numbers.

summary: Wrote the docs page for the default 90 day range of v2 searches together with Sam, including the response header and two example requests.
body:
Sam and I wrote the page for the docs. It says that a v2 search without a time range covers the last 90 days, and that the response contains a header with the range that was applied.

I wrote two examples: one without a range, with the header in the answer, and one with an explicit range of two years. Sam rewrote my text to be shorter and added a sentence on how to search all time on purpose.

We did not publish yet. The page waits until the alias scheme is decided, because the limits may change.

summary: Discussed the alias switch at the month change with Tobias and agreed on a cron job that creates next month's index three days early.
body:
Tobias proposed that a job creates the next monthly index three days before the month ends, with its settings and mapping, and adds it to the read alias at once. The write alias moves at midnight UTC with one atomic alias action.

That avoids a gap and makes it easy to test. I checked that an atomic alias update with remove and add in one request is supported on our cluster version. It is.

Tobias will write the job and I will write the test that runs it on staging with a fake month change. A failed create must page the on-call, since writes would fail on the first of the month.

summary: Wrote the month-change runbook for the monthly search indexes: create, verify the alias, switch, and a manual fallback if the cron job fails.
body:
Started the day by turning the discussion with Tobias into a runbook. It lists the steps for the month change: the cron job creates next month's index three days early, a check confirms the document mapping matches the previous month, and the alias for writes moves at midnight UTC.

The runbook also has a manual fallback. If the new index is missing at the alert time, the on-call runs the creation script by hand with the month as an argument. The script is safe to run twice, so there is no risk in a second run.

I added the exact commands and the expected output of each check, so that nobody has to read the script to know what a good result looks like. Tobias read it and asked for one more line about how to roll the write alias back. I added it with the curl call.

What is left: a dry run on staging across a real month change, which is planned for the end of this week. Sam will get a short version of the page for the support notes.

summary: Added a per-key limit override to the admin console API and found that the Redis lookup cache kept the old limit for up to the full TTL after a change.
body:
Lena asked for a way to change the limit of an API key from the admin console, so I added the endpoint that writes the new value to Postgres. The limiter reads the limit through a Redis lookup cache with a TTL of 10 minutes.

In a test on staging I changed a limit from 100 to 20 requests per second and the limiter kept using 100 for almost the whole TTL. For support this is confusing, because a customer who asks for a lower limit expects it right away.

The fix is that the endpoint now deletes the cache key of that API key after the Postgres write. If the delete fails, the endpoint still returns success but logs a warning, since the TTL will correct it anyway.

I wrote two tests: one for the change with a delete, and one where the Redis delete throws. Both pass. The key naming follows the existing prefix, so no new prefix shows up in the memory report.

Next step is the response header that tells clients their current limit, which Sam wants for the docs.

summary: Dry-ran the month change of the monthly search indexes on staging with a faked clock, and the alias switch worked, but the alert for a missing index fired late.
body:
Ran the month-change runbook on staging with a faked clock set to a few minutes before midnight. The cron job created the new index, the mapping check passed and the write alias moved on time.

Queries over a range that crossed the month boundary returned the same counts as before the switch. I compared 20 saved queries from the staging set and all matched.

The problem was the alert. I deleted the new index on purpose to test it, and the alert took 12 minutes to fire, because the check runs every 10 minutes and the rule waits for two failed checks. For a three day lead time that is fine, but for the last day it is too slow.

I changed the rule to fire after one failed check in the last 24 hours before the month change and left the two check rule for earlier days. Tobias reviewed the Prometheus rule change and approved it.

The runbook has one more note now about the faked clock, so the next person can repeat the test.

summary: Found that the Postgres autovacuum on the audit log lagged behind after the partition switch and tuned it per partition, which cleared the dead tuple backlog.
body:
The Grafana panel for dead tuples showed the audit log growing in dead rows since the partition switch. Autovacuum was running, but the older partitions are rarely written, and the settings I had were tuned for the old single table.

I looked at pg_stat_user_tables for the partitions. The current month had 2.1 million dead tuples and the vacuum ran only every few hours, because the scale factor was too large for a table of that size.

I set a lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and a higher cost limit on the current partition only, and left the old ones alone. Old partitions get a single manual vacuum freeze once they are closed, and I added that step to the month-change script of the audit log.

After two hours the dead tuples of the current partition dropped below 50 thousand. Query times on the admin console audit page did not change, since the index work of last week already covered them.

I also wrote a short note in the Postgres page of our docs, so that the setting is not removed later by mistake. Nothing else is open on this.

summary: Added the rate limit header to responses and a docs example, so customers see their current per-key limit and the remaining requests.
body:
Added the header with the limit and the remaining count to every API response, taken from the same lookup the limiter already does. No extra Redis call is needed.

For keys without their own limit the header shows the global value. I wrote tests for both cases and for a key that has just been changed.

Sam helped with the docs: one example request with the headers in the response, and a short text about what to do when the remaining count reaches zero. We kept the wording simple and did not promise exact numbers during a limit change.

The next step is to check the overhead on the p99 latency of the search API after the deploy.

summary: Checked the p99 of the search API after the rate limit header change and found a small rise caused by an unneeded JSON parse of the cached limit entry.
body:
After the deploy to production I compared the p99 latency of the search API for two hours before and after. The p99 rose from 182 ms to 191 ms, which is small but outside the normal noise of that hour.

I profiled one instance with the Node inspector for ten minutes. The limiter parsed the cached limit entry as JSON on every request, and then the header code parsed it again through a helper.

I changed the lookup so that it returns the parsed object once, and the header code uses that object. I also moved the number formatting out of the hot path.

The tests still pass. I ran a load test on staging with 500 requests per second for five minutes. The p99 matched the numbers from before the header change within 2 ms.

I deployed it in the afternoon and watched the panel for an hour. The p99 is back to 183 ms.

One thing I did not do is store the entry as a plain string in Redis. That would save more, but it changes the key format, and it is not worth a migration now. I noted the idea in the branch todo list.

Next is a look at how the limiter behaves when Redis is slow, since the lookup is now in every request path.

summary: Wrote a fallback for the limiter when the Redis lookup of the key limit times out: it uses the global limit and counts the event in a metric.
body:
Looking at the request path, the limit lookup waits for Redis with the default client timeout of one second, and a slow Redis would slow every search request.

I set a timeout of 50 ms for this lookup only. On a timeout, the limiter uses the global limit and increments a counter, limiter_lookup_timeouts_total.

I tested this on staging by pausing the Redis container for a few seconds. Requests stayed fast and the counter rose. After the resume everything went back to normal without a restart.

I added a Grafana panel next to the limiter panels and an alert for more than 20 timeouts per minute for five minutes. Mara looked at the change and asked that the timeout be a config value. I made it one with 50 ms as the default.

summary: Started the ingest batching design: the worker should write events to Postgres and ClickHouse in groups, and I measured how large the groups are today.
body:
Began work on the ingest-batching topic. The worker now writes each message from the queue as its own insert in one path, and groups only in the ClickHouse loader. I wanted real numbers before changing anything.

I added a temporary log line and collected one hour of production traffic from one worker. The median group has 1 event on the Postgres path and about 400 on the ClickHouse path, which has its own buffer.

The Postgres path is the expensive one. At peak it makes about 900 small inserts per second per worker, and the commit time dominates.

The plan is to collect up to 200 events or 50 ms, whichever comes first, and write them in one transaction using COPY or a multi-row insert. I looked at both. COPY is faster, but conflicts on the event id are harder to handle, so I chose the multi-row insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for the first version.

I wrote the interface for the batcher with a flush function and a context for shutdown. On shutdown the worker must flush before it commits the offsets to Redpanda, otherwise events are lost, and I added a comment about this in the code.

There are no tests yet beyond the empty batch case. Tomorrow I will write the tests for the size limit, the time limit and the shutdown order.

I also asked Tobias whether the database has room for larger transactions. He thinks it does, and wants to see the WAL rate in the first staging test.

summary: Wrote the batcher tests for size, time and shutdown, and a partial failure case showed that one bad event failed the whole group, so the worker now splits and retries it.
body:
Wrote the tests for the new batcher. The size limit and the time limit passed on the first run, and so did the shutdown flush with offsets committed only afterwards.

The partial failure test was the interesting one. I put one event with an invalid value into a group of 200. The multi-row insert failed for the whole group, and all 200 events went back to the queue and failed again, which is a poison message loop.

The fix is a fallback: when a group fails with a data error, the worker splits it in half and tries each half. This repeats until single events are left, and the single bad event goes to the dead letter topic with the error text.

Connection errors are not data errors. For those the group is retried with the existing backoff of the worker and is not split, otherwise a short network problem would produce many small inserts.

I added tests for both kinds of errors. With one bad event in 200 the split needs 9 inserts in total, which is acceptable for a rare case.

I also added a metric for the number of splits and one for the group size, so the staging test can show how the batcher behaves.

Tomorrow I will run it on staging against the replayed traffic of one hour and look at the WAL rate for Tobias.

summary: Ran the replayed hour of production traffic through the batching worker on staging and saw 14 times fewer commits, with the WAL rate lower by about a third.
body:
Replayed one hour of recorded production traffic on staging with the batching worker and with the old worker, one after the other.

The old worker made about 3.1 million commits in the hour. The batching worker made 220 thousand, a factor of 14, with a median group of 61 events at this traffic level.

The WAL rate was lower by about a third, which Tobias wanted to see. CPU on the staging database dropped from 46 to 29 percent.

The event counts in Postgres matched the input exactly, and the dead letter topic had the 12 invalid events that the old worker also rejected.

summary: Looked at the latency of single events with batching and found the 50 ms wait adds a visible delay at low traffic, so the wait now shortens when the queue is empty.
body:
With batching the staging test looked good for throughput, but I also wanted to know how long a single event waits. At night traffic is low, and a group often waits the full 50 ms before it is written.

I measured the time from ingest accept to the row being visible in Postgres. At peak the median was 31 ms. At low traffic it was 58 ms, up from 6 ms with the old worker.

Nothing breaks, but the dashboard for the live view of the customers shows events a bit later, and some customers watch that closely. I did not want to make the product feel slower in quiet hours.

The change is that the batcher flushes early when the queue has no more messages ready. It uses the poll result of the Redpanda client to know that. A group is then written as soon as the worker has nothing else to add.

I repeated the measurement. The median at low traffic is 9 ms now, and at peak it is unchanged at 31 ms, since the groups still fill up there.

The test for the time limit needed a change, because it assumed that the batcher always waits. I added a fake poll source to the test and checked both behaviors.

One more point: the early flush produces smaller groups at medium traffic. I looked at the commit count at a third of the peak rate and it was still 9 times lower than the old worker, which is fine.

Next I will write the rollout plan with a config switch per worker, so Tobias can enable it on one instance first.

summary: Wrote the rollout plan for the batching worker with a switch per instance and the metrics to watch, and reviewed it with Tobias and Mara.
body:
Wrote the rollout plan for the batching worker. The batching is behind an environment variable, so each ECS task can run old or new code paths without a new image.

The plan has four steps. First one task out of six runs with batching for a day. Then three tasks for a day. Then all tasks, and the old path stays in the code for one more week.

For each step I listed what to watch. These are the commit rate, the group size, the number of splits, the dead letter count, the consumer lag in Redpanda, and the time from accept to visible row.

I also wrote down what counts as a reason to go back. The reasons are consumer lag above 30 seconds for five minutes, or the dead letter count rising faster than before, or any mismatch in the nightly count check between the queue and Postgres.

Tobias asked for the Terraform variable to be added, so the switch can be set per task definition and not by hand in the console. I added the variable in the module and he will review the change in his next block.

Mara looked at the shutdown handling. She asked what happens when ECS kills a task after the grace period while a group is still being written. The flush runs within the stop timeout, but I had not set it explicitly. We set the stop timeout of the task to 60 seconds, and the flush has a limit of 20 seconds.

She also pointed out that the offsets commit must follow only a successful write, and that is already tested.

I added both points to the plan. The first step is planned for tomorrow morning, in a quiet hour.

Open question: whether the batch size should be a config value too. For now it stays in code, and we will change it only if the metrics ask for it.

summary: Switched one of six ingest tasks to the batching worker in production and compared it with the others for three hours; counts matched and the commit rate dropped.
body:
Started step one of the rollout: one ingest task out of six with batching enabled through the environment variable.

I watched it for three hours, which includes the late morning peak. The commit rate of that task is about 12 times lower than that of the others, and the group median at peak was 58 events.

Consumer lag stayed under 2 seconds on all partitions, the same as before. The dead letter count of that task was 3 events, and all three also fail on the old path when replayed.

I ran the count check by hand for the three hours. The number of events in the topic and the number of rows in Postgres for the partitions that this task served matched.

The time from accept to visible row had a median of 28 ms at peak, and 8 ms in the quiet period before it. That matches the staging numbers.

One surprise: the memory of the batching task grew by about 40 MB compared with the others. This comes from the buffer of up to 200 events and the larger transactions. It is well within the task limit, but I noted it.

I did not see any split events in production. The split counter stayed at zero for the whole time.

Tobias checked the WAL rate on the production database and saw a small drop that fits one task of six. He approved the next step.

Tomorrow the plan is to enable three tasks. I will leave the first task as it is overnight and read the nightly count check in the morning before I change anything.

summary: Dashboard queries for the largest customer moved to the new ClickHouse materialized view for hourly counts, cutting the p95 from 9 s to under 400 ms.
body:
The first rewritten dashboard query went live behind a flag for the biggest customer. It reads from the hourly counts materialized view instead of scanning the raw events table. The view is keyed by customer id, event type and hour, and uses SummingMergeTree.

I compared old and new results for 200 random time ranges. 197 matched exactly. The three that differed were ranges that cut through the current hour, where the view had not merged yet. Reading with sum() and GROUP BY fixed that, because the unmerged parts add up correctly.

The p95 for the events-over-time panel fell from about 9 s to under 400 ms. The top-event-types panel is still slow because it needs distinct counts, and that needs a different view.

The flag stays on for this one customer for a few days. Next steps are the distinct-count view and moving the other panels over. Mara will check the Go side that the loader writes the fields the view needs.

One leftover: the view definition lives only in a SQL file I ran by hand. It should go into the migrations folder so staging and production cannot drift apart. I added a ticket for it.

summary: Moved the ClickHouse view definitions into the migrations folder and added a check that fails CI if staging and production schemas differ.
body:
Yesterday's hourly counts view was only a SQL file I had run by hand. I turned it into numbered migration files under db/clickhouse/migrations, with an up file for each.

A small Go runner applies them in order and records the applied names in a table called schema_migrations. I ran it against an empty local ClickHouse and then against staging, where it detected the view as already present and skipped it.

The CI check dumps SHOW CREATE TABLE for every table and view in staging and compares it to a dump from a fresh database built from the migrations. It failed once on purpose when I added a column by hand, so I know it works.

Still open: the production run is for later today with Tobias watching. Rollback files are empty for now because dropping a view is trivial.

summary: Built the distinct-count view for the top-event-types panel using uniqCombinedState, and found that it needs the AggregatingMergeTree engine, not SummingMergeTree.
body:
The top event types panel still timed out for the large customers, so I built a second materialized view for distinct users per event type per day. My first attempt reused the engine of the hourly view, SummingMergeTree. The numbers were wrong: distinct counts cannot be summed across parts, and users seen on two merge runs got counted twice.

I switched to AggregatingMergeTree with an AggregateFunction(uniqCombined, String) column and wrote it with uniqCombinedState(user_id). Reading uses uniqCombinedMerge and GROUP BY. The results are approximate, with an error under 1 percent in my tests.

I checked the error against exact uniq on three customers over 30 days. The worst case was 0.7 percent, on the largest customer. That is fine for a dashboard, but the export endpoint promises exact numbers, so it keeps using the raw table.

The view fills only new data. I wrote the backfill as an INSERT SELECT in daily chunks, so one failing day does not restart everything. I ran it for the first 20 days on staging. Each chunk took about 40 s for the largest customer.

Two things came up. First, the day boundary is UTC in the view, but some customers expect their local time zone in the dashboard. Lena said the console already sends a time zone parameter. For now the panel rounds to UTC days and shows a note. Second, the query for a 90 day range reads about 90 rows per event type instead of 40 million raw events, which is the whole point.

Next: run the rest of the backfill in the evening, then switch the panel behind the flag.

summary: Ran the distinct-count backfill on staging for the remaining days; two chunks failed on memory and went through after a smaller chunk size.
body:
I started the rest of the backfill on staging after dinner, one INSERT SELECT per day. Days 21 to 60 went through. Two chunks, both from the busiest week of the largest customer, failed with a memory limit exceeded error at about 10 GB.

The cause was GROUP BY with a high-cardinality key over a whole day. I split those two days into six-hour chunks and set max_bytes_before_external_group_by to 4 GB. They finished in 2 and 3 minutes.

I changed the script so the chunk size is a parameter and it logs the row count per chunk. Counts in the view now match the raw table for all days checked, using the exact uniq on a sample of 10 days.

Production will take longer, about 18 months of data. I estimated 6 hours at the staging rate. I will ask Tobias for a quiet window so the dashboards are not hit by it.

Nothing was changed in the app yet. The flag is still off.

summary: Switched the top-event-types panel to the distinct-count view for one customer and found a gap: events backfilled out of order were missing from the view.
body:
Late in the evening I turned on the flag for the large customer on staging and compared the panel against the raw numbers. Most values matched, but event type checkout_failed was low by about 3 percent on two days.

I looked at the loader. Those days were part of the old Postgres backfill, which inserts rows directly into the raw table through a different path. The materialized view only fires on inserts through the table it is attached to, and that path wrote to a staging copy that was swapped in later with EXCHANGE TABLES. The swap moved the data but not the view trigger.

So the rows existed but never went through the view. The fix is to run the view backfill after every bulk load, not only once. I did that for the two affected days and the numbers matched.

I wrote this into the backfill notes in the repo: any data that comes in by a path other than the normal loader needs a manual view backfill for its date range. I also added a check script that compares counts per day between the raw table and the views and prints days that differ by more than 0.1 percent.

I ran the check script on all 60 days of staging. Only those two days had differed.

An open point is whether the old backfill code should write through the main table instead. That would be slower but safer. I will ask Mara tomorrow because she wrote it.

The flag stays on for staging only. Production waits for the check script to run clean there.

summary: Mara and I agreed the old-event backfill will write through the main table; the swap approach is dropped for ClickHouse loads.
body:
I discussed the missing view rows with Mara this morning. She had used the swap because it kept the table small and fast to query while loading. The cost was the views, as seen yesterday.

We decided that the backfill writes through the main table in batches of 100k rows, sorted by the partition key. In a test with 5 million rows this was about 25 percent slower than the swap, but the views were filled at the same time, and no second pass was needed.

Mara changed the backfill tool to take a mode flag. The default is now direct. The swap mode is still in the code, but prints a warning that views will not be filled.

I ran the new mode on staging for a customer with 12 million events. It took 14 minutes and the check script showed zero differing days.

Next is the production run, planned with Tobias for tomorrow evening.

summary: Production backfill of the hourly and distinct views started for the first third of customers, no dashboard impact seen in Grafana.
body:
Tobias and I started the production run at the quiet time of early evening. He watched ClickHouse CPU and the insert queue in Grafana while I ran the tool for the 13 smallest customers first.

These finished in 35 minutes. CPU on the ClickHouse node stayed under 40 percent, and the dashboard query latency did not move. The merge queue grew a little during the run and recovered within ten minutes.

Then I started the middle group of 14 customers. One of them has a field with very long values, and the tool hit a limit on the row size in its batch. I lowered the batch from 100k to 20k rows for this customer, and it went through.

The check script after each group showed no differing days, except one day for a customer who also sent events during the run. That difference was 0.08 percent and went away on the second check, once the merges finished.

The largest 13 customers are left. They hold about 80 percent of the data, so Tobias suggested we do them over two evenings and keep the CPU under 60 percent. I added a pause option to the tool that waits when the merge queue is above a threshold.

The flag for the hourly view is on for the first group. The customers did not report anything.

Notes for the next session: the tool should log its progress to a file, since my terminal scrollback was the only record this time. I will add that first.

summary: Added a progress file and resume to the backfill tool, then finished the first of two evenings of large-customer backfill in production.
body:
I started by fixing the lack of a record. The backfill tool now writes one line per finished chunk to a progress file: customer, day, rows, seconds. When started again, it reads this file and skips finished chunks.

I tested the resume by killing the process halfway through a customer on staging. The restart picked up at the next chunk and the final counts matched the raw table.

Then the production run for the large customers. The pause option from yesterday worked as planned: it triggered four times when the merge queue went above 200 parts and waited about a minute each time.

Seven customers finished, with the two largest remaining. The largest alone took 2 hours 10 minutes for the hourly view and 1 hour 40 minutes for the distinct view.

While it ran I read the slow query log of ClickHouse. Two queries from the console, for the funnel panel, scan the full raw table. They will need their own view, which is next on the list after the backfill.

A question from Lena: can the panel show a message while the backfill is not finished for a customer? I told her the flag is per customer and stays off until the check script is clean, so no message is needed.

One small problem: the check script takes about 6 minutes for the largest customer because it runs exact counts. I will limit it to sampled days for the routine check and keep the full run for the final one.

summary: Finished the production backfill for the two largest customers and turned on the flags; the dashboard p95 for them dropped from 11 s to 0.5 s.
body:
The last two customers were the biggest ones, and the run took most of the afternoon. I started it at the same time as the first coffee and kept an eye on the merge queue.

The pause option triggered six times. Total time for the second largest was 1 hour 20 minutes and for the largest 2 hours 30 minutes, so a bit more than yesterday's estimate.

The full check script ran clean for both. I ran it in the background with the exact counts, and it took 9 minutes for the biggest one. No day differed by more than 0.02 percent.

Then I switched on the flags. The numbers before and after, from the Grafana panel of the search API timings:
- events over time: p95 from 11 s to 0.5 s
- top event types: p95 from 14 s to 0.6 s
- error rate panel: p95 from 8 s, unchanged, since it is not yet moved

The customer success side, Sam, forwarded a message from the largest customer's admin, who said the dashboard felt instant. I did not reply except to say thanks.

I looked at the error rate panel next. It uses a ratio of two counts with a filter on a JSON field, and the filter is the slow part. Extracting the field at insert time into its own column would help, but that changes the table. I wrote the idea into the ticket and will discuss it with Mara before touching the schema.

The funnel panel needs a window function over sessions. I do not see a simple view for it. I will try a pre-aggregated table of session paths.

Cleanup: removed the temporary staging copies from the first backfill tests, about 90 GB. Updated the backfill notes with the final procedure and the memory settings. Open: schema change for the error panel.

summary: Extracted the status field into its own ClickHouse column with a default and a mutation for old rows; the error rate panel now takes 0.7 s.
body:
Mara agreed to the schema change this morning, with one condition: do it as a normal migration and not by hand. I wrote migration 0007, which adds a LowCardinality(String) column named status with the default empty string.

The loader now fills the column from the JSON payload at insert time. For old rows I used ALTER TABLE UPDATE as a mutation, in partitions of one month, to avoid one huge mutation. On staging the mutation for the largest customer ran 25 minutes.

The error rate view reads the new column. A first version used the default empty value for rows that had not been mutated yet, and those rows were counted as successful. I fixed this by checking system.mutations for pending ones before turning on the flag. The check is now part of the check script.

After the mutation finished on staging, I compared the new panel with the old query for 30 ranges. All matched. The p95 went from 8 s to 0.7 s.

In production I started the mutation for the oldest partitions only, to see the disk effect. Disk use rose by 6 GB temporarily and fell after the merges. The rest will run tomorrow.

Lena noticed that the console shows status values with different case, such as Error and error. That is a data issue from two customers' apps. I did not normalize it in the column; the loader keeps what was sent. I added a lowercase in the view instead.

Open: the funnel panel, and the rest of the mutation tomorrow.

summary: Finished the status column mutation in production and switched the error rate panel on for every customer.
body:
The remaining partitions of the mutation ran in the morning, one month at a time. Total time was about 3 hours, with the disk rising by at most 11 GB.

I checked system.mutations afterwards. No pending entries and no failed ones. The check script counted zero rows with an empty status among rows where the payload had one.

I then turned on the flag for all customers. The p95 of the error rate panel in Grafana is 0.6 s overall, and the worst customer is at 1.1 s.

One customer has a payload with the status nested under a different key, so their panel shows no errors. Sam asked them, and they will send a sample. I will adapt the loader rule per customer, if the sample is simple.

Next is the funnel panel.

summary: Looked at the funnel panel queries and decided on a per-session table; the first draft schema is in the ticket.
body:
The funnel panel takes the ordered steps a customer defines and counts sessions that went through them. Today's query uses windowFunnel on the raw events. On the big customers it reads 30 days of events and takes 20 s or more.

My idea is a table with one row per session and day: customer, session id, the list of event types with timestamps as arrays, and first and last time. A materialized view builds it. windowFunnel can run on the arrays after an arrayJoin, but that is almost as costly.

A simpler approach is to store per session a compact string of step codes, and to match the funnel by position. That needs the steps to be fixed, which they are not.

I wrote both in the ticket with the numbers from a test on staging. The array table is 4 percent of the raw size. Mara will look at it tomorrow.

summary: Mara reviewed the session table draft and suggested capping sessions at 500 events and sorting by session start; adopted both.
body:
Mara read the ticket and replied in the afternoon. Her point was that some sessions come from bots and hold tens of thousands of events. Arrays of that size would hurt merges.

We will cap at 500 events per session in the view and set a flag column, truncated, for sessions that were cut. The funnel panel can show them as approximate.

She also suggested the ORDER BY of the table start with customer and the day of the session start, so that range queries by day read few granules. That fits how the panel queries.

I built the table and the view on staging and loaded 7 days. Size is 3.5 percent of the raw data for the same days.

Tomorrow I rewrite the funnel query to run on it and compare the results.

summary: Rewrote the funnel query on the session table; results match the raw query on 28 of 30 test funnels, and the two mismatches are explained by truncated sessions.
body:
I rewrote the funnel panel query to read the session table. It uses arrayFilter and arrayFirstIndex on the step arrays, and counts sessions by the deepest step reached in the given order.

The test set was 30 funnels taken from the saved funnels of real customers, each over 7 days. I ran the old and the new query and compared the counts per step.

28 matched exactly. Two differed, both for the same customer, by 1 to 2 percent in the later steps. The sessions in question had more than 500 events, so the truncation cut off later steps. That is expected, and the panel will show the approximate marker.

Timing on staging for the largest customer over 30 days:
- old query: 22 s
- new query: 1.4 s

There were two bugs on the way. The first was that the step timestamps were in arrays of DateTime64, and my comparison used seconds, so steps within the same second came out in the wrong order. The second was that events with the same timestamp need a stable tie-break. I used the event sequence number from the loader, which the table already had.

I wrote a unit test for the second case, with three events in one millisecond, and it fails without the sequence number.

The backfill for the session table is the same tool as before. I added a mode for it and started it on staging for 60 days, which takes about 50 minutes for the biggest customer.

Lena has to change the console only for the approximate marker. I sent her the field name, truncated, and an example response.

Not done: production. I want one more day of staging data with real traffic first, and I want the check script to compare session counts, which it does not yet. That is the next small task.

summary: Extended the check script to compare session counts and backfilled the session table in production for the small and medium customers.
body:
First the check script: it now counts distinct sessions per day in the raw table and in the session table and reports days that differ. Sessions that cross midnight are assigned to the day of their first event in both, so the numbers should match exactly.

On staging it showed three differing days. All three were days where the loader had restarted after a deploy and a session was split into two rows. The merge of those rows needs the same key, and my key included the batch id by mistake. I removed the batch id from the sorting key in a new migration and rebuilt the table on staging.

After the rebuild the check ran clean for all 60 days.

Then production. I ran the backfill for the 27 small and medium customers, in the same way as before with the pause option and the progress file. It took 1 hour 50 minutes in total. The CPU stayed under 45 percent.
