The check script was clean for all of them except one day for one customer, with 2 sessions of difference. I looked at them: both had events arriving late, 30 hours after the first one, after the backfill had passed the day. A second run of that day fixed it.

The late events point out a limit. Late events can change a session after the fact, and the view only adds new rows. With AggregatingMergeTree this is fine for the aggregated tables, but the arrays are merged with groupArray states, so it should work as well. I tested by inserting a late event on staging, and the array grew as expected.

Open: the 13 large customers, planned for the next two evenings. The funnel flag is still off in production.

summary: Large-customer backfill of the session table, first evening: 8 of 13 done, and the biggest customer's sessions are heavier than predicted.
body:
I started the large customers after the dinner break, with Tobias reachable but not watching. The pause threshold was the same as before.

Eight customers finished in 2 hours 40 minutes. For the ninth, the biggest, the progress file shows each day taking 15 minutes instead of the expected 6. The cause is the session cap: it is applied in the view, but the backfill reads the arrays and sorts them first, which is the heavy part for bot sessions.

I stopped the run for that customer and added a filter to the backfill query: sessions with more than 5000 events are cut early with limit by. That brought a day down to 7 minutes.

Before restarting I checked that cutting early gives the same first 500 events as cutting late. It does, since both sort by sequence number first. I tested this on three days of staging data.

The biggest customer will have its 400 days done tomorrow evening. The merge queue is quiet now, and disk use is up by 40 GB, which is within the plan.

I also noted the issue in the backfill notes. Remaining work: biggest customers tomorrow, then flags on, then the check script on everything.

A side note from reading the logs: the loader logs a warning for about 0.1 percent of events saying the session id is empty. Those events land in a session called empty. I will ask Mara whether the apps of those customers can fix it, or if the loader should drop them from the session table.

summary: Finished the session backfill in production and switched on the funnel panel for all customers; the p95 is 1.2 s against 20 s before.
body:
The biggest customer finished in the afternoon after the early cut. The remaining four large customers ran in the shadow of that and took 1 hour in total.

The check script compared sessions per day for all customers. It was clean, except for the empty session id events, which are all in a single session per day and were excluded from the comparison on both sides.

I then turned on the flag. Panel numbers from Grafana over the first hours:
- funnel p95: 1.2 s overall, 2.3 s for the largest customer
- the old p95 was above 20 s with timeouts for 4 customers

Lena's console change for the approximate marker was already deployed, and it shows the marker for 0.4 percent of the sessions.

Mara answered about the empty session id: two customers use an old SDK that does not send it. The loader will drop those from the session table with a counter metric, and Sam will ask the customers to update.

The analytics dashboards are now all on the new views. Left from this topic: cleaning up the old queries and removing the Postgres analytics indexes, which are now unused. I will check pg_stat_user_indexes first.

summary: Checked pg_stat_user_indexes on the events table and found 6 indexes without scans in the last weeks; dropped 4 and kept 2 that the audit log reads.
body:
Now that the dashboards read from ClickHouse, I looked at which Postgres indexes on the events table are still used. The stats view has been running since the last restart, 19 days ago, so there is a decent window.

Six indexes had zero scans. Four of them were built for the old dashboard queries, on customer and type, on customer and day, on the status field and a partial one for errors. These I dropped, on staging first and then in production with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

The other two without scans are on the account id and the created time. The monthly audit job and the export tool run only once a month, and may not have run during the window. I kept them, and left a comment in the migration notes.

The freed space was 38 GB, which will help the autovacuum as well because there are fewer indexes to maintain on each write. Insert time for the importer, measured on a 1 million row file, fell from 41 s to 33 s.

One thing I noticed in the same view: the table is still the main store for the raw events of the search indexing path, so it cannot be removed. The reindex job reads it nightly.

I ran the explain on the slowest of the old dashboard queries to confirm nothing calls them any more. The search for the query text in the code found two admin scripts with them. Both are old and I deleted them in a commit.

Next is to look at the vacuum settings for the same table, since the dead tuple count was high in the stats.

summary: Autovacuum on the events table was falling behind with 30 percent dead tuples; lowered its scale factor for that table and it caught up in two hours.
body:
The stats from yesterday showed 30 percent dead tuples on the events table, about 90 million rows. The default scale factor of 0.2 means autovacuum waits until 20 percent of the table is dead, which for a table of this size is a very long time.

I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 and the threshold to 50000 for this table with ALTER TABLE SET. Cost limit stays the default so that vacuum does not hit the importer too hard.

Autovacuum started within a minute and ran for about two hours. I watched pg_stat_progress_vacuum. The dead tuple share fell to 2 percent, and the table size did not shrink, which is normal without a full rewrite.

I did not do a VACUUM FULL, because it locks the table. The free space inside will be reused by new rows.

I wrote the setting into the Terraform notes of the database, as a table level parameter in the migration file, so it is not lost in a rebuild. Then I added a Grafana panel for dead tuples per table, from the postgres exporter.

Next check is in a week to see that the share stays low.

summary: Tried moving the audit log table to a partitioned layout by month, got it working on staging, but stopped because the unique constraint on the id would have to include the partition key.
body:
The audit log grows by about 2 million rows a month, and queries for a single customer and time range are slowing down. I tried declarative partitioning by month on created_at as a first step.

On staging I created the new partitioned table, copied 14 months of data with INSERT SELECT and compared counts. The copy took 11 minutes. The range queries became faster, from 800 ms to 90 ms for a month of one customer, as partition pruning worked.

Then the problem. The table has a primary key on the id, and other tables reference the id from the audit entries, for example the comments feature of the console. In a partitioned table the unique constraint has to include the partition key, so the key becomes id plus created_at, and the foreign keys would need the time as well.

Changing the references touches the console code from Lena and the export queries. That is more than I wanted for this step, and the gain can be reached differently. A composite index on customer and created_at would give most of the benefit.

I tested that: with the new index on the unpartitioned table, the same query took 140 ms. That is close enough for now.

So I dropped the staging copy, and created the index in production with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which took 6 minutes and added 1.1 GB. I checked a customer query in the console afterwards, and it is fast.

The partitioning idea stays in the notes for the time when the export for compliance needs it. I will think again then.

summary: Started the schema registry design: a table for event schemas with versions and a compatibility check on registration, planned in the schema-registry branch.
body:
The customers' event shapes change over time, and the ingest worker only validates against one fixed schema. The registry should let a customer register named schemas with versions, and let the worker check events against the latest one.

I created the branch and a worktree for it. First the data model in Postgres: tables schemas, with customer, name and the current version, and schema_versions with the JSON schema document, a hash and the created time. The hash makes registering the same document twice a no-op.

Compatibility is the interesting part. I defined it as backward compatible: a new version may add optional fields, but not remove a field or change a type, and may not make an optional field required. I wrote the check as a function that walks both documents and returns a list of violations with their paths.

I wrote 24 tests for the check, with cases like a type change from integer to number, an added required field and a nested object change. The nested case failed at first because my walk did not descend into arrays of objects. Fixed.

The API is one endpoint to register, POST /v1/schemas/{name}/versions, which returns 409 with the violations when the check fails. Reading is a GET of the latest or a given version.

I have not yet connected the worker. It should cache the latest schema per customer in memory and refresh every minute, to avoid a database lookup per batch. That is the next step.

Mara will review the data model tomorrow.

summary: Mara's review of the schema registry model asked for soft deletes and a limit on schema size; both added in the branch.
body:
Mara read the migration and the compatibility function this morning. She had two requests.

First, a way to retire a version without losing it, because customers' old events refer to them. I added a deleted_at column to schema_versions, and the read endpoints skip retired versions unless a query parameter says otherwise. The latest-version lookup ignores them as well.

Second, a limit on the size of the document. A huge schema would be loaded into memory by every worker. I set a limit of 256 KB and the API returns 413 above it. I also cap the nesting depth at 20 levels in the check, to avoid slow walks.

She also asked about concurrent registrations of the same name. Two requests could both read version 3 and both write version 4. I added a unique constraint on name and version number, and the second request now gets a conflict and retries once in the handler by reading again. A test with two parallel requests passes.

The tests are 31 now and all green. I rebased the branch on main, where Lena had changed the migration numbering, and renumbered mine.

summary: Connected the ingest worker to the schema registry with an in-memory cache and a validate-only mode that counts violations without rejecting events.
body:
The worker now loads the latest schema of a customer on first use and keeps it in a map with a 60 second refresh. A failed refresh keeps the old entry and logs a warning, so a database blip cannot stop ingest.

I did not want to reject events on day one. The new mode, validate-only, runs the JSON schema validation and increments a Prometheus counter labelled by customer and schema name when an event violates it. The event goes through as before.

Performance was the worry. I benchmarked with the library gojsonschema on a batch of 1000 events with a mid-sized schema: 38 ms. That is about 20 percent more per batch than before, which is too much for the large customers. I compiled the schema once per version instead of per refresh, and the time fell to 22 ms. A typed fast path for the flat schemas would help further, but I will wait for real numbers.

On staging I replayed an hour of the real stream with schemas registered for three customers. The counter showed 0.3 percent violations for one of them, mostly a field sent as a string instead of a number. That is just what the registry should find.

Worker memory rose by 12 MB with 40 schemas loaded, which is fine.

Tests: a unit test for the cache refresh with a failing store, and one for the validate-only mode that checks the event still passes. Both are in.

Next: a flag per customer to switch from validate-only to reject, and an entry in the admin console for the violations. Lena will need the counter data from an endpoint.

summary: Added a read endpoint for schema violation counts per customer and day, fed from a small Postgres table that the worker flushes every minute.
body:
Prometheus counters are good for alerts but cannot be queried by the console for a history by customer and schema. So the worker now keeps counts in memory and flushes them once a minute to a table schema_violations with customer, schema, day and count, using an upsert that adds to the count.

The flush is one batched statement per minute per worker, so the write load is small. I checked it on staging with four workers: about 160 rows a minute, no lock waits.

The endpoint is GET /v1/schemas/{name}/violations with a from and to day. It returns counts per day and the top three violated paths, which the worker also records in a small map, capped at 20 paths per schema and day to bound memory.

I sent Lena the response shape. She will build a table in the console next week.

A test covers the upsert adding to existing rows, and one covers the cap on paths. Open: the flag to reject events.

summary: Added a per-schema breakdown to the violation counts endpoint, so customers can see which event type breaks its schema and not just a daily total.
body:
The endpoint from yesterday only returned counts per customer and day, which Sam said is not enough to tell a customer what to fix. I added a schema_id and version column to the small Postgres table the worker flushes every minute. The primary key now covers customer, day, schema_id and version.

The worker keeps a map of counters per schema and flushes it in one multi-row upsert. A flush with 200 distinct schemas took 6 ms on staging, which is fine. The read endpoint takes an optional schema_id filter and sorts by count descending.

I wrote tests for the upsert with concurrent flushes from two workers, and the sums were right. The old rows have no schema id, so a migration puts them under a placeholder value of 0 and the endpoint hides that bucket by default. Next is a field-level reason for each violation, which needs a short code list that Mara and I still have to agree on.

summary: Defined short reason codes for schema violations (missing field, wrong type, unknown field, too long) and the worker now counts each code separately in validate-only mode.
body:
Mara and I talked through the code list in the ticket this morning. We settled on four codes: missing_required, type_mismatch, unknown_field and value_too_long. Anything else goes to other, and I want to see how large that bucket gets before adding more.

The validator used to return a bool and a message string. I changed it to return a small struct with the code and the field path, and the message is built only when a sample is stored. That keeps the hot path free of string formatting. A benchmark on a 500 event batch showed no measurable change, 1.9 ms before and 1.9 ms after.

The counters table got a reason column and the primary key grew again. I kept the flush as a single upsert. The read endpoint now groups by reason when asked, with a query parameter named by.

I replayed one hour of staging traffic through the worker. About 3 percent of events violated something, and nearly all of those were type_mismatch on a timestamp field sent as a string by one test customer. The other bucket was empty, which is a good sign for the list.

One snag: unknown_field is noisy, because customers often add fields we never registered. I made it count separately and not weigh in any future rejection rule. Next I need to store a few sample payloads per violation so support can see real examples.

summary: Stored up to five sample violating payloads per schema and reason, truncated and with values masked, after Sam asked for real examples for support.
body:
Sam asked for examples because a count alone does not help a customer who says their data is fine. I added a table violation_samples with customer, schema_id, reason, the field path, a masked copy of the payload and a created time. The worker writes a sample only when fewer than five exist for that combination in the last day.

Masking was the part that took thought. I replace every string value with its length in the form <str:12> and keep numbers as the type name only. The structure and the field names remain, which is what support needs. Payloads are cut at 2 KB.

The check for the number of existing samples would have cost a query per violation. Instead each worker keeps a local counter per combination, reset every hour, and the table has a unique index that caps duplicates by a bucket number. Two workers can therefore store up to ten samples in the worst case, and I accepted that.

On staging I sent a batch with 1000 broken events from a script. The table ended with 5 rows for the combination, with no slowdown in the ingest latency graph. The p99 stayed at 41 ms.

The read endpoint got a samples sub-route. Lena will want it in the admin console later, but that is not planned yet. I wrote the API description in the docs draft and sent it to Sam for a read.

summary: Added a per-schema breakdown to the schema registry's violation counts endpoint after support asked which event types break their schemas most, not only a daily total.
body:
Sam asked yesterday for something finer than the daily total on the violation counts endpoint, because customers wrote in asking which of their event types was the problem. I added a schema_id dimension to the query and to the response, so each day now lists counts per schema name and version. The worker already flushed counts per customer and day, so the first step was widening the Postgres table with a schema_id column and changing the primary key to (customer_id, day, schema_id).

The migration ran on staging in under a second because the table is small. The worker flush now groups by schema in memory and writes one upsert per group, which went from one row per minute to at most a few dozen rows per minute for a busy customer. I checked that against the largest customer on staging and the flush stayed under 20 ms.

The endpoint takes an optional schema filter and returns the top 20 schemas by count when none is given. Old rows without a schema id are reported under an 'unknown' bucket so the totals still match the old numbers. I compared the sum of the per-schema counts with the old daily totals for three customers and they matched exactly.

Mara reviewed the change and asked for a limit on the number of schemas returned, which is the top 20 above. Still open: the counts do not yet say why an event failed, only which schema it belongs to. The reason codes are the next step, and I will keep the same table and add a second dimension to it.

summary: Ran the first enforce-mode test on staging, rejecting events with missing required fields, and found the rejection response lacked the batch index so clients could not tell which events failed.
body:
I added an enforce flag per customer to the registry settings. When it is on, the worker rejects events that fail with missing_required or type_mismatch, and still only counts the other codes. The flag is off for every customer, and I turned it on for the staging test account only.

The first run showed a problem. The ingest API answered the whole batch with a 422 and a single message, so a client sending 500 events could not know which ones were bad. That would make the feature unusable for real customers.

I changed the response to a 207 style body with a list of failures, each with the index in the batch, the reason code and the field path. The good events in the batch are still accepted. Mara pointed out in review that partial acceptance changes the contract for clients who assume all or nothing, so I made it a documented opt-in through a header, and the default stays all or nothing with the failure list in the 422 body.

Tests added:
- a batch with 3 bad events out of 50
- a batch where every event is bad
- the header off and on

All passed. I also checked that the rejected events are counted in the violation table, so the numbers do not drop once enforcement starts. One open point is the rate limiter, which counts rejected events against the customer limit. I think that is right, but I will ask Mara tomorrow before I decide.

summary: Decided with Mara that rejected events count against the rate limit, then wrote the migration guide for customers who want to switch from validate-only to enforce mode.
body:
Mara and I settled the open question from yesterday. Rejected events do count against the limit, because the work of parsing and validating them is real, and a client in a loop with a broken payload should be slowed down. We wrote that into the docs as well.

The rest of the day went into the guide for customers. It describes three steps. First leave validate-only on for at least a week and read the violation counts. Second, fix the senders until missing_required and type_mismatch are near zero. Third, ask support to switch on enforce for the account.

Sam read the draft and asked for a table of the reason codes with an example each, and for a note about the opt-in header for partial acceptance. I added both. I also added a short section on how to read the sample payloads, with the masked format explained.

While writing I tried the examples against staging, and one curl example had the wrong header name. I fixed it in the guide and added a test that runs the documented examples, so the docs cannot drift from the API.

The docs build had a link check that failed on the new page because the anchors are generated from headings, and I had renamed one. That took twenty minutes to find.

Still to do before any customer gets enforce mode: a switch in the admin console, or at least a support script. For now I wrote a script in the tools folder that flips the flag and writes an audit log entry. Mara will review it tomorrow. After that I want to pick two friendly customers for a pilot.

summary: Reviewed Mara's support script for the enforce flag and asked for a confirmation prompt and a dry run; she added both and it is merged into the branch.
body:
The script flips the enforce flag for one customer and writes an audit log entry. My review had three points. It should show the current violation counts before asking for confirmation, it should have a dry run mode, and it should refuse to run if the customer has no validate-only history of at least seven days.

Mara added all three and also a rollback command that turns the flag off and logs the reason. I ran it on staging against the test account. The dry run printed the counts and exited, the real run asked for the customer name to be typed, and the audit entry appeared with the right user.

One small bug: the seven day check used the creation time of the schema and not the first violation count, so a customer with an old schema but no data would pass. We changed it to look at the counters table. Merged into schema-registry.

summary: Started a two-customer enforce pilot in production after the counts looked clean, and saw the first rejections within an hour, all from one misconfigured sender.
body:
The two pilot customers were chosen from the violation counts. Both had been in validate-only mode for more than three weeks and their missing_required and type_mismatch counts were under 0.1 percent of events. I told them by email through Sam and turned enforce on for both at midday with the support script.

In the first hour the worker rejected 212 events for one of them. All came from a single sender, an old mobile app version that sent the user id as a number where the schema says string. The customer did not know that version was still in use. Sam wrote to them with a sample payload from the samples table, which worked as intended.

The ingest latency was unchanged and the error rate panel showed the expected small 422 increase for that customer only. The second customer had zero rejections.

I added a Grafana panel for rejections per customer and reason, fed from the same counters table through the existing Postgres data source. An alert is not set yet, because the right threshold is unclear with only two customers. I will watch for a few days and then decide.

One thing I noticed is that the customer with the old app could be helped by a coercion rule that turns numbers into strings for declared string fields. That is a product decision, so I wrote it up as a question in the ticket and did not build anything.

summary: Pilot week review: three days of data show rejections falling from 212 to 9 an hour as the customer fixed their sender, and no complaints, so enforce can go to the next group.
body:
I looked at the rejection panel and the counters table for the pilot. The first customer went from 212 rejected events per hour on the first day to 9 per hour now, after they updated the old app. The second customer stayed at zero. No support tickets were opened about the feature.

I also checked the side effects. Ingest p99 for both customers is within normal range at 38 to 45 ms. The sample table has about 40 rows in total, so there is no growth worry. The counters table is small too.

The coercion question from last week got an answer. Mara and I think no, because silent coercion makes the schema meaningless, and the customer fixed the app anyway. I closed that point in the ticket.

Next group is the list of customers with clean counts for at least two weeks. I ran a query and found 11 of them. I will not switch them all at once. The plan:
- four customers this week
- four next week
- the remaining three after a look at the numbers

Sam will send the guide to each of them first and wait for a reply or three days of silence. I also added the alert that I had held back. It fires when a customer has more than 1000 rejections in an hour, and it goes to the Slack channel and not to PagerDuty, because a customer error is not an outage.

One remaining item is the admin console switch. Lena has room next week, so I wrote a small spec with the endpoint, which already exists, and the permissions needed.

summary: Tracked down slow dashboard loads for one mid-size customer to a ClickHouse query that skipped the hourly view because of a timezone conversion in the filter.
body:
Sam forwarded a complaint that the main dashboard of a mid-size customer took 6 seconds to load, while others take under a second. The customer has the flag for the hourly counts view, so it should have been fast.

I ran the panel query by hand with EXPLAIN. It read the raw table, not the materialized view. The reason was that the API converted the customer's local time range with toTimeZone in the WHERE clause, which made the query not match the view's hour buckets. The other customers use UTC, so nobody had seen it.

The fix is to convert the range boundaries in the API, round them to whole hours, and send plain DateTime values to ClickHouse. For time zones with a 30 or 45 minute offset the buckets do not line up, so the API falls back to the raw table for those. There is one such customer, in India, and I checked that its volume is small enough.

After the change the p95 for the customer went from 6.1 s to 0.45 s on staging with a copy of their data. I added a test with three time zones, including one with a half hour offset, that checks which table the query uses by reading the generated SQL.

I deployed it to production in the afternoon and watched the panel in Grafana. The p95 for that customer dropped to 0.5 s within minutes. I also searched the code for other places that use toTimeZone in filters and found one in the CSV export, which is not performance critical, so I left it.

The lesson for the notes: any new panel needs a check that the view is actually used, so I added a log line with the table name to the slow query log.

summary: Switched enforce mode on for four more customers after Sam's mails went out, with no rejections above the alert threshold in the first day.
body:
Sam sent the guide to the four customers from the list and two replied with thanks, the others did not answer in three days, as planned. I ran the support script in dry run mode first for each and read the counts. All four had under 0.05 percent violations.

I then switched them on one after the other with the real run, and each wrote its audit entry. Over the first day the rejection panel showed 14 events in total, all from one customer with a test sender. The alert did not fire.

The next four are for next week. Lena has taken the admin console switch into her sprint.

summary: Made the registry validator cheaper by compiling each schema once per version instead of per batch, cutting worker CPU in validate-only mode by about a third.
body:
After the enforce pilot started, the CPU graph of the ingest workers showed validation as a visible share of each batch. A pprof profile on staging confirmed it: about 28 percent of the time in the hot path went into building validators from the stored schema JSON, which the worker did again for every batch. I changed the in-memory cache so that it holds the compiled validator, keyed by schema id and version, and not the raw document.

The first attempt used a single shared validator with a mutex, and it made things worse under parallel batches, because the workers waited on each other. The second version builds one immutable compiled validator per version, which is safe to use from many goroutines without locking. Cache entries are dropped when the registry reports a new version, using the same refresh the worker already does every 30 seconds.

I ran the replay of one hour of real traffic from staging through the old and the new code. The violation counts were identical for every reason code, so the behavior did not change. CPU per worker dropped from about 61 percent to 41 percent at the same event rate, and the p99 of the batch handling time went from 38 ms to 24 ms.

One unexpected finding was that a schema with many optional fields compiled slowly, about 4 ms each time. That explains why one customer's workers had looked worse than the others. The cache is bounded to 500 compiled validators for now, and I added a counter for cache misses so that we can see if the bound is too small. Mara will review the branch tomorrow, and after that the change goes out together with the next worker release.

summary: Memory graph of the ingest workers stays flat for a day after the cache bound, and the last four enforce customers were switched on without issues.
body:
Tobias confirmed that the memory of the workers is flat since the deploy, at about 480 MB instead of the climb of 40 MB per day. I will keep the ticket open for another week before closing it.

The four customers of the second group got enforce today. Dry runs showed counts below 0.1 percent for all of them. One had 0.09 percent, mostly unknown_field, which does not reject anyway, so I went ahead.

I looked at the rejection numbers in the afternoon and saw 31 rejections for one customer, from a sender that omitted a required field on a rare event type. I opened the sample table, found the payload shape, and Sam passed it on. The customer fixed it the same evening.

Lena's admin console switch is in review. I read the endpoint code again and added a check that the caller has the admin role for the customer. Remaining after this are the last three customers, which have noisier data, and I want to look at their counts together with Mara before touching them.

summary: Reviewed Lena's admin console switch for enforce mode and asked for the violation counts to show next to the toggle so nobody enables it blind.
body:
Lena's pull request adds a toggle on the customer page that calls the enforce endpoint. It works and the permission handling is right, but the toggle sat alone with no context.

My review asked for the last seven days of counts per reason, shown next to the toggle, with a warning when missing_required plus type_mismatch is above 0.5 percent. The data comes from the endpoint I wrote earlier, so no backend change was needed. She added a small bar chart and the warning in a few hours.

I also asked for a confirmation dialog that names the customer, like the support script does. She had that already, but with the wrong text, which she fixed.

One thing I found when I tried it on staging: the toggle did not write the audit entry the script writes, because the endpoint only set the flag. I moved the audit write into the endpoint so every path through it is logged, and removed the duplicate from the script. Tests for both paths pass. Merged into the branch after that, and the console release is planned for next week.

summary: Looked at the three remaining customers' violation counts with Mara and decided to keep two in validate-only mode until they change their senders.
body:
The last three customers have noisier data. Their counts were 1.2, 2.8 and 0.3 percent for missing_required plus type_mismatch. The third is fine and can go on soon.

For the other two, switching on would reject thousands of events a day. We looked at the samples: one has a batch job that sends null for a required field, the other has two event types where a number field arrives as a string. Both are fixable on their side, so Sam will write to them with the samples attached.

Mara suggested a grace period setting, where enforce rejects only events with a timestamp after a chosen day. It is simple to add, but I decided against it for now since the customers can fix quickly and the setting adds a path we must test. I put it in the ticket as an option if they do not move.

The third customer gets enforce tomorrow after a final dry run.

summary: Closed the schema registry rollout for ten customers, and wrote down what is left: two customers in validate-only mode, a leaner validator, and docs for the console toggle.
body:
The third customer of the last group went on enforce this morning, after the dry run showed 0.2 percent. That makes ten of twelve customers with enforce active. The two others are waiting for their own fixes.

I went through the ticket and wrote a closing summary. The registry stores schemas with versions and soft deletes, the worker validates with a bounded cache, violations are counted by reason, samples are stored masked, and enforce can be toggled by the script or in the console. The alert for more than 1000 rejections an hour goes to Slack.

Open points:
- the two customers still in validate-only mode
- the size of compiled validators for schemas with many optional fields
- docs for the console toggle, which Sam will write after Lena's release

I also checked the numbers of the whole feature over the last two weeks. About 0.4 percent of events across enforced customers were rejected in the first days and 0.05 percent now. Ingest p99 did not move. The counters table has 18000 rows and the samples table 160, so storage is not a concern.

Memory in the workers is still flat according to Tobias. I closed that ticket. The branch is ready to merge once the console release is done, and I will ask Mara for a last look at the migration files before that.

summary: Mara's last review of the registry migrations found a missing index on the samples table for the lookup by customer and schema; added and merged the branch.
body:
Mara read the migration files one more time and asked how the samples sub-route finds its rows. It filtered by customer and schema_id, and the table only had an index on the primary key, which is a serial id. With 160 rows it is invisible, but it would grow.

I added an index on customer, schema_id and created time descending. I checked the plan with EXPLAIN on staging with 100000 generated rows, and it used the index with 0.3 ms against 18 ms for the sequential scan.

She also noticed the counters table down migration did not drop the new reason column in the right order. I fixed it and ran up and down on a fresh database twice.

After the CI run was green, we merged schema-registry into main. The production migration ran in a few seconds, since the indexes are on small tables. I watched the Postgres graphs for a quarter of an hour and saw nothing unusual.

summary: Wrote the docs page for the admin console enforce toggle: what it does, what customers see in the violation counts, and how to switch back to validate-only.
body:
Lena's toggle is merged and Sam asked for a docs page before more customers see it. I wrote the page in the public docs repo, starting with a short explanation of validate-only and enforce mode, and what happens to a rejected event in each. The page includes the rejection response with the batch index, since that was the thing clients missed in the first staging test.

A section follows on reading the violation counts, with the per-schema breakdown and the reason codes: missing field, wrong type, unknown field and too long. I added a worked example where a customer finds one event type with a rising count of wrong type, fixes the sender and watches the count fall. The numbers are taken from the pilot week with the customer name removed.

I also wrote down that rejected events count against the rate limit, as Mara and I decided, because customers will otherwise wonder why the limit moves. The last section explains how to switch back to validate-only from the console, which takes effect within about a minute because of the worker cache refresh. Sam read it and asked for a shorter intro, so I cut it from six sentences to three. The page is merged and linked from the migration guide.

summary: Added a 'preview' hint to the docs and console text for enforce mode, plus a link from the violation counts view to the sample payloads for each schema.
body:
Right after the docs page, I went through the console text that Lena wrote for the toggle, because it and the docs should say the same thing. Her label said 'Strict mode' while the docs and the API say 'enforce', and customers would search for the word they saw. We agreed on 'Enforce mode' in the console, with 'strict' only in a tooltip. Lena changed the label and the tooltip in her branch.

The second change was a link from each row of the per-schema counts to the stored sample payloads. Until now, the samples were only reachable through the support script, and Sam wanted customers to see them without opening a ticket. The endpoint exists already, so the change was a small one in the console: each row has a 'show examples' link that opens up to five masked payloads with the reason code.

While testing it, I noticed that samples for a schema with no violations returned an empty array with status 200, which is right, but the console showed a blank panel. I added the text 'No violations seen for this schema'. Another small finding was that long payloads were cut off in the middle of a UTF-8 character on one sample. The truncation in the worker counts bytes, so I changed it to cut on a character boundary and added a test with a multi-byte string.

Both changes are in the branch. The docs page now gets a screenshot of the examples view, which Sam will take on staging. Nothing else is left on the console side except the two customers who stay in validate-only mode.

summary: Planned the removal of the in-memory fallback and the old counters in the schema registry worker code, and cleaned up the validate-only code paths that enforce mode made redundant.
body:
The rollout is done for ten customers, so tonight I used the quiet time to clean up the worker code in the registry branch. There were three leftovers: the first version of the violation counter that wrote one row per event, the in-memory fallback used when the registry could not be reached, and a flag that switched off validation altogether. I went through each and decided what to do.

The old per-event counter was already unused since the batched flush replaced it, so I deleted it with its tests. The flag that disabled validation was never turned on in production, but it was useful during the pilot as a safety switch, so I kept it and renamed it to make clear what it does. The fallback was the interesting one: when the registry is unreachable, the worker used to accept everything without counting. I changed it to keep the last known schemas for up to an hour, and after that to accept events and increment a separate 'registry unavailable' counter.

I tested this on staging by blocking the registry table with a lock for ten minutes. Workers kept validating from the cached schemas, and the new counter stayed at zero, as it should. After I raised the time limit in a test to force the fallback, the counter rose and events were accepted. Then I released the lock and the workers picked up fresh schemas on the next refresh.

I added a Prometheus counter and a Grafana panel for registry unavailability, next to the violation panels. An alert is not set up yet, since a few seconds of failure is normal during a database failover, and I want to look at a week of data before choosing a threshold. The unit tests grew by eleven cases, and the full suite runs in the same two minutes as before.

One attempt did not work out. I tried to replace the hand-written schema diff in the compatibility check with a library, hoping to delete 300 lines. It reported some compatible changes as breaking, such as adding an optional field with a default, so I dropped it and kept our own code. The branch is ready for Mara's look tomorrow. What is left after that is the leaner validator idea and the two validate-only customers.

summary: Checked the Redis key naming of the search API caches and wrote a short convention, after finding three different prefix styles in use.
body:
While reading the cache hit numbers last week I saw that the search API keys use three styles: 'search:v1:', 'srch_' and a bare customer id with a colon. That makes the per-prefix reports in Grafana awkward, and it makes it hard to find which code path writes which key. This morning I listed the key patterns with SCAN on a replica and counted them. About 70 percent follow the first style, 20 percent the second, and the rest are leftovers from the old code path that wrote keys without a TTL.

I wrote a short convention in the repo docs: service, purpose, version, customer id, then the hash of the query, separated by colons, for example 'search:results:v2:123:ab12'. Every key must be written through one helper that also takes the TTL as a required argument, so a key without an expiry cannot be created by accident. The helper is about 25 lines in the shared cache module.

I moved the dashboard summary cache and the query results cache to the helper, and left the rest for later because each move changes the key and empties that cache once. For the two moved caches I did it at a quiet hour, and the hit rate was back to normal within 20 minutes. Mara agreed with the convention and will use it for the rate limit counters when she next touches them. The remaining three code paths are listed in the ticket, in order of memory use.

summary: Investigated Redis memory growth from the query cache keys and found that keys without a TTL made up 22 percent of the memory, written by an old code path in the search API.
body:
Tobias pointed out that Redis memory crept up by about 1 GB over two weeks. I sampled the keyspace with SCAN and the MEMORY USAGE command on a replica, 20000 keys, and grouped them by prefix.

The query cache prefix qc: had proper TTLs. A prefix named sq: had no TTL on any key and made up 22 percent of the memory. It came from an older code path in the search API, the saved search counts, that used SET without EX. The path had been moved to a new key prefix months ago, but a fallback branch still wrote the old one.

I removed the fallback in the code and wrote a script that deletes the sq: keys in batches of 1000 with a short pause. I ran it on staging first. In production it freed about 1.3 GB and the memory graph dropped accordingly, and no latency change appeared in the search API.

I also added a test that scans the source for Redis SET calls without an expiry, with an allow list for the session store. It found two other places, both for counters in the rate limiter, which are meant to be short lived but rely on a separate EXPIRE call. I left those as they are.

The key naming is a bit of a mess, with sq:, qc: and a few with no prefix. I wrote a short naming rule in the docs folder: a service prefix, a purpose, then the customer id. Changing the old ones would need a migration, so the rule applies to new keys only.

summary: Reviewed the Redis hit rate per cache prefix and found the dashboard summary cache at 31 percent hits because its key included a timestamp with seconds.
body:
After the memory cleanup I wanted to see how well each cache prefix works. I added a hit and miss counter per prefix in the search API and exposed it to Prometheus, then let it run for a few hours before looking.

The query cache had 74 percent hits, which is fine. The dashboard summary cache was at 31 percent. I read the key builder and found that the key included the request time range in full precision. The dashboard sends now as the end of the range, so every request produced a new key within a second.

The fix rounds the end of the range down to the full minute before building the key, and the summary is allowed to be up to a minute old. I asked Sam whether customers would notice and she said no, since the panels refresh every five minutes anyway.

After the deploy the hit rate of that prefix rose to 88 percent over an hour. The ClickHouse queries per second from the summary panels dropped by about a half in Grafana, which was a nice side effect.

One thing to watch is that rounding makes many clients ask for the same key at the same moment when the minute turns, so a burst of misses can arrive together. I added a short lock with SET NX and a 5 second TTL, so only one request recomputes and the others wait for it. The test with 50 parallel requests showed one computation.

I wrote the results in the ticket. A look at the other prefixes with low hit rates is next, and there are two more under 50 percent.

summary: Removed the old in-memory fallback and the legacy counters from the schema registry worker code, which enforce mode had made dead code.
body: Started from the cleanup plan written two days ago. Deleted the in-memory fallback path in the worker's registry client, since the cached lookup with the Postgres read is the only path now. The three old counters that fed the first violation table were removed along with their flush goroutine. Go tests for the worker still pass, and the diff is about 340 lines removed against 40 added. I checked the Grafana panels and none of them used the old counter names. The branch is ready for Mara to look at tomorrow.

summary: Found that the Redis connection count of the search API grows by about 20 per deploy because the old pool is never closed on config reload.
body:
Sam had noticed the Redis client list getting long after deploys, so I looked at it with CLIENT LIST on the staging instance. Connections were tagged by the client name we set, and the search API showed 60 connections after three reloads where one pool should hold 10. The config reload handler built a new ioredis client and dropped the reference to the old one without calling quit.

I added a close of the old client after the new one answers a ping. I also set a client name that includes the process id, so a leak is easier to see next time. After five reloads on staging the count stays at 10. The production fix goes out with tomorrow's deploy. What is left is a Grafana panel for connected clients per service, which I will ask Tobias to add to the Redis dashboard.

No user impact so far, as the pool is far below the server limit. It would have become a problem with more frequent deploys.

summary: Wrote the first draft of the per-API-key rate limit design, with a sliding window in Redis and limits stored in Postgres next to the key.
body:
Sat down with the current limiter code, which counts per customer with fixed windows of one minute. Customers with several keys complain that one noisy integration uses up the budget of all others. The draft gives each API key its own counter, with the customer limit as an upper bound over all keys.

Counters stay in Redis as a sorted set per key and window, with names following the prefix convention from last week. Limits live in a new column set on the api_keys table in Postgres, with a default taken from the plan. The limiter reads them through a small cache with a 60 second TTL.

Open questions: what response headers to send, and whether rejected schema events count, which we decided yes two weeks ago. A sorted set per key costs more memory than the fixed counters, so I estimated about 40 MB for the current number of keys. I put the draft into the docs folder of the branch and asked Mara to comment.

summary: Built the per-key limiter prototype and measured it at about 0.4 ms per check on staging, which is acceptable, but the sorted set approach needs a cleanup job.
body:
Following the morning draft, I wrote the prototype of the per-key limiter in the rate limiter module. Each check runs one Lua script that removes old entries, counts the rest, adds the new request and sets a TTL on the key.

The script is atomic, so two workers cannot both pass at the limit. I wrote a test with 200 parallel requests against a limit of 100 and exactly 100 passed.

I then ran a load test against staging with 2,000 requests per second spread over 300 keys. The median cost of a check was 0.4 ms and the 99th percentile 1.3 ms. CPU on the Redis instance stayed under 15 percent.

Memory was the weak point. At a limit of 1,000 requests per minute, a busy key holds up to 1,000 entries, about 50 KB. For our largest keys that is fine, but a flood of requests over the limit also adds entries unless I skip adding rejected ones. I changed the script to not add rejected requests, which caps the set at the limit.

Keys of departed customers get cleaned by the TTL, so no cleanup job is needed after all. I wrote that into the notes. Still open are the response headers and the admin console field for the limit. I will start with the headers next, and ask Lena how she wants the console field to look.

summary: Added RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers to the ingest and search responses, and documented them in the public API docs.
body: The limiter now returns the three headers on every response, not only on 429. Remaining is computed in the same Lua script, so no extra round trip is needed. Retry-After is the number of seconds until the oldest entry leaves the window, rounded up. I added tests for the header values at the limit and just below it. The docs page for rate limits got a short section with an example response and advice for clients to wait for Retry-After instead of retrying at once. Sam read it and asked for a sentence on how rejected events count, which I added. Lena has not yet answered about the console field.

summary: Reproduced the slow search for customers with long query strings and traced it to the query parser expanding every term across all fields before boosts are applied.
body:
A support ticket from one large customer said searches with 15 or more terms take over 4 seconds. I took their query from the logs and ran it against staging with the profile flag on.

The OpenSearch profile showed 38 sub-queries per term, one for each indexed field. With 15 terms this gives more than 500 clauses. The parser in the search API builds a multi_match for every term and only afterwards applies the boost map.

I first tried to cut the field list by customer, since most customers use only a few fields. That reduced the clauses, but the field list needs a lookup for each request and it went stale when a customer added a field.

The better fix is to group terms into one query_string per field group. I changed the parser so that terms share a single multi_match with type cross_fields, and the boosts go into the fields list. This produces 38 clauses regardless of the term count.

On the customer's query the time fell from 4.2 seconds to 380 ms. For short queries of one to three terms the difference is small, about 10 ms.

I checked that the result order stays close. On 200 sampled queries, the top 10 results were the same in 171 cases. In the other cases the differences came from the scoring of cross_fields, and they looked reasonable on a manual check of ten of them.

I did not want to merge this without Mara's view on the ranking, so I wrote down the 29 differing queries in a file for review. Next I will add a test with a long query so that the clause count cannot grow again. The parser change is in the search-v2 branch.

summary: Rewrote the search query parser to apply field boosts before term expansion, which cut the expanded clause count for long queries from about 400 to about 40 on staging.
body:
Following the finding that the parser expanded every term across all fields before boosts were applied, I changed the order in the parser: boosts are resolved first, and each term is expanded only across the fields that carry a boost or are in the customer's default field list. The change is in the query builder module of the search API and a small part of the boost lookup.

On the staging data, a query with 60 terms used to produce about 400 clauses and now produces about 40. The p95 latency for that query shape fell from 1.9 seconds to 310 ms. Short queries were not affected, and their latency stayed within noise.

The new clause shape changes the ranking, because the old version scored each term as a best match over all fields and the new one uses cross_fields over the selected set. I compared the top 10 results for 200 recorded customer queries between old and new. 171 were identical, 24 differed by swapped neighbours, and 5 differed more. Most of the larger differences were exact phrase queries, which now rank lower than before.

I wrote the five cases and the swapped ones into a sheet for Mara to review. The unit tests for the parser needed updating because they asserted the old clause structure, and I rewrote them to assert on the result sets instead. The highlighter still takes the expanded term list and shows wrong fragments for the new shape; I noted that and did not touch it yet. Next is Mara's review of the ranking differences and a decision on the phrase queries.

summary: Mara reviewed the cross_fields ranking differences and accepted them, except for exact phrase queries, which now get a separate phrase clause with a higher boost.
body:
Mara went through the file of 29 queries with different top-10 results. In 22 of them she judged the new order as good or better. In seven, all quoted phrase queries, the old order was clearly better, because the cross_fields scoring spreads the match over fields and loses the phrase proximity.

We agreed to keep cross_fields for plain terms and to treat quoted phrases separately. The parser now pulls quoted parts out first and builds a match_phrase clause for each, with a boost of 3 on the message field and 1.5 on the others. The plain terms go into the shared multi_match as before.

I changed the parser tests for this. One test checks that a query with one quoted phrase and two plain terms gives one phrase clause per boosted field and one multi_match. Another checks that an unbalanced quote is treated as plain text and does not throw.

The unbalanced quote case was a bug in my first version, which dropped everything after the quote. Mara found it by pasting a query from a customer ticket.

After the change I ran the 200 sampled queries again. Now 189 have an identical top 10, and the 11 others are again plain-term cases with small score differences.

Latency stays good: the long query takes 410 ms, and phrase queries take about 25 ms more than without a phrase, which is fine.

Open is the effect on the highlight code, which reads the old clause structure to find the matched terms. I will check the highlight output tomorrow with Lena, since the console shows it. If it breaks, the highlighter needs its own query object. Not merged yet.

summary: Fixed the search highlighter for the new query shape by passing it the original term list, and then found a second bug with quoted phrases that contain regex characters.
body:
Lena had checked the admin console search with the branch build and saw highlights missing for plain terms. As feared, the highlighter walked the clause tree to find matched terms, and with a single multi_match there was nothing to walk.

I changed the parser to return an object with the query body and the list of terms and phrases it used. The highlighter now takes that list and builds its highlight_query from it, instead of reading the body. This also removed about 80 lines of tree walking code.

I wrote tests for plain terms, phrases and a mix. All of them pass.

While testing with odd input I found a second problem. A quoted phrase such as "error (code 500)" produced a highlight query that threw a parse error, because the phrase was put into a regexp-style field. The cause was that the phrase went through the same escape function as terms for prefix matching, and that function leaves parentheses alone.

I replaced it with a separate escape for phrases that only handles the quote and the backslash, since match_phrase does not interpret other characters. Prefix terms keep the old escape.

I also tried a set of 40 strange queries taken from the logs: emoji, very long words, only punctuation, empty quotes. Three of them gave errors. Empty quotes created a phrase clause with an empty string, which OpenSearch rejects. Only punctuation led to an empty term list. For both I now return a match_none query, and the API answers with zero results and not a 500.

After these fixes all 40 queries answer. I checked the console with Lena over a call: highlights work for plain terms, phrases and both.

What remains before merging is a run of the full search test suite on staging data, and a note in the docs that quoted phrases now rank higher. The reindex is not needed, since the change only touches the query side. I will do the suite run tomorrow morning.

summary: Full search suite passed on staging data and the parser change is merged into the search-v2 branch, with a docs note about phrase ranking.
body: The run covered 412 tests, including the new clause count and phrase cases, and all passed in 6 minutes. I compared the p95 latency of the 200 sampled queries before and after: 640 ms before and 190 ms after. The docs page on search syntax now says that quoted phrases rank above matches of single terms. Sam reread it and fixed two wording problems. Mara approved the pull request and I merged it into the branch. Next is the per-field boost configuration per customer.

summary: Looked at the Postgres slow query log and found that the audit log listing for the console sorts 2 million rows because the index is on the wrong column order.
body:
Lena asked why the audit log page in the admin console takes several seconds for the biggest customer. The slow query log shows the listing query at about 3.1 seconds. It filters by customer_id and orders by created_at descending, but the existing index is on (created_at, customer_id).

The planner scans the index backwards and filters, which reads far too many rows for a customer with few recent entries. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 2.1 million rows removed by filter.

I created an index on (customer_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on staging first. The query then takes 4 ms. Staging has a copy of the production data from last week, so the numbers should be close.

Before dropping the old index I checked pg_stat_user_indexes, because the audit log reads may use it. The old one still has scans from a nightly job that deletes by created_at, so I keep it. The new index adds about 180 MB. I will create it in production tonight outside the busy hours.

summary: Created the (customer_id, created_at desc) index on the production audit log table without locks, and the console listing now answers in under 10 ms.
body: Ran CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the quiet hour. It took 9 minutes and I watched pg_stat_activity for blocked sessions, and there were none. The index is 176 MB. After ANALYZE the same listing query takes 6 ms in production, down from 3.1 seconds. The console page now loads at once for the large customer. I told Lena and closed the ticket from support.

summary: Wrote the console field for the per-key rate limit together with Lena, with a validation that the key limit cannot exceed the customer limit.
body:
Lena had answered about the console field, so we paired for an hour on the API. The keys endpoint now accepts an optional limit_per_minute, and returns the effective limit, which is the key value or the plan default.

Validation happens in the API and not only in the console. A value above the customer limit gives a 422 with a message that names the customer limit. A value below 10 is also rejected, since a limit that low breaks most integrations and was probably a typo.

Changes to the limit write an entry into the audit log with the old and new value and the user who made it. This was Mara's request in the draft review.

The limiter reads the new column through its 60 second cache. That means a change takes up to a minute to apply, which we put into the help text of the field. Lena found it acceptable.

I added API tests for the three cases: valid value, too high, too low. Lena wrote the console form with a number input and the effective limit shown as grey text when the field is empty.

What is left is a migration for the column on production and the default for existing keys, which stays null so they follow the plan. I will prepare the migration next.

summary: Migration for the per-key limit column ran on staging, and a load test showed the limiter keeps the customer total correct when keys share a budget.
body:
The migration adds a nullable integer column to api_keys, with a check constraint for the minimum of 10. It ran on staging in under a second, since a nullable column without default needs no table rewrite. I also wrote the down migration and tested it.

Then I tested the interaction of key limits and customer limit. A customer with a limit of 600 per minute had three keys, with limits of 300, 300 and unset. I sent traffic through all three at the same time.

The result matched what we planned. Each limited key stopped at 300. The unset key could use what was left of the customer budget. The total never went over 600 in any one-minute window, which I checked from the request logs with a small script.

There was one edge case. When the customer limit is reached first, the response said the key limit was exceeded, because the check order was key first. I changed the order of the checks so that the customer limit is checked first, and the header values then show the one that actually applies. A test covers it.

I also looked at Redis memory during the test. The key counters used 11 MB for 300 keys, in line with the estimate of 40 MB for all keys.

Open points are the docs for the limit field and a note in the migration guide for customers with many keys. Sam will take the docs. Tobias should run the production migration in the next deploy.

summary: Investigated why the nightly reindex job takes 3 hours, and found that it refreshes the index after every bulk request instead of once at the end.
body:
The reindex job has grown from 90 minutes to 3 hours over the last months. I read through the job code and watched one run on staging with the OpenSearch tasks API.

The job reads events from Postgres in pages of 5,000 and sends each page as a bulk request. The bulk call sets refresh to wait_for, which makes every request wait for a refresh cycle. With about 2,400 pages per run, this adds up.

I changed the bulk call to use no refresh, and the job sets refresh_interval to -1 on the new index at the start and restores it to 1s at the end, followed by a single explicit refresh. This is the usual way to load an index in bulk.

On staging the run went from 52 minutes to 21 minutes for the staging data set. That is a 60 percent reduction, so production should go from 3 hours to about 70 minutes.

I added a safety step. If the job fails halfway, a finally block restores the refresh interval, because otherwise the index would never become searchable. I tested this by killing the job in the middle and the setting came back.

I also raised the page size from 5,000 to 8,000 as a test, but the gain was only 2 percent and memory use went up, so I left it at 5,000.

The job still reads from Postgres with an offset, which gets slow at high offsets. Keyset paging would be better, and I noted it as a next step. For now I will let the change run on staging for two nights before it goes to production.

summary: Replaced offset paging with keyset paging in the reindex job and the Postgres read time per page stays flat instead of growing with the offset.
body:
Following the note from this morning, I changed the page query of the reindex job to use WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000. The old version used OFFSET, and the last pages took 1.8 seconds each against 40 ms for the first ones.

With keyset paging every page takes about 40 ms on staging. The total read time for the run went from 11 minutes to 3 minutes.

The job needs the last id to resume after a failure, so I store it in a small Redis key with a 2 day TTL, under the job prefix from the naming convention. If the key is missing, the job starts from the beginning.

One detail was the sort order. Events are inserted by several workers, so ids are not strictly in time order, but they are unique and increasing within the table, which is all that keyset paging needs. A test with inserts during a run confirmed that no rows are skipped.

I ran the whole job on staging and it took 17 minutes. The result has the same document count as the old version, 4,812,330, and I compared a sample of 1,000 documents by field hash and found no differences.

The next step is the production run, which I plan after two clean nights on staging.

summary: Looked at the Redis memory of the session store after Lena saw logouts, and found session keys with a 30 day TTL that nobody renews on activity.
body:
Lena reported that a few admin console users were logged out after exactly 30 days, even though they use the console daily. The session store keeps one key per session in Redis with a TTL of 30 days, set when the session is created.

The session middleware only reads the key and never extends the TTL. So the session ends 30 days after login, no matter how active the user is. This was the intended behaviour at first, but nobody wants it now.

I changed the middleware to call EXPIRE on each request, but at most once per hour per session, to avoid writes on every call. A timestamp inside the session value tells when the last renewal happened.

I tested it with a short TTL of 2 minutes on staging, and an active session stayed alive across 10 minutes while an idle one ended. The write rate on Redis from this change is small, about 20 extra commands per second at peak.

I also looked at the memory used by sessions: 14 MB for about 9,000 keys, so nothing to worry about. The fix goes out with the next deploy and I told Lena.

summary: Tried the lightweight query parser library for the search API, dropped it after it could not handle our field boost syntax, and kept the hand-written parser.
body: Wanted to see whether a maintained parser library could replace part of the hand-written query parser in the search API. I picked the one with the best reputation for search syntax and wrote an adapter in a scratch branch. It parsed plain terms and quoted phrases well. It failed on our field syntax like message^2:error, which it read as a single term, and the grammar could not be extended without forking it. Making it work would cost more than the 300 lines it would replace. I dropped the experiment and noted the reasons in the docs folder, so nobody tries it again without a new reason.

summary: Production reindex ran with the new refresh and keyset changes and finished in 64 minutes instead of 3 hours, with the same document count as before.
body:
After two clean nights on staging I enabled the changes for production. I watched the run from the start. The refresh interval was set to -1 at the beginning, and I confirmed with the settings API that it came back to 1s at the end.

The job ran 64 minutes. Search latency during the run did not change noticeably, and the query p95 stayed around 190 ms. The final document count matched the Postgres count at the start of the run, with the difference of a few hundred events that were inserted during the run, which the next run picks up.

Tobias asked whether the shorter run frees time before the backup window. It does, the job now ends well before. Nothing to change in the schedule for now.

summary: Wrote the per-field boost configuration for customers, stored as JSON in Postgres, and found that unknown field names were silently ignored until validation was added.
body:
The search-v2 plan includes boosts per field that a customer can set, for example to make the title field count more than the body. I started with the storage. A new table search_settings holds one row per customer with a JSONB column for the boost map and a version number.

The API gets two endpoints: one to read the effective boosts and one to replace them. The effective boosts are the default map with the customer's values laid over it.

In the first test I sent a map with a misspelled field, titel, and it was accepted. The parser then built a clause for a field that does not exist, and OpenSearch ignored it without any error. The customer would have seen no effect and no message.

I added validation against the list of indexed fields. The list comes from the index mapping, cached in memory for five minutes. Unknown names return a 422 that lists the unknown names and the valid ones.

Boost values are limited to 0.1 through 10. A value of 0 would remove the field from scoring, which is not what a boost should do, and very large values make all other fields irrelevant.

I also thought about caching. The search API caches the boost map per customer in Redis for 60 seconds, using a key with the customer id and the settings version. A change bumps the version, so old cache entries are simply not read any more and expire.

Tests cover the default, an override, an unknown field, out-of-range values and the cache version change. All pass.

Next I will check with Lena what the console needs. She suggested a simple list of fields with sliders, and I think a number input is easier to test. We will decide when she has a mock.

summary: Reviewed Mara's rate-limit change for the ingest API and asked for the key limit lookup to fall back to the plan default when Postgres is slow, which she added.
body:
Mara had wired the new per-key limiter into the ingest API and asked me to review. The logic is right: it reads the key limit through the cache, runs the Lua script and sets the headers.

My main concern was the cache miss path. On a miss, the limiter reads the key limit from Postgres in the request path. If Postgres is slow, every ingest request waits on it, and ingest is the part that must stay fast.

I asked for a timeout of 50 ms on that read. When it fires, the limiter uses the plan default for that request and logs a warning with a counter. Mara added this, plus a metric rate_limit_lookup_fallback_total.

I also asked for a test for the case where Redis is unreachable. The agreed behaviour is to let the request through and count it, since dropping data because the limiter is down would be worse than being too generous for a short time. Mara had this already, and the test covers it.

A smaller point was the log line on each rejected request, which would be noisy during a flood. We changed it to log once per key per minute and count the rest in a metric.

I ran the branch on staging with the load test again, 2,000 requests per second over 300 keys. The p99 of the whole ingest request went from 14 ms to 15 ms, so the added cost is small.

One more thing I checked was the interplay with the schema rejection count. Rejected events count against the limit as decided, and the test with 10 percent invalid events shows the right totals.

After her changes I approved the pull request. It will go to production together with the migration, and Tobias will run it in the deploy.

summary: Deployed the per-key rate limits to production with the migration and watched the first hours: no unexpected 429s, and the lookup fallback counter stayed at zero.
body:
Tobias ran the migration at the start of the deploy and the new ingest and search images went out afterwards. All keys have a null limit, so the behaviour for existing customers is unchanged until someone sets a value.

I watched the dashboards for the first three hours. The share of 429 responses stayed at 0.2 percent, the same as the days before. The new fallback counter showed zero, so the Postgres reads were fast enough.

Redis memory for the limiter keys rose by 9 MB, and the command rate by about 1,800 per second, which matches the load test. Redis CPU went from 8 to 11 percent. That is fine, but I put it on the list to watch when more customers set key limits.

I set a limit on one test key of our own account to 20 per minute and sent 50 requests. The first 20 passed and the rest got 429 with a correct Retry-After. The audit log has the entry for the limit change with my user.

Sam is writing the customer mail about the new setting, and the docs page is live. One question from support came up: whether a key limit applies to the batch or to the events inside it. It applies to requests, as before, and I added a line to the docs to say that.

What remains is a look after a week at which customers set limits and whether any of them hit them.

summary: Went through the Postgres connection use of the admin console API and cut the pool from 40 to 15 per instance after finding that most connections sat idle.
body:
Tobias pointed out that Postgres is close to its max_connections at peak, with 190 of 200 in use. I looked at pg_stat_activity grouped by application name to see who holds them.

The admin console API holds 3 instances times 40 connections, which is 120. At the busiest time only about 12 of the 40 per instance were active, and the others were idle. The pool size was set long ago when the console did more work in the request path.

I looked at the pool metrics for a week. The maximum number of connections in use at the same time per instance was 14, and the wait time for a connection was zero.

I changed the pool maximum to 15 and the idle timeout to 30 seconds, so the pool also shrinks after a burst. I then ran the console's test suite and a load test with 200 parallel users on staging. The wait time stayed under 2 ms and no request failed.

The change frees 75 connections in total. That gives room for the ingest workers to grow without raising max_connections, which would cost memory on the database host.

I considered adding PgBouncer for this, but with 75 connections freed it is not needed now. I wrote the option into the notes for the case that the number of services grows.

The config change is in the Terraform variables of the console service, and Tobias will apply it. After applying I will look at the connection graph again.

summary: Wrote the console UI for per-field boosts with Lena, using number inputs, and found that saving an unchanged form bumped the settings version and emptied the Redis cache entries.
body:
Lena had a mock with sliders, and we agreed to use number inputs with a reset button per field, because sliders are hard to set to 0.1 steps and hard to test. The form lists the fields from the mapping endpoint with the default boost next to each one.

We wired it to the two endpoints from earlier this week. Loading works. Saving sends the whole map, and the API replaces the row.

During testing I noticed that pressing save without a change still bumped the version number. Since the Redis cache key includes the version, every save made all cached boost maps for that customer unreadable, and the next requests had to load from Postgres. It is not a large cost for one customer, but it is wasteful and makes the version number meaningless as a change counter.

I changed the API to compare the new map with the stored one, after filling in defaults, and to return the current row without a write if they are equal. A test covers the unchanged case and the case where only a default value is sent explicitly, which also counts as unchanged.

Another small bug was in the console. The form sent values as strings, and the API accepted "2" as 2, which hid the type problem. I made the API strict and let the console convert with Number before sending.

Lena also added a warning text when a boost is above 5, saying that other fields might become hard to find. I like it, since customers will not know the effects.

We tested the form on staging with three different customer accounts and the effect on the ranking is visible in the sample searches. The title boost of 4 moved matching documents up as expected.

What remains is the docs page for the boost settings, and a check of how the settings survive the reindex. They live in Postgres and not in the index, so they should, but I will test it after the next reindex.

summary: Checked the boost settings across a staging reindex and wrote the docs page, then listed what is left for search-v2: synonyms and the rollout plan.
body:
I ran the reindex job on staging and then searched with a customer whose title boost is 4. The ranking was the same before and after the run, which confirms that the boosts are read at query time from Postgres and not stored in the index. I also deleted the Redis cache entries by hand during the test, and the next request filled them again with the right values.

Then I wrote the docs page for the boost settings. It explains what a boost is, the allowed range of 0.1 through 10, the delay of up to a minute until a change applies, and two examples with a before and after of a result list. Sam reviewed the text and asked me to add a section on how to go back to the defaults, which is the reset button or an empty map through the API.

I took the time to go through the open points of the search-v2 branch:
- Synonyms per customer are not started. Mara thinks they need a change of the analyzer, which means a reindex with a new mapping.
- The rollout of the new parser is planned behind a flag per customer, so we can switch back quickly if a customer sees worse results.
- The p95 latency target of 200 ms is met on the sampled queries, but I want a longer comparison on live traffic with the flag.
- The tests for the highlighter should run in CI with a real OpenSearch container, now they use a mock for part of the cases.
