I set the keepalive in the shared options to 30 seconds, below both values. After the deploy to staging there were no warnings for an hour.

I also wrote the two values into a comment in the options module so that the next change to either of them is made with the other in mind.

The change is small but touches the shared module, so I told Tobias. No production deploy until the rate limit work goes out together with it.

summary: Wired the per-key limiter into the ingest gateway and the search API, with new response headers showing the key limit and the account limit
body:
Both services now call the limiter with the API key id and the account id. The key id comes from the authentication step, which already runs before the limiter, so no new lookup was needed.

For the headers I kept the existing X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset for the limit that is closest to being used up, because existing clients read them. I added X-RateLimit-Scope with the value key or account so a client can tell which one applies. Mara agreed with this in chat.

The 429 body now says which scope was exceeded and when to retry. Retry-After is set in whole seconds. I checked that our own ingest client library, which retries on 429, reads Retry-After correctly with the new response, and it does.

Tests:
- integration test in the search API for both scopes
- integration test in the gateway with a batch request
- header test for a key without a row

The gateway test found a bug: batch requests count by number of events, and I had passed the request count as the cost. The cost argument is now the event count, and the Lua script adds it as a number instead of 1. The script test was extended for that.

I ran the full suite on staging, 238 tests, all passing. A load test of 5 minutes with three keys under one account showed the right split: the noisy key was limited at its own value and the other two were not affected.

What is left is the admin console part for setting limits, which Lena will build, and the rollout. I plan to deploy behind a flag so that the old counting stays available for a quick return.

summary: Built the admin API for reading and setting per-key rate limits, with audit entries for every change and validation against the account ceiling
body:
The console needs endpoints to list limits for an account's keys, set one and delete one. I added them to the console API under /accounts/:id/key-limits.

Validation was the main part. A key limit above the account limit is useless, so it is refused with a clear message. Lowering the account limit below an existing key limit is allowed, but the response lists the keys that are now capped by the account. I decided not to block this because support may need to lower an account quickly.

Every change writes an audit entry with the old and new value and the user. I reused the helper from the schema registry work for this, which saved some time. A test reads the audit log after a set and a delete.

Permissions: only the roles admin and support can write. Customers' own users can only read their own account's limits. I tested a customer token against another account and got a 403, as it should.

There was one problem with the cache. The 30 second limit cache in each service means the console shows the new value at once but enforcement lags up to half a minute. I added a note to the API response and the docs rather than build invalidation, since a Redis pub/sub for this seemed too much for the value.

Lena has the shape and starts the console page tomorrow. Sam will write the docs section once the page exists.

Tests: 19 new ones, all passing with the suite at 257 tests.

summary: Rolled the per-key limiter out to production behind a flag for one customer and watched the counters and 429 rate through the morning peak
body:
I deployed the branch to production with the flag off, and everything stayed the same for an hour. Then I turned the flag on for one mid-size customer who had asked for the feature, with three keys.

I watched Redis during the morning peak. Commands per second rose by about 3 percent for that customer's traffic, which is the second counter. Latency of the limiter script stayed under 0.1 ms at p99. The connection count did not change.

The 429 rate for the customer was 0.2 percent before and 0.2 percent after, so nothing was blocked that was not blocked earlier. I then set a low limit of 50 per minute on one test key to confirm enforcement. Requests with that key got 429 with scope key, while the other two keys went on without errors. I removed the test limit afterwards.

One detail: the overshoot at the deploy that I had expected did not happen, because the flag was off during the rollout.

I sent the customer a short message through Sam. If tomorrow is also quiet, I will enable the flag for everyone and remove the old counting after a week.

summary: Turned the per-key limiter on for all customers and checked that 429 counts and Redis load stayed in line with last week
body:
The first customer had a clean day, so I switched the flag on for all accounts at the start of the day. I compared the 429 rate per account with the same hours of last week. Of the 40 accounts, 38 were identical within noise. Two accounts had a few more rejections, and both turned out to be clients that retry fast on errors; those hit the account limit as before.

Redis commands per second went up 4 percent overall, memory did not change visibly, since the counters are small and expire. I checked a sample of rl: keys and each had a TTL.

I also tested what happens when Redis is slow. With an added 200 ms delay on staging the limiter times out after its 50 ms budget and lets the request through, which is the behavior we chose for the old limiter too.

The flag stays for a week as the way back. Lena's page for the limits is in review.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console page for key limits, then merged the rate-limits branch and removed the old counting code after finding no use of it in logs
body:
Lena's page shows the keys of an account with their limits, a form to set one and a delete button. I tried it on staging and found three things. The form accepted a limit of 0, which would block a key completely; the API refuses it but the page showed a generic error. I asked for the API message to be shown as it is.

Second, the page did not show that a key without a row uses the account limit. It showed an empty field. She changed it to show the account value in grey with the text "inherited". Third, after saving, the list did not refresh. She fixed that with a refetch.

On the backend side I looked at the logs for the old limiter path. The flag had been on for all customers for a week with no fallback use, and no one asked for a return. I removed the old counting function, the flag and its tests, which deleted about 180 lines.

Before the merge I ran the full suite and the load test again. 257 tests passed. The load test with 200 clients showed the same numbers as before.

I also updated the limiter section of the architecture notes: key naming, the two-counter script, the 30 second cache and the fail-open behavior on timeout. Mara checked the notes and added the rule that a new key family in Redis needs a TTL from the start, a result of the settings cache problem found earlier.

The branch was merged after Lena's fixes and deployed. I watched the first hour in production: no errors, and the console page worked for a real account.

Sam is writing the docs section now. One point left: we should tell the customers who use several keys that they can now set limits themselves. Sam will draft that message.

summary: Investigated why the search API p99 latency rose in the evening and found slow Postgres lookups of account settings that bypassed the cache
body:
Grafana showed the search API p99 going from 180 ms to 420 ms between 18:00 and 20:00 for three days in a row. Search itself on OpenSearch was steady at about 60 ms, so the time was elsewhere.

I added timing around the pipeline steps on staging and replayed an evening sample of requests. The slow part was the account settings lookup, which usually comes from Redis. For a group of requests it went to Postgres, because the cache key included a locale field that one client library sends in a different case. So "en-US" and "en-us" made two keys, and one of them was never warm.

In Postgres the lookup itself took 3 ms, but under the evening load the connection pool queue added up to 200 ms.

The fix was to lower-case the locale when building the key. I also looked at the key family naming and added the version to it so that a change in format cannot mix old and new entries.

After the deploy the cache hit rate for settings went from 91 percent to 99.4 percent. I checked the evening hours the next morning in the metrics of staging replay, and the p99 estimate fell back to 190 ms.

I also made the pool queue time visible: a new Prometheus histogram for the wait time of the Postgres pool in the search API.

Still open: why only that client sends a different case. I asked Sam to find out which customer uses it so we can tell them, but it is not urgent.

summary: Confirmed in production that the settings cache fix brought the evening search latency down and added an alert on the Postgres pool wait time
body:
The fix went out this afternoon, and the first evening peak is over. The p99 of the search API stayed between 170 and 200 ms for the whole evening, compared to 420 ms on the three days before.

The hit rate for the settings cache was 99.5 percent at peak. The Postgres pool wait histogram showed a p99 of 4 ms, where my replay had shown up to 200 ms.

I added an alert rule in the alerts repository: if the p99 of the pool wait is above 50 ms for 10 minutes, it sends a warning to the channel, not to PagerDuty. I chose 50 ms because the normal value is under 10. The rule has a test in the rule test suite.

I also went through other cache keys built from client input. Two more used raw header values, the API version and the timezone. I normalized both in the same way and added a unit test for the key builder with mixed-case input.

The key builder now lives in one function for the search API, and the lint rule from the Redis work blocks building keys by string concatenation outside of it. It found one place in the rate limiter test helper, which I changed.

Sam found the customer with the different locale case; it is an old mobile app. No action needed.

The ticket for the latency can be closed. I will look at the hit rates of the other key families next week.

summary: Wrote the notes on cache key rules after the locale bug so that new keys are built the same way and carry a version and a TTL
body:
After the latency fix I wrote a short page in the repository docs about cache keys. It has the rules in one place.

Keys are built only through the key builder function. Input from clients is normalized before it enters a key: lower case, trimmed, and for free text a hash. Every key family has a version prefix and a TTL set in the same call that writes the value. A family without a TTL needs a reason in the code review.

I listed the current families with their TTLs: settings 10 minutes, query results 60 seconds, rate limit counters by window, session store 8 hours. Mara checked the list and added one family that I had missed.

The page links to the lint rules, so people can see how they are enforced.

summary: Looked at Redis memory growth over the last month and found the query result cache grew with the number of distinct filters, not with traffic
body:
Tobias asked why used memory in Redis went from 3.1 GB to 4.4 GB in a month while traffic grew only 6 percent. I sampled keys by family with SCAN, not KEYS, and summed their sizes.

The query result family took 2.6 GB, up from 1.4 GB. Its keys include the full filter set, and a new dashboard filter that customers use allows free text, so there are many more distinct keys with few repeat hits. The hit rate of that family was only 34 percent for those queries.

Most of that memory is useless, since those results are rarely read again within the 60 second TTL. I did not change the TTL. Instead I tested a rule to cache only queries that are seen a second time: the first request writes a small marker, the second one writes the result.

On a staging replay the memory of the family dropped by 55 percent while the overall hit rate fell by only 1.5 points.

I have not deployed it. I want Mara to look at the extra latency for the second request, which now pays for one more write. We will decide tomorrow.

summary: Deployed the second-hit rule for the query result cache after Mara's review and saw the memory of that key family fall by half in a few hours
body:
Mara reviewed the change and had two points. The marker key should have a short TTL of 30 seconds so the markers do not pile up, and the rule must be off for queries that are known to be expensive, because for those a first-time cache write is worth it. We have a list of those dashboard queries, so I added a flag per query type.

I made both changes and added tests for a repeated query, a single query and an expensive query. The suite passed.

The deploy went out at midday. Over the next four hours the query family shrank from 2.6 GB to 1.3 GB as old keys expired. Total Redis memory went to 3.2 GB. The hit rate of the family stayed at 34 percent for the free-text queries and rose slightly for the rest, since they no longer share space with one-off results.

I measured the latency effect on the second request. It is 0.4 ms more at p50 and the same at p99, which is nothing next to the search itself.

The connection count stayed at its usual value and no errors appeared.

I added the marker family to the docs list of cache keys with its 30 second TTL. Tobias will keep an eye on the memory graph through the week.

Idea for later: a limit on the length of free text in the filter, but that is a product decision, so I asked Lena whether the console needs it.

summary: Started the cost review of the OpenSearch cluster, listing node sizes, storage per customer and unused indices before any change is made
body:
Tobias asked for a view of what the search cluster costs and where the money goes. Before suggesting anything I wanted numbers, so I spent the morning collecting them from the cluster APIs and the AWS cost reports.

The cluster has 6 data nodes and 3 small master nodes. The data nodes make up about 78 percent of the search bill. Storage use is 5.8 TB for primary data and the same again for replicas.

Per customer, the three largest take 61 percent of the storage. One of them alone holds 1.4 TB, and about 40 percent of that is events older than a year that are searched rarely. I checked the query logs: in the last 90 days only 2 percent of that customer's searches touched events older than 6 months.

I also found 11 indices with no queries for more than 60 days. Seven of them are test indices from the search v2 work and the benchmark runs, together 190 GB. Four belong to customers who have left. I listed them with their sizes and last query time, but I did not delete anything, because deleting is irreversible and I want Mara to confirm the customer ones.

The heap use of the data nodes is around 62 percent, and CPU stays under 35 percent except during the nightly reindex. That suggests the nodes are bigger than the queries need, but the reindex peak and the shard plan make it unclear how much we could shrink. A smaller node count would also mean larger shards each.

I wrote the findings in a table in the planning doc, with a column for the possible saving and one for the risk:
- delete unused indices: small saving, low risk
- shorter replica count for old data: medium saving, medium risk
- smaller nodes: large saving, needs the new shard layout first

The last point ties the cost work to the plan for the shard layout by month. With monthly shards, old months can sit on cheaper settings, so I will not touch node sizes now.

Next step: ask Mara about the four customer indices and the test ones.

summary: Deleted the seven test indices from the search v2 work after checking nothing reads them, and kept the four customer indices until Mara answers
body:
Mara confirmed in chat that the seven test indices can go. Before deleting I checked the aliases and the query logs again; none had an alias, and the last query on each was more than two months old. I also grepped the repositories for their names, since a config or a script could still point to one. One staging script mentioned two of them, so I fixed it to use the current index names.

I took a snapshot of the seven indices to S3 first, which cost almost nothing, then deleted them. The cluster freed 190 GB of primary storage, and the used storage graph dropped as expected. The cluster health stayed green and the heap use did not move.

For the four indices of former customers, Mara said she wants to check the contracts for the data retention period. Sam will find out. So they stay for now.

The estimated saving of this step is small, about 3 percent of the storage bill, but it is free and finished. I updated the table in the planning doc.

summary: Measured what a lower replica count for old search data would save and what it would risk, using a staging copy of the largest customer's index
body:
Of the cost ideas, setting the replica count to zero for old events looked most promising, so I tested it before proposing it. The largest customer's index on staging is a copy from last month, 1.4 TB with one replica.

I worked out the cases. If a node fails, a shard without replica is lost until it is restored from a snapshot. Restoring a 40 GB shard from S3 took 11 minutes in a test on staging. During that time searches over the affected data return partial results, and the API reports that in a header if shards fail. I checked that the search API passes the shard failure information on, and it does, in the existing partial flag.

The other effect is search load. With no replicas, all queries on those shards go to one node. I replayed a day of the customer's queries against the staging index with and without the replica for the old data. The p50 stayed the same at 58 ms. The p99 went from 210 to 260 ms for queries across the old data, which is acceptable given how rare they are.

The saving, projected to production, is about 1.9 TB of storage, which is roughly 14 percent of the search storage cost.

My concern is that this change belongs to the shard layout plan. If the migration to monthly shards is done on top of different replica settings, the two changes interact, and a mistake in one would be hard to see. So I would do the replica change after the migration, when the months are separate and we can set replicas per month.

I also looked at the snapshot schedule. It runs every six hours and keeps 14 days. For old data that does not change, a daily snapshot would be enough, which saves S3 requests and a little storage. This is independent of the layout, so we can do it now.

I wrote down the numbers and the recommendation in the planning doc:
- snapshots daily for old indices now
- replica change after the monthly shard migration
- node size decision after both

Tobias read it and agreed with the order. He will change the snapshot policy in Terraform, and I will review the pull request.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's snapshot policy change in Terraform and tested a restore from the new schedule on staging to be sure old indices come back correctly
body:
Tobias's pull request changes the snapshot policy in two parts: indices older than 60 days are snapshotted once a day at 03:30, and the recent ones every six hours as before. Retention stays at 14 days for both.

I reviewed the Terraform diff. The policy is defined with an index pattern, and old and new indices are told apart by a naming rule, so I checked that the pattern matches what we have. The current names include the customer and a creation stamp. The pattern for old indices used a date range that does not work with wildcards, so a policy would have matched nothing. I explained that in the review, and Tobias changed it to use an alias that the nightly job moves indices into after 60 days.

That made me look at the nightly job. It does not move indices today, so Tobias added a small step that updates the alias after the reindex finishes. I read the code. It handles a missing alias and an index that is already in it.

The real test was a restore. On staging I applied the new policy, waited for a snapshot of an old index, then deleted the index and restored it from the snapshot. The 40 GB index came back in 11 minutes, green, with the same document count and the same checksum on a sample of 1,000 documents.

I also tested a restore of a recent index from the six-hour schedule to make sure that the split did not break it. It worked in the same way.

One issue came up: the policy has a limit on running snapshots, and the daily one for old indices started at the same time as the nightly reindex window. That is the window the backup work has clashed with before. I asked Tobias to shift the daily snapshot to a time clear of the reindex job. He moved it to 04:30 after we looked at the durations of the last week; the reindex has always finished by 03:15.

After these changes I approved the pull request. Tobias applied it to production in the afternoon. The first run is tonight, and I will look at it in the morning.

The saving of this step will be small, about 2 percent, but the policy is clearer now, and the alias is useful for the replica change later.

summary: Checked the first night of the new snapshot policy and drew up the list of costs that remain for the search cluster, ordered by what depends on the shard plan
body:
The daily snapshot of the old indices ran at 04:30 and finished in 38 minutes. It did not overlap with the reindex job, which ended at 03:05. The recent indices kept their six-hour runs and all of them succeeded. The snapshot storage in S3 is slightly lower already.

I checked that the alias for old indices got its members. After the nightly job, 142 indices were in it and 9 were not, because they were newer than 60 days. That matches the data.

With this done, I went back to the cost table and sorted the remaining items by dependency.

Independent of the shard plan:
- the four customer indices, waiting for the contract answer
- the ClickHouse and Postgres side, which is not part of this review
- the EBS volume type of the data nodes, which I have not looked at yet

Dependent on the shard plan:
- replicas by month
- node count and size
- cheaper storage for old months

I looked at the EBS item now. The data nodes use gp3 volumes with the default throughput. The disk metrics show an average of 80 MB/s at the reindex peak, far under the volume limit, and IOPS use is below 15 percent. Provisioned values could be lowered a little, saving perhaps 4 percent of the storage bill. The risk is that a restore or a reindex with the new layout needs more throughput than today. So I decided to leave this too until the migration has been planned in detail.

I had one more look at the reindex job's duration, since it will be part of the plan. It has grown from 1 hour 40 to 2 hours 10 over three months. The growth is in line with the data. With monthly shards it could process months in parallel, but that is a plan for later.

I wrote a summary for the lead at the top of the planning doc: what is done, what it saved (about 5 percent of search cost so far), and the one decision we need, which is to start the monthly shard design before touching nodes or replicas.

Tobias will draft the shard sizing next week, with a target of 30 to 50 GB per shard. I will provide the query pattern data by customer and age that I collected for this review.

summary: Collected the query age data by customer for the shard plan: how many searches reach back more than one, three and six months
body:
For the monthly shard layout Tobias needs to know how far back searches reach. I took the search API logs of the last 90 days and counted, per customer, the share of queries whose time filter starts before one, three and six months ago.

Across all customers, 71 percent of queries stay within the last month, 90 percent within three months and 97 percent within six. Queries with no time filter count as reaching back to the start, and they are 4 percent of the total, so I listed them separately. Most come from two customers using a saved search without a range.

The three largest customers differ. One has 83 percent in the last month, and another has only 52 percent, because its compliance team searches old events often. That matters for the layout, because that customer would hit many monthly shards per query.

I saved the table as a CSV in the planning folder together with the query that produced it, so that the numbers can be repeated. I sent Tobias the link and the note about the unbounded queries.

summary: Turned the query age data into a first draft of the monthly shard layout: most searches stay within three months, but two large customers reach back much further.
body:
The age numbers from two days ago showed that about 91 percent of searches touch only the last three months. Two large customers are the exception: one has 14 percent of its searches reaching back more than six months, and that customer drives most of the old-data reads.

I drafted a layout with one index per month and an alias per customer that carries a filter on the customer id. Hot months get more shards, and older months get fewer. The first sizing used the current index of the largest customer as a base. A month of its data is about 60 GB, so five primary shards keeps each shard near 12 GB.

I wrote the math in a doc in the repo. The main open point is the alias count. With 40 customers and 24 months of history we would have about a thousand aliases, which the cluster state can hold, but I want to confirm that on staging before it goes into a plan.

The reindex job also needs a change, because today it walks one index per customer. In the new layout it would walk months. I listed the places in the job that assume a customer index name: three functions and one config file.

I did not touch any code today. The draft is only a doc with numbers and a list of questions for Mara, mainly about whether the per-customer routing should stay. Next step is a staging test with a copy of two months of data.

summary: Created 24 monthly indices on staging with 40 customer aliases and found that search latency stayed flat while the cluster state grew by only a few megabytes.
body:
Following the draft from this morning, I built the monthly layout on staging. A script created 24 indices named by month and an alias for each of the 40 customers with a term filter on the customer id. The script is idempotent, so I could run it several times while tuning.

I loaded the two largest customers into it by reindexing from the existing customer indices. The load took about 50 minutes, mostly limited by the reindex throttle I had set to protect the staging nodes.

Then I replayed 20 minutes of real search traffic, captured from production last week, through the aliases. The p50 stayed within 3 ms of the old layout. The p99 was 12 percent higher on queries that reach across more than six months, which is what we expected, since they fan out to more indices.

The cluster state grew from 4.1 MB to 6.8 MB with all aliases. That is fine for now. I checked the master node heap during the load and it did not move.

One problem showed up. Filtered aliases do not route queries to a single shard, so every search hits all shards of the month. I tried custom routing by customer id, and it fixed the fan out for small customers, but the largest customer then put most of a month on one shard. I left routing off for now.

I wrote down both results in the doc. The next question for Mara is whether to split the largest customer into its own index family. I also want a look at the replay for the old-data queries.

summary: Asked Mara about routing and the big customer, and her answer is to keep routing off and give the largest customer its own monthly index family.
body:
I took the routing result to Mara this evening. She read the staging numbers and agreed that custom routing is not worth it, since it creates one hot shard for the customer that matters most.

Her proposal is a second family of monthly indices for the largest customer only, with its own shard count, and an alias for that customer pointing at that family. All other customers share the common monthly indices. That keeps the alias filter cost low for the many small customers, and the large customer queries one index per month without a filter.

I checked how this affects the reindex job. It needs a mapping from customer to family, which could be a small table in Postgres. Mara would rather have it as a config file in the repo, because the list is short and changes rarely, and a change then goes through review. I agreed.

We also talked about what to do when a second customer grows large enough. The rule we wrote down is that a customer moves to its own family when it exceeds 25 percent of a month's data. The reindex job would need a way to move a customer's old months, and we left that for a later step.

I updated the plan doc with the family idea, the config format and the move rule. I also listed the work in order: the config loader, the index naming helper, the reindex change, the alias management script. None of it has been started in code yet. Tomorrow I begin with the naming helper because everything else depends on it.

summary: Wrote the index naming helper and its tests for the monthly layout, covering the shared family, the dedicated family and month boundaries in UTC.
body:
I started the code today with the helper that turns a customer and a timestamp into an index name. It lives in the search package next to the existing index utilities.

The helper reads the family config, which maps a customer id to a family name. Customers not in the file get the shared family. The index name is the family name plus the year and month, taken in UTC. I picked UTC deliberately because the events are stored in UTC, and local months would shift events between indices.

The tests cover these cases:
- an event at the last second of a month goes to that month's index
- an event one second later goes to the next month
- a customer in the dedicated family gets the dedicated name
- an unknown customer gets the shared name
- a malformed config entry fails at load time and not at query time

The last case found a bug in my first version. A customer id with an uppercase letter was written into the index name, and OpenSearch refuses uppercase index names. I now reject such ids when the config loads, and lowercase ids are the only valid ones.

I also added a function that lists all index names a time range touches. The search layer will use it to build the list of indices for a query, so a one-week search does not fan out to all 24 months. It handles the range edges the same way as the helper.

All tests pass locally. I did not wire anything into the search API yet. The next step is the config loader that reads the file at startup, with validation and a clear error message.

summary: Added the family config loader for the monthly layout with startup validation, so a bad customer entry stops the service with a readable message.
body:
The loader reads a YAML file from the repo and builds the map from customer id to family. It runs once at startup and when the service gets a reload signal.

Validation checks that ids are lowercase, that no customer appears twice, and that each family name has a shard count in the same file. A duplicate or a missing shard count aborts the start with a message that names the line.

I tested a reload with a broken file. The service kept the old map and logged the error, which is what I want, since a bad edit should not take search down.

Still open is where the file lives in deployments. For now it is baked into the image, and Tobias may want it in a mounted config instead. I will ask him.

summary: Tobias said the family config can stay in the image, since it changes rarely and a deploy gives an audit trail, so no mounted config is needed.
body:
I asked Tobias how he wants the family file delivered. His view is that a mounted config adds a second place to change things, and the Terraform side has no good home for it.

A change in the image goes through review and a normal deploy, and the deploy log shows who changed it and when. That is the audit trail we want. The reload signal still works for local testing.

He asked for one thing: the service should log the loaded family count and a hash of the file at startup, so he can see in the logs which version runs. I added both lines.

summary: Changed the reindex job to walk monthly indices and tested it on staging; it needed a fix because aliases made it count documents twice for the shared family.
body:
Today I changed the nightly reindex job so that it works on monthly indices rather than customer indices. It now asks the naming helper for the indices of the range it must rebuild and processes them one at a time.

The first staging run finished, but the document counts did not match the source. The shared family had about 4 percent more documents than expected. The cause was that my verification step counted through the customer aliases, and a few test documents had been indexed once per alias during the earlier load. Counting directly on the indices showed the right number.

That meant the verification step was wrong, not the data. I changed it to compare counts per index, and then also per customer using a filter on the customer id, so a mismatch shows which customer is off.

The second run was clean. For the two large customers the job took 38 minutes, compared to 52 minutes before, because the monthly indices are smaller and the bulk requests are more even.

I also looked at what happens when the job fails in the middle of a month. Each index is built under a temporary name and swapped in at the end, which stays the same as before. A failed run leaves a temporary index that the next run deletes first. I tested that by killing the job after three indices, and the next run cleaned up and finished.

One detail remains. The job still writes its progress marker per customer, and now it needs one per index. I started that change but did not finish it, so the job is not safe to run in production yet. The change and a test for resuming are the first things tomorrow.

summary: Finished the progress marker per index in the reindex job, so a killed run resumes at the first unfinished month instead of starting over.
body:
The marker is now a small record in Postgres keyed by index name and run id. It is written when the swap of an index has finished and not before.

I tested the resume by killing the job after four months and starting it again. It skipped the four and continued with the fifth. A run with a new id ignores the old markers, as it should.

The records are removed seven days after the run. I added that to the job's cleanup step. The job still must not run in production, because the alias management script is not written.

summary: Wrote the alias management script that creates and checks customer aliases for the monthly indices, with a dry-run mode that only prints what it would change.
body:
The script reads the family config and the list of existing indices, and works out which aliases should exist. It then prints a plan of aliases to add and to remove.

After Mara's earlier comment about the schema registry backfill, I made dry-run the default. A real change needs an explicit flag. That seemed the safer choice for a script that touches every customer's search.

Applying a plan uses one alias request with all actions, so the switch is atomic. I confirmed on staging that a search during the apply never saw a missing alias.

I ran it against the staging layout and the plan was empty, which is right, since I built that layout with the earlier script. Then I deleted three aliases by hand and the plan listed exactly these three.

The old script from the first test is now redundant, and I will remove it with the branch cleanup. Next is a full rehearsal on staging with all customers.

summary: Rehearsed the whole monthly layout on staging with all 40 customers, and the run finished clean in about two hours with matching counts and no failed searches.
body:
This evening I ran the full path on staging for the first time: config, reindex, alias script and then a search replay.

The reindex of all customers took 1 hour 52 minutes. The per-index count check passed for all 24 months, and the per-customer check passed for all 40 customers. The dedicated family for the largest customer was built with eight shards per month, and the shared family with five.

The alias script then created 40 aliases. The plan afterwards was empty, so the second pass found nothing to change.

I replayed one hour of production search traffic through the aliases. Results:
- 0 errors out of about 18,000 requests
- p50 within 2 ms of the old layout
- p99 8 percent higher overall, concentrated in searches over more than six months
- the largest customer was faster by 15 percent at p99, since its alias needs no filter

I compared the top ten results for a sample of 500 queries between the old and the new layout. 497 matched exactly. The three differences were ties in score, where the order of equal results changed. That is harmless, but I noted it, since scores depend on the shard statistics and will shift a little in the new layout.

The heap use on the data nodes was slightly lower than before, which is what I hoped for with smaller shards.

Nothing is blocking. What is missing is a rollback plan for production, since the migration is not reversible after the old indices are removed. I will write that next, and I want Tobias to check the disk headroom, because both layouts exist side by side during the move.

summary: Wrote the rollback plan for the shard migration: keep the old customer indices for fourteen days and switch aliases back in one request if searches go wrong.
body:
The plan starts from the fact that old and new indices exist at the same time during the move. The rule is that nothing from the old layout is deleted until the new one has served production for fourteen days.

Switching back is one alias request, since the customer aliases are the only thing the search API sees. I wrote that request as a script and tested it on staging. It took under a second and searches continued without errors.

The plan covers three kinds of problem. A wrong result for one customer means switching just that customer back. A latency problem across all customers means switching all of them. A data problem in a month means rebuilding that month with the reindex job.

One gap showed up. New events written during the move must go to both layouts, otherwise a switch back would miss them. The ingest side writes through the index name helper, so I added a dual-write option that writes to the old and new names. It is off by default.

I tested dual-write on staging with a stream of test events for 30 minutes. Counts matched in both layouts.

Disk is the other cost. Tobias estimated that both layouts together need about 1.6 times the current storage for two weeks. He will check that the cluster has room, and if not, the move would go in batches of customers.

I put the plan in the repo docs next to the layout draft, and asked Mara to review it.

summary: Mara reviewed the migration plan and asked for a per-customer order and a check gate between steps; the plan now moves the smallest customers first.
body:
Mara read the rollback plan this morning and had three requests.

First, move customers in order of size, smallest first, so that the first steps carry little risk and test the whole path. Second, put a check gate between steps, a script that compares counts and a sample of searches before the next customer starts. Third, write down who decides to continue, so the move does not run unattended.

I changed the plan for all three. The order is now a list in the config, and the first five customers are small test-like accounts that agreed to be early.

The gate script was the main work. For one customer it does the following:
- compares document counts per month between old and new
- runs 200 recent queries of that customer against both and compares the top ten
- compares p99 for the sample
- prints pass or fail with the reasons

I ran it on staging for five customers. Four passed. One failed on the count, and the cause was a document that had been deleted from the old index after the reindex and was still in the new one. In production this would be handled by the dual-write plan, which also writes deletes, and I checked that the deletes were missing from dual-write.

That was a real bug. I added delete handling to the dual-write path and tested it with a stream of inserts and deletes on staging. The counts then matched for all five.

The decision rule is that the user and Mara both look at the gate output of the first five customers before the large ones go. I wrote it in the plan.

summary: Tested a failed move halfway on staging, killing the reindex and the dual-write in turns, and fixed two ways the gate script could pass on incomplete data.
body:
Before the plan can be trusted, I wanted to see what happens when things break in the middle. I used staging with ten customers and injured the move in four ways.

First, I killed the reindex job during a month. The temporary index stayed, and the next run removed it and continued. That worked as designed.

Second, I stopped the dual-write for ten minutes and then started it again. The gate script showed a count mismatch for the busy customers and failed correctly.

Third, I made one month's index smaller on purpose by deleting some documents. The gate failed on that month. Good.

Fourth, I made a month missing entirely. The gate passed, which was wrong. It compared counts only for months that existed in both layouts, and a missing month was skipped. I changed it to compare the set of months first and fail when they differ.

While looking at this I found a second hole. The query comparison used the most recent queries, and for a quiet customer the sample could have fewer than 200 queries and still pass with, say, 3. I added a minimum sample size, and if the customer has less, the gate now uses a fixed set of synthetic queries from the test fixtures and says so.

After both fixes I repeated all four injuries and the gate failed on all of them, except the first, where nothing is wrong at the end.

I also timed the apply of aliases for ten customers in one request. It took 0.4 seconds. The remaining risk is the disk headroom, and Tobias's answer is still to come.

summary: Tobias confirmed the cluster has disk room for both layouts if customers move in groups of ten, and I added the batch size to the migration config.
body:
Tobias looked at the disk numbers yesterday and came back this morning. The data nodes are at 54 percent. With both layouts the peak would be about 87 percent if all customers moved at once, which is above the watermark where the cluster starts to refuse writes to shards.

Moving in groups of ten keeps the peak around 71 percent. The old indices of a group stay for the fourteen days, so disk grows with each group, and by the fourth group we would be back at the high number. He therefore suggested one of two options: add a node for the migration period, or shorten the keep time for the first groups.

I proposed to shorten the keep time to seven days for the groups of small customers, since their data is small and a rebuild is fast. The large customers would keep the fourteen days. Tobias agreed that this is enough, and he will still add a temporary node as a cushion, which costs about a week of one node.

I added two things to the config: a batch size and a keep time per customer. The cleanup script reads the keep time and refuses to remove an index that is younger.

I tested the cleanup on staging with an index that was too young. It refused and logged the reason. With a old enough index it removed it.

The batch order is now: five small customers, then groups of ten by size, and the largest customer last on its own. I also added a disk check to the gate script. It fails if the data nodes are above 75 percent before a group starts.

The plan is complete as far as I can see. What remains is a review by Mara and a date.

summary: Mara approved the migration plan with one change: the largest customer goes last and only after a full week without incidents on the other groups.
body:
Mara read the final version of the plan and approved it. Her one change was about the largest customer. It carries most of the traffic and most of the data, so it should wait until the other groups have run a full week with no incidents.

I added that as an explicit condition in the plan, and the gate for the last group now asks for confirmation that the week has passed.

She also asked that the alert on search p99 be tightened during the migration period, from 800 ms to 600 ms, so a slowdown shows up early. I will do this when the first group starts and put it back later.

No date is set. The migration is waiting for the temporary node from Tobias.

summary: Wrote the Grafana dashboard for the shard migration with per-group counts, gate results and search latency by layout, so progress is visible during the move.
body:
This evening I built the dashboard we will watch during the migration. The search service now tags each request metric with the layout that served it, old or new. That was a small change in the alias lookup and I tested it on staging.

The dashboard has five rows:
- migration progress: customers per group in old layout, in new layout, and in dual-write
- gate results: the last result for each customer with the reason when it failed
- search latency: p50 and p99 by layout, with the alert threshold drawn as a line
- cluster: disk use per data node, heap use, and shard count
- errors: search errors by layout and by customer

The gate script needed a way to publish its results. I made it write a Prometheus metric through the push gateway, with labels for customer and result. A failed gate sets the value to zero and the reason goes into a label, which is a bit rough, but it works.

I tested the whole dashboard on staging by moving three customers while the replay ran. The progress row followed the move within a minute. The latency rows showed the layout difference I expected, about 8 percent at p99.

One panel was wrong at first. The error rate by layout divided by total requests of all layouts, and so looked tiny. I changed it to divide by the requests of the same layout.

I also exported the dashboard as JSON into the repo, under the monitoring folder, so it is deployed like the other dashboards, and I asked Tobias to look at it. He will check the alert rule file too, since the alerts have been in code since last year.

The tool side of the migration is ready on staging. What is missing is only the temporary node and the go from Mara and the user.

summary: Found that the alert rule change for the migration period was missing in the alert code, and added a rule with a lower threshold that can be switched on by a flag.
body:
Tobias reviewed the dashboard and pointed out that the lower p99 threshold we planned could not be set in the Grafana UI, because alerts live in code. I looked at the alert rule files in the monitoring repo.

The search latency rule has a fixed threshold of 800 ms for five minutes. I added a second rule with 600 ms and a label that marks it as a migration rule. A variable in the rule file switches it on, and the normal rule stays as it is.

Another point came out of the review. The rule paged the on-call, but a migration rule that fires at 600 ms would page during normal evening peaks for the large customers. I checked the last four weeks of p99 data. The 600 ms line was crossed on six evenings, always by less than a minute.

So I set the duration of the migration rule to ten minutes with a warning level that goes to the chat channel. A page happens only if the 800 ms rule fires. That was Tobias's suggestion and I agree.

I tested the rules with the Prometheus rule tester and a series of synthetic values. The migration rule fired after ten minutes at 650 ms and not at a short spike. The normal rule was not changed.

Tobias merged the change after a second look. The flag is off for now, and it will be turned on with the first group.

summary: Looked at the Redis memory report for the week and found the session store grew because of a missing TTL on keys from the old login path.
body:
The weekly memory report showed that the session key family had grown by 30 percent in a month while the number of active users stayed flat. I counted keys by prefix with a scan on the replica.

There were about 410,000 session keys, but only around 9,000 users logged in during the last week. Most of the extra keys had no TTL at all. I checked the TTL of a sample of 1,000 and 62 percent returned no expiry.

The cause was in the old login path of the admin console. It still wrote the session with a plain set and no expiry, and only the new path used a set with a TTL. Both paths are live, because an old redirect still goes through the first one.

I changed the old path to use the same helper as the new one, with the 12 hour TTL. Then I wrote a one-off script that sets a TTL on session keys that have none, based on the last-access field inside the value. Keys not accessed for more than 12 hours get a TTL of one minute, so they are cleaned up soon, and the others get the rest of the 12 hours.

I ran the script in dry mode against production and it listed 255,000 keys to be changed. Nothing is applied yet. Lena should confirm that no one needs a session older than 12 hours, for example a kiosk display.

summary: Applied the session TTL script after Lena confirmed no long sessions are needed, and Redis memory dropped by about 380 MB over the next hours.
body:
Lena answered early: the console has no kiosk mode, and the longest session anyone should have is the 12 hours already in the product docs. She did mention one dashboard wall display used by a customer, but it uses an API key and not a session.

I ran the script in production in batches of 5,000 keys with a short pause between them, to keep the load on Redis low. The whole run took about 25 minutes. The command latency graph stayed flat, with a small bump of 0.2 ms during the batches.

The result over the next hours:
- session keys went from 410,000 to about 14,000
- used memory fell from 2.9 GB to 2.5 GB
- the number of keys without TTL in the session family went to zero

I checked that nobody was logged out by mistake. The login error rate stayed the same, and a count of 401 responses from the console API did not move. I also logged in with an old session that I had kept in a browser from the day before, and it was still valid, as it had been used within the 12 hours.

Then I added a check to the key naming notes from last month. Every new key family must be written through the helper that takes a TTL, and the helper refuses a zero. The old direct writes in the console code were found with a search through the repo. There were two more, both in rarely used paths, and I converted them as well.

I also wrote a small Prometheus gauge from the memory report script, the share of keys without TTL per family, so this kind of growth is visible earlier. It is at zero for all families except the rate limiter counters, which are meant to be reset by the limiter itself.

The old login redirect still exists. I asked Lena whether it can be removed, and she will check the links in the docs.

summary: Lena checked the old login redirect and found two links in the public docs that still use it, so the redirect stays until the docs are changed.
body:
Lena searched the console code and the public docs for the old redirect. The console no longer uses it, but two pages in the public docs link to it, and Sam wrote one of them.

She will fix the two links this week. After that I can look at the access log for the redirect for two weeks, and remove it if nothing calls it.

In the meantime the redirect writes sessions through the helper with the TTL, so it does no harm. I noted the removal as a follow-up in the journal for the console.

summary: Checked the Redis session key count after one night and it stayed at about 15,000, so the TTL fix holds and the memory is stable.
body:
I looked at the key counts again this morning. The session family has 15,200 keys, which fits the number of users active in the last 12 hours.

Used memory is 2.5 GB and has not moved since yesterday. The share-of-keys-without-TTL gauge shows zero for sessions, and there is only the limiter family above zero, as expected.

The 401 rate of the console API was the same as on the days before. No user has reported a logout. I think this topic can be closed, except for the redirect removal.

summary: Reviewed the Postgres slow query log for the week and found an unindexed lookup of audit entries by actor that ran several hundred times a day.
body:
The weekly slow query report showed one query near the top: audit entries filtered by actor id and ordered by time. It ran about 600 times a day and took between 400 and 900 ms each, because it scanned the audit table.

The source is the console page that shows what a user did. I checked the table and it has indexes on the customer and on the time, but none on the actor.

I created an index on actor id and time, descending, using the concurrent option so writes are not blocked. On staging with a copy of the table the query went from 620 ms to 3 ms.

The table is large, and the index will add about 1.2 GB. I looked at the disk of the database and there is plenty of room. I plan to create the index in production tomorrow morning when the load is low.

summary: Created the actor index on the production audit table and watched the write latency and replication lag, which stayed normal while the build ran for about 14 minutes.
body:
I ran the concurrent index build in production at a quiet time. Before starting I noted the baseline: the audit insert latency was about 1.1 ms at p50, and the replica lag was under 200 ms.

The build took 14 minutes. During it the insert latency rose to 1.4 ms at p50 and then returned. The replica lag peaked at 1.8 seconds and came back within two minutes after the end of the build. No alert fired.

After the build I checked that the index was valid, since a concurrent build can leave an invalid index when it fails. The check query showed it as valid. Then I ran the slow query by hand in production and it took 4 ms.

The slow query report for the rest of the day no longer listed it. The console page for user activity loads quickly now, and Lena confirmed it feels faster in the admin console.

I also looked at the second item of the report, a lookup of settings by account. It is cached in most paths, and the remaining calls come from a batch job that runs at night. That is not a priority.

One more thing: I used the occasion to check the unused indexes view for the audit table. There are two old indexes with zero scans in the last months. I did not remove them. I will ask Mara whether the audit export planned for later could use them.

I wrote the index and the reason into the database notes so that the next person who looks at the table knows why it is there.

summary: Asked Mara about the two unused audit indexes, and she wants to keep one for the compliance export and drop the other, which I scheduled after a final check.
body:
Mara looked at the two indexes with no scans. One is on the event type and the other on the customer and the event type together.

Her view is that the customer and event type index will be needed by the compliance export that is planned for later, since exports will filter by customer and type. The index on event type alone is covered by the other one and has no use.

Before dropping the single one, I checked the statistics once more. It had zero scans since the last statistics reset, and that reset was 45 days ago, so the evidence is decent but not long. I also searched the code for queries filtering by event type alone and found none outside tests.

So the plan is to drop it. Dropping an index takes a short lock, so I will do it with the concurrent option to avoid blocking writes. It will free about 700 MB.

I kept the index definition in a migration file with a down step, so it can be recreated if some forgotten query turns up. The down step creates it concurrently as well.

The drop is scheduled for tomorrow at a quiet hour. I will watch the slow query report for a few days after it.

summary: Dropped the unused audit index after a last check of the query plans and the compliance export, and the write latency on the audit table improved slightly.
body:
Mara wanted one of the two unused audit indexes kept for the compliance export and the other dropped. This session did the final check before the drop.

First I read pg_stat_user_indexes on production for the audit table. The index on (tenant_id, created_at, action) had zero scans since the stats reset two weeks ago. The index on (action, created_at) had a few scans, all from the export dry run last week.

I then ran EXPLAIN on the export query with the first index hidden in a transaction on staging. The plan did not change, because the export uses the (action, created_at) index. So that one stays and the other one goes.

I also searched the repository for queries that filter by tenant_id and created_at together. The only hit was an old admin console report that Lena says nobody has opened since the new dashboards. I told her it would be slower afterwards, and she agreed.

Before the drop I saved the index definition in the migration folder, so it can be rebuilt in about 14 minutes if needed. I ran DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY during the quiet hours of the afternoon, and it finished in a few seconds.

After the drop I watched the insert rate and the replication lag for 40 minutes. The lag stayed under one second. The average insert time on the audit table fell from about 2.1 ms to 1.8 ms, and the table's index size shrank by roughly 1.2 GB.

I added a note to the audit table section of the docs about which index serves which query. What remains is to check the slow query log again at the end of the week, in case the old report shows up there.

summary: Read the Redis connection counts per service for a week and found the search API opens far more connections than it uses, which is the first step for the pool review.
body:
The Redis connection count has crept up in the dashboards, so I started a review of how many connections each service holds. I used the CLIENT LIST output from a quiet hour and the Prometheus series for the last seven days.

The search API holds about 120 connections across its tasks, but the peak number in use at the same time was 23. The admin console holds 30 for the session store and uses fewer than 10. The rate limiter in the ingest API is the only client that stays busy, with about 40 connections all in use during peaks.

The search API creates a new pool per Fastify plugin, and two plugins both create their own. That explains the doubled count. I found it in src/cache/client.ts and src/ratelimit/redis.ts.

I did not change anything yet. First I want a plan that shares one client per process and sets a max for each pool. I wrote the numbers into the pool review note, with the peak values next to the current settings.

Next step is to try the shared client on staging with the load script and watch the connection count and the latency of cache reads.

summary: Merged the two Redis clients of the search API into one shared client on staging, and the connection count fell from 120 to 62 with the same cache latency.
body:
Following the review from earlier today, I changed the search API to create one Redis client at startup and pass it to both the cache plugin and the rate limiter helper. The change is small: a new module src/cache/shared.ts and two call sites.

On staging I ran the usual load script for 30 minutes. The connection count went from 120 to 62 across the tasks, and the p95 of a cache read stayed at 1.4 ms, the same as before. No errors showed up in the logs.

One detail: the rate limiter used a separate database number, so I kept the key prefix and used a second client only for that. That is why the count is not lower.

I opened the change for Mara to review. It is not for production until the pool maximum is decided, which is the next topic.

summary: Wrote down the key naming rules for Redis after finding five different prefix styles in use, and renamed the cache keys of the search API behind a version prefix.
body:
While reading the key space for the connection review I found five styles of key names: cache:, c/, search_cache_, sess: and a few keys with no prefix at all. This makes it hard to see which service owns which key and to delete a group safely.

I wrote a short rule in the docs: service name, then purpose, then a version, then the identifier, separated by colons, for example search:q:v2:<hash>. Sessions and rate limiter counters keep their current names, since renaming them would log users out or reset the counters, and they already follow a clear pattern.

For the search API cache I changed the key builder in src/cache/keys.ts to use the new form. Old keys will simply expire, since all of them have a TTL of an hour or less. I checked that with a scan of 10,000 keys on staging, and none had a TTL above 3600 seconds.

The hit rate dropped to near zero right after the deploy on staging and was back to the normal 71 percent after about 40 minutes. I expect the same on production. I will deploy it at a quiet time tomorrow and watch the hit rate graph.

The three keys without prefix come from an old script of the importer. I opened a small task to fix it.

summary: Deployed the new Redis key names to production and the cache hit rate recovered in 45 minutes, then found the importer script still writes the unprefixed keys.
body:
I deployed the key naming change at the quiet time before lunch. Before it I wrote down the baseline: hit rate 72 percent, Redis memory 2.9 GB, and p95 of search latency 180 ms.

Right after the deploy the hit rate fell to about 4 percent, as expected, and search latency went up to 310 ms at the p95 for the first 15 minutes. Then it improved steadily. After 45 minutes the hit rate was 70 percent and the latency was back at 185 ms.

Memory went up by about 400 MB while old and new keys lived side by side, and then it dropped again as the old ones expired. The peak was 3.3 GB, which is within the limit of the instance, but it was closer than I liked. I noted that a rename of this kind needs a check on memory first.

Then I looked at the three unprefixed keys. They come from the importer script scripts/import_status.py, which stores a progress counter per import job. They have no TTL, and there are 212 of them. I checked with Mara and they are not used by anything after an import ends.

I changed the script to write import:status:v1:<job> with a TTL of seven days. I deleted the old 212 keys after saving their names to a file. A scan afterwards showed no key without a known prefix.

The rules doc now lists the keys that are exempt from the new form, with the reason for each. Tomorrow I will check the hit rate once more after the daily peak.

summary: Planned the Redis version upgrade: read the release notes, listed the commands and settings we use that changed, and chose a staging rehearsal before touching production.
body:
The managed Redis is one minor version behind the current stable release, and the provider will retire the old one later in the year. I started the plan for the upgrade today.

First I read the release notes between our version and the target. Most changes are fixes and new commands. Two items need a closer look: a change in how the client output buffer limits are counted for replicas, and a change to the default of one persistence setting. I wrote down both in the upgrade note.

Then I searched the code for the commands we use. The list is short: GET, SET with EX, INCR, EXPIRE, SCAN, a few HSET calls in the rate limiter, and one Lua script for the sliding window. None of them changed in the notes. The Lua script uses only redis.call and tonumber, so it should work as is.

I checked the client libraries. The ioredis version in the search API is recent enough. The Go client in the ingest API is two minor versions old, and its changelog says the target server version is supported since a version we already have.

The plan has four steps. First, upgrade a staging instance and run the load script and the rate limiter tests. Second, create a replica of production with the new version and compare the memory use and the INFO output. Third, ask Tobias for a change window and do the production upgrade with the provider's tool. Fourth, watch the dashboards for a day.

I asked Tobias about the window. He said the provider does the switch with a short failover of about 30 seconds, and that the ingest rate limiter must treat a failed Redis call as allow, which it does already, but I want to test that on staging with a forced failover.

I also wrote the rollback: the provider keeps a snapshot from before the upgrade, and restoring it takes around 20 minutes, with the loss of counters and cache, which is acceptable. Sessions would be lost, though, so users would need to log in again. I told Lena about that.

Next is the staging upgrade tomorrow.

summary: Upgraded the staging Redis to the new version and the load script and rate limiter tests passed, with no change in latency or memory.
body:
I upgraded the staging Redis instance with the provider's tool. The failover took 27 seconds and the service came back without manual steps.

After that I ran the full load script for an hour, the rate limiter tests and the session tests of the admin console. All passed. The p95 of a cache read was 1.3 ms against 1.4 before, which is within noise. Memory use for the same data set was 1.1 GB on both versions.

I also checked the two items from the release notes. The replica output buffer change does not matter, since we have no replicas on staging and the production one is small. The persistence default is only used when a setting is missing, and our parameter group sets it.

The Lua script for the sliding window gave the same results as before on a test of 5,000 calls that I compared with the stored output.

Next I want to test a forced failover while the ingest test load runs, to confirm that the limiter allows requests when Redis is not there.

summary: Forced a Redis failover during an ingest load test on staging and found the limiter allowed requests as planned, but the connection pool took 40 seconds to recover.
body:
The goal was to prove that the ingest API stays up when Redis fails over during the version upgrade. I started the ingest load at 500 requests per second on staging and triggered a failover of the Redis instance.

The result was mixed. No request failed. The rate limiter logged failed Redis calls and let the requests through, which is the intended behavior. The p95 latency of ingest went from 22 ms to 35 ms for about a minute.

The pool was slower to recover than expected. After the failover, the Go client held broken connections and each one failed once with a read timeout before it was replaced. The log showed 64 errors in the first 40 seconds, then none.

The cause is the read timeout of 2 seconds in the limiter client config. During the failover each call waited the full 2 seconds before giving up. A call that waits that long also holds a request open, which is the reason for the higher latency.

I changed the read timeout to 200 ms and the dial timeout to 500 ms in the staging config and ran the test again. This time the latency effect was a short bump to 28 ms, and the error count was 61 but all of them fast. The limiter's normal calls take under 2 ms, so 200 ms is a safe value.

I will bring the timeout change into the production config with its own review, and I want it deployed before the upgrade window. I told Mara what I found, because the limiter code belongs to her and she knows the edge cases better.

summary: Mara reviewed the limiter timeout change and asked for a circuit breaker flag instead of only shorter timeouts; the first version of it is written and tested.
body:
Mara looked at the timeout change from this morning. She agreed with 200 ms but pointed out that during a longer Redis outage each request would still try the call and fail fast, which adds a little load and log noise. She asked for a simple breaker: after 20 failures in 5 seconds, skip Redis for 10 seconds and allow requests, then try again.

I wrote it in the limiter module as a small struct with an atomic counter and a timestamp. It is behind a config flag, off by default, so we can turn it on in production after the upgrade and see how it behaves. I did not want to add a new library for this, since the logic is about 40 lines.

I wrote tests for four cases: failures below the threshold, failures above it, recovery after the pause, and a single success resetting the counter. I used a fake clock to avoid sleeping in tests. All four pass, and the race detector found nothing when I ran them with -race 200 times.

On staging I repeated the failover test with the flag on. The errors fell from 61 to 20, since after the threshold the calls were skipped. The latency bump was barely visible, and after the pause the limiter used Redis again without trouble.

One thing I noticed is that while the breaker is open, the limits are not enforced at all. For a few seconds that is acceptable, but a customer could burst. I put a metric on the number of skipped checks, so we can see it in Grafana and alert on a long open period.

I added the metric and a panel to the limiter dashboard. Mara will review the final code tomorrow. After that the timeout and the breaker go to production, and then the upgrade window can be set.

summary: Wrote the limiter breaker metric into the alert code, then spent the evening on a failed attempt to use a Redis pipeline for the cache reads, which gave no gain and was dropped.
body:
Two things today, one finished and one not.

The finished one is the alert. The breaker metric counts skipped checks. I added a rule in the alert code that warns when the breaker has been open for more than 60 seconds in total during five minutes. I tested it with the promtool unit test format, with a series that opens and closes, and the rule fires only in the long case. The change is in the alerts folder and passed the lint in CI.

The second part was an idea from the connection review. The search API reads several cache keys for one request, up to six, one after the other. I thought a pipeline or MGET would cut the round trips and the latency. So I tried it on a branch of the main checkout.

First I measured how often it matters. In a sample of 10,000 requests from the logs, 38 percent read more than one key, and the average was 2.6 keys. At 1.3 ms per read, the best case saving is about 2 ms per request.

Then I wrote the change with MGET for keys that are known up front. This turned out to be a smaller part than I expected, since in most flows the second key depends on the first result. Only one flow, the dashboard summary, reads independent keys.

I benchmarked that flow on staging. The p50 went from 9.1 ms to 8.8 ms and the p95 stayed at 17 ms. The difference is within noise, since the rest of the time is the OpenSearch query and the JSON work. I ran it three times to be sure.

The code got more complicated: the cache helper needed a second function for batches, a different miss handling, and new tests. For a gain of 0.3 ms this is not worth keeping, so I dropped the branch and wrote the numbers into the pool review note. The conclusion there is that the cache round trips are not our latency problem.

The open question is where the search latency does come from. The next step is to look at the OpenSearch time per query type, which fits the work on the shard layout.

summary: Prepared the limiter timeout change for production: addressed Mara's review comment and planned the rollout with the breaker flag off.
body:
Mara approved the limiter timeout change after a small comment about a log message, which I fixed. The change sets a read timeout of 200 ms and a dial timeout of 500 ms on the limiter's Redis client, and includes the breaker code behind a flag. I did not deploy it yet.

To be sure about the rollout, I went through the ingest dashboards for the last evening peak and wrote down the baseline. The p95 latency of ingest stayed at 21 to 24 ms, the Redis error count was zero, and the limiter's skipped check metric was flat at zero. I added these numbers to the task so that I can compare them after the deploy. The new alert for the breaker shows as healthy in staging.

The plan is to deploy the limiter client to production with the breaker flag off, and to watch the dashboards through one evening peak before anything else changes. After that, Tobias can set the window for the Redis upgrade. I will propose the early morning, since the load is lowest then, and turn the breaker flag on after the upgrade, not before, so that only one thing changes at a time. I wrote this order into the rollout notes and sent them to Tobias and Mara.

summary: Did the production Redis upgrade in a short window; the failover took 31 seconds, the limiter behaved as designed and the cache recovered within the hour.
body:
Tobias and I did the Redis upgrade in the window we agreed on. Before starting I took a manual snapshot and noted the baseline: 14,800 session keys, 2.8 GB memory, cache hit rate 70 percent.

The provider's tool started the switch and the failover took 31 seconds. During that time the ingest API logged fast Redis errors, 58 in total, and let requests through. The p95 latency of ingest rose to 30 ms for about a minute and then went back to 22 ms. No client saw an error.

The search API reconnected without help. The admin console is the part I worried about, since sessions live in Redis. The snapshot restore after the failover kept the sessions, because the provider's switch carries the data over. Lena checked a login and an old session and both worked.

The cache hit rate stayed at 70 percent, because the data moved with the instance. So the cold cache I had feared did not happen. Memory is 2.8 GB, as before.

After the upgrade I checked INFO for the new version, the persistence setting, and the replica status. All were as in the staging test. The slow log had three entries, all from a SCAN that I started myself.

Then I turned on the breaker flag for the ingest limiter in the config and deployed it. I watched the skipped check metric for an hour, and it stayed at zero, which is correct, since Redis is healthy. To see it work I did a controlled test on one staging task, and the breaker opened and closed as in the earlier tests.

Things left over: the Go client could be updated, but that is separate. I also want to remove the old note about the previous version from the runbook and put in the new version number and the failover time we measured. I did that right away, with the 31 seconds in it.

I will check the dashboards again tomorrow morning, after the night jobs, and then close the upgrade task.

summary: Checked Redis the morning after the upgrade, closed the task, then went through the Postgres vacuum report and found the events settings table bloated by a nightly update job.
body:
The first thing was the Redis check. After the night jobs the hit rate was 71 percent, memory 2.7 GB, and the breaker metric was still zero. No new errors in any service. I closed the upgrade task and added the final numbers to it.

The second thing was the weekly look at Postgres. I read the vacuum report and the table sizes. Most tables are healthy. One stood out: account_settings has 3,000 live rows but its size on disk is 1.9 GB, and the dead tuple count is high even after autovacuum runs.

I searched for what writes to it. A nightly job in the admin backend updates a last_seen column for every account, even when the value did not change. That makes a new row version for each of the 3,000 rows each night, and also for the large JSON settings column, which is stored out of line. The job does that in one transaction, so autovacuum cannot clean the old versions until it finishes.

The fix has two parts. First, change the update to touch only the rows where last_seen differs by more than a day. This cuts the updates to a few hundred per night. Second, move last_seen into its own small table, so that updates do not copy the large settings. The second part is a schema change and needs more care, so I did the first part today.

I changed the query in jobs/touch_accounts.ts and ran it on staging. The count of updated rows fell from 3,000 to 412 for a typical day. I checked the plan, and it uses the primary key with a filter, which is fine at this size.

For the existing bloat I decided to use pg_repack in a quiet period rather than VACUUM FULL, because VACUUM FULL locks the table and the admin console reads from it all the time. I tested pg_repack on a staging copy, and it took 40 seconds and the table went from 1.9 GB to 38 MB.

I have not run it on production yet. I asked Tobias whether the extension is available on the managed instance, and he will check. If it is not, then we have to plan a short lock window.

I wrote down the second part, the small last_seen table, as a task with the migration steps. It can wait, since the first part already removes most of the problem.

Tomorrow I will deploy the job change and see how the dead tuple count behaves over a night.

summary: Deployed the account touch job change and saw only 390 rows updated in the night run, with the dead tuples of account_settings no longer growing.
body:
I deployed the job change this morning and checked the result of the night run. The job updated 390 rows instead of 3,000, and ran in 0.4 seconds instead of 6.

In pg_stat_user_tables the dead tuple count of account_settings was 640 after the run, and autovacuum cleaned it within the hour. Before it was above 9,000 each morning.

Tobias answered about pg_repack: the extension is available on the managed instance in the version we have. He wants to run it himself in a quiet period, since he knows the monitoring of the instance. I sent him the staging results and the command I used.

The table size is still 1.9 GB until the repack. I do not expect it to grow now. I will check again at the end of the week.

summary: Tobias ran pg_repack on account_settings, and the table shrank from 1.9 GB to 40 MB without a visible effect on the admin console.
body:
Tobias ran pg_repack on account_settings in the evening, when the admin console has little traffic. I watched the dashboards with him.

The repack took 52 seconds. During that time the lock was held only at the start and the end, for under a second each. The admin console reads showed no errors, and the p95 latency of the settings endpoint stayed at 12 ms. Replication lag peaked at 1.4 seconds and went back to under 200 ms.
