The table went from 1.9 GB to 40 MB, and its indexes from 210 MB to 6 MB. Because the settings are read on nearly every request, I also looked at the cache effect: the Postgres buffer hit rate for the table is now 100 percent, since it fits in memory easily.

Afterwards I checked the other tables for the same pattern. I listed all tables where the size on disk is more than 20 times the estimated live data. Two more came up: the sessions_archive table, which is mostly deleted rows after the purge job, and notification_state. The first is 600 MB for 40,000 live rows, the second is 90 MB for 800 rows.

Both are smaller problems. For sessions_archive the purge job deletes in a big batch and autovacuum then has a lot to do. I plan to change the purge to run in chunks of 5,000 rows, and I will write that as the next step. For notification_state I looked at the writes: a heartbeat updates the same rows every ten seconds. That is a design problem, and these values would better live in Redis with a short TTL. Lena wrote this code, so I asked her whether the console reads it anywhere except the notification badge.

She said it is read only by the badge and a debug page, so moving it is easy. We agreed to do that after the current work. I put it on the list with a note about the key name following the new naming rule: console:notif:v1:<account>.

The repack is documented in the runbook with the exact command and the checks, so the next one can be done by anyone on the team.

summary: Changed the sessions archive purge to delete in chunks, tested it against a copy of production data, and found that the chunked delete is slower but no longer builds up bloat.
body:
The purge job for sessions_archive deleted everything older than 90 days in one statement. On production that is about 30,000 rows each night, which creates a lot of dead tuples in a short time, and the table had grown to 600 MB.

I rewrote the job in jobs/purge_sessions.ts to delete in chunks of 5,000 rows, with a short pause of 200 ms between chunks. The ids come from a select with LIMIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so two runs cannot fight over the same rows.

I tested it on a staging copy restored from last night's backup. The old version took 3.1 seconds and left 31,000 dead tuples. The new version took 9.4 seconds with 6 chunks, and autovacuum cleaned up as it went, so the dead tuple count after the run was under 4,000. The slowdown does not matter for a night job.

One mistake along the way: my first version used OFFSET to move through the rows, and it skipped rows after each delete because the set changes. I found that when the test showed 11,000 rows left. The fix was to always select the first 5,000 matching rows again, which is correct, since the deleted rows no longer match.

I added a test with 12,500 rows that checks that all old rows are gone, the new rows are untouched, and the job returns the right count. It runs against a temporary schema in CI.

For the existing bloat I will ask Tobias to run pg_repack again on the table, since the procedure is now written down. The table is small enough for a quick job.

I also want to log the chunk count and the duration, so a change in the data volume shows up. I added a log line with both, and a Prometheus gauge for the rows deleted per run.

The change is deployed to staging, and the production deploy is planned for tomorrow, after Mara reviews it. The notification_state move to Redis is the next piece, and I will start it after the review.

summary: Moved the notification heartbeat state from Postgres to Redis with a short TTL, after Lena confirmed the badge and the debug page are the only readers.
body:
The notification_state table gets an update every ten seconds per open console, and that was creating dead tuples for 800 rows. Redis is a better place for this, since the values are short-lived.

The change has three parts. In the backend I replaced the UPDATE with SET console:notif:v1:<account> and EX 60. The badge endpoint reads the key, and if it is missing it returns the default state, which is what happens now for a new account. The debug page does the same.

Lena reviewed the console side and noticed that the badge treats a missing row as unknown and shows a gray dot. With the new TTL, a closed console would also show gray after a minute, which is the better behavior, since the old table kept the last state forever and showed a green dot for accounts that were gone. She called it a fix, not a regression.

The second part is the migration. I did not want to copy the old data, since it is stale by nature. The deploy only switches the code, and the table stays until we are sure. I added a note to drop it in two weeks.

The third part is tests. I wrote one for the key format, one for the TTL being set, and one that simulates Redis being down, where the badge returns the default and does not raise an error. This last one found a bug: the first version threw on a failed read and the endpoint returned 500. I wrapped the read in a try with a logged warning and the test passes now.

On staging I opened three consoles and watched the keys with a scan. They appeared with a TTL near 60 and refreshed every ten seconds. After closing them, the keys disappeared after a minute. Redis memory for these keys is a few kilobytes.

I deployed it to production in the afternoon. The write rate to Postgres dropped by about 8 updates per second, and the dead tuples of the table are no longer growing. The old table stays for now.

summary: Deployed the chunked sessions purge to production after Mara's review and checked the first run, which finished in 10 seconds with few dead tuples.
body:
Mara reviewed the purge change and only asked for the chunk size to come from a config value instead of a constant. I changed that, with 5,000 as the default, and she approved.

I deployed it in the afternoon and started the job by hand once to see the effect, since the nightly run is hours away. It deleted 28,400 rows in 6 chunks and took 10 seconds. The log line and the gauge worked.

After the run, the dead tuple count for sessions_archive was 2,900, and autovacuum cleaned it in a few minutes. Replication lag did not move.

I asked Tobias to schedule a pg_repack of the table. It will bring the 600 MB down to a few megabytes. I will check the nightly run tomorrow morning.

summary: Looked into why the search API p95 is high at the start of each hour and found a scheduled export job from one customer that sends many large queries at once.
body:
The latency graph for the search API shows a small spike at the beginning of every hour, with the p95 going from 180 ms to about 400 ms for two or three minutes. It is not large, but it shows every day, so I looked for the cause.

I took the request logs for the last two days and grouped them by API key and minute. At the start of each hour one key sends about 150 requests within 90 seconds. The key belongs to one of the larger customers, and the requests are almost all the same query shape with different time ranges, each one asking for up to 10,000 hits.

That explains the spike. The queries are heavy, the cache does not help since every range differs, and they use up the search thread pool on a few OpenSearch nodes at the same time. Other customers' queries wait in the queue during that time.

I checked the limits. The key has the normal rate limit per minute, which allows the burst, so the limiter does nothing here. The per-key limits we want to add on the rate-limits branch would be too coarse to help, since the number of requests is fine, but the cost of each is high.

There are a few options. We can ask the customer to spread the export over the hour, which is the cheapest. We can offer a proper export endpoint with scroll or search_after, which is the right answer for 10,000 hits per query. Or we can weigh the limiter by the cost of a query, which is a larger change.

I wrote the three options with a short estimate of work for each into the latency note. I think the first one should come now, and the second one later. The shard plan may also help, because a monthly index limits the data a time range query has to touch, so these queries should become cheaper after the migration.

I sent the customer's key id and the pattern to Sam, who is the contact for support, and asked her to talk to the customer about spreading the requests. I did not name any queries or data, only the timing and the volume.

Next I will check how much of the spike is from this key by excluding it from a day of data, and see whether anything else is left.

summary: Excluded the hourly export key from a day of latency data and found the spike almost disappears, so the export burst is the main cause.
body:
To test the finding from last night, I recomputed the search p95 per minute for the last day without the requests of the export key.

Without them, the hourly spike falls from 400 ms to about 195 ms, which is within the normal noise of 180 ms. So the export is responsible for nearly all of it.

I also looked at a second effect. In the minutes after the burst, the cache hit rate dips by about 3 points, because the export queries fill the cache with keys that are never used again. They have a TTL of an hour, so they use memory for no gain.

I asked Sam to tell me when she has talked to the customer. In the meantime I added a small change to the cache layer to skip caching for requests with a size above 5,000 hits, since those almost never repeat. I will deploy it after review.

summary: Wrote and tested the cache skip rule for very large search requests, and measured that the hit rate after the hourly burst now stays flat on staging.
body:
The export queries ask for up to 10,000 hits and do not repeat, so storing their results in Redis only costs memory and pushes out useful keys. I added a rule in the cache layer of the search API to skip both the read and the write when the requested size is above a threshold.

The threshold is a config value, set to 5,000 for now. I chose it from the request log: 99.2 percent of all requests ask for 100 hits or fewer, and the next group starts at 1,000. Only the export key goes above 5,000.

The change is in src/cache/policy.ts, a small function shouldCache(request) that returns false for large sizes and for requests with a flag that says no-cache, which the admin console already sends for the live view. I moved that second check into the same function, because it was done in two other places and one of them had a bug where the header was compared case sensitive.

I wrote tests for four cases: a normal request, a large request, the no-cache header in different cases, and a size exactly at the threshold, which is cached. All pass.

On staging I replayed an hour of production requests, including a recorded burst from the export key. Before the change, the hit rate went from 71 percent to 66 percent after the burst and needed about 25 minutes to recover. After the change it stayed at 71 percent through the whole replay.

Memory used by search keys was 90 MB lower at the end of the replay, which is the share the large responses took. On production I expect a similar drop, though the exact amount will depend on how much the customer sends.

One thing I checked is that the skip does not hide the load from our metrics. The request counter still counts these requests, and I added a label for cache skipped, so we can see how often it happens.

I opened the change for review. Mara will look at it tomorrow. The spike in latency itself is not solved by this, because the queries still hit OpenSearch. That depends on the customer talk and the shard layout.

summary: Sam talked to the export customer, who agreed to spread the requests over the hour, and I drafted the proposal for a proper export endpoint with search_after.
body:
Sam called the customer's technical contact. They did not know the bursts were hurting other users and agreed to spread their export jobs over the full hour with a small delay between requests. They plan to change their scheduler within the week.

Sam also asked if there is a better way for them to get all hits for a time range. This is a good question, because 150 queries of 10,000 hits each is the wrong tool. I drafted a short proposal for an export endpoint in the search API.

The idea is a request that takes the same filter as the normal search and returns pages of 1,000 hits with a cursor, built on search_after with a point in time on OpenSearch. This keeps the order stable even if new events arrive while the export runs, and the server keeps no state apart from the point in time, which expires after a few minutes.

There are some details to decide. The cursor must contain the point in time id and the last sort values, and it should be signed so a client cannot change the filter between pages. I suggest an HMAC with a key from the secrets store, which we already use for the pagination links of the admin console.

The rate limit for the endpoint should be per page, with a lower number than the normal search, for example 30 pages per minute per key. That gives a customer 30,000 hits per minute, which is more than the 150 queries gave at the peak, but it is spread evenly.

With monthly indices, the point in time would cover only the indices that match the time range. This is one more reason to keep the shard migration in the plan, because the cost of such an export would then be proportional to the range asked for.

I listed what needs to be done: the endpoint and cursor, the docs with an example for the public API page, tests with a few million documents on staging, and a note for Sam to give to customers. I estimated about four days of work.

I did not start it. I asked the user whether this should come before or after the migration steps, since both touch the search code. Until the answer comes, I will deploy the cache change once it is reviewed and watch the next hourly spikes to see whether the customer's change works.

summary: Mara approved the cache skip rule, and after the deploy the cache hit rate held at 70 percent through the hourly burst for the first time.
body:
Mara reviewed the cache policy change and asked for one more test, with a size given as a string in the query parameters, which the API turns into a number before the cache check. I added it and found the function received the number as expected, so no code change was needed.

I deployed it before lunch. For the next hourly burst I watched the cache panel. The hit rate stayed at 70 percent through the whole burst, where it dropped by 5 points the day before.

Redis memory for search keys was about 110 MB lower after two hours than the day before at the same time. The label for cache skipped shows 140 requests in the burst, which matches the export key.

The p95 spike still shows, as expected, at about 390 ms. The customer has not changed their scheduler yet. I will look again in a few days.

summary: Checked the second hourly burst after the customer changed their scheduler, and the search p95 spike is gone, so the export is spread out now.
body:
The customer deployed their new scheduler overnight. This morning I looked at the search latency for the last three hourly marks. The p95 stays between 178 and 190 ms at the start of the hour, with no spike.

The export key now sends about 3 requests per minute across the hour, with the same total volume. The cache skip rule still applies to them, and the cache hit rate is steady at 70 percent.

So the problem is solved for now. The export endpoint proposal stays open as a later improvement, and I wrote the result into the latency note for the record.

summary: Worked on the proposal for the export endpoint with search_after and listed the open questions before asking where it fits in the plan.
body: I reopened the proposal for the export endpoint with search_after in the search notes and read it through again after the customer changed their scheduler. The hourly spike is gone for now, so the endpoint is no longer urgent, but the customer will still need it if their volume grows. I wrote down the open questions: how to sign the cursor so a client cannot forge a position, and what page rate limit to apply per API key so one export cannot crowd out normal search traffic. I also sketched how the point in time would work. If the search index is later split by month, the point in time could cover only the months in the requested range, which keeps it small, so the endpoint will probably depend on that layout. I have not decided that yet. I wrote a short question for the user about whether the endpoint should come before or after the planned shard layout work, since both need the same few days of care. I left the task list as it is until the answer comes. I also checked that the cache skip rule is still holding the hit rate flat through the hourly window, and it is. Nothing else was needed from this session.

summary: Started the review of the ClickHouse materialized views for the dashboards and found two that nobody reads and one that doubles the insert work for a single customer.
body:
I began the quarterly look at the materialized views in ClickHouse, because the insert latency of the loader has crept up a little over the last weeks. I listed all views with their source tables and read the query log for a week to see which ones the dashboard queries actually hit.

Two views, daily_events_by_source_v1 and hourly_errors_old, had zero reads in seven days. Both were left over from the first rewrite of the dashboard queries. Their definitions still match the current schema, so nothing is broken, they just cost work on every insert.

The third finding was more interesting. A view called per_customer_top_fields keeps a map of field counts for every customer, but only one large customer has a dashboard panel that uses it. For that customer the map grows to a few thousand keys per hour, and the view takes the largest share of insert time on the events table.

I measured the insert time with and without the views on a copy of the table on staging, using a replay of one hour of the real stream. Without the two unused views the insert time per block dropped by about 9 percent. Without the third view it dropped by a further 18 percent.

I did not drop anything yet. I wrote the list into the task with the query log evidence and asked Lena whether the admin console still has any panel that reads the old views, since she knows the console code better than I do. She wants to grep the frontend and the saved dashboard definitions.

For the third view I think the better option is to keep it but cap the map to the top 200 fields, since the panel shows only the top 20. That needs a change to the panel query too, so it is a separate step. Next I will wait for Lena's answer, then detach the two unused views first, as detaching is easy to undo, and drop them after a week.

summary: Lena found no reader of the two old views in the console, so I detached them on production and insert time per block fell by about 8 percent.
body:
Lena replied after lunch that neither daily_events_by_source_v1 nor hourly_errors_old appears in the console code or in any saved dashboard definition. She also checked the docs examples, which only use the current views.

I detached both views from the insert path on production, which keeps the data and only stops new rows from flowing in. Before doing so I saved the create statements in the repo under the ops folder, so that recreating them takes one command.

I watched the insert time per block for the loader through the afternoon. It fell from about 310 ms to 285 ms on average, which is close to the 9 percent from the staging test. The merge backlog on the events table also got a little shorter.

Then I looked at the capped version of per_customer_top_fields. The new definition keeps the top 200 fields per customer and hour using a topK aggregate. I built it on staging next to the old one and compared the numbers for the large customer's panel. The top 20 fields were identical in all 24 hourly buckets I checked, and the counts differed by under 1 percent, which is the expected error of the approximate aggregate.

The panel query needs a small change to read the new state column. I wrote it and tested it against staging, but I did not deploy it. Lena wants to review the panel change because the console caches the query text.

Open items: the new capped view must be backfilled for the large customer before the old one is detached, and the backfill of one customer's history may take a few hours. I put that in the plan for tomorrow. The two detached views stay for a week and then get dropped.

summary: Backfilled the capped top-fields view for the large customer on production in about two hours, and its numbers match the old view for the last 30 days.
body:
I ran the backfill of the new per_customer_top_fields_v2 view for the large customer. I did it in daily chunks, with a pause between chunks, so that it would not compete with the loader for merges.

The backfill covered the full retention of 13 months. It took about two hours, and the loader insert time stayed within 5 percent of normal during that time. The CPU of the ClickHouse nodes peaked at 61 percent, which is fine.

After the backfill I compared the old and new views for the last 30 days. For each day I took the top 20 fields from both and compared the order. 29 of 30 days were identical. On one day two fields in places 19 and 20 were swapped, because their counts were nearly equal. That is within the error I expected.

I also checked the size on disk. The new view uses about 4 percent of the space of the old one, since it stores only 200 keys per hour instead of the full map.

The panel change is still waiting for Lena's review, so the console still reads the old view. I did not detach the old view yet.

Next steps are the review, the deploy of the panel query, a few days of watching, and then detaching and dropping the old view.

summary: Lena reviewed the panel query change and asked for a fallback to the old view, so I added a flag, deployed it, and the large customer's panel now reads the capped view.
body:
Lena went through the panel query change this afternoon. Her main worry was the cached query text in the console: if the cache has the old text, the panel would keep reading the old view for the cache lifetime. That is harmless for correctness, but it would make my measurements confusing.

She also asked for a way to switch back without a deploy. I added a setting in the console config, top_fields_source, with the values v1 and v2. The default is v2 for the large customer only, and v1 for everyone else, since the other customers do not have the panel enabled anyway.

I wrote two tests for the query builder. One checks that v1 produces the old query text byte for byte, the other that v2 produces the new one with the state column. Both pass in CI.

After the deploy I opened the panel for the large customer and compared it with a screenshot from yesterday. The top 20 list looked the same, with one swap in places 19 and 20 as seen in the backfill check. The query time of the panel went from 1.4 s to 0.3 s, which was a nice side effect, because the new view reads far fewer rows.

I also cleared the Redis keys for the panel cache with the versioned prefix, so that no stale text stayed around. The hit rate of the dashboard cache dipped for about ten minutes and then recovered.

I will watch the panel for three days. If no one reports anything, the old view gets detached, and a week later dropped together with the two views from earlier. Sam will tell the customer's contact that the panel got faster, in case they noticed a difference.

No open problems at the moment.

summary: Dropped nothing today, but checked the panel and the insert time after a full day on the capped view, and both look good.
body:
I looked at the large customer's top fields panel again this morning, after one full day on the capped view. No complaints from Sam or the customer's contact came in.

The panel query time stayed at about 0.3 s across the day, also during the evening peak. The loader insert time per block averaged 262 ms, down from 310 ms before the view work started.

I checked the console error log for the setting top_fields_source and found no errors or fallbacks to v1. The old view still receives inserts and is not read by anything now.

The plan stays as it was: two more days of watching, then detach the old view.

summary: Detached the old per_customer_top_fields view after three quiet days and noted that dropping the three detached views is set for next week.
body:
Three days have passed since the panel moved to the capped view, and there were no reports and no fallbacks to v1 in the logs. I detached per_customer_top_fields from the insert path on production.

The insert time per block fell once more, from 262 ms to 241 ms, which is the biggest single step of this whole cleanup. In total the loader is now about 22 percent faster per block than at the start of the review.

I saved the create statement of the old view next to the other two in the ops folder and added a short note on how to recreate and backfill it, including the chunked backfill script I used for the new one.

The three detached views still hold data on disk, about 140 GB together, mostly the old per customer map. I set a reminder in the task to drop them next week, after the week of waiting I promised. If something unexpected reads them, the error will show up in the query log as a missing table, and the recreate steps are ready.

I also wrote a short section in the ClickHouse notes: before adding a view, check what it costs per insert, and add a reader check to the quarterly review. Mara read it and added a line asking that every new view names its panel or query in the comment of its definition. I did that for the existing views as well.

summary: Looked into a spike of slow Postgres queries on the settings tables after the evening deploy and found a missing index on the new notification preferences lookup.
body:
The slow query log showed a group of queries at about 400 ms on the notification_preferences table, starting right after the evening deploy of the console. Before that deploy the same lookup did not exist, so the timing matched.

The query reads preferences by account and channel. The table has roughly 600,000 rows, and the planner used a sequential scan because the only index is on the primary key. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed 380 ms and 600,000 rows scanned for a result of one row.

I first thought it might be bloat like the account_settings case from last week, so I checked the vacuum statistics. The table is clean, with few dead tuples, so it was only the missing index.

I wrote a migration for a unique index on account_id and channel. The pair should be unique by design, but I checked for duplicates first and found 11 rows that violated it, all from a test account of Lena's that was created during the feature work. I asked her, and she said to delete them.

I deleted those rows and built the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on production. The build took about 40 seconds. Write latency and replication lag stayed normal while it ran.

After the build the same query ran in 0.2 ms. The slow query group disappeared from the log within the next hour.

I also added a check to the migration review list: any new lookup by a column pair needs an index, with an EXPLAIN on a copy with production-like row counts. Mara agreed to put it into the pull request template.

Nothing is left open on this one, apart from the template change by Mara.

summary: Dropped the three detached ClickHouse views after a clean week and freed about 140 GB, with no missing table errors in the query log.
body:
This was the planned cleanup at the end of the views review. I first searched the ClickHouse query log of the last seven days for the names of the three detached views and found no reads and no errors.

I also searched the repository, the Terraform files and the alert rules for the names, and found only the saved create statements in the ops folder and a mention in an old note of mine. No dashboards or scripts use them.

Then I dropped the views one by one, in the order of size, and checked the disk use after each step. The first was the old map view, which freed about 120 GB. The other two together freed about 20 GB.

The parts were removed in the background and the disk use of the nodes went down from 71 percent to 64 percent over about twenty minutes. Merges were not slower during that time.

After the drops I ran a last check of the dashboard queries for the three biggest customers, to be sure that none of them failed. All finished in their normal time.

I closed the task and wrote the summary into the notes: the loader is about 22 percent faster per block, the disk use is lower by 7 points, and the large customer's panel is faster by a factor of four.

The quarterly review stays as a recurring task, and I set the next one for three months from now. Tobias asked if the disk saving would let us delay the next storage increase, and I said probably by a couple of months, depending on growth.

summary: Started a draft of the plan for the schema registry compatibility checks and found that the current check treats a removed optional field as a breaking change.
body:
I opened the work on the compatibility checks of the schema registry today. The question from Mara was why a customer got a rejection when they removed an optional field from their event schema, since our docs say optional fields can be removed.

I read the checker code and found the cause. The rule for backward compatibility compares the field sets of the old and new schema and reports every field that is only in the old one as removed. It does not look at whether the field was required. So the docs and the code disagree, and the code is the stricter one.

I wrote four test cases that describe the behavior I think is right. Removing an optional field is allowed. Removing a required field is breaking. Changing an optional field to required is breaking. Changing a type from integer to string is breaking, but integer to number is allowed. Three of the four failed against the current checker, as expected.

Then I changed the checker to look at the required list of the old schema. The change is about 25 lines in the compare module. All four tests pass, and the older 38 tests of the registry still pass.

I am not sure about one case: removing an optional field that has a default value that the consumers might rely on. The docs do not say. I wrote it down as a question for Mara, since it affects how the workers read old events.

I also looked at the customer's actual rejection in the audit log. Their change removed two optional fields and added one, and with the new checker it would have been accepted. I will not tell Sam yet, because the fix is not merged, but I noted the case so that she can answer the customer after the release.

Next step is Mara's answer on the default value case, and then a pull request with the tests and the checker change.

summary: Mara answered the default value question for the schema registry: removal is allowed, but the registry must warn, so I added a warning level to the checker.
body:
Mara replied this morning on the open case. Removing an optional field that has a default is allowed, since the workers fill in the default when the field is missing in new events. Old events keep their stored value, so nothing breaks.

She did ask for a warning in the response, so that the customer sees that a default is dropped. I added a warnings list to the result of the compatibility check, separate from the errors, and the removal of a field with a default adds one entry.

The API response now has a warnings array, and it is empty in all other cases. I checked that the existing clients of the endpoint ignore unknown fields. The admin console shows only errors for now, and Lena said she will show warnings in a later change.

I added two tests for the warning and opened the pull request with all six new tests and the checker change.

summary: Reviewed the alert rules for the ClickHouse loader after the views cleanup and replaced a fixed insert time threshold with one based on a rolling baseline.
body:
The views cleanup lowered the insert time per block from about 310 ms to 241 ms, and I noticed that the alert for slow inserts still fires at 600 ms. With the new baseline that threshold is far too loose, because a real regression would have to more than double the time before anybody hears about it.

I looked at a month of data from Prometheus to see how the insert time behaves. During the nightly backfills and the rollup job the time rises to about 400 ms for short periods, and on normal days it stays below 320 ms. So a fixed threshold at, say, 350 ms would flap every night.

I wrote a rule based on the ratio of the current five minute average to the average of the same hour over the last seven days. The alert fires when the ratio is above 1.6 for fifteen minutes. This takes the nightly rise into account, because it is part of the baseline for that hour.

The alert rules live in code since the move last year, so the change is a pull request with the rule and a unit test file. The test feeds three series into promtool: a normal day, a day with the nightly peak, and a day with a regression of 70 percent. The rule stays quiet on the first two and fires on the third.

I also kept the old 600 ms rule as a second, critical alert, since it protects against a case where the baseline itself has drifted. Its severity stays the same.

Mara reviewed the pull request and asked me to add the runbook link to the new alert and to say in the description what to check first. I wrote that the first check is the merge backlog on the events table, then the loader logs, then the number of active views.

After the merge I looked at the rule on the Prometheus page, and it evaluates without errors. The ratio was at 0.97 at the time.

I will watch for false alarms for a week and note them in the task. If there are none, I will do the same for the query time alert of the dashboards, which also has a fixed threshold.

summary: Started search v2 with a new query parser in its own worktree: tokenizer and AST for field:value, quoted phrases and AND/OR/NOT are in, boosts come later.
body:
Created the search-v2 worktree and began the new query parser for the search API. The v1 parser was a chain of regexes that broke on nested quotes, so this one is a small tokenizer plus a recursive descent parser that builds an AST.

Supported so far: field:value, quoted phrases, AND/OR/NOT with parentheses, and a leading minus for exclusion. Unknown fields are kept as plain text instead of raising an error, which matches what v1 did for customers who paste log lines.

Wrote 38 unit tests in src/search/parser.test.ts, taken partly from real queries in the access log of the search API. Two of them fail: an unterminated quote and a trailing OR. I decided that both should be parsed leniently and left that for the next step.

The AST is not yet translated to OpenSearch queries. That translator comes next, and per-field boosts will hang off it. Nothing is deployed.

summary: Made the new parser lenient on unterminated quotes and trailing operators, and wrote the AST to OpenSearch translator; 41 of 41 parser tests pass and 12 translator snapshots exist.
body:
Continued in the search-v2 worktree. The two failing parser tests from the morning were fixed by treating an unterminated quote as running to the end of the input, and by dropping a trailing AND or OR with a warning flag on the result.

The translator in src/search/translate.ts turns the AST into a bool query. AND maps to must, OR to should with minimum_should_match 1, NOT to must_not. Phrases become match_phrase and bare words go to a multi_match over the default fields.

One decision: field:value on a keyword field uses a term query, but on a text field it uses match. I get the field types from the index mapping, which is cached in memory for 5 minutes. Without that cache every query did an extra call to OpenSearch.

I wrote 12 snapshot tests for the generated queries and checked them by hand against the expected JSON. One bug showed up: nested parentheses with NOT produced an empty must_not array, which OpenSearch rejects. The translator now omits empty clauses.

Open points: wildcards are not supported yet, and the boosts are still fixed numbers in the code. Tomorrow I will run the parser against a sample of a few thousand real queries and compare the hit counts with v1.

summary: Replayed 4,000 real customer queries through the v2 parser: 96 percent give the same hit count as v1, and the differences are mostly cases where v1 was wrong.
body:
Evening session to check the parser against reality. I took 4,000 queries from the search API log of last week, stripped customer identifiers and replayed them against a staging copy of the index with both v1 and v2.

Result: 3,842 queries returned the same count, 158 differed. I sorted the 158 by hand in batches.

- 71 had quoted phrases containing a colon, which v1 split into a field query. v2 is right here.
- 49 used lowercase and or not as words. v1 treated them as operators, v2 treats only uppercase as operators. This is a behaviour change that must go in the docs.
- 22 had a leading wildcard, which v2 does not support yet and which therefore returned fewer hits.
- 16 were real bugs on my side with escaped parentheses.

I fixed the escaping bug and added tests for it. The wildcard case needs a decision: leading wildcards are expensive in OpenSearch, so I lean towards allowing only trailing wildcards and telling customers.

I also timed the parsing itself. The median is 0.04 ms and the slowest query took 1.1 ms, so the parser is not a concern.

Next steps: ask Sam to note the lowercase operator change for the docs, and start on per-field boosts.

summary: Added configurable per-field boosts to search v2, stored per customer in Postgres and cached in Redis for ten minutes; the default is title 3, message 1.5, the rest 1.
body:
Worked in the search-v2 worktree on the boosts. Each customer can now set a weight per field, and the translator applies it as field^weight in the multi_match clause.

Storage: a new table search_field_boosts with customer_id, field and weight, and a check that the weight is between 0.1 and 10. The migration is small and ran on staging in under a second. The search API reads the rows through a Redis key of the form boosts:v2:<customer_id> with a TTL of 10 minutes, and the settings endpoint of the admin console deletes that key on write.

Defaults apply when a customer has no rows: title 3, message 1.5, everything else 1. I picked these from a look at which fields the large customers query most often.

A test with a fake Redis checks the invalidation path. I also found that a weight of 0 was accepted by the API layer even though the table rejects it, so the validation now lives in both places.

Lena will need an endpoint shape for the settings page. I wrote it up in the branch README: GET and PUT on /v2/settings/boosts with a map of field to weight.

summary: Looked into why the nightly reindex takes 3 hours 40 minutes and found that it re-reads every event from Postgres in pages of 500, which is the main cost.
body:
Read through the reindex job to see what dominates its runtime. A full run takes 3 hours 40 minutes at the moment, and customers are asking about freshness after big imports.

I added timing logs for one customer with 9 million events. Reading from Postgres in pages of 500 with OFFSET took 61 percent of the time, and the bulk calls to OpenSearch took 33 percent. OFFSET pagination gets slower the deeper it goes, which fits what we see.

The fix I propose is keyset pagination on (customer_id, id) with pages of 5,000. I tried it by hand on a copy and the read phase dropped from 2 hours 15 minutes to about 25 minutes for that customer.

The bulk size should also change, since 500 documents per bulk request is small. I will test 2,000 later and watch the rejections from OpenSearch.

I have not changed the job yet. The plan is to do the keyset change first, since it is the larger win and easy to review.

summary: Switched the reindex job to keyset pagination with 5,000-row pages; a full staging run now takes 1 hour 20 minutes instead of 3 hours 40 minutes, and counts match.
body:
Implemented the keyset pagination in the reindex job as planned this morning. The query now reads WHERE (customer_id, id) > ($1, $2) ORDER BY customer_id, id LIMIT 5000, and the job remembers the last pair per page.

A full run on staging took 1 hour 20 minutes, against 3 hours 40 minutes before. I compared document counts per customer between the old and the new index afterwards, and all 40 customers match. I also compared a random sample of 200 documents field by field with no differences.

While doing this I found a second problem. The job had no checkpoint, so a crash at hour three meant starting from zero. I added a small table reindex_progress with the last key per customer, and the job resumes from it. I tested that by killing the process halfway through, and it picked up at the right place.

The bulk size test: 2,000 documents per request worked, 5,000 gave a few 429 responses from OpenSearch. I kept 2,000.

One thing I did not like: the job still holds one Postgres connection for the whole run, which shows up as a long transaction. Setting the isolation to read committed and closing the cursor between pages fixed the long transaction warning.

Not done: the job still runs at the old time and has not been deployed to production. Tobias should check the ECS task memory, because the larger pages use about 300 MB more.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why a customer's search for error codes with dashes returns nothing: the standard analyzer splits on the dash, and the v2 parser needs a phrase for it.
body:
Sam asked in support why a customer searching for ERR-4012 got no hits although the event exists. I reproduced it on staging.

The standard analyzer splits ERR-4012 into the tokens err and 4012. In v1 the query was sent as a bare word, which matched on either token and gave noise. In the v2 parser a dash inside a word is read as one token, which is then analyzed into two tokens joined by AND, and the field holds the code under a keyword mapping, so nothing matches.

Workaround for the customer: put the code in quotes, or use the field search code:ERR-4012, which uses the keyword field.

A better fix is to have the translator add a should clause on the keyword subfield for any bare token that contains a dash or a dot. I wrote this as a task in the branch notes rather than doing it now.

I gave Sam a short text for the customer.

summary: Added the keyword-subfield fallback for bare tokens with dashes or dots to the v2 translator, which fixes codes like ERR-4012 and IP addresses without quotes.
body:
Did the fix noted this afternoon. In translate.ts, a bare token that contains a dash, dot or underscore now becomes a bool should with two parts: the normal multi_match and a term query on the .keyword subfield of the default fields.

The boost of the keyword match is double the boost of the text match, so an exact code ranks above partial token matches. I checked this on staging with the customer's data: ERR-4012 now returns the 214 events with that exact code first, then 3 loosely related ones.

IP addresses were also broken the same way, and 10.2.3.4 now works without quotes. Version strings like 2.14.1 do too.

Tests: 9 new snapshot tests, and the old 12 needed one change where a dotted word appeared. Total is 62 passing.

A side effect is that queries get a bit larger. For a query with five dashed tokens the JSON grows from 1.2 KB to 3.4 KB. I measured the latency on staging and saw no difference above noise.

I still want to check how this behaves with the per-field boosts of the customers, since a customer who sets message to 10 will multiply the keyword boost too. That is acceptable for now but I will keep it in mind.

summary: Rate limiter work started: read the current Redis counter code and decided to move from one limit per customer to per-API-key limits using a sliding window.
body:
Started the rate-limits branch with a read-through of the current limiter. Today it keeps one counter per customer, using INCR with an expiry of 60 seconds on a fixed window.

Problems with that: a customer with several API keys cannot isolate a noisy integration, and fixed windows allow double bursts at the window edge. Two customers asked for per-key limits.

Design decision: a sliding window counter with two buckets per key, the current and the previous minute, weighted by the elapsed fraction. It needs only two keys per API key and no sorted sets, which keeps Redis memory small. The key name will be rl:v2:<key_id>:<minute>.

A Lua script will do the check and increment in one call so there is no race between workers. I wrote a first version of the script and a test against a local Redis.

The limits themselves will live in Postgres next to the API key, with a default taken from the customer plan. The next step is the schema for that and the lookup cache.

summary: Added the api_key_limits table and a lookup with a 60-second cache; keys without a row fall back to the limit of the customer plan.
body:
Continued the rate-limits branch. The migration adds api_key_limits with key_id, requests_per_minute and burst, and a foreign key to api_keys with cascade on delete.

The lookup function first checks a small in-process cache with a 60-second TTL, then Postgres. I considered putting the limits in Redis as well but an in-process cache is enough, since a limit change taking a minute to apply is fine.

If there is no row, the limit of the plan is used: 600 per minute for the small plan, 3,000 for the large one. Those values come from the existing plan config and I did not change them.

Tests cover the fallback, the cache expiry using a fake clock, and a deleted key. All 14 pass. Next is wiring the Lua script into the Fastify hook and returning the right headers.

summary: Wired the sliding-window Lua script into the Fastify hook and added the RateLimit headers and a 429 body; load test shows 0.3 ms median overhead.
body:
The Fastify onRequest hook now resolves the API key, loads its limit and calls the Lua script through the shared Redis client. The script returns allowed, remaining and the seconds until reset.

Responses carry RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset. A rejected request gets 429 with a JSON body that names the key id and the limit, and a Retry-After header. The old per-customer limiter stays active in parallel behind a flag, so we can compare.

I load tested on staging with 200 concurrent clients at 5,000 requests per second for 5 minutes. The median overhead of the limiter was 0.3 ms and the 99th percentile 1.4 ms. Redis showed about 9,000 commands per second and no memory growth, because the keys expire after two minutes.

One bug: when the clock of a worker was slightly ahead, the previous-bucket weight became negative. I clamp the elapsed fraction to the range 0 to 1 now.

Open: what to do when Redis is unreachable. At the moment the hook fails open and logs a warning. I think that is right for an ingest-adjacent API but I will ask Tobias what he thinks.

summary: Decided with Tobias that the limiter fails open when Redis is down but only for 30 seconds of errors, after which it falls back to a local in-memory limit.
body:
Talked it through with Tobias in the morning and then implemented the result in the rate-limits branch. Failing open forever would let a Redis outage turn into an unlimited flood on the search API, and failing closed would take customers down for a cache problem.

The compromise: on a Redis error the hook allows the request and counts the error. If errors last longer than 30 seconds, the hook switches to a local token bucket per process, using one fifth of the configured limit since we run about five tasks. When Redis answers again the hook goes back to the shared script.

I wrote this as a small state machine in limiter-state.ts with three states: normal, open and local. The transitions are tested with a fake clock and a fake client that fails on command. There are 11 tests for it.

I also added two Prometheus metrics, limiter_redis_errors_total and limiter_state, and a Grafana panel on the API dashboard that shows the state over time.

The local bucket is approximate, and that is fine, since it only runs in an emergency. A real Redis outage test on staging, by blocking the port, showed the switch after 31 seconds and the return within 2 seconds of unblocking.

Still to do: the admin console page for setting limits per key, which needs Lena.

summary: Gave Lena the API shape for per-key limits and reviewed her console form; validation rules for burst and requests per minute are now shared in one schema.
body:
Met Lena about the admin console page for per-key limits. I proposed GET and PUT on /admin/keys/:id/limits with requests_per_minute and burst, and DELETE to go back to the plan default.

She built the form quickly. In review I found that the console validated burst against a different maximum (1,000) than the backend (5,000). To stop that from happening again, I moved the rules into a zod schema in the shared package that both sides import. Now the limits are: requests_per_minute from 1 to 100,000, burst from 1 to 5,000, and burst may not be larger than requests_per_minute times 2.

Other review notes: the form should show the effective limit, including the plan default, so a customer who has no override sees what applies. Lena added a small text that says default (plan) in that case. The delete button now asks for a confirmation.

I wrote the endpoints in src/admin/key-limits.ts and each change writes a line to the audit log with the old and new values and the user. The audit entry uses the existing helper, so no schema change was needed.

Backend tests: 8 new, all pass. Console tests are Lena's and passed on her side.

Next: roll out to staging with the old limiter still on, then compare counts of rejected requests between the two for a few days.

summary: Staging now runs both limiters side by side; the first hour shows the new one rejecting 0.4 percent of requests and the old one 0.9 percent.
body:
Enabled the per-key limiter on staging in shadow mode, so both limiters count and only the old one enforces. I added a log line when they disagree.

After an hour of the replayed traffic, the old limiter rejected 0.9 percent of requests and the new one 0.4 percent. The difference is as expected: the old fixed window punished bursts at the window edge. In 31 cases the new one would have rejected a request the old one allowed, and all of those came from one key with a very low override that I set in a test.

I will let it run through the night and check the numbers again.

summary: Overnight shadow data looks right, so the per-key limiter enforces on production for the two customers who asked; the old limiter stays behind the flag for a week.
body:
Evening check of the shadow run on staging: 11 hours, 2.1 million requests, no unexplained disagreements. The only cases where the limiters differed were the edge bursts, and the one test key.

I then deployed the branch to production with the new limiter in shadow mode for everybody, and enforcing for the two customers who asked for per-key limits. The flag is per customer in the settings table, so enabling it for others is one row.

Checks after deploy:
- limiter_state stayed at normal on all tasks.
- Redis command rate went up by about 6 percent, which is what I expected from the Lua calls.
- Median latency of the search API did not change.
- The p99 rose by 0.8 ms, within the load test result.

One of the two customers set 120 requests per minute on a key used by a cron job. The job sends 100 requests in a burst every minute, so burst is set to 150 to be safe, and I told them what the headers mean.

I wrote the customer-facing text for the docs on limits and headers and handed it to Sam. It includes the 429 body, Retry-After and a short example with curl.

Plan for the next week: look at the shadow disagreements each day, then switch everybody over and remove the old limiter code after two quiet weeks.

summary: Added wildcard support to the search v2 parser, trailing only, and a clear error message for leading wildcards instead of an empty result.
body:
Back in the search-v2 worktree to settle the wildcard question from the replay. Leading wildcards force OpenSearch to scan every term, which is a risk for the larger indexes, so v2 allows only trailing wildcards such as err*.

The parser now produces a prefix node for a word ending with an asterisk. The translator maps it to a prefix query on the keyword subfield and a wildcard on the text field, with a minimum of 2 characters before the asterisk. A query with a leading wildcard returns a 400 with the message that leading wildcards are not supported and a hint to use a trailing one.

The v1 behaviour was to accept leading wildcards, so this is a break for a few customers. In the replay, 22 of 4,000 queries used them. I will tell Sam so the support team can prepare an answer.

Tests added: 7 for prefix handling, 3 for the error. Everything passes, 69 in total.

I also checked the cost of a prefix query with 3 characters on the largest index: 38 ms median, which is fine.

summary: Looked at Redis memory after the boosts and limiter went live: used memory rose from 2.1 GB to 2.4 GB, mostly from the new boost and limiter keys.
body:
Checked the Redis dashboard because two new key families went into use this week. Used memory went from 2.1 GB to 2.4 GB.

Sampling with SCAN and MEMORY USAGE showed the split: the rl:v2 keys take about 140 MB, since there are two per active API key and they live for two minutes, and the boosts:v2 keys about 20 MB. The rest of the growth comes from the query cache, which grows with traffic anyway.

Nothing needs action, but the key naming is not uniform: older keys use colons and some use underscores. I wrote down the naming rule, family:version:id, in the repo docs and listed the three old families that break it. Renaming them would need a migration with a dual read, so I leave it for later.

I also noted the TTLs: the boosts at 10 minutes, the limiter at 2 minutes, and the query cache at 5 minutes.

summary: Moved the alert rules of the ingest API into code as the first step of alerts-as-code: 14 rules now live in a YAML file, rendered and checked in CI.
body:
Started moving the Prometheus alert rules out of the Grafana UI and into the repository. The first group is the ingest API, which has 14 rules.

I exported the existing rules, cleaned them up and wrote them to alerts/ingest.yaml. Each rule has a name, an expression, a for duration, a severity and a runbook link. A small script renders them into the Prometheus rule format, and CI runs promtool check rules on the output.

During the export I found that three rules had no runbook, and two had a threshold that nobody could explain. One of those was the queue lag alert at 10,000 messages, which pages at night. Looking at the last three months of data, the lag was above 10,000 eleven times for under a minute each. I changed the for duration from 0 to 5 minutes, which removes the false pages and still catches a real backlog.

Tobias will review the severity levels, because he is the one woken up. I kept every rule that existed, so the move is purely mechanical apart from the lag change.

Next: the same for the search API and the Redis alerts, then switch the deployment so Prometheus loads the rendered files and not the UI rules.

summary: Search API and Redis alert rules are in code too, 31 rules in total, and CI now fails when a rule has no runbook link or an unknown severity.
body:
Continued the alerts-as-code work with the search API (9 rules) and Redis (8 rules). The files are alerts/search.yaml and alerts/redis.yaml, in the same format as the ingest rules.

I added checks to the CI script: every rule needs a runbook URL, the severity must be page, ticket or info, and the for duration must not be zero for a page-level rule. The last one would have caught the queue lag rule from before.

Two of the Redis rules were duplicates, memory over 90 percent and memory over 90 percent for 5 minutes. I kept the second.

Runbooks: I wrote short ones for the five alerts that had none, with the first three things to check and the command to run. For the connection count alert it says to look at the pool size in the service config and the client list in Redis.

The total is 31 rules in code. Prometheus is still loading the UI versions, and the switch will happen when Tobias has read the severity levels. I do not want two sets active at the same time, so the switch has to be one change.

One annoyance: promtool does not check that the metric names exist. A typo in a metric name passes CI and then the rule never fires. I am thinking about a check against a list of metric names scraped from staging, but did not build it.

summary: Tobias approved the severity levels with two changes, and Prometheus now loads the 31 rules from the repository; the UI rules are disabled but not deleted yet.
body:
Tobias reviewed the alert files this morning. He changed two things: the Redis memory alert goes from page to ticket below 95 percent, and the search API error rate alert needs a 10 minute window instead of 5 because of the reindex noise.

After those edits I deployed the change. Prometheus now mounts the rendered rule files, and the old rules defined in the Grafana UI were disabled. I did not delete them, so there is a quick way back.

Verification: I listed the loaded rules through the Prometheus API and got 31, the same names as the files. To prove the pipeline fires, I lowered a test rule threshold on staging and saw the alert reach Alertmanager within a minute, and PagerDuty received it with the runbook link in the details.

One thing went wrong. The label for the team was missing in the rendered output of two rules, so those alerts routed to the default receiver. The renderer now fails when the team label is absent, and I fixed the two.

I plan to delete the UI rules after a week without surprises. After that the remaining groups, which are the ClickHouse and the queue alerts, can follow.

summary: Wrote the metric-name check for the alert files: CI compares every metric in the rules with a list scraped from staging, and found one typo in an existing rule.
body:
Built the check I was thinking about last time. A script scrapes the metric names from the staging Prometheus and writes them to a file, metrics-known.txt, which is committed. CI parses the expressions of the rules, takes out the metric names and fails when one is not in the list.

The parsing uses the PromQL parser library of Prometheus through a small Go program, since regexes would be fragile with functions and label matchers. It was only about 60 lines.

On the first run it found a real problem: the rule for the ingest consumer lag used redpanda_consumer_lag, while the actual metric is redpanda_kafka_consumer_group_lag. So that alert had never fired, since it was moved from the UI, and probably had not before either. I fixed the name and tested the rule on staging by pausing a consumer, and it fired after the for window.

The list must stay current. A weekly job refreshes it and opens a change if names appeared or disappeared, so removal of a metric is visible to a reviewer.

I told Tobias about the lag alert. It is worth thinking about whether we missed real backlogs in the past, but the logs for that are gone.

summary: Ran the first full reindex with the new keyset job on production overnight data: 1 hour 35 minutes, counts match, and OpenSearch showed no rejections.
body:
The reindex job with keyset pagination, checkpointing and bulk size 2,000 ran on production last night for the first time, so I read the results this morning.

Total time was 1 hour 35 minutes, against 3 hours 40 minutes before. It is slower than on staging because the production index is larger and other traffic competes. The read phase from Postgres took 28 minutes and the bulk phase most of the rest.

Checks: the document counts per customer match the live index for all 40 customers, and OpenSearch showed zero rejected bulk requests. The Postgres side showed no long transaction warning, and the replication lag stayed under 2 seconds.

ECS task memory peaked at 710 MB out of 1 GB. That is closer than I like, and I asked Tobias to raise the limit to 1.5 GB in Terraform before the next growth in data.

One small find: the checkpoint table kept rows for customers who had been deleted. The job now removes them at the end of a successful run.

The branch is ready for review. After it is merged, the job is a good base for the new shard layout later, because the keyset reading does not depend on the index layout.

summary: Merged the search-v2 parser, boosts and reindex changes after Mara's review; the v1 query path stays for one month behind a flag per customer.
body:
Mara reviewed the search-v2 branch this afternoon. She had comments on three things: the in-memory mapping cache needed a way to be cleared when a mapping changes, the 400 message for leading wildcards should name the offending token, and the boost migration should be reversible.

I fixed all three. The cache now has a clear function that the reindex job calls at the end, the error includes the token, and the migration has a down step that drops search_field_boosts.

After merge I deployed with a per-customer flag, search_engine_version, defaulting to v1. I switched it to v2 for our own test account and for one small customer who asked for the boosts. Customers move over in groups, and the flag can be set back at once if there are problems.

The v1 code stays for a month. Sam has the list of behaviour changes: lowercase operators, no leading wildcards, and the dash handling.

Next up: look at the latency of v2 for the largest customers before moving them.

summary: Removed the v1 query path flag for three small customers after a week of clean search v2 results, and logged what the remaining flags cover.
body:
Went through the per-customer flags that keep the v1 query path alive after the merge of search v2. Three small customers had no differences in hit counts in the shadow comparison, so their flag now points to v2 only. Eleven customers still run v1 for some queries.

For each remaining customer I checked the query log for syntax that v2 treats differently. The main cases are leading wildcards, which v2 rejects with an error message, and unbalanced parentheses. Two customers use leading wildcards in saved searches; both are in the list for Sam to contact.

Added a small script, scripts/v2_diff_report.ts, that replays the last 24 hours of queries of one customer through both paths and prints the hit count differences. It takes about 40 seconds per customer on staging. Output is a CSV with query text, v1 hits, v2 hits and the first differing document id.

Ran it for all 11 customers. Seven show zero differences, three show fewer than 0.5 percent, and one shows 3 percent. The 3 percent customer sends queries with a trailing backslash escape that v1 swallowed and v2 treats as a literal. That is a parser bug on our side, not a customer problem.

Opened a ticket for the backslash case and wrote a failing test for it in the parser tests. The fix is small: the tokenizer should consume a backslash before a quote or colon only. I did not touch it yet because Mara is reviewing the tokenizer for the highlight work.

The flags stay in place for now. The plan is to switch the seven clean customers tomorrow, then the rest once the backslash fix is in. The month limit set at the merge still applies, so there are about three weeks left.

summary: Fixed the backslash escape bug in the search v2 tokenizer; the customer with 3 percent hit count differences now matches v1 exactly.
body:
Picked up the ticket from three days ago. The tokenizer treated a backslash before any character as an escape, which dropped the backslash and joined tokens. The rule is now narrower: a backslash escapes only a quote, a colon, a backslash or a parenthesis. Everything else stays literal.

Added 9 test cases in the parser tests, including the failing one from the ticket. All 50 parser tests pass and the 12 translator snapshots did not change.

Replayed the day of queries of the affected customer through the diff script. Hit counts now match v1 on all but 2 of 6,300 queries. Both remaining ones are cases where v1 treated an unterminated quote as a phrase and v2 is lenient and drops it, which is the behaviour we chose earlier.

Switched the seven clean customers to v2 only. Watched the search API error rate and p95 latency for an hour: no change in errors, and p95 went from 180 ms to 170 ms, within noise.

Next step is the remaining four customers once Sam has talked to the two that use leading wildcards.

summary: Answered Sam on why a customer sees different result order after the v2 switch: per-field boosts changed the scoring, not the matching.
body:
Sam asked why a customer reported the same search returning the same hits but in a different order since the switch. I compared the explain output of one query on both paths.

On v1 all fields had the same weight. On v2 the default boosts are title 3 and message 1.5, so documents with the term in the title now sort above documents with it only in a long message. The hit count is the same, only the ranking differs.

This is intended, but the customer's events have a title field that is mostly a constant service name. For them a title boost makes no sense, since every event matches on it.

The boosts are stored per customer in Postgres, so I set title to 1 for that customer with the existing admin endpoint. The Redis cache for boosts has a ten-minute TTL, so the change was live after that time. I asked Sam to check with the customer that the order is what they expect.

I also wrote a short paragraph for the docs that explains the default boosts and how support can change them. Sam will fold it into the search guide.

summary: Switched the four last customers to search v2 after Sam confirmed the two leading wildcard users accept the error message.
body:
Sam talked to both customers who use leading wildcards in saved searches. One rewrote the searches to use the keyword field, the other said the new error message is clear and they will change them this week.

Switched the last four customers to v2 only. The flags are still in the code, but no customer needs v1 any more. I will remove the v1 path after the month of the flag runs out.

Watched the search API for an hour afterwards. Error rate stayed at 0.02 percent, p95 at 170 ms. OpenSearch showed no rejected requests.

One small find: the v1 path still builds its own cache keys with a prefix that nothing else uses. When v1 goes, those keys will expire on their own, so no cleanup job is needed.

Next is the removal of the v1 code in about two weeks, and the highlight work Mara has in review.

summary: Wrote the plan for the audit log retention report that Sam needs for a customer questionnaire, using a read-only Postgres query.
body:
Sam got a compliance questionnaire from a larger customer that asks how long audit log entries are kept and who can read them. I checked the audit log table instead of answering from memory.

The table keeps entries without a limit at the moment. There is no deletion job. The oldest row is from about 640 days ago and the table has 18 million rows, around 9 GB with indexes.

Access is through the admin console only, for users with the auditor role. Five accounts have it. I listed them for Sam without names in the notes, only the count.

Sam can answer that entries are kept indefinitely and are read-only from the console. I suggested we talk about a retention period before the next questionnaire, since an open-ended table will keep growing by about 400 MB per month.

No code changed in this session.

summary: Added an index on audit_log(customer_id, created_at) after the console audit page took 6 seconds for the biggest customer.
body:
While looking at the audit table for Sam, I opened the audit page in the console for our largest customer and it took about 6 seconds to load. The query filters by customer_id and sorts by created_at descending, and only had an index on created_at.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a scan of the created_at index with a filter that threw away most rows. For that customer it read about 2.1 million rows to return 50.

Created the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on staging first. It took 48 seconds and added 380 MB. The same page now loads in 40 ms in staging.

Ran the same on production in the quiet hour. It took 1 minute 50 seconds and no lock waits showed up in the Postgres logs. The page now takes 55 ms for the large customer.

Checked that the old created_at index is still used by the retention-style queries from the admin tools, so it stays. Wrote the migration file so that fresh environments get the index too.

The page for the smaller customers was fast before and is unchanged.

summary: Prepared the removal of the old per-customer rate limiter by checking per-key enforcement results and listing what the old flag still covers.
body:
The old per-customer limiter has stayed behind its flag since the per-key limiter went live for two customers. Since then the per-key limiter has been switched on for more customers in steps, and no support tickets about wrong 429s have come in. Today I went through the data before touching any code, because the flag removal should only happen when the numbers are clean.

I compared the 429 counts from the per-key limiter with the old counters for the customers that run both. For the customers on both paths the two agree within a few requests per hour, and the differences come from requests at the edge of a window. I also read the Fastify hook again and listed where the old flag is still checked: two places in the hook and one in the test setup.

The old counters use a key prefix of their own and a TTL of 60 seconds, so they should vanish on their own once nothing writes them. I wrote down a SCAN count on that prefix to run before and after the change, so I can confirm that none are left. I also noted the Redis used memory today as a baseline, so that any drop can be matched to the old keys later.

The rate limit tests currently pass, 38 of 38, with the flag in both positions. I sketched which tests exist only for the old path and could go away with it, about 30 lines of changes in the tests.

One open point: the Grafana panel for the old limiter will show no data after the cleanup. I will ask Tobias before the change, since he owns the dashboards folder. The plan is to enable the per-key limiter for the remaining customers first, wait a few more days, and only then remove the old code.

summary: Started the highlight feature for search v2 results: the translator now asks OpenSearch for highlights on boosted fields and the API returns snippets.
body:
Mara's review of the tokenizer came back with small comments, which I fixed first: one rename and one missing test for an empty phrase.

Then started highlights. The translator adds a highlight block for the fields title and message with fragment size 150 and two fragments. Tags are marked with a simple marker pair instead of HTML, so that the console can decide how to render them.

The search API response gets a new optional field, highlights, as a map from field to a list of snippets. It is only returned when the client passes include=highlights, so existing clients do not change.

On staging, a query with 100 results got 9 ms slower on average with highlights, which is fine. For very long messages of over 100 KB the highlighter is slow, so I set the highlight limit to 50,000 characters.

Snapshot tests for the translator were updated, 12 of 12 pass, and I added 3 API tests. Lena needs the response shape to render it, so I wrote the shape into the API doc draft.

Next: wait for Lena's rendering and test a phrase query with highlights.

summary: Lena rendered the search highlights in the console and found that phrase queries highlight each word separately; a one-line option fixed it.
body:
Lena built the snippet rendering in the console from the shape in the doc and sent a screenshot where a phrase like "connection reset" had both words marked separately across the snippet, not as one phrase.

The cause was the default highlighter settings, which mark terms and not phrase matches. Setting phrase matching on for the highlight block in the translator fixed it.

Checked three other query types: field:value, wildcards and AND/OR. All of them highlight correctly. Updated one snapshot.

Lena's rendering is merged on her side behind a console flag for now.

summary: Redis memory check after the highlight and limiter changes: 2.4 GB used, with the boost keys and a forgotten session key family as the largest groups.
body:
Did a routine look at Redis memory since it has been creeping up. Used memory is 2.4 GB of 4 GB, about the same as after the boosts went live, so the rate limiter cleanup balanced the growth.

To find the biggest groups I sampled keys with SCAN and the MEMORY USAGE command, on a replica to avoid load on the primary. Sample size was 50,000 keys.

The breakdown by prefix: session store 41 percent, query cache 33 percent, limiter 9 percent, boosts 6 percent and the rest in small groups.

One group stood out: keys named tmp:export:* with no TTL. About 12,000 of them, 90 MB in total. They come from a CSV export helper in the console that wrote its progress and forgot to set an expiry.

The helper is in the admin console code. I added an expiry of one hour to the write and wrote a one-off script to delete the old keys. I ran it on the replica sample first to check the pattern, and then on the primary in batches of 500 with a short sleep.

After the run, 12,140 keys were deleted and used memory fell by 92 MB.

I also renamed nothing else; the key naming is inconsistent between teams, with some using colons and some dots, and I wrote a short note in the repository docs with the rule that new keys use colons and need a TTL unless there is a written reason.

No change in latency was visible. Next check is in a month.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's Terraform change for the OpenSearch data nodes and asked for a snapshot repository setting to stay explicit.
body:
Tobias opened a Terraform pull request that changes the OpenSearch data node instance type for more memory. I reviewed it as the user of the cluster.

The plan output showed a rolling replacement of the three data nodes. That is fine in the quiet hours, but the nightly reindex job runs during that period, so I asked him to schedule the change after the reindex ends.

The diff also dropped the explicit snapshot repository setting, which the module now takes from a default. I asked to keep it explicit, because a different default would silently change where the backups go.

He agreed to both. I approved with those two changes.

It is worth remembering that the search v2 boosts do not depend on the node type, so there is no application change needed.

Nothing was applied in this session.

summary: Designed the schema registry check for the ingest API: events are validated against versioned JSON schemas fetched from a registry service with a local cache.
body:
Started the design for the schema registry on its branch. The aim is that every event type has a versioned schema, and the ingest API can reject or tag events that do not match, instead of the checks being spread over customer-specific code.

Today's state: the event schema is one big JSON schema file in the ingest worker repository. Changes need a deploy of the worker, and customers cannot see which version they send against.

The design has three parts. A registry table in Postgres with event type, version, schema body and status (draft, active, deprecated). A small read API in the Fastify service. A cache in the ingest worker that loads active schemas at start and refreshes every minute.

I decided on compatibility rules: a new version may add optional fields, but may not remove fields or change types. The registry checks this on publish by comparing the old and new schema.

For validation mode I proposed three per event type: off, warn and enforce. In warn mode the event is accepted and a counter goes up, in enforce mode it is rejected with a 422 and a message that names the path of the failing field.

Tobias raised a question about the cost of validation in the hot path. I measured a quick prototype with a Go JSON schema library on 100,000 sample events from staging: 11 microseconds per event on average for the current schema, which is acceptable next to the network cost.

Open questions: how customers learn about their schema errors, and whether the registry should have a console page. I put both on the list for Lena and Sam.

Wrote the design as a markdown file in the branch and created the migration for the registry table, not yet applied. Next step is the compatibility checker.

summary: Wrote the schema compatibility checker for the registry with 24 test cases; it rejects removed fields, type changes and new required fields.
body:
Today's work on the registry branch was the compatibility checker that runs when a new schema version is published.

The checker walks the old and new schema and reports a list of problems. It is written in TypeScript since the registry API lives in the Fastify service. The rules: a removed property is a breaking change, a changed type is breaking, a property newly added to required is breaking, and a narrowed enum is breaking. Widening an enum, adding optional properties and loosening a string length are allowed.

The first version handled only top-level properties. Real event schemas have nested objects and arrays of objects, so I made the walk recursive and gave each problem a JSON pointer path like /properties/user/properties/id.

One case took thought: a type that changes from integer to number. It looks like a widening but the Go validator in the ingest worker reads integers into int64 fields in some consumers. I decided to treat it as breaking for now and write down why in the test name.

Wrote 24 test cases from examples taken from the real schema history of the repository, including the three times the schema changed in the past, which the checker now classifies correctly as two compatible and one breaking.

The publish endpoint calls the checker and returns 409 with the list of problems if the change is breaking. An override flag exists for admins, with a reason stored in the audit log.

All tests pass. The migration was applied on staging, and I published the current production schema as version 1 for the first event type to try the flow.

Next: the Go side, with the cache and the three modes.

summary: Built the schema cache in the Go ingest worker with warn and enforce modes; staging shows a clean warn run on live-like traffic.
body:
The ingest worker now has a schema cache package. At start it fetches all active schemas from the registry API, compiles them and keeps them in memory. A goroutine refreshes every 60 seconds with an If-None-Match header, so unchanged schemas cost almost nothing.
