If the registry is not reachable at start, the worker falls back to the schema file that is still in the repository, and logs a warning. If a refresh fails later, it keeps the schemas it has. I wanted that so that a registry outage cannot stop ingest.

The validation hook sits after parsing and before the batch goes to the queue. The mode comes from the registry per event type. In warn mode it increments a Prometheus counter, schema_validation_failures_total, labelled by event type and mode, and does not touch the event.

In enforce mode the whole batch item is rejected and the response lists the index of the event and the path of the failure. A batch with some bad events still accepts the good ones, which matches the existing partial success behaviour.

Benchmarked with the staging replay: 40,000 events per second on one worker with validation, against 43,000 without. That is a 7 percent drop, more than the prototype suggested because of allocation. I cached the compiled schema per event type and avoided a second parse, which brought it to 42,000.

Ran warn mode on staging for an hour with replayed production-like traffic. The counter stayed at zero for five event types, and showed 0.8 percent failures for one type. That type has an old field format that the schema does not describe.

I will look at that type tomorrow and decide if the schema or the data is wrong.

summary: Traced the 0.8 percent warn failures of one event type to a timestamp field sent both as number and as string; the schema now allows both.
body:
The event type with failures in warn mode on staging had one field, occurred_at, that the schema declared as a string in ISO format.

I pulled 200 failing events from the replay log. About 70 percent of the failures had the timestamp as a number in epoch milliseconds, the rest had an empty string. The numbers come from an older SDK version that customers still run.

The ingest worker already normalizes the number format downstream, so the data is handled correctly. The schema was wrong, not the data.

Published version 2 of the schema for that type with occurred_at as either a string with date-time format or an integer. The compatibility checker accepted it as a widening.

The empty string is a different matter. Normalizing code treats it as missing and uses the receive time. I left it as a failure in the schema, because it is probably a bug in the SDK, and told Sam so that support can tell the customers.

After the new version loaded, the failure rate in warn mode went from 0.8 percent to 0.05 percent on staging.

Still to do is a way for customers to see their warn counts.

summary: Production warn mode for the schema registry is on for all event types; first hour shows 0.03 percent failures and no latency change.
body:
Deployed the registry API and the worker change to production with every event type in warn mode. The registry holds version 1 of all schemas, plus version 2 for the timestamp case.

Before the deploy I checked that the fallback works: I stopped the registry service in staging and restarted a worker. It started with the file schemas and logged the warning, as intended. I then started the registry again and the worker picked up the schemas within a minute.

The rollout was a rolling update of the ECS service. During the deploy, one task failed its health check because the registry fetch took 4 seconds on the first call and the check timeout is 3. I made the initial fetch part of the start before the health endpoint opens, and the next deploy passed.

In the first hour of production, 0.03 percent of events failed validation in warn mode. By event type, almost all came from two customers with the empty string timestamps. The ingest latency p95 did not change, 62 ms before and after.

I added a Grafana panel for the failure counter by event type and customer. The customer label is a hash of the id so that the metric cardinality stays small, about 40 values.

Plan for enforce: wait a week in warn, tell the two customers, then switch types with zero failures to enforce first.

One thing I did not do: a console page for schemas. That waits for Lena.

summary: Answered Sam's question on whether enforce mode would reject a whole batch: it rejects only the bad events and the response lists them.
body:
Sam asked, for a customer call, what happens to a batch of 500 events if one fails the schema in enforce mode.

I tested it on staging with a batch of 5 events where the third had a wrong type. The response was 207-style partial success in our format: accepted 4, rejected 1, with an errors array that has the index 2 and the path /properties/amount with the message expected number, got string.

The four good events went into the queue as usual. Nothing is retried by the server; the client should resend only the rejected ones after fixing them.

I gave Sam the example response to paste into the docs. Enforce is not on for anyone yet, so this is for the later rollout.

summary: Profiled the search API p95 after the v2 switch and found the boost lookup hitting Postgres on every cache miss in a thundering pattern.
body:
The search API p95 had a weekly bump at the time the ten-minute boost cache keys expire together after a restart. I looked at it because the metrics showed short peaks of 400 ms against the normal 170 ms.

The boosts of a customer are cached in Redis with a ten-minute TTL. After a deploy, all customers' keys are created within the same minutes and so they expire together, and then many concurrent requests miss at once. Each one queries Postgres for the same row.

I confirmed it with the Postgres statistics: the boosts query showed 900 calls in one second at the peak, for 40 customers.

Two fixes. First, a random jitter of plus or minus 20 percent on the TTL, so keys no longer expire together. Second, an in-process single-flight so that concurrent misses in one API instance share a single Postgres query.

Implemented both in the boost lookup module. The single-flight is a small map of promises keyed by customer id, removed when the promise settles.

Tested with a load script that expires 40 keys and sends 200 concurrent requests. Before: 612 Postgres calls. After: 40, one per customer, per instance, and with 3 instances at most 120.

Unit tests cover that a failing lookup does not stay in the map and that the jitter stays in range. 14 tests pass in this module.

Deployed to staging in the afternoon. The peak in the p95 did not show again after a forced restart. I will watch production after the next deploy, and then close the ticket.

summary: Wrote the first version of the audit export design for compliance: scheduled NDJSON files to a customer S3 bucket, signed, with a manifest.
body:
Started planning the audit export that came out of the compliance questionnaire. A customer wants their audit log delivered to their own storage on a schedule, so they can keep it in their own systems.

The requirements I gathered from Sam: daily delivery, a file format that is easy to load into other tools, proof that files were not changed, and no access for us to anything else in their bucket.

Decisions so far. The format is NDJSON, one audit entry per line, gzip compressed, with one file per day and customer. Each day's file comes with a manifest that lists the file name, the row count, the first and last entry id and a SHA-256 of the file. The manifest is signed with an HMAC key per customer, stored in the secrets manager.

Delivery goes by an IAM role in the customer's account that we assume, limited to PutObject on one prefix. The customer creates the role from a template we give them. We never get read access.

The job reads from Postgres. With the new index on customer_id and created_at, the daily slice for the largest customer is a range scan, and I measured it at 1.3 seconds for about 40,000 rows on staging.

There is a subtle issue: entries can be written late, with a created_at before the end of the day, after the job has run. To avoid gaps I decided to export by entry id range instead of by time, and keep the last exported id per customer in a table.

Failure handling: if the upload fails, the job keeps the last id and tries again at the next run. Files are named by id range, so an upload repeated after a partial failure overwrites the same object.

I made the branch audit-export from main and wrote the design document plus the table migration for export_state, with customer id, last id, last success time and last error.

Next step is the job itself, with a dry run mode that writes to a local directory.

summary: Implemented the audit export job with a local dry run: 40,000 rows export in 2 seconds, manifest and HMAC verify, and a resume after a forced failure works.
body:
Built the export job on the audit-export branch. It is a Node script run by the existing scheduler, one customer at a time, and it takes a sink: a local directory for dry run or the S3 sink.

The job reads the export_state row, selects entries with id greater than last_id in order, in pages of 10,000 with keyset pagination, and streams them through gzip into the sink. Memory stays flat at about 80 MB because nothing is held in full.

File names follow the id range, such as audit-000123400-000127399.ndjson.gz. The manifest is a small JSON with the same range, row count and SHA-256, and a signature field with an HMAC over the other fields.

Wrote a verify command that takes a file and manifest and checks the hash, the count and the signature. I use it in the tests, and customers could use it too, so I documented the algorithm in the design file.

Tests: 18 pass. They cover an empty range which produces no file, a range crossing the page size, and a failure in the sink halfway, after which last_id must not change and the next run must produce the same file name.

In the failure test I used a sink that throws after 5,000 rows. The state stayed the same, and the second run, with a normal sink, wrote the full file. This is the property I was after.

On staging data for the largest customer, a run of 40,000 rows took 2.1 seconds and the file is 1.4 MB.

One issue found during the run: the audit table has rows with a null actor for system actions, and my NDJSON writer dropped null fields. Customers would see inconsistent shapes, so I now write explicit nulls.

The S3 sink is a stub. The next step is the role assumption and a test in a sandbox bucket that Tobias will set up.

summary: Tobias set up a sandbox account and bucket, and the S3 sink of the audit export now uploads with an assumed role and per-object checksums.
body:
Tobias made a sandbox bucket in a separate account with the role template we plan to give customers. It allows only PutObject under one prefix and requires the checksum header.

I wrote the S3 sink on the audit-export branch. It assumes the role with STS using the customer's role ARN and an external id, so that the role cannot be used by other parties, and uploads with the SHA-256 checksum sent as a header. S3 verifies the checksum and rejects mismatches.

The first upload failed with AccessDenied. The template required the external id as a condition and my call used the session name only. Passing the external id in the assume role call fixed it.

The manifest is uploaded after the data file, so the presence of a manifest means that the data file is complete. That order matters for customers who watch for manifests to trigger loading.

Ran a full export of the sandbox customer, four daily files. All verified with the verify command from the bucket contents. I also tested a role with a wrong external id and the job recorded the error in export_state and exited cleanly.

I want a metric for the age of the last successful export per customer, so an alert can fire when it is older than 36 hours. I will add that with the alert rules in code, which keeps the runbook link rule in CI happy.

summary: Added the export age metric and an alert rule in code for the audit export, with a runbook page, and CI accepts it.
body:
Added the metric audit_export_last_success_age_seconds to the export job, written through the pushgateway at the end of every run, per customer hash. Customers that have never exported are not reported.

Wrote the alert rule in the alerts YAML: it fires at warning severity when the age is over 36 hours for 15 minutes, and at critical when it is over 72 hours. The expression has a clause so that customers who paused their export do not alert; there is a paused flag in export_state which the job also reports.

CI first failed on the new rule because the metric was not in the staging scrape list. I ran the job on staging once so the pushgateway had it, regenerated the list and the metric check passed.

The runbook link rule also applies. I wrote a short page in the runbook folder: what the alert means, how to see the last error in export_state, the three usual causes (role removed by the customer, external id mismatch, bucket policy changed) and how to rerun for one customer.

Reviewed with Tobias, who asked that the critical alert page only during working hours since the customer can fix nothing at night on our side. I set the critical to route to the working-hours channel, not to PagerDuty.

Tests of the rule are in the rule unit test file: one for firing, one for the paused clause. Both pass.

Still open: a console form for customers to enter their role ARN, which belongs to Lena, and the docs for the role template, which belong to Sam.

summary: Gave Lena the API for audit export settings and reviewed her console form; the role ARN is validated by format and by a test upload.
body:
Lena started the console form for audit export. I gave her the API shape: a GET and PUT for the export settings of a customer with the role ARN, the external id, the bucket prefix, the paused flag and the last status.

The external id is created by us and shown read-only, so the customer can put it into the role trust policy. I did not let customers choose it.

Validation: the ARN must match the role ARN pattern and the account id in it must not be one of our own accounts. On save, the API can run a test upload of a small marker object, and returns the result in the response. If the test fails, the settings are saved as paused with the error, so nothing breaks the nightly job.

In the review of her form I asked for two things: show the last error text from export_state, and disable the save button while the test upload runs, since it takes up to 5 seconds. She did both in the same hour.

The API tests are 11 and pass, with STS and S3 mocked. A sandbox run with Tobias's bucket also passed, with the marker file visible in the bucket.

Next is Sam's docs for the role template, then a pilot with one customer who asked for it.

summary: Ran the audit export against the sandbox bucket for a full day of rows and fixed a manifest bug where the last file's row count was off by one
body:
Ran the audit export end to end against Tobias's sandbox bucket with a copy of the largest customer's audit rows. The job produced 9 files and a manifest, and the verify command rejected the manifest because the last file reported one row too many.

The cause was the resume logic. After a restart it counted the boundary row of the previous file again when it wrote the manifest entry. The row itself was exported once, only the count was wrong. I changed the counter to take the number from the written file instead of the running total.

Added a test that kills the job right at a file boundary and resumes, then compares the manifest counts with the NDJSON line counts. It passes now. The HMAC check passed before and after the fix.

The full run took 41 seconds for 610,000 rows, and memory stayed under 120 MB because rows are streamed from a Postgres cursor. Still open: a schedule per customer and a clear error when the assumed role is revoked. Those come next, probably tomorrow.

summary: Added per-customer schedules to the audit export and a clear failed state when the customer's role can no longer be assumed
body:
Built the scheduler part of the audit export. Each customer has a setting for daily or weekly export, and a small loop picks up the customers that are due and starts one job per customer, at most three in parallel.

The first version stored the next run time in the settings row. That broke when two scheduler instances ran together in staging, because both took the same customer. I switched to a claim with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a jobs table, and the double runs went away in a test with four instances.

For revoked roles, the STS call returns AccessDenied. The job used to retry this five times and then log an error nobody read. Now it is treated as a permanent failure: the job state becomes failed_auth, no retries, and the export age metric keeps growing, so the alert from yesterday fires after the threshold.

Transient errors such as timeouts and 503 from S3 still retry with backoff, up to 6 attempts. I wrote tests for both paths with a fake S3 server. Lena needs one new field from the API, last_error_kind, to show the state in the console. I added it and told her. Next step is a review by Mara.

summary: Mara reviewed the audit export and found that the signing key was read from the environment on every file; it is loaded once now and rotation is documented
body:
Mara went through the audit export branch this morning. Her main point was the signing key: the HMAC key was read from the environment for every file, and a rotation would have mixed keys inside one export without a trace.

I changed the job to load the key once at start and write a key id into the manifest. The verify command now looks up the key by id, so old exports stay verifiable after a rotation. I added a test with two keys.

Her second point was that the NDJSON rows contain the internal user id and the customer wants the email. We decided to keep the id and add a lookup file in the export, because the audit log should not change after the fact. Sam will mention this in the docs.

Smaller items: a constant for the file size limit instead of a literal, and a log line without the bucket name in the error path. Both done. Mara approved with these changes. Remaining before merge: the docs page and a trial with the first real customer from Sam's list.

summary: Answered Sam on how long audit exports stay in the customer bucket: nebula never deletes them, the customer's own lifecycle rules decide
body:
Sam asked for the questionnaire what happens to the exported files. The export only writes objects. It has no delete permission in the role policy we give customers, and I confirmed this in the policy template in the repository.

So the retention of exported files is the customer's choice, for example an S3 lifecycle rule on their bucket. The audit log in Postgres itself keeps rows as before.

I wrote two sentences for Sam's answer and added the role policy example to the docs draft so he can quote it. He will ask the customer whether they want a prefix per month.

summary: Wrote the audit export docs page and ran a real trial for the first customer; it exported 1.2 million rows in 3 minutes, and a prefix naming issue came up
body:
Spent the first part of the afternoon on the docs page for the audit export. It covers the settings, the role policy, the file layout, the manifest and the verify command with an example.

Then Sam and I ran the trial with the first customer, who has a bucket in their own AWS account. Their admin created the role from our template. The test upload in the console form passed on the first try.

I started a manual export of the full audit history. It produced 1.2 million rows in 3 minutes 10 seconds, split into 24 files of about 50 MB. The manifest verified with the command from the docs.

The customer's admin noticed that all files land under one prefix with the export date, and their tooling wants one prefix per month of the rows. That is a reasonable wish. I added an optional prefix template with {year} and {month} placeholders in the settings.

The first draft of the template code used the export time, not the row time. That would have put old rows into the current month. I fixed it to use the created_at of the first row in each file, and files now split at month borders.

The split made some files small, with 3,000 rows. That is acceptable. A test covers a month border inside a batch.

I updated the docs with the placeholders. Lena will add the field to the form tomorrow. After that the branch can merge. I also noted in the branch description that the weekly schedule is untested with real data, because no customer has chosen it yet.

summary: Merged the audit export branch after a last CI run, and the daily schedule is on for the first customer
body:
Rebased the audit export branch on main, ran CI, and merged it. Mara had approved it earlier, and the month prefix change was small enough that she only looked at the diff.

Lena's form field for the prefix template went in this morning, so the console shows it. I enabled the daily schedule for the first customer in production.

The first scheduled run is tonight. I added a line in the on-call notes that the alert for export age fires after 30 hours, and that the runbook says to check the role first.

I will look at the result tomorrow.

summary: The first scheduled audit export ran fine, then I looked at Redis memory after the session store cleanup and found the boost keys still the largest group
body:
The first scheduled audit export ran at 02:00 and wrote 3 files with 41,000 rows. The manifest verifies, and the customer's admin confirmed that the files appeared under the month prefix.

The afternoon went to Redis. A week ago we removed the forgotten session key family, so I checked memory again. Used memory is 2.2 GB, down from 2.4 GB. The biggest group is now the boost lookup cache with about 0.6 GB, then the query cache.

I looked at the key naming. The boost keys are named boost:{customer}:{field}:{hash}, and the hash part makes many keys that are used once. A sample of 10,000 keys showed that 38 percent were read only one time before their TTL ran out.

The TTL of the boost keys is 24 hours. A shorter TTL would save memory, but the thundering pattern from the profile last week showed that the boost lookup hits Postgres on a miss. A shorter TTL would make that worse.

So I decided not to touch the TTL yet. A better fix is to cache the boosts per customer and field without the query hash, because the boost values do not depend on the query. That would cut the number of keys a lot.

I wrote this down as a ticket with the numbers. The change needs a small piece of code in the search API and a one-time cleanup of the old key pattern, which expires on its own after 24 hours.

I also checked connection counts. Peak is 31 connections from the search API and 12 from the admin console. That leaves room.

Next: implement the per-field boost cache and measure the memory and the Postgres query rate before and after. I will also ask Tobias whether the Grafana panel for key counts per prefix can be added.

summary: Changed the boost cache to key by customer and field only, which cut boost keys from about 410,000 to 2,600 in staging
body:
Implemented the boost cache change in the search API. The key is now boost:{customer}:{field}, and it stores the full boost table for that field. The query hash is gone from the key.

In staging with a replay of a day of production queries, the number of boost keys dropped from about 410,000 to 2,600. Memory for the group went from 0.6 GB equivalent to a few MB.

I also added a lock per key on a miss, so that only one request loads from Postgres and the others wait up to 200 ms. This addresses the thundering pattern. The Postgres query rate for boosts in the replay fell from 90 per second at the worst moment to 4.

One test failed because it expected the old key name. I updated it. The next step is a production rollout behind a flag, then the cleanup of old keys by their TTL.

summary: Rolled out the new boost cache to production for half the traffic and saw search p95 drop from 310 ms to 270 ms
body:
Turned the flag on for half of the search API traffic at 13:30. For the first hour I watched the p95, the Postgres query rate and the Redis key count.

The p95 of the search API went from 310 ms to 270 ms on the flagged half. The boost query rate on Postgres fell as in staging. There were no errors in the logs.

Redis key count grew a little at first and then fell, as the old boost keys began to expire. I expect the full effect tomorrow, when the 24 hour TTL has passed.

One surprise: a customer who changed their boosts in the console still saw the old values for a short time. The save path did not delete the new key. I added the delete of boost:{customer}:{field} to the save handler and deployed it. A test covers it.

I will move to 100 percent tomorrow if the numbers hold.

summary: Moved the new boost cache to all traffic; Redis used memory is 1.7 GB and the boost group is gone from the top five
body:
The half rollout held overnight, so I set the flag to all traffic this morning. Redis used memory is now 1.7 GB, down from 2.2 GB two days ago.

The boost group is no longer among the five largest. The query cache is the largest now at about 0.5 GB.

Search p95 is 268 ms over the last three hours. The Postgres boost query rate stays under 5 per second.

I removed the flag from the code and deleted the old key pattern from the code paths. I also updated the key naming page in the repository docs. Next I want to look at the hit rate of the query cache.

summary: Measured the query cache hit rate by customer and found that two customers with unique timestamps in queries make up most of the misses
body:
Looked at the query cache hit rate. The overall hit rate is 54 percent, which is lower than I expected.

I added a counter per customer to the search API for hits and misses, deployed it, and waited a few hours. The data shows two customers with hit rates under 10 percent. Together they send about 45 percent of all queries.

A sample of their queries showed the reason. Their dashboards put the current time in a range filter, down to the second, so every query is new and the cache key never repeats. Other customers round the range to the hour or the minute.

Options I considered:
- Round time ranges in the cache key to a minute on the server side.
- Ask the two customers to round in their clients.
- Leave it.

Rounding in the key is cheap, but it can return a result that is up to a minute old, which changes the semantics. For a dashboard that is fine, for an exact search it is not. I would limit it to ranges whose end is within the last minute of now.

I wrote the proposal and the sample queries into a ticket and asked Sam to check with the two customers whether a minute of delay is acceptable. I did not change the code yet.

A side result: the cache TTL is 5 minutes for all customers, and for dashboards that refresh each minute even a 5 minute TTL is not used, since the keys never repeat.

Next step is Sam's answer, then a small experiment on staging.

summary: Sam got the OK from both customers for one minute of delay, and the rounded cache key lifted the hit rate in staging from 8 to 71 percent for their queries
body:
Sam came back late this afternoon: both customers accept results that are up to one minute old on their live dashboards. One asked that exact searches with a fixed end time stay unchanged, which was my plan anyway.

I implemented the rounding in the cache key builder of the search API. If the end of a time range is within 60 seconds of the current time, the key uses the end rounded down to the minute. Ranges with a fixed end in the past are left alone. The same rule applies to the start when it is given as a relative value.

The unit tests cover the border: end exactly at now, end 61 seconds ago, no end at all, and a range in the future. The last case gave a wrong key at first, since a future end is not within 60 seconds in the past. I changed the check to an absolute difference.

Then I replayed a day of queries from the two customers in staging. The hit rate for their queries rose from 8 to 71 percent. The p95 for these queries fell from 420 ms to 95 ms in the replay, because most now come from Redis.

I added a response header, X-Cache-Rounded, that says when the rounding was used. This helps Sam when a customer asks why a result looks old.

There is a cost on the Redis side. More hits mean the keys stay, and the query cache grows. I estimated it from the replay at 120 MB more, which is fine given the 1.7 GB used today.

I put the rounding behind a per-customer setting, off by default, so that it only applies to those two customers at first. Mara reviewed the diff quickly and had one comment about the header name, which stays.

The plan for tomorrow is to turn it on for the first customer in the morning and check the numbers by afternoon. I will write down the semantics in the docs as well, in a short section for Sam.

summary: Turned on rounded cache keys for both customers; the production hit rate for them is 66 percent and Redis grew by 90 MB, as estimated
body:
Enabled the rounding setting for the first customer at 09:20 and for the second at 10:15, after the first showed no problems. I watched the dashboards for both.

The hit rate for the first customer rose from 7 to 68 percent within the hour, and for the second from 9 to 64 percent. The overall hit rate went from 54 to 71 percent.

Search p95 over all traffic fell from 268 ms to 205 ms. OpenSearch query load fell too: the search request rate to the cluster dropped by about 30 percent, which is visible in the Grafana panel of the data nodes.

Redis used memory grew from 1.7 GB to 1.79 GB, close to the estimate of 120 MB. Key counts rose accordingly. The connection count did not change.

One issue appeared at noon. The second customer reported that a count on their dashboard was one minute behind a value they saw in another tool. This is the accepted delay, and I showed Sam the X-Cache-Rounded header so he could explain it. He answered the customer, who was satisfied.

I also checked what happens at the minute border. At second 0 of a new minute, all dashboards of a customer miss at once, and the load goes to OpenSearch in a burst. The panel shows a small spike each minute, with 40 parallel queries at most. This is acceptable, but I added a lock per key as with the boosts, so that identical queries wait for one result instead of running in parallel.

The lock needed some care. If the loading request fails, the waiting ones must not wait the whole timeout. I made the lock holder release on error and the waiters then run their own query. A test with a failing backend covers this.

After the lock was deployed the burst at the minute border fell from 40 to about 6 parallel queries.

I wrote the semantics of the rounding in the docs section for Sam: what it does, which ranges are affected, the header, and how to switch it off per customer.

One more thing I want to do: check whether other customers would profit. A scan of the cache miss counters shows three more with a hit rate under 30 percent, but their queries have different reasons, mostly large result pages. I will look at them separately later this week.

Status: the experiment is a success and stays on. The ticket is closed.

summary: Looked at the three other low-hit-rate customers and found one uses a random sort seed in each query, which cannot be cached without changing its meaning
body:
Took the three customers with a hit rate under 30 percent from the scan and looked at their queries one by one.

The first sends a random seed in the sort parameter for a sample view. Each query is meant to differ, so caching would change the meaning. I left it alone and noted it as expected.

The second uses very large page sizes of 5,000 hits and pages through by offset. The keys repeat, but the results are over the size limit for the cache, 256 KB, so they are not stored. Raising the limit would cost memory. I found that the limit was set long ago without a reason, and a gzip of the value would bring most of these under it. I did not change it today, only wrote a ticket.

The third has a hit rate of 28 percent because the customer has 400 saved searches that each run only once a day. Nothing to fix there.

So the result is one ticket for compressing big cache values. I estimated that it would add a CPU cost of about 2 ms per large response, which is small compared with the query time. Mara thought it was fine to try when time allows.

I also cleaned up the per-customer counters in the search API. The label cardinality in Prometheus was 40 customers times 3 results, which is small, but I renamed the metric to follow the naming check from the alert files. The CI check for the names passed.

No production change today except the metric name.

summary: Tried a Redis client library with built-in pooling to replace our own pool code, and dropped it after it doubled connection counts in the staging load test
body:
Tried one of the newer Redis client libraries for the search API, because it promises automatic pooling and pipelining, and our own pool code is old and I wanted to delete it.

The port took about two hours. The API is close to what we use, and the tests passed with small changes.

Then I ran the staging load test. With the new library the search API held 62 connections at peak instead of 31. The library opens a connection per pipeline when several run at once, and the setting to limit this did not behave as documented: the limit was applied per node, not per client, and it was ignored when the pipeline mode was on.

I tried two other settings and read the source for the pool part. A fix would need a patch to the library, and a doubled connection count is a risk, since the Redis server has a connection limit shared with the admin console and the rate limiter.

I decided to drop it and went back to the old client. The branch with the port is deleted, and I wrote the findings in the ticket so nobody repeats the test: peak connections, the setting that did not work and the version that I tried.

Nothing changed in production.

summary: Started the loader-retry work: large file imports restart from the beginning after a failure, so I wrote down where the loader keeps its state
body:
Started on the document loader for large files. The problem is that an import of a 4 GB NDJSON file that fails after 90 percent starts from the beginning when the user submits it again.

I read through the loader code to find where state is kept. The reader streams the file from S3 in chunks of 8 MB, parses lines, and sends batches of 500 events to the ingest API. The only state is in memory: the offset and the count of lines sent.

The plan is to write a checkpoint after each acknowledged batch: the byte offset of the next line, the line count, and the file etag. The checkpoint goes to a Postgres table, import_checkpoints, one row per import job, updated at most every 5 seconds so that the database is not hit for each batch.

On a restart the loader checks the etag. If the file changed, it starts from the beginning and logs a warning. If not, it seeks to the offset with a ranged GET.

A subtle issue is duplicates. A batch may be sent and acknowledged but the checkpoint not yet written when the process dies. After the restart the batch is sent again. The ingest API deduplicates by event id for 10 minutes, but the checkpoint interval could be longer than that. So I will write the checkpoint at least every 60 seconds and keep the batch ids stable, derived from the file offset, and then the API dedup works for any restart inside the window.

I created the branch loader-retry and the migration for the table. Nothing is running yet.

For tomorrow: the checkpoint writer and a test that kills the loader in the middle.

summary: Implemented checkpoints in the loader and a kill test that resumes a 1 GB file at the right offset with no lost and no extra events
body:
Wrote the checkpoint writer and the resume path in the loader this afternoon.

The writer runs in its own goroutine and takes the latest acknowledged offset from a channel. It writes to import_checkpoints at most every 5 seconds, and on a clean finish it writes a final row with state done.

The resume path reads the row at the start. If the etag matches, it uses a ranged GET from the stored offset. A first bug: the offset I stored was the end of the last batch in bytes, but the parser had read ahead inside the chunk, so after a resume the first line was cut in half. I changed it to store the offset of the first byte after the last acknowledged line, computed from line lengths, not from the reader position.

The batch ids are now a hash of the job id and the starting offset of the batch. A resumed run sends the same ids as the first run for the same batches.

The kill test: generate 1 GB of NDJSON with 2.1 million events with sequence numbers, run the loader against a fake ingest server, kill it at a random time, restart, and repeat three times. At the end the fake server checks that every sequence number arrived at least once and that after dedup there are no extras. It passed in 20 random runs, and each run took about 40 seconds.

One more case: when the fake server returns 503 for a batch, the loader retries it with backoff. This already existed, but the checkpoint must not advance beyond a failed batch. The test covers that with a server that fails every 50th batch.

The retry policy is 5 attempts with jittered backoff from 500 ms to 8 seconds. After that the job is marked failed with the checkpoint kept, so that a later submit continues. I made that explicit in the job state instead of deleting the checkpoint.

Open points are the cleanup of old checkpoint rows and the interaction with the admin console, which shows only running or failed today. The console needs a state for resumable. I will tell Lena.

summary: Added cleanup for old checkpoints and a resumable state in the import API, and asked Lena for a console label
body:
Two small pieces for the loader-retry branch today.

First, the cleanup. Checkpoint rows for finished imports are deleted after 7 days by a daily job. Failed imports keep their row for 30 days, so that a customer can still continue after a long weekend. The job logs the number of deleted rows. A test with rows of different age checks both rules.

Second, the import API now returns state resumable for a failed job that has a checkpoint, with the percent done, from offset divided by file size. For a failed job without a checkpoint it returns failed as before.

I added a POST to resume a job, which starts the loader with the job id. It refuses when the job is running, and returns 409. A test covers it.

I wrote to Lena with the new state and the percent field. She will show a Resume button and the percent in the import table. She wanted to know if the button should be shown to all users or only admins. Imports can be started by any user with the write role, so the same role is right.

I also tried the resume against a real 3 GB file in staging. I killed the worker at about 60 percent and restarted. The loader continued from 1.8 GB and finished in 2 minutes 5 seconds, against 3 minutes 20 seconds for the complete run.

Next step: Mara's review, and a short note for Sam about what customers can expect.

summary: Mara's review of loader-retry found a race between the checkpoint goroutine and the final write; fixed, and the branch is merged
body:
Mara reviewed the loader-retry branch in the morning and found one real problem. When the loader finishes, the final write of state done and the periodic writer can run at the same time, and an older offset could be written after done. The job would then look resumable although it was complete.

I reproduced it by making the periodic writer slow with a sleep in a test. The state flipped back to resumable in 3 of 20 runs.

The fix has two parts. The final write now stops the writer goroutine first and waits for it to exit, and the SQL update has a condition that it never changes a row from done to another state. The second part protects against any other case.

She also asked about the ranged GET after a resume: what if S3 returns a different size than the stored one? I had checked the etag but not the size. I added a size check as well and a test with a changed size and the same etag, which can not happen on S3 in practice but costs nothing.

The third comment was about the name of the table. She preferred import_progress, since the table also stores the state. I did not agree: the table stores checkpoints, and the state is a column for the cleanup rule. We left the name.

After the changes CI passed, and Mara approved. I merged the branch into main and ran the migration in staging first, then in production. It was a new table, so the migration took a few milliseconds.

I watched the first real imports after the deploy. Three small imports ran and wrote checkpoint rows, and the cleanup job ran at the next schedule. No errors.

For Sam I wrote a short text for the docs: large imports can be resumed after a failure from the last saved position, the Resume button appears in the console, duplicates are avoided by the ingest dedup within the window, and files that change between runs start over.

What remains is the ingest dedup window. If a customer waits more than 10 minutes to resume, the batches from just before the failure could be counted twice. I want to measure how often this could happen and perhaps extend the window, but that touches the ingest worker, so I will discuss it with Tobias first.

summary: Looked into the 10 minute dedup window for resumed imports: with 24 hours of imports it could double up to 60 events, and a longer window costs Redis memory
body:
Followed up on the open point from the loader merge: the ingest dedup window of 10 minutes.

The dedup keys live in Redis as dedup:{batch id} with a TTL of 600 seconds. A resumed import that starts later than this can send again the batches between the last checkpoint and the point of failure. Since checkpoints are written every 5 seconds, that is at most a few batches of 500 events.

I took the data of the last 60 days from the loader logs and counted resumes: 14 in total, 9 within 10 minutes and 5 later. For the 5 late ones, I computed the batches between the last checkpoint and the failure. The worst case was 3 batches, 1,500 events. In total this could have given up to 60 events doubled for the whole period per resume, depending on timing, and the real number was probably lower.

Next question: what does a longer window cost? There are about 2,000 batches per second at peak. With a 24 hour TTL the keys would grow to a very large count. A rough calculation gave 170 million keys at peak rates, so that is out of the question. Even one hour is 7 million keys, or about 700 MB, too much given 1.8 GB total.

An alternative is to dedup only the loader batches in a different way. Loader batches have a stable id that includes the job id and the offset. The ingest API could store those ids in a separate key family with a long TTL, since loader traffic is a small share, about 1 percent of batches. That would be around 20 per second, and a 24 hour TTL would give 1.7 million keys, about 170 MB. This is still sizable.

A third option is to dedup in the loader itself: on resume, ask the ingest API which offsets were acknowledged beyond the checkpoint. That needs a new endpoint and is more work.

I talked to Tobias in chat. He prefers to avoid more Redis use and suggested to make the events idempotent by event id in the store. The ClickHouse loader already has a block-level dedup for inserted blocks, which helps within a short window only.

We decided to do nothing now. The numbers show at most a few thousand duplicate events per year across all customers, against billions of events. I wrote the analysis in the ticket and closed it as accepted. If a customer asks for exact counts after a resume, Sam can use the offset-based export check.

summary: Answered Sam on whether a resumed import can create duplicates: rarely, only if resumed after 10 minutes, and at most a few batches
body:
Sam asked for the support docs whether a resumed import can create duplicates. The short answer is yes, but rarely.

The resume sends the same batch ids, and the ingest API ignores a repeated id for 10 minutes. If the customer resumes later, the last few batches before the failure can be counted twice, up to about 1,500 events per resume.

In the last 60 days there were 5 such cases out of 14 resumes. I gave him the numbers from the analysis and a sentence he can use. He will add a note to the docs and tell customers with strict counts to resume within 10 minutes or to contact support.

summary: Started ingest-batching: the worker writes each event to ClickHouse with its own insert call, so I measured the cost and designed a batch buffer
body:
Opened the ingest-batching branch. The reason is cost and load: the Go ingest worker writes events to the analytics store one block per message, so a busy partition makes many small inserts, and ClickHouse has to merge the resulting small parts.

I first measured the current state on production metrics. At peak the workers make about 3,800 inserts per second in total, with a median of 42 rows per insert. The number of active parts in the biggest table reaches 410 at peak, and the background merges use a visible share of CPU on the nodes.

The design is a buffer per table in each worker. Events collect until one of three limits is reached: 5,000 rows, 8 MB, or 1 second since the first event in the buffer. Then the worker flushes one insert. The offset of the queue message is committed only after the flush succeeded, so that a crash loses nothing and the messages are read again.

That gives at-least-once semantics, and the duplicates after a crash must be handled. The ClickHouse insert dedup works on identical blocks within a window, but only if the block is formed the same way after a restart. A different batch composition would break it. So I will tie the dedup token to the queue offsets: the token for a flush is the partition and the first and last offset. The insert setting insert_deduplication_token is made for this.

Backpressure is the other part. If the buffer is full while a flush is slow, the worker must stop reading from the queue and not grow memory. I plan a bounded channel of two buffers: one filling, one flushing.

I wrote the skeleton of the buffer with the three limits and unit tests with a fake clock for the time limit. The tests cover a flush by size, by bytes and by time, and the case when two limits are hit at once. One test failed because the timer was not reset after a size flush, so the next flush came too early. I fixed that.

I also wrote down what to measure after the rollout: the number of inserts per second, the median rows per insert, active parts, the end-to-end latency from ingest to queryable, and the worker memory. The latency will rise by up to 1 second, which is acceptable for dashboards, and I will tell Sam so that he can answer questions.

Next step is the offset commit with the dedup token and a crash test in staging.

summary: Wired the dedup token to queue offsets in the batch buffer and a crash test in staging produced no duplicate rows in 30 kills
body:
Finished the offset handling for the batch buffer. Each flush now sends an insert with a dedup token made of the topic partition and the first and last offset of the batch. The commit to Redpanda happens after the insert returns.

For the crash test I ran the worker in staging with a producer that sends numbered events, and a script that kills the worker with SIGKILL at random times. After 30 kills, I counted rows by sequence number in ClickHouse. All numbers were present and there were no duplicates.

One case needed attention. After a restart the worker may read from the last commit, and the new batches can be cut differently because the 1 second timer fires at another point. Then the token differs from the first attempt and dedup does not help. In the test this happened in 4 of the 30 kills, and the rows still did not double. The reason is that I made the buffer cut batches at offset boundaries aligned to multiples of 500 within a partition, so the first batch after a restart ends at the next boundary and is the same as before, if the failed flush started at an aligned offset.

That is a bit subtle, and I wrote it into a comment and a test. It means that small time-based flushes are shorter, but they always end at an aligned offset or contain the rest up to it.

I am not fully sure about this under all rebalances, when a partition moves to another worker. I added a rebalance test with two workers and a forced move. It passed, but I want more runs before the production rollout.

summary: Ran the batching worker for a few hours on a staging copy of production traffic: inserts fell from 3,800 to 190 per second and active parts stayed under 40
body:
Ran the new worker in staging against a mirror of the production event stream for about three hours.

The insert rate fell from 3,800 per second, measured in production, to 190 per second in staging at the same event rate. The median rows per insert rose from 42 to 2,900. Active parts in the largest table stayed under 40, against 410 before.

End-to-end latency from ingest to queryable had a median of 0.6 seconds and a p99 of 1.4 seconds. The worker memory was 180 MB, with no growth.

I also checked what happens when ClickHouse is slow. I added a delay of 5 seconds to inserts with a proxy. The queue lag grew, the worker stopped reading as designed, and memory stayed flat. After the delay was removed the lag cleared in about a minute.

One finding: for the smallest event types the 1 second timer is the only limit that fires, so they flush one tiny insert per second per partition. With 12 partitions this is still small. I noted that we could raise the time limit for low volume types, but did not change it.

Next step is a production rollout on one worker first, then all, with the metrics I listed. I will do it tomorrow morning, when traffic is low and Tobias is online.

summary: Finished the ingest-batching work: a flush on shutdown, a size and time limit for the buffer, and a rollback switch, so the branch is ready for Mara's review.
body:
The staging run from the afternoon looked good, so this session closed the remaining gaps in the batch buffer. First, the worker now flushes the buffer on SIGTERM. Before, a deploy during the staging test lost the last partial batch, because the process exited before the timer fired. The fix drains the buffer, waits for the insert to be acknowledged and only then commits the queue offsets.

Second, the buffer has two limits: 5,000 rows or 800 ms, whichever comes first. I tried 2,000 rows and 2 seconds first. The 2 second wait made the freshness of the dashboards visibly worse for small customers, so I dropped it. With 800 ms the p99 delay from queue to ClickHouse was 1.1 seconds in staging.

Third, a config flag INGEST_BATCH_ENABLED falls back to the old single insert path. I kept the old path on purpose for the first week in production. A test covers both paths with the same fixture of 20,000 events and compares the rows in ClickHouse.

I also added metrics: batch size histogram, flush reason (size, time, shutdown) and insert latency. The Grafana panel is a copy of the loader panel with the new names. One thing left: a backpressure case where ClickHouse answers slowly and the buffer fills. For now the worker stops reading from the queue when two batches are in flight. I will test this with a slowed ClickHouse tomorrow and then ask Mara to review.

summary: Tested ingest-batching with a deliberately slow ClickHouse: the buffer stops reading from the queue as designed, and lag recovers by itself in about four minutes.
body:
I added a delay of 2 seconds to every insert on the staging ClickHouse with a small proxy and ran the normal replay of production traffic. The worker reached two batches in flight, stopped reading from Redpanda and memory stayed flat at about 180 MB per worker. Consumer lag grew to 90,000 messages.

After I removed the delay, the lag was gone in about four minutes. No rows were lost and the dedup token kept the count exact; I compared the row counts with the source topic.

One problem showed up: the health check of the worker reported unhealthy while it was paused, since it looked at the time of the last commit. The load balancer would have taken such workers out. I changed the check to look at the last successful flush or an empty buffer, with a note in the code. A test now covers this case.

Next is the review by Mara, and I wrote the description of the pull request with the numbers from the staging run.

summary: Mara's early review of ingest-batching asked for a cap on rows per customer in a batch, so one noisy tenant cannot starve the flush of others.
body:
Mara read the branch this morning. Her main point: the buffer is shared across tenants, and a customer sending a huge burst can fill the 5,000 row limit alone, which makes everyone else wait for the next flush. I checked the staging numbers and she is right in theory; in practice the delay stayed under 1.2 seconds.

We agreed on a small change: a flush also triggers when one tenant holds more than 60 percent of the buffer. She also asked for the flag name to match the other worker flags, so it is NEBULA_INGEST_BATCH now. Two smaller comments were about log lines in the hot path, which I turned to debug level.

I will do the changes this evening.

summary: Applied Mara's review notes to ingest-batching, added the per-tenant flush trigger and a test with a noisy tenant; the branch is merged and the flag is off in production.
body:
The change for the tenant share was small. The buffer keeps a count per tenant, and when one passes 60 percent of the row limit, it flushes right away. I wrote a test with one tenant sending 9,000 events and three small ones sending 20 each. The small tenants' events reached ClickHouse within 300 ms, compared to 800 ms before.

I renamed the flag to NEBULA_INGEST_BATCH and updated the Terraform variables so the ECS task definitions carry it, off by default. Tobias checked the plan output and found that I had put the variable in only one of the two services; fixed.

The log lines went to debug. After that I ran the full test suite and the staging replay one more time: 190 inserts per second, active parts under 40, same as before the changes.

Mara approved, CI was green and I merged the branch. Production still uses the single insert path. The plan is to turn the flag on for one worker first tomorrow, watch parts and lag for a few hours, and then widen it.

I also wrote the rollout steps into the runbook page, including how to turn it off: set the flag to false and redeploy, which takes about six minutes. A last note for myself: the dashboard for ClickHouse parts needs an alert threshold at 150 parts, which does not exist yet. That is for the next session.

summary: Turned on batching for one production ingest worker and watched it for the morning: inserts per second fell by 95 percent for that worker and nothing was lost.
body:
At 08:00 I set the flag on a single ECS task out of six. The other five kept the old path, which made a good comparison on the same traffic.

Results after three hours: the batching task issued about 40 inserts per second, the others about 640 each. Active parts in ClickHouse dropped a little already with one task. Consumer lag stayed at zero. Insert latency was 35 ms median, 120 ms at p99.

I checked correctness with a query that counts events per minute by event id for the window and compared it with the source count from the Redpanda offsets. The numbers matched for the task's partitions. I also ran a duplicate check on the dedup token; zero duplicates.

One surprise: memory per task went from 150 MB to 260 MB. That is within the limit of 512 MB, but I want to see it at peak time. Another is that the first flush after a start was slow, 900 ms, due to a cold connection; I added a warm-up ping.

I added the alert for ClickHouse active parts at 150 with a warning at 100. The rule is in the alert code repository and CI accepted it.

Next: widen to three tasks tomorrow if the peak looks fine. Tobias knows the plan and will watch the on-call channel.

summary: Peak traffic with batching on one task looked fine, with memory at 310 MB, so batching is on for three of six production workers now.
body:
The peak is around 11:00, so I waited for it. The single batching task reached 310 MB and then stayed there. The limit is 512 MB, so there is room. Flush reasons were mostly size at peak and mostly time at night, which is what I expected.

I turned the flag on for two more tasks. Lag stayed at zero. Active parts went from about 70 to 45 across the table.

I plan the other three for tomorrow, but not at the same time as the Terraform change that Tobias has planned.

summary: Debugged the audit log page in the admin console that showed duplicate rows for page two: the cursor used created_at alone, and rows with equal timestamps were skipped or repeated.
body:
Lena reported that on the audit log page, a few rows appeared twice when going to the next page, and others never appeared at all. I could reproduce it with the staging data, where a bulk action writes 200 audit rows in the same millisecond.

The query in the search API used WHERE created_at < $cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. With equal timestamps, rows at the page border are skipped, since the cursor is strictly less. When I changed it to less-or-equal, the same rows repeated instead.

The fix is a compound cursor of created_at and id. The query is now WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC. The cursor is base64 of both values. Old cursors with a single value still work: if the id is missing, the code uses the max id, which is slightly wrong only for those rare rows and is acceptable for a link that lives a few minutes.

I checked the plan in Postgres. Without a matching index, the query used a sort. I added an index on audit_log (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. On the staging copy with 8 million rows, the page query went from 180 ms to 4 ms. In production the table has about 31 million rows, so the build will take a while, and I scheduled it for the evening.

I wrote a test that inserts 500 rows with the same timestamp and walks through all pages; it checks that every id appears exactly once. It failed before the change and passes now.

Lena does not need to change anything in the console, since the cursor is opaque to her code. I told her in the channel and asked her to retest with her bulk action.

Open: the export of the audit log (the audit-export branch) uses its own pagination by id range, so it was not affected. I checked this by reading the job code once more.

summary: Built the audit log index on production Postgres with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; it took 11 minutes, did not block writes, and the page query is fast now.
body:
I started the build at 12:30 because the load on the primary is low at noon on the audit table. I watched pg_stat_progress_create_index in a second terminal. The phases went through as usual: the build of the index, then the wait for old transactions, then the second scan.

It finished in 11 minutes. Writes to the audit log kept flowing; the insert latency in Grafana did not change. The index is about 2.1 GB. I checked that it is valid with a query on pg_index (indisvalid is true).

The page query in production now takes 3 to 6 ms with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, down from around 150 ms. I deleted the old index on (customer_id, created_at), since the new one covers it, and that freed about 1.4 GB.

Lena confirmed that her test with the bulk action shows each row once.

summary: Turned on batching for all six production ingest workers; lag stayed at zero through the evening peak and ClickHouse active parts settled near 30.
body:
Three more tasks got the flag in the morning, but I held back for the afternoon until Tobias had finished his Terraform change, which touched the same service. After his apply at 17:30 I turned on the last three tasks one by one, with ten minutes between them.

I watched four things: consumer lag, active parts, insert latency and memory per task. Lag stayed at zero. Active parts fell from around 70 at the start of the week to about 30. Insert latency was 40 ms median and 140 ms at p99. Memory per task peaked at 330 MB.

I ran the count comparison again for one hour of traffic across all partitions: source offsets against rows in ClickHouse by dedup token. Both were 4.82 million, with no duplicates.

One minor issue: the metric for batch size was reported per worker, but the Grafana panel summed it, so it looked like 30,000 rows per batch. I changed the panel to use the average.

Now the old single insert path is only a fallback behind the flag. I will keep it for a week and then remove it in a cleanup commit, as I wrote in the runbook.

I also wrote a short entry for Sam in the docs notes: the freshness of dashboards after ingest is up to about one second, as before for the customers, so nothing changes for the public docs.

Next: a look at the cost; ClickHouse CPU should drop with fewer parts, and I want a number for it next week.

summary: Started the rate-limits work: wrote down how the Redis limiter counts today, per customer only, and designed per-API-key limits with a sliding window.
body:
The current limiter is a fixed window counter in Redis, one key per customer and minute, incremented with INCR and given an expiry. It works but has two problems that customers have raised through Sam: a key that leaks or loops can use the whole quota of a customer, and the fixed window allows double bursts at the window border.

I read the code in the search API and the ingest API and found that both use the same small module, which is good. The design: keys become rate:{customer}:{apikey}:{window}, and a second level counts the customer total as now. A request must pass both. The limit per key is optional and set in the settings table in Postgres; no setting means only the customer limit.

For the window I looked at a sliding window with two counters (current and previous window, weighted by the position in the window). It needs two reads and one INCR, which I can do in a Lua script to keep it atomic and in one round trip. The error against a true sliding window is small, under about 5 percent in my quick simulation with random arrivals.

I considered a token bucket, but the explanation to customers is harder, and our docs speak of requests per minute. So I stayed with the sliding window.

Memory: with about 40 customers and, say, 300 active keys, two counters each per minute with a 120 second expiry is tiny, well under 1 MB. I wrote the estimate in the design note anyway.

The response headers need work too: X-RateLimit-Remaining should show the lower of the key and customer values, and a new X-RateLimit-Scope says which one applied.

I created the branch rate-limits and committed the design note and a spike of the Lua script with a unit test against a local Redis. The test replays 1,000 timed requests and checks the counts. Next step is the settings table and the API for the console.

summary: Implemented the sliding window Lua script and the per-key settings table for the limiter, with tests that include a Redis restart and two clock-skewed clients.
body:
The script takes the key prefix, the limit, the window length and the current time from the Redis server clock (TIME), so API nodes with different clocks agree. I had first passed the time from the node, and the skew test with a 2 second offset showed a wrong count at window borders; that is why it uses TIME now.

The script returns three values: allowed, remaining and reset seconds. It sets an expiry of twice the window on both counters. I tested it with 10,000 requests from 4 simulated clients and a limit of 100 per minute: it allowed 100 to 104 per minute, which fits the expected error of the weighted window.

The settings table api_key_limits has api_key_id, requests_per_minute and a created_by column. A migration adds it, and a partial index is not needed for so few rows. The search API loads the limits into a small in-process cache for 30 seconds, so a change in the console is live within half a minute, and no Postgres query runs per request.

I also tested what happens when Redis is not reachable. The existing behavior is fail open with a log line and a counter, and I kept that for both levels. A test with a stopped Redis container confirms it, and another with a restart shows the counts start at zero afterwards, which is fine.

The headers are done: X-RateLimit-Remaining carries the lower value, and X-RateLimit-Scope is key or customer. The existing tests for the headers needed small changes, since they compared the full header set.

I did not touch the docs yet; that needs Sam. Next steps: the console API for the limits, Lena's form, and a load test in staging with real key counts.

summary: Answered Sam on whether a per-key limit can exceed the customer limit: it can be set higher, but it never raises the total, because both levels must pass.
body:
Sam asked this for a customer who wants one key with 'unlimited' use. I explained that the customer limit stays the hard ceiling in the new design: a request is allowed only if both the key and the customer counters have room. So a key limit above the customer limit has no effect beyond it.

If a customer needs more in total, the customer limit must be raised, which is a setting that Sam can request through the normal change. I suggested that the console warns when a key limit is higher than the customer limit, and I noted that for Lena's form.

Sam will add one sentence to the docs draft once the feature is ready.

summary: Load tested the per-key limiter in staging with 300 keys and found the Lua script adds 0.4 ms at p50, but a hot key made one Redis command stall the pool for 40 ms at p99.
body:
I used the replay tool with the production traffic shape, 300 API keys, and a profile where 3 keys send most of the requests. The limiter script added about 0.4 ms at p50 and 1.1 ms at p95 to a request, which is acceptable.

The p99 was worse than I wanted: 40 ms. I looked at the Redis slowlog and at the connection pool metrics. The script itself ran in microseconds. The delay came from the pool: the limiter and the query cache share the same pool, and a burst of cache reads for the large customers occupied the connections, so limiter calls waited for a free one.

I tried two things. First, a separate small pool for the limiter, 8 connections. This brought the p99 down to 6 ms. Second, I tried pipelining the two counters into one round trip; it made no difference once the pool was separate, so I dropped it to keep the code simple.

The cost of the separate pool is 8 more connections per API node. With 4 nodes that is 32 more on the Redis side. I checked the current connection count in Grafana, which is around 140 at peak out of a limit that is much higher, so there is room.

I also checked the key naming: the keys are short, and the TTL of twice the window leaves about 600 keys at any moment, so memory use is unchanged to the megabyte.

The pool size is configurable through RATE_POOL_SIZE. I will leave the default at 8 and revisit it if the p99 grows with more customers.

Next: the console API for editing the limits and a test for the 30 second cache so that a change shows the new limit in the response headers. Then Lena can start on the form. I told her the endpoint shape in the channel: GET and PUT on /admin/keys/:id/limit.

summary: Added the admin endpoints for per-key limits with validation and audit log entries, and told Lena the shape so she can build the form.
body:
The endpoints are GET and PUT on /admin/keys/:id/limit, and DELETE to remove the limit. PUT takes requests_per_minute as an integer from 1 to 1,000,000. Values outside return 422 with a message that the console can show directly.

Every change writes an audit log row with the old and new values and the admin user. I used the same helper as the other settings, so the new rows appear in the audit log page that I fixed last week, and in the export.

The warning for a key limit above the customer limit is part of the GET response as a field warnings, so the console does not need to compare the numbers on its own.

Tests cover the validation, permissions (support users may read, only admins write) and the audit rows. I also ran the whole suite, which passed.

Lena has the endpoint description and will build the form tomorrow.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console form for per-key limits and rolled the limiter to staging with a canary customer; a stale 30 second cache confused the first manual test.
body:
Lena's form shows the current limit, the effective limit (the lower of key and customer) and the warning text. I reviewed it in the browser. Two comments: the number input accepted a minus sign before the server rejected it, so she added min and max, and the empty value should send DELETE instead of PUT with zero. She fixed both within the hour.

I deployed the branch to staging and set a limit of 20 per minute on one key of a test customer. My first manual test still allowed 60 requests in a minute. After some confusion I remembered the 30 second cache of limits in the API node; the second test, after waiting, showed 20 allowed and then 429. I added a line to the console form's help text saying that changes apply within 30 seconds, and put the same in the design note.

To check the sliding window by hand I sent requests with a small script at a steady pace and printed the headers. The Remaining value went down by one per request and the Reset value counted down correctly. At the window border, the allowed count did not double, which was the whole point.

I also tested a key limit for a key belonging to a different customer by mistake, using the endpoint with a wrong id: the API answered 404, not 403, to avoid leaking that the key exists. That is the same behavior as the other admin routes.

Then Sam and I picked a canary: a customer with 12 keys and a history of one runaway job. Sam will ask them whether they want a limit on the job's key. Nothing is on in production yet.

Remaining: the docs, the Prometheus counter for 429 by scope (done in code, the panel is not), and a look at how the ingest client of one big customer reacts to the new headers. I will read their client code in the public SDK repository tomorrow.

summary: Checked the public SDK's handling of 429 and found it retries with a fixed one second delay and ignores the reset header, so I made it use the header with jitter.
body:
The SDK for the ingest client retries on 429 and 503 up to five times with a fixed delay of one second. With per-key limits, many clients of one customer could hit the limit together and then all retry at the same moment, which is a thundering herd on the limiter.

I changed the retry delay: it uses the X-RateLimit-Reset value when present, otherwise exponential backoff starting at 500 ms, and in both cases adds random jitter of up to 25 percent. The maximum is 30 seconds. The number of attempts stays at five.

A test with a fake server that answers 429 with reset 2 shows waits of between 2.0 and 2.5 seconds. Another test checks that the backoff without a header grows 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and then stops.

The change is backward compatible: older servers without the header produce the backoff. I wrote a note for the changelog and told Sam so that the docs mention the new behavior.

I will release a minor version of the SDK after the limiter is on in production, so the header exists when the client starts to rely on it.

summary: Enabled per-key limits in production behind a flag for the canary customer and watched the first day of traffic; no false 429s, and the 429 counter by scope works.
body:
The merge of the rate-limits branch was approved by Mara this morning after one comment about the name of the pool setting, which is now RATE_LIMIT_POOL_SIZE. I deployed the build with the flag RATE_KEY_LIMITS off, then turned it on only for the canary customer.

First I checked that nothing changed for everyone else. The customer limit path gave the same results as before: the 429 rate was identical to the day before within noise, about 0.02 percent of requests, nearly all from two customers who are known to be above their limits.

For the canary, Sam had talked to the customer, who chose a limit of 600 per minute for the key of the runaway job. I set it in the console, which was the first real use of Lena's form. It worked and left an audit row.

In the next hours the job's key reached the limit three times and got 429 with scope key, and the customer's other eleven keys were not affected at all. That is the case the feature is for. The customer total never reached its own limit during these hours.

The new Prometheus counter splits 429 by scope, and I built the panel: two lines, key and customer. I put it next to the existing request panels. I also added an alert, only a warning, if more than 5 percent of requests of one key are limited for 10 minutes, since that likely means a wrong limit.

The separate pool for the limiter showed up as 8 connections per API node in the Redis client list, 32 in total, as planned. The p99 of the limiter calls was 3 ms.

One thing I found by reading the logs: a client of the canary retried 429s immediately, without any delay, which is not our SDK. It made about 200 requests in a second against the limit. The limiter handled it without trouble, but I told Sam to mention the Retry-After and reset headers in the answer to the customer.

Next: wait a few days, then enable for the other customers who ask. The docs page is the last open item.

summary: Rolled the per-key limiter out from the canary customer to ten more customers and fixed a hot-key stall by caching the settings lookup locally for five seconds.
body:
The canary customer ran for several days without a false 429, so I widened the flag to ten more customers this afternoon. Before that I went back to the load test result from last week, where a hot key made one Redis command stall the pool for 40 ms at p99. The cause was that every request for a hot key read the per-key settings from Redis before running the Lua script, so the same hash was hit twice per request. I added a small in-process cache of the settings with a five second TTL, keyed by API key, in limiter/settings.ts. The admin endpoints now publish a short invalidation message so a changed limit reaches all API processes within a second in the normal case. The five second TTL is the worst case if that message is lost.

I repeated the staging load test with 300 keys and one hot key sending 2,000 requests per second. The p99 stall dropped from 40 ms to 6 ms, and the Redis command rate for the limiter fell by about 45 percent. The p50 cost of the script stayed at 0.4 ms. I also checked that the stale cache cannot let a key pass the customer level, because the customer limit is checked separately and is not cached. A test covers a lowered limit: the new value takes effect after the invalidation message, and after at most five seconds without it.

In production, the ten customers were picked with Sam, who knew which ones had asked for per-key limits. I watched the 429 counter by scope for two hours and saw only key-scope 429s for two customers that were really over their limit. Redis memory grew by less than 5 MB for the new limiter keys. Next I want to write the rollout plan for all customers and ask Sam to announce the feature in the docs.

summary: Wrote the rollout plan for per-key limits to all customers, with a docs section and a rollback step, and Sam reviewed the wording of the customer announcement.
body:
After the widened rollout from earlier today looked stable, I wrote the plan for the remaining customers. The plan has three waves: ten customers, then twenty, then the rest, with at least one full day between waves. Each wave has a check list: no unexplained 429s in the scope counter, limiter latency at p99 under 10 ms, and Redis memory growth below 20 MB. If any check fails, the flag goes off for that wave and the limiter falls back to the customer level only, which is the old behavior.

I tested that rollback in staging by turning the flag off while traffic ran. Requests moved to customer-only counting within one cache period, and the per-key counters expired on their own. Turning the flag on again started the keys from empty windows, so for a short time a key can send a little more than its limit. I wrote that down in the plan as a known and accepted effect.

Sam read the draft of the docs section and the announcement text. Sam asked for a clearer explanation of what a customer sees when both levels apply, so I added an example: a customer limit of 1,000 per minute with two keys at 600 each, where the total still stops at 1,000. I also added the reset header and the jitter advice for the SDK, since the SDK change from last week ships in the same release. Sam will publish the docs page when the second wave starts. Tobias was asked to add the limiter latency panel to the Grafana board so the wave checks are in one place, and he said he would do it tomorrow.

summary: Tried a schema registry client library for the event schema checks and dropped it after it needed a running service for every unit test and added 300 ms to worker start.
body:
I started the day on the schema registry topic by evaluating an off-the-shelf Go client that fetches and caches schemas and validates events against them. The idea was to save writing our own cache and compatibility checks.

It looked good in the README. In practice, three things went wrong. First, every unit test of the worker that touched validation needed a registry endpoint, and the library has no in-memory mode, so I wrote a small fake HTTP server, which was already more code than a cache. Second, the worker start took 300 ms longer, since the library fetches all schemas eagerly. Third, its compatibility modes are named differently from the rules we want: backward only for the optional fields, and forward for new event types. The mapping would have been a source of mistakes.

I spent about three hours on this and then stopped. The decision is to write our own small registry client: a versioned schema table in Postgres, an in-process cache with a short TTL, and a compatibility check function that is a pure function and easy to test.

I did start that part and got the table and the check function. The table schema_versions has subject, version, schema JSON, compat_mode and created_at, with a unique index on subject and version. The check function compares two schemas and returns a list of violations, such as a removed required field, a changed type or a new required field without default. I wrote 24 test cases from the real history of our event schemas, taking each past change and checking that the function would have said the right thing. Two of the historical changes would have been blocked, and both were known mistakes from the first year.
