Tomorrow: the HTTP endpoints for registering a schema and a CI step that runs the check on schema changes in a pull request. The library branch is deleted and I noted in the design doc why it was dropped.

summary: Built the schema registry endpoints and a CI check that fails a pull request when an event schema change breaks compatibility; the first run found a real problem in an open branch.
body:
The registry has three endpoints in the search API service for now: POST /schemas/:subject to register a version, GET /schemas/:subject/latest and GET /schemas/:subject/:version. Registering runs the compatibility check against the latest version and answers 409 with the list of violations if it fails. A force flag exists, but only for admins, and it writes an audit row.

The worker side is a small client with a cache of 60 seconds. It loads one subject at a time on first use, so there is no eager fetch and the worker start time is unchanged. I measured the start before and after: 410 ms and 412 ms.

For CI I wrote a script that reads the schema files in the repository, compares each changed file with the version on the main branch using the same check function, and prints violations as annotations on the pull request. It runs in about 4 seconds. To test it I used the open pull requests. One of them, an old change from Mara for the session event, makes a field required without a default. The check flagged it correctly; she had not yet noticed that old clients would break, and she will change it to optional.

I added a few cases that the check function got wrong at first. A type change from integer to number is compatible in one direction only, and in backward mode it is allowed. Enum values added are allowed in forward mode, but removed values never. The nested object case, a field inside an array of objects, was missing, and I added recursion. The test count is now 41.

I also thought about how the registry is seeded: a one-time script loads the current schemas of all event types as version 1 with the mode backward. I ran it on staging and found 19 subjects. Two had a leftover field that does not appear in the code any more; I left them as they are and noted them for later cleanup.

Permissions: only the CI service account and admins may register. Reads are open to workers.

Next steps are the production seed, a metric for cache misses, and a short doc for the team about the workflow: change the file, open the pull request, CI checks, merge registers the version.

summary: Seeded the schema registry in production and wired registration into the merge pipeline; all 19 subjects are at version 1 and the worker reads them from the cache.
body:
I ran the seed script on production in the afternoon. It created 19 subjects at version 1 with backward compatibility. I verified with the GET endpoint for each subject that the stored schema equals the file in the main branch; a small loop compared the hashes, and all 19 matched.

Then I added a step to the merge pipeline: after a merge to main, any changed schema file is registered as the next version using the CI service account. If the check passes in the pull request, it passes here too, so a failure at this stage would mean someone merged around CI, and the step stops the deploy.

The worker now logs the schema version it used for validation in debug mode, and the cache miss counter is in Prometheus. After the deploy, the miss rate was 19 in the first minute (one per subject) and then zero, as expected.

I wrote the short team doc with the workflow and told Mara and Lena in the channel. Open: the two subjects with leftover fields, and whether the console should show the schema versions to customers, which I will raise with the lead of the product discussion later.

summary: Added a registry compatibility mode per subject and a dry-run endpoint, so authors can test a schema change before opening a pull request
body:
After seeding the registry, the first question from Mara was how a team checks a change before the CI job fails it. I added a dry-run endpoint, POST /subjects/:name/check, that returns the compatibility verdict and the list of breaking fields without registering anything.

Each subject now has a compatibility mode: backward, which is the default, or none. The none mode exists only for two internal debug subjects and needs an audit log entry to set. I wrote it as a column on the subjects table with a check constraint, so a typo cannot create a third mode.

The breaking-field report was the hard part. The first version said only 'incompatible', which is useless in a review. It now names the path, for example payload.items[].price changed from number to string, and the rule that failed.

I wrote 24 tests for the rules: added optional field, added required field, removed field, type widening, enum value removed and nested arrays. Two cases surprised me. Adding a required field with a default passed in my first draft, but old workers would not know the default, so it is rejected now.

The CI job calls the same endpoint, so the local result and the pipeline result cannot differ. I added a short section to the registry README with the curl command.

Not done yet: the worker still reads schemas only at start, so a new version needs a worker restart. Next I want a cache refresh with a version check, and I will write that down as a separate task for tomorrow.

summary: Made workers refresh schemas from the registry every 60 seconds with a version check, so a new schema version no longer needs a restart
body:
Workers loaded all 19 subjects at start and never again. A new version therefore only took effect after the next deploy, which is fragile.

I added a background refresher in the worker that asks the registry for a small version map every 60 seconds. Only subjects whose version changed are fetched in full. The request is one cheap call with an ETag, and the registry answers 304 most of the time.

If the registry is down, the worker keeps the schemas it has and logs a warning once per minute, not on every event. I tested this by stopping the registry in staging for ten minutes while a replay of production traffic ran. Nothing was rejected and nothing was slow.

An unknown event version is still handled as before: the event goes to the dead letter topic with a reason. I added a counter, schema_refresh_total, split by result, and a Grafana panel next to the existing worker panels.

One bug showed up in the test. The refresher swapped the whole map while a validation held a pointer to the old one, which was harmless, but the race detector complained about an unsynchronized write. I switched to an atomic pointer swap and the complaint went away.

Next is a note in the docs for Sam about when a schema change becomes active.

summary: Investigated why the search API p95 rose to 420 ms on Redis cache misses and found the cache key included the full query object with unordered fields
body:
Tobias pointed out that the search API p95 had crept up from about 250 ms to 420 ms over two weeks, while the load stayed flat. I started with the cache hit rate in Grafana, which had fallen from 71 percent to 48 percent in the same period.

I pulled a sample of 2,000 cache keys from Redis with SCAN and compared them. The same logical query appeared under several keys. The key was built from JSON.stringify of the query object, and the console sends the filter fields in a different order depending on which control the user touched last. Two identical searches therefore missed each other.

I wrote a small script that normalizes the sample and counted the distinct keys. 2,000 keys collapsed to 1,310, so about a third of them were duplicates. That fits the lost hit rate.

The fix is a canonical form: sort object keys recursively, drop empty filters and lowercase the sort direction, then hash it with sha1. The key prefix stays search:v1:, but I bumped it to search:v2: so old keys are never mixed with new ones and expire on their own through their TTLs.

I also checked that the customer id is part of the key before hashing. It is, and I added a test that two customers with the same query never share a key, because that would be a data leak.

I deployed it to staging and replayed an hour of production queries. The hit rate was 69 percent after a warm-up of about ten minutes, and p95 was 270 ms.

Two things remain. The warm-up after a deploy empties the effective cache for a short time, so I will deploy it at a quiet hour. And the memory use of Redis will rise a little as the new keys fill in, so I will watch it for a day after production.

summary: Deployed the canonical cache key for search to production in the quiet hour; hit rate climbed from 48 to 66 percent and p95 fell to 285 ms
body:
I deployed the search:v2 cache key change after the evening peak, when traffic is about a fifth of the day's maximum.

The hit rate started at zero as expected, since the new prefix has no entries. After 15 minutes it was at 40 percent, and after an hour at 61 percent. By the end of the session it was at 66 percent. The search API p95 went from 420 ms to 285 ms.

Redis memory grew from 3.1 GB to 3.4 GB while the old and new keys lived side by side. The old keys have a TTL of one hour, so they were gone before I finished checking. I wrote down the figure so that we know what the cache needs: about 3.2 GB at the current key count.

I looked at the slowest remaining misses. They are mostly wide date ranges with a full text clause, which really are slow in OpenSearch, so no key change helps there. Those are a topic for the shard layout plan.

I left the old key builder in the code behind no flag. It is simply deleted. If something goes wrong, a revert of the commit is a clean way back.

I told Tobias in the team channel and put the before and after numbers in the ticket. I will look at the graphs again tomorrow morning.

summary: Wrote the first outline of the new search index shard layout, by month instead of by customer, with the size per shard and the main risks
body:
The large customers make a few shards of the search index much bigger than the rest. The biggest customer shard holds about 190 GB, while the median is 6 GB. Queries across a time range hit that shard hard, and the nightly reindex job takes its time on it.

I wrote a document with the proposal: one index per month, with a fixed number of primary shards, and an alias per customer with a filter on the customer id. With 13 months of searchable data, that is 13 indices. The size per shard would be near 25 GB, which is in the range the OpenSearch guidance recommends.

I listed the risks:
- Aliases with filters cost a little on every query. I want a measurement before I promise anything.
- A customer delete now means a delete by query across many indices, instead of dropping one index.
- The reindex job needs a new loop, and it must be idempotent so it can run twice.
- Boosts from the search-v2 work depend on the mapping, which must be identical across all months.

I did not start any migration. This is only the plan and the questions that need answers first. I asked Tobias for a rough cost of the extra nodes if the shard count grows from 12 to 26.

Next step is a benchmark on a staging copy with one month of real data and the alias filter, so I can see the query latency before we choose the shard count.

summary: Measured filtered-alias query latency on a staging copy of the search index: about 6 ms extra at p50, which is acceptable for the planned layout
body:
I built the staging copy from last month's data of five customers, about 140 GB, as one monthly index with 4 primary shards. Then I created a filtered alias per customer.

I replayed 5,000 real queries from the search API log against the old layout and against the alias. The p50 was 38 ms on the old layout and 44 ms on the alias. The p95 was 210 ms and 224 ms. So the alias filter costs about 6 ms at the median, and it is smaller at the tail.

A surprise came from routing. Without a routing key, every query goes to all shards of the monthly index. With routing by customer id, the query hits one shard, and the p95 fell to 150 ms. That is better than the old layout. The cost is that very large customers can again make one shard hot, so routing should be used only for customers under a size limit.

I noted that the routing value must be set at index time, which means the reindex job has to know the rule. I wrote this into the plan with the limit as an open question.

I also checked the mapping: dynamic fields from event payloads grow the mapping per month. A template with a fixed field limit of 1,000 keeps this under control.

I will ask Mara to review the plan before I do more, since she wrote the reindex loop.

summary: Mara reviewed the shard layout plan and asked for a rule for large customers and a delete procedure; both are now in the document
body:
Mara read the plan and the benchmark and had four comments. The most useful one was that routing by customer id would make the hot shard problem return for the three largest customers, so they need a different rule.

We agreed on this: customers below 50 GB per month are routed by id to one shard. The three above get a dedicated alias to a set of routing values, spread over 4 shards by a hash of customer id and day. I added the rule to the document with the size limit as a setting, not a constant.

Her second comment was about deletes. A customer who leaves must be removed within 30 days by contract. A delete by query over 13 indices is slow and leaves segments with deleted documents. I wrote a procedure: run the delete by query, then a force merge of only the deleted-heavy segments in a quiet window. I flagged that this needs a test on staging, which is not done.

The third point was to keep the reindex job idempotent by writing documents with the event id as the document id. That is already the case, and I noted it.

The fourth was to ask whether the search-v2 boosts depend on index settings. They only depend on the mapping, so a shared template is enough.

I updated the plan and sent it to Tobias for the node cost. He said he will answer tomorrow. I am not going to touch production for this until the delete test is done.

summary: Found why Redis memory climbed by 600 MB in a week: the rate limiter wrote per-key window keys without a TTL on one code path
body:
Tobias saw the Redis memory graph rising slowly and asked if the new per-key limits were the cause. I looked at key counts by prefix using SCAN with a sample, and the prefix rl:key: had 1.9 million keys, far more than the number of active API keys, which is about 3,000.

The sliding window script sets an expiry with each call, but the path for a rejected request returned early, before the EXPIRE call. Keys that only ever saw rejections, for example a client that is blocked all day, never got a TTL if they were created by a rejected call. I confirmed it with the TTL command on twenty sample keys, which returned -1 for eleven of them.

The fix moves the expiry to the start of the script, so every path sets it. I wrote a test for the rejected-first case, which failed before the change and passed after.

For the keys already there, I wrote a one-time cleanup script that scans rl:key:, and sets a TTL of 120 seconds on keys without one. It ran for six minutes against production at a low scan count and did not move the command latency.

Memory fell from 4.0 GB to 3.4 GB over the next hour. I will check the key count again tomorrow.

summary: Deployed the limiter TTL fix and confirmed with a key count check that rl:key: stays near 3,000 keys
body:
I deployed the Lua script change to production with the normal pipeline. Because the script is loaded by its SHA, I checked that all six workers had picked up the new version. Two of them still used the old one for a minute until the script cache refreshed, which is fine because both versions give the same answers.

After an hour I sampled the prefix again. rl:key: held 3,200 keys and no key had a TTL of -1 in a sample of 500. After the evening peak it was 3,400, which is plausible for the active keys with a 120 second window.

I added a Prometheus gauge for the key count of this prefix, fed by a small job that uses a scan every five minutes, and an alert when it exceeds 20,000. That is far above normal but well below a harmful level.

I also noted in the rate limits document that every new Lua path must set the expiry first. A short comment now sits at the top of the script too.

The ticket is closed. The memory graph is flat, around 3.3 GB.

summary: Slow Postgres query on the audit log export list: a missing composite index and a sort on text; fixed with an index built concurrently, 9 s down to 40 ms
body:
Sam reported that the page in the admin console listing past audit exports took several seconds to load for the largest customer. I ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the query from the API log.

The plan was a sequential scan over 8.4 million audit rows, filtered by customer and then sorted by created_at and id. It took 9.1 seconds. The existing index covered only customer_id, so Postgres had to sort everything it found.

I considered a partial index, but the query is used for all customers, so I built a composite index on (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It took 14 minutes on production and did not block writes. I checked pg_stat_progress_create_index while it ran and watched replication lag, which stayed under a second.

After the build the plan used an index scan with no separate sort, and the query ran in 40 ms. The buffers hit count fell from about 310,000 to 60.

I also found that the old customer_id-only index is now redundant for this query and mostly for others. I did not drop it yet. First I want to check pg_stat_user_indexes for a week to see whether anything still uses it.

I answered Sam that the page should be fast now and asked her to say if any customer still sees delays.

summary: Tried replacing the hand-written Redis pool settings with a pooling helper library and dropped it after it hid connection errors from our metrics
body:
I wanted to see if a small helper library for Redis connection handling could replace our own wrapper, which is about 200 lines and has had a few bugs. The library promised automatic reconnect, health checks and metrics.

I spent the afternoon on a branch in the search API. The reconnect worked well in a manual test where I restarted Redis. But two things did not.

First, the library swallowed the errors during reconnect and only exposed a total counter, so our metric that counts failed commands per type went flat. That would blind the alerts we have for Redis problems.

Second, the pool settings were global. We need a small pool for the session store and a larger one for the cache, and the library offered only one pool per process. A workaround with two client instances worked but doubled the idle connections.

I measured the startup and the latency. Both were the same as now, so there was no gain in performance. The only benefit would have been less code, and that does not outweigh the lost visibility.

I dropped the branch and wrote a short note in the repo docs about why, so the next person does not repeat it. Our own wrapper stays. I did add one thing from the experiment: a log line at reconnect time, which the wrapper lacked.

summary: Wrote the plan for moving the nightly reindex job to the monthly index layout, with a backfill order, a dual-write phase and a rollback at each step
body:
With the benchmark and Mara's review done, the open part was how to get from the customer shards to the monthly indices without a gap in search. I wrote the migration plan in the document and went through it with the reindex code open.

The phases are:
1. Create the monthly index template and the empty indices for 13 months.
2. Backfill, starting with the newest month, from the source events, writing with the event id as document id.
3. Dual write: the ingest path indexes into both layouts for a period.
4. Switch the search API read path per customer with a flag.
5. Remove the old shards after a holding period.

For each phase I wrote what we check and how we go back. In phase 3 the check is a count comparison per customer per month between old and new, with a tolerance of zero for closed months. Rollback is just turning off the dual write and deleting the new indices.

The nightly reindex job needs a change too. Today it loops over customers. It will loop over months and then customers, and it must not run on both layouts at once or it doubles the load on the cluster. I noted that the job's schedule needs a look as well, because the backup window is close to it.

For the backfill speed I estimated from the benchmark: about 40 GB per hour with 4 bulk workers, so 13 months of 2.1 TB would take about 53 hours. That is manageable if it runs over a weekend at a reduced rate.

The plan lists three open decisions: the shard count per month, the size limit for routing, and who is on call during the switch. I asked Tobias about the last one.

Nothing here is started. This session was only the written plan.

summary: Answered Sam on how long a changed event schema takes to reach production workers: at most about a minute after the merge pipeline registers it
body:
Sam asked for a sentence for the docs: when does a new schema version take effect for customers?

I checked the chain. The merge pipeline registers the new version right after the merge. Workers refresh every 60 seconds with a version check, so each one picks it up within about a minute. Then the worker accepts events of the new version.

There are two caveats I told her about. A worker that cannot reach the registry keeps its old schemas, so a registry outage delays the change but never breaks ingest. And events of the new version sent before a worker has refreshed go to the dead letter topic, with the reason unknown version. They can be replayed.

So the advice for customers is to send events of a new version only after the announcement, not right after the merge. I suggested that the docs say a few minutes of margin.

She will add this to the docs page on schema versions. I also gave her the dead letter replay command in case a customer asks.

summary: Added alerts for registry refresh failures and dead letter growth, with thresholds taken from a week of normal values
body:
The schema refresher and the dead letter topic had no alerts, only panels. I looked at the last week of values to choose thresholds that do not cry wolf.

schema_refresh_total with result error was zero on all days except two short blips of three errors, both during a deploy of the registry. The dead letter topic gets 5 to 15 events per hour, mostly from one customer with a bad client.

I wrote three rules in the alert code repository:
- Refresh errors above 5 per 10 minutes on any worker, warning level.
- No successful refresh for 15 minutes on any worker, page level.
- Dead letter rate above 200 per hour for 30 minutes, warning level.

The second rule matters most, because a worker with an old schema can silently reject new events. I tested the rules with promtool against recorded data and with a synthetic series that crosses each threshold.

Each rule has a runbook link. I wrote the runbook text: check the registry health, check network from the task, and if needed restart the worker.

The alerts went through the normal review. Tobias approved them and they are active. The page-level rule goes to the on-call only in working hours until we see how it behaves.

summary: Postgres autovacuum fell behind on the events metadata table; tuned per-table settings and a manual vacuum cut dead tuples from 31 to 4 percent
body:
A Grafana panel showed dead tuples climbing on the table that holds import job state. About 31 percent of its rows were dead, and the queries on it were getting slower.

The table has a lot of updates, since each import job updates its progress every few seconds. The default autovacuum threshold is 20 percent of the table, which for a big table means a long wait. I looked at pg_stat_user_tables and saw the last autovacuum was almost a day old.

I set per-table parameters: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.02 and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit 1000 for this table. I then ran a manual VACUUM (VERBOSE) in a quiet time. It took 6 minutes and removed 2.4 million dead tuples. The table size on disk did not shrink, which is normal, but the new updates now reuse the space.

I also asked if the progress update frequency was needed. The loader writes it every 2 seconds. Changing that to 10 seconds would cut the churn by 80 percent. I made the change, since the console only polls every 15 seconds anyway.

After two hours the dead tuple share was 4 percent and the autovacuum had run twice on its own. I will check again in a few days.

summary: Looked into a customer's complaint of missing dashboard data and found their client sent events with timestamps in the future that the materialized view skipped
body:
Sam forwarded a ticket: a customer's dashboard showed no events for the last day, though they said they were sending. The ingest logs showed accepted batches at a normal rate, so the data was not lost at the API.

I queried ClickHouse directly for the customer. The raw events were there: 410,000 rows for the day. The daily rollup view showed zero. So the problem was between the table and the materialized view.

The cause was in the timestamps. Their client had a clock that ran 26 hours ahead, so the events were stored with a day that is tomorrow. The dashboard asks for today and earlier, so those rows never matched. The view itself worked, since the rollup for tomorrow existed.

We do not want to reject such events, because the ingest should be tolerant. But we can show them. I proposed two changes: a warning field in the ingest response when the timestamp is more than an hour in the future, and a note in the console for the customer when more than 1 percent of events are in the future.

I implemented the response warning, a small change in the validation step, with a test. The console note I described for Lena in a ticket.

I told Sam what to answer: the data is there, the client clock is wrong, and here is how to check it. She will also send the customer the documented NTP advice. Once their clock is fixed the new events will appear on the right day. The old rows stay on their future day, unless the customer asks us to shift them, which would be a manual job.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console change that shows the future timestamp warning; asked for a threshold from config and it is merged
body:
Lena built the notice in the console that appears when more than 1 percent of a customer's events carry timestamps in the future. I reviewed the pull request this evening.

The component itself was clean and the text was clear. I had two comments. The 1 percent threshold was a constant in the component, but the backend already has the value in the settings, so the console should read it from the API. Otherwise the two would drift apart.

The second was about the query. She calculated the share on the client from a list of events, which would be wrong with paging. I pointed to the new field in the stats endpoint, which returns the share directly.

She fixed both within the hour. I tried it in staging with a test customer whose events I had shifted by a day, and the notice showed up and went away after the clock was fixed in my test data.

The pull request is merged. It goes out with tomorrow's console deploy. I added a line to the ticket so Sam knows where the text lives if she wants to change the wording.

summary: Built the monthly index template and the backfill tool for the new search layout and ran it on one small month in staging, 31 GB in 52 minutes
body:
After the plan was reviewed, I started on the tools, still only on staging. The production cluster is untouched.

First the index template. It fixes the mapping for all monthly indices, with the field limit at 1,000, 4 primary shards and 1 replica, and the same analyzers as the current index, so that the search-v2 boosts behave the same. I put it into the Terraform repository as a JSON file and a small script, so that it is applied the same way everywhere.

Second, the backfill tool, a Go command with these flags: month, customer filter, worker count and rate limit. It reads the source events for one month, builds the documents and writes bulk requests of 5,000 documents. The document id is the event id, so a second run overwrites and does not duplicate. It writes a checkpoint file per month and customer, so a stopped run continues where it ended.

The routing rule from the plan is built in. For customers under the size limit it sets the routing to the customer id. For the large ones it uses the hash of customer id and day.

I ran it on a small month, 31 GB, with 4 workers. It took 52 minutes, which is about 36 GB per hour and close to the estimate. I then compared the document counts per customer between the source and the new index. They matched for all 19 customers in that month.

One problem: the bulk requests sometimes got 429 from OpenSearch when the write queue filled. The tool now backs off with jitter and halves its batch size on repeated rejects. After that, no request failed.

I also tried a query across the alias for a customer, and the results were the same as from the old layout for a set of 200 queries. Ranking differences were zero in the top 10.

Next I want to test the delete procedure on staging, as Mara asked, and then the dual write in the ingest path.

summary: Tested the customer delete procedure on the staging monthly indices: delete by query plus a targeted merge removed all rows, but took 38 minutes for 6 months
body:
Mara had asked for a test of removing a customer from the monthly layout. I used a staging customer with 6 months of data, about 9 GB.

The delete by query over the alias with the customer filter ran as a task. It deleted 3.1 million documents in 22 minutes. Searching for the customer afterwards returned nothing, but the index size had not changed, as expected, because deleted documents stay in the segments.

Then I ran a force merge with only_expunge_deletes on the six indices, one at a time. This took 16 minutes in total and the size dropped by 8.6 GB. The cluster load rose noticeably during the merge, so it should be done in a quiet window.

Total time was 38 minutes for 9 GB. For a big customer, I would expect hours. That is within the 30 days of the contract, but I wrote down that it must run as a job with a progress view, not by hand.

I added the numbers to the plan. The next step is the dual write.

summary: Dropped the unused customer_id-only index on the audit table after a week of stats showed zero scans
body:
A week ago I built the composite index for the audit export list and left the old single column index in place. I checked pg_stat_user_indexes today.

The old index had zero scans since the stats were last reset, and the composite one had about 90,000. Since the composite index starts with customer_id, it also serves queries that filter only by customer.

I dropped the old one with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It finished at once and the writes were not affected. The table's total index size fell by 410 MB, and the insert rate in the audit log is a little better.

I wrote the migration so that staging and production match, and noted the reason in the migration file. If a query turns up that needs the old index, it is a short rebuild.

summary: Implemented the dual write for the new search layout in the ingest indexing path behind a flag, with a failure counter for the new side that does not block the old
body:
The dual write sends each indexed event to the old customer shard and to the right monthly index. I added it to the indexing step as a second writer behind a flag, off by default.

The old write stays the primary. If it fails, the event is handled as before, with a retry and then the dead letter topic. The new write is best effort in this phase: if it fails, a counter, search_dualwrite_errors_total, goes up and a record with the event id goes to a small repair topic. The reason is that a problem in the new layout must never cost a customer an event.

The repair topic is read by a tool that is the backfill tool in a different mode. It rewrites the documents by id, so it is safe to repeat.

I wrote tests for four cases: both succeed, only the new fails, only the old fails, and both fail. I also tested the routing rule for a small and a large customer.

In staging I ran it with the flag on for an hour of replayed traffic. The error counter was 0, and the count per customer matched on both sides. The extra indexing load was about 30 percent on the staging cluster, which tells me the production cluster needs a look at its capacity before this runs there.

I did not turn it on in production. I asked Tobias about the capacity. The flag is documented in the plan.

summary: Tobias estimated the search cluster headroom for dual writing: 2 more data nodes are needed during the migration, about 11 percent more monthly cost
body:
Tobias came back with the capacity numbers. The current cluster runs at about 55 percent CPU at the evening peak. With a dual write adding roughly 30 percent to indexing, plus the backfill, the peak would pass 80 percent, which is too high.

His proposal is two more data nodes for the migration period only, in the same instance type. That adds around 11 percent to the monthly search cost while they run. After the old layout is removed, he thinks the cluster can shrink again, since the shard sizes are better balanced.

I asked about the disk. The new indices need space next to the old ones for about the same volume, so the disk usage roughly doubles for the data of 13 months. He confirmed that the volumes have room for about 70 percent more.

We agreed to add the nodes through Terraform before the dual write goes on in production, and to keep the backfill rate low in the first run. I added his figures and the agreed order to the plan document.

summary: Investigated an on-call page for Redis latency and found a single large key listing job scanning with a high count; changed it to smaller batches
body:
The on-call page this evening said Redis command latency p99 was above 25 ms for ten minutes. I looked at the slowlog first and found the SCAN commands from the key-count job I had added for the limiter gauge. They used a count of 10,000, which is much larger than I meant.

I had written the job with the count as a default of the client library, and the library default for that call was bigger than I assumed. Each scan call blocked Redis for several ms, and the job ran several of them back to back across the whole keyspace, not just the limiter prefix.

I changed the job in two ways. It now uses a MATCH pattern for the prefix with a count of 200, and it sleeps 20 ms between calls. A full pass takes about 40 seconds and the slowlog stays clean.

I deployed it, and the p99 fell back to 2 ms within a minute. The page resolved on its own.

The lesson for the notes: every scan job needs an explicit count and a pause. I added a comment to the job and a line to the Redis runbook. I also checked the other jobs that use scan, and the cleanup script from last week was the only other one, and it was already set low.

summary: Prepared the search dual write for one small customer in production and checked the flag, the counters and the saved searches in staging before turning it on.
body:
The two extra nodes were in place since the morning, so I spent the evening getting ready to enable the dual write flag for one small customer with about 40,000 events a day. I did not turn it on yet.

First I went through the flag path once more in the ingest indexing path. The failure counter for the new side is exported and shows 0 in Grafana, and I added a panel for the indexing latency split by old and new side. I also wrote an alert rule that pages only if the new side fails more than 1 percent of writes for ten minutes, since the new side must never block the old one. I tested this in staging by pointing the new side at a closed index, and the old side kept indexing normally while the counter rose.

Then I wrote the comparison script I want to use after the evening peak. It counts the documents for a day in the old shard and in the new monthly index, and it runs a list of saved searches against both layouts and compares the top 10 results. I built a list of 50 saved searches for the chosen customer from its real query log and ran the script against staging data, where the counts matched and the top 10 were the same in all cases.

I checked the cluster CPU, which was at 52 percent during the peak, so I expect the extra load from a single small customer to be negligible. Tomorrow I plan to enable the flag for that customer before the peak, watch the error counter and the latency, and run the comparison afterwards. If it looks clean, I will add four more small customers and a medium one later. The backfill of older months comes only after the dual write has run a few days, so I don't mix the two.

summary: Prepared the backfill of older months for the first small customers into the monthly search indices, and checked the template and mappings after a staging dry run turned up a field that changed type.
body:
Four more small customers were on the dual write after yesterday's check, and the counts matched again. Today I prepared the backfill of their older months with the backfill tool, set up for 2 workers and a low rate limit, to keep the cluster calm. I did not start it against production yet. I ran it only against the staging monthly indices with a copy of the data of two of the customers.

The first customer went through staging without a problem: 12 months, 3.4 GB, 11 minutes. The second one failed in month 7 with a mapper_parsing_exception. A payload field called amount had been a number for months and then a string in a few events after a client change. The monthly index had already mapped it as a number, so the string events were rejected.

The old layout had the same problem in principle, but it handled it with an ignore_malformed setting that I did not carry over when I wrote the new template. I checked the old mapping and confirmed that the setting was there. That was my omission.

I wrote the fix for the dynamic template for payload fields, adding ignore_malformed, and applied it to the staging indices only. Existing indices keep their old mapping, so for the affected staging month I deleted the index, recreated it with the new template and ran that month again. The count matched the source: 214,330 documents. The production template is not changed yet. I put the change in a review for tomorrow.

I also started a check in the backfill tool: before it starts, it compares the template settings with the old index settings for a list of important keys and stops if they differ. That would have caught this problem. It still needs tests for the case of a missing key.

The ignored malformed values are counted by OpenSearch in the index stats, so I added that number to a Grafana panel. For the staging copy of the second customer it was 37 documents, which is small. Next I will check whether any customer has large amounts of malformed values, because those would be invisible in search, and then plan the production run for the small customers.

summary: Prepared the backfill of the older months for the second group of small customers into the monthly search indices and checked the plan against what the first group showed.
body:
After the mapping conflict fix of this morning, I went through what the backfill for the next eight small customers would need. The tool is the same one that handled the first small customers, and I read through its logs from that run to see where it spent its time. A full pass over eight customers' months looked like about 70 minutes in staging-sized batches, so I planned to start with the oldest month of each customer and work forward.

For the checks, I wrote a small script that compares document counts per customer between the old per-customer index and the new monthly index, one month at a time. I ran it only on the customers already covered by the dual write, as a trial of the script itself. For two months the counts differed by a few hundred at first. The cause was the dual write still catching up with the evening peak, and a second count an hour later matched. I will leave an hour between the backfill and the final count for each month.

The type-change template rule held in a test on sample documents: the payload field that used to be a number and later a string is mapped as keyword with a numeric sub-field, and no document was rejected. I also added the backfill failure counter to a Grafana panel so it is visible during the run.

The tool writes a progress file per customer, so a rerun skips finished months. I tested that by killing it halfway on a small sample and restarting; it resumed at the right month and did not double any document, because document ids are deterministic.

Open points: the medium customers have months of 40 GB and more, and the tool needs a throttle for them so the search latency does not suffer. I will add a bulk size and pause setting next. Tobias should watch the data node CPU while the medium customers run.

Next step is to start the backfill for the eight small customers, then the throttle, then a dry run on one medium customer in staging. Nothing is switched for readers yet; the search API still reads the old indices.

summary: Added a throttle to the search backfill tool, with bulk size and pause between bulks, and it keeps search p95 flat in a staging test with a medium customer.
body:
The backfill of medium customers would have hit the same data nodes that serve live queries, so I added two settings to the tool: bulk size in documents and a pause in milliseconds between bulks. The defaults are 2,000 documents and 200 ms.

I also added a check that reads the search thread pool queue from the cluster stats before each bulk. If the queue is above a limit, the tool waits and tries again. The limit is configurable and starts at 20.

Test in staging: I replayed a query load of 40 requests per second from a recorded sample and ran the backfill of one 38 GB month at the same time. With the defaults the p95 of the search API stayed at 280 ms, the same as without the backfill. With the pause at zero and bulk size 10,000 it rose to 510 ms, so the throttle does matter.

The backfill itself took 97 minutes for that month with the defaults, against 52 minutes for the 31 GB month earlier without the throttle. That is slow but acceptable. With six medium customers of several months each, the plan is to run it at night over several days.

I wrote the settings into the runbook of the migration plan, with the values to start with and what to look at in Grafana: queue size, p95 of the search API, and CPU of the data nodes.

Not done: a pause button that stops the tool cleanly from outside. For now it stops on SIGTERM after the current bulk, which is enough.

Next: Tobias reviews the node CPU numbers from the staging test, then the first medium customer goes into production tonight.

summary: Prepared the first medium customer backfill into the monthly search indices: tested the throttle settings in staging, checked the old data for odd field names and planned the overnight run.
body:
I prepared the backfill for the first medium customer, which covers 7 months and about 190 GB. Nothing was run in production yet. The plan is to start in the evening at the low point of traffic, with bulk size 2,000 and pause 200 ms, the values that kept search p95 flat in the staging test.

In staging I ran the throttled tool against a copy of the three newest months of this customer and watched the search p95, the thread pool queue and the node CPU. The p95 stayed between 270 and 295 ms, the queue peaked at 6 and node CPU stayed under 55 percent. The throttle check had to wait only a few times. I think these numbers are good enough to go ahead, but the production cluster has more load from other customers, so I will keep the dashboards open during the run and stop it if p95 rises clearly.

I also looked at what could be rejected. The new template marks event_type as required for routing in the monthly index, while the old index accepted documents without it. I ran a count query on the old index for this customer and found a small number of documents in the oldest month with no event_type field. They seem to come from an early client version that sent a different field name for a few weeks. The ingest path today normalizes it, but the old data was never fixed.

Options are to relax the template or to map the old field name to event_type in the backfill tool. I lean toward the second, because the template rule is useful for the new data. I started a small transform step in the tool with a list of field renames per customer. It is not finished and not tested on real data yet.

I also began a summary line at the end of the tool run that prints rejects per month and per reason, so that I do not rely only on totals. Next: finish the transform step, test it in staging on the oldest month, and then start the production run for this customer.

summary: Answered Sam on how a customer can export their own search results, and pointed to the existing export endpoint and its 10,000 row limit.
body:
Sam asked whether a customer can get the results of a search as a file, because a customer asked support for it.

The answer is yes. The search API has an export endpoint that takes the same query as the search and returns NDJSON or CSV. It is limited to 10,000 rows per request, and above that the customer has to page with the cursor parameter. The limit is in the search API config and I did not change it.

I checked the public docs and found that the export endpoint is described, but the cursor paging is not. I wrote a short paragraph with a curl example and sent it to Sam to put into the docs.

I also noted that the export does not apply the per-field boosts of search v2, because the order does not matter for a file. Sam will mention that in the docs too, since a customer might compare the order with the console.

Nothing else changed in the code today.

summary: Fixed a Postgres slow query in the admin console's API key list, which sorted a join on text; a new index and a rewrite brought it from 2.4 s to 30 ms.
body:
Lena reported that the API keys page of the admin console takes several seconds to load for the large customers. I found the query in the slow query log: it joins api_keys with a last-used table and sorts by the key name as text.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on the last-used table, which has about 9 million rows, followed by a sort on disk. Total time was 2.4 s for a customer with 1,800 keys.

The last-used table keeps one row per use, though the console only needs the latest. I rewrote the query to take the latest row per key with a lateral join that uses an index on (key_id, used_at desc). That index did not exist, so I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It took 6 minutes on production and I saw no lock waits.

I also changed the sort: the console sorts by the lowercase name, so the query now sorts on lower(name) and a small expression index on the api_keys table covers it. For one customer it was 1,800 rows, so the effect of this one is small, but it avoids the disk sort.

Result: 30 ms for the same customer, and the plan uses an index scan in both parts. I tested three other large customers and all were below 60 ms.

The last-used table is the real problem: it grows without limit. I opened a ticket to keep only the latest row per key plus a short history, and to delete the rest in a nightly job. That is not part of this fix.

The change is deployed; Lena confirmed the page loads without delay.

summary: Checked Redis memory after the limiter TTL fix and found the search cache keys now dominate, with no key without a TTL in a full scan of the cache database.
body:
Two weeks after the limiter TTL fix I did a full check of Redis memory. Used memory is 1.9 GB and has been flat for ten days.

I scanned the keyspace with a small script, in batches of 200 to keep the load low, and grouped the keys by prefix. The search cache prefix holds 71 percent of the memory, the sessions 14 percent, the rate limiter 6 percent and the rest is small stuff.

I also counted keys without a TTL per prefix. Only the sessions prefix has some, and those are the console sessions that are refreshed by the application on use. All other prefixes have a TTL on every key.

The limiter prefix rl:key: stays near 3,000 keys, as expected after the fix. I will keep the Grafana panel for the key count.

Next I want to look at the size of single cache values for search, because a few of them are large. That is for another session.

summary: Looked at the size of cached search results in Redis and found that 3 percent of the values are over 200 KB; capped the number of cached hits per query at 50.
body:
Following the memory check, I sampled 5,000 search cache values and looked at their sizes. The median is 8 KB, the p99 is 180 KB, and about 3 percent are over 200 KB. The largest was 1.4 MB.

The big values are queries with a large page size, where the customer asks for 500 hits including the full event body. They are rarely repeated, so they take memory and rarely give a hit. I measured the hit rate for values over 200 KB and it was 9 percent, against 66 percent overall.

I changed the cache writer to skip caching when the page size is above 50 hits, and for the others it stays as is. The skip is counted in a new metric, search_cache_skipped_total, so I can see how often it applies.

I deployed it to staging first and ran the recorded query sample. The overall hit rate there dropped by 0.4 points, which is small, and the memory of the cache prefix dropped by 22 percent.

Then I deployed to production in the late evening. After the first hour, the skip counter shows about 3 percent of requests, in line with the sample. Hit rate is 65.6 percent.

I will look at the memory curve in a few days to see the real effect after the TTL has turned over the old keys.

summary: Wrote the cutover plan for moving search reads to the monthly indices, with small customers first, a per-customer flag and a count comparison before each switch.
body:
The backfill of the small customers is still running, and the dual write has only just been turned on for the first of them. Before any reads move, I wrote the cutover plan so the order is settled while the data is still filling in.

Reads go through the search API, which builds the index name from the customer. I plan to add a per-customer flag, read_layout, with the values old and monthly. The search API would resolve the flag from the settings, which are cached locally for a short time, so a switch should take effect within seconds and could be reversed as fast. I have not written that code yet; this session was only the design.

Order: first the five smallest customers, then the rest of the small ones, then the medium customers once their backfill is complete. The large customers come last and need the rule for large customers from the earlier plan.

Before each switch there will be a check: counts per month must match between the layouts, and a sample of 200 recorded queries must return the same hit ids in the first page. I do not expect differences from the new boosts, since search v2 applies the same boosts on both layouts.

After a switch I would watch p95, error rate and the empty-result rate of the customer for one day before the next group goes.

The rollback is to set the flag back to old. The dual write has to continue until all customers have been on monthly for two weeks, so the old indices stay complete.

Risks I wrote down: the filtered alias adds about 6 ms at p50 in a first test, and some customers with many months may have slower alias resolution. I will measure that with the first group.

I sent the plan to Mara for review and asked Tobias to confirm the node headroom for the read load on the new indices.

summary: Implemented the per-customer read_layout flag in the search API and the query comparison script; both are tested in staging and not yet used in production.
body:
I built the first part of the cutover plan: the flag and the comparison script.

In the search API, the index resolver now reads read_layout from the customer settings. For old it returns the per-customer index as before, for monthly it returns the alias of the customer on the monthly indices, filtered by customer id. The default stays old, so nothing changes without a flag.

Unit tests cover the resolver for both values and for a missing setting. I also added a test that an unknown value falls back to old and logs a warning, rather than failing the query.

The comparison script takes a customer and a file of recorded queries. For each query it runs both layouts and compares the total hit count and the ids of the first page. It prints the differences with the query text. I ran it in staging for three customers with 200 queries each.

Two customers had no differences. The third had 7 queries with different hit ids at positions 8 to 10. The scores there were equal, and the order of ties depends on the shard where the document is, which differs between the layouts. That is not a real difference, but it would confuse the check, so I changed the script to compare the first page as sets when the scores are tied.

With that change all three customers pass.

I also added the layout to the search API log lines and as a label on the latency histogram, so the Grafana panel can show both layouts side by side.

Not yet done: the admin console shows the customer's settings, and Lena needs to add the flag as read-only there so that support can see it. I opened the request.

Next is the review by Mara and then the switch of the first five customers.

summary: Prepared the first switch of five small customers to the monthly search indices: count checks, a query comparison and a fix for one backfilled month, with the switch itself still ahead.
body:
After Mara's review of the read_layout flag and the comparison script, I spent the afternoon getting the first group ready. I have not set the flag for any customer yet, and all customers still read from the old layout.

I picked the five smallest customers for the first group and ran the count check for them. All months matched, including the months from the first backfill. Then I ran the comparison script with 200 recorded queries per customer against both layouts in staging and against the production clusters in read-only mode. Four customers showed no differences. The fifth had 3 queries that returned fewer hits on the monthly layout. I looked into it and found that one month had been backfilled before the type fix, so 3 documents with a string in the changed field were missing from the monthly index. I reran that month with the template rule, and the check for that customer then passed.

I also prepared the Grafana board. It now shows the error rate, the empty-result rate and the p50 and p95 latency per layout, split by customer, so a change after a switch is easy to see. In staging the p50 on the monthly layout was about 6 ms higher than on the old one, so I wrote 6 ms down as the number to expect and anything much above it as a reason to stop.

I also noticed that the first query to an alias in staging took about 600 ms, because the alias was not yet in the cluster's cache. It was gone after a minute. I will warm the aliases with one query per customer before the switch, so no customer sees it.

I told Sam the plan: five customers first, one at a time with ten minutes between them, and a rollback that is a flag change which engineering does. Sam will add a note to the internal support doc once the switch has really happened.

Tomorrow, if the day stays quiet, I will repeat the count check right before the first switch and then go through the five customers in order.

summary: Traced 212 documents with a missing event type in the first medium customer backfill to an old client version, and planned a default fix in the backfill tool.
body:
The first medium customer backfill left 212 documents without an event type in the monthly indices, so I looked at the source rows in the old customer-based index. All of them came from one week, from before the schema registry made the field required, when an old client version sent batches without a type. The old layout accepted them because its mapping did not require the field, and the new template rule rejects nothing but also does not fill it.

I wrote down the plan for the backfill tool: a rule that sets the type to unknown for documents without one and writes a counter of how many it touched. I tried the rule on a copy of the affected month in staging, and the counts matched the old layout, with 212 documents carrying the unknown type. The production month has not been touched yet, and I will re-run it after a review of the rule. The dual write path is not affected, since current events always have a type. Next I will check the other medium customers for the same gap before their backfill starts, with a count query per month.

summary: Designed and tested a bounded retry with backoff for the new side of the search dual write, limited to 429 bulk rejections, and left the production rollout for later.
body:
The 41 lost documents of last week showed that the new side of the dual write drops a bulk on a rejection. The old side is the one that matters for the customer, so a failure there is handled by the existing queue logic. For the new side I wanted a bounded retry, and today I wrote it and tested it, without turning it on anywhere in production.

In the indexing path I added a retry only for the rejection status 429 from OpenSearch, which means the write queue is full. Other errors, like mapping errors, are not retried because they would fail again. The retry waits 200 ms, then 800 ms, then 3 s, with random jitter of up to 25 percent. After the third try the bulk is dropped and the failure counter increases, as before.

The retry runs in a separate goroutine with a small buffer of 64 bulks, so it does not hold up the old side. If the buffer is full, the bulk is dropped and counted under a different label, dropped_full, so I can tell the two cases apart.

Tests: a unit test with a fake client that returns 429 twice and then succeeds, one where it always returns 429, and one for a mapping error that must not retry. I also ran a staging test with a bulk load that produces rejections on purpose by reducing the write queue size. In that test 96 percent of the rejected bulks succeeded after a retry, and the rest were counted as failed.

The change is behind the same flag as the dual write, and that flag is still off for the monthly indices in production, so nothing is deployed yet. I wrote down what to watch in the first hour after the rollout: the retry count, the two drop labels and the failure counter. The count check before any switch stays, as the retry is bounded and does not give a guarantee. The ingest-batching work on the worker side is separate and does not touch this code.

summary: Prepared the last seven small customers for the switch to the monthly search layout and checked the alias cost for customers with many months, without switching anyone yet.
body:
I ran the count check and the failure counter check for the seven customers left in the small group. All counts matched and the counters were at zero since the retry change on the dual write. Eight small customers are in the group that is already prepared, and these seven are the last ones. No small customer reads from the monthly indices yet. I have not switched any of them, and the first switch of five small customers is still ahead. The plan is to do it in two steps with a half hour in between, and to look at the error rate and the latency per layout after each step.

I also went through the latency numbers from the staging comparison runs on the monthly layout. For the test queries, p50 is about 6 ms higher than on the old layout and p95 is about 18 ms higher. The empty-result rate is the same, which is what I wanted to see before touching any production customer.

One customer with many months, 31, has a p95 of 260 ms in the comparison, which is higher than the others. The alias resolution with 31 indices costs more. I noted that for the rule for large customers: customers with many months might need a different alias setup, and I will write up the findings so the rule is ready before the large customers come up.

The medium customers are still being backfilled, and three of them have finished. They come after the small group, so I did not touch them today. Next I will switch the small customers following the two-step plan.

summary: Wrote down the findings on alias cost for customers with many months and proposed a rolling alias for the latest 6 months in addition to the full one.
body:
The customer with 31 months had a p95 of 260 ms on the monthly layout. I took a look at why.

I ran the slow queries against staging copy of this customer's data. The query itself is fast in each index, about 4 ms. The cost comes from the search touching 31 indices, each with a shard, and the coordinating node merging 31 partial results. For queries with a time filter of the last 7 days, the search still goes to all indices, because the alias does not know about the time range.

The API already adds a range filter on the timestamp, and OpenSearch can skip shards whose range cannot match, but only when the field is indexed with the can_match phase active for the request. In our case this works only for the pre-filter step above a threshold of shards, which is 128 by default, so with 31 it does not trigger.

Two options:
- Lower the pre_filter_shard_size for these requests, so shards are skipped early.
- Add a second alias for the latest 6 months, and let the API use it when the time filter is inside that range.

I tested the first option in staging. With pre_filter_shard_size set to 1 the p95 for this customer went from 260 to 215 ms, with a small overhead for the customers with few months. The second option gave 170 ms, but needs the API to decide on the alias, and the alias needs a job to roll it every month.

My proposal is to do the first one now for all, because it is a request parameter, and to build the rolling alias for the large customers later. I wrote this into the plan document and asked Mara for her view.

summary: Prepared the pre_filter_shard_size setting for search requests on the monthly layout and tested it in staging; the production rollout is still ahead.
body:
Mara agreed to the first option from the alias analysis, so I started on the change, but only in code and staging today.

In the search API, the request builder now sets pre_filter_shard_size to 1 when the layout is monthly. It is behind a config value, search.prefilter_shards, so that I can change it later without a deployment of code. For the old layout nothing changes. The flag is off by default and nothing in production reads it yet.

I tested it in staging with the recorded query sample of three customers with 6, 14 and 31 months. The results at p95 were 120 to 118 ms, 175 to 160 ms and 260 to 215 ms. For the customer with 6 months the difference is within the noise, as expected. The coordinating node CPU in staging went down by about 4 percent, as fewer shards are searched.

I looked for side effects. The pre-filter phase adds a round trip to the shards, which adds a few milliseconds when no shard can be skipped. For a query without a time filter, which is rare, p50 went up by 2 ms in staging. I think this is acceptable, but I want to see it with real traffic before I say so for sure.

I also checked that the results are the same. The comparison script ran for the 31-month customer with 300 queries and found no differences in the totals or the first page.

Open: the rolling alias for large customers. It is in the plan, but it is not needed for the small and medium ones. I will decide when the large customers are next.

Next: write the rollout steps for the setting, pick a quiet window for the first customers on the monthly layout, and watch p95 and the coordinating node CPU while I switch it on. After that come the medium customers: three are ready for the count check, and the other three finish their backfill in the next nights.

summary: Prepared the switch of the three finished medium customers to monthly search reads: ran the count checks and the 300-query comparison, and planned the shard sizing for the heaviest month.
body:
Three of the medium customers had finished their backfill, so today I ran the checks that come before a switch. I did not switch any of them yet.

The count check passed for two. For the third, the current month was short by 6 documents, and the dual write failure counter showed 6 dropped_full events during a burst. I reran the current month for it, and the counts matched afterwards.

The comparison script with 300 queries per customer found no differences in hit totals or ids for any of the three. That part looks clean.

While looking at the third customer's indices to decide the order, I noticed that its largest month holds 62 GB in a single primary shard, because the template uses one primary shard per monthly index. Queries that hit that month will probably be slower, since one shard does all the work for it. The old layout had the data spread over several shards in the customer index. The plan has a rule for large customers, but it was written for the large ones, not for medium ones with a heavy month.

I tried a split of a copy of the 62 GB index to 3 shards in staging with the split API. It needs the index to be read-only for the time, and it took 41 minutes. The same test queries went from 300 to 245 ms on the split copy, compared with the single shard copy.

Plan: change the template so the shard count depends on the expected monthly size, stored per customer, and do that first, since new months matter most. Then split the existing big months of this customer in a quiet window. I will switch the three customers one at a time with 30 minutes between them, and I want to hold the third until its heavy month is sorted out, or at least watch its p95 against the agreed limit of 400 ms. I told Tobias about the split window.

summary: Changed the monthly index template so the primary shard count follows the expected monthly size per customer, with one shard per 25 GB.
body:
Following the oversized shard of the medium customer, I changed how new monthly indices are created.

The template now reads an expected size from the customer settings, and a small job that creates the next month's indices before the month starts picks the shard count as the size divided by 25 GB, rounded up, with a minimum of one. For customers without a value the default is one shard.

I filled in values for the six medium customers based on their last three months. The customer with the 62 GB month gets 3 shards for the next month.

I tested the job in staging for next month's indices and checked the resulting settings with the cat indices API. The shard counts were as expected. The existing months are not changed by this, and the split is still to be done.

summary: Planned the split of the oversized 62 GB monthly index of the medium customer into 3 shards and checked the disk space, the runbook steps and the comparison script, without running anything yet.
body:
I prepared the split of the oversized monthly index for the medium customer, which I want to do in a quiet window late in the evening, when traffic is at its lowest. Nothing has been split yet. Today was only the preparation.

The plan has these steps: set the index to read-only through the block setting, run the split API from 1 to 3 shards into a new index, wait for green, compare counts, then move the alias to the new index and remove the old one after a check. The customer's reads are served from the alias, so the API should not notice the switch. I checked how the dual write behaves: it sends current writes to the current month, which is a different index, so the read-only block on this month should not affect any live write. I read through the write path once more to be sure about this, and I will watch the write rejections during the split.

I also looked at the cost of the split on the cluster. The split needs free disk equal to the index size on the nodes, and one node has only 30 percent free. For a 62 GB index this is fine, but the allocation decides where the new shards go, so I want to see the disk numbers again just before I start. For the large customers this will be a real limit and must be checked in advance. I added a disk check to the runbook as a first step.

I wrote the split commands into the runbook so that Tobias can run them too, and I ran the comparison script with 300 queries for the customer against the current index to have a baseline: p95 is about 300 ms and p50 is about 52 ms. After the split I will run the same script again and compare counts, which are 118,402,331 documents now.

The plan for the old index is to keep it for a day after the alias move, without the alias pointing to it, in case something turns up. Two other months of the customer, 38 and 41 GB, would be split into 2 shards each in the same way afterwards.

Next: do the split of the 62 GB month in the window, then the two smaller months, then the other three medium customers go through the checks.

summary: Reviewed the first part of Mara's audit export branch, found that the export reads the whole audit table without a keyset and asked for a cursor on id and time.
body:
Mara asked for a review of the audit-export branch. The compliance export lets a customer download their audit log for a time range as a file.

What I looked at: the export query, the file writer, the endpoint and the tests. The file writer streams NDJSON and gzip, which is good, because it keeps the memory flat. The endpoint authenticates with the customer's admin key and checks the scope.

Main problem: the query uses OFFSET and LIMIT for paging through the table. For a customer with 4 million audit rows, the later pages get slow, because Postgres has to skip all earlier rows. I tested it on a staging copy: page 1 took 12 ms, page 400 took 1.9 s, and the whole export would take 14 minutes. It also can skip or repeat rows when new audit entries come in during the export.

I asked for keyset paging on (created_at, id), which uses the composite index that we built recently for the list. The next page starts where the last one ended, so each page costs the same. I wrote the query in my review comment:

WHERE (created_at, id) > ($1, $2) AND customer_id = $3 ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 5000

Second point: the export is synchronous in the HTTP request. For large ranges, the load balancer timeout of 60 s will cut the connection. I suggested to make the export a job that writes the file to object storage and gives the customer a link, with the state in a table. Mara said she had planned that as a second step, and we agreed that it may come in the same branch before the merge.

Smaller points: the file name has the customer id but not the range; the time range limit is not checked, so someone can ask for ten years; and the error response on a bad range is a 500 where it should be a 400 with a message.

What I liked: the tests use a seeded table with 50,000 rows and compare the file content with the expected output, including a customer boundary check, so that no other customer's rows are in the file.

I approved with changes, with the keyset paging as a must and the job as a before-merge item. Mara will push the update next week and I will look at it again.

summary: Mara's audit export now pages by keyset and the same staging customer exports in 31 seconds instead of 14 minutes; I found one tie-break bug at equal timestamps.
body:
Mara pushed the keyset change to the audit-export branch and I reviewed again and ran it on the staging copy.

The test customer with 4 million audit rows now exports in 31 seconds. Each page of 5,000 rows takes about 35 ms, and it does not grow with the position. The memory of the process stays at 90 MB during the export.

I then tried edge cases. One was an export while new audit rows are written. I ran a script that inserts 20 rows per second during the export. The file contained all rows that existed at the start and some of the new ones, but no duplicates, which is the behavior we want. The export also records the upper bound of the time range at the start, so a later row is not included.

The bug I found: the row comparison for the next page uses (created_at, id) but the id is a UUID in this table, and the ORDER BY is on created_at and id as text in one place and as uuid in another. With equal timestamps, which happen when a batch action writes several rows in the same transaction, the order differed, and 3 rows were skipped in my test of 1,000 rows with the same timestamp.

The fix is to use the same type in both places. I wrote a failing test first, with 1,000 rows of identical created_at, and Mara changed the cast. The test passes now, and the count matches exactly.

The job part is in the branch too. The export creates a row in an export_jobs table with the state queued, running, done or failed, a worker picks it up and writes the file to the object store, and the customer gets a signed link that is valid for 24 hours. I tested the whole flow in staging: a request, a poll, the link and the download. The file's checksum matched the one in the table.

What is still open:
- The cleanup of old files after 7 days is not there yet; the bucket has a lifecycle rule in the plan, but Tobias has not added it.
- The 400 response on a bad range is fixed, and the limit is 2 years.
- The docs for the endpoint are missing, and Sam will write them when the branch is merged.

I approved the branch for merge after the lifecycle rule exists. I asked Tobias for it in the infrastructure repo.

summary: Checked the backfills of the last three medium customers and prepared their switch to monthly search reads, which I have not done yet.
body:
The backfills of the last three medium customers finished over the nights, so I started with the checks and left the switch for later.

Before anything else I ran the rejects summary of the backfill tool for each customer. Two customers had no rejects. The third had 58 rejects in a month from a payload field that was an object in some old events and a string in others. The template rule for the type change did not cover that case, because it was an object. I added a rule to map the field as flattened, reran that month, and had 0 rejects.

The count check passed for all three, and the failure counters were at zero. The comparison script ran with 300 queries per customer and found no differences.

I looked at the month sizes, because of the earlier experience with oversized shards. One customer had months of 55 GB and 48 GB in a single shard, and the other two were below 30 GB. I wrote down the two big months as candidates for a split into 2 shards each and went through the runbook steps for a split in the quiet window of the evening. I have not run any split yet. I want the split done before the reads move, so the latency does not rise the way it did for the earlier customer.

I also prepared the switch itself: the read flag change for the three customers, with 30 minutes planned between them, and a list of the p95 and p50 dashboards I will watch. The three customers still read from the old indices, and the dual write continues, so nothing has to be rolled back.

Tobias looked at the node disk and CPU as a baseline before the splits. Disk use is at 61 percent with the two extra nodes, CPU peak at 58 percent. He said that is fine for now, but the large customers will need another look at the disk, since their months are several hundred GB.

I updated the migration document with the check results and the plan for the splits.

Next: do the two splits in the evening window, then switch the three customers one at a time and compare the latency.

summary: Measured month sizes of the five large customers for the shard layout; the biggest month is 410 GB, which will need 17 shards by the 25 GB rule.
body:
I queried the old indices for the five large customers and summed the size per month for the last 12 months.

The largest month is 410 GB for the biggest customer. The 25 GB per shard rule would give 17 primary shards for it, which is a lot for one index but not unusual. The other four customers have peak months of 120, 95, 80 and 66 GB, which gives 5, 4, 4 and 3 shards.

The growth over the year is about 3 percent per month for the biggest one, so the sizes will not change the picture soon.

The alias question remains open: with 12 or more months of 17 shards, a customer alias covers about 150 shards. The pre-filter setting helps, and the rolling alias for the latest 6 months probably becomes necessary here. I will test it on the 120 GB customer first, as that is the lowest risk of the five. I noted these numbers in the plan document.

summary: Measured the five large customers' months against the 25 GB rule and drafted a migration order that starts with the one with the smallest biggest month
body:
Yesterday's measurement gave the biggest month as 410 GB, so today I turned the numbers into a plan for the five large customers. Together they have 140 monthly indices by the current data, and with the 25 GB rule that adds up to 402 primary shards. The old layout had 5 big per-customer indices with 60 shards in all.

The shard count is the concern. Tobias had said the cluster is comfortable up to about 1,000 shards per node group with the current heap, so 402 is fine for the data nodes, but the cluster state gets bigger and the mapping updates get slower. I checked the cluster state size in staging with 300 test indices and it was 38 MB, which is acceptable.

The order I proposed: the customer whose biggest month is 96 GB goes first, since it needs at most 4 shards per month and a problem would be cheap to fix. Then the two with biggest months near 200 GB. The customer with the 410 GB month goes last, because its backfill needs a throttled run over several nights.

I also estimated backfill time at the throttled rate we use now. For the 410 GB month it is about 9 hours, and the whole large group about 6 nights if one customer is done per night. I wrote this into the planning doc and left open the question of whether to split the 17-shard months further by event type.

Next step is a staging test of one large month with 17 shards to see the query fan-out cost.

summary: Staging test of a 410 GB month on 17 shards: query fan-out adds latency for narrow queries, so a routing key by event type is worth testing
body:
Built a staging copy of the largest month with 17 primary shards using the backfill tool and ran the standard query set of 40 queries against it. Wide queries over the whole month were faster than on the old layout, 1.9 s against 3.1 s at p95. Narrow queries with a filter on one event type got slower: 85 ms against 52 ms at p50, because every query still hits all 17 shards.
