The cause is plain fan-out. Each shard has a fixed cost for the request, and a narrow query gains nothing from having 17 of them. The same effect showed up on the medium customers, only smaller.

I tried custom routing by event type in the template, so that documents of one type land on a subset of shards. With routing on, the narrow queries dropped to 61 ms at p50. The downside is that a very common event type makes uneven shards. In the test the biggest type made one group of shards 2.4 times the size of the others.

So the result is mixed. Routing helps narrow queries and hurts balance. I did not change the template yet. I wrote down the numbers and will ask Mara whether the search API can tell from the query when routing applies, since it already parses the type filter.

Open: routing partition size and how the delete procedure works with routed documents.

summary: Mara confirmed the search API parser knows the event type filter before the request goes out, so routing by type is possible without a new query path
body:
Asked Mara about the routing idea over chat and then looked at the parser together. The v2 query parser already extracts a list of event types from the filter part into a field on the parsed query. It is used today for the boosts. So passing it as a routing value is a small change, about 20 lines in the request builder.

Two cases need a rule. A query with several types would go to the union of the routed shard groups, which OpenSearch supports by a comma separated routing value. A query without a type filter has no routing and goes to all shards, as now.

Mara raised a fair point: if a customer sends a new event type that was never seen, the routing value just hashes to some shards, which is fine for correctness. Only the balance is affected.

I will implement it behind a flag in the request builder and compare in staging with the large month again. Not touching the template until the numbers are in. Mara will review the builder change tomorrow.

summary: Implemented the optional routing value in the search request builder behind a flag, with a unit test for single, multiple and missing event types
body:
Added the routing value to the request builder in the search API. When the flag search_route_by_type is on and the parsed query has event types, the builder sets the routing parameter to the comma joined list. Without types, nothing is set.

Tests cover three cases: one type, three types, and no type. A fourth test checks that the flag off leaves the request exactly as before, which I compared by snapshot against the existing request fixtures. All pass.

One detail came up: the types in the parsed query are lower cased by the parser, but the ingest side writes the original case into the routing value if routing is on at index time. That would make the values differ for any customer with mixed case types. I normalized to lower case in the builder and added a note to do the same in the indexing path before routing is turned on in a template.

The flag is off in all environments. Staging comparison is next.

summary: Compared routed and unrouted queries on the staging large month: narrow queries went from 85 to 58 ms at p50, wide queries stayed the same
body:
Turned on the flag in staging and rebuilt the large month with routing by lower cased event type at index time. Ran the same 40 queries three times each.

Narrow queries with one type: p50 58 ms, p95 140 ms, against 85 and 210 before. Queries with three types: p50 71 ms. Queries without a type: unchanged, 1.9 s at p95 for the wide ones.

Shard balance is the cost. The largest shard is 2.1 times the average. The single most common event type makes up 38 percent of that customer's events and all of them go to the same small group of shards. With 17 shards that is a hot spot, but the 25 GB rule still holds for the average, and the largest shard came out at 41 GB.

A possible fix is routing partition size in the template, which spreads one routing value over several shards. I will try a partition size of 3 next. This is a staging test only.

summary: Routing partition size of 3 evened out the large month shards to 1.3 times the average, with narrow queries at 64 ms p50
body:
Set the index routing partition size to 3 in the staging template and rebuilt the large month. The biggest shard is now 1.3 times the average, 32 GB, which is much closer to the rule. Narrow queries run at 64 ms p50 and 155 ms p95, slightly slower than without partitioning, since each type now spans 3 shards instead of one group, but still better than the unrouted 85 ms.

One thing to know: with a partition size set, the number of shards has to be a multiple-compatible setting. OpenSearch checks that routing_partition_size is smaller than the number of shards, and the template for small months with 1 shard would fail. So the setting must only apply for months with more than 3 shards. I put the setting into a second template with higher priority that matches only the large customers' indices.

The delete by query test still passes on the routed month, as deletes search all shards by customer.

Tomorrow I will write up the routing decision for the other large customers.

summary: Answered Sam's question about what customers will notice when the monthly index layout goes live, and drafted a short note for support.
body:
Sam asked whether customers will see anything different once the customers read from the monthly indices. The migration has not started in production yet. So far only the staging runs and the planning exist, and the first production backfill is still ahead. I explained what the plan looks like from the customer side: results, order and the export endpoint should not change. The staging comparisons gave the same hits in the same order for the test queries, and the p95 difference was a few milliseconds, not something a customer would notice.

The one visible difference will be the index names in internal logs and in the debug output of the admin console. They will carry a year-month suffix after the customer name. I told Sam to expect that and to note it in the support docs now, so nobody takes it for an error when it shows up in tickets. I also said we would tell the support channel before each customer is switched, so Sam can match any ticket to the migration order. Sam will draft the note, and I will check it before it goes into the docs.

summary: Wrote and tested the large-customer template with routing partitions and ran the first large customer's oldest 8 months into staging in one pass
body:
Wrote the second index template for large customers: shard count follows the 25 GB rule, routing partition size 3 for anything over 3 shards, and the same mapping rules as the small template including the fix for the payload field that changed type. A script generates the primary shard count from the measured month size, and I checked it against the table from the measurement: the biggest month gets 17, the smaller ones 2 to 9.

Then I ran the backfill tool for the large customer with the smallest biggest month, for its oldest 8 months, into staging with the production throttle settings. It took 3 hours 10 minutes for 214 GB. The counts match in all months.

Two findings. First, the tool did not set the routing value, because it copied documents with the plain bulk action. Documents landed on shards by id hash, which is not what the template expects for routed queries. Queries with routing returned only part of the documents. I found this when the narrow query count came out at 61 percent of the expected number. The fix was one line in the bulk action builder to add the lower cased event type as routing. I reran the 8 months and the counts match now for routed queries too.

Second, the same lower case rule must be in the indexing path of the dual write. I checked the code and it uses the raw event type. I changed it to lower case, with a test, but behind the same flag so nothing changes for the existing monthly indices.

The lesson for the plan: any new write path must set routing the same way, or the routed queries lose documents silently. I added this to the cutover checklist as a count comparison with routing on.

Not done: production backfill. The next step is a review of the routing change by Mara and then a first production night for the smallest large customer.

summary: Mara's review of the audit export: the cursor works, but the file is built in memory and a 2 million row export used 1.8 GB of heap
body:
Reviewed the next part of the audit export branch. The keyset paging from last week holds, and the tie-break fix is in. I ran the export for the largest staging customer with 2 million audit rows and watched memory of the export process.

The heap went up to 1.8 GB, because the code collects all pages into one array and then serializes to CSV. Production tasks for the export job have a 1 GB limit, so this would be killed. I asked Mara to stream the pages into the output as they arrive.

She made the change in the afternoon: each page is written to a gzip stream that goes straight to the S3 upload with multipart parts of 8 MB. I ran the same export again: heap stayed under 140 MB, runtime 4 minutes 20 seconds, and the file is 96 MB compressed.

I checked the output for correctness. Row count matches the table count for the period, the order is by time and id, and the header line is there. One difference: timestamps were written in local time of the process in one path, and in UTC in the other, the one used by the streaming path. The compliance format should be UTC, so I told Mara and she fixed the remaining path and added a test with a timezone set in the test environment.

Open points: the export of a customer with zero rows writes only the header and should probably still produce a file, which it does. Failure in the middle of the upload leaves an incomplete multipart upload, so we need a lifecycle rule for aborted uploads on the bucket. I will ask Tobias for it.

The branch is closer to done. What is left is the signed link for the download and the audit entry for the export itself.

summary: Asked Tobias for a bucket lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after 2 days, for the audit export
body: Wrote the request to Tobias with the reason: the streaming audit export uses multipart uploads, and a job that dies in the middle leaves parts that are billed but never visible. He added the rule to the Terraform of the export bucket this morning, abort after 2 days, and applied it to staging first. I checked with the CLI that the rule is listed on the bucket. Production apply follows in the normal Terraform run. I also checked that there are no old incomplete uploads in staging, and there are none. Nothing else needed from my side.

summary: Mara's review of the routing change: she accepted it and asked for a metric that counts routed against unrouted search requests
body: Mara reviewed the routing change in the request builder and the backfill tool. She accepted both and had one request: a Prometheus counter with a label routed true or false, so that after the cutover we can see how many queries benefit and spot a drop that would mean the parser stopped finding types. I added search_requests_total with that label in the builder and a panel in the search Grafana board. In staging the panel shows about 70 percent routed in the replayed query set. No other changes were needed.

summary: Prepared the first production backfill for the smallest large customer's oldest 12 months into the monthly layout and tested the routing setup in staging.
body:
Spent the evening getting ready for the first production backfill of the smallest large customer, planned for the next night after the evening peak. The plan is the same throttle as for the medium customers: a bulk size of 500 and a 400 ms pause between bulks. The backfill tool now sets the routing value on each document, and I checked that in staging by loading two months and reading back a sample of documents with a routed query.

I wrote down the count comparison I will run afterwards: counts per month against the old layout, plus a routed narrow query for the three most common event types. I also added a panel to the Grafana board that shows search p95 for all customers next to the bulk rate, so a slowdown during the run is visible at a glance. The template for large customers is applied in staging only. Applying it in production is the first step tomorrow, and I wrote the steps down so Tobias can check them.

From the staging run I estimate about 4 hours for 290 GB. If p95 for other customers moves by more than 15 ms, I will stop the tool and halve the bulk size. Nothing has been written to the monthly layout in production yet. The remaining months of this customer would take two more nights after that.

summary: Compared counts for the smallest large customer's backfill and found 9 documents in one month that exist only in the old layout, which I plan to investigate next.
body:
The second and third nights of backfill finished all months of the first large customer. The per-month count comparison showed one mismatch: 9 documents missing from the monthly index of a month three months back. Every other month matched exactly, including the routed queries.

I looked at the dual write failure counter history for that period. The 9 documents were written on a day before the retry with backoff was added to the dual write, and the counter shows one rejected bulk of 9 documents at that time. So the new side most likely lost them, as we feared back then, and the backfill had already passed this month before that day's writes, which explains the gap.

I have not changed anything in the index yet. The backfill tool has a skip-existing mode that only adds documents whose id is missing, and I read through its code to confirm it does not touch documents that are already there and that it handles a single month on its own. I wrote down the command for that one month and the expected result, 9 added documents and equal counts afterwards, so I can check it against the output when I run it.

The gap also raises a wider question. If one rejected bulk slipped through, other customers may have the same problem. I exported the failure counter history for the whole period since the dual write started and began going through it day by day. It shows a few more days with rejected bulks, all of them before the retry change. I have not yet matched them to customers. Some of those customers may already read from the new layout, and that would make them more urgent than the large one.

Next I will map each of those days to its customer and months, then decide the order of the skip-existing runs. I also want to add a skip-existing run just before the switch to the cutover checklist. I will talk to Sam once I know which customers are affected, in case a ticket comes in about missing events.

summary: Prepared the first large customer for the switch to monthly search reads by comparing counts, replaying a day of real queries against both layouts and writing down the plan, without switching yet.
body:
The first large customer was nearly ready: the backfill had finished, the 9 missing documents from the rejected bulk were fixed, and the skip-existing run was clean. Before any switch I wanted proof that the two layouts agree, so I replayed its last day of real search queries against both layouts with the comparison script. 18,400 queries, and the hit counts were identical in all of them. The top ten results matched in all but 3 queries, where equal scores lead to a different order. That already happens between runs on the old layout, so it is not a layout effect.

I did not change the read_layout flag for this customer. The flag stays on the old layout for now. The plan is to set it after the evening peak, so that I can watch the first traffic of the next morning as well. I also wrote down what to look at in the first hour: p95 against the value of the week before at the same time of day, the routed share (74 percent of this customer's queries could be routed), query errors and the search thread pool queue on the data nodes. Narrow queries with routing should be the main gain, but the shard count per search request will be higher, so the queue is the number I care about most.

One thing I found while reading the code: the Redis cache key for search results includes the index layout name. A switch will therefore invalidate this customer's cached results, and the hit rate, now around 61 percent, will dip until the cache fills again. I will schedule the switch for the quiet time so the dip happens when nobody searches, and I added the point to the checklist.

Next: decide the exact time of the switch with Mara, and look at the two customers with the biggest months near 200 GB, whose backfill is not yet planned in detail.

summary: Prepared the morning check of the first large customer's move to monthly search reads by listing which boards and numbers to compare, without any switch having happened yet.
body: Looked at the boards for the first large customer to set a baseline before the switch. The morning peak ran with p95 between 380 and 400 ms on the old per-customer layout, and that is the number I will compare against later. The Redis hit rate for its search keys sits at 60 percent. I wrote down the key naming of the search cache, because the new routing will change the key names and I expect a short dip in the hit rate that has nothing to do with the data. The routed counter Mara asked for is in place and shows 73 percent of this customer's requests as routed in the staging replay, so I noted which requests are still unrouted and why. No errors and no slow query log entries beyond the normal few. I told Tobias what CPU load the data nodes usually have at peak, so he can tell if anything differs later. The backfill of the second large customer starts tonight, and I checked the disk space on the data nodes for it.

summary: Dropped the alias per customer for old months from the search request path and used a month range filter on the index list instead, which cut the request setup time
body:
While reading the traces of the large customer I noticed that the request setup in the search API takes 14 ms at p50 for customers with many months. The cause is the alias: the full alias of a customer with 40 months resolves to 40 indices on every request, and the cluster resolves the alias expression each time.

The idea was to send the explicit index list instead, built in the API from the time range of the query. A query for the last 7 days only needs the current and the previous month. I implemented a function in the request builder that takes the time range and returns the list of monthly index names for the customer, clipped to the months that exist. The list of existing months comes from a small cache in memory, refreshed every 5 minutes from the cat indices call.

Results in staging with the 31 month customer: for a 7 day query, shards searched fell from 74 to 5, and p50 went from 96 to 41 ms. For an unbounded query nothing changes, it still uses the full alias.

The risk is a month that was just created and is not yet in the memory list. A document written at the start of a new month could be missed for up to 5 minutes. I handled this by always adding the current month and the next month to the list when the range reaches today. A test covers the month change with a mocked clock.

I also thought about the rolling alias for the latest 6 months that I proposed earlier. The explicit list makes it unnecessary for time bounded queries, so I will not build the rolling alias unless the numbers say otherwise.

The change is behind a flag, off by default. I will test it against the replay of real queries tomorrow and compare counts for all ranges used by the dashboards.

summary: Replayed a day of real queries against the explicit month list: counts equal in all but 6 queries, which all had a range that ended in the future
body: Ran the replay for the large customer and two medium ones with the explicit index list flag on and compared hit counts with the alias path. Of 41,000 queries, 6 differed. All six had an upper time bound some hours in the future, set by a client with a clock that runs ahead. The month clipping logic cut the list at the current month when the bound was in the next month but the next month index did not exist yet, which is correct, but the old alias path returned the same documents, so the difference was in the count of an empty next month. Looking closer, the real difference was a document with a timestamp in the future, written by the same client, which lives in the next month index that the dual write had already created. My list included the next month only when the range reached today, not when it went beyond. I changed the rule to include every existing month up to the end of the range. After that, all 41,000 matched.

summary: Prepared the rollout of the explicit month list for the customers on the monthly layout and checked the replay and the empty-range case before switching anything.
body:
With the replay of a day of real queries clean, I did not turn the flag on for anyone today. Instead I wrote down the order for the rollout: first the 6 medium customers at midday, then the whole group on the monthly layout after the evening peak has been checked, with a watch on the boards until the peak is over.

I took the numbers from the shadow runs to see what to expect. On the replay, the explicit month list lowered the count of shards searched per request by about 60 percent on average, and in the shadow queries p50 went from 74 to about 55 ms and p95 from 310 to about 275 ms. For the customer with 31 months the p95 in the shadow run was around 150 ms against 212 ms now. These are shadow numbers only, so I wrote them in the plan as a hope and not as a result.

The dashboards of the admin console use time bounded queries with ranges of 24 hours to 30 days, and these should gain the most. Lena asked whether the activity panel of the console would get faster; I told her it should, but only after the flag is on, and that I will tell her when it is.

One problem showed up in the replay. A query with a range starting before the customer's first month gave an empty result. The month list clip returns an empty list when the range lies entirely before the first existing index, and the builder then sends an empty index expression. The expression is always prefixed with the customer name, so the empty list leaves only the prefix wildcard, which matches this customer only. No data of other customers is exposed, and the result was empty because of the time filter. Still I do not like an empty list falling through to a wildcard. I changed the builder in my branch to return an immediate empty response when the list is empty, and added a test for it. I searched the logs of the last two hours for requests with this shape: 11 of them, all with ranges before the first month, and the new code returns the empty result for all 11.

What is left: the rollout itself, and the large customers once their backfill is done; two are in progress. I also need to decide what to do with the month list cache when a customer is deleted, since its entry would stay for 5 minutes. That is harmless, but I will make the delete procedure clear it.

summary: Wrote the runbook for the large-customer switch to monthly search reads, with a count comparison, shadow queries, a fixed order of steps and a rollback that takes about 10 minutes.
body:
The first large customer is the one the procedure is modelled on, and the next two are close to their own switches, so I wrote down the procedure while it is fresh. The runbook is in the repo docs folder next to the small-customer one, and it replaces the ad hoc notes in my scratch file.

The steps, in order:
1. Run the backfill with skip-existing until a second run reports zero documents written.
2. Run the count comparison script per month and per event type, not only per month. The 9 missing documents found in the first large customer's backfill would have shown up a day earlier that way.
3. Turn on shadow queries for one full day and replay them against both layouts. Differences must be explained one by one. The known case is a range that ends in the future.
4. Switch the read_layout flag at night, in the quiet window, and watch p95 and the cache hit rate for the first two hours.
5. Check again the next morning through the peak before the old indices of that customer are touched.

The rollback is the flag set back to the old layout. It takes effect within one config reload, and I measured about 10 minutes until the cache was warm again in staging. The dual write stays on for at least 7 days after the switch, so the old side has all new documents and a rollback loses nothing. I added this as a hard rule, because the old indices are the only fallback.

I also listed the checks that stop the switch: a count difference above zero after the skip-existing run, a p95 rise of more than 100 ms in the shadow phase, or a bulk rejection counter on the new side that is not flat. Tobias read the draft and asked for the cluster headroom to be checked before each switch, so that is now step zero with a link to his estimate for the two extra data nodes.

Not done yet: the runbook has no section for deleting the old indices after the dual write period. That depends on the customer delete procedure test, which took 38 minutes for 6 months in staging, and I want to write that part after the first real deletion.

summary: Backfill of large customers two and three into the monthly layout is under way, with counts checked month by month on the finished months and the switch planned for later.
body:
The backfill of the two large customers with the biggest months of about 200 GB has been running for the last four nights and is nearly done. Customer two has 26 months, 1.1 TB, customer three has 33 months, 1.6 TB. The throttle stayed at 500 per bulk with a 400 ms pause. I raised the pause to 600 ms for the hours between 08:00 and 20:00, because the tool had to run in the day for one month that did not finish at night.

Counts per month match the old layout for every month that is finished. Two months of customer three are still being filled, and I will compare them when they are done. Before any switch I will run a skip-existing pass to find gaps. I also compared the routed narrow queries for the 5 most common event types per customer on the finished months, and they match so far.

Shard sizes: the template followed the 25 GB rule, and the biggest month of customer three has 9 shards with the largest at 31 GB, 1.2 times the average. With routing partition size 3 the balance looks fine for all months. Two months of customer two have a single event type that makes up 60 percent of the data. In these months the largest shard is 1.6 times the average, still acceptable at 38 GB.

I started replaying a day of queries against both layouts for the pair. The first 52,000 queries for customer two gave identical hit counts. The replay for customer three is still running, and the first batch shows 9 queries with different order for equal scores, same as in earlier comparisons.

The switch is not done yet. I plan it for the quiet time, one customer per night, so that the cache dip does not hit the daytime. I wrote the order of steps and the rollback step, which is setting the flag back to the old layout and takes effect within a minute, since the flag is read per request.

Still to do: finish the last months, run the skip-existing pass, and then the last two large customers, including the 410 GB month. I decided to start its backfill with the oldest months and to leave the biggest month for last, in two parts split by date range, so that a failure does not cost a whole night.

summary: Prepared the night switch of large customer two to monthly search reads: counts checked, shadow queries compared and the rollback steps rehearsed
body: Spent the afternoon getting customer two ready for the switch to monthly reads, which is planned for tonight at about 03:10, when its traffic is lowest. I counted documents per month against the old per-customer layout and all months match after the last skip-existing run, with no gaps in the gap file. I then ran the shadow queries from a day of its real traffic against the monthly indices: the counts are equal in all but a few queries, and those all have a range that ends in the future, the same pattern as before. The read_layout flag for customer two is still off, and I have only written down the exact command and the value to set. I rehearsed the rollback from the runbook on the staging copy and it took about 10 minutes, as written. I set the thresholds for the morning check: p95 above 520 ms for the first hours or a cache hit rate under 40 percent means rollback. Last week's p95 at the same hours is about 520 ms, which I saved as the baseline. Tobias will be on call and has the rollback steps. Customer three comes after customer two, once the morning numbers look good.

summary: Looked at an on-call page for the Redis memory use and found that the month list cache keys were not the cause; the growth came from a session key prefix without cleanup
body:
The memory alert for the Redis cache database fired at 80 percent used in the afternoon. My first thought was my own change, the explicit month list, but that one lives in the API process memory and not in Redis, so it could not be the cause.

A scan of key prefixes by count and size showed the search cache at 52 percent, the rate limiter counters at 9 percent, and the session store at 31 percent, up from about 18 percent a month ago. Sessions have a TTL of 7 days, but the key count grew linearly. I sampled 2,000 session keys and looked at the TTL: all had one. So the keys are valid, there are just many.

The reason was in the admin console: a health check script from a monitoring tool logged in on every run, every 30 seconds, and each login created a new session. That makes 2,880 sessions a day, and each lives 7 days, so about 20,000 extra sessions. They are small, 1.4 KB each, but together 28 MB, which does not explain 13 percent of memory alone. The rest was the audit data attached to each session, an array with the last permissions, 6 KB per session. Together about 150 MB.

I changed the health check to use the unauthenticated status endpoint, and deleted the sessions of the monitoring user with a scan and delete by user id in batches of 200. Memory fell to 61 percent within a minute. Lena will look at whether the session needs the permissions array at all.

I added a gauge for the session key count to the Redis board, so that growth is visible earlier. The alert threshold stays at 80 percent.

summary: Prepared the switch of large customer three to monthly reads: ran the last skip-existing pass, checked counts and wrote down the plan for the night.
body:
Prepared the switch for the customer with 33 months. In the afternoon I ran the last skip-existing pass for the current month, which added 41 documents that arrived since the backfill, as expected for a live month with dual write on, and found that they were in the new side already. So no loss, just late comparison.

I replayed a day of this customer's real queries against the monthly indices in shadow mode. Counts were equal for all queries. The share of requests that the router would send to a single month is 77 percent, higher than for the other customers, since its dashboards filter on event type most of the time. In the shadow runs the search thread pool queue stayed empty and the data node CPU looked unchanged.

One thing I noticed: this customer has the longest range queries, 12 months and more, and after the switch they will search the full list of indices, so for these requests the shard count is high, up to 140 shards. Their latency is 2.4 s at p95 today. I want to compare it after the switch and did not find a way to make it better before then. It is the case to watch for the 410 GB customer, which has the same query habits.

I went through the runbook with the 'what to watch' thresholds and the rollback, which takes about 10 minutes, and set the flag change for 03:00 tonight. I have not set the flag yet. The last two large customers remain after this one; I will start the oldest months of the next one once this switch is checked, and keep the biggest month for the end.

summary: Wrote a draft 'what to watch' sheet for the large customer switches to monthly search reads, with the checks and the thresholds that would trigger a rollback.
body:
The runbook from a few days ago covers the steps of the switch to monthly search reads, but not what to look at once a switch is done. The first customers have not been switched yet, so I wrote a one page sheet that sits next to the runbook, so whoever is on call at night does not have to guess. It lists five metrics: p95 and p50 of the search API for the customer, the cache hit rate, the share of routed requests, the rejection rate of the search cluster, and the Redis memory use.

For each metric the sheet has a first guess at a normal range. I took the numbers from the shadow queries and from the rollout of the explicit month list, since there is no real switch to measure yet. For p95 I expect a drop of 80 to 130 ms within the first hour, so a rise of more than 10 percent over the old value counts as a warning. For the cache hit rate I expect a dip after the switch, because the keys change, and a recovery within a day, so a dip below 35 percent for more than two hours is the line for now. For the routed share I used the metric Mara asked for in her review; it should be above 90 percent for customers whose queries mostly carry an event type.

I added the rollback rules in plain words. One flag turns the customer back to the old layout and it takes about 10 minutes to take effect. Roll back if p95 is above the old value for 30 minutes, if the count comparison after the switch shows any difference that is not a future range, or if the rejection rate goes above 1 percent. A single warning does not mean a rollback; two warnings at once do.

I replayed the thresholds against the shadow query results and against the logs of the explicit month list rollout. Nothing in them would have triggered a rollback, but the sample is small, so the numbers are marked as provisional and I will adjust them after the first night. I also wrote down a likely false alarm: the count comparison may show a few differences for queries with a range that ends in the future. These look like timing races, not lost data, and the sheet says to ignore them if the count is off by only a few documents.

One open point is the order of checks in the first ten minutes. I put the count comparison first, because a data problem is worse than a slow query, then the p95 and the routed share. Tobias should read the sheet before the first switch, and I will ask him whether the Grafana panel can show all five metrics on one board. I started a draft of that board with the existing panels and left the cache and Redis ones for later.

summary: Counted documents per month for the fourth large customer after the first backfill pass: small months match, the 14 shard month is 0.02 percent short.
body:
I compared counts between the old per-customer index and the new monthly indices for the six months that finished this morning. Five of them match exactly. The month with 14 shards is short by 1,140 documents out of about 5.2 million.

I looked at the missing ids. They all fall into a ten minute window, which is the time when the bulk queue was full and the cluster rejected requests before I lowered the concurrency. The job logged the rejections but treated them as retried, and some of the retries gave up after the limit.

I reran that month with skip-existing and the count is equal now. It is the same kind of gap as the 9 documents found on the first large customer, only larger because of the rejections.

To avoid this, I changed the job so that a bulk that gives up after its retries makes the job exit non-zero and write the month and window to a file. Before, it only logged a warning. A count comparison stays a required step before any switch.

The night run for the two largest months is queued for 22:00.

summary: Added a non-zero exit and a gap file to the backfill job when a bulk gives up after its retries, with a test that uses a fake cluster that always rejects.
body:
The backfill job used to log a warning when a bulk gave up, and the run still ended with success. That hid the 1,140 missing documents this morning until I counted.

The change collects the failed bulks in a list with month, first id and last id. At the end the job writes them to a gap file and exits with code 2. The next run can read the gap file and only process these ranges, which is much faster than a full skip-existing pass over a big month.

The test starts the job against a fake client that rejects every bulk. It checks the exit code, the content of the gap file and that no documents were reported as written. A second test lets the fake client reject only the first two attempts and checks that the job ends with code 0 and an empty gap file.

I did not touch the retry count or the backoff, only what happens after the last attempt. Both tests pass and the job is ready for tonight's run.

summary: Prepared tonight's backfill run for the 14 and 17 shard months of the fourth large customer: ordering, concurrency limit and the alert on the gap file.
body:
I planned the night run for the 14 and 17 shard months of the fourth large customer and got everything ready before starting it later. The two jobs will run one after the other, not in parallel, so that the bulk concurrency stays at 4 for the cluster as a whole. The 14 shard month goes first because it is smaller, and the 17 shard month follows once it is done.

Before leaving it, I looked at the numbers from the last test pass on a small month. It wrote at about 18k documents per second with no rejections, and heap use on the data nodes stayed between 55 and 60 percent. The indexing queue never went above 30. I took these as the baseline to compare with tonight, and a higher queue or heap use means I lower the concurrency.

I also set up an alert on the gap file so that the job pages me on exit code 2. I tested it once with the fake cluster that always rejects, and the page arrived within a minute. I will check the result in the morning together with the counts per month and per type.

summary: Night run finished early for the 14 shard month, with the 17 shard month still running; counts for the first match and the gap file is empty.
body:
The 14 shard month finished after 4 hours 10 minutes. The gap file is empty and the job exited with code 0. I compared counts with the old index and they are equal, including a comparison per event type, which I added because routing depends on the type value.

The per event type counts matter because a document with a missing or wrongly normalized type would be indexed with a different routing value. It would still be counted, but narrow queries would not find it. All types match for this month.

I also ran 200 narrow queries from the sample of real queries against the new month, routed and unrouted, and compared the hits. They are equal for all 200.

The 17 shard month started at 01:30 and was at about 40 percent when I looked. The rate is a little lower, around 16k per second, because the documents of this month are larger on average. At this rate it ends around 06:00.

I will not start anything else on the cluster tonight. In the morning I count, rerun the gaps if there are any, and then plan the shadow queries for this customer.

summary: Checked the finished 17 shard month of the fourth large customer and turned on shadow queries against the monthly layout.
body:
The 17 shard month of the fourth large customer finished with zero gaps. The job ended at 05:50 with exit code 0 and an empty gap file. Total time was about 4.4 hours, shorter than the estimate.

I compared counts for the whole customer. All 41 months are equal, and the per event type counts match for the two big months. I did not compare per type for every small month; the sample of five I checked was equal.

I turned on shadow queries for this customer at 08:20. Each real query is run against the monthly layout in the background, and the hit counts and the time are logged. The answer for the user still comes from the old index.

In the first 10 minutes there were about 900 shadow queries and no count differences. The latency of the shadow queries is a little above the real ones, which is expected because the monthly caches are cold.

I will leave the shadow mode on for a day, as the runbook says, and check the differences tomorrow morning. The switch is planned for tomorrow night if the log is clean.

summary: Reviewed Mara's change that streams the audit export to a multipart upload; heap for a 2 million row export dropped from 1.8 GB to about 90 MB, but the final part is not flushed on an error.
body:
Mara changed the export so that it writes rows into a buffer of 8 MB and uploads each full buffer as a part. This replaces the file that was built in memory. I ran it on the staging customer with 2 million rows, and the heap peak was around 90 MB. The export time is the same as before, about 31 seconds.

I found one real problem. When the database cursor fails in the middle, for example on a timeout, the code throws before it completes or aborts the upload. The parts stay in the bucket as an incomplete upload. This is the reason I asked Tobias for the lifecycle rule last week, but the rule only removes them after 2 days, and the code should clean up itself too.

I asked Mara to wrap the loop in a try and call abort on the upload in the error case, and to write a test with a cursor that fails after the third page.

Smaller points: the part size should be a setting and not a constant, and the last part may be smaller than 5 MB, which is fine for S3 but needs a comment, because the next reader will wonder.

She agreed to all three and will push the changes today. I will look at them again tomorrow.

summary: Checked the shadow query log for the fourth large customer after a day: 38,000 queries, 3 differences, all with a range that ends in the future, the same known case as before.
body:
The shadow log has 38,412 queries from the last 24 hours. Three of them returned different counts between the old and the monthly layout.

All three have a time range whose end lies in the future. This is the case I already saw on the replay for the explicit month list: the old index answers for the whole range, while the month list stops at the current month and the future months do not exist yet. The counts differ by documents that arrived after the shadow query started, so it is a race and not a gap. I reran the three by hand a minute later and the counts were equal.

Latency: the shadow queries had a p95 of 410 ms against 560 ms on the old layout for the same queries. The new layout is better here, in line with the other customers.

I also looked at the slowest 20 shadow queries. Seventeen are wide queries over more than 12 months with no event type, which cannot use routing. They fan out to many shards and take 900 ms to 1.4 seconds, but they are as slow on the old layout.

The log is clean enough for the switch. I will do it tonight at the usual quiet time and keep the rollback ready.

summary: Told Sam that the three queries with a different count in the shadow log are timing differences and not lost data, and gave her wording for a customer who asks.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel whether the fourth large customer could see wrong counts after the switch tonight. I explained the three differences in the shadow log: the search range ended in the future, and the counts differed by documents that arrived during the query. A repeat a minute later gave equal numbers.

I wrote a short text for her: counts of a search that includes the current moment can change by a few documents between two runs, because new events are still arriving, and this is the same on the old layout. If a customer shows a difference that stays after a minute, she should send me the query and the time.

She will add the text to the support notes for the monthly layout.

summary: Prepared the switch of the fourth large customer to monthly search reads: counts match for all 41 months, and the flag flip is planned for later tonight.
body:
I went through the runbook step by step for the fourth large customer, but I did not flip anything yet. First a count comparison for all 41 months, which was equal. Then I read the shadow log again: p50 of 44 ms and p95 of 430 ms on the monthly layout, against a p95 of 560 ms on the current layout, with no errors in the shadow replies.

I planned one last skip-existing run for the current month, because documents keep arriving since the backfill. A dry run showed about 200 new documents to write. I will run it right before the switch so the gap is as small as possible, and I will check the count again after it.

I also thought about the query cache. The keys include the month list, so after the switch the old keys will not be used any more and the hit rate will fall for a while. In the earlier switches it fell from about 63 percent to about 51 and climbed back in under an hour. I told Sam to expect a short slower period and wrote it into the switch notes.

For the cluster I set up a Grafana panel with the rejection rate and the search thread pool queue on the data nodes, since the new reads add fan-out. The limit I will watch is a queue well under the configured maximum, and any rejection at all means I stop.

The old index stays for 14 days as the runbook says, and writes go to both layouts. The rollback is one flag and takes about 10 minutes to be effective for all running workers. I wrote the exact command into the notes so it can be done quickly by anyone on the on-call.

Tomorrow morning I will decide on the exact time of the switch for tonight or the next night, depending on the traffic. After the fourth customer only the fifth large customer is left, with its 60 months and the biggest total size, and I will plan it separately.

summary: Measured the fifth large customer's layout needs: 63 months, 9.1 TB in total, and the biggest three months need 17, 15 and 15 shards; the backfill would take about 9 nights at the current rate.
body:
After the switch I looked at the last customer. I took month sizes from the cat indices output of the old index with a per month count query and an average document size, and checked the result against the real sizes of the already finished months of the other customers, where the estimate was off by under 6 percent.

The fifth customer has 63 months and about 9.1 TB in total. The three biggest months are 410, 365 and 360 GB, so 17, 15 and 15 shards by the 25 GB rule. The other months are mostly under 150 GB.

At 16 to 18k documents per second with concurrency 4, the whole backfill is about 9 nights. That is too long if it blocks everything else, since the same cluster serves production reads for this customer, which are the heaviest.

Options I wrote down:
- Raise concurrency to 6 at night between 23:00 and 05:00, when read load is a quarter of the peak. This may give about 25 percent more throughput, but I would need to watch the rejections.
- Run the small months during the day with a low concurrency of 2 and keep the big nights for the three biggest months.
- Skip months older than 13 months for the first step, since the analytics rollups cover them and the search of old months is rare. I need to check this with the real query log before deciding.

I pulled the query log of the last 30 days. Only 4 percent of this customer's searches touch months older than 13 months, but those customers are exactly the ones who use search for compliance questions, so I do not want them slower or broken. I will keep all months but order them by recency, so the switch can be done in two stages if needed.

Next step is a test of concurrency 6 on staging with the 365 GB month copy.

summary: Staging test of bulk concurrency 6 on a 365 GB month: throughput went from 17k to 21k documents per second, and the rejection rate stayed at 0.3 percent, which is too high for production.
body:
I loaded the copy of the second biggest month of the fifth customer into staging with concurrency 4 as a baseline, and then with 6. Staging has the same node type as production but three data nodes instead of six, so the absolute numbers are lower and I only look at the relation.

At concurrency 4: 17k documents per second, zero rejections. At concurrency 6: 21k per second, so 24 percent more, but the cluster rejected 0.3 percent of the bulks. The retries took care of them, with no gap in the end, but each retry adds backoff time, and on production the reads of this customer are served by the same nodes.

I also tried concurrency 5, which gave 19.5k per second and 0.05 percent rejections. That looks like the better trade, but with half the nodes the staging result is not a promise for production.

Decision for now: use concurrency 4 during the day with the small months and 5 at night, and watch the rejection rate on the first night. If it stays under 0.05 percent I keep it. The job already aborts and writes a gap file if retries are exhausted, so the failure mode is safe.

Tomorrow I will start with the 40 oldest small months.

summary: Planned the first backfill night for the fifth large customer's monthly search layout and prepared the settings for the 38 oldest, small months.
body:
Prepared the first night of the backfill for the fifth large customer. The plan is to write the 38 oldest months, which are small, between 8 and 70 GB each, at bulk concurrency 5. The job is set to start at 23:00, and from the earlier size measurements I expect it to be done a little before 05:00.

I set the limit for the rejection rate on the cluster at 0.1 percent. Staging with concurrency 6 gave 0.3 percent, which is too high, so concurrency 5 is the value I want to try first. The job should stop and write the failed bulks into the gap file if the rate goes above the limit, and a bulk that gives up must not make the exit code 0. I tested this on a small month in staging with an artificial failure, and the gap file was filled as expected.

For the morning I wrote a check script. It compares the document count by month between the old layout and the new one, and for a random sample of 6 months it also compares the counts per event type.

One thing I looked at in advance: the shadow queries of the earlier customers found events with an empty event type. They are indexed with the default routing value, the same as in the old layout. I will check the oldest months of this customer for the same case, because they come from a very early version of the customer's app. If there are such documents, I will add a note about the default routing value to the runbook.

I also asked Tobias to watch the cluster dashboards during the night, since the job runs while the nightly reindex of other customers is paused. The three big months are for later nights, one after another, once the small ones show how the cluster behaves.

summary: Analyzed the search cache after the fourth large customer's switch and found that keys for closed months waste memory, then tested a TTL rule on replayed traffic without rolling it out.
body:
Looked at the cache hit rate of the search API after the fourth switch: it is stable at 61 percent, but keys for months that are no longer current never get hits again and should have a shorter TTL.

I went through the Redis keys of the search cache by prefix with a SCAN on a replica, sampled 50,000 keys and grouped them by the month part of the key and the TTL.

The cache key contains the explicit month list, so a query over the last 3 months has a different key every month. Keys that contain a month that closed more than 2 months ago get hits only from the same repeated dashboards, and a large part of the keys, about 34 percent of the sample, had a TTL of 24 hours and were hit only once.

This is not a memory problem right now; the used memory is at 58 percent of the limit. But the cache holds a lot of entries that cost memory and give nothing, and it will matter more when the last large customer is switched, since its queries are the largest results.

I tried a rule in the cache layer: if a query range ends before the start of the current month, the result is final, so it gets a TTL of 7 days, but only if it was already requested twice, and otherwise 1 hour. I tested it on a copy of 1 hour of production traffic with a local Redis. The hit rate in the replay went from 61 to 63 percent, and the number of keys fell by 22 percent.

I did not roll this out yet. The rule counts requests, and the counter needs its own key, which doubles the keys for single requests. I need a cheaper way, for example a small counting structure per day, or a decision on the query hash only. I will look at this next week.

Separately, the key naming for the counter would need to follow the prefix scheme of the cache, so that the cleanup tools find it. I wrote that down in the notes of the cache layer.

summary: Planned the night of the three biggest months of the fifth large customer's backfill and prepared the job settings and the checks for the morning.
body:
I prepared the night run for the three biggest months of the fifth large customer, to be done in sequence: the 360 GB month, then the 365 GB month, then the 410 GB month. The job is not started yet. I plan to start it at 22:30 and to set the concurrency to 4 for these months, since the shards are larger and one bulk touches more of them.

For the estimate I used the earlier nights. The smaller months ran at concurrency 5 with rejections at 0.02 percent, and the staging test of concurrency 6 on a 365 GB month showed 0.3 percent rejections, which is too high. So 4 looks like the safe choice for the large shards. From the staging throughput I expect about 6 hours for each of the first two months and 7 to 8 hours for the 410 GB month. That means the last month would run into the start of the day load.

Because of this I wrote down what to watch. The read latency of the customer on the old layout is at a p95 of about 560 ms now, and the alert limit is 800 ms. If the p95 goes clearly above 600 ms in the morning, I will lower the concurrency of the running job to 2 through the setting file, which the job reads every minute. I checked that the file is read correctly by changing a value in staging and looking at the log of the job.

I also prepared the checks for the next morning: the gap file should be empty, the counts for the three months should match, and the counts per event type should match too.

For the plan I will think about a rule for the runbook: the biggest month probably needs a start before 21:00, so that it is done before the morning. I will decide this after the real run. The remaining months are smaller, so the next nights should be shorter.

summary: Prepared the backfill of the last 22 months for the fifth large customer, with the first 20 months written and the gap handling tested, so the shadow queries can be planned.
body:
The last nights covered the first 20 of the remaining 22 months. I ran them at concurrency 5, in blocks sorted by month from oldest to newest. The 54th month is still open. Two bulks gave up there, because the cluster was doing a segment merge on the node that held the shard of that month, and the job wrote a gap file with a range of 14 ids.

I have not run the job again with the gap file as input yet. I tried it on a copy of the gap file in staging against a small month, and it wrote the documents in about one second. Documents that already exist in the target are skipped, so I expect the net gap to be smaller than 14, and I will only know the real number after the run in production. Month 60 has not been written yet, and I expect the same kind of gap there, so I will keep the gap-file run ready for it.

The count comparison by month is clean for the 20 months written so far. Per event type counts match for the 12 months I checked in detail, among them the three biggest.

The size on the cluster of the new layout is now 8.3 TB with the replicas counted once, for the months written so far. The estimate for the full customer was 9.1 TB. I expect the final number to be a little above it, because the routing partitions make the large months not perfectly even.

I checked the disk use on the data nodes. The highest node is at 71 percent and the lowest at 63 percent. With the old index still there, we have a little room, but I would not want to go above 78 percent. This is the reason to keep the 14 days for the old index of the other customers and not more.

Next step: run the gap file for month 54, write the last two months, and compare the counts for all 63 months. Only then will I turn on the shadow queries. This customer has the highest query load, about 3 times the one of customer four, so the shadow queries will also double the read load on the cluster. I plan to start with a shadow share of 50 percent for the first hours and raise it if the cluster is calm.

summary: Shadow queries for the fifth large customer ran for 5 hours at 50 percent: 31,000 queries and 9 count differences, 8 with a future range and one real one with a missing event type.
body:
I looked at the log after 5 hours. The shadow share of 50 percent gave 31,284 queries, the cluster was calm, the queue of the search thread pool peaked at 20 and the rejections were zero. I raised the share to 100 percent at noon.

Nine queries had different counts. Eight of them end in the future and are the known race. The ninth is real: the query filters on an event type and returned 41 fewer documents on the monthly layout.

The cause is the empty event type documents of month 22 that I noted a few days ago. This query had a filter with a list of two types and a 'missing' option, which the old layout resolved with a must_not exists clause. The request builder with routing sees a list of types and routes only to those types, and so it skips the default routing value where the empty type documents sit.

So the routing flag leaks for the case 'missing' together with a type list. Narrow queries of this kind are rare, only 1 in 5,000 in the log, but they would return wrong answers.

I changed the request builder so that if the filter includes the missing option it does not set a routing value and fans out to all shards of the month. I added a unit test for that case, next to the tests for single, multiple and missing event types. Then I replayed the query and got the same count as the old layout.

I will let the shadow queries run overnight with this fix to see if more such cases exist. Mara should look at the change for the parser side, in case it has the same assumption on the 'missing' option somewhere else.

summary: Asked Mara to check the search parser for other places that treat a missing event type as a normal value, after the shadow query found a routing leak.
body:
I wrote Mara a message with the case: a filter on a list of event types together with the 'missing' option returned 41 fewer documents on the monthly layout. The cause was in the request builder, where the routing value was computed from the type list only.

I told her what I changed in the builder: if 'missing' is in the filter, no routing value is set. The unit test covers this case.

The question for her is whether the parser or the saved search feature, or the dashboards that run through the search API, have other places that read the list of types and decide something from it. I especially mean the cache key, which uses the type list, and the per customer type allowlist.

She replied that the cache key builds from the normalized filter object and not the list, so it includes the missing option. She will look at the allowlist and tell me this afternoon.

summary: Mara found that the type allowlist ignores the missing option, which is fine because it only limits visible types, and no other place in the parser needs a change.
body:
Mara went through the parser, the saved searches and the allowlist code and sent me the result.

The cache key uses the normalized filter, so a query with the missing option has a different key than the same one without. That is right, and I confirmed it by a test that builds both keys and compares them.

The allowlist per customer limits which event types a user may see. It runs after the parse and removes types that are not allowed from the list. It does not touch the missing option, because documents with no type are visible to everyone of that customer. That is the existing behavior and not a bug.

The saved searches store the filter as the user typed it. They go through the same parser, so they pick up the builder fix without a migration.

I asked her about the dashboards. They do not use the search API for event counts; they use the analytics store, so they are not affected.

She suggested adding the 'missing' case to the replay set of real queries, because the replay is how we find these cases. I created a file with the 6 queries of this kind from the log of the last 30 days and put it into the replay folder. All of them give equal counts now.

The shadow log is the final check. I will read it tomorrow morning. If it is clean, the switch of customer five can be planned for the night after.

summary: Read the overnight shadow log of customer five after the routing fix: 74,000 queries and only the known future range races, so I scheduled the switch for the night after tomorrow.
body:
The shadow ran at 100 percent from noon on. I read the log at the end of the evening, since the peak of this customer is in the afternoon and the evening is calm. It has 74,310 queries, 11 count differences.

All 11 end in the future. I reran them by hand and the counts match. There is no further difference with the missing option, so the fix in the request builder holds.

Latency for the shadow queries: p95 of 520 ms against 640 ms on the old layout. That is lower than for the other customers in absolute terms, but this customer is the largest, so I expect the final p95 after the switch to be around 480 to 500 ms.

I picked the night after tomorrow for the switch. Tomorrow night I will run a last skip-existing pass for the newest two months, to catch the documents that came in during the shadow days. Then the count comparison and the flag. I told Tobias, since he is on call that night, and gave him the rollback steps of the runbook.

summary: Prepared the last skip-existing pass for customer five and planned the count comparison and the dual write check, without running the pass or the switch yet.
body:
I planned the last skip-existing pass for customer five, which will start at 22:00 tonight. I expect it to write only the documents of the last two months, the ones that arrived after the backfill. The older months should get zero new documents, since their sources are closed, and I wrote that expectation into the notes so a surprise is easy to see.

I prepared the count comparison for all 63 months. For the two newest months I added a per event type check, because they are the ones that can still change. I tested the script on a small slice of the older months and it ran cleanly, so the full run should be short.

I also wrote the check for the dual write. It counts the documents that live ingest sends to the new layout and to the old index during a window of 10 minutes, and the two numbers must be the same. I tried it on staging with a small test stream and the numbers matched.

The disk use on the data nodes is at 72 percent on the highest node, which is fine for the pass but leaves little room. The old indices of customers one to four are to be deleted in the next days, so there will be room again. I wrote the order and the days in the planning notes and asked Tobias to look at them.

The switch itself is not decided for a night yet. I will pick the time after I have read the results of the pass and the comparison. The plan is to follow the steps of the runbook, and the rollback stays one flag.

summary: Checked the Redis memory after the shadow load of customer five: used memory rose from 58 to 66 percent, driven by the duplicate cache keys of the shadow reads, which I turned off for the cache.
body:
The on-call dashboard showed the Redis memory at 66 percent in the morning, up from 58 percent a few days ago. I looked at the key counts by prefix. The search cache prefix had grown by about 1.4 million keys.

The cause is the shadow mode. Each shadow query is run against the monthly layout through the normal search path, and the path writes its result into the cache under the key of the monthly list. For customer five the volume is large, so the cache got a second copy of each result.

The shadow results are never read, since the user gets the answer from the old layout until the switch. So these keys cost memory and give nothing. I changed the shadow path to skip the cache write, with a flag in the call and a unit test that checks no set is called for a shadow query.

The keys already written are still there. They have a TTL of 24 hours, so they will go away on their own. I did not delete them by hand, since after the switch tomorrow the same keys would be useful for the cache warm-up.

The memory should go back to about 60 percent after one day. I will look at it after the switch.

summary: Sent Tobias the switch plan for customer five tonight, with the steps, the times, the metrics to watch and the single flag for the rollback.
body:
I wrote a page for Tobias, who is on call tonight. It lists the steps: the count comparison at 21:30, the last skip-existing run for the current month, the flag flip at about 21:50, and then 30 minutes of watching.

The metrics to watch are p95 of the search API for the customer, with a warning above 600 ms, the rejection rate on the cluster, the cache hit rate, which is expected to dip to about 50 percent and recover in 40 minutes, and the Redis memory.

The rollback is to set the flag for the customer back to the old layout. It takes about 10 minutes until all workers read the new value. The dual write continues, so no data is lost in either direction.

I will do the switch myself, and he only needs the page if something looks wrong while I am not at the keyboard.

summary: Prepared the night switch of the fifth large customer to monthly search reads: the final checks are done and the plan is ready, but the switch has not run.
body:
The switch is planned for tonight with Tobias on call. This evening I went through the checklist so that the steps are clear before we start. The plan is to begin in the early evening with the shadow reads turned off for the cache, and then to flip the single flag for the customer's read path.

I ran the count comparison for all 63 months again and every month is equal, including the three biggest ones with 17, 15 and 15 shards. I also replayed the last hour of real queries against both layouts and found 2 differences, both with a range that ends in the future, the known timing case. I decided to accept that case for the switch and not to chase it further tonight.

For the cache I expect a dip in the first minutes after the switch, as with the earlier customers, with the hit rate recovering within about half an hour. Redis memory stands at 61 percent. The shadow cache change from this morning kept it flat in the last test, so I do not expect growth during the window. No bulk writes are scheduled in parallel, so the rejection rate on the cluster should stay at zero.

Tobias will watch the load balancer and the OpenSearch heap on the data nodes. We agreed that he calls the rollback if the heap goes over 80 percent or the p95 for this customer goes above the current 640 ms for more than ten minutes. The rollback is the same single flag.

What is left: the switch itself tonight, then a check of the p95 and the count differences a few hours later. The old per-customer indices stay as a safety net for two more weeks after the switch. I will write the closing note for the large customer phase afterwards, with the numbers for all five customers in one table.

summary: Prepared the night switch of customer five to monthly search reads and checked that the plan and rollback flag were ready, before the switch itself.
body:
I went through the dashboards one more time before going to bed, to be sure the plan for tonight's switch of customer five holds. The p95 for customer five has stayed at 465 to 480 ms in the busiest hour of the night, when its batch jobs query the search API on the per-customer index. That is the baseline I will compare against after the switch.

Cache hit rate for customer five is 60 percent, close to the 61 percent of customer four. Keys for old months are not hit, as expected for this layout, so the shorter TTL for non-current months is still open. I wrote it down as a task for after the switch and have not changed it yet.

The count comparison job that I scheduled every hour found no differences in its last three runs. The shadow log shows only the known future range cases, 4 in three hours, which matches the earlier nights.

No pages came in for Redis or OpenSearch. I asked Tobias to confirm the rollback path: the old per-customer indices are still in place, and the single flag is the only thing that would have to change to go back. He confirmed both, and I added the flag name and the times to the plan I sent him.

The switch has not run yet. Next is the switch itself in the night window, then the summary table of all five switches and the TTL change for old month keys.

summary: Started collecting the numbers of the five large customer switches for a summary table, with the p95 and cache dip figures still to be checked against the dashboards.
body:
I started the summary table in the docs folder. Four of the five customers are already switched and the fifth is planned, so the table is a draft and the last row is still empty. I took the numbers from the earlier entries and from the dashboards, and for each customer I listed the months, the shards of the biggest month, the backfill nights and the p95 before the switch.

The p95 before values are 450 ms for customer one, 520 for two, 610 for three, 560 for four and 640 for five. The after values for customers one to four are in the draft, but I have not compared them with the dashboards yet, and for customer five there is nothing to enter because the switch has not run. The cache dip lengths are also only noted for the first four customers, and I am not sure the dashboards show the start of each dip clearly enough to read them to the minute.

The backfill time grew with the data size. Customer five took the longest because of the three biggest months, and I planned about 9 nights at first. I want to see whether running the larger months in sequence makes it faster before I write that down.

The rejection rate was 0.02 percent at concurrency 5 for the customers so far. The test with concurrency 6 gave more throughput but 0.3 percent rejections, so we stay at 5.

The count differences in the shadow logs were nearly all queries with a range that ends in the future. One real difference came from a missing event type in the routing, which was fixed for customer five.

I started a short section with lessons: run skip-existing before every switch, turn off the cache for shadow reads, and keep the gap file in the backfill job. Sam will use the table for the customer notes later, so I will ask Mara to read it once the numbers are complete.

summary: Set the TTL for month list and result keys of non-current months to 6 hours instead of 24, and the Redis memory growth from search keys stopped in staging.
body:
Last week I saw that keys for months that are no longer current never get hits again. They stayed in Redis for the full TTL of 24 hours and filled memory for nothing.

The change is in the cache module of the search API. The key builder now knows whether the month of a query is the current one. For current months the TTL stays at 60 seconds for results, and for the month list at 24 hours. For all other months the result keys get 6 hours.

I first tried a TTL of 1 hour. In staging with a replay of a day of queries, the hit rate fell from 61 to 54 percent, because dashboards that look at the last three months reuse the same keys during the day. At 6 hours the hit rate was 60 percent, so I kept 6.

The memory effect was visible: after a replay of one day, the number of search keys was 22 percent lower than with 24 hours.

I added unit tests for the key builder with a fake clock around the month border. One test failed at first because the border was computed in local time, so I switched it to UTC.

The change also needed a note in the key naming doc, since the TTL is part of the contract for people who look at keys by hand. I wrote it there.

I did not roll this out yet. The plan is to deploy it tomorrow morning to one instance and compare the hit rate and the memory for a few hours.

summary: Deployed the shorter TTL for old months to one search instance: hit rate is 60 percent against 61 on the others, and its key count grows more slowly.
body:
I deployed the TTL change to one of the four search API instances at 10:50. They share the same Redis, so I compared by key prefix, since the instance writes the keys with a tag in the metrics.

After an hour the hit rate of the instance was 60 percent and of the others 61 percent. That is within the normal noise between instances.

The count of new keys with a long TTL per minute fell, as expected, because requests for old months now write keys with the short one. Memory of Redis rose by 0.3 points in two hours, against 0.9 points the same time yesterday.

One thing surprised me. A dashboard of customer two asks for the last 12 months every 5 minutes, and its keys expire after 6 hours, so it sees one miss per 6 hours per month. That is cheap, so it does not matter.

I also checked the p95 of the instance, to see if more misses hurt: 438 ms against 441 ms on the others. No difference.

I wanted to see the effect on a busy hour too, so I let it run through the lunch peak. Hit rate stayed at 60 percent and no errors appeared in the logs.

The decision is to roll it out to all instances this afternoon. Before that I asked Mara to look at the key builder, because she wrote the first version. She found nothing wrong but suggested a constant for the 6 hours instead of the literal. I changed it and ran the tests again.

Next step is the rollout and a look at memory tomorrow. If the growth stays low, the Redis memory alert threshold for the search keys can stay where it is.

summary: Rolled out the 6 hour TTL for old months to all search instances; Redis memory grew 0.4 points overnight instead of about 1, and the hit rate is unchanged.
body:
The rollout went out yesterday evening and I checked the numbers this afternoon. Memory of Redis went from 62.1 to 62.5 percent over the night, where it had grown about one point per night before.

The hit rate of the search API stayed at 60 to 61 percent. The p95 stayed near 440 ms across customers that already read from the monthly layout.

The session key prefix without cleanup, found a few days ago, still adds growth on its own. I opened a ticket for it with the numbers, because it is the larger part now: about 0.3 points per night come from there.

I also looked at the config flag for the shadow read cache switch. For the large customers that have been switched so far, the shadow reads have been running without new count differences, and the flag no longer changes anything for them, so I wrote a note to remove it in a later change and left it in place for now.

The old per-customer indices stay for another week. Then Tobias and I will go through them and decide which ones to delete.

summary: Fixed the missing cleanup of the session key prefix in the admin console: sessions now get a sliding TTL of 14 days, and a one-time scan removed 410,000 stale keys.
body:
The session store of the admin console writes keys with the prefix sess:, and nothing ever deleted them if a user did not log out. Memory grew by about 0.3 points per night from these keys.

The fix has two parts. First, the session middleware sets a TTL of 14 days on every write and refreshes it on use, so active users do not get logged out. Second, a one-time script scans for keys of this prefix without a TTL and sets one based on the last access field in the value.

I ran the script first in staging with a copy of the key space. It found 410,000 keys without a TTL there. In production the count was similar, and I used SCAN with a count of 500 and a short pause to keep the load low. The run took 11 minutes and Redis latency stayed under 2 ms.

Keys with a last access older than 14 days were deleted at once, which was 372,000 of them. The rest got a TTL. Memory fell from 62.8 to 59.9 percent.

Lena checked that the admin console login still works, and that a session that is 13 days old survives one more request. It does.

One problem: some old keys have no last access field at all. I gave these a TTL of 3 days and logged the count, which was 1,900. I will look at the log next week to see if someone complained.

I added the TTL to the key naming doc and a test for the middleware with a fake Redis. The ticket from earlier is closed.

What is left is an alert for keys without a TTL in the sess: prefix, which Tobias may add to Prometheus.

summary: Planned the deletion of the old per-customer indices for the first large customer after a week of monthly reads, and prepared the snapshot and the count comparison without deleting anything.
body:
The first large customer switched to monthly reads the longest ago, so it is the first candidate for cleaning up the old per-customer indices. I did not delete anything today. I wanted the plan written down and the checks ready before touching the cluster.

I went through the runbook and wrote the order of steps in the ticket: run the count comparison for all months, take a snapshot of the old indices to the backup bucket, then delete the indices one by one with a pause between them while watching the cluster health. I ran the count comparison once on staging data to check the script, and it printed equal counts for every month there. The production run is still to come, and so is the snapshot.

I also looked at the disk use on the data nodes, which is at 71 percent. Deleting the indices of this customer should free a good part of that, but I only have a rough size from the index list and will write down the real number after the work. I asked Tobias to check the monthly cost effect at the end of the month, and he agreed.

The plan for the other customers is to follow every other day, so the cluster does not have to rebalance too much at once. I added that to the ticket and left the first deletion for a later session, after one more look at the rollback logs of the last week.

summary: Prepared the deletion of the old indices of large customer two by comparing counts and taking a snapshot, with the deletion itself still to come.
body:
Followed the same steps as for customer one, and this time stopped before any deletion. The first step was the count comparison between the old per-customer indices and the monthly reads for customer two, and the numbers matched for every index.
