The snapshot to the backup bucket took 55 minutes because customer two has more data than customer one. I restored one small index from it into a scratch index on the cluster and compared the document count and a handful of sample documents, and they were identical. The cluster stayed green during the snapshot and disk use on the data nodes stayed at about 70 percent.

I wrote the deletion plan in the runbook: delete in small steps of a few indices each, check cluster health and search latency after every step, and let shard rebalancing finish before the next step. I asked Mara to read it before I start, and she wanted the p95 baseline written in the note. The p95 for customer two is at 430 ms today, so that is the number to compare with afterwards. Customer three comes next, in two days.

summary: Looked at a slow Postgres query in the admin console that lists API keys per customer; an index on (customer_id, created_at) cut it from 900 ms to 6 ms.
body:
Lena reported that the API key page of the admin console takes about a second to load for the large customers. I found the query in the slow log: it filters by customer_id and sorts by created_at, and Postgres did a sequential scan on the api_keys table with a sort.

The table has 380,000 rows because revoked keys are never deleted. An EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed 900 ms.

I added an index on (customer_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so no lock was held on writes. The build took 4 seconds.

After that the same query took 6 ms and the plan used an index scan. I wrote the migration file and tested it on staging first.

The revoked keys could be archived, but that is a separate task, and I noted it in the backlog.

summary: Wrote the plan to archive revoked API keys out of Postgres, with a retention of 90 days and a table for the audit trail, and Mara agreed to the steps.
body:
After the index fix this morning, the question was whether to keep 380,000 revoked keys in the main table. Most are revoked because customers rotate keys, and nobody needs them after the audit window.

The plan has four steps. First, add a revoked_at column index, since the archive job selects by it. Second, a job that copies keys revoked more than 90 days ago into api_keys_archive in batches of 1,000. Third, delete the copied rows in the same transaction. Fourth, run vacuum on the table after the first big run.

The audit log refers to keys by id, so I checked that nothing joins to api_keys for revoked ones. The audit export has one join, and it uses a left join, so missing rows would only show an empty name. I will change it to read from both tables with a union view, to keep exports correct.

Mara pointed out that the rate limiter loads keys at startup from the same table and filters by status. That is fine, but she asked for a check that the limiter does not load archived ones by mistake. I added it to the test list.

We talked about whether to hash the key values in the archive. They are already stored as hashes, so no change is needed there.

I estimate that about 310,000 rows move on the first run. Table size is 120 MB now and would fall to about 25 MB after vacuum. This is small, so the point is more about clean queries than space.

The next step is to write the job and the union view, and test them on a staging copy of the data. I want to run the first archive in the early morning when load is lowest.

One open point: how long to keep the archive. For now it is without a limit, and Sam will ask what the contracts say.

summary: Wrote the archive job for revoked API keys and tested it on staging: 308,000 rows moved in 9 minutes, and the union view returns the same rows as before.
body:
I wrote the job as a small Node script that runs batches of 1,000 rows inside one transaction each, with a short pause between them. It selects by revoked_at older than 90 days and uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so two runs would not collide.

On the staging copy, it moved 308,000 rows in 9 minutes. The main table fell to 72,000 rows. The union view api_keys_all returns 380,000 rows, the same as the table before.

I changed the audit export query to use the view and ran the export tests of the audit-export branch against it. All passed. The rate limiter test that checks that archived keys are not loaded also passed.

A problem came up in the first run: the job failed with a unique constraint error on the archive table, because I had run it twice after an interrupt. I made the insert use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and delete only rows that were confirmed in the archive.

Production run is planned for tomorrow at 05:00.

summary: Ran the weekly archive task for revoked API keys on production for the first time: 1.9 million rows moved in 38 minutes, and the key lookup and the union view gave identical results.
body:
Ran the weekly archive task by hand on production this afternoon, after Tobias deployed the narrowed task role. The task selects revoked keys older than 90 days, copies them into the archive table, checks the copy and only then deletes from the live table. Before the run I took a Postgres snapshot and wrote down the row counts of both tables: 2,214,000 revoked keys in total, of which 1.9 million were older than 90 days.

The job worked in batches of 5,000 rows with a pause of 200 ms between batches. That kept the replication lag under 1.5 seconds the whole time, and the admin console showed no slow requests. The full run took 38 minutes, which is a bit more than the staging rate suggested, because the production table has more indexes to maintain.

After the run I compared the counts: live table plus archive table equal the count from before, to the row. I also ran the union view against a saved list of 500 random key hashes from before the move, and every key was found with the same customer, creation time and revoke time. The auth path that checks a presented key reads only the live table, and the revoked keys it needs are all younger than 90 days, so it was not touched. The API key list of the admin console reads through the union view and returned the same page for the three customers I tried, including the one with 140,000 revoked keys.

The first autovacuum on the live table started about 10 minutes after the end and took 6 minutes. Table size on disk did not shrink yet, as expected, since a plain vacuum does not give the space back to the system. I wrote a note to plan a rewrite of the table in a quiet window, but it is not urgent because the index on (customer_id, created_at) is now much smaller. Still open: the cleanup job for keys older than 12 months, which comes next, and an alert if the weekly task has not run for 8 days. The task is scheduled for the next weekly slot and I will check its log then.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's Terraform change for the weekly archive task and found that the task role could delete from every table; narrowed it to the two key tables.
body:
The change adds a scheduled ECS task that runs the archive job once a week. The schedule and the container definition were fine, with the cron expression in UTC and a timeout of 30 minutes.

The database user was the problem. The task used the same Postgres user as the admin console backend, which has delete rights on most tables, including the audit log. A bug in the job could in theory delete from something it should not.

I created a role archive_job with select, insert and delete on api_keys and insert and select on api_keys_archive, and nothing else. Tobias put the new secret in Secrets Manager and changed the task definition to read it.

I tested the role in staging. The job ran and moved test rows. A deliberate delete from audit_log failed with a permission denied error, which is what I wanted to see.

The first scheduled run needed one more fix. The job read the connection string from the wrong variable name, and the task exited with code 1 after 2 seconds. The log showed it clearly. After the rename in the task definition it ran and moved 0 rows, as all old keys were already archived.

Tobias added a CloudWatch alarm for a task exit code other than 0. I added a Prometheus metric push at the end of the job for the number of rows, though the push gateway is not used elsewhere, so we will see if it fits.

One point I have not solved: if the job is killed halfway, the next run starts clean because every batch is its own transaction, so that is safe.

The review is done and the change is merged. Next is Sam's answer about retention, then I can close this topic.

summary: Sam confirmed from the contracts that revoked API keys must be kept for 12 months, so the archive gets a cleanup job after that and the plan note is updated.
body:
Sam read the contracts of the large customers and the standard terms. The standard terms say that records of access credentials are kept for the audit period of 12 months after revocation. Two large customers have 24 months in their contracts.

So the archive cannot be kept forever, and it must not be cut at 12 months either, because of the two contracts. I decided on 25 months for all, which is simple and covers both. The cost is tiny, since the archive has about 310,000 rows.

I wrote a second step in the weekly job: delete rows from api_keys_archive where revoked_at is older than 25 months, in batches of 1,000. At this time nothing is that old, so the first runs will do nothing. A unit test with a fake clock checks the cutoff exactly at 25 months.

The archive_job role needed a delete right on the archive table, so I added it and updated the Terraform for the role grant. I reread the grants after the change, and the role still has no access to the audit log.

I also changed the metric to report both counts, archived and purged.

The doc of the data retention in the wiki had no line for API keys, so I wrote one with the three periods: 90 days in the main table, 25 months in the archive, then deleted. Sam will link it from the customer FAQ.

One question from Mara: should the purge write a line to the audit log? I think yes, one line per run with the count, not per key. I added that, and the audit entry has the job name and the cutoff.

I ran the job in staging with test data that I aged by changing revoked_at. It purged 120 rows and wrote one audit line. Next is the production deploy of the new image, which Tobias does with the normal pipeline this afternoon.

summary: Looked into why the nightly OpenSearch snapshot grew from 40 to 75 minutes, found that the snapshot policy also covers the old per-customer indices, and planned a narrower policy without applying it.
body:
Tobias noticed that the nightly snapshot to the backup bucket takes almost twice as long as two weeks ago. He asked me to look because it now ends close to the start of the reindex job.

I listed the snapshot contents. The policy includes all indices with the pattern events-*, and that matches the old per-customer indices, including the ones for customers three, four and five that we have not yet deleted, as well as the large indices of the busiest customers.

The old per-customer indices are still what search runs on today, so they stay in the nightly policy until we have a reason to change that. The snapshot is incremental on segment level, so unchanged data is cheap to copy, but the listing and the consistency checks of about 4,000 shards still take time. In a test run against a copy of the repository settings, skipping the three customers already shortened the listing step noticeably, so those three are the first candidates once their deletion is decided.

The backfill nights are the other part. After a backfill the first snapshot must copy all the new segments, which accounts for 20 to 30 minutes on those nights. That part cannot be avoided, but it explains why the duration jumps around.

My plan is to look at narrowing the snapshot policy to the indices that still change, plus the small config indices, and to take a one-time final snapshot of the indices for customers three, four and five under a separate name before anything is removed. I wrote the candidate pattern down but did not apply it. My first draft was events-x*, which would also match a test index of Mara's, so I need to include the dash in the final pattern and check the match list before saving.

Before changing anything I want to restore one index of a small customer from the existing snapshot into a test cluster, to confirm that the snapshots are usable at all. I prepared the test cluster and the restore command for that, and did not run it yet.

If the narrower policy works, I expect the nightly run to drop to roughly 30 to 40 minutes, which would leave a safe gap before the reindex job. I started a note for the runbook of the snapshot policy.

What is left is the decision about the old indices for customers three, four and five, nothing is deleted. I also asked Tobias to add an alert if the snapshot takes more than 60 minutes.

summary: Wrote the cleanup job that deletes archived revoked API keys after 12 months, with a dry run mode, and tested it on staging against a copy of the archive table.
body:
Wrote the cleanup job for the archive table of revoked API keys, because Sam's contract check said the keys must be kept for 12 months and not longer. The job deletes rows whose revoke time is older than 12 months, in batches of 2,000 with a short pause, so the table does not lock for long. It has a dry run mode that only prints the count per customer and the oldest and newest revoke time that would go. That is the mode I used first on staging, with a copy of the archive table that holds 308,000 rows.

The dry run said 41,200 rows would be deleted, and a plain count query with the same condition gave the same number. The real run took under 2 minutes and the count afterwards was 266,800 rows, which is the difference exactly. I added a test with a fake clock that checks a key revoked just inside the limit stays and one just outside goes. A second test checks that the job refuses to run if the retention value is set below 12 months, so a typo in the config cannot delete data early. The audit trail table is not touched by the job, as the plan says, because it keeps only the key id and the time of the revoke. Tobias still needs to add the job to the weekly task in Terraform, with the same narrow role for the two key tables. I will ask him for that tomorrow and run the dry run on production before the first real run.

summary: Wrote a dry-run-only plan and a draft script for checking, snapshotting and deleting old per-customer search indices, and did not delete anything yet.
body:
The shard migration to the monthly layout is still only a plan, and no old index has been touched. Today I prepared the tooling for the cleanup that will come later, so the steps are written down and tested before they are used on real data.

The script takes a customer id and runs the steps in a fixed order: a count comparison for every month, with an abort on any difference; a snapshot with a name that includes the customer id; a check that the snapshot state is SUCCESS; then the deletion of old indices in batches of 5 with a 60 second pause. At this point only the first three steps can run against a cluster. The deletion step is behind a flag that I left switched off, and the code refuses to enable it without a second explicit confirmation.

The script has a dry run mode that prints the plan and the counts without changing anything. I ran it against the staging copy of one customer and it listed 63 months and 212 old indices that would be in scope. Nothing was deleted and nothing was snapshotted.

One bug showed up in the dry run. For months with a missing event type, the counts from the old and the new layout were compared with different filters, and the script reported a difference for 1 month. The old query treated a missing type as an empty value. I made both sides use the same filter, the one from the routing fix of last week.

I also made the script refuse to run if a shadow query log from the last 24 hours shows differences other than the future range case. This is a bit strict, but deleting cannot be undone, so I preferred that.

Mara reviewed the draft and asked for a lock so two runs cannot overlap. I used a Redis key with a TTL of 4 hours and the job name, set with NX. If the script dies, the lock expires.

I wrote a test with a fake cluster client that returns a different count for one month, and the script stops before the snapshot. A second test checks that a failed snapshot stops before the deletion.

Next I will agree with Mara and Tobias on which customer goes first and how long the safety net period should be, and I will write that into the plan note before any real run.

summary: Search v2 query parser now handles quoted phrases, field prefixes and negation, with 41 parser tests passing against the old grammar's fixtures
body:
Worked in the search-v2 worktree on the new query parser. The old parser split on whitespace and lost quoted phrases whenever a field prefix was present, so `user:"john smith"` became two terms. The new one is a small recursive descent parser in src/search/parser.ts that produces an AST, and a separate step turns the AST into an OpenSearch bool query.

Supported syntax now: bare terms, quoted phrases, `field:value`, `-term` and `-field:value` for negation, and `AND`/`OR` with parentheses. Unknown fields raise a ParseError with the column of the offending token instead of silently searching everything.

I replayed the 41 fixture queries from the old test suite. 38 gave the same bool query as before. The three that differed were all cases where the old output was wrong, for example a negation that was dropped inside a phrase. I updated those fixtures and noted why in the commit message.

One open point is wildcards. The old parser passed `*` through to OpenSearch untouched, and some customers use prefix searches like `host:web-*`. I kept that for the trailing position only, and a leading wildcard now returns a clear error because it is very slow on the big indices.

Next is per-field boosts, which need the parser output to carry the field name. The AST already does, so that should be small. I did not touch the reindex job today.

summary: Search v2 now parses range filters and wildcards, and the parser rejects a leading wildcard that scanned the whole index in a test, with 58 parser tests passing
body:
Worked on the next step of the search v2 query parser, after quoted phrases, field prefixes and negation were done. The new parts are range filters such as size:[100 TO 500] and trailing wildcards on terms. Both are translated into the OpenSearch query DSL by the same builder that handles the boosts.

The first version of the wildcard support accepted a leading wildcard too, like *error. On the large test index this query took 11 seconds and touched every shard, so the parser now returns a clear 400 with a message that says leading wildcards are not allowed. Trailing wildcards need at least three characters before the star, which keeps the cost in a range we can accept.

Ranges needed more care than expected. The old grammar treated brackets as plain text, so I went through the fixtures from the old grammar and found 6 that contained brackets in normal messages. Those now parse as plain terms when they are not in the form field:[a TO b], and I added them as regression tests.

Dates in ranges accept the ISO format only, and a malformed bound gives an error that names the field and the bad value. I first tried to be lenient and guess formats, but that made two ambiguous cases return different results, so I dropped it. The parser test count went from 41 to 58, all passing, and the parser runs on the 200 recorded queries without a change in the parsed output for the old syntax.

What is left is the error format in the API response, which should carry the position of the problem in the query string, and a note in the docs for Sam about the wildcard limit. Next I will start on the per-field boosts, which depend on this builder.

summary: Per-key rate limit counters on Redis now use a sliding window in a Lua script, replacing the fixed window that allowed double bursts at the boundary
body:
Started the rate-limits branch work on counters per API key. The current limiter uses a fixed window with INCR and EXPIRE, which lets a client send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next.

I wrote a Lua script that keeps a sorted set per key, trims entries older than the window, counts what remains and adds the new request in one atomic call. The script is loaded once with SCRIPT LOAD and called by its SHA, with a fallback to EVAL if Redis answers NOSCRIPT after a restart.

Key naming is `rl:{key_id}:{route_group}`. The curly braces keep the future option of a clustered Redis open. TTL on each key is the window length plus a few seconds.

Tested with a small load script at 500 requests per second against one key with a limit of 100 per minute. The fixed window let 198 through in a 70 second span, the sliding window let 100 through in any 60 seconds. The memory cost is higher: roughly 60 bytes per request in the window, so for a limit of 1000 per minute that is about 60 KB per active key. With 40 customers and a few keys each, that is fine.

Still to do: the limits need to be configurable per key in Postgres, and the admin console needs a field for it. I will ask Lena about the form next time. Also the 429 response should carry a Retry-After header computed from the oldest entry in the set.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why dashboard numbers differ slightly from CSV exports: the exports use event time, dashboards use ingest time
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer saw 12,408 events in a dashboard for one hour and 12,391 in the CSV export of the same hour. I checked the queries behind both.

The dashboard materialized views in ClickHouse bucket by ingest time, while the export endpoint filters on the event's own timestamp field. Events from mobile apps often arrive minutes late, so a few land in the next hour's bucket on the dashboard.

This is not a bug, but it is not documented either. I wrote a short paragraph for the docs draft in Sam's folder explaining both timestamps and which view uses which. I also suggested a docs example with a late-arriving event.

Sam will reply to the customer. I did not change any queries.

summary: Per-field boosts for search v2 are in: title and message fields weigh higher than metadata, configured by a small JSON file per index
body:
Continued in the search-v2 worktree. Boosts are read from config/boosts.json and applied when the AST is turned into the bool query, as `field^weight` in a multi_match for bare terms.

Defaults: message 3, title 2, tags 1.5, everything else 1. A customer can override these later through the index settings, but that is not part of this step.

I checked relevance with 20 saved queries from support tickets. In 16 the expected document is now in the top three, up from 9 before. Two of the failures were caused by tokenization of hyphenated hostnames, which is a separate analyzer issue I wrote down for later.

The unit tests cover the boost output for phrases, negation and field-specific terms. Field-specific terms do not get a boost, because the user already chose the field.

summary: Admin console showed stale API key limits because the React query cache never invalidated after saving; fixed with an explicit invalidate
body:
Lena reported that after editing a key's limit the console still showed the old value until a reload. The mutation hook in the console saved to the API but never invalidated the keys query.

I added the invalidate call in onSuccess and an optimistic update so the field does not flicker. Lena had already prepared the form, so I only touched the hook.

I also found that the API returned the limit as a string for keys created before a migration, which made the number input empty. I normalized it in the serializer.

Checked manually in staging with three keys. No tests added in the console, as Lena is moving that area to a new test setup soon.

summary: Reviewed Mara's pull request for the schema registry compatibility check; two changes requested around how optional fields are treated
body:
Reviewed the compatibility checker on the schema-registry branch. It compares a new event schema version with the latest registered one and rejects breaking changes.

The logic is sound for removed fields and type changes. Two problems I asked her to fix. First, adding a new required field was classed as compatible, but old producers would then send events that fail validation, so it has to be breaking unless a default exists. Second, changing an optional field to required was not caught at all.

I also suggested the error output list every incompatibility instead of stopping at the first one, since users will otherwise fix them one by one and resubmit.

The test file is good and has 27 cases. I asked for four more covering the two bugs above and nested objects. Mara agreed and will push changes tomorrow.

No code from me in this session, only review comments.

summary: Tobias and I checked the ECS task sizes for ingest workers: memory was oversized by about 40 percent, so the tasks go from 4 GB to 3 GB
body:
Looked at Prometheus memory metrics for ingest workers over the last two weeks. The peak resident memory was 1.8 GB and the typical value 1.2 GB, in tasks given 4 GB.

Tobias prepared the Terraform change. Going to 3 GB leaves a margin of more than 1 GB over the peak. CPU stays as it is.

We rolled it out to one of the services first and watched for an hour: no restarts, memory flat, no change in ingest latency. Then the rest followed.

Expected saving is a small but real part of the monthly ECS bill. I will note the number once the billing data shows a full week.

summary: Per-key rate limiter load test on a staging Redis showed 4,200 checks per second per instance with p99 under 3 ms, enough for the current peak with a wide margin
body:
Ran a load test of the new per-key rate limiter against the staging Redis, to see whether the Lua script holds up before the settings move to Postgres. The test replayed the key distribution of last week's real traffic, with a few hot keys and a long tail of quiet ones. One limiter instance handled about 4,200 checks per second, with a p99 of 2.8 ms for the script itself. The busiest real hour needs roughly a tenth of that.

Memory per key was small, around 300 bytes for a window with 100 entries, so 5,000 active keys use well under 2 MB. I did see the p99 rise to 9 ms when I pushed to 8,000 per second, and the cause was the connection pool of the test client, not Redis. The Redis CPU stayed below 30 percent during all runs. Next I will write down the numbers in the rollout notes and check the key naming with Tobias, so the limiter keys are easy to find in the monitoring.

summary: Wrote the first version of the nightly reindex for search v2 so it builds into a new index and swaps an alias, instead of rewriting in place
body:
The current nightly reindex deletes and rebuilds documents in the live index, which means search results are incomplete for part of the night. For search v2 I changed the job to write into a fresh index and switch an alias at the end.

Steps: create `events-v2-<run id>` with the current mapping, stream documents from Postgres in batches of 2,000 using the bulk API, refresh, compare the document count against the source, then update the alias `events-v2` in one atomic actions call. The previous index stays for one day so there is a way back.

On the staging copy with 3.1 million documents the job took 11 minutes, against 8 minutes for the old in-place job. The extra time is the larger index being written with replicas set to 0 and then raised to 1 after the load, which I think is a good trade.

The count check fails the job if the difference is more than 0.1 percent. In a first test I got a 0.4 percent difference and traced it to rows inserted while the job was running. I changed the check to use a snapshot of the maximum row id taken at the start.

Cleanup of old indices is a separate small function that keeps the two newest. I tested it against staging and it removed the right ones.

Not done yet: alerting when the job fails, and the cron entry. Both come next. I will also check how the job behaves with the boosts config, since the mapping is created per run.

summary: Added a failure alert and a last-success metric for the search v2 reindex job, so a silent skip now pages within 26 hours
body:
The reindex job now writes a Prometheus gauge, reindex_last_success_timestamp, through the pushgateway when it finishes with matching counts.

The alert rule fires when the value is older than 26 hours. It is defined in the alert rules repository, which is code already since the move of the rules.

I also added a counter for failures by reason: count mismatch, bulk errors, alias swap failure. This should make the first look at a page faster.

Tested by stopping the job halfway on staging. The alert went pending after the threshold as expected. The cron entry in the Terraform scheduled task is still the old one for the old job, so I left it for the next step.

summary: Redis memory on the cache instance grew to 78 percent; found that dashboard cache keys had no TTL and added a 15 minute one
body:
Tobias saw the Redis memory alarm creeping up. Using SCAN with a sample and MEMORY USAGE I found that about 60 percent of the memory belonged to keys with the prefix `dash:` that had no expiry at all.

The dashboard query cache wrote with SET but without EX, a leftover from the first implementation where the cache was invalidated by hand. Nothing did the invalidation anymore after the ClickHouse move.

I set a TTL of 15 minutes in the cache helper, which matches how fresh the materialized views are. For the keys that exist already I ran a one-off script that sets EXPIRE 900 on all `dash:*` keys, going through them in batches of 500 with a short pause.

Memory dropped from 78 to 41 percent within the hour. The cache hit rate went from 91 to 88 percent, which I accept.

I also renamed the prefix pattern in the docs of the cache helper so the key naming is `dash:{tenant}:{view}:{hash}`. Old and new names are the same, I only wrote it down. A check in code review is wanted so no cache write goes in without a TTL; I added a lint-style test that fails if the helper is called without one.

summary: Rate-limit settings per API key now live in a Postgres table with a migration, and the limiter reads them through a short-lived Redis cache
body:
Next step in the rate-limits branch: limits per key were hard-coded defaults. I added a table api_key_limits with key_id, requests_per_minute, burst and updated_at, and a migration that fills one row for each existing key from the plan default.

The limiter looks up the limit on each request, which would hit Postgres too often. So the lookup goes through Redis with the key `rlcfg:{key_id}` and a TTL of 60 seconds. A change in the admin console writes to Postgres and deletes the cache key, so changes apply at once in the common case.

I wrote tests for three paths: key with a row, key without a row falling back to the plan default, and a changed value after cache deletion. All pass.

A concern I checked: if Redis is down the lookup falls back to Postgres directly, and the limiter itself fails open. This was already the behavior for the counters, and I kept it, but I added a log line and a counter so we see it happening.

A load test at 2,000 requests per second across 50 keys showed the config lookup adding under 1 ms at p95. Postgres saw about 1 query per key per minute, as intended.

Still to do: the Retry-After header and the console form. Lena needs the API shape, which I wrote into the branch description.

summary: Added Retry-After and X-RateLimit headers to 429 responses; the value is taken from the oldest entry in the sliding window
body:
The limiter now returns three headers on every response for keyed requests: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset. On 429 there is also Retry-After in whole seconds.

To compute these the Lua script returns a small array: allowed flag, count in the window and the score of the oldest entry. Retry-After is the oldest score plus the window length minus now, rounded up, and never less than 1.

I had one bug: Reset was computed from the server clock of the Fastify process, while scores come from the Redis TIME command inside the script. With some clock skew in staging the header was off by two seconds. I now use the time returned by the script in both places.

Tests: a unit test for the header math with fixed numbers, and an integration test that exhausts a limit of 5 and checks the header values. Both pass.

The public API docs need a paragraph on these headers. I wrote a draft and left it for Sam to edit into the docs style, with a curl example that shows a 429.

summary: Tried a third party OpenSearch client library for the search API and dropped it: it hid error bodies and added 30 ms per request in our test
body:
The idea was to replace our thin wrapper around the OpenSearch HTTP API with a maintained client library, to get typed queries and built-in connection handling.

I tried it in a scratch branch for most of the afternoon. The typed query builder did not support some of the bool query shapes our parser produces, such as nested should clauses with minimum_should_match as a string, so I needed casts everywhere.

Error handling was the bigger problem. On a 400 from OpenSearch the library threw a generic error with only the status text, and the response body that says which field failed was only available through an internal property. Our support tickets depend on that message.

Then I measured. Against staging with 200 identical queries, our wrapper had a median of 18 ms and the library 49 ms. Part of that was its default of a sniffing request on start and a compression setting I could change, but after turning those off it was still at 33 ms. I did not find the rest in the time I had.

I decided to drop the experiment. Our wrapper is about 120 lines and works. I noted the numbers in the scratch branch README, then deleted the branch.

One useful thing came out of it: the wrapper had no timeout on the HTTP agent. I added a 10 second request timeout and a test with a mocked slow server.

summary: Per-key rate limits are finished: the console form from Lena works against the new API, and docs and a rollout plan are ready
body:
Today closed out the rate-limits branch work. Lena's form in the admin console now saves requests per minute and burst for each key, and the page shows the current usage from a new read endpoint.

I built the endpoint in the Fastify API. It reads the sliding window set for the key, returns the count and the limit, and requires the admin role. Usage is shown as a small bar in the console. Lena adjusted the styling and added validation: limits must be integers between 10 and 100,000 per minute.

I tested end to end on staging with three keys. Changing a limit applied within a second, thanks to the cache key deletion. Setting a limit below the current usage immediately returned 429 for the next request, which is the right behavior.

Rollout plan: first deploy the migration, which only adds a table and fills defaults. Second deploy the limiter code with the old fixed values as fallback. Third turn on enforcement per customer, starting with two small ones, and watch the 429 rate in Grafana. Tobias added a dashboard panel for 429 count per key.

One risk is that large customers send bursts at the top of the hour. For these the burst value is set at 5 times the per-minute rate in the migration defaults. I asked the user to confirm the numbers for the three largest customers.

Sam has the docs draft with headers and the limits table. The branch is ready for review by Mara tomorrow.

summary: Postgres slow query on the accounts settings page traced to a missing index on settings(account_id, key); the query dropped from 480 ms to 3 ms
body:
The pg_stat_statements top list showed a query on the settings table taking 480 ms on average. It filters by account_id and key, and the table has no index on either, only the primary key on id.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirmed a sequential scan over about 900,000 rows. This table grew after the per-index settings were added.

I created a unique index on (account_id, key) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, after checking that there were no duplicates. There were 14, all old test rows of one account, which I removed after asking Mara.

After the index the same query takes 3 ms. I added the index as a migration so staging and production stay in line.

summary: Wrote a design note for the audit log schema changes needed for compliance export, listing the fields auditors asked for
body:
Sam collected the requests of two customers who need an audit export. I went through them and compared with what the audit_log table stores today.

Missing today: the source IP of the actor, the API key id when the action came from the API, and a before/after snapshot of changed settings. The actor email and timestamps are there.

I wrote a design note proposing three new nullable columns and a JSONB column for the diff. Old rows keep nulls, and the export marks those fields as not recorded instead of leaving them blank.

I also noted a size concern. The table is about 40 GB, so adding JSONB diffs will grow it faster. Partitioning by month is an option, which would also make retention simpler. I did not decide that yet and wrote both options with rough sizes.

Next is to talk with the user about which option to take before any migration is written.

summary: Search v2 queries are now behind a flag per customer, and the first two customers run on v2 with identical result counts on 200 replayed queries
body:
Prepared the switch from the old search to v2. A flag in the settings table, search_v2_enabled, decides per account which parser and index alias is used. The default is off.

To check quality before turning anything on, I replayed 200 real queries from the access log of two small customers against both the old and the new path in staging, which has copies of their data. I compared result counts and the first ten ids.

Results: for 171 queries both gave exactly the same ids in the same order. For 24 the counts matched but the order differed, which is expected because of the boosts. For 5 the counts differed. I looked at each of them. Three had phrases with punctuation that the old analyzer split differently, and two used a leading wildcard which now gives an error, as planned.

For the leading wildcard errors I wrote a clear message and put it in the docs draft. The hyphenated hostname problem from before is the same analyzer issue. I added a custom analyzer with a word delimiter filter in the v2 mapping. After that, two of the three punctuation cases matched the old results too.

Latency on the same replay: old path median 52 ms, v2 median 41 ms, p95 140 ms against 118 ms. I think the alias with replicas helps here.

Plan: turn on v2 for the two customers tomorrow morning, keep the flag as an instant way back, and look at support tickets for a week. Then widen in steps. I told Sam which customers they are so support knows.

One thing to remember is that the reindex job must create the new analyzer in every run, since the mapping is built each time. I tested it and the first run on staging produced the right analysis for hostnames.

summary: Search v2 is on for the two pilot customers, with no errors in the first hours and a response time about 20 percent lower
body:
Turned on search_v2_enabled for the two pilot accounts this afternoon, after the user agreed.

In the first two hours there were 312 searches from them. No 5xx errors, two 400 responses from leading wildcard queries with the new message. The median latency was 39 ms.

I watched the OpenSearch cluster too. CPU stayed flat and the new index had no rejected requests in the search thread pool.

Sam knows to forward any ticket about results order. I will look at the numbers again tomorrow.

summary: Mara's schema registry changes landed after fixes, and I checked the new compatibility errors against five real schema updates from last month
body:
Mara pushed the fixes from the review: new required fields without a default are now breaking, optional to required is caught, and the checker lists every incompatibility in one run.

To see how it behaves on reality, I took five real schema updates that customers made last month from the audit log and ran them through the checker. Four were accepted, as they were at the time. One was now rejected, because a field went from optional to required. That change did cause a few validation errors for a customer back then, so the new check would have caught it.

I also tried a nested object where a child field was removed. The error path was printed as `payload.device.os`, which is clear enough.

The branch tests pass with 31 cases. The remaining work is the HTTP endpoint for registering schemas and the storage of versions in Postgres, which Mara has started.

summary: Decided to partition the audit log by month and wrote the migration plus a backfill that moves 40 GB in small batches without locking writers
body:
After talking with the user, we chose monthly partitioning for audit_log, which also fits the export work and makes dropping old data a cheap operation. The new columns from the design note are included in the same change.

The approach avoids a long lock. I created a new partitioned table audit_log_p with the same columns plus source_ip, api_key_id and diff JSONB. Partitions are created by a small function for the months that exist in the data and two months ahead. A trigger on the old table copies each new insert into the new table, so both stay in line during the move.

The backfill is a script that copies rows by id range, 20,000 rows per batch, with a pause of 200 ms between batches and a check of replication lag after each one. If lag goes above 5 seconds it waits. I ran it on a staging copy of the table first. The 40 GB copy took about 3 hours and 10 minutes there. Production has more traffic, so I expect more, maybe five hours.

I checked the result on staging with row counts per month and a checksum on the id and created_at columns for each partition. All matched. The indexes are created on the partitions after the copy, which was much faster than keeping them during the copy, about 25 minutes in total.

A surprise came from a foreign key. One table references audit_log(id), and a partitioned table needs the partition key in its primary key. I changed the primary key to (id, created_at) and dropped the foreign key, since nothing really depends on it. I confirmed with Mara that no code relies on that constraint.

The switch is a short transaction at the end: take a lock, copy the last rows, rename the tables, drop the trigger. I timed it on staging at under 2 seconds.

The next step is to run the backfill on production overnight. The schedule is tonight at low traffic, and I wrote the commands and the rollback in the runbook: rename back and keep the old table for one week. Tobias will watch the disk usage graph because the new table needs another 40 GB temporarily.

summary: The overnight audit_log backfill started on production and was at 22 percent after the first check, with replication lag staying under 2 seconds
body:
Started the backfill script on production a bit before eight in the evening, in a tmux session on the bastion host, with logging to a file.

After the first hour the script had copied 22 percent of the rows. Throughput was about 11,000 rows per second, a bit below the staging number, as expected. Replication lag never went above 2 seconds, so the pause logic did not trigger.

Tobias confirmed the disk usage graph: the volume went from 61 to 68 percent so far, and we have headroom to 85 percent. He set a temporary alert at 80 percent to be safe.

The insert trigger on the old table works. I checked that new rows from the last ten minutes were present in the new table with the same ids.

One small issue: the script printed progress every 1,000 batches, which is too rare to see a stall. I changed that to every 100 without restarting by using the log level setting that the script rereads. I did not touch the logic.

Tomorrow morning I will verify counts and checksums per partition, then do the switch if all matches. I left the notes in the runbook where Mara can find them in case something happens while I am away.

summary: Audit log backfill finished and verified, the table switch took 1.4 seconds, and the old table stays for a week as the way back
body:
The backfill had finished a little after four in the night, so it took about eight hours, longer than the five I estimated. The slower part was the second half, where the larger rows from 2 years of settings diffs sit. No errors in the log, and replication lag stayed under 4 seconds at its worst.

Verification came first. I compared row counts for every monthly partition against the old table and they matched, 100 percent. The checksum on id and created_at matched for each partition as well. I also compared 10,000 random rows by full content and found no differences.

Then the switch. I took the lock, copied the rows that the trigger had not yet covered at that point, which was none, renamed audit_log to audit_log_old and audit_log_p to audit_log, and dropped the trigger. The transaction took 1.4 seconds. The application logged two slow inserts of about a second during that time and nothing failed.

After the switch I checked that the audit writes go to the right partition, that the admin console audit page loads, and that the usual query by account and time range uses partition pruning. EXPLAIN showed only the one or two relevant partitions being scanned. The page load went from 900 ms to 180 ms for a customer with a long history.

I created the next partitions through the function and added a monthly cron job in the scheduled tasks, so partitions exist ahead of time. An alert fires if the newest partition is less than 20 days ahead.

Audit_log_old stays for a week, and then I will drop it to free the 40 GB. I wrote that in the runbook with the date given as relative to the switch. Autovacuum settings I set earlier for the old table were applied to the new partitions through a table-level default on the parent.

Next, the audit export work can start on the new columns. First I need to start the audit-export branch and write the export format with Sam, since the customers want CSV and a signed manifest.

summary: Search v2 reindex ran its first full build on a production copy: 14.2 million documents in 38 minutes, and the alias swap left no failed queries during a replay
body:
Ran the new reindex job from last week against a snapshot of the production data, to see real timing before it goes on the nightly schedule. It built into a fresh index and swapped the alias at the end, as designed. The build took 38 minutes for 14.2 million documents, with bulk requests of 2,000 documents.

While the swap happened I replayed 500 queries per minute against the alias. Zero queries failed and none returned an empty result during the swap. The old index stayed in place for rollback.

Two things came up. First, the refresh interval was still at one second during the bulk load, which slowed indexing. Setting it to -1 during the build and restoring it afterwards cut the time from 52 to 38 minutes. Second, replica count was copied from the old index, so the build wrote every document twice. Building with zero replicas and adding them after the swap brought the cluster load down visibly in Grafana.

I put both settings into the job config and added a step that restores them even when the build fails halfway. A test now covers that restore step. Left to do: delete old indices after three successful nights, and add a check that the new index document count is within 1 percent of the source table before the swap. Mara will review the config change tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam: the 429 responses for API keys come from the per-key limiter, and the old global limit only applies to keys without their own settings
body:
Sam asked why one customer saw 429 errors although their new per-key limit was higher than their traffic. I looked at the limiter logs. The customer had two keys, and only one had a row in the settings table. The second key fell back to the global default of 100 requests per second.

The fallback is intended, but the console did not show it. I told Sam how to read the effective limit from the key detail API. I also opened a small ticket for Lena to show the word default next to a limit that is not set per key.

No code change today.

summary: Audit export first working version writes NDJSON files by account and time range, streaming 2 million rows in 90 seconds with flat memory
body:
Started the audit export for compliance, based on the field list from the design note. The export reads the monthly partitions of audit_log, so a time range only touches the partitions it needs.

The first version is a command in the backend that takes an account id, a start and an end, and writes NDJSON to a file. It uses a server-side cursor with batches of 5,000 rows. I first tried loading a month at once, and memory went to 1.8 GB for a large account. With the cursor it stays around 120 MB.

Test with the largest customer: 2 million rows in 90 seconds. The output includes actor, action, target, ip, and the before and after values that the auditors asked for. The ip column was null for older rows, since it was added later. I kept null in the export instead of inventing a value, and documented it in the file header record.

I added a checksum line at the end of each file, a SHA-256 of all rows, so the auditors can verify that a file was not changed. Unit tests cover empty ranges, a range across a partition boundary and rows with unicode in the target field.

Open points: the export should run as a background job and not block the console, and the file needs a place to be stored with an expiry. Next step is the job and the S3 location. I also need to ask Sam whether the auditors want CSV as well.

summary: Audit export now runs as a background job with progress in Postgres and writes finished files to S3 with a 14 day lifecycle rule
body:
Moved the export from a command to a job. A new table audit_exports holds the id, account, range, status, row count and the S3 key. The worker picks up rows with status queued, updates the row count every 10,000 rows and sets done or failed at the end.

Files go to a dedicated S3 prefix. Tobias added a lifecycle rule in Terraform that deletes them after 14 days, and the bucket policy only allows the backend role to read them.

Download happens through a presigned URL that is valid for 15 minutes. I decided against streaming through the API, because large files would hold connections for a long time.

One bug: when two exports for the same account ran at once, both used the same temp file name and one corrupted the other. The name now includes the export id. A test starts two jobs in parallel and compares the checksums.

Failure handling is simple for now. A failed job is marked failed with the error text, and the user can start it again. Resume from the last row would be nice, but exports are short enough that it is not worth it yet.

Next: an API endpoint to create and list exports, and a permission check so only account admins can use it.

summary: Added the export API endpoints with admin-only permission and an audit log entry for every export, since exports of the audit log should be audited too
body:
Built POST and GET endpoints for exports in the Fastify API. Creating an export validates the range, which must be at most 13 months, and rejects overlapping duplicates that are still queued.

The permission check uses the existing role field, and only account admins pass. A test with a member role returns 403, and a test with another account's export id returns 404 and not 403, so ids do not leak.

Every export request writes its own row to the audit log, with the range and the requesting user. Mara pointed out this is what an auditor would ask first, and it was a two-line change.

The list endpoint pages by id, and the response never includes the S3 key, only a download link that is created on request. I wrote the endpoint docs for Sam with an example request and response.

One annoyance: the range validation used local time in one place and UTC in another, which made a range ending at midnight off by a day. Everything is UTC now, and a test pins that.

Lena will take the console side next week. I left a short note with the response shapes in the branch.

summary: Redis memory on the cache instance fell from 78 to 61 percent after the 15 minute TTL on dashboard keys, and the remaining growth is from search suggestion keys
body:
Checked the cache instance after the TTL change from a few days ago. Memory went from 78 to 61 percent and has been flat for two days. The key count dropped by about a third.

I sampled keys by prefix with SCAN and sizes from MEMORY USAGE. Dashboard keys are now small in total. The biggest remaining group is the search suggestion cache, with about 400,000 keys and no TTL. Each holds a small JSON list, but they add up to 1.1 GB.

No change yet. I want to know how often the suggestion keys are read before choosing a TTL. I added a counter for hits per prefix, so tomorrow there is data.

summary: Search v2 pilot got a third customer, and a field boost bug showed up: the boost file was read once at start so edits needed a restart, fixed with a reload on change
body:
Turned on search v2 for a third customer, a larger one with about 4 million events. Result counts on 200 replayed queries matched v1, and the response time was 18 percent lower.

While tuning their boosts I found a bug. The per-index boost JSON was read once at process start, so my edits did nothing until a restart. That made me think for an hour that the boost values had no effect.

The fix is a file watcher with a check of the modification time every 30 seconds. On a parse error, the loader keeps the old config and logs the error with the file name and line. A broken file should not take search down.

I wrote three tests. A valid change is picked up. An invalid change keeps the old values. A deleted file keeps the old values.

The boost values for the new customer: title 3.0, message 2.0, tags 1.5, metadata 1.0. I compared ranking on ten queries that their support team gave us. In seven the top result was the one they expected, and in v1 it was five of ten.

Two of the remaining misses are queries with a typo. Fuzzy matching is not in v2 yet, so I added it to the list. The third miss was a query where the expected document was older and ranking favored newer ones. I will look at a recency factor, but only as an option, because some customers want pure relevance.

Watch the error rate tomorrow. Nothing in the logs so far, and p99 stayed at 210 ms.

summary: Postgres autovacuum on the events metadata table was starting too late; lowering its scale factor to 0.02 cut dead tuples from 9 million to under 1 million
body:
A Grafana panel showed dead tuples growing on a busy table, up to 9 million, with autovacuum running only every few hours. The default scale factor of 0.2 means the vacuum waits for 20 percent of a large table to change.

I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 for that table only, with ALTER TABLE, and raised the cost limit slightly. After a day, dead tuples stay under 1 million and the vacuum runs about every 40 minutes, each run short.

No effect on write latency was visible. I will look at two other large tables for the same pattern next week.

summary: Wrote the first loader-retry design: large file loads resume from the last committed chunk instead of starting over, with backoff for 5xx from the ingest API
body:
Started on the document loader for large files. Today a failed load of a 6 GB file starts again from the beginning, and last week one customer file failed three times at 80 percent because of a short ingest API error.

The design splits the file into chunks of 10,000 events. After each accepted chunk, the loader writes the chunk number and a byte offset to a small state file next to the job. On restart it reads the state and seeks to the offset.

Retries use exponential backoff starting at 500 ms, doubling up to 30 seconds, with jitter, and a limit of 8 attempts per chunk. Only 5xx responses, timeouts and connection resets are retried. A 400 stops the load at once, because repeating bad data does not help.

Idempotency matters, since a chunk may be accepted but the answer lost. The ingest API already deduplicates by event id for 10 minutes, so a repeated chunk is safe. I checked this in the ingest code and wrote it into the design note.

I created the branch and a skeleton with the state file reader and writer plus three tests for it. Next step is the backoff and the error classification.

summary: Loader retry now classifies errors and backs off with jitter, and a test with a fake server that fails every third request completes a 100 chunk file
body:
Implemented the error classification and the backoff in the loader. Timeouts, resets and 502, 503, 504 are retried. 429 is retried too, and the loader respects the Retry-After header when present, which we added to the rate limiter some days ago.

Backoff starts at 500 ms and doubles up to 30 seconds with full jitter. After 8 failed attempts on one chunk the load stops and keeps its state, so a manual restart continues there.

For tests I wrote a small fake ingest server that fails every third request with 503. A file of 100 chunks loads fully, with 49 retries in total, and no chunk is lost or duplicated in the receiver's log. A second test kills the loader process in the middle and starts it again. It resumes at the right chunk.

One bug found: the state file was written after the chunk was sent but not flushed to disk, so a hard kill could repeat a chunk. It is fsynced now. Repeats are harmless because of deduplication, but I prefer the state to be right.

To do: a log line per retry with the chunk number and reason, and a try with a real 6 GB file in staging.

summary: Staging run of the loader with a real 6 GB file survived two forced ingest restarts and finished in 41 minutes, resuming correctly both times
body:
Ran the loader branch in staging with a 6 GB NDJSON file from the failed customer load. While it ran, Tobias restarted the staging ingest service twice.

Both times the loader logged a connection reset, retried chunk 212 and 389 with backoff, and continued. The total time was 41 minutes, with about 3 minutes lost to the waiting.

I compared the event count in staging against the file line count: 12,480,331 on both sides. No duplicates after deduplication by event id.

The retry log lines are in now. Each has the chunk number, the attempt, the reason and the wait time, which makes support questions easy to answer.

Memory stayed below 90 MB for the entire run, since the loader streams the file and holds only one chunk.

One gap: if the source file changes between a run and its restart, the offset is wrong. I added the file size and a hash of the first megabyte to the state file and refuse to resume if they differ.

summary: Merged the loader retry branch after review by Mara, with one change: the max attempts is now a setting and not a constant
body:
Mara reviewed the loader pull request this morning. Her main comment was that 8 attempts is a guess and large customers may want more. I moved it into a setting with the default of 8 and the same for the maximum backoff.

She also asked about the fsync cost on every chunk. I measured it: about 4 ms per chunk on the staging disk, against several seconds per chunk for the network, so it stays.

A second comment was about a log line that printed the full chunk URL including an API key in a query parameter. That was a real problem. The log now masks the key, and I searched the other loader logging for the same pattern and found none.

Tests all pass, 23 for the loader, including the new ones for settings. The docs for Sam have a short section on what happens when a load fails and how to continue it.

After merge I started the deploy of the loader to production. Nothing else is in the release. I will watch the first real large loads this week.

summary: Search suggestion keys in Redis are read mostly within an hour of being written, so they get a 2 hour TTL, which should free about 1 GB
body:
The hit counters per prefix I added two days ago gave data. For the suggestion keys, 94 percent of hits come within 60 minutes of the write, and almost none after 6 hours.

I chose a TTL of 2 hours to keep a margin. The change is in the suggestion cache write function, one line plus a constant, and a test that checks the TTL is set.

Existing keys have no TTL, so they will not expire by themselves. I wrote a small script that walks the prefix with SCAN in batches of 500 and sets the TTL on old keys. I ran it on staging first, then on production with a pause between batches. It took 11 minutes.

Memory on the cache instance dropped from 61 to 44 percent over the following half hour. Hit rate for suggestions did not change in a visible way.

Key naming: the suggestion keys are named sugg:{account}:{hash}, which fits the other prefixes. I added the TTL to the key list document.

summary: Alert rule for the reindex job fired a false alarm because the last-success metric reset on deploy; the metric now persists in a Pushgateway-free way using a Postgres row
body:
The failure alert for the search v2 reindex job paged this morning even though the job had succeeded. The cause was that the last-success metric lived only in process memory, and a deploy during the night restarted the service and reset it to zero.

I changed the job to write the time of its last success to a row in Postgres, and the metrics endpoint reads that row on each scrape. After a restart the value is still right.

I tested it by running the job, restarting the service and checking the gauge in Prometheus. It kept the earlier timestamp.

The alert threshold of 26 hours stays. I also added a note in the alert description with the first thing to check, the job log, and the command to start the job by hand.

Sam was on call and was woken at 04:10 by this, so I told him about the cause and the fix.

summary: Console form for audit exports from Lena is wired to the API; testing found the range picker allowed 14 months, so the limit is checked on both sides now
body:
Lena finished the console page for audit exports, and I tested it against the staging API. It has a range picker, a list of past exports with status, and a download button.

The first problem: the picker allowed a range of 14 months while the API accepts 13. The user would only see a generic error. We agreed that the form limits the picker to 13 months and the API keeps its check, with a clear error message text that the form shows as it is.

The second problem was the status refresh. The list polled every second, which is more than needed. It polls every 5 seconds while an export is running and stops when none is.

I ran an export of 6 months for the large test account. It took 48 seconds, the row count updated during that time, and the download gave a file with the right checksum line. I verified the checksum by hand with sha256sum over the rows.

A third issue was that a failed export showed the raw error text from the backend. Lena replaced it with a short message, and the details stay in the log.

Access check from the console: a member user does not see the menu entry, and a direct URL gives the 403 page.

For docs, Sam asked for screenshots. I gave him the staging link and a test account.

Still open: the question of CSV. Sam asked the auditors' contact and the answer is that NDJSON is fine as long as there is a description of the fields. I wrote that description today.

summary: Audit export went to production, and the first real export by a customer admin, 3.1 million rows, finished in 2 minutes with no load impact on the primary
body:
Deployed the audit export to production in the morning release. The migration for audit_exports ran in under a second.

To keep the load off the primary, the export reads from the replica. I checked that the cursor works there. A long read on a replica can be cancelled by replication conflicts, so I set max_standby_streaming_delay a bit higher for it, 60 seconds, after talking with Tobias.

The first real export came from a customer admin in the afternoon. It was 3.1 million rows over 9 months, and it finished in 2 minutes and 5 seconds. Replication lag on the replica stayed under 1 second, and primary CPU did not move.

I looked at the audit log for the export request itself, and it was there with the range and user.

One detail I noticed: file sizes are about 900 MB for such a range. The download over a slow connection could take longer than the 15 minute presigned URL, but the URL is only needed to start the download, so it should be fine.

Sam will tell the customer success contact that the feature is live. I wrote a short entry in the docs changelog.

What is left on this branch is only polish: compress files with gzip to save size, and an email when an export is ready.

summary: Gzip for audit export files cut sizes by 87 percent, and downloads now come as .ndjson.gz with the checksum computed over the uncompressed rows
body:
Added gzip compression to the audit export writer. A 900 MB file is now 118 MB, a reduction of 87 percent, and the writing time went up by only about 15 percent.

The checksum question needed a decision. Computing it over the compressed bytes would change if the compression level changed, but over the rows it stays stable. I kept the checksum over the uncompressed rows, as in the first version, and put a line in the description of the format that explains how to check it with zcat and sha256sum.

I tried zstd first because it is faster. Auditors' tools often handle gzip but not zstd, so I stayed with gzip, level 6. Level 9 gave only 2 percent more.

Tests: the file decompresses to the same rows as before, and a truncated file fails the gzip check, which is a nice property for a partial upload. I also checked the multipart upload to S3, because the writer now streams compressed data and the part size must be at least 5 MB. The writer buffers 8 MB per part.

Old export files in the bucket stay as they are and expire in 14 days.

I deployed it in the evening. One export ran after the deploy and the numbers matched my staging run.

Next is the email on completion, which needs a template from Sam.

summary: Sent the audit export ready email through the existing mail service, with a download link to the console and no file link in the mail itself
body:
Implemented the email for finished exports. The worker puts a mail job on the existing queue of the mail service when an export is done or failed.

The mail contains the range, the row count and a link to the console page of the export. It does not contain a presigned URL. Mails can be forwarded, and the console link needs a login and an admin role, which is the safer way.

Sam supplied the text. For a failed export the mail says that it failed and that the user can start it again, without technical details.

Test: an export in staging sent the mail within 3 seconds of finishing, and the link opened the right page. A test with a mail service that is down shows the export itself stays done, since the mail job is separate.

This closes the list for the audit export branch except the final review by Tobias, who wants to look at the bucket policy once more.

summary: Search v2 fuzzy matching added with a maximum edit distance of 1 for terms of 5 or more characters, which fixed 3 of the 4 typo queries from the pilot customers
body:
Started the typo work that was on the list since the third pilot customer. OpenSearch supports fuzziness in match queries, so the work is mostly in the parser output and in limiting the cost.

Rules I chose: terms of 1 to 4 characters get no fuzziness, since an edit there changes the meaning too much. Terms of 5 or more get an edit distance of 1. Distance 2 matched a lot of unrelated documents in my tests and doubled the response time.

Prefix length is set to 2, which means the first two characters must be right. This is a cheap way to keep the cost down, because the engine does not expand all terms.

Quoted phrases and field-prefixed exact terms are not fuzzy. A user who quotes something wants exactly that, and the parser tests have a case for each of these.

I took the 4 typo queries from the pilot customers. Three now return the expected document in the top 3, and the fourth had two typos in one word, which distance 1 does not cover. I left that one.

Performance on 200 replayed queries: median went from 38 to 44 ms, p99 from 210 to 265 ms. That is a visible cost, so fuzziness is a flag on the customer settings and not default.

I wrote 12 new parser tests, including one for a term of exactly 5 characters and one for unicode terms with accents. The accented case found a problem: the edit distance counts the combined characters differently in two forms of the same letter. The query text is normalized to NFC now before parsing.

The docs need a paragraph on fuzzy search. I will draft it and give it to Sam. Next is the recency factor, only as an option per index.

summary: Recency option for search v2 added as a per-index decay function, and on the pilot data it moved the newest relevant documents up without hurting exact title matches
body:
Built the optional recency factor. It uses a gauss decay on the event timestamp inside a function_score query, with a scale of 7 days, an offset of 1 day and a decay of 0.5. All four values are in the per-index JSON file next to the boosts, and without them there is no decay at all.

The main concern was that decay would push an old exact match below recent weak ones. I tested with the 10 queries from the third pilot customer and 30 more from the other two. Combining it with the field boosts as multiplication was too strong. A weight of 0.5 on the decay part fixed that, and exact title matches stayed in the top 3 in every case.

One of the earlier misses, where the expected document was old and recent ones ranked above it, is still a miss with decay on, as expected. That customer wants pure relevance, so they will keep it off.

Performance is a minor matter. The decay adds about 3 ms to the median.

Implementation notes: the field must be a date type in the mapping, and one old index had it as a keyword, from the first version. The reindex fixes that, but until then the loader refuses to enable decay for that index and logs a clear error. A test covers it.

I also found that the boost file reload I fixed some days ago works for the new keys too, so changing the scale does not need a restart.

The decision for the customers: decay is available on request, off by default. I will write this into the docs next to fuzziness.

For the next days: the reindex job runs nightly, and the pilot customers should get the fuzzy flag turned on for a week to see the effect on real traffic. I put a reminder to check the query logs for the zero-result rate, which is the number that should fall.

summary: Postgres connection count on the main database crept to 410 of 500 after the audit export and search deploys, traced to idle pools in two services
body:
Late in the day the connection graph in Grafana showed 410 of 500 connections used, up from about 300 a week ago. That is close enough to matter, because a spike during a deploy could hit the limit.

I listed connections by application_name from pg_stat_activity. The audit export worker held 40 idle connections, because its pool minimum was set to 40 by a copy of the API settings. The search API had also grown its pool when I raised the maximum for the replay tests, and never lowered it.

Changes: the export worker pool is min 2, max 10, since it runs a few jobs at a time. The search API pool is back to max 20. Both have an idle timeout of 60 seconds so that unused connections are closed.

After the deploy, the count went down to 290 within ten minutes. I let it run for an hour and watched it during a burst of traffic, where it peaked at 330.

I also thought about PgBouncer, which Tobias suggested earlier. It would help, but it brings a change in how prepared statements work, and I do not want to mix that into today. I added it to the list for later, with the numbers from today as the reason.

A small alert was added: warn at 400 connections, page at 460. Before, there was only the page at 480, which leaves no time.

The settings of all services are in one table in the wiki now, with the pool sizes, so a copy-paste of a value is easy to see.

Nothing was broken by the high count, and no errors showed up in the logs. It was only a margin issue, found by looking at the graph.

summary: Tobias reviewed the audit export bucket policy and found it too broad for list access; the export prefix is now the only one the backend role can list
body:
Tobias went through the Terraform for the audit export bucket today. He found that the backend role had s3:ListBucket on the whole bucket, while it only needs the export prefix.

The policy now uses a condition on s3:prefix, so listing works only below the export path. Reading and writing objects were already limited to the prefix.

Tobias also asked for server-side encryption with a bucket key and a deny rule for requests without TLS. Both are added. The encryption was a default in the account, but he wanted it explicit in the code, so a change of the account default does not matter.

I ran the export tests in staging against the changed policy. Upload, presigned download and the lifecycle rule all still work. A try to list the root of the bucket with the backend role gives AccessDenied, which is what we want.

Plan applied by Tobias in staging first and production an hour later. No change in behavior for users.

With this the review of the audit export branch is done. I merged it after the checks passed.

The list of what the feature contains, for the release notes: export by range up to 13 months, NDJSON with gzip, checksum, email on completion, admin only, every export logged. Sam has the text.

One thing for later: a retention of the export records themselves. The table grows by a row per export, which is small, but a cleanup after a year is cleaner. I added a note to the backlog.

Tomorrow I come back to the search work.

summary: Zero-result rate for the three pilot customers fell from 6.1 to 3.8 percent in a week with fuzzy matching on, and no customer reported worse results
body:
Looked at the query logs of the pilot customers, a week after fuzzy matching went on for them. Zero-result queries were 6.1 percent of all before, and are 3.8 percent now.

I looked at a sample of 100 queries that now return results but did not before. Seventy-one were plain typos where the match is clearly what the user meant. Eighteen were plausible. Eleven looked like noise, such as an id with one digit different, which matched another record. That last group worries me a bit, since for ids a near match is wrong.

A fix is to turn off fuzziness for fields marked as identifiers in the index config. I added a fuzzy boolean per field, default true, and set it to false for trace_id and user_id in the pilot indices. A test checks that a one-character difference in trace_id returns nothing.

Latency over the week: median 43 ms, p99 258 ms. Both are close to my test numbers.

No support tickets about worse results came in, Sam confirmed. One customer wrote that search felt more forgiving.

The plan is to offer fuzzy matching to the next five customers after the next reindex, since the new field setting needs the mapping from the nightly build. I will prepare the list with Sam.

summary: Dropped an attempt to generate the search boost JSON from the console UI: validation rules were too tangled, so the file stays hand-edited with a schema check in CI
body:
I spent about two hours on a prototype where Lena's admin console would edit the per-index boost file through a form. The idea was that support could change boosts without a developer.

The trouble was validation. Boost values depend on the mapping of each index, since a field has to exist and have the right type, and the decay settings need a date field. The form had to know the mapping, and I ended up copying mapping rules into the frontend. That would get out of date quickly.

I stopped there. The prototype is not merged, and I deleted the branch of it.

What I did instead is simpler. A JSON schema for the boost file, and a CI step that validates every file in the repo against the schema and also against the current mapping fixtures. A wrong field name now fails the build with a message that names the file and the field.

I checked it by breaking a file on purpose in three ways: an unknown field, a negative boost and a decay on a keyword field. All three failed CI with a readable message.

Sam can still ask for a change, and a developer edits the file. For the number of customers we have, that is fine.

summary: Search v2 pilot got a per-field boost schema check in CI, and the first bad boost file it caught had a negative weight that would have silently flipped ranking
body:
After dropping the console generator for boosts, I added the schema check to CI today. It validates the hand-edited boosts JSON: field names must exist in the index mapping, weights must be between 0.1 and 10, and no field may appear twice.

I wrote the schema with Ajv in the search API repo, in `boosts.schema.json`. The mapping check needs the index mapping, so CI loads a snapshot of it from `fixtures/mapping.json`. That snapshot has to be refreshed whenever the mapping changes, which I noted in the README.

To test it I ran the check against the three pilot customer boost files. Two passed. The third, from the newest pilot, had a weight of -1 on the `tags` field. Someone had probably meant to demote tags, but OpenSearch rejects negative boosts on some query types and the reload code logged a warning and kept the old file. So the edit never took effect and nobody noticed.

I fixed the file to 0.5, which does what was intended. I also made the reload code log at error level when a file fails validation, because a warning was too quiet.

The check takes about 300 ms in CI. It also runs as a pre-commit hook for people who want it locally, but I did not make that mandatory.

Left to do: tell Sam, who edits some of these files for customers, how to read the validation error output. I will write a short section for the docs tomorrow. Mara reviewed the schema and asked for a maximum on the number of fields per file, so I set it to 40.

Next is checking that the reload path behaves the same when the file is replaced in place versus written by rename, since the two pilots deploy differently.

summary: Documented how to read the boost file validation errors for Sam, with three real examples from today's CI failures and what to change in each
body:
Wrote the docs section on the boost file check that I promised Sam. It lives in the internal docs next to the search v2 pilot notes.
