It lists the three error kinds the schema check produces: unknown field, weight out of range, and duplicate field. Each has a real message copied from the failures I provoked yesterday, plus the one-line fix.

Sam read it and asked what happens when a customer wants a field that is not in the mapping yet. The answer is that the mapping change comes first, through a reindex, and the boost file follows. I added that as a short note with a warning that CI will reject the file until the mapping snapshot in the repo is updated.

I also added a small table of sensible weight ranges from the pilots. Titles sit around 3 to 5, body text at 1, and tags at 0.5 to 1.5. These are only starting points, and I said so in the text.

Sam found one confusing sentence about the reload, which reads the file on change. I rewrote it to say that edits take effect within a few seconds and no restart is needed.

Nothing in code changed in this session. The next step is the rename versus in-place replacement test for the reload.

summary: The boost file reload misses atomic renames, since the watcher followed the old inode, and now watches the directory so both deploy styles work
body:
I tested the reload with the two ways the pilot customers deploy their boost files. In-place edits worked. Atomic replacement by writing a temp file and renaming it did not: the watcher stayed on the old file and never fired.

The cause was that the watcher was attached to the file path, which on Linux follows the inode. After a rename the path points to a new inode and the old one is gone, so no more events arrive. That explains a report from the third pilot last week, where an edit took effect only after a deploy.

The fix watches the containing directory instead and filters events by file name. On create, rename or write events for our file, it debounces for 200 ms and then reloads. The debounce matters because editors often emit several events per save.

I wrote tests for four cases: in-place write, rename over the file, delete followed by create, and an invalid file. In the invalid case the old boosts stay active and an error is logged. All four pass locally and in CI.

On staging I changed a weight with both methods and watched the query explain output. The new weight showed up within about a second each time.

One side effect: the directory watcher also sees other files in the config directory. The filter ignores them, but the debounce timer was shared, so I made it per file. Mara reviewed the change and was fine with it.

It goes out with the next search API deploy this afternoon. I will check the pilot customers' logs for reload messages after that.

summary: Postgres slow query review found the audit log list endpoint scanning a month partition without the account filter, and a composite index brought it from 2.1 s to 40 ms
body:
Lena reported that the audit log page in the admin console felt slow for the larger accounts. I pulled the slowest queries from pg_stat_statements and the audit list query was at the top, with a mean of 2.1 seconds.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed it scanning the whole partition for the current month and filtering on account_id afterwards. The old index was on (created_at) only, and that made sense before the partitioning, when the table was queried mostly by time.

I created a composite index on (account_id, created_at DESC) on the partitions. It was created concurrently, one partition at a time, to avoid blocking writers. Each build took between 1 and 4 minutes, and the largest partition added about 3 GB.

After that the query uses an index scan and the mean dropped to 40 ms. For the biggest account it is around 90 ms, because they have many rows per page.

The new partitions need the same index. The monthly partition creation job did not include it, so I changed the job to create it with the partition. I checked it by creating next month's partition on staging.

I also found an index on (event_kind) that has not been used for months according to pg_stat_user_indexes. I did not drop it yet. I will watch it for another two weeks and decide then.

The old pre-partition table from the audit migration is still there as the way back, and I left its indexes alone.

Lena checked the console page and confirmed the list loads instantly now. The export job was not affected, as it streams with its own cursor query.

summary: Redis memory on the cache instance is flat at 58 percent after the suggestion TTL change, and the biggest key group is now dashboard query results
body:
Checked Redis memory after the 2 hour TTL on search suggestion keys had been live for two days. The cache instance sits at 58 percent, down from 61, and the curve is flat over the last 36 hours.

I sampled the keyspace with `--bigkeys` and a scan that sums MEMORY USAGE by key prefix, on a replica to keep the load off the primary. The result by prefix:

- `dash:` query results, about 41 percent of the used memory
- `sugg:` suggestions, about 17 percent
- `sess:` sessions, about 12 percent
- the rest is rate limiter counters and small things

The dashboard group is the largest but it is bounded by the 15 minute TTL, so it follows traffic rather than growing. The suggestion group dropped by roughly a gigabyte as predicted.

One oddity: a handful of `dash:` keys are over 5 MB each. They belong to the largest customer and hold wide result tables. Compressing them before the write might help, but the CPU cost on the search API is unknown. I noted it as an idea and did not try it.

Key naming also has a small problem. Some older keys have no prefix colon structure, like `ratelimit_key_abc`, and they are hard to count in the scan. A renaming would need a migration for live counters, which is not worth it now. New keys follow the `group:id` form.

No change to the setup today. The next look at the memory graph is in a week.

summary: Wrote the ingest client retry guide for customers after two support tickets about duplicate events, explaining the batch id header that makes retries safe
body:
Sam forwarded two tickets from customers who saw duplicate events after their own client retried a timed-out batch. Both used a home-grown client that resends the same batch when a response is slow.

The ingest API already supports a batch id header, and a repeated id within 24 hours is acknowledged but not written twice. That was in the API reference but only in one line, so neither customer knew about it.

I wrote a longer section for the public docs. It explains why a timeout does not mean the batch failed, how to generate a stable id per batch, and a backoff schedule: start at 500 ms, double, cap at 30 seconds, with jitter. It states that 429 and 5xx responses are safe to retry, while 400 and 413 are not.

I added short examples in curl and in Python. I ran both against staging, including a forced resend, and confirmed the second send returned 200 with the `duplicate: true` flag and the event count stayed the same.

One gap showed up in testing: the dedupe window is kept in Redis, so a flush of that instance would reopen the window. This is acceptable and I added a note that the guarantee is best effort for 24 hours.

Sam will send the link to the two customers and review the wording tomorrow.

summary: Per-key rate limit settings now have an admin console form and an API, after a week of editing them by SQL, with validation that rejects limits above the plan
body:
Per-key limits have been set by hand in SQL since the rate-limits branch landed, and Sam asked twice for a way that does not need an engineer. Today I built the API side and Lena built the form.

The endpoint is `PUT /admin/keys/:id/limits`. It takes requests per second and a burst value. The service validates three things: both are positive integers, burst is at least the rate, and the rate does not exceed the account's plan ceiling. Violations return 422 with a message naming the field.

The settings go to the Postgres table that the limiter already reads, and the limiter picks changes up from a Redis pub/sub message, so changes apply within a second without restarting anything. I tested that by setting a limit of 5 per second on a test key, sending 50 requests and seeing 429 after the burst, then raising it and seeing the requests pass.

While testing I found that deleting a limit row left the old value cached in the limiter process. The fall back to the global default only happened after a restart. I fixed it so a delete publishes the same message, and added a test for it.

Every change writes an audit log entry with the old and new values and the admin who made it. That went in without trouble using the same helper as the exports.

Lena's form shows the current values and the plan ceiling next to the input. She added a confirmation step when the new limit is more than 5 times the old one, which seemed sensible to me.

Open points: bulk editing for customers with many keys, and a display of the actual current usage next to the limit. Both are for later. Mara will review the PR tomorrow morning.

summary: Mara's review of the rate limit console change found a race between the delete message and a limit update, which is fixed with a version number on each row
body:
Mara reviewed the per-key limit API and form and raised one real issue. If an admin updated a limit and another admin deleted it a moment later, the two pub/sub messages could arrive at a limiter process in the wrong order and leave the deleted value active.

I reproduced it with a test that publishes the two messages in reverse order. The limiter ended with the updated value although the row was gone.

The fix adds a version column to the limits table, incremented on every change including deletes, which are now soft deletes with a flag. The message carries the version, and a limiter process ignores any message with a version lower than the one it has for that key. A periodic full reload every 5 minutes remains as a safety net.

That needed a migration. The column has a default of 1 and the table is small, a few hundred rows, so it ran in milliseconds. I tested the migration on a staging copy and on the way down.

I also changed the form's save so that it sends the version it loaded. If the server has a newer one, it answers 409 and the console shows a message to reload. Lena changed the form for that in an hour.

Mara also asked about the plan ceiling lookup, which is read on every update. It hits Postgres, but updates are rare, so no cache is needed.

Other review comments were small: a naming change from `rps` to `rate_per_second` in the API, and an extra test for burst smaller than rate. Both are done.

All tests pass and the change is merged. Deploy is planned for this afternoon, and I will watch the 429 rate for the larger customers for a day afterwards.

One more thing I checked: the audit entries for the updates contain the version too. That helps with later questions about who changed what first.

summary: Rate limit console change is in production, and the 429 rate for the big customers did not move in the first hours
body:
Deployed the per-key limit API and form after lunch. The migration for the version column ran in under a second.

I watched the 429 rate in Grafana per account for the five largest customers. It stayed at the same level as the same hours the day before, below 0.1 percent for all of them.

Sam used the form to raise the limit for one customer who had asked for more headroom, from 200 to 400 requests per second. The change showed in the audit log and the limiter used it within a second.

No errors in the search or ingest logs related to the change. I will check again tomorrow morning.

summary: Postgres connection count dropped from 410 to 260 after setting pool maximums in the two services with idle pools
body:
Followed up on the connection count that had crept up to 410 of 500. The two services were the audit export worker and the search API, and both used pool defaults of 50 connections per process with no idle timeout.

I set the maximum to 10 for the export worker, which runs two processes, and 15 for the search API, which runs six. Both now close idle connections after 60 seconds. Neither service had ever needed more than 6 at once according to the pool metrics.

After the deploy the count fell to 260 within ten minutes and stays there. Query latency in both services is unchanged.

I added a Grafana panel for connections by application name, which needed `application_name` set in the connection strings. Both services now set it.

I also lowered the alert threshold from 450 to 380, so there is more warning than before. Tobias agreed with the number when I asked.

The ingest worker still has a large pool, but it uses it. I left it alone.

summary: Search v2 pilot grew to five customers, and a synonym file for one of them exposed that the analyzer applied synonyms at index time, forcing a reindex to change them
body:
Two more customers joined the search v2 pilot, so five now run on v2. The queries replayed from their old traffic gave the same result counts for four of them, and the fifth had 3 percent more results, which comes from the fuzzy matching and looked fine.

The fifth customer also sent a synonym list for product names, around 120 pairs. I added them to the analyzer for their index and found that the analyzer in the v2 mapping applies synonyms at index time. That means any later change to the list needs a full reindex of that customer's documents. For a customer with 3 million documents this takes about 8 minutes, which is acceptable but not nice.

I looked at moving the synonyms to query time with a search analyzer. It works for single-word synonyms. Multi-word synonyms like `usb c` and `usb-c` behave less predictably, and two of the 120 pairs gave strange scoring in tests.

I decided to use the search analyzer approach for single words and keep the few multi-word pairs out for now. Sam will tell the customer which pairs are left out and why.

The reload of the synonym file without a reindex needs the index to be closed and reopened, or the update analyzers API. I tested the latter on staging and it works for search-time analyzers.

I wrote down the rule in the pilot notes: single-word synonyms at query time, multi-word later.

Tomorrow I will replay the customer's queries again with the new setup and compare results.

summary: Replay of the fifth pilot customer's queries with query-time synonyms gave the expected hits, and the zero-result rate fell from 7.4 to 5.0 percent
body:
I replayed 300 queries from the fifth pilot customer against staging with the synonym file at query time. Result counts went up for 41 queries, which were the ones using product name variants, and none went down.

The zero-result rate on the replay fell from 7.4 percent to 5.0 percent. The remaining zero results are mostly typos beyond one edit and product codes that do not exist.

I also checked for ranking damage. Exact title matches still ranked first in all sample queries I looked at, 25 of them by hand.

Updating the synonym file through the update analyzers API worked without closing the index. Search latency did not change in a visible way.

The customer will go live on the new setup this week once Sam confirms the list of left-out pairs with them.

summary: Started the ingest worker batch write change: the worker now collects events for up to 50 ms or 500 events before one insert, which cut write calls by a factor of 40 in a local test
body:
Today I started the ingest-batching work. Until now the worker wrote each event batch it consumed from Redpanda as separate inserts, and with many small batches this means many round trips to the store.

The new design adds a buffer per partition consumer. It flushes when it holds 500 events or when 50 ms have passed since the first event arrived in the buffer, whichever comes first. The flush writes one multi-row insert.

I wrote the buffer in `worker/batcher.go` with a clock interface so tests do not depend on real time. Tests cover size flush, time flush, flush on shutdown and an insert failure.

The failure case needed thought. On a failed insert the offsets of the buffered events must not be committed. I made the commit happen only after the flush returns successfully, so a crash replays the buffer. That means at-least-once delivery, as before, and the dedupe on event id in the store handles duplicates.

In a local test with a generator sending 20,000 small batches of 10 events each, the number of insert calls fell from 20,000 to about 500. That is a factor of 40. End-to-end latency from produce to stored rose by a median of 28 ms, as expected from the wait.

There are open questions: the right flush interval for the low-priority topic, where the latency matters less and a longer wait would batch more, and the memory per buffer when events are large. I set a byte limit of 4 MB as a third flush condition.

Nothing is deployed yet. Next I want a load test on staging with the real event mix and a check of the consumer lag.

summary: Batching worker rollout on the ingest path started with a canary plan, and a flush bug on shutdown that lost the last partial batch was found and fixed before any production task ran it
body:
Before the canary of the batching worker, I read through the shutdown path of the ingest worker and found a real problem. On SIGTERM the worker stopped its consumer loop but never flushed the buffer that collects events for up to 50 ms or 500 events. Any events still in that buffer were lost, although their queue offsets had been marked as done.

I reproduced it locally with a script that sends 10,000 events and kills the worker at random moments. In 20 runs, 14 lost between 1 and 380 events. That is the kind of loss that would only show up as a vague customer complaint about missing events after a deploy.

The fix has two parts. The shutdown handler now stops reading, flushes the buffer with a 5 second timeout and only then commits the offsets. The offset commit also moved to after the insert returns, so a crash between the two causes a redelivery and not a loss. Redelivery is safe because the insert is keyed on the event id and ignores duplicates.

I added a test that fills the buffer with 300 events, sends the shutdown signal and checks that all 300 are in the store and the committed offset matches. I ran the kill script again 50 times with zero lost events and at most 12 duplicates that the key rejected. The ECS stop timeout was 30 seconds, which is enough for the flush, so Terraform did not need a change.

I also added a metric for the number of events flushed on shutdown and a log line with the count, so we can see it during real deploys. Mara reviewed the diff and asked for the timeout to be a setting, which I changed. The canary on one production task is planned for tomorrow morning. If the lag stays equal and the insert calls drop as in the local test, the rest of the tasks follow after that.

summary: Search v2 pilot customers got a short note on how fuzzy matching and the recency option behave, written from the real queries of the pilot so support has answers ready
body:
Wrote a one page note for the five pilot customers and for Sam about how search v2 behaves now. It covers the fuzzy matching, the recency decay and the per-field boosts, each with a plain explanation and one real query from the pilot data.

For fuzzy matching, the note says that terms of 5 or more characters tolerate one typo and shorter terms must match exactly. I included the example of a misspelled product name that now finds the right documents. I also listed the case that still fails, a typo in the first two letters, because the pilot customers had asked about it.

The recency section explains that newer documents move up only when the text relevance is similar, so an exact title match from last year still wins over a weak match from yesterday. I checked this claim against 30 replayed queries before writing it and it held in all of them.

Sam read the draft and asked for a short list of what to answer when a customer says results changed. We added three standard answers with the flag name to check per customer. The note goes out to the pilot customers tomorrow, and the same text moves into the docs once the pilot ends.

summary: Canary of the batching worker on one production task ran for two hours with equal lag and a 36x drop in insert calls, so the rollout to the rest starts tomorrow
body:
I deployed the batching worker to one of the production ingest worker tasks and let it run for two hours during the busiest part of the morning.

Consumer lag on its partitions was the same as on the old tasks, with p99 around 150 ms. Insert calls per second were 36 times lower than on a comparable old task. CPU was at 28 percent against 52.

I compared stored event counts for the partitions the canary handled against the produced counts from Redpanda offsets, and they matched. No duplicates beyond what the dedupe removes were seen, and the dedupe counter did not rise in a notable way.

One log message needs cleaning up: the buffer logs at info level on each timer flush, which gave thousands of lines per minute. I moved it to debug and kept a summary line once per minute.

The rollout of the rest is for tomorrow morning, task by task, with Tobias watching the load balancer side. I will keep the old image tag ready in case.

summary: Full rollout of the batching worker finished with no lag increase, and the primary store write load fell by about two thirds, which also reduced the replication lag spikes
body:
The rollout of the batching worker went to all ingest worker tasks this morning, one task at a time with five minutes between them. Tobias watched the load balancer and the queue.

Nothing unusual came up. Consumer lag stayed below 250 ms at p99 on all partitions throughout, and the highest single value was 410 ms, during a task restart.

The effect on the store was larger than I expected. Write operations per second fell from about 9,000 to 2,800, which is a drop of roughly two thirds. The disk write throughput fell less, about 20 percent, since the bytes are the same.

Postgres replication lag also looked better. The metadata writes for the ingest path were batched in the same flush, and the short spikes of 3 to 4 seconds that appeared each evening did not appear today. I do not want to claim a cause from one day, so I will compare over a week.

I checked the low priority topic as well. Its flush interval is still 50 ms, and a longer one would batch more. I tried 200 ms on one task, which cut inserts for that topic by half again with no complaints from the lag alerts. I made that a setting for the low priority topic and set it to 200 ms in Terraform.

A problem I found at the end of the day: the metric for buffer fill level used a label with the partition and the task id, which produced many series. Prometheus memory grew a little. I removed the task id label from that metric, since the instance label already identifies it.

The dashboards for the ingest worker got two new panels, flush size distribution and flush reason, the latter showing size, timer, bytes and shutdown. In the first hours the timer flushes are 70 percent for most partitions and size flushes dominate on the page view partition.

Remaining work: a runbook entry about what to do when the buffer fill alert fires, and the decision about whether the batch change needs a note in the customer-facing docs. I think not, as the ingest API behavior has not changed. The branch can be merged after a week of observation.

summary: Attempted to replace the hand-written Redis key helper with a typed key library and dropped it after it doubled the allocations in the rate limiter hot path
body:
I tried a small refactor to make Redis key naming safer: replace the string concatenation helpers with a typed key builder library that I found, so that a key can only be built with its group and the right id types.

The idea was to end the inconsistent names like `ratelimit_key_abc` next to `dash:abc`. The library builds keys from a template and checks them at compile time.

I converted the search suggestion and dashboard code first, and it worked. Then I converted the rate limiter, which builds a key on every request. A benchmark showed 2 allocations per key become 5, and the time per key rose from 90 ns to 310 ns. At the request rates of the ingest API this adds up to measurable CPU, and the limiter is the hottest path in the service.

I looked for a way around it, with a pooled buffer inside the library, but it would need a fork. I did not want to own a fork of a small library for a naming convention.

I reverted the limiter change and then the others, because having two styles would make the naming worse. The branch is deleted. What I kept is a short list of rules in the repo docs about key names, `group:id` with lower case groups, and a lint test that scans for key literals not following it in new code.

The lint test found three existing places with off-pattern keys. They are old counters with live data, so I left them and put them in an allow list with a comment.

Mara had suggested the library, and I told her the numbers. She agreed to keep the helper functions. Tests pass and nothing was deployed.

summary: A week of data confirms the batching change: replication lag spikes are gone and the evening peak write rate is 2.9k per second, so the branch is ready to merge
body:
Reviewed seven days of metrics after the batching rollout.

Consumer lag p99 stayed below 300 ms every day. The write rate in the evening peak is about 2,900 per second, against 9,400 before. The replication lag spikes of 3 to 4 seconds disappeared completely, and the maximum in the week was 1.3 seconds.

The buffer fill alert fired once, during a restart of the store for a minor patch by Tobias. It cleared in under a minute, and the runbook entry I wrote says exactly that case is expected.

I also looked at the dedupe counter. It is at the same level as before the change, so the replays after restarts are not causing more duplicates.

Mara reviewed the final diff and asked for one thing, a comment in `batcher.go` explaining why offsets are committed only after the flush. I added it, and the branch is merged.

summary: Search API latency review found the suggestion endpoint making one OpenSearch call per keystroke without a cache, and a 30 second cache on prefixes cut calls by 45 percent
body:
I looked at the latency of the search API with the traces from the last week. The suggestion endpoint had the worst p99, around 380 ms, while normal search was at 140.

The console and some customer apps call it on each keystroke. Each call became a separate OpenSearch query, even when many users typed the same prefixes, which is common for the first two or three letters.

I added a cache in Redis for suggestion results keyed by customer, index and prefix, under the `sugg:` group, with a TTL of 30 seconds. The short TTL keeps new documents visible quickly, and it matters less than the hit rate on short prefixes.

After a few hours in production, the hit rate was 45 percent overall. It was 70 percent for prefixes of up to 3 characters and about 20 percent for longer ones. Calls to OpenSearch for suggestions fell by the same amount.

The p99 for the endpoint fell from 380 to 210 ms. Cached responses return in about 4 ms.

I checked the memory use, since this adds keys to the instance. With the small TTL the increase was under 100 MB, and the instance stayed at 58 percent.

The cache key includes the boost file version, so a boost change does not return stale ordering. I tested that by changing a weight and querying again.

What is not done is a limit for very long prefixes, which are rarely repeated and fill the cache with entries that never hit. I will cache only up to 12 characters.

summary: Wrote the plan for the new search index shard layout by month instead of by customer, with the reasons, the open risks and a stepwise migration outline
body:
I spent the session writing the plan for the new shard layout of the search index. Today the index is split by customer, and the largest customers have shards much bigger than the rest, while small customers share shards with unbalanced load.

The proposal is monthly indexes, with an alias per customer and a filter on customer id. Old months can be made read only and merged into fewer shards, and they can be dropped when retention ends, without delete-by-query work.

Benefits I listed in the plan:
- shard sizes stay predictable, around 30 to 40 GB
- retention becomes dropping an index
- recent months, which most queries hit, sit on fewer shards
- the nightly reindex can work on one month instead of a whole customer

The risks are more real. Queries without a time range would have to hit every month, and some customers search over their whole history. With 24 monthly indexes a query touches 24 shards in the worst case, and I estimated the cost with a test on the staging copy: a full history query went from 140 to about 230 ms. That is a real cost, and a cache or a time range default in the console may take care of part of it.

A second risk is the number of shards in the cluster. 12 customers of the large kind times months would be too many if we kept per-customer indexes, so the filter alias approach is needed, and the filter adds a small cost per query.

The migration outline has five steps: create the monthly indexes and templates, dual write new documents to both layouts, backfill month by month, switch reads per customer with a flag as for search v2, and drop the old indexes after a hold period. Each step has a way back.

I also noted that the search v2 mapping should be final before this starts, so we do not reindex twice. Mara and Tobias will read the plan and comment, and Tobias needs to size the cluster storage for the dual write period, when the data takes twice the space.

Nothing is started. I put the plan in the repo docs folder as `search-shards.md`.

summary: Tobias estimated the storage for the dual write period of the shard migration at 1.9 times current, which fits in the cluster only if two large customers move last
body:
Tobias read the shard plan and calculated the storage need during the dual write period. The current index data is about 2.1 TB with replicas. During dual write and backfill the old and new layouts both exist, so the maximum is close to 1.9 times that, around 4 TB.

The cluster has 5 TB of disk, and with the watermark at 85 percent that leaves 4.25 TB. It fits, but with little room. He suggested moving the two largest customers last, so the old data of the others can be dropped first and free space as we go.

I added that to the plan as an ordering rule. He also proposed a disk alert at 75 percent for the period, and I added it to the list of prerequisites.

Mara commented that the dedicated backfill should use the existing reindex job code with a month filter, instead of a new tool. That seemed right to me and I changed the outline accordingly.

Open question: should the hold period of the old indexes be one week or two? Given the disk, one week is more realistic.

summary: Alert for Redis memory above 80 percent fired twice at night from a cache warm-up job, so the job now spreads its writes over 20 minutes instead of one burst
body:
The Redis memory alert paged on-call twice last night, at 80 percent each time, and cleared within ten minutes. Looking at the graphs, the jumps matched the start of the nightly dashboard cache warm-up, which writes the results for the main dashboards of all customers in one burst.

The job computes about 4,000 result sets and writes them right away. Memory rose by 1.6 GB in two minutes, then fell back as the previous day's keys expired and the older entries were replaced.

I changed the job to write in 40 groups with 30 seconds between them, so the whole warm-up takes 20 minutes. Memory now rises in small steps and the peak is at 66 percent.

The results of the warm-up are the same, and the dashboards are still ready before the first customers log in, which is around 06:00 for the earliest ones. The job finishes at 02:40.

I considered raising the alert threshold to 85, but a burst-driven alert is a sign of a real load pattern. I kept the threshold.

I also added a metric for the duration of the warm-up job and its last success, kept in the Postgres row like the reindex job does, so a failing job gets noticed.

Tobias had no objections. I will check the graph tomorrow after the next run.

summary: Merged the first customer-facing note on query-time synonyms into the search docs, listing single-word synonyms as supported and multi-word pairs as not yet
body:
Wrote the docs page for synonyms in search v2, with Sam reading along. It says that a synonym file can be supplied per customer, that single-word synonyms apply at query time and changes appear within a few seconds, and that multi-word pairs are not yet supported.

I explained with an example why multi-word pairs are hard: `usb c` and `usb-c` are tokenized differently, so the scores come out strange. We say they are planned but have no date.

Sam added a short checklist for support to use when a customer sends a list, covering the format, the size limit of 500 pairs and how long it takes to apply.

The page is merged and published in the internal docs. The public version follows after the pilot ends.

summary: Search v2 multi-word synonym pairs prototyped at query time by expanding phrases into a bool query, and the first pilot replay shows hits for 'hard drive' style pairs
body:
The synonym note from last week listed multi-word pairs as not yet supported, so today started on that. The analyzer's synonym graph filter already handles single words at query time, but pairs like 'hard drive' and 'disk' broke phrase positions.

The prototype expands a multi-word synonym in the query parser into a bool query with a match_phrase clause for each side. The change is in the parser module of the search-v2 branch, about 120 lines plus tests. It reads the same synonym file as before, so no reindex is needed.

Replayed 2,000 real queries from the fifth pilot customer. 31 queries contained a multi-word synonym, and 27 of them now return the expected documents. The 4 that still fail have three-word phrases where the phrase clause outranks the exact match.

Query latency on the replay went from a median of 38 ms to 41 ms, which is acceptable. The worst case was a query with 4 synonym expansions at 96 ms. The expansion count is not capped yet, and that is the first thing to add.

Next steps are a cap of 5 expansions per query, a test for the three-word case, and a check that boosts still apply to each clause. Sam gets the updated note once the pilot customer confirms the results.

summary: Postgres autovacuum on the audit log partitions was lagging because the scale factor was too high for the large tables, and a per-table setting fixed the dead tuple build-up
body:
Mara noticed the audit log list endpoint getting slower again, though the new composite index was in place. pg_stat_user_tables showed about 18 percent dead tuples on the current month partition, and autovacuum had not touched it for two days.

The default scale factor of 0.2 means a table with tens of millions of rows waits very long before vacuum starts. I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 on the audit log partitions and a threshold of 5000 through the partition creation script, so new months inherit it.

Ran a manual vacuum on the current partition. It took 6 minutes and the dead tuples fell to under 1 percent. The list endpoint went from 180 ms back to 45 ms at the 95th percentile.

Added a Grafana panel for dead tuple ratio per partition. An alert at 10 percent is still to do.

summary: Capped query-time synonym expansion at 5 per query in search v2, and the three-word phrase case now ranks the exact match first
body:
Followed up on this morning's prototype. The parser now stops expanding after 5 synonym matches in a query and logs a counter metric when the cap is hit, so we can see whether it matters for real traffic.

The three-word failures came from the phrase clause for the synonym side having the same boost as the original term. I gave the original clause a boost of 1.5 and the synonym clauses 1.0. After that, all 4 remaining failing queries from the replay returned the exact match first.

Added 9 unit tests, including one with 8 synonyms in one query to check the cap, and one for the interaction with per-field boosts. The boost schema check in CI still passes, as the boost file format did not change.

The worst-case latency in the replay dropped from 96 ms to 61 ms with the cap. I sent the replay results to the fifth pilot customer's contact via Sam and asked for confirmation on their own synonym list. The documentation change is waiting on that answer.

summary: Redis key naming review found three prefixes in use for the same session data, and a migration plan with a dual-read period was written before touching anything
body:
While looking at the biggest key groups in Redis, I found that session data for the admin console is stored under sess:, session: and admin_sess: depending on which code path created it. The oldest prefix comes from the first version of the console, and the other two are from later refactors.

A SCAN with a sample over the session instance showed 61 percent of keys under session:, 33 percent under sess: and 6 percent under admin_sess:. The smaller groups are mostly keys from users who have not logged in since the change.

The risk is a change that logs everybody out. So the plan is as follows:
- Write only to session: from now on.
- Read session:, then fall back to the other two prefixes.
- After the longest session TTL has passed (7 days), remove the fallback reads.
- Delete leftover keys with a script that runs in small batches.

Lena confirmed that the console never reads the keys directly, only through the session helper, so the change is in one file. I wrote the helper change and tests against a local Redis, but did not deploy it.

One question remains: the rate limiter keys use a different naming scheme again, with the API key id in the middle. I left that out on purpose, as the hot path was just measured and a rename there would need a counter reset. The plan is in the repo under docs/redis-keys.md, and Tobias will check it tomorrow.

summary: Wrote and merged the redis session key fallback helper, with the first production hour showing no extra logouts and a fallback read rate of 38 percent
body:
After the plan this evening, Tobias read the document and had no objections, so the change went out. The helper now writes only to session: and reads in order session:, sess:, admin_sess:.

The change was small:
- sessionKey() returns the canonical prefix.
- getSession() tries each prefix and, on a hit in an old one, copies the value to the new key with the remaining TTL.
- A counter metric records which prefix served each read.

Copying on read is useful because active users migrate on their own, and the fallback rate should fall quickly. If I had only changed the write path, sessions would have stayed under the old keys for the full 7 days.

One detail: the copy has to keep the remaining TTL and not reset it, otherwise sessions would live longer than intended. I used PTTL and then SET with PX, and a test covers a key with 90 seconds left.

Deployed through the normal pipeline at about 18:30. In the first hour the logout rate in the console logs was the same as the day before. The fallback read rate started at 61 percent and was 38 percent at the end of the hour. The Redis command rate rose by about 3 percent because of the extra GETs.

I did not touch the rate limiter keys. The cleanup script is not written, and it has to wait until the fallback reads are close to zero. I'll check the metric again tomorrow morning and write a note on the removal date in the plan document.

summary: Looked into why the schema registry compatibility check accepted a field type change from int to string, and found the check only compared field names
body:
A test event with a changed field type passed the compatibility check in the schema-registry branch, which should not have happened. Reading the checker, I found it compares the set of field names and the required flags, but never the types.

The fix compares types per field with a small table of allowed widenings: int to long, and float to double. Anything else, like int to string, is rejected as incompatible in backward mode. Nested objects are compared recursively.

I added 14 test cases, 6 of which failed before the fix. I also ran the checker over the 212 schema versions already in the registry from the last months to see whether any history would now fail. Two versions of the checkout event had changed a field from int to string and would be flagged.

Those two are old and the consumers were updated at the time, so I added an explicit allow list entry for them with a comment. The rest of the history passes. Mara will review the branch tomorrow.

summary: Mara reviewed the schema registry type check and asked for the widening table to be configurable per subject, which was left for a later change
body:
Mara went through the type comparison change in the schema-registry branch this morning. She agreed with the logic and the tests, and asked about the two allow list entries for the old checkout event versions.

Her main request was that the widening table should be configurable per subject, since one customer-specific schema might want to allow int to string. I argued against it for now: nobody has asked for it, and each exception would weaken the guarantee for consumers. We agreed to keep the fixed table and revisit if a real case appears.

She also found that the error message for a rejected change named only the field, not the old and new types. I changed it to print both, for example 'field amount: int -> string not allowed'. The change is merged into the branch.

summary: Schema registry type widening is now configurable per subject, so the registry no longer treats every int to long change the same way, and the table is validated at load
body:
Mara's review of the type check asked for the widening table to be configurable per subject, and this session did that change. Until now the allowed widenings (int to long, float to double) lived as a constant in the compatibility module, and every subject got the same rules.

Each subject can now carry an optional widening block in its registry settings. When it is missing, the default table applies, so existing subjects behave exactly as before. A subject can list extra allowed pairs or switch widening off completely, which the billing events subject needs, because its consumers parse amounts as strict integers.

The table is validated when the settings load. An unknown type name or a pair that narrows a type (long to int) is rejected with an error that names the subject and the offending pair. I added that after the first test config with a typo was accepted and then silently ignored, which is the same kind of failure that let int to string through last week.

The tests cover the default table, a subject with widening off, a subject with an extra pair, and the narrowing rejection. A replay of the last 300 real schema submissions from the staging registry gave the same verdicts as before for all of them, so no existing producer is affected.

Left for later: the console does not show the widening table yet, so for now it is edited in the settings file. Sam asked for a short docs section on it, which comes after Mara has looked at the final version.

summary: Search v2 query parser now rejects unbalanced quotes with a clear error instead of silently dropping the last term, found while testing synonym phrases
body:
While testing the multi-word synonym expansion, one of my test queries had a missing closing quote, for example title:"hard drive. The parser treated the rest as a phrase to the end of the string, but a code path for the synonym expansion dropped the last token. The result was a query that returned documents for 'hard' only.

There are two things to decide: what should an unbalanced quote do, and how do old v1 queries behave. In v1 the quote was ignored and the terms were searched as separate words. Customers' integrations may rely on that.

I chose to keep the v1 behavior in compatibility mode and to return a 400 with a message in v2 mode: 'unbalanced quote at position 6'. The pilot customers all use v2 mode explicitly, so a 400 only affects them. I checked the pilot query logs of the last month: 3 of about 41,000 queries had an unbalanced quote, all from one customer's search box where users type freely.

That customer's search box would show an error for those users, which is worse than an approximate result. So I added a third option: the parser option lenient_quotes, default off, that closes the quote at the end of the string. I will ask the customer through Sam whether they want it on.

Tests added:
- unbalanced quote strict mode returns 400
- lenient mode closes the quote
- v1 mode ignores the quote
- escaped quote inside a phrase is balanced

All pass. The branch now also has a changelog entry for the parser behavior.

summary: Grafana alert for Postgres dead tuple ratio above 10 percent added to the alert rules in code, with a one-hour pending period to avoid noise
body:
Finished the alert that was left open after the autovacuum change. The rule is in the alerts repo, in the Postgres group, and uses the dead tuple ratio from the exporter per table, ignoring tables under 100k rows.

I set the pending period to one hour. Autovacuum runs can take a while on the big partitions, and a shorter period would page for normal work. Severity is warning, which goes to the Slack channel and not to PagerDuty.

Tested the rule by checking the expression against the last week of data. It would have fired once, for the audit log partition two days ago, which matches what we saw. The rule file passes the lint step in CI. Tobias merged it after a short look.

summary: Audit export now streams large account exports in chunks of 10k rows, bringing peak memory of the export task from 2.3 GB to 310 MB for the largest customer
body:
The export for the largest customer's audit log, about 14 million rows for the requested range, had been failing twice a week with out of memory kills on the export task. The cause was simple: the job loaded the result of the query into an array before writing the file.

The new version uses a server-side cursor with a fetch size of 10,000 rows. Each chunk is serialized to NDJSON, gzipped on the fly and written to the multipart upload of the export bucket. A part is uploaded whenever the buffer reaches 16 MB.

Several things needed care:
- The cursor needs a transaction, so the export holds a snapshot for its whole run. For the largest export this is about 11 minutes. I checked that it does not block vacuum in a harmful way, since the audit log is append-only and old rows are rarely changed.
- If the task is killed in the middle, the multipart upload must be aborted. I added an abort in the error handler and a lifecycle rule on the bucket for incomplete uploads after one day. Tobias applied the rule in Terraform.
- The checksum of the file is now computed while streaming and written to the manifest, not in a second pass.

Tested with a generated account of 14 million rows on staging. The run took 11 minutes 20 seconds, peak memory was 310 MB, and the result file had the same checksum as the old implementation on a smaller account of 200k rows. The old code needed 2.3 GB at the largest size.

One point I did not solve: the progress shown in the console is still a fake estimate based on elapsed time. A count query up front would cost too much on the largest tables, so for now the console says 'running'. Lena knows about it. The change is on the audit-export branch and ready for review by Mara.

summary: Mara's review of the streaming audit export found that a cancelled export left the cursor transaction open, and the fix closes it in a finally block with a test
body:
Mara reviewed the streaming export this morning and asked a good question: what happens when the user cancels an export in the console while the cursor is open. I had tested kills of the task, but not the cancel message path.

She was right. The cancel handler set a flag that the loop checked only after fetching the next chunk, and then returned without closing the cursor or rolling back. The connection went back to the pool inside an open transaction. On staging I reproduced it: after a cancel, pg_stat_activity showed the connection as 'idle in transaction' until the pool recycled it, about 10 minutes.

An idle transaction holding a snapshot is exactly what we do not want on the main database, because it can hold back vacuum. The fix:
- The export function wraps the whole run in try and finally.
- The finally block closes the cursor, rolls back the transaction and aborts the multipart upload if it was not completed.
- The cancel flag is checked before each fetch, and also the fetch itself is given a statement timeout of 60 seconds.

I wrote a test that starts an export of 50k rows with a chunk size of 1,000, cancels after 3 chunks and asserts that no session of the export user remains in pg_stat_activity and that the upload was aborted. It failed before the fix and passes now.

Mara had two smaller comments. The first was a variable name that suggested bytes while it held rows, and the second was a missing log line with the export id when the upload is aborted. Both are done.

I also asked Tobias to add an alert for connections idle in transaction for more than 5 minutes, because it would have caught this on staging. He will do it next to the dead tuple rule. Mara approved the branch after the fixes, and the merge is planned for tomorrow after one more run on the large staging account.

summary: Dry run of the Redis session key migration showed that the old prefixes cover about 9 percent of live sessions, so the dual-read period can be shorter than planned
body:
Before touching the session keys again, I ran the counting script from the naming review against the production Redis in read-only mode. It scans with a small count per call and sleeps between batches, so the load on the instance stayed unnoticeable in Grafana.

Result: of roughly 61k session keys, about 9 percent still use one of the two older prefixes. The rest already use the current one. Most of the old keys belong to sessions that the console refreshes on every visit, so they move to the new prefix by themselves within a few days of normal use.

Because of that, the plan of a two-week dual-read period looked too careful. The session TTL is 7 days, so after one week every active session has been rewritten under the new prefix, and what remains is only keys that expire anyway. I changed the plan to a read fallback for 8 days and then removal of the fallback code.

I also checked that no other service reads sessions. Only the console backend does, and the search API only reads the signed cookie, so nothing else needs the fallback.

One odd finding: a few hundred keys have the old prefix and a TTL of under a minute, which looks like logout in progress. They were ignored in the count.

Next step is the fallback helper itself with a metric for the fallback read rate, so the end of the migration can be seen in a graph and not guessed. Mara will review it.

summary: Dry run count of old Redis session keys found 2,300 without a TTL, all created by a script from the console's first version, and they were removed in batches
body:
Counted again before running the cleanup script. Most of the old-prefix keys were gone or about to expire, but 2,300 keys under sess: had no TTL at all. A TTL check on a sample of 100 showed they all had the same format and the same field set, with no user id.

They look like they come from the first console version's login test script, which wrote sessions for load testing and never set an expiry. I found the script in the old repo history. The keys held no real user data, only test accounts.

I ran the cleanup script in real mode. It deleted 2,300 keys in 5 batches of 500, with a pause of 200 ms between batches. Redis latency did not change in Grafana, and the command rate stayed flat. After the run a second dry run counted zero keys under both old prefixes.

I wrote a short note in docs/redis-keys.md that the cleanup is done and that the load test script was deleted from the old repo, so it cannot create keys again. The plan document now says 'done' at the top.

The rate limiter key scheme remains as it is. If it is ever changed, it needs a window where counters reset, which the big customers could notice as a short period of looser limits.

summary: Merged the streaming audit export after a final run on the large staging account, and added a progress estimate from table statistics for the console
body:
The final staging run of the streaming export on the generated account with 14 million rows finished in 10 minutes 50 seconds, peak memory 305 MB. No sessions were left in pg_stat_activity after the run, and one cancelled run as well. Mara agreed to the merge, and it is on the main branch now.

After the merge I looked at the progress problem that Lena raised. A count query is too slow, but the planner statistics give an estimate of rows for the range cheaply. I use EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) on the export query and read the plan rows value. It takes about 3 ms.

The estimate is not exact. On four test accounts the estimate was off by between -12 and +35 percent compared with the true count. So the console must not show an exact percentage that could pass 100. The export job now writes progress as rows exported over the estimate, capped at 99 percent until the job completes.

Details:
- The estimate is stored in the export record when the job starts.
- The progress value is updated after each chunk, so every 10k rows.
- Lena changed the console bar to show 'about N percent' and to switch to 'finishing' at 99.

One case I checked: a very selective filter on event type, where the planner estimate can be far off. For that one the estimate was 40 rows when the real count was 9,000. The progress would then jump to the cap at once. I added a rule that if the exported rows exceed the estimate, the console shows an indeterminate bar instead. Lena had to add this state to the component, and it was a small change.

Tests cover the estimate parsing and the cap. The export docs for Sam say that the percentage is approximate. Next on this branch is the compliance report format, which a customer asked about.

summary: Tried a streaming JSON parser library for the document loader and dropped it after it was 20 percent slower than the current approach on large NDJSON files
body:
The loader-retry branch has a part that reads large files, and one idea was to replace the line-by-line parsing with a streaming JSON parser library that promised lower memory use. I tried it for an afternoon against a set of files from real customers.

The test set had three files: 200 MB, 1.1 GB and 3.4 GB of NDJSON. The current code reads a line, parses it and passes it on. The library parses tokens from a stream and builds objects on demand.

Results for the 1.1 GB file:
- current code: 41 seconds, peak memory 180 MB
- library: 50 seconds, peak memory 175 MB

So memory hardly changed, since the current code already holds one line at a time, and the library was about 20 percent slower. On the 3.4 GB file the difference was the same. The library also had no good way to report the line number of a bad record, which our error report to customers needs.

I considered patching the line counting in, but it would mean carrying a fork of the library for a gain that does not exist. So I dropped it and reverted the branch changes that touched the parser. The commit message for the revert lists these numbers so the idea is not tried again by accident.

The actual memory spikes of the loader were from something else. While profiling I saw that the retry queue keeps the full text of failed records, and a file with many bad records holds all of them in memory. Storing only the line offset and reading it again on retry would fix this. That is the next step, and I wrote a ticket-style note in the branch's TODO file.

summary: Postgres idle in transaction alert added at 5 minutes for the main database, next to the dead tuple rule, after the audit export cancel bug
body:
Tobias added the alert I asked for after the cancel bug in the export. It counts connections in state 'idle in transaction' per application name, and fires when any has been in that state for more than 5 minutes.

I checked the expression against two weeks of history. It would have fired three times, twice for a reporting script that holds a transaction open while waiting for a human prompt, and once for the export staging test. The reporting script now closes its transaction before the prompt, which is a one-line change.

The rule is a warning and goes to Slack. After the reporting fix there are no false positives in the last day.

summary: Loader retry queue now stores line offsets instead of full records, and a test file with 200k bad lines dropped from 1.4 GB to 90 MB of memory
body:
Followed up on the finding from this afternoon. The retry queue of the document loader kept the full text of each failed record, which for a file with many bad lines grew without bound.

The queue entry is now an object with the file id, the byte offset and the length of the line, plus the attempt count and next retry time. On retry the loader reads the bytes from the stored file with a range read and parses again.

I generated a 600 MB test file where one line in three is invalid for a reason that is transient in the test setup. With 200k failing lines the old version peaked at 1.4 GB, the new one at 90 MB. The total run time was about the same, with the range reads adding 4 percent.

The backoff stays at the same settings as before: 1 second doubling to a maximum of 60 seconds, 6 attempts. Tests cover the offset logic with multi-byte characters at line borders, which was the tricky part, since offsets must be in bytes.

summary: Planned the dual write period of the search shard migration in detail, with a table of which writes go where and the checks before each switch; nothing has been started.
body:
Wrote the next level of detail for the shard migration plan from the earlier document, concentrating on the dual write period, as that is where most of the risk is. Nothing has started, and this is only the plan.

The core idea is that during the migration every indexing write goes to the old per-customer shards and to the new monthly shards. Reads stay on the old layout until a customer is switched. The steps in order:
1. Create the monthly indices with the new mapping and the same analyzers, with replicas set to 0 for the bulk load.
2. Turn on dual write in the indexing service behind a flag per customer.
3. Backfill the history of each customer in monthly chunks, newest month first.
4. Compare document counts and a sample of 1,000 documents per customer between old and new.
5. Switch reads for the customer with a flag, and watch the latency and zero-result rate for a day.
6. Turn off dual write for that customer and delete the old shard data after a grace period.

The things that worry me are these. First, deletes and updates during the backfill: a document updated in the old layout after its month was copied must also be updated in the new one, which the dual write covers only if it is on before the backfill starts. So step 2 must come before step 3. Second, the document ids must be identical in both layouts, otherwise the comparison cannot work. I checked that ids are derived from the event id, so they are.

Third, routing. In the old layout the customer id is the routing key, so queries touch one shard. In the monthly layout a query over a long range touches many shards. Tobias's earlier estimate said that the dual write period needs 1.9 times the storage, so the two large customers go last.

I listed the checks before each switch as a short table in the document, with the expected values, such as count difference zero, sample mismatch zero and p95 latency not more than 10 percent above the old layout. The order of customers is: the smallest pilot customers first, then the middle ones, then the two large ones.

Open question for tomorrow: whether the nightly reindex job should write to both layouts during the migration, or be paused. I lean toward pausing it for migrated customers, but want Tobias's view on the schedule.

summary: Looked at the cache hit rate of dashboard query results in Redis, which sits at 62 percent, and found that the key includes a timestamp rounded to the second
body:
The biggest key group in the Redis cache instance is dashboard query results, and its hit rate has been about 62 percent for weeks. I wanted to see whether keys that should be shared are not.

Looking at a sample of 500 keys for one customer, I found that the key includes the end of the time range as a full timestamp. The console sends 'now' as the end of the range, and the API turns it into the current second. Two users opening the same dashboard one second apart get different keys, so there is no hit.

The fix is to round the end of the range down to a bucket before it goes into the key. I chose 30 seconds for ranges under one day and 5 minutes for longer ranges. The result may be up to a bucket old, which is fine for dashboards that already refresh every minute.

I first tried a single 60 second bucket for all ranges. It gave a better hit rate but made the 'last 15 minutes' view visibly stale, with the newest points missing, so I dropped that.

The change is in the key builder of the search API cache module. I wrote unit tests for the bucket logic including a range that crosses a bucket border, and replayed one hour of production dashboard requests against a local instance. The replayed hit rate went from 61 percent to 84 percent.

Memory should drop too, since fewer distinct keys are written. I will deploy this tomorrow morning and compare memory and hit rate over a day. TTLs of the results are unchanged at 60 seconds.

summary: Dashboard cache key bucketing is in production and the hit rate rose from 62 to 81 percent, while the dashboard result key group shrank by a third
body:
The bucketing change from two days ago went out in the morning. I compared a full day of numbers with the day before at the same hour range.

Hit rate for dashboard query results rose from 62 to 81 percent, a bit below the 84 percent of the replay, as real traffic has more unique ranges than the replay hour. The number of keys in the group fell by about a third, and Redis memory on the cache instance went from 58 to 51 percent.

The Postgres and ClickHouse load from dashboard queries also dropped. The ClickHouse query count for dashboards fell by roughly 20 percent in the busy hours, and the p95 of the dashboard endpoint went from 410 ms to 290 ms.

One customer's contact wrote to Sam that the 'last 15 minutes' chart showed a point missing at the right edge. I checked: with a bucket of 30 seconds the newest data can be up to 30 seconds old plus the 60 second TTL, so the edge can lag by a minute and a half in the worst case. The chart looked correct, only a little behind.

I decided to shorten the TTL for ranges under one hour from 60 to 30 seconds, which keeps the worst case at one minute. The hit rate dropped by about 2 points in a test, which I accept. Sam answered the customer with an explanation of the delay.

Still open is a way for the console to tell the user how fresh the data is. Lena thinks a small 'updated 20 s ago' label would be enough, and I will give her the timestamp in the response header.

summary: Search v2 per-field boosts now load from a per-customer config file, and a replay of 2,000 real queries shows the title boost moves 14 percent of top hits
body:
Boosts were hard-coded in the query builder, which blocked the two customers who asked for heavier weight on the title field. I moved them into a per-customer config in the settings table, with defaults applied when a field is missing. The config is read once per request through the existing settings cache.

To see the effect I replayed 2,000 real queries from the pilot customer with title boost 3 and with the default of 1. In 14 percent of the queries the first hit changed. Most changes looked right when I read a sample of 40, but 6 of them promoted short titles that only matched a stop word.

I added a validation step that rejects boosts below 0 or above 10, because a test with 50 gave absurd rankings. The error message names the field and the allowed range.

The unit tests cover the default case, the override case and a missing field. One test failed at first because the config cache returned a stale object after an update. I fixed it by clearing the key on write.

What is left is a UI for the boosts in the admin console, which Lena will do. The stop word issue needs a decision from me about whether stop words should count at all in boosted fields. I will bring it to the next planning session with the six example queries.

summary: Rate limit per API key now returns a Retry-After header computed from the Redis window, and clients that honor it cut rejected calls by about 60 percent in staging
body:
The per-key limiter returned a plain 429 with no hint about when to come back, so some client libraries retried at once and made the pressure worse. I changed the limiter to compute the seconds until the current window ends and send that as Retry-After.

The computation reads the TTL of the counter key that already exists, so there is no extra Redis call on the hot path. When the TTL is missing or negative, the header falls back to 1 second.

In staging I ran the load script with two client modes. The naive client ignores the header and retries after 100 ms. The polite client waits for the header value. Rejected calls per minute fell from about 5,400 to 2,100 with the polite client, which is a drop of around 60 percent.

I also noticed that the counter increments and the expiry were two commands. A crash between them could leave a counter without a TTL. I put both into one small Lua script, and the test with a killed process no longer leaves orphan keys.

Sam needs a paragraph in the public docs about the header and the recommended client behavior. I wrote the first draft of it and left it in the docs branch for review. The next step is the per-key override for the three customers with higher limits.

summary: Per-key overrides for rate limits are stored in Postgres and cached in Redis for 60 seconds, so a limit change takes effect within a minute without a deploy
body:
Three customers have contracts with higher limits, and until now their limits lived in an environment variable that needed a deploy to change. I added a table api_key_limits with the key id, requests per minute and a burst value. The limiter looks up the override and falls back to the plan default.

The lookup goes through Redis with a 60 second TTL on a key named limits:key:<id>. A miss reads Postgres and writes the result back, including a negative result so keys without an override do not hit the database on every request.

The first version cached only positive results, and the staging test showed 800 Postgres reads per second from one noisy key. Caching the negative case brought that to about 1 per minute per key.

Mara reviewed it and asked that the table has a check constraint so burst cannot be lower than the rate. I added it with a migration and a test that expects the insert to fail.

One thing I did not do is invalidate the cache on update. The 60 second delay is acceptable for now, and I wrote that in the code comment and in the docs draft. If a customer complains, an explicit delete of the key from the console endpoint is a small change.

Next I want to expose the limits in the admin console, which needs a small read endpoint. I opened a ticket for Lena with the response shape.

summary: Postgres slow query log showed the console's audit search scanning a whole partition, and a composite index on account and created time brought it from 3.1 seconds to 40 ms
body:
Support reported that searching the audit log in the console took several seconds for large accounts. I pulled the slow query log for the last day and found one statement responsible for most of the time: a filter on account_id and a created_at range, with an order by created_at desc.

EXPLAIN showed a scan over the index on created_at alone, filtering account_id row by row. For the largest account that meant reading about 2 million rows to return 50.

I created an index on (account_id, created_at desc) concurrently on the staging copy first. The same query dropped from 3.1 seconds to 40 ms. On production the concurrent build took 11 minutes for the largest partitions and did not block writes.

I watched replication lag during the build and it stayed under 2 seconds. The old single column index is still used by the retention job, so I kept it.

The new index adds about 6 percent to the table size. That is fine for the disk we have. I will check again next week that the planner still picks it after the autovacuum settings from earlier this week have done their work.

summary: Reindex job for search v2 now skips unchanged documents by comparing a content hash, which cut a full staging run from 52 minutes to 19
body:
The nightly reindex rewrote every document even when nothing had changed, which was most of them. I added a content hash field to the indexed documents, computed from the fields that are searchable, and the job now compares it before writing.

To read the hashes the job scrolls through the index with only the id and hash fields. That scroll is cheap compared with the writes. Documents with a different hash or no hash go to the bulk writer as before.

On the staging cluster, with a copy of about 40 percent of the production data, a full run went from 52 minutes to 19. About 93 percent of the documents were skipped.

There was a bug in the first version: the hash included the boost config version, so a boost change made all documents look changed. I removed that from the hash input because boosts apply at query time anyway. A test now checks that changing a boost does not alter the hash.

The first run on a real index still has to write everything because no hashes exist yet. I plan to run that on a weekend window and watch the bulk rejections.

Open question: deleted documents. The job removes them in a separate pass and I have not touched that. It still reads the full id list and I want to look at it next.

summary: Search v2 reindex now writes per-field boosts into the index mapping metadata, and a staging run confirmed that a boost change no longer forces a full reindex of unchanged documents
body:
Boost changes in search v2 used to mean a full reindex, because the boost values were baked into the documents at index time. Following the content hash change, the open question was whether a boost edit should invalidate the hash. It should not, since the document content is identical. So the boosts now live in the query layer and the mapping metadata, and the hash covers only the document fields.

The work was in three places. The reindex job reads the boost config version and records it next to the index alias, but does not mix it into the hash. The query builder loads the per-customer boost file and applies the values when it builds the bool query. A small check at startup compares the config version in the file with the one recorded for the alias, and logs a warning if they differ.

On staging I changed the title boost for one test customer from 2.0 to 3.0 and ran the reindex. It skipped all 1.2M unchanged documents and finished in 41 seconds, instead of the 19 minutes of a full run. The replay of 2,000 queries then showed the new ranking right away, with 9 percent of top hits moved by the change.

One case failed at first. Documents with a renamed field were skipped, because the hash looked only at values and not at field names. The fix includes the field names in the hash input, and a test with a renamed field now passes. Next is a run on the largest customer's staging copy, then a note in the search docs about how a boost change takes effect.

summary: Loader retry now backs off per file with jitter and gives up after 6 attempts, and a test with a flaky storage mock shows no thundering herd when 50 files fail together
body:
When the object storage had a short hiccup, all loader jobs retried at the same moment and failed again together. The retry delay was a fixed 5 seconds. I replaced it with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds, doubling each time, with random jitter of up to 30 percent.

After 6 attempts the file is marked failed and moved to the failed list that Sam can see in the console, with the last error message. Before, it kept trying forever and blocked a worker slot.

For testing I wrote a storage mock that fails the first N calls for each file. With 50 files failing together, the old code produced a burst of 50 requests every 5 seconds. The new code spreads them so the maximum in any one second was 9.

One case needed care: a failure in the middle of a large file. The retry restarts from the saved line offset, not from the beginning, which was part of the offsets change from last week. I added a test that kills the stream at line 120,000 and checks that the final count of records is exact with no duplicates.

The jitter uses a seeded random source in tests so they are repeatable. I had a first version using the global source and it made one test flaky, so I changed it before pushing.

The remaining piece is a metric for the number of retries per file, so we can see if some customers send files that often fail. I will add it tomorrow.

summary: Added a Prometheus counter for loader retries by reason, and the first afternoon shows 80 percent of retries are storage timeouts rather than bad input
body:
The retry metric I planned is in: loader_retries_total with labels for the reason, which can be timeout, throttled, parse or other. The labels are fixed, so the series count stays small.

After a few hours in production, 80 percent of the retries were storage timeouts, 15 percent throttling and 5 percent parse errors. I had expected more parse errors from customer files, so this changes where to look.

The timeouts came mostly from one customer who uploads files of several GB. The read timeout was 30 seconds, which is short for that size. I raised it to 90 seconds for files above 1 GB only.

I added a panel to the loader dashboard in Grafana, and the rule for an alert on a retry rate above 5 per minute is written but not turned on yet, until I know the normal level.

summary: Search v2 parser handles field-scoped phrases like title:'hard drive' and negation, and a grammar test file of 140 cases passes against the old behavior where it should
body:
Customers had asked for queries that limit a phrase to one field and exclude terms with a minus sign. The parser from earlier work handled fields and phrases separately, and the combination produced a wrong tree. I reworked that part of the grammar so a field prefix can apply to a term, a phrase or a parenthesized group.

Negation is the second part. A leading minus on a term or phrase becomes a must_not clause. A query of only negative parts is a special case, because OpenSearch returns nothing for it. I add a match_all as the positive clause in that case.

To be sure I did not break old queries, I built a test file of 140 cases. Seventy of them come from real queries in the logs of the pilot customer, and the rest are hand-written edge cases. For the real queries, the expected tree is the one the old parser produced. Of those, 68 are the same, and the two differences are both queries with a stray minus in the middle of a word, like e-mail. The old parser kept it and the new one first split it.

I fixed that by only treating a minus as negation at the start of a token. Hyphenated words stay one token, and that case is now in the test file.

I also checked the interaction with the synonym expansion from last week. The expansion cap of 5 still applies after negation, and a negated phrase is not expanded, since expanding an exclusion would hide too many results. I wrote that rule in a comment and a test.

Performance was measured on the parser alone: 140 cases parse in 6 ms in total, so there is no concern there.

The error messages for the new syntax are still basic. For an unclosed parenthesis the message says only unexpected end of input. I will improve it next, in the same way as the quote error.

Sam will need examples for the docs. I listed five that work and two that are rejected in the pull request description.

summary: Parser errors in search v2 now include the position and a short excerpt, so an unclosed parenthesis reports where the group began
body:
The error for an unclosed parenthesis was only unexpected end of input, which told customers nothing in a long query. The parser now records the position of each opening token and reports the position of the one left open, with an excerpt of up to 20 characters around it.

For a query like (title:disk AND (size:large the message says unclosed group at position 17, near (size:large. The same shape is used for the unbalanced quote error from last week, so the console can show them in one way.

I added 11 tests for the messages, including a query with multibyte characters, where the position must count characters, not bytes. The first version counted bytes and the test caught it.

The API returns these as a 400 with a code field called query_syntax and the position as a number, so the console can highlight the place. Lena has the field description. The docs list the error codes now.

There is one more case I left open: a closing parenthesis without an opening one. It reports as an unexpected token for now, which is fine.

summary: Postgres minor version upgrade on staging went through with no changes in query plans for the ten heaviest queries, so the production window is booked for next week
body:
Tobias upgraded the staging database to the newest minor release of version 16 this morning. I compared EXPLAIN output for the ten heaviest queries from the slow log before and after, and the plans were identical for all ten, with timings within 3 percent.

I also ran the full integration suite and the audit export on the large staging account. Both passed, and the export took the same time as before.

The production window is next week in the quiet hours. Tobias will do a snapshot before, and the rollback plan is to restore the snapshot, which takes about 40 minutes. I added the ten queries as a script in the repo so we can run the same check on production afterwards.

summary: Schema registry now stores a compatibility mode per subject, and a field removal is rejected under backward mode with the field name in the error
body:
Until now the registry applied one global rule, which was too strict for some customers and too loose for others. I added a compatibility_mode column on subjects with the values backward, forward and none, and backward as the default for existing subjects.
