The check function takes the mode and the two schema versions. Under backward mode a removed required field is rejected, and an added field must have a default. Under forward mode the logic is reversed. Under none every change is accepted but is still recorded in the version history.

The error now lists every violation, not just the first, with the field name and the reason. Mara asked for this in review, since people had been fixing one problem at a time.

The widening table from the earlier change is respected in all modes. An int to long change passes where the table allows it, and int to string fails everywhere.

I wrote 24 tests, one per rule and mode. I also wrote a migration that sets the mode for existing subjects, and ran it on a copy of production data to check that it takes under a second.

The endpoint for changing the mode is not done. It needs an audit log entry for each change, which I will do next, because a mode change is an important decision to be able to trace.

summary: Mode changes in the schema registry are written to the audit log with the old and new value, and the console endpoint requires the admin role
body:
A change of compatibility mode can let breaking schemas through, so it has to be traceable. I added the endpoint PUT /subjects/:name/mode, which checks the admin role, validates the value and writes the change in one transaction together with an audit log row.

The audit row has the actor, the subject, the old mode, the new mode and the request id. Using one transaction means there is no state where the mode changed without a log entry. A test forces the audit insert to fail and checks that the mode stays the same.

I first tried to write the audit entry through the shared audit helper, which runs on its own connection. That broke the transaction guarantee, so I added a variant of the helper that takes the transaction client. The shared helper now calls the same code with its own client.

For permissions I reused the role check from the console API. A user without the admin role gets 403, and a missing subject gets 404. Tests cover both.

Mara reviewed the change and found that setting the same mode again wrote a pointless audit row. It now returns 200 without writing when nothing changes.

I also updated the docs page on compatibility with a short table of what each mode allows, and asked Sam to read it for clarity, since it will be used by customers.

What is left is a view in the console, a read-only list of subjects with their mode, for Lena. I gave her the response format. After that I want to check how the registry behaves when two people change the mode at once. I think the last write wins, which is acceptable, but I want a test that says it.

summary: Cache warm-up job for the search suggestion prefixes now skips prefixes under 3 characters, which removed 70 percent of its Redis writes with no change in hit rate
body:
The warm-up job wrote suggestion results for every prefix from the log, including one and two character ones. Those are rarely repeated in the same form and fill the key space with entries that live only 30 seconds.

I added a minimum length of 3. In the first hour after the deploy, writes from the job fell by 70 percent. The hit rate of the suggestion cache stayed at 54 percent, the same as before.

The number of keys in the suggestion group dropped from about 90,000 to 31,000 at peak. That helps the memory graph a little, though the main use is elsewhere.

I made the minimum a setting so it can be tested at 2 later if the suggestions behave differently.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's Terraform change for the ingest task sizes and asked for the memory headroom to stay at 30 percent, which he accepted after checking the last month of graphs
body:
Tobias proposed lowering the memory of the ingest tasks from 4 GB to 3 GB to save cost. I looked at the peak memory graphs for the last month. The highest value was 2.4 GB, during a large batch from one customer.

3 GB would leave 20 percent headroom, which I thought was thin for spikes. I asked for 30 percent, so 3.5 GB would be the size.

He checked the numbers and agreed, and he also found that the batching change from earlier lowered the average memory a bit, so the saving at 3.5 GB is still about 8 percent of the ingest cost. The plan output showed only the task definition changing.

He will roll it out one service at a time and watch the memory graph for two days between steps. I will look at the graph on my side too.

summary: The ingest client library now retries only on 429 and 503 with the server's Retry-After, and no longer retries 400 errors, which had been repeated three times for nothing
body:
A customer's logs showed that our client library retried a 400 response three times before giving up. A 400 means the batch is invalid, so each retry fails the same way and only adds load.

I changed the retry rule to cover only 429, 502, 503 and 504, plus network errors before a response. For 429 and 503 the client uses the Retry-After header if present. Otherwise it uses its own backoff.

Tests use a local server that returns each status code in turn and count the calls. The 400 case now makes exactly one call. I released a patch version and wrote the change in the changelog, so customers know why the behavior changed.

summary: Dual-read of the Redis session keys ended after the old prefixes fell below 1 percent of reads, and the fallback code and the old key patterns were removed
body:
The fallback helper from last week kept reading the old prefixes when the new key was missing. I looked at the metric for the fallback read rate this morning, and it had fallen from 38 percent to 0.7 percent, which matches the sessions that expired by themselves.

Before removing the helper, I checked that no code outside the session module used the old prefixes. A search through the repo found two places: a test fixture and a small admin script that lists sessions. I changed both to the new prefix.

The removal itself is a deletion of about 80 lines and the helper's tests. The session module now reads and writes one key pattern. I kept the metric name but it is gone from the code, so the Grafana panel will show no data. I removed the panel too.

The remaining old keys are the ones with a TTL that will expire within the session lifetime of 24 hours. I did not delete them by hand, because the count was only a few hundred, and a script could remove active sessions by mistake.

I deployed to staging first and logged in and out with five test users on different browsers. Then I ran the console end to end tests, which passed. The production deploy was done in the rolling way and I watched the logout rate for an hour. It stayed at its usual level of about 0.4 percent of requests.

One more thing I noticed is that the session key still includes the user agent hash, which makes a session invalid when a browser updates. That was in the design from the first version. It is a separate question and I added a note to the backlog for Lena and me to decide.

The memory of the session key group fell by about 4 percent, since the dual write is gone. That is small but I wrote it down.

Next I want to look at the key naming of the remaining groups once more, now that the session part is clean, and write a short document with the rules so new keys follow the same pattern.

summary: Wrote the Redis key naming rules into the docs folder after the session cleanup, with the six groups in use, their TTLs and an example for each
body:
After the session cleanup I wrote down what the key groups are, so nobody has to guess. The document lists six groups: session, query cache, dashboard results, rate limit counters, limits overrides and suggestion cache.

For each group the table gives the key pattern, the TTL, who writes it and who reads it. The pattern is always group:scope:id, with lowercase names and colons only as separators. An example line follows each pattern.

While writing I found that the limits overrides group uses limits:key:<id>, which does not fit the same scope idea. I left it as is, because changing it would need a migration and the group is small, but I noted the exception in the document.

I also added a rule that every new key must have a TTL, because of the 2,300 keys without one that were found earlier. A small test helper in the Redis module now throws in tests if a set is called without an expiry.

Tobias read the document and asked to add the memory estimate per group, which I did from the latest numbers.

summary: Alert rule for audit export failures added to the alert rules in code, firing when more than 2 exports fail within 30 minutes
body:
The audit export had no alert, and a failed export is only noticed when a customer asks. I added a counter for failed exports by reason in the export task and a rule in the alert rules repository.

The rule fires when more than 2 exports fail in 30 minutes. A single failure is often a cancel by the user, which the code already counts as cancelled, not failed.

I tested the rule with the promtool unit test format, with a series that crosses the threshold and one that stays below it. Both pass. The alert goes to the normal channel, not to the pager, since an export failure is not urgent.

summary: Audit export now signs the finished file with an HMAC and writes the checksum next to it, so compliance reviewers can check that a file was not altered after export
body:
Compliance asked for a way to prove that an export file is unchanged. I added an HMAC with SHA-256 over the file content, computed while streaming, so it does not need a second pass over the data.

The key comes from the secrets store and has a key id, which is written in the manifest together with the checksum, the row count and the time of export. Rotating the key means old files can still be checked with the old key id.

I wrote a small command line tool, audit-verify, that takes the file and the manifest and prints ok or the mismatch. A test changes one byte in a sample file and checks that the tool fails.

The streaming memory stayed at about 310 MB, as the hash state is tiny. The largest export took 2 percent longer.

The docs for the auditors still need to be written.

summary: Ingest batching worker now flushes on size, age or shutdown, and a graceful stop test confirms no events are lost when a task receives SIGTERM mid-batch
body:
During rollouts of the ingest workers, tasks get a SIGTERM and I wanted proof that the batching buffer is flushed before exit. I reread the shutdown path and found that the flush on stop was called, but the context it used was already cancelled, so the insert could fail.

I changed the shutdown to use a fresh context with a 10 second timeout for the final flush. The ECS stop timeout is 30 seconds, so there is room.

For the test I wrote an integration test with a local Redpanda and Postgres. It sends 5,000 events, stops the worker with SIGTERM when about half are in the buffer, and then counts the rows. Before the fix the count was short by up to 400. After the fix it is exact in 20 out of 20 runs.

The offset commit has to come after the insert. I checked the order in the code and it was right, so after a failed flush the messages would be read again. A second test makes the insert fail on purpose and confirms that the messages come again after restart.

I also looked at the flush triggers. The size trigger is 500 events, the age trigger 200 ms. Under low traffic the age trigger fires most of the time, which is why the insert count dropped less at night in the rollout data.

The branch was already merged, so this went in as a small follow-up from the main checkout. Mara reviewed it in ten minutes and had one question about the timeout value, which I answered with the stop timeout numbers.

A metric for the size of the final flush at shutdown would show how much is normally in the buffer. I added a gauge for it and it shows up in the dashboard next to the batch size panel.

I will watch the next production rollout and look at that gauge.

summary: Search API p99 latency fell from 780 ms to 410 ms after the per-customer query cache keys were normalized, and the cache hit rate for search results rose to 47 percent
body:
The search result cache was keyed on the raw query string plus the options, so two queries that differ only in spacing or letter case missed each other. I looked at the logs of one busy customer and saw many such pairs.

I added a normalization step before the key is built: trim, collapse whitespace, lowercase the terms outside of quotes, and sort the filter parameters. Quoted phrases keep their case, because a quoted match is case-sensitive in one field.

The key is now a hash of the normalized query, the customer id, the boost config version and the page. Including the boost config version means a boost change makes old entries unreachable without any delete.

Before the deploy the hit rate was 31 percent. After one day it was 47 percent. The p99 latency of the search endpoint fell from 780 ms to 410 ms, and the p50 stayed near 90 ms, as the misses are the same as before.

The TTL of these entries is 5 minutes. I thought of raising it, but new documents appear within seconds for the customers and they notice stale results, so I left it.

There was one problem in the first deploy on staging. The sort of filter parameters changed the order of results for a query with repeated parameters, as the order had meaning for one filter type. I found that in the tests and kept the order for that type.

Memory in the search result key group grew by about 6 percent, which is acceptable. I told Tobias, since he watches Redis memory.

I wrote the normalization rules in the search docs for the team, not for customers.

An open point is the case of queries with a date range ending at now. They have a different key every second, as the dashboard queries had. I want to apply the same rounding that fixed the dashboards, and I will do that next.

summary: Rounded the now-based date ranges in search cache keys to the minute, and the hit rate for those queries went from near zero to 38 percent in the first evening
body:
Following up on the normalization from this morning, queries with a range like the last 24 hours use now as the end, so the key changed every second. I measured it on the logs: of all search queries, 19 percent have such a range, and almost none of them hit the cache.

I applied the same approach as for the dashboard results: the end of the range is rounded down to the minute in the key. The query that goes to OpenSearch still uses the exact time, so the results are correct. Only the cache identity is bucketed.

This means a cached result can be up to a minute old for those queries. I checked it with Sam, who talks to customers, and he said that a delay of one minute is not a problem for search, as the dashboards already work like that.

In the first evening the hit rate for queries with a relative range went from about 1 percent to 38 percent. The overall search hit rate moved from 47 to 53 percent.

I added a test with a fake clock: two requests 20 seconds apart in the same minute share a key, and two requests across a minute boundary do not.

A risk I thought about is the burst at each minute boundary, when all the keys of popular queries become invalid at once. The graph for OpenSearch load shows small peaks at the start of each minute, about 15 percent over the base. That is fine for now, though it could grow with traffic.

A way to soften it would be a random offset per customer for the bucket start. I wrote the idea in the notes but did not build it, since the effect is small today.

I also checked the Redis memory graph at the end of the evening. The key group for search results grew by about 2 percent since this morning, which is within what I expected from more entries being kept.

Tomorrow I will look at the hit rate again with a full day of traffic, and decide whether the bucket should be 30 seconds for the customers who want fresher results.

summary: Search v2 query parser now supports boolean groups with field scopes inside parentheses, and a 160 case grammar file passes, with two intended differences from v1 listed
body:
Continued the parser work from last week. The open gap was groups such as (title:disk OR body:drive) AND NOT status:deleted, which the parser flattened wrongly when a field scope sat inside a group.

The cause was that the scope was applied at tokenization time instead of at the node level. I moved the scope into the AST node and let children inherit it unless they carry their own. This touched parser/scope.ts and parser/ast.ts.

The grammar test file grew from 140 to 160 cases. All pass against the old behavior except two, and both differences are intended. First, v1 treated a lone minus before a quoted phrase as part of the term, while v2 treats it as negation. Second, v1 silently dropped an empty group, while v2 returns a parse error with the position.

I wrote both differences into the docs of the parser as a short list, so Sam can put them in the public API notes later.

I also replayed 2,000 real queries from the staging log. 11 of them parse differently now, and I read all 11. Nine are the minus case, and two are queries with unbalanced quotes that v1 accepted by guessing. For the unbalanced quotes the error excerpt now points at the opening quote.

Nothing is deployed to production. Next is the boost interaction: a field-scoped term should not get the boost of other fields. I will check that with the replay set tomorrow.

summary: Search v2 parser now treats a leading wildcard as an explicit error with a hint, after the slow tail traced to such queries, and the old behavior stays behind a flag
body: Yesterday's look at the search latency tail showed that wildcards at the start of a term cause most of the slow calls. This morning the v2 parser got a rule for them. A term like *drive now produces a parse error that says leading wildcards are not supported and suggests the suffix form or a field-scoped prefix. The reason is that OpenSearch has to scan the whole term dictionary for such a pattern, and no cache key helps when every customer types a different one. I kept the old behavior behind a per-customer flag called allow_leading_wildcard, because two customers have saved searches that depend on it. The grammar test file got 11 new cases, so it has 171 now, and all pass. I also checked the logs of the last week: 4 percent of calls used a leading wildcard, and 90 percent of those came from three API keys. Sam will write to those customers with the suggested forms before the default changes. The error text was reviewed against the position and excerpt format from the earlier parser error work, and it fits. A staging replay of 2,000 real queries shows the p99 falls from 410 to 290 ms when the flag is off. The next step is a release note for the docs and a date for switching the default.

summary: Postgres vacuum on the audit log table was tuned per table after dead tuples kept growing, and the bloat dropped from 38 percent to 9 percent over a morning
body: The dead tuple alert fired twice last week for the audit log table, and the cause was that autovacuum could not keep up with the update rate of the export status rows. The table lives in the main Postgres database, so bloat there also slows the console's audit search. I started by measuring with pgstattuple: 38 percent of the table was dead space, and the biggest index was 2.4 times larger than it needed to be. The default autovacuum scale factor of 0.2 meant the vacuum started only after millions of rows were dead. I set the scale factor to 0.02 for this table and raised the cost limit so each run finishes faster. The first run after the change took 11 minutes and did not disturb the query latency of the console. I then rebuilt the two bloated indexes with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY during the quiet hours of the morning. The rebuild needed extra disk, about 6 GB, and the volume had enough room. After both steps the bloat measured 9 percent. The slow query log showed no new entries while the rebuild ran. I also looked at whether the export status updates could be fewer. The export worker wrote a progress row every 2 seconds, and a write every 10 seconds is enough for the progress estimate in the console. Changing that is a small code change and I did it in the same session. This cut the update rate by 80 percent. The per-table settings were added to the Terraform-managed parameter notes in the docs folder. The dead tuple rule stays as it is, and I will check the graph again in three days. If the numbers hold, the same settings go to the two other write-heavy tables.

summary: Per-field boosts in search v2 no longer leak across field-scoped terms, and a replay of 2,000 queries shows the top hits move for 9 percent instead of 14
body:
The problem from yesterday was that a term scoped to one field, like title:disk, still received the boost of other fields when the same word appeared in an unscoped part of the query. That inflated the title boost effect on mixed queries.

I changed the query builder so that each clause carries its own boost list. A scoped clause uses only the boost of its field, and an unscoped clause uses the multi-field boost from the customer config. The change is in query/build.ts, with about 90 lines moved.

I replayed the same 2,000 real queries as before against the old and new builder. With the old one, 14 percent of top hits changed under the title boost. With the fix it is 9 percent. I looked at 40 of the changed cases by hand. 31 look better, 6 are neutral, and 3 look worse, all of them short queries with one very common word.

For the three worse ones, I checked whether a minimum term weight would help. It helped one and hurt another, so I left it out for now and wrote the three queries into the notes for later.

Tests: the 160 grammar cases still pass, and I added 12 builder tests for mixed scoped and unscoped clauses. The staging index was reindexed only for one customer to check that the mapping metadata still carries the boosts, and it does.

Next I want the boost config validated on load, because a typo in a field name is silently ignored today. I will do that in a separate change.

summary: Boost config for search v2 is validated on load now, and an unknown field name stops the load with the file and line instead of being ignored
body:
A typo in a field name of the per-customer boost file was silently ignored, which meant a customer had no boost and nobody saw it. I added a validation step that checks every field against the index mapping.

An unknown field now stops the load with an error that names the file, the line and the closest known field, for example: unknown field titel, did you mean title. Negative boosts and values above 10 are also rejected.

I ran the validator over all 40 customer files in staging. Two files had typos: one with titel and one with a field that was renamed in the mapping last quarter. I fixed both files and told Sam, since one of those customers had asked about weak results.

There are 9 new tests. The validation runs in CI as well, so a bad file cannot merge.

summary: Redis memory use of the rate limiter keys was measured and the sliding window counters take 40 percent less space after switching to a compact encoding
body: The memory graph for Redis showed a slow rise over the last month, and the rate limiter counters were the largest key group after the session keys. Each window was stored as a sorted set with one member per request, which is costly for keys with high limits. I wrote a script that samples 5,000 keys with MEMORY USAGE and grouped the result by key pattern. The sorted sets of the limiter averaged 3.1 KB, against 180 bytes for a plain counter. For the fixed-size buckets the limiter can use a hash with one field per sub-window, which keeps the sliding behavior within 1 second of precision. I built this in a branch and ran the limiter test file of 90 cases against it, and all passed. In staging the key group shrank by 40 percent for a replayed hour of production traffic. The Retry-After value still comes from the same window, so clients see no change. The rollout needs a dual read for one window length, so old keys expire by themselves, and I planned this for next week.

summary: Loader retry for large files now resumes from the last committed line offset after a restart, and a kill test mid-file on a 2 GB NDJSON file loses nothing and duplicates nothing
body:
Until now the loader retried a failed file from the start of the retry queue entry, but after a worker restart it lost the position and began the whole file again. That doubled the work for big files.

The retry queue already stores line offsets instead of records. I added a checkpoint that writes the last committed offset together with the batch commit, in one Postgres transaction. On restart the loader reads the checkpoint and seeks to that offset.

Testing: a 2 GB NDJSON file with 4 million lines, killed at random points with SIGKILL, 25 runs. Every run ended with exactly 4 million events and no duplicates, checked by the event id uniqueness count. The worst case lost the work since the last checkpoint, which is at most 5,000 lines.

One case needed care. When the kill came between the batch commit and the checkpoint write, there was a window for duplicates. Because both are in one transaction, the window is gone. I confirmed it with a fault injection that aborts after the batch insert.

The checkpoint interval is 5,000 lines by default. I measured the overhead at under 1 percent of the load time.

Left to do: the cleanup of old checkpoints when a file finishes, which I will do tomorrow, and a metric for resumed files.

summary: Schema registry now rejects a subject name with unsafe characters and the console shows the rule, after a test subject with a slash broke the audit log search
body: A test subject named with a slash was created in staging last week, and the audit log search of the console could not find its entries because the path parser split the name. The root cause was that the registry accepted any string as a subject name. I added a validation rule that allows letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores up to 120 characters. The error message names the first bad character and its position, in the same style as the parser errors. Existing subjects in production were checked with a query, and all 214 names pass the rule, so no migration is needed. The clone feature from earlier this week uses the same check for the new name. I added 18 test cases for the rule, including unicode letters and an empty name. The console form now shows the allowed characters under the input field, and Lena reviewed the text. The audit log entry for a rejected create includes the attempted name, escaped, so it can be searched. One open question is whether to allow a slash for namespaced subjects later. For now the answer is no, and the docs page says so.

summary: Ingest worker memory graphs were checked after the batching changes and the heap stays flat over a 12 hour soak, so the headroom of 30 percent holds
body: After the adaptive flush age went to the canary, I wanted to know that bigger batches under load do not make the heap grow. I ran a 12 hour soak in staging at twice the normal event rate. The Go heap in the worker stayed between 410 and 460 MB, and the resident size of the task stayed under 70 percent of its limit. That matches the 30 percent headroom that Tobias and I agreed on in the Terraform review. I also looked at the garbage collector pauses, and the longest was 6 ms. One thing showed up in the profile: the batch buffer was reallocated on each flush. I changed it to reuse a slice with a fixed capacity, which cut allocations per batch by 35 percent. The soak was repeated with this change and showed the same flat shape. The change is small and goes out with the next release.

summary: Loader retry now records the failure reason per file in its state table, so the console can show why a large file is waiting instead of only that it is waiting
body: Sam asked why a customer's 1.5 GB import showed as waiting for two hours, and the answer was only visible in the logs. The retry state of the loader held the attempt count and the next time, but not the reason. I added a reason column to the state table with values such as storage_timeout, bad_input and rate_limited, matching the labels of the Prometheus counter from last week. The loader writes the reason on every failed attempt and clears it on success. A small migration added the column with a default of unknown, so old rows stay valid. The console endpoint now returns the reason and the next attempt time, and Lena will show it in the import list. I wrote tests for the three reasons and for a file that changes reason between attempts. The 50 file failure test still shows no thundering herd, and the state table size grows by only a few bytes per row. For the customer in question, the logs showed storage timeouts on the third attempt, and the file went through on the fifth. After the give-up limit of 6 attempts, the reason stays visible, so support can tell a customer what to fix. The next step is a short text in the docs that explains each reason, which Sam will write from the labels.

summary: Wrote the full test plan for the search shard migration dual write, with failure cases for each stage and the checks that must be green before each switch.
body:
Following the dual write plan from last week, I wrote the test plan for each step. The goal is that no switch happens without a check that can be run and read by someone else on call.

The plan has four stages: dual write on, shadow reads compared, read switch per customer, and old write off. For each stage I listed what can go wrong and how we would see it.

Examples of the failure cases:
- A write to the new layout fails while the old one succeeds. The writer logs the event id into a repair queue, and a counter goes up.
- The shadow read returns a different hit count. The comparison job stores both queries and the diff.
- A reindex runs during dual write. The job must write to both layouts or be paused.

The third case is the one I worried about most. The nightly reindex writes a lot, and if it only wrote to the old layout, the new one would drift. I decided that the reindex gets a flag for the target layouts, and that it is blocked from running without the flag once dual write is on.

For the read switch, the gate is that the hit counts match on 99.5 percent of a 10,000 query sample, and that every difference is explained by the ordering of ties. I wrote a script outline for the comparison.

Nothing in the index changes today. There are no code changes, only the plan in the docs folder, and no shard has been touched. Mara will review the repair queue design, since she knows the writer best. I also listed the dashboards we need before the first stage: write lag, repair queue size and the shadow diff rate.

summary: Ingest batching worker flush age is now adaptive to queue depth, and p95 end-to-end write latency fell from 1.9 to 1.2 seconds in a staging load test
body:
With a fixed flush age of 2 seconds, a quiet queue made events wait for a full batch or the full age. At low load that added latency for no reason.

I made the flush age depend on the topic backlog. If the backlog is under 500 events, the worker flushes after 200 ms. Above 5,000 it uses the full 2 seconds and the size limit, so batches stay large under load. Between those values it scales linearly.

A staging load test used a mixed profile: a quiet phase, a burst of 10 times the rate, and a quiet phase again. The p95 latency from API accept to stored event fell from 1.9 to 1.2 seconds over the whole run. During the burst the batch sizes stayed the same as before, around 4,000 events.

Postgres write calls rose by 15 percent in the quiet phases, as expected, and are still far from any limit.

The graceful stop test from last week still passes. I added a test for the scaling function with boundary values. Next I want to try the same on the production canary task for a day before the full rollout.

summary: Tried moving the console's session store reads to a Redis pipeline and rolled it back, because the saving was only 0.3 ms per request and the code got harder to read
body:
Lena wondered if the console made too many round trips to Redis per request. I looked at a trace and saw three reads for one page load: the session, the role and a feature flag.

I tried a pipeline that fetches all three in one round trip. In staging the saving was 0.3 ms per request on average, which is nothing next to the 80 ms of the page. The change also made the session middleware depend on the other two, which made tests awkward.

I rolled the change back and kept the notes in the branch description. No other changes were needed. The three reads stay as they are.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long a Retry-After value can be: the limiter caps it at the window length, so it never exceeds 60 seconds for the default plan
body:
Sam asked for the docs how large Retry-After can get. I read the limiter code: the value is the time to the end of the current window, capped at the window length. The default plan uses 60 second windows, so 60 is the maximum.

For custom plans the window can be longer, up to 10 minutes, and so can the header. I gave Sam the two numbers and an example response for the docs.

summary: Dashboard queries for the large customers were checked after the cache key change, and the slowest panel now answers in 1.4 seconds on a cache miss and 30 ms on a hit
body:
After the hit rate rose to 81 percent, I wanted to know what a miss costs for the slowest dashboards. I took the five slowest panels of the largest customers and ran each cold, five times.

The slowest panel, the event type breakdown over 90 days, took 1.4 seconds on a miss. The others were between 0.4 and 1.1 seconds. All of these read from the ClickHouse materialized views and not from the raw events.

On a hit, the answer came from Redis in about 30 ms, including the API overhead.

I checked the TTLs of the dashboard result group, which are 5 minutes for short ranges and 30 minutes for ranges over 30 days. The numbers fit what customers expect from the freshness. I did not change anything.

One observation for later: the 90 day panel has a bucket boundary at midnight UTC, and the cache entries all expire together for some customers. A little jitter on the TTL would spread that. I wrote it down as a small task.

summary: Audit export gained a resume option after a cancel: a cancelled export continues from the last written chunk and the HMAC covers the whole file, verified on the large staging account
body:
Compliance asked what happens when an export is cancelled at minute 15 of 17. Until now it had to start again. I added a resume option that continues from the last written chunk.

The export writes chunks of 50,000 rows and records the last chunk index and the last row key in a small state row. A resumed export reads that state, seeks to the key and appends. The state row is removed when the export finishes.

The HMAC was the tricky part. It has to cover the whole file, not only the appended part. I keep the running HMAC state serialized in the state row, so a resumed export continues the same computation. I checked this by comparing the result of a resumed export with an uninterrupted one of the same data: the checksums were identical in 10 of 10 runs.

The idle in transaction alert from last week matters here. The cancel path now closes its cursor and transaction before it writes the state, so the connection is not left open. I confirmed with pg_stat_activity during a cancel that no session stays idle in transaction.

There is one limit. If the data changes between cancel and resume, rows could be missed or doubled. The export uses a snapshot timestamp stored in the state row and filters on it, so rows created later are not part of the file. Rows updated later are exported as of their state at resume time, which I documented.

The console shows a Resume button for cancelled exports newer than 24 hours. Lena will review the button text. Tests: 14 new, including a cancel during the last chunk and a cancel before the first one.

summary: Schema registry subjects can now be cloned with their compatibility mode and version history, and a clone of a 30 version subject keeps ids and order in tests
body:
Mara's team of customers asked for a way to copy a subject to a new name, for a test environment, without losing the history. I added a clone endpoint to the registry.

The clone copies all versions in order with new global ids, but the version numbers stay the same, so version 7 of the source is version 7 of the clone. The compatibility mode is copied too, and the audit log writes one entry for the clone with the source and target names.

The first version used one transaction per version. For a 30 version subject that took 1.8 seconds and left half-copied subjects when it failed in the middle. I moved it to a single transaction, which takes 0.4 seconds and either completes or leaves nothing.

Checks in the endpoint:
- the target name must not exist
- the caller needs the admin role, as for mode changes
- a subject with more than 200 versions is refused with a clear error, for now

The 200 limit is a guess to protect the transaction size. I tested a 150 version subject and it took 2 seconds, so the limit looks safe.

A test compares the schemas of source and clone byte by byte, and checks the order of the versions and that the mode is the same. Another test confirms that a failed clone, forced by a duplicate in the middle, leaves no target subject.

The references between subjects are not rewritten. If subject A refers to B, the clone of A still refers to B. That is what the customers wanted, but I put it in the endpoint docs so nobody is surprised.

Next is a console button, which Lena can add once the endpoint is merged.

summary: Looked at the search API p99 after the cache key fixes: the remaining slow tail comes from queries with wildcards at the start of a term, 4 percent of calls but half of the slow ones
body:
After p99 fell to 410 ms, I wanted to know what the rest of the tail is. I took one day of search API logs and sorted the calls above 400 ms by query shape.

Two shapes make up most of it. Queries with a leading wildcard, like *error, are 4 percent of calls but about half of the slow ones, with a median of 900 ms. They cannot use the term index well, and OpenSearch has to scan the term dictionary.

The second shape is very wide date ranges over unfiltered full text, about 1 percent of calls, with a median of 700 ms.

I tested two ideas on staging. The first was an extra reversed-term field for leading wildcards, so *error becomes a prefix query on the reversed text. It brought the median for that shape from 900 to 120 ms. It costs about 12 percent more index size for that field.

The second was to refuse leading wildcards for customers on small plans. Sam says that would break some saved searches, so I did not go further.

The index size matters because of the planned shard layout by month. A 12 percent bigger index for one field is acceptable, but I want to apply the field only to the message and title fields, not to every text field. With only those two, the growth is about 5 percent.

I have not changed the production mapping. The reversed field would need a reindex, and that should wait for the shard migration, so we do the reindex once. I wrote this into the migration plan as a prerequisite to decide.

The parser needs a small change too, to rewrite a leading wildcard into the reversed query. I made a draft in the search-v2 branch with 8 tests, but it is not merged. The wide date range case needs a different fix and I did not start on it.

summary: Reindex job for search v2 now writes to a target layout flag, which the dual write plan needs, and refuses to run without one once dual write is switched on
body:
The test plan for the shard migration had a gap: the nightly reindex would only write to the old layout. I implemented the flag that I described there.

The job takes a targets setting with the values old, new or both. If the dual write switch in the settings table is on, a run without an explicit targets value stops at the start with an error that says why. That is on purpose, so that nobody starts a reindex by hand and lets the layouts drift.

The content hash skip still works per layout. Each layout stores its own hash, so a document that is up to date in the old layout but missing in the new one is written to the new one only. I had to change the hash lookup to take the layout name. That touched reindex/hashes.ts and the mapping metadata writer.

I ran the job on staging in four ways:
- targets old with dual write off: as before, 19 minutes for a full run
- targets both on an empty new layout: 31 minutes, since everything is written to the new side
- targets both again: 21 minutes, because only unchanged checks happen on both sides
- no targets with dual write on: stopped with the error, as intended

The second run shows the cost of filling a new layout, and it is a useful number for planning. The third shows that the skip works across both layouts.

One issue came up: the metadata of boosts is written per layout as well, and the new layout test index did not have the metadata field. I added it to the new mapping template.

Tests: 11 new, plus the old ones. I will ask Mara to review the hash lookup change, since it touches the part she wrote. After that, the repair queue is the next piece.

summary: Redis client in the search API now reuses connections per worker instead of opening one per request batch, and connection count at peak dropped from 38 to 22 in staging
body:
The connection graph of Redis showed that the search API opened and closed connections in bursts. At staging peak there were 38 connections for 4 workers, which is more than needed.

The cause was a helper that created a client for each cache warm-up batch, and the client was closed afterwards. I changed it to use the shared client of the worker. The shared client has a small pool of its own with a fixed maximum.

Staging load test with the usual profile: peak connections went from 38 to 22, and the latency of cache reads did not change. Reconnect events fell to almost zero.

I checked the shutdown path, because a shared client must be closed once. The worker closes it after the server stops accepting, and a test confirms no open handles remain.

Production rollout will follow with the next regular release. I wrote the connection numbers in the notes, so we can compare them afterwards.

summary: Added jitter of up to 10 percent to the TTL of long-range dashboard cache entries, so entries of one customer no longer expire at the same moment
body:
I wrote down last week that the 90 day panels expire together. Today I added jitter to the TTL of the dashboard result group for ranges over 30 days.

The TTL is now 30 minutes plus a random value of up to 3 minutes, chosen when the entry is written. Short ranges stay at 5 minutes without jitter, because they are cheap to recompute.

I checked the effect in staging with a script that opens the five slowest dashboards of one customer every minute for two hours. Before the change the misses came in clusters: all five at once, every 30 minutes. After it they spread over the 3 minute window, and the peak load on ClickHouse for that customer fell by about 60 percent.

The overall hit rate did not change, still around 81 percent.

The key naming docs list the TTL for this group, and I updated the line to say 30 minutes plus jitter. A unit test checks that the jitter stays within the bounds. Nothing else in the cache code was touched.

summary: Per-key rate limit overrides now have an expiry date in Postgres, so a temporary raise for a customer ends by itself, and the Redis cache respects the shorter of 60 seconds and the expiry
body:
Support often raises the limit of a key for a launch or a data import and then forgets to lower it. Sam asked for temporary overrides.

I added an expires_at column to the overrides table, nullable, with a migration that needs no lock because the column has no default. The limiter reads the override through the Redis cache with a 60 second TTL. For an override with an expiry, the cache TTL is the smaller of 60 seconds and the time to the expiry. Otherwise a cached value could outlive the override by up to a minute.

When an override has expired, the limiter falls back to the plan limit. A background job deletes expired rows once an hour, and writes an audit log entry for each deletion with the key and the old limit.

Testing needed some care with time. I used an injectable clock in the limiter and wrote tests for these cases:
- an override that expires in 10 seconds is used and then dropped
- an override with no expiry behaves as before
- an override already expired at read time is ignored
- clock skew of a few seconds between the console and the API does not give a wrong result

In staging I set an override to expire in 2 minutes and watched a client call at a steady rate. The rejected calls started exactly when the override ended, within the 60 second cache bound.

The console endpoint takes an optional expiry in the request. Lena will add a date field to the form. Sam will write the docs, and I gave her the behavior at the boundary: at the moment of expiry the plan limit applies at once for new cache reads.

I also considered a notification before expiry, but left it out. It can be added later if support asks.

summary: Ingest batching canary ran a day in production with the adaptive flush age: batch sizes under load are unchanged and p95 write latency is 1.3 seconds against 1.9 before
body:
The canary task with the adaptive flush age has run since this morning on about 10 percent of the partitions. I compared it with the other tasks over six hours.

The p95 latency from accept to stored event was 1.3 seconds on the canary and 1.9 on the rest. During the afternoon peak the canary batch sizes were the same as the others, around 4,000 events, so the size limit still rules under load.

Postgres write calls from the canary were 14 percent higher than from the other tasks over the whole period, close to the 15 percent from staging. The database CPU did not move in a way that I could see.

I also checked shutdown. Tobias redeployed the canary twice for an unrelated change, and the events counted before and after matched, with no loss. The flush on shutdown worked as in the test.

One small finding: right after a restart the backlog is not known for the first second, and the worker used the short flush age. This created a few small batches. I made the worker use the long age until the first backlog reading arrives. A test covers that.

I plan to roll out to all tasks in the next release if tomorrow's numbers look the same.

summary: Search v2 parser now reports the position of a syntax error in a query, and the console shows a caret under the broken character instead of a generic 400
body:
Until now a malformed query in search v2 returned a plain 400 with the text 'invalid query'. Support had asked for something better after three tickets last week where customers could not find a missing parenthesis.

The parser now keeps the offset of the token where it gave up and returns it as `error.position` together with a short expected-token list. The search API passes this through unchanged. The console formats it as the query with a caret under the offset.

The grammar file got 22 new error cases, one for each kind of failure: unclosed group, dangling operator, empty field scope and so on. All 182 cases pass. Two messages were reworded because they named internal token types that mean nothing to a customer.

The v1 parser is untouched. Lena still has to look at the caret rendering for queries longer than the input box, where the caret drifts when the text wraps. That is the next step.

summary: Postgres slow query review found the audit log listing doing a sort on 4 million rows, and a composite index cut it from 2.1 seconds to 40 ms
body:
The slow query log of the last week showed one statement far ahead of the others: the audit log listing in the console, filtered by account and ordered by created_at descending. The planner used the account index and then sorted about 4 million rows for the largest customer.

I added an index on (account_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so there was no lock on the table. Build time on production was 6 minutes. The explain output now shows an index scan with no sort, and the listing for the large customer answers in 40 ms instead of 2.1 seconds.

The old single column index on account_id is now mostly redundant. I did not drop it yet; I want to watch the index usage statistics for a week first. The extra index adds about 380 MB, which is fine.

Tobias was told, because the disk graph will show a small step.

summary: Redis memory by key group was measured on production, and the dashboard cache keys take 61 percent of the memory, more than all other groups together
body:
Mara asked yesterday where the Redis memory goes, so I ran a sampling scan over the keyspace with the key naming rules as groups. The scan used SCAN with a small count and a pause, so it did not disturb the instance.

Result by group: dashboard cache 61 percent, search result cache 18 percent, session 9 percent, rate limiter 7 percent, the rest 5 percent. The dashboard entries are large because they hold the full series for long ranges, with a median of 38 KB.

Two ideas came out of it. The first is compressing the long-range dashboard values before the write, which a quick test shrank by about 70 percent. The second is shortening their TTL, but that would lower the hit rate, so I left it alone.

No change was made. I wrote the numbers into the notes for the cache planning and will try the compression on staging next.

summary: Dashboard cache values are compressed with zstd on staging, memory of that group fell 64 percent, and the extra CPU in the search API is below 2 percent
body:
Following the memory measurement of this morning, I added compression to the long-range dashboard cache writes in the TypeScript search API. Values above 4 KB are compressed with zstd at level 3, and a one byte marker in front tells the reader whether a value is compressed.

The marker matters for the rollout. Old uncompressed values are still read correctly, so there is no flush and no need for a switch at one moment.

On staging with a replay of a day of dashboard traffic, the memory of the dashboard group fell from 2.3 GB to 0.83 GB. That is 64 percent. The CPU of the API tasks rose by 1.6 percent at peak. The time to read and decompress a typical 38 KB value is 0.2 ms, which is below the noise of the network.

I also checked the p99 of the slowest dashboard panel on a cache hit. It stayed at 30 ms.

Tests added: a roundtrip test for values on both sides of the 4 KB threshold, and a test that a value with an unknown marker is treated as a miss and not as an error. The second one came from a worry that a bad value would break a whole dashboard.

Next step is a canary on one task in production, probably tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question on whether a customer can see which API key made a rate limited request: yes, in the audit log, but only for the last 30 days
body:
Sam asked this for a support ticket. A customer had hit 429 responses and wanted to know which of their keys caused it.

The limiter writes a rate limit event to the audit log with the key id, not the key itself. The console shows it under Audit, filter type 'rate_limit'. The events are kept 30 days in Postgres.

Older events are not available. The counters in Redis only live for the window length, so they cannot help either.

I suggested to Sam to tell the customer to filter by key id and to mention the 30 day limit. I also wrote one paragraph for the docs.

summary: Terraform plan for the ECS ingest service showed an unexpected change to the health check grace period, traced to a module default that Tobias had updated
body:
While preparing a small change to the ingest task definition, `terraform plan` showed that the health check grace period of the service would drop from 120 to 60 seconds. I had not touched it.

The cause was in the shared service module. Tobias changed its default last week for another service, and the ingest service relied on the old default instead of setting the value itself.

I set the value explicitly to 120 in the ingest service. The plan is clean now, with only my intended change. I told Tobias, and he will check whether other services have the same hidden dependency on module defaults.

I did not apply anything beyond my own change.

summary: Canary of compressed dashboard cache values ran on one production task for a day: hit rate unchanged, memory growth of that group slowed, no decode errors
body:
The compression change went to one of the six search API tasks yesterday evening, and I looked at it this afternoon after a full day of traffic.

Correctness first. The decode error counter stayed at zero. The counter for unknown markers is also zero, which is expected, because nothing writes other markers yet. Mixed reads worked: the canary task read old uncompressed values written by the other tasks and the other way around, since the other tasks can still read only uncompressed values. Wait, that second direction should have failed, and it did for a short time. The other five tasks do not know the marker and treated a compressed value as broken JSON, and they counted it as a cache miss and recomputed it.

This was a mistake in my rollout plan. The effect was small, but it showed up as a lower hit rate on those five tasks: from 52 to 44 percent for dashboard panels during the canary. Nothing was wrong for customers, only a bit slower on some panels.

The fix is to roll out in two steps. First a version that can read both formats but still writes plain values. Then, after all tasks run it, the version that writes compressed values. I changed the code with a flag `dashboard_cache_compress_write`, default off.

Numbers from the canary task itself: the memory of the keys it wrote was 66 percent smaller than comparable keys. Its CPU was 1.8 percent higher than the others. The p99 on a hit stayed at 30 ms.

Plan: deploy the read-both version to all tasks tomorrow, wait a day, then switch the flag on for one task and then for all. I added this to the rollout notes with the reason, so the order is not forgotten.

summary: Read-both version of the dashboard cache deployed to all search API tasks, with the write flag still off, and the hit rate is back at 52 percent
body:
I deployed the read-both version to all six tasks of the search API in the afternoon. The deployment was a normal rolling one and took 14 minutes.

After the roll, the dashboard hit rate returned to 52 percent, as before the canary of last week. The earlier dip was gone because the one task that wrote compressed values had been taken out of the flag the day before. The decode error counter is zero on all tasks.

A check I added: a small script that reads 500 random dashboard keys and reports how many have the marker. Today it reports 0 percent, which is right while the flag is off.

Tomorrow the flag goes on for one task. If the numbers are as good as the first canary, the rest follows two days later.

One open point is the cache entries of the biggest customer, which are over 200 KB for some panels. I want to look at how well they compress separately.

summary: Compression flag for dashboard cache writes turned on for one task, and after two hours its keys are 65 percent smaller with no errors
body:
Today's step of the compression rollout: `dashboard_cache_compress_write` was switched on for one task. All tasks can read both formats now, so this time no other task was affected.

After two hours the sample script found 17 percent of the dashboard keys with the marker, which fits one task out of six writing for a while. The new keys are on average 65 percent smaller than old ones of the same panels. Decode errors stay at zero, and the miss rate did not move.

CPU of the canary task is 1.7 percent above the others, as in staging.

I looked at the large customer panels too. The 200 KB values shrink to about 52 KB, which is a smaller gain than the typical case because they hold mostly numbers with high entropy. I think it is still fine.

I will leave it on this one task overnight and decide on the others in the morning.

summary: Search v2 field boost config can now be reloaded without a restart, and a bad file leaves the running boosts in place with a logged error
body:
The boost config of search v2 was loaded once at start. Changing a boost meant a rolling restart of the search API, which is too heavy for a tuning loop.

I added a reload on SIGHUP and on a `POST /admin/boosts/reload` call that only the console service account can use. The new file goes through the same validation as at start, the one that stops on an unknown field name. If validation fails, the old boosts stay active, the error with file and line is logged, and the endpoint returns 422 with the same text.

The swap itself is one assignment of an immutable object, so a query in flight never sees half of the old and half of the new boosts.

Tests: a reload with a valid file changes the ranking of a fixed query set, a reload with an unknown field keeps the old ranking, and 200 parallel queries during a reload give only results from one of the two configs.

Open: the console has no button for it yet. Lena can add one later, and for now the call is documented in the runbook.

summary: Dashboard cache compression is on for all search API tasks after a clean night on the canary, and the dashboard group should shrink as old keys expire
body:
The canary task had a clean night: no decode errors, no change of the hit rate, and CPU within 2 percent of the others. So I turned the write flag on for the remaining five tasks.

Memory will not drop at once. Old uncompressed values stay until their TTL ends, and the long-range ones have TTLs of up to a day with jitter. I expect most of the effect by tomorrow evening.

I wrote down the expected result in the notes: the dashboard group should go from 61 percent of Redis memory to about 35 percent of today's total, and the total from 3.8 GB to about 2.6 GB.

If something looks wrong, switching the flag off is enough, because the readers handle both formats.

summary: Postgres autovacuum settings reviewed for the events metadata tables, and the two busiest tables now have their own thresholds after a bloat check showed 27 percent dead space
body:
The weekly bloat check, a query over pg_stat_user_tables and an estimate from pgstattuple on a sample, flagged two tables. One is the API key usage table and the other is the import jobs table of the batch importer. Dead space was 27 percent on the first and 19 percent on the second.

Both tables are updated very often by small writes, and the global autovacuum scale factor of 0.2 means vacuum starts only after a fifth of the rows are dead. For a table of 30 million rows that is far too late.

I set per table values: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.02 and autovacuum_vacuum_threshold 5000 for the usage table, and 0.05 for the import jobs table. I also raised the cost limit for them a little, so that a vacuum run finishes in a few minutes instead of being throttled for half an hour.

The change was made with ALTER TABLE ... SET, which needs only a short lock. No restart, no maintenance window.

I watched the first vacuum on the usage table. It started within two minutes, ran for 4 minutes and removed about 8 million dead tuples. The I/O graphs of the database show a small bump during the run and nothing else.

The space is not returned to the operating system by a normal vacuum, so the file size stays. The tables will reuse the space, which is what matters. A full rewrite with pg_repack would shrink the files, but I decided it is not worth it for now, since the disk is at 41 percent.

I also looked at long running transactions, because they block vacuum from cleaning. There was one idle in transaction session from the console, open for two hours. It came from a debugging connection of mine, and I closed it. To catch such cases in the future I set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10 minutes for the console role.

Plan: look at the bloat numbers again in a week. If they are below 10 percent, the same settings go to the other tables with heavy updates, which is a short list.

summary: Loader retry now backs off with jitter after a failed chunk upload, and a test with a flaky object store shows that 98 percent of large files finish without manual action
body:
The loader retried a failed chunk upload at once, up to five times. During a short problem of the object store last week this made things worse, because many files retried in the same second.

I changed the delay to exponential backoff starting at 500 ms, with a factor of 2, a cap of 30 seconds and a random jitter of up to 25 percent. The attempt limit stays at five for a single chunk, but the file as a whole may now go back to the waiting state and be picked up again later, which was already the behavior of the state table.

To test it, I wrote a small fake object store that fails 30 percent of requests, in bursts of a few seconds. A run of 200 files of 50 MB to 2 GB each gave this result: 196 finished without help, 4 ended in the waiting state with the reason recorded and finished on the second pass. So 98 percent finish in the first pass, and all finish in the end. Before the change the same test gave 71 percent in the first pass.

The resume from the last committed line offset, written some days ago, was exercised too. No file was loaded twice, and the line counts match the sources.

One detail I had to fix: the backoff sleep held a worker slot, so five files in backoff blocked the pool. The sleeping chunk now releases its slot and re-queues itself with a not-before time.

The console shows the next attempt time next to the failure reason, which helps Sam to answer questions about files that are waiting. That was a small addition to the state table: a `next_attempt_at` column.

Next step is a production canary on the import queue of one customer with big NDJSON files.

summary: Looked into why the Redis client in the ingest API reconnects every few minutes and found an idle timeout on the load balancer path, fixed with a keepalive
body:
Prometheus showed small bursts of new Redis connections from the ingest tasks every four to five minutes, always about the same number. That did not match any traffic pattern.

The first guess was the connection pool recycling its connections by max lifetime. The setting is 30 minutes, so it was not that. The second guess was a server side timeout, but the Redis `timeout` setting is 0.

The client logs at debug level told the rest: 'read ECONNRESET' on connections that had been idle for about 300 seconds, which is not a Redis behavior. Between the tasks and Redis there is a network path with a connection tracking idle limit of 350 seconds on one hop, and the ingest tasks use few connections, so some of them are really idle for that long during the quiet hours.

The fix is a TCP keepalive on the client sockets with a first probe after 60 seconds, and the same for the rate limiter client. In the Go ingest code the dialer got KeepAlive: 60s. The search API in TypeScript already set a keepalive, which is why only the ingest side showed the problem.

I deployed to staging first, where I can see the same pattern with a quiet load. After two hours the reconnect bursts were gone. In production after the rolling deploy the bursts also stopped, and the count of new connections per hour went from about 700 to about 40.

There was a side effect I did not plan. The first request after each reset used to fail once and be retried by the client, and these single retries are gone now too. The ingest p99 did not change in a visible way, because it is dominated by other things.

I wrote the finding into the infrastructure notes with the 350 second figure, so that Tobias has it when he changes the network setup. The same limit may apply to the Postgres connections, which I did not check.

Open question: whether the pool should send a cheap PING on borrow after a long idle time as a second safety. I decided against it for now, because the keepalive solves the cause.

summary: Per key rate limit headers now include the remaining quota on every response, not only on 429, and the public API docs describe them
body:
Customers had asked for the remaining quota on successful calls, so that their clients can slow down before they hit the limit. Until today the limiter sent Retry-After only with a 429.

The middleware now adds three headers to each response: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, the last in seconds until the window resets. The values come from the same sliding window counter that makes the decision, so there is no extra Redis call. The counter read was already part of the Lua script, and the script now returns the remaining count along with the allowed flag.

Two edge cases got tests. With a temporary override that has an expiry, the limit in the header is the override value until it expires, and then the plan value. If the override ends in the middle of a window, the header follows the shorter of the two, as the cache already does.

The second case is a key that is not limited at all, such as internal service keys. These get no headers, which is simpler than inventing a large number.

The response size grows by about 90 bytes. For batch endpoints with small responses this is visible but unimportant.

I updated the docs page for rate limits with a table of the headers and an example of a client that sleeps until the reset time when Remaining is 0. Sam read it and asked for a note that the values are per key and not per account, which I added.

Next I will check the load test for the limiter to see if the changed script has an effect on latency. Early numbers from staging show 0.05 ms more per call.

summary: Search index shard planning note: by month layout needs about 36 shards for 13 months with the biggest customer, and the sizes per shard are uneven
body:
I worked on the sizing for the planned layout of the search index, which will split by month instead of by customer. This was desk work with queries over the index stats, no change in the system.

The current index has 12 shards. By customer means that the three largest customers hold 70 percent of the data, and their shards are far bigger than the rest. By month, each month would be spread evenly across customers, but the months differ: the last month is 1.4 times the size of the oldest ones because event volume grew.

With the 13 month retention of the analytics side as a guide, and keeping the search side for the same span, I estimated 13 monthly indices with 3 primary shards each, so 39 shards. Each shard comes to roughly 25 to 35 GB, which sits in the range that is good for OpenSearch.

A downside I noted is the query fan out. A search over a full range touches all 39 shards, where before it touched the shards of one customer. The query cache and the filter on customer should keep this acceptable, but it has to be measured on a copy.

I wrote the table of shard sizes into the planning doc, with the question for Tobias about the memory of the data nodes. He will answer when he has looked at the heap numbers.

summary: Audit export for large accounts now streams in chunks of 50,000 rows with a server side cursor, and peak memory of the export task fell from 2.6 GB to 310 MB
body:
The audit export for compliance builds a file from the audit log of an account. For the biggest account, with 38 million rows over its retention, the export task read the result into memory in pages, but kept all pages until the end for the checksum step. Last week it was killed twice by the memory limit of the ECS task.

The cause was in how the HMAC and the file writer were connected. The writer wanted the whole buffer to compute the signature in one call. HMAC can be updated incrementally, so this was not needed.

What I changed:
- The query uses a server side cursor (DECLARE ... CURSOR) inside a read only transaction, fetching 50,000 rows at a time.
- Each chunk is serialized, written to the file, and fed into the HMAC with update(), then dropped.
- The resume option keeps its behavior. The last written chunk number is stored in the state row after each flush, and on resume the cursor is reopened with a keyset condition on (created_at, id), not with OFFSET.
- The final HMAC covers the whole file, as before.

The keyset condition needed the composite index on (account_id, created_at, id). The one added recently has created_at descending, and Postgres can scan it backwards, so no new index was necessary. I checked the plan: it is an index scan, with the cursor opening in 12 ms.

Measurements on the large staging account, a copy with 38 million rows: the export takes 21 minutes, which is 3 minutes more than before because of the smaller chunks and the flushes. Peak memory is 310 MB where it was 2.6 GB. The CPU of the task is flat at about 35 percent.

Verification: the signature of the new file is valid with the reviewer tool, and the content hash matches that of a file made by the old code from a frozen snapshot, line by line. The cancel and resume test was repeated, three cancels at random points, and each time the result matched.

One thing I noticed and did not fix: with a cursor, the transaction stays open for the whole export, 21 minutes. That holds back vacuum on the audit log a bit. The table is append mostly, so the effect is small, but I set a statement timeout of 30 minutes on the export role to prevent runaway cases.

Next I will lower the ECS memory of the export task from 4 GB to 1 GB, which saves cost, after one more week of observation.

summary: Search API wildcard handling: trailing wildcards are capped at a prefix length of 3, and the slow tail from wildcard queries dropped, with p99 at 360 ms in staging replay
body:
The remaining slow tail of the search API was traced to wildcard queries some time ago. Leading wildcards are an explicit error in search v2 now. This session was about trailing and middle wildcards, which still can be expensive when the prefix is very short, like `a*`.

I replayed one day of real queries against a staging copy and sorted by time. Queries with a prefix shorter than 3 characters before the wildcard were 2.2 percent of the calls, but they made up 31 percent of the time spent in OpenSearch, because they expand to a very large number of terms.

The rule I added to the v2 parser: a wildcard term needs at least 3 literal characters before the first wildcard. Otherwise the parser returns an error with a hint, in the same format as the leading wildcard error, with the position from the work of two weeks ago. Like the other one, it is behind a flag that restores the old behavior, `allow_short_prefix`, for customers who depend on it.

I looked for customers who depend on it. The audit of the query logs shows two accounts that send short prefix queries regularly, both from an autocomplete box in their own product. For them I set the flag on, and I will write to Sam so that he can ask whether a longer minimum is possible on their side.

Results of the replay after the change, with the flag off for all except the two accounts:
- p50 went from 38 ms to 36 ms
- p95 from 190 ms to 150 ms
- p99 from 780 ms in the old state, 410 ms after the cache work, to 360 ms now
- OpenSearch CPU on the data nodes down by 9 percent in the replay

The errors returned for the rejected queries were 1.9 percent of the calls in the replay. That is higher than I would like. Looking at them, most come from the same few clients which send a single letter and a star while the user is typing. Those clients get an error with a hint and not a result, and that may look like a regression to them.

Because of that I decided not to turn the rule on everywhere at once. Plan: log-only mode for a week, where the parser accepts the query but counts it and logs the account. Then decide with the real numbers which accounts need the flag.

I added the log-only mode as a third value of the setting: off, log, enforce. The default is log. Tests cover all three values, and the grammar file has 6 new cases for the prefix rule. All 188 pass.

summary: Tried a different Redis client library for the search API and dropped it after benchmarks showed no gain over the current one and a worse reconnect behavior
body:
Mara had seen a newer Redis client for Node with a promising benchmark page, so I tried it on a branch of the search API for half a day.

The benchmark used our own access pattern: mostly GET of 1 to 40 KB values, some MGET, and the Lua script of the limiter. With 50 concurrent requests and a local Redis, the new library gave 3 percent more throughput, which is inside the noise. On staging with the network in between it was identical.

The reconnect behavior was the problem. After I killed the Redis connection on purpose, the new client queued commands without a limit while it was reconnecting, and memory of the process grew by 400 MB in a minute. The current client fails fast with an error that we already handle as a cache miss. Setting a queue limit was possible, but the semantics differ and the limiter would need extra code.

So there is no reason to switch. I deleted the branch and wrote two lines in the notes with the result, so the question does not come back in a few months.

summary: Schema registry compatibility check now reports every incompatible change in a new version, not only the first, and the console lists them in one table
body:
Until now the compatibility check for a new schema version stopped at the first incompatible change. Users fixed one problem, submitted again and found the next, which cost several rounds for big schemas.

The checker now walks the whole diff and collects all findings. Each has a path in the schema, the kind of change (field removed, type narrowed, required added, enum value removed) and the compatibility mode that forbids it. The API returns them as a list with a count, limited to 100 findings, and a flag if there were more.

Some details that needed care:
- A removed field inside a nested object that was itself added as new is not a finding, so the walk must skip new subtrees.
- For the backward and forward mode, the same change can be a finding in one mode and fine in the other. Each finding carries the modes, to avoid confusion for subjects set to a full mode.
- The order is stable, sorted by path, so that two submissions give the same output and a diff of results is useful.

The console, which is Lena's part, got a small table in the failure dialog. I only changed the API contract and gave her an example response. She had the table running in an hour.

Tests: 14 new cases for the checker, including a schema with 40 breaking changes to check the limit, and the old single finding test now expects a list of one. The existing 120 tests pass.

One case I could not resolve cleanly: a type change from integer to number is compatible in one direction only, and our rules list it as a finding in backward mode. This matches the old behavior, so I left it, and added a line to the docs.

summary: Ingest batching: a stuck partition no longer blocks the flush of the others, after a test showed one slow commit delaying all batches by up to 8 seconds
body:
During a staging soak with a fault injected into one partition, the p95 write latency went up for all event types, not only the slow one. The injected fault was a delay of 8 seconds on the commit of one partition. The expectation was that only that partition's batches would wait.

The reason was in the flush loop of the batching worker. One goroutine iterated over all open batches and flushed the ready ones in turn, and a flush included the commit. A slow commit therefore held the loop, and all other batches that had reached their size or age had to wait behind it.

The change: each partition now has its own flusher goroutine with its own timer, and the shared loop is gone. The flush rules stay the same, size, age (adaptive to queue depth) or shutdown. A limited semaphore of 8 keeps the number of parallel commits to the database bounded, so that many flushers do not overload Postgres at the same moment. That limit was an explicit decision, because the old loop had a natural limit of one and I did not want to remove it without a replacement.

The graceful stop test of two weeks ago had to be updated. At shutdown, all flushers get the stop signal, flush their open batch and report back, and the process waits for all of them with a timeout of 25 seconds, which is below the ECS stop timeout of 30. The test with SIGTERM in the middle of a batch passes, with no events lost, and I added a variant where one partition's commit is slow, which ends within the timeout and reports the batch as not flushed instead of hanging. In that case the events stay in the queue and are read again after the restart, since the offset was not committed.

Results of the same soak with the fault:
- healthy partitions: p95 write latency 1.2 seconds, the same as without a fault
- slow partition: p95 about 9 seconds, which is the injected delay
- semaphore wait time in the metrics: below 5 ms at the 99th percentile

Heap in the 12 hour soak is flat again; the added goroutines cost very little, I measured 2 KB per flusher.

I added two metrics: flush duration per partition and the semaphore wait time. A dashboard row in Grafana shows them together, since a growing wait would be the first sign that the limit of 8 is too low.

Next step is a production canary like the one before, with the same checks on batch sizes and latency.

summary: Console session store keys checked after the cleanup: no keys with the old prefixes remain, and the session TTL is 8 hours with a sliding refresh
body:
Sam asked in the morning how long a user stays logged in to the console, and I wanted to answer from the real data instead of from memory of the code.

I scanned the session key group in Redis. All keys use the current prefix, and there are no keys left with the old patterns that the dual read once handled. The count is 212 sessions today.

The TTL is 8 hours from the last request, as the middleware refreshes it on use, but at most once per 5 minutes to avoid a write on every call. So a user who works all day stays in, and a user who leaves for the evening is logged out by the next morning.

I told Sam this, and also that there is no fixed maximum session age. If compliance wants an absolute limit, for example 24 hours, that would be a small change in the middleware. He will ask and tell me.

summary: Ingest API Redis keepalive fix was checked after a day in production: reconnects fell from about one every four minutes per task to none, and the error log is quiet
body:
The keepalive change from the last days was verified on all ingest API tasks after a full day of traffic. Before the change each task logged a reconnect to Redis every three to five minutes, always after a quiet spell on the connection.
