The cause was an idle timeout on the load balancer path that dropped the connection without a close.

I counted the reconnect log lines per task for the day before and the day after the deploy. Before: 280 to 340 lines per task per day. After: zero on 11 of 12 tasks, and one on the twelfth, which came right after a task restart and not from an idle drop. The Redis client error counter in Grafana, which used to show small bursts of failed commands at each reconnect, is flat.

I also looked at the rate limiter, because it is the main user of that connection in the ingest API. Before, the limiter fell back to its local counters for about 200 ms after each reconnect, and the share of requests judged on local counters was around 0.4 percent. That share is now below 0.01 percent. So the limits are applied more evenly across tasks, which was a side effect nobody had measured before.

The keepalive interval is 30 seconds, well under the idle timeout of the load balancer path. I tried 15 seconds on one task for two hours as a comparison and saw no difference in the reconnect count, so the 30 seconds stays and the extra packets are avoided. The TCP keepalive settings of the host were not touched; only the client option is used.

One open item: the search API uses a different client setup and never showed this pattern, but I wrote a note to check its idle behavior the next time the connection pool is reviewed. Nothing else is planned for this topic, and the ticket for the reconnects is closed.

summary: Rate limit overrides by plan: a migration moved 31 hard coded plan limits from the code into a Postgres table, and the limiter reads them with a 60 second cache
body:
The plan limits of the rate limiter, such as requests per minute for default, business and large, lived in a constants file in the API code. Every change needed a deploy, and support could not see them anywhere.

This session moved them into a Postgres table `rate_limit_plans` with the plan name, the window length, the limit, and a version column. The migration inserts the 31 current values, taken from the constants by a script, and a test compares the table with the old file so that no number was copied wrong. All 31 match.

The limiter reads the plan row through the same small cache as the per key overrides. The cache holds a row for 60 seconds, so a change in the table takes effect within a minute without any restart. If Postgres is not reachable, the limiter uses the last cached row for up to 10 minutes and then falls back to the compiled default for the plan, with a warning in the log. I wanted the limiter to never fail open or closed because of a database hiccup.

The order of checks stays: a per key override with an unexpired date wins, then the plan row, then the default.

The constants file stays for now as the fallback source. I did not want to delete it in the same change. A test makes sure that it and the migration data agree, and it fails if somebody changes only one of them.

The console has no form for editing the plan table, and this is intentionally left out. For now changes go through a reviewed SQL file. Lena and I talked about a form for later, but there is no need yet, since plan limits change maybe twice a year.

Verification on staging: I changed the limit of a test plan from 600 to 60 per minute in the table, and within 60 seconds a loop of requests started to receive 429 after the 60th call. I changed it back and the 429s stopped. The headers I added last week show the new limit as well.

Load test of the limiter: the added cache lookup costs nothing measurable, 0.01 ms in the average.

summary: Loader retry canary on one customer's big NDJSON queue finished 41 files, with 3 waiting once and then done, and the state table shows the reasons and the next attempt
body:
The canary of the backoff change ran on the import queue of one customer who uploads large NDJSON files every night. I looked at the result this afternoon after two nights.

The numbers: 41 files, between 300 MB and 3.1 GB, 118 GB in total. 38 of them finished in the first pass. Three went to the waiting state once. Two of those had a chunk upload that failed five times in a row during a short slow period of the object store, and the third had a timeout while the parser was reading a very long line of 14 MB. All three were picked up again at the time stored in `next_attempt_at` and finished on the second pass.

The state table shows what I hoped. Each waiting file has the failure reason, such as 'chunk upload failed: timeout after 30s', and the time of the next attempt, and the console displays both. Sam checked a waiting file in the console during the second night and could tell the customer why it was waiting and when it would continue, without asking me.

Correctness checks: the line counts of the loaded data match the files for all 41, and a comparison of event ids shows no duplicates. The resume offsets worked after the waiting state, and in the second case the file restarted from the committed offset and not from the beginning.

The jitter looks good in the metrics. The retries of the two files with upload failures were spread over 11 seconds and did not start in the same second, and worker slots were free while they waited, as designed.

One thing I found is a wrong message. The long line of 14 MB gave 'timeout' as the reason, but the real cause is a limit of the line reader at 16 MB buffer with a slower path above 8 MB. The timeout was a symptom. This is not harmful but misleading, and I opened a note to give a separate reason 'long line' with the size.

Next steps: fix the reason text, then enable the new backoff for all customers in the next release, one queue group at a time.

summary: Loader retry state table got a reason column with a fixed set of codes, so support can filter waiting files by cause instead of reading free text
body:
Sam had asked how to tell why a large file was waiting, and the free text in the state table was hard to filter. Added a reason_code column with five values: store_timeout, store_throttled, checksum_mismatch, source_gone and unknown. A migration backfilled the 41 rows from the canary by matching on the old message text.

The retry code now sets the code at the point where the failure is classified, so there is no string matching later. The console list shows the code as a small label next to the next attempt time.

One row stayed unknown after the backfill because its message had been truncated. I left it as it was. Next I want a count per reason on the Grafana panel for the loader.

summary: Dual write for search v2 ran in staging for the first time and the two indexes differ in 0.4 percent of documents, mostly from a field that the new analyzer lowercases
body:
Switched on dual write in staging with the target layout flag set, and replayed a day of ingest traffic through it. After the replay I compared document counts and a hash of the stored source per document between the old and the new index.

Counts matched. The hash differed for about 0.4 percent of the documents. I sampled 200 of them and nearly all had a customer_ref field where the new analyzer lowercases the value in the stored source copy. That is a bug in the mapping, since the source should be kept as it came in.

The rest of the differences were documents whose write to the new index failed once and went through on the second attempt. The old index had them earlier by a few hundred milliseconds, which is fine, but my comparison job ran too early and counted them.

Fixed the comparison to wait 30 seconds after the last write. The mapping fix is a small change to the normalizer on the field and needs a reindex of the staging copy. I started that reindex and it will take most of the night.

Tomorrow I will rerun the comparison. If the difference is below 0.01 percent, the next step is dual write on one production task.

summary: Staging comparison of the two search indexes is down to 3 differing documents out of 1.1 million after the normalizer fix and a full reindex
body:
The staging reindex finished overnight, so I reran the comparison with the 30 second wait. Of 1.1 million documents, 3 differ. That is far below the limit I set yesterday.

All three were documents with a customer_ref that contains a trailing space. The old path trimmed it and the new one keeps it. I checked the ingest schema, and it does not say whether the space is allowed. Mara said the trim in the old path was an accident of the old client library, so the new behavior is the right one. I wrote that into the notes for the cutover.

I also looked at the write latency of dual write in staging. The p95 of an index request went from 38 ms to 61 ms, since each document is now written twice. The ingest path does not wait for the second write, so the user facing latency is unchanged. The queue lag stayed flat during the replay.

Open points before production:
- a switch to turn off the second write without a deploy
- a metric for failed second writes
- a decision about what happens when the new index is red

I added the first two today. For the third I proposed that failures of the second write are logged and counted but never block the first. Mara agreed. The production canary on one task is planned for tomorrow.

summary: Postgres slow query log showed the console's customer settings lookup running 900 times a minute, and a 30 second cache in the console API cut that to 30
body:
Looked at the slow query log after a note from Lena that the console felt sluggish on the settings page. The query itself was fast at 3 ms, but the same lookup by customer id ran about 900 times a minute because every widget on the page called it separately.

Added a small in-process cache with a 30 second TTL in the console API, keyed by customer id. Writes to settings clear the entry on the same task. Other tasks may show old settings for up to 30 seconds, which Lena accepted for this page.

After the deploy the lookup count dropped to about 30 per minute and the page load fell from 1.4 to 0.8 seconds in her test. No change was needed in Postgres.

summary: Production canary of search dual write on one task: second writes succeed at 99.97 percent, and the failures are all bulk rejections that clear on the next attempt
body:
Turned on dual write on a single search API task in production with the switch added last night. The goal was to see real traffic against the new layout flag before widening it.

For the first hour I watched three things: the failed second write counter, the queue lag and the index request latency on the new index. Queue lag did not move. The latency of the second write was a little higher than in staging, with p95 at 74 ms.

The second write succeeded for 99.97 percent of documents. The rest, about 1 in 3,000, failed with a bulk rejection error from the new index, which means its write queue was briefly full. Each of these went through on the next attempt a few seconds later. The new index was only given the settings of staging, with a refresh interval of one second. I raised it to 5 seconds, since nothing reads the new index yet, and the rejections fell to almost none in the following hour.

I compared a sample of 5,000 documents between the two indexes by hash, and all matched. I also checked that the extra write did not change CPU on the task in a visible way. It rose from 31 to 34 percent.

Risks I still see are the disk use of the new index, which will be double until the cutover, and the case where the new index goes red. For the second one the failure path only logs and counts, as agreed, and I tested it by closing the index on staging. The task kept serving and the counter rose.

Tomorrow I will keep it on one task through a full day of traffic and then widen it to a third of the tasks if the counters stay quiet.

summary: Rate limit counter keys in Redis were renamed to include the plan version, and a read-both period keeps limits correct while old keys expire
body:
The per key limiter stores its counters in Redis under names like rl:{key}:{window}. With plan limits now in a table, a change of a plan's limit should start a fresh counter, or a customer who was just raised could still be blocked by an old count. So I added the plan version to the key name: rl:v{n}:{key}:{window}.

The change was done in the limiter module in three steps. First, the key builder takes the version from the cached plan row. Second, the limiter reads the new key and, if it does not exist, also the old one, and uses the larger of the two counts. Third, writes go only to the new key.

The read-both step matters because a deploy replaces tasks one by one. For a few minutes some tasks write old keys and some new ones, and without it a customer could get double the quota in that window. The window windows are at most 60 seconds, so the old keys expire by themselves.

Tests covered the plan change case, the deploy overlap case and a missing plan row, where the limiter falls back to the default plan and logs it. I added a test that checks that two different versions never share a counter.

In staging I ran the load script with 200 keys at their limits and changed a plan midway. The counters restarted at the change and no request was wrongly blocked. The key count in Redis rose by about 6,000 during the overlap, which is small.

I deployed it to production in the evening with the read-both on. In an hour the 429 rate was unchanged at 0.7 percent of requests. The read of the old key can be removed in a week once I have checked that no task writes the old names. I put a reminder into the branch notes.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long a rejected batch stays visible to customers: the ingest API keeps the rejection reason for 7 days in Postgres
body:
Sam asked what a customer can see when a whole batch is rejected for a schema error, and for how long. I read the ingest code and the table to be sure.

The rejection is stored in the batch_rejections table with the batch id, the customer, the error code and the first 20 offending events. A cleanup job removes rows after 7 days. The console shows the last 100 rejections per customer and the public API has the same list at the rejections endpoint.

The docs say 14 days, which is wrong. I opened a change to the docs text and told Sam, who will check the wording. Should the time be 14 days, that is a one line change in the cleanup job, but I did not make it.

summary: Ingest batching flush age was made configurable per event type after the low-volume types showed up as high latency in the canary data
body:
Looking at the canary data from last week again, I noticed that p95 write latency was good overall but poor for the low-volume event types, where batches wait for the flush age before they go out. The adaptive flush age is computed per worker, not per type, so a quiet type inherits the age of a busy one.

The change adds a map of event type to maximum flush age in the worker config. If a type is not listed, the adaptive value is used as before. Listed types use the smaller of their value and the adaptive one.

I looked at which types are quiet. Six of the eleven types get fewer than 20 events per second. For those I set 200 ms as a first value. The busy types keep the adaptive logic.

Tests:
- a unit test for the min logic with an unlisted type
- a unit test with a listed type and a high adaptive value
- a test that reloading the config changes the age without dropping buffered events

The last one found a bug. On reload the old buffers were replaced by empty ones, so up to one batch per type could have been lost. I changed the reload to flush before the swap and the test passes.

On staging with the replay of an hour of traffic, the p95 for the quiet types fell from 1.7 seconds to 0.4. The busy types did not change. The average batch size of the quiet types dropped from 42 to 9 events, which means more commits for them, but the commit rate stayed well inside the limit of the queue.

I plan a one task canary tomorrow and will watch the commit rate on the quiet partitions in particular.

summary: Ingest batching canary with per-type flush ages ran a day: quiet types dropped from 1.7 to 0.5 seconds p95, and commit rate rose 12 percent without strain
body:
The per-type flush age went to one production task in the morning and ran through the full day. I checked it at several points, and wrote down the numbers in the evening.

For the six quiet types, the p95 write latency fell from 1.7 seconds on the other tasks to 0.5 seconds on the canary. The busy types were the same on both, at about 1.3 seconds. So the change does what it should and leaves the rest alone.

The cost is more commits. On the canary the commit rate to the queue was 12 percent higher than on a comparable task. The broker's request latency stayed flat, with p99 around 9 ms, so there was no strain. I also looked at CPU on the task, which was 2 points higher.

One thing to check was the stuck partition fix of last week. In the afternoon one partition had a slow commit of about 5 seconds, and the other partitions flushed normally in the meantime. That worked as intended and it was good to see it in production, not only in the test.

I found one oddity. The batch size histogram has a new small peak at one event per batch for a type called session_end. Looking at the data, session_end events come singly with long gaps, so with a short flush age each goes out alone. That is expected, but it means 200 ms is about right and I should not go lower.

Before widening, I want to talk to Tobias about the broker side, since he watches its load. I wrote him a short note with the numbers. If he is fine with it, I will roll it out to a third of the tasks tomorrow and all of them at the end of the week.

Left to do: a Grafana panel for flush age per type, and a line in the runbook for how to change the values.

summary: Redis memory check after dashboard cache compression: the dashboard key group fell from 61 to 34 percent of used memory
body:
The compression went to all tasks about a week ago, so the old uncompressed keys should have mostly expired by now. I measured memory by key group again with the same script as before.

The dashboard cache group is at 34 percent of used memory, down from 61. In absolute terms total used memory fell from 9.8 GB to 6.9 GB. The other groups did not change much. The session store is now the second largest at 22 percent.

The long TTL entries with jitter are still shrinking, since they live up to a day. I expect a bit more to go over the next days, but the big step is done.

One small thing: 0.3 percent of dashboard keys are still uncompressed. They come from a batch job that writes through an old helper. I opened a task to switch it to the shared cache client.

summary: Wrote the remaining-quota header tests for the rate limiter edge case where a key has no plan row, so the header shows the default plan's numbers
body:
A review comment on the header change said the remaining quota is unclear when a key has no plan row. The limiter falls back to the default plan, but the header code read the plan directly and returned nothing in that case.

I moved both onto the same resolved plan object. Now the header and the limit always agree. Added three tests: no plan row, an expired override and a plan change in the middle of a window.

All pass locally. The change is small and is waiting for review by Mara.

summary: Console audit log page was slow to open for accounts with long histories, and a default filter of the last 7 days made it open in under a second
body:
Lena reported that the audit log page takes several seconds to open for the largest account. The index added last week helped the query, but the page still asked for the full count of rows to draw the pager.

I changed the page to open with a 7 day filter and to show only next and previous, without the total. The count query is gone from the default path. A user can still pick a wider range, which runs the count in the background.

On the largest account the page now opens in 0.7 seconds against 4 before. Lena will adjust the pager design on her side.

summary: Search v2 dual write now runs on a third of production tasks, with the new index at 180 GB and failed second writes still below 0.05 percent
body:
After a full day on one task with quiet counters, I widened dual write to a third of the search API tasks this morning. The point was to see whether the new index copes with three times the write rate.

Its size is 180 GB at this point, against 96 GB of the old layout for the same content. That is more than I expected. The reason is that the new layout is built from the monthly pieces and each carries its own overhead, and that segments have not been merged yet. I forced a merge on the oldest pieces and size fell by about 15 percent.

Failed second writes are at 0.04 percent, again bulk rejections that clear on the next attempt. Write latency p95 on the new index is 81 ms.

I also ran a set of 2,000 recorded queries against both indexes and compared the first ten hits. For 96.8 percent of the queries the lists are identical. The differences come from scoring, since the new index has different shard counts and so different term statistics. For a sample of 50 of the differing queries I read the results by hand and found none that was clearly worse.

Things to do:
- check disk headroom on the data nodes, since the double use will last until the cutover
- decide whether to use a search type with global statistics for the comparison
- widen to all tasks if tomorrow is quiet

I asked Tobias about the disk. He says there is room for about three more weeks at this rate, which is enough, but it should be on the plan. I added a line to the cutover notes with that deadline.

The branch notes are updated with the numbers so far.

summary: Loader retry now treats a checksum mismatch as a reason to re-download the part once before giving up, which saved 5 of 6 files that had failed on bad chunks
body:
Looking at the failed files in the state table, six had the reason checksum_mismatch. The loader used to count that as a normal failure and back off, and after the maximum attempts it gave up on the file.

I looked at the logs of the six. Five had a bad part on the first download, and the same part was fine when fetched again by hand. So a mismatch is often a transient fault on the path, not a bad file.

The change: on a mismatch the loader drops the part from its local buffer and fetches only that part again, once, before it counts a failure. If the second fetch fails too, it goes into the normal back off. The attempt counter is not touched by the first re-fetch, but a separate counter in the state row records it, so support can see it.

Tests:
- one mismatch then success
- two mismatches in a row
- a mismatch on the last part of a file

The last test found a bug, where the final part is shorter and the buffer size check was wrong, so the re-fetch asked for too many bytes. Fixed.

I then replayed the six failed files on staging against a copy of the data. Five finished and one failed twice with the same part, which is a real damaged upload. That is the right outcome, and its state row shows the reason and the next attempt.

I will let this go with the next deploy of the loader. A graph of re-fetches per day would be useful, and I put it on the list.

summary: Looked at a cache hit rate dip in the search API overnight and found it came from a customer's bulk export script that used unique query strings
body:
The hit rate of the query cache fell from 52 to 44 percent for about two hours overnight. The key group metrics showed a jump in new keys, all from one customer's API key.

The queries were identical except for a timestamp parameter the script added to each call. So each one missed and wrote a new key. The keys had a 60 second TTL and did no harm to memory.

Nothing to fix on our side. Sam will tell the customer to drop the parameter. I did not change the cache key normalization, since the parameter is a legitimate part of the query for some endpoints.

summary: Search v2 dual write is on all production tasks, and a global statistics comparison shows the score differences between layouts were only a shard-count effect
body:
With another quiet day behind it, dual write went to all search API tasks in the morning. Failed second writes stayed at 0.04 percent and queue lag was flat through the rollout.

The open question from yesterday was whether the differing result lists come from the layout or from something worse. I reran the 2,000 recorded queries against both indexes using the search type that gathers term statistics across all shards before scoring. With that, 99.6 percent of the first-ten lists are identical. The remaining 8 queries differ in ties, where two documents have the same score and the order depends on the internal id.

So the earlier 3.2 percent was a shard-count effect. In normal use the new layout will have a different statistics profile, and the results will move a little for some queries. For the cutover I decided to keep the normal search type, since the global one costs an extra round trip and adds about 15 ms at p50 in staging.

To keep the order of ties stable, I proposed sorting on a secondary key, the event id, in the v2 query builder. I made that change on the branch with a test that checks two documents with the same score come back in the same order on repeated calls.

Disk on the data nodes: the new index is now 205 GB, and the old one 98 GB. After the forced merges it will settle lower. Tobias has the disk alert at 80 percent and we are at 61.

What is left before a cutover plan: a read shadow, where a share of real queries is also sent to the new index and the results are compared in the background, and a rollback path. I wrote a first design of the read shadow with a sample rate of 2 percent and a timeout of 300 ms, so it cannot slow anything down. I will build it tomorrow.

summary: Audit export gained a manifest file with row counts and a checksum per chunk, so compliance reviewers can check that nothing was dropped in a large export
body:
The chunked export works well on memory, but a reviewer asked how they could know that all rows arrived. I added a manifest to the export archive.

The manifest is a JSON file with the export parameters, the time range, the number of chunks and, for each chunk, the first and last row id, the row count and a SHA-256 checksum. The export task writes the entry for a chunk right after the chunk file is complete, and the manifest is closed at the end with a total row count.

The total comes from a separate count query, run inside the same transaction snapshot as the cursor. That is important, because otherwise rows written during the export could make the numbers disagree. I used a repeatable read transaction for the whole export, which the cursor needed anyway.

A small verify command was added to the CLI. It reads the archive, recomputes the checksums and compares the counts. I tried it on an export of 3.1 million rows. The export took 4 minutes and the verify 1.5.

Two edge cases got tests: an empty range, which gives a manifest with zero chunks, and an export that was cancelled, which leaves a manifest marked incomplete.

I wrote a short section for Sam about the manifest for the compliance docs. The next step is a signature on the manifest, which needs a decision about keys, and that I left open.

summary: Postgres minor version upgrade on staging went through cleanly, and the reports query plans are unchanged, so production can follow next week
body:
Tobias applied the latest minor release of Postgres 16 on the staging database this morning, and I did the checks afterwards. This is only a minor update within the same major version.

What I checked:
- the extension versions, which are all unchanged
- the settings in the config, which are identical after the restart
- replication lag to the replica, which was back to under 100 ms within a minute
- the plans of the ten slowest queries from the review of last week

For the plans I used EXPLAIN on each of the ten with the same parameters before and after, and compared the output. Nine are identical. The tenth, the audit log listing, shows the same index but a slightly different row estimate, which has no effect on the cost choice.

I also ran the integration tests of the console API and the ingest API against staging, and all passed. The ingest suite takes about 11 minutes.

The release notes mention a fix for a vacuum problem with some index types, which does not affect us, and a fix in the logical replication code, which we do not use.

A failover test on staging was done by Tobias, and the replica took over in 22 seconds. Applications reconnected without errors after the retry in the client library.

The plan for production is to do the replica first, then fail over, then the old primary, in a quiet hour. Tobias will write the steps into the runbook. We agreed to do it next week and not on a day with a deploy of the search API.

No changes to the code were needed. I added the new version to the notes of the infrastructure repository.

summary: Built the read shadow for search v2: 2 percent of real queries also go to the new index, and the first hours show 98.9 percent identical top ten lists
body:
The read shadow is in the search API behind a flag. For a sampled share of queries, after the answer to the user is sent, the same query is run against the new index with a 300 ms timeout. The two top-ten lists are compared and the result goes to a counter and, for differences, a log line with the query id.

Design points that I kept:
- the shadow call never delays the response, since it starts after the reply is written
- a failed or timed out shadow call counts as its own outcome, not as a difference
- the sample rate is a flag that can change without a deploy
- customer queries are not logged in full, only a hash and the customer id

The sample rate is 2 percent. That comes to about 14 shadow queries per second across the tasks, which the new index handles easily. Its search latency p50 is 21 ms and p99 140 ms.

After four hours with the flag on: 98.9 percent of compared lists are identical, 0.8 percent differ in order only, 0.3 percent differ in membership. The timeouts are 0.1 percent.

I looked at the 0.3 percent. Most are queries with the new parser's handling of quoted phrases mixed with wildcards, where the old path was looser. These are intended changes of v2. A few have a customer-specific field boost that is only set in the old config. I found that two customers have boosts in the old config that were not copied. I added them to the v2 boost file, and the config reload took them without a restart.

The unchanged items are the cutover plan and the rollback path. For the rollback, the simple thing is to keep dual write on for a week after the switch, so that the old index stays current. That costs disk but little else.

Tomorrow I will let the shadow run through a full day and raise the rate to 5 percent if latency stays flat. I also want to group the differing queries by customer to see if one customer stands out.

summary: Dropped an attempt to generate the admin console API client from an OpenAPI file, because the generated types for union fields were too loose to be useful
body:
Lena and I wanted to stop writing the console's API client by hand, so I tried a generator on the OpenAPI file that the Fastify routes already produce. I spent most of the afternoon on it.

The basic calls came out fine. The problem was the fields that can have several shapes, such as the rate limit override, which is either a number or an object with an expiry. The generator turned these into a loose type that allows anything, so the compiler no longer caught the mistakes that the hand-written types do catch.

I tried two ways around it. One was to rewrite the schema with discriminator fields, which would have changed the public API shape and is not something to do for a tool. The other was a post-processing script to patch the types, and that was already 80 lines long and brittle after the first three endpoints.

I decided to stop. The hand-written client is about 600 lines and changes slowly, so the saving would be small. I reverted the branch work and kept one useful piece: a script that checks that the hand-written client covers every route in the OpenAPI file. It found two routes that the client does not call, both internal.

I told Lena and wrote the reason into the notes of the console repository, so that nobody tries it again without a different generator.

summary: Search v2 read shadow at 5 percent for a day: top ten lists match for 99.1 percent of queries, and the differences by customer are spread evenly
body:
I raised the shadow sample rate from 2 to 5 percent in the morning after the first day looked fine, and let it run for most of the day. Then I went through the numbers.

Overall, 99.1 percent of the compared lists are identical, 0.6 percent differ only in order and 0.3 percent in membership. The share of timeouts is 0.1 percent and does not rise at the higher rate. The new index's p99 stays at about 150 ms.

I grouped the differing queries by customer to see if one stands out. No customer has more than 2 percent of its queries differing, and the largest customer is at 0.9. So there is no sign of a problem with one data shape.

I read 40 queries of the membership group by hand. Of those, 28 involve the quoted phrase handling of the new parser, 7 involve a field that the new analyzer splits differently on hyphens, and 5 I could not explain at first. For the five, the cause was documents that arrived in the last seconds before the comparison and were present in one index only. I changed the shadow to skip the comparison when the newest hit is less than 5 seconds old, which removes this noise.

The hyphen case deserves a decision. The new analyzer splits part-number-12 into three tokens, the old one kept it as one. Searching for the whole string works in both, but a search for just number now hits in v2. For logs with hyphenated ids, that could be surprising. I will ask Mara whether to add a keyword subfield for these fields, which keeps the old behaviour at a small cost of index size.

Cutover planning so far:
- keep dual write for a week after the switch
- switch reads by customer, starting with internal and two small ones
- keep the old index until the end of the week

I wrote this into the plan document and asked Tobias for a review of the disk and node numbers.

summary: Redis version upgrade rehearsed on staging: the minor version bump kept all data and the clients reconnected, but the session store showed one failed write during the failover
body:
Tobias and I rehearsed the Redis minor version upgrade on staging today. The setup is a primary with one replica, and the plan is to upgrade the replica, fail over and then upgrade the old primary.

The steps went as planned. The replica was upgraded first and caught up in seconds. The failover took about 9 seconds, and the clients reconnected without a manual action. I watched the search API, the ingest API and the console during the failover.

The search API cache clients logged connection errors for about 10 seconds and then recovered, and cache misses were served from the database. The hit rate returned to its normal level within three minutes. The ingest API's keepalive fix meant its connections came back at once.

The console was the one to look at. Its session store had one failed write during the failover, which showed up as a user being asked to sign in again. In the test it was our own test user. In production with sliding refresh it could affect any user who is active at that moment, but only once, and only if the write lands in the window.

I looked at the code. The session write has no retry when the connection drops. A single retry after a short pause would cover the failover window, and Lena agreed to add it, since the console is her code. It is a plain retry of one call, with a 200 ms pause and a limit of two attempts.

I also checked:
- memory use before and after, which is the same within 1 percent
- the key counts per group, which are unchanged
- the TTLs on a sample of keys, which are preserved
- the rate limiter counters, which kept counting without a reset

The slow log had nothing new. The rate limiter reads continued during the failover with 40 errors in total, and the limiter lets requests pass when it cannot reach Redis, which is the intended behaviour.

The plan is to do production after Lena's change is deployed, and in a quiet hour. Tobias will write the steps into the runbook.

summary: Search v2 read shadow went to 10 percent, and the remaining top ten differences trace to tie-breaking between equal scores, so a stable secondary sort by document id was added
body:
After the 5 percent shadow looked even, the read shadow was raised to 10 percent of real queries this afternoon. Top ten lists matched for 99.2 percent of queries, which is close to the last step.

I pulled 200 of the differing queries and compared them by hand with a small script. In 171 of them the two lists held the same documents, with two or more documents sharing exactly the same score and appearing in a different order. The old layout broke ties by shard order, and the new layout does it by segment order, so neither is wrong.

The other 29 were real differences. Most had a short query with one common term, where the per-field boosts of the new parser weigh the title a bit more than the old query did. That is intended and was in the plan for search v2.

To make results stable for customers, I added a secondary sort by document id in the new query builder. This is applied only when scores are equal, so it does not change relevance. It costs almost nothing, and p95 in the shadow stayed at 112 ms against 118 ms for the old index.

I also checked that the shadow path does not touch the response. The shadow call is fire and forget with a 2 second timeout, and a timeout only increments a counter. The counter stayed at 0.03 percent over the afternoon.

Next step is to rerun the comparison tomorrow with the tie-break in place and count only the true differences. If that number stays under one percent, I will write the cutover plan with Tobias, including how to flip reads per customer. The unresolved item is the 29 queries with boost effects, which I will send to Sam so support knows what to say if a customer notices.

summary: Redis session store write failure during the failover rehearsal came from the client giving up after one attempt, and a single bounded retry on session writes removed it in staging
body:
The rehearsal of the Redis minor version upgrade showed one failed session write during the failover. I looked at the console session code today to see why.

The session store used the client default, which gives up after one attempt when the connection drops. The failover took about 4 seconds, and a login that landed in that window got an error.

I added a retry for session writes only, with two attempts and a 300 ms pause between them. Reads were left alone, because a failed read just asks the user to log in again.

I ran the failover on staging five more times with a script that logged in every 200 ms. There were no failed writes in any of the five runs. One login took 540 ms instead of the usual 40 ms.

The production upgrade is still planned for next week. Tobias wants the window outside the busiest hours, so I will check the traffic graph with him before we pick the time.

summary: Production Postgres minor upgrade went through in the quiet window with 40 seconds of failover, and the reports query plans and the slow query log look the same as before
body:
Tobias and I did the Postgres minor version upgrade on production this afternoon, after the clean staging run of last week. We used the standby first, then failed over.

The steps were: upgrade the standby, wait for replication to catch up, promote it, and upgrade the old primary as the new standby. Writes were refused for about 40 seconds during the switch. The ingest API kept accepting batches into the queue the whole time, so no customer saw errors.

After the switch I compared the plans of the ten heaviest queries from the slow query log, including the reports query. All ten had the same plans as before, and the timings were within 5 percent.

I ran analyze on the larger tables, since the statistics are rebuilt after a restart. Autovacuum was running normally on the events related tables within the hour.

One small thing: the console showed a short burst of connection errors right after the failover, because its pool held dead connections. They cleared within a minute. I added a note to the runbook that the pool in the console API should be recycled after a failover.

Nothing else is open. I will look at the slow query log again tomorrow morning to be sure nothing new shows up.

summary: Rate limits per key got a dry run mode that logs what would be blocked, and a day of staging replay showed 14 keys that would hit their limit under the new plan values
body:
For the rate-limits work I added a dry run mode to the limiter. When it is on, a request over the limit is let through, but a log line and a counter record that it would have been blocked.

The mode is set per plan in the Postgres table of plan limits, so we can test a new value on one plan only. The limiter reads that table with its 60 second cache, so a change takes effect within a minute.

I replayed a day of production request logs against staging with the new plan values in dry run mode. Of 612 active keys, 14 would have been blocked at least once. Nine of them were over by less than 5 percent for a few minutes.

The other five were real heavy users. Two belong to a large customer whose export script sends bursts at the start of every hour. Burst allowance for that plan may need to be larger, so I will talk to the user about it.

I also checked the headers in dry run mode. The remaining quota header still shows the real numbers, and the response has no sign that a limit was passed.

Next I will write the list of the 14 keys with their customers for Sam, so support can warn them before the limits are enforced.

summary: Search v2 read shadow with the stable tie-break shows 99.7 percent matching top ten lists, and the cutover plan was written with a per-customer switch and a fast way back
body:
The comparison reran over the weekend with the secondary sort by document id, and the numbers are in. Of about 410,000 shadowed queries, 99.7 percent had an identical top ten list. The 0.3 percent left are the boost effects we expected.

I split the differing queries by customer. No customer had more than 1.1 percent, and the largest customers were all below 0.5 percent. So there is no sign that one data shape is handled badly by the new analyzer.

With that, I wrote the cutover plan. It is short, and Tobias read it this morning.

The core is a per-customer setting in Postgres, search_backend, with the values old, shadow and new. The search API reads it through the same 30 second cache that the console uses for customer settings. A switch therefore takes effect within a minute and goes back just as fast.

The order of the switch: first our own test account, then three small customers who agreed to it, then the rest in groups of ten. Between groups we wait a day and look at p99, error rate and the support inbox.

Dual write stays on during the whole cutover. That is the main reason the way back is safe: the old index is never behind. It will only be turned off after two weeks without a switch back.

Open points from the review:
- Tobias asked about the disk use while both indexes are written. The new one is 180 GB, the old one 210 GB, and there is room for 40 percent more on the nodes.
- Sam wants a short text for customers about slightly different order of results. I will draft it with her.
- The nightly reindex has to rebuild both indexes during the cutover, which doubles its run time to about 3 hours.

I also added a metric by backend to the search API dashboard, so the latency of old and new can be seen side by side. Tomorrow I will switch the test account and run our own query set through it.

summary: Switched the test account to the new search index and ran the saved query set, with all 480 queries returning and a median latency of 71 ms against 88 ms before
body:
The first real switch of search v2 happened this morning, on our own test account. I set search_backend to new in Postgres and waited for the cache to pick it up.

Then I ran the saved query set of 480 queries that we collected over the last months. It has plain words, phrases, field filters, wildcards and a few bad queries on purpose. All 480 returned, and the 12 bad ones gave the same error messages as before.

Median latency was 71 ms, against 88 ms on the old index for the same set. P99 was 290 ms against 360 ms in the earlier staging replay. The gain comes mostly from the smaller index and fewer shards per query.

Two results looked wrong at first. A phrase query with a hyphen found fewer documents on the new index. The new analyzer splits on hyphens, and the old one kept them in one token, so the phrase needed a different match.

I checked the parser, and the phrase is handled as intended, but the old behavior found exact hyphenated codes more reliably. I decided to add the hyphen case to the query parser: a quoted phrase with a hyphen now also matches the joined token. After this, the count matched the old index again.

I added the case to the query set as a regression test, with the expected counts. The parser tests pass, 212 of 212.

The switch back was tested too. I set the value to old, and after 35 seconds queries went to the old index again. No request failed in between.

Next step is the three small customers. I will send the text to Sam first, since she knows who agreed to it.

summary: Loader retry state table cleanup job now removes finished rows after 30 days, and the table fell from 2.1 million rows to 380,000 in the first run
body:
The loader retry state table has kept every row since the canary started. It grew to 2.1 million rows, and the support filter by reason got slower, so I added a cleanup job.

The job deletes rows in state done after 30 days. Rows that are waiting or failed stay until someone handles them, because support needs them for questions.

It deletes in chunks of 5,000 rows with a short pause, to not hold locks on the table. The first run took 11 minutes and removed 1.7 million rows. Autovacuum followed and the table size on disk went from 1.4 GB to 300 MB after a manual vacuum.

I checked that the support filter by reason now answers in about 40 ms. Before it took 700 ms for the most common code.

The job runs nightly at 03:30 as a scheduled task, and logs the number of deleted rows. I added a counter for this to the Grafana board of the loader.

One open question is whether failed rows should be archived after a longer time. I will ask Sam what she needs for old cases.

summary: Answered Sam on why a large NDJSON file shows waiting in the console: the loader waits for the retry time, and the reason code tells whether it is the customer's source or our side
body:
Sam asked why one customer's large NDJSON file had shown waiting in the console for almost an hour. I looked at the state table.

The file had hit a timeout from the customer's storage server three times. Each wait is longer than the last, and the third was 20 minutes. The reason code was source_timeout, so the cause was on the customer's side.

I told Sam that source_timeout and source_http_5xx mean that the customer's server is the problem, and that our own codes start with internal_. She can filter by these prefixes in the console now.

The file finished at the fifth attempt. I wrote the short explanation into the support docs page so she can reuse it.

summary: Switched three small customers to the new search index and watched a full day, with no errors, p99 lower by about 20 percent, and one question from a customer about result order
body:
Three small customers who had agreed were switched to search v2 this morning, by setting search_backend to new for each of them. Dual write stayed on, so the old index was kept current.

I watched the dashboard by backend during the day. The error rate of the three was 0.00 percent, the same as before. P99 for their queries was 280 ms on average, against 350 ms in the weeks before.

Cache hit rate in Redis for their search keys dropped at first, from 62 to 41 percent, because the cache key includes the backend name and the first queries were all cold. It was back at 60 percent by the afternoon. I did not change the key naming, since the separation is useful when a customer is switched back.

At about 14:00 one of the customers wrote to support. They noticed that two documents with the same score were in a different order than the day before. Sam asked me what to say.

The cause is the tie-break by document id. The old layout ordered ties by shard, which could change when a reindex ran. I wrote this down in plain words and Sam sent it. The customer was fine with it, and said the order is now the same on every repeat of the query, which they liked.

I also looked for slow queries on the new index. The slowest 20 of the day were all wildcard queries with long terms, and all took under 900 ms. The prefix cap of 3 is working as it should.

One point for the next group: the shard sizes on the new index are uneven for one of the three customers, with one shard 3 times larger than the others. This is part of why the plan for a new shard layout by month exists, so I noted it there.

Tomorrow the groups of ten are planned. Before that, I want to read the support inbox once more in the morning, and compare the error counts of both backends.

summary: Audit export manifest check tool now validates a downloaded export against its manifest and reported a clean result on a 4 million row test export
body:
Compliance reviewers can read the manifest, but they had no easy way to check it, so I wrote a small check tool for the audit export.

It reads the manifest file, then each chunk, counts the rows and computes the checksum. It compares both with the manifest and prints one line per chunk.

I ran it on a test export of 4 million rows in 41 chunks. All chunks matched, and the run took 2 minutes 10 seconds on my laptop.

To be sure the tool can fail, I changed one byte in a chunk and removed a row from another. It reported a checksum mismatch for the first and a row count mismatch for the second, with the chunk names.

The tool is a single command in the repository, with a short readme. I will give it to Sam for the compliance docs.

summary: Ingest batching flush age was raised for the largest event type after a canary showed too many small commits, and commit rate fell by 9 percent
body:
The per-type flush ages of the last days worked well for quiet types, but the canary data showed a different problem for the busiest type. Its batches were flushed by age at 0.5 seconds with only about 60 percent of the target size.

This gave many small commits. The commit rate for that type was higher than needed, and the p95 commit time rose a little at peak.

I set the flush age for that type to 0.9 seconds and left the batch size target as it was. On the canary task, batches reached 93 percent of target size on average.

Total commit rate fell by 9 percent over three hours. Latency for that type from the API to the queue rose from 0.6 to 0.95 seconds at p95, which is inside what customers are told in the docs.

I will let the canary run through the evening peak and decide tomorrow whether to roll it to all tasks.

summary: Redis memory growth in the search cache group was traced to long TTLs on rarely repeated queries, and a shorter TTL for those keys cut the group by a third
body:
Memory use in Redis crept up over the last two weeks, and the search cache key group was the biggest part of it, at 38 percent of used memory.

I sampled the keys with a scan and looked at their TTLs and hit counts from the cache metrics. Most keys had a TTL of 6 hours, and about 70 percent of them were read only once.

These were queries with unique strings, such as the bulk export scripts we saw before, and queries with timestamps in the filters. They fill memory and never help.

I changed the TTL rule in the search API. A query that has a time filter with a precise timestamp, or a result set over 500 documents, gets 20 minutes. All others keep 6 hours.

After a day on staging with replayed traffic, the group was a third smaller. The hit rate fell from 61 to 59 percent, which is within the noise.

I will roll it to production tomorrow and watch memory and hit rate for a few days.

summary: Schema registry gained a deprecation flag for fields, with a warning in the console and in the API response, and 6 existing fields were marked as a first test
body:
A request from Sam and from two customers led to this: they wanted to mark a field as deprecated in the schema registry without removing it. I added a deprecated flag with an optional message to the field definition.

The flag is stored in the registry table in Postgres, in a new column with default false. The migration was small and ran in under a second on staging.

The compatibility check treats a deprecation as compatible. Removing a deprecated field is still treated as a breaking change, so the old rule stays in place. I added tests for both cases, and the suite has 148 tests passing.

The registry API now returns the flag and the message in the schema document. The ingest API does not reject events with deprecated fields, but it adds a header, X-Nebula-Deprecated, with the field names when a batch uses any of them.

I limited this header to the first 5 field names, to keep header sizes small. A batch with more shows 5 names and a count.

In the console, the schema page shows a small badge by the field and the message on hover. Lena looked at the layout and asked for a muted color so it does not look like an error. I changed it to grey with a text label.

As a first test I marked 6 fields in our own staging schema. Events using them returned the header, and the console showed the badge. The check for compatible versions still listed no problems.

One thing that I found along the way: the diff view in the console did not show a change in the flag, because it compared only types and names. I fixed this and added the flag to the diff.

What is left is the docs text and a decision about how long a field stays deprecated before removal. I will ask the user whether we want a fixed period.

summary: Switched the first group of ten customers to search v2 with no rise in errors, and one customer with very long queries needed the query length limit raised from 512 to 1024 characters
body:
The first group of ten customers was switched to the new search index at 09:30. I set search_backend to new for all ten and watched the dashboards by backend through the day.

The overall numbers were good. The error rate stayed at 0.01 percent, the same as before. P99 for the group was 310 ms, down from 395 ms last week, and the median was 68 ms.

At 11:40 an alert fired for one customer, with a rise in 400 responses from the search API. The customer sends very long queries, built from lists of ids with OR between them. Some reached 700 characters.

The new parser has a length limit of 512 characters, which the old query path never had. The limit was set while building the parser to guard against abuse, and nobody had checked it against real queries.

I looked at the query logs of all customers for the last month. The longest legitimate query was 940 characters, from this customer. Ninety-nine percent are under 120.

I raised the limit to 1024 characters, and added a clause limit of 64 per query as the better guard. The clause limit protects against costly queries, while the length does not. The parser tests were extended, with 218 of 218 passing.

After the deploy at 13:10 the 400 responses stopped. I told the customer through Sam that it was fixed on our side.

Other things I checked:
- Redis cache hit rate for the group recovered to 58 percent by the afternoon.
- The slowest queries were again long wildcards, none over 1 second.
- Disk use on the nodes with both indexes is at 61 percent.

The support inbox had one more message, about the order of equal scores, which Sam answered with the text from before.

The plan says to wait a day before the next group. Tomorrow I will check the clause limit metric to see if any customer comes near 64. I also want to write the clause limit into the public API docs, since it is now a real limit.

summary: Ingest batching rolled out to all tasks with the longer flush age for the busiest type, and the commit rate dropped 9 percent while latency stayed inside the documented limits
body:
After a full day on the canary, the 0.9 second flush age for the busiest event type looked right, so I rolled the setting to all ingest tasks this afternoon.

The rollout was done in three steps of a third of the tasks each, with 20 minutes between steps. I looked at commit rate, queue lag and the 5xx rate after each step.

The commit rate for that type fell by 9 percent overall, as on the canary. Batches reached on average 91 percent of the target size, up from 60 percent.

Queue lag in Redpanda stayed under 200 ms at the busiest time. The p95 latency from the API to the queue for that type was 0.94 seconds, which is under the 1.5 seconds in our docs.

One thing I watched for was the stuck partition case from last week. Another test with one slow commit showed that only that partition waited, and the others flushed on time.

After the rollout I removed the old fixed flush age from the code path. It had stayed as a fallback, but all event types now have a configured value, and the fallback only hid mistakes. A missing value now fails at start with a clear message.

The config test that checks every event type has a flush age was added to the suite. It found one test type in staging without a value, which I fixed.

The next step is to look at the batch size target itself, since the busiest type now reaches it most of the time. That is a small experiment for another day.

summary: Redis minor version upgrade went through on production in the quiet window with 5 seconds of failover and no failed session writes, thanks to the bounded retry
body:
Tobias and I did the Redis minor version upgrade this evening, in the window we had picked from the traffic graph.

We upgraded the replica, waited for sync, and failed over. The failover took about 5 seconds, a little longer than on staging.

Session writes in the console had no failures. The log showed 3 writes that needed the second attempt, which means the retry from last week did its job. Login latency for those was about 0.5 seconds.

The ingest API and the rate limiter reconnected without help. The limiter failed open for 5 seconds as designed, and the counter of passed unchecked requests shows 1,900 requests, which is normal for this length.

Memory use was unchanged after the upgrade, and the key counts of all groups matched the numbers before. I checked the dashboard cache and the rate limit keys by hand.

One item is left. The old replica is still running, and we will remove it after two days if nothing odd shows up.

summary: Search v2 clause limit metric shows the largest customer queries at 31 clauses, so the limit of 64 stays, and the public API docs now list both query limits
body:
Today I read the clause limit metric that was added with the length change. Over the day, the highest clause count in any query of the switched customers was 31, from the customer with the id lists. The 99th percentile was 4.

The limit of 64 is therefore twice the largest real use, and I left it. It still blocks the machine generated queries with hundreds of clauses that cost a lot on the shards.

I wrote the two limits into the public API docs for search: 1024 characters and 64 clauses per query. The error message for each case is also shown, with the same text the API returns.

Sam read the page and asked for an example of what to do when a list of ids is too long. I added one that splits the list in batches and merges the results on the client.

The second group of ten customers is planned for tomorrow morning. Error rate and latency for the first group were stable all day, with p99 at 305 ms.

I also checked disk use on the nodes. It is at 62 percent with both indexes, so there is room until the old index goes away.

summary: Per-field boosts for the search v2 parser now apply to title and tags, but the score of exact phrase matches dropped, so a phrase clause was added to the generated query
body:
Late session on the boost work in search-v2. The parser turns a user query into a bool query with one match clause per boosted field, and title^3 and tags^2 worked as planned. The problem was that exact phrase matches in the body field ranked below loose matches in tags.

I added a match_phrase clause with a boost of 1.5 for quoted terms. The fixture set of 40 queries now gives the expected top result in 37 cases; before it was 31. The three remaining misses are all queries with a trailing wildcard, which the parser still rewrites in the old way.

I did not touch the reindex mapping. The boosts live in the query, not in the index, so no reindex is needed. Next step is the wildcard case and then a comparison against v1 on real customer queries from the logs.

summary: Wildcard terms in the v2 query parser now become prefix queries with a minimum length of 3, which fixed the last three fixture misses and removed a slow leading-wildcard path
body:
Continued the search-v2 parser work from last night. The three fixture misses were all caused by trailing wildcards being rewritten into a query_string clause that ignored the per-field boosts.

The parser now emits a prefix clause per boosted field. A term shorter than 3 characters before the star is rejected with a 400 and a message that says why. Leading wildcards are refused too, because on the large customers' indexes they took up to 4 seconds in a test.

Changes:
- src/search/parser/wildcard.ts is new, with 14 unit tests.
- src/search/parser/build.ts calls it instead of the old rewrite.
- The error shape follows the one in the API docs for invalid queries.

The fixture set is now 40 of 40. I then ran 500 real queries from last week's search log through both v1 and v2 and compared the top 10 results. 412 were identical in the top 3, 61 differed in order only, and 27 differed in content. I looked at 10 of the 27 by hand. In 8 of them v2 was clearly better because of the title boost; in 2 it was worse, both queries with many short terms.

I wrote the 2 bad cases into a notes file in the branch. A decision on minimum_should_match is needed next. I will ask Lena whether the admin console search box passes raw user text or already splits it, since that changes what the parser sees.

summary: Set minimum_should_match to 75 percent for queries with more than three terms, which fixed both bad many-term cases from the v1 versus v2 comparison
body:
The two worse cases in the comparison were queries with five and seven short terms. With the default of one matching term, v2 returned documents that matched only a common word in a boosted field.

I tried three settings on the 500 logged queries: 50, 75 and 100 percent. At 100 percent too many queries returned nothing; 14 percent of them. At 50 the two bad cases stayed bad. At 75 both were fixed and only 2 percent of queries returned empty, all of which also returned empty in v1.

The rule only applies above three terms. Short queries keep the default. It is a single constant in build.ts with a comment that points to the comparison numbers.

Lena confirmed that the console passes raw text, so the parser keeps handling the splitting. I added 6 tests. Still open: how to treat quoted phrases combined with loose terms, which I will look at after lunch.

summary: Mixed queries with a quoted phrase and loose terms now require the phrase and score the loose terms, matching what the v1 users expected
body:
In v1, a quoted phrase was mandatory and the loose terms only raised the score. The first v2 version treated all of it as one should group, so the phrase could be missing from results.

The parser now puts each quoted phrase into a must clause and the loose terms into the should group with the 75 percent rule from this morning. For a query that has only phrases there is no should group at all.

I added 9 tests for the mixed cases, including two phrases, a phrase with a negated term, and an unbalanced quote. The unbalanced quote is treated as a plain term and the quote character is dropped. All 55 parser tests pass.

Next is a small load test of the new queries against the staging index. I want to see that the extra must clauses do not change latency by much.

summary: Staging load test of the v2 queries showed p95 of 180 ms against 150 ms for v1, with the extra cost coming from the prefix clauses on four fields
body:
I ran the load test against the staging index with a copy of one large customer's data, about 38 million events. The query mix was the 500 logged queries replayed at 40 requests per second for ten minutes.

Results for v1: p50 41 ms, p95 150 ms, p99 310 ms. For v2: p50 47 ms, p95 180 ms, p99 360 ms. The difference is mostly the prefix clauses. When I limited prefix clauses to title and tags only, p95 fell to 160 ms.

I made that the default, since body prefix matches were rarely useful in the comparison. The setting is a list in the parser config, so it can be widened later.

The cache hit rate in Redis was low during the test, because the replay used distinct queries. I did not change anything in the cache. Next is the reindex job, which needs the new analyzer for the tags field.

summary: Added a keyword sub-field with a lowercase normalizer for tags to the index mapping, so the tags boost matches regardless of case, and the reindex dry run passed on staging
body:
Tags were stored as plain keyword fields, so a search for Billing did not match the tag billing. The fix is a normalizer on the field, which needs a new mapping and therefore a reindex.

I changed the mapping template in the reindex job and added the sub-field tags.norm. The parser now boosts tags.norm instead of tags. The old field stays for exact filters in the console.

I ran the reindex on the staging copy. It took 52 minutes for 38 million events with 4 workers, similar to the old mapping. A check script compared document counts per day and found no differences.

Before production, the template change needs to be reviewed by Mara, since she wrote the alias swap at the end of the job. I opened the review and noted the staging numbers in it.

summary: Mara reviewed the mapping change for tags and asked for the alias swap to check the document count before switching, which is now in the reindex job
body:
Mara's review found one real issue. The alias swap at the end of the reindex job switched to the new index even if the count was much lower than the old one, for example after a worker crash.

I added a check: the swap only happens if the new index has at least 99.5 percent of the documents of the old one, and otherwise the job exits with an error and pages nobody, but writes a line to the job log and a metric. Mara asked for the metric so that Grafana can show it.

I added the metric reindex_count_ratio and a panel on the existing search dashboard. A test with a mocked client covers three cases: 100 percent, 99.6 percent and 90 percent.

The review is approved. The production reindex will run in the nightly slot tonight.

summary: The first nightly reindex with the new tags mapping finished in 2 hours 10 minutes and the swap worked, but one customer index had 0.3 percent more documents than expected
body:
I checked the job log in the morning. The reindex ran for all 40 customer indexes and the alias swap went through for all of them. Total time was 2 hours 10 minutes, about 15 minutes longer than the last run with the old mapping.

The new count ratio metric showed 1.000 for 39 indexes. One index, from a mid-sized customer, showed 1.003. That means the new index had 0.3 percent more documents than the old one, which should not happen in a reindex.

I looked into it. The old index was reindexed from Postgres events by the job while ingest continued, so events that arrived after the old index was last updated but before the reindex read them show up as extra. The old index is refreshed by a lagging indexer. The lag for this customer was about 6 minutes at the time because of a burst.

So the difference is expected and not data duplication. To be sure, I ran a query for duplicate event ids in the new index and found none. I also checked three random documents against Postgres.

The check in the swap uses a lower bound only, so a ratio above 1 is fine. I left it as it is and added a sentence to the job's README about this case.

Then I switched the search API to the new field names in the parser, behind the flag search_v2_tags, and turned it on for our internal account. The results for our own test queries looked right.

Next is a gradual rollout to customers. I asked Sam to tell the support channel that the ranking of search results will change a little and to collect reports.

summary: Rolled the search_v2_tags flag out to five small customers and saw no change in error rate or latency in Grafana over a few hours
body:
Turned the flag on for five small customers chosen with Sam, ones who use search often but have small indexes. The error rate of the search API stayed at 0.1 percent, and p95 stayed within 10 ms of the normal value.

One customer wrote to support asking why a search for an old project tag now shows it first. That is the intended boost on tags, and Sam answered with a short explanation.

I did not roll out further today. The plan is to add 10 more customers tomorrow and the large ones at the end of the week, after one more check of the cache keys: the Redis cache key for search results does not contain the parser version, so after a flag change a customer can see cached v1 results for up to the TTL of 10 minutes.

I wrote this down as a task. The fix is to add the flag state to the key.

summary: Added the parser version to the Redis cache key of search results and checked key naming across the search API so old and new results never mix
body:
The cache key for search results was search:{customer}:{hash of query}. When the flag changes, results from the other parser version can be served from cache until the TTL ends. It is harmless for the five customers, but it would be confusing during the wider rollout.

The new key is search:v{parser}:{customer}:{hash}. The parser version comes from the same place as the flag decision, so there is one source of truth. Old keys are not deleted; they expire with their 10 minute TTL.

While I was there I listed all key patterns in the search API:
- search:* for results
- suggest:* for the query suggestions, TTL 1 hour
- facets:* for the facet counts, TTL 5 minutes

The suggestions and facets do not depend on the parser, so I left them alone. The key naming is not consistent, since the rate limiter uses rl: and the console sessions use sess:, but they are separate concerns and I did not rename anything.

I wrote a test that calls the search API twice with the flag changed in between and checks that the second response is not the cached one. I also ran the full suite, which passed.

In production I watched the keyspace size for an hour after the deploy. It grew by about 2 percent, as expected, and then went back as the old keys expired.

After that I turned the flag on for 10 more customers. No errors. Tomorrow the larger customers get it, one at a time, and I will start with the one that has the biggest index because it is the best test for latency.

summary: Turned search v2 on for the largest customer and p95 went from 420 ms to 460 ms, which is acceptable, but a cold cache after the flag change caused a short spike
body:
The largest customer has an index of about 900 million events, so I expected the latency to be the hardest test. I turned the flag on at 08:00 while traffic was still low.

For the first ten minutes the p95 was 1.1 seconds, because the new cache keys were empty and the search API had to ask OpenSearch for everything. After that it settled. Over the first two hours, p95 was 460 ms against 420 ms the day before, and p99 was 900 ms against 840 ms.

The cause of the spike is the cache key change from yesterday. I should have warmed the cache before the flag change. For the next large customers I will use a small script that replays their top 200 queries from the log right after the flag is on.

I wrote that script. It reads the search log of the last day, takes the most frequent queries per customer, and sends them through the API with a low rate of 5 requests per second. It took about 40 seconds for 200 queries.

The error rate stayed at 0.1 percent. There was one 400 error from a query that begins with a star, which the new parser rejects on purpose. The customer's integration sends such queries from a saved search. I told Sam so that support can contact them.

The saved search could be handled by the parser by dropping the leading star silently, but I decided against that. The 400 has a clear message, and silent changes of meaning are worse.

Then I checked the memory use of the OpenSearch data nodes: no change. The heap stayed at 62 percent.

I also looked at the suggestion endpoint, which still uses the v1 code. It is not in scope for this branch. I opened a note for later.

Tomorrow the next three large customers get the flag, with the warm script. After that, only the last five remain, and then I can remove the flag.

summary: Ran the warm-up script before turning on search v2 for three more large customers, and no latency spike appeared this time
body:
With the script from yesterday the rollout was calm. For each customer I ran the warm-up, waited for it to finish, and then turned the flag on.

The three customers have indexes of 120, 200 and 350 million events. The p95 before the flag was 210, 260 and 330 ms. After it was 225, 270 and 355 ms. There was no spike in the first minutes.

One of the customers has a lot of queries with quoted phrases, and the new must clause made some of them return fewer results than before. I looked at three of those queries. In all three, v1 had returned documents without the full phrase, so the new behavior is the correct one. I told Sam in case the customer asks.

The remaining customers are five of the largest ones. I will do them on the next working session. I also noted that the flag code can be removed after one week without incident.

No other changes today. Cleaned up the warm-up script's output and added it to the scripts folder with a short usage note.

summary: Investigated why Redis memory grew by 18 percent in a week and found the facets cache keys had no TTL set on one code path, fixed and verified after a day of expiry
body:
While checking the keyspace after the parser change I saw that Redis used 18 percent more memory than a week ago. The new cache key explained about 2 percent. The rest needed a closer look.

I sampled keys with SCAN and the TYPE and TTL commands, 20,000 keys at a time. Most keys of the pattern facets:* had a TTL of -1, which means no expiry. The facets code has two paths: the normal one uses SET with EX, and the path for a facet with a date range used SET and then EXPIRE in a second call. When the second call failed, for example on a connection reset, the key stayed forever. More likely, a refactor three weeks ago had dropped the EXPIRE on the date range path completely. The git log showed that this was the case.

I fixed the path to use SET with EX in one call, which also removes the gap between the two commands. I added a test that checks the TTL of the key after a date range facet.

Then I needed to clean up the keys without a TTL. I wrote a small script that scans for facets:* keys with TTL -1 and sets a TTL of 5 minutes on them. I ran it first in dry run mode and it counted 1.9 million keys. Then I ran it for real at a limited rate of 2,000 keys per second, so it did not load Redis.

The memory graph went down over the next hour. Used memory fell from 6.1 GB to 5.2 GB, which is below the level of a week ago.

To avoid the problem coming back I added an alert on the share of sampled keys without TTL. A job samples 1,000 keys each hour and exports the metric key_no_ttl_ratio. The alert fires above 5 percent for 3 hours. Some key patterns are meant to have no TTL, such as the sessions in some modes, so the sampler skips sess: and rl:.

Tobias looked at the alert rule in the alert repository and approved it. It is in the code-based rules, so it deploys with the next run of the pipeline.

I checked the hit rate for facets: it rose from 61 to 64 percent, because the date range facets are now cached for a fixed time and not stuck. Not a big change, but in the right direction.

Tomorrow I come back to the last five large customers for search v2.

summary: Search v2 is on for all customers; the last five large ones went through without a problem, and the plan is to remove the flag code after a week
body:
Finished the rollout of search v2 today. I did the five largest customers one after the other, with the warm-up script before each and a pause of 20 minutes between them to watch the graphs.

Numbers for the five, p95 before and after the flag: 380 to 400, 450 to 470, 520 to 560, 610 to 640 and 700 to 760 ms. The increase is in the range of 5 to 8 percent, which matches the tests on staging. The error rate stayed at 0.1 percent for all of them.

One issue came up with the fourth customer. Their API client sends the query in a field called q and a second field called filter with a Lucene style string. The parser handled the filter correctly, but the combination of q with a quoted phrase and a filter on a keyword field produced a 500, not a result. The logs showed a TypeError in build.ts because the filter was an empty string and the code called .trim() on undefined when the field was missing in one branch.

I fixed it by normalizing both fields at the start of the function and added a test for an empty filter, a missing filter and a filter with only spaces. Deployed the fix within 20 minutes. During that time there were 63 failed requests for that customer, all with the same stack trace. I wrote to Sam so that she could inform the customer if they asked.

After the fix I replayed the 63 failed requests from the log against the API and all of them returned 200.

Then I looked at the whole v2 rollout once more. Flag on for all 40 customers. The search dashboard shows p95 over all customers at 240 ms against 225 ms before the rollout. The Redis hit rate for search results is 38 percent, a little lower than the 41 percent before, since the cache keys changed and the warm-up only covers the top 200 queries.

The plan from here:
- keep the flag for one week in case a customer needs a rollback
- then remove the flag and the v1 parser code
- update the API docs with the notes about wildcards and the minimum length
