I started on the docs part and wrote the section about wildcards with three examples, which Sam will review for language. The text says that leading wildcards are rejected and prefix terms need at least 3 characters.

One more thing I noticed: the suggestion endpoint still uses the v1 code. I added it to the list of work after the flag removal.

summary: Sam reviewed the wildcard docs for search v2 and asked for an error response example, which I added together with a table of the new query syntax
body:
Sam's review of the docs section was useful. Her main point was that a developer who gets a 400 for a short prefix wants to see the exact response, not only a sentence about it.

I added an example with the request, the status and the JSON body of the error, using the same shape as the other invalid query errors. I also changed the sentence about the minimum length so that it names the number 3 in the first line.

Then I wrote a table of the query syntax in v2:
- plain terms: matched in all boosted fields
- quoted phrase: required
- minus before a term: excluded
- trailing star: prefix, at least 3 characters
- field:value: exact match on keyword fields

Sam also pointed out that the old docs said that a leading star works. I checked and removed that line, and added a note to the changelog page that this changed with v2.

The docs build passed, including the link checker. I published the preview and sent the link to Sam for a last look. After that I will merge the docs change together with the flag removal next week.

The examples in the docs are tested against staging by a small script. All 12 returned the documented result.

summary: Looked at the slowest Postgres queries of the week and found that the audit log listing in the console does a sequential scan on 22 million rows
body:
Weekly look at pg_stat_statements. The top entry by total time was the audit log listing of the admin console, with a mean of 1.4 seconds per call, called about 900 times a day.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on audit_log with 22 million rows. The query filters by customer_id and orders by created_at descending with a limit of 50. There was an index on customer_id alone, but the planner preferred the scan because many customers have a lot of rows and the sort was expensive.

A composite index on (customer_id, created_at desc) fixes the plan. I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on staging first. It took 4 minutes and used 600 MB. The query then ran in 3 ms.

For production I will create it in the quiet time at night. The old single column index becomes redundant, but I will drop it only after a week to be sure no other query needs it.

I also noted that the audit export branch will read this table in bulk, so the new index helps there too, but I need to check that the export does not use the same ordering.

summary: Created the composite audit log index in production, listing time fell from 1.4 s to 4 ms, and wrote down the rollout checks for the flag removal of search v2
body:
The index was built at 02:30 by a scheduled command I started yesterday evening. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY took 6 minutes in production and used 640 MB. I checked pg_stat_progress_create_index during the run and there were no lock waits.

In the morning the audit listing showed a mean of 4 ms in pg_stat_statements after the reset. The console page for the audit log now opens at once, where before it needed more than a second for customers with a long history. Lena noticed it before I told her and asked what had changed.

The table size on disk grew by 640 MB and the autovacuum did its normal work. I looked at the dead tuples and bloat of the table afterward and found nothing unusual.

Then I moved on to the flag removal of search v2. The flag has now been on for all customers for a few days. I wrote a checklist for the removal so it does not depend on my memory:
- check the error rate of the search API for the last 7 days, expected 0.1 percent
- check support tickets that mention search results
- delete the flag from the config and the code
- delete the v1 parser and its tests
- delete the old cache key pattern from the notes
- publish the docs change

I looked at the first two points now. The error rate over seven days was between 0.09 and 0.12 percent, with no increase after the rollout. Support had two tickets about search ranking and none about missing results. Both were explained by the title boost, and one customer asked whether the boost can be changed per customer. That is a feature request, and I put it on the list for later, but not for this branch.

I started on the code removal in the branch. The v1 parser is about 400 lines, and 11 tests only use it. I deleted them and the flag checks. The code now has one path, which is easier to read.

As I removed the flag I noticed that the warm-up script refers to the flag in a comment, so I updated it too.

I did not merge yet. The PR is open and waits for Mara's review, and the deploy will be tomorrow morning when traffic is low.

summary: Merged and deployed the removal of the v1 search parser; the first hours show the same latency and error rate, and the old cache keys are gone from Redis
body:
Mara approved the PR with one comment about a leftover config key, which I removed. The deploy ran at 06:30 in the quiet time.

After the deploy I watched four things for several hours: error rate, p95 latency, cache hit rate and the memory of Redis. Error rate stayed at 0.1 percent. P95 over all customers was 238 ms. The hit rate for search results was 39 percent.

The old key pattern search:{customer}:{hash} was not used anymore after the flag was on for everybody, so those keys had already expired. I verified it with a SCAN for the pattern and the result was empty. So there was nothing to clean up in Redis.

The docs change was published afterwards, with the wildcard section, the syntax table and the changelog note. Sam checked the page and found a typo, which I fixed in a small follow-up.

Then I started to look at the suggestion endpoint, the last part that uses v1 logic. It uses a prefix query on the title field with a size of 10. The change to the v2 mapping is small: it can use the tags.norm field too. I wrote a prototype and compared the output with the current one on 200 logged prefixes. 170 were the same, and in 30 the new one added tags as suggestions. I do not know yet if the customers want tags in the suggestions, so I will ask Lena what the console does with them.

The console shows the suggestions in a dropdown with no label for the type, so tags mixed with titles could confuse users. I think the answer is a separate section in the dropdown, but this is a design question for Lena. I wrote the question in our channel with a screenshot of the proposed output.

This finishes the main work on search v2. What remains:
- the suggestions, depending on the answer of Lena
- a per-customer boost setting, as a possible feature
- one more look at the reindex time, which grew by 15 minutes

I closed the branch tasks for the parser, the mapping and the rollout.

summary: Lena answered that the console dropdown can show sections, so suggestions get a type field in the response and tags are shown under their own label
body:
Lena replied that the dropdown component already supports grouped options, because the saved searches use it. She needs a type field per suggestion, with the values title and tag.

I changed the suggestion endpoint to return objects with text and type, and kept the old plain list under a query parameter, compat=1, for API customers who use the endpoint directly. The docs for the endpoint now mention both shapes.

Tests: 8 new ones for the two shapes and the mixed result. All pass. Lena will take the new response in the console next week.

summary: Reindex time grew from 1h55 to 2h10 after the tags mapping, and profiling showed the new normalizer is not the cause but the bulk size of 500 documents is too small
body:
I looked at why the nightly reindex got slower. A first guess was the lowercase normalizer on tags.norm. I tested that on staging by indexing 5 million documents with and without the sub-field. The difference was 3 percent, which does not explain 15 minutes out of 115.

Then I looked at the bulk size. The job sends bulk requests of 500 documents. The OpenSearch node stats showed many small bulk requests and the bulk queue was rarely full, so the nodes were waiting for the job, not the other way round. The CPU on the job's workers was at 70 percent, mostly for JSON serialization.

I tried bulk sizes of 1,000, 2,000 and 5,000 on the staging index with 38 million documents and 4 workers:
- 500: 52 minutes
- 1,000: 45 minutes
- 2,000: 41 minutes
- 5,000: 43 minutes, with two rejected bulks at the end

So 2,000 is the best value. At 5,000 the nodes started to reject requests with 429, which the job retries with backoff, so it is slower and riskier.

I set the bulk size to 2,000 in the job config and added a limit of the payload size of 10 MB, since some customers have very large events and 2,000 of them could exceed the HTTP limit of the cluster. The job flushes when either limit is reached.

I also looked at the number of workers. With 6 workers on staging the time was 38 minutes but the search latency during the run rose by 20 percent, which I do not want during the early morning traffic of some European customers. I left it at 4.

The next nightly run will show the real effect in production. I expect about 1h45. I noted in the job README the numbers of the test, so that the next person knows why 2,000 and 4 workers.

Tomorrow I check the result and then close the reindex topic.

summary: The nightly reindex now takes 1h42 with the larger bulk size, and the count ratio stayed at 1.000 for all indexes
body:
I checked the job log. The run took 1 hour 42 minutes, 28 minutes less than before the change and 13 less than the time before the tags mapping. No bulk was rejected, and the retry counter of the job was 0.

The count ratio metric was 1.000 for all 40 indexes this time, since there was no burst of ingest lag. The search latency in the time of the run stayed normal, p95 within 5 ms of the usual.

The OpenSearch heap on the data nodes peaked at 68 percent during the run, against 66 before, which is fine.

I closed the topic. I wrote the numbers in the job README and removed the staging indexes of the tests to free the disk, about 120 GB.

summary: Dropped the old single column index on audit_log customer_id after a week without any use, freeing 480 MB
body:
The check of pg_stat_user_indexes showed idx_scan for the old index had stayed at the same value for the whole week, so no query used it. The composite index covers every query on that column.

I dropped it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the quiet time. It finished at once, and the table size fell by 480 MB. No query got slower, which I checked in pg_stat_statements an hour later.

The audit export branch will need the table too, but it reads by customer and time, which the composite index serves.

summary: Tried to speed up the admin console login by caching the user lookup in Redis, measured a gain of only 12 ms, and abandoned the change
body:
Lena said the login of the admin console feels slow, so I measured it. The login request took about 190 ms in total. A trace showed 45 ms for the password hash check, 60 ms for two Postgres queries (user and account settings) and the rest in session creation and network.

My idea was to cache the user and settings lookup in Redis for 60 seconds. I built a prototype with a key pattern user:{id} and tested it on staging with 1,000 logins. The median went from 190 to 178 ms, a gain of 12 ms. The hit rate was low in any case, because most users log in once or twice per day, so a 60 second TTL rarely helps. A longer TTL would risk stale permissions after a change of the role, which I do not want for an admin tool.

Then I looked at what makes up the 60 ms of Postgres time. The two queries ran one after another. I merged them into a single query with a join, which brought it down to 25 ms and needs no cache at all. The total median after that was 155 ms.

So the Redis change is dropped. I deleted the branch of the prototype, but kept the numbers in a note in the repo's docs folder in case somebody has the same idea again.

The join change has a test that checks that a user without account settings still gets the default settings, since that case uses a left join and returned null in the first version of my query. I found it by a test with a new user and fixed it by coalescing the settings with the defaults in code.

I also looked at the password hash. 45 ms is by design, the cost factor is chosen on purpose and I did not touch it.

Lena tried the staging console and said the login felt faster, though 35 ms is hardly something a person sees. The slow feeling may come from the first page after login, which loads the dashboard list. I will look at that separately, since it is a frontend and API question and I should talk with Lena about what it fetches.

The change with the join is merged and deployed in the afternoon. No errors in the logs.

summary: The first page after the console login makes seven API calls in sequence; Lena will batch them, and I added one endpoint that returns the dashboard list with the settings
body:
Lena and I looked at the network panel of the console after login. Seven API calls ran one after the other: user, account, settings, dashboard list, alert list, saved searches and a usage summary. Together they took 1.1 seconds, which is where the slow feeling comes from.

Three of them can be answered by one call, so I added GET /console/bootstrap on the API side. It returns the user, the account, the settings and the dashboard list in a single response, using two Postgres queries run in parallel. The median on staging was 70 ms.

Lena will change the console to call this endpoint first and to load alerts, saved searches and the usage summary in parallel afterwards. She expects the first page to be ready in about 400 ms.

I wrote tests for the endpoint, including a user without dashboards. The docs for the internal API got a short entry. Review is with Mara.

summary: Console login now needs three API calls instead of seven after Lena switched the first page to the new dashboard-list endpoint, cutting first paint by about 400 ms
body:
Lena merged her change this afternoon so the first page after login uses the dashboard list endpoint I added earlier. I measured it on staging with the browser network panel. Before, the seven calls ran in sequence and took about 900 ms in total. Now there are three calls, two of them in parallel, and the total is about 500 ms.

The remaining sequential call is the session check, which has to come first. I looked at whether the settings call can be folded into it, but the response would carry data that most pages do not need, so I left it alone.

One small issue: the new endpoint returned the dashboards without their sort order, so the console showed them in creation order. I fixed the query to order by the position column and added a test with three dashboards in shuffled positions.

Next step is to watch the p95 of the endpoint in Grafana for a day. It joins settings and dashboards in Postgres, and I want to be sure it does not turn slow for customers with many dashboards.

summary: Wrote a plan for the audit export for compliance: NDJSON files per customer and day, signed manifest, and a cursor on the audit log so large exports can resume
body:
Spent the session on the design for the audit export, because two customers asked for a regular export of their audit log for their own compliance reviews. Nothing is built yet, this is the plan.

The export writes one NDJSON file per customer and per day into an S3 bucket owned by us, with a manifest file that lists each file, its row count and a SHA-256 checksum. The manifest is signed with a key kept in Secrets Manager, so the customer can check that nothing was changed afterwards.

The audit_log table has 22 million rows, so the export must not scan it with offsets. I will page with a cursor on (created_at, id), which the composite index from last week already supports. I checked with EXPLAIN that a page of 5000 rows by that cursor is an index range scan and takes a few milliseconds.

Open questions I wrote down:
- Whether the customer can pull the files by a presigned URL or whether we push to their bucket. Pull is simpler, push is what one customer asked for.
- How long we keep the exported files. I suggest 30 days.
- Whether the export includes entries written by our own staff in support sessions. I will ask Sam.

I created the branch audit-export and committed the plan as a markdown file in docs/. Tomorrow I will start with the cursor reader and a test with a million generated rows.

summary: Sam answered that staff support actions must be in the audit export, marked with an actor type, so the export schema gets an actor_type field
body:
Asked Sam about support actions in the export. Sam checked with two customers and the answer is yes: they want to see every change, including the ones our staff made while helping them. They also want to tell them apart from their own users.

So the export schema gets an actor_type field with the values user, api_key and staff. The audit_log table has no such column, but the actor id has a prefix, so the export can derive it. I looked at the data: all 22 million rows have a known prefix, except about 3000 old rows from the first import of the admin console. Those get actor_type user.

I updated the plan file in the branch with the field list and the rule for the old rows. Sam will write the customer-facing description of the fields for the docs once the schema is fixed.

summary: Built the cursor reader for the audit export; a test with one million generated rows exports in 41 seconds with flat memory use
body:
Started the implementation in the audit-export branch. The first piece is the cursor reader, which takes a customer id and a day range and yields pages of rows ordered by (created_at, id).

The reader is in TypeScript next to the other jobs. It keeps the last created_at and id of each page and uses a row comparison in the where clause, so Postgres can use the composite index. I first wrote it with a plain created_at > $1 and saw that rows with the same timestamp were skipped. The test caught it, because the generated data has many rows in the same millisecond. The row comparison fixed that.

The test loads one million rows for one customer into a local Postgres and exports them. Result:
- 41 seconds in total with a page size of 5000.
- Memory stays at about 90 MB, because pages are written to the output stream and dropped.
- The row count matches and no id appears twice.

I also tried a page size of 20000. It was only 4 seconds faster, and the memory went up to 210 MB, so I kept 5000.

The writer for NDJSON and the manifest is not done. Tomorrow I will build the file splitting per day and the checksum. I also have to decide what happens when the job dies in the middle of a day: the plan is to restart that day's file from the start, which is simple and safe.

summary: Audit export now writes per-day NDJSON files with checksums and a signed manifest, and a killed job restarts the day cleanly without duplicate rows
body:
Continued in the audit-export branch with the writer and the manifest.

The writer opens one file per customer and day, in a temp path, and streams the pages into it through a gzip stream. When the day is done it computes the SHA-256, uploads the file to the bucket under customer/day/ and records the file in the manifest. The temp file is deleted after the upload.

The manifest is a JSON file with the list of files, row counts, checksums and the actor_type rules version. It is signed with an HMAC using a key from Secrets Manager. I used HMAC because the customers verify with a script we give them, and a shared key is enough for the first version. A public key signature may come later if a customer asks.

The restart case:
- The job writes a state row in Postgres for each day with the status started or done.
- On restart, every day that is not done is exported again from the beginning, and the file in S3 is overwritten.
- The manifest is written last, only when all days are done.

I tested it by killing the process in the middle of the third day of a five day export. The second run exported the days 3 to 5 again, and the manifest listed five files with the right counts. I compared the files to a run without a kill and they were byte for byte the same after gunzip.

One thing I found: gzip output is not deterministic when the mtime header is set, so the checksums of two runs differed. I set the mtime to zero in the gzip options.

Left for tomorrow: a CLI to start an export, and the schedule. I also want a limit on how many exports run at the same time, because a large customer export will hit the database.

summary: Added a concurrency limit of two audit exports at a time and a read replica option, after a test export raised Postgres CPU to 60 percent on staging
body:
Ran an export of a large generated customer on staging to see what it does to the database. Postgres CPU went from 15 to 60 percent for the 3 minutes it ran, and the console listing of the audit log became slower while it ran. That is too much for a job that will be scheduled for many customers.

Two changes in the audit-export branch:
- A limit of two exports at the same time, enforced by a Postgres advisory lock with a slot number. A third job waits and tries again after 30 seconds.
- A config value for the database URL of the export, so it can point to a read replica. On staging I pointed it to the replica and the CPU of the primary stayed under 20 percent.

The replica lag was 0.2 seconds during the run, which does not matter for a day-old export. I do not export the current day anyway, only completed days.

I asked Tobias in chat whether production has a replica with room for this. He said there is one, used by the reports, and it has enough CPU in the night. So the schedule will be at night, with the replica.

Tomorrow: the CLI and the schedule.

summary: Added the export CLI and a nightly schedule for the audit export, with a per-customer setting in the console database that turns it on
body:
The CLI is done: it takes a customer id, a from day and a to day, and starts the export. It prints the manifest location at the end. For the nightly run there is a small scheduler entry that exports the previous day for every customer that has the setting audit_export_enabled.

The setting is a new column in the customer settings table, default false. The migration is small and I ran it on staging. Nothing uses the column except the export, so there is no risk for the other code.

I wrote tests for the scheduler:
- A customer without the setting is skipped.
- A customer with a failed day is retried the next night, together with the new day.
- A day without any audit rows still produces an empty file, so the customer can see the day was checked.

The empty file question took some time. I first skipped empty days, but then the manifest has holes and a customer cannot tell a hole from a failure. I decided on the empty file with a row count of zero.

The next step is a review by Mara. I opened the pull request and asked her to look at the advisory lock part in particular. After that I will switch it on for the first customer who asked.

summary: Mara reviewed the audit export and found that the advisory lock was never released when a job threw, which would have blocked slots until the connection closed
body:
Mara reviewed the pull request this morning and found a real bug. When an export threw an error between taking the advisory lock and the finally block, my code released the lock on a different pooled connection. Advisory locks belong to the session, so the lock stayed on the first connection and the slot was blocked until that connection was recycled.

I reproduced it with a test that throws in the third page. After two such failures both slots were taken and the next export waited forever.

The fix: the export now takes one dedicated connection from the pool for the whole job and takes and releases the lock on it. The connection is returned to the pool only after the unlock. Mara also suggested a lock timeout so a stuck job cannot hold a slot for hours, so I added a maximum of 3 hours, after which the job is stopped.

Other comments from her:
- Rename the state table column from ok to status, which I did.
- Log the customer id in each log line of the job, also done.

I pushed the changes and she approved. I will merge tomorrow after one more run on staging with the failing test case.

summary: Merged the audit export and switched it on for the first customer; the first nightly run is planned for tonight and the checks are written down
body:
After one more run on staging with injected failures, I merged the audit-export branch and deployed it. All migrations were already applied, so the deploy was only the new job and the scheduler entry.

I switched the setting on for the customer who asked first. This is a mid-size customer with about 1.2 million audit rows in total, so the first run should be quick. Because the schedule exports only the previous day, I also started a manual export of the last 90 days for them with the CLI. It finished in 2 minutes 20 seconds, with 90 files and a manifest. I downloaded them and checked three things:
- The sum of the row counts in the manifest equals a count query on the replica for the same range.
- The checksum of two random files matched.
- The verify script Sam is writing for the docs accepted the manifest signature.

Checks for tonight, so the next session knows what to look at:
- The scheduler started the job after midnight UTC.
- The Postgres CPU on the replica stayed below 40 percent.
- A file for yesterday exists and the manifest was updated.

I also noticed that the manifest is rewritten for every night, so it grows. At 365 files it is still small, so I left it as it is. If a customer keeps it for years, we may need one manifest per month.

summary: The first nightly audit export ran in the right window, produced yesterday's file and kept replica CPU at 25 percent
body:
Looked at the result of the first scheduled export of last night. The job started a few minutes after midnight UTC, took 14 seconds and wrote the file for the previous day plus the updated manifest.

The numbers: 3800 rows in the day file, replica CPU peaked at 25 percent, and no entry in the error log. The manifest has 91 files now, matching the 90 days of the manual run plus the new one.

Sam's verify script accepted the new manifest too. I told Sam the format is stable now, so the docs page can be finished. Next I will enable the setting for the second customer, who has about ten times as much audit data.

summary: Enabled the audit export for the second, larger customer; the 90 day backfill took 19 minutes and the nightly run needed no change
body:
The second customer has about 14 million audit rows, so I wanted to watch this one closely. I switched the setting on and started the backfill of 90 days by the CLI, running on the replica in the evening.

Results of the backfill:
- 19 minutes in total for 90 days, about 4.1 million rows.
- Replica CPU between 35 and 50 percent during the run, replica lag below 1 second.
- Peak memory of the job was 110 MB.
- The files are between 2 and 9 MB each after compression.

The row count check against the replica matched in total and for each day. The console listing on the primary was not affected, I measured it during the run and it stayed at 4 ms for the first page.

One small finding: the CLI printed the progress for each page, which made the output very long. I changed it to print once per finished day. I also added the elapsed time per day, which will help if a customer later reports a slow export.

Tomorrow I will write a Grafana panel for the export duration and the number of failed days, and an alert for a day that failed twice in a row. After that the audit-export topic is done, apart from the docs from Sam.

summary: Added export metrics, a Grafana panel and an alert for failed audit export days, then started to read the loader code for the retry plan for large files
body:
First the finish of the audit export. I added three Prometheus metrics to the job: the duration per day, the number of exported rows and the number of failed days, each with the customer id as a label. With about 40 customers the label count is fine. The Grafana panel shows the duration as a heat map and the failed days as a single number with a red threshold at 1.

The alert rule is in the rules-as-code repository, as all of them are now. It fires when a customer has a failed day twice in a row, which means the nightly retry also failed. It pages nobody, it goes to the normal chat channel, because a late export is not urgent. I tested it by making a failure on staging for two nights in the metrics with a fake gauge, and the alert fired after the second evaluation. I removed the fake data afterwards.

Then I merged those changes and the audit export topic is closed on my side.

The second part of the session was the start of the loader work. Large file imports through the document loader fail now and then, mostly files above 2 GB, because one failed request in the middle of the file makes the whole load fail and the customer has to start again. Support had four such cases in the last month. I created the loader-retry branch and read the code before changing anything.

What I found:
- The loader reads the file in chunks of 8 MB and posts each chunk to the ingest API.
- A non-200 answer throws and ends the load.
- There is no record of which chunk was the last one accepted, so there is no way to continue.
- The ingest API has no idempotency key, so posting a chunk twice would create duplicates.

The last point is the important one. A retry is only safe if a repeated chunk is recognized. My first idea is a chunk id made from the file hash and the chunk number, sent as a header, and a short-lived record in Redis of accepted chunk ids. I wrote this into a notes file in the branch and will discuss it with Mara tomorrow, because she knows the ingest side better.

summary: Mara preferred a dedup record in Postgres over Redis for the loader chunk ids, because a lost key would silently create duplicates
body:
Talked with Mara about the chunk id idea. She agreed with the header, but not with Redis for the record of accepted chunks. If a Redis key expires or the instance restarts, a retried chunk would be accepted twice and nobody would notice. For event data that is worse than a failed load.

Her suggestion is a small table in Postgres, load_chunks, with the load id and the chunk number as primary key, written in the same transaction as the batch is handed to the queue, or at least before the answer is sent. An insert that hits the primary key means the chunk is already accepted, and the API answers 200 without queuing it again. Old rows can be deleted after 14 days.

I agreed, mostly because the volume is low: one row per 8 MB chunk. I updated the notes in the branch. The next step is the migration for the table and the header handling in the ingest API.

summary: Added the load_chunks table and the chunk id header to the ingest API, with an insert that decides if a chunk is new, and tests for the duplicate case
body:
Implemented the server side in the loader-retry branch. The migration creates load_chunks with load_id, chunk_no, accepted_at and a primary key on the first two. I ran it on staging, and it was instant because the table is new.

In the ingest API, a request with the header X-Chunk-Id (load id and number) now does an insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING before queuing. If no row was inserted, the answer is 200 with a field duplicate set to true, and nothing is queued. Requests without the header work as before.

Tests:
- First post of a chunk is queued once.
- Second post of the same chunk gives 200, duplicate true, and the queue count stays at one.
- Two parallel posts of the same chunk result in exactly one queued batch.

One open point: if the insert succeeds but the queue write fails, the chunk is marked accepted but was never queued. I need to put the insert and the queue write in an order that cannot lose data. I will look at that tomorrow before I touch the client.

summary: Fixed the lost chunk case in the ingest API by deleting the load_chunks row when the queue write fails, and checked it with an injected queue error
body:
The problem from yesterday: a chunk could be recorded as accepted and then fail at the queue, so a retry would be treated as a duplicate and the data would be lost.

I considered a transaction that spans both, but the queue is Redpanda and cannot take part in a Postgres transaction. The simple option is to keep the order insert first, queue second, and when the queue write fails, delete the row and answer 503 so the client retries. If the delete itself fails, the row stays, which is the bad case, so I added a second safeguard: the row has a status column, pending at the insert and done after the queue write. A pending row older than two minutes counts as not accepted, and a retry takes it over by an update.

Tests I added:
- Queue error injected: the answer is 503 and a retry is queued.
- Queue error and delete error together: the retry after two minutes is queued, and one before that gets a 409 so the client waits.
- Normal case still gives one queued batch.

All pass. The extra status column needed a second migration, which I ran on staging.

summary: The loader client now retries failed chunks with backoff and a chunk id, and resumes from the last accepted chunk after a crash, tested on a 3 GB file
body:
Now the client side of the loader-retry branch. The loader sends the X-Chunk-Id header, made from the SHA-256 of the file and the chunk number. Hashing a 3 GB file takes about 9 seconds, which is fine compared to the upload.

Retry rules I implemented:
- Retry on network errors, 429, 502, 503 and 504, and on 409 from the pending case.
- Exponential backoff starting at 1 second, doubling up to 30 seconds, with random jitter of up to 25 percent.
- At most 6 attempts per chunk, then the load stops with a clear message that names the chunk number.
- A 400 is never retried, since the data itself is wrong.
- If a 429 has a Retry-After header, the client waits that long.

For the resume: the loader writes a small state file next to the input with the load id and the last chunk that was answered with 200. After a crash, running the same command again finds the file and starts after that chunk. If the file hash differs, it ignores the state file and starts a new load.

Testing on staging with a 3 GB generated NDJSON file. I used a proxy that returned 503 for every tenth request and killed the loader at chunk 150 of 384. Results:
- All chunks went through with at most two attempts each.
- After the kill, the second run started at chunk 151.
- The final event count was exactly the number of lines in the file, without duplicates.

It took 11 minutes in total, compared to 8 minutes without failures. The retries are the main cost. Tomorrow I will add the progress output and update the docs for support, because Sam will need to explain the resume to customers.

summary: Wrote a short support note for the loader resume and added progress output with the chunk number and an estimated time left
body:
Added a progress line to the loader that prints the chunk number out of the total, the throughput in MB per second and an estimate of the time left. The estimate uses the average of the last 20 chunks, because the first chunks are slower while connections warm up.

I also wrote a short note for Sam with the facts support needs:
- If a load fails, run the same command again and it continues.
- The state file sits next to the input file and has the suffix .loadstate. Deleting it forces a new load.
- A repeated chunk is never stored twice, so running the command again is always safe.
- After 6 failed attempts on one chunk the load stops, and the message names the chunk so the support can tell us.

Sam read it and asked what happens when the customer moves the file. The state file is found by the file hash and the directory, so a moved file starts a new load. A new load with the same content is deduplicated only per load id, so it would create the events twice. I wrote that down as a known limit. It is rare, but I will think about making the load id depend on the content alone.

summary: Made the load id depend on the file content so a moved file resumes safely, and found that old duplicate rows in load_chunks cleanup would have deleted live loads
body:
Followed up on the limit I noted yesterday. The load id used to be random and stored in the state file, so a moved or copied file got a new id and the dedup did not apply. I changed the id to a hash of the file hash and the customer id. Now the same file loaded twice for one customer gives the same chunk ids, and the second load answers duplicate for every chunk.

That raises a product question: a customer may want to load the same file again on purpose, for example after deleting events. I added a flag --force-new that adds a random salt to the load id. Without the flag, the CLI tells the customer that the file was already loaded and shows when. I asked Sam, and the support agrees that this is the better default, because most repeated loads are mistakes.

While I wrote the cleanup job for load_chunks, which deletes rows after 14 days, I found a mistake in my first draft. It deleted by accepted_at, but for a load that runs for more than 14 days, which is possible with a paused large import, it would delete the early chunks and then a resume would load them again. I changed the cleanup to delete a load only when its last accepted_at is older than 14 days, using a group by load id.

Tests I added for the cleanup:
- A finished load older than 14 days is removed completely.
- A load with an early chunk of 20 days ago and a new chunk of yesterday stays.
- Pending rows older than a day are removed, since they are abandoned.

I also ran the content-hash approach on a 3 GB file moved to another directory, and the resume worked from the right chunk.

One more thing: hashing the whole file before sending delays the start by 9 seconds. For small files it is negligible. I decided not to optimize this.

Still open: the review by Mara, and the rollout plan. The server side can go first, since it ignores requests without the header.

summary: Mara approved the loader-retry pull request with two small comments, and the server side with the chunk table is deployed to production
body:
Mara reviewed the loader-retry branch. She approved it and had two comments. The first was to log the load id and chunk number when a duplicate is answered, so support can see it in the logs. The second was to cap the Retry-After wait at 60 seconds in the client, since a bad value could stall a load for hours. I did both.

I deployed the server part first, as planned: the two migrations and the ingest API change. The API ignores requests without the header, so old clients are not affected. After the deploy I watched the error rate and latency of the ingest API for an hour, and nothing changed. The load_chunks table has only the test rows from staging, so it is empty in production.

The client release is tomorrow.

summary: Released the loader client with resume and retries, and the first customer load of 2.4 GB finished with two retried chunks and no duplicates
body:
Released the new loader client in the morning and told support. Then I checked the first real use, which came in the afternoon: a customer loading a 2.4 GB NDJSON file with about 6.1 million events.

From the logs and the load_chunks table:
- 307 chunks were accepted.
- Two chunks needed a second attempt, both after a 502 from the load balancer.
- No chunk was answered as duplicate, so nothing was repeated after an accepted answer.
- The load took 9 minutes.

I compared the number of events in the store with the number of lines the customer gave us, and the counts are the same. Before the change, a load like this could fail at any chunk and start again from zero, which is what happened to this customer last month, according to Sam.

One thing I saw in the Grafana panel of the ingest API: the 502 answers from the load balancer came in a short burst of about 10 seconds. It looks like a worker restart during a deploy of another service, not our code. I asked Tobias whether the deploys are rolling and he confirmed that the workers drain for 30 seconds, but the load balancer deregistration delay is only 10. He will look at making them match.

Small follow-ups for me:
- The docs page for the loader needs the new flags. Sam will do it with my note.
- The state file suffix should be mentioned in the error message after six failed attempts, so the customer knows what to keep. I added this now.

I think the loader-retry topic is done. I will keep the branch open for a few days in case the first real loads show something odd, and then delete it.

summary: Planned a cleanup of the Redis key names in the search API after finding three different naming styles, and wrote the rename list without touching production yet
body:
While looking at the Redis memory graph for another reason, I scanned the key names of the search API and found three styles that grew over time: search:v2:{customer}:{hash}, facets_{customer}, and sug/{customer}/{prefix}. It makes it hard to see in a key sample what belongs to what, and it makes per-feature memory counts by prefix unreliable.

I wrote a proposal for one scheme: nebula:{service}:{feature}:{customer}:{hash}. Examples: nebula:search:results:123:ab12, nebula:search:facets:123, nebula:search:suggest:123:ab. The parser version stays in the results key as part of the feature name, so old and new results still never mix.

A rename in production has a risk. If the code writes new keys and reads old ones, or the other way round, the cache is cold for a while and the Postgres and OpenSearch load goes up. The last time a cold cache caused a short latency spike, when search v2 was turned on for the largest customer. So the plan has steps:
- Step 1: the code reads both names, writes the new one. Old keys expire with their TTL.
- Step 2: after the longest TTL (24 hours for facets), the code reads only the new name.
- Step 3: a script deletes any remaining old keys by a scan of the old patterns.

I counted the keys per pattern on a sample with SCAN: about 2.1 million results keys, 38,000 facets keys, and 410,000 suggestion keys. The suggestion keys are the largest group by count but small in bytes.

I also looked at where the key strings are built in the code. There are 14 places, and 5 of them build the key by hand instead of the helper function. I made a list. A first cleanup that moves all of them to the helper, with no change to the names, is a safe step on its own, so I started that. I changed 9 of the 14 places today, and the tests for the search API pass. The remaining five are in the suggestion code, which has its own tests that I have to extend first.

I did not deploy anything. I will finish the helper change tomorrow, and then ask Mara to look at the plan before step 1.

summary: Moved all Redis key building in the search API to one helper without changing any names, and Mara agreed with the three step rename plan
body:
Finished the helper change from yesterday. The five remaining places in the suggestion code now call the key helper. Before I touched them I extended the suggestion tests so that they assert the exact key strings, so any accidental change in a name would fail a test. That found one difference already: one path lowercased the customer prefix and another did not, which means the same suggestion was cached twice under two keys. I kept the lowercase version for both. It is a small change in the names, but it only merges duplicates, and the old keys expire by their TTL.

I deployed the helper change in the morning. I compared the number of keys per pattern before and after on production with a SCAN sample, and the pattern counts were close to what they were. The cache hit rate of suggestions went from 61 to 64 percent over the afternoon, which is the effect of the merged duplicates, a nice side effect.

Mara read the rename plan and agreed with the three steps. Her points:
- Do the rename for the facets first, since they have the smallest key count and the longest TTL, and the cold cache is cheap there.
- Keep a counter metric for reads that hit the old name, so we can see when step 2 is safe instead of waiting for 24 hours by the clock.
- Do not do the results keys in the same week as the shard layout planning, so that a cache problem is not mixed up with an index problem.

The last point is good. The new shard layout needs a plan of its own, and I want to avoid two changes that both show up as latency changes. I will do the facets rename next week and leave the results keys to later.

I added the metric for old-name reads to the helper code now, a Prometheus counter with the feature as a label. It is only active when the dual read is on, which is not the case yet.

summary: Measured the Postgres vacuum behaviour on the audit_log table after the export work and found autovacuum keeps up, so no settings change is needed
body:
After the audit export started to read the table every night, I wanted to be sure that it does not cause bloat or hold back vacuum. A long read on the replica can delay vacuum on the primary if hot_standby_feedback is on, so I checked that setting. It is on for the replica, so the question is real.

What I looked at in pg_stat_user_tables and the Grafana panel for the database:
- audit_log has 22 million rows, about 1.5 percent dead tuples, and the last autovacuum finished 3 hours ago.
- The export reads from the replica for 14 to 20 minutes at night, and the oldest transaction age on the primary did not go above 25 minutes in the last week.
- Table and index size grew by 2 percent in a week, which is the normal rate of new audit rows.

The audit log is append-only, so there are almost no updates or deletes, and vacuum has little to do apart from freezing. I decided not to change autovacuum settings. I wrote the numbers in the ops notes, so that a later session can compare if the picture changes.

One thing to remember: if the exports ever get much longer, for example when many customers turn them on, the replica feedback could matter. I added a Grafana alert on the oldest transaction age above 2 hours for the primary, since that is cheap and useful in general.

summary: Tried a typed client library for the OpenSearch calls in the search API, hit incompatibilities with our query builder, and went back to the plain client
body:
I spent the afternoon on an experiment: replacing the hand-written request objects in the search API with a typed query builder library, hoping to catch mistakes in the generated queries at compile time. The v2 parser creates quite complex bool queries, and a typo in a field name only shows up at runtime today.

What I did: added the library on a branch from main, and converted the prefix clause and the phrase clause generation to it. The unit tests of those parts passed after about an hour of fixing types.

Then the problems:
- The library has no type for the minimum_should_match string form we use, such as 75%, only for numbers, so I needed casts that remove the benefit.
- The per-field boost syntax with the caret in the fields list is not supported for multi_match, and I would have had to split it into several clauses, which changes the scoring.
- The generated JSON of the converted code differed from the old one in key order and in two default values it adds, and the cache key of the results is made from the query JSON. That would have meant a cold cache for all customers.

The scoring one is the deciding point. I do not want to change relevance as a side effect of a typing exercise. I abandoned the change and deleted the branch.

What I will do instead is smaller: a plain TypeScript type for the field names that the parser may use, taken from the mapping file, so that a typo in a field name fails at compile time. I wrote this as an idea in the notes, and have not started.

summary: Added a compile-time type for the searchable field names, generated from the index mapping, and it already caught one wrong field name in a test fixture
body:
Did the smaller idea from yesterday. A small script reads the OpenSearch mapping file in the repository and writes a TypeScript file with a union type of all field names, including sub-fields such as tags.keyword. It runs as part of the build, so the type is never out of date against the mapping.

The parser and the boost configuration now use this type for field names. The change touches 11 places, and no generated query changed, which I checked by comparing the JSON of the 60 fixture queries before and after. They are identical, so the cache keys stay as they are.

The compiler caught one problem immediately: a fixture used the field name title_text, and the mapping has no such field. It was a leftover from the v1 days, and the test passed only because the fixture expected a no-match. I fixed the fixture to use title and checked that the expected result is still right.

I also wrote a short note in the contributing doc about the generated file and how to run the script. Merged after the tests and the build passed.

summary: Wrote the three step plan for the search API Redis key rename: dual read first, then dual write, then drop the old names after the TTLs have run out
body:
After the key builder helper of this morning, I wrote down the rename in detail. Step one makes the helper read the new name and fall back to the old one. Step two writes only the new name. Step three removes the fallback once the longest TTL has passed.

The longest TTL among the affected keys is 24 hours, for the saved query cache, so step three can follow one day after step two. The shortest is 60 seconds for the autocomplete keys, which can switch at once.

I counted the keys on staging with a SCAN over the three prefixes: about 41,000 keys, of which 30,000 belong to the autocomplete cache. That cache is cheap to lose, so the rename of those keys does not need a fallback. For the session keys of the admin console I did not plan a rename at all, because Lena's code reads them directly and a change would log everybody out.

I added a test that builds every key type through the helper and checks the new prefix. Another test checks that the fallback read returns the same value for both names. Both pass.

Mara asked for a metric that counts how often the fallback is used, so we can see when step three is safe. I added a counter called search_cache_key_fallback_total. Production is untouched so far. Step one goes out tomorrow with the normal deploy, and I will check the counter after a few hours.

summary: Deployed step one of the Redis key rename in the search API and the fallback counter fell to near zero within two hours as the cache refilled under the new names
body:
The helper now reads the new key name first and falls back to the old name. It went out with the morning deploy.

At first the fallback counter showed about 70 percent of reads, which is expected: no key existed under the new names yet. After one hour it was at 22 percent and after two hours under 2 percent. The remaining fallbacks come from the saved query cache with its 24 hour TTL.

Cache hit rate stayed within one point of the usual 83 percent. Search API p95 latency did not move. Redis memory grew by about 90 MB, because both name sets exist for a while, and that is within the headroom we have.

Step two, writing only the new names, is planned for tomorrow. I do not want to do it on the same day as step one, so a problem has a clean point to be traced to.

summary: Found that the search API autocomplete cache keys had no customer id in two code paths, which could have shown one customer's suggestions to another, and fixed both
body:
While checking the new key helper against the old call sites, I found that two code paths of the autocomplete cache built the key from the field name and the prefix typed, without the customer id. These were the paths for the global tags field and for the saved filters. The old naming styles hid this, because the keys looked different from the others and nobody had compared them.

I first checked whether data could really have leaked. The cached value is the list of suggested values for the prefix. For the tags field the list is built from the customer's own index, so two customers typing the same prefix could have received each other's tags.

I looked at the logs of the last 30 days for the cache key pattern and counted 212 cases where two different customers had hit the same key within its TTL of 60 seconds. I could not tell from the logs if the content differed, so I treated all of them as possible exposures.

The fix is in the helper: the customer id is now a required argument of every key builder, and the type system refuses a call without it. That makes this class of mistake a compile error. I added a test that scans all key builders and fails if a key has no customer segment, except the explicitly listed global ones.

The fix was deployed after a review by Mara. Because the keys are new, the wrong old entries are no longer read. I flushed the old autocomplete keys by prefix to be safe.

I told Sam about the 212 cases, with the list of customers involved, so support can decide if a note to customers is needed. Most of the cases were small customers with generic tags like 'prod'. I wrote down the finding in the internal notes with the log queries I used.

summary: Finished steps two and three of the Redis key rename in the search API, with the old key names removed and the fallback code deleted
body:
Step two went out this evening: the helper writes only the new names now. The fallback counter was already near zero, so no read path depended on the old names.

I had planned a day between step two and three, but the long TTL keys, the saved query cache with 24 hours, are the only reason for the wait. To avoid waiting, I deleted the old saved query keys by prefix with a script that works in batches of 500 with a short pause. It removed 11,300 keys in under a minute and Redis latency stayed flat in Grafana.

Before the deletion I ran the script in dry mode on staging and compared the count with the SCAN result: 4,120 keys, the same in both. On production I ran dry mode first too and checked the prefix list line by line against the rename list from last week.

After the deletion the fallback code in the helper became dead code. I removed it together with the counter and its Grafana panel. The diff is small, about 60 lines removed.

Results after the change:
- Redis memory down by about 130 MB compared with the time both name sets existed
- cache hit rate 84 percent, one point higher than before the rename, probably because the keys with the missing customer id no longer collide
- no change in p95 latency

Mara reviewed the pull request quickly. One comment asked for a short document that lists the key types, their TTLs and who owns them. I wrote it as a table in the repo docs folder with eleven key types.

One open point: the admin console keys for sessions still follow a different style and belong to Lena's code. We agreed not to touch them. The rename is done.

summary: Ran the Redis key rename plan past the production traffic numbers and found one cache family, the facet counts, that needs a longer dual read window than the rest
body:
Before the key rename goes further, I checked the plan against what production actually holds in Redis. I sampled the key space with SCAN on a replica, counted keys per prefix and read the TTLs of each family. The autocomplete, query result and session lookup keys all have TTLs of 15 minutes or less, so the dual read window for them can be short.

The facet count keys are different. They are written by a nightly warm-up job and have a TTL of 26 hours, and a few of them are only rebuilt once a week for small customers. If step one of the plan ended after a few hours, those customers would see a cold cache and a burst of facet queries on OpenSearch the next morning. I changed the plan so that the dual read stays on for at least 30 hours before dual write begins.

I also found that the warm-up job builds its keys with its own string formatting and not with the new helper. That would have kept writing old names after the rename. I listed the job in the plan as an extra change to be done together with step two, and added a test that fails if any file under the search API source builds a key without the helper.

The memory estimate is fine: during the dual period the key count grows by about 35 percent, which is roughly 190 MB on a node that sits at 41 percent of its memory. I wrote the numbers into the plan so Mara can see them when she reviews it. Still open is whether to delete the old facet keys by hand after the switch or let their TTL run out; I lean towards letting them expire, because a manual delete adds risk for no gain. Next I will ask Mara about the longer window and then start step one with the helper change for the warm-up job.

summary: Looked at the slowest Postgres queries of the week with pg_stat_statements and found that the accounts usage report scans the whole events counter table
body: The top entry in pg_stat_statements by total time was the usage report query for the admin console, 1.9 seconds per call on average and called about 600 times a day. It scans the whole counters table because the filter on month has no matching index. I did not change anything yet. I wrote the EXPLAIN output into a note and planned an index on (customer_id, month) for tomorrow, to be tested on staging first. The next entries on the list were all under 100 ms.

summary: Added the (customer_id, month) index for the usage report and the query went from 1.9 seconds to 14 ms on staging, with a clean rollout in production
body:
Yesterday's finding was the usage report query scanning the whole counters table. Today I created the index on staging with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and ran the same query against a copy of the production data.

The plan changed from a sequential scan over 38 million rows to an index scan. Execution time dropped from 1.9 seconds to 14 ms. The index is 820 MB, which is acceptable for the gain.

Before production I checked the write cost. The counters table gets about 2,000 upserts per second at peak. On staging I replayed a recorded batch of upserts with and without the index and saw a 3 percent increase in time per upsert. That is small.

In production I built the index in the afternoon, outside the peak hours of the ingest. The build took 11 minutes. I watched the replication lag on the replica during that time and it stayed under 2 seconds.

After the build I ran ANALYZE on the table, then looked at pg_stat_statements again after two hours: the report query now has a mean of 16 ms, and the total time per day fell from 19 minutes to under 10 seconds.

One side effect: the console usage page loaded faster, and Lena noticed that the loading spinner no longer shows. I wrote the index into the migrations folder so staging and production stay the same.

Next I want to check whether the second slowest query, the audit log listing with a free text filter, needs something similar. It is much faster, so it is not urgent.

summary: Stopped the search API sending a full OpenSearch request per autocomplete keystroke by adding a 150 ms debounce and a prefix cache, cutting requests by about 60 percent
body:
The OpenSearch cluster graph showed a steady load from autocomplete requests, many of them for prefixes of a few letters that were replaced by the next keystroke before the answer came back. I looked at the access logs of one hour and found that a typical session sends 5 requests for a word of 6 letters.

The first change is in the console: Lena added a debounce of 150 ms to the input field, so a fast typist sends one request instead of five. She tested it with the slowest and fastest typing she could do and it did not feel slower.

The second change is in the search API. A request for a prefix that is longer than three letters now checks whether the shorter prefix result is cached and can be filtered locally, if that result was not cut by the size limit. If the shorter result was cut at 20 entries, it cannot be used, because entries might be missing. I wrote a test for this case since it is easy to get wrong.

In staging I replayed the logged hour of requests. OpenSearch requests fell from 14,200 to 5,600, which is 60 percent less. The responses matched in all but 3 cases, and in those 3 the local filter returned the same entries in a different order. I fixed the order by sorting on the same score field.

Production results after the deploy, measured for two hours:
- OpenSearch search thread pool queue stayed at 0
- autocomplete p95 went from 85 ms to 31 ms
- Redis memory grew by 20 MB for the new prefix keys

The new keys use the key helper and have the customer id in them, and a TTL of 60 seconds like the other autocomplete keys. I added them as a row in the key table.

One thing I did not do: a larger rewrite to use a completion suggester in OpenSearch. It would need a new mapping and a reindex, so I wrote it down as an idea for search v2 and did not start.

summary: Added a Prometheus alert for the autocomplete queue in OpenSearch and a Grafana panel showing the share of autocomplete requests served from the prefix cache
body:
After the autocomplete change I wanted to see if it stays good. I added a panel with the share of autocomplete requests that were answered from the prefix cache, and today it shows around 58 percent. A second panel shows the OpenSearch search queue length next to it.

The new alert fires if the search queue is above 10 for five minutes. I tested it on staging by running a load script with many parallel searches, and the alert fired after five minutes and cleared after the script stopped.

The alert goes to the normal channel, not to PagerDuty. Tobias agreed that a page would be too much for a queue that only means slower searches.

summary: Started the schema registry work for event versions: wrote the compatibility rules and a first check that rejects a field type change on the same version
body:
Mara and I talked through what the registry must guarantee, and I wrote the rules in the branch docs. A new version of an event schema may add optional fields, and may not remove a field or change its type. A type change needs a new event type name. These rules are strict, but customers send events from apps that are updated slowly, so we prefer a clear error to a quiet breakage.

I built the first compatibility check as a function that takes the old and the new schema and returns a list of violations. It handles these cases:
- a removed field
- a changed type, including a change from integer to number
- a field that was optional and became required
- a changed enum where a value was removed

The change from integer to number was a discussion. Technically it is widening and JSON does not distinguish them, but our ClickHouse columns do, and the loader would fail on the existing integer column. So it counts as a violation.

I wrote 24 test cases from the real schema history of the last year. I took all 31 changes the customers had made so far and ran them through the check. 29 passed and 2 were flagged, both type changes of a field called duration. I looked at them: in one case the customer fixed a wrong type from string to integer, and our ingest had already been coercing it. That means the rule would have rejected a change that was harmless in practice.

We decided to keep the rule and add an explicit override flag that support can set per schema, with an audit log entry for each use. I did not build the override yet, only a placeholder in the check result.

The next step is the storage of versions in Postgres and the API for registering a schema. I sketched the table: schema_versions with the event type, the version number, the JSON schema, the creator and the time. Mara wants a unique constraint on the event type and version, and I agree.

Nothing is deployed. The branch has the check and the tests, and everything passes locally.

summary: Added the schema_versions table and the register endpoint to the schema registry, and registering an incompatible schema now returns a 409 with the list of violations
body:
The table has the event type, the version number, the schema document, the creator and the creation time, with a unique constraint on the event type and the version number, as Mara asked. The migration is in the branch and ran on staging.

The endpoint registers a new version. It loads the latest version for the event type, runs the compatibility check and stores the new schema as the next version number if no violations exist. If there are violations, it answers 409 with the list.

To avoid two parallel registrations getting the same version number, the insert takes the number inside a transaction with a lock on the event type row. I tested with 20 parallel requests for the same event type, and exactly one got each number, with no duplicates and no gaps.

I also made registering the same schema twice return the existing version instead of creating a new one. Customers' deploy scripts call the endpoint at each start and would otherwise create a new version each time.

Tests cover the happy path, the conflict, the repeated registration and the parallel case. All pass. The next step is reading a schema in the ingest API, which needs a cache so the check does not hit Postgres per batch.

summary: Wrote the ingest API side of the schema registry as a cached lookup with a 30 second refresh, and measured 0.02 ms added per batch
body:
The ingest API needs to know the latest schema version of an event type for each batch. A Postgres query per batch is out of the question, since the ingest handles thousands of batches per second at peak.

I implemented an in-process cache in the Go worker code that holds all schemas for the event types, loaded at start and refreshed every 30 seconds. The refresh asks only for versions newer than the highest known one, so it is a cheap query. I considered Redis for this, but the process cache is simpler and has no network hop. A stale value of up to 30 seconds is fine, as a new schema version only adds optional fields.

If the refresh fails, the old values stay in use and a counter is increased. The worker does not stop. At start, if the first load fails, the worker retries with backoff and does not accept batches until it has the schemas, because accepting without validation would defeat the purpose.

I measured the cost with a benchmark on a batch of 500 events: the lookup adds 0.02 ms per batch, which is not visible. The validation itself is not part of this change. It is only the lookup and the cache.

Three tests cover the refresh, the failure case and the start without a database. One test found a data race on the map during refresh, and I fixed it by swapping the whole map with an atomic pointer instead of locking.

The ingest does not use the schemas to reject anything yet. That will come in a separate step with a shadow mode, so we can see how many batches would be rejected before the first real rejection. I wrote that plan into the branch notes.

summary: Shadow validation in the ingest worker found that 0.7 percent of events on staging replay would fail their schema, mostly missing required fields from one old SDK
body:
I added the shadow mode to the schema lookup of the last session. The worker validates each event against the latest schema and only increments a counter with the event type and the reason. No event is rejected.

I replayed one hour of recorded production traffic through staging. Of 4.1 million events, 28,700 would fail validation, which is 0.7 percent. That is more than I hoped for.

Looking at the reasons:
- 21,000 missing required field user_agent
- 5,200 wrong type on the field duration
- 2,500 other

The missing user_agent comes almost entirely from one old version of a customer's mobile SDK. I found the customer by the API key and told Sam, who will contact them. The duration case is the one that I saw in the history before.

Because of these numbers, we cannot switch to rejection now. The plan is to make user_agent optional in the schema for that event type, since the field is not needed by any dashboard, and to keep the shadow counter on in production for a week before deciding.

summary: Turned on the schema shadow validation counter in production and its first hour shows 0.4 percent of events that would fail, lower than the replay
body:
The deploy went out in the evening with the shadow mode only counting. There is no effect on the ingest path besides the lookup cost I measured before.

After one hour, 0.4 percent of events would fail validation, with the same two main reasons as on staging, missing user_agent and the duration type. The share is lower than the replay probably because the replay hour was during the busy time of the mobile customer.

I added a Grafana panel with the failing share per event type. I also set no alert for now. The panel will be reviewed in a week, and then we decide about the switch to rejection.

summary: Looked into why the OpenSearch nightly reindex takes more memory on one node, and found a customer index with very large documents that skews the bulk batches
body:
Tobias pointed out that one OpenSearch data node uses far more heap during the nightly reindex than the others, with a peak of 82 percent against 60 percent on the rest. I started with the bulk requests, since the bulk size was changed a few days ago to a larger value.

The bulk size is counted in documents, 2,000 per request now. For most indexes that is about 4 MB per request. But one large customer has events with big attachment fields, and their documents average 180 KB, so a bulk of 2,000 documents is about 360 MB. That explains the heap peak, and it also explains why the node that holds the primary shards of that index is the one that struggles.

I checked the size distribution of the documents in that index. The median is 3 KB, but the 99th percentile is 400 KB. A small number of documents with huge fields makes the average high.

The fix is to limit the bulk by bytes as well as by count. I changed the reindex job so that a bulk request is sent when it reaches 2,000 documents or 10 MB, whichever comes first. The code change is about 30 lines in the batch builder.

I tested on staging with a copy of that index. Before: peak heap 79 percent on the node. After: 61 percent. The reindex time for that index went from 21 minutes to 24 minutes, which is a small cost.

For the other indexes the byte limit is never reached, so their time did not change. I compared the total: 1h42 before, 1h44 after, which is within the normal variation.

I also thought about truncating the large attachment fields in the index, since they are not searchable in any useful way. That is a product question, so I wrote a note for Sam to ask the customer. The mapping is not changed.

The change is merged and will run tonight. I will look at the heap graph tomorrow morning.

summary: The first reindex with the 10 MB bulk limit ran last night with a heap peak of 63 percent on the busiest node and the same document counts in all indexes
body:
I checked the Grafana graphs for the reindex window. The busiest node peaked at 63 percent heap, down from 82 percent. The other nodes were at their usual levels.

The reindex took 1h45, two minutes more than the average of the last week, as expected from the staging test. The count ratio between the old and the new index was 1.000 for every index.

No further change is needed. I will leave the byte limit at 10 MB. Sam still has to ask the customer about the large fields.

summary: Designed the per-key rate limit configuration for the rate-limits branch, with a default tier, per-key overrides in Postgres and a Redis counter per key and window
body:
Rate limits per API key are the next step after the global limits. I started the branch and wrote the design first, since the rate limiter runs on every request and mistakes are expensive.

The configuration has three levels. A default tier applies to every key without an override. A customer can have a plan tier, such as standard or large, with higher limits. A single key can have an override, which wins over the others. All of it lives in Postgres: a table rate_limit_tiers and a nullable tier reference and override columns on the api_keys table.

The counters stay in Redis, with one key per API key and time window, using the fixed window approach that the global limiter already uses. The key names follow the new key helper and the customer id is part of the key. The TTL is two windows so late counters can still be read for the response headers.

The limiter should not query Postgres per request. I plan an in-process cache of the limits per key with a refresh of 60 seconds, like the schema cache in the ingest worker. A change of a limit in the console then takes up to a minute to apply. I think that is acceptable, and Lena agrees, but the console should say so next to the field.

We talked about what to do when Redis is not reachable. The global limiter currently lets requests pass and counts a failure metric. I keep this for the per-key limit. A limit that blocks all traffic when its store is down is a worse failure than briefly missing limits.

The response headers will show the limit, the remaining count and the reset time for the key limit. For rejected requests, status 429 with a Retry-After header, as before.

Open questions for Mara:
- whether bursts above the limit are allowed for a short time, which would need a token bucket instead of fixed windows
- how the limits apply to batch size: one request with 5,000 events or 5,000 requests

I wrote both down in the branch notes. I lean towards counting requests and keeping a separate maximum batch size, as it is today. The first code step is the table and the cache.

summary: Mara answered the rate limit questions: fixed windows are fine for now and limits count requests, with the batch size cap kept separate
body:
I went through the two open questions of the design with Mara. On bursts she said fixed windows are enough for the first version, because the customers who complain about limits mostly have steady traffic, and a token bucket can be added later without a change of the configuration tables.

On counting, she agreed with requests plus the existing batch size cap. Counting events would punish customers who batch well, which we want to encourage.

She added one request: the limit values must be visible in the response headers from the start, so Sam can ask a customer to look at their own responses when they report a problem. That was already in the design.

I updated the branch notes with the decisions. Then I wrote the migration for rate_limit_tiers with three rows, default, standard and large, and the nullable columns on api_keys. It ran on staging without problems. The limit values are placeholders that Mara will fix after looking at the traffic of the biggest customers.

summary: Built the in-process limits cache and the per-key counter check for rate-limits, with a load test showing 0.15 ms added per request and correct 429 behaviour
body:
The limiter now resolves the limit of an API key from an in-process cache, which is filled from Postgres at start and refreshed every 60 seconds. The refresh loads only the keys changed since the last one, using an updated_at column that I added with the migration.

The resolution order is the key override, then the tier of the customer, then the default. I wrote a table test with 12 combinations, including null overrides and a deleted tier. A deleted tier falls back to the default, and logs a warning.

The counter check uses one Redis call per request: INCR on the window key, and an EXPIRE when the result is 1. I changed this into a small Lua script so both happen in one round trip and a crash between them cannot leave a key without TTL. A key without TTL would count forever and block a customer, so this was worth the script.

Response headers are set on every request: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset. On rejection the status is 429 with Retry-After in seconds until the window end.

The load test ran on staging with 200 parallel clients at 5,000 requests per second for 10 minutes. The added latency was 0.15 ms at the median and 0.6 ms at p99, almost all of it the Redis round trip. The CPU of the API workers rose by 2 percent.

I tested the failure case by blocking the Redis port during the test. Requests continued to pass, the failure counter rose, and the limits worked again once the port was open. No request was rejected wrongly.

Two things I found and fixed on the way. The Reset header was off by one second at the window border because I used the wrong rounding, and the cache refresh did not remove keys that were deleted in Postgres. For the second one I added a periodic full refresh every 10 minutes, as a simple way to drop them.

The branch is ready for Mara to review. The placeholder limits are still in the tiers table, and I will not deploy before she sets the real values.

summary: Mara reviewed rate-limits, asked for the Lua script to be loaded once with EVALSHA, and set real tier values after reading the traffic of the ten largest customers
body:
Mara reviewed the branch this afternoon and had three comments. The most important one was the Lua script: I sent the full script text with each call, which costs bytes and parsing on every request. She asked me to load it once and call it by its hash with EVALSHA, and to reload on a NOSCRIPT error.

I changed it. The limiter loads the script at start, keeps the hash, and calls EVALSHA. If Redis answers NOSCRIPT, which can happen after a restart or failover, it loads the script again and repeats the call once. I tested this by running SCRIPT FLUSH on staging during the load test, and saw a handful of reloads and no failed requests.

Her second comment was about the log level of the fallback to the default tier. It should be a warning only once per key and minute, otherwise a deleted tier fills the log. I added a small rate-limited logger.

The third was a naming comment on the headers cache. I renamed it.

Then we looked at the limit values. I pulled the request rates per API key for the last 30 days, taking the peak minute of each day. For the ten largest customers, the highest peak was 1,900 requests per minute, and the median of their peaks was 700. For the typical customer the peak is below 120 per minute.

Mara set these values:
- default: 300 requests per minute
- standard: 600
- large: 3,000

The default is above the peak of nearly all small customers, so they will not notice it. The largest customer got the large tier with room of 50 percent over their peak.
