I wrote the values into a migration and assigned the tiers: the ten large customers to large, the others to default. Standard stays unused for now. The console field for the override is Lena's work and comes next week.

We agreed on a gradual start. First week, the limiter runs in log-only mode in production: it counts and logs what it would reject, but passes everything. Then we turn on rejection. The log-only flag is a setting in the environment, not in the database, so it can be changed quickly.

The branch is approved and merged with the flag set to log-only. I will deploy it tomorrow morning.

summary: Deployed the per-key rate limit in log-only mode and the first four hours show 31 keys that would have been limited, all from two customers' test scripts
body:
The deploy went out in the morning with the log-only flag set. Latency of the ingest and search APIs did not change, and the Redis call count rose by one per request, as designed.

After four hours I counted the keys that would have been rejected. There are 31, all belonging to two customers. For the first customer, the keys are used in a load test script that sends 900 requests per minute against the default tier of 300. I know it is a test because the user agent says so and the event type is called loadtest. The second customer has a nightly job that sends a burst for 3 minutes at 500 per minute.

Neither of them is in the large tier. I do not want to raise their limits without asking, so I wrote to Sam with the details and suggested that she ask both customers. For the second one the burst is real traffic, so the standard tier at 600 would be right.

I also checked the headers by calling the API with curl from my machine. The values are right, and the Reset time matches the end of the window.

The Redis memory increase for the counters is small, about 4 MB, because the keys live for two windows only. Hit rate of the query cache is unchanged.

The plan for the week is to look at the log counts each day, with the list of would-be rejected keys, and to switch the flag after the two customers have answered. I added a Grafana panel for the would-reject counter by customer to make the daily look easy.

One small issue came up. The log lines for would-be rejections include the full API key. That is bad in logs. I changed the line to log only the key id, and the first 4 characters. The fix is deployed as well, and the old log lines will fall out of retention in two weeks. I noted in the incident notes that no one outside the team can read those logs.

summary: Sam heard back from the first customer: the loadtest script is theirs and can be slowed down, so no tier change is needed for them
body: Sam wrote to the contact of the first customer, and the answer came quickly. The load test script belongs to their platform team, who run it by hand before releases. They will lower the rate to 250 requests per minute, or ask for a temporary increase if they need more. I told Sam that a temporary override on a key is possible with the console field next week, or with a direct update by me before that. That leaves the second customer with the nightly burst.

summary: Moved the second customer to the standard tier after confirming their nightly burst, and added the override field and a help text to the admin console with Lena
body:
The second customer answered Sam: the nightly job is a real import of the day's data, it sends about 500 requests per minute for 3 minutes, and they cannot easily change it. I set their keys to the standard tier with a migration-style SQL file that is kept in the repo, so the change has a history. It applies after the next 60 second refresh of the cache. I checked the would-reject counter after 5 minutes and the customer's keys were no longer in the list.

With that, the log-only phase has no more known false positives. The 31 keys from earlier are now only the load test of the first customer.

Lena built the console part this afternoon, and I reviewed it. The API key detail page has a new section with the tier of the customer and an optional override field for requests per minute. The field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 10,000, and an empty field means no override. Under the field, a help text says that changes may take up to one minute to apply. That was the thing we promised in the design.

On the server side, I added the endpoint that the console calls. It checks that the user is an admin of the customer, validates the number and writes the override. It also writes an entry into the audit log with the old and the new value, the key id and the user. That uses the audit log from the earlier work, with actor type user. When support changes a limit, the actor type is staff, so the audit export shows it as Sam wanted.

Tests cover the validation, the permission check and the audit entry. One test found that an override of 0 was accepted by the endpoint, which would block the key completely. I changed the minimum to 1 on the server, not only in the form.

We tried the whole path on staging. Setting an override of 5 on a test key and sending 10 requests gave 5 successful responses and 5 with status 429 and a correct Retry-After, once the cache refreshed. Removing the override brought the default back after a minute.

The remaining steps are to look at the would-reject list for two more days and then to switch the flag to enforcement. I also want a short customer note about the headers and the limits, which Sam will write from my notes in the branch.

summary: Rate-limits went fully live after the log-only phase: 429s are enforced for all keys, with a Retry-After header and a per-key usage panel in Grafana
body:
After the log-only period and the two customer conversations, I switched the per-key rate limit from log mode to enforcing mode. The switch is one config flag in the search API, and I rolled it out to a tenth of the traffic first, then to everything over about an hour.

The 429 response now carries a Retry-After header computed from the end of the fixed window. Before this, the response only had the error body. Mara had asked for the header in review, and the first customer script that hit the limit in staging backed off correctly once it was there.

I added a Grafana panel with requests per key against the limit, for the top 20 keys. A second panel counts 429s per tier. The panel queries come from the Prometheus counters that were already exported in log-only mode, so there was no new instrumentation.

In the first hour of enforcement there were 12 429s, all from one key that belongs to the customer who moved to the standard tier. I checked their override in Postgres and it had been saved with the old tier id, because the admin console wrote the field only on the second save. I fixed the row by hand and filed the console bug with Lena.

The Redis counters behave as designed. Key count for the rate limiter stayed under 3,000 and the memory use did not move in a way I could see. The EVALSHA script is loaded once per connection and I saw no NOSCRIPT errors after a Redis restart in staging.

Still open: the docs page for limits, which Sam will write next week from my notes, and a decision on whether the batch size cap should return its own error code. I left the cap as it is for now.

summary: Wrote the public docs page for API rate limits with Sam, including the tiers, the 429 body and a backoff example that customers can copy
body:
Sam and I wrote the rate limit page for the public API docs today. I gave Sam the tier table, the window length and the exact 429 body, and Sam rewrote it in the plain style of the other pages.

The page has four parts: what is counted (requests, not events), the tiers and how to ask for a change, the headers on a response, and what to do after a 429. The batch size cap is described in a separate short section so nobody confuses the two limits.

For the backoff example I used a small Python snippet and a curl loop. Both read Retry-After and wait at least that long, with a little jitter. Sam ran both against staging with a low test limit and they behaved correctly.

Sam found one confusing point: the limit window is fixed, so a client can send a burst at the end of one window and another at the start of the next. We added a sentence about that instead of changing the design, since Mara had agreed fixed windows are fine for now.

The page is merged and live. Sam will point the two customers who asked about limits to it.

summary: Looked at why the Redis memory graph climbs every morning and traced it to the facet count cache family, whose TTL was set to a full day
body:
The Redis memory graph has a ramp every morning, from about 2.1 GB to 3.4 GB, and Mara asked me to see whether it is a leak.

I sampled keys with SCAN and the MEMORY USAGE command on a replica, grouped by prefix. The facet count family accounts for roughly 60 percent of the growth. Each entry is small, but there are many, because the key includes the full filter combination.

The TTL for that family is 24 hours, a value left from the first version of the cache. After the key rename of last week, the facet keys are written in a new format, so the cache is not leaking: the memory simply fills until the oldest keys run out of time.

I checked the hit rate by age of the key. Entries older than 2 hours account for under 3 percent of hits. So a TTL of 2 hours would lose almost nothing.

I have not changed anything in production. I wrote the proposal in the cache notes: 2 hour TTL for facet counts, then watch the hit rate and memory for three days. Mara agreed and I will deploy it after lunch tomorrow.

summary: Cut the facet count TTL from 24 hours to 2 hours and the morning memory ramp in Redis flattened, with the hit rate down by only 0.4 points
body:
Deployed the TTL change for the facet count cache family. It was one constant in the key helper, so the diff was tiny, and I added a test that checks the TTL of each family against a table.

Old keys keep their old TTL until they run out. To avoid waiting a day for the memory to fall, I ran a one-off script that lowered the TTL of existing facet keys to 2 hours with EXPIRE, in batches of 500 with a short pause between batches so that Redis latency stayed flat. It processed about 1.1 million keys in 9 minutes.

Result after the first afternoon: Redis memory fell from 3.3 GB to 2.2 GB and stayed there. The cache hit rate for facets moved from 71.8 to 71.4 percent, which is within the normal daily swing.

I also checked the p95 of the search API facet endpoint. It did not change, still about 85 ms.

While doing this I saw that the autocomplete prefix cache has a TTL of 6 hours with the same pattern of old entries that are rarely used. I wrote that down as a follow up and did not touch it. Tomorrow I will check the morning ramp once more and then close the task.

summary: Confirmed the morning Redis memory ramp is gone after the facet TTL change and closed the cache memory task
body:
Checked the Redis memory graph for the first full night and morning since the TTL change. The ramp is gone: memory rose from 2.0 GB to 2.3 GB during the morning peak and stayed flat after that.

The hit rate for the facet family is 71.5 percent, as expected. The search API latency graphs show no change.

I added a short note to the cache documentation about why the TTLs are what they are, with the hit-rate-by-age numbers as evidence. The next person who looks at the TTLs can then decide from data.

The prefix cache TTL follow up stays on the list, low priority.

summary: Started the batch write path in the ingest worker on a new branch: one multi-row insert per batch instead of one insert per event, with a first benchmark
body:
Began the ingest-batching work. Today the worker still writes each event of a batch with its own insert, and under load the database round trips dominate the time. I worked in a worktree of the ingest-batching branch.

First I measured the current state. With a replay of one hour of production traffic against staging, the worker handled about 9,500 events per second per instance, and 70 percent of the time of a batch was spent waiting for Postgres.

The change builds one multi-row INSERT per batch, with the rows grouped by target table. I used pgx's CopyFrom for the large batches and a plain multi-row insert for batches under 50 rows, because CopyFrom has a fixed cost that does not pay off for small ones.

The tricky part is error handling. Before, one bad event failed alone. With a multi-row insert, one constraint violation fails the whole statement. I made the worker catch the error, split the batch in halves and try again until the bad event is alone, then send it to the dead letter topic. That keeps the good events moving.

The first benchmark shows about 31,000 events per second per instance with a batch of 500, and the share of time waiting for Postgres fell to 25 percent.

Things not done yet: the dead letter path has only one unit test, the ordering guarantee within a partition needs a closer look, and the batch size should be configurable. I wrote these as TODO items in the branch description.

I also noticed the transaction is now larger, so I want to look at lock times on the events table before this goes anywhere near production. The next session will run the replay with concurrent writers.

summary: Ran the ingest-batching replay with four concurrent workers and found no lock waits, but the split-and-retry path doubled latency for batches with a bad event
body:
Ran the replay with four worker instances writing to the same staging Postgres. The events table showed no lock waits above 5 ms in pg_stat_activity, and the throughput scaled to about 118,000 events per second in total.

Then I injected bad events at 1 percent, to test the split path. A batch with one bad event needs about 9 splits to isolate it (log2 of 500), and the batch latency rose from 40 ms to 85 ms. For a normal day this is rare, since the schema check in front of the worker rejects most bad events.

I changed the split to first check the error detail from Postgres. When the error names a row (many constraint errors do), the worker removes that row at once and retries once. The split is only the fallback. With that the latency for a batch with one bad event is 52 ms.

Event order within a partition is kept, because the worker processes one batch at a time per partition and removes the bad row without moving the others.

Next: make the batch size configurable and write the dead letter tests.

summary: Made the ingest batch size configurable per environment and added three tests for the dead letter path of the batched writer
body:
Added the INGEST_BATCH_MAX setting, with a default of 500 and a hard upper limit of 2,000, checked at startup. The worker logs the value when it starts so it is easy to see in the ECS logs.

The three new tests cover a batch with one bad row, a batch with all rows bad, and a batch where Postgres returns a connection error halfway. The last one must not send anything to the dead letter topic, since the whole batch should be tried again. It did at first: the error handler treated every error as a bad row. I fixed it by checking for the SQLSTATE class 23 only.

All tests pass. I pushed the branch and asked Mara for a review tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the staging rollout plan for batched ingest writes: one instance first, then half, with a flag to go back to single inserts
body:
Wrote the rollout plan for ingest-batching so Mara can review it with the code.

The code keeps the old single-insert path behind a flag, INGEST_BATCHED_WRITES. On staging the flag is already on. In production the plan is to turn it on for one of the six worker instances for a day, compare error counts and dead letter volume with the others, then half, then all.

The things to watch are: dead letter topic rate, write latency p95 per batch, Postgres CPU, and the lag of the queue consumer groups. I prepared a Grafana dashboard with these four side by side, split by instance.

The rollback is turning the flag off, which needs a restart of the instance, about a minute. That is fast enough, since the data format is not changed by this work.

One risk I listed: a larger transaction holds row locks longer. The staging test says it is fine, but staging has less variety in the data than production, so I would not skip the one-instance day.

summary: Mara reviewed ingest-batching and found an ordering bug: the dead letter write could overtake good rows when the split happened across two table groups
body:
Mara went through the ingest-batching pull request this morning and asked good questions. The most important one was about ordering when a batch contains events for more than one table.

She was right. The writer groups rows by target table and writes the groups one after the other. If the second group has a bad row, the code sends it to the dead letter topic while the first group is already committed. That is acceptable for ordering inside one table, but I also had the code write the dead letter record before the later groups finished, and in one case that meant a consumer saw the dead letter record before its sibling events.

I reproduced it with a test that uses two tables and a bad row in the second. The fix collects dead letter records during the batch and sends them after all groups are written. The order of the good rows is not changed.

Mara's other comments:
- the CopyFrom threshold of 50 rows should be a named constant, not a literal in two places,
- the split fallback needs a maximum depth so a bug in the error parser cannot loop,
- the log line for each split is too noisy at info level.

I did all three. The max depth is 12, which covers a batch of 2,000 with some room, and the log line is now at debug level with a counter for splits exported to Prometheus instead.

I also added a property-style test that generates random batches with random bad rows and checks that the good rows are all written exactly once and the bad rows all end up in the dead letter topic once. It ran 2,000 random cases and found one more problem: when the same event id appears twice in one batch, the second insert hits the unique key and was counted as a bad row. The old single-insert path treated that as a normal duplicate and skipped it. I made the batched path use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for the event id, to match the old behavior.

After these changes the random test passes. I asked Mara to take another look tomorrow. The rollout plan stays as written.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why a customer saw duplicate events after a load: the file had repeated rows and our importer deduplicates only by event id
body:
Sam asked about a customer who said that a CSV load created duplicates. I looked at the load record and the events table.

The file had 48,000 rows. In the table there were 48,000 events, so nothing was added twice by us. But 1,900 of them had the same content with different event ids. The customer's export tool generates a new id for each row on every run, and they had run the export twice and joined the files.

Our importer deduplicates by event id only, as the docs say. A content-based dedupe would be costly and wrong for events that legitimately repeat, like two identical page views in the same second.

I wrote the answer for Sam: what happened, why we do not remove them, and two options for the customer. They can send their own stable ids, or use the delete by load id endpoint to remove the second load. I tested the delete endpoint on staging to be sure it works for loads of that size, and it took 6 seconds.

I suggested Sam add a paragraph to the importer docs on how ids work.

summary: Wrote the audit log retention job for Postgres: old rows move to compressed monthly files in S3 and the table stays under 20 GB
body:
The audit_log table has grown to 31 GB and the export work made it clear that most rows are never read after 90 days. I wrote a retention job that moves old rows out.

The job runs nightly. It picks all rows older than 90 days, writes them into one NDJSON file per month, compresses the file with zstd, uploads it to the audit archive bucket, checks the object size and the row count in the file against the database, and only then deletes the rows from Postgres.

Deletion happens in batches of 5,000 rows by primary key range, with a pause of 200 ms, so autovacuum and replication can keep up. I checked the replication lag on staging during a test run and it never went above 300 ms.

The first staging run archived 11 months of data, 4.2 million rows, into 11 files with a total of 310 MB. That is about 14 percent of the size in Postgres, mostly because of the repeated JSON keys.

The verification step caught a bug in my first version: the row count of the file was off by one for months where a row had a timestamp exactly at midnight, because the month boundary used a closed interval at both ends. I changed it to a half-open interval.

What is still open: the audit export for compliance reads from Postgres, so it needs to know about the archive for ranges older than 90 days. That is a bigger change and I want to talk to Mara before I start. For now the job is only on staging, with a dry-run flag that logs what it would do.

I also wrote a restore script that loads a month file back into a table with the same shape. It is small and I tested it with one file.

summary: Made the audit export read both Postgres and the S3 archive so ranges older than 90 days still export, and tested a 14-month export end to end
body:
Mara and I agreed this morning that the export should hide the archive from the customer: they ask for a date range and get one file, whatever the source.

The export code now splits the range at the 90 day boundary. The recent part comes from Postgres as before, with the same streaming query. The older part is read from the monthly archive files in S3, with a ranged GET and a streaming zstd decoder, and filtered by the customer id on the fly.

The filter by customer is the weak spot. The monthly files hold all customers, so a request for one customer reads the whole month file. For the largest months that is about 40 MB compressed, which is fine, but it grows. I considered one file per customer and month, and decided against it for now: it would create 40 times more files and the job would be more complex. I put a note in the design document to revisit it if a month file goes over 500 MB.

Tested end to end on staging with a 14 month export for a test customer with 600,000 audit rows. It took 48 seconds and the output file was identical to the one made before the retention job ran, which I checked with a checksum of the sorted lines.

Ordering: the old part and the new part are both ordered by timestamp and the join between them is at a boundary, so the final file is in order.

Two bugs found on the way. First, the zstd decoder was not closed on an early client disconnect, which leaked a goroutine. I added a context cancel. Second, the S3 client used the default timeout of the SDK, which is too long for a stuck download, so I set 30 seconds per read.

Tests added: a range entirely in the archive, a range entirely recent, a range across the boundary, and a missing month file, which must return a clear error and not a partial export without a warning.

Next step is Lena's part: the admin console shows the export size estimate, which needs the archive row counts.

summary: Switched on the ingest-batching flag for one of six production workers; after four hours its error rate matches the others and its write latency is 3 times lower
body:
Mara approved ingest-batching after the second look, so I merged and deployed it with the flag off, then turned INGEST_BATCHED_WRITES on for worker 1 of 6 at about the start of the afternoon. I watched the comparison dashboard.

After four hours, worker 1 had written about 41 million events. Its error rate was 0.00 percent, same as the others. The dead letter topic got 212 records from it, in line with the share of traffic it handled, and the others together sent 1,090.

Write latency p95 per batch: 18 ms on worker 1 and 57 ms on the others. Postgres CPU did not change in a visible way, which I think is because the load was smaller than the replay.

I looked at lock waits on the events table in the middle of the busiest hour. The longest wait I saw was 4 ms.

One surprise: the memory of worker 1 is about 18 percent higher. Each batch holds the rows for the multi-row statement and the copy buffers at the same time. It is well within the container limit, but I noted it for the next step.

The queue consumer lag for the partitions handled by worker 1 was lower than for the others, which is the point of the change.

Decision: leave it a full day on one worker, as planned. Tomorrow I will check the night traffic, where the nightly importers produce very large batches, and then go to three workers if nothing is odd.

I also updated the runbook with the flag name and the restart step to go back, so whoever is on call knows what to do if the dead letter rate jumps.

summary: Night traffic on the batched worker looked clean, so batching is on for three of six workers, and the dead letter rate is still proportional
body:
Checked worker 1 after the night, when the importers send the big batches. No errors, no restarts. The biggest batch it wrote was 2,000 rows in 94 ms.

The memory of worker 1 peaked at 410 MB against 350 MB for the others, so the extra is stable and not growing.

I turned the flag on for workers 2 and 3 as well. Two deploys, ten minutes apart, to keep at least four workers able to take traffic at any time.

In the two hours since then, the dead letter rate per worker is the same on all six. Write latency p95 for the three batched workers is 20 ms, for the three others 55 ms.

Postgres CPU went down from about 46 to 38 percent on average, as three of six workers now send far fewer statements.

I also talked with Tobias about the connection count. With batching each worker needs fewer concurrent connections, so the pool size per worker can be reduced from 20 to 12 later. He will change it in Terraform after all workers are on the new path, not before.

Next: all six workers tomorrow if the day stays quiet.

summary: Finished the ingest-batching rollout to all six workers and measured a 40 percent lower Postgres CPU, with the connection pool cut to 12 by Tobias
body:
The flag went on for workers 4 to 6 this morning after a quiet night on the first three. I did it one worker at a time, with a check of the dead letter rate between each.

Numbers for the whole fleet after four hours:
- Postgres CPU: average 27 percent, down from 46 before the rollout, which is about 40 percent lower
- write latency p95 per batch: 21 ms, from 57 ms
- queue consumer lag: peak 1.1 seconds, from 6.4 seconds in the same hour of the day before
- dead letter records: 0.03 percent of events, same as before

Tobias then changed the pool size per worker from 20 to 12 in Terraform and applied it with a rolling restart. The pool wait time metric stayed at zero. Total connections to Postgres fell from 140 to 90, which gives room for the reports queries.

I also removed the old single-insert path from the code? No: I kept it for now, behind the flag, for two weeks in case something unexpected shows up in the monthly import runs. I put a reminder in the task list to delete it later.

One issue turned up in the afternoon. The nightly importer for the biggest customer sends batches with many repeated event ids, since it re-sends the last hour on each run. With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING these are skipped, but Postgres still takes the time to check them, and the statement for that customer takes 300 ms instead of 90. It is not a problem now, but I wrote it into the notes as something to watch.

Wrote the summary of the work in the project notes with the numbers above. The branch is merged and done, apart from removing the old path.

summary: Planned the search-v2 field boost config: boosts per field and per customer, stored in Postgres and read by the query parser, with a first parser change
body:
Started planning the per-field boosts for search v2 and made a first code change in a worktree of the search-v2 branch.

Today the search API ranks with fixed boosts in code: title 3, body 1, tags 2. Two customers have asked for something else, for example one wants the ticket id field to outrank everything because their agents search by id.

The design: a table field_boosts with customer_id, field name and a boost value, with defaults for customers without rows. The search API loads the rows for a customer into an in-process cache with a 60 second refresh, like the rate limits cache, and the query parser reads from it when it builds the multi_match clause.

The field names are validated against the generated type of searchable fields from the index mapping, so a boost for a field that does not exist is rejected with a clear error when it is saved, not when somebody searches.

The allowed range is 0.1 to 10. I asked Mara in a comment whether a wider range makes sense, and she thought 0.1 to 10 is plenty since boosts multiply with the relevance score and big values give strange results.

In the parser I changed the part that builds the field list. It takes the boosts as an argument, defaults to the old constants and produces fields like title^3 or ticket_id^8. Unit tests cover the defaults, an override and an unknown field.

I ran a small relevance check with 40 saved queries from the support team and the default boosts. The top 5 results are identical to the old code for all 40, so the refactor is safe.

Not done: the migration for the table, the admin console form (Lena) and the effect of boosts on the autocomplete, which uses a separate query. I decided autocomplete stays with fixed boosts for the first version.

Tomorrow: migration and the API endpoint to set the boosts.

summary: Added the field_boosts migration and the PUT endpoint for boosts, with validation and an audit log entry for every change
body:
Wrote the migration for the field_boosts table, with a unique index on customer id and field name, and a check constraint for the 0.1 to 10 range as a second line of defence behind the API validation.

The endpoint is PUT on the customer boosts resource and replaces the whole set for the customer in one transaction. I chose replace over patch so a customer never has half of a configuration. An empty list resets to the defaults.

Every change writes an audit log entry with the old and new set, which also makes it visible in the audit export.

Validation errors list all problems at once, not only the first: an unknown field, a boost out of range and a duplicate field are reported together.

I tested it on staging with a customer that has the ticket id case and the result in the search was as wanted. I sent Lena the response format for the console form.

summary: Reviewed the search-v2 parser on real query logs and found that quoted phrases with a trailing wildcard were parsed as two terms, so the parser now handles them as one
body:
Took a sample of 20,000 real queries from the search API logs of the last two weeks and ran them through the new search-v2 parser next to the old one, to see where the results differ before any customer is switched. Most queries parse the same way. 312 of them differ, and I went through all of them by hand.

The biggest group, 184 queries, were quoted phrases followed by a wildcard, such as "payment failed" err*. The new parser split the phrase and the wildcard into two separate terms and dropped the quotes. That changed the match from a phrase match to an any-word match, which returns far too many hits.

The cause was in the tokenizer in the parser: after a closing quote it started a new token without checking whether a wildcard character came right behind it. I fixed this by letting the phrase token carry an optional prefix flag, and the OpenSearch query builder now emits a match_phrase_prefix clause for it. I added 14 test cases for quotes, wildcards and escaped quotes in the parser test file.

The second group, 61 queries, differed because of field names written in upper case, like Status:500. The old parser lowercased them silently. The new one rejected them with a parse error. Rejecting is wrong here because customers already use these queries in saved searches, so I made field names case-insensitive and used the generated field type from the index mapping for the lookup.

The remaining 67 differences were queries with unbalanced quotes. The old parser ignored the broken quote and the new one returns a clear 400 with the position of the error. I kept the 400, and Mara can say if she wants a softer fallback. After the fixes, the replay shows 9 differing queries, all of them unbalanced quotes. Next I want to repeat the replay on the queries of the two largest customers, since their saved searches are the most complex.

summary: Pruned the unused staging databases and sped up the upgrade script to run extension updates only where the extensions exist, cutting the run from 25 to 6 minutes
body:
Following the first look this morning, I listed the 14 databases on the staging instance. Nine are old test databases from earlier benchmark and migration work, and five are in use. I asked Tobias, and he agreed that the nine can go after a dump to S3.

I dumped each one with pg_dump in custom format and uploaded them to the archive bucket with a short README listing the origin of each. Then I dropped them. Staging disk use went down by 38 GB.

The upgrade script was also wasteful in another way: it ran every extension update in every database, even where the extension was not installed, and each failure was logged and retried twice. I changed it to query pg_extension first and only update what exists and is behind the available version.

I ran the upgrade on a staging copy restored from a snapshot, to be safe. Total time was 6 minutes, and most of it was the restart and the checkpoint.

The script now also checks the replication state before it begins and refuses to run if a replica is more than 10 seconds behind, which would have been useful on the last real upgrade.

Tobias will use the new script for the production minor upgrade. I wrote the steps down in the runbook, including the check that the version after the upgrade is what we expect, by reading it from SHOW server_version in each database.

One point I want to keep an eye on: the planner statistics are reset by some upgrades, and queries may be slow until the next analyze. The script runs ANALYZE on the main tables at the end, with the largest table last so the small ones are quick.

Open: nothing blocking. The production upgrade is not scheduled yet.

summary: Built the boost form in the admin console API contract with Lena and ran a relevance comparison on two customers that showed the ticket id boost helps
body:
Spent the morning with Lena on the boosts form in the admin console. She had a first version of the form from the response format I sent, and we went through the edge cases together.

Things we changed:
- the form shows the default boost next to each field as a hint, so the customer sees what they change from,
- field names come from a new endpoint that lists searchable fields for a customer, taken from the generated mapping type, instead of a list copied into the frontend,
- saving shows the validation errors per field, which works because the API returns all problems at once.

I added the endpoint for the field list. It is small, but I made sure it only lists fields the customer can see, since some fields are internal to our own tooling.

In the afternoon I wanted evidence that boosts do what we think. I took the two customers who asked for them and ran 60 of their real queries from the last week, with and without the requested boosts, on a staging copy of their indexes.

For the customer with the ticket id case, 23 of the 60 queries were id lookups. With the default boosts, the right document was first in 14 of those 23. With ticket_id^8 it was first in 22 of 23. The one miss was a query with a typo in the id.

For the second customer, who wanted the title boost lowered to 1, the result was less clear. The top result changed in 17 of 60 queries and I could not say that it was better. I asked Sam to get a few examples confirmed by the customer before we apply it for them.

One thing to fix: the cache refresh of 60 seconds means a customer who saves a boost waits up to a minute to see it. The console now says so in a small text under the save button. A cache flush on save is possible but needs a message to all API instances, so I postponed it.

Next: wait for Sam's answer and write the docs for boosts.

summary: Wrote the plan for the search-v2 reindex with boosts and the new parser, including how to switch customers over one at a time with a dual query check
body:
Mara asked for a written plan for rolling out search v2 before more code goes in, so I spent the session on that, in a worktree of the search-v2 branch.

What changes for a customer: the new query parser (phrases, minus terms, field filters), the per-field boosts, and a reindex because two fields change their analyzer. The analyzer change is the reason this cannot be only a flag.

The plan has four phases:
1. Build the v2 index next to the v1 index for each customer, using the nightly reindex job with a target suffix. Disk use goes up by the size of the customer index while both exist, so we start with the small customers.
2. Shadow mode: the search API runs the saved queries on both and logs where the top 10 differ. I wrote the comparison as a small job that stores the counts per customer in Postgres.
3. Switch per customer with a setting in the accounts table, readable in the console, so Sam can tell a customer what version they are on.
4. Drop the v1 index a week after the last customer has moved.

Risks I listed:
- the reindex of the three large customers takes hours and competes with the nightly job for heap, so they need their own window,
- the parser accepts more syntax, and a query that used to be a plain text search may now be read as a filter, for example a minus at the start of a word. I wrote down a rule that a minus counts as an operator only after a space and before a term,
- the Redis cache keys for search results must include the version, or customers would see old-style results after the switch. I added the version to the key helper in a small commit and tested that the keys differ.

I also estimated the disk: for the 40 customers the v2 indexes add about 210 GB on the OpenSearch nodes at the peak, which fits in the current volumes with 30 percent left. Tobias should confirm that number, so I sent it to him.

For the shadow comparison, I wrote the first version of the job and ran it on three small customers on staging. The top 10 lists were identical for 94 percent of queries, and the rest differed because of the boosts and the analyzer, as expected.

Next: the docs for the new syntax, and the first real customer reindex.

summary: Checked the disk graphs for the analytics store before the retention change and confirmed the raw events grow by about 40 GB a month, mostly from three large customers
body:
Before changing anything about retention, I pulled the disk usage of the analytics store for the last six months. Growth is almost linear at 40 GB a month, with no step changes. Three customers produce 58 percent of the raw events.

I also ran a query to see how much of the old data the dashboards touch. Nothing in the current dashboards reads raw events older than 13 months; the longest range is the yearly view, which uses daily counts. That gives room for a retention cut.

I wrote the numbers into the retention task so Tobias and Mara can check them. The next step is a draft of the rollup table and the job that drops old partitions. I did not touch production today.

summary: Drafted the daily rollup table for the analytics store and checked that the yearly dashboard queries return the same numbers from rollups as from raw events
body:
The retention plan needs daily rollups, so I started with the table design. The rollup keeps one row per customer, event type and day, with the event count, the unique user estimate and the sum of the numeric properties the dashboards use. It is filled by a materialized view from the raw table.

To test it, I took the yearly dashboard queries and ran each in two versions: one on raw events and one on the rollup. I did this for the ten largest customers and for 12 months of data. Counts and sums were identical.

The unique user numbers differed by up to 0.8 percent, because the rollup uses an approximate distinct count. Two customers care about that figure in their reports. I noted it for Sam, who will tell them before the change goes live.

I also found that the property sums overflowed for one customer's byte counter in a 32 bit column. I changed the column to 64 bit in the draft and reran the check, which now passes.

Still open: the backfill of rollups for months that are already in the raw table, and the drop job. I will write both next. No production changes were made in this session.

summary: Wrote the partition drop job for raw analytics events, with a dry run mode that lists what would go and a guard that refuses to drop a month without a finished rollup
body:
The drop job runs on the first day of each month and removes the raw partition that is now 14 months old. I wrote it as a small Go command in the maintenance tools, with a dry run flag as the default.

The important guard is a check that the rollup for every day of that month exists and that its event counts match the raw partition within zero difference. If a single day is missing or differs, the job stops and pages nobody but writes an error log line and a Grafana counter. I preferred a failed run over a lost month.

I tested it on the staging copy with 15 months of data. The dry run listed one partition of 41 GB. With a day of rollup deleted on purpose, it refused, as intended.

One thing I changed: the first version used the partition name to calculate the age, which is fragile if a partition is renamed. It now reads the min and max date from the partition metadata.

Next is the live backfill of rollups and a review by Tobias on the disk side.

summary: Answered Sam's question on what customers lose with the shorter retention: raw event search stays, but raw analytics queries older than 13 months return daily rollups only
body:
Sam asked what to tell customers about the retention change. I wrote the answer from what the system does, so it can go into the docs.

What stays the same: full text search runs on OpenSearch and has its own retention, which is not touched. The dashboards for ranges of up to 13 months read raw events as before. Longer ranges already show daily numbers.

What changes: in the analytics store, events older than 13 months exist only as daily rollups per event type. A customer cannot run a query by single user, or by a property that is not in the rollup, for such a range. The export of raw analytics events for old ranges will return an empty set.

I checked the last 30 days of query logs for the analytics API. Of 212,000 queries, 61 reached back more than 13 months, and they came from four keys. Two of those were the yearly dashboards. The other two were scripts of one customer; Sam will write to them directly.

I also listed the unique user difference of up to 0.8 percent. Sam will add a sentence to the help page. No code changed in this session, only the text for Sam and a note in the task.

summary: The analytics store keeps the raw events for 13 months now, and older events only as daily rollups, after the backfill and the first live drop check
body:
I switched the retention on in production today. First I ran the rollup backfill for all months that were still in the raw table. It took 52 minutes and did not disturb the dashboards; query p95 stayed at 340 ms during the run.

Then I ran the drop job in dry run mode on production. It found the one partition older than 13 months, 43 GB, and the guard confirmed that all its days had rollups with equal counts. I ran it for real. Disk use fell by 43 GB.

Tobias checked the disk graph and agreed that the growth is now flat after the drop, as the raw events of a month go away on the first day of the 14th month. The job is set in the scheduler, and a Grafana alert fires if the guard refuses.

Sam has sent the notice to the four customers whose queries reached further back. The help page now has the sentence about the approximate unique user counts.

Open: watch the first scheduled run next month, and check that the restore notes mention that dropped raw events cannot be restored from the store, only from the S3 backups of the last 30 days.

summary: Looked at the slow query log in Postgres and found the settings list endpoint doing a sequential scan on a table that grew past 2 million rows, fixed with a composite index
body:
The slow query log showed one statement over 800 ms several hundred times a day: the settings list for the admin console, filtered by account and sorted by update time. The table has grown to 2.1 million rows because of the per-key rate limit overrides and old versions of settings.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan with a sort. I added a composite index on account id and updated at, descending, created with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so that writes were not blocked. It took four minutes.

Afterwards the same statement took 3 ms. The index is 90 MB, which is fine.

I also checked whether autovacuum keeps up with this table. It does; dead tuples stay under 2 percent. I did not change any vacuum settings.

The migration file is in the repository and was applied to staging first. Lena confirmed that the settings page of the console loads noticeably faster now. Nothing else to do for this one.

summary: Tried a different Redis client library for the session store to cut connection use and dropped it after it showed no gain and broke pipelining in the search API
body:
I tried a lighter Redis client for the session store of the admin console, hoping for fewer connections per process. The idea was to replace the current client in one service only.

In a staging test with 300 simulated sessions, the connection count was the same as before, 8 per process, and the latency per call was within noise. The library also handled pipelined commands differently; the search API test suite failed in two places where we send batches of cache reads.

I looked for a configuration that would fix it, but the differences were in how errors are returned inside a pipeline, and fixing that would mean changing our cache code for no benefit. So I reverted the change and deleted the branch.

The connection count is better handled by the pool size settings, which I will look at separately. Nothing changed in production.

summary: Reviewed the ingest-batching logs after a week at full rollout and found the dead letter rate steady at 0.02 percent, with no ordering problems since Mara's fix
body:
A week after the ingest-batching rollout reached all six workers, I went through the logs and metrics. The dead letter rate is 0.02 percent of events, the same as before batching. All of it comes from malformed payloads of two customers.

I checked the ordering issue Mara found in review. I wrote a query that compares the sequence numbers of dead letter writes against the good rows of the same batch. Over the week, no case was found where a dead letter row was written before good rows of its batch.

Write latency is still about 3 times lower than before, and Postgres CPU stays 40 percent lower. The connection pool of 12 has never been full.

I removed the single insert flag from the worker config in the staging environment, but kept it in production for one more week in case of a rollback. Next I will remove the old code path.

summary: Removed the single-insert code path from the ingest worker now that batching has run a week cleanly, and cut about 300 lines and two config keys
body:
Since the batched write path has been stable, I removed the old one-insert-per-event path. The worker had both, selected by a flag, and several tests ran twice for the two modes.

The diff removes about 300 lines, the flag, and a config key for the old pool size. The batch size setting stays. I also simplified the dead letter code, which had a branch just for the single insert mode.

Tests: the suite now runs in 41 seconds instead of 70, because duplicated cases are gone. I ran the replay of a day of traffic on staging, and the row counts matched the source.

Mara reviewed it quickly and only asked to keep a note in the runbook on how to roll back, which is now to deploy the previous image. The change is deployed to one worker so far. I will roll it out to the rest tomorrow if the metrics stay the same.

summary: Finished rolling out the ingest worker without the single insert path to all six workers, with no change in error rate or latency
body:
The cleaned worker image went to the other five workers one after another during the evening. I waited 20 minutes between steps and watched error rate, write latency and the dead letter counter.

All three stayed where they were. Write latency p95 is 11 ms on every worker, and the dead letter rate is 0.02 percent.

I updated the runbook with the rollback step and removed the old flag from the Terraform variables. Tobias applied the plan, which only removed an environment variable.

The ingest-batching branch can be merged and closed. Remaining small item: the dashboard still has a panel for the single insert mode, which I will delete tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the loader retry design for large files: per-chunk retries with backoff, a resume marker in Postgres and a cap on total attempts
body:
The document loader fails whole files when one chunk hits a timeout, and for files over 500 MB that means starting again from the beginning. I wrote a design for the loader-retry branch.

The file is split into chunks of 16 MB. Each chunk is retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds and with jitter. Errors that are not transient, like a parse error, are not retried and go straight to the failed list.

Progress is stored as a resume marker in Postgres: the file id, the last committed chunk and a checksum of the chunks so far. When a job restarts, it reads the marker and continues from the next chunk. If the checksum of the source file changed, the marker is dropped and the job starts fresh.

A total cap of 40 attempts per file stops endless loops on a broken source. After the cap, the file goes to a failed state with the last error text, and Sam can see it in the admin console.

Open questions: whether the marker table needs cleanup after success. I propose deleting rows 7 days after completion. I will start on the code tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the first loader-retry step: a resume marker table in Postgres and the chunk splitter, so a failed large file can continue from its last good chunk
body:
This was the first coding session on loader-retry after the design note from earlier this week. The goal was the groundwork only: a place to remember how far a file got, and a loader that cuts a file into chunks it can count. The retries themselves come next.

I added a migration for a table called loader_markers. It has the file id, the customer id, the schema version, the index of the last chunk that was written, a total chunk count, an attempt counter and an updated_at column. The primary key is the file id, and there is an index on updated_at for the cleanup job we will need later. The migration ran on the staging copy in under a second, since the table is new and empty.

The chunk splitter was the harder part. The old loader read a file as one stream and wrote events as it went, so a failure at 80 percent meant starting from zero. The new splitter cuts NDJSON files at line boundaries into chunks of 5,000 events, and it records the byte offset where each chunk starts. For CSV files it has to respect quoted fields that contain newlines, so I used the existing CSV reader and counted records instead of lines. That removed a bug I had in my first version, which split a record in half on a customer file with multi-line notes.

Each chunk now writes its events and updates the marker in the same Postgres transaction. That way the marker can never say a chunk is done when its rows are missing, and it cannot lag behind the rows either. I checked this by killing the loader process in the middle of a chunk, three times, and the marker pointed at the last complete chunk every time. No duplicate events appeared, because the events keep their ids and the insert already ignores repeats by event id.

I also stored the schema version in the marker when the file is first seen. A resumed run will compare it with the current version and refuse to continue if they differ. The check is not written yet, only the column, so I left a TODO in the loader and a note in the branch description.

Tests: six new unit tests for the splitter, covering empty files, a file with exactly one chunk, a file ending without a newline, quoted newlines in CSV, a very long single line, and a file whose last chunk is short. One integration test loads a 60,000 event file, stops after chunk 7 and checks the marker. All pass locally. Loading the same 60,000 event file takes about 4 percent longer than before, which comes from the extra marker update per chunk, and I accept that for now.

Next steps are the per-chunk retry with backoff, then the cap on total attempts, then a cleanup job for old markers. I will ask Mara to look at the transaction handling first, because it is the part that is easiest to get wrong.

summary: Added per-chunk retries with jittered backoff to the loader and found that timeouts from the object store needed a separate, longer deadline than parse errors
body:
Today I wrote the retry part of the loader-retry branch. Each chunk is attempted up to 5 times; the delay starts at 2 seconds, doubles and has up to 25 percent jitter. A total cap of 40 attempts per file is counted in the marker row.

The errors are sorted into transient and permanent. Transient are network resets, 503 from S3, and database deadlocks. Permanent are parse errors and schema violations. A permanent error fails the chunk at once and the file goes to the failed state with the line number.

While testing with a fault injecting proxy in front of S3, I saw that a slow response was counted as a failure after 10 seconds, even though 16 MB chunks sometimes take 12 to 15 seconds from a busy region. That led to retries that were not needed. I gave the read its own deadline of 45 seconds, separate from the connection deadline of 5 seconds.

Results of the proxy test with 10 percent injected failures: 50 files of 300 MB, all 50 completed. The average number of retried chunks per file was 2.1. Without the new logic, 46 of 50 files failed at some point.

I also added a metric for retried chunks and one for files in the failed state, and a log line for each retry with the chunk index and error class.

Next: the failed state view for the console, which needs a small API call, and a review from Mara.

summary: Mara reviewed loader-retry and asked for the marker cleanup job and a check that a resumed file still has the same schema version as the first attempt
body:
Mara went through the loader-retry branch this afternoon. She liked the transaction around chunk and marker, and the separate deadlines.

She raised two points. First, if the schema version changes between the first attempt and the resume, the chunks would be written under two versions. The loader should store the schema version in the marker and refuse to resume if it differs, then restart the file from zero. I added that.

Second, the marker rows need cleanup. I wrote a small job that deletes rows of completed files after 7 days and failed ones after 30 days, so that Sam can still look at failures. It runs nightly and deletes in batches of 1000.

She also asked about a hard limit on the backoff delay. The longest delay is 32 seconds now, which I made explicit in the config.

Tests pass. One more review round is needed tomorrow for the changed marker format.

summary: Looked at the Redis memory graph for the session store and found it steady at 38 percent with sessions expiring on time, so no change is needed
body:
Sam asked whether the session store was growing, because a support customer complained about being logged out. I checked the Redis memory by key family. Sessions use 1.1 GB, about 38 percent of the instance, and this has not moved in a month.

The session keys have a TTL of 12 hours that is refreshed on activity. I sampled 1000 keys and all of them had a TTL set. Nothing lives forever.

The logout of that customer was caused by a password change, which ends all sessions on purpose. I told Sam.

No change was made.

summary: Merged loader-retry after a staged rollout: the loader resumed 14 interrupted files in the first test batch of real customer uploads without a restart from zero
body:
After the second review round, Mara approved the loader-retry branch and I merged it. I rolled it out in two steps: staging in the morning, and production loader instances in the evening.

For the first real test, Sam asked a customer with large monthly exports to upload their batch of 60 files, from 200 MB to 1.4 GB. During the load, an S3 slowdown caused 14 chunk failures across 9 files. All 9 files resumed from their marker and finished. The longest wait was a chunk that needed 3 attempts and about 14 seconds in delays.

The row count of the loaded files matches the customer's own count of 48.2 million events. I also checked duplicates by event id, and found none.

One thing I noticed: the progress bar in the console showed percentages that jumped back after a retry, because it calculated from the attempt count. I changed it to read the marker's byte offset. Lena reviewed the small change in the API response.

Metrics: retried chunks were 0.9 percent of all chunks, and no file reached the cap. The failed state counter is 0.

The docs for the loader now say that a failed upload can be started again and will resume where it stopped, if the source file is unchanged. Sam will add that to the help page.

Remaining: watch for a week, then remove the old whole file retry code, which is still in as a fallback.

summary: Planned the cost review of AWS spend: listed the ten largest line items and found that NAT gateway traffic and idle staging instances are the quick wins
body:
I started the cost work with a look at the last three months of the AWS bill, grouped by service and by tag. Total spend grew 9 percent over the period, while customer volume grew about 6 percent.

The ten largest items are ECS compute, RDS, OpenSearch, the load balancer, NAT gateway data, S3, ClickHouse instances, Redis, data transfer, and CloudWatch logs. The first three make up 61 percent.

Two quick wins stood out. NAT gateway data cost is high because the workers pull container images and call S3 through the NAT; an S3 gateway endpoint in the VPC removes most of it. And the staging environment runs the full set of services all night and at weekends, with a cost of roughly 11 percent of the production bill.

Other candidates are longer log retention than needed in CloudWatch, and OpenSearch nodes that run at 30 percent heap. The last one is bound to the shard layout work that may come later, so I left it.

I wrote the list into the cost task with the estimated saving for each: the S3 endpoint at about 700 per month, the staging schedule at about 1,100, and the log retention at 250. Tobias will own the Terraform for the endpoint and the schedule.

No changes yet to the infrastructure. I asked Tobias whether the staging data needs to survive the nightly stop, and he said the databases can be stopped and started but the ClickHouse volume should stay.

summary: Added the S3 gateway endpoint and a night schedule for staging in Terraform with Tobias, and the NAT gateway traffic fell by 70 percent within a day
body:
Tobias and I wrote the Terraform for the two cost items. The S3 gateway endpoint is attached to the route tables of the private subnets, and a bucket policy check confirmed that the workers still reach their buckets.

The plan showed three resources added and two route tables changed. We applied it in staging first. A test load went through, and the NAT bytes for S3 dropped to near zero in the staging VPC. In the afternoon we applied it to production, and in the following hours the NAT gateway traffic went down by about 70 percent.

For staging we added a scheduled stop at 20:00 and start at 07:00 on working days, and full stop at weekends. It covers the ECS services and the Postgres and Redis instances of staging. The ClickHouse volume stays, as Tobias said, and only its instance is stopped.

A wrinkle: the first morning start failed because the Redis instance came up after the services, and they crashed on connect. We changed the order, so the data stores start first and the services start 10 minutes later.

Also, the developers sometimes need staging late. I added a small script that starts it by hand and a note in the README.

The saving is expected at about 1,800 per month together. I will check the bill at the end of the month to confirm. Next is the CloudWatch log retention.

summary: Set CloudWatch log retention per log group and found that the ingest access logs were the main cost, now kept 14 days with older logs going to cheap S3 storage
body:
CloudWatch costs were the third item on the cost list. I listed all log groups with their stored size and retention. Most had no expiry set. The ingest access log group alone held 2.3 TB.

I set retention in Terraform: 14 days for access logs, 30 days for application logs and 90 days for the audit related ones. For access logs, I added a subscription that sends them to S3 through Firehose, where they go to infrequent access storage after 30 days and are deleted after a year. Compliance asked for a year of access records, so we could not just drop them.

The old data was removed by the retention change over the next day. The stored size fell from 3.1 TB to about 0.5 TB. The ingestion cost stays, because the logs are still written.

To reduce that too, I looked at the debug logs of the ingest API. A line per accepted batch was written at info level, which gave 40 percent of the log volume. I changed it to a counter metric and kept the line at debug level only. Mara confirmed no alert rule uses that line.

The estimated saving is 600 per month from storage and 300 from ingestion. I will check it with the next bill.

summary: Wrote a Redis key naming guide after finding three families with different prefix styles, and renamed the oldest one with a dual read for a day
body:
While reading the Redis memory by key family for the cost work, I noticed the keys use three naming styles: colon separated with the service first, underscore separated, and some with the customer id at the front. This makes it hard to scan by pattern and to see who owns what.

I wrote a short guide in the docs: service, family, customer id, then the rest, separated by colons, for example search:facets:1042:abc. It also says that every family must have a TTL, and that the TTL is stated in the code next to the key builder.

The oldest family is the query cache, with keys like qc_1042_hash. I changed the key builder in the search API so that new writes use the new style, and reads try the new key and then the old one. After a day the old keys expire by their TTL of one hour, so no migration job is needed.

I checked the hit rate during the change. It dropped from 71 to 66 percent for about an hour, then went back to 71 as the new keys filled up.

The dual read can be removed tomorrow. The other two families stay as they are until they are touched for another reason. I added a lint test that checks that new key builders follow the guide, which already caught one in a branch of Lena's.

summary: Removed the dual read after the query cache rename and wrote up the day's work on cost and Redis keys, with Tobias checking the first numbers of the staging schedule
body:
The old query cache keys have all expired, as the Redis key count by pattern shows zero for the old prefix. I removed the dual read from the search API, and the code is simpler now: one key builder, one lookup. The hit rate stayed at 71 percent after the deploy.

Tobias looked at the first days of the staging schedule. The staging compute hours fell by 62 percent, which is a little less than the 65 expected, because two developers started it by hand on two evenings. That is fine.

I also went through the cost task list again. Done: the S3 endpoint, the staging schedule, the log retention and the debug log change. Open: the OpenSearch node sizes and the RDS instance class. Both depend on other work, one on the planned shard layout for the search index and the other on the Postgres load after batching, which dropped by 40 percent.

For RDS, I looked at the CPU and memory over the last month. CPU peaks at 28 percent now and the memory is mostly cache. A smaller class would still give a margin, but a change needs a failover, so I asked Tobias to plan it for a quiet night and to try it first on the staging copy.

I wrote a summary for the team with the savings so far: about 3,400 per month from the changes that are live. The bill of the next month will show if it holds.

Tomorrow: the RDS plan with Tobias, and a look at the S3 lifecycle rules for old exports.

summary: Wrote the S3 lifecycle rules for export and archive buckets: temporary exports expire after 7 days and audit archive files move to infrequent access after 60 days
body:
I looked at the S3 buckets for the cost task. The export bucket, where customers download their audit and event exports, had files from months ago, because nothing deleted them. It held 480 GB.

I added lifecycle rules in Terraform. Export files expire after 7 days, which matches the link validity in the console. Incomplete multipart uploads are aborted after 2 days. The audit archive written by the retention job moves to infrequent access after 60 days but is never deleted.

Before applying, I checked with Sam that no customer relies on an old link. The links expire after 24 hours anyway, so nobody does.

The plan was applied in the afternoon. The first expiry run removed 430 GB, and the estimated saving is 10 to 15 dollars a month for the exports and a bit more as the archive grows.

summary: Checked the RDS downsizing plan with Tobias on the staging copy: the smaller class held the replayed load with CPU at 41 percent, so the change is scheduled for a quiet night
body:
Tobias restored a snapshot of production to a staging instance of the smaller class, and I replayed a busy hour of traffic against it with the batched writes. CPU peaked at 41 percent, and write latency p95 was 13 ms, against 11 ms on the current class.

The memory was enough for the working set; the buffer cache hit rate stayed at 99.4 percent. The slow query log stayed quiet except for the reports query, which is slow on both.

The change needs a failover of about 60 to 90 seconds. The ingest workers keep events in the queue during that time, so nothing should be lost, and Tobias will announce the window to Sam for the customers' status page.

We agreed on a quiet night this week, with Tobias doing the change and me watching the queue lag. The saving is about 900 per month.

summary: Ran the RDS downsize on the quiet night window and watched CPU and connections; the smaller class held at about 45 percent CPU with no slow query alerts.
body:
Tobias and I ran the planned RDS class change in the quiet window after the staging replay from last week. The failover took 94 seconds, and the ingest workers reconnected on their own because the pool settings from the batching rollout allow that.

After the change I watched CPU, connections and replica lag for two hours. CPU sat between 40 and 48 percent, connections stayed under 30, and replica lag never passed 1 second. The slow query log showed nothing new.

One thing came up: the nightly vacuum on the events metadata table ran about 20 percent longer than before. It still finished well before the backup window, so I left it as is.

The saving is about a third of the database line item, which matches the estimate from the cost review. Tobias will keep the old class snapshot for a week in case we need to go back. I added a note to the Grafana database board with the time of the change, so later graphs are easy to read.

summary: Wrote the Terraform change for the S3 gateway endpoint policy so that only our buckets are reachable through it, after finding it allowed all buckets in the account.
body:
While reading the endpoint we added in the cost work, I saw that the policy was the default full access one. That is not a bug in traffic terms, but it allows any bucket reachable by the role, which is wider than needed.

I wrote a policy that lists the export, archive, loader upload and log buckets by name. The plan showed one in-place change and nothing to recreate.

Before applying I grepped the ingest and loader code for bucket names to be sure none was missing. I found one, the temporary bucket of the document loader, which was not in my first list, so I added it.

Applied it to staging first. A loader run with a large file and an export both worked. Production follows tomorrow once Tobias has looked at the plan.

summary: Investigated why the search API p95 latency crept up on Redis cache misses and found a query cache key that included a timestamp, so it never hit; fixed the key and saw hit rate rise.
body:
Lena noticed that a dashboard widget in the admin console felt slow, and the search API p95 had risen from 180 to 260 ms over two weeks. I started with the cache hit rate in Grafana. It had dropped from about 71 percent to 52 percent over the same time.

I listed the key families in Redis with a sampled scan, following the naming guide from the other day. One family, the saved search results, had keys that ended in a number that changed every minute. A look at the code showed that the saved search handler added the current time rounded to the minute into the key, a leftover from a debugging change.

That meant each saved search was cached under a new key every minute, and each old key just sat there until its TTL ran out. It also explains part of the Redis memory growth I saw in the graph earlier.

The fix removes the time from the key and uses the TTL of 60 seconds that was already set. I added a unit test that builds the key twice with a second between and checks that both are equal.

Before deploying I ran a replay of one hour of real query logs against staging. Hit rate on that replay went from 49 to 74 percent. I deployed it to production in the afternoon.

Two hours later the hit rate was at 70 percent and p95 was 195 ms. Redis memory dropped by about 8 percent as the old keys expired.

I did not touch the other key families. One, the facet counts, has a TTL of 10 minutes that might be too long for customers who ingest a lot, but that is a question for another day. I wrote it down as an open item with the numbers I had.

Next I will check the hit rate again tomorrow after the daily traffic peak.

summary: Answered Sam's question about how long a failed large file upload can be resumed: the resume marker is kept 7 days, and a changed schema version forces a restart.
body:
Sam asked for the support docs how long a customer can resume a failed large file load, and what happens afterwards. I checked the loader-retry code and the cleanup job that Mara asked for in review.

The resume marker stays in Postgres for 7 days after the last chunk attempt. After that the cleanup job removes it, and the next upload of the same file starts from zero.

If the schema version of the customer changed between the first attempt and the resume, the loader refuses to resume and says so in the load status. That is the check from the review, and it needs a new upload from the start.

I also checked the cap on attempts. A chunk is tried at most 6 times, and after that the file is marked failed with the last error text. The customer sees this in the admin console.

I wrote the answer in plain words and Sam added it to the draft page of the docs. I suggested that the page also show the error texts for timeouts and parse errors, since support gets asked about those most.

summary: Tried a Redis memory report per key family to find what grows, and found the facet counts family holds 31 percent of memory with a 10 minute TTL.
body:
I wrote a small script that samples keys in Redis and sums their size by key family, using the prefixes from the naming guide. The goal was to know where memory goes before anyone proposes a bigger instance.

Results from a sample of 200,000 keys: facet counts 31 percent, query cache 27 percent, rate limiter counters 9 percent, sessions 19 percent, rest 14 percent.

The facet counts are large because each entry holds the full list of values for a field. For three big customers, one entry can be over 200 KB.

I tried storing them compressed. It cut size by 60 percent, but added about 4 ms per read on the search API, which is too much for the autocomplete path. I dropped that idea for now.

A cheaper option is to cap the number of values stored per field at 500, since the console only shows the top ones. I wrote that down for Lena to check whether the console needs more.

summary: Capped facet count values at 500 per field after Lena confirmed the console only shows the top 50, and Redis memory fell by about 20 percent.
body:
Lena checked the admin console and confirmed that facets show the top 50 values, with a search box that queries the search API directly. So the cached list never needs more than a few hundred values.

I changed the facet builder to keep the top 500 by count and drop the rest before writing to Redis. A test checks that the order is by count and that ties are stable.

I also kept the old behaviour behind a config flag for a week, so we can go back without a deploy. The flag is off by default.

After the deploy to production I watched the memory graph. Over one hour, as old entries expired, memory fell from 61 to 49 percent of the instance. The facet family went from 31 percent of memory to about 9 percent.

The search API p95 did not change. Autocomplete stayed at the same speed.

One customer reported that a facet for a field with many distinct values looked incomplete. That was the search box case, and I checked that it works as designed. I told Sam so that support can say it.

Next I will remove the flag next week if nothing else turns up.

summary: Started the alert rules review for the ingest API: found 4 rules with no runbook link and 2 that have never fired, and wrote a list of what to fix.
body:
The alert rules are in code since earlier this year, so I could review them in one pass. I went through each rule in the repo for the ingest API and the workers.

Four rules had no runbook link in the annotations. They are the queue lag, the dead letter rate, the worker restart count and the 5xx rate. These are the ones the on-call would need at night.

Two rules have never fired in the last year, according to the Prometheus history. One checks a metric name that was renamed in the batching change, so it can never fire. That is a real bug.

The other one has a threshold of 95 percent for disk use on the workers, which is never reached since the logs go to CloudWatch. I suggest 80 percent.

I wrote the list into a ticket with a proposed order. The renamed metric comes first, then the runbook links. I did not change any rule yet.

summary: Fixed the dead alert on the renamed batch metric and added runbook links to the four ingest alerts, with a test that every alert rule has a runbook annotation.
body:
I started with the broken rule. After the batching change the metric for the insert duration was renamed from ingest_insert_seconds to ingest_batch_insert_seconds, and the alert still used the old one. I fixed the expression and used promtool to test it against a series with a slow batch.

The test file now has a case where batch inserts take 4 seconds for 5 minutes, and the alert has to fire. It did.

Then I wrote the runbook pages for the four alerts that had none. Each page has what the alert means, the first three things to check and who to call. For the queue lag I included the command to look at consumer lag per partition in Redpanda.

For the dead letter rate I wrote the usual level of 0.02 percent and that a jump over 0.5 percent means a bad batch from one customer, not an outage.

I added a CI check that reads all rule files and fails if a rule with severity page has no runbook annotation. It found one more rule that I had missed, the Redis connection alert, which I fixed.

The disk alert threshold went to 80 percent as proposed. Tobias reviewed and agreed.

Open: the rule that never fired is still unclear. I could not find any reason for it, and will leave it for now.

summary: Looked at a slow Postgres query in the audit log list and added a partial index on tenant and created time, which cut the query from 1.8 s to 40 ms.
body:
Support reported that the audit log page in the admin console was slow for one large customer. I found the query in the slow log: it filters by tenant and a time range and sorts by created time, descending.

EXPLAIN showed an index scan on tenant only, followed by a sort of about 600,000 rows. The query took 1.8 seconds.

I added a composite index on tenant and created time descending. On a copy of the production data the plan became an index scan with no sort, and the time was 40 ms.

The index build on production used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and took about 6 minutes without locking writes. I watched the replica lag during it, which stayed under 2 seconds.

The old tenant-only index is now redundant. I will drop it after a week, when I have checked that no other query needs it.

summary: Planned the audit export for compliance: formats, signing, size limits and delivery through S3, and wrote the first step, the export job table and a streaming reader.
body:
A customer in a regulated field asked for a full export of their audit log, and two others have asked since. I wrote a plan before coding. The export covers a time range for one tenant and is delivered as NDJSON, optionally CSV, in a file on S3 with a signed URL that lasts 24 hours.

The file is signed with a checksum file next to it, so the customer can check that nothing changed. The sha256 is enough for now, a real signature can come later if somebody asks.

Size is the main risk. The biggest tenant has about 9 million audit rows. The reader must stream, not load into memory. I decided on a keyset cursor over created time and id, in pages of 5,000 rows.

The temporary exports go into the export bucket, where the lifecycle rule expires them after 7 days, as set up last week.

I then wrote the first step. A migration adds an export_jobs table with tenant, range, format, status, row count, checksum and an error column. A second part is the streaming reader with the keyset cursor.

Tests cover an empty range, a range with exactly one page, and a range with rows that share the same created time. The last case was the interesting one, since a cursor on time alone would skip rows. With id as tiebreak it returns all.
