On the production-size copy the reader went through 9 million rows in 3 minutes 40 seconds, with memory flat at about 60 MB.

Next steps are the job runner, the upload to S3 and the endpoint in the admin API. I will ask Lena about the console button when the endpoint exists.

summary: Added the export job runner to audit-export: it writes the file to S3 in parts, records the checksum and marks failed jobs with the error, and was tested with the big tenant.
body:
The runner picks up jobs with status queued, one at a time per tenant, and sets them to running. It reads through the streaming reader and writes NDJSON through a multipart upload to the export bucket, in parts of 16 MB.

While writing, it computes the sha256 and stores it with the row count when done. A small checksum file is uploaded next to the data file.

For failures I made the runner abort the multipart upload and set status failed with the error text. A crash in the middle leaves the job in running, so I added a reaper that sets jobs running for over 2 hours back to queued, since a rerun is safe.

I tested with the biggest tenant, 9 million rows. The export took 6 minutes and the file was 3.1 GB. The checksum matched the one I computed with the command line tool.

One problem was that the signed URL helper used the default expiry of 1 hour. I changed it to 24 hours for exports.

summary: Added the audit export endpoints and a row level check that a user can only export their own tenant, then agreed the console flow with Lena.
body:
I added POST for creating an export and GET for status and the download link in the admin API. Creating needs the admin role, and the tenant comes from the session, not from the request body.

That last point I tested on purpose. A test sends a request with another tenant id in the body, and expects it to be ignored. Another test asks for the status of a job from a different tenant and expects a 404, not a 403, so ids do not leak.

I also limited exports to 3 running or queued per tenant, and a range of at most 400 days per request. Larger ranges must be split. The error text says so.

Every export request writes an audit log entry itself, with the range and format. It seemed right that exporting the audit log is audited.

With Lena I agreed the console flow. A form with range and format, then a list of exports with status, and a download link when done. She will build it against the contract this week.

Mara will review the branch tomorrow.

summary: Debugged a rate limiter bug where counters for API keys with colons in the name collided, found it through a customer report, and fixed the key format with a dual read for one day.
body:
A customer reported getting 429 responses although their traffic was far below their limit. I looked at the limiter counters in Redis for their key and saw a count much higher than their own requests.

The counter key was built as the prefix, the API key name and the window, joined by colons. This customer had two keys named team and team:eu, and the window part of one key looked like the name part of the other. So the counters for team:eu and team in a certain window ended up as the same Redis key.

I reproduced it in a unit test with those two names. Before the fix the test showed the shared counter. It was a real collision, and it only affects keys with a colon in the name. I found 3 such keys among all customers.

The fix uses the key id, which is a UUID, instead of the name in the Redis key. That follows the naming guide, which I had written but this family predates.

To avoid resetting the windows on deploy, I did a dual read for a day: the limiter reads the new key and, if it is missing, the old key, and writes only the new one. The worst case is a short extra allowance, which is fine.

I deployed it in the evening and checked the 429 rate for the three affected customers. It went to zero for the one who had complained.

I also scanned the other key families for the same pattern, names with free text inside a colon joined key. The saved searches family uses a name of the search. I checked that names there can contain colons and found the same risk. I opened a ticket for it but did not fix it today.

I wrote to Sam so that support can tell the customer the cause and that it is solved.

Tomorrow I will remove the dual read and the old key code.

summary: Reviewed the audit-export branch changes with Mara and fixed three comments: a missing index on export jobs, the checksum file name and a test for the reaper.
body:
Mara reviewed the branch in the afternoon and left comments that I went through one by one.

First, the export_jobs table is read by tenant and status in the runner, and I had no index for it. With few rows it does not matter now, but she was right that it will. I added an index on status and tenant.

Second, the checksum file was named after the job id, while the data file was named after the tenant and range. A customer who downloads both would not see that they belong together. Both files now share a base name, with .ndjson and .sha256 as endings.

Third, she asked for a test for the reaper, the part that returns stuck jobs to queued. I wrote one with a job whose start time is 3 hours old, and one with 30 minutes. Only the first must be reset. It passed.

She also wondered whether the 400 days limit should be configurable. I kept it as a constant for now, since a config key is one more thing to document, and we can change it when the first customer needs more.

A question from her about the CSV format: how are nested fields in the audit details written? I had flattened them with dots. I added a test and a line in the docs draft.

After the changes the CI was green. Mara approved with one remaining note on logging the row count every 100,000 rows, which I added as well.

Next is a staged rollout with a test tenant, then the first customer who asked.

summary: Planned the removal of the rate limiter dual read after a day of checks and investigated the same colon problem in the saved search keys.
body:
The limiter counters have been running on the UUID keys for a day. I checked the 429 rate across all customers and it was unchanged except for the drop for the three affected keys. That is the result I wanted before touching the fallback, so I wrote down the plan to remove the old key read and its test in a small follow-up change, and I did not merge anything yet. I want Mara to look at the diff first, since she wrote the first version of the fallback.

Then I picked up the ticket from yesterday about saved search keys. The key uses the name of the search, which users can write freely, including colons and spaces. Two searches could in theory share a key, for example one named a:b under one tenant and one named b under a tenant ending in a. In practice the tenant id is a UUID, so a real collision is unlikely, but a name with a colon would still break the prefix scans that the memory script uses. I reproduced the broken scan on staging with a search named with two colons and saw it skipped the key.

I sketched the fix: build the key from the search id instead of the name. This cache has a 60 second TTL, so I decided a dual read is not needed, because the cache would simply refill within a minute. I noted that the hit rate, which is about 70 percent now, will dip for a minute after the deploy, and I will watch it on the dashboard when the change goes out.

I also drafted a rule for the naming guide: never put free text from users in a key, only ids. I left it as a draft until the key change is reviewed.

summary: Ran a staged audit export for the first customer who asked, found the CSV had a wrong column order for rows without details, and fixed it before delivery.
body:
After the rollout of audit-export to production, I created the first real export for the customer in the regulated field, a range of 11 months with about 2.3 million rows, in CSV as they requested.

The job took 2 minutes and the file looked right at first. When I opened it in a spreadsheet to check, I saw that some rows had the columns shifted. These were rows with no details field.

The cause was in the CSV writer. The header was built from the first row it saw, and for rows without details the writer skipped the empty column instead of writing an empty value. So the number of fields was lower than the header.

I fixed the writer to use a fixed header list: id, tenant, actor, action, target, created, details. Missing values are written as empty strings. I added a test with three rows, one without details, one without actor and one complete.

I reran the export, checked that every row has 7 fields with a small script, and compared the row count with the database count. Both were 2,311,408.

I sent the signed link to Sam to forward to the customer, along with the checksum file and a short explanation of how to verify it with sha256sum. The link lasts 24 hours.

summary: Planned the search index shard layout problem for the first time: measured shard sizes per customer and found three customers hold 64 percent of the data in 3 of 24 shards.
body:
Search latency for the large customers has been uneven, so I pulled the shard stats from OpenSearch to see how the data is spread. The index is sharded by customer, with 24 shards in total.

The numbers were clear. Three customers hold 64 percent of the documents, and each of them sits in one shard. Those shards are between 70 and 95 GB, while most others are under 5 GB.

The large shards explain two things we have seen. Queries for the big customers are slower, with p95 near 400 ms against 120 ms for the rest. And the nightly reindex takes most of its time on these shards, since one shard is handled by one thread.

I sketched two alternatives. One is more shards for the big customers using routing. The other is sharding by month, so each shard holds a bounded amount of data, and queries over a time range touch only some shards. Most of our queries use a time filter, so by month looks better.

The downside of the month layout is that queries without a time range must hit all shards, and that deleting a customer's data is harder. I listed what I know about each.

I wrote this as a short document with the numbers and asked Tobias to think about the cluster side, since more shards means more memory for the cluster state. No decision yet, and no migration, only the plan.

summary: Wrote a script to estimate query fan-out under a by-month shard layout from real query logs: 83 percent of queries have a time filter of 30 days or less.
body:
To see whether sharding by month is realistic, I needed to know how many shards a typical query would touch. I wrote a script that reads a week of search API query logs and extracts the time filter of each query.

The logs hold about 4.2 million queries for that week. Of those, 83 percent have a time filter of 30 days or less, so they would touch one or two monthly shards. Another 9 percent have a filter up to 12 months, and 8 percent have no time filter at all.

The 8 percent are not small. Looking closer, most of them come from the admin console's global search box and from two customers' integrations that search by a ticket id. For ticket ids, a lookup that first reads a small id-to-month table could avoid the full fan-out. That is one idea for later.

I also estimated the cost for the full fan-out queries. With 12 monthly shards for a year of data, such a query hits 12 shards instead of 1. For the large customers that is similar in total work, but split in parallel, so latency may even be lower.

The script is in the tools folder with a README, so Tobias can rerun it with other windows.

Next I want to know how the index size would look after a year. That depends on the retention in the search index, which I need to ask about.

summary: Dropped the redundant tenant-only index on the audit log after a week with no queries using it, and the table writes got a little faster.
body:
A week ago I added the composite index on tenant and created time. Today I checked pg_stat_user_indexes for the old tenant-only index. It showed zero scans since the new index was created, while the new one had about 80,000.

Before dropping I also checked that no migration or admin query hint refers to the old index by name. A grep found nothing.

I dropped it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY during the day. It freed 410 MB. The insert time for audit rows went from about 1.1 ms to 0.9 ms in the metrics, a small but measurable change.

summary: Asked about how long the search index keeps events for the shard plan and found the raw event search has no retention, only the analytics store has the 13 months.
body:
For the by-month shard plan I needed to know how big the index will get over time, so I checked what the retention covers. The change from last week of the analytics store applies only to ClickHouse. It does not delete anything from OpenSearch.

I looked at the nightly reindex job and the delete paths. The search index keeps all events as long as the customer account exists, and the only removal is the customer deletion. So the raw event search stays whole, as I told Sam in the answer about what customers lose.

That means the index grows without limit. Today it holds 3.4 TB across all shards, and it grew about 6 percent in the last month.

For month shards this means the number of shards grows by one per month, and old ones are never merged away. I noted a possible plan: force merge shards older than two months into read-only, which saves memory.

I added these findings to the plan document and asked the user whether a retention for search is wanted. It is a product question, not mine.

summary: Upgraded the Redis minor version on staging and ran the load test; latency and memory looked the same and the upgrade is planned for production next week.
body:
Tobias prepared a new Redis minor version image with security fixes, and I used staging to test it. The upgrade was in place with a short restart, and the staging admin console had to log in again, since sessions are in Redis on that instance as well.

I ran the query replay from last week, with one hour of real search queries, and a separate script that hits the rate limiter. Latency p99 for cache reads was 1.4 ms before and 1.4 ms after. Memory for the same data was within 1 percent.

I also checked the connection behaviour, since we had trouble with the pool before. The client reconnected after the restart in under a second and no errors were logged by the search API.

One point for the production plan: the restart logs out all admin console users. I will choose a time at night and tell Sam, so support can warn customers. Tobias will do the production step.

summary: Wrote a design for per-key rate limit overrides on the rate-limits branch, with the table, the cache of overrides in Redis and a first working endpoint for admins.
body:
Several customers have asked for higher limits for a single API key, for example for a nightly import, without raising the limit for the whole account. At the moment this means a code change, which is wrong.

I wrote the design first. An overrides table in Postgres holds the key id, the limit per minute, an optional burst size, a reason and an expiry time. An override without expiry is not allowed, so temporary raises do not stay forever by accident.

The limiter reads the override from Redis, where it is cached for 5 minutes under a key with the key id, following the guide. On a miss it reads Postgres and writes the result, including a marker for no override, so that most keys do not hit Postgres each time.

When an admin changes an override, the endpoint deletes the Redis key, so the new limit applies at once and not after 5 minutes.

I then wrote the migration and the endpoints: PUT to set an override, DELETE to remove it and GET to list overrides of a tenant. Validation checks that the limit is between 1 and 10 times the plan limit, and that the expiry is at most 90 days away.

Each change goes into the audit log with the old and new values, as for the field boosts.

Tests cover the cases of an expired override, a deleted override with a stale cache entry and a limit over the maximum. The second one found a bug: I deleted the cache key before committing the Postgres change, so a read in between could cache the old value again. I moved the delete after the commit.

After that, the limiter code uses the override when present. I tested it in staging with a key at limit 10 per minute and an override of 50. The requests 11 to 50 passed and the 51st got a 429.

Sam asked for text for the docs, which I will write once the console part is planned.

Next steps are the burst handling and metrics for overridden keys, so we can see which keys use their raised limits.

summary: Added metrics and a Grafana panel for rate limit overrides, showing per key usage against the raised limit and the count of overrides that expire within 7 days.
body:
To see how overrides are used, I added two Prometheus metrics. One counts requests per override key and outcome, allowed or limited. The other is a gauge of the active overrides, with a label for days until expiry in buckets.

I took care of the label cardinality. Using the key id as a label for all keys would create thousands of series, so only keys with an override get their own label, and there are at most a few dozen of them.

The Grafana panel shows the usage as a share of the raised limit, and a table of overrides that expire within 7 days. The second one is for Sam, who will tell customers before a raise ends.

I also added an alert at low severity if an override key is limited more than 5 percent of the time, which means the raise is too small. It has a runbook link, as the new CI check demands.

A test in promtool covers the alert with a series of 10 percent limited requests. It fires after 15 minutes as intended.

One open question is the burst size. The first version uses the same burst as the plan, scaled by the factor of the override. I think that is fine until a customer says otherwise.

summary: Wrote the plan for moving the search index to monthly shards: naming, alias handling, and a dry run on a copy of the smallest customer's data.
body:
Started from the fan-out estimate of last week and turned it into a plan with steps. Indices will be named events-YYYY-MM with a write alias for the current month and a read alias per customer that carries a filter on the tenant id.

The plan has five steps. First, create the index template with the new shard count. Second, write a reindex script that copies one customer at a time. Third, switch the read alias. Fourth, check document counts against the old index. Fifth, delete the old shards after a week.

Open question: the three large customers have months with more than 200 GB, so one shard per month will be too big for them. I noted that the template needs a per-month override for shard count, and that the number must be set before the index is created, because it cannot be changed later.

I ran a dry run of the reindex script against a copy of the smallest customer on staging. It copied 1.2 million documents in about 4 minutes, and the counts matched. The script does not yet handle documents with a missing timestamp, so 31 documents went to a fallback index named events-unknown. I will check with Mara where these come from.

Next: size the per-month override for the big customers and write down the cutover order. No production change has been made.

summary: Found that 31 documents without a timestamp came from an old batch importer path and decided to fill them from the ingest time field instead of a fallback index.
body:
Followed up on the 31 documents that landed in events-unknown during the dry run. Asked Mara and she remembered that the first version of the CSV importer did not set the event time when the column was empty, so those rows only have the ingest time.

I searched the staging copy and then the production index with a count query for documents with no event_time. Production has 4,212 of them across 6 customers, all written in the first months after launch. None were created in the last year.

Two options were considered. One was to keep a fallback index for such documents. The other was to fill event_time from ingest_time during the reindex. The fallback index would need its own alias and its own queries, and customers could not find these events with a time filter. So I chose the fill, and the script now sets a flag field, time_inferred, to true on those documents.

I changed the reindex script and re-ran the dry run. All 1.2 million documents landed in monthly indices, the fallback index stayed empty, and the flagged documents were 31 as before.

I also added a test with three documents, one without event_time, to the script's test file. It passes.

Still open: whether the console should show the flag. I will ask Lena, but I think it is not needed. The production reindex has not started.

summary: Sized the monthly shards for the three large customers and found that two need four shards for their busiest months, which the index template can now express.
body:
Used the shard size report from the earlier session and grouped the data by customer and month. For most customers a month is under 20 GB, so one primary shard fits well. The three large customers are different.

Customer A has months between 90 and 140 GB. Customer B has months up to 210 GB. Customer C is steady at about 60 GB. My target is a shard of 30 to 50 GB, so A needs 3, B needs 4 and C needs 2.

A single template cannot know the customer if the index holds all customers of a month. That was the point I got stuck on. Two ways out came up. Option one: one index per month for all customers, with shard count by total size. Option two: separate monthly indices for the three large customers and one shared monthly index for the rest.

I wrote the numbers down for both. Option one gives a total of about 400 GB per month, so 8 shards, and the big customers share them with everyone else. Query routing by tenant id keeps a query on one or two shards. Option two gives more indices, and the alias logic is more complex.

I chose option one with custom routing on the tenant id, because it keeps the alias layer simple. The routing key puts a customer on a fixed subset of shards, so it must be tested for skew. I wrote a quick script that hashes the 40 tenant ids into 8 shards, and the largest shard got 19 percent of the data, which is acceptable.

I wrote the template with 8 shards and a routing requirement. Not applied to any cluster yet.

Next: test the template on staging with the load from the dry-run copy and compare query latency to the old layout.

summary: Loaded the staging copy into the monthly layout and compared query latency: queries with a 30 day filter ran about 2.4 times faster at p95.
body:
Applied the template with 8 shards and tenant routing on staging, then loaded a copy of about 60 million documents from three customers with the reindex script. It took just under two hours.

For the comparison I replayed 5,000 queries from the real query log, once against the old per-customer index and once against the new monthly one. The replay ran with 8 parallel clients.

Results for queries with a time filter of 30 days or less: p50 went from 38 ms to 19 ms and p95 from 410 ms to 170 ms. For queries without any time filter the new layout was slower, p95 520 ms against 450 ms, because they must touch every monthly index.

The slower group is about 17 percent of queries according to the earlier fan-out script. I think that is acceptable, but I want to look at what those queries are. Many are probably saved searches from the console that Lena could give a default time range.

The doc counts per customer matched in the old and new layout. Heap use on the staging nodes was a little lower.

I wrote the numbers into the plan document. Next: ask Lena about default time ranges and check how the nightly reindex job must change, because it reads the old index names.

summary: Went through the nightly reindex job to see what must change for monthly indices and found three places that hardcode the per-customer index name.
body:
Read the nightly reindex job from start to end, since it will be the first thing to break when the index names change. It lives in the search API repository, under jobs/reindex.

I found three places where the old name pattern events-<tenant> is built by string concatenation: the function that lists indices to rebuild, the one that creates the temporary target index, and the alias swap at the end. There is also a fourth, softer dependency: the job's log lines parse the tenant from the index name for the metrics label.

The job today rebuilds one customer at a time into a new index and swaps the alias. With monthly indices this changes a lot. A rebuild would be per month, and the old months almost never change, so a nightly rebuild of all months would be wasteful. My proposal is that the job rebuilds only the current and the previous month, and that older months are rebuilt only on request with a flag.

I wrote a small helper module, indexNames.ts, with functions for the monthly name, the alias names and the parse of a tenant from a name. The three hardcoded places now call it. For now the helper still produces the old pattern, behind a setting, so the code can be merged before the migration and nothing changes in production.

Tests for the helper pass, and the job still runs on staging with the old pattern. I also ran it with the setting on the new pattern against the staging copy, and the alias swap worked for the current month.

One problem remains: the job takes a lock per tenant in Redis, and with monthly indices the lock key would be per month. I left a comment and did not change the lock yet.

Next: decide the lock key, then ask Tobias about the backup window and index snapshots for the new layout.

summary: Changed the reindex lock to be per tenant and month and ran the job on staging with the new naming for the current and previous month, which took 11 minutes instead of 52.
body:
Picked up the open point from the last session, the Redis lock of the reindex job. Today the key is reindex:lock:<tenant>, with a TTL of 2 hours. With monthly indices a job per month could run in parallel, but I decided against it to keep the load on the cluster predictable.

So the key stays per tenant, and the job loops over the months for that tenant in order. This means no change in the lock itself, only a rule: the lock is held for the whole loop, and the TTL is refreshed after each month. I added the refresh call and a test with a fake clock.

Then I changed the job to rebuild only the current and the previous month by default. A flag, --months, takes a list or a range for the older ones. The default needs a safety check: if a month index does not exist, the job creates it from the template rather than failing.

I ran the job on staging with the new naming setting on. Before the change a full nightly run for the three staging customers took 52 minutes. Now it takes 11 minutes, and most of that is the current month. Document counts after the run matched the source database counts.

One bug showed up. The job computed the previous month from the local time zone of the container, while the indices use UTC. On the first day of the month at night this would pick the wrong month. I changed the code to use UTC everywhere and added a test with a timestamp at 23:30 on the last day of a month.

A second smaller thing: the log line that parsed the tenant from the index name now uses the helper, and the metric label is correct again.

What is left is the migration runbook: the order of customers, the checks after each one, and the rollback. I will write it next and ask Tobias to read it.

summary: Wrote the first draft of the shard migration runbook, with the customer order, the checks after each step and the rollback by switching the alias back.
body:
Wrote the runbook as a document in the repository under docs/search-migration. It starts with the smallest customers so that mistakes cost little, and ends with the three large ones.

For each customer the steps are: copy into monthly indices, compare document counts and a sample of 200 random documents, switch the read alias, watch p95 latency and error rate for one hour, and only then continue. The old index stays for 7 days.

Rollback is the alias switch back to the old index, which takes seconds. The weak point is writes during the migration. New events go to the old index until the cutover, and I wrote a step that replays the events of the copy window afterwards.

I left the timing open. Tobias should read it, especially the snapshot step and the disk space needed, since both layouts exist side by side for a week.

summary: Tobias reviewed the shard migration runbook and found that disk space would run out with both layouts side by side, so the order of customers now includes deleting old indices early.
body:
Tobias read the runbook and checked the disk numbers against the cluster. The data nodes are at 58 percent today. Keeping the old and the new layout for a week for all customers would push them past 85 percent, where OpenSearch stops allocating shards.

We changed the plan in two ways. First, the old index of a customer is deleted after 2 days instead of 7, once the checks are green and a snapshot exists. Second, the three large customers go one at a time with a gap of at least a day in between.

Tobias also asked for a snapshot before each customer, so that the rollback after the deletion of the old index is a restore and not only an alias switch. I added the step and the expected duration, about 20 minutes for the largest.

I updated the document and the disk table. We will ask Mara for a look at the replay step for writes, because she knows the ingest side best.

summary: Looked at the Redis memory growth after the facet cap and found that saved search results keep a TTL of one day, which is the next largest key family.
body:
After the facet count cap of last week, Redis memory fell, but I wanted to know what is next. I ran the per-family memory report on production at a quiet time. It samples keys with the MEMORY USAGE command and groups them by prefix, and it does not block.

The result: the query cache is still the largest family at 38 percent. Second is saved search results at 17 percent, then session data at 11 percent, the rate limiter counters at 9 percent, and the rest is small.

The saved search results have a TTL of 24 hours. I checked in the search API code why. A comment says the console shows the same result when a user reopens a saved search the same day. I looked at the access log of those keys with a counter on staging for a day. 91 percent of the reads happen within 30 minutes of the write, and almost none after 4 hours.

So a TTL of 4 hours should keep nearly all the hits. I did not change it right away, because Lena may rely on it in the console for a feature I do not know about. I wrote her a message with the numbers.

I also looked at the session store. Sessions have a sliding TTL of 30 days, and there are about 9,000 sessions for 40 customers. Many belong to people who left. The TTL is a product decision, so I only noted it.

Next step: wait for Lena's answer, then change the TTL on staging and look at the hit rate for a day.

summary: Lena confirmed the console does not rely on day-old saved search results, so the TTL is 4 hours on staging and the hit rate stayed at 88 percent.
body:
Lena answered the question about saved search results: the console reloads the result on every open anyway and uses the cache only as a speed-up. She had no objection to a shorter TTL.

I changed the TTL constant in the search API from 24 hours to 4 hours and deployed to staging. To get useful numbers I replayed one day of recorded console traffic at fast speed, in about 40 minutes, with the same read pattern as production.

The hit rate for this family was 88 percent with the 4 hour TTL. With the 24 hour TTL the same replay gave 90 percent. The memory for the family dropped by 71 percent in the staging instance.

The small loss of hit rate is not worth the memory, so I opened the change for review. The change is two lines and a test that checks the TTL is set on write.

I also noticed that the code writes the key and the TTL in two separate commands. If the process dies between them, the key stays forever. I changed it to a single SET with the EX option. A scan on production showed 212 saved search keys with no TTL at all, probably from exactly this case. I wrote a one-off script to set a TTL on them and ran it on staging first.

summary: Merged the saved search TTL change and cleaned the 212 keys without a TTL in production, then watched memory and hit rate for two hours.
body:
The review of the TTL change came back with one comment from Mara: log the TTL in the debug output of the cache layer so that it can be seen in a trace. I added that and merged.

After the deploy to production I ran the cleanup script for the keys without a TTL. It scans with SCAN in batches of 500, checks the TTL, and sets 4 hours on keys of the saved search family where it is missing. It found 212 keys, as expected, and set the TTL on all of them. It made no other change.

I then watched Grafana for two hours. Redis memory fell from 61 percent of the instance to 55 percent over that time, as the old keys with the long TTL expired or were rewritten. The hit rate of the family went from 90 to 87 percent, and the p95 of the search API did not change.

The commands per second stayed flat, so the new shorter TTL did not cause a burst of recomputation.

One more point from the scan: the same two-step write of key and TTL exists in the facet cache and in the rate limit override cache. I checked both. The facet cache uses SET with EX already. The override cache has the two-step write, so I opened a small ticket for it, since overrides are new and still on the rate-limits branch.

Next: look at the query cache, the largest family, and see whether its key space has duplicates after the key rename from last week.

summary: Checked the query cache key space for duplicates after the rename and found none, but 6 percent of keys belong to queries that ran only once.
body:
Sampled 20,000 keys of the query cache family and normalized each key by removing the tenant and the hash. I wanted to know whether the rename of last week left old and new names side by side. It did not: all sampled keys use the new prefix.

Then I counted how often each key was read before it expired, using the debug counter I had added on staging. 6 percent of the keys were written and never read again. These are queries with very specific filters, mostly from API clients that search for one event id.

One idea was to skip caching for queries that filter on a single id. It would save little memory, because those results are small. I dropped the idea and made a note.

So the query cache is in good shape. The memory work can pause here.

summary: Fixed the two-step write of key and TTL in the rate limit override cache on the rate-limits branch and added a test that kills the write between the commands.
body:
Worked on the ticket from this morning, in the worktree of the rate-limits branch. The override cache wrote the value with SET and then called EXPIRE in a second command. If the process died in between, an override without a TTL would stay in Redis, and a key would keep a raised limit longer than the admin chose.

I changed the write to SET with EX, and the same for the refresh path. The expiry of an override is a timestamp in the database, so the TTL is computed as the remaining seconds, with a minimum of 1 second so that a just-expired override is not stored forever by a zero value.

That last point mattered. Redis rejects EX 0 with an error, and the old code would have swallowed the error of the zero EXPIRE. I added a guard for TTL values at or below zero: such an override is not cached at all and the database is read instead.

The test uses a fake Redis client that fails after the first command of a pair. With the old code the key stayed. With the new code a single command is sent, so there is nothing to kill. I kept the test in a more general form: it asserts that every write to the override cache has an expiry argument.

I also ran the override endpoint by hand on staging. I created an override with a 90 second expiry, checked the TTL with the TTL command, which showed 89, and saw the key vanish after 90 seconds, after which the limit fell back to the default.

The branch tests pass. Next: handle the case where an admin shortens an override, which must lower the TTL in the cache too.

summary: Handled shortening of an override on the rate-limits branch: the cache entry is now rewritten with the new TTL, and a delete on removal prevents a stale higher limit.
body:
Continued on the rate-limits branch with the case left open this afternoon. An admin can change the expiry of an override. The first version only updated the database row, so the cache kept the old value and the old TTL until it expired. If the admin made the override shorter or removed it, the key kept its raised limit for as long as the old TTL.

I changed the update and delete handlers so that they write through. On update, the handler sets the cache entry again with the new value and the new remaining TTL. On delete, it deletes the key. The order is: database first, cache second, so a failure in the cache leaves the database right.

Because a failed cache write would leave a stale entry, I added a short fallback. If the cache command fails, the handler logs a warning with the key id and the limiter reads overrides with a maximum cache age of 60 seconds. For that I store the write time in the cached value, and the limiter ignores values older than 60 seconds when the flag is on. It is cheap, and it bounds the damage.

Tests: update to a shorter expiry, update to a longer one, delete, and a cache failure on delete. All four pass. I ran the rate limiter benchmark again and the added check on the age costs less than 1 microsecond per call.

I wrote a note for Mara, who reviews this branch, and listed the four cases in the pull request text.

Next: the admin endpoint for listing overrides and the console view are still open.

summary: Answered Sam's question about what happens to a rate limit override when its API key is rotated: the override follows the key id, so it survives the rotation.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel what happens to a raised limit when a customer rotates an API key. I read the code on the rate-limits branch to be sure.

The override is stored against the key id, not the secret value. A rotation creates a new secret for the same key id, so the override stays active until its own expiry. If the customer deletes the key and creates a new one, that is a new key id, and the override is gone.

I told Sam this and gave the one case to watch for in support: a customer who deletes and re-creates a key to rotate it will lose a raised limit and may report it as a bug. For that case, an admin can create the override again from the console, or support can ask us.

Sam will add two lines to the support docs. I suggested wording that tells customers to use the rotate function and not delete and create.

summary: Wrote the replay step for events written during a shard copy window and tested it on staging with a simulated ingest of 300 events per second, with no events lost.
body:
The runbook still had an open point: new events arrive while a customer is being copied into monthly indices. Without a fix they go only to the old index, and the copy misses them. Today I built the replay step.

The approach uses the ingest time. Before the copy starts, the script records a start timestamp. After the copy and before the alias switch, it queries the old index for documents with ingest_time at or after the start timestamp, and writes them to the new monthly index with the same document id. Since ids are the same, a document written twice is overwritten, not duplicated.

I tested with a load generator on staging that sends 300 events per second for one test tenant, which is more than the largest real customer at peak, about 180. During a copy of 10 million documents, the generator wrote about 70,000 events. After the replay the new index had 10,070,000 documents and the old one had the same count.

There was one problem in the first run. The count differed by 212 documents. The cause was the refresh interval: the replay query ran before the last writes were visible. Setting an explicit refresh on the old index before the replay query fixed it, and two more runs matched exactly.

A second edge case: a second replay is needed right before the alias switch, because the first replay takes time too. I made the script loop. It repeats the replay with the last end timestamp until the number of new documents is under 100, and then switches the alias in the same step as a last small replay. The loop converged in three rounds in the test: 70,000, 1,900 and 40.

For documents that are updated, not only created, the ingest time is not enough. Events are append-only in our schema, so updates do not exist for events. I checked the schema registry to be sure, and no event type allows updates.

I also wrote the metric names for the script: documents copied, documents replayed, rounds, and duration. They go to Prometheus through the push gateway, since the script is a short job.

Updated the runbook with the replay step, and asked Mara to review the script. The next piece is the check after the switch, comparing the counts per month between the database and the index.

summary: Mara reviewed the replay script and asked for a hard stop if the loop does not converge in 6 rounds, which is now in the code with an alert-friendly exit code.
body:
Mara read the replay script and had two comments. First, the loop had no upper limit. If the load was very high, the rounds might never get under 100 new documents, and the script would run forever with the alias unswitched. I added a limit of 6 rounds. After that, the script stops with exit code 3 and a clear message, and nothing is switched.

Second, she asked that the message include the number of documents of the last round, so the person on call can see how far from converged it was. Done.

I added a test with a fake source that always returns 500 new documents, and it exits with code 3 after 6 rounds. Merged after her approval.

summary: Built the post-switch check that compares per-month document counts between Postgres events metadata and the monthly indices, and ran it on the staging copy with zero differences.
body:
After the replay step, the runbook needs a check that says the copy is complete. I built a script for it today.

There is no full event table in Postgres anymore for analytics, but the raw events that go into search are counted in a metadata table, with one row per tenant, month and event type. The ingest worker updates it in batches. That makes a cheap source of truth, though it is only as exact as the worker's counting.

The script reads the counts for a tenant from Postgres and runs a count query per month on the index, using the tenant routing so that it hits only the right shards. It prints a table with both numbers and the difference, and exits with code 1 if any difference is not zero.

On the staging copy, the first run showed differences in 3 of 31 months. The differences were between 1 and 4 documents. I looked at the cause. The metadata table counts events when the worker accepts the batch, but the search index only gets events that pass the second validation step. A few events were rejected there and counted anyway.

That is a small data quality issue on the ingest side. I did not want to change the counting right now, because it touches the ingest worker. Instead, I made the check tolerant in a defined way. A difference is allowed up to 0.01 percent of the month's count, with a minimum allowance of 5 documents. The tolerance is printed in the table so nobody forgets it exists.

With the tolerance, the staging run passes. I also ran a deliberate failure test: I deleted 200 documents from one month of the new index, and the check caught it and exited with code 1.

I then looked at how the count query performs for the largest customer. 14 months took 2.1 seconds in total, so it is fine to run after each customer.

I wrote a ticket for the rejected-but-counted events so that Mara can decide on it, and linked the numbers. For the runbook, the check is now step 6 of 8, between the alias switch and the one hour observation.

Next: the observation step needs a dashboard in Grafana that shows the latency and error rate per alias, so that old and new can be compared side by side.

summary: Built a Grafana dashboard that compares search latency and errors for the old and the new index aliases, using a label for the layout on the existing search API metrics.
body:
The runbook says to watch p95 latency and error rate for one hour after each switch, and for that old and new must be comparable. The search API metrics did not have a label for which layout served a request.

I added a label, layout, with the values legacy and monthly, to the request duration histogram and the error counter. It is set from the alias that the query used. The cardinality is tiny, two values.

Then I made a dashboard with four panels: p50 and p95 by layout, error rate by layout, requests per second by layout, and the count of queries that touch more than 3 monthly indices, which is the fan-out. The dashboard has a variable for the tenant.

I tested it on staging with the replayed traffic from earlier in the week. Both layouts showed data, since the copied tenants were split between them, and the numbers matched what I saw in the replay earlier.

The dashboard json is in the repository under grafana/, and Tobias will import it with the rest.

summary: Wrote up the day's search migration work: replay step, count check and dashboard are done, and the open items are the rejected-event counting and the first production customer.
body:
Summary of the day for the record. The replay script for events written during a copy is done and tested with a load of 300 events per second, with no events lost and a stop after 6 rounds that does not converge. Mara reviewed it.

The count check against the metadata table is done. It has a tolerance of 0.01 percent with a minimum of 5 documents, because the ingest worker counts a few events that the second validation rejects. A ticket for that is with Mara.

The Grafana dashboard for old against new layouts is done, and the metrics have a layout label.

Still open: the choice of the first production customer, which I would pick from the smallest ones with an active console user so a problem would show quickly, and a rehearsal of the full runbook on staging from start to end, with Tobias watching the disk. I plan both for after the weekend.

summary: Added counting of rejected events to the shard migration replay and check, so events the new index refuses show up as numbers instead of silent gaps.
body:
The open item from the replay work was that events refused by the new monthly indices were not counted anywhere. In the staging runs the replay loop only logged a warning per rejected bulk item, so the count check could not tell a rejected event from a lost one. I added a counter per tenant and month that the replay script and the reindex job both increment, with the rejection reason as a label.

To test it I fed staging a few hundred events with a bad field type and 12 events whose month had no index. The first group was counted as mapping errors and the second as missing target. Both showed up in the output of the post-switch check next to the document counts, so a difference between Postgres and the index can now be explained line by line.

One surprise was that the bulk API returns a rejection for a whole item when the alias points at two indices during the copy window. The script treated that as a transient error and retried it up to the round limit, which wasted rounds. I now classify that case as a write alias problem and stop at once with the exit code Mara asked for.

The next step is to add the rejected counts to the Grafana dashboard and to write the expected value, zero, into the runbook check. Then the first production customer can be prepared.

summary: Picked the first customer for the shard migration with Sam's help and wrote down the reasons: small, an active console user and no open support case.
body:
Went through the customer list with the data sizes. Sam checked the support queue and told me which customers have open cases or a planned import this week, so that we do not move the index under someone who is just loading a large file.

Five customers were excluded for that reason. Of the rest, I looked at those under 5 GB with a console user active in the last week, because a problem in search would be noticed fast by a real person and not only by metrics.

The choice is a customer with 3.4 GB in 19 months. It has one console user who searches daily, according to the access log, and uses saved searches, which are a good test of the cache change from earlier this week. The saved search keys include the index alias, I checked, so they do not need a flush.

I wrote the choice and the reasons into the runbook, with a rollback contact, which is Sam for the customer message and Tobias for the cluster.

I also thought about the order after that. After the first one succeeds, the next four small customers can go on the same day, one after another with the one hour observation each. Then the medium ones, then the three large ones with a day between them.

One question that came up in the talk with Sam: do we tell customers? We decided on no message for the small customers, since nothing changes for them if it works. For the large three, Sam will prepare a short note to send the day before, in case of a slower search for some minutes at the alias switch. In the rehearsal the switch itself did not cause any visible gap, but a note costs little.

Open: the date. Tobias wants a quiet night and no deploys of the ingest side in the same period, and I want the on-call to know. I will agree it with both of them.

summary: Walked through the first production customer's index data with Sam's list of support contacts and checked that the migration night does not collide with their known batch import.
body:
After the customer was picked, I looked at how they actually use nebula, so the migration night does not hurt them. Their ingest logs show a steady 20 to 40 events per second with one larger NDJSON import that arrives shortly after midnight on most nights. That is exactly the time the runbook had in mind for the copy window.

I asked Sam whether the customer had said anything about the import time. Sam confirmed it comes from a scheduled job on their side and that they have no contact person at night, so we agreed to avoid that window. The migration is now planned for an hour after the import normally ends, and the replay step covers the short overlap if the import runs late.

I also checked the data size. The customer has about 1.3 million documents spread over 9 months, which is small enough that the copy should take well under half an hour on staging timings. The count check per month will run right after the switch and the old indices stay until the next morning.

I wrote these points into the runbook under the customer's name, with the import time and the rule to postpone if the import is still running at the planned start. The plan can now go to Tobias and Mara.

summary: Sent the plan for the first production migration to Tobias and Mara for a last look, with the customer, the order, the quiet night and the rollback contact.
body:
Collected everything from this week into one message in the team channel for Tobias and Mara. It has the runbook link, the dashboard link, the chosen first customer with 3.4 GB, the rehearsal numbers and the list of what changed in the tools after the rehearsal.

The changes after the rehearsal are the snapshot id as a required argument, the refresh interval reset, the tolerance of the count check and the six round limit of the replay. I also listed the open points: the console default of 90 days from Lena, which does not block the first customers, and the ticket for rejected events that are counted.

I proposed a quiet night for the first customer, with no ingest deploys during that time. Tobias will confirm the window and the snapshot space, and Mara will read the replay and count scripts once more. Nothing has been run on production yet.

summary: Ran the first dry run of the monthly shard migration on a production-sized copy of the smallest customer and it finished in 14 minutes with matching counts.
body:
Restored last night's snapshot of the first customer's index into the staging cluster and ran the migration script end to end with the new alias handling. The copy took 9 minutes, the replay step 3 minutes and the count check 2 minutes. The per-month document counts matched Postgres events metadata in every month, and the rejected-event counter stayed at zero.

One thing showed up in the log: the script created the monthly index for next month too early, because the month boundary used local time and not UTC. It did no harm on staging, but an event written just after midnight UTC could have landed in the wrong index. I changed the boundary to UTC and added a unit test with timestamps one second before and after the boundary.

I also checked disk use on the staging data nodes during the copy. The peak was 1.7 times the size of the old index, which fits the numbers in Tobias's reviewed runbook. Next is a second dry run with a simulated ingest running, so the replay is tested with real traffic shape.

summary: Second dry run with simulated ingest worked, but the replay needed 4 rounds to converge, close to the limit of 6 that Mara asked for.
body:
Ran the migration on the staging copy again, now with the ingest simulator writing 300 events per second for the customer during the copy. The copy window was 9 minutes, so about 160000 events arrived in it. The replay converged in 4 rounds, with the last round replaying 11 events.

Four rounds is more than I expected. Looking at the rounds, the first one took 70 seconds because it read the events by ingest time and sorted them in memory. I changed it to page through by sequence id, and the first round dropped to 22 seconds. With that the loop converged in 3 rounds in a second run.

The hard stop at 6 rounds stays as it is. I wrote down in the runbook that a customer with more than 1000 events per second needs a quiet window or a longer copy gap. The count check showed zero differences after both runs.

summary: Looked into why p99 search latency on the staging monthly layout is worse than p95 suggests and found a few queries that hit twelve monthly indices at once.
body:
The latency dashboard for the old and new aliases showed p95 about 2.4 times better on the new layout, but p99 was only 1.3 times better. I pulled the slowest 200 queries from the staging run and grouped them by time filter. Most of the slow ones had no time filter or a filter of a year or more, so they fan out over twelve or more monthly indices.

This matches the earlier fan-out estimate: 83 percent of queries have a filter of 30 days or less, and the rest are the slow tail. On the old layout those queries touched one index per customer, so they were not slower than average. On the new layout each one pays for twelve small searches and a merge.

I did not change anything in the search API yet. Options are a default time filter in the console, a cap on the fan-out with a clear error, or a rollup index for long ranges. I wrote the three options with rough costs into the plan document and will ask Lena what the console sends by default.

summary: Asked Lena what time range the console sends by default and found two screens that send no time filter at all, which explains most of the slow tail on the monthly layout.
body:
I sent Lena the list of slow queries from the staging run and asked which screens produce them. She looked through the console code in the afternoon and came back with two answers.

The first is the event detail lookup by id. It sends no time filter, because the id is unique. This one is cheap even on twelve indices when the search is a term query on the id, so it is not the real problem.

The second is the saved search screen. A saved search stores its query but no time range, and when it is opened it runs over all time. Lena said that about a third of saved searches of the large customers are like this. These are the queries in the slow tail.

I checked this against the query log of the last week. Of the queries with no time filter, 61 percent came from saved searches and 24 percent from the id lookup. The rest were API users.

We talked about the fix. Lena proposed that a saved search without a range gets a default of 30 days in the console and shows a note that the range can be widened. This changes behaviour for users, so Sam should tell the customers in the docs. I think it is the right choice, because all-time searches over the raw events were already slow on the old layout for the large customers.

The API stays as it is. A cap on fan-out would break existing integrations, and I do not want to do that during the migration. I wrote the decision into the plan: the console gets the default range, the API gets a warning header when a query touches more than 6 indices, and we revisit after the first three customers. Lena will make the console change on her side this week, and I will add the header in the search API tomorrow.

summary: Added the fan-out warning header to the search API and a metric for queries that touch more than six monthly indices.
body:
The search API now reads the number of indices from the resolved alias before it runs a query. If the number is more than 6, the response gets a header x-nebula-index-fanout with the count and a short hint to narrow the time range. The header is only added when the monthly layout is active for the customer, so it does nothing in production today.

I added a Prometheus counter, search_fanout_queries_total, with labels for the layout and a bucket for the fan-out size. The buckets are 1, 2 to 6, 7 to 12 and more than 12. The metric is also shown in the old-versus-new Grafana dashboard as a stacked panel, so we can see how many queries pay for the wide merge.

The tests cover three cases: a query with a 7 day filter, a query with a filter of a year and a query without a filter. They run against a small local OpenSearch with 14 monthly indices. The first run of the third test failed, because the test helper created the indices with the old naming. I fixed the helper to use the monthly name function from the migration code, so there is one source for the naming.

I checked that the header does not break the console. Lena's client ignores unknown headers, and the public API docs say clients must ignore them as well. I still asked Sam to add a line about the new header to the API docs before the first customer moves.

The change is merged to the main branch behind the layout check. Next step is the review of the plan by Tobias and Mara, which I sent last night.

summary: Tobias and Mara answered the first migration plan with two changes: a pause switch for the replay and a check of Redis cache keys that include the index name.
body:
Both replies were in this morning. Tobias liked the quiet night and the rollback contact, and asked for a pause switch in the replay script, so that he can stop it from the on-call laptop without killing the process. I will add a flag file that the loop checks at the start of each round.

Mara asked a question I had not thought about: do any cached query results use the index name in their key? I grepped the key builder in the search API. The query cache key is built from tenant, a hash of the normalized query and the alias name, and the alias stays the same after the switch. So cached results would stay valid and also be served after the switch, which is what we want, because the content is the same.

There is one exception. The facet cache uses the physical index name when it records the facet cap, which was added a few weeks ago. That key would be wrong after the switch and would just be a miss, so nothing breaks, but the hit rate would drop for that customer for a while. I changed the key to use the alias name and added a test.

I also updated the runbook with both points. The flag file path is in the section about the replay, and the key change is in the list of things to check after the first customer. After that the plan has no open questions, so I will schedule the first production night for the customer with Sam tomorrow.

summary: Added the pause flag to the replay loop and tested pause, resume and a hard stop on staging, including the exit codes that the alert uses.
body:
The replay loop now checks for a flag file at the start of every round. If the file exists, the loop logs that it is paused, sleeps 10 seconds and checks again. When the file is removed, it goes on at the same sequence id. A pause is not counted as a round, so it does not trigger the hard stop at 6 rounds.

I first wrote the check at the end of a round, but then a pause during a long round would have started only after it. Moving it to the start was simple, and I also added a check inside the paging loop every 50 pages so a long round can be paused in the middle.

Tests on staging, with the simulator at 300 events per second:
- pause after round 1, wait 2 minutes, resume: converged in 3 rounds, zero differences
- pause and never resume: the script waits and the alert fires after the maximum pause time of 30 minutes, with exit code 4
- a simulated burst that never converges: exit code 3 after round 6, as Mara asked

The exit code 4 is new. I added it to the table in the runbook next to the existing codes and to the alert rule for the job, which was in the alert rules repository. The alert text now says whether the job stopped because of a pause timeout or because it did not converge, because the first one needs a human to resume and the second needs a decision.

I also noticed that the script wrote its progress only to stdout. For the production night I want it in the log group as well, so Tobias can follow it. I changed the logger to write JSON lines and checked that the ECS log driver picks them up in staging. The remaining work for the day is the scheduling with Sam.

summary: Agreed with Sam on the first migration night for the small customer and wrote the contact steps into the runbook.
body:
Sam checked the support calendar and the customer's known activity. The night after tomorrow is quiet, and the customer's batch import runs on the first day of the month, which is not close. We set the start of the copy to 23:30 UTC, so the replay and the check are finished before the customer's morning.

Sam will send a short note to the customer's contact two days before, saying that a search maintenance may make results a bit slower for a few minutes. I wrote the text with him and kept it free of internal words, so it says nothing about shards.

The runbook now has a contact section. It lists who is awake on the night: me for the migration, Tobias on call for infrastructure, and Sam reachable in the morning for the customer. It also says who decides on a rollback, which is me, and that the rollback is the switch of the alias back to the old index.

One open point is the old index. Tobias wanted to delete it early because of disk space, but for the first customer I want to keep it for 48 hours, since the data is small. I added that exception in the runbook with the size, 6 GB, so the disk numbers still hold.

summary: Rewrote the rate limit override expiry job on the rate-limits branch so it removes cache entries and rows in one pass and handles a crash between the two.
body:
The expiry job for per-key rate limit overrides had a gap. It deleted the expired rows from the table first and then the cache entries in Redis. If the process died between the two, the cache entry kept the raised limit until its own TTL ended, and nobody could see why from the table.

I changed the order. The job now selects the expired ids, deletes the cache entries first and then the rows. If it dies after the cache step, the rows are still there and the next run finds them again, so the work is repeated, which is safe because deleting a missing key is not an error.

I added a test that kills the job between the two steps and runs it again. The first version of the test passed for the wrong reason, because the fake Redis client in the test returned 0 for the delete and the job treated that as a failure and stopped before the table step. I changed the job to ignore the count and only fail on a connection error.

Also fixed in this pass:
- the job read the clock once per row, now once per run, so a long run does not shift the cutoff
- the batch size is 200 ids per cycle, because the first draft used one big IN list
- a log line with the number of removed overrides per run

I ran the job against staging with 1500 generated overrides, half of them expired. It finished in 3 seconds and the table and the cache agreed afterwards. The metric for overrides that expire within 7 days from the Grafana panel went down as expected. Still open is the admin endpoint to list expired overrides for a short time, which Sam asked for.

summary: Added a short grace listing of expired overrides to the admin endpoint for Sam, kept for 7 days in a separate table.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel whether she can see which overrides ended recently, because customers sometimes write in when their raised limit stops and they are surprised. Right now the expiry job deletes the row, and the information is gone.

I added a table, rate_limit_override_history, with the key id, the old limit, the start, the end and the reason for the end, either expired or removed by an admin. The expiry job and the delete endpoint write a row there in the same transaction as they delete the override. A cleanup job removes history rows older than 7 days, and it uses the same loop as the expiry job.

The admin endpoint got a query parameter, state=ended, that returns the history rows. I kept it read-only and behind the existing admin role check. The response has the same shape as the active list, plus the end time and reason.

Tests cover the transaction, so a failed history insert keeps the override, and the cleanup of old rows. I ran the migration on staging and checked the explain output for the lookup by key id, which uses the new index on the key id and end time.

I told Sam where to find it and asked her to say if 7 days is too short. She said it is fine for support cases, but she would like a note in the docs about it. I put that on her list for the docs work.

summary: Looked at Postgres autovacuum on the events metadata table after a slow report query and set a lower scale factor for that table only.
body:
The reports query that Mara watches ran 3 times slower this afternoon than in the morning. I looked at pg_stat_user_tables and saw that the events metadata table had 18 percent dead tuples, because the default autovacuum threshold of 20 percent is high for a table with 90 million rows.

I did not run a manual vacuum on production in the middle of the day. Instead I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit higher for this table only, with ALTER TABLE. The next autovacuum started within minutes, ran for 26 minutes and removed about 16 million dead tuples.

After that the reports query went back to its normal time. The index sizes stayed large, so I noted a reindex of two indexes for a quiet night. I checked the size with pg_relation_size and one index was 40 percent bigger than a fresh one in the staging copy.

I also checked the I/O graph during the vacuum. Read IOPS rose but stayed under half of the limit, and the ingest latency did not change. I set an alert on dead tuple ratio above 10 percent for the three biggest tables, because the problem was only seen through a slow query.

The cause is the update pattern from the migration check, which updates a status column on many rows. I will look at whether the column can live in a separate small table later.

summary: Ran a safe reindex of two bloated Postgres indexes with concurrent builds and the query time on the reports query improved by about a fifth.
body:
Because the earlier vacuum left the two indexes on the events metadata table large, I rebuilt them tonight. I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY with a new name, then dropped the old one, so no write lock was held. The first index was 11 GB and the new one 7.4 GB. The second went from 6.2 GB to 4.9 GB.

The build of the bigger one took 38 minutes. During the build, the ingest latency stayed flat, and the Postgres CPU went up by about 15 percent. I paused the build once for a few minutes when a deploy was running, and nothing was lost.

One problem came up. The first attempt to drop the old index failed, because a unique constraint depended on it. I could not drop it directly, so I created the new unique index first and used ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX in a short transaction, then dropped the old constraint. That needed a brief lock of less than a second. I checked in the pg_locks view that no long query was waiting.

Results on the reports query, five runs each before and after:
- before: median 2.9 seconds
- after: median 2.3 seconds

That is roughly a fifth faster. It is less than I hoped, so the main cost is probably in the sort and not in the index scan. I saved the explain plans in the notes. A later step may be a partial index for the active status rows.

I wrote the exact steps for the unique constraint swap in the Postgres notes, because the next bloated index will have the same dependency.

summary: Prepared the first production migration night for the small customer to the monthly shard layout: staging rehearsal, checks and the plan with Tobias, with nothing run on production yet.
body:
Spent the day getting ready for the first production migration night for the small customer. The run is planned for 23:30 UTC, with Tobias on call. Earlier I tested the pause flag path on staging again, including pause, resume and a hard stop, and checked that the exit codes match what the alert expects.

I rehearsed the copy of a staging index of similar size into the monthly layout. The index has about 2.1 million documents over 19 months, so the plan is 19 monthly indices with one shard each. The copy on staging took 7 minutes. I wrote a small script that compares the settings the index template puts on every monthly index with the staging copy, and it showed no differences.

The replay loop on staging converged in 3 rounds with the rejected-event counter at zero. I prepared the count check, which compares the per-month document counts with the Postgres events metadata, and a set of 50 sample queries taken from the customer's real query log. The script will run them against both aliases and compare hit ids and ordering. I expect ties in score to come out in a different order, so I added a note in the script to list those separately and not count them as failures.

For the switch I prepared one alias update request with two actions, remove the old index and add the new ones, so there is no moment without an alias. I also built the old-versus-new dashboard so I can watch error rate and p95 latency for the customer.

Things that did not go as planned:
- the log line from the replay did not include the customer name in the first round on staging, so I am fixing that before tonight
- the facet cache key change still needs a check on staging for misses

The old index will be kept for 48 hours after the switch. I will write timings into the runbook after the run, so the next customers have real numbers. Nothing has been touched in production yet.

summary: Prepared the check of the first customer's morning traffic for the monthly search layout and planned the next small customers, with no migration done yet.
body:
I looked at the dashboard for the first small customer to decide what to compare once their users are online. I wrote down the baseline from the old layout: p95 search latency in the morning hours was 185 ms last week, with no errors. I also noted the fan-out metric, which counts how many indices a query touches, as the number to watch once the customer moves.

The facet cache keys are built from the alias name, so the hit rate should not change when the alias is repointed. I took a snapshot of the current hit rate and of Redis memory so I can see later whether anything moves.

While going through the saved searches of this customer I found one without a date range. On a monthly layout it would touch every index, so I expect a slow query there. Lena's console does not set a default range yet, so I added a note to her list and checked that the response header with the fan-out count is ready in the search API.

I wrote to Sam that the first night is still ahead, that the customer does not have to be told anything beyond the agreed contact steps, and that I would report after the night. The next customers are three small ones. I plan them in two steps, one per night, so that anything unusual can be seen before the next.

summary: Wrote the plan for the next three small customers on the monthly shard layout, with one night each and a script that refuses to switch the alias if the count check shows any difference.
body:
The runbook for the first production night was written for one run by hand. I turned it into something that can run three times with different input. The migration script now takes a customer id and a list of months, and it writes a result file with timings, counts and the replay rounds. So far I have only run it against the staging copy, and nothing has been started on production for these customers.

I added a rule that the script does not switch the alias if the count check has any difference or the rejected-event counter is above zero. When I rehearsed the first night I imagined making that decision by hand, and I would rather have the script refuse to go on, with an exit code and a message. A person can still force it with a flag, but only after reading the difference list.

The order of the next customers is based on size, and on what Sam knows about them:
- customer B: 3 GB, mostly API access, no console users
- customer C: 5 GB, a batch import every night at 02:00 UTC, so the copy must be done before that
- customer D: 8 GB, a support case closed last week

For C, I planned the start at 20:00 UTC, so the migration is finished before the import. If the replay is not done by 01:30, the script pauses itself and I decide. I also asked Tobias to check that the import job does not write directly to the old index name. He said it uses the alias, so it is fine.

Disk space: if the old indexes are deleted early, after 48 hours, the peak across the three is 14 GB on the data nodes, well under the free space Tobias reported. I added a line to the plan with the free space check before each night, as a command to run and a threshold of 40 GB.

The plan is in the repository next to the runbook. I also drafted a dashboard panel that will list migrated customers, so the state is visible without reading notes, and it will be filled in once the nights have run.

summary: Prepared the migration of customer B to the monthly layout with a dry run of the new stop rules, and left the production run for a later night.
body:
Customer B has 3 GB of data over 14 months and almost no console users, so it is the right one to go first after the small test index. I did not start the production run today. I spent the evening on the script and on the checks around it.

I started a dry run at 21:00 UTC against a copy of B's data on staging, with the new version of the script that takes the customer id and writes a result file. The free space check passed on the staging nodes, and I added a line to the plan that production needs at least 200 GB free on the data nodes before a real run begins. The copy on staging took 5 minutes. The replay converged in 2 rounds with 9 and 0 events, and the count check showed zero differences over 14 months, which is what I want to see again in production.

One thing I had not seen before: the script's check of the index template found that the template version on production was one number behind staging. The difference was a comment-only change, so it is harmless, but the script printed a warning that I think is useful. I made the template version part of the result file, and I will bring production to the same version before the real run.

I also tested the pause flag during the replay on staging. I created the file, saw the log line about the pause, waited a minute and removed the file. The loop went on from the same sequence id, so the stop rules work as written.

For latency I looked at B's traffic from last week. It is low, about 40 requests in an hour, so p95 will be hard to read after the switch. I will compare the old and new dashboards for errors instead and not trust the percentile alone.

I wrote down that the old index of B must be kept for 48 hours after the real switch and added a calendar note and a runbook entry as a template, so it is not forgotten when customers C and D follow in the same week.

Next is the real run for B tomorrow evening, and I will check the schedule of the nightly import with Sam in the morning so the two do not overlap.

summary: Prepared customer C for the monthly shard layout by reading the import tool's code, and found that its verification step reads the document count from the old index name, which needs a fix first.
body:
I planned the run for customer C at 20:00 UTC, so that it would finish well before the nightly import at 02:00. Before starting anything I wanted to know what else touches the customer's index, so I went through the import tool's code. Tobias had said that the import job uses the alias, and that is true for writes. But the import tool also has a verification step at its end that reads the document count through the cat API with the old physical index name.

That matters because after a migration the old name stays for 48 hours but no longer receives writes. The verification would then report a wrong count and mark the import as failed. Nothing has been switched for C yet, so the problem is only on paper for now.

The tool is a small Go program that Mara wrote. The count call is in verify.go, and it builds the index name from the customer id with the old pattern. The fix is to use the alias name in that call. A count through the alias sums over all monthly indices, so it gives the total. I changed the line and ran the tool's tests, which passed. Then I tested it on the staging copy of C with a sample file of 1000 events. The count after the import went up by 1000 as expected.

I told Mara what I changed, because it is her code, and asked her to review it before anything is deployed. She replied that she would have caught it in review and asked me to grep for other places that build the old pattern.
