I did that: the reindex job was already fixed, and one script in the admin tools folder used it for a one-off cleanup. I changed that too and put both changes in the same review.

The migration of C is not started. It waits for the fixed tool to be deployed, and I will do the free space check and the copy once that is done, in a window that leaves enough room before the import. For customer D, I added the grep for the old name pattern to the migration checklist, so that every customer migration starts with it.

summary: Prepared the deletion of the first customer's old search index and checked that nothing uses it, without deleting anything.
body:
The 48 hours for the first customer's old index end later today, so I spent this session preparing the deletion and did not delete anything. I checked the OpenSearch search slow log and the request stats for the index name. There had been no reads or writes since the switch except my own comparison queries.

I also looked for the old name in the config of the console and in the cron jobs of the new AWS-style definitions in Terraform, and found nothing. The check commands are saved in a small script, so they can be run again right before the deletion and give the same answer.

I started a runbook step for the deletion. It lists the check commands, the delete index call and the disk graph to watch afterwards. The graph should show about 6 GB of free space coming back, and I wrote that number into the step so I can compare it with the real result later. The index stays in place until the 48 hours have passed and I have run the checks once more. Customer B's deletion would follow the day after, and C's the day after that.

summary: Prepared the migration of customer D, the largest of the four small customers, to the monthly search layout and studied its ingest pattern, without starting the copy.
body:
Customer D has 8 GB over 26 months. I ran the new grep for the old index name pattern first and found nothing new. Then I did a dry run of the script against a copy of D's mapping on the staging cluster, with no real data moved and no alias switched. The free space check on the production cluster showed 198 GB, which is plenty for the copy.

I wrote down what the copy should do for D. Earlier customers took 5 to 11 minutes in the test runs. The chunked copy replays the last three months at the end, and the script stops on any count difference or when a replay round finds more than the hard stop of 6 events. D is the largest of the four small ones, so I expect more replay rounds than for the others, and I want to watch the first one closely.

I looked at D's ingest pattern in Grafana. It sends large batches every 10 minutes. If one of them lands in the last minutes of the copy, the replay will need more rounds. For customers with such a pattern, the script could wait for a gap between batches before it starts the last copy step. I put this idea into the notes as an option and did not change the script, because the current rules already stop safely when the replay does not converge.

I also picked 100 sample queries from D's log and saved them, so that the comparison of hit ids and ordering between the old and the new alias can run right after the switch. Earlier comparisons showed small ordering differences only where scores were equal, so I will treat those as expected.

D has two console users, so I checked their usual hours and picked a night slot when they are not active. I wrote the slot into the runbook. The next step is to run the migration in that slot, then review the results of all four customers with Mara and Tobias before the medium customers and then the three large ones.

summary: Prepared the review of the planned first four customer migrations to the monthly search layout, with the open questions for the medium customers, and moved no customer yet.
body:
I started the review document for the small customers, but no customer has been moved to the monthly layout yet, so there are no real timings or latency numbers to put in it. I built the table with empty columns for size, copy time, replay rounds, count differences and the rejected-event counter. I filled in only what I knew from staging: the sizes of the four small customers, from about 2 to 8 GB, and the staging estimate of about 2.4 times faster for search latency at p95.

I also wrote the list of things to check in the first runs, based on what I found while reading the script and the tests:
- the import tool must count through the alias and not through the old index name
- the month boundary in the script should use UTC and not local time
- the facet cache key should not use the physical index name
- the replay may need more rounds for a customer with large periodic batches

Then I thought about the medium customers, who have 20 to 60 GB. A copy of that size would take roughly 30 to 90 minutes by my estimate from the staging runs, and the replay may not converge in 6 rounds without a quiet window. I wrote down two ideas. The first is to wait for a gap in the ingest for a customer, based on the batch times of the last 24 hours. The second is to run the copy in month chunks, oldest first, so only the current month needs the replay.

I tried the chunk idea on staging with the data of customer D. The old months copied without any replay, and the current month needed a replay of only 90 events. The total time was the same, but the window where replay matters was much smaller.

I sent the draft and the two ideas to Mara and Tobias. Mara will check the chunk idea for late events, because the batch importer can write into older months when a customer uploads an old file. For that case I will plan a final replay for the last 3 months, not only the current one.

summary: Mara's late-event case from the batch importer changed the plan for the chunked copy: the replay routes every event by its timestamp, and a new test covers it.
body:
Mara read the review and confirmed the late-event case. The batch importer for CSV and NDJSON files can write events with old timestamps, and customers do upload files that are a few weeks old. If the copy of an old month is already done, such an event would land in the old index but not in the new monthly index. Wait, the alias only points at the new indices after the switch, so the problem is the events written to the old layout during the copy, with an old timestamp.

To cover it, I changed the plan for the chunked copy. The old months are copied first, oldest to newest. The replay step then reads all events written since the copy started, with a sequence id above the starting mark, and routes each of them to its monthly index by timestamp. This is what the replay was meant to do, but I had assumed that all replayed events belong to the current month.

I checked the replay code and the routing was already by timestamp, so the code needed only a test. I wrote one with 5 events in 4 different months arriving during a simulated copy, and it passed. The count check runs the comparison for all months only after the end, which is still right, so I left it alone.

I also added the count of months touched by the replay to the result file, so we can see how many old months get late events. That number will be good to know for later customers.

For the wait for a gap in the ingest, I wrote a small function that reads the batch times of the last 24 hours from the ingest metrics in Prometheus and finds the next gap of at least 90 seconds. It is optional, behind a flag. I tested it on staging with the data of D, and it picked a gap about 4 minutes after the start.

I also talked with Tobias about disk space for the medium customers. At 60 GB, the peak with both layouts is 1.7 times, so about 100 GB for one customer. The data nodes have 190 GB free, so only one medium customer can be in flight at a time, and the old indices should go within 24 hours for those, not 48. He agreed. No medium customer has been moved yet.

summary: Checked reads and writes on the old search indices of customers B and C after their 48 hours and prepared the deletion without deleting anything yet.
body:
The 48 hours for customers B and C ended today. I checked reads and writes against the old index names, using the index stats and the slow log, and saw no activity after the switch except from my own comparisons.

For C, I looked closely at the import at 02:00, because the verification step had been the problem. Last night's import went through, so the fix works in production, and I saw its count line in the log.

I did not delete anything yet. I wrote down the expected result so I can compare it afterwards: the old index of B should free about 3 GB and the old index of C about 5 GB, which are the sizes in the result files. I also planned to delete them one at a time with the delete index API and to wait between the two to watch the cluster state.

While reading the runbook step I found one thing to change: the check commands should use the cat indices API with the byte flag, so the sizes are comparable with the result files. I changed the commands in the runbook text and tested them on a small index.

Disk space on the data nodes is at 208 GB free for now, and I noted this as the number to compare with after the deletion. D's old index has to stay until its own 48 hours end, so it is not part of this.

I also looked at the migrated customers panel on the dashboard. It counts the customers on the monthly layout, and the remaining count has to be right before I touch it, so I wrote down which customers are still on the old layout and left the three large ones at the end of the list. The deletion is planned for tomorrow morning, after a last look at the slow log.

summary: Planned the next phase of the search shard migration: wrote down what is ready for the medium customers and what is still open, with no new customer moved yet in this session.
body:
Wrote up the plan for the search shard migration before the medium customers start. The four small customers are already on the monthly layout, and this session only prepared the next stage. Nothing was copied or switched today.

What is ready for the medium customers:
- the chunked copy, oldest months first, with the replay for the last 3 months at the end
- routing of replayed events by timestamp, with a test for late events in old months
- an optional wait for a gap in the ingest
- the stop rule if the count check shows a difference or events were rejected

I went through the stop rule again with the numbers from the earlier small runs and wrote it into the runbook in plain words, so that whoever runs a night does not have to guess when to halt.

What is open: the console default of 30 days for saved searches, which Lena is working on, and the line in the API docs about the fan-out header, which is Sam's. Neither blocks the next customers, but the large ones will need the console change, because their saved searches would otherwise fan out over many indices.

The next steps are to pick the first medium customer with Sam, check disk space for one in-flight customer at a time, and plan a quiet night for the first run. I want the first medium run to be a customer with no nightly batch, to see the replay at a bigger size without another variable. I also listed the questions to ask Sam about import times so the choice is ready when we talk.

summary: Planned the medium customer wave of the shard migration: three customers, two nights each, with the chunked copy and a stop on any count difference.
body:
Went through the list of medium customers with the numbers from the four small migrations. Their indices are 10 to 40 times larger, so the copy takes hours instead of minutes, and the old plan of one night per customer no longer fits.

The chunked copy that Mara asked for splits the copy by month. That means a night can stop after any chunk and continue the next night. I wrote this into the plan: night one copies the older months, night two copies the recent months, replays the last three months and switches the alias.

I estimated the copy time from the dry run on customer D. It copied about 2.1 GB in 5 minutes. The smallest medium customer has 38 GB, so the estimate is about 90 minutes plus replay. The largest of the three has 120 GB, which is about 5 hours, so it needs the two-night split.

The disk is the other limit. During the copy, old and new indices exist side by side, so the cluster needs room for twice the customer's data. I checked the current free space and it is enough for one medium customer at a time but not for two at once. The plan therefore runs the customers strictly one after another.

I also added a rule for the old indices: they are deleted after 48 hours, as before, but only when the disk graph is below the threshold in the runbook. Otherwise the next customer waits.

Open points are the order of the customers and the quiet night for each. I will ask Sam for the batch import times and the support contacts of the three. The plan is not sent yet, since it needs Tobias's check of the disk numbers first.

summary: Sam sent the batch import times and contacts for the three medium customers, and one of them imports at night, so the order of the nights changed.
body:
Sam answered the questions from yesterday with a list. For each of the three medium customers it has the import times, the main contact and whether they have an open support case.

Customer E runs a large NDJSON import every night at about 02:00. That collides with a copy of several hours and would produce a lot of late events. I moved E to the last place, and we will ask them whether the import can pause for one night.

Customer F has no regular import and only light traffic on weekends, so it goes first. Customer G has an open support case about a slow dashboard, which is not about search. Sam thinks it is safe, but we will close the case first so that a complaint is not mixed with the migration.

I changed the plan: F first, then G, then E. I wrote the contact steps for each into the runbook. The plan now only needs the disk check from Tobias before it goes out to the team.

summary: Tobias confirmed the disk numbers for the medium wave and asked for a free-space check in the script before every chunk, which is now in the copy step.
body:
Tobias looked at the disk plan this morning. His own numbers match mine: one medium customer at a time fits, and two do not. He added that the cluster grows on the days when the nightly reindex runs, so the free space I measured is slightly too good.

He asked for a check in the script itself and not only in the runbook. Before each chunk, the copy step now reads the free space of the data nodes and compares it with the size of the chunk times 1.5. If the space is smaller, the script stops with its own exit code, so the alert can tell it from a count difference.

I wrote the check as a small function in the migration script and a test for it. The test uses a fake cluster stats response with three cases: enough space, too little space, and a node that does not answer. The last case also stops, because an unknown state should not continue.

I ran the copy on the staging copy of customer F with the check on. It passed on all 36 chunks, and the extra calls cost about 40 ms per chunk, which does not matter.

The free-space exit code is 14. I added it to the alert description so that whoever is on call knows that it means waiting, not a problem with the data. I also noted it in the runbook next to the exit codes of the pause switch.

Next is a full dry run of F on a production-sized copy, and after that the real night.

summary: Dry run of customer F on a production-sized copy took 84 minutes and the replay converged in 3 rounds with matching counts.
body:
Ran the full dry run for customer F on a copy of its production index, about 38 GB. The copy was chunked by month, 36 chunks in total, and I let it run without pausing.

The copy took 71 minutes. Replay needed 3 rounds, the last one with 212 events, and then the count check compared per-month document counts with Postgres. All 36 months matched, and the rejected-event counter showed 0.

Total time was 84 minutes, close to my estimate of 90. The slowest chunks were the three most recent months, which hold about 40 percent of the data. That fits the shape of the customer, whose traffic grew over the last year.

I watched the cluster during the run. Indexing latency on the data nodes went up a little, but search p95 stayed under 120 ms for the other customers. I will still ask Tobias whether we should lower the copy rate for the larger customers.

One thing was odd. The count for the oldest month was off by 2 at first, and then it matched after a refresh. The check ran right after the last bulk call, before the refresh interval. I added an explicit refresh before the check, since a flapping check would train people to ignore it.

The dry run is good enough for the real night. I will ask Mara to look at the numbers before we schedule it.

summary: Found why the count check was off by 2 after the last bulk call: it ran before the index refresh, and the script now refreshes first and waits for it.
body:
Followed up on the small difference in the oldest month from the dry run. I wanted to be sure that it was only timing and not a lost document.

I reran only that month on the staging copy and took the count at three points: right after the last bulk call, after an explicit refresh and after the normal refresh interval of one second. The first count was 2 lower, the other two matched.

So the documents were there, but not yet visible. The check used the count API, which only sees refreshed segments. In the earlier migrations the copy ended with a replay round that gave enough time, so we never saw it. The chunked copy ends faster.

The fix is in two places. The script calls refresh on the new monthly indices before the check, and it waits for the call to return. The check itself also retries the count once after two seconds when it finds a difference, but only to log a warning; it still fails the night if the second count differs.

I wrote a test with a mock client that returns a lower count at first and the right one after the refresh call. It shows that the check fails when the refresh is not called, so the order is protected.

I also added a line to the runbook that explains why the check calls refresh. The old migrations are not affected, since their counts were verified after a longer wait.

summary: Mara reviewed the dry run numbers, asked for a lower copy rate on busy hours, and the script now takes a rate limit that changes with the time of day.
body:
Mara read the dry run summary and had two remarks. The replay rounds are fine at 3, but she did not like that search p95 of other customers moved during the copy, even if it stayed under the limit.

Her idea was a rate limit on the copy that is lower in the busy hours of the console, between 08:00 and 18:00, and higher at night. I added a setting with two values, a day rate and a night rate, in documents per second. The script reads the current hour in UTC and picks one.

The night rate stays as it was in the dry run. The day rate is a third of it. Nobody wants to run a copy in the day if it can be avoided, but a chunk that runs over into the morning should not hurt the customers.

I tested the switch with a fake clock: before the boundary, after the boundary and exactly on it. The rate changes between two bulk calls, not in the middle of a call. For a pause, the pause flag still wins over everything.

Mara also asked what happens if the clock on the machine is wrong. The script runs on a build host with the same time source as the rest, so I accept that. I noted it in the code comment.

Then I did a second dry run of F with a start time at 07:30 on purpose, to see the change. The rate dropped at 08:00 as intended, and the search p95 for the other customers stayed flat. The run took 96 minutes instead of 84.

The plan for F is now ready, and I will write the night into the runbook next.

summary: Prepared the real migration of customer F to the monthly layout with a full rehearsal on a production-sized copy and a checklist for the night session.
body:
Spent the evening getting ready for the real migration of customer F, which is planned for tomorrow night. Sam had already told the contact of F, and there was no open case, so I wrote down the start time of 19:10, so that the copy would be done well before the night rate would matter.

I ran the whole procedure once more on the production-sized copy to check the time. The copy of the 36 monthly chunks took 68 minutes. The free-space check passed every time, with the lowest margin at about 2.3 times the chunk size, which is enough for Tobias. After the copy, the replay needed 3 rounds, the last with 140 events, and that is the number I expect in the real run.

The count check ran with the refresh in front, and all months matched. The rejected-event counter showed 1 on the copy. I looked at it and it was an event with a timestamp in the far future, which the old index accepts and the new one refuses because the month does not exist yet. I wrote the event id into the migration notes and sent it to Mara, since it is a data quality question and not a migration problem.

I also went through the steps after the copy. The script switches the alias at the end, and I plan to watch the dashboard for the old and new aliases for 30 minutes. For comparison I noted the current p95 of 130 ms on the old layout. I expect the fan-out header on a small share of the queries, those from the screen without a time filter, and I added that to the checklist so it does not look like an error.

As Tobias asked earlier, I listed the Redis keys that contain the index name. The cache keys of F should be rebuilt by the first queries, and I will check that the hit rate goes back to the old value.

The old index is to stay for 48 hours. Its deletion goes into the calendar of the runbook, with the disk threshold as a condition. Next after F is customer G, after its support case is closed.

One small thing: the log of the script printed the chunk list twice because of a leftover debug line. I removed it, and it did not affect anything.

summary: Prepared the first night of customer G's migration to the monthly layout: checked disk space on the nodes, planned the chunk order and agreed the stop conditions with the team.
body:
Prepared the first night of customer G, since the support case was closed two days ago and Sam gave the go for the night session.

The plan is to start the copy at 19:30 and copy the older months first, in 40 chunks. I went through the disk graph of the nodes this morning. They have less room than before, because the old index of F is still there and the nightly snapshot staging takes some space. The old index of F is not yet past its 48 hours, so I cannot delete it today. I wrote down the numbers and estimated that G may reach the free-space check before the end of the copy.

That is acceptable. If the script stops with exit code 14, that is the stop that we want. The alert describes the code as waiting, and nobody has to touch the data. The copy is resumable from the chunk list, so the finished chunks stay and the second night continues from the next one. I checked this once more on the staging cluster by stopping a small copy by hand and resuming it, and the counts matched.

I also wrote the plan for the second night: the remaining chunks, the replay of the last three months and the alias switch. The switch waits for the second night in any case. Sam knows the order and will tell G's contact that search stays on the old index until then.

I started a short runbook page with the reason for a stop on free space, so the next person sees that it is normal and what to check first. One thing to improve: the script could print how much space it needs before it starts, so that we do not find out in the middle. I will add a pre-flight line for that after the first night.

summary: Added a pre-flight check that prints the space needed for the whole customer before the first chunk starts and refuses to start if it is clearly too much.
body:
After the stop on customer G, I added a pre-flight step to the migration script. It sums the size of all old monthly source data of the customer, multiplies it by 1.2 for the new indices and compares it with the free space across the data nodes.

If the free space is less than the sum, the script refuses to start and prints both numbers. If it is between the sum and twice the sum, it starts but prints a warning. The per-chunk check stays as before.

I tested the three cases with the fake cluster stats. For G's remaining chunks it now prints 23 GB needed against 61 GB free, which is fine. The runbook has a new line saying that a refusal at the start means freeing space first.

summary: Prepared the second night of customer G's migration by checking the space, planning the resume from chunk 22 and agreeing the replay limit with Mara.
body:
The first night of G stopped for free space after 54 GB, so today was about getting the second night ready. The copy is planned to resume from chunk 22, and 19 chunks are left, covering the last of the 40 months.

I ran the new pre-flight check against G's remaining chunks. It prints the space needed for the whole customer, and the line showed enough room on the data volumes for the rest of the copy. I still left a margin of about 15 percent and cleaned up two scratch directories from the first night, which freed a few more GB.

I went over the replay plan with Mara. The limit stays at 6 rounds, and she wants the last round under about 500 events. G has more evening traffic than F, so I expect the last rounds to be larger than in F's migration, and I planned the copy to start at 19:20 to catch the quieter part of the evening.

I also wrote down the checks for tonight: refresh the index and wait for it before the count check, compare the counts for all 40 months, and look at the rejected events. The alias switch is not part of tonight's plan until the counts match, and the old index stays untouched until then. A calendar entry for deleting the old index after the 48 hours will only be made once the switch is done.

summary: Asked E to pause their nightly import for one night and, because they cannot, planned the copy of E around the import with an extra replay of the import window.
body:
Customer E is the last of the medium wave, and its NDJSON import runs every night at 02:00. Sam asked their contact whether the import could pause for one night. The answer came back this morning: it cannot, because their own pipeline depends on the result in the morning.

So the migration has to live with the import. I looked at the import from the last 14 nights in the ingest logs. It writes between 02:00 and 02:50 and about 1.1 million events, mostly into the current month and the month before.

The chunked copy is useful here. The older months do not get new events from the import, except a few late ones, and these are covered by the replay of the last three months. So the plan is to copy the older months in the evening and leave the two newest months for after the import.

The night looks like this. At 19:30 the copy of the older chunks starts. At about 01:30 the script pauses by the pause flag, which I will set by a timer. At 03:00, after the import, it resumes with the two newest months, then replays and checks.

I added a scheduled pause to the script, which takes a start and an end time for a window where nothing is copied. Inside the window the script sleeps and checks the pause flag every 30 seconds. I tested it with a window of five minutes on staging and the resume worked from the same chunk.

The risk is that the import writes during the copy of the two newest months if it runs late. The replay would catch it, but it could need more rounds. I set the plan so that the script also stops if the replay needs more than 6 rounds, which is the rule already.

I sent the plan to Mara and Tobias. Sam will tell E that the night is on, and that no change is needed from their side. If the import is late, I will see it in the ingest metrics before I resume.

summary: Planned the night migration of customer E around its nightly import window, with a pause and an extra replay, and prepared the script settings.
body:
Customer E is the last one of the medium wave, and its nightly import makes it harder than F and G. I spent the morning planning the copy around that import instead of running it.

E's import usually starts at 02:00 and ends before 03:00, about 1.2 million events. They cannot move it, so the plan is to start the copy of the older months in the evening, pause the script at 01:30 and resume it at 03:00 after a look at the ingest metrics. The two newest months hold most of the data and will be copied after the pause, because that is when the import events land in the old index.

I set the script to use the time-of-day copy rate that Mara asked for, with the lowest rate during the import. I also wrote the pause and resume times into the run config so nobody has to remember them. The replay is the part I worry about: events written during the import window will have to be replayed, and I expect more rounds than for F. I raised the replay limit check in the script to 6 rounds and made it print the number of events left after each round, so I can see if it converges.

I also checked the disk numbers for E. The pre-flight check says the space is enough with a margin, so no stop for free space should be needed. I wrote down the count check per month and the p95 and cache hit rate baselines for E, to compare after the alias switch.

I wrote a short note for Sam in case E asks about slower search during the night, and I put the deletion of the old index into the plan as a calendar item for 48 hours after the switch. Nothing was started today. The copy begins this evening.

summary: Planned how to handle the rejected events seen in the migration rehearsals for F and E, with Mara deciding the rule for future timestamps and a default for the missing type.
body:
Mara went through the notes on the rejected events from the rehearsals for F and E and answered them. There were two kinds that mattered: timestamps far in the future, and a missing type field. Nothing else showed up in the notes.

For the timestamps, the old index accepts them, but the planned monthly layout has no index for a month that far ahead, so those events would have nowhere to go. Her proposal is that the ingest API clamps timestamps more than one day in the future to the ingest time and keeps the original value in an extra field. That would be a change on her side in the ingest API, not part of the migration, and she has not started it.

For the missing type, the mapping requires the field and the ingest validation should already refuse such events. She found that an old client version skipped the validation, which explains where they came from. The plan for the replay is a default type of unknown, with a counter, so that the event is not lost.

I wrote the default into the replay script and prepared the matching change in the check. The check should count these events as expected differences and list them, while any other difference still fails. I tried the script on a small sample from the staging copy of E, and the rejected counter for the missing type case dropped to 0 there. The two far-future events would stay rejected until Mara's change exists, so I noted them in the checklist for the night session as a known leftover. A full rerun on the staging copy is still to do.

summary: Planned what the five large customers will need for the search index migration: disk, copy time, replay limit and the console screens, and sent the notes to the team.
body:
Today I looked at the numbers from the medium wave and wrote down what the five large customers need before any of them is touched. The old indices of F, G and E are still there, and I did not delete anything. Their 48 hours are not over for all three, and I want to check the access logs of the old index names and the Redis keys for them first, so that is planned for later.

The disk graph shows the free space on the data nodes is still below the level before the medium wave, because the old indices of the migrated customers are still on the nodes. I compared the sizes of those three indices with the runbook, 38 GB, 54 GB and 61 GB, and they match within a few percent. I will put the real values into the runbook once the cleanup has happened.

Then I wrote down what the large customers need. There are five of them, from 150 GB to over 600 GB. The numbers from the medium wave do not simply scale.

First, the disk: a customer with 600 GB needs more than the cluster has free, even with one at a time, and the old indices of the medium customers take space as well. Tobias has to add nodes, or we have to copy by chunk and delete the old months as we go. The second is risky, because the rollback would then be incomplete. I prefer the extra nodes.

Second, the copy time. At the rate from the dry runs, 600 GB takes about 20 hours, so it needs several nights with the scheduled pause and also a rate that does not hurt the other customers.

Third, the replay. The large customers have constant traffic and no quiet night. The late event replay of the last three months may need more than 6 rounds. I want Mara's opinion on a higher limit or a short write stop.

Fourth, the fan-out. The large customers use more screens without a time filter, and Lena has to fix them before the switch, or the tail latency will be worse than now.

I put these four points into a short document and sent it to the team. Nothing is decided yet.

summary: Planned a check of the Redis search cache keys before the search index moves to the monthly layout, and wrote down what to measure.
body:
Prepared for the search index migration by looking at how Redis is used by the search API, because the cache keys contain the index name. When a customer moves to the monthly layout, the keys with the old index name will never be asked for again, so I wanted to know how much room they could take.

I listed the keys by prefix with a scan, not with a blocking command, and counted them for the current layout. About 41,000 keys carry index names of the customers in the first group of the plan, together about 180 MB. Redis memory is at 64 percent, so it is not a problem today. The number will grow once the large customers are in the plan, so I wrote down the count and the size as a baseline to compare with later.

The TTL of the search cache keys is 6 hours for result pages and 24 hours for the facet counts. I checked a sample of keys and the oldest one was 23 hours old, so the TTLs are applied as expected. My expectation is that old keys will disappear by themselves within a day after a switch, and that no cleanup job will be needed. I thought about deleting the old keys at the alias switch, but it would add a step to the script and one more way to fail, for a gain of a few hundred MB for one day. I will decide after the first real switch and, for now, only added a note about it to the plan.

I also found a detail to watch. The facet keys for the new aliases will have a slightly different name format, with the layout label at the end, so a facet query right after a switch will probably miss the cache for a while. I expect a dip in the hit rate of about 15 minutes after each switch, and I added a panel to the Grafana board so that we can see it.

The memory graph is stable. I will look at it again before the migration starts and write down the numbers next to the baseline.

summary: Talked with Lena about giving the two console screens without a time filter a default range, and planned a 30-day default with a chip that clears it.
body:
Talked with Lena about the two screens that send no time filter. They are the saved searches page and the event detail lookup by id. On the planned monthly layout, both would touch all indices of a customer.

For the lookup by id, the answer was easy. The id contains the creation time, so the console can derive the month and send a time range of that month plus the one before. Lena said it is a small change in the query builder.

The saved searches page is harder. Saved searches can be old, and users expect them to find old events. Her proposal is a default of 30 days with a visible chip that says so and one click to clear it. That keeps the old behavior possible, but makes the common case cheap.

I measured the effect on a staging copy of the monthly layout with a replay of one day of console queries. With the 30-day default, the share of queries that touch more than six indices went from 9 percent to under 1 percent. The p99 of the replay dropped from 410 ms to 190 ms.

I also asked Sam whether a default can surprise customers. He thinks the chip is enough, and he will add one line to the docs of the saved searches page.

Lena will make the change in the admin console in the coming days, behind a flag, so that it is ready before any large customer is moved. Once it is in, I will watch the fan-out metric before and after. Until then, the plan keeps the warning header in the API, and the large customers are not scheduled for the new layout.

summary: Batch writes in the ingest worker now flush on size or a 200 ms timer, whichever comes first, and the first load test shows fewer Postgres round trips
body:
Started the day on the ingest-batching branch. The worker used to write each event batch from the queue with its own insert. It now collects records in a buffer and flushes at 500 rows or after 200 ms.

The flush logic lives in worker/writer/batcher.go. I added a unit test for the timer path, because the first version never flushed a half-full buffer when traffic stopped. Fixed that by resetting the timer after each flush instead of only after each append.

A local load test with the recorded stream showed round trips to the database dropped from about 1 per batch to 1 per 6 batches. The p99 write latency has not been measured yet. Next step is to run the same test on staging and look at the commit offsets in Redpanda, since offsets must only move after a successful flush.

summary: Commit offsets in the batching writer were advancing before the flush finished, so a crash could lose events; the offset now moves only after the insert commits
body:
Reviewed the batching writer on staging and found a real problem. The consumer marked offsets as soon as a record entered the buffer. If the worker was killed between append and flush, up to 500 events were gone for good.

Reproduced it by sending SIGKILL to a worker during a load test and comparing the event count in Postgres with the count produced. 212 events were missing in the first run.

The fix keeps a list of pending offsets per partition in the batcher. After the insert transaction commits, only the highest contiguous offset per partition is marked. A failed flush leaves the offsets alone, so the records are consumed again.

This makes duplicates possible after a crash, so I checked the unique key on (tenant_id, event_id). The insert already uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so duplicates are dropped silently. I re-ran the kill test five times and the counts matched every time.

I also added a metric, ingest_batch_pending_offsets, so Grafana shows how many offsets are waiting. Still open: the flush has no backoff when Postgres is slow, so it hammers the database. That is the next item for this branch.

summary: Asked whether the Redis session store and the query cache share a connection pool; they do, which explains some of the contention seen in the admin console
body:
Mara asked why admin console logins slow down while a big dashboard query runs. I read the Fastify setup in the search API and the console backend.

Both the session store and the query cache get their client from the same factory in lib/redis.ts. The factory creates one pool, with a default size of 10. A burst of cache reads therefore queues behind session lookups and the other way round.

I did not change anything yet. The plan is to give sessions their own client with a small pool, keep the cache on a larger one, and name the keys with separate prefixes, session: and qcache:, which is already the case. I wrote the finding into the ticket so Mara can decide on pool sizes.

One caveat: I could only see the pool settings in code, not the real connection counts. Tobias has the Prometheus view for that.

summary: Added jittered backoff to the batching writer's flush, so a slow Postgres no longer gets hammered; staging load test held steady at 4x normal traffic
body:
Continued on ingest-batching with the open item from earlier: what the writer does when a flush fails or is slow.

Before, a failed flush retried immediately in a loop. Now it waits 50 ms, doubling up to 2 s, with random jitter of plus or minus 20 percent. While waiting, the consumer pauses the partitions it owns, so the buffer cannot grow without limit. The buffer has a hard cap of 5000 records.

I wrote tests with a fake database that fails N times. They cover three cases: recovery after two failures, the cap being hit and the pause working, and a context cancel during a wait. The cancel test found a goroutine leak in the timer code. The fix was one defer.

Then a staging run. I sent 4x the normal traffic for 30 minutes and injected a 10 second database stall in the middle. The pending offsets metric rose to about 3800, the partitions paused, and everything drained within 40 seconds after the stall ended. No events were lost and the duplicate count was 0.

What remains is the batch size tuning. The 500 rows and 200 ms are guesses. I will try a few values tomorrow and compare commit time per row.

summary: Postgres autovacuum on the audit_log table lagged behind; lowered the scale factor for that table and dead tuples fell from 9 million to under 200 thousand
body:
The evening check of the Postgres dashboards showed dead tuples on audit_log at about 9 million, and the last autovacuum was long ago. The table is append mostly, but the retention job deletes old rows in bulk, and that creates the dead tuples.

The global autovacuum scale factor of 0.2 meant the vacuum waited for tens of millions of changes. I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 for audit_log only, with ALTER TABLE, and wrote the change into the migration folder so it is not lost.

I started a manual VACUUM (ANALYZE) once to catch up. It took 14 minutes and did not block writes. Afterwards the dead tuples were under 200 thousand, and the table size on disk stopped growing.

To do: the retention job should delete in smaller chunks. I noted it for later.

summary: Tried a Go generics based pool for the batch buffers and dropped it: allocation numbers did not improve and the code got harder to read
body:
Late session on a small experiment in the ingest worker. The idea was to reuse the batch buffers through a generic sync.Pool wrapper, to cut garbage collection work after the batching change.

I wrote the wrapper in worker/internal/pool and swapped it in for the slice allocation in the batcher. Then I ran the benchmark with -benchmem. Allocations per flush went from 41 to 39, and the GC pause in the 10 minute load test did not change in any way I could measure.

The pooled slices also need careful resetting, otherwise stale events leak into the next batch. That needed extra tests, and the wrapper made the batcher harder to follow.

I reverted the branch changes with git restore and kept only the benchmark file, since it is useful for later. The GC cost is simply not where the time goes. Postgres commit time is, and that is the tuning I planned for tomorrow.

summary: Measured the ingest worker's Postgres insert path before batching: one INSERT per event at about 2,300 rows/s per worker, with round trips as the bottleneck, so batching is the next step
body:
Before touching the worker, I wanted a baseline for the single-row insert path. I wrote a small Go benchmark in cmd/ingest-bench that replays a captured slice of 400 thousand real events against a staging Postgres and reports rows per second, p95 insert latency and round trips.

With one INSERT per event, a single worker reached about 2,300 rows/s. The p95 insert latency was 6.8 ms, and nearly all of that was network and commit time, not the work of Postgres itself. CPU on the database stayed under 30 percent during the run, so the database was not the limit.

I then ran the same replay with four workers in parallel. Throughput went up to about 7,900 rows/s, not the 9,200 that linear scaling would give, and the p95 rose to 11 ms. The lock wait on the events indexes was small, but WAL sync time grew with every added worker.

I also tried a quick throwaway variant that wrapped 50 inserts in one transaction. That alone gave about 9,000 rows/s for one worker, which suggests that per-statement commits are the main cost. I did not keep that code, because it ignored offsets and failure handling.

The open question is the commit offset. The queue offset must move only after the batch is committed, otherwise a crash can lose events. I wrote this down as a requirement in the branch notes, together with the idea of flushing on both row count and a timer so quiet partitions do not hold events for long.

Next I will write the batch buffer with a unit test for the empty timer tick. After that I will rerun this benchmark against it, so the before and after numbers come from the same replay file. I saved the replay slice and the benchmark flags in the repo README for that comparison.

summary: Reviewed Mara's rate-limit config change for per-key limits and found that burst size was applied per second instead of per window, which would let keys exceed their quota
body:
Mara asked for a review of her work on the rate-limits branch. The change adds a limits table in Postgres and reads the per-key quota in the limiter, with the counters in Redis.

Most of it was fine. The migration is reversible, the admin API validates the numbers, and the cache for limits has a TTL of 60 seconds.

The problem was in limiter/window.ts. The burst value from the table was used as the bucket capacity, but the refill rate was derived with the window length in seconds where the code expected milliseconds. A key with 600 requests per minute got a refill of 600 per second.

I wrote a test that makes 1000 calls in two seconds for such a key. Before the fix 1000 passed, and the right answer is about 20. I put the test into the review as a suggestion.

Mara fixed the unit conversion in a follow-up commit, and the test now passes. I also asked her to log the limit that was applied on each rejection, because support will ask customers which limit they hit.

One open question is what happens when the limits table is unreachable. At the moment the limiter falls back to the default quota. I think that is right, but we should say so in the docs. I left a note for Sam.

summary: Answered Lena's question on why dashboards for one customer showed old numbers: the query cache TTL was 15 minutes for the summary key, not the 2 minutes in the docs
body:
Lena saw a customer dashboard that lagged behind the live event count. She asked if the frontend was caching.

The frontend was not. I traced the request to the search API and looked at the keys in Redis with SCAN, for the prefix qcache:summary:. Their TTL was 900 seconds.

In the code, services/summary.ts sets the TTL from a constant, SUMMARY_TTL, which was 900. The public docs say data is at most two minutes old. The constant was raised during a load problem some months ago and not lowered again.

I set it back to 120 seconds and left the other keys alone. Cache hit rate for summaries will go down somewhat, so I will check it over the next days.

I told Lena what happened, and Sam got a line for the docs check.

summary: Wrote the first version of the batch buffer for the ingest worker: it flushes on row count or timer, with a unit test for the empty timer tick and a size flush
body:
This afternoon I implemented the buffer that sits between the Redpanda consumer and the Postgres writer in the ingest worker. It collects events in a slice with a fixed capacity and hands the whole slice to the writer when the row limit is reached or when the timer fires, whichever comes first. The limits come from two new settings, BATCH_MAX_ROWS and BATCH_MAX_WAIT, with defaults of 1000 and 100 ms.

The first version had a bug in the timer handling. After a size flush the old timer was still running, so the next batch was flushed early with only a few rows. I fixed it by resetting the timer on every flush and by draining its channel when Stop returned false. A test now covers that case.

I added two more tests: a timer tick with an empty buffer must not call the writer, and a burst of 2500 rows must give two size flushes and one timer flush for the rest. All tests pass with the race detector on.

The writer still inserts rows one transaction per flush using a multi-row INSERT. The commit of the offsets is not changed yet and still happens right after the hand-off, which I know is wrong for crash safety. I left a TODO with the exact place in consumer.go and will do it as the next step, before any load test on staging.

I ran a quick local run with a generated stream of 200 thousand events. Postgres statements dropped from about 200 thousand to about 210, which looks right for 1000 rows. I will not trust that number until staging confirms it.

summary: Added gzip and a checksum manifest to the audit export; the manifest is the last line of the stream and includes row count and SHA-256 of the data
body:
Continued on audit-export. Two features today: compression and the manifest.

Gzip is negotiated through Accept-Encoding. I use zlib with level 4 in the pipeline. On the 4 million row test the file shrank from 1.1 GB to 97 MB, and the export took 91 seconds instead of 78. That is an acceptable price.

The manifest is trickier. The auditors want a way to see that the file is complete and unchanged. The handler keeps a running SHA-256 over the uncompressed lines and a row counter. At the end it writes one extra line with type manifest, the row count, the range, the hash and the time of export. A reader can strip that line and check the hash of the rest.

I wrote a small verify script in scripts/verify-audit-export.js for Sam to hand to customers. It reads a file, handles gzip, recomputes the hash and compares it. It prints OK or the difference in rows.

One bug came up in testing. If the client disconnected, the handler still wrote the manifest to a closed stream and logged an unhandled error. I now listen for the close event and skip the manifest, and I log the export as aborted.

The export is now also written into audit_log itself, with the actor, the range and the row count. That was the access record I planned.

Tests pass: 14 new ones. Next I want to look at what happens when two large exports run at once for one tenant, and probably limit it to one at a time per tenant with a Redis lock.

summary: Limited audit exports to one at a time per tenant with a Redis lock; the lock has a TTL and a heartbeat so a crashed export cannot block a tenant for long
body:
Today's work on audit-export was the concurrency limit. Two parallel exports of a large tenant would hold two database cursors and two long streams, and the database does not need that.

The lock is a Redis key, lock:audit-export:<tenant_id>, set with NX and a TTL of 60 seconds. The value is a random token. While the export runs, a timer extends the TTL every 20 seconds, but only if the stored token still equals ours. I did that with a small Lua script, so the compare and the expire happen in one step.

Release works the same way: delete only if the token matches. This avoids the classic problem where a slow export finishes after its lock expired and deletes the lock of a newer export.

If a second request arrives, the endpoint answers 429 with a Retry-After of 30 and a short message that an export is already running. I picked 429 and not 409, because clients and the support docs already know how to treat 429.

Tests:
- two parallel requests, the second gets 429
- a crash simulated by killing the first handler without release; the second request succeeds after the TTL passes
- a long export longer than the TTL keeps its lock through the heartbeat

I used a shortened TTL of 3 seconds in the tests, set through an option, so they run fast.

One decision for the lead to confirm: the lock is per tenant, not per API key. I think per tenant is right, since the load lands on the same rows. Another point is that the Redis client for the lock uses the shared cache pool. Given what I found about contention earlier this week, I used the small separate client that I created for sessions, and added a third name for locks. It is only two connections.

The branch needs a docs page next. I wrote an outline of the sections for Sam: the format, the cursor, the manifest, the limits and the verify script.

summary: Split the Redis clients in the search API into separate pools for sessions, cache and locks; the console login latency stopped following dashboard bursts
body:
This follows the finding from two days ago that sessions and the query cache shared one pool of 10 connections.

lib/redis.ts now exports three factories: sessionClient with a pool of 5, cacheClient with 20 and lockClient with 2. Each one sets a connection name through CLIENT SETNAME, so that CLIENT LIST shows which part of the app owns a connection. That will help the next time someone looks at the connection count.

I moved all call sites by hand. There were 23 of them, and the compiler found the ones I missed, because I removed the old default export.

Testing on staging: I ran the dashboard burst script with 200 parallel summary requests while another script logged into the console every second. Before the change the login took 400 to 900 ms during the burst. After it, 40 to 70 ms, the same as with no load.

Total connections from one search API task went from 10 to 27. With the current number of tasks this is still well below the server limit, but I wrote the arithmetic into the pull request so it is not forgotten when the task count grows.

Tobias should check the connection graph after the deploy. I will look at it tomorrow morning too.

summary: Wrote the audit export docs page with a worked example, the verify script usage and the 429 behaviour; Sam will review the wording for customers
body:
Wrote docs/api/audit-export.md in the public docs repository, following the outline from yesterday.

The page covers the request parameters, the NDJSON format of a row, the cursor token and how to continue a cut-off download. I included a full curl example that downloads a day of the log with gzip and writes it to a file. I ran every command against staging to make sure the output on the page is real.

The manifest section explains the last line and how to check it. I added the verify script with a short run:

node verify-audit-export.js export.ndjson.gz
OK 48213 rows, sha256 matches

The limits section says one export at a time per tenant, and shows the 429 response with the Retry-After header. I also wrote what a client should do: wait, then start again with the cursor.

While writing I noticed that the endpoint accepts ranges up to any size, but the docs say nothing about that. I added a note that very large ranges are best split by month, and I put a ticket on the board to decide whether to enforce a maximum.

Sam gets the page for a wording review, especially the compliance terms, which I am not sure I used in the way the auditors do. I did not merge the docs yet.

summary: Staging connection counts after the Redis client split look as expected: 27 per search API task, no refused connections, and cache hit rate unchanged
body:
Checked the Grafana panels the morning after the deploy, as planned.

Connections per search API task settled at 27, split into 5 for sessions, 20 for cache and 2 for locks, which CLIENT LIST confirmed through the connection names. The sum over all tasks is about a fifth of the server limit.

The cache hit rate stayed at 71 percent, so the split did not change caching behaviour. Summary keys now expire after 2 minutes, and their hit rate dropped from 88 to 74 percent, which matches what I expected from the shorter TTL.

No refused connections and no timeouts in the logs. I closed the ticket and told Tobias he does not need to do anything.

summary: Reviewed the loader-retry design for large files: chunk-level retries with a stored offset are better than restarting the whole file, and I wrote down the plan
body:
Planning session for the loader-retry branch, no code yet. The document loader fails on large files today when a single request to the storage backend times out, and the whole file starts again. For a 6 GB file that can mean an hour lost.

I went through the loader code in loader/fetch.ts and loader/parse.ts. The parser already works on chunks of 8 MB, so the natural unit for a retry is the chunk. The plan:
- keep the byte offset of the last chunk that was fully parsed and handed to the next stage
- on a failure, request the file again with a Range header starting at that offset
- use backoff of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds with jitter, and give up after five attempts
- distinguish errors: a timeout or a 5xx is retried, a 403 or 404 is not

A problem is records that cross a chunk boundary. The parser keeps a partial line in a buffer. The offset I store must be the start of that partial line, not the end of the chunk, otherwise a retry would lose or cut a record. I wrote this down as the main rule and added a test idea for it: a file whose lines are all exactly the chunk size plus one byte.

Another question is progress reporting. The admin console shows a percentage per import, and on a retry it must not go backwards. I will keep the maximum.

I checked that the storage backend supports Range requests for these objects. It does, and I confirmed it with a curl -r call on a test file.

Next session: implement the offset tracking and the error classification, in this order, with tests first.

summary: Implemented offset tracking and error classification in the loader, with tests for the chunk boundary case; retries themselves are not wired in yet
body:
Late session on loader-retry, following the plan from earlier today.

First the error classification, in loader/errors.ts. A function isRetryable takes the error and returns true for timeouts, connection resets, DNS failures and HTTP 500, 502, 503 and 504, and false for 4xx codes and for parse errors. Unknown errors are not retried, on the principle that a wrong retry on a corrupt file only wastes time. Eleven table-driven tests cover it.

Then the offset tracking in parse.ts. The parser now exposes resumeOffset, which is the byte position of the start of the buffered partial line, or the end of the last chunk if the buffer is empty. I wrote the boundary test: a generated file where every line is chunk size plus one byte, and another where lines are exactly the chunk size. Both give correct resume offsets, and the first version had an off by one for the second file. The fix was to count the newline byte as part of the line.

The retry loop is not connected yet. That comes next, together with the progress rule so the percentage never goes down. All tests run green locally.

summary: Wired the chunk retry loop into the loader with backoff and Range requests; a simulated storage failure at 70 percent of a 2 GB file now costs seconds, not a restart
body:
Connected the pieces on loader-retry. The fetch stage now runs inside a loop. On a retryable error it waits with backoff, 1 second doubling to 16, plus up to 25 percent jitter, then requests the file again with a Range header starting at resumeOffset. After five failed attempts in a row it fails the import with the last error.

The attempt counter resets whenever a chunk is parsed successfully, so a file that has several short outages over a long download does not run out of attempts.

For the test I built a small HTTP server that cuts the connection at 70 percent of a 2 GB file, once. Before the change the import started again from zero and took 11 minutes in total. Now the loader resumed after 1 second and the whole import took 7 minutes, with the row count correct.

Progress is the maximum of the old value and the new one, so the console percentage stays monotonic.

Open: a log line for each retry with the attempt, offset and error, and a counter metric. I will add those in the next session.

summary: Added retry logging and a loader_chunk_retries_total metric, labeled by error class, so support can see why an import was slow
body:
Small follow-up on loader-retry. Each retry now logs one line with the import id, attempt number, resume offset, wait time and error class. A Prometheus counter, loader_chunk_retries_total, has a label for the class: timeout, reset, server or other.

I kept the labels coarse on purpose, because a label with the raw error message would create many series. I checked the metric on a local run with the failing server and it shows up on the metrics endpoint. A Grafana panel will come with the review.

summary: Reviewed the loader-retry branch with Tobias's questions about memory use on resume; found the old response stream was not destroyed on retry and fixed the leak
body:
Tobias reviewed the loader-retry pull request and asked what happens to memory when a file has many retries. Good question, and I tested it instead of guessing.

I ran the failing storage server so that it cut the connection every 200 MB of a 4 GB file, which gives about 20 retries. The Node process memory grew by about 30 MB per retry and never came down. After 20 retries it had grown by 600 MB.

The cause was in fetch.ts. When a request failed, the code started a new request but never destroyed the old response stream. The old stream kept its buffers and its socket. Both stayed alive until the process ended.

The fix is to call destroy on the old stream in a finally block before the next attempt, and to remove the listeners that had been attached to it. I also made the abort controller of each attempt abort when the attempt ends, so the socket is released immediately.

After the fix I ran the same test. Memory rose and fell with the chunks, and stayed within about 150 MB for the whole file. I wrote a regression test that checks the number of open handles after five forced retries, using process.getActiveResourcesInfo. It fails on the old code and passes now.

Tobias also asked about the maximum total time for an import with retries. At five attempts with the longest wait of 16 seconds, one outage costs at most 31 seconds of waiting, but there is no overall limit. I added a total deadline of 30 minutes spent in retries per import, configurable. After that the import fails with a clear message.

He asked, too, if the imports in progress survive a deploy of the worker. They do not, and neither did they before. Persisting the offset in Postgres would allow that, but I think it is a separate piece of work. I wrote a ticket for it and did not expand this branch.

The branch is ready for another look from Tobias tomorrow. All 31 tests pass.

summary: Merged the ingest-batching branch after Mara's review; the worker on staging runs with 1000 rows and 100 ms and production deploy is set for the early morning
body:
Mara finished reviewing ingest-batching. She had three comments. One asked for the buffer cap to be an environment variable too, which I did: INGEST_BATCH_MAX_PENDING with a default of 5000. The second asked for a clearer name for the pending offsets metric, and I kept it after we agreed the dashboard already uses it. The third was a typo.

Before merging I ran the kill test again on the final code, five times, with SIGKILL at random moments under 3x traffic. The event count in Postgres matched the produced count each time, and the duplicates were removed by the unique key.

I also ran the full test suite with the race detector, 212 tests, all passing. Then I squashed the commits into four with sensible messages and merged into main.

The deploy plan for production, agreed with Tobias:
- release in the early morning when traffic is lowest
- roll one ECS task first and watch commit time and the pending offsets for 20 minutes
- then the rest in two steps
- if the p99 write latency is worse than before, set INGEST_BATCH_ROWS to 1, which behaves like the old code, without a new build

The last point is a useful safety net that I tested on staging today. With rows set to 1 the writer flushes every record and the numbers matched the old version.

I wrote the dashboard panel for Grafana with commit time per row and the pending offsets, so the rollout can be watched on one screen. The expected effect in production is a drop in database load of about half for the write path, as measured on staging, but the real number will only be known after the rollout.

summary: Planned the first steps for per-customer limits in the admin console with Lena: a form, a usage bar and a clear message when the key is throttled
body:
Planning session with Lena for the admin console side of the rate-limits branch. Mara's backend now stores a limit per API key, but the console shows nothing of it.

We agreed on three pieces:
- a form on the key detail page to set requests per minute and burst, with validation that matches the backend: burst not smaller than the per-minute value divided by 60, and a maximum set by the plan of the customer
- a usage bar showing the share of the limit used in the last minute, read from a new endpoint that returns the counters from Redis
- a readable message in the console when a request of the test tool is throttled, with the limit that applied and the time until the next free slot

I looked at the Redis counters to see what the usage endpoint can read. The counters are keyed per API key and per window, with a TTL of two windows, so the current and the previous window are available. That is enough for a bar, and not for a history. A history would need Prometheus or a table in Postgres. We decided against it for the first version, because nobody has asked for it.

For the endpoint I wrote a short spec in the pull request: GET /v1/keys/:id/usage returns limit, used, window_ends_at. It reads two keys with MGET, so there is one round trip. It must be cached for at most five seconds per key, to protect Redis from a console tab left open with polling.

Lena raised the point that polling every second is more than needed. We settled on every 10 seconds, with a pause when the tab is hidden.

A question we left open is whether support users may change limits or only read them. Sam should tell us how support handles these requests today. I wrote the question into the ticket.

Lena starts with the form tomorrow. I begin with the usage endpoint and its tests, and we meet to connect the two when both are done.

summary: Production deploy of the batching writer ran early; insert rate per worker rose from about 2,300 to 11,000 rows/s and Postgres round trips fell sharply
body:
The ingest-batching deploy went out at the start of the quiet window, one ECS task at a time. I watched the Grafana panels for the first worker for twenty minutes before letting the rest roll. Insert throughput per worker went from about 2,300 rows/s to roughly 11,000 rows/s at the same CPU.

Postgres round trips per second dropped by about 85 percent, which is what the design promised. The p99 of the ingest API did not change, so customers should see no difference except that lag in the queue drains faster after bursts. Consumer lag on the Redpanda topic peaked at 1,800 messages during the deploy and went back to zero within a minute of the last task restarting.

One thing I checked on purpose was the offset commit. After the fix from last week, offsets move only after the insert commits, and I confirmed this by killing one task in the middle of a flush. The restarted task replayed a few hundred events, and the unique key on the event id absorbed the duplicates, so the row count matched the source.

The flush timer settings are 1000 rows and 100 ms, as on staging. In production the size flush fires most of the time during the day, and the timer flush dominates at night. I looked at the batch size histogram and the median batch was 640 rows at midday, so there is room before the size limit matters.

There was one noisy moment. Two workers logged a slow flush warning at 3 seconds when an autovacuum started on the events table. The jittered backoff did its job and nothing was dropped. I left the warning threshold alone for now.

Next I want to add a metric for batch size and flush reason, so we can tune the numbers with real data instead of guessing. I also told Mara the deploy was clean so she can close the branch checklist. I will look at the dashboards again tomorrow morning after the daytime peak.

summary: Watched the first night of the batching writer in production: no lost events, steady lag and fewer Postgres connections, with one slow flush on the audit table to look at
body:
I checked the ingest worker late in the evening, after the production deploy of the batching writer had run for a full busy period. The goal was to confirm that the offset fix from the earlier session holds under real traffic, not only in the staging load test.

The consumer lag on the Redpanda topic stayed under 400 messages at the peak, where before the deploy it climbed to a few thousand in the same hours. I compared the count of events accepted by the ingest API with the rows inserted in Postgres over a four hour window, and the two numbers matched exactly. I also restarted one worker by hand with a SIGTERM during the peak, and after it came back the row count still matched, with no gap and no duplicates.

Postgres active connections from the workers dropped from about 140 to 60. The p99 of the flush time was 38 ms, well under the 100 ms timer. There was one outlier: a single flush took 1.9 seconds at around the busiest minute, and it coincided with the autovacuum run on the audit_log table. The jittered backoff kicked in once, the retry succeeded, and the log shows no error after that.

The flush size histogram shows that most flushes are triggered by the timer at night and by the row count in the busy hours, as expected. The batch size rarely goes above 800 rows, so the limit of 1000 is not the one that matters yet. I left both values as they are.

Open items:
- Watch the flush time on the audit table for another few days and see if the slow flush repeats.
- Add a Grafana panel for flush duration and batch size, so Tobias can see it without reading logs.
- Write down in the runbook how to drain a worker safely, since the SIGTERM test worked.

Next step is the panel and the runbook note tomorrow morning.

summary: Looked at why the admin jobs page is slow: the loader jobs query sorts four million rows without a useful index, so I added a composite index and the page loads in 300 ms
body:
The admin jobs page had been getting slower for weeks, and Lena asked me to look before building more on it. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the main query in the console. It filters by tenant and orders by created_at descending with a limit of 50.

The plan showed a sequential scan over the loader jobs table, which has about four million rows, followed by a sort. The query took 2.4 seconds on a copy of production data. The existing index was on tenant_id alone, but the planner did not use it because most of the rows belong to three large tenants.

I created a composite index on tenant_id and created_at descending. On the copy, the plan changed to an index scan with no sort, and the query dropped to about 12 ms. In the console, the page now loads in about 300 ms, and most of that is the front end.

Building the index on production took a short while. I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes to the table were not blocked. The loader kept running during the build, and I saw no lock waits in the logs. The index is about 280 MB on disk.

This fixes the symptom but not the cause. The table keeps growing, because nothing ever deletes old job records. The purge job after 90 days that I planned yesterday is still the right fix, and the index will get smaller when it runs.

I also checked the count query behind the pagination, which still does a full count and takes about 400 ms. It is not a problem yet. I noted it in the ticket, with the suggestion to switch to a next-page cursor if the table grows again.

I told Lena the page is fast now and she can go on with the filters. The purge job comes next.

summary: Per-customer limits form in the admin console: Lena built the layout, I added the API endpoints for reading and updating a key's limit and current usage
body:
Following the plan from yesterday, I worked on the backend half of the per-customer limits screen while Lena did the form. Two endpoints in the Fastify service: GET /admin/keys/:id/limits returns the configured limit, the window and the current usage, and PUT updates the limit.

Usage comes from the Redis counters the rate limiter already keeps. The read only needs the current window's counter and its TTL, so no new keys are needed. I made sure the endpoint does not create a counter if none exists.

Validation was the fiddly part. A limit must be a positive integer, the window must be one of 1 s, 10 s or 60 s, and the burst must not exceed the limit per window. After the burst bug found in review last week, I added a test that sets burst equal to limit and one that exceeds it.

Updates are written to Postgres first and then pushed to Redis, so a failure in Redis leaves the stored setting correct. The limiter reloads settings every 30 seconds anyway.

Lena's form already calls the GET endpoint against staging. The usage bar shows the right percentage, and the throttled message is the next step.

summary: Answered Sam's question about whether the 429 response tells a customer when to retry: it does, through Retry-After, but only for window-based limits
body:
Sam asked for the docs whether a throttled client learns how long to wait. I checked the limiter code to be sure.

When a key exceeds its limit the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header, in whole seconds, computed from the remaining TTL of the window counter. The JSON body also has a retry_after_ms field.

There is one exception. If a request is rejected by the burst check and not the window check, the header is set to 1, because the burst bucket refills continuously. That is a rough value, not an exact one.

I suggested wording for Sam: clients should wait at least the number of seconds in Retry-After and add some jitter. I also pointed to the example in the audit export docs, which already shows the same pattern. Sam will fold it into the API docs page.

summary: Wrote the purge job for old loader job records: it deletes in batches of 5,000 after 90 days and keeps failed jobs longer, tested against a copy of production
body:
I implemented the purge job for the loader job records, following the plan from earlier this week. It is a small script in the admin service that runs nightly and deletes rows older than 90 days. Failed jobs are kept for 180 days, because support likes to look back at them when a customer asks why an import broke.

The delete runs in batches of 5,000 rows with a short pause between batches. A single large delete would create a lot of dead tuples at once and lock rows the loader still needs. With batches, the job takes longer but the table stays responsive. I put the batch size and the pause in the config so that Tobias can change them without a deploy.

I tested it on a copy of production data. The copy has about 4.1 million rows, and 3.2 million of them are older than 90 days. The job removed them in about 11 minutes, and I watched the query latency of the jobs page during the run. It stayed under 400 ms the whole time.

After the purge, I ran a manual vacuum on the copy. The table went from 1.9 GB to about 420 MB. On production, autovacuum will do the work, but the first run will leave a lot of dead tuples, so I will run the first vacuum by hand.

I added tests for the cutoff, for the failed job exception and for a batch that is smaller than the limit. One test caught an off-by-one in the cutoff date, where jobs exactly at 90 days were deleted. That is fixed.

The job writes a line to the audit log with the number of deleted rows. Mara asked for this so that deletions are traceable. I did not enable it in production yet. First I want Sam to confirm that the 90 and 180 days are acceptable for the customer docs.

Next step is the production deploy of the job, behind a flag.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long a customer's loader job history is visible: 90 days for successful jobs and 180 for failed ones once the purge job is on
body:
Sam asked what to write in the docs about how long customers can see their import history. I answered from the purge job I just wrote. Successful loader jobs will be visible for 90 days, and failed jobs for 180 days.

I explained that the purge is not live yet, so today the history goes back further, in some cases more than a year. The first run will remove everything older than the limit in one night. A customer who relies on old records should export them before the flag goes on.

Sam asked whether the records can be recovered afterwards. They cannot, apart from the normal Postgres backups, and restoring a few rows from a backup is a manual job that I would rather avoid. The docs should therefore say clearly that the history is not an archive.

I suggested a line in the release notes a week before the flag goes on. Sam will write it and show it to me. I also pointed to the audit log entry that records how many rows each night's purge removed, in case a customer asks.

summary: Redis memory on the cache instance grew 30 percent in a week; most of it is summary keys for dashboards with long TTLs, so the TTL policy needs a look
body:
Checked the Redis memory graph after Tobias noticed the cache instance at 62 percent. Used memory grew about 30 percent over the last week with no rise in traffic.

I sampled keys with SCAN and MEMORY USAGE. The biggest group is the dashboard summary keys, under the prefix q:summary:, which are large JSON blobs of up to 80 KB each. Their TTL is 15 minutes, as found last week, but customers with auto-refreshing dashboards keep recreating them with different parameters.

The key names include the full filter string, so tiny filter changes produce separate keys. About 40 percent of the summary keys were referenced only once.

I wrote down two options: normalize the filter order in the key, and store the blobs compressed. Normalizing is cheap and I will try it first. Compression costs CPU in the search API and I want numbers before deciding.

summary: Production deploy of the purge job went out behind a flag; the first run removed 3.1 million loader job rows in 12 minutes and the jobs page stayed fast
body:
The purge job for loader job records is deployed, and I turned the flag on for one run in the quiet window. Sam had confirmed the 90 and 180 day limits and the release note went out a week ago for the customers who had asked, so I did not wait longer. Before the run I took a snapshot of the instance, just in case.
