The job removed about 3.1 million rows in 12 minutes. The batches of 5,000 with a pause of 100 ms worked as on the copy. I watched Postgres CPU and replication lag in Grafana, and neither moved by more than a few percent. The loader kept importing files through the whole run, and I saw no lock waits.

The jobs page in the admin console stayed under 400 ms during the run and went to about 250 ms afterwards. The query plan used the new composite index the whole time. The table now has about 900 thousand rows.

After the run I started a manual vacuum on the table. It took about four minutes, and the table shrank on disk from 1.9 GB to about 480 MB after it. The index shrank too, from 280 MB to about 70 MB. Autovacuum would have caught up eventually, but doing it by hand removed the bloat at once.

I checked the audit log entry. It says 3,104,882 rows deleted with the cutoff for both classes of jobs, which matches the count I took before the run. Mara looked at it and was happy with the format.

One small thing I noticed is that the cron for the job runs in UTC, and the reindex job for the search index runs close to it. They do not conflict now, but I wrote a note in the runbook so nobody puts a heavy job in the same hour.

The flag stays on, and the job will run every night now. I will look at the row counts in a few days to see that the steady state is a few thousand rows per night. The ticket for the purge is closed, and the count query for the pagination remains as a small open item.

summary: Planned the next step for per-key rate limits: limit changes should apply at once, so I compared pushing updates through Redis pub/sub against shorter polling
body:
The load test showed that limit updates take up to 30 seconds to apply, and the admin form says so. Mara and I want something better, so I spent the morning on options. The first is to shorten the polling interval of each API task from 30 seconds to 5 seconds. The second is to publish a message on a Redis channel whenever a limit changes, and let the tasks refresh the key right away.

Polling is simple, and it needs no new moving part. The cost is the load on Postgres, because every task would read the limits table six times as often. With about 30 tasks that is still only a few queries per second, and the table is small. So the load is not a real objection.

Pub/sub gives an instant update, but a task that misses a message, for instance during a reconnect, keeps the old limit until the next full refresh. I would need both mechanisms anyway, polling as the safety net and pub/sub for speed. That is more code and more ways to fail, for a gain of a few seconds.

I also asked what customers actually need. Sam said that in support the usual case is raising a limit after a customer complains, and waiting 5 seconds is no problem for them. Nobody asked for an instant change.

So I decided on the shorter polling and no pub/sub. I wrote the decision and the reasons in the design doc, so that the question does not come back. I will change the interval, make it a setting, and rerun the load test to check that the update delay is now under 6 seconds. The form text then says that changes apply within a few seconds.

summary: Answered Tobias on whether the Redis version upgrade can wait: the current version is supported for months, so it goes after the shard layout planning
body:
Tobias asked if the Redis minor version upgrade should be done this sprint. I looked at the release notes and our version's support status.

The current version still receives security fixes, and none of the fixed issues touch features we use: plain strings, hashes, sorted sets and a few locks with TTLs. The newer version has better memory reporting for hashes, which would be nice but is not needed.

The risk is mostly operational. The upgrade means a failover on the managed instance and a brief connection drop, and the search API pools reconnect after that, as we saw in the staging tests of the client split.

My suggestion was to do it in a quiet window after the search index shard planning is finished, so we do not change two things at once. Tobias agreed and put it in the backlog.

summary: Started the schema registry compatibility check for event type changes: it now rejects removing a required field, with the rules written as small testable functions
body:
Worked on the schema-registry branch. The registry stores a versioned JSON schema per event type, and until now a new version was accepted if it parsed. Customers' senders break when a required field disappears, so the check has to catch that.

I wrote the compatibility rules as separate small functions: field removed, required field added without a default, type changed, enum value removed. Each returns a list of violations with the field path, so the API can answer with a precise message.

The first rule set is backward compatibility: events valid under the old schema must be valid under the new one. Adding an optional field passes, adding a required field without a default fails, and widening an integer to a number passes.

The tests use fixtures from three real event types, trimmed. One surprise was nested objects: an optional parent with a required child. A new required child inside an optional parent is compatible, since events without the parent stay valid, and I encoded that in a test.

The publish endpoint is not wired to the check yet. That is tomorrow's step, along with a dry-run mode so customers can test a schema change without publishing it.

summary: Wired the compatibility check into the schema publish endpoint, with a dry_run flag that returns the violations without storing the new version
body:
The publish endpoint of the registry now runs the compatibility rules before storing a version. On violations it answers 409 with the list, each entry having the rule name and the field path.

I added a dry_run query parameter. With it, the endpoint runs the same checks and returns 200 with an empty list or the 409 body, but never writes. Sam asked for this so support can test changes with customers.

Tests cover both modes and the case where the event type has no previous version, which always passes. The audit log records published versions, and I made sure a dry run writes no audit entry.

summary: Wrote the first load test for the rate limiter with per-key limits and found that limit updates took up to 30 seconds to apply, so the admin form now says so
body:
Built a k6-style load script for the limiter on staging, with 50 keys at different limits. Goal was to check that each key is throttled at its own configured rate and no more.

The results were right for steady limits. Keys at 100 per 10 s were throttled at 100 plus a small tolerance, and keys at 1000 per 10 s likewise. The p99 added latency of the limiter stayed at about 1.5 ms.

The interesting case was changing a limit mid-test. The limiter reloads settings every 30 seconds, so a raised limit stayed in force for up to half a minute at the old value. That is not a bug in itself, but it would confuse a customer who changes a limit and tests it right away.

I considered a pub/sub message to reload immediately. That adds a new moving part and Redis connection use, and the pools were just split, so I chose not to do it. Instead Lena changed the form to show a note that changes apply within 30 seconds.

I also found that the usage bar reads the counter at request time and does not reflect requests in flight, which is fine.

The load script is committed under tools/loadtest so Mara can reuse it.

summary: Loader memory after chunk retries holds steady at about 180 MB on a 4 GB file in staging, and a retry storm test showed no growth after the stream fix
body:
Ran a longer memory test on the loader-retry branch work that was merged to main. The test loads a 4 GB NDJSON file from storage with a fault injector that fails 5 percent of the range requests.

Memory stayed at about 180 MB resident throughout, with the heap flat after the first minute. Before the stream destroy fix, the same run climbed past 900 MB, so the fix does its job.

The number of retries was 212 over the run, all of the class transient network, and the loader_chunk_retries_total metric matched that. No chunk needed more than three attempts.

I also tried a harsher run with 40 percent failure. The loader slowed a lot, as expected, and gave up on two chunks after the configured five attempts, then reported the file as failed with the stored offset. A rerun resumed at that offset and finished.

One gap: when the job is cancelled by the user during a backoff sleep, the sleep is not interrupted and the job finishes a few seconds late. I made the sleep abortable with the job's abort signal and added a test.

The branch is clean now. Remaining are the docs for support about reading the retry metric.

summary: Checked cache hit rate after three days: the summary keys hold at 77 percent through the busy period, so the key change is done
body:
As planned, I looked at the Redis graphs three days after the key normalization deploy. Hit rate on the summary keys stayed between 76 and 78 percent, including the busiest hours.

Memory has been flat at about 18 percent below the old peak. Key count is lower and no new key prefixes appeared.

I closed the note on this topic. Compression of the blobs is not needed for now.

summary: Reviewed Mara's schema-registry change for enum handling and found that adding an enum value was flagged as incompatible, which would block harmless updates
body:
Mara changed the compatibility rules to cover enums, and I reviewed the diff. The intent was right: removing an enum value must fail because old events may use it.

The code compared the sets in the wrong direction, though. A new schema with an extra value was reported as a violation, while a removed value passed in one path. I wrote two tests to show it, one for adding and one for removing a value, and the first failed.

Mara fixed the comparison. We discussed what adding a value means for consumers: senders are fine, but readers of the events, such as the dashboards, may meet unknown values. For now we treat it as compatible and add a warning field to the response, not an error.

I also asked for the nested enum case, where an enum is inside an array of objects, to be tested. She added it.

The branch is ready to merge after one more look at the error messages, which still print the internal rule name in a few places.

summary: Changed the limit refresh interval to 5 seconds and reran the load test: updates now apply within 6 seconds and Postgres load from the polling is negligible
body:
I made the refresh interval for per-key limits a setting and set it to 5 seconds, following the decision from two days ago. The change is in the limiter's config loader and takes about 15 lines. I added a test that uses a fake clock to check that a changed limit shows up after one interval.

Then I reran the rate limiter load test on staging, with the same key set as the first time. The slowest update I saw was 5.8 seconds, and the median was about 2.6 seconds. Before the change the slowest was just under 30 seconds.

I watched Postgres during the test. The limits query went from about one per second to about six per second across all tasks, and its mean time stayed at 0.4 ms. It does not show up in the slow query log and does not matter for CPU.

The limiter itself held up as before, with no change in the rejection counts for keys under their quota. I checked a key at exactly its limit, and the 429 came at the right request in every run. The Retry-After value was also correct for window limits.

I changed the text of the admin form to say that changes apply within a few seconds. Lena reviewed the wording and merged the front end part. The change is on staging, and production deploy is planned for tomorrow after Mara has looked at the diff.

summary: Tried a Postgres connection pooler in front of the search API settings queries and abandoned it: the queries are rare and the extra hop only added latency
body:
Following the Postgres load discussion, I tried putting a pooler in front of the database for the search API's settings and account reads. The idea was to cut connection counts on the primary.

I set up the pooler on staging in transaction mode and pointed one search API task at it. The connection count on the primary did fall, from 38 to 12 for that task group.

The benefits ended there. The settings queries run a few times per minute per task and are cached in Redis, so they were never a real load. Latency per query rose by about 2 ms because of the extra hop.

Worse, transaction mode broke the prepared statements that the Postgres client library uses by default. I had to turn them off, and that made a few other queries measurably slower. Session mode would avoid the problem but would remove the benefit.

I decided to drop the experiment. The real connection users are the ingest workers, which the batching change already helped, since fewer round trips mean connections are held shorter.

I removed the staging pooler and wrote a short note in the journal notes so the idea is not repeated without a different reason.

summary: Production deploy of the schema registry checks went through; the first real publish by a customer was a compatible change and passed
body:
Deployed the schema-registry branch work to production in the afternoon. The migration for the stored versions needed nothing new, so the deploy was a plain rollout.

I ran a dry run against a real event type with a removed required field and got the 409 with the right path. A publish of a harmless optional field was accepted and shows in the audit log.

Later a customer published a new version through the API. It added an optional field, passed the check, and no support ticket followed.

Sam updated the docs page with the dry run. I will look at rejected publishes next week to see which messages confuse people.

summary: Planned the retention of old loader job records in Postgres: a table of 4 million rows is slowing the admin jobs page, so a purge job after 90 days is the proposal
body:
Lena noticed that the jobs page in the admin console loads slowly for the biggest tenants. The table behind it, loader_jobs, has about 4 million rows, many of them finished jobs over a year old.

The query sorts by created_at with a tenant filter and the planner uses the right index, but pages deep in the list still cost time. Most users never look beyond the first page, so the cost is mostly in the count query for the pager.

My proposal is a nightly purge of finished job records older than 90 days, with a summary row per tenant and month kept for the usage report. Failed jobs stay for 180 days since support looks at them.

I also suggested replacing the exact count with an estimate beyond 10,000 rows. Lena is fine with 'more than 10,000' in the pager.

Next step is to check with Sam whether support needs older records, then write the purge job in small batches to keep autovacuum calm.

summary: Per-key rate limit admin form shipped to staging: Lena's usage bar reads from the new endpoint and a throttled key shows a clear message with the refresh delay
body:
Lena and I spent the early afternoon on the last pieces of the per-customer limits screen. The usage bar reads current usage from the endpoint I added last week, and it now turns amber at 80 percent of the limit and red once the key is throttled.

The throttled message used to be a generic error. It now says the key is over its limit, shows the window, and mentions that changes to the limit apply within about 6 seconds. That matches the 5 second polling interval we settled on.

I found one bug while clicking through: a limit of 0 was accepted by the form and effectively blocked the key. The API now rejects values below 1 with a 422 and a message, and the form shows it inline. I added a test for the boundary.

Lena also asked whether the usage bar should count rejected requests. I decided it should not, because the customer would otherwise see usage above 100 percent and think the limit was broken. The counter in Redis only increments on accepted requests, so no change was needed.

We checked the key naming of the counters, since the admin endpoint reads them directly. They use the rl:{key_id}:{window} pattern, and the endpoint now builds the name through the same helper as the limiter, so the two cannot drift apart.

Staging deploy went fine. I created a test key with a limit of 10 per minute and drove it with a small script; the bar followed within a refresh and the 429 carried Retry-After as expected.

Left for tomorrow: a confirmation dialog when lowering a limit below current usage, and Sam's review of the wording. Production comes after that.

summary: Answered Sam: a customer who lowers a key's limit below current usage is throttled right away, and the form will warn before saving
body:
Sam asked what happens when a customer lowers a limit while the key is already above the new value. The next request after the refresh, within about 6 seconds, gets a 429, because the counter for the window is already past the new limit.

Nothing is reset, and the counter stays as it is until the window ends. For window-based limits Retry-After then points to the end of that window.

This surprised Sam, so I wrote it down as a case for the docs. I also added the confirmation dialog to tomorrow's list, with text saying that the key will be throttled until the window ends.

Sam will add one sentence to the limits page of the docs.

summary: Looked into the slow flush on the audit table seen during the first night of the batching writer: a missing index on the foreign key made the multi-row insert wait on lock checks
body:
The first night of the batching writer in production showed one slow flush on the audit table, about 1.8 seconds against the usual 40 ms. I wanted to know whether this was a one-off or something that would grow.

I pulled the Postgres logs for that minute with log_min_duration_statement lowered on staging and replayed a similar batch. The slow statement was the multi-row insert into audit_log with 1000 rows. The plan showed time spent in the trigger that checks the foreign key to accounts.

The cause was not the foreign key itself but an autovacuum run on audit_log that started at the same moment. It held the table busy while the insert waited for buffer space. The table is big, around 60 million rows, and autovacuum had fallen behind on it.

Two changes came out of this. First, I lowered the autovacuum scale factor for audit_log to 0.02 so it runs more often with less work per run. Second, I checked the batch size for this one table: 1000 rows is fine, so I left it.

I also looked at whether the audit table should keep going through the same writer as events. It should, because the audit entries have the same loss requirements, and the only difference is the volume, which is small.

After the setting change I replayed the batch ten times on staging with a manual vacuum running in parallel. The worst flush was 210 ms, which is acceptable.

I will watch the flush duration panel in Grafana for the next few nights. If a slow flush shows up again, the next step is to look at partitioning the audit table by month, but I do not want to do that yet.

summary: Added a confirmation dialog for lowering a limit below current usage and updated the limits page text after Sam's review
body:
Lena built the dialog and I wired it to the usage endpoint. When the new limit is below the current usage in the window, the form shows a warning that the key will be throttled until the window ends, and the user has to confirm.

Sam reviewed the wording of the limits docs page. Two changes: the term window is now explained with an example of 60 seconds, and the section about Retry-After says plainly that it only appears for window-based limits.

I added a test for the dialog logic itself, covering exact equality, which should not warn, and one above and below usage. The first version warned on equality, which was an off-by-one.

We also checked the screen in the narrow layout that support uses on their laptops. The usage bar overflowed by a few pixels, and Lena fixed it with a min-width.

Production deploy of the admin form is planned for tomorrow morning, together with the endpoints. The rate-limits branch has two open items: the load test with 10,000 keys and a short note for the on-call about how to raise a limit by hand.

summary: Load test of the rate limiter with 10,000 keys showed Redis latency stays under 2 ms at 20k requests/s, but the limit polling query was fetching all keys every 5 seconds
body:
I extended last week's load test to 10,000 API keys with mixed limits to see how the limiter behaves at the scale of our largest customers combined. The request rate was 20,000 per second spread evenly over the keys.

Redis command latency stayed under 2 ms at p99 and CPU on the instance was around 25 percent. The counters for the keys use little memory, about 6 MB in total, so the limiter is not the cause of the memory growth we saw on the cache instance.

The weak spot was the polling for limit changes. Every task fetched the limits of all keys every 5 seconds, so with 10,000 keys it ran a query returning 10,000 rows each time, on each task. Postgres handled it, but it was a waste and it would grow with the customer count.

I changed the query to fetch only rows with an updated_at newer than the last poll, and added an index on updated_at. A task now keeps its limits in memory and merges the changes. On startup it does one full load.

There was a bug in the first version: deleted keys never left the in-memory map. I added a soft delete flag to the query so that revoked keys are removed on the next poll. A test covers that.

After the change the polling query returns 0 to 3 rows in the usual case and takes under 1 ms. I reran the full test and the update latency still came out at about 6 seconds.

Next step is the short on-call note and the production deploy of the form.

summary: Production deploy of per-key rate limits and the admin limits form went out; first customer change applied within 5 seconds and no 429 spike followed
body:
The rate-limits branch went to production this morning after Mara reviewed the incremental polling change. The deploy had two steps: the API with the new endpoints first, then the admin console with the form.

I watched the 429 rate in Grafana during and after the rollout. It stayed at the usual baseline of a few per minute, all from keys that were already throttled before. No new keys were throttled by the change.

Sam changed the limit of one real customer who had asked for a higher limit last week. The change applied in about 5 seconds, measured by watching the counter's limit field in the debug endpoint. The customer's traffic went up as they expected and nothing else moved.

One small issue came up. The usage bar showed 0 for keys that had not made a request in the current window, which is correct but looked odd next to a limit. Lena changed it to show 0 of the limit explicitly.

The on-call note is written and sits in the runbook. It says how to raise a limit with the admin form, what to do if the form is down, and how to read the counter by key in Redis. It does not suggest touching the counters themselves.

I also cleaned up the branch. The leftover feature flag for the polling was removed, since the flag stayed on everywhere. The branch is ready to be closed.

What is left in this area is a daily report of keys that hit their limit more than 100 times, which Sam asked for to help with sales conversations. I will plan it next week.

summary: Looked at Redis key naming for the dashboard summary keys; a prefix by customer and version makes it possible to drop one customer's cache without a scan
body:
The summary keys for dashboards are named by a hash of the query, which makes it impossible to find the keys of one customer. When support asked for a cache reset for a single customer last week, we had to scan the whole keyspace.

I changed the naming to sum:v2:{customer_id}:{hash}. The version part lets us change the format later without old keys being read by new code. The old keys expire on their own with their TTLs.

For dropping a customer's cache I used a set per customer that holds its key names, with the same TTL as the longest key. Deleting is then one read and one multi-delete, not a scan. The set costs a little memory, about 40 bytes per key.

I measured the effect on staging with a copy of the dashboard traffic. The hit rate was the same as before, 77 percent in the busy period, and memory per key went up by about 4 percent. That is a fair price.

The write path has a small race: a key can be created just after the delete. For the support case this is fine, because the next dashboard view fills the key with fresh data anyway.

Production deploy is planned for the next quiet window.

summary: Schema registry: enum value additions are now compatible, but removing one still is not; Mara's change merged with a fix for the nested enum case
body:
Following the review from two days ago, Mara's schema-registry change for enums needed one more round. Adding an enum value was flagged as incompatible, and her change fixed the top-level case.

I tested nested objects with an enum inside an array of objects and found it still failed. The rule function compared the enum lists but only for fields at the top level, so the nested path was skipped and then treated as a type change.

The fix was to make the walk over the schema recursive, with a path string for the violation message. The messages now read events.items[].status: enum value removed, which is something a customer can act on.

I wrote tests for four cases: adding a value, removing a value, reordering values, and an enum turning into a plain string. Reordering is compatible. An enum turning into a string is compatible for readers but we decided to flag it as a warning, not an error, since consumers that generate code from the schema may break.

The dry_run flag returns warnings and errors in separate lists now. Existing clients that only read the violations list see errors only, so the response stays backward compatible.

Mara merged her branch after the changes and the checks passed in CI. A customer-facing page about what counts as compatible is the next small item, and Sam will draft it from the rules in the code.

One open point: required fields with defaults. Adding a required field with a default is currently rejected. I think it should be allowed, but I want Mara's opinion first.

summary: Answered Tobias: the loader memory on resume is bounded by chunk size times concurrency, about 180 MB with the current settings, so the ECS task limit has room
body:
Tobias asked how large the loader tasks need to be on ECS before he sets the limits in Terraform. I looked at the staging numbers again.

Memory is bounded by chunk size times the number of concurrent chunks, plus the parser buffers. With 8 MB chunks and 4 in flight, the chunk buffers are about 32 MB. The rest is the parser and the Node runtime.

The measured plateau was about 180 MB on a 4 GB file, and it did not move in the retry storm test after the stream fix. I told him 512 MB per task gives plenty of room, and that 1 GB would be generous.

He also asked about the case where several large files run in one task. The loader processes one file per job and a task takes two jobs at a time, so the worst case is about 360 MB.

He will set 512 MB and an alert at 80 percent so we see if anything grows. No code change was needed.

summary: Checked why a customer's NDJSON import stalled at 40 percent: the file had a single 30 MB line, which the parser rejected, and the loader reported it as a retryable error
body:
Support passed on an import that sat at 40 percent for an hour. The loader log showed the same chunk retried again and again with the error class set to unknown.

The file contained one line of about 30 MB, an event with a large embedded blob. The line parser has a maximum line length of 10 MB and threw an error that my error classification had not covered, so it fell into the default class, which is retryable.

Retrying could never help here, because the data is the same each time. I added a new error class, line_too_long, which is permanent and fails the job at once with a message that names the line number.

I also reviewed the other errors that fall into unknown. A look at the metric loader_chunk_retries_total over the last weeks showed only this one in meaningful amounts, so no other class needed to be added.

The maximum retries per chunk is 5, so the job would have stopped by itself eventually, but only after a long time with backoff. A permanent failure should not wait for that.

I asked Sam to tell the customer the line number and the limit. The limit is on the docs page for the importer, but it did not mention lines, so I added one sentence.

summary: Planned the daily report of API keys that hit their limit often: a Redis counter per key and day, a small job that writes the top keys to Postgres, and a view in the admin console
body:
Sam asked for a report of keys that are throttled a lot, so that sales can talk to customers who have outgrown their limit. I spent the evening on the design.

The limiter already knows when it rejects a request. I would add one increment on a counter named rl:hits:{key_id}:{day}, with a TTL of 3 days. It adds one Redis command per rejected request, not per request, so the extra load is tiny.

A job runs once per night and reads the counters of the day that just ended. It writes the keys with more than 100 hits to a table in Postgres: key id, customer, day, count. The table is small, a few hundred rows per day at most.

For reading the counters, scanning is not needed. The job takes the list of keys from Postgres and reads the counters in pipelines of 500. With 40 customers and some hundreds of keys this is fast.

The admin console gets a page with a table sorted by count, with a filter by customer. Lena said she can do it in an afternoon once the endpoint exists.

I considered computing the report from the access logs instead. It would be possible, but the logs are in another system and the query is slow, so the counter is simpler.

Open questions: should the threshold be configurable per customer? Sam thinks a global value is enough for now. I agreed, because we can change it later with one line.

I wrote the plan into the branch notes and created the tasks. Start of the work is tomorrow.

summary: Allowed adding a required field with a default in the schema registry, after Mara agreed that old events stay valid because readers fill the default
body:
I asked Mara about required fields with defaults, and she agreed that they should be allowed. A producer that does not send the new field is still valid, since the reader supplies the default.

I changed the rule function. Adding a required field is compatible only if a default is set. Without a default it is still rejected, with the message that names the field and says a default is missing.

There was a catch with the type of the default. A default of null on a non-nullable field passed the check and then broke the validation of the stored event. I added a check that the default matches the field type, with tests for strings, numbers, booleans and arrays.

The dry_run endpoint returns this case as a violation with a clear text. Sam will include it in the compatibility page.

The change is small and went into the schema-registry branch today.

summary: Implemented the nightly counter job and the endpoint for throttled keys; the first run on staging produced the expected rows and took 400 ms
body:
I started the throttle report with the limiter side. A rejected request now increments rl:hits:{key_id}:{day} with a TTL of 3 days. The call is made after the rejection response is prepared, so it cannot slow the caller, and an error in it is logged and ignored.

The nightly job reads the counters in pipelines of 500 keys and writes rows over the threshold to a new table, throttled_keys_daily. The threshold comes from a setting with a default of 100. I used an upsert on key id and day, so a rerun of the job does not make duplicates.

On staging I drove a few keys over their limits with the load script and then ran the job by hand. It wrote the expected rows and finished in about 400 ms with 600 keys. The counters for keys without hits do not exist, so the pipeline returns nil for them, which I first mishandled and counted as an error. A test covers it now.

The endpoint returns the rows of the last 30 days, with filters for customer and minimum count, and pages of 50. It joins to the customer table for the name. The query uses the primary key order, so no extra index was needed.

One detail: the day boundary is in UTC for the counters. Customers think in their own time zones, but for a sales report this is fine, and the page says so.

The job is scheduled with the same mechanism as the purge job. Lena starts on the page tomorrow, and I will review her pull request. I also need to add the job to the alert rules for missed runs.

summary: Started the plan for the new search index shard layout by month: measured shard sizes per customer and found that three large customers hold 70 percent of the data
body:
The planning for the new shard layout started today. The current layout has one shard group per customer, which made sense at first, but the large customers have shards that are far bigger than the rest and the small customers have many nearly empty shards.

I pulled the shard sizes from the cat API. The index has 12 shards in the current layout on the largest group. Three customers hold about 70 percent of the data. Their biggest shards are over 60 GB, while the median shard is under 2 GB.

Searches by a large customer hit those big shards and are the slow ones in the latency panel. Merges and reindex runs on them take much longer too, and the nightly reindex job spends most of its time there.

The idea of splitting by month is that each shard covers a period and shards stay at a similar size. Queries nearly always have a time range, so most of them only touch a few shards. Old months become read-only and can be merged once.

Things I want to know before deciding:
- how many queries have no time range at all
- how the routing by customer would work, so that customers do not see each other's data
- how long a reindex of the full dataset takes into the new layout

For the first point I took a day of search API logs from staging replayed traffic. About 8 percent of the queries have no time range, and the default in the API adds the last 30 days, so most of those are already limited.

The second point needs routing by a customer key in the index, plus a filter in the query. I will write down how the search API enforces the filter, since a mistake there would be a data leak.

I wrote these findings into the planning document and asked Tobias for the cost of the extra nodes during the reindex.

summary: Tobias estimated the temporary cost of the reindex into the new layout: two extra data nodes for about a week, which is acceptable
body:
Tobias replied with his numbers for running the old and new layout side by side. We need two extra data nodes for the duration of the reindex, and he estimates about a week including the verification.

The cost is small compared with a month of the current cluster, and he said he can create the nodes with Terraform in under an hour. He asked that we keep the old index until the new one has been in use for a few days.

I noted that this means disk space for both copies. He confirmed the disks have room, with about 35 percent free now.

The next step is the routing design, and I will write it tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the routing and filter design for the monthly shard layout and tested on staging that a missing customer filter is rejected by the search API before the query reaches OpenSearch
body:
The important risk of the month layout is that shards hold several customers, so the customer filter must always be applied. I spent the afternoon on how the search API guarantees that.

The design has three layers. First, the query builder adds the customer term filter itself, and callers cannot pass a raw query without it. Second, a final check in the function that sends the request verifies that the filter is present in the body and throws if not. Third, the index has an alias per customer with a filter in the alias, so even a bug in the first two layers cannot reach other data.

The aliases are the strongest protection. With 40 customers it is manageable, and creating one is part of the customer setup that already exists. I tested an alias with a filter and a routing value on staging and it behaved as expected.

I then tried to break it. A query body built by hand without the filter was rejected by the check with an error. A query through the alias without a filter returned only that customer's documents, as intended. A query with a filter for a different customer through the alias returned nothing.

For performance, the routing value sends queries by a customer to a subset of shards. In the monthly layout this is combined with the time range, so most queries touch one to three shards. I measured this on a test index with synthetic data of similar shape and p95 dropped from about 420 ms to 150 ms for a large customer.

The test data is smaller than production, so I treat these numbers as indicative only. I wrote that into the document.

Next I need to decide how many primary shards per month and how to handle the current month, which is still being written. I will look at that after the first part of the planning has been reviewed by Tobias and Mara.

summary: Daily throttled-keys page works in the admin console: Lena's table reads my endpoint, and I fixed a pagination bug that skipped rows on equal counts
body:
Lena finished the page for throttled keys and I reviewed her pull request in the evening. The table shows customer, key, day and hit count, with filters for customer and minimum count, and a link from each key to its limit form, so sales can raise a limit directly.

While testing I noticed that page two started with a row that was already visible on page one. The cause was in my endpoint: it sorted by count only, and rows with equal counts have no stable order. Offset paging then repeats or skips rows.

I added the day and the key id as tiebreakers to the sort. The page boundaries are now stable. I wrote a test with 120 rows, all with the same count, and check that paging returns each row exactly once.

Lena's code was fine. One suggestion was to keep the filter values in the URL, so a filtered view can be shared with Sam. She did it in a few minutes.

We checked the empty state. With no throttled keys the page shows a short note instead of an empty table, which Sam liked.

I also added the alert for a missed run of the nightly job. It fires if no rows or marker has been written by 03:00 UTC. It is in the alert rules repository as code, with a link to the runbook.

The job's marker is a row in a small table with the run time and the number of keys read. That is easier to check than looking at the output, since a quiet night legitimately produces no rows.

Staging has the page now, and production deploy is planned for tomorrow with the counter change. After that the rate-limits branch can close.

summary: Decided the shard counts for the monthly layout: 3 primaries per month for large customers' data and a shared month index for small ones, after measuring document counts per month
body:
Today's planning step was how many primary shards each monthly index gets. I pulled document counts and sizes per month from the last year of the current index.

The volume is uneven. A month of data for the three large customers together is about 90 GB, and the other 37 customers together add about 25 GB. If everything goes into one index per month, the large customers dominate it.

The proposal is two kinds of monthly indices. Large customers get their own monthly index with 3 primary shards, which gives about 10 GB per shard, a good size for fast merges. The small customers share one monthly index with 2 primary shards, routed by customer.

I checked the alternative of a single index per month with 5 shards. It is simpler, but the large customers' queries would then compete with all the others for the same shards, and the routing would send the small ones to the same shards as the large ones. The two-kind layout costs more setup but isolates the heavy users.

A customer can move from the shared to the dedicated kind when it grows. Moving means a reindex of its documents, which we can do with the same tool as the main migration. I wrote that this is a manual operation for now.

For the current month, writes go to the newest index, and we use rollover by size as a safety so a single index cannot grow beyond 30 GB per shard.

Mara raised a point in review: the nightly reindex job assumes one index per customer. It will need changes to iterate the monthly indices, and the job should only reindex the months where documents changed. I added that as a separate task.

Open items:
- a template for the monthly indices with the right mappings, from the search-v2 mapping
- the alias naming, which I propose as search-{customer}-read and search-{customer}-write
- a dry run of the migration on a staging copy

Tobias will review the document tomorrow. I did not start any migration step in production and the plan says that this only happens after the staging dry run has passed twice.

summary: Production deploy of the throttle counters and report page went out; the first nightly run found 4 keys above 100 hits, all from one customer already known to sales
body:
The deploy of the counter, the nightly job and the admin page went to production this morning. I watched Redis command rates before and after and saw no visible change, since only rejected requests add a command.

The nightly job ran for the first time at its scheduled time and wrote 4 rows. All 4 keys belong to one customer who has been throttled for days, and Sam already had them on his list for a talk about a higher limit. That showed the report was right.

The missed run alert is active. I tested it on staging by pausing the job, and it fired after the grace period and resolved after a manual run.

The rate-limits branch is closed now. The remaining wish is a weekly summary mail to sales, which I put in the backlog because Sam said the page is enough for now.

I also updated the runbook with the report and the threshold setting.

summary: Staging dry run of the shard migration tool on a 10 percent sample copied 1.2 million documents correctly, but the alias filter was missing for one customer with a space in its name
body:
I built a first version of the migration tool for the new layout, based on the reindex API with a scripted loop per customer and month. Today I ran it on staging with a sample of about 10 percent of the data.

The tool creates the monthly indices from the template, reindexes by customer and month with a query on the event timestamp, and creates the aliases at the end. It copied 1.2 million documents in about 25 minutes. Document counts per customer and month matched the source in all cases except one.

The exception was a customer whose name contains a space. The alias name was built from the display name and the alias creation failed, so that customer had data in the new index but no alias with a filter. A query through the search API fell back to the customer filter only, which still returned correct data, but the protection of the alias was missing.

The fix is to build alias names from the customer id, not the name. I changed that in the tool and in the search API helper. A test now creates a customer with spaces and unusual characters and checks that the alias exists and carries the filter.

I also found that the tool did not verify the counts itself. I added a verification step that compares counts per customer and month between old and new and exits with an error if there is any difference. It also samples 200 random documents and compares their fields.

The reindex speed was lower than I hoped for. I tried a higher number of slices, and 8 slices raised the throughput by about 60 percent with no visible load problem on staging. For production I will use that, but I need Tobias to confirm that the extra nodes can take the load.

Second dry run is planned after the fixes, with a copy closer to the real size. The plan says two clean runs are needed before anything starts in production.

I wrote the results into the planning document.

summary: Adapted the nightly reindex job to iterate monthly indices and skip months without changes; on staging it finished in 9 minutes instead of 38
body:
Following Mara's remark, I changed the nightly reindex job so it can work with the monthly layout. The old version assumed one index per customer and rebuilt all of it each night.

The new version lists the monthly indices of each customer, and for each month it compares the highest update timestamp in Postgres with a marker stored from the last run. Months without changes are skipped. In practice only the current month and sometimes the one before change.

On the staging copy the job went from 38 minutes to 9 minutes, since most of the time was spent on old months that never change. A shorter run should also reduce the load around the backup window, which is something I want to look at again once the job is in production and we can see real timings.

One problem came up in testing. A late event with an old timestamp updates a document in an old month, and the marker based on the event time would miss it. I switched the marker to the ingest time of the document, so a late event marks its old month as changed.

I wrote tests for late events, for a month with no documents, and for a customer who has just been created and has no markers yet. The last case reindexes everything for that customer, which is the right behavior.

The markers live in a small Postgres table with customer, month and last run. It is tiny, and I added the primary key on the first two columns.

The job still works with the old layout through a setting, so the change can go to production before the migration. That keeps the deploys separate. I will deploy it only after Mara has reviewed it, so for now it stays on the branch and on staging.

summary: Redis memory on the cache instance fell about 12 percent a few days after the summary key change, as old-format keys expired by their TTLs
body:
I checked the Redis memory graph again. After the key naming change, the old keys without customer prefix expire by their TTLs, and the memory on the cache instance fell about 12 percent compared with last week.

The per-customer sets add some memory, but much less than the old keys release. The hit rate stayed at 77 percent.

The longest TTL on the summary keys is still 7 days, and a share of the keys are read only once. I will look at which dashboards produce those, but that is a task for next week.

I added the memory numbers to the planning notes for the Redis version upgrade.

summary: Shard migration tool now builds the alias filter from the customer id instead of the name, so the customer with a space in its name is covered on the 10 percent sample
body:
The dry run earlier today missed the alias filter for one customer whose name contains a space. The tool built the filter from the display name and passed it unquoted. I changed it to use the numeric customer id everywhere, and the name is only used in log lines.

I added a test with three names: one with a space, one with a quote, and one with unicode letters. All three produce a valid alias with a term filter on customer_id. Then I reran the dry run on staging with the same 10 percent sample.

The run copied 1.2 million documents again and every customer now has an alias. I compared document counts per customer between the old index and the new monthly indices, and they match for all 40 customers. Search results for ten saved queries gave the same top 20 hits in both layouts, apart from two ties that came back in a different order.

The tie order is a known effect of different shard counts, so I did not chase it. The next step is a run on a 50 percent sample with timing, then a plan for the cutover window with Tobias. I also noted in the plan that the alias creation must happen before any traffic is switched.

summary: Ran the shard migration on a 50 percent sample in staging: it took 41 minutes and the copy rate dropped near the end because the large customers' months were last
body:
I started the 50 percent sample migration on staging at the start of the morning, with the fixed alias logic from last night. It copied about 6.1 million documents in 41 minutes. The rate started at roughly 3,800 documents per second and fell to about 1,900 in the last ten minutes.

The slowdown came from the order of work. The tool went through customers alphabetically, and the three large customers happen to sit late in the alphabet, so their big months ran at the end with only one worker busy. I changed the scheduler to sort tasks by document count, largest first, and to hand them to a pool of four workers.

I reran the same sample with the new order. It finished in 27 minutes and the rate stayed above 3,200 documents per second the whole time. OpenSearch bulk rejections were zero in both runs, so the bulk size of 2,000 documents is fine.

I checked document counts per customer and per month again, and they match. I also checked that the refresh interval is restored to the normal value after the run, because the tool sets it to 30 seconds while copying. It was restored.

One open point is the deletion of the old by-customer indices. I do not want the tool to do it, so it only prints the list. The next step is to write down the cutover order with Tobias and to test the rollback of an alias switch on staging.

summary: Answered Sam: a customer's API key that is throttled sees HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header of one to five seconds, and the docs say so now
body:
Sam asked what a customer sees when a key hits its limit, because two support tickets this week described it differently. I read the middleware and tested it on staging with a key limited to 5 requests per second.

The response is HTTP 429 with a JSON body that has an error code, the limit and the key id. The Retry-After header holds the seconds until the current window ends, so between 1 and 5 with the present window settings. Requests after the window starts again go through normally.

The two tickets differed because one customer's client library ignores the header and retries after a fixed 30 seconds. That customer saw a long pause, while the other saw short ones. This is not a bug on our side.

I wrote a short section for the public API docs about the 429 response, the header and a suggestion to honor it. Sam reviewed the wording and changed two sentences to be clearer for non-native readers. The page is merged and will go out with the next docs build.

summary: Wrote the cutover and rollback plan for the monthly shard layout: alias switch per customer, old indices kept for 7 days, and a check list after each switch
body:
Together with Tobias's cost estimate, the staging runs give enough to write the real plan. I wrote it as a document in the repo, next to the migration tool, so it can be reviewed in a pull request.

The plan goes in four phases. First, the tool copies a customer's data into the monthly indices while the old by-customer index still takes writes. Second, a catch-up pass copies the documents that arrived since the first copy, using the ingest timestamp. Third, the search alias of that customer switches to the monthly indices in one atomic alias update. Fourth, the old index stays for 7 days and is then deleted by hand.

I chose to go per customer, starting with the small ones, so a mistake affects one customer. The three large customers come last, one per night, and the nightly reindex job must be paused for them.

Checks after each switch:
- document count per customer matches within 0.01 percent
- ten saved queries return the same top hits
- p95 latency of the search API for that customer is not above the value of the week before
- no 4xx from the missing customer filter rule

Rollback is the same alias update in the other direction, and it works as long as the old index exists and the writes during the new phase went to both. That means dual writes in the indexing path, which I have not built yet. I listed it as the main open item and estimated one day of work.

I also noted a risk: the catch-up pass reads by timestamp, and events with a late timestamp could be missed. The count check should find that, but a second catch-up before the switch is cheap, so I added it. Tobias will review the plan tomorrow.

summary: Built the dual write in the indexing path so new events reach both the old customer index and the monthly index, with a flag per customer to turn it on
body:
The rollback in the cutover plan needs both layouts to receive new events during a migration, so I built the dual write today. The change is in the indexer that reads from the queue and sends bulk requests to OpenSearch.

For each event the indexer now computes two targets when the customer flag dual_write is on: the old by-customer index and the monthly index from the event time. It adds both actions to the same bulk request. If one item of the pair fails, the indexer logs it with both targets and retries just that item, so the other copy is not written twice. Document ids are the event ids, so a repeated write overwrites and does not duplicate.

The flag lives in the settings table in Postgres and the indexer reads it through a small cache with a 30 second refresh. I first thought of Redis for this, but the settings are few and the table is already read by other code, so I kept it simple.

Tests:
- unit tests for the target calculation, including an event right at a month boundary in UTC
- an integration test with a local OpenSearch that sends 1,000 events and checks both indices
- a test where the monthly index rejects one item and the retry fixes it

On staging I turned the flag on for two customers and sent a replayed stream of 200,000 events. Both indices matched exactly. Indexing throughput fell by about 35 percent per worker, which is expected because the bulk request is twice as large, and the queue lag stayed under 3 seconds.

The cost on production needs thought. Dual write for the three large customers at the same time would likely push the indexers to their limit, so the plan to do one customer at a time matters. I added this to the plan document. Next step is a review of the change by Mara and a production deploy with all flags off.

summary: Reviewed Tobias's Terraform change for the extra OpenSearch data nodes and asked for a tag on the nodes so the temporary cost can be found and removed after the migration
body:
Tobias opened a pull request that adds two data nodes to the OpenSearch domain for the reindex week. I read the plan output and the variables.

The change itself is small: the instance count goes from 6 to 8 with the same instance type and the same volume size. The plan shows an in-place change with a blue and green deployment, which on AWS means the domain copies data to a new set of nodes. That takes hours and puts load on the cluster, so I asked him to run it in the early night and not during the busy period.

I asked for two more things. First, a tag temporary_until on the domain so the cost report shows the extra spend and someone sees the date to remove it. Second, an output that prints the node count, so a later change does not silently keep the larger size. He agreed to both and pushed an update within the hour.

I also checked that the disk watermarks are still fine with eight nodes. The new layout has more small shards, and I counted about 1,100 shards across all indices in the plan, which is below the limit of roughly 1,000 per node with the node count we will have.

Approved the pull request. Tobias will apply it tonight and I will check the cluster health tomorrow morning before the next migration run.

summary: Cluster health after the node increase is green with 8 data nodes, and shard rebalancing finished in about 3 hours without search errors
body:
Checked the OpenSearch domain first thing, after Tobias applied the change last night. Status is green, 8 data nodes, no unassigned shards. The blue and green step finished a little after 02:00, according to the domain events.

I looked at the search API error rate during the window and it was flat at 0.02 percent, the same as the days before. The p95 latency rose from 180 ms to about 260 ms for roughly 40 minutes while data moved and then came back. That matches what Tobias expected.

Heap use on the new nodes sits around 55 percent and the disks are at 38 percent, so there is room for the temporary copy of the large customers' data. I saved a screenshot of the dashboard panels into the plan document so we can compare later.

summary: Deployed the dual write to production with all flags off, then turned it on for one small customer and found the monthly index template was missing a mapping for a date field
body:
I deployed the dual write change in the morning with all customer flags off. The indexer metrics did not change, which was the purpose: same throughput, same lag of about 1 second.

Then I picked the smallest customer, about 90,000 documents, and turned dual_write on for it. Within a minute the indexer logged mapping errors for the monthly index: the field received_at was dynamically mapped as text on the first document that carried it as a string without a timezone. The by-customer index has an explicit mapping for it as date, but the template of the monthly indices did not have it.

The cause was how I created the template for the monthly layout. I copied the settings and the main mappings, but left out three fields that were added to the old template later: received_at, source_version and the nested attributes object. I compared the two templates field by field and found exactly those three.

Fix:
- added the three fields to the monthly template
- deleted the single monthly index that had the wrong mapping, since it held only a few minutes of dual-written data
- added a test that compares the field list of both templates and fails on any difference that is not listed as intended

After that I turned the flag on again. No errors for 20 minutes, and the document counts in both indices match for the new events. The backfill pass for that customer will run later.

The staging runs did not show this because the staging template was created by the migration tool from the old index mapping directly, and production uses the Terraform template. That difference is itself a problem, so I wrote a note to make the tool use the same template file in both places. For now the new test covers the gap.

summary: Prepared the copy of the smallest customer's history to the monthly shard layout and checked the dry run against the plan, without switching anything in production
body:
With the missing date mapping fixed in the monthly index template and the dual write running for about five hours, I prepared the first copy for the smallest customer. I did not run it against the live alias. I ran the copy tool in dry-run mode, which reads the customer's documents and reports what it would write without creating anything. It counted 90,412 documents that would go into four monthly indices, and the estimate for the real copy was about two minutes.

Then I wrote the catch-up step. It uses the ingest timestamp taken at the start of the first copy, so that documents written during the copy window are picked up afterwards. I tested the timestamp filter on a staging index with a small bulk import running, and it found the expected few hundred documents on the first pass and none on the second.

I also turned the checks from the plan into a script, so that nobody has to do them by hand after each switch:
- count per customer in both layouts
- ten saved queries, comparing the top 20 hits
- p95 latency for the customer before and after
- a look at rejections from the customer filter rule

I ran the script against the staging copy and fixed one problem: it compared hit order too strictly, so equal scores showed up as differences. It now accepts a different order within the same score.

I also wrote the alias switch as a single update call, so the customer never sees a state with two indices or none. The old index stays for 7 days and the dual write stays on until then, so a rollback is still possible.

Next is the real copy for the smallest customer, and after that the other small customers in batches of five. I want Sam to tell the two customers with the most support contact that a short change is coming, even though they should not notice it.

summary: Looked at why the Redis cache instance shows 300 more client connections than the app pools should open, and found the admin console opens one connection per session store call
body:
The Redis dashboard showed about 480 connected clients, while the search API and ingest pools together should use fewer than 200. I listed clients with CLIENT LIST and grouped them by the name and address.

About 290 belonged to the admin console. Its session store middleware creates a new client for each request when the session lookup misses the first time, and the old client is closed only after an idle timeout of 60 seconds. At normal traffic that adds up to a few hundred open connections.

I did not change the code yet. The fix is to share a single client in the middleware, and Lena owns that part of the console, so I wrote the finding and the line of the file into a ticket for her. In the meantime the idle timeout is not a risk, since we are far from the server limit.

I also added a client name for each service in the connection setup, so the next listing is easier to read.

summary: Prepared the next batch of five small customers for the monthly layout in a dry run, and found that one customer's saved query could change order on equal scores
body:
I prepared the migration for five more small customers and ran it as a dry run only, with no copy to production and no alias changes. Together they hold about 410,000 documents. I estimated the copy at around 7 minutes with four workers, based on the earlier batches, and checked the plan against the skip list so the customer with the long import is not touched again.

While preparing, I ran the saved query check on staging against copies of the five customers' data in both layouts. The check passed for four. For the fifth, one query returned the same set of 20 hits but in a different order on positions 6 to 9. I looked at the scores and they were equal for those four documents, so the order came from the shard and the internal document id. In the old layout the customer had one shard, and in the new shared month index the shards are mixed.

I do not think this is a defect, but customers sometimes see a result order as stable. As a cheap fix I added a tiebreak on the event id in the search API sort when scores are equal. That makes the order the same across layouts and also between repeated queries. I tested it on staging with the same query and got identical lists in both layouts.

The tiebreak adds a sort key to every query. I measured on staging with the query set of 500 queries, and the p95 changed from 112 to 114 ms, which I accept. The change is in a pull request waiting for Mara's review, and it is not deployed yet.

The real run for the five customers is planned for later, after the tiebreak is in production, so the alias switch does not change anything the customers can see. Remaining are about 25 customers, then the three large ones, and the large ones need the pause of the nightly reindex.

summary: Wrote the Redis key naming guide for the team after the summary key change, with the prefix format, TTL rules and how to drop one customer's cache without a scan
body:
The key change of the last weeks worked well, so I put the rules into a short guide in the docs folder of the repo. Without it the next feature will invent its own format.

The guide says that every key starts with a service prefix, then the customer id, then a version number, then the name, for example nebula:search:c123:v2:summary. The version is raised when the format of the cached value changes, so old keys are simply not read and expire by their TTLs. This is the same thing that lowered the memory by about 12 percent after the last change.

TTL rules:
- every key written by the app must have a TTL, and the helper function refuses a write without one
- summary and dashboard keys use 10 minutes to 1 hour
- rate limit counters use the window length plus a margin
- session keys follow the session lifetime of 8 hours

For dropping one customer's cache there is a small set per customer that holds the names of its keys, and the helper deletes the keys in that set. I described the cost: one extra write per cache fill, and the set has the same TTL as the longest key it points to.

I also listed what not to do. No KEYS command in production code, and no keys with user input in them without a hash, since search queries can be long and contain spaces.

Mara read it and suggested adding an example of a bad key from the old code, so I added one. The guide is merged. A follow-up is a lint rule that checks the prefix in new code, which I put on the list without a date.

summary: Tried a lint rule that checks Redis key prefixes in TypeScript and dropped it: the rule could not see keys built from variables, so it flagged half of the correct code
body:
After writing the key naming guide, I wanted to enforce the prefix with an ESLint rule. The plan was to look at the first argument of the Redis helper calls and check that a string literal starts with the service prefix.

I built a first version in an hour. It worked for literals, but most of our keys are built with template strings and a key builder function, for example key(customerId, 'summary'). The rule could not follow the function, so it either skipped all of those calls and checked nothing useful, or flagged them all.

I tried a second approach with type information, with a branded string type for keys that only the key builder can create. That would be solid, but it needs changes in about 60 call sites across the search API and the admin console, and some are in Lena's code. The gain does not justify that now, since the helper already refuses writes without a TTL and the builder is the normal path.

I removed the rule and left a note in the guide that the key builder must be used. Maybe a review checklist item is enough. Nothing else changed.

summary: Planned the next batch of the monthly layout migration, checked the tool against a running import, and prepared a skip for customers with active loader jobs.
body:
The evening was spent on preparing the next batch of customers for the monthly layout. The batch under discussion had twelve customers with about 2.2 million documents together. I did not copy anything in production; I ran the whole plan against staging with a replayed copy of their data to see how long it would take and how the catch-up passes would behave.

The dry run on staging took about 19 minutes for the copy. For eleven of the twelve customers, the simulated catch-up passes found small numbers and the second pass found none, which is what we want to see before touching production.

One customer looked different. Its first simulated catch-up found 4,100 documents and the second still found 380. I checked the loader job table in Postgres and saw that this customer had an NDJSON import running. The importer writes documents continuously, so there is no quiet moment, and the catch-up cannot converge to zero while the import runs. The dual write covers new documents, so data would not be lost, but the pass would never settle.

I decided that this customer should be skipped in the real batch and run after the import ends. To avoid doing this by hand, I added a check in the migration tool: if the customer has a running loader job, the tool prints a message and skips them. I tested it on staging with the customer in question and with a customer without a job, and both behaved as expected.

I also read through the check list for the count check and the saved queries once more, so that the eleven other customers can be switched in one run with the alias switch and half an hour of watching error rate and latency.

Status: nothing in this batch is switched yet. The tool is ready, the skip works, and I will look at the import tomorrow to see when it is expected to finish.

summary: Planned the migration of the three large customers: one per night, reindex paused, a catch-up with timestamps and a limit on indexer throughput so the queue lag stays under 10 seconds
body:
The small and medium customers are mostly done, so I used the evening to plan the part with risk. The three large customers together hold about 70 percent of the data, around 190 million documents, so the copy takes hours and the dual write takes real capacity.

From the staging runs I estimated the copy speed at 3,200 documents per second with four workers, so the biggest customer with 90 million documents needs around 8 hours. The dual write for that customer adds about 40 percent of load on the indexers, because it has the highest ingest rate of all.

The plan I wrote down:
- one customer per night, starting after the busy period of the customer ends, with the largest last
- the nightly reindex job skips the customer that is being migrated, using a skip list option I will add
- the tool throttles itself when the queue lag is above 10 seconds, so ingest keeps priority
- two catch-up passes before the switch, as for the small ones
- after the switch the old index stays for 7 days, and the dual write stays on as well

The throttle needs the lag metric. Prometheus has it, so the tool queries it every 30 seconds and pauses the workers when the value is too high. I will build this first, since it protects the ingest path.

Two risks. The first is disk space on the data nodes: both copies of a large customer exist for a week, and with the extra nodes the disks stay under 60 percent in my estimate, but I want an alert at 70. The second is the cost of a rollback after the old index is deleted, which is a full copy again. That is why the old index stays for 7 days.

Tobias will check the disk estimate against the real volumes, and I will ask him to add the alert. The first large customer is planned in two nights, after the throttle works.

summary: Built the lag-based throttle and the skip list option in the migration tool and tested them on staging with a replayed ingest burst
body:
Today I implemented the two things the large customer plan needs. The tool queries Prometheus for the indexer queue lag every 30 seconds. When the value is above 10 seconds it pauses the copy workers, and it resumes when the lag is below 5 seconds. The two thresholds avoid flapping.

The second part is a skip list option for the nightly reindex job. It reads a list of customer ids from the settings table and leaves their indices out, both old and monthly. Without this the reindex could rewrite a customer's index in the middle of a copy and the counts would not match.

To test the throttle I replayed a burst on staging: 50,000 events per minute for ten minutes, on top of a running copy. The lag rose above 10 seconds after about three minutes, the tool logged that it paused, and the lag fell back under 5 seconds in 40 seconds. The copy then resumed. Over the ten minutes the copy ran for about 60 percent of the time, and the lag peaked at 14 seconds, since the pause only takes effect at the next check.

I shortened the check interval to 10 seconds and repeated the burst. The peak was then 11 seconds, which is acceptable.

The skip list was tested with a unit test and one run of the reindex on staging with two customers on the list. Both were skipped and the log shows them. The reindex time with the monthly layout stayed at about 9 minutes.

Open items: the disk alert from Tobias and the customer with the running import. I checked and the import finished last night, so that customer can go in the next small batch.

summary: Prepared the customer with the long import for the monthly shard layout with a trial copy into a scratch index, and planned the alias switch for later.
body:
The import of that customer finished overnight, according to the loader job table, and no other job was running for them. I did not touch the production alias. Instead I ran a trial copy of about 1.3 million documents into a scratch index with the same mappings as the monthly layout. It took 7 minutes.

The first catch-up pass on the scratch index found 210 documents that had arrived during the copy, and a second pass found none. Counts matched the old index and the saved queries returned the same results. One query had a different order because of equal scores, the same thing we saw with another customer, so I added it to the list of known differences for the check list.

Nothing has been switched for this customer yet, and the production alias still points to the old index. The plan is to do the small batch of 18 customers first, then the three large ones, one per night. For this customer I wrote down the steps for the alias switch and for keeping the old index for a week as a way back, and I will decide on the switch after the batch review with Tobias.

summary: Prepared the last small batch of 18 customers for the monthly shard layout, fixed a tool crash on a customer name with a percent sign, and wrote the check list for the first large customer
body:
The last small batch has 18 customers and about 3.4 million documents in total. I did a dry run in the morning on staging with the throttle on, and the tool estimated a copy of around half an hour. In the dry run the throttle paused the workers twice for under a minute each, when a customer's batch import raised the queue lag. That is the behavior I want, so I left the thresholds as they are.

The dry run also found a bug. For one customer the tool crashed after the copy with a parse error in the log summary step. The customer name contained a percent sign, and the summary line was built with a format string that read it as a placeholder. The copy itself had finished, so no data was affected, but the tool exited before the catch-up. I fixed the line to pass the name as an argument, added a test with a percent sign in the name, and ran the catch-up for that customer separately on staging. After the fix, all counts matched.

The saved queries passed for all 18 on staging. The plan for production is to switch the aliases in groups of six with a pause of 10 minutes between groups, watching the error rate and the p95 latency of the search API. I have not started the production batch yet. It is scheduled for the next quiet window, and no customer has been moved to the monthly layout in production so far; everyone stays on the layout by customer until then.

The three large customers are the real test, so I also wrote a check list for the first one:
- skip list entry for the customer in the reindex job
- dual write on at least a day before the copy, to have the index in the monthly layout growing
- disk alert at 70 percent active on the data nodes
- a person on call who knows the plan, which will be me, with Tobias as backup
- the lag throttle thresholds at 10 and 5 seconds
- the alias switch only after two clean catch-up passes and a manual look at the dashboards

I also asked Sam to prepare a short note for the support channel in case the large customer reports slow searches during the copy. Tobias confirmed that the disk alert is in and tested it by lowering the threshold for a minute.

summary: Looked into a Postgres slow query on the admin jobs page: the loader job table scan took 1.8 seconds, and a partial index on active jobs brought it to 12 ms
body:
Lena reported that the jobs page in the admin console feels slow again, even after the paging fix. I took the query from the Fastify logs and ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of production data in staging.

The query lists the jobs of a customer ordered by creation time, with a filter on status in ('running', 'queued', 'failed'). The table has about 4 million rows, and most are old finished jobs. The planner used the index on customer_id and then sorted and filtered about 90,000 rows for the big customers. Total time was 1.8 seconds for the largest customer.

I tried three things:
- a composite index on (customer_id, created_at desc): the time fell to 400 ms, but the filter still read many rows
- a partial index on (customer_id, created_at desc) where status in the three active states: 12 ms
- both together: no gain over the partial index alone

The partial index is small, since only a few thousand rows are in those states at any time, so it adds almost nothing to the write cost. I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on production to avoid blocking the loader writes. It took 40 seconds and the table stayed usable.

The page needs the finished jobs as well, with a filter for them. For that view the composite index is enough, and the query there is paged, so it reads only 50 rows. I did not add the composite index, to save space, and I will watch it.

I checked pg_stat_statements the next hour: the mean time of the query fell from 1.6 seconds to 15 ms and the calls per minute did not change. Lena confirmed that the page loads quickly now.

The retention purge of old job records that I planned two weeks ago would help here too. I have not built it yet, so the table is still at 4 million rows. I put it as the next small item, after the large customer migration.

summary: Answered Mara: the dual write does not change event ids, so the loader retry safe-write behavior still applies and a retried chunk overwrites instead of duplicating
body:
Mara asked whether the dual write in the indexer could produce duplicates when the loader retries a failed chunk. I checked the code path from the loader to the queue to the indexer.

The loader assigns an event id per document when it reads the file, and the id is the same on a retry of the chunk. The indexer uses that id as the document id in both targets. So a retried chunk overwrites the earlier copy in the old and in the monthly index.

One case needs attention: if the event time differs on a retry, the monthly index could change. The loader takes the event time from the file and not from the clock, so it does not differ. I confirmed it with a test that replays one chunk twice and counts documents in both indices. Both showed the same count.

summary: Dual write for the first large customer has run for a day: the indexer lag peaks at 4 seconds and the monthly indices hold 6.1 million new documents matching the old index
body:
The dual write for the first large customer went on last night. I looked at the dashboards at midday. The indexer queue lag peaks at 4 seconds in the busy hours and is about 1 second otherwise, so the extra load is fine.

I compared counts of documents since the flag was turned on, by the ingest timestamp. Old index: 6,118,402. Monthly indices: 6,118,402. A second check with an aggregation by hour gave the same buckets for all 24 hours.
