Disk use on the data nodes rose by 2 percentage points, as estimated, and the 70 percent alert is quiet. The full copy is planned for tonight after the customer's busy period.

summary: Wrote the Redis memory checklist for on-call after Tobias asked what to look at when the cache instance climbs: biggest key groups, TTL coverage and the client output buffers
body:
Tobias asked for a short list for on-call, since the Redis memory alert fired twice last month and each time someone looked at different things. I wrote a page in the runbook with the order of checks.

First, INFO memory: used memory, the peak and the fragmentation ratio. A ratio above 1.5 points to fragmentation and not data growth. Second, the key count and the share of keys that have a TTL, from INFO keyspace, where the expires number should be close to the key count for the cache instance. Third, a sample of keys by prefix with redis-cli --memkeys or a scan on a replica, never a scan on the primary at busy times.

For sizes, the guide points to the prefixes of the naming guide: summary keys, rate counters, sessions. The summary keys are the biggest group at about 60 percent of the memory, and a customer-wide drop with the key set is the fast fix when one customer's data grows.

The last check is client output buffers, with CLIENT LIST and the omem column, because a slow subscriber can hold a lot of memory. We do not use pub/sub on the cache instance now, but the check costs nothing.

I added what to do for each result: raise the version number of a key group, shorten a TTL, drop one customer, or scale the instance, and who to call. Tobias reviewed it and asked for the current numbers of a normal day, so I added them: about 3.1 GB used, 2.4 million keys, 99.8 percent with a TTL.

summary: Prepared the copy of the first large customer's history to the monthly layout: checked the tool on staging, set the skip list entry and planned the run for after their busy period.
body:
The first large customer's dual write had run for more than a day, so today was about getting ready to copy their history to the monthly layout. I did not start the copy itself.

I added the customer to the skip list entry so the nightly reindex job leaves them alone, and I checked that the job log shows the entry as read. Then I ran the tool on staging with a sample of about 2 million documents. It wrote them into monthly indices with 3 primaries each, and the counts matched after one catch-up pass.

I looked at the throttle settings. The workers pause when the queue lag goes over 10 seconds and resume when it falls under 5. On staging I forced a lag spike with a test import, and the workers paused and resumed as expected. I am still not sure how a batch import from another customer will push the lag in production, so I will watch the lag graph during the run and keep the pause limit as it is.

I estimated the disk use. The monthly indices for this customer should add about 10 percent of the data node disk, which would take use from 38 to around 49 percent, below the alert. I wrote that number in the run notes so I can compare it later.

I also found that one of the saved queries sorts by a field with null values, and the null order can differ between the layouts. I tested a missing value option of _last in the sort on staging and the lists are the same. The change will go in before the production run.

The plan is to start after their busy period, run the catch-up passes until one finds nothing, then check the counts and the saved queries. The alias stays on the old index until I have looked at the latency with a fresh mind.

summary: Prepared the switch of the first large customer's alias to the monthly layout by checking the earlier copy and writing the plan, without changing the alias.
body:
I looked at the results of the copy of the first large customer's history again this afternoon and found nothing new: counts match, the dual write is in sync, and the disk is at 49 percent. The indexer lag stayed low for the whole day.

I went through the check list for the first large customer line by line and ran the parts that can be run before a switch. The saved queries return the same hits on the old index and on the monthly indices. The filter rule for their API keys gives the same answers on both. The cache hit rate for their summary keys does not depend on the layout, since the cache sits above the search layer, so I do not expect it to move.

I also measured the old layout as a baseline. The p95 for this customer was 340 ms over the last week. My guess is that a query for a recent time range will touch only the last one or two monthly indices instead of all of the customer's data in one large index, but that is only a guess until I see it in production. I did not change the alias. The switch is planned for the quiet time of their morning, in one alias update, and I will watch the search API for an hour afterwards.

The old index and the dual write will stay for 7 days after the switch. Tobias agreed to be on backup. The second large customer comes after this one, with the same checklist.

summary: Second large customer's dual write has run overnight: the indexer lag stays under 6 seconds and the monthly indices match the old index document for document
body: Turned on the dual write for the second large customer yesterday evening and checked it this evening after about a day of traffic. The monthly indices hold 4.8 million new documents, and the count matches the old customer index exactly in a per-month comparison. Indexer lag peaked at 6 seconds during the afternoon import window, still under the 10 second limit from the plan, and the queue drained within a minute after each peak. I also compared a sample of 2,000 document ids by hash of the source field and found no differences. The one oddity was a burst of mapping warnings for a custom date field, which turned out to be the same missing mapping we fixed in the template for the first small customer, so I checked that this customer's months carry the fixed template and they do. Redis latency for the cache stayed flat, so the extra indexing load did not leak into the query cache. Next is the history copy for this customer, which I scheduled for tomorrow night with the lag throttle at the same setting as for the first large customer. After the copy, a catch-up pass and the alias switch follow the check list, and the old index stays for 7 days.

summary: Prepared the copy of the second large customer's history to the monthly layout: checked the dual write, the throttle settings and the plan for the night run, without starting the copy.
body:
The dual write for the second large customer had been running for two days, so I used the morning to prepare the copy and did not start it. The indexer lag in that time stayed under 9 seconds, below the target of 10 seconds. The monthly indices for the customer already held all new documents from the start of the dual write.

I planned the copy for the night, after the reindex job is paused. The migration tool will run with the lag-based throttle set to a limit of 10 seconds. I tested the throttle on a small slice of one month in a scratch index. It paused the workers when I raised the lag by hand and resumed them after the lag fell. I also reread the first large customer's run, where the throttle paused the workers four times, and expect a few more pauses here because of the customer's size and the bursts from one of its apps.

I counted the old customer index per month, so that the comparison afterwards is not only a total. There are 26 months. I wrote the counts into a sheet next to the planned catch-up pass. One thing to watch: an old bulk import used generated ids in its first version, so the old index may hold duplicates by event id. The tool writes with the event id as the document id, so the second write overwrites the first, and a monthly index with a slightly higher or lower count than the old one needs a look before it is called a mismatch.

I also checked that the mapping of the date field that caused trouble with the first small customer is in the index template. The template fix from last week is there, so new monthly indices of this customer will get it.

I told Tobias the time of the run. He will watch the CPU on the data nodes in Grafana and said the limits he planned should be enough. Next is the start of the copy tonight. The review with the customer's top ten saved queries on both layouts comes after it, and the third large customer, whose dual write is not yet on, stays last.

summary: Compared the saved queries of the second large customer on old and new layout: nine of ten return the same hits, one differs by order because of equal scores
body:
Ran the ten most used saved queries of the second large customer against both the old customer index and the monthly alias. Nine of them returned the same hits in the same order. One returned the same set of hits but in a different order for results with equal scores.

This is the same effect that showed up with the small customer last week. Scores are computed per shard, and with a different shard layout the term statistics differ a little. The ordering for equal scores falls back to the internal document order, which is not stable between layouts.

I looked at the query. It sorts by relevance only, and the customer uses it in a dashboard widget that shows the top 20 errors. A change in the order inside the group of equal scores would be visible there. I added a secondary sort on the event timestamp, newest first, to the query builder when no sort is given by the client.

This changes the behavior for all customers on the monthly layout, so I checked with Lena whether the console sends its own sort. It does for the table view, but not for the widget. The widget now gets stable results on both layouts.

I ran the ten queries again and all ten matched in order. I wrote a note for Sam, because customers may ask why an order changed, and the answer is that the order of equal scores is now by time.

The tie break is in the main checkout and has a unit test with two documents of equal score. It is deployed with the next release this afternoon, before the alias switch.

summary: Prepared the cutover of the second large customer's alias to the monthly layout: ran the check list against the dual write and wrote down the rollback steps, without switching anything yet.
body:
The release with the sort tie break went out at noon. After that I started on the cutover plan for the second large customer, which we agreed last week: first the check list against the new monthly indices, then the switch itself later, after Mara has had a look at it.

The alias is still on the old customer index. I only ran the checks and wrote the steps down. The old index stays in place for 7 days after the switch with the dual write still on, so a rollback would be only a switch back, and I put that into the plan as the first line.

The check list passed in order on the dual write side. First, the document counts for the last 30 days matched on both sides. Second, the ten saved queries returned the same hits, except one that differs in order because of equal scores, which the tie break release should now settle. Third, the search error rate stayed at the usual 0.02 percent. Fourth, the indexer lag was under 6 seconds for the last hour.

I also ran the wide time range queries of this customer against the monthly indices on the side, with the old alias untouched. The p95 of that sample was clearly lower than what the customer sees today, around 230 ms against 410 ms, but a sample from my laptop script is not the same as live traffic, so I do not trust it yet.

One query type looks a little slower: a count over the whole history went from 1.1 seconds to about 1.4 seconds, because it has to visit 26 indices. The customer uses it rarely, and I decided not to do anything about it for now.

I asked Mara in the team channel to check how her loader picks the alias for writes, because it writes into this customer's data. She will run a test import of 5,000 documents once we have a date for the switch.

Open point: I still need to recount how many of the 40 customers are on the new layout from the tool's report, because my own count in the notes does not agree with it. I will do that tomorrow.

summary: Turned on the dual write for the third large customer and found the indexer lag rises to 14 seconds in its evening burst, above the 10 second target
body:
The third large customer is the one with the most steady traffic, around 900 events a second in the evening. I turned on its dual write flag at 15:20 and watched the first half hour.

The lag stayed under 5 seconds until 15:50. Then the customer's batch jobs started and the lag climbed to 14 seconds for about 6 minutes. That is above the limit of 10 seconds in the plan. Since the dual write doubles the writes for this customer, the indexer does twice the bulk requests.

I looked at the bulk size. The indexing path sends batches of 500 documents to each target. For the monthly indices the documents of one batch are spread over up to two months, so the bulk request has to split. The split is cheap, but the bulk requests to the monthly side were small, around 120 documents on average, because the grouping happens after the batch is cut.

I changed the grouping so that the batch for the monthly side is collected up to 500 documents per index before it is sent, with a flush after 1 second. On staging with a replayed burst the lag peak fell from 14 to 7 seconds.

I did not deploy it yet. The change touches the indexing path for all customers with the flag on, which now means 21 customers. I asked Mara to read the diff, because she knows that code best.

The dual write stays on for the third customer meanwhile. I will check the lag in the evening burst again and decide about the history copy for tomorrow night.

summary: Mara reviewed the grouping change in the indexing path and found a case where documents of the flush window could be lost on a worker restart
body:
Mara read the diff of the bulk grouping change and left three comments. Two were about names. The third was a real problem.

With the flush after 1 second, documents wait in a buffer in the worker. If the worker is stopped during a deploy, the buffer is lost unless it is flushed on shutdown. The old code did not buffer, so this case did not exist. For the old index the writes are still direct, but for the monthly side the loss would mean a gap that the catch-up pass has to find later.

I added a flush on the shutdown signal with a timeout of 5 seconds, and a test that stops the worker with 300 documents in the buffer and checks that they arrive. The test failed before the fix and passed after it.

Mara also asked what happens if the flush fails. Now the failed batch goes back to the normal retry path of the indexer, with the same event ids, so a second write overwrites. That is the same safe-write behavior as in the loader.

I will deploy it tomorrow morning in a quiet hour and not at the end of the day.

summary: Looked at the Redis cache hit rate by key group and found the summary keys at 91 percent while the saved-query keys sit at 54 percent
body:
I took the hit and miss counters per key prefix from the cache metrics for the last 7 days. The key naming guide from last week makes this possible, because every group has a prefix.

The summary keys are at 91 percent hits, which is good after the key change. The saved-query keys are at 54 percent. They have a TTL of 60 seconds, and most customers run a saved query less often than once a minute, so most reads find an expired key.

I checked the data. For the 10 customers with the most saved-query traffic, the median time between two runs of the same query is 3 minutes. A TTL of 5 minutes would raise the hits to around 80 percent in my estimate from the logs. The risk is that a customer sees results that are up to 5 minutes old, and for dashboards that is fine. For the alert queries it is not.

So I will split the group: alert queries keep 60 seconds, dashboard queries get 5 minutes. This needs a different prefix for the two, and I will write that change tomorrow. I noted the numbers in the cache tuning doc.

summary: Answered Sam's question about a possible drop in document totals for the second large customer, and explained why it could happen once the monthly layout is in place.
body:
Sam asked in the channel what to tell a customer who might write to support about a lower document total after the move to the monthly layout. Nothing has been switched for the second large customer yet, so no customer has seen a drop. Sam wanted an answer ready before the cutover.

I looked at the customer's count check from the dual write. The old index holds both copies of 12 events from an early bulk import that used generated ids. The monthly layout writes with the event id, so in the new index the second copy replaces the first. After the switch, the total will be 12 lower.

No data will be lost. I compared the 12 pairs by hand and both copies of each pair have the same content. I gave Sam a draft text for the customer to use only if they ask after the cutover: the total is 12 lower because of duplicates from the first import that the new layout does not keep.

Sam asked if this can happen with other customers. It can, wherever old imports used generated ids. The migration report lists the difference per customer, and so far only this one shows a gap. I added a note to the cutover check list to read that line of the report before each alias switch, and Sam saved the draft text in the support notes.

summary: Deployed the bulk grouping change with the shutdown flush; the third customer's evening lag peak is 6 seconds now instead of 14
body:
The deploy went out at 17:40 in the quiet hour between the two traffic peaks. I stopped the old workers one by one and checked the log line for the shutdown flush. Each worker flushed between 0 and 212 documents, and no flush failed.

After the deploy I compared the document counts of the third customer between the old index and the monthly indices for the last two hours. They matched. That means the flush on shutdown worked, since 212 documents were in a buffer at one point.

The lag of the evening burst is the real result. At 18:05 the batch jobs of the customer started, and the lag peaked at 6 seconds. Before the change it was 14. The bulk requests to the monthly side now average 430 documents.

The CPU of the data nodes went down a little as well, around 5 percent, because there are fewer bulk requests. Tobias saw that in Grafana and asked if he can lower the alert limit for the bulk queue. I said to wait one week to see the normal range first.

The history copy for the third customer is planned for tomorrow night with the reindex job paused. This is the biggest one at about 74 million documents, so I expect around 6 hours. I prepared the skip list so that the months of the last 2 days are left for the catch-up pass.

I put the check list into the ticket and asked Tobias to be reachable at night in case the nodes show disk pressure.

summary: Split the saved-query cache keys into alert and dashboard groups, with 60 second and 5 minute TTLs, and updated the key naming guide
body:
Implemented what I planned after the hit rate check. The saved-query cache now has two prefixes. Queries that belong to an alert rule use the prefix for alerts with a TTL of 60 seconds. Queries from dashboards use the dashboard prefix with a TTL of 5 minutes.

The search API decides by a flag that the caller passes. The alert evaluator already identifies itself with a header, so I used that. Everything else, including the console, is a dashboard query. I did not want a guess based on the query text.

There was one thing to fix in the key builder. It built the prefix from the group name and the customer id, and the new group names needed a version number to follow the guide. I added it, and the tests for the key format passed after I updated the expected strings.

The old keys of the group expire by their 60 second TTL, so there is nothing to delete. I checked this in a staging Redis with a scan of the prefix, which is fine on staging, and found none left after two minutes.

On staging I replayed an hour of query traffic from the logs. The hit rate of the dashboard group was 78 percent and that of the alert group stayed at 52 percent, as expected. The memory for the group grew by about 40 MB on staging, so I estimate 400 to 500 MB in production. The cache instance has room for this, since memory fell by 12 percent last week after the summary key change.

I wrote a paragraph in the key naming guide that explains the two groups and the rule for choosing a TTL: the TTL must be shorter than the time a customer accepts stale data for that use. Lena read it and asked that the console show a hint with the age of the result. She will think about it, and it is not planned.

Tomorrow morning I deploy this together with a watch on the Redis memory graph for the first hours. If the memory climbs more than 1 GB I roll the TTL back to 60 seconds, which is one setting.

summary: Prepared the night run for the third large customer: skip list, throttle limit of 8 seconds and a message to Tobias with the stop conditions
body:
Prepared the history copy for the third customer, which is the largest one at about 74 million documents.

The skip list holds the two most recent months for the catch-up pass, since they get writes all the time. The throttle limit for the queue lag is 8 seconds for this run, a little under the 10 second target, to keep a margin.

I wrote the stop conditions into a message to Tobias. Stop if the disk use of any data node goes above 80 percent, if search errors go above 0.1 percent for 5 minutes, or if the lag stays above 10 seconds for more than 10 minutes after a pause.

The reindex job is paused until 07:00. I checked the schedule, and the nightly job normally starts later in the night, so I set the pause in the scheduler and did not rely on memory. The old indices stay for 7 days after the alias switch as planned.

summary: Prepared the copy of the third large customer's history to the monthly layout: planned the night run, the throttle and the checks, with nothing copied yet.
body:
The night run is planned for 01:00 and I used the morning to get it ready. I read the log of the dry run on the test cluster and checked the numbers from it.

The throttle is set to pause the workers when the indexing lag goes over 8 seconds. In the dry run on a small slice it paused them three times, always when another customer's bulk import was running, so the throttle does what it should. I wrote the stop conditions for Tobias in a message: stop if the lag stays over 8 seconds for more than 15 minutes, or if disk use on any data node goes over 80 percent. Today the fullest data node is at 58 percent, so there is room for the extra copy.

The tool will copy about 74 million documents by my estimate from the count on the old layout. I made a skip list for two months where the customer has odd date values, and those two months will be handled in a catch-up pass after the main copy. The plan is to run catch-up passes until one finds no new documents, and then to take the counts per month.

For the checks after the copy I wrote a small script that compares the counts per month in both layouts and picks 2,000 random documents by id to compare the full content. I tested it on the dry run slice, and it found the date field mapping that was missing in the first template, which I fixed in the template before anything else.

One open point is that the oldest months will be very small, since the customer started small, but they get 3 primaries each per the shard decision. I do not want to change the shard count now. A shrink of the old months can be looked at after the migration is done, as it is cheap for indices that nobody writes to.

The next steps are the night run, then the saved query comparison, and only after that the alias switch. The temporary extra nodes must stay until the old indices are deleted, since the data will exist twice until then.

summary: Compared the saved queries of the third large customer on both layouts and all ten matched, so the alias switch is ready to be planned for later today.
body:
Ran the ten most used saved queries of the third customer against the old index and the monthly alias. All ten returned the same hits in the same order, and the tie break on timestamp from the earlier change did its work.

I also ran three of the slowest queries from the slow log of the last week, wide ranges over a whole year with an aggregation. They returned equal results, and the monthly side was faster by 30 to 45 percent.

The console's table view uses its own sort, so I opened the customer's three dashboards in a test session and the widgets showed the same numbers. Nothing blocks the switch, which is still planned for after the afternoon traffic peak at about 17:00, so the first hour on the new layout is a calm one.

summary: Prepared the copy of the third large customer's history to the monthly layout: planned the night run, the throttle and the checks, with nothing copied yet.
body:
I did not copy anything today. This session was about getting the third large customer's move to the monthly layout ready, and the copy itself is planned for tonight's window.

The plan is to run the copy shard by shard, so search keeps working for this customer the whole time. I wrote the order of the shards, with the biggest months first, so that a problem shows up early. The throttle is set so that indexer lag stays under 8 seconds. If it goes over that for more than a few minutes, the run pauses by itself. I wrote down the stop conditions and sent them to Tobias, so that whoever is on call knows when to stop the run and what to check.

I also prepared the checks that will run after the copy. They compare counts for the last 30 days between the old and the new index, and they run the customer's ten saved queries on both layouts, comparing hits and order. The search error rate on the old layout is at 0.02 percent now, and that is the number I will compare against later.

I built a skip list for documents that are known duplicates from old imports. This customer has more of them than the other two, and I would rather the copy not carry them over. Sam will need to know that the document total may change for this customer, so I added a line about it to the ticket.

I looked at latency with replayed queries against the two other customers' data on the new layout, to know what to expect. This customer has the widest time ranges of the three, so I hope for the biggest gain, but I have no real numbers and will not quote any. Sam asked for latency figures for the status text, and I told her they can only come after the copy and the switch have run for a while.

The dual write is not on yet for this customer. I will turn it on when the copy starts. Tobias knows that the extra data nodes stay until the old indices are gone.

summary: Wrote a script that checks the alias table against the customer list in Postgres and found that the migration report's count of 40 hid a customer with two accounts.
body:
I wrote a small script that reads the alias table from OpenSearch and compares it with the customer list in Postgres. The migration tool's report said 40 of 40, so I wanted a check that does not depend on the tool.

The script found 39 customers with a monthly alias and 40 customers in Postgres. I looked at the one without. It is a customer with two accounts, a production one and a test one, that share a company name. The tool had deduplicated by name for its report, which is why it counted 40 while it had migrated only one of the two accounts.

That is related to the problem with the space in a customer name that I fixed three weeks ago. The alias filter now uses the customer id, but the report still grouped by name. I changed the report to group by id.

The test account is small, with 8,000 documents. I did not start its migration today. I only checked how the standard run would behave for it: the estimate is about 20 seconds for the copy, and the saved query check would have only two queries for this account. I will run it in the next session, after I have told Mara, because her loader tests write into this account and I want her to know when the target indices change.

I also asked myself whether the other numbers I gave in the last days are right. The earlier counts of 19 and 21 customers came from the same report. I checked the history of the alias table, and the numbers were right in terms of accounts, since the duplicate name was only in the group that I migrate last.

The dual write for the test account has not been turned on, which should be fine for such a small account, because a history copy and a catch-up pass should take only a minute and no important traffic runs there.

I added the script to the migration tools folder and put it on the check list as the last step. I put the finding in the ticket, with a note that the count of 40 is not final until the script shows 40 of 40 from the alias table itself.

summary: Deployed the saved-query TTL split and watched Redis memory: it grew by 430 MB in the first hour and then stayed flat
body:
Deployed the change with the two saved-query key groups at 13:20. I watched the Redis memory graph of the cache instance for the next hour, with the rollback of the TTL ready.

Memory grew by 430 MB in the first hour, which is within my estimate of 400 to 500 MB. After that the curve went flat, as the keys of the 5 minute group started to expire as fast as new ones were written. I did not need the rollback.

The hit rate of the dashboard group moved to 76 percent after an hour, and the alert group stayed at 52 percent. The estimate was 78 percent, so it is very close.

The load on the search API went down too. Cache misses cause real searches, and the number of searches for saved queries per minute fell by 35 percent. The search p95 over all customers went from 210 ms to 185 ms in this hour.

There is one thing to watch. Customers may notice dashboards that are up to 5 minutes old. I asked Sam to tell me if support tickets mention old data in dashboards.

summary: Checked the Postgres slow query log and found the audit log search taking 900 ms because its filter on actor and time had no combined index
body:
Went through the slow query log of the last two days. Most entries are known. One new one is the audit log search of the admin console, with an average of 900 ms.

The query filters on the actor and on a time range and sorts by time. The audit table has an index on the actor and a separate one on the time, and the planner picks one of them and filters the rest, so it reads many rows.

I created a combined index on actor and time, in descending time order, with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so the table stays writable. It took 4 minutes on the 28 million rows and added 1.1 GB.

After that the same query took 14 ms in EXPLAIN ANALYZE. I dropped the old single index on the actor, because the new one covers it, which saves 600 MB. The single index on the time stays, since another query uses it.

I will check the slow log again tomorrow.

summary: Tried a connection pool wrapper for the admin console session store and dropped it: it cut connections only by 40 and made logins slower
body:
The admin console opens one Redis connection per session store call, which I found a few days ago and which adds around 300 connections to the cache instance. I tried a small pool library for the session store to bring this down.

The library keeps a fixed number of connections and queues the calls. On staging it worked at first and the number of connections from the console fell. But the saving was small in the real test. Under a replay of the login traffic, the console still held about 260 connections, only 40 fewer than before.

The reason is how the session middleware creates its client. It makes a separate client for every worker process, and each client opened its own pool, so the library's pool size multiplied by the number of workers. I could have set the size to 1 per worker, but then the logins were slower. The login p95 went from 180 ms to 310 ms under the replay, because calls waited in the queue.

I looked at the other option, which is to share one client across the session store calls in a worker. This needs a change in how Lena's code creates the store. The simple version is a module-level client, with a single connection that pipelines the commands.

I dropped the library, since it did not help and added a dependency. I removed the branch and wrote the findings in the ticket. Then I did the simple version of the shared client in a test branch, and in staging the connections of the console went down to 24 with a login p95 of 175 ms.

I have not merged it. It touches the session code of the console, so Lena needs to review it, and the session store needs a check that reconnects work after a Redis restart. I will test that tomorrow by restarting the staging Redis during a login replay.

I told Lena about the finding and the plan. She said the middleware allows passing a client, so the change fits. She will read the diff after the reconnect test.

summary: Reconnect test of the shared session client passed on staging after a fix for a missing error handler, and Lena approved the change
body:
I ran the reconnect test for the shared Redis client of the admin console. The plan was to restart the staging Redis during a replay of login traffic and see what the console does.

The first run failed. After the restart the shared client emitted an error event, and nobody listened to it. In Node this error event is thrown as an exception when there is no handler, and the console worker crashed. The ECS service restarted it, so users on staging would have seen a short outage of the console after every Redis restart.

The old code had the same problem in principle, but each of its short-lived clients was gone before the restart, so it rarely showed up. The shared client lives long and meets every restart.

I added an error handler that logs the error with a rate limit, so a down Redis does not fill the log with thousands of lines. The client's own reconnect strategy was set to a delay that grows from 50 ms to 2 seconds.

The second run was good. During the 8 seconds in which Redis was down, the login calls returned errors with a clear message, and after the restart the logins worked again within 2 seconds. No worker crashed. The session data was still there, as the session store has no dependence on the connection.

I added an automated test for it with a fake server that closes the connection, and it runs in 3 seconds.

Lena read the diff and had two comments. One was about the delay constant, which should be configurable, and I moved it to the settings file. The other was about a log message with the session id in it. That is a privacy problem, so I removed the id from the message and kept only the first 4 characters.

She approved it. I merged it and deployed to production at the end of the session. The connection count of the cache instance fell from about 780 to 520 within a few minutes, as the old console workers were replaced.

I keep watching the number of connections tomorrow. The remaining 220 more than the app pools should open are not explained by the console alone, and I want to look at the worker's connections next.

summary: Looked at the remaining excess Redis connections and found the rate limiter opens a new client for every API key batch job
body:
After the console fix, the cache instance still shows about 220 connections more than the pools of the apps should open. I listed the connections by client name and by address with CLIENT LIST on a read replica of the config, which is safe, and grouped the output.

The largest group is the report job for throttle counters that I deployed two weeks ago. It runs nightly and creates one client for each customer, 40 in total, and never closes them. They stay open until the process stops, which is the next deploy. That accounts for about 160 connections. The rest are the ingest workers, whose pool is as configured.

The fix is small. The job should use one client for the whole run and close it at the end. I changed it and added a close in a finally block, so errors do not leave the connection open.

I ran the job on staging. It opened one connection, and the number went back to the base level after it finished. The run time did not change, 11 seconds for the 40 customers.

I will deploy this with the next release. The connection count in production should fall to about 360 once the job has run again.

summary: Prepared the removal of the first large customer's old search index by checking counts and looking for anything still pointing at it, without deleting or switching anything.
body:
The first large customer was switched to the monthly layout seven days before the others, so its old index will be the first one to be removed. The seven days of dual write are not over yet, so today I only prepared the cleanup and changed nothing on the cluster. I started with a comparison of the counts for the last 30 days between the old index and the monthly indices.

I searched the application logs and the config of the services for the old index name. Nothing used it except the dual write itself. The nightly reindex job reads its targets from the alias table, so it does not touch the old index either. I wrote the names of the two places that still write to it into the ticket, so the removal of the dual write flag can be checked against that list.

The counts are close but not equal. The monthly indices hold about 3,000 documents more than the old index for the period since the switch. I traced it to events that arrived while a test of the dual write flag was running on staging and went only to the monthly side. This looks harmless, but I want the numbers explained before the old index is touched, so I will repeat the comparison right before the cleanup.

I also looked at how the delete call would behave. The cluster has a wildcard protection in its settings, so the index has to be named in full. This protects from deleting by pattern by mistake, so I will not change it. I added the full index name to the cleanup plan, together with a first step of making a snapshot into the snapshot repository, so there is a way back for another week.

The other two large customers follow as their seven days end. I put the dates as reminders in the ticket in relative form: the second customer in 2 days and the third in 3 days.

I also checked the memory of the Redis cache, to be sure that the later deletion cannot change the cache keys of the customer. The cache keys of the summaries do not contain the index name, so nothing should change there. The connection count went down as planned after the job fix, from 520 to 370.

summary: Read the log of last night's reindex job on the per-customer layout, found it too noisy, and planned the log cleanup and the next steps for the search index shards.
body:
I read the log of last night's reindex job. It finished in 38 minutes, which is the same as the weeks before. The cleanup of the first large customer's old index freed space but did not change the run time, because the job still walks every customer index in full. In the first test on staging, with a sample of the data, the job on the planned monthly layout took 9 minutes, and that is the only number I have for the new layout so far. The monthly layout is still a plan, and no production shard has been moved.

The idea for the plan is that the job would iterate over monthly indices and skip the months without changes. On a normal night only the current and the previous month have changes, so it would read very little. The saving would not depend on the size of the large customers any more, which is the point of the new layout. I wrote this down in the plan document with the staging numbers, and marked clearly that the production effect is a guess.

One detail I noticed is the log. It prints one line for every skipped customer index and alias, around 1,100 lines per night, and that hides the lines that matter. I changed the log level of the skip lines to debug, and added one summary line with the number of indices skipped and processed per customer group. I checked it on staging and the output was short and readable.

I also checked the OpenSearch cluster at the end of the run. Indexing during the reindex raised the CPU on the data nodes to about 70 percent, as in the weeks before. I told Tobias the numbers and that the extra nodes stay for now, because the old indices of the two other large customers are still there and their dual write period is not over.

The reindex start time is still the usual one. Tobias mentioned that it overlaps with the backup window in some weeks, which is a topic for another day, and I did not touch it.

Next are the deletes of the second and third old indices when their days are over, then a check of the shard sizes for the plan of the monthly layout, and then the removal of the dual write code from the indexing path.

summary: Wrote the cleanup plan for the old per-customer search indices as a script and a runbook checklist, with an archive snapshot before any deletion and nothing deleted yet.
body:
Wrote the cleanup plan for the old per-customer search indices as a script and a runbook checklist: delete only after seven days of matching counts, with an archive snapshot first.

No customer's old index has been touched yet. The first large customer is the one I am preparing now, and the same procedure has to run for the other two large customers and then the 37 small ones. I wrote it down as a script plus a checklist in the runbook instead of leaving it in my head.

For each customer the script compares the document count of the old index with the sum of the monthly indices for that customer. It also runs the ten saved queries on both layouts and prints hit counts. It refuses to continue if the counts differ by more than the number of documents written in the last minute. This margin was needed because the dual write was still running for some customers when I tested it.

I tested the script against the first large customer's data from the snapshot. It correctly reported a match. I then changed one monthly index count by hand on staging and it stopped with a clear message, which is what I wanted.

The seven day wait is a rule I set for this cleanup. The first large customer is the furthest along, and I still want to check its counts once more before I do anything. The second large customer switched its alias five days ago, so its dual write has two more days to run. The third switched only two days ago. The small customers were switched in batches, and the oldest batch is already past seven days. The plan only says when each one becomes eligible.

I also added a step that takes a snapshot of the old index into the archive bucket before deletion. It costs a few dollars per large customer and gives a way back if a customer later says documents are missing. Tobias asked that the snapshot be kept for 30 days and then deleted by a lifecycle rule, and I added that to the Terraform for the bucket.

Open points: the script does not yet remove the dual write flag, which is still a manual step in the settings table. I will add it once the first two deletions have gone through by hand. Next is the cleanup check for the first large customer and for the oldest batch of small customers, followed by the second large customer once its dual write has run its full time.

summary: Prepared the cleanup of the old per-customer indices for the first batch of 12 small customers: ran the count check and looked into one mismatch, but deleted nothing yet
body:
I ran the count check script on the oldest batch of small customers, the ones that moved more than a week ago. All 12 passed on the first run. Their saved queries matched in hits and order, so the batch looks ready for cleanup.

I only ran the script in dry-run mode. It lists the old indices, estimates the space and takes no snapshots. The estimate came to about 41 GB on the search cluster. Disk use on the data nodes is at 71 percent, so the cleanup would give more room before the next planned node change, but I decided to wait until the checks are fully done.

One customer needed attention. Its old index had 3,112 documents more than the monthly indices. I looked at it before going further. They were test events with an event type that the new indexer drops on purpose, a rule from the schema registry work. I checked three of them by id and the type was the one on the drop list. I added the exception to the script as a per-customer allowance that must be written down in the runbook. The runbook entry is still a draft, and Mara will read it before the allowance is used for real.

I also checked the dual write flag for the 12 customers in the settings table. It is still set, and the indexer still writes to the old indices for them. The lag graph is steady. I will remove the flag only together with the cleanup, not before.

Next: a snapshot test restore on staging for one of the old indices, then the real cleanup of this batch, then the second large customer in two days, and then the remaining small customers in batches. I told Sam that customers may see a higher storage figure in the console for now, because it counts the old duplicates until they are deleted.

summary: Found that the nightly reindex job still builds its target list from a static file of customer index names and planned a change to read the targets from the alias table instead.
body:
While going through the log of last night's reindex job I saw that it had logged a warning of the form index not found for each of 12 customers. The job still built its list of targets from a static file of customer index names, written before the work on the monthly layout began. The count check for the first batch of small customers was still going on, and the old indices of those customers were still in place, so I first wanted to know where the warnings came from.

The warnings did no harm, because the job skips a missing index. But each one bumped an alert counter that does not page anyone, and the counter would grow with every index we remove later under the cleanup plan. I decided to change the job so it asks the alias table for its targets instead of reading the file. The idea is that it takes whatever the alias points to, an old per-customer index or a monthly one, so it keeps working while both layouts exist side by side.

I started a draft and ran it on staging. The target count matched the alias table at 40 customers, and the job time did not change. I have not merged anything. Mara wants to look at how the draft handles a customer with two accounts, because those have two aliases, and I will ask her to try it on the two customers we know about. I also plan to remove the static file in the same commit, so nobody edits it by mistake, but only after she has signed off.

summary: Redis memory climbed to 78 percent after the TTL split settled; the biggest growth is the dashboard saved-query keys with their 5 minute TTL
body:
Tobias saw the Redis memory graph at 78 percent in the morning and asked if it was a problem. I used the checklist from last week.

Biggest key groups by sampled size: dashboard saved-query keys at 31 percent of the memory, summary keys at 22 percent, rate limiter counters at 4 percent, sessions at 6 percent. Before the TTL split the saved-query keys were one group at about 25 percent. The dashboard group is bigger because 5 minutes keeps more distinct results alive than the old behavior did for some customers.

TTL coverage was 99.7 percent. The keys without TTL were a small set of old debug keys from a test script, 1,900 keys and 14 MB. I deleted them and added the script's prefix to the guide as forbidden.

The client output buffers were small, the largest at 2 MB. So the memory is real data, not a leak.

The hit rate of the dashboard group is 73 percent now, up from 54. I think the memory is a fair price, but I do not want it to keep growing with every customer. I looked at result sizes: some dashboard results are over 200 KB because they carry the full hit list with highlight fragments, and the dashboard only uses the counts and the first ten.

I tried a quick experiment on staging: store only the counts and the first ten hits for dashboard keys. The key group size fell by 62 percent in a replay of an hour of traffic. The dashboards looked the same to Lena when she checked three customers.

I did not deploy it yet. The change touches the result serializer, which the alert queries also use, and I want Mara to look at it first. I wrote the ticket and the replay numbers. Meanwhile I raised the memory alarm threshold from 75 to 82 percent so on-call is not woken by a known state, and wrote the reason into the alert description.

summary: Mara reviewed the dashboard result trimming and wanted a separate key suffix for it so alert queries keep full results
body:
Mara read the serializer change this afternoon. Her main point was correct: alert queries read the same cached result and some of them use the highlight fragments in the notification text. Trimming results by key group would work today, but a later change to the alert text would break quietly.

We agreed on a small change. The trimmed form is stored under its own suffix, so dashboard keys end in :t and the reader asks for exactly that form. There is no shared meaning of a key with two shapes. I updated the key naming guide with the suffix.

She also found that my replay compared sizes but not content. I wrote a check that reads each replayed dashboard result in the old form and the trimmed form and compares counts and the first ten hit ids. Across 4,200 replayed requests, zero differences.

I will deploy tomorrow morning, when the cache is busy and I can watch it. The plan is to deploy, watch memory for an hour, and expect the dashboard group to drop as old keys expire within 5 minutes.

summary: Deployed the trimmed dashboard cache results and Redis memory fell from 78 to 61 percent within ten minutes, with the hit rate unchanged at 73 percent
body:
I deployed the trimmed result form with the :t suffix at the start of the busy period. The cache graph was open on the second screen the whole time.

The old dashboard keys expired in 5 minutes as expected. Memory fell from 78 percent to 61 percent in ten minutes and stayed there for the hour I watched. The dashboard group dropped from 31 percent to 12 percent of the memory.

The hit rate stayed at 73 percent. For a short moment it fell to 58 percent right after the deploy, because the new keys were cold, and it recovered in about six minutes. That matches the expected warm-up.

I checked the alert queries, since Mara's worry was about them. The test alert with highlight text on staging still produced the full notification. The production alert queries kept their old key form and hit rates did not move.

One small problem: the dashboard in the admin console showed a blank hit list for one customer for about two minutes. The cause was a client call that asked for the full form of the key and found the trimmed one. It was Lena's preview widget for the first ten hits. It read the dashboard key with the old suffix. I fixed it to read :t and she merged it.

I lowered the memory alarm back from 82 to 75 percent, as the value now has comfortable room. Tobias agreed. I added a note to the Redis checklist that the dashboard group is the one to check first.

What is left: the same trimming idea for the summary keys, which are 22 percent. I looked at their size and they are already small per key, with many keys. So the better lever is the TTL, not the size. I will leave them for now.

summary: Prepared the cleanup of the second large customer's old search index: ran the count check as a dry run and tested the snapshot restore on staging, deleted nothing.
body:
The second large customer is at six days since its alias switch, and the dual write has run the whole time. I did not run the cleanup script today. The plan says seven days of matching counts, so any delete waits until tomorrow at the earliest, and the monthly layout for the rest of the index is still only a plan.

I ran the count check as a dry run to see where we stand. The old index has 52,104,331 documents and the monthly indices have 52,104,331. The ten saved queries match in hits and order. I expected a difference from the old import duplicates, but the old index was also cleaned of them at the time of the copy. I confirmed that in the copy notes from that day.

I checked the archive bucket for the snapshot. The lifecycle rule for 30 days is on the prefix, so a snapshot taken tomorrow will expire correctly. I did not take the snapshot yet, because I want it to be the last step before a delete. The old index is about 118 GB, and the data nodes are at 64 percent disk use. I estimated that removing it would free enough room for the next shard layout work without adding nodes, and I put that estimate in the plan document.

Tobias asked if the snapshot restore works. I tested it on staging with a small customer's snapshot: the restore took 3 minutes and the counts matched. I attached the restore command to the runbook.

I also looked at the indexer. It writes each document twice for this customer because of the dual write, and the lag graph for the customer's evening burst shows about 6 seconds. I expect it to drop after the flag is removed, but I will only know after the cleanup.

The third large customer reaches its seventh day in four days. Then the remaining small customers follow.

summary: Looked into Sam's question about a customer with two accounts seeing two different document totals in the console, and found nothing wrong with the data.
body:
Sam asked why a customer with two accounts sees two different document totals in the console. The customer had written to support after the alias table check last week, and Sam wanted a clear answer before replying.

Each account has its own index and its own alias, as before. The monthly layout is still only a plan, and the draft is not final. So the totals shown in the console are per account, which gives two numbers, not one wrong one. The customer would see a sum only if they asked support for a combined report.

I checked the customer's data to be sure. Account A has 4.2 million documents and account B has 1.1 million. The sum matches the old combined total minus the duplicates that were removed during the earlier cleanup of the old indices. So nothing is missing.

Sam wrote a short paragraph for the help page. I read it and corrected one point: the totals are per account, not per customer, and the console label says account. Lena offered to show the sum in a tooltip. We left that as a possible later change, because it needs a new query in the console and nobody has asked for it yet.

summary: Tried a Postgres index on the audit log actor and time filter and the search went from 900 ms to 14 ms
body:
The slow audit log search from the slow query log had no combined index on actor and time. I created one on staging with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on (actor_id, created_at DESC). Build time on the staging copy of 31 million rows was 2 minutes.

The same search dropped from 900 ms to 14 ms in the plan, with an index scan instead of a sequential scan. The index is 640 MB. I checked that inserts into the audit log are not noticeably slower: the batch insert test was 3 percent slower, which I accept.

I will run the same statement on production tomorrow morning when load is low, and check for locks while it builds.

summary: Built the audit log index on production without blocking writes; the actor and time search now takes 15 ms and the build took 6 minutes
body:
I ran CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the production audit log table early this morning. The build took 6 minutes for 44 million rows. I watched pg_locks during the build and saw no waiting writers.

After the build the index is 910 MB. The audit log search in the admin console now returns in 15 ms in the slow query log sample. I removed the entry from the list of known slow queries.

The insert rate was unchanged in the metrics. I will look at table bloat at the next vacuum review.

summary: Found the rate limiter opens a new Redis client for every API key batch job and changed it to one shared client with a pool of 10
body:
Last week I found that the rate limiter opens a new client for each API key batch job. Today I fixed it.

The batch job that refreshes the limits per key creates a client inside its loop, once per key group. With 40 customers and several keys each, it opened up to 120 connections in the minutes of the refresh, and some of them stayed open until the garbage collection closed them. The connection graph had a visible comb pattern at the half hour, which matched the job.

The change moves the client creation to the module level and uses one client with a pool of 10 connections for the job. The job code now only borrows it. I removed the closing calls from the job, since the client lives as long as the process, and added a close on shutdown.

I tested it on staging with the refresh at the half hour. Peak connections from the limiter fell from 118 to 11. The refresh time went from 4.1 seconds to 2.6 seconds, since opening connections was most of the time.

One issue came up in the test: when I restarted Redis on staging during the refresh, the job threw an unhandled error and the process stopped. The shared client from last week had a handler for this, and the new one did not. I copied the same error handler and reconnect strategy, with a maximum delay of 2 seconds, and repeated the test. The job logged the error, reconnected after 1.2 seconds and finished.

Lena reviewed the change because the rate limiter shares the client factory with the session store. She asked that the pool size be a setting, not a number in the code. I added RATE_LIMIT_POOL_SIZE with default 10.

I deployed it to production in the afternoon. After the first half hour refresh, the comb pattern in the connection graph was gone and the peak was 14 connections for the limiter. Total Redis connections fell from 310 to 205 at the busiest time.

Next I want to look at the remaining connection users, which are the search API workers and the ingest rate checks.

summary: Counted Redis connections by client name and found the search API workers hold 96 idle connections each at the quiet hours
body:
After the rate limiter fix, total connections still sit at 205 at the busy time. I used CLIENT LIST grouped by name to see who holds them.

Result in the busy period: search API 112, ingest rate checks 41, admin console sessions 22, rate limiter 14, others 16. At the quiet hours the search API still holds 96, so most of its connections are idle most of the time.

The search API client has a minimum pool size of 24 per process and runs 4 processes, which gives 96. The minimum was set a long time ago, when the cache was used for every request. Today most requests are served in under a millisecond from a few connections.

I looked at the pool statistics for a day: the peak number of connections in use at one time was 9 per process, and the 99th percentile was 5. So the minimum of 24 is far too high. I tried a minimum of 4 and a maximum of 16 on staging with a load test of twice the normal traffic. The p95 latency of the cache calls stayed at 1.1 ms and no waits for a connection were logged.

I am careful here because of the connection pool problem of the earlier weeks. The limit on the Redis side is what we hit, not the client side. If many processes grow to their maximum at once, the sum matters. With 4 processes at 16 the worst case is 64, still lower than 112.

The change has two settings, REDIS_POOL_MIN and REDIS_POOL_MAX. I wrote them into the service config and the runbook. I will deploy this on one process first and watch.

I also noticed that the ingest rate check opens a connection per worker task, 41 in all, and that it is a different code base from the Go workers' shared pool. That is a bigger change and I put it on the list for Mara, who owns that code.

What I did not touch: the session store, which is already on the shared client after last week's fix.

summary: Deployed the smaller search API Redis pool to one process, then to all four; total connections at the busy hour fell from 205 to 118
body:
I deployed the minimum of 4 and maximum of 16 to one search API process late in the morning and watched for 40 minutes. The cache call latency was the same, and the connections of that process went from 24 to 6.

Then I rolled it to the other three. Total Redis connections at the busy hour fell from 205 to 118. At the quiet hours they are about 60.

I checked the logs for waits for a connection. In two hours there were none. The highest number in use at one time was 11 on one process during a burst of dashboard loads, below the new maximum of 16.

The Redis memory used by the connections themselves fell by a small amount, about 20 MB, which is not meaningful.

I kept the old values in the notes in case we need to go back. The rate limiter and search API are now fixed. The rest is the ingest rate checks, which I handed to Mara with the numbers.

One thing to remember is that when the number of API processes goes up, the sum of maximum connections should be checked. I added a line with the formula to the checklist.

summary: Wrote the shard layout plan for the monthly search index: 12 shards per month for large customers is too many, so the draft proposes 3 and a rollover by size
body:
I started the written plan for the new shard layout of the search index, which has to be ready before any migration. This is a plan only, nothing is changed in the cluster.

The current layout is one index per customer, and the plan describes the move to monthly indices, which is not started. The test template I used for the monthly indices gives each one 12 shards. That was a quick first choice for the tests, and it is too many for small customers, where a month holds a few hundred thousand documents.

I collected the sizes of the data over the last three months, cut by month as the new layout would cut it. The median monthly slice is 2.3 GB, the largest is 61 GB for the third large customer. A good shard size for our queries is between 10 and 40 GB. With 12 shards the median shard would be 190 MB, which wastes memory for the shard metadata and slows searches that have to visit every shard.

The proposal has three tiers. Small customers, under 10 GB a month, get 1 shard. Medium customers get 3 shards. Large customers get up to 6 shards, and a rollover to a second index in the month if the first goes over 40 GB per shard.

I estimated the effect. The number of shards on the cluster would fall from about 5,800 to about 1,900 compared with the 12-shard layout. Heap use on the data nodes for shard metadata would fall by an estimated 35 percent. I got that from the per-shard overhead measured on staging.

Risks I wrote down: a customer that grows quickly from small to large within a month and ends with a large shard. The rollover rule covers it. Another risk is that queries across many months touch many indices. With fewer shards each, that is actually cheaper.

The method for the move would be a reindex per month into a new index with the chosen shard count, then an alias swap. I counted the time using our measured copy speed of about 12 million documents per hour per customer: about 4 days of copy for everything, if run at night with the throttle.

I listed open questions for Tobias: whether the cluster can hold both copies during the move, and whether the snapshot schedule needs a pause. For Mara: how the indexer finds the target index, and whether it needs a change for the rollover.

I shared the draft with the team. I did not ask for a decision yet.

summary: Tried the 3-shard layout for the monthly index on a copy of the largest customer's data: shard sizes came out even and p95 search latency matched the 12-shard test
body: Created a test monthly index for the largest customer on the staging cluster with 3 primary shards instead of the 12 from the first plan, and loaded one month of its documents, about 9 million. Shard sizes came out at 11.2, 11.6 and 11.4 GB, so the routing spreads the documents evenly and no shard is hot. I ran the ten saved queries of that customer and a set of 200 queries sampled from the search API log against both the 3-shard and the 12-shard version. The p95 latency was 185 ms with 3 shards and 191 ms with 12, which is within noise. The 12-shard version used about 14 percent more heap on the data nodes, from the extra segment and shard overhead. The draft proposes a rollover at 30 GB per shard, and with these sizes a busy month would roll over once, which is fine. Not tested yet: a month with a burst of imports, where one shard could grow much faster than the rest. Next I will write the rollover condition into the plan and ask Mara how the indexer should pick the write index after a rollover.

summary: Mara found that the indexer picks the target index by the month of the event time, so a rollover needs a small lookup and a new write alias
body:
Mara looked at the indexer code for the plan. It computes the target index name from the customer and the month of the event time. For a rollover it needs a different way, because two indices would belong to the same month.

We discussed two ways. One is a write alias per customer and month, which points to the current index, and the rollover moves the alias. The other is a lookup table in Postgres. She prefers the alias because OpenSearch already supports rollover on size and the indexer does not need any new state.

The catch is late events. An event for last month must go to last month's write alias, and that must still exist. We decided that the write alias for a month stays for 40 days after the month ends, which covers the late arrival window we saw in the ingest data, where 99.99 percent of events arrive within 30 days.

She will change the indexer to use the alias name. I will add the template and rollover policy to the plan, with the size limit of 40 GB per shard.

One more point from her: the bulk grouping change from last week groups documents by target index. With an alias it groups by alias, which is fine and even creates fewer groups. She will check that the shutdown flush still works with the new grouping.

I updated the plan with the alias approach and the 40 day rule, and wrote down the open point for the flush check.

summary: Dropped a trial of a Redis client library with automatic pipelining after it made the p95 cache latency worse by 0.4 ms
body:
I tried a different Redis client library for the search API for an hour, since it promises automatic pipelining of commands. On staging with the replay of an hour of traffic, p95 cache latency went from 1.1 to 1.5 ms, and p99 from 2.3 to 3.9 ms.

The reason is that each request makes only one or two cache calls, so there is little to batch, and the library waits a short time to collect commands. I tried its setting for the wait and the result was not better at the lowest value. Reverted, no code kept.

summary: Ingest worker batch writes: raised the flush size from 500 to 2,000 events and found that Postgres commit time per batch stays flat up to 1,500
body:
Today's work on the ingest worker was to measure the batch size for writes. This is a step in the batching work and the numbers decide the setting.

The worker takes events from the queue and writes them in batches to the store. The flush size has been 500 events or 200 ms, whichever comes first. I wanted to know whether a larger batch reduces the load on the database without hurting the latency of the pipeline.

Setup: staging, with a replay of one busy hour of real traffic from the stream, at 3,400 events per second. I ran five flush sizes: 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000 and 3,000, each for 20 minutes.

Results for commit time per batch: 500 events took 11 ms, 1,000 took 14 ms, 1,500 took 18 ms, 2,000 took 31 ms and 3,000 took 58 ms. Up to 1,500 the time grows slowly. Beyond that it grows faster, because the batch no longer fits into the statement size we use for the multi-row insert and the driver splits it.

The commits per second fell from 6.8 at 500 to 2.3 at 1,500. Database CPU on staging fell from 34 to 21 percent between those two.

The end to end latency, from queue to stored, had a p95 of 240 ms at 500. At 1,500 it was 310 ms, because events wait for the flush. With the time limit of 200 ms the flush happens earlier at lower traffic, so the effect is smaller at night.

So the best choice looks like 1,500 events with a 150 ms limit. I tried that combination for another 20 minutes: p95 latency 262 ms, commit time 17 ms, database CPU 22 percent.

A failure to note: at 3,000 the worker's memory rose by 180 MB and one worker was killed by the memory limit of the task, which shows that large batches have a cost on the worker side too. I did not investigate it further, since that size is not in the running.

The next step is a failure test. If a worker dies with a batch in memory, the events must not be lost: offsets are committed only after the write. I checked that this is the case in the code and Mara will review it. I will write the test for a killed worker tomorrow.

I put the numbers into a table in the branch notes so the decision is visible.

summary: Wrote the killed-worker test for batch writes: after a kill in the middle of a flush, the replayed batch stores each event once
body:
I wrote the test for the case that worried Mara: a worker is killed while a batch of 1,500 events is in memory or in the middle of the write.

The test starts a worker against a local queue and database, sends 20,000 events with ids, and kills the process with SIGKILL at a random point, five times in a run. Then it starts the worker again and waits until the queue is empty. At the end it counts the rows and compares the ids.

In the first run the count was correct but the test showed 212 events written twice. The offset is committed after the write, so a kill between the write and the commit replays the batch, and the insert had no conflict handling on the event id.

The store insert already uses the event id as key in the loader path, where a retried chunk overwrites. The ingest worker path used a plain insert. I changed it to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING, which makes a replay harmless.

After the change I ran the test 30 times with kills at random points. Every run ended with exactly 20,000 rows and no duplicates. The insert is a little slower with the conflict clause: commit time at 1,500 events went from 17 to 18 ms.

I sent the change to Mara for review, with the test. The settings are 1,500 events and 150 ms, still on staging. The deploy to production is planned for the next quiet period, with a flag to go back to the old size.

summary: Answered Lena: the saved-query cache keys use the customer id and a hash of the query, so a customer's keys can be cleared by prefix without touching others
body:
Lena asked how to clear the cached saved queries for one customer from the admin console, for a support case.

The key format from the naming guide is sq:{group}:{customer_id}:{hash}, where group is alert or dashboard. So the prefix sq:dashboard:{customer_id}: and sq:alert:{customer_id}: select exactly one customer's keys.

I warned her not to use KEYS on production. The right way is SCAN with a MATCH pattern and a count of 500, in a loop, and UNLINK for the deletion. I wrote a small helper in the admin API that does this and returns the number of keys removed.

I tested it on staging with a customer that had 340 keys, and it removed all of them in 60 ms. The new :t suffix keys are covered, since they share the prefix.

She will add a button for support to the console and Sam will write the instructions.

summary: Checked vacuum on the Postgres events and audit tables after the new index and found the autovacuum threshold too high for the audit log
body:
I looked at the table bloat I had promised to check after the audit log index. The audit log table has 44 million rows and about 9 percent dead tuples, which is higher than I like. The autovacuum scale factor is the default 0.2, so it starts only after about 8.8 million dead rows.

The audit log is mostly appended to, but the compliance flag updates old rows, which creates dead tuples in bursts. Vacuum runs rarely and then for a long time.

I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 for this table only, and the analyze scale factor to 0.01. With that the vacuum starts after about 880,000 dead rows. I used ALTER TABLE ... SET, so nothing else is affected.

I watched the first run that evening. It took 4 minutes and removed 1.1 million dead tuples. The size of the table and its indexes dropped by 380 MB. IO on the database stayed within the normal range during the run.

I will look at the dead tuple ratio again in a week. The events table is not affected, since it no longer holds the analytics events and has few updates.

summary: Deployed batch writes with 1,500 events and 150 ms to production behind a flag; database commits fell from 6.5 to 2.4 per second and latency rose by 60 ms at p95
body:
Mara approved the batch write change and the killed worker test, so I deployed it in the quiet period of the morning. The flag INGEST_BATCH_SIZE controls it and the old value of 500 is one config change away.

I started with one worker of the pool, which takes about a quarter of the traffic. For the first 30 minutes I watched four graphs: queue lag, commit time, database CPU and the error rate. The queue lag stayed near 1 second. Commit time per batch was 19 ms on production, a little above staging because the table is larger.

Then I moved the other workers over, one at a time, with ten minutes between them. At full traffic the numbers were these. Database commits per second fell from 6.5 to 2.4. Database CPU fell from 38 to 24 percent in the busy hour. The p95 latency from queue to stored rose from 250 to 310 ms, which is the cost I expected and within the target of 500 ms.

The error rate stayed at zero. No batch was split by the driver in the logs.

I also checked what happens at the end of a burst. When the traffic falls, the 150 ms limit makes small batches, and I saw batches of 20 to 80 events at night, so there is no waiting for a full batch.

One surprise was that the Redpanda consumer lag per partition became uneven. Two partitions of the busiest event type showed up to 3 seconds, while the others had 1. That comes from the larger batches being committed less often on these partitions. It is within the target, but I added it to the dashboard as a panel to watch.

I wrote to Tobias about the lower database load. With it he can postpone the planned instance size increase for Postgres by a few months, and the cost saving is about 300 dollars a month for now.

The flag stays for a week. If nothing happens, I remove it and make 1,500 the default in the code.

Next: a test of the shutdown during deployment, with the worker getting SIGTERM, since the ECS deploys stop workers that way.

summary: Tested the SIGTERM shutdown of the ingest worker with a full batch in memory and found it flushes in 90 ms, within the ECS stop timeout of 30 seconds
body:
ECS stops tasks with SIGTERM and waits 30 seconds before it sends SIGKILL, so the worker has to flush the batch in memory within that time. The earlier test killed with SIGKILL. This one tests the normal case.

I wrote the test to send 1,400 events, just under the batch size, and then SIGTERM before the flush timer fires. The worker should stop reading, flush the batch, commit the offsets and exit with code 0.

First run: it exited with code 0 but 1,400 events were missing from the store. The worker stopped the consumer loop and then the flush function was skipped, because the shutdown handler set a flag that the flush checked, and the flag said the worker was closing. A bug from the batching change itself.

I changed the order. The handler first stops the consumer, then calls flush with a forced flag that ignores the closing state, then commits offsets, then closes the connections. I also gave the flush its own timeout of 10 seconds, so a database problem does not hold the task until SIGKILL.

Second run: all 1,400 events were stored, the offsets were committed and the exit code was 0. The flush time was 90 ms. I repeated 20 runs with different batch fill levels from 1 to 1,500 and all passed.

I also tested a database that is not reachable during the shutdown. The flush fails after the 10 seconds, the worker exits with code 1 without committing, and the events are replayed by the next worker, where the conflict clause makes it safe.

This bug was only in staging and in the one canary window. On production the workers had been deployed with the flag for the morning, and the rolling deploy of this afternoon had not happened yet. I checked the logs of the morning deploys and found that 3 workers had been stopped by the first rollout. Their final batches were replayed from the queue. I compared the event counts for the window and found no missing events, since the offsets had not been committed.

I sent the fix to Mara and will deploy it after her review.

summary: Mara reviewed the shutdown flush fix, asked for one more test with a slow database, and approved after it passed
body:
Mara read the shutdown change in the evening and agreed with the order of steps. Her question was about the 10 second flush timeout: what if the database answers slowly but does not fail, say 8 seconds for a commit.

I added a test with a proxy that delays the database responses by 8 seconds. The flush completed in 8.2 seconds, the offsets were committed and the worker exited with code 0, within the 30 second stop time. With a delay of 12 seconds, the flush timed out at 10, the worker exited with code 1 and the batch was replayed with no duplicates.

She also asked that the log line at shutdown include the number of events flushed. I added it, in the form shutdown flush: 1400 events, 90 ms.

She approved the change. I will deploy it tomorrow with the next rollout and check the shutdown lines in the logs for the first workers that stop. Then the flag for the batch size can go in a week.

summary: Ran the batch write flag at full traffic for a day and the commit rate held at 2.4 per second, with p95 ingest latency up 58 ms as predicted
body:
After the production deploy this morning I watched the batch writes behind the flag for a full day on all ingest workers. Database commits stayed near 2.4 per second at the busy hour, against 6.5 before. The p95 ingest latency rose by 58 ms, which matches the 60 ms seen on the first day.

I checked the batch size histogram in Grafana. At the busy hour most flushes hit the 1,500 event limit. At night most flushes come from the 150 ms timer and carry 40 to 200 events. That is the intended behavior.

I looked for duplicates with a count of event ids per hour in Postgres and found none. The killed-worker test from yesterday covers the replay case, and a real worker restart during the deploy showed no duplicates either.
