One open point is the p99 latency, which rose from 210 to 340 ms for small customers whose events wait for the timer. I wrote it down for Mara. We could lower the timer to 100 ms for low volume keys, but I did not change anything tonight. Next I will compare the Postgres write load at the peak with last week and decide when to remove the flag.

summary: Noted the p99 ingest latency rise for small customers after batching and proposed a 100 ms timer, left unchanged until Mara has seen the numbers
body:
Wrote up the p99 finding from the batch write rollout. For customers sending under 20 events per second, the batch waits for the 150 ms timer, so the p99 went from 210 to 340 ms.

I sketched two options. The first is a 100 ms timer for everyone, which would cut the wait but give about 30 percent more commits at night. The second is a timer that depends on the recent event rate, which is more code and harder to test.

I prefer the first option for now because the extra commits are still far below the old rate. I put the table of p99 by customer size into the ticket. The large customers are not affected, since their batches fill before the timer fires.

No code change was made. Mara will look at the numbers tomorrow and pick one.

summary: Mara chose the 100 ms timer; deployed it and measured p99 for small customers dropping from 340 to 270 ms with commits still well under the old rate
body:
Mara read the ticket this morning and picked the simple option, a 100 ms flush timer for all workers. I changed the default in the worker config and kept the size limit at 1,500 events.

The change went to staging first. I replayed a recorded low volume stream of about 15 events per second for 30 minutes. The p99 latency was 262 ms, and commits ran at 9 per second for that stream.

Then I deployed to production on one worker, watched it for 40 minutes and rolled it to the other three. The production numbers after an hour were these:

- p99 for small customers: 270 ms, down from 340
- p95 overall: 55 ms above the pre-batching level
- database commits at the busy hour: 2.6 per second
- night commits: up by about 25 percent over the 150 ms timer

The p99 did not return to the old 210 ms, because the timer itself adds up to 100 ms. For the small customers this is still inside the 500 ms that the docs promise, so I did not look at it any further.

I also checked the Postgres commit time graph. The write latency per commit stayed flat, so the database has room. Sam asked whether customers would see any difference. The answer is no, since the API returns after the batch is stored, and the acknowledgement time stays well below the documented limit.

The flag stays on. I plan to remove it after the weekend if the numbers keep their shape.

summary: Removed the batch write flag from the ingest worker after three quiet days and deleted the old single-event write path from the code
body:
The batch write numbers were stable for three days, with no duplicates, no alert and no customer report. So I removed the feature flag today.

The diff deletes the old per-event insert function and the flag check in the worker setup. It also removes two tests that only covered the old path. The killed-worker test and the SIGTERM test stay.

I ran the full ingest test suite locally, then on staging, where it took 4 minutes. Production got the new build on one worker first and then on the rest. Nothing changed in the graphs after the deploy, as expected.

One leftover is the README of the worker, which still described the old insert. I updated it with the 1,500 event and 100 ms limits and a note on how the replay after a crash works.

The batching work is done. The next ingest topic is the client side retry, but that waits until the search index plan moves forward.

summary: Wrote the rollover lookup for the monthly search index so the indexer picks a write alias by event month and size, working on staging with the 3-shard layout
body:
Following Mara's note about the indexer, I started the lookup that decides the target index for an event. Before, the indexer built the index name from the customer and the month of the event time. With rollover, a month can have several indices.

The new code keeps a small table in Postgres with one row per customer and month: the current write alias, the number of the index and its size at the last check. The indexer reads it into memory and refreshes it every 30 seconds.

The rollover rule is simple. When an index passes 40 GB, a new one is created with the next number, and the write alias moves to it. Reads go through a search alias that covers all indices of the month, so the search API does not change.

I tested on staging with the copy of the largest customer's data. I loaded it at 5 times the normal speed. The index rolled over twice, and the counts matched the source afterward. There were no failed bulk requests.

A problem showed up with events that arrive late for an old month. They go to the last index of that month, which may be closed to writes. I made the lookup fall back to the newest index of that month and reopen the write alias if needed. This has a test now.

Still open are the cleanup of empty indices and a metric for the rollover count. Tomorrow I will add both.

summary: Added a rollover counter and an empty index cleanup to the indexer lookup after staging showed two leftover empty indices from failed rollovers
body:
The staging run from this morning left two empty indices, created by rollovers that were interrupted when I restarted the indexer. They did no harm but would pile up.

I added a cleanup step to the nightly job. It deletes an index only if it has zero documents, is not the write target, and is older than one hour. I also added a Prometheus counter for rollovers per customer and a gauge for the largest index size.

The cleanup is tested against a staging cluster with the two leftovers, and it removed both. A dry run mode logs what would be deleted, and I will use it first in production.

summary: Investigated why Redis memory rose again by 6 points over the weekend and traced it to rate limiter counters that were missing a TTL after the shared client change
body:
Redis memory was at 67 percent this afternoon, after being at 61 following the dashboard trimming deploy. I looked at where the growth came from.

I sampled keys with SCAN and grouped them by prefix. The cache keys were stable. The rate limiter keys, with the prefix rl:, had grown from about 40,000 to 310,000.

The cause was in the change I made last week for the shared client. The batch job counters were created with INCR, and the EXPIRE call was in a second command that ran only in the old per-job client code path. After the change to the shared client, that path was skipped, so the counters had no TTL.

I checked a few keys with the TTL command and got -1 for the new ones, which confirms it. The fix sets the counter and its expiry in one small Lua script, so the two cannot be separated. I wrote a test that creates a counter and checks that its TTL is positive.

I then needed to clean up the keys already there. I wrote a script that scans for rl: keys with no TTL and sets a 1 hour expiry on them. I ran it on staging first. Then I ran it in production in pieces of 5,000 keys with a short pause, so it did not slow other commands.

After the cleanup the key count fell to 41,000 and memory to 62 percent. The limiter behavior stayed the same, because the windows are 1 minute.

I added an alert for the number of keys without TTL under the rl: prefix. The deploy of the fix went out at the end of the day. Mara will review the Lua script tomorrow.

summary: Mara reviewed the rate limiter Lua script and asked for the TTL to be set only on first creation, which fixed a window drift in the test
body:
Mara found that the script reset the expiry on every increment, so a busy key would never expire and the window would slide. I changed it to set the expiry only when the counter returns 1.

The test for the window now sends requests across the minute boundary and checks that the counter resets. It failed with the old script and passes with the new one. The new version is deployed and Mara approved it.

summary: Checked the ingest client retry settings and found the SDK retries on 400 responses, which wastes requests on malformed batches
body:
While reading the ingest client code for another reason I saw that the retry policy covers every non-2xx response, including 400. A malformed batch is sent three times and fails each time.

I counted in the access logs: about 1,900 requests per day are repeats of a 400. This is small against the total, but a few customers produce most of them.

I changed the policy to retry only on 429, 502, 503, 504 and network errors, with backoff and a limit of 4 tries. A test covers each status code. I did not yet release the SDK. Sam will check the docs for the retry description first.

summary: Built the first version of the audit log export query with a cursor and tested it on the largest customer's 14 million rows in 3 minutes
body:
Started on the compliance export of the audit log. The need is simple: a customer can ask for all audit entries in a period as a file, and the export must not lock or slow the main database.

I wrote the query with keyset paging on the actor and time index that I built last week. Each page reads 5,000 rows ordered by time and id, and the next page starts after the last id. This avoids the slow OFFSET paging.

The export writes NDJSON to a temp file and streams it to S3 in parts. I tested on the largest customer, which has 14 million audit rows for the period. The run took 3 minutes and used about 180 MB of memory in the worker.

I watched Postgres during the run. CPU stayed under 20 percent and the replica lag was below one second, because the query runs on the read replica. The index was used in every page, confirmed with EXPLAIN on a sample.

There were two problems. First, rows with identical timestamps were skipped at a page border in an early version, because I compared only the time. Using the pair of time and id fixed it, and the row count matches the table now. Second, the S3 part upload failed once with a timeout. I added a retry for the part with a short backoff.

The file format has fields for actor, action, target, time and the source IP. Lena asked for the export to appear as a button in the admin console, so I wrote the API shape in the ticket: a POST that starts a job, and a GET that returns its state and a signed link.

Next steps are the job table, the signed link expiry and a limit of one running export per customer.

summary: Added the export job table and a limit of one running export per customer, with signed links valid for 24 hours
body:
Created the table audit_export_jobs with customer, period, state, file key and timestamps. The states are queued, running, done and failed.

A partial unique index allows only one queued or running job per customer. A second request gets a 409 with the id of the running job. I tested this with two parallel requests.

The signed link uses the S3 presign with a 24 hour expiry. A done job whose link has expired gets a fresh link on the next GET, as long as the file still exists. Files are deleted after 7 days by a bucket rule.

The worker marks a job failed when the process dies, using a heartbeat column that the job runner checks every minute. I tested by killing the worker mid export, and the job moved to failed after 90 seconds.

summary: Found and fixed a Postgres autovacuum setting for the audit log table so dead rows stay under 5 percent, and wrote down the new per-table values
body:
Two days ago I saw that the autovacuum threshold was too high for the audit log. Today I made the change.

The table has 90 million rows and the default scale factor of 0.2 means vacuum starts only after 18 million dead rows. The audit log is mostly appended, but the redaction job updates old rows, so dead rows pile up in bursts. The last check showed 11 percent dead rows.

I set the per-table values: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 and the cost limit to 800 for this table only. For the events table I looked at the same numbers and left them alone, since it is append only and its dead row share is under 1 percent.

I applied the setting with ALTER TABLE during the quiet hours. The first vacuum ran for 22 minutes. I watched the I/O graphs in Grafana and the read latency of other queries did not change. After it the dead row share was 0.4 percent.

The index on actor and time got smaller as well, from 3.1 GB to 2.6 GB after the vacuum cleaned the pages. The export query was a bit faster on the test customer, 2 minutes 40 seconds instead of 3 minutes.

I also wrote a Grafana panel for the dead row share of the five biggest tables, with an alert at 10 percent for an hour. The values for each table are written in the infrastructure docs.

I did not run a full VACUUM, since that locks the table. The bloat is low enough that it is not needed. Mara will check the alert thresholds tomorrow.

summary: Started the schema registry validation step: events are checked against the registered schema version at ingest, and an unknown version gets a 422 on staging
body:
Today I worked on the first validation step of the schema registry. The registry stores the event schemas with a version per event type. The ingest API should check each event against the version it names.

I added a validation call in the ingest API before the batch goes on to the queue. The schema is loaded from the registry service and cached in memory for 5 minutes per type and version. A miss triggers a fetch, and a failed fetch uses the last cached copy, so a registry outage does not stop ingest.

For an invalid event the API returns a 422 with the index of the event in the batch and the path of the failing field. I decided that a batch is rejected as a whole, because partial acceptance made the retry logic of clients hard to explain. Sam agreed that this is easier to document.

On staging I sent 100,000 events from a recorded stream. The validation added 0.3 ms per event at p95, which is small compared with the batch latency. The memory of the API process grew by 40 MB for the cached schemas.

Three problems came up:

- Two older event types have no registered version. I registered version 1 for both from the existing schema files.
- One customer sends an extra field called ts_local that the schema does not list. The schema allows extra fields now, with a warning counter.
- The JSON schema library was slow on deep nesting. I compiled the schemas once and reused them, which cut the time in half.

The next step is a feature flag per customer so the validation can be turned on slowly. I will also write a test with a batch that has one bad event in the middle.

summary: Added a per-customer flag for schema validation and a test with one bad event in the middle of a batch, then enabled it for the internal test account
body:
I built the flag in the settings table in Postgres, with the values off, warn and enforce. The ingest API reads it through the same cache as other customer settings.

In warn mode an invalid event is counted and logged but the batch goes through. In enforce mode the batch is rejected with the 422. The default is off.

The test sends a batch of 50 events where event 23 has a string in a number field. In enforce mode the response is a 422 naming index 23 and the path, and none of the 50 is stored. In warn mode all 50 are stored and the counter goes up by one.

I turned on warn mode for our internal test account in production and sent a few thousand events. The counter and logs behaved as expected. Tomorrow I will pick two small customers who agreed to a trial and ask Sam to write to them.

summary: Checked the Redis key count by prefix after the weekend and found all groups stable, with the rl: keys at 43,000 and memory at 62 percent
body:
A routine check after the TTL fix for the rate limiter. I scanned Redis keys and grouped them by prefix.

The saved-query keys were at 210,000, the session keys at 8,400, and the rl: keys at 43,000. All of them move within a few percent from last week. The alert for keys without TTL did not fire.

Memory was 62 percent at the busy hour and 55 at night. The hit rate was 73 percent, as before. Connections at the busy hour were 118. I made no change.

summary: Began the loader retry work: the document loader now resumes a large file from the last committed chunk instead of starting over after a failure
body:
The document loader reads large NDJSON and CSV files from S3 and writes events in chunks. Today a customer file of 6 GB failed at 80 percent because of a network error, and the whole load started again from zero. This is the problem the loader-retry branch is meant to solve.

I added a small progress record per load in Postgres. It holds the file key, the byte offset of the last committed chunk and the number of rows stored. The offset is written in the same transaction as the chunk, so the two cannot differ.

On a failure the loader retries the chunk up to 5 times with backoff, which starts at 1 second and doubles. If all tries fail, the load is marked paused and keeps its offset. A later start of the same load reads the record and seeks to the offset with an S3 range request.

I tested with a 1 GB file and a fault injection that cut the connection at random points. In ten runs, each one finished, and the final row count matched the file every time. With no resume, the same test took 4 times longer on average.

One edge case is a chunk border in the middle of a line. The loader now moves the offset only to the end of a complete line, and the next read starts at the next byte after the newline. A test covers CSV files with quoted newlines, which are the hard case. For those I use the CSV parser state to find the real end of a record.

The remaining work is a command to list paused loads and a cleanup of old progress records.

summary: Handled the quoted newline case in the loader resume and added a command to list and resume paused loads
body:
The quoted newline case from this morning needed more work than I thought. A CSV record can contain a newline inside quotes, so cutting at a newline is wrong.

I changed the loader so the offset is stored only at record ends, as reported by the parser after each complete record, not at line ends. The chunk writer commits after a count of records and records the byte position of the parser at that moment. A test file with 2,000 multi-line records, cut at random positions by the fault injector, loaded with the right count in 50 of 50 runs.

Then I added two commands to the loader tool. The first, list-paused, shows file key, offset, percent done and the last error. The second, resume, takes a load id and continues it.

I also found that the progress record was never deleted after a successful load. I now delete it when the load finishes, and a nightly cleanup removes paused records older than 14 days with a log line for each.

One more issue: the S3 range request needs the file to be unchanged. If the file was replaced between the failure and the resume, the offsets would point into different content. I store the ETag of the file in the record and compare it before resuming. A mismatch makes the load fail with a clear message asking for a restart.

Tested the ETag check by replacing the test file between runs. It failed as intended. The branch is ready for review by Mara tomorrow.

summary: Looked at search API p95 latency by endpoint and found the suggest endpoint at 180 ms, mostly waiting on a Redis call per keystroke
body:
I broke down the search API latency by endpoint in Grafana. Search itself is at 95 ms p95, but the suggest endpoint used by the admin console is at 180 ms.

A trace of one request showed two Redis round trips for a suggest call: one for the customer settings, one for the cached suggestions. Each costs about 1 ms on the wire but the settings call was also waiting for a connection from the pool at busy times.

I merged the two reads into one pipeline call. On staging the p95 fell from 180 to 131 ms. I did not deploy yet, because Lena wants to check the console behavior with the debounce first.

summary: Reviewed the loader retry branch with Mara, fixed two findings, and ran the 6 GB customer file through it with three injected failures
body:
Mara reviewed the loader-retry branch this afternoon and had two findings that I fixed before the test run.

The first was that the backoff had no jitter. With several loads failing at the same network event, they would all retry at the same moment. I added a random jitter of up to 30 percent of the delay. The second was that the retry count was per chunk but never reset, so a load with many small failures could pause even though it made progress. Now the count resets after each chunk that commits.

After the fixes I ran the real 6 GB customer file on staging. I injected three failures by blocking the S3 endpoint for 20 seconds at about 25, 60 and 90 percent. The loader retried each time. The first two blocks were shorter than the total backoff, so the loader recovered by itself. The third was a long one, so it paused after 5 tries.

I resumed it with the command and it continued from the stored offset. The final row count was 31,204,118, which matches the line count of the file. The total time was 38 minutes, with 4 minutes lost to the pauses and waits.

I looked at the memory use too. It stayed at 210 MB, flat across chunks. There was no growth after a resume.

Mara also asked about duplicate rows if a chunk commits but the process dies before it records progress. Because the offset is written in the same transaction as the chunk, this cannot happen. I wrote a test that kills the process between the insert and the commit, and the row count matched after resume.

The logs now include the load id and the chunk number in every retry line, which will help with support questions. I updated the loader docs with the resume commands and the ETag rule. Mara approved the branch. I plan to merge it tomorrow morning and deploy during the quiet hours.

summary: Merged the loader retry branch and deployed it, then ran the first real customer load with it: 2.3 GB finished with one automatic retry
body:
After Mara's approval I merged loader-retry into main this evening and deployed the loader service. The deploy was one task replaced at a time, and no load was running at that moment.

The first real use came an hour later. Sam had a customer who needed to import 2.3 GB of NDJSON history, and she started it with the standard tool. I watched the logs.

At about 40 percent the S3 read timed out. The loader logged the retry with the chunk number, waited 1.2 seconds with jitter, and went on. The rest of the file loaded without a problem. The total time was 14 minutes, and the row count matched the file at 9,870,552 rows.

What I checked after the load:

- the progress record was deleted at the end
- the audit log shows one entry for the load
- no paused loads are listed
- the Postgres commit time for the chunks stayed in the usual range

I also thought about what the customer sees. Before, a failure sent them an error mail and they needed support to start again. Now a short failure is invisible, and a long one leaves a paused load that support can resume with one command. I wrote a short note for Sam with the two commands and an example of the output of list-paused.

There is one more thing for the future. The retry limit of 5 is a constant in the code, and a customer on a bad connection may need more. I do not want a config option yet, as we have no case for it. I added a line to the backlog to look at this if support sees a paused load that would have worked with more tries.

The branch work is complete. I will watch the loader metrics over the next days.

summary: Deployed the merged suggest endpoint pipeline change after Lena confirmed the console debounce, and p95 settled at 128 ms
body:
Lena checked the admin console and confirmed that the debounce there is 150 ms, so the console does not send a request per keystroke. The change is safe to deploy.

I deployed it to one search API process first, then to all four. The suggest p95 went from 180 to 128 ms. The Redis commands per second from the search API fell by about 12 percent. Connections did not change.

I saw no errors after the deploy, and the cache hit rate stayed at 73 percent.

summary: Wrote the plan for the next batch of old per-customer index deletions, with the count checks scripted so each customer needs no manual comparison
body:
So far the count check before deleting an old per-customer index was done by hand: query the old index, query the alias on the monthly layout, compare. For the next 30 small customers I wanted this scripted.

The script takes a customer id and does these steps. It counts documents in the old index and in the monthly alias, filtered by the customer id. It compares the two numbers and also compares the count per month. It writes a result line with both numbers and a pass or fail.

A first dry run on staging for five customers passed for four. The fifth failed with a difference of 212 documents. I looked at it and found that the old index still received writes from a client that used a cached alias. The dual write flag was gone, but one old ingest worker image was still running in staging. After I stopped it and waited an hour, the counts matched.

This showed that the script should also check that the old index has had no writes for some time. I added a check on the indexing total from the index stats, taken twice with one hour in between. If the number changed, the customer fails with the message that the old index is still written to.

The plan for the deletion has these rules:

- seven days of passing checks, as before
- deletion in groups of ten customers
- a snapshot of the group's indices kept for 14 days, as a safety net
- one group per day, in the morning hours

I estimated that the 30 customers hold about 90 GB, so the cluster gets that much space back. The disk use of the search cluster is at 71 percent now, and this would bring it near 60.

I shared the plan with Tobias, because the snapshots go to the new bucket. He confirmed that the bucket has room. Tomorrow I start the daily checks for the first group.

summary: Prepared the first group of ten old customer indices for deletion by running the scripted count checks and testing a snapshot restore, without deleting anything yet
body:
This morning I ran the scripted count check for the first group of ten customers. All ten had passed for seven days in a row, and the script showed no writes to the old indices in the last hour.

I took the snapshot of the ten indices to the new bucket. It took 6 minutes and the snapshot status said SUCCESS with no failed shards. I tested the restore of one small index under another name on staging to be sure that the snapshot is usable. The restored document count matched the original.

I did not delete anything yet. I want Mara to read the script output first, and I want one more look at the nightly reindex job. Last time it logged warnings for deleted indices that were still in its list. Its config still reads the per-customer index names for these ten, so a deletion today would bring the same warnings back. I wrote a short change that makes it read the aliases for this group, and I will test it on staging tonight. I checked the run time of the last night run and it was 7 minutes, which is the baseline to compare against.

I also checked that the search results for the ten customers work against the current indices. I ran a saved query for each of them against the API, and every response had a total matching the count in the script. Sam looked at two of the accounts in the console and saw no difference, which gives us a reference for later.

A small problem came from the Grafana panel for the index sizes. It has a fixed list of index names, so indices that disappear would show as zero. I changed it to use a pattern, so removed indices will drop out of the panel.

By my estimate the group frees about 31 GB, but two of the customers were smaller than their reported size, which included replicas I did not count, so the real number may be lower. The search cluster disk use is at 68 percent. The last group has the two customers with two accounts, and I will look at those more carefully because their totals are split over two aliases.

summary: Prepared the second group of ten old per-customer index deletions, ran only the scripted count checks in dry-run mode and found a mismatch of 212 documents for one customer.
body:
Followed the plan written two days ago for the second group of ten old customer indices. This time I ran the deletion script in dry-run mode only, so nothing was removed. The script compares document counts between each old index and the matching slice of the monthly index, and it reports a mismatch instead of continuing. Nine of the ten matched at once. One customer showed 212 fewer documents in the monthly index than in the old one.

I marked that index as held back and looked at the difference. The 212 documents were events with a missing event month. The rollover lookup writes such events to the current month alias instead of the month of the event. That is a bug in the lookup from last week, not a problem in the data. The documents are all there, but in the wrong monthly index, so the count by month slice did not match.

I changed the lookup to fall back to the received time when the event month is missing, and wrote a small test with three such events. It passes locally. I have not yet moved the 212 documents. I wrote the reindex call into the plan as a step for later, with a count check before and after it.

I also wrote down the sizes of the nine clean indices, about 28 GB in total, so the disk numbers can be compared after the deletion. The deletion itself waits until the fix is deployed and the dry run is repeated on the held index.

Next is a review of the fix with Mara. After that, the third group holds two of the larger customers, so I will check the cluster disk headroom before planning it.

summary: Explained to Sam why saved-query results sometimes show old counts: the Redis cache TTL for dashboard queries is 300 seconds and the console does not show cache age
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer saw a dashboard count that was lower than the number in their own export. I looked at the request in the logs. The dashboard query was served from the Redis query cache, and the entry was 4 minutes old when the customer looked.

The TTL for dashboard query results is 300 seconds. That is a deliberate setting from the time the ClickHouse dashboards got fast enough to run often. Raw search results use 60 seconds. The customer had loaded a file just before, and the loader writes events in chunks, so the count grew while the cache entry was still valid.

I wrote a short answer for Sam that he can reuse. Counts can lag up to 5 minutes after an import, a refresh in the console does not bypass the cache, and the export always reads fresh data. I also noted that the console shows no sign of cache age, which causes this question about once a month.

I suggested to Lena to show a small label such as updated 3 minutes ago on the dashboard card. The response already carries a cached-at field, so it would need only a console change. Lena will look at it next week.

summary: Checked the new audit export signed links end to end on staging and found the link host was the internal name, so the downloads failed from outside
body:
Ran a full export of the staging audit log for the test account and opened the signed link from a laptop outside the VPN. The download failed with a name resolution error. The job had stored the link with the internal service host, which is only visible inside the network.

The link builder took the host from the request that created the job. In the console that request comes through the internal proxy, so the wrong host was recorded. I changed it to read a public base URL from the service config and added the value to the staging and production settings.

After the change, the link worked from outside and the signature check rejected a link with one changed character, as it should. A link older than 24 hours also returned the expected 410. I added a test for the builder with the proxy header set.

Still open is the size limit for a single file. The largest customer produces about 2 GB of CSV, and I want to split it into parts of 500 MB before the link goes to customers.

summary: Split large audit exports into parts of 500 MB with one signed link per part, and the 14 million row export now finishes as five files
body:
Built the part splitting for the audit export that I noted this morning. The export job writes rows to a part file and starts a new one when the file passes 500 MB, closing at a row boundary so no row is cut in two. Each part gets its own object key and the job record keeps a list of parts with row ranges.

The cursor query was not changed. Only the writer was. The first version kept the whole part in memory before upload, and the memory of the export worker went above 1.2 GB on the large customer. I changed it to stream into a multipart upload, and the peak went down to about 180 MB.

I ran the largest customer's 14 million rows on staging. It produced five parts of about 480 MB and took 3 minutes 20 seconds, a little slower than the single file because of the uploads. The row counts of the parts add up to exactly the count in the table.

The console needs to show a list of links instead of one, which I wrote up for Lena as a small API change. The response keeps the old single link field filled with the first part for now, so nothing breaks while the console is updated.

To do: a test for a crash in the middle of a part, since the job must resume from the last finished part and not start over.

summary: Found that the export job resume re-wrote the last finished part, so a crash would give one duplicate part; fixed it by recording the part after the upload completes
body:
I wrote the crash test I had on the list for the audit export. The test kills the export worker while it uploads part 3 of 5 and then restarts the job. The result had six parts, and part 3 appeared twice with the same row range under two keys.

The cause was the order of the steps. The job recorded the part in the table before the upload was complete, so after the restart it saw the part as done, but the upload was missing, and then it wrote the range again in a new part and recorded that too. I changed the order: upload first, record the part in the same transaction that moves the cursor position.

With this order, a crash leaves at worst an orphan object in storage that no record points to. I added a lifecycle rule on the export prefix that deletes objects after 3 days, which also cleans up those orphans.

The test now passes with five parts and no repeated range. I ran it ten times with the kill at different moments, such as during the first part and right after the last one, and all ten passed. Mara will review the branch tomorrow.

summary: Looked at Redis memory by key group after the cleanup of rate limiter TTLs and found the cache group has grown to 31 percent, mostly saved-query results
body:
Checked memory use after the TTL fix for the rate limiter counters from a few days ago. Total use is at 58 percent, down from 62. The rl: keys went from 43,000 to 39,000 and are stable now, as the counters expire with their window.

The largest group is now the query cache with 31 percent of memory. I sampled 2,000 keys of that group with a scan and looked at their sizes. Most saved-query results are small, but about 3 percent of keys hold more than 200 KB each, and those hold about a third of the group.

The large ones are dashboard results for the two biggest customers with many breakdown columns. They are valid for 300 seconds, so they do not pile up for long, but they are written again and again by many users with different filters.

I listed three options. First, compress values above 50 KB. Second, do not cache results above a size limit. Third, narrow the cache key so that equal queries from different users share an entry. The third is the most useful, but the filter order is currently part of the key hash, and that is the reason for many duplicates.

I tried a test of normalizing the filter order on a copy of last hour's queries. The number of distinct keys fell by 18 percent. I will write that into a change for the cache key function and keep the customer prefix first, so the clearing by prefix still works. No change was deployed in this session.

summary: Normalized the filter order in the query cache key and checked the effect: hit rate for dashboard queries rose from 61 to 68 percent on staging replay
body:
Implemented the key normalization I measured earlier today. The cache key is built from the customer id, the endpoint and a hash of the query. Before the hash, the filters are now sorted by field name and the values of in-lists are sorted too. Everything else in the query stays as it was, so no two different queries can share a key.

The risky part was the in-lists. A list of values is a set for the search, but for one endpoint the order of the values decides the order of the result columns. I read the code of that endpoint and found that it is the compare view of the dashboard. For this endpoint the sort of values is skipped, and I added a comment and a test for that case.

I wrote tests for sorted filters, for the compare view, for nested filters and for an empty filter. All pass. The customer id is still the first part of the key, so the prefix clearing that Lena asked about keeps working, and I added a test for that too.

Then I replayed one hour of production queries against staging with a cold cache. The hit rate for dashboard queries was 61 percent with the old key and 68 percent with the new one. The number of distinct keys fell by 18 percent, as in the first measure. The search endpoints did not change much, which is normal since their queries rarely repeat.

One point to watch: after the deploy, all old keys are a miss at once, so the first minutes will show more load on ClickHouse. The dashboards of the large customers are the heaviest, so I plan to deploy in the quiet hours of the morning, not at midday.

The change is in review. Mara has the pull request, and I asked her to look at the in-list case in particular.

summary: Mara approved the audit export branch with one comment about the part list size, and it was merged and deployed to production for the internal account
body:
Mara went through the audit export branch this morning. She was fine with the cursor query and the crash safe order of upload and record. Her only comment was about the part list. A job with a very long export could hold hundreds of parts in one JSON column, and she wanted a limit.

I checked the numbers. At 500 MB per part, even a 100 GB export would give 200 parts, and the biggest customer is at 2 GB. So the column stays small in practice. But a limit is cheap, so I added a maximum of 400 parts per job, and a job that would go over it fails with a clear error message instead of writing on.

I also added a test that sets the part size very small so that the limit triggers, and the job ends in the failed state with the reason in the record. The test passed on the first run.

After the second review round, I merged the branch. The deploy went through the normal pipeline to staging, then to production. I started an export for the internal account on production, which has about 90,000 audit rows. It finished in 6 seconds with one part, and the link worked from outside.

The next step is a customer who asked for the export for their compliance review. Sam will contact them, and I will watch the first real export on production. For now the feature is enabled only for the internal account, with a per-customer flag as for the schema validation.

summary: Deployed the normalized cache key in the early morning and watched the first hour: the miss spike was short and ClickHouse CPU peaked at 55 percent
body:
Deployed the cache key change shortly after nine, outside of the busiest hours of the customers in Europe. Before the deploy I looked at the ClickHouse CPU as a baseline, which usually sits near 30 percent in this time of the morning.

Right after the deploy, all dashboard queries were a miss, as I expected. The CPU of ClickHouse rose to 55 percent within three minutes and stayed there for about eight minutes. Then it fell back as the cache filled again. No query timed out, and the p95 of the dashboard endpoint went from 210 ms to 640 ms for those minutes and then back.

After one hour, the hit rate of the dashboard queries was at 66 percent, and after two hours at 68 percent, in line with the replay. The key count in Redis for the query cache group fell by about 15 percent compared with the same hour yesterday.

I did not see any wrong results. To be sure, I picked ten dashboard queries with filters in different order, ran them as two users and compared the answers. They were equal, and the second one was a hit.

I will check the memory share of the cache group again in a few days. If it is still near 30 percent, the next step is compressing the large values.

summary: Started the first batch of the schema registry validation for real customers by enabling it for two small ones and watching the 422 rate for a day
body:
After the staging tests of the validation step from the last week, I enabled the per-customer flag for two small customers who send a simple and stable event shape. Sam had asked them in advance and they agreed. Both use the official SDK, which sets the schema version in each batch.

I wrote a Grafana panel for the rate of 422 responses by customer and by reason, so unknown version, missing required field and wrong type are separate lines. Without it, we would only have seen the total.

In the first three hours, customer A sent about 41,000 events and had zero rejections. Customer B sent about 9,000 events and had 14 rejections, all with the reason wrong type. The field was a user id that the customer's app sends as a number in some code paths and as a string in others.

The rejection is correct by the registered schema, but the customer would lose those events, because the SDK drops a batch after the 422. I talked this through with Mara in chat. We decided that for the first weeks the validation should have a log only mode, where the event is stored and the problem is counted, and the reject mode is turned on only after the customer fixed the code.

I will build that mode next. For customer B I set the flag back to off in the meantime, so no events are lost, and Sam will tell them about the number type.

summary: After a day of schema validation on two small customers the 422 rate was under 0.2 percent, so it was enabled for five more with a clear error body
body: Checked the schema registry validation for the two small customers after a full day. Of about 310,000 events, 480 were rejected with 422, and almost all came from one SDK version that sends a field as a string instead of a number. The 422 body now names the event index, the field and the registered schema version, which the customer's developer asked for in a support thread. Ingest p95 did not move, since the schema lookup is cached in the worker for 60 seconds. I enabled the flag for five more small customers and told Sam what the new error looks like so support can answer questions. The next step is a week of watching the 422 counts per customer before any large customer gets it.

summary: Investigated a slow Postgres query on the settings table behind the console login and found a missing index on the lower-cased email
body:
Lena reported that the login screen of the admin console sometimes took more than two seconds. I looked at the Postgres slow query log for the last day and found one query that appeared 300 times with an average of 1.4 seconds. It looks up an account by the lower-cased email address.

The explain output showed a sequential scan on the accounts table. The table has only about 6,000 rows, so the scan alone should take a few milliseconds. But the query also joins the settings table, and for that join Postgres chose a nested loop with a sequential scan for each row, because the statistics were old.

I ran analyze on both tables by hand and the plan changed to an index scan on the settings side, with 3 ms. The accounts side still scanned, because the existing index is on the email column as written, not on lower(email).

I created an index on lower(email) with the concurrent option, which took a few seconds, and then the plan used it. The same query then ran in under 1 ms. I added the index to the migration files as well, so a fresh database has it.

The autovacuum settings of the accounts table are default, which is fine for its size, but the analyze threshold is why the statistics were old. I will leave it for now.

summary: Answered Tobias about the ECS task memory for the ingest workers: the peak after batching is 410 MB, so the 1 GB task size has room
body:
Tobias asked whether the ingest worker tasks could be made smaller to save cost, now that batching is in. I looked at the memory graphs of the last week for all workers.

The resident memory peak was 410 MB, reached while a batch of 1,500 events sat in memory together with the incoming requests. The average is about 260 MB. Before the batching change, the peak was about 340 MB, so batching added roughly 70 MB.

The task is set to 1 GB. Going down to 512 MB would leave only 100 MB of headroom over the peak, and a burst from a large customer could push it over, which ends the task with an out of memory kill. A kill in the middle of a flush is safe because of the replay test, but it still costs a restart and a latency spike.

My suggestion was 768 MB, which is a saving of about a quarter of the memory cost for these tasks. Tobias will make the change in Terraform for staging first and watch it for a week.

summary: Planned the monthly index shard layout in detail: a table of customer sizes, the proposed shard counts per month and the order of the migration steps
body:
Wrote the working plan for the new search index layout, where events go to one index per month and not one per customer. This is still a plan only, and nothing in production will change in this step.

First the sizes. I pulled the document counts and store sizes of all customer indices, plus the monthly indices we are testing on staging. The total across production is about 1.9 TB. The five largest customers make up 71 percent of it. The smallest 20 customers together are under 2 percent.

The current layout gives each customer their own index with a shard count chosen at the time of sign up. That produced about 160 shards for 40 customers, many of them tiny. The cluster pays for each shard with heap and with cluster state, and the small ones are the reason the cluster state updates got slow.

For the monthly layout, I looked at the shard size. A good range is 20 to 50 GB per shard. The newest months hold about 110 GB, so 3 shards would be about 37 GB each, which fits. Older months with less data would be 1 or 2 shards. This is the rule the rollover lookup already uses: size and event month.

There are risks that I wrote down. Customer isolation gets weaker, since a filter on customer id replaces the separate index, and this makes the filtered alias important. Deleting one customer's data becomes a delete by query and not an index drop. And the per-customer boosts of search v2 need to work on the filtered alias, so I need to test them.

The order of the steps is this. One, finish the deletion of the old customer indices that are already copied. Two, create the filtered aliases for all customers on staging and run the query test set against them. Three, migrate the months from newest to oldest, since the newest are read most. Four, switch the search API to the aliases per customer. Five, delete the old indices after a check of the counts, as with the current group.

I asked Mara to look at the risk about the delete by query for customers who leave. She will think about whether we need a separate index for the customers with legal deletion terms.

summary: Ran the search query test set against filtered aliases on staging and found two boost differences, both caused by the shared index statistics
body:
Built the filtered aliases for ten customers on the staging cluster. Each alias points to the monthly indices and filters on the customer id, with a routing value so that a query touches fewer shards. Then I ran the query test set from the search v2 work against both layouts and compared the results.

The test set has 400 queries with expected top results, collected from real customers and cleaned of personal data. For 396 queries, the top 10 were identical in both layouts. Four differed, in two groups.

The first group, two queries, differed in the order of rank 3 and 4. The scores were nearly equal in the old layout, and the new one has a different term frequency, because the statistics are now counted over all customers in the monthly index and not for one customer. A word that is rare for one customer may be common for all. This is expected, and the order was still reasonable.

The second group was more interesting. Two queries with a boost on the title field gave a different top result. The cause was the same, a word like invoice which is frequent in the whole index and so has a low weight, while it was rare and strong for the small customer. The boost still works, but its effect is weaker for such words.

Options for this are the search type with distributed term statistics, which costs one more round trip, or a higher boost for small customers. I tried the first on staging. The four differences shrank to one, and the latency went up by about 9 ms at p95. That is a cost I do not like for all queries.

I also ran the latency comparison on staging. With routing, the p95 of the test set was 95 ms on the monthly layout and 112 ms on the current one, because queries touch fewer shards on average. So the new layout looks faster in general, at least on staging.

My conclusion is to plan with the default statistics and accept the small ranking differences, unless a customer complains. I wrote the four queries into a list of known differences, so that the next test run does not flag them again. Nothing has been changed on production. I will show the results to Mara and Sam, since Sam hears the complaints first.

summary: Reviewed the Redis connection pool settings of the search API after the key naming cleanup and found idle connections held at 120, far above need
body:
Looked at the Redis client connections after a Grafana panel showed 120 connections from the search API while the busiest hour only needed about 30 at the same time. The extra ones were idle, but each connection costs memory on the server and counts toward the connection limit.

I read the client config. The pool had a minimum of 40 idle connections per process, and there are three search API processes per task and a few tasks. That is where 120 came from. The minimum was set a long time ago when the first cache layer was added, to avoid connection setup latency after quiet periods.

I changed the minimum to 8 per process and set the idle timeout to 60 seconds. On staging, I ran a load test with a ramp from zero to the normal peak in 30 seconds to see whether the connection setup showed in the latency. The p95 rose by 2 ms during the ramp only, and p99 by 6 ms. That is acceptable.

Then I checked the other users of Redis. The rate limiter, which sits in the ingest API, uses its own pool with 20 connections and is busy all the time, so I left it alone. The admin console uses Redis for sessions with a pool of 10, also fine.

I deployed the search API change to production in the afternoon. The total connection count from the search API fell from 120 to 41 within a few minutes, and the p95 of the search endpoints did not move. The server side connected client count fell by the same number.

I wrote the new values in the runbook page for Redis and added a line that the numbers must be checked against the process count when the number of tasks grows. A note for the future: if the number of API tasks doubles, the peak connection count doubles too, so the limit on the server should be checked then.

The next point I want to look at is whether the suggest endpoint could share a connection per request and not take one per keystroke, but that is for another day.

summary: Tested the rate limit per API key on staging with a burst of 2,000 requests and found the limiter allowed 2,140, a 7 percent overshoot at the window edge
body:
Ran a burst test for the per-key rate limits. The limit for the test key was 1,000 requests per minute, and the test sent 2,000 requests in 10 seconds across two windows, so about 1,000 should pass and 1,000 be rejected with 429.

The test measured 1,070 accepted for the first window and 1,070 over the two windows combined within 10 seconds, which overshoots near the window edge. The fixed window counter allows a full limit just before the edge and a full limit just after it. That is the usual behavior of the method and I expected some of it.

The larger part of the overshoot, though, came from a second reason. Two ingest tasks check the counter at nearly the same time, and with the Lua script each one is atomic, so that is not the cause. The cause was the clock: the window key is built from the task's local time, and the two tasks differed by about 400 ms, so for 400 ms they used different keys.

I changed the script to take the time from Redis with the TIME command inside the script and build the key there. That removes the clock difference between tasks. The overshoot at the edge from the fixed window method remains and is documented.

After the change, the same test gave 1,000 accepted in the first window exactly, and in the edge case at most 2,000 across the edge as the method allows. I ran it five times and the numbers were the same each time.

Mara reviews the Lua change tomorrow. A sliding window would remove the edge effect, but it costs more memory per key, and after the recent TTL problem I do not want to add keys without need.

summary: Wrote the first part of the migration plan for the infrastructure to the new AWS accounts: inventory of cron jobs, secrets and scheduled tasks to move
body:
Tobias and I began the preparation for moving the infrastructure to the new AWS accounts. My part today was the inventory of what runs on a schedule and what secrets it needs, because those are the things that fail without anyone noticing a missing piece.

I went through the Terraform code, the ECS scheduled tasks and the crontab of the utility host. I found 17 scheduled jobs. Seven are on EventBridge schedules, such as the nightly reindex, the backup copy and the export cleanup. Nine are cron entries on the utility host. One is a GitHub Actions schedule for the dependency scan.

For each job I wrote down the schedule, what it needs, which secret or role it uses, and whether it can run twice without harm. Three jobs must never run in both accounts at once: the nightly reindex, the daily rollup of the analytics events and the certificate check. For those, the plan is to switch them off in the old account before they are switched on in the new one, and to write the exact order in the checklist.

The secrets are the second list. There are 31 entries in Secrets Manager. Five are only used by humans or by the old pipeline and can be left behind. For the other 26, I noted which service reads them, so Tobias can create them in the new account and set the policies by service and not by hand.

I found two surprises. One cron entry on the utility host calls a script in a home directory of a person who left, and the script is not in the repository. I copied it into the repository after reading it, and it is a small cleanup of old upload files. Also, the Redis password is read by a startup script from a file on the host and not from Secrets Manager.

I put both things on the list for Tobias. The first needs to become a scheduled task in code. The second needs to move into Secrets Manager before the migration, or the new hosts will not start.

The inventory is a table in the infrastructure docs. I asked Tobias to read it tomorrow and add what I do not know, such as the things set up in the console by hand. Next is the order of the move: which services first, and what runs in both accounts for a short time.

summary: Mara approved the per-key rate limit script after asking for a test of the Redis TIME call under a replica read, which passed
body:
Mara reviewed the Lua change for the rate limits. She liked the removal of the task clock from the key. Her question was whether TIME inside a script is safe, since in older Redis versions a script that calls a non-deterministic command could not write afterward.

I checked the version we run and the script flags. The Redis version we use allows it, because scripts are replicated by their effects and not by their source. So the write after TIME is allowed. I wrote this in a comment in the script, with the version number, so the next reader does not have to ask.

She also asked about reads from a replica. The limiter only talks to the primary, but the test showed me that I never tested what happens when the client is configured for replica reads by mistake. I added a test where the script is called against a read-only connection and checked the error. It failed loudly with a read-only error and the ingest API treated this as limiter unavailable and let the request pass, which is the intended fail-open behavior.

Two more details: she asked for the metric name of the overshoot counter to follow the other limiter metrics, and for the 429 body to include the retry-after seconds. I changed the name and found that the header was already set but the body was not. Now both carry the value.

After these changes, she approved. I merged the branch and deployed the ingest API change to staging. For production, I want to wait for the quiet hours, since the limiter is on the path of every write.

summary: Deployed the rate limit script change to production at low traffic and compared 429 counts per key before and after, with no unexpected changes
body:
Deployed the per-key rate limit change to production early in the morning, when ingest traffic is at its lowest. The limiter is on the path of every write, so I watched the error rate and the latency of the ingest API closely during the roll out.

The roll out goes task by task. During the roll out, old and new tasks ran together for about six minutes. That was the one moment of worry, because old tasks build the window key from their own clock and new ones from the Redis time. For a short time, the same key could be counted in two ways. In practice, this means a customer could get a few requests more than the limit during the switch, which is harmless. I checked afterward that no key was left without a TTL, and the count of rl: keys without one was zero.

Then I compared the 429 responses. I took the hour after the deploy and the same hour a week ago, and grouped by API key. 38 keys had any 429 at all. In most cases the numbers were within 10 percent. Two keys had clearly more rejections than a week ago, and I looked at both.

The first belongs to a customer who runs a big import every morning. Last week the import ran at a different time, and this morning it was larger, so the difference comes from the customer. The second one was a test key of our own that I used in the burst test yesterday. So no unexpected change.

The ingest latency did not change at the p95 level. The p99 was 4 ms lower than a week ago, though this may be noise. The Redis commands per second from the limiter did not change either, as the script does the same number of calls. TIME is one more command inside the script, not one more round trip.

I updated the docs page for the API limits. It now says that the limit is counted per fixed window of 60 seconds, that the burst across a window edge can reach twice the limit, and that the 429 body carries a retry-after value in seconds. Sam will read it and put the part about the edge into the customer-facing docs in simpler words.

The branch is done for this period. What is left is the per-key limit setting in the console, where Lena wants to show the current limit and the usage of the last hour. I will give her the endpoint data tomorrow.

summary: Gave Lena the usage endpoint for the console: current limit, requests in the last hour per key, and rejected count, read from Redis counters
body:
Lena needs data for a small panel on the API key page of the console. I added an endpoint to the admin API that returns the limit, the used count in the current window, and the 429 count of the last hour for one key.

The current window count is read straight from the limiter key. The rejected count did not exist per key, so the script now increments a small counter with a one hour bucket and a TTL of two hours whenever it rejects. I made sure the TTL is set on the first creation only, as Mara asked before for the other keys.

The endpoint needs the customer to own the key, which is checked with the same middleware as the other key routes. I added a test for a key of another customer, and it returns 404 and not 403, so it does not tell anything about key ids.

I sent Lena the response format as an example JSON in the pull request. She said she can build the panel with it, and she asked for the hourly numbers in a list, which I may add later if the panel needs a small chart.

summary: Tried a Go library for faster JSON decoding in the ingest worker and dropped it after it gained only 6 percent on the real batch sample
body:
The profile of the ingest worker shows JSON decoding at about 22 percent of the CPU time, so I tried a faster decoder library that promises two to three times the speed of the standard one. The goal was to lower the CPU cost of the workers, a part of the cost work.

I wrote a benchmark with 5,000 real batches taken from the sample set of events, with the personal data replaced. The standard decoder took 31 ms per 1,000 events. The new library took 24 ms in the plain case, which is a gain of 22 percent of the decode time, but only about 5 percent of the total CPU.

Then I ran it on the whole worker on staging for an hour at replayed production load. The total CPU fell by 6 percent. That is within the noise of the daily load, and the saving would be less than one task out of the fleet.

There were costs too. The library does not give the same error messages on bad input, and our 400 responses quote the position of the error. I would have had to wrap the library, and for some malformed batches it accepted input that the standard one rejects, such as a trailing comma in one case. A change in what we accept is a risk for the schema validation work.

I decided not to adopt it. I removed the branch and wrote the numbers in the cost notes, so nobody repeats the test. The bigger part of the CPU is in the writes and the compression of the responses, which I will look at later.

summary: Looked at gzip compression of ingest API responses and requests: lowering the level from 6 to 3 cut worker CPU by 4 percent with the payload only 3 percent larger
body:
After the decoder test showed that JSON was not the main CPU cost, I profiled the worker again, this time looking at the compression. The ingest API takes gzip requests from many SDKs and compresses its own responses, and together the gzip code took 17 percent of the CPU in the profile.

The response bodies are small, usually under 200 bytes, so compression of them gives almost nothing. The ingest API was set to compress all responses above 0 bytes. I changed the threshold to 1 KB. This alone removed a part of the CPU cost, though the response compression was the smaller part.

The larger part is the decompression of the request batches, which we cannot avoid, and the compression of the batches that the worker sends to Redpanda. For the second one, I tested compression levels on a sample of 2,000 batches. Level 6 gave a ratio of 7.1 and level 3 gave 6.9, with about 35 percent less time per batch. Level 1 gave 6.2, which costs too much in size.

I deployed the settings to staging with level 3 and the 1 KB threshold, and replayed an hour of load. The CPU of the workers fell by 4 percent. The bytes written to the topic rose by 3 percent, which is a very small cost for the broker disk.

Tobias looked at the broker disk numbers. The retention is short enough that 3 percent more does not matter, and he agreed with the change. I deployed it to production in the afternoon. The CPU is down by 4 percent there as well, in the first two hours of traffic, and the lag of the queue stayed at zero.

This is a small win, but it is real, and it needed only two settings. The next place to look is the number of tasks at night, where the traffic is low and the fleet is the same size as at noon. Tobias will say what the scaling rules allow in the new accounts, so I will not touch that now.

summary: Continued the infrastructure move plan with Tobias: ordered the services into three waves, moved the Redis password into Secrets Manager and tested a host boot without the file
body:
Today I worked on the second part of the move to the new AWS accounts, after Tobias read the inventory and added six things set up by hand in the console. Among them were two security group rules and a DNS record that existed nowhere in Terraform. He is putting them into code first, which is a good result of the list.

We agreed on the order of the move in three waves. Wave one holds the services that nobody notices: the export cleanup, the dependency scan, the documentation site and the staging environment. Wave two holds the internal parts: Redpanda, the workers and the schedulers. Wave three holds the parts that customers touch: the load balancer, the ingest API, the search API and the console. The databases are a separate step, because Postgres and ClickHouse hold the data and need a longer plan with a replica in the new account.

For each wave there is a short checklist with a check that proves it works, such as a test batch through ingest or a query through the search API. Each check has a name of the person who runs it. The rollback is to switch the DNS back, and that works as long as the old accounts are not touched.

The second task was the Redis password I found on the host in a file. I created a secret in Secrets Manager, gave the task roles the read policy for it and changed the startup script of the utility host to read the secret by the AWS CLI. The ECS services already got their secret by the task definition, so only the host needed this.

To test it, I started a new utility host from the image on staging, with the file removed. The first boot failed because the instance role did not have the policy, and the error was a clear access denied. After Tobias added the policy, the host booted and the cron jobs could reach Redis. I ran the nightly cleanup by hand on that host and it worked.

Then I did the same for the script from the home directory of the person who left. It is now in the repository as a scheduled task in the Terraform code and runs at the same hour as before, on staging at first. The cron entry on the old host is still there. It will be removed when wave one is done, so that the job does not run twice.

Still open are the cron entries that run on the utility host, nine of them. Tobias wants to move all of them to EventBridge scheduled tasks before the move, so the host becomes less important. We will do three a day, starting with the least risky ones.

summary: Moved the first three cron jobs from the utility host to scheduled ECS tasks in Terraform and verified one run of each on staging, with the old entries disabled
body:
Started the cron move with the three least risky jobs: the export file cleanup, the stale session cleanup in Postgres and the weekly report of the disk use of the search cluster. All three are small and safe to run twice, which I had written down in the inventory.

For each job, I wrote a task definition that uses the same image as the service, with a different command, and a schedule rule in Terraform. The roles are narrow: the cleanup of exports can only list and delete in the export prefix, and the session cleanup reads only the Postgres secret. I did not copy the broad role of the host, since the point of the move is to be able to see what each job needs.

On staging, I applied the code and started each task once by hand. The export cleanup deleted 14 objects older than three days. The session cleanup removed 2,300 old rows in 0.4 seconds. The disk report ran, but posted its message to the wrong channel, because the channel name was set in an environment file on the host that I had not carried over. I put it in the task definition and ran it again, and the message arrived in the right place.

I also made sure that logs of the scheduled tasks go to the same log group naming as the services, so the alert for failed jobs picks them up. I tested it by making the session cleanup fail on purpose, with a wrong secret name. The log line appeared and the alert rule fired within two minutes, then I corrected it.

After one run of each looked right, I disabled the three crontab entries on the staging utility host by commenting them out, with a note of the date of the move in words, not as a date in the file, and the name of the task that replaced them. I did this on staging only. For production, the same steps follow after one day of watching the staging runs.

A note for the next session: the next three are the backup copy check, the audit table partition creation and the certificate check. The last one must not run in both places, so I will turn off the cron entry in the same step as I enable the schedule. I also want to add the job names to the on-call runbook, because the on-call person will look for the cron entries on the host in the old way and will not find them.

summary: Moved the next two cron jobs, the nightly usage rollup and the temp file cleanup, to scheduled ECS tasks and checked one run of each on staging
body: Continued the infrastructure move with the cron jobs from the utility host. The usage rollup and the temp file cleanup now run as scheduled ECS tasks defined in Terraform, with the same schedule as before. Both ran once on staging and wrote the expected output; the rollup produced the same row counts as the old job for the previous night. The old crontab entries are commented out, not deleted, so Tobias can switch back in a minute if needed. Six cron jobs are left, and the two that touch the audit log need a closer look because they use a local socket to Postgres. Next step is to write the list of environment variables each job reads.

summary: Wrote the list of environment variables and secrets each remaining cron job reads, and found two jobs that still read a password from a file on the utility host
body: Went through the six remaining cron jobs one by one and wrote down every environment variable, file path and secret each one touches. Four of them are clean and only need the Postgres URL from Secrets Manager. Two, the audit log compaction and the old export cleanup, read a database password from a file under the home directory of the deploy user. That file would not exist in the new account. I changed both scripts to read the password from the environment and added the secret reference to the task definitions. The list is in the migration plan document now, with a column for the wave in which each job moves. Tobias will review the Terraform tomorrow.

summary: Profiled the ingest worker batch writer after a rise in Postgres insert time for the audit table and found the commit per batch was the cost, not the row count
body:
Mara noticed that the p95 of the audit table insert in the ingest worker went from 9 ms to 21 ms over the last two weeks. I started by checking whether the row count per batch had grown. It had not; the median batch is still about 180 rows. I then turned on the statement log for one worker on staging and replayed an hour of real batches.

The replay showed that each batch did three separate commits: one for the audit rows, one for the account counters and one for the last-seen timestamp. Each commit waits for the WAL flush, and the disk on the Postgres host has been busier since the audit export went out. The three writes are independent of each other in terms of data, but they were never put in one transaction.

I put the three writes into one transaction in the batch writer, in the main checkout of the worker, because the change is small and not part of the batching branch itself. On the replay the p95 dropped from 21 ms to 10 ms. The account counters are still updated at the same moment as before, so the console shows no difference.

One risk is that a failure in the timestamp update now rolls back the audit rows. I made the timestamp update tolerate a failure and log it, since it is only a hint for the console. A unit test covers that path. I did not deploy yet; it goes out in the next window after Mara looks at the diff. I will also look at the account counters later, because a single row there is updated by every batch of a large customer and may need a different design.

summary: Built the part-level checksum for audit exports so customers can verify each downloaded part, and tested it with the five-part 14 million row export
body:
Sam asked for a way for compliance teams to verify that the export files they download are complete and unchanged. I added a SHA-256 checksum per part to the audit export job. The checksum is computed while the part is streamed to S3, so there is no second read of the 500 MB file.

The checksums are stored in the same record as the part list, right after the upload completes, which matches the fix from the resume bug last week. A crash between the upload and the record write now leaves the part to be re-uploaded, which is the safe side. The export result endpoint returns the checksum next to each signed link.

I tested with the 14 million row export on staging. It finished as five parts, and I downloaded all five and compared the checksums with sha256sum on the command line. All five matched. I then flipped one byte in a copy of part three and the comparison failed as expected.

The manifest file that lists the parts got a new field for the checksum. Old manifests without it still parse, and I added a test for that. I wrote a short paragraph for the public docs describing the command to verify a part; Sam will edit the wording.

Open points: the checksum covers the compressed file, not the rows, so a customer who recompresses cannot compare. That is acceptable for now. Next I want to add the total row count per part to the manifest, because Mara asked for it in the review.

summary: Added the row count per part to the audit export manifest and found that the count was off by one for parts that end on a page boundary
body:
Following the review comment from Mara, I added the row count to each entry in the audit export manifest, so a customer can check that the sum of the parts equals the total reported by the console. The first implementation counted rows as they were written to the part file.

On the 14 million row test export the sum of the parts was 14,000,004 against a total of 14,000,000 from a count query. Four parts too many. I looked at where the extra rows came from. Each part boundary is cut when the file reaches 500 MB, and the cursor reads the audit table in pages of 10,000 rows. When a page ended exactly on the boundary, the next part started by re-reading the last row of the page, because the cursor was restarted from the last id inclusive instead of exclusive.

This would have meant a duplicate row at the start of four parts, and it would have been in production data for the internal account that is already running on the export. I checked the internal account export from the day before and it did have one duplicate, in the second part.

The fix changes the cursor condition to a strict greater-than on the id. I added a test with a page size that divides the part size evenly, which is the case that exposed it. After the fix the sum of the five parts is exactly 14,000,000, and the manifest matches the count query.

I re-ran the internal account export and sent the new files to Mara to compare against the old ones. The only difference was the single duplicate row. I wrote down in the branch notes that the earlier export had a duplicate. Nothing outside the company received it, since only the internal account has the export enabled. The change is ready for review.

summary: Reviewed the first full day of the cache key change in Redis and ClickHouse and found the hit rate stable at 68 percent with one customer far below
body:
The normalized cache key has been in production for a day now, and I used the evening to look at the numbers in detail instead of only the dashboard average. The overall hit rate for dashboard queries is 68 percent, which is the value we saw on the staging replay, so the change behaves as predicted.

The average hides a spread. I broke the hit rate down by customer using the key prefix. Most customers sit between 64 and 75 percent. One mid-size customer is at 31 percent. That customer has many saved queries with a relative time filter, like the last 24 hours, and the filter is part of the key as a literal timestamp. Two requests a minute apart therefore never share a key.

I checked the query code. The time filter is rounded to the minute in the search API but not in the dashboard path. Rounding to the minute would still give poor reuse for a 300 second TTL, since a new key appears each minute. Rounding to five minutes matches the TTL and costs at most five minutes of staleness at the edge, which is within what the console already shows, since results can be up to 300 seconds old.

I prototyped the rounding on staging and replayed the traffic of that customer. The hit rate went from 31 to 59 percent. ClickHouse CPU for that customer's queries dropped by about a third in the replay.

I did not deploy this. Rounding changes what the user sees at the edge of the window, and Lena should know before it changes the console behavior. I wrote her a short note with the example and the replay numbers. I also noted the memory effect: fewer distinct keys means a smaller cache group in Redis, which was at 31 percent of memory last time I looked. Tomorrow I will check the key count after a day of the rounding on staging.

summary: Moved the audit log compaction and export cleanup jobs to ECS scheduled tasks and ran both on staging against the Postgres replica
body:
After fixing the password handling this morning, I moved the two remaining jobs that touch the audit log to scheduled ECS tasks. The compaction job merges old audit rows into daily summaries, and the export cleanup deletes expired export parts from S3 and the part records from Postgres.
