The compaction job used a local socket to Postgres on the utility host. In ECS it connects over the network with the URL from Secrets Manager. I set a statement timeout of 60 seconds so that a slow query cannot hold a connection for long, since the task has no human watching it.

On staging I ran the compaction once against a copy of last week's audit data. It produced 412 daily summaries and the counts matched the old job's output from the same data, which I compared with a checksum query. The cleanup run deleted 38 expired parts and left the unexpired ones. I verified in S3 that the object count went down by exactly 38.

One difference: the old job wrote its log to a file on the host, which nobody read. The tasks now log to CloudWatch with the same log group naming as the other scheduled tasks, so Tobias can find them in one place. I added an alert on a non-zero exit code of either task through the same rule that already covers the first five.

The old crontab entries are disabled but still present. Four jobs remain on the utility host, all in the third wave, and they depend on the move of the OpenSearch snapshot role. That is next, together with Tobias.

summary: Explained the plan for the OpenSearch snapshot role in the new AWS account with Tobias and moved the snapshot cron job with a test restore into a scratch index
body:
The last four cron jobs on the utility host all relate to the search cluster, and the one that matters most is the snapshot job. It writes snapshots of the indices to an S3 bucket, and the cluster needs an IAM role that is allowed to write to that bucket. In the new account the role and the bucket have different names, so the cluster has to register a new snapshot repository.

Tobias created the bucket and the role in Terraform. I registered the repository on the cluster with the new bucket name and ran a manual snapshot of one small customer index. It finished in 40 seconds. Then I did the part that is easy to skip: a restore. I restored that snapshot into a scratch index with a different name and compared the document count with the source index. Both had 1,208,331 documents. I then ran a few of the query test set queries against the scratch index and the results matched.

With that confirmed, I moved the snapshot job itself to a scheduled ECS task. The old job used the aws cli on the host with the instance profile. The task now uses a task role, which Tobias scoped to the two buckets, old and new, during the move, so both repositories can be read. Retention is the same as before, 14 daily snapshots, and I wrote it into the task as an explicit parameter instead of a default in a script.

There is one thing to watch. The first full snapshot to a new repository has to copy everything, since snapshots are incremental only within a repository. On this cluster that is several hundred gigabytes. I scheduled the first full run for the night so that it does not compete with the reindex job. If it is not finished by the time the backup window starts, we will look at it in the morning.

The remaining three jobs are the index statistics report, the alias check and the old index report. They only read from the cluster and are quick to move. I will do them next and then update the plan document with the status of the waves.

summary: Checked the first full snapshot to the new repository, then moved the last three search cron jobs and closed the cron part of the migration plan
body:
The first full snapshot to the new repository finished overnight in 2 hours 40 minutes, before the backup window opened. The size in S3 is 612 GB, about what the old repository holds. I listed the snapshots through the API and the state is SUCCESS with zero failed shards.

As a second check I restored one mid-size customer index from the new repository into a scratch index and compared document counts and a sample of 200 documents by id. All matched. I deleted the scratch index afterwards so it does not leave a shard behind on the cluster.

Then I moved the three remaining jobs: the index statistics report, the alias check and the old index report. They only read from the cluster, so the work was mostly the task definitions and the credentials. The alias check gave a different result in the first run on staging, because it compared aliases against a list in a file on the utility host that was out of date. I moved that list into the repository next to the task and regenerated it from the cluster. Now the job checks against a file that is under review like everything else.

For each of the 14 cron jobs I now have a scheduled task, a run on staging and an alert on failure. I ran the full list once in order on staging and wrote the result in the plan: all 14 exit zero. The old crontab on the utility host has every entry disabled.

Tobias will let the old entries stay disabled for a week before removing the host from the plan. If a task fails in that week, we can switch an entry back quickly. I also listed what is not covered by cron: the two systemd timers on the utility host for log rotation. They are not ours in a strict sense, but they go away with the host, so they need a replacement. Logs now go to CloudWatch, so rotation is not needed in the new setup, and I noted that.

The cron part of the migration plan is closed. Next is the move of the secrets that are not yet in Secrets Manager, starting with a list of where each one is read.

summary: Listed every secret still outside Secrets Manager and found five, two of them read by the loader in places the plan had not covered
body:
I went through the repositories and the Terraform state to find secrets that are still stored somewhere else: environment files, SSM parameters with plain strings, or values pasted into task definitions. I found five. The ClickHouse password for the loader and the dashboards, the OpenSearch service user password, the PagerDuty integration key, the SMTP credentials for the console, and the signing key for the audit export links.

Two of these, the ClickHouse password and the signing key, are read by the loader code in a second place that the plan did not list: a small admin script used for backfills. It reads the values from the environment of whoever runs it. I changed the script to fetch them from Secrets Manager by name, so it works from a task or from a laptop with the right role.

The signing key needs care. If the key changes, signed links already sent to customers stop working. I decided to copy the same value to the new secret and not rotate it during the move; a rotation can be a separate step with a notice. I wrote this down in the plan so nobody rotates it by accident.

I created the five secrets in the new account with the same names as the old ones plus a prefix, and left the values to be filled by Tobias, since I should not hold them. The list and the readers of each are in the plan.

summary: Rounded the relative time filter to five minutes in the dashboard cache key on staging and measured the key count in Redis after a day
body:
Lena had no objection to the rounding after reading my note, as long as the console shows the time of the result, which it does not do today. She will add a small label later. I put the rounding into the dashboard query path for relative filters such as the last 24 hours and the last 7 days, using five minute steps.

I ran the change on staging for a day with the replayed production traffic. The overall dashboard hit rate in the replay moved from 68 to 73 percent. For the customer that was at 31 percent it is now 58 percent, close to the prototype. Customers with only absolute time ranges are not affected, as expected.

The effect on Redis memory is the part I wanted to see. The count of keys in the cache group dropped by 22 percent compared with the day before on staging, and the memory of the group by about the same amount. The sizes of single values did not change. I checked the keys by pattern to make sure the rounding did not merge queries that should differ, and I compared the results for 300 random queries with and without the rounding: all the same except for rows in the final five minute window, which is the expected difference.

One case needed a fix. A query with the filter now minus 1 hour and a sort by time showed a row that was 4 minutes newer than the end of the rounded window. It is not wrong, but it made the result differ between a cache hit and a miss. I made the upper bound of the window open, as it is in the search API, so both agree.

I wrote the change up for Mara. The rollout will be like the key change: early in the morning, with ClickHouse CPU on the screen for the first hour.

summary: Answered Sam on why export links expire after 24 hours and how a customer can ask for a new one without running the export again
body:
Sam got a question from a customer whose compliance person opened an export link two days after it was created and got an access denied error. The signed links of the audit export are valid for 24 hours, which was chosen to limit how long a leaked link is useful. The files themselves stay in S3 for seven days before the cleanup job removes them.

The result endpoint can create new signed links for an existing export without running it again, as long as the files are still there. In the console this is the button called refresh links, which Lena built. Sam did not know about it, and it is not in the docs. I checked that it works for an export that is five days old on staging, and it returned new links with a fresh 24 hour validity and the same checksums.

After seven days the cleanup removes the files and the customer has to start a new export. I gave Sam a short text for the docs that says this, with the three time limits. She will add it to the audit export page.

summary: Put the three batch writes into one transaction in the ingest worker and deployed it at low traffic, which cut the audit insert p95 from 21 to 10 ms
body:
Mara reviewed the diff from last week's profiling and had one request: a metric for the number of times the timestamp update fails, so a silent failure does not pile up. I added a counter with the name of the worker and the reason, and a Grafana panel next to the insert latency.

The deploy went out at low traffic in two steps. First one worker out of the six, with the change, for 30 minutes, while I compared it with the others. Its audit insert p95 was 10 ms against 21 ms on the rest. Postgres commits per second from the worker group fell visibly, since each batch now has one commit instead of three.

Then I rolled the other five. The WAL flush wait on the Postgres host dropped by about a third in the following hour, which also helped the console queries that share the disk. The failure counter for the timestamp stayed at zero.

I watched two things that could go wrong. One is a longer transaction holding row locks on the account counters row. I checked pg_stat_activity during a busy period and the longest transaction was 38 ms, with no lock waits. The other is the end to end delay between an event arriving and the audit row being visible, which I measured by comparing the event timestamp with the insert time. It did not change.

The account counters remain a point of contention for the largest customer, since every batch updates the same row. That is not a problem at today's volume, but with the batching branch the batches get larger and fewer, which helps. I added a note to the ingest batching list to look at counters again after the next volume increase.

Nothing left to do for this change except to remove the single worker flag I used for the test, which I did.

summary: Tested the audit export part checksum and row count manifest in the review with Mara and fixed one finding about the manifest version field
body:
Mara reviewed the branch with the part checksums, the row counts and the cursor fix. She ran the 14 million row export on staging herself and verified the manifest by script: the sum of the row counts was 14,000,000 and all five checksums matched the files she downloaded.

Her one finding was that the manifest has no version field. Old manifests have no checksum and no row count, new ones have both, and a reader has to guess which it is by looking for the keys. That works today but would become a problem the next time a field is added. I added a version number to the manifest, set to 2 for the new format, and treated a missing version as 1 in the reader. A test covers both.

She also asked about the exports that were already made for the internal account with the cursor bug. I explained that I had re-run the one from the day before and that only the internal account had used the feature. She was fine with that.

I pushed the fix and she approved. The merge is planned for the morning, together with a deploy to the internal account first. Customers get the feature only after Sam has updated the docs about the verification command, which she is doing this week.

summary: Deployed the five minute rounding of relative time filters to production early in the morning and watched ClickHouse CPU and the hit rate for the first hour
body:
The rounding of relative time filters in the dashboard cache key went to production at the quiet time before the first customers wake up. As with the earlier key change, a short miss spike was expected, because the new keys start empty.

First ten minutes: the hit rate for dashboard queries dropped to 40 percent, as predicted, and ClickHouse CPU rose from 30 to 52 percent. By minute 25 the hit rate was back at 65 percent and CPU at 38 percent. After an hour the hit rate was 72 percent, close to the 73 percent from the staging replay.

The customer that was at 31 percent is now at 57 percent. Their dashboards had been the slowest in the console, and Lena checked one of them: the load time of the main dashboard went from about 4.1 seconds to 1.8 seconds on a warm cache.

I watched Redis during the hour as well. The number of keys in the cache group fell by 20 percent compared with the previous day, and the memory of the group fell by a similar share. No increase in connection count or command latency. The slowlog was empty.

I checked the error rate of the dashboard endpoints and it stayed flat, at 0.1 percent, which is the usual level. I also ran my 300 query comparison against production for a few customers who agreed in advance, and only the edge rows differed.

One remaining item is the label for the age of results in the console, which Lena will build. I will also write a short summary in the docs for Sam, so that support can explain what a five minute window means when a customer sees a count that differs from an export. The work on the cache key is finished for now.

summary: Merged the audit export branch with the manifest version and deployed it to the internal account, then ran a full export and verified every part by script
body:
After Mara's approval I merged the audit export branch with the part checksums, row counts, manifest version and the cursor fix. The deploy went to production for the internal account only, where the feature is already enabled.

To be sure about the production setup I ran a full export of the internal account's audit log. It was 2.1 million rows and finished as one part, which is the normal case for small accounts. I then made an export with a part size set to 50 MB through an internal parameter, so I got 11 parts from the same data. That tested the multi part path in production without needing a large account.

I wrote a short script that downloads all parts through the signed links and checks each against the checksum in the manifest, then sums the row counts. For both exports all the checksums matched and the sums were equal to a count query. The manifest version was 2.

I also checked the signed link host, since that was a problem on staging last week. The links use the public host name, and the downloads worked from my laptop outside the VPN.

The duplicate row problem from before is gone: the 11 part export has no repeated ids, which I checked with a sort and uniq on the ids from the files.

What remains before customers get it: the docs from Sam about verifying a part, and a decision about which customers get it first. The user wants two customers who asked for it. I will prepare the flag change for those two, and watch the first export of each.

summary: Looked at why the idle Redis connections of the search API stayed high after the pool settings change and found a second client created per request in one route.
body:
Earlier I reduced the pool settings of the search API after seeing 120 idle connections. After the deploy the number went down to 70, not to the 20 I expected. Something else was holding connections.

I listed the clients on the Redis server with CLIENT LIST and grouped them by the name that the search API sets on its connections. Fifty of them had a name that did not match the main pool. They belonged to a route for saved query previews, where a helper created a new Redis client for each call and closed it only on success. On errors the client was left open until the idle timeout of 300 seconds.

This is a small leak that shows up when a preview query fails, for instance with a bad filter. Customers who try queries in the console produce many such errors. I changed the helper to use the shared client from the pool and wrote a test that sends 100 failing preview requests and checks that the connection count on a test Redis does not grow.

On staging, after the change, the idle connections sit at 21 with the same traffic replay. The total connections are also steadier over the day.

I did not touch the size limit of the pool in this change, because the leak was the cause and not the limit. The fix is a small change in one route, and I put it up for review by Mara. After the deploy I will compare the connection count at the busy hour with the old numbers.

summary: Reviewed the five new secrets with Tobias and confirmed which service reads each one, then marked the secrets step of the migration as ready to fill
body:
Tobias and I went through the list of the five secrets that I had created empty in the new account. For each one we checked three things: the name, which task roles can read it, and which service reads it.

The SMTP credentials were read by the console only, so only the console task role gets access. The PagerDuty key is needed by the alert forwarder and nothing else. The ClickHouse password has the most readers: the loader, the dashboards service and the backfill script. We gave each of those roles read access and nothing broader.

Tobias found one problem: the signing key secret had the wrong resource policy in my Terraform and would have let the whole account read it. We fixed it to name the audit export role only.

He will fill in the values from the old account. The plan now has the step marked ready, with the order: fill, test a boot of each service on staging with the new secrets, then switch production in the wave order.

summary: Tested boot of each service on staging with the secrets read from the new account and found the console failed on a missing SMTP port setting
body:
With the values filled in by Tobias, I tested each service on staging reading its secrets from the new account instead of the old one. The order followed the waves: the ingest workers, the loader, the dashboards service, the search API, then the console.

The ingest workers booted and passed the health check, and a batch of test events went through to the queue and the store. The loader started and processed a small NDJSON file. For this I used a 40 MB sample and it finished without a retry. The dashboards service connected to ClickHouse with the new password and answered a dashboard query. The search API connected to OpenSearch with the service user and to Redis with the password that had moved earlier.

The console failed to send mail. The log showed a connection refused on port 25. The old setup had the SMTP host and port both in an environment file, and I had copied only the user and password into the new secret. The port was missing, so the client fell back to the default. I added the host and port as fields in the secret JSON and changed the console config to read them, with a clear error at startup if either is missing, instead of silently using a default.

After that the console sent a password reset mail on staging, and I checked that it arrived with the right links.

The PagerDuty key I tested by sending a test alert through the forwarder, and it appeared on the test service in PagerDuty with the right label. The audit export signing key was tested by creating a signed link on staging and opening it. It worked and the signature matched one created with the old secret, which is what I wanted, since the value is the same.

All five secrets work. I updated the plan with the result and the missing port. Production follows the waves, starting with the ingest workers when Tobias is ready.

summary: Prepared the saved query preview fix for the Redis client leak with Mara and tested it on staging, with the idle connections of the search API still at 70 on production.
body:
Mara reviewed the change that makes the saved query preview route use the shared Redis client. She asked for one thing: the failing request test should also cover a timeout, not only a bad filter, since a timeout leaves the client in a different state. I added the case with a slow query that hits the timeout, and the test still shows no growth in the connections.

She approved the change, but I did not deploy it. The traffic was high in the afternoon and I did not want to touch the search API during the busy hours. I wrote down the plan for the rollout: deploy in a quiet period, then watch the connections to Redis from the search API for two hours. For the comparison I saved the current numbers. The count of idle connections from the API is 70 over the busy hours. On staging with the change the number settled at 22, and I expect something close to that on production, with the total of all services lower by about 50.

I checked CLIENT LIST again for connection names. On production the group of unnamed clients from the preview route is still there, and on staging it is gone. The command latency of the Redis server is normal and the slowlog is empty, so there is nothing else to chase right now.

One side effect to think about: after the change, preview requests will share the pool with the normal queries. A burst of previews could use up the pool and slow the main search. At the current volume the pool should have enough room, since the busy hour peak is well under the maximum. I started a gauge for pool usage in the search API so we can see it if it changes, and it is not deployed yet.

Next step is the deploy in the quiet period, then a look at the pool gauge to see the real peak.

summary: Migration of cron jobs to the new AWS account: moved the audit cleanup, prepared the nightly reindex, and found two jobs still pointing at old secret paths
body:
Continued the move of scheduled jobs into the new AWS accounts. Tobias had already created the account and the ECS cluster, so this session was about the cron definitions in Terraform. Wrote the definitions for the nightly reindex trigger and the audit log cleanup job first, and kept the reindex schedule exactly as it was in the old account.

The audit cleanup ran fine in a manual run. The reindex task read its OpenSearch password from the old secret path and failed with AccessDenied on the first try in a dry run against staging. Fixed the path in the task definition and ran it again; it finished without errors and the duration looked about the same as before. I left the schedule itself untouched for now.

While going through the list I found two more jobs that still referenced secrets in the old account: the weekly CSV export for one large customer and the session cleanup for the admin console. Neither is critical, but the export would have failed silently on the next run. Changed both and added a short check script, scripts/check-secret-paths.sh, that greps the task definitions for the old account id.

The script found nothing else. I also compared the list of enabled schedules in the old account with the new one. Eleven jobs in the old account, nine in the new one. The two missing ones are the old test-data refresh and a metrics snapshot nobody uses; I left them out on purpose and noted that in the migration checklist.

Open: the Redis snapshot job still runs in the old account and needs Tobias for the bucket policy. Tomorrow I plan to enable the reindex trigger in the new account, move the remaining jobs and compare logs from one full night in both accounts before turning the old schedules off.

summary: Secrets inventory for the account migration: 37 secrets listed, 6 still missing in the new account, copy script written but not run yet
body:
Late session on the secrets for the new AWS accounts. Listed every secret the ECS tasks and cron jobs read, using the task definitions in Terraform as the source and not the console, since the console had a few leftovers.

Result: 37 secrets in use. 31 exist already in the new account's Secrets Manager. Six are missing: the Redpanda SASL password for the admin tools, the PagerDuty integration key, two customer webhook signing keys, the Grafana API token and the OpenSearch snapshot role credentials.

Wrote a small script, scripts/copy-secrets.sh, that reads a secret from the old account and writes it to the new one with the same name prefix changed. It has a dry-run mode that prints names and value lengths only, never values. The dry run listed all six correctly.

I did not run it for real. The webhook signing keys are used by customers to verify our calls, so they must not change by accident. I will ask Tobias to check the KMS key policy first, because the new account uses a different key and a copy may fail on decrypt.

Also noted that the PagerDuty key should probably be rotated after the move rather than copied. That is a decision for tomorrow.

summary: Copied the six missing secrets to the new account after Tobias fixed the KMS policy; webhook signing keys verified byte for byte by hash
body:
Tobias fixed the KMS key policy overnight, so the copy of the six missing secrets could run. I ran scripts/copy-secrets.sh without the dry-run flag.

Five copied cleanly. The OpenSearch snapshot role credentials failed once with a decrypt error, because the role was attached to the wrong key alias. After Tobias changed it, the second run worked.

For the two webhook signing keys I compared SHA-256 hashes of the values in both accounts and they matched. The PagerDuty key was copied as is, and I put a rotation task on the list for after the migration.

Next is to start the ingest workers' staging copy in the new account with these secrets and watch the logs for access errors.

summary: Postgres slow query on the audit log list: missing composite index on tenant and created_at, query went from 2.8 s to 40 ms
body:
Mara reported that the audit log page in the admin console was slow for the two largest customers. I looked at pg_stat_statements and found the list query as the top entry by total time, with a mean of 2.8 seconds.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on audit_log filtered by tenant_id with a sort on created_at. The table has about 61 million rows. There was an index on tenant_id alone, but the planner preferred the scan because of the sort.

Created a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. The build took 14 minutes and did not block writes. After it, the same query ran in about 40 ms.

I also checked that the old single-column index is now redundant. I did not drop it yet, since the retention job uses it for a delete by tenant. Added the migration file under db/migrations and a note to look at the retention query next.

The console page now loads in under a second for both customers. Lena confirmed on her side.

One thing to watch: the new index adds about 3 GB. Disk is fine for now.

summary: Started the ingest-batching branch: the worker now groups events into batched Postgres and queue writes, first benchmark shows 2.3x higher throughput
body:
Started work on the ingest-batching branch. Until now the ingest worker wrote each event of an incoming batch separately to its sink, which costs a round trip per event and shows up in the CPU profile.

The first step was a small batcher in internal/sink/batcher.go. It collects events until either 500 events or 50 ms have passed, then flushes them as one write. It runs one goroutine per sink and takes events over a channel.

Flush on shutdown was the first thing I got wrong. The worker exited on SIGTERM and dropped whatever was in the channel. I added a drain step that closes the channel, waits for the goroutine and flushes the rest. A unit test now sends 1,200 events, cancels the context and checks that all 1,200 arrive.

Backpressure came next. When the sink is slow, the channel fills and the HTTP handler blocks. I kept the channel size at 2,000, which gives a visible delay to clients instead of an unbounded queue in memory. Timeouts of the handler stay as they are.

The benchmark ran on the staging setup with a recorded stream of 5 million events. Before: about 38,000 events per second per worker. After: about 87,000, which is 2.3 times more. CPU per event dropped by around 45 percent.

Latency of a single event got worse in the quiet case, up to 50 ms extra. For the real traffic this is acceptable, but I want to make the wait time configurable per customer tier later.

Open points: partial failure of a batch. If one event in a flush is rejected, the whole flush currently reports an error. I need to decide whether to split and retry or to report per event. Tomorrow I will write the per-event result handling and talk to Mara about the error codes the API returns to clients.

summary: Per-event results in the batched flush: failed events are now split out and reported, the rest of the batch goes through
body:
Continued on ingest-batching. The open problem from the earlier session was a batch flush where one event is rejected by the sink, for example for a schema violation that slipped past validation.

Mara and I agreed on the behaviour: the API keeps its 207-style response with a list of per-event results, and accepted events must not be lost because of a bad neighbour. So the batcher now tries the full flush first. If it fails with a data error, it bisects: halves the batch and flushes each half, until the bad events are alone. Those are returned as rejected, the others are written.

The bisection costs extra writes only in the failure case. In a test with 1 bad event in 500 it needed 10 flushes, which is fine. For a transient error, like a connection reset, it does not bisect but returns the whole batch to the normal retry path with backoff.

Distinguishing the two needed a small error classification in internal/sink/errors.go. Postgres error classes 22 and 23 count as data errors; everything else is transient. I wrote table tests for it with the codes I could think of.

A mistake on the way: my first version of the bisection reused the slice and modified the original, so the results mapped to the wrong events. A test with three bad events at different positions caught it. I now copy the index map before splitting.

Re-ran the benchmark with 0.1 percent bad events. Throughput was 81,000 events per second, so the failure path costs about 7 percent. Without bad events nothing changed.

Next: make flush size and wait time configurable and add Prometheus metrics for batch size and flush duration, so that Tobias can see them in Grafana.

summary: Added batch size and flush duration metrics to the ingest worker, plus a Grafana panel for the new batching behaviour
body:
Added Prometheus metrics to the batcher: a histogram for the number of events per flush, a histogram for flush duration, and a counter for flushes by outcome (ok, split, transient_error). Labels are the sink name only, to keep cardinality low.

The histogram buckets for batch size are 1, 10, 50, 100, 250, 500. Flush duration buckets run from 1 ms to 2 s. I first used the default buckets and the quantiles were useless for the fast flushes.

Then I built a Grafana panel group in the ingest dashboard: p50 and p95 of batch size, p95 flush time and the rate of split flushes. Dashboards are in code in the repo, so the JSON went into the dashboards folder.

On staging the median batch size under the replay was 500, which means the size limit triggers and not the timer. That is what we want at load. In the quiet phase the median fell to about 12.

Nothing else changed in behaviour. Next is the config for flush size and wait time.

summary: Flush size and wait time of the ingest batcher are configurable by env var and tier; defaults kept at 500 events and 50 ms
body:
Made the batcher settings configurable. Two new settings, INGEST_BATCH_MAX_EVENTS and INGEST_BATCH_MAX_WAIT, are read at startup in the worker config. Defaults stay at 500 and 50 ms.

There is also a per-tier override. The idea from last session was that small customers who send a few events at a time should not wait 50 ms for a flush. The tier comes from the account settings that the worker already caches. For the lowest tier I set the wait to 10 ms.

The override needed one batcher per sink and tier, not just per sink. That meant a small map of batchers created lazily, guarded by a mutex. I kept it simple and did not use sync.Map, since the map is read far more often than written and the lock is held for a few nanoseconds.

Validation of the config: negative values and a wait above 1 second are rejected at startup with a clear message. A test covers both.

I ran the staging replay with three tiers mixed. Throughput stayed at about 85,000 events per second per worker. The p95 added latency for the small tier fell from 52 ms to 11 ms.

There is a side effect: more batchers means more small flushes for the quiet tier, so the flush count went up by 18 percent. The sink handled it.

Still to do: load test with a real size distribution of customers, and a review by Mara before merging.

summary: Mara reviewed ingest-batching and found a shutdown race in the tier batcher map; fixed and covered with a test under the race detector
body:
Mara's review of the ingest-batching branch came back with five comments. Four were small: naming, a missing comment on the bisect function, a log line at the wrong level and a constant that should be in the config package.

The fifth was real. During shutdown, the drain step iterates over the map of tier batchers while a late request can still create a new batcher. That is a race, and the new batcher may never be flushed. Mara found it by reading, not by a failing test.

I wrote a test that starts the shutdown and sends requests from 20 goroutines at the same time, and ran it with go test -race -count=50. It failed 3 times out of 50, with a data race report on the map.

The fix is a closed flag guarded by the same mutex as the map. After shutdown starts, getBatcher returns an error, and the handler answers 503 with a Retry-After header. The drain step takes the lock, sets the flag, copies the batchers out and then flushes them without the lock held.

With the fix the test passed 200 runs in a row.

I also applied the four small comments. One of them, the log level, was a good catch: the split flush logged at error and would have paged us for harmless events. It is now a warning with a counter.

The branch is ready for a second look. I will run a longer soak test in staging overnight, 8 hours of replayed traffic, and check memory and goroutine counts in the morning.

summary: Overnight soak test of ingest-batching came out clean: flat memory, goroutines stable at 140, no lost events in the count comparison
body:
Looked at the results of the 8 hour soak test of the ingest-batching branch on staging. The replay sent about 2.4 billion events in total.

Memory of the worker stayed flat at around 410 MB. The goroutine count settled at 140 after the first minutes and did not grow. No restarts happened.

To check for lost events I compared the number sent by the replay tool with the number in the queue topic and the sink. Both matched exactly, apart from 2,300 events the replay had marked as intentionally invalid, which were rejected as expected.

The p95 flush time was 14 ms, and the split rate stayed below 0.2 percent. A short spike of flush time at one point matched a vacuum on the staging database.

I told Mara the results and asked for the approval. Plan is to merge today and roll out to one worker group in production tomorrow.

summary: Redis memory use grew 30 percent in two weeks; the cause is a new cache key per search filter combination, not a leak
body:
Tobias noticed that Redis memory use on the main cluster went from about 5.1 GB to 6.6 GB in two weeks and asked me to look before it hits the alarm level.

I sampled keys with SCAN and grouped them by prefix. The prefix search:result: made up 71 percent of the memory. Two weeks ago it was 52 percent.

The cause was the change to the search API that added the filter set to the cache key. Before, the key had query and tenant only. Now each different combination of filters produces a new key, and customers with the dashboard filter panel create many of them. No leak: the number of keys grows and then flattens as the TTL of one hour expires old ones.

I checked the hit rate for these keys from the metrics. It is only 9 percent for the filtered ones, against 46 percent for the plain ones. So most of the new memory buys almost nothing.

Proposal: cache filtered queries with a TTL of 5 minutes instead of 60 and keep the long TTL for plain queries. I wrote that down in the ticket and did not change it yet, because Lena wants to check whether the console re-sends the same filters often.

Also renamed nothing for now; the key naming is fine, only the TTL differs.

summary: Merged ingest-batching and rolled it out to the first production worker group; throughput up, CPU down, one config mistake caught in the canary
body:
Merged the ingest-batching branch after Mara's approval and started the rollout. The plan was one worker group first, as a canary, then the rest if the numbers hold.

The deploy goes through the normal pipeline. I set the canary group to 25 percent of the ingest tasks, using the weights on the load balancer target groups.

The first ten minutes looked wrong. The p95 request latency of the canary was 70 ms higher than the rest. I looked at the task environment and found the cause: the per-tier override was not set, because the new variable names had a typo in the Terraform file, INGEST_BATCH_MAX_WAIT_MS instead of INGEST_BATCH_MAX_WAIT. The worker fell back to the default of 50 ms for all tiers, and the small tier felt it.

I fixed the name in Terraform, applied it, and the canary tasks restarted. Latency then matched the rest within 5 ms.

After an hour I compared the two groups. CPU of the canary tasks was 38 percent lower for the same traffic. Events per second per task were about 2 times higher at the peak of the hour. The error rate was the same, 0.02 percent.

The split flush counter showed 11 splits in the hour. I looked at them in the logs. All were customer events with a timestamp in the far future that the sink rejects, so the bisection did its job and only those events were reported.

I also checked the queue lag in Redpanda for the topic. It stayed under 200 ms, no change.

I raised the canary to 50 percent and left it for the afternoon. Memory per task was 420 MB, as in staging.

Things left: raise to 100 percent tomorrow if the night is calm, then remove the old per-event code path. I will keep the old path behind a flag for one week in case something odd appears with large customers.

I wrote the rollout state in the team channel so that Tobias knows the target group weights are not at the usual values.

summary: Lena asked whether the console resends identical filters; answer from the access logs is yes, in 62 percent of filtered searches within 5 minutes
body:
Lena asked a question about the filtered search cache: does the admin console send the same filter set repeatedly within a short time? This decides whether a 5 minute TTL for filtered queries still gives hits.

I looked at the search API access logs of one busy day and hashed query, tenant and filters. Of all filtered searches, 62 percent were a repeat of an identical request within 5 minutes. Within 60 minutes it was only 68 percent. So the long TTL adds just 6 points of repeats.

The reason is the console behaviour: the dashboard refreshes every 30 seconds and re-sends the same request, and people rarely come back to an old filter after leaving.

That supports the proposal. I changed the TTL of filtered result keys to 300 seconds in the search API config, behind the existing setting SEARCH_CACHE_TTL_FILTERED. Plain queries keep 3600.

I will check Redis memory again in two days.

summary: Ingest-batching at 100 percent in production after a calm night; old per-event path stays behind a flag for a week
body:
The night with the canary at 50 percent was calm: no alerts, error rate unchanged at 0.02 percent, queue lag under 200 ms. So I raised the weights to 100 percent in the evening.

The load balancer shifted traffic in steps of 25 percent every ten minutes. I watched CPU, latency and the split counter between steps. Nothing moved apart from the expected drop of CPU.

After the full rollout the average CPU of the ingest tasks went from 61 to 37 percent at the evening peak. That gives room to reduce the number of tasks. I did not do that yet; Tobias wants to see a few days of data first, and the cost work is on his list anyway.

The flag for the old path, INGEST_LEGACY_WRITE, is off in all groups. I left the code in place for a week.

Next: cleanup of the old path after the week.

summary: Dropped the redundant tenant_id-only index on audit_log after checking the retention delete uses the new composite index
body:
Followed up on the audit log index from a few days ago. The question was whether the old single-column index on tenant_id could go, since the retention job deletes by tenant and I had not checked its plan.

Ran EXPLAIN on the retention delete with a typical tenant and date filter. The planner now uses the composite index on (tenant_id, created_at) with an index range scan, so the old index is not needed.

I also looked at pg_stat_user_indexes. The old index had zero scans since the composite one went in. Dropped it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a migration, and freed about 1.4 GB.

The retention job ran in the evening and finished in 6 minutes, about as before. No other query changed.

summary: Planned the new shard layout for the search index: shards by month instead of by customer, with a sizing estimate and open questions
body:
Spent the morning on a written plan for the new shard layout of the search index. Today the index has one shard group per customer. The large customers have shards of over 80 GB, while some small customers have shards of a few hundred MB, and the shard count on the cluster is higher than it should be.

The proposal is to shard by month: one index per month with a fixed number of primary shards, and a customer filter in the query. Old months become read only and can be merged and moved to cheaper nodes.

Sizing: the current data is about 1.9 TB across 410 shards. With monthly indices of 12 primary shards each, targeting 30 to 40 GB per shard, the total would be roughly 60 shards for the live months, plus the history. That is much easier for the cluster state.

Benefits I listed: fewer shards, simple retention (drop a month), and better balance. Costs: queries for one customer must now hit shards of several months, and a customer filter on every query. Routing by customer can reduce the fan-out, so I want to test routing by tenant id inside each month.

Risks: the nightly reindex job assumes one index per customer and must be rewritten. The search API builds index names in one function, src/search/indexName.ts, which helps. Per-customer deletion for data protection requests becomes a delete by query, which is slower.

Questions for the team: how many months of history must stay searchable at full speed? Sam says support rarely looks past 6 months. Tobias should say what the node layout can take.

I also thought about how to migrate. The safest way is to dual write for some days, backfill month by month, then switch reads per customer with a flag. Rollback is flipping the flag back.

I wrote all this in docs/plans/search-shards.md and asked Tobias and Mara to comment. No code yet.

summary: Cost review of the ECS fleet found the ingest and search services oversized; right-sizing task CPU and memory should save about 18 percent of compute with no latency change.
body:
Spent the session on the AWS cost work, starting with a pull of the last 30 days of usage per service from Cost Explorer and the ECS container metrics from Prometheus. The goal was to find the services that pay for capacity they never use.

The ingest workers were the largest line. They run at 2 vCPU and 4 GB per task, but p95 CPU over the month was 31 percent and p95 memory was 1.6 GB. The search API tasks looked similar, with 28 percent CPU and 1.1 GB of 2 GB. The admin console backend is already small and was left alone.

I wrote a small script, tools/cost/rightsize.ts, that reads the Prometheus peaks and proposes a task size with 40 percent headroom over the p99 values. For ingest it proposed 1 vCPU and 2.5 GB, for search 1 vCPU and 1.5 GB. The script prints the monthly saving per service, and the total came to about 18 percent of the compute bill.

Before changing anything I checked the worst moments, not only the averages. The nightly reindex pushes the search tasks to 64 percent CPU for about 40 minutes, which still fits within the new size. The ingest peak during the large customer's batch import hit 58 percent on the smaller size in a test with replayed traffic, with no growth in queue lag.

I also looked at the NAT gateway and cross-zone traffic. About 9 percent of the bill is data transfer between zones for the Redpanda consumers, which is a separate topic. I noted it for Tobias rather than touching it now.

The Terraform change is a pull request with only the task definition values, so it is easy to revert. I did not apply it. Tobias wants to roll it out to one worker group first, since the infrastructure migration to the new accounts is still going on and he does not want two big changes mixed together.

Next steps: Tobias reviews the pull request, the ingest group at 25 percent gets the new size, and I compare lag and error rates for two days before the rest follows. After that I will look at the reserved capacity for Postgres and the idle OpenSearch nodes.

summary: Removed the legacy per-event write path from the ingest worker after a week with no use; the flag and 380 lines of code are gone
body:
A week has passed since ingest-batching went to 100 percent, and the INGEST_LEGACY_WRITE flag was never turned on. Time to remove the old code.

I checked first that no environment sets the flag: grepped Terraform, the task definitions in both accounts, and the staging overrides. None did.

Then I deleted the old write function, its tests, and the flag handling in the config. The diff removes 380 lines and adds 40, mostly test changes for the new path. A helper that only the old code used, for per-event retries with jitter, also went away. The batch retry has its own backoff.

Ran the unit tests and the staging replay once more. Throughput was the same, 86,000 events per second per task.

I updated the docs page for the worker settings and removed the flag from it. The changelog got a line.

Tobias has seen that CPU is low enough and wants to cut the number of ingest tasks from 12 to 8. I suggested 9 first, so that one task failure still leaves room at the evening peak.

summary: Production Postgres minor upgrade done through replica failover; 40 seconds of write errors during the switch, no data issue
body:
Did the production minor upgrade of Postgres 16 in the quiet window. The steps followed the runbook from yesterday.

First I upgraded the replica and let it catch up; replication lag was under one second. Then Tobias triggered the failover, and the upgraded replica became primary.

The switch took longer than I had planned. For about 40 seconds the API had write errors, because the connection pools kept old connections to the former primary. The pool settings for reconnects were too patient. Reads from the replica endpoint were fine.

After the failover I upgraded the old primary and reattached it as a replica. It caught up in 12 minutes.

I ran a count check on the audit_log and accounts tables on both nodes, and the numbers agreed. pg_stat_statements was reset by the upgrade, which is expected.

Follow up: lower the pool's max connection lifetime to 5 minutes so that failovers heal faster. I wrote that in the ticket.

summary: Started the shard plan work: a script that sizes monthly indices from the real data and shows that 4 customers dominate the shard count
body:
Mara and Tobias commented on the shard plan and the main wish was numbers from the real data and not the rough estimate. So I wrote a script, scripts/shard-sizing.ts, that reads the _cat/shards and _cat/indices output and groups document counts and store size by customer and by month of the event timestamp.

The script samples with a query per month using a date histogram aggregation, since the index itself has no month split. For the 41 customers it took about 9 minutes against the production cluster. I limited the request rate so that search latency did not change; the p95 stayed within 5 ms of normal.

Results: the total is 1.9 TB, as in the plan. Four customers hold 64 percent of the data. The biggest one alone is 27 percent, about 510 GB.

With a monthly index and 12 primary shards, a month for the large customers would be about 40 GB per shard in the busiest months. The most recent month is also the largest in all cases, because the volume grew over time. That means the 12 shard figure holds only for now, and I should leave room to raise the shard count for future months. Monthly indices make that simple, since each new month can have its own number.

The median customer has 11 GB in total, which is under one shard of the new layout per month. For these customers, routing by tenant puts all their data of a month on one shard, so a search touches one shard per month and not twelve.

For the largest customer routing is bad: it would concentrate 40 GB on one shard. For those four I plan to leave routing off, or to use routing with a small number of virtual buckets per tenant. I wrote this as an open decision.

I added a table with these numbers to docs/plans/search-shards.md. Sam gave an answer on the history: 6 months at full speed is enough, 13 months must stay searchable, and older events are covered by the rollup rule, so no search is needed for them.

Next step: a test index with one month of the largest customer, to measure query latency with and without routing.

summary: Test index for the new shard layout: one month of the largest customer loaded, p95 query latency 120 ms with bucketed routing against 310 ms without
body:
Built a test index on the staging OpenSearch cluster for the shard plan. It holds one month of events of the largest customer, about 38 GB, with 12 primary shards, as in the plan.

Loading used the existing reindex code with a new target name and a time filter. It took about 2 hours 10 minutes. I had to lower the bulk size from 5,000 to 2,000 documents, because a few documents with long text fields hit the request size limit and gave 413 errors.

Then I ran a set of 60 real queries from the search API logs for that customer, in three variants: no routing, routing by tenant id, and routing by tenant id plus a bucket number from a hash of the event id modulo 4.

Results, p95 over 5 runs of the set:
- no routing: 310 ms, all 12 shards queried
- routing by tenant only: 95 ms, but one shard held almost all the data and its size was 38 GB with the CPU of one node high
- tenant plus 4 buckets: 120 ms, 4 shards queried, data spread over 4 shards of about 9.5 GB

So bucketed routing gives most of the benefit and avoids a single hot shard. I will take this as the plan for the four large customers. Small customers can use plain tenant routing.

The bucket count should be stored per customer in the settings table in Postgres, so that it can be changed for new months without breaking old ones. I noted that the index name function and the query builder both need the bucket count.

I also tried the queries with the new parser of search-v2 for a check, and the results were the same, so the parser does not interact with the routing.

Things I did not test: the effect of concurrent queries from several customers on the shared shards. That needs a load test. I put it into the plan.

Summary posted to the team channel with the numbers. Tobias will check the node layout for the monthly indices.

summary: Postgres connection pool lifetime set to 5 minutes for the API services; a staged failover test healed in 6 seconds instead of 40
body:
Followed up on the failover issue from the Postgres upgrade. The API services keep connections for a long time, and after a failover they kept using dead ones until timeouts hit.

I set the maximum connection lifetime of the pool to 5 minutes and the idle timeout to 60 seconds in the shared database config. I also turned on a health check on borrow for the pool of the search API.

To test, Tobias triggered a controlled failover on staging while a load script wrote rows every 100 ms. With the old settings I had measured 40 seconds of errors in production. With the new ones the errors lasted 6 seconds.

The remaining 6 seconds are the DNS change of the endpoint. Lowering the TTL of the record to 5 seconds might shorten it; Tobias will look.

summary: Dropped the unused sessions_archive table after a backup and a check of every query reference
body:
Dropped sessions_archive, the unused table I had found during the vacuum check. Before doing so I grepped all repos for the name and looked in pg_stat_user_tables. The table had no reads or writes since the last statistics reset, and the only match in code was a migration that creates it.

I took a dump of the table first, about 4.2 GB compressed to 600 MB, and put it in the cold backup bucket with a note in the runbook.

The drop itself was a migration with DROP TABLE. It freed 11 GB, which also removed it from the daily backups and shortened the base backup by a few minutes.

No errors appeared in the logs after the change.

summary: Redis hit rate for filtered search keys went from 9 to 41 percent after the shorter TTL, and memory fell from 6.6 to 5.3 GB
body:
Checked the effect of the shorter TTL for filtered search queries, a few days after the change.

Memory on the main Redis cluster dropped from 6.6 GB to 5.3 GB. The prefix search:result: now takes 54 percent of the memory, down from 71.

The hit rate of the filtered keys rose from 9 to 41 percent. The reason is probably that fewer stale keys crowd the dataset and the console's 30 second refresh gets repeat hits within the 5 minutes.

Search latency for filtered queries did not change, p95 at 180 ms before and after. The plain queries are unchanged.

I will leave the setting as it is and recheck in two weeks when the usage of the new filter panel grows. No change to key names was needed.

summary: Draft of the monthly index naming and query changes for search: index names, routing bucket lookup, and the dual write plan are written down
body:
Worked on the design in code form for the shard plan, without changing production. I wrote the details of how the search API would address monthly indices.

Index naming: events-YYYY-MM style, with the month taken from the event timestamp, and an alias events-read that covers the live months. The function in src/search/indexName.ts gets a second variant that takes a time range and returns the list of monthly indices to query. For a default 30 day search it returns two names.

Routing: the query builder asks a small lookup for the customer's bucket count, cached in Redis under a key like search:buckets:<tenant> with a TTL of 10 minutes. For one bucket it sends routing=<tenant>; for more it sends a comma separated list of tenant:bucket values.

Dual write: the ingest side would write into both the old per-customer index and the new monthly one, controlled by a per-customer flag. The indexer is a separate worker, so the ingest API itself does not change. The cost is about 40 percent more indexing load during the dual phase, which Tobias thinks the cluster can take if we do the large customers one at a time.

Backfill: month by month, newest first, using the reindex code with the target changed. The earlier test had 2 hours 10 minutes for 38 GB, so the full 1.9 TB would be roughly 4 days of runtime at that speed, and we can run it in parallel.

Switching reads: a flag per customer in the settings table, with the old path as fallback. We would compare result counts for the same query on both paths during the dual period and log mismatches.

I listed the tests needed: a unit test for the index list for ranges across a year border, one for the routing string, and an integration test on staging that compares old and new results for 200 sampled queries.

I did not start the implementation. The plan is waiting for Tobias and his node layout answer, and Mara wants to review the dual write before it begins.

summary: Dual write to the old and new search indices is in a feature flag: documents go to both layouts, and a count check compares them every ten minutes
body:
Implemented the dual write from the plan of this morning. The search indexer now writes each document to the customer-based index and to the monthly index, controlled by the flag search_dual_write. The flag is off by default and can be set per tenant.

The monthly index name comes from the event timestamp, for example events-m-<bucket>, and the routing bucket comes from the lookup table written earlier today. A failure on the new index does not fail the old write; it is logged with the tenant and document id and counted in a new Prometheus counter, dual_write_new_failures.

Added a small checker script that compares document counts per tenant and month between old and new indices every ten minutes. On the test cluster with the largest customer's month loaded, the counts matched exactly after 40 000 documents.

One problem: documents with a missing timestamp had no month. I made them go to a catch-all index named events-m-undated and logged a warning. There were 12 of those in the test data, all from an old CSV import.

Unit tests cover the name building, the flag per tenant and the case of a failing new write. Not done yet: bulk requests are still split per index in a naive way, so bulk size doubles the request count. That is the next step. The flag stays off in production until the bulk path is fixed.

summary: Bulk indexing for the dual write now groups documents per target index, so request count dropped from 2x to about 1.1x of the old path
body:
Rewrote the bulk part of the dual write so that one batch is split into groups by target index and each group goes out as one bulk request. Before, every document produced two single actions in two separate requests, which doubled the load on the OpenSearch coordinators in the test.

With the grouping, a batch of 500 documents from one tenant spanning two months makes three requests: one for the old index and two for the monthly ones. Over a replay of one day of the test tenant the request count was 1.1 times the old path.

I also set a concurrency limit of 4 bulk requests in flight per indexer, because the first run without it pushed bulk queue rejections up to 30 per minute on the test cluster. With the limit there were none.

Tests were extended for mixed month batches and for partial bulk failures, where the response items are matched back to the documents by position. Mara will look at this tomorrow, as she wrote the original indexer.

summary: Sized and wrote the plan to backfill old documents into monthly indices: oldest months first, tenants by size, throttled to protect search latency
body:
Wrote the backfill plan for the monthly indices, so it is ready before the real migration starts. The dual write only covers new documents; everything older has to be copied.

The numbers from the sizing script: about 1.9 billion documents in total, 4 large customers holding around 70 percent of them. At the throughput measured on the test cluster, roughly 9 000 documents per second with the throttle on, a full copy would take close to 2.5 days. That is acceptable if it runs in the background.

The plan has these rules:
- Copy by month, oldest first, because old months get no new writes and can be verified once.
- Small tenants first, to find problems cheaply; the four large ones last.
- Use a scroll with a fixed sort on the document id, and a resumable checkpoint per tenant and month stored in Postgres.
- Pause automatically when the p95 of the search API goes above 400 ms for five minutes.
- Verify each finished month with a count and a sample hash of 1 000 documents.

Open questions: whether to refresh intervals should be set to -1 during the copy (probably yes, and reset after), and what to do with documents that were deleted during the copy. For the second one my idea is to run a final delete reconciliation pass after the dual write has been on for a week.

I also noted that the reindex job at night must not run against a month that is being copied. It needs a lock row in the same Postgres table. Did not code anything today, only the document and the table definition.

summary: Redis client in the search API reconnected in a storm after a short network blip on the test stack; added jittered backoff and the storm stopped
body:
While testing the dual write on the test stack, Tobias restarted a network component and the search API lost its Redis connections for about 8 seconds. When the network came back, all 30 pool connections reconnected at the same instant and the Redis log showed a burst of 30 connects in one millisecond, followed by a second burst when the first handshake timeouts hit.

The cause is the client option for reconnects: it used a fixed delay of 200 ms with no jitter, so all connections kept the same rhythm. I changed it to exponential backoff starting at 100 ms, capped at 3 seconds, with up to 50 percent random jitter.

Repeated the blip three times with the new settings. The reconnects spread over about 1.5 seconds and no burst was seen. Requests during the blip fell back to uncached search, as designed, and the error rate was 0 percent; latency went up to about 600 ms for the 8 seconds.

I also added a metric for reconnect count per minute and a Grafana panel next to the pool panel. The same backoff settings should be applied in the admin console session client, but that is Lena's code. I wrote her a note with the three option names. The pool size itself was not touched.

summary: Admin console session store now uses the same Redis reconnect backoff; Lena applied the three options and the test with a killed connection passed
body:
Lena picked up the note from earlier and changed the session store client of the admin console. She asked me to check it, so I ran the test: killed the Redis connections on the test stack with a client kill command and watched the console.

Before the change, the console showed a login redirect for about 4 seconds, because the session lookup failed and was treated as no session. After the change the lookup waits for a reconnect for up to 1 second and only then fails. In ten kills, no user was thrown to the login page.

One detail we found: the lookup timeout had to be shorter than the load balancer idle timeout, or the user would see a gateway error instead. 1 second is far below it, so fine.

She merged it. Nothing else changed in the session keys or their TTLs.

summary: Tried a generated TypeScript client for the public API from the OpenAPI file; output was too loose in types, so I dropped it and kept the hand-written examples
body:
Spent the evening on an experiment for the API docs: generating a TypeScript client from our OpenAPI file with a popular generator, so the docs could show examples that are always correct.

The generator ran fine, but the result had problems. Every event payload field came out as an unknown-valued record, because our schema uses open objects for customer fields. The search query parameter, which can be a string or a structured object, was generated as a union with 6 branches, and two of them were wrong. Fixing this would need changes to the spec with custom extension keys in about 40 places.

I also looked at the bundle size: 380 KB for a client that does four calls. The hand-written client in the docs examples is 6 KB.

Decision: dropped the generator. I wrote down in the docs repo notes why, so nobody tries it again without a reason. The one useful result is that the generator found 3 places where the spec disagrees with the real API: a field marked required that is optional, and two wrong response codes. I fixed those in the spec and sent the change to Sam for the docs review.

No code from the experiment was kept.

summary: Mara reviewed the dual write and found two real problems: deleted documents are not mirrored, and the month is taken from ingest time for updates; both fixed
body:
Mara reviewed the search-v2 dual write branch this morning, going through it with me on a call. She found two problems that the tests had not covered.

First, deletes. The indexer mirrored index and update operations, but a delete only went to the old index. A deleted document would stay forever in the monthly index and show up in searches after the switch. I added the delete to the dual path. Because the document id alone does not tell the month, the delete needs the timestamp. The delete request carries it in most cases, but not for the retention job. For that job I added a lookup of the month from the old index document before the delete, and a fallback that sends the delete to all monthly indices of the tenant using a bulk delete with ignore-missing.

Second, updates. The month for an update was taken from the time of the update, not from the event timestamp. An updated document would have been written to a new month and existed twice. I changed it so the month always comes from the event timestamp stored in the document, and the update path reads it from the payload or from the old document.

We also talked about ordering. If a delete overtakes the index operation of the same document through the queue, the old index has the same problem today, so this is not new. Mara still wants a test for it; I wrote one that applies the operations in reversed order on the test cluster.

Tests added: delete mirrored, delete without a timestamp, update across a month border, reversed order. All pass. The checker script showed 0 difference on the test tenant after a replay with 2 000 deletes mixed in.

Mara also asked to rename the flag to match our naming, so it is search_monthly_dual_write now. Remaining before any production use: the backfill tool, and a decision about when to switch reads. We agreed to discuss the read switch at the start of next week.

summary: Wrote the Redis cache key migration for the monthly search layout: keys now carry the index month, and old keys expire on their own TTL instead of a purge
body:
The monthly layout changes which index a result comes from, so the search API cache keys needed to know the month. Before, a key was built from tenant, query hash and filter hash. A result cached before a tenant switched to the monthly indices could be served after the switch, which is wrong for a short time.

I added a layout version and the month range to the key: search:v2:{tenant}:{months}:{queryhash}. The old keys are not deleted. They keep their normal TTL of 5 minutes for filtered searches and 1 hour for unfiltered ones, so they are gone within the hour. I considered a scripted purge with SCAN, but it adds load on Redis for no gain.

The key builder lives in one function in the search API, src/cache/keys.ts, and I changed only that function and its callers in two files. The unit tests cover the tenants that are on the old layout and the ones on the new layout, and a query that spans three months gives a key with the full range.

One thing found on the way: the console sent date ranges as local times, so two identical searches produced different month ranges around midnight. I normalized the range to UTC before building the key. This also helps the hit rate a little.

On the test stack, a run of 2,000 recorded searches gave the same hit rate as before for the old layout tenants. For the five tenants on dual write, the keys were correct, and no result crossed layouts. Still open: Mara wants a metric split by layout, so I will add a label to the hit rate counter next. After that I want to run the same replay with the 15 mid-size tenants before the production switch.

summary: Wrote the backfill tool skeleton for monthly search indices with a Postgres checkpoint table and the tenant and month work queue
body:
Started the backfill tool from the plan of two days ago. It is a Node script in the search repo, run as a one-off ECS task.

The checkpoint table backfill_progress has tenant_id, month, last_id, status and updated_at, with a unique key on tenant and month. The work queue is built at start from the sizing script output, small tenants first and oldest months first.

The copy loop uses a search_after on document id and sends bulk requests of 1 000 documents to the monthly index. It saves the checkpoint after every bulk. Killing the process and restarting continued at the right place in my test, with no duplicates, since the ids are the same and the write is idempotent.

The pause rule on search p95 is not built yet. Neither is the verification of a finished month. Both are next.

summary: Backfill tool pauses itself when the search p95 is high and verifies each month with a count and a sample hash
body:
Added the two missing parts of the backfill tool. The throttle reads the p95 of the search API from Prometheus every 30 seconds. When it is above 400 ms for five minutes, the tool stops taking new batches and waits until the value is under 300 ms for two minutes. The two thresholds avoid flapping.

Tested it by running load on the test search API while the backfill ran. The tool paused after about five minutes and continued once the load stopped. The log lines show the reason and the measured value.

The verification runs after the last batch of a month: count in old index with a date range filter against count in the monthly index, then a sample of 1 000 ids hashed over their source fields. A difference marks the month as failed in the checkpoint table, with the numbers in a column, and the tool goes on to the next one.

I found one false alarm in the test: documents in the old index with a timestamp in the future, 4 of them, fell into a different month than their range filter. The filter now uses the same month function as the indexer.

Still to do is the lock row against the nightly reindex.

summary: Lock row for the nightly reindex and the backfill added; the reindex skips months being copied and the first small tenant ran through the full path
body:
Built the lock between the backfill and the nightly reindex job. The table backfill_locks has a row per tenant and month while the backfill works on it. The reindex job checks it before touching a tenant's monthly index and skips the locked ones, with a log line and a counter. It picks them up the next night.

A decision I made: the lock is a row with a heartbeat column, not a database advisory lock. The backfill runs on ECS and a killed task would leave an advisory lock only until the connection drops, which is fine, but a visible row is easier for the support and for Tobias to inspect. A lock counts as stale after 10 minutes without heartbeat.

Then I ran the full path with a small tenant in the test cluster: 41 000 documents over 14 months.
- All 14 months copied and verified.
- Total time 6 seconds, as the throttle did not trigger.
- Dual write was on at the same time with a live replay, and the checker showed no difference at the end.
- One run of the reindex job during the copy skipped 2 locked months and handled the rest.

The job's skip logic needed a fix, because the first version treated a skip as a failure and the job exit code was 1. Now a skip is counted as success with a warning.

Next I want a run with a mid-size tenant to measure real throughput, and a plan for the first production step, which will be the dual write for the 5 smallest tenants.

summary: Alert rules in code: added a rule for Redis reconnect rate and one for backfill pauses, with tests in the rule test suite
body:
Added two alert rules to the alert-rules-as-code repo. The first fires when the Redis client reconnect count of any service is above 20 per minute for 5 minutes, a sign that the network or Redis is unstable. It uses the metric I added a few days ago.

The second fires when the backfill tool has been paused by the throttle for more than 30 minutes, since a long pause means the search API is under stress or the threshold is wrong. It routes to Slack only, not to PagerDuty, as it is not urgent.

Both rules have unit tests using the promtool test format with synthetic series. For the reconnect rule there are cases for a short spike that must not fire and a steady rate that must fire. The CI check for the rules passed.

I also went through the existing rules to see which still point to the old account labels from the infrastructure migration. Three of them used the old account id in a label matcher and would never fire. I fixed them and checked with a query that the series exist now. This was a real find: one of the three was the disk space warning for the OpenSearch nodes.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why search results for a customer looked stale: the cache TTL for filtered keys is 5 minutes, not a bug
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer saw new events missing from a filtered search for a few minutes. I looked at the request logs for the customer's key. The search was a cache hit with an age of 3 minutes 40 seconds.

This is the shorter TTL for filtered search keys set two days ago, five minutes. Before it was longer, so the effect is actually smaller than it was. Unfiltered searches have a 30 second TTL and the customer's new events appeared there right away.

I gave Sam a short text for the docs and for support answers: filtered searches can be up to five minutes behind, unfiltered ones up to 30 seconds, and a changed filter always gives a fresh result. Sam will put it in the search section of the public docs.

We also talked about a cache bypass header for customers who need exact results. Not decided; I noted it as an idea for the rate-limits work, since a bypass would need its own limit.

summary: Started the Redis minor version upgrade on the test stack: replica first, then failover; clients reconnected cleanly with the new backoff
body:
Prepared the Redis minor version upgrade for the production instance. First the test stack, which has the same topology of one primary and one replica.

Steps done:
- Read the release notes for the target version; no changes in the commands we use and no change in defaults that touch our configuration.
- Took a snapshot of the test primary.
- Upgraded the replica and checked that replication caught up, offset difference 0.
- Triggered a failover so the upgraded node became the primary, then upgraded the old primary.

During the failover the services lost their connections for about 5 seconds. The search API and the admin console both reconnected with the jittered backoff, with no burst on the new primary, and the error rate stayed at 0 because uncached searches went through. The rate limiter fell back to its local counters for the 5 seconds, as designed.

Memory use of the same dataset was the same before and after, within 1 percent. The key count matched.

Tobias will plan the window for production. I proposed a quiet time in the early morning, and a rollback by restoring the snapshot onto a new instance if something is wrong. I wrote the runbook with these steps and the checks after each one.

summary: Prepared the first production step of the monthly index dual write for the five smallest tenants, with the flag still off and the checks lined up.
body:
Went through the plan for switching on search_monthly_dual_write for the five smallest tenants, which together hold about 0.3 percent of the documents, so a problem would be cheap. The flag is still off. Mara is going to do the flag check before anything is switched on, and I wrote down the order of steps so we do not skip one.

I created the monthly indices on the test stack with the settings from the plan: 1 shard per tenant bucket where small, 1 replica, refresh interval 5 seconds. I also checked the index templates against the index names, and they applied correctly. The same creation script will be used in production, and I read through it twice for the tenant bucket naming.

I looked at the traffic of the five tenants to see what the checker has to handle. Tenant 4 sends events with timestamps up to 6 hours in the past, so at month borders its writes will land in the previous month. That means a tenant can have 2 open monthly indices at the same time, and the checker script must compare both. I changed it to do that and ran it against the test stack with replayed events from tenant 4; the difference was 0 in the replay.

I estimated the cost of the extra bulk request in the worker at a few milliseconds per batch and added a panel for indexing latency next to the dual_write_new_failures counter, so both are visible in one place on the dashboard.

The backfill for the five tenants is not run yet. It should wait until the live writes have been seen for a while.

Plan for the next days: switch the flag on for the five tenants after Mara's check, watch the failure counter and the checker for a week, then run the backfill, and only then think about 15 mid-size tenants. No change to reads; all queries keep going to the old indices.

summary: Production Redis minor upgrade done through replica failover in the early window; 6 seconds of reconnects, no user-visible errors, hit rate recovered in minutes
body:
Did the Redis minor upgrade on production with Tobias on the call, following the runbook from the test stack.

Timeline of the window:
- 06:00 snapshot of the primary taken and checked to restore on a scratch instance. Restore worked, key count matched within the writes since then.
- 06:10 upgraded the replica, replication offset caught up in 40 seconds.
- 06:20 failover to the upgraded node. Services lost their connections for about 6 seconds.
- 06:30 upgraded the former primary and rejoined it as the replica.

What we saw in the services: the search API and the console reconnected without a burst, which the reconnect panel confirmed, with a peak of 31 reconnects in the one minute and none after.
