The rate limiter used local counters during the gap, and the counters were back to the shared ones in the next window. Searches fell back to uncached, so p95 went from 90 ms to 480 ms for those seconds and then back.

The cache was not lost, as the replica had the data. The hit rate for filtered keys dipped from 41 to 36 percent for ten minutes and recovered. Memory use was at 5.3 GB before and after.

One thing that did not go well: the Grafana Redis dashboard lost the instance label after the failover, because it matched the primary by hostname. I changed the panels to use the role label instead.

Alert check: the new reconnect-rate alert did not fire, as the rate stayed below 20 for five minutes. That is the right outcome for a planned event, but I am not sure the threshold is not too lenient for an unplanned one. I will watch the first real case.

All finished at 06:45. Tobias deleted the scratch instance. The runbook got two corrections about the order of the label update.

summary: Dropped the dual write idea of a separate flag for deletes after Mara's test showed the combined flag is enough; code simplified
body:
While preparing the next tenants for the dual write, I looked at the delete path again. Last week I added a separate sub-flag for the mirrored deletes so they could be switched off alone. In practice there is no case where we would want writes mirrored but not deletes, since that leaves ghost documents.

Mara agreed in the review comment. I removed the sub-flag and the branch in the code that read it, 45 lines in total, and the config entry.

Ran the delete tests again, including the reversed order test. All green. The checker showed no difference on the five tenants.

summary: Postgres slow query on the settings API: N+1 loading of API key limits; one join query replaced 40 queries per request
body:
The slow query log showed the settings API list endpoint with up to 40 small queries per request, one per API key to load its limits. For a tenant with 400 keys the endpoint took 1.9 seconds.

I rewrote the loader as a single query with a left join on the limits table, and grouped the rows in code. The index on the key id in the limits table already existed. The endpoint now takes 70 ms for the same tenant and does 2 queries.

I added a test with 50 keys that counts the queries through the query logger, so a regression would fail the test. It matters for the rate-limits work too, since that adds a field to the same table.

The response format is unchanged; I compared the JSON of old and new for 5 tenants and they were equal.

summary: Per-key rate limit config reads now go through a small in-process cache with a 30 second TTL, cutting Postgres reads of the limits table by 95 percent
body:
On the rate-limits branch, the limiter looked up the limit of an API key in Postgres for each request that missed the Redis counter cache. That produced about 900 reads per second in the load test, nearly all for the same few hundred keys.

I added an in-process cache in the Fastify service with a 30 second TTL and a maximum of 5 000 keys. A change of a limit in the settings API is therefore visible after at most 30 seconds, which I documented in the endpoint description. The settings API also sends a publish message on a Redis channel, and the services drop the key from their cache when they get it, so normally the change shows up at once.

Load test result: reads of the limits table went from 900 to 40 per second, and the limiter's added latency fell from 4 ms to under 1 ms at p95.

A test covers the TTL, the invalidation by message and the size cap. Next is the response header for the remaining quota.

summary: Rate limit response headers added: limit, remaining and reset on every response, and Retry-After on 429; docs example drafted with Sam
body:
Added the headers to the API responses on the rate-limits branch. Every response now has X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, where reset is the number of seconds to the end of the window. A 429 response also carries Retry-After with the same number of seconds.

The values come from the counter the limiter already updates, so there is no extra Redis call. I checked this with the command stats on the test Redis: the number of commands per request stayed at 2.

One edge case: when Redis is unreachable and the limiter uses local counters, the remaining value is only the local view. In that case I leave out the Remaining and Reset headers instead of sending a wrong number, and send only Limit.

Wrote the tests for the three states: normal, limit exceeded and fallback. Then I sat with Sam and drafted the docs section. It has a short explanation, a table of the headers, and a client example in 12 lines that waits for Retry-After on a 429 and tries again at most 3 times, with the wait capped at 60 seconds.

Sam asked whether clients should add jitter on top of Retry-After. I think yes for the batch importers that run in parallel, so the example adds up to 20 percent random delay. Sam will review the wording tomorrow.

summary: Docs review by Sam on the rate limit page came back with three wording fixes and one real question about burst limits; fixed and answered
body:
Sam reviewed the rate limit section and sent back four points. Three were wording: the reset header was described as a timestamp, though it is seconds; the 429 example used a wrong status text; and the terms key and token were mixed.

The real question was about bursts: does a customer get a short burst above the limit? Today the limiter uses a fixed window of one minute, so a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next. I wrote this into the page as a known behaviour. A sliding window would fix it and cost more Redis work; we leave it for later.

Fixed all four and Sam approved.

summary: Prepared the dual write for 15 mid-size tenants and tested the month function against documents with future timestamps, before any backfill.
body:
Spent the evening preparing the next step of the search index plan: the dual write for the 15 mid-size tenants, with document counts between 1 and 20 million each. Nothing was switched on yet. I listed the tenants and checked their sizes, and wrote down the order for the backfill queue, small tenants first. The tool's throttle is set to pause when the search p95 touches 400 ms, and I tested the pause and resume on a staging copy, where it paused twice and resumed on its own. The throughput estimate stays at 9 000 documents per second, and I will compare it with a real run later.

While reading through sample data I found a problem for the verification step. A few documents from a customer client with a wrong clock have a timestamp a few hours after the time of the import. The old index filter by date range includes them in the month of the data, but the month function in the indexer rounds on the UTC border and would put them into the next month. That means the plain count per month can differ by a few documents at the borders, even when the data is correct by the rule.

I drafted a second verification step that counts with the same month function, using a scripted field in the query. On a staging copy it is about 4 times slower for big months, so the plan is to use it only when the plain count differs. I wrote a test with a handful of border documents and it passes. The big four tenants will need a night with low traffic, and I started a short note for Tobias about the window. The backfill itself is planned for another day.

summary: Cache hit rate report for search: unfiltered 78 percent, filtered 43 percent after the TTL change; key naming cleaned up for the monthly layout
body:
Pulled the weekly numbers for the search cache. The hit rate for unfiltered keys is 78 percent and for filtered keys 43 percent, stable since the TTL change. Memory use of Redis is 5.2 GB, flat for the week.

Because the search index will have a monthly layout, the cache keys need a look. Today a key looks like search:v1:<tenant>:<hash of the query>, with no index in it. After the move the results are the same for the same query, so the keys can stay the same, which is good: no cold cache at the switch. I confirmed this by checking that the hash is computed from the query and the tenant only, not from the index name.

I did find that two services build the key with different ordering of the filter fields, so the same search can produce two keys. I fixed the ordering with a sorted list of fields in one shared helper and used it in both. Expected effect is a few points more hits. The old keys expire by their TTL.

I added a test with filters in two orders that must give the same key.

summary: Audit export design check: the compliance export of 10 million rows streams from Postgres in 2 minutes with a cursor, memory flat at 90 MB
body:
Started with a measurement for the audit export, to see whether the streaming approach is fast enough before building more. I wrote a test script that reads the audit log of the largest tenant, 10 million rows, with a server-side cursor in chunks of 5 000, and writes NDJSON through a gzip stream to a local file.

Results on a replica:
- 2 minutes 5 seconds in total.
- Memory of the process flat at about 90 MB.
- Output file 410 MB compressed.
- Replica lag during the run stayed under 1 second.

I tried a larger chunk of 50 000 as well, and it was not faster, only 400 MB of memory, so 5 000 stays.

The query uses the composite index on tenant and created_at, so the order is stable and the export can continue after a failure from the last created_at and id. I will use that for resume.

Open points: where the file goes (an S3 bucket in the new account with a short-lived signed URL), and whether the customer gets a notification. The notification part is for Lena's console work. Next I write the export job and the signed URL endpoint.

summary: Audit export job built: resumable streaming to S3 with checksum, signed URL endpoint, and a failure test that killed the job mid-way and continued correctly
body:
Built the first complete version of the audit export on the audit-export branch.

The job takes a tenant and a time range from a row in an export_jobs table in Postgres, with states queued, running, done and failed. A worker picks up a queued row with a lock that skips rows locked by others, so two workers do not take the same job.

It streams the rows with the cursor approach from this morning, writes gzip NDJSON and uploads to S3 with a multipart upload, in parts of 16 MB. After each part it saves the last created_at, the last id and the part number in the job row. If the task dies, the next worker finds the running row with a heartbeat older than 2 minutes and continues from the saved position, using the stored upload id.

The finished file gets a SHA-256 checksum, stored in the job row and as S3 object metadata. The endpoint GET /exports/:id returns the state, and for a done job a signed URL valid for 15 minutes. A new URL can be requested at any time while the file exists.

Tests:
- Unit tests for the state changes and the resume position.
- An integration test on the test stack with 200 000 rows, where I killed the worker after the third part. The next worker continued, and the final file had exactly 200 000 lines with no duplicate and the same checksum as an uninterrupted run.
- A test where the tenant of the requester differs from the job tenant; the endpoint answered 404, not 403, to avoid showing that the job exists.

Two problems came up on the way. The multipart upload must have parts of at least 5 MB except the last, and a tiny export with 3 MB got an error until I switched to a single put for small files. Also the first resume test failed since the heartbeat timestamp used the local clock of the worker; I now use the database time.

Not done: the cleanup of old files, which should follow the lifecycle rule of the bucket at 7 days, and the export of the audit entries of deleted users, whose handling Mara and I still have to agree on. Next step is the lifecycle rule with Tobias and a run against a copy of the largest tenant.

summary: Audit export now has a per-tenant row cap and a progress endpoint, and a 10 million row run stayed at 90 MB of memory and finished in just under 3 minutes
body:
After the resumable export job from earlier today, I spent the afternoon on the parts a support person needs when a customer asks for an export. First I added a progress endpoint. It returns rows written, the last cursor position and a state of running, done or failed. The job updates its checkpoint row in Postgres every 50,000 rows, and the endpoint reads that row.

The second change was a row cap per export request. Without it, one tenant with a very wide time range could hold a cursor open for a long time. The default cap is 20 million rows, and it can be raised per tenant in the settings table. When the cap is hit, the job stops cleanly, marks the file as partial and says so in the status text.

I also changed the cursor to use a server side cursor inside a read-only transaction with a short snapshot. This is the same pattern as the report job fix from the vacuum problem, so the export does not hold back cleanup on the events metadata table. I checked pg_stat_activity during a run, and the transaction age stayed below the length of the export.

For the test I ran a 10 million row export on the test stack. It took 2 minutes 50 seconds, and the process memory stayed at about 90 MB. The checksum of the file matched the one stored in the job record. I then killed the worker at about 60 percent and started it again. It continued from the checkpoint, and the final file had no duplicate rows. I verified that by sorting and comparing the row ids.

One problem showed up with the signed URL endpoint. It accepted a request for a file that was still being written and returned a URL for a partial object. It now returns 409 until the job state is done. I added a test for that case. Next I want Mara to review the endpoint shapes, and Sam needs a short text for the docs about the cap and the partial state.

summary: Export files in the audit bucket now expire after 7 days through a lifecycle rule in Terraform, and the console text says so
body:
Added the lifecycle rule for the audit export prefix in the Terraform module: objects are deleted 7 days after creation, and incomplete multipart uploads are aborted after 2 days. The plan showed only the new rule, nothing else changed in the bucket.

Applied it on the test account first and uploaded a file with a back-dated tag to check. The rule showed up in the bucket settings as expected. S3 runs lifecycle rules once a day, so I could not see the delete happen in the session, and I will look tomorrow morning.

The signed URL lifetime is 24 hours, much shorter than the file lifetime, so a user who needs the file again requests a new link and gets the same file until it is deleted. Wrote that in the console help text. Lena will check the wording when she is next in the export page.

Still open: the audit log itself is not touched by this rule, only the export copies.

summary: The lifecycle rule worked: the back-dated test export file was gone this morning, and the incomplete multipart uploads are cleaned up too
body:
Checked the test bucket after the daily lifecycle run. The back-dated test file was deleted, and the files with a normal age were still there. The abort rule for incomplete multipart uploads also cleared two leftovers from my killed-job test of yesterday.

That closes the retention point of the audit export. Applied the same Terraform change to production with Tobias watching the plan; it changed one resource. Nothing else in the audit export needs a decision before review.

What is left on this branch: Mara's review of the job code, a short runbook for Sam on how to hand an export link to a customer, and the question about per-customer keys, which is parked.

summary: Planned the fix for documents with future timestamps in the monthly index backfill, after two months failed verification last week.
body:
The two months that failed verification last week had documents with a timestamp in the future, up to 3 days ahead, caused by customer clocks. The monthly index is chosen by the event timestamp, so those documents would land in the next month's index and the count for the source month came out off.

I wrote down the options: reject such documents, clamp the month to the ingest month, or keep them where the timestamp says. Rejecting would lose data. Keeping them breaks the count check, because the old layout has no such idea. I lean towards clamping: the month would be min(timestamp month, ingest month), and the original timestamp stays in the document untouched. The same rule should go into the dual write path, so live traffic and any later backfill agree. I wrote the rule into the design notes and asked Mara to read it before I touch the code.

To check the idea, I ran the month selection on the two failed months in a dry run, without writing anything. With the clamp, the expected counts per source month matched the old layout. I also pulled 500 sample documents per month and prepared the hash comparison script, so it is ready for the real run. I have not re-run any backfill yet; the 15 mid-size tenants stay in the queue until the rule is reviewed.

I started a test for the dual write suite with a document dated 3 days ahead; it fails for now, as expected, because the rule is not in the code. Next is a report of how many documents in production have a future timestamp at all, to see if clamping would touch many.

summary: Counted future-dated documents in production: 0.03 percent of the last month, nearly all from three tenants with bad device clocks
body:
Ran a query on the old index counting documents whose timestamp is later than ingest time plus one minute, for the last 30 days. The result was 0.03 percent of documents, about 41,000 of 130 million. Three tenants account for 92 percent of them.

So clamping touches very little, and it only matters for counts at a month border. I wrote the numbers in the shard layout notes so nobody is surprised later when a month count differs by a handful of documents.

Sam asked whether we should tell the three tenants. I think it is worth a note from support, since their dashboards in the analytics store also show events from the future. Sam will write it in plain words. I gave Sam the three tenant ids and a sample of five events each.

Nothing changed in code in this session. The next step in the plan is the dual write for the large tenants, which needs a bigger throttle budget.

summary: Large tenants in the dual write plan need 6 hours of backfill each; set a per-tenant throttle and a night window so search latency stays under the alert line
body:
Estimated the backfill for the 10 largest tenants from the document counts and the measured speed of the tool, about 9,000 documents per second when not paused. The biggest tenant has 410 million documents, which is about 12 hours without pauses and likely 18 with them. Too long for one night.

Changes made to the tool:
- Work items are now one tenant and one month, so a night window can stop cleanly at an item border.
- Added a window setting: the tool runs between 22:00 and 06:00 UTC and finishes the current item before it stops.
- The throttle is per tenant, a cap of 4,000 documents per second for the largest ones, so a single tenant cannot use all of the bulk capacity.

Tested on the test stack with a loaded copy of a mid-size tenant, with the window set to 10 minutes. It stopped at an item border and resumed on the next run from the checkpoint table with no duplicate work. The count check passed.

Open point: the nightly reindex also runs in the night window, and the lock row protects the months being copied, but the two jobs compete for bulk capacity. Talked it over with Tobias; he will look at the OpenSearch write queue graphs before we start the big tenants. I will not start them before that. Also wrote the plan into the notes, with the order of the tenants by size, smallest first.

summary: Tobias checked the OpenSearch write queue during a reindex test and saw no rejections, so the big tenants can run in the night window
body:
Tobias and I looked at the write thread pool graphs from the last three nights of the nightly reindex. The queue peaked at 120 of 200 slots, with zero rejected requests. With the backfill at the 4,000 per second cap on top, my estimate is about 160 slots, still under the limit.

To be sure, we ran the backfill for one mid-size tenant at the same time as the reindex on the test stack. Peak queue was 150, no rejections, and search p95 stayed under 180 ms.

Decision: start the largest tenants in the night window, one at a time, and keep a hand on the pause rule. Tobias added a panel with the write queue next to the backfill pauses panel in Grafana, so one look shows both.

No code changed today.

summary: Postgres vacuum on the events metadata table was stuck behind a long transaction from a report job; the job now uses a short snapshot and bloat is shrinking
body:
The table with event metadata had grown to 38 GB with about 40 percent bloat. Autovacuum ran but did not remove dead rows, and pg_stat_activity showed why: a reporting job held a transaction open for 3 hours, which pinned the oldest transaction id.

The job read a big result set through a cursor inside one transaction. I changed it to read in pages of 50,000 rows by primary key, each page in its own short transaction. It is slightly slower, 14 minutes instead of 11, but no transaction lives longer than a few seconds.

After the next deploy I started a manual vacuum, and dead tuples fell from 22 million to 1.4 million within an hour. I did not run a full rewrite of the table, since it takes a lock. A plain vacuum makes the space reusable, and the table will stop growing, which is enough for now.

Also added an alert for any transaction older than 30 minutes, with a note in the rule on how to find the owner. It has a test in the rule test suite. Open: check the bloat again next week to see whether the size really stays flat.

summary: Redis memory for the rate limiter keys is flat at 0.4 GB; checked key counts and TTLs after Sam asked why usage grew last month
body:
Sam asked whether Redis memory growth last month meant something was wrong. I looked at memory by key prefix with a sampled scan. The search cache is the biggest part at 4.9 GB, sessions 0.3 GB, rate limiter counters 0.4 GB.

The growth came from the cache, caused by the new monthly key names being written next to the old ones. The old keys expire by their own TTL, so the total will fall when the old keys are gone. The last old keys should expire within a day or so.

Checked the rate limiter counters too. Every counter has a TTL equal to its window, and I found no key without one in a sample of 20,000. The count of keys follows the number of active API keys, which is what we want.

Answered Sam with a short paragraph and the graph. No change in config.

summary: Loader retry design for large files: failed chunks are retried with backoff and a per-file budget, and the state survives a worker restart
body:
Started the design for retries in the document loader, since large files of 2 GB and more fail half way when the source host drops the connection. Today the whole file starts again, which wastes up to an hour.

The design in short:
- A file is split into chunks of 64 MB by byte range, each with an id and a status in a Postgres table: pending, running, done, failed.
- A failed chunk is retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff, starting at 2 seconds and capped at 60, with jitter.
- A per-file budget of 20 retries in total, so a broken source fails the file instead of looping.
- The status table is the source of truth. A restarted worker picks up running chunks older than a lease time of 10 minutes and pending ones.

The chunk boundary needs care for NDJSON: a range can cut a line. The reader for chunk n skips the partial first line, and reads past its end to finish the last line, unless n is 0. That makes every line belong to exactly one chunk. Wrote a small test with a file of 1,000 lines and random cut points, and it passed for 200 random layouts.

I also thought about CSV with quoted newlines. A line-based cut does not work there, since a quoted field can contain a newline. For now the loader keeps whole-file mode for CSV with quotes and uses chunks only for NDJSON and plain CSV. I wrote that as a known limit in the design note and will ask Mara whether it is acceptable for the first version.

No production code yet, only the migration for the status table and the chunk reader with its test. Next is the worker loop that takes chunks from the table.

summary: Mara accepted the CSV limit for the loader, and the chunk worker loop now claims chunks with a lease and runs two in parallel per file
body:
Mara read the design note and agreed that quoted CSV can stay in whole-file mode for the first version, since most large customer files are NDJSON. She asked for a counter metric of files that take the whole-file path, so we can see if it matters later. Added it.

Built the worker loop. A worker claims a chunk with an update that sets status to running and a lease expiry, using skip locked so two workers never take the same row. On success it writes done, on error it writes the attempt count and the next try time from the backoff.

Runs two chunks of a file in parallel for now. More would be faster, but the source host of the biggest customer limits connections, and I want to see real behaviour first.

Test: a fake source that fails every third request. A 640 MB test file loaded fully, with 11 retries in total, and the row count matched. Killing the worker mid-chunk and starting it again continued after the lease passed, which I shortened to 5 seconds for the test.

Open: what happens to rows already written by a failed chunk. Next entry covers it.

summary: Chunk retries could write rows twice; the loader now writes each chunk in one transaction with a chunk id, so a retry replaces the earlier partial result
body:
Thought through the open point and then proved it with a test: a chunk that fails after writing half of its rows leaves them in the table, and the retry writes them again. In my fake source test with a failure after 500 rows the final count was 640 plus 500 extra.

The earlier run missed this because the fake source failed on the request, before any row was written. Changed the fake to fail in the middle of a chunk and the duplicates showed at once.

Options considered:
- Delete rows with the chunk id before the retry. Simple, but needs the chunk id on every row and an index on it.
- Write each chunk inside one transaction, so a failure rolls it back. No cleanup is needed.
- Make the writes idempotent through a unique key on the event id, so duplicates are ignored.

I took the transaction, because a chunk of 64 MB is about 200,000 rows, which Postgres handles well in one transaction. The unique event id is also a good idea, but it already exists for events and is not available for all document types, so I did not rely on it.

The cost is that a failure at the end of a chunk loses up to a minute of work. That is acceptable.

Re-ran the mid-chunk failure test: 640 rows expected, 640 found, with 14 retries. Also ran a test with a worker killed during the commit, and the chunk was either complete or absent after restart.

Looked at the transaction length against the new alert for transactions older than 30 minutes. A chunk takes about 40 seconds, so no alert. Left to do: the backoff settings in config, and a status page in the console for Lena, with the count of retries per file.

summary: Loader retry settings moved to config with safe defaults and a hard cap, and a failed file now reports which chunk and why
body:
Moved the backoff numbers into the loader config: base delay 2 seconds, cap 60, 5 attempts per chunk, 20 per file. Each can be set per customer, because one customer's source host is flaky and another's is solid. Values above 10 attempts per chunk are refused when the config loads, to avoid a loop that runs for hours.

When a file fails because the budget ran out, the error now names the chunk number, its byte range, the attempt count and the last error text, for example connection reset at 41 percent of the chunk. Before it said only that loading had failed.

Wrote tests for the config limits and for the error text. Sam will use the text in support answers, so I kept it plain.

Next is the status data for Lena's page.

summary: Tried a streaming parser library to speed up NDJSON chunk reads; it was slower on real files with long lines, so I dropped it and kept the standard decoder
body:
Chunk reading is now the slowest part of a load, at about 38 MB per second per chunk, so I tried a streaming JSON library that promised several times faster parsing. I made a branch of the chunk reader that used it and ran it on three real files from customers.

Results in MB per second against the standard decoder:
- Short lines, 200 bytes average: 61 against 38, a clear gain.
- Medium lines, 2 KB: 44 against 39, a small gain.
- Long lines, 40 KB with big nested arrays: 29 against 37, slower.

The biggest customer sends the long lines, and these are exactly the files where loading takes hours, so the gain would be in the wrong place. The library also allocates more per line there, and the worker memory went from 300 MB to 520 MB in the long line test.

I also checked error behaviour. On a broken line the library stops the stream and gives an offset that is hard to map back to a line, while the standard decoder gives a line we can report. That matters for the new error messages.

Decision: drop it. I left the benchmark script in the repository under tools with a note, so nobody tries again without the numbers. The branch with the library is deleted.

A cheaper idea that I measured: the reader used a 4 KB buffer, and raising it to 1 MB gave 38 to 47 MB per second on all three files, with no other change. Kept that one. The memory cost is 2 MB per running chunk.

Left for tomorrow: the status data for the console and a full run on the largest real file in the test stack.

summary: Status data for the console: the loader exposes chunk counts, retries and the last error per file, and Lena has the endpoint shape
body:
Added a status endpoint in the loader service that returns, per file: chunks total, done, running, failed, retries used and the last error text with its chunk number. It reads from the chunk status table with one grouped query, which takes about 3 ms for a file of 200 chunks.

I wrote the shape of the response in the API notes and sent it to Lena. She wants a progress bar that counts done chunks, and a line with the retries when there are any. The data supports both.

One decision: the retry count shows the total for the file, but the budget limit is not shown, since it is an internal setting that we may change. Lena agreed.

Added tests for a file with no chunks, a finished file and a failed file. All three pass.

summary: Full loader run on the largest real file in the test stack: 3.4 GB loaded in 31 minutes with 9 retries, row count matched, against 52 minutes and a failed run before
body:
Ran the new chunked loader on a copy of the largest customer's file, 3.4 GB of NDJSON with long lines, from a test host that I set to drop about 1 in 40 connections. The old loader failed on this setup twice before the end and took 52 minutes on the run that got through.

The new run finished in 31 minutes. It used 9 retries, 8 on the first attempt of a chunk and one chunk that needed two. The row count in Postgres matched the line count of the file, 7,912,044 on both sides. The sample check of 1,000 random lines by event id found all of them with the same content.

Worker memory stayed at about 330 MB. Two chunks ran in parallel, as configured. Tried four in parallel after that: 23 minutes, but the test host started to refuse new connections, which is the problem we expect on the real source. So the default stays at 2, and a customer setting allows more for sources that cope.

Some things I saw in the logs:
- The backoff with jitter spread the retries well, and no two chunks retried in the same second.
- A chunk that failed near its end lost its whole transaction, about 35 seconds of work, as designed.
- The lease of 10 minutes was never needed, since no worker died in this run.

Then I killed the worker at about 60 percent and started it again. It waited for the lease, took the running chunks back and finished. The final count still matched, and no chunk was loaded twice.

What is left before a review: the runbook for support, and a flag to switch the new loader on per customer. I will make the flag first and turn it on for the customers with the biggest files.

summary: Loader flag per customer added; chunked mode is off by default and turned on for the two customers with files over 2 GB
body:
Added a customer setting for chunked loading, off by default. With it off, the old whole-file path runs unchanged, so a rollback is only a setting change.

Turned it on for the two customers with the largest files, after checking their last uploads in the log: both are NDJSON, so the chunk path applies. The next upload from each will use it.

The metric for files on the whole-file path shows 3 percent today, all quoted CSV. The test for the flag covers both settings. Next step is the runbook for Sam.

summary: Wrote the loader runbook for Sam: how to read a failed file's error, when to retry by hand, and when to ask for a bigger budget
body:
Wrote a one-page runbook for support on the chunked loader. It explains the status values and what the error text means, for example a connection reset points to the source host, and a parse error with a line number points to the customer's file.

It also says when to retry by hand: only if the source problem is fixed. A manual retry starts the failed chunks again and keeps the done ones, so it is cheap. If a file fails twice for the same chunk, the runbook says to ask a developer, since the budget may need a raise for that customer.

Sam read it and asked for an example with real numbers, so I added the 3.4 GB case with its 9 retries as an example of normal behaviour. Sam also asked what the progress bar shows during a wait for the backoff. It stays where it is, and the status says running, which I wrote down.

The runbook is in the docs folder of the repository and linked from the console help.

summary: Mara's review of the loader retry branch: two requested changes, a missing index on the chunk table and a lease check that used local time instead of database time
body:
Mara reviewed the branch and found two real problems.

First, the claim query for chunks filtered on status and lease expiry without a supporting index. With 200 chunks per file it was fine, but with many files running the table scan would show up. Added an index on status and lease expiry, and the plan for the claim query now uses it.

Second, the lease expiry was computed from the worker's own clock, while the check used the database clock. With a small clock difference between hosts a worker could lose its chunk early or hold it too long. Both now use now() from Postgres, in the same statement.

She also suggested a test where two workers claim at the same time. I wrote one with 8 workers and 100 chunks, and every chunk was claimed exactly once.

All three changes are in and the tests pass. Mara will look once more tomorrow.

summary: Search latency check after the monthly dual write reached 40 tenants: p95 unchanged for reads, bulk indexing cost matches the estimate, one slow aggregation found
body:
Looked at the search API numbers after the dual write grew from 15 to 40 tenants, since the dual write adds load on the indexing side and the plan says reads must not suffer. Compared the last 7 days against the 7 before.

Read latency: p50 22 ms before and 22 ms after, p95 140 ms before and 143 ms after, p99 410 ms before and 420 ms after. Those are within the normal day-to-day noise on the dashboard.

Indexing: the bulk request count is 1.1x of the old path, as measured in the test, and the document write rate on the cluster rose by about 38 percent, which is close to the share of tenants now mirrored. The write thread pool peak was 130 of 200, no rejections.

The count check that compares the two layouts every ten minutes reported 3 mismatches in the week. I looked at each. Two were documents updated during the check window, and the check found them equal on the next run. The third was a deleted document from a tenant that was switched on that very hour, and it was fixed by the delete mirroring that Mara asked for.

While looking at slow queries I found one real problem: an aggregation for a facet count on the field with many distinct values, with p95 of 1.9 seconds, on one large tenant. It exists in both layouts, so it is not caused by the dual write. The cause is a terms aggregation with size 10000 where the console shows 20. Dropped the size to 100 in the search API for that call and the p95 fell to 160 ms. The console only shows the top 20, so 100 is plenty.

Two things I did not do. I did not touch the cache TTL, since the hit rate is stable. And I did not extend the dual write to more tenants yet; that waits for the backfill of the large tenants. Next entries will be about starting that backfill for the first large tenant in the night window.

summary: Started the backfill for the first large tenant in the night window; first two months verified, pauses so far at 2 and each under 3 minutes
body:
Started the first large tenant, 120 million documents, with the cap at 4,000 documents per second, oldest months first. Watched the first hour on the Grafana panel that has the write queue next to the pauses.

Two months finished and both passed the count and the sample hash check. The tool paused twice when search p95 went over the line, each under 3 minutes, and it resumed on its own.

Write queue peak was 110 of 200, no rejections. The window will end at 06:00 UTC, and the tool will stop at an item border and continue tomorrow night.

No problems so far. I will check the checkpoint table in the morning to see how far it got.

summary: Redis memory by prefix after the old search keys expired: total down to 4.6 GB, the cache part 4.2 GB, all inside the plan
body:
Checked Redis memory again now that the old-format search keys should be gone. Total used memory is 4.6 GB, down from 5.3 GB after the TTL change. The search cache is 4.2 GB, sessions 0.2 GB, rate limiter 0.2 GB.

Counted keys with the old naming pattern in a sampled scan of 50,000 keys and found none. The monthly key format is the only one left.

The hit rate for filtered keys is 44 percent and unfiltered 79 percent, which is within a point of the last report. So the key change cost us nothing.

Wrote the numbers into the cache notes. The one thing I would still like is a dashboard panel with memory by prefix, since I had to do the scan by hand. I made a small script that writes the numbers to Prometheus once an hour, and a panel on top of it. The scan samples, so the load on Redis is small, a few hundred milliseconds of work per run.

No change to Redis config.

summary: Checked the Redis key counts for the search cache after the monthly key change; the old-format keys are nearly gone and the new keys follow the naming plan
body:
I looked at the Redis keyspace for the search cache this morning, because the monthly key format has been live for about a week. The old keys had a TTL of 5 minutes for filtered searches and longer for unfiltered ones, so they were expected to disappear without a purge. A scan with a count limit over a sample of the keyspace found old-format keys at under 0.5 percent of the total. All of those had a remaining TTL below an hour.

The new keys carry the index month in the name, as planned. I checked 2,000 random keys and every one matched the pattern of prefix, tenant, month and query hash. No key was without a TTL, which was the thing I most wanted to confirm.

Key count per month looks as expected. The current month holds about 70 percent of the keys, the previous month about 22 percent, and older months share the rest. That matches how customers search, mostly recent data.

I also compared the hit rate before and after the format change. Filtered keys are at 43 percent and unfiltered at 78 percent, unchanged within one point, so the change did not cost anything. Memory use of the cache part stayed within the plan.

I wrote the numbers into the shard layout plan document, so that the later steps can refer to them. Nothing needs to change in the code, and I will check once more after the next tenants join the dual write.

summary: Wrote the Postgres bloat follow-up: events metadata table size is flat at 38 GB after a week and dead tuples stay under 2 million, so no rewrite is needed
body:
Checked the events metadata table a week after the report job was changed to short transactions. Size is 38 GB, the same as before, so the table stopped growing. Dead tuples are 1.6 million, and autovacuum now keeps up, with a run about every 40 minutes.

The old bloat of about 15 GB is still inside the table as free space, which new rows reuse. A full rewrite would give the disk space back, but it needs a lock, and the table is on the write path. I do not think it is worth the risk for disk we have enough of, so I decided against a rewrite.

The new alert for transactions older than 30 minutes fired once, from a manual query of mine that I forgot to close. It did what it should: the message named the user and the query start time, and I found it in a minute.

One more thing I checked was the index sizes. The index on the event timestamp is 9 GB and has 30 percent bloat. A concurrent reindex of that one index is safe and needs no long lock, so I ran it in the quiet window. It took 22 minutes and the index is now 6.3 GB. Query plans on it did not change.

Wrote the numbers into the database notes, with the rule that a full table rewrite needs a decision from the lead and a maintenance window. Next check on this table is in a month.

summary: Second large tenant backfill started in the night window; the first one finished and verified, with search p95 inside the alert line throughout
body:
The first large tenant finished its backfill overnight. All months verified against the Postgres counts, and the pauses stayed at 2 in total, each under 3 minutes. Search p95 never went above the alert line, so the throttle from last week held.

I started the second large tenant this morning, which is about 30 percent bigger. The throttle stays the same and the run is queued for the next night window, since a daytime run would compete with the dashboards.

Before queueing it I checked the per-month document counts for this tenant. Two months are much larger than the rest, because of a bulk import the customer did a year ago. Those two months will take about twice as long, so the plan now says 8 hours instead of 6.

I also checked that the verification script handles the clamped future timestamps. It does, and it reports them as a separate count instead of as mismatches. That count was 212 for the first tenant, which fits the 0.03 percent figure.

Tobias looked at the OpenSearch heap during the first run. Peak was 71 percent, which is fine. He asked that the second run does not overlap with the snapshot job, so I moved the start to 23:30.

Next step is to read the verification report tomorrow morning and decide if the third large tenant can run on the following night.

summary: Evening check of the second backfill: it is progressing on schedule with no pauses so far and search latency is flat
body:
I looked at the second large tenant backfill at the start of the night window. Four months were done, all verified, and there had been no pauses yet.

Search p95 on the dashboard was flat at the usual evening level. The OpenSearch write queue had no rejections.

The two oversized months come later in the run. I left the throttle unchanged and set an alert on the pause count so that I get a message if it goes above 5.

Nothing else to do tonight. I will read the report in the morning.

summary: Redis connection count per service measured after a slow afternoon; the search API holds many idle connections and the pool minimum is lowered
body:
Sam reported that the console felt slow around the middle of the afternoon, so I looked at Redis first. The command latency was fine, but the connection count was at 310, higher than I expected for our traffic.

Breaking it down by client name showed that the search API used 140 of them. Each Fastify instance kept a pool with a minimum of 20 idle connections, and we run seven instances. Most of those connections never did anything.

The ingest rate limiter used 90, which is in line with its workers. The console session store used 60.

I lowered the pool minimum for the search API from 20 to 4 and kept the maximum as it was. After a rolling restart the total went down to 190, and the p95 of the cache GET calls stayed the same.

The slow afternoon did not come from Redis. The console request that Sam saw was a Postgres query on the audit log page without a tenant index on one filter. I wrote that down as a follow-up and did not fix it today.

The pool change is in the config of the search API only. The other services are untouched. I will check the connection count again in two days to see whether it creeps up.

summary: Verification report for the second large tenant: all months match, two oversized months took 2.1 times longer, no pauses above 3 minutes
body:
The second large tenant backfill finished before the window closed. The report shows every month with a matching document count against Postgres.

The two oversized months took 2.1 times as long as an average month. The total run time was 7 hours 40 minutes, a little below the new estimate.

There were 3 pauses, each under 3 minutes. The future timestamp clamp touched 540 documents.

Search p95 stayed under the alert line for the whole run. The highest value was 8 percent above the normal level, during one of the pauses recovery.

The third large tenant can run tonight. It is the largest one, so I will ask Tobias to be reachable in case the heap goes up.

summary: Audit log page filter was slow without a tenant index; the new composite index brought the query from 4 seconds to 30 milliseconds
body:
Yesterday I wrote down that the audit log page in the console was slow. Today I looked at it properly with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query behind the page.

The query filters by tenant, action and a time range, and orders by time descending. The planner used the index on time and then filtered the rest, which scanned about 2 million rows for a large tenant. The runtime was 4 seconds.

I created a composite index on tenant id, action and time descending. I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so the writes of the audit log were not blocked, and it took 9 minutes on the production table.

After that the same query ran in 30 milliseconds. The page for the largest tenant loads in under half a second now.

I checked the cost: the index is 1.1 GB, and the insert rate of the audit log did not change in a measurable way. The table gets about 40 inserts per second at peak.

There was also an old index on tenant id alone that the new one makes redundant. I did not drop it yet, because I want to see a week of statistics first. The pg_stat_user_indexes view will show whether it is still used.

I told Lena the page is fast now, since she had a ticket open for it. She will close it after she checks the console herself.

The migration file is in the main checkout, with the concurrent create and a note that it must not run inside a transaction.

summary: Retry budget for the ingest client library reviewed: the default of 5 attempts with jitter is kept, but the maximum wait is capped at 20 seconds
body:
A customer asked in a support ticket why their client sometimes waited for more than a minute after a 503. I looked at the retry settings in our ingest client library.

The library retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff and full jitter. The base is 500 milliseconds and the factor is 2, but there was no cap, so the later waits could reach 16 seconds each, and with jitter and the connection timeout the total could pass a minute.

I added a cap of 20 seconds for the total wait and kept the 5 attempts. The jitter stays, because without it clients that fail together retry together.

A test with a fake server that always returns 503 now ends after at most 19 seconds, where it needed 58 before. A second test checks that a 429 uses the Retry-After header instead of the backoff, which was already the case.

I wrote the change in the changelog of the library and a short note for Sam, so the docs say what the real maximum wait is.

The customer gets a new version of the library. I do not expect other changes to behavior, because most requests succeed at the first attempt.

summary: Third large tenant backfill started; its biggest month is four times average, so I split that month into two runs to keep the pauses short
body:
The third large tenant is the largest we have, and its documents are spread unevenly over the months. I looked at the counts before starting.

One month has four times the average count, from a campaign the customer ran. A single run on that month would hold the throttle at a high write rate for a long time, so I split it into two halves by day of month.

The backfill tool takes a time range now, not only a month. That was a small change: the range goes into the scroll query and the verification uses the same range. I tested it on a small tenant with two half-month runs and the count matched a single run.

I started the run in the night window. The plan is 11 hours, so it may need a second night, and the tool continues from the last verified range.

Tobias is reachable tonight. I asked him to watch the heap and the merge queue of OpenSearch, since this tenant is large enough to show a problem if there is one.

I also moved the alert on pause count to 8 for this tenant because the large month will cause more pauses by design.

If the heap goes over 80 percent, the run should be stopped and the throttle lowered. That is written in the runbook note in the ticket.

I will check the first verified months in the morning.

summary: Postgres minor version upgrade planned for the test stack first: the release notes show no changes to the planner, and the test run is set for tomorrow
body:
Tobias asked me to plan the next minor Postgres 16 upgrade. I read the release notes for the versions between ours and the newest one.

There are security fixes and a few bug fixes for replication and for the autovacuum. Nothing about planner changes, which is what I looked at most.

The plan is to upgrade the test stack first, run our reports query set and the audit export test, and compare the timings with the numbers from the current version. Then the staging database, then production in a quiet hour.

The query set has 24 queries with their current timings in a file. I made a script that runs all of them 5 times and writes the median to a table, so the comparison is easy.

I ran the script on the current test stack to have a baseline from today. The slowest query is the monthly report at 1.8 seconds.

The production upgrade needs a restart of the primary, which means about 30 seconds of failed writes unless the failover is used. Tobias will use the replica promotion so the gap is shorter. We will send a notice to the customers with the maintenance time anyway.

Tomorrow Tobias upgrades the test stack, and I run the script again.

summary: Per-key rate limit overrides for two large customers added to the limiter config, with a test for the burst behavior and a docs sentence for Sam
body:
Two large customers asked for higher limits on their API keys. The rate limit branch already supports per-key limits, so this was a config and test task.

The overrides live in a table in Postgres and the limiter loads them into Redis with a TTL of 10 minutes. Changing a value takes at most 10 minutes to apply, unless we delete the cached key by hand.

I added the two overrides: 3000 requests per minute for the first customer and 5000 for the second, with the burst at 20 percent of the limit. The default is 1000 with the same burst rule.

A new test sends a burst at the limit plus the burst allowance and checks that the next request gets a 429 with the correct Retry-After. It also checks that the headers show the override limit and not the default.

While testing I found that the remaining header showed a negative number for one request at the edge, because two requests were counted at nearly the same time. The counter is atomic, but the header was computed from the value before the second increment. I changed it to use the value returned by the increment and the header is never below zero now.

I deployed it to staging, where the test with the override keys passed. Production follows after the review by Mara.

For Sam I wrote one sentence for the docs: custom limits are set by us on request and apply within ten minutes.

The key names of the override cache follow the naming scheme with the prefix rl:override and the key id, and the memory is negligible.

summary: Mara reviewed the rate limit overrides and asked for an audit log entry on every change; added and tested
body:
Mara reviewed the override change this afternoon. She had one request: every change of a limit must go into the audit log, because support changes them by hand and nobody could tell later who did it.

I added an audit entry with the key id, old limit, new limit and the user who made the change. The entry is written in the same transaction as the update, so there is no change without a record.

A test covers the update and the rollback case: when the update fails, no audit row stays. Both pass.

She also asked about the 10 minute TTL. I explained that a delete of the cached key applies a change at once, and I added that as a helper command in the admin scripts.

She approved after the changes. I will deploy to production tomorrow morning.

summary: Test stack upgraded to the new Postgres minor version; all 24 reports queries are within 3 percent of the baseline
body:
Tobias upgraded the test stack database to the newest minor version of Postgres 16 this afternoon. I ran the query set script right after.

All 24 queries are within 3 percent of the baseline medians, and 9 of them are slightly faster. The monthly report is 1.8 seconds, the same as before.

I also ran the audit export test with 10 million rows. It finished in under 3 minutes with memory flat, as before.

The plans of the five slowest queries are identical to the baseline plans, checked with EXPLAIN. No planner change shows up.

Staging is next. Tobias will do it tomorrow, and I will run the script there too.

summary: Third large tenant backfill: half of the months verified, the split big month passed in two runs, and the heap peaked at 74 percent
body:
This evening I looked at the progress of the third large tenant backfill. Seven of the 14 months were verified and the run is on schedule for a second night.

The oversized month ran as two half-month ranges. Both ranges matched the Postgres counts and the sum of the two equals the month total I computed before. The pauses for that month were 4 and 5, each below 3 minutes.

Tobias reported the OpenSearch heap peaked at 74 percent, which is under the 80 percent line. The merge queue stayed short.

Search p95 was up 11 percent at the peak, which is within the alert line but more than for the other two tenants. I lowered the throttle by 10 percent for the rest of the night to be careful. The estimated finish moves by about an hour.

I wrote the change of the throttle into the ticket so the numbers can be compared later.

One issue turned up: the verification step for a half-month range reads the count with a filter on the timestamp in the local timezone of the tool host, and the host runs in UTC, so there was no wrong result. But I noticed the filter does not state the timezone, so I added the explicit UTC to the query. Nothing changed in the output, but it will not break if someone runs the tool on a laptop.

Tomorrow I read the final report and then decide the order of the remaining large tenants.

After that, the dual write covers all tenants except the biggest two, and the plan for the cutover of reads starts.

summary: Third large tenant backfill finished and verified; all 14 months match, with 1,900 future timestamps clamped to the ingest month
body:
The third large tenant backfill finished in the second night window. All 14 months match the Postgres counts, including the two half-month ranges.

The clamp of future timestamps touched 1,900 documents, nearly all from the one device clock problem we saw before. The count is reported separately and the verification does not count them as mismatches.

The total run time was 12 hours 20 minutes with the lowered throttle. Pauses: 17 in total, none longer than 3 minutes.

Search p95 was inside the alert line for the whole run. The heap peak was 74 percent, as reported yesterday.

Two large tenants are left. Both are smaller than this one, so the plan stays the same. I will queue the next one tonight.

I added the final numbers to the plan document, so the estimate for the last two is based on measured rates: about 9 hours for each.

summary: Staging database upgraded to the new Postgres minor version; query set within 2 percent of baseline and production is set for the quiet hour tonight
body:
Tobias upgraded staging this morning and I ran the query set script there. All queries are within 2 percent of the baseline, and the plans match.

Staging has a copy of production data from last week, so the numbers are more realistic than the test stack. The monthly report is 2.4 seconds, the same as before the upgrade.

We also ran the replica promotion procedure on staging to measure the write gap. It was 11 seconds, which is shorter than the 30 seconds for a plain restart.

The notice to customers went out yesterday with the maintenance time of tonight. Tobias will do the production upgrade with the promotion, and I will run the script right after.

The rollback plan is the old replica, which stays on the previous version until tomorrow. If something looks wrong, we promote it back.

I checked that the application connection strings use the writer endpoint and not an instance name. They do, so no config change is needed.

The only open point is the ingest workers, which hold long connections. Tobias will restart them after the promotion so they reconnect cleanly.

summary: Redis cache hit rate for the search API checked after the pool change: filtered queries at 45 percent, unfiltered at 79 percent, connections at 190 and stable
body:
Two days after lowering the pool minimum for the search API, I checked Redis again. The total connection count is 190 and it did not creep up.

Cache hit rates for search: unfiltered 79 percent and filtered 45 percent. Both are a little above the numbers from last week, which come from the TTL change and not from the pool.

The p95 of cache GET calls is the same as before the change, so the smaller pool had no effect on latency.

I looked at the filtered queries a bit more, because 45 percent is still low. Many filtered queries include a time range with the current minute in it, so the cache key is different on every call. That is why they do not hit.

A fix would be to round the end of the range to the start of the minute for cache purposes only. The results would be at most 60 seconds old, which is within the TTL anyway.

I tried the rounding on staging with a replay of one hour of production queries. The filtered hit rate went from 44 to 61 percent.

The risk is that a user who just ingested an event does not see it in a repeated query for up to a minute. That is already true for the TTL, but I want Lena to confirm that the console does not promise live results on that page.

I wrote the proposal in the ticket and did not change production.

summary: Production Postgres minor upgrade done last night with an 11 second write gap; queries match the baseline and the old replica is kept for a day
body:
Tobias did the production upgrade in the quiet hour with the replica promotion. The write gap was 11 seconds, as in staging, and the ingest clients retried through it without lost batches.

I ran the query set script right after. All 24 queries were within 3 percent of the baseline. The monthly report took 2.1 seconds.

The ingest workers were restarted and reconnected without errors. The error rate on the ingest API was back to normal within a minute.

The old replica stays on the previous version for a day as the rollback path. Tobias will remove it tomorrow if nothing looks off.

I checked autovacuum activity on the events metadata table after the upgrade. It runs as before, and dead tuples are below 2 million.

summary: Fourth large tenant backfill started in the night window with the same throttle and a 9 hour estimate
body:
The fourth large tenant backfill started tonight at 23:30. The estimate is 9 hours, based on the rate of the third tenant.

I used the throttle from the last run after the reduction, since that kept p95 low. The tool continues from the last verified range if it is stopped.

Before starting, I checked that the snapshot job does not overlap with the window. It runs at 03:00 and takes 20 minutes, so I accepted one overlap and watched the heap during the first snapshot of the earlier runs. It stayed under 75 percent.

The alert on pause count is at 8 for this run. Tobias is reachable.

This tenant has no unusually large month, so I did not split any ranges. The biggest month is 1.6 times the average.

The verification report will be ready in the morning.

One thing for later: after the last large tenant, the next step is the read cutover plan. I started a short outline in the document with the tenant order, a flag per tenant for reads, and a fallback to the old layout.

summary: Fourth large tenant backfill verified: 11 months match, 5 pauses, and the snapshot overlap raised the heap by only 2 points
body:
The fourth large tenant backfill finished in 8 hours 50 minutes. All 11 months match the Postgres counts, and the clamp touched 130 documents.

There were 5 pauses, each under 3 minutes. Search p95 stayed within the alert line, with a peak 6 percent above the normal level.

The snapshot overlap at 03:00 raised the heap by 2 points for about 20 minutes, to 72 percent. That is not a problem, so the last large tenant can run in the same window.

One tenant is left in the plan, the second largest. It has an unusual number of small documents, so the estimate by size may be too low. I will count the documents per month before starting and compare it with the rate of the other runs.

I updated the plan document with the measured numbers of all four runs, in a table with run time, pauses, peak p95 and peak heap.

summary: Count of the last large tenant's documents shows 2.3 times the volume of the fourth, so its backfill is planned for two nights
body:
I counted the documents per month for the last large tenant before starting its backfill. The total is 2.3 times the fourth tenant, because it has many small documents from a monitoring integration.

At the measured rate this means about 20 hours. I split it over two nights with a break in the day, and the tool resumes from the last verified month.

Bulk indexing cost per document is lower for small documents in batches, so the real time may be shorter. I will adjust after the first night.

The throttle stays the same. The heap alert is unchanged.

I also let Tobias know about the two nights so he does not schedule maintenance in the window.

The first night starts at 23:30 as before.

summary: Rounded cache keys for filtered search queries went to production after Lena confirmed the console does not promise live results; hit rate rose from 45 to 60 percent
body:
Lena confirmed that the search page of the console does not promise live results. It already shows a note that results can be a minute behind, so the rounding of the query range for cache keys is acceptable.

The change rounds the end of a relative time range down to the start of the minute when the cache key is built. The query sent to OpenSearch is not changed, so results are still exact for the first call. Only repeated calls within the TTL can be a little older.

I added unit tests for the key builder: two calls in the same minute produce the same key, and calls in different minutes differ. Absolute time ranges are not rounded, because a user who picks fixed times expects exact results.

I deployed it in the afternoon with a feature flag, first at 10 percent of the traffic. The filtered hit rate for that part was 59 percent after an hour.

I raised the flag to 100 percent after checking error rates and latency. p95 for filtered queries went down by 18 percent because more of them were answered from the cache.

Redis memory grew by 0.1 GB, as the new keys are shared by more requests and the old ones expire by TTL. That is inside the plan.

The key naming follows the monthly layout scheme from last week, and I added a line about the rounding to the key naming document.

Sam asked whether support should tell customers about the minute of delay. I suggested one sentence in the docs under the search page. He will draft it.

After a full day I will check the hit rates again and decide if the flag can be removed.

summary: Last large tenant backfill: first night finished 9 of 16 months, all verified, with the small-document volume faster than estimated
body:
The first night of the last large tenant backfill finished 9 of 16 months, all verified against the Postgres counts. That is faster than the plan, which expected 8.

Small documents index at a better rate per document, as I guessed. The estimate for the remaining months is now 7 hours, so the second night should be enough.

Pauses: 6, each under 3 minutes. Search p95 peak was 7 percent above normal and the heap peaked at 73 percent.

The clamp of future timestamps touched 20 documents, much fewer than the other tenants.

The second night starts as planned.

summary: Last large tenant backfill complete after the second night, so the dual write now covers every tenant; next is the read cutover plan
body:
The second night finished the last 7 months of the last large tenant. All 16 months match the Postgres counts.

With this run the dual write to the monthly layout covers every tenant, and the backfill is complete. Total pauses across all large tenants were about 35, none longer than 3 minutes.

Search p95 stayed within the alert line for all five large runs. The highest heap value was 74 percent.

I updated the plan document with the final table. It has run time, pauses, peak p95 and peak heap for each large tenant.

The next step is the read cutover plan. I will write the order of tenants, the per-tenant flag, the comparison of results between old and new layouts for a sample of queries, and the fallback.

I will review it with Tobias and Mara before anything is switched. The migration of the index itself is separate and has not started.

summary: Read cutover plan for search written: shadow reads on the monthly layout for 10 percent of queries first, with a diff report before any tenant is switched
body:
With the dual write now covering every tenant, I wrote the read cutover plan today. Reads stay on the per-customer indexes until the monthly indexes have answered shadow queries for a full week.

Step one is shadow reads: the search API sends 10 percent of queries to both layouts, returns the old result and logs a diff of hit counts, top 10 ids and total time. The diff goes to a small table in Postgres so Sam can look at it without Grafana.

Step two is a per-tenant switch in the settings table, starting with the five smallest tenants. The large tenants come last, one per day, in the morning when Mara is online.

Step three is the rollback. The switch is a single setting, and the old indexes stay untouched for two weeks after the last tenant moves. I did not plan to delete anything before that.

Open points I listed: the boost settings are stored per index, so I need to confirm that the monthly indexes carry the same per-field boosts as the search-v2 parser expects. Also, queries with a date range over many months fan out to many indexes, and I do not yet know how slow a 13 month range is. I estimated 13 sub-requests but have no measurement.

I asked Mara to review the plan tomorrow. Next is the shadow read code in the search API, behind a flag that is off by default.

summary: Shadow read flag added to the search API behind a default-off setting; with it off, the request path is unchanged and the tests pass
body:
Started the shadow read code from the cutover plan. In the search API, a new setting shadow_read_percent defaults to 0 and is read from the settings cache.

When it is above 0, a request is picked by a hash of the request id, so the same request is not sampled twice on retry. The picked request runs the monthly query after the response is sent, so the user does not wait for it.

The monthly query builder takes the date range, lists the month indexes that overlap it and builds one multi-index search. I reused the search-v2 parser output, so both layouts see the same parsed query.

The diff is not written yet. For now the shadow result is only logged with its took time.

I added two tests: flag at 0 never calls the shadow path, and flag at 100 calls it once per request. Both pass, and the full search suite passes in 3 minutes.

Next is the diff table and the writer.

summary: Redis memory by prefix checked this morning: total 4.5 GB and the rate limiter counters stay under 200 MB, so the plan holds
body:
Routine check of Redis memory by key prefix, since the search cache keys changed last week and I wanted to see the steady state.

Total used memory is 4.5 GB. The search cache prefix is 4.1 GB, the session store 190 MB and the rate limiter counters 170 MB. Everything else together is under 40 MB.

The counters grew a little after the per-key overrides for the two large customers, because those keys now carry a second window. The growth is about 12 MB, which is fine.

I also scanned a sample of 10,000 keys for missing TTLs. Everything in the search and session prefixes has one. Two old debug keys from the migration of the accounts had none, and I deleted them by hand.

Nothing to change. I will repeat the check after the shadow reads start, because they may add a few cache keys for the monthly layout.

summary: Shadow read diff table and writer done: each sampled request stores hit count difference, top 10 overlap and both took times
body:
Finished the diff writer for the shadow reads. The table search_shadow_diff in Postgres has the tenant, a hash of the query, hits_old, hits_new, top10_overlap, took_old_ms, took_new_ms and a created_at column. It has an index on tenant and created_at, since Sam's questions will almost always be per tenant.

The writer does not write to Postgres per request. It collects rows in memory and flushes every 5 seconds or at 200 rows, whichever comes first. If the flush fails, it drops the batch and counts the drop in a metric. Losing diff rows is acceptable, slowing the search API is not.

I ran it against staging with the flag at 100 and a replay of 20,000 real queries from the log. Result: 19,640 rows match in hit count and top 10. 360 rows differ, and I looked at the first 30 of them.

Twenty-two are queries with a date range ending in the current month, where the monthly index has a few documents that the old index does not have yet, because the dual write lags by a second or two. That is expected and harmless.

The other eight are queries with a phrase and a boost on the title field, where the order of the top 10 differs in places 8 to 10 only. I suspect the scoring differences from different shard statistics, since the monthly shards hold fewer documents. I will compare the scores later.

Next is to turn the flag on at 1 percent in production tomorrow and look at real traffic.

summary: Mara reviewed the cutover plan and asked for a per-tenant diff view and a stop rule if the new layout is slower than the old one
body:
Mara read the cutover plan and left three comments.

First, she wants a stop rule written down: if the median took time of the new layout is more than 30 percent above the old one for any tenant over a day, that tenant does not move. I added it to the plan with that number.

Second, she asked for a view of the diff table by tenant, so we can see which tenants have more differences. I will add a saved query for it.

Third, she asked what happens to saved searches in the admin console, which store an index name for some old entries. I had not checked that. I will ask Lena tomorrow.

summary: Asked Lena about saved searches in the console: they store a tenant and a query string, not an index name, so the layout change does not touch them
body:
Following Mara's question I asked Lena about saved searches in the admin console.

She checked the code and the table. Saved searches store the tenant id, the query string and the filters. The index name is never stored, and the search API resolves it on each call. The few old rows with an index name in a legacy column are ignored by the code since the search API v1 was dropped.

So the layout change does not touch them. I added a line to the plan and closed the comment.

summary: Slow aggregation from the latency check traced to a terms aggregation on a high-cardinality field; a cardinality cap and a cached result bring it from 2.8 s to 300 ms
body:
The latency check last week found one slow aggregation, and I spent the afternoon on it. It is the facet for the user_agent field in the console's event view, and it took 2.8 seconds at p95 for the three large tenants.

The cause is a terms aggregation with size 500 on a field with roughly 400,000 distinct values per month. Each shard builds its own top list, and the coordinating node merges them. With the monthly layout there are more shards per query, so the merge cost grew too.

I tried three things.

1. Lower the size to 50. The console only shows 20 values, so nothing visible changes. This gave 1.6 seconds.
2. Add the shard_size parameter at 100, so shards do less work. This gave 1.1 seconds, with slightly less exact counts for the tail.
3. Cache the result in Redis for 5 minutes, with the key built from tenant, time range rounded to the hour and filters. The key follows the naming plan for the search cache, under the same prefix. A cache hit takes 300 ms including the API overhead.

I kept all three. The first call is about 1.1 seconds, and later ones within 5 minutes take 300 ms. I checked with Lena that the console shows the facet as a sidebar list and that exact counts in the tail are not promised anywhere. She said the label already says top values.

One side effect to watch: the cache key count for the search prefix will grow a little, since each tenant, range and filter combination gets its own key. I estimated 20,000 extra keys at most, about 40 MB.

I added a test that two requests with ranges within the same hour hit the same key, and one that a different filter gives a different key. Both pass.

I did not touch the other aggregations, because they are all under 400 ms. The change goes out with tomorrow's deploy. Then I will look at the p95 for this facet again after two days.

summary: Ingest client library: added a test and a docs note for the capped maximum wait of 20 seconds, after Sam found the docs still said unlimited
body:
Sam pointed out that the public docs for the ingest client library still say the wait between attempts grows without a limit. That was true before the review a few days ago, when I capped it at 20 seconds.

I fixed the docs first. The section now says: 5 attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, each wait at most 20 seconds, so a batch can take about 60 seconds in the worst case before the client gives up and returns the error to the caller.

Then I looked at whether the cap is tested. It was not. I wrote a unit test with a fake clock that forces 5 failures and checks the sequence of waits. The jitter is seeded in the test, so the values are fixed. The waits are 1, 2, 4, 8 and then 16 seconds before jitter, so the cap of 20 is never reached with 5 attempts and the defaults. To test the cap I added a second case with the base set to 10 seconds, where the waits become 10, 20, 20, 20 after the cap.

While I was there I noticed that the jitter can push a wait above the cap by up to 25 percent. The cap is applied before the jitter. I changed the order so the cap is applied after the jitter and updated the test. The docs say at most 20 seconds, so the code should do that.

The library has a changelog file. I added an entry for the patch release and bumped the version. The release is on the list for tomorrow. I did not publish it today because Mara wants to look at the order change.

I checked the two sample apps in the docs repository. Both use the defaults, so nothing changes for them.

Sam will update the support macro that quotes the retry behavior to customers.

summary: Mara approved the jitter order change in the ingest client library; the patch release goes out tomorrow morning
body:
Mara reviewed the change that applies the 20 second cap after the jitter. She approved it with one comment: the test with the seeded jitter should also assert the maximum over 1,000 draws, not only the fixed sequence.

I added that test. It draws 1,000 waits with the base at 10 seconds and checks that none is above 20 seconds and that at least one is above 15, so we know the jitter still spreads the waits.

All tests pass. The release is set for tomorrow morning, and the changelog and docs are ready.

summary: Postgres autovacuum check on the audit log table: dead tuples are low and the new tenant index did not change the vacuum time
body:
Checked the audit log table after the composite index went in. Autovacuum last ran 6 hours ago and took 41 seconds, about the same as before the index.

Dead tuples are at 12,000 on a table with 9 million rows. The table is mostly insert only, so that is expected.

The index adds 410 MB. The table is 3.1 GB, so I consider that fine. Nothing to change.

summary: First production shadow reads at 1 percent: 4,100 samples, 98.7 percent identical top 10, and the new layout is faster for short ranges but slower for ranges over 6 months
body:
Turned shadow_read_percent to 1 in production at midday and let it run through the afternoon. By evening the diff table had 4,100 rows.

Hit counts match exactly in 97.9 percent of the rows. Most of the rest are the one-to-two second lag of the dual write for documents of the current month. When I exclude queries that touch the last 5 minutes, the match rate is 99.6 percent.

The top 10 overlap is complete in 98.7 percent of the rows. I looked at the remaining rows by tenant. They are spread over many tenants, with no single tenant standing out, and they match the boost-order differences I saw in staging for positions 8 to 10.
