Times are the interesting part. For date ranges up to one month, the new layout has a median of 38 ms against 52 ms for the old one. For ranges of 1 to 6 months it is about equal. For ranges over 6 months it is slower: the median is 190 ms against 130 ms, and p95 is 640 ms against 410 ms.

That is the fan-out I worried about in the plan. A 13 month range hits 13 indexes, each with its own shards, and the coordinating node pays for it. Mara's stop rule is a 30 percent increase in the median, and the long ranges are at 46 percent. But only 6 percent of the real queries use ranges over 6 months. The overall median is better with the new layout.

I see two options for the long ranges:

- Use a coarser rollup index for ranges that start more than 6 months back. This is a lot of work and I do not like it yet.
- Reduce the number of shards per monthly index for old months, since old months do not take writes. A force merge and a shrink to one shard per old month index could remove most of the overhead.

I will try the second option on one old month in staging tomorrow and compare. I wrote the numbers into the plan under a new section. I also left the flag at 1 percent overnight and will raise it to 5 if tomorrow's numbers look the same.

summary: Evening plan review: wrote the order of the read cutover by tenant size, the checks before each move and who is awake, and listed the long range slowness as the one open risk
body:
I used the evening to turn the cutover plan into a checklist that someone else could follow, since Tobias or Sam may need to read it while I am away.

The order of the tenants is by document count, smallest first. The first group is the five smallest tenants, switched on the same morning once the diff report for the last 24 hours shows a hit count match above 99 percent for them. The second group is the next 15 tenants, 5 per day. The third group is the 15 mid-size tenants, 3 per day. The five large tenants come last, one per day, each in the morning with Mara online.

The checks before each move are the same every time:

1. The diff report for the tenant, last 24 hours, has at least 500 samples. If the tenant has fewer, we raise the sample rate for it only.
2. The hit count match is above 99 percent without the last 5 minutes.
3. The median took time is not more than 30 percent above the old layout.
4. The dual write lag metric is under 3 seconds.
5. The backfill verification for the tenant is marked done in the tracking sheet.

The rollback is the single setting for the tenant, and it takes effect after the settings cache refreshes, which is 30 seconds. I tested that on staging today. The switch back took 31 seconds, and the next request used the old layout.

I also wrote what to watch after each move: the search p95 in Grafana, the error rate on the search API, and the cache hit rate, because the cache keys do not depend on the layout and so should keep their hit rate. If the hit rate drops after a move, that points to a key bug, and we stop.

The one open risk is the long date ranges. The plan says that the first group does not start before the shrink test of old months has a result. I wrote that as a blocking item at the top.

I also noted a smaller item: the shadow diff table will grow, and I set a delete job for rows older than 14 days, so it cannot become a Postgres size problem. The job is a plain SQL delete in the nightly maintenance script and I tested it on staging.

Mara has the document and will comment tomorrow.

summary: Shrink test of an old month index in staging: one shard instead of five cut the long range median from 190 ms to 120 ms
body:
Ran the test I planned. In staging I took the monthly index for a month 9 months back, set it read only, force merged it to one segment and shrank it from five shards to one.

Then I replayed 2,000 queries with date ranges over 6 months against the old layout and the shrunk monthly layout. Median took time: old layout 135 ms, monthly before the shrink 192 ms, monthly after the shrink of all months older than 3 months 121 ms. P95 went from 650 ms to 380 ms, and the old layout was at 420 ms.

So shrinking old months more than fixes the long ranges. The shrunk indexes are also smaller on disk by about 8 percent, because the merge removes deleted documents.

The cost is a job that runs each month: when a month is 3 months old, set it read only, merge and shrink it. I will write that as a step in the nightly reindex job's neighbor script, not inside the reindex job itself.

The shrink needs a copy of the shards on one node first, which took 14 minutes for this month in staging. For production months with the large tenants, I expect more. I will schedule it outside the backup window.

I told Mara the result and unblocked the item in the plan.

summary: Wrote the monthly shrink job for old search indexes, with a dry run mode that prints which months it would touch and a guard against running during the backup window
body:
Wrote the script for the monthly shrink job in the search tooling folder. It takes the list of monthly indexes, picks those older than 3 months that still have more than one shard, and for each one does four steps: set read only, move a copy of every shard to one node, force merge to one segment and shrink to one shard.

The dry run mode, which is the default, only prints the list and the expected disk use. I added the real mode as a flag, so nobody shrinks an index by accident.

The guard checks the clock and refuses to start inside the backup window, and it also refuses to run if the cluster status is not green. It also checks that the free disk on the target node is at least twice the size of the biggest shard of the index, since the copy needs room.

One mistake I found in my first draft: I set the index read only before moving the copy, and when the copy failed, the index stayed read only. For old months that is harmless, but I changed the script to remove the read only block in a cleanup step when anything fails after it was set.

Tests: the pure parts, such as selecting months by age and computing the disk estimate, have unit tests. The cluster steps I tested on staging with two months, and both ended as one shard with a green status.

The dry run on production lists 10 months, with an estimated 380 GB of copying in total. I did not run the real mode. I will ask Tobias about the disk headroom on the data nodes before I set a date.

I added the job to the plan as a monthly step and as a prerequisite for the first tenant group.

summary: Tobias confirmed the data nodes have 40 percent free disk, enough for the shrink copies if the months run one at a time
body:
Asked Tobias about disk headroom for the shrink job. He checked the data nodes: free disk is 40 percent on all of them, and the largest old month index has shards of about 22 GB.

He said one month at a time is safe, and he does not want two in parallel. The script already runs one index at a time.

He also asked to run it outside business hours and to tell him before the first real run, so he can watch the disk graphs. I will do that.

summary: Real shrink run on the two oldest production months at quiet hour: both ended green with one shard, 9 percent smaller, and search latency stayed flat
body:
With Tobias watching the disk graphs, I ran the shrink job in real mode on the two oldest monthly indexes in the evening, after the busiest traffic had passed.

The first month took 23 minutes, and the second 19 minutes. Both ended with one shard and a green cluster status. The disk use of the first dropped from 61 GB to 56 GB, the second from 54 GB to 49 GB.

During the run, the free disk on the target node fell by at most 26 GB and came back after the old shards were removed. Search p95 in Grafana did not move, and the indexing rate of the dual write stayed the same, because these months take no writes.

I checked the shrunk indexes with a count query against the old per-customer layout for three tenants. The counts match.

One thing I did not expect: the job printed a warning that the index settings kept the old number_of_routing_shards, which only matters if somebody wants to split the index again. We do not, so I ignored it, and put the line in the notes.

Next I will run the other eight old months over the next nights, two per night. Then I rerun the long range shadow comparison.

summary: Chose a two-month-per-night schedule for the remaining shrinks and added a Grafana panel for free disk per data node so the runs can be watched
body:
Set up the schedule for the remaining eight old months. The shrink job will run at the quiet hour with two months per night, one after the other, and stop if free disk on any data node falls below 25 percent.

The 25 percent line is a new check I added to the script. Before, it only checked the target node at the start. Now it re-checks before each index. I tested it on staging by setting the line to 90 percent, and the job stopped before the first index as intended.

For watching, I added a Grafana panel with the free disk per data node and a marker for each shrink run, using an annotation the script writes at start and end. Tobias looked at it and asked for the disk line at 25 percent to be drawn on the graph, so I added it.

The schedule goes into the normal cron on the tooling host, and it uses the secret that the search tooling already has. I did not add anything new there.

Nothing was run in this session. The first scheduled night is tonight.

summary: Cache keys for shadow reads reviewed: the shadow path must not write to the search cache, and a bug that did so for 1 percent of requests is fixed
body:
While checking Redis key counts after the first day of shadow reads, I saw more new search cache keys than I expected: about 3,000 more than the number of distinct queries would explain.

I looked at the code. The shadow path calls the same query function as the normal path, and that function writes its result to the cache. So every shadow request wrote the monthly layout result under the normal cache key. The key does not include the layout, so a user who asked the same query a minute later could get the monthly result from the cache, not the old layout result.

The impact was small. The results are almost the same, as the diff table shows, and the flag was only at 1 percent. But it breaks the point of the shadow reads, since the diff would stop being a clean comparison if the cache served the monthly result for the old path.

The fix: the query function gets a parameter use_cache, and the shadow path passes false. It reads no cache and writes no cache. I added a test that runs a shadow request and then checks that no new key exists in a fake Redis.

I deleted the affected keys. I could find them because the shadow path sets a field in the stored value that the normal path does not set, so a scan with a check on that field found 3,212 keys. I removed them in batches of 500 with a short pause.

After the fix and the delete, the key count is back to the expected level. The hit rate of filtered queries did not change visibly, 60 percent before and after.

There is also a lesson for the later switch per tenant: when a tenant moves to the new layout, the cache keys of that tenant should stay valid, since the results are nearly the same. But if the boost order differs in positions 8 to 10, a user may see a different order after a cache expiry. I think that is acceptable, and I wrote it in the plan so that Sam can say it in the docs if a customer asks.

The fix is in tomorrow's deploy together with the aggregation change.

summary: First scheduled shrink night finished: two more old months are one shard each and the disk never went below 33 percent free
body:
Checked the result of the first scheduled shrink night. Both months ended with one shard and a green status. The runs took 24 and 21 minutes.

The lowest free disk on any data node during the run was 33 percent, well above the stop line of 25 percent. The annotations show up in the Grafana panel as planned.

Four old months are done now, six remain. Search p95 stayed flat overnight.

summary: Postgres slow query review: the reports page query with a sort on created_at moved to a partial index, cutting it from 1.9 s to 60 ms for the large tenants
body:
Sam forwarded a complaint from a large customer that the reports page in the console takes two seconds to open. I looked at the slow query log and found the query behind it.

It selects the latest 50 reports for a tenant with status not equal to archived, sorted by created_at descending. The table has an index on tenant_id and one on created_at, and the planner picks the created_at index, walks it backwards and filters by tenant. For a large tenant it finds its 50 rows fast, but for tenants with few reports it scans a long way, and the p95 shows it.

The EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the large tenant showed 1.9 seconds, with 410,000 rows removed by the filter. That is the problem: the planner thinks the tenant is more common than it is.

I tried a few things on a copy of the data from staging:

1. A composite index on tenant_id and created_at descending. The query dropped to 80 ms.
2. The same index as a partial index with where status is not archived. The query dropped to 60 ms, and the index is 40 percent smaller, because most old reports are archived.
3. Raising the statistics target for tenant_id. This did not change the plan.

I chose the partial index. The query in the code must have the same condition in its where clause, or the planner will not use the index, so I checked the query builder. It uses status not equal to archived in exactly this form, and I added a comment next to it so nobody changes the condition without the index.

I created the index in production with create index concurrently during a quiet hour. It took 4 minutes and did not block writes. The old created_at index is still used by the cleanup job, so I kept it.

After the index I ran the query again for five tenants, including the one that complained: 60 ms for the large one, 3 ms for the small ones.

I checked the write cost. The reports table gets about 200 inserts a minute, and the extra index did not move the insert time in a visible way.

I wrote back to Sam that the page should open fast now, and asked him to confirm with the customer. The index definition is in the migrations folder with the same name as in production, so staging and production do not drift.

One follow-up: the audit log page had the same pattern a few days ago, and I fixed it with a composite index. Maybe there are more pages with sort and tenant filter. I will grep the slow query log for the next days for queries with order by created_at and a tenant filter.

summary: Shadow reads raised to 5 percent: 21,000 samples, long range median now 118 ms against 131 ms on the old layout after the shrinks
body:
Raised shadow_read_percent to 5 now that six old months are shrunk. By the afternoon the diff table had 21,000 new rows.

The hit count match is 99.5 percent without the last 5 minutes, and the top 10 overlap is complete in 98.9 percent, so the picture is the same as at 1 percent.

Times for ranges over 6 months: the median is 118 ms on the monthly layout against 131 ms on the old one, and p95 is 400 ms against 415 ms. The slowness from the fan-out is gone for the shrunk months. Four old months are still not shrunk, and queries that reach them are slower, as I could see by splitting the samples by the oldest month in the range.

For ranges up to a month, the monthly layout is still faster, with a median of 36 ms against 51 ms.

By tenant, the five smallest tenants have 700 or more samples each, so they pass the first check of the checklist. Two of them have a hit count match of 99.2 percent, which is above the 99 line.

I am not switching any tenant until the last four months are shrunk, which is in two nights, and until Mara has seen the numbers. I will send her the saved query for the tenant view.

summary: Redis client upgrade attempt in the search API rolled back: the new minor version of the library changed how it closes idle connections and the count climbed from 190 to 330
body:
I tried a minor version upgrade of the Redis client library in the search API today, hoping for a fix for a reconnect bug that the release notes mention. It is rolled back, and the library stays on the old version for now.

The upgrade itself was simple. The API did not change, the tests passed, and staging looked normal in the first hour.

I deployed it to production at midday to one of the three search API tasks as a canary. For the first hour the canary looked fine. Then in the afternoon, when the traffic pattern changes, the connection count of the canary climbed. The three tasks together were at 190 connections before. With the canary they reached 330 after two hours, and the canary alone held about 140 of them while it carried a third of the traffic.

I looked at the library's changelog again and found the reason. A new default for the idle timeout of the pool: the pool no longer closes idle connections after the old default, but keeps them until the pool minimum is applied. We lowered the pool minimum a few days ago because the search API held many idle connections. The new default seems to bypass part of that tuning.

I tried setting the idle timeout explicitly in our config. That brought the canary down to 95 connections in the test, but one of the options in the doc is marked as changing in the next minor version, and I do not want to build on it.

The decision was to roll back the canary and leave the library alone. The reconnect bug from the release notes does not affect us, as far as I can tell. We have not seen the symptom in the logs for months.

The rollback was a redeploy of the previous image, and the count went back to 190 within ten minutes.

I wrote a note in the dependency file to wait for the next minor version, and a line in the tracking sheet to check its release notes for the idle timeout default. I also told Tobias, since the connection count also matters for the Redis server limit.

This was a quiet failure, and the only cost was the afternoon. I did not touch the pool maximum, which stays as set.

summary: Mara looked at the shadow numbers and agreed to start with the five smallest tenants once the last four old months are shrunk
body:
Sent Mara the saved query and the numbers from the 5 percent run. She looked at the per-tenant view and at the long range split.

Her comments: she agrees that the first group can start after the last four months are shrunk, and she wants the first switch on a morning when she is online. She also asked that I keep the shadow reads running at 5 percent for the tenants that have already moved, so the diff keeps being recorded and we notice if the new layout drifts.

That needs a small change, since the shadow path should then run the old layout for moved tenants. I added it to the list for tomorrow.

summary: Shadow reads now run in both directions: for tenants on the new layout the shadow path queries the old indexes, so the diff keeps working after a move
body:
Implemented Mara's request. The shadow path used to be fixed: the normal path answers from the old layout, and the shadow path asks the monthly layout. For a tenant that has moved, that would compare the monthly layout with itself.

The code now looks up the tenant's layout setting and picks the other layout for the shadow query. The diff table got a column primary_layout, so rows from before and after a move can be told apart and the saved query can group by it. The column has a default of old, so existing rows are right without a rewrite.

The diff compares hits and top 10 in both directions in the same way, and the field names hits_old and hits_new keep their meaning: old is the per-customer layout and new is the monthly one, whatever answered the user. I wrote that in a comment, since otherwise it reads wrongly.

Tests: four cases, one for each layout with the flag on and off. I also added a test for a tenant whose layout setting is missing, which falls back to old. All pass, and the search suite takes 3 minutes as before.

On staging I set one test tenant to the new layout and replayed 5,000 queries. The primary_layout column read new for those rows, the old indexes answered the shadow queries, and the match rate was the same 99.5 percent as in the other direction.

The cache path still ignores the shadow, as fixed yesterday. I checked that again with the fake Redis test.

The change goes out tomorrow with the next deploy. The remaining item before the first group is the last four shrinks, which run in two nights.

summary: Second scheduled shrink night done: two more months are single shard, with two months left for tomorrow night
body:
Checked the second scheduled night of the shrink job. Both months ended as one shard with a green status, and the runs took 25 and 22 minutes.

The lowest free disk was 34 percent, so the stop line was never close. Eight old months are done and two remain. Search p95 stayed flat.

summary: Shrink job guard checked against the backup window after a close call in the schedule: runs now abort cleanly if they overlap and resume the next night
body:
While reading tonight's shrink schedule I noticed that the second month of a night could start close to the backup window if the first month ran long. I added a check before each month, not only at job start, that compares the expected duration with the time left before the window.

If the month would not finish in time, the job stops and logs which months are left. A dry run in staging with a fake window of 20 minutes showed the stop at the right place and a clean exit code.

The next night picks up the remaining months without any manual step. Tobias was told about the change in the infrastructure channel. Tomorrow the last two old months run under this check.

summary: Wrote the per-tenant diff view for shadow reads that Mara asked for, with a stop rule that pauses sampling if the new layout is slower for a tenant
body:
Mara asked for two things in the cutover review: a diff view per tenant and a rule that stops the move if the new layout is slower. Both are in now.

The view is a Fastify route on the search API that reads the shadow diff table and groups by tenant and by range bucket: under 1 month, 1 to 6 months, over 6 months. For each group it returns sample count, share of identical top 10, median hit count difference and the median took time on both layouts. I kept the query on an index over tenant and sampled time, so it answers in about 80 ms for the 21,000 samples we have.

The stop rule is a small job that runs every 10 minutes. It compares the p50 and p95 took time of the new layout with the old one per tenant and bucket, and needs at least 200 samples in a bucket before it judges. If the new layout is slower by more than 15 percent at p95 in any bucket, it sets a flag for that tenant and writes a line to the log and to the Grafana annotations.

The flag does not change any traffic yet. It only blocks the cutover script, which checks it before moving a tenant. I tested with synthetic rows where the new layout was 30 percent slower and the flag was set after one run.

I added unit tests for the threshold edges: exactly 15 percent does not trigger, 15.1 does. A test for too few samples confirms the job stays silent.

Open: the 15 percent is a guess. With the real numbers of the long ranges it would currently not trigger, since the new layout is 118 ms against 131 ms. Mara will look at the view tomorrow and say if she wants a lower threshold for the large tenants.

summary: Postgres vacuum and bloat check on the settings tables found nothing worth acting on, so no change is planned for now
body:
Looked at the accounts and settings tables because the nightly backup got a little slower last week. Bloat estimates are under 6 percent on every table, and dead tuples are low.

Autovacuum ran on the settings tables within the last hour each time, and the longest run was 40 seconds. The backup time rose mostly because the audit log table grew, which is expected.

I did not change any vacuum setting. I wrote the numbers down so that the next check has a base to compare against. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Third shrink night finished with the last two old months at one shard each; free disk stayed above 35 percent on all data nodes
body:
The overnight shrink run processed the last two old months. Both ended green, and the shard count of each is one now. All old months before the recent window are single shard.

The disk panel showed the lowest free value of 35 percent on one data node during the copy, and it went back to 41 percent after the old shards were dropped. The guard against the backup window did not trigger.

Search latency stayed flat during the run according to the Grafana dashboard. This was the condition Mara set for starting with the smallest tenants, so it is met. I will tell her this morning and ask for her call on the start day.

summary: Mara agreed to move the five smallest tenants to the monthly layout, starting with the smallest, one per day with a check after each
body:
Talked through the start with Mara this morning. The shrinks are done, shadow reads are at 5 percent with no bucket where the new layout is slower, and the diff view is in use.

The agreed plan: one tenant per day, the smallest first. Before a move the script checks the stop flag, the share of identical top 10 (at least 98 percent for that tenant) and the free disk. After the move the shadow path queries the old indexes in the other direction, as built last week, so the diff continues.

We agreed on a 24 hour wait before the next tenant, so that a slow problem at night shows up. If a tenant shows problems, the script switches it back, and the dual write makes this safe since the old indexes stay written.

Lena will be told which tenants move on which day, since they may ask her in the console support channel. I wrote the list with tenant sizes into the plan document. The first move is planned for tomorrow morning.

summary: Redis memory by key prefix after the cache key rounding: the search cache is 2.1 GB, TTL of the filter keys cut from 1 hour to 20 minutes with no hit rate loss
body:
Ran the memory by prefix check again because the rounded cache keys from last week changed the key count. Total use is 4.6 GB. The search cache prefix is 2.1 GB, sessions 0.9 GB, the rate limiter counters under 200 MB and the rest is small prefixes.

The filtered search keys were the largest part of the cache: about 1.1 GB for 380,000 keys. With the rounding, many queries share a key, but each key still lived for one hour, and a sample of key ages showed that most keys are read in the first 15 minutes or never again.

I changed the TTL of the filter keys from 1 hour to 20 minutes in the cache module. The unfiltered query keys keep their TTL.

What I watched after the deploy:
- Hit rate of filtered queries stayed at 60 percent over two hours, the same as before.
- Key count for the prefix fell from 380,000 to about 150,000.
- Memory of that prefix fell from 1.1 GB to 450 MB.
- No change in the p95 latency of the search API.

I also checked for keys without any TTL, since a bug could leave some. The scan found 212 keys without TTL, all from an old debug prefix of a script. I deleted them and removed the script's write.

The key naming document got a line saying that every new prefix needs a TTL and an owner. Next I will look at the session prefix, which grows more than the number of active users explains.

summary: Session keys in Redis grew faster than active users; found that the console refreshed the session TTL on every poll, fixed with a refresh at most once a minute
body:
The session prefix is 0.9 GB for about 600 active users, which is too much. Looking at a few keys showed the size was fine, around 1.4 KB each, but the count was 640,000.

The cause was in the console session middleware: each request wrote the session again to extend the TTL, and the old sessions of the same user were not replaced, because the session id was rotated on each write for one code path. That path is the dashboard polling, every 15 seconds.

I changed the middleware so that the TTL is extended at most once a minute per session, using a timestamp inside the session, and the id is only rotated at login. Lena reviewed the change since it touches the console.

After the deploy the write rate to Redis from the console fell by about 70 percent. The old keys expire by their TTL over the next day, so the count will fall without a cleanup. I will check the prefix size again tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why a customer sees a short delay in search results after an import: the index refresh is one second plus the queue time
body:
Sam asked for a sentence for the docs: a customer imported a file and searched at once and saw nothing. I checked the path. An event goes through the queue, the worker, then the bulk write to OpenSearch, and the index refresh interval is one second.

In normal load the whole path takes 2 to 4 seconds at p95. During a big import the queue time dominates, and I saw up to 40 seconds for a file of 2 million events.

Suggested the wording: results usually appear within a few seconds, and after large imports it can take a minute. Sam took this into the docs draft and will ask Lena to put a short hint in the import dialog.

summary: Prepared the first tenant move to the monthly search layout: the pre-move checks are scripted and tested on a copy, and the smallest tenant is planned for the next quiet window
body:
I spent this morning getting ready to move the smallest tenant to the monthly search layout. Nothing has been switched yet, and the tenant still reads from the old indexes.

The move script now runs three checks before it does anything. It looks at the stop flag, which has to be clear. It reads the identical top 10 share from the diff view, and I set the threshold at 99 percent over at least 1,500 samples. The last run for this tenant gave 99.1 percent over 1,900 samples, so it is above the line. It also checks the free disk, which has to be above 35 percent on every data node. The lowest node is at 38 percent right now.

The move itself is a single switch in the tenant setting that makes the search API read from the monthly indexes. I ran the script in dry-run mode against a copy of the settings. It printed the change it would make and took about 4 seconds. The settings cache in the search API should pick up a change within a minute, and I checked the cache TTL in the code to confirm that.

I also looked at the saved searches, since a switch of the read path could break them. Lena confirmed they store tenant and query only, with no index names. So I expect a saved query from this tenant to return the same hits after the move. I wrote that test search down in the plan document, so I can run it right after the switch and compare it with the result I took today.

I added a section to the plan document with the order of steps, the numbers to compare (request count, median and p95 took time, shadow path diff) and the rollback, which is to set the tenant setting back. Mara read it and had no objections.

The plan is to move the tenant in the next quiet window, then watch the error logs and the diff view for a few hours before deciding about the next tenant.

summary: Added a layout_move audit log entry type and a Grafana annotation to the cutover script, tested on staging, ahead of the first tenant move to the monthly search layout.
body:
Sam asked last week how support can know which layout a tenant is on when a customer reports a strange result. Today I added an audit log entry type, layout_move, to be written by the cutover script with the tenant, the direction, the time and the operator name. The audit log is in Postgres, so this needed one enum value and a small migration. It ran in under a second on staging.

The admin console already lists audit entries by type, so the new type shows up without a change. Lena checked that an unknown type does not break the filter list; it displays the raw name, and she will give it a nicer label later.

I also made the script write a Grafana annotation for each move, so the latency graphs show the moment of the switch. A test run of the script against staging in dry mode produced both the audit entry and the annotation, and the operator name was filled in correctly.

The last shrink night left the disk free space above 35 percent on all data nodes, so the plan holds. Mara and I agreed to start with the smallest tenant and move one per day, with a check after each. For the first move I want a quiet hour, so I will look at the traffic graph at 14:00 and pick the slot then. I also prepared the diff view sample set of 2,600 queries for that tenant, and the stop flag is clear and tested. Nothing has been moved yet; the first move comes after the traffic check.

summary: Postgres slow query review of the week: the audit log export count query and the tenant list query were slow, the second one fixed with an index
body:
Went through the slow query log of the last week. Four queries were above 500 ms more than ten times. Two of them are the same count query of the audit log page, one is a batch job and one is the tenant list in the admin console.

The tenant list query sorted by last activity and joined the settings table. Explain showed a sequential scan on the settings table with 40 tenants times many setting rows, 350 ms on average. An index on the settings table by tenant and key brought the plan to an index scan and the time to 6 ms. The index builds in a few seconds, so I created it with the concurrent option in the migration.

The audit log count query counts all rows for the filter to show a total on the page. For the large tenants this took 800 ms to 1.4 s. Options I considered:
- A cached count with a short TTL in Redis.
- An estimate from the planner statistics.
- Removing the exact total and showing 'more than 10,000'.

I did not decide alone, because it changes what the page shows. I wrote the three options and the times in a note for Lena, who owns the page. The batch job query is a nightly job and 600 ms is no problem.

I also checked that the new index did not slow down the writes to the settings table; the settings table gets under 50 writes a day, so it does not matter.

Nothing was changed for the audit log count yet. Lena will answer tomorrow, and then I will do the one she prefers.

summary: Prepared the second tenant move to the monthly layout: the pre-checks ran on 1,400 samples and the differences came from tie order, so the move waits for the quiet hour
body:
The second smallest tenant is the next one for the monthly layout. The traffic graph showed a low point at 14:00, so I planned the move for that quiet hour and ran the checks ahead of time. The stop flag is clear, free disk is 38 percent, and the top 10 over 1,400 samples is 98.8 percent identical between the old and the new layout. The move itself has not been started.

The lower identical share than the first tenant made me look at the differing samples. 17 of the 1,400 differed in the order of the lower hits of the top 10, with equal scores. This is the tie order between shards, and with the monthly layout the tie break goes by index name. It is not a real difference in the results.

I compared median took time and p95 on the test queries against the current numbers: the median is 55 ms and p95 is 205 ms on the old layout. These are the numbers I will compare against in the first hour after the move, together with the error rate.

I wrote a note in the plan document about the ties so that nobody is surprised by the diff numbers of the next tenants. Should it matter, a tie break on the event id can be added to the query, but customers have not asked for a stable order of equal hits. I will leave it for now. Next is the move itself, and then watching the first hour.

summary: Tried a streaming JSON parser in the ingest API to cut allocations, measured a 6 percent gain and dropped it because the error messages for bad batches got worse
body:
The profile of the ingest API under the load test showed that JSON decoding of the batches is the top allocation source, so I tried a streaming decoder library as a drop-in for the standard one in the batch handler.

Setup: the load test with the recorded batch sizes, 30 minutes per run, three runs per variant, on the staging ECS tasks with the same size as production.

Results:
- Allocations per request fell by 31 percent.
- CPU of the API tasks fell by about 6 percent at the same request rate.
- p95 latency of the ingest call did not change in a way I could separate from the noise between runs.

The problem showed up in the tests for bad input. The standard decoder reports the offset and the field of a type error. The streaming library reports a generic syntax error for the batch without an offset in several cases, for example a number where a string is expected inside a nested object. Our API returns this message to the customer, and Sam says that support relies on the offset when customers send a broken batch.

I tried to rebuild the offset by decoding the failed batch again with the standard decoder only on the error path. That works, but it adds code and a second decode of a batch of up to 5 MB on the error path, and it makes two parsers with different rules for what is valid. One test input with a trailing comma was accepted by the new library and rejected by the old one, which would change behavior for customers.

With a gain of 6 percent CPU and these two risks I decided to drop it. The branch of the experiment is deleted, and the numbers are in this entry. If CPU becomes a problem in the ingest tasks, the batch writes already planned are a better lever. Nothing was changed in production.

summary: Lena chose the 'more than 10,000' display for the audit log total; the exact count query is gone from the page load
body:
Lena answered the note about the audit log count. She prefers to show 'more than 10,000' once the filter matches that many rows, and the exact number below that. Customers look at the first page and the filters, not at the total.

I changed the query to count with a limit of 10,001 rows inside a subselect. For the large tenants this takes 9 ms instead of 800 ms to 1.4 s. For small results the number is exact as before.

The API returns a flag for 'capped', and Lena changed the label in the console. Tests cover the exact cases of 0, 10,000 and 10,001 rows.

summary: Third tenant move held back for a day after the diff view showed a low top 10 match; the cause was a stale alias, not the layout.
body:
Before the third move the script refused to run: the identical top 10 share for this tenant was 94.6 percent, under the 98 percent needed. I looked at the diff view for the tenant and then at the stored samples.

The differing samples had a pattern. Almost all were queries with a date filter on the last 30 days, and the old layout returned more hits. The hit count difference was positive, between 3 and 40 hits.

I first suspected the monthly layout was missing documents, which would have been serious. I checked the document counts per month for the tenant on both sides, and they matched to the document. So the data was not the problem.

The next suspect was the query building. The shadow path builds the monthly index list from the date range. For ranges that start in the previous month, the list used the month of the end date and the month before, but the filter 'last 30 days' is computed on each side at slightly different times, since the shadow query runs after the main one. That would only cause tiny differences, not 40 hits.

The real cause was in the alias of the old layout. The tenant has a per-customer alias with a filter on a field that was renamed two years ago, and a few hundred old documents are not returned by the alias on the old layout. The monthly layout has no such alias and returns them. So the new layout is more complete here.

I confirmed with a direct query on the old index with and without the alias filter: the difference was 212 documents, exactly matching the extra hits.

This is not a bug of the new layout, but it is a visible change for the customer. I asked Sam to check whether the customer ever reported missing events. The move waits until Sam answers, and I wrote the 212 documents and the alias in the plan document. Tomorrow I will decide with Mara whether to fix the alias on the old layout, which no longer matters after the move, or to just move.

summary: Wrote the ingest client library docs for the batch size limit and the jitter, and added an example that shows the capped wait with the three retry attempts
body:
Sam's docs review pointed out that the client library page explains the retry settings but not the batch limits, which customers hit first. I wrote the missing part and an example that matches the real behavior.

The batch limit section says a batch can have up to 5,000 events or 5 MB, whichever comes first, and that larger batches get a 413 response with the limit named in the message. I checked the limit values in the ingest API config before writing them, since the docs once had an old number.

The example sends a batch against a server that answers 503 twice and then 200. The output shows the three attempts, the waits with jitter, and the cap of 20 seconds that the last patch release added. I ran the example against the staging API with a fault switch and pasted the real output, with the random waits marked as examples.

Facts I checked while writing:
- Default attempts are 3, and the first wait is about 500 ms with jitter.
- The wait doubles per attempt and stops at the cap.
- The client does not retry on 400 or 413, only on 429, 502, 503 and 504 and on connection errors.
- A 429 with a Retry-After header uses the header value, up to the cap.

The last point was not documented at all. I tested it with a fake server that sent Retry-After 3 and the client waited three seconds.

Sam read the page and asked to explain what a customer should do if all attempts fail. I added a short paragraph: keep the batch, wait, and send it again later; the events carry ids, so a repeated batch does not create duplicates within the dedupe window of 24 hours. I checked the dedupe window in the worker code and it is 24 hours.

The page is in the docs repo as a pull request. Sam will review the wording, and I will fix the remaining comments tomorrow.

summary: Decided with Mara to move the third tenant to the monthly layout anyway, because the extra 212 documents are old events the alias hid and Sam found no customer report about them.
body:
Sam checked the support history of the third tenant and found nothing about missing events. The customer has never asked about events from before the field rename, so no one relies on them being hidden or shown.

Mara and I looked at the numbers together. The hit count differences are all positive, from the old documents the alias filter hid, and they only appear for queries whose date range reaches back before the rename. For recent ranges, the top 10 matches. We agreed that the new layout showing complete data is the right result and that the old alias is just a historic mistake. So the decision is to go ahead with this tenant when its turn comes.

To keep the stop rule useful, I changed the diff job so that it can mark a known cause per tenant. For this tenant, samples whose old-layout result excludes the documents of the renamed field are counted as explained, and do not lower the identical share. The rule is a filter on the tenant and a date, and it is stored in the settings, so it is visible and can be removed.

With the explained samples excluded, the share is 99.0 percent over 2,100 samples, above the limit. That is the number I will check again before the move.

For the plan of the move, the checks I want to see are:
- Free disk above the limit; it was 39 percent at the last look.
- A clean first half hour on the shadow load, with no errors.
- Median latency close to the old layout, which is 50 ms today.
- Long range queries in line with the other tenants, around 130 ms.

I picked a quiet period for it, the same as for the second tenant.

I also searched the other tenants for the same alias issue, using the alias filter on all customer aliases. Only one more alias has a filter like this, for a tenant that is fourth in the order. I wrote this into the plan so it is no surprise when its turn comes.

I will tell Lena that the third tenant might show a few more old events in the console for long ranges. She does not expect questions.

summary: Session prefix in Redis fell from 640,000 to 9,100 keys after the TTL fix, memory of the prefix is now 38 MB
body:
Checked the session prefix as planned. The old rotated sessions expired by their TTL, and the count is 9,100 for about 600 active users, which is the expected size.

The prefix now uses 38 MB instead of 0.9 GB. Total Redis memory is 3.8 GB. The write rate from the console is lower than before the fix, and the Redis latency graph shows a lower p99.

No user reported logouts. I closed the topic in the plan and noted the numbers for later comparisons.

summary: Prepared the fourth tenant's move to the monthly search layout after finding why its diff came in under the limit, and left the move itself for later.
body:
The fourth tenant in the order has the second alias with a filter, as I found earlier. The diff for it showed 96.8 percent identical, under the limit, so the script refused to run the move, as designed.

I ran the direct query on the old index with and without the alias filter again. The difference was 61 documents, which matches the extra hits in the differing samples. It is the same cause as with the third tenant: documents from before a field rename that the alias hid.

I drafted an explained-samples rule for this tenant. It lets a sample count as matching when the only difference is a document that the alias filter hid and that is older than the rename. With the rule applied in a dry run, the share was 99.2 percent over 1,700 samples. That is over the limit, but I did not change the script's settings or run anything against the live index.

Mara had agreed to this kind of rule for the third tenant, so I did not ask her again about the idea. I wrote her a line with the 61 documents, the dry run number and the rule text, so she can object before the move.

I also checked the baseline for the later comparison: the median is 66 ms and p95 is 250 ms on the old layout for this tenant, and the free disk is 39 percent, enough for the extra copy.

One tenant is left in the first five after this one. Its alias has no filter, so I expect a plain diff. I plan to move the fourth tenant first, if Mara has no objection and the night is quiet.

summary: Redis version upgrade to the next minor release in staging: no change in the connection count or the latency, production is planned for a quiet hour
body:
Upgraded the staging Redis to the next minor version of the same major line. Tobias changed the version in the Terraform module, and the node was replaced at 12:30 with a short outage in staging only.

Checks I ran afterwards:
- The connection count of the search API, which went wrong with the client library change, stayed at 190, the same as before.
- The latency of the cache reads and writes in the load test was equal, p99 at 1.2 ms.
- The memory use for the same data set was the same within 1 percent.
- The rate limiter script worked and the counters matched.

I also read the release notes for changes that could affect us. The notes list a fix for a rare crash with a certain command and some changes in the slow log format. Our monitoring reads the slow log with a parser, so I ran it against the new format. It still parsed all lines.

I asked Tobias for the production step. The plan is a replica first, then a switch in a quiet hour, with the connection pool at its limit watched. He will do it on the next quiet morning, and I will watch the graphs with him.

summary: Prepared the fifth small tenant for the move to the monthly search layout: checks run and the plan written down, nothing switched yet.
body:
The fifth tenant's checks passed without any special rule: 99.3 percent identical top 10 over 1,600 samples, stop flag clear, free disk 39 percent. I did not run the move yet. The plain diff showed no stale alias and no hidden filter, so nothing needs the kind of decision we made for the third and fourth tenants.

Before the switch I looked at the baseline for this tenant on the old layout. In the last 20 minutes of a normal quiet period it brought about 70 requests, no errors, and a median of 40 ms. That is the number the move will be measured against, and I saved it next to the diff report so the comparison is easy later.

The tenants that are already on the new layout give a consistent picture over the last days: median took times equal or a little lower, p95 equal, long ranges at about 130 ms. No customer contacted support about search results, and Sam confirmed that again today.

I checked with a dry run on staging that the script will write the audit entry and the Grafana annotation when the switch runs, and that no import is running for this tenant. The move is planned for the next quiet slot, after Mara has seen the diff report.

After that comes the question of how fast to go for the middle-sized tenants. I started a draft of a proposal for Mara with the order, the disk need for each one and the wait time between moves.

summary: Wrote the proposal for moving the middle-sized tenants to the monthly search layout: two per day with a 12 hour check, the stop rule per tenant, and the disk and shadow load numbers behind it
body:
No tenant has been moved to the monthly layout yet, so I wrote the proposal for the first group of 15 middle-sized tenants, for Mara to review before anything is switched.

The main question was the pace. A one-tenant-per-day pace would be slow for 15 tenants, so I looked at what limits it: the disk for the new monthly writes, the load of the shadow reads in both directions, and the attention needed for the checks.

Disk: the dual write already writes both layouts, so a move does not need more disk. The shrunk old months freed about 9 percent, and the lowest data node has 38 percent free. The middle group has about 22 percent of all documents, and all of it is already in the new indexes.

Shadow load: at 5 percent sampling, the shadow queries add about 4 percent to the search cluster load. The sampling rate per tenant is the same, so the load does not grow with the number of tenants. I checked the CPU graph of the data nodes, which stays under 45 percent in the busy hours.

Checks: the script already checks the flag, the identical share and the disk. The new element for the middle group is a rule for the aliases with filters. I ran the alias scan on all customer aliases again, and none of the middle tenants has one. So no explained-samples rules are expected.

The proposal says:
- Two tenants per day, one in the morning and one in the afternoon, always in a quiet hour for the tenant.
- A 12 hour check before the next pair, with the stop flag, the error rate and the p95 per bucket.
- A pause of two days after the first pair, to make sure that the larger traffic does not show a slow problem.
- A switch back for any tenant whose p95 is more than 15 percent over the old layout in a bucket.

I also listed the risk that the middle tenants have more long range queries, since they have more history. There is no data from real moved tenants yet. To get a first number I ran the long range queries of the middle tenants from the shadow samples only: 3,800 samples, median 140 ms new against 151 ms old.

The large tenants stay out of this proposal. Their plan is a separate one, after the middle group is done. I sent the proposal to Mara and will go through her comments tomorrow.

summary: Production Redis minor upgrade done by Tobias in a quiet hour: the replica switch took 6 seconds and the connection count held at 190
body:
Tobias and I did the production Redis upgrade at 16:00 after the staging check. He upgraded the replica first, let it catch up, then switched over.

What we saw:
- The switch took 6 seconds, in which the search API served cache misses from OpenSearch and the console sessions kept working, since the clients reconnected.
- The connection count of the search API stayed at 190 after the reconnect, and the ingest workers' count did not move.
- Cache hit rate dropped for two minutes and came back to 60 percent for filtered queries.
- The p99 of the Redis commands is 1.2 ms, same as before.

The rate limiter counters survived the switch because the replica had them. A short check of three API keys showed the counters continued from their values.

Tobias then upgraded the former primary and it joined as the replica. All done in 25 minutes. I wrote the versions and times in the infrastructure notes. No follow-up is needed except the usual watching of the memory graph for a day.

summary: Mara's review of the middle tenants proposal: she wants one pair per day first, a lower stop threshold of 10 percent, and a report of the long range numbers per tenant
body:
Mara read the proposal and sent comments. She agrees with the order and the checks, but has three changes.

First, the pace: she wants one pair per day for the first week and only then more, since the middle tenants have real traffic and she prefers to see a few days of data. I changed the plan to one pair per day for the first five days. That moves 10 tenants in five days and the last five later.

Second, the stop threshold: 15 percent at p95 is too loose for tenants with many queries. She asked for 10 percent for tenants with more than 5,000 queries a day. I changed the stop job so that the threshold depends on the query volume of the tenant over the last day. The setting is in the config with both values. Tests cover the switch at 5,000 queries and the rule that the minimum sample count is unchanged.

Third, a report of long range numbers per tenant, since long ranges were the one open risk. I added a table to the diff view and an export as CSV for the plan document. For each tenant it shows the share of queries over 6 months, and the median and p95 on both layouts.

I ran the new report on the existing data. The five moved tenants have a long range share of 2 to 7 percent, with medians equal to the old layout within 10 ms. For the middle tenants the share from the shadow samples is 5 to 14 percent, which is why Mara wanted this.

One more point she raised was who is awake during a move. The pairs are in the morning and the afternoon, in working hours, and I am on the on-call list for the week, so a problem would reach me. She wants the PagerDuty alert for the search error rate to include the tenant name; I checked and it already does.

The plan document has the new version. The first pair of the middle group can start the day after tomorrow, once the Redis graph shows a stable day.

summary: Search latency check at the end of the week: p95 of the search API is 190 ms, the slowest remaining route is the tenant facet query at 640 ms
body:
Looked at the search API latency by route over the last week to see what else is slow while the layout work goes on. The overall p95 is 190 ms, down from 230 ms a month ago, mostly from the cache key rounding and the shrunk old months.

By route, the slowest is the facet query that fills the filter sidebar in the console: p95 640 ms and median 210 ms. It runs a terms aggregation on three fields for each page load of the search page, and the result rarely changes within a minute.

I tried a cache of the facet result for 60 seconds keyed by tenant, query and the three fields, in the same cache module as the search results. On staging with replayed traffic, the hit rate was 38 percent and the p95 of the route fell to 410 ms. The hit rate is lower than for search results since the facet queries carry the free text of the user.

I did not deploy it yet. A cache for facets means that the numbers in the sidebar can be 60 seconds old while the hit list is live, and Lena should decide if that is acceptable. I wrote her the numbers and a screenshot of how the two would look together.

The other routes are fine: the saved search list is 30 ms and the suggestion route is 90 ms at p95.

While at it I checked the cost of the shadow reads in the same numbers. They do not appear in the route latency, since they run after the response is sent, and the CPU graph shows the 4 percent expected. Next step is Lena's answer on the facet cache, and then the first pair of middle tenants.

summary: Wrote the runbook for moving a tenant to the monthly search layout, with checks before, the switch step and the way back, so anyone on the team can do a move.
body:
Until now the steps for a tenant move were only in the proposal and in the heads of the user and Mara. Five small tenants were prepared with checks and a written plan, but nothing was switched yet, so the runbook is written from the plan and from the staging notes. It now lives in the docs folder of the repo and has three parts.

Before the move: confirm the shadow diff for the tenant is above 90 percent on the top 10 match, check that free disk on every data node is above 35 percent, and make sure no import is running for the tenant. The import check is a query on the loader job table in Postgres that must return zero rows.

The switch: set the tenant flag in the settings table, wait for the search API config reload (it takes up to 30 seconds), then run one known query per route and compare the index names in the response debug header. The audit log entry for the layout move is written by the flag change itself, so nobody has to add it by hand.

The way back: flip the flag again. The plan is to keep the old indexes for 14 days after a move, so the old layout stays complete and current as long as the double write is on. The double write goes through the reindex path, and the runbook says to check its lag before a rollback, because a lag over a few minutes means the old index misses recent events.

I added a short list of what to look at in the first 12 hours: the per-tenant diff view, the p95 for the tenant, and the error rate on the search route. The stop rule from Mara's review is written in as a 10 percent threshold.

Sam read the draft and asked for a plain sentence on what customers may notice. The answer is nothing, except that a few old documents hidden by stale aliases can show up in results. That sentence is in now. Next is the dry run of the runbook by Tobias on the staging cluster.

summary: Dry run of the move runbook on staging found two wrong steps and a missing check for running imports; fixed in the runbook and the flag script, and the script now refuses to switch during an import
body:
Tobias followed the new runbook on the staging cluster without help from me, to see where it fails for someone who did not write it. He took about 40 minutes for one tenant, and found three problems.

First, the runbook named the settings column wrongly: the flag is search_layout and not layout_version. He lost ten minutes on that before he found it in the schema. Fixed in the text.

Second, the wait for the config reload was written as 30 seconds, but on staging the reload is slower because the poll interval is 60 seconds there. I changed the text to say to look at the config version in the debug header instead of waiting a fixed time. That is safer on production too.

Third, and the one that matters: nothing stopped him from switching a tenant while an import was running. The runbook only said to check it by hand. During his dry run a small CSV import was in flight and the new events went to the old index only for about two minutes, which the diff view showed as a dip. No data was lost, because the double write covers it, but the check should not depend on a person.

I changed the flag script in scripts/tenant-layout. It now queries the loader job table and exits with a clear message if the tenant has a job in state running or queued. There is an override flag, --force, for the case where the import is stuck, and it writes the reason into the audit log entry.

I added three tests for the script: no job, a running job, and a queued job with the force flag. They run against a throwaway Postgres in the test setup, which takes about 4 seconds.

Tobias also suggested printing the old index names and the planned deletion date at the end of a move, so support can answer a question about the old data. That is done as well, and the date is the move plus 14 days.

The runbook is now version 2. The next dry run is not needed, but Tobias will do the first production move of the middle tenants with me watching, once Mara has seen the long range numbers report.

summary: Redis memory by prefix after the session fix: total used memory dropped from 6.4 GB to 5.1 GB, and the rate limiter counters are now the second largest prefix
body:
I looked at the Redis memory again after the session key fix of two days ago, to see what is left to trim. The command was a scan with a sample of the key sizes, grouped by the first two parts of the key name.

Total used memory went from 6.4 GB to 5.1 GB. The session prefix is small now. The search cache stays at 2.1 GB, as expected, and the rate limiter counters are the second largest at about 900 MB.

The counters looked too big for what they do, so I checked how many keys they have. There are 3.1 million, because the limiter writes one key per API key per window of one minute, and the windows are kept with a TTL of 24 hours although only the last 5 minutes are ever read. The 24 hours came from the first version of the limiter, when the dashboards showed the usage per day from these keys. That feature moved to ClickHouse long ago.

I did not change it yet. The limiter is also in the rate-limits work of earlier months and I want Mara to confirm that nothing reads the old windows. I wrote the question into the team notes with the key pattern and the code search result, which shows two readers: the limiter itself and an old admin script.

The rest of the memory is small things: the facet cache at 300 MB, the import progress keys at 80 MB, and some leftover keys from a feature flag experiment that have no TTL, about 12,000 keys. I deleted the flag keys by hand after checking the names in the code.

Next step is a TTL cut for the limiter windows once Mara answers.

summary: Mara confirmed nobody reads the old rate limiter windows; TTL cut from 24 hours to 10 minutes, with a keys count of 3.1 million falling to about 260,000 within the hour
body:
Mara answered the question from yesterday: the admin script that reads old windows was for a usage report that Sam stopped using last year, and it can go. I deleted the script and its entry in the scripts readme.

The change is small. In the limiter module the TTL for a window key is now 10 minutes instead of 24 hours. The read side looks at the current and the last 4 windows, so 10 minutes leaves a margin of 5 minutes. I added a test that sets the clock forward by 6 minutes and checks that the count of the first window is no longer seen, and one that checks the limiter still blocks a key that sends 100 requests in a minute.

I deployed it in the quiet hour before noon. The key count of the limiter prefix started to fall as soon as the old keys expired, but only the keys written after the deploy get the new TTL. The old ones keep the 24 hours. So I ran a one-time script that sets the TTL of the old keys to 10 minutes, in batches of 5,000 with a pause of 50 ms between batches, so the Redis latency does not move.

Results after an hour: 3.1 million keys fell to about 260,000, memory of the prefix from 900 MB to 75 MB, and total used memory is now 4.3 GB. The p99 command latency on Redis stayed at 1.2 ms during the cleanup, and the connection count stayed at 190.

The limiter behaved the same in the logs: the number of 429 responses per hour was within the normal range.

I put the new numbers on the Grafana memory panel as annotations so the drop is easy to explain later. The next topic for Redis is the key naming, where a few old prefixes still have no common pattern.

summary: Answered Sam about why the tenant facet query is the slowest search route: it counts over all fields without a filter, and the monthly layout will help but not fix it
body:
Sam asked why one customer sees the tenant facet in the console load slowly, sometimes over half a second. I looked at the route, which showed up as the slowest one in the latency check at the end of last week at 640 ms.

The facet query asks OpenSearch for counts of five fields over the whole tenant, with no time range, because the console shows an overview of all data. For a large tenant that means touching every shard of the tenant index. The cache helps for repeated calls, with a TTL of 20 minutes, but the first call after the TTL is always slow.

The monthly layout should help in two ways. Small and middle tenants will have fewer, smaller shards to touch, and old months are single shard after the shrinks. For the large tenants it does not reduce the work much, since they have data in every month.

I told Sam that the delay is expected for the first call, and gave him a short text for customers: the overview refreshes every 20 minutes and the first load after that can take a second. A real fix would be to compute the counts in a background job and store them, which I wrote down as an idea for later, not planned yet.

Sam will put the text into the support notes. No code change today.

summary: Wrote the query-report script for Mara's per tenant long range numbers of the search layout test, so the plan for the first pair of middle tenants can be discussed once the table is ready.
body:
Mara asked for a report of the long range numbers per tenant before the middle tenants are planned. I wrote a script that reads the shadow samples from the last 5 days and prints median, p95 and the top 10 match for three query classes: short range (up to 7 days), medium (up to 90 days) and long range (over 90 days). The samples come from the shadow runs, where each query is sent to both the customer layout and the monthly layout, so the two sets of numbers are for the same queries.

The script is query-report in the tools folder of the search API. It reads the samples from the shadow table in Postgres, groups by tenant and class, and writes a Markdown table and a CSV. I ran it on a small sample first, to check the grouping, and the class borders were off by one day for queries that end exactly at 90 days. I fixed that and added a test with three such queries.

I also decided what goes into every row: tenant, class, sample count, median and p95 for both layouts, the difference in percent, and the top 10 match. The sample count is there because the smallest tenant has only about 640 samples in 5 days, so its numbers will be noisy, and I did not want anybody to read too much into them.

One open point is the top 10 match for the tenant with the alias that hid 212 documents on the old layout. That was decided last week, but the match will be lower for that tenant, so I added a note column to the table where I can write the reason.

The full run over all tenants is still ahead. I plan to run it in the next hours, send the table to Mara, and ask her which two tenants of the middle group should go first. The move itself needs the disk check on the data nodes before any date is set.

summary: Free disk check before the first middle tenant pair: all data nodes above 38 percent free, and the two tenants add about 140 GB for the new indexes during the double write
body:
Before the first pair of middle tenants moves, I checked the disk space on the data nodes. The runbook asks for more than 35 percent free on every node, and the double write needs extra room for the new indexes while the old ones stay for 14 days.

The lowest node has 38.4 percent free, the others are between 41 and 47 percent. The two tenants have 96 GB and 44 GB of data on the old layout. With one replica the new indexes add about 140 GB in total across the nodes, which would bring the lowest node to about 35 percent. That is too close to the limit.

The shrinks of the old months freed space earlier, but the old indexes of the five small tenants are still there for their 14 days. The first of them will be deleted tomorrow, which gives back about 6 GB on each node. I decided to move only one of the two tenants tomorrow and the second one the day after, which is still one pair in two days and keeps the margin.

I wrote this into the plan and told Mara. Tobias will watch the disk panel during the move. No change to the cluster today.

summary: Fixed the console search box sending a query on every keystroke after Lena saw the request rate in the logs; the debounce was lost in a refactor and is back with a test
body:
Lena noticed in the search API logs that one admin session produced about 40 requests in 10 seconds while typing a query. The console search box should wait 300 ms after the last keystroke before it sends.

I looked at the history of the component. The debounce was there until a refactor two months ago that moved the input state into a custom hook. The new hook calls the search function inside the change handler directly, and the debounced version was only used by the old component, so the wrapper was dropped by accident. Nobody saw it because the cache absorbed most of the duplicate calls, which also explains why the hit rate of the search cache looked fine.

The fix is in the hook: the value is stored at once for the input, and a second state with the debounced value, updated by a timer of 300 ms, feeds the query. I also made the previous request abort when a new one starts, using the abort controller, so slow old answers cannot overwrite new ones. That was a second bug, visible as a flicker of results when typing fast.

Tests: Lena's component tests use fake timers. I added three cases: typing five characters in 200 ms sends one request, typing with a pause of 400 ms sends two, and an older response arriving late is ignored. All pass, and the full console test run takes 52 seconds as before.

I checked in the staging console by hand. Typing a 12 character query sends one request now, and the network panel shows the aborted ones when I type with pauses.

On production, the search request rate from the console should drop. I will compare the count per hour tomorrow with the same hour a week ago, since the cache hit rate will probably fall a little, because fewer duplicate keys mean fewer free hits. That is fine.

Lena reviewed the change and approved with one comment about the name of the hook state, which I changed. It is merged and will go out with the afternoon deploy.

summary: Went through the Redis key names and wrote the naming rule: app, purpose, tenant, then the id, with a list of seven old prefixes to rename and three that can stay
body:
The Redis key names grew over three years and the memory work of the last days showed that finding a prefix is harder than it should be. Today I made a list of all prefixes with a sample of keys per prefix and who writes them.

There are 14 prefixes. Four follow a pattern that was never written down: service name, purpose, tenant id, then the rest, like search:cache:t123:abc. Seven use their own order, for example t123:facets or cache_search_t123, and three are from the console session library with names fixed by the library.

The rule I wrote into the docs folder is: service, purpose, tenant, then the id or hash, separated by colons, all lower case. Keys that belong to no tenant use a dash in place of the tenant. The reason is practical: with a fixed order, one scan pattern gives the memory of a tenant or of a purpose, and a delete by tenant is one pattern.

The seven old prefixes to rename are the facet cache, two import progress keys, the rate limiter windows, the feature flag cache, the audit export status and the schema registry lock. The three that stay are the session keys of the library and its two helper keys.

Renaming keys in a running system needs care. For caches, the simplest way is to change the code to write the new name and let the old keys expire by their TTL, which is at most 20 minutes for the facet cache. For the limiter, the windows live 10 minutes now, since the change of two days ago, so the same works. The import progress keys and the audit export status live for hours, and a rename in the middle of a job would lose the progress, so for those the code reads the new name first and the old name as fallback for one release.

I wrote a small helper, redisKey(service, purpose, tenant, id), in the shared package and a lint rule that flags string concatenation with a colon in a call to a Redis client method. The lint rule found 23 places, of which I changed the 9 in the search API today and put the rest into the task list for Mara's service.

The tests for the helper cover the lower case rule and the dash for no tenant. Next is the rename of the facet cache and the limiter keys, one pull request each.

summary: Prepared the first middle tenant move to the monthly layout with Tobias: import check, diff view and disk margin all reviewed, and the runbook walked through step by step.
body:
This was the preparation for the first move of a middle-sized tenant, the one with 44 GB, planned for the quiet hour before noon. I went through the runbook line by line with Tobias, who will be on the disk and cluster panels during the move.

First I checked the import state. The import check returned no running jobs for the tenant, and I asked Sam to tell the customer contact that no large file import should start in the quiet hour. The diff view for the tenant showed a top 10 match of 97.9 percent between the old and the new layout. The shadow sample count was high enough, 4,800 samples over the last days, so the comparison is solid enough to start.

I read the flag script again and ran it in dry mode. It printed the old index names with the planned deletion date and did not switch anything. I also checked how the config version reaches the search API tasks: the version in the debug header should change within about 20 seconds on all tasks, and I wrote down the known queries per route that I will run right after the switch.

For the numbers I wrote down the baselines from the shadow path: short range median 52 ms and long range median 197 ms on the old layout, p95 around 470 ms, and an error rate of 0.02 percent on the route. These are the values to compare against in the first hours.

The disk on the lowest node is at 38.4 percent free. The double write will need extra space for the new indexes, so Tobias and I agreed on a stop point: if the lowest node goes under 35 percent, we stop and clean up before going on. He also wants to see the number again in the morning before the second tenant.

One small finding in the diff view: a few shadow samples showed a 1,100 ms time on the old layout, all the same query shape, a wildcard on a text field. It looks slow on both layouts, so it should not count against the move. I added a note to the runbook to filter that shape out of the comparison.

The move itself is still to be done in the quiet hour, and the night check is set up to run afterwards as usual.

summary: Read the planning notes for the middle tenant move and the disk margin, and set up the second tenant of the pair for the afternoon quiet hour, with nothing moved yet
body:
I went through the prepared material this morning before anything is started. The per-tenant diff view is ready, and the stop rule from Mara's review is written into the runbook: stop if the new layout is more than 10 percent slower than the old one for the tenant. The diff baseline for the five tenants from the long range report is loaded, so the first hours of any move can be compared against it.

The long range class is where I looked closest, since Mara asked for it. In the report the medians on the monthly layout were equal or faster for all five tenants, and I copied the old layout medians, 195 ms for the long range class, into the check sheet so that the later numbers have something to be read against.

The disk figure is the open point. The lowest data node shows 36.8 percent free this morning. That is below the 38 percent I wanted before a double write, because the old indexes of the smallest of the five tenants are still waiting for their scheduled deletion date. Tobias looked at it from his side and agrees. The second tenant, 96 GB, can only go if the free number is back above the limit by the quiet hour, so the decision is left for then.

The audit log entry for the layout move is written as a template with the time and the old index deletion date. Sam checked that the text shows in the support view of the console and that it is understandable, and asked for one clearer sentence about what the customer sees, which I changed.

One side question: the wildcard query shape that is slow on both layouts. I only noted it in the backlog. A short note in the docs for customers about leading wildcards might be worth it, but I will look at it later, after the moves.

summary: Prepared the second middle tenant, 96 GB, for the move to the monthly layout in the evening quiet window; the disk check took longer than planned and the move itself is still ahead
body:
I planned the move of the second tenant of the pair for the quiet window of the evening, but it started later than planned because I waited for the disk check to settle after the deletion of an old index of a small tenant. The lowest node had 37.2 percent free before I stopped to prepare.

I went through the runbook steps one by one and did not run the flag script. The import check on the new indexes passed, and the diff before the move was 98.4 percent on 6,100 samples. The flag script is ready to print the old index names and a deletion date 14 days out, but I only ran it in dry mode to see the output. The config version has not been changed on any task yet.

I compared the old layout with the shadow path numbers of the first tenant to know what to expect. The short range median was 47 ms against 58 ms there, medium range 120 against 124 ms, long range 214 against 218 ms. This second tenant is the largest one planned so far in the middle group, with data in 38 months. A long range query will go to up to 38 indexes with one shard each, where the old layout had a few big ones with more shards. I expect the work to be spread over fewer parallel tasks, so the long range p95 may be only equal and not better. For middle tenants that is an acceptable trade, since the gain on short range queries covers the most frequent use. I wrote the concern down for Mara, because it matters for the large tenants later.

A possible improvement is to merge the old months into yearly indexes after 12 months, but that is a layout question and not part of this work. I only put the idea in the notes.

The disk is the real risk. With 140 GB of new indexes during the double write for the pair, I calculated that the lowest node may fall to about 35.6 percent, above the limit of 35 but not by much. I asked Tobias to watch it overnight once the move starts, and he agreed to clean the old index of the first small tenant a day early if it goes below 35.2.
