The stop rule is set up in the sampling job to check every hour, with the threshold at 10 percent slower than the old layout. I tested it on the earlier numbers and it stayed quiet. The report for Mara with the long range numbers will come after the night check.

summary: Report to Mara on the first middle pair: short range 15 to 20 percent faster, long range equal for the largest tenant, and a proposal to hold the next pair until the yearly merge idea is checked
body:
I wrote the long range report that Mara asked for, now with the two middle tenants, using the query-report script from earlier this week. The night check for the second tenant was clean, and the disk on the lowest node recovered to 36.3 percent without help.

The numbers over the first 12 hours for the first middle tenant (44 GB): short range median 41 against 52 ms, medium 109 against 118 ms, long range 183 against 195 ms. For the second one (96 GB): short range 47 against 58 ms, medium 120 against 124 ms, long range 214 against 218 ms, with a p95 of 690 against 684 ms.

The pattern is the same as in the first five tenants, only less strong. The bigger the tenant and the more months it has, the less the long range gains. The old layout had a few large indexes, and a long range query used all shards of them in parallel. The new layout has one small shard per month, so a long range query touches many indexes, each cheap, and the coordination cost grows with the count.

I tested that idea quickly on the staging cluster with a copy of the second tenant. A long range query over 38 monthly indexes spent about 30 ms of the 214 ms in the coordinating node on merging results. Merging the months older than 12 months into yearly indexes would cut the index count from 38 to about 15 for this tenant, and the estimate is a gain of 10 to 15 ms. That is small, and I did not build it.

My proposal in the report: continue with the next pair as planned, since the short range gain is real and the long range is not worse. But hold the third pair until Mara has decided whether the large tenants need the yearly merge in the plan, because those are the ones where the count of indexes will hurt.

I also listed the risks: the disk margin on the lowest node, which stays near 36 percent while old indexes wait for their 14 days, and the wildcard query shape that is slow on both layouts.

Mara will read it today and answer in the team notes. In the meantime the stop rule and the hourly sampling run for both tenants.

summary: Mara's decision on the middle tenants: continue with the next pair, skip the yearly merge for now, and revisit it with real numbers when the first large tenant is planned
body:
Mara read the report and wrote her decision into the team notes, and we talked about it for a few minutes.

She agrees that the next pair of middle tenants moves as planned, one per day, with the same checks. She does not want the yearly merge in the plan now, because the gain of 10 to 15 ms is inside the noise of the shadow samples and the merge adds a second job type to the layout, with its own failure cases. Her words were roughly that a clean monthly layout is easier to reason about for the rest of the team than a clever one.

She wants one thing added: the report must show the number of monthly indexes per tenant touched by the long range class, so that when the large tenants come, the cost of the count is visible and not guessed. I added a column to the query-report script that reads the index count from the debug header of the shadow samples. For the two middle tenants it is 12 and 38 on average for the long range class.

The stop rule stays at 10 percent. Mara also asked that the disk margin goes into the stop rule for the moves, not only the runbook. I extended the flag script: it now reads the free disk percentage of the lowest node from the cluster stats API and refuses to move when it is under 35.5 percent, with an override that needs a reason like the import one.

I tested the check with a fake stats response in two unit tests, one at 35.4 and one at 35.6 percent.

The next pair is the third and fourth middle tenant by size, 120 GB and 150 GB. With the old indexes of the five small tenants about to be deleted, the disk margin should be better by tomorrow evening. I will start the third middle tenant only if the script allows it.

The topic of the yearly merge stays in the notes with the numbers, so it is easy to find later.

summary: Renamed the facet cache and rate limiter Redis keys to the new naming rule in two pull requests; old keys expired within 20 minutes and the memory and hit rate stayed the same
body:
Two pull requests for the first part of the Redis key rename, following the rule written two days ago: service, purpose, tenant, then the id.

The first one is the facet cache. The old keys looked like t123:facets:abc and the new ones are search:facets:t123:abc, built with the redisKey helper. The TTL of the facet keys is 20 minutes, so I did not add a fallback read. The old keys simply expire. For the first 20 minutes after the deploy the hit rate falls, since the new names are empty, and then it comes back. I deployed in the quiet hour to keep the effect small.

The second one is the rate limiter windows. The old names were rl_{apikey}_{minute} and the new ones are search:ratelimit:-:{apikey}:{minute}, where the dash means that the key has no tenant. A rename in the limiter has one risk: the counters of the current window are lost at the deploy, so a client could send up to twice its limit in one minute during the switch. The limits are not strict security limits, and I checked with Mara that this is acceptable for one minute. The window TTL is 10 minutes since the change of last week, so the old keys disappeared fast.

Results from the Grafana panels after the deploy: the facet cache hit rate dropped from 71 to 22 percent in the first five minutes and was back at 69 percent after 25 minutes. The facet route p95 went up to 1.3 seconds during that time, which matches the cold cache, and came back to 640 ms. No timeouts.

The limiter: the number of 429 responses in the minute of the deploy was 14 against a normal 10 to 20, so no visible effect. The key count of the limiter prefix is about 260,000 as before, and memory used by it is 75 MB.

Total Redis memory is 4.3 GB, the connection count 190, and the p99 command latency 1.2 ms. No change there.

I also found that a scan pattern with the new names now gives the memory of one tenant in one command. I tried it for the tenant that moved to the monthly layout this week, and it takes 4 seconds on the full keyspace. I added the command to the Redis notes in the docs folder.

Still open: the import progress keys, the audit export status and the schema registry lock, which need the fallback read for one release. Those will be the next pull request. The lint rule now reports 14 places in the search API instead of 23, and the rest belong to Mara's service.

summary: Planned the move of the third middle tenant, 120 GB, to the monthly layout and checked the disk margin and the flag script, with the move itself left for the next quiet hour
body:
After two quiet days with no moves, I prepared the third middle tenant for the quiet hour of the next morning. The old indexes of three of the five small tenants had been deleted since the last move, so the disk margin on the lowest node was back to 38.9 percent free. The new check in the flag script read that number from the stats API and would allow the move without an override. I ran the script in dry mode only. It printed the plan and the old index names with a deletion date 14 days out, and it did not touch the flag.

Before the move I went through the preconditions. No imports were running. The diff on the shadow path was at 98.6 percent on 7,300 samples, and the shadow job was healthy. I also checked how fast the config version spreads. In the last test it changed on all tasks within 22 seconds, which is fast enough for the stop rule to work.

I then reread the numbers from the earlier moves to know what to expect. Short range was clearly faster, medium was about equal, and long range was equal or slightly worse. The index count column in the report is the main thing to watch. For this tenant I expected it to be the highest so far, since its data spans the most months. That means the long range gain will probably be gone, as the earlier finding suggested.

I also looked again at the wildcard query shape I noted earlier. This tenant has it too: a query with a leading wildcard on the message field, taking 900 to 1,400 ms on the old layout. The cause is that a leading wildcard cannot use the term index and scans all terms of the field. Customers use it to search for the end of an id. I wrote a short paragraph for the public docs that suggests searching for the full token or using the id field filter, and gave it to Sam to review. No code change in the search path.

Tobias will watch the lowest node during the double write. The move itself is planned for the quiet hour, and the night check comes after it.

summary: Checked the night results for the third middle tenant's move to the monthly layout, found the disk margin too low for the fourth tenant, and held that move until the margin recovers.
body:
The night check for the third middle tenant was clean. The diff held between 98.3 and 98.7 percent, the hourly stop rule never fired, and the long range median over 12 hours was 232 ms against 238 ms on the old layout.

For the fourth tenant, I ran the flag script as a dry check first, and it refused. The lowest node was at 35.4 percent free, just under the 35.5 limit that Mara asked for, because the double write of the third tenant was still settling and a merge on one node was running. This is what the check is for. I did not override it. I will wait until the merge is done and run the script again, and only then plan the move for a quiet hour. Nothing about the fourth tenant has been started.

The tenant has 150 GB of data, and the index count for the long range class would be 44, the highest so far. Before any move the diff on the old layout was 98.9 percent on 8,200 samples. The flag change and the config reload should go as before, about 24 seconds on all tasks, so I prepared the change and the notes but did not touch the flag.

For the report to Mara I collected the numbers of the third tenant and the expected index count of 44. I do not think the larger count needs action yet. If the next, larger tenants show 5 percent or more on the long range class, the yearly merge idea comes back into the plan, and the numbers for it are in the notes.

While watching the third tenant's double write I saw that the lowest node went down to 34.9 percent for about 20 minutes, under the limit for a moment, because the script only checks before the move and not during. Tobias saw the alert on the disk panel and did nothing, since the number recovered. I wrote down a task to make the double write phase check the margin, or to spread the new indexes more evenly across nodes, since the lowest node seems to carry more shards than the others.

summary: Checked why one data node carries more shards than the others: the allocation weights favor the node with the most free space, which keeps it filling up, so I set a shard count limit per node
body:
The disk number of the lowest node went under 35 percent during the double write of the last move. I looked at why it is always the same node.

The shard counts per node are 214, 198, 201 and 187 for the four data nodes, and the node with 214 is the one that runs lowest. The index shrinks of the last weeks moved shards around, and the default allocation tries to balance by shard count and disk, but a node with more shards than the others stays that way as long as the balance is inside the threshold.

Tobias and I changed the setting for the total shards per node in the index settings of the new monthly indexes, so that no node takes more than a fixed number of shards of one index, and asked the cluster to rebalance. The rebalance moved 11 shards from the node with the most to the one with the fewest over about 25 minutes, with the recovery speed limited to the usual 40 MB per second.

The counts after the rebalance are 203, 201, 200 and 196, and the free disk of the lowest node went from 35.8 to 37.4 percent. The search latency did not change during the move, as the p95 stayed at 190 ms.

We did not touch the old indexes of the tenants on the old layout, since they are going away over the next weeks.

The flag script was not changed. The check before a move stays, and with the more even nodes the margin during the double write should be larger. I will watch it at the next move.

summary: Redis import progress keys renamed to the new scheme with a one release fallback read; a test covers a job that starts before the deploy and ends after it
body:
This is the second part of the Redis key rename. The import progress keys are written by the loader and read by the console, and they live for hours, so a plain rename would lose the progress of running imports.

Old name: import:{jobid}:progress. New name: loader:progress:{tenant}:{jobid}. The writer now writes only the new name. The reader tries the new name first and then the old name as a fallback. The fallback stays for one release and then I remove it, with a note in the task list.

The case that needed a test is a job that starts before the deploy and ends after it. The job writes progress under the old name until the worker restarts, and the worker restart is part of the deploy, so the job continues after the restart under the new name, starting from the saved offset in Postgres. The console, with the fallback, would show the old progress for a moment and then the new one. The test starts a job, writes the old key by hand, switches the writer to the new name and checks that the reader shows a progress value that never goes back.

I also changed the audit export status key and the schema registry lock to the new names. The lock is the one where a rename can do harm, because two holders with different names could both think they own the lock. I made the lock acquire check both names for the one release, and wrote a test with two clients, one old and one new, that cannot both acquire.

The lint rule is down to 6 places in the search API, all in test files. Mara's service keeps its list of 14.

I deployed in the quiet hour. Two imports were running, and both finished with the right counts. The console showed progress without a jump back.

summary: Prepared the fifth middle tenant, 180 GB, for the move to the monthly layout and checked the disk number, the pre checks and the plan for the double write phase before starting anything.
body:
With the shard rebalance of two days ago, the fifth middle tenant, 180 GB, is next in line. I did not move it yet. I wanted the numbers and the checks ready first, so the move can go in the quiet hour of the next morning.

The disk check in the flag script reads 38.1 percent free on the lowest node and would allow the move. I ran it twice, an hour apart, to see whether the number was stable, and it was. I expect the lowest node to go down a little during the double write phase, but not below 35, because the shard counts are more even now. I told Tobias which hour the move is planned for so that he knows what to expect on the disk graphs.

The pre checks I ran as a dry run were the usual ones. There are no running imports for this tenant. The diff job sits at 98.5 percent on 9,000 samples, and the shadow job is healthy. I also timed the config reload on a staging copy, which took 23 seconds on all tasks. I checked that the audit log entry will carry the old index deletion date, as in the earlier moves.

Then I looked at what to watch afterwards. The number I said I would watch is the index count column, which was 44 after the fourth tenant. The stop rule for long range p95 is 10 percent slower, and I wrote it at the top of the report page so that I read the numbers against it. The long range class has few samples for this tenant, about 700 in six hours, so I prepared a set of 200 long range queries that I can run against staging copies of both layouts, three times each, if the production numbers look doubtful.

I also drafted the section for Mara in the weekly report, with empty cells for the latency table. The yearly merge idea stays in the notes, and I will not start any change on it until she has decided. The sixth tenant waits until this one has had its night check.

summary: Wrote the numbers for the yearly merge question: with 46 indexes the coordination cost is 35 ms of 281 ms, and merging old months would recover about 20 ms, for Mara to decide
body:
Following the finding on the fifth middle tenant, I measured the coordination cost on staging to give Mara a number to decide with. The staging copy of the tenant has all 46 monthly indexes.

For a long range query, the profile output shows the time spent on the shards and the time on the coordinating node. Over 100 queries the median total was 281 ms, of which 35 ms was spent on the coordinating node for merging and reducing the results from 46 shards. The remaining time is the shard work, mostly in parallel.

I then built a test copy where the months older than 12 months are merged into yearly indexes with one shard each. That cut the index count from 46 to 17. The same 100 queries had a median of 262 ms, with 19 ms on the coordinating node. So the gain is about 19 ms, 7 percent of the long range time, which is about the size of the difference to the old layout.

The cost of the merge is not small. A yearly index has to be built by a reindex of 12 monthly indexes, which for this tenant takes about 40 minutes and about 25 GB of extra disk during the build. Later events for old months would need a rule too, because late events with an old timestamp can arrive, and they would go to a closed yearly index. In the monthly layout they go to the month, which stays open.

My summary for Mara: the merge recovers the long range gap for the middle tenants, but adds a job, extra disk use and a rule for late events. The gap is 4 to 7 percent on a class that is 9 percent of the queries. For the large tenants the index count will be 50 to 60, and the effect will be a bit larger.

I recommend not building it now, moving the remaining middle tenants, and looking again with the first large tenant's shadow numbers. I put this into the team notes with the profile outputs attached. The decision is Mara's.

summary: Looked into the 6 percent slower long range p95 after the fifth middle tenant move and traced it to two slow shards on the node with the oldest disks
body:
While preparing the fifth middle tenant, 180 GB, for the move to the monthly layout, I looked into the 6 percent slower long range p95 that I had noted on the earlier tenants. The slow queries all touched the same two monthly indexes. Those two indexes were placed on the node with the oldest disks.

I compared the per-shard query times from the search slow log. The two shards took about 1.4 times as long as the rest on the same query. The shards on the other nodes were equal to the old layout.

The even spread limit I set earlier today would force the shards of the fifth tenant onto that node as well, because the other nodes are at their count limit. So the limit works, but it ignores that nodes differ in speed. I did not change the limit.

I wrote down three options: raise the limit by one for the faster nodes, move the two shards by hand, or accept the 6 percent. A manual move is cheap, but it would be undone by the next rebalance. Raising the limit by one is the simplest, and the disk numbers allow it.

For the fifth tenant I checked the disk number and the pre checks, and went through the plan for the double write phase. I did not start the move yet, because the placement question should be answered first.

I will talk to Tobias about the node types before changing anything. For the report to Mara I started a note with the per-shard table. The sixth tenant waits until this question is answered.

summary: Asked Tobias about the data nodes: two of the five are the older instance type, which explains the slow shards of the fifth middle tenant
body:
Tobias confirmed in the infrastructure channel that two data nodes are still the older instance type. They were never replaced because the migration of the accounts took priority. The disks on them are slower for random reads.

That matches the slow log numbers from this afternoon. The two slow shards of the fifth tenant sat on one of those nodes. The earlier tenants happened to land mostly on the newer nodes.

He can replace the two nodes, but not before next week, and the plan needs one node at a time to keep the free disk above the limit. I asked him for the rough cost. He said the new type is cheaper per hour, so it is not a cost problem, only a time problem.

Until then I will keep the shard limit, since it still keeps the disks from filling. I will not move the next tenant to a layout that depends on luck. The sixth tenant waits until I know where its shards will land.

I added the node type column to the check output of the flag script. Now the dry run prints the expected node for each new shard.

summary: Drafted the weekly report on the monthly layout plan, with the numbers so far, the open questions and a proposal for the larger tenants.
body:
I started the report for Mara on the monthly layout. It has one table per tenant with short range and long range medians, p95 and the diff to the old layout, taken from the test runs on the staging copy of the index. The short range queries look faster in all the runs, between 12 and 20 percent, but I wrote clearly that these are staging numbers and not production.

Long range is equal for most of the tenants I tested. One tenant shows p95 about 6 percent slower with the even shard spread. I traced it to two slow shards that sit on one node, and I put the per-shard table in the report. I asked Tobias about the data nodes and he confirmed that two of the five are the older instance type, which explains the slow shards.

The report also has the disk numbers. I checked the lowest node and it stays above 36 percent free in the plan for the double write phase. The shard limit per node does what I wanted, and the spread is more even than at the start of the week.

I listed the open questions: whether to wait for the node replacement before moving the next tenants, and whether the yearly merge matters. For the merge I repeated the 35 ms of 281 ms coordination cost and the 20 ms gain with 46 indexes. I did not give an opinion because the numbers are small.

My proposal is to hold the next tenant until the node replacement and to use the time to prepare the checks for the large tenants. The large ones are 400 GB and more, and the double write needs a different disk plan.

I sent the draft in the evening and I expect the answer tomorrow. No production tenant has been moved yet.

summary: Mara agreed to hold the sixth tenant until the two old data nodes are replaced, and asked for a disk plan for the large tenants in the meantime
body:
Mara read the report and answered this morning. She agrees with waiting for the node replacement. A 6 percent slower tenant is not a problem, but another one placed on the same nodes would be.

She asked for a disk plan for the large tenants. The largest is about 520 GB, and the double write needs the new indexes next to the old ones for at least a day. With the current free space that would push the lowest node below 30 percent.

She also asked that I do not move two large tenants close to each other. I will write that into the runbook as a rule.

I started the disk plan with the current numbers per node. The new node type has larger disks, so the plan depends on the replacement. I will finish it when Tobias gives me the dates.

summary: Went through the Postgres slow query log and found the audit log listing doing a sequential scan on 21 million rows; a composite index brought it from 4.8 s to 40 ms
body:
Sam reported that the audit log page in the admin console takes several seconds for the larger customers. I looked at the slow query log of Postgres and found the query behind it. It filters by tenant and sorts by creation time, and it had a plan with a sequential scan.

The audit table has 21 million rows now. There was an index on tenant only, and one on the creation time only. The planner picked neither for the combined filter and sort, and the sort spilled to disk.

I wrote an index on tenant and creation time descending. I created it with the concurrent option on staging first. On staging the query went from 4.8 s to 40 ms for the largest tenant.

Then I checked the size. The index is 1.3 GB on the production sized copy. That is fine for the disk, but it adds some cost to every audit write. I measured the insert rate on staging with a loop of 50,000 inserts. It was 3 percent slower, which is acceptable.

I also looked at the old tenant only index. The new index covers its queries, so the old one is redundant. I did not drop it yet. I want one week of the usage statistics from the index views first, to be sure nothing else uses it.

The migration file is in the pull request, with the concurrent creation, because a normal index build would lock writes to the audit table. Mara reviewed the SQL and asked to add a comment about why it is concurrent, which I did.

I will deploy it tomorrow in a quiet hour and check the plan again in production. After a week I will look at dropping the old index.

summary: Deployed the audit log composite index in production: build took 11 minutes, the listing for the largest tenant now answers in 55 ms
body:
The audit index went out tonight in the quiet window. The concurrent build took 11 minutes and no writes were blocked. I watched the lock view during the build and saw no waits.

After the build I ran the explain for the listing query on the largest tenant. The plan uses the new index, and the execution time was 55 ms. This is a bit slower than on staging, which is normal because of the cache state.

I asked Sam to open the page for three of the larger customers. All three loaded at once. She will tell me if anyone reports a slow page.

The insert rate on the audit table did not change in the Grafana panel. Next check is in a week for the old index.

summary: Looked at autovacuum on the events metadata tables: dead tuple counts were high on two tables, so I lowered the scale factor for them and the bloat is falling
body:
While checking the audit table I saw that the dead tuple counts of two other tables were high. They are the import jobs table and the settings history table. Both get many updates.

The import jobs table had 38 percent dead tuples. Autovacuum ran on it, but only after the default 20 percent threshold of a large table, and it was slow to finish because of the cost limit. The table is only 4 GB, but it was 7 GB on disk.

I set a lower scale factor of 2 percent for these two tables with a table level setting. I did not change the global defaults, because the other tables are fine. I also raised the cost limit for them a little.

After two hours the autovacuum had run three times on the import jobs table. The dead tuple share fell to 4 percent. The disk size stays at 7 GB because a normal vacuum does not give space back, which is expected.

I thought about a full rewrite to get the space back, but it would lock the table and the table is used by the importer. The extra 3 GB is not a problem. I left it.

I wrote the setting in the database notes with the reason, and a query that shows the dead tuple share per table. I added a Grafana panel for the dead tuples of these tables, so a regression shows up.

Next I will check the same numbers in a week.

summary: Tried a connection pooler library for the search API Postgres access and dropped it: the saving was small and prepared statements broke
body:
The search API opens many Postgres connections during peaks, and I wanted to see whether an external pooling library in the Node process would help. I picked one with good reviews and wired it in behind a flag on a branch off main.

On staging with the load script the connection count dropped from 60 to 34. The latency of the settings queries did not change. So the gain was only fewer connections, and the database has room for them.

Then the errors started. Some queries failed with an error about prepared statements that did not exist. The library runs in transaction mode, and our query layer uses named prepared statements. Turning them off in the query layer meant changing about 40 call sites.

I tried the session mode of the library instead. That works with the prepared statements, but then the connection count was 57 again, so there was no gain at all.

I considered rewriting the call sites, but 40 places for a small gain is not worth the risk. Postgres is not near its connection limit, as the peak is about 40 percent of the maximum.

I dropped the branch and wrote the result in the notes: what I tried, the two counts, and the prepared statement problem, so nobody repeats it. If the connection count becomes a problem later, a pooler on the infrastructure side is a better place, and I will mention it to Tobias.

I deleted the flag from the config and checked that main has no leftovers.

summary: Tobias gave dates for replacing the two old data nodes: one next week, the other three days later, one at a time with the shard limit kept
body:
Tobias sent the plan for the node replacement. The first old node goes next week, and the second three days after that. He replaces one node at a time and waits for the cluster to be green before the next.

The shards of the old node move to the others while it is drained. With the shard limit per node, there is a risk that the move stalls, because the others are at the limit. I asked him to raise the limit by one during the drain. He agreed and will lower it afterwards.

The free disk is the other question. The remaining nodes must take the data of the drained one. I calculated that the lowest node would be at about 33 percent free at the worst time. That is above the 30 percent line, but not by much.

So no tenant moves happen during the replacement days. I added this to the plan and to the runbook as a rule.

summary: Wrote the disk plan for the large tenants: with the new node type the double write of the 520 GB tenant fits at 34 percent free, but only if no other move runs
body:
With Tobias's dates, I could finish the disk plan for the large tenants. The new nodes have 1.5 times the disk of the old ones. After both replacements the cluster has about 40 percent more total space.

I took the current sizes of the four large tenants: 310, 380, 450 and 520 GB. The double write needs the new monthly indexes next to the old ones. The monthly layout is a bit larger in total, about 8 percent more than the old indexes because of the per-index overhead.

For the largest tenant the double write needs about 560 GB of extra space, spread over five data nodes. That is about 112 GB per node. With the new nodes the lowest node stays at 34 percent free in my calculation.

For the old layout I assumed that the old indexes are deleted only after a 12 hour check. For the large tenants Mara asked for 24 hours, so I used 24 hours.

I listed three rules in the plan:
- one large tenant at a time, and no middle tenant move on the same day,
- a free disk check above 36 percent before the start,
- a pause of the nightly reindex job, or a check that it does not overlap with the double write.

The reindex job is the part I had not thought about before. It writes a lot during the night and it needs space too. Its start time is still where it was, and it has to be checked against the moves as well. I also wondered whether it overlaps with the backup window; I did not look into that yet and left it as a note for later.

I also thought about a slower option: moving the large tenants month by month in the double write, so only part of the data is doubled at a time. It would lower the peak disk to about 200 GB extra in total, but the move would last a week and the flag script does not support partial moves. I noted it as a fallback and did not build it.

I sent the plan to Mara for review. The open number is the exact size of the new nodes, which Tobias will confirm when the first one is ready.

summary: Redis cache hit rate for the search API fell from 71 to 64 percent after the key rename; the cause was a tenant prefix that was lowercased in one place only
body:
The hit rate panel showed a drop of about 7 points since the rename of the facet cache keys last week. I first thought it was a TTL problem, but the TTL values were the same as before.

I compared the keys written by the API with the keys it read. For a group of tenants the writer used the tenant id as it is stored, and the reader used a lowercased form. The old key scheme did not include the tenant in that part of the key, so it never showed.

Tenants with capital letters in the id were the ones with misses. There are six of them, and two are among the larger customers, which explains the size of the drop.

I fixed it by using one helper function for both sides, and removed the local lowercasing. I added a test that builds the key for a tenant with capital letters and checks that the writer and reader give the same result.

After the deploy the hit rate went back to 70 percent within an hour. The old wrong keys expire by their TTL, so I left them.

I will add a check of the hit rate per tenant to the dashboard, so a case like this shows up faster.

summary: Answered Lena's question about the Redis session store: sessions use their own prefix with a 12 hour sliding TTL, and logging out deletes the key at once
body:
Lena asked how long a console session lives in Redis and what happens at logout, because she is building the session expiry notice.

Sessions are stored under the session prefix with the tenant and user in the key. The TTL is 12 hours and it is renewed on each request, so it slides. After 12 hours without activity the key is gone.

At logout the key is deleted directly, so the session ends at once and does not wait for the TTL. I checked the code path and a test covers it.

I told her the console cannot ask Redis for the exact remaining time without a new API route. A simple choice is to show the notice after 11 hours of inactivity in the browser. She will do it that way.

summary: Reviewed the Redis memory by prefix after the rate limiter change: total is 4.7 GB, and the import progress keys are now the largest group after the cache
body:
I ran the memory by prefix report again to see where things stand after the session and rate limiter fixes of the last days. Total used memory is 4.7 GB, down from 6.4 GB at the start of the week.

The largest group is still the query cache at 2.6 GB. Then the import progress keys at 540 MB, then the rate limiter counters at 310 MB, and the sessions at 38 MB.

The import progress keys surprised me. There are about 900,000 of them, but only a few dozen imports run at a time. I sampled 200 keys and looked at their TTL. About 60 percent had no TTL at all.

The cause is the old code of the importer. When a job fails in a certain step, the progress key is written once more after the TTL was set, and the new write has no TTL. This only happens on the failure path, which is why nobody saw it.

I wrote a fix that sets the TTL in the same command as the write. I used a set with expiry instead of a set followed by an expire. A test now covers the failure path of a job.

For the existing keys without a TTL I wrote a small script that scans the prefix and sets a 7 day TTL on them. I ran it on staging first. It found 410,000 keys without TTL and the script took 3 minutes at a low rate.

I ran it in production at the end of the day, with a pause between batches so the main thread was not blocked. The latency panel did not move. Memory of the prefix will fall over the next days as the keys expire.

I will check the number again in a week. The pull request for the importer is merged.

summary: Wrote a short note for Sam on how to read the search latency panel, with what the p95 and the facet route line mean for a customer question
body:
Sam asked for help to answer customers who ask whether search is slow. I wrote a note for the docs folder with the panel explained.

The main line is the p95 of the search API, currently about 190 ms. It means that 19 of 20 requests are faster than that. A customer who sees a slow search once is not necessarily in the slow group.

The second line is the tenant facet route, at about 640 ms. It is the slowest and it counts over many fields. It is expected to be slow, and the monthly layout helps a little.

I added when to ask the team: if the p95 stays above 300 ms for 10 minutes, or if one tenant is far above the others in the per-tenant panel. Sam can look at both without any access to the cluster.

She read it and asked for an example of a per-tenant check. I added a screenshot description with the panel name and the filter to use.

summary: Replacement of the first old data node started: drained in 2 hours 40 minutes with the shard limit raised by one, and the cluster stayed green
body:
Tobias started the replacement of the first old data node early this morning. I watched the cluster with him. Before the start he raised the shard limit per node by one, as agreed.

The drain took 2 hours 40 minutes. The shards moved to the other four nodes. The cluster was yellow for a short time and went back to green when the last shard was done.

The free disk of the lowest node fell to 35.2 percent at the worst time. That is above my calculation of 33 percent, because the node had a bit more free space than I assumed.

Search latency stayed normal during the drain. The p95 went up by about 15 ms for 20 minutes while the largest shards moved, and then came back.

The new node joined in the middle of the morning. It took shards at the normal rate, and the shard limit is back to the old value. The new node is the faster type and it has the larger disk.

No tenant moves ran today. The second node is planned for the day after tomorrow.

summary: After the first node replacement the slow shards of the fifth middle tenant moved to the new node, and its test queries on the monthly test layout went from 6 percent slower to 2 percent faster.
body:
The shards of the fifth middle tenant were on the old node that was replaced this morning. During the drain they were moved, and two of them are now on the new node.

I ran the long range query set again for this tenant against both the current layout and the monthly test copy of the index that I keep for the comparison. The set has 40 queries and I ran it three times to reduce the noise. The p95 on the monthly test copy is now 2 percent faster than on the current layout.

The median is about 4 percent faster. Before it was equal, so this is a small gain.

This supports the explanation about the node type. The layout itself was not the problem. The older disks were. The production index is still split by customer, and nothing about it has changed, so this is only a comparison on the test copy.

I updated the table in the report to Mara with a new column for the result after the node replacement. I kept the old numbers visible, so the history is clear.

The second old node is still in the cluster. I expect the numbers of other tenants with shards there to improve too, but only two tenants have shards there, and I will run the same set for them after the replacement.

I also checked with the dry run, using the node type column, where the sixth tenant would put its shards in the planned layout. The output shows two of its shards on the new node and the others on the newer ones, so it is fine, but I still wait for the second node as planned.

summary: Fixed a console bug where the audit log page showed the same page twice when scrolling fast, caused by an offset based cursor and new rows arriving
body:
Lena found that the audit log page in the console sometimes shows the same row twice when a user scrolls quickly. I reproduced it on staging with a script that writes audit rows while the page loads.

The API used an offset for paging. When a new row arrives between two requests, all rows shift by one, so the first row of the next page is the last row of the previous one.

I changed the route to use a cursor based on the creation time and the id. The query asks for rows older than the cursor. This works well with the new composite index from last week, as the index can serve both the filter and the order.

The response now has a next cursor field. The old offset parameter still works for one release, because the export script of a customer uses it. I wrote a note for Sam about the change.

On the console side Lena changed the hook to pass the cursor. It was a small change of about 20 lines. I ran the script again with 500 new rows during the scroll and there were no duplicates.

I added a test with rows that have the same creation time, because the id must break the tie. That case failed in my first version, where I used only the time. The final cursor has both.

The explain for the new query shows the index scan with 0.3 ms for the first page. The change is deployed to staging, and I will move it to production after Lena's review.

summary: Profiled the nightly reindex job on staging, found it reads each tenant's documents in small pages, and tested larger page and bulk sizes to cut the run time.
body:
The nightly reindex job has grown from about 2 hours a few months ago to 3 hours 20 minutes. The job overlaps with the backup window, which is a separate problem, so I wanted to know first if the run time alone can be reduced.

I profiled one run on staging. Most of the time was waiting for Postgres pages. The job reads the documents of each tenant in pages of 500 rows and sends each page to OpenSearch as a bulk request. The database round trip per page was about 40 ms, and with many pages this adds up.

I tried a page size of 5,000 rows and a bulk request of 2,500 documents. At first I tried 10,000 rows, but the memory of the job went up to 1.8 GB, which is too much for the task size. With 5,000 the memory is 700 MB, and the run on staging took 2 hours 5 minutes, instead of 3 hours 20 minutes. Staging has about 60 percent of the production data, so the production gain should be similar.

Then I checked the result. I compared document counts per tenant between the old and the new run, and they were equal. I also compared a sample of 1,000 documents by hash and found no difference.

I also looked at the bulk errors. With the larger bulk requests there were a few rejected requests because the write queue of OpenSearch was full. The job already retries those, but the count of retries went from 3 to 41 per run. This does not change the result, but it shows that the cluster is busy at that time. I lowered the bulk size to 1,500 to reduce the rejections. The retries fell to 9 per run and the run time rose by only 4 minutes.

The job writes to the old and new layout for the moved tenants, so the bulk traffic is higher than it looks. That is part of why the queue is busy.

The change is a config value and a small code change. It is only tested on staging so far. I plan to put it in the next release and look at the first night run after that. I still need to talk with Tobias about the possible overlap with the double write of the large tenants.

summary: Postgres minor version upgrade on staging done: no plan changes in the 30 slowest queries, and production is planned with Tobias for a quiet hour
body:
Tobias upgraded the staging Postgres to the newest minor release of version 16 this morning, and I checked the effects. A minor release should not change plans, but I wanted to be sure after the problems we had with planning before.

I took the 30 slowest queries of the last month from the slow query log and ran the explain on each of them before and after the upgrade on staging. I saved the plans as text and compared them with a diff.

All 30 plans are the same in shape. The estimated costs differ by less than 1 percent in a few of them, which comes from fresh statistics after the restart.

I also ran the test suite of the search API and the importer against staging. All tests passed. The audit log listing with the new index is as fast as before.

The release notes mention two fixes that touch us. One is a fix for a crash with a certain kind of parallel query, and one is a fix in the logical replication. We do not use logical replication, but the crash fix is the reason to upgrade soon.

I checked the extensions too. The two we use are compatible and they loaded without a warning.

I asked Tobias to do the production upgrade in the quiet hour tomorrow night. The downtime is expected to be one minute, because of the restart. I wrote the steps and the way back in the notes: a snapshot before the start, and a check list after it.

After the upgrade I will rerun the same set of explains in production and compare the plans in the same way.

summary: Production Postgres minor upgrade by Tobias: the restart took 48 seconds and the 30 query plans are unchanged
body:
Tobias did the production upgrade tonight after the snapshot. The restart took 48 seconds, and the API returned a few errors in that time, which the clients retried successfully.

I ran the explain set for the 30 slowest queries right after. All plans have the same shape as on staging and as before the upgrade. The audit log listing still uses the new composite index.

The replica caught up within a minute. The connection count of the search API came back to its normal value of about 40 after the restart.

summary: Wrote a script that checks the rate limiter counters in Redis against the API gateway logs and found that two API keys were counted twice
body:
Mara asked me to confirm that the rate limiter counts requests correctly, after we cut the window TTL. I wrote a script that takes one hour of the gateway logs and counts requests per API key, then compares the totals with the counters in Redis for the same window.

For 38 of 40 tenants, the numbers were equal within 1 percent. For two API keys the Redis counter was almost exactly double the log count.

I looked at the code path for those keys. Both keys belong to customers who send requests through two regions, and the middleware runs once at the edge and once at the search API. The edge one is meant to skip keys that were already counted, using a header. The header check compared the value as a string against a boolean, and so it failed for keys with a certain flag.

The effect is that those two customers reach their limit at half the traffic that they should. Neither of them had complained, since their traffic is far below the limit, but one of them was at 40 percent of the limit at peak, so it was close to being a problem.

I wrote the fix to parse the header value properly. A test sends a request with the header set to true and to false, and checks the counter. The old code failed the first case.

I deployed the fix to staging and ran the script again with a replay of the logs. All 40 tenants now match within 1 percent.

The script is useful as a regular check, so I put it into the tools folder with a short README. It needs read access to the gateway logs and to Redis, and it runs in about a minute for one hour of data. I set it to run weekly and to post a message when a key differs by more than 5 percent.

Mara reviewed the fix and the script. She asked me to also tell the two customers through Sam, which I did with a short description she can use. The production deploy is planned for tomorrow morning.

summary: Deployed the rate limiter header fix to production; the counters of the two affected keys dropped to half and the weekly check shows all 40 tenants within 1 percent
body:
The fix for the double counting went to production this evening. I watched the counters of the two affected API keys in Redis during the first hour. They fell to about half of their old rate, which is what the gateway logs show.

I ran the comparison script right after the deploy against the last hour. All 40 tenants are within 1 percent of the log counts. The biggest difference was 0.8 percent, and it came from requests that were in flight at the window edge.

The memory of the rate limiter prefix did not change, since the number of keys is the same. Only the values were different.

Sam told the two customers. One of them answered that they had noticed some strange limit warnings last month and were glad to hear the cause.

I set up the weekly run of the check and tested the message to the team channel with a fake difference. It arrived and the text was clear.

One open point is the old counters that were doubled. They are in windows of 10 minutes now, so they are already gone. Nothing to clean up.

I will look at the first weekly result next week.

summary: Wrote a nightly check that compares the rate limiter counters in Redis with the gateway logs and alerts when a tenant drifts by more than 2 percent
body:
After the double counting of two API keys, I turned the one-off script into a nightly job. It reads the counters from Redis for every API key and compares them with the request counts in the API gateway logs for the same window.

The job writes one row per tenant into a small Postgres table and pushes the maximum drift as a Prometheus gauge. The alert fires when any tenant is above 2 percent for two nights in a row. One night is not enough, because the log export is sometimes late by a few minutes.

I ran it against the last 7 days of data. All 40 tenants were within 1 percent, except the two fixed keys, which show the old doubled values before the fix and normal values after it.

The job needs the gateway logs in the new bucket layout. I used the path from Tobias's account migration notes and it worked on the first try. The Redis scan uses the rate limiter prefix only and a count of 500 per call, so it does not hurt the server. It took 14 seconds on production.

Still open: a dashboard panel for the gauge. I will add it with the other alert panels. Lena does not need anything from this.

summary: Replacement of the second old data node done: drain took 2 hours 20 minutes, cluster stayed green and the shard spread is now even on all five nodes
body:
Tobias replaced the second old data node this morning, a few days earlier than he planned. I watched the drain from the search side.

The drain took 2 hours 20 minutes with the shard limit raised by one for the time of the move. The cluster stayed green the whole time and the search API p95 did not move beyond its normal range.

After the node joined, the allocator spread the shards in about 40 minutes. The five nodes now hold 9, 9, 9, 9 and 8 shards, and the lowest free disk is 41 percent. Before, the lowest was 37 percent.

I put the shard limit per node back to the normal value after the move. I checked the setting with the cluster settings call and it reads as expected.

With all five nodes on the new type, the condition Mara set for the sixth tenant is met. I will check long range latency on the fifth middle tenant again this afternoon to confirm that the number from the first replacement still holds, and then ask Mara about the sixth tenant.

summary: Planned the comparison of the monthly layout for the next middle tenant and wrote down what to measure before asking Mara about moving it
body:
Prepared the comparison for the next middle tenant that could go to the monthly layout, since nothing of it has been moved yet. The plan is to take the last 24 hours of real traffic for that tenant on the old layout and keep it as the baseline, so that the numbers after a move can be set next to it.

I pulled the baseline for the short range and the long range queries from the Grafana panels and saved them in the layout report. Short range p95 is 98 ms and long range p95 is 283 ms. I also exported the per shard times of the long range query. One shard is 2.3 times slower than the median, and it sits on one of the old data nodes. That matches the loss we saw in the earlier tests, so I added a line to the report saying the cause is known and tied to those nodes.

I wrote down the checks to run after a move: the disk free percentage on each node, the index count column, the per shard spread of the long range query, and a comparison after 10 hours and again after 24 hours. I put the threshold for the spread at 10 percent between shards.

Next is asking Mara if the sixth tenant can go once the second old data node is out, and agreeing with her on a quiet hour for it.

summary: Wrote a nightly check that compares the rate limiter counters in Redis with the gateway logs and alerts when a tenant drifts by more than 2 percent
body:
After the double counting of two API keys that I found last week, I did not want to rely on a weekly manual look, so I turned the one-off script into a nightly job. It reads the counters for every tenant from Redis and sums the matching requests from the API gateway logs for the same window. The window is the last full day, cut at the same hour the counters roll over, because an earlier version of the script compared different cuts and showed false drift.

For each tenant the job computes the relative difference and writes it to a Prometheus gauge named rate_limiter_drift_ratio. An alert rule fires when a tenant is above 2 percent for two nights in a row, and a single night only goes to the Slack channel for the team. I chose 2 percent because on the last 14 nights of staging data the normal noise was below 0.6 percent, and the double count of the two keys was around 100 percent.

The gateway logs are read from the S3 export, so the job does not touch the production gateway. It takes about 4 minutes for all 40 tenants and uses a single Redis connection with a SCAN over the counter prefix, so it does not add pressure to the pool. Small tenants with fewer than 200 requests a day are skipped for the percent rule, because one request already moves them by more than 2 percent. For those I compare the absolute difference and alert only above 5 requests.

I ran it against the last two weeks of data and it reported all 40 tenants within 1 percent, which matches the weekly check. I also fed it a copy of the old buggy counters and it flagged both affected keys at once. The cron entry is in the new account setup and the alert rule is in the alert rules repository. Next I want to add the drift gauge to the rate limit panel in Grafana, so Sam can see it when a customer asks about a limit that looked wrong.

summary: Planned the move of the sixth tenant (210 GB) to the monthly layout and checked disk space on the data nodes, but did not start the copy yet.
body:
Prepared the move of the sixth tenant, 210 GB, to the monthly layout. I ran the disk check script first. It showed the lowest node at 40.2 percent free, which is enough for the double write, and the index count column reads 52 for this tenant's planned monthly indices.

I did not start the copy. From the sizes of the earlier tenants I estimated that the copy would take about 3 hours and that the lowest node would drop to around 37 percent free during the double write. That is still above the limit we agreed on, but I want to watch it live, so I will begin after Mara has read the plan.

I wrote down the order of the steps: copy to the monthly indices, compare document counts on every monthly index, switch the flag only if the difference is zero, and compare the short range and long range p95 after a few hours, because the first queries hit cold caches.

The old index should stay for 48 hours after the switch, as agreed with Mara, and the night check should run as for the earlier tenants. I added these steps to the checklist in the runbook so the next tenant uses the same list.

summary: Went through the Redis key TTLs by prefix and found three groups with no TTL at all, about 310 MB of stale keys, so I added TTLs and a cleanup for the old ones
body:
While looking at the memory by prefix last week I saw that the total did not fall at night as much as the traffic does. Today I listed every prefix with its key count and how many keys have a TTL.

Most groups are fine. The cache prefixes all have TTLs between 5 minutes and 6 hours, the session keys have the 12 hour sliding TTL and the rate limiter counters expire with their window.

Three groups had keys without any TTL: old export job status keys, a set of per tenant feature flag snapshots from a test last year, and the import progress keys of finished jobs from before the rename. Together they were 310 MB and about 640 thousand keys.

I checked each group in the code. The export status keys were written with a plain set call in one place and never got an expiry. I fixed that to a 7 day TTL. The flag snapshots were not read anywhere, so they were deleted with a scan and delete script with a count of 200 per call, run slowly so it would not block Redis.

The finished import progress keys now get a 3 day TTL when a job ends. The old ones from before the rename I deleted with the same script after checking that no running job used them.

The number of keys fell from 5.1 million to 4.5 million, and used memory from 4.7 GB to 4.4 GB. The hit rate of the search cache stayed at 64 percent, as expected since none of these keys are in its path.

I added a small check to the weekly report script that lists any prefix with more than 1 percent of keys without a TTL. Still to do: the 64 percent hit rate itself, where the lowercase prefix fix is not yet deployed everywhere.

summary: Fixed the lowercase tenant prefix in the last two places that built cache keys, and the search cache hit rate came back from 64 to 70 percent
body:
The hit rate drop after the key rename was caused by a tenant prefix that was lowercased in one place only. I fixed that place last week, but a search of the code today found two more spots that build keys by hand.

One is in the facet route, the other in the suggest route. Both used the raw tenant id from the request, while the writer used the lowercased one. For tenants with capital letters in their ids this meant a miss every time.

I replaced the hand built keys with the shared key builder, which lowercases once, and added a unit test with a tenant id in mixed case for each route. The test fails on the old code.

After deploying, I watched the hit rate for two hours. It went from 64 percent to 70 percent, and the facet route alone from 52 to 68 percent. Before the rename the overall number was 71 percent, so we are almost back.

The remaining 1 point is probably from entries that expired during the switch. I will look at the rate again tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why a customer sees search results from a deleted event: the delete reaches OpenSearch within one minute, but the cached page can live for 5 minutes
body:
Sam asked this morning why a customer saw a deleted event still in the search results, and wanted a sentence to send back. I traced the path of a delete to give a real answer. The delete request goes to the ingest API, then through the queue, and a worker removes the document from OpenSearch. In the logs of the customer's case this took 38 seconds from request to the document being gone, and the usual figure is under one minute.

The search API caches result pages in Redis, though, keyed by tenant, query and page. The TTL of those pages is 5 minutes, and a delete does not remove them. So a customer who ran the same query within the 5 minutes before the delete can see the old page for up to that long, even after OpenSearch no longer has the document. A new query or a different page number goes to OpenSearch and shows the right result.

I checked the case with the customer's tenant and found a page cached 3 minutes before the delete, which fits. I considered clearing the cache of the tenant on every delete, but for a tenant that deletes in bulk this would empty the cache and the hit rate, now at 70 percent, would drop. For now I did not change anything, since the delay is short and documented.

For Sam I wrote a short answer: the deleted event disappears from search within a minute, and an identical search made just before can show it for up to 5 minutes. A page refresh does not help, but a changed query does. I also added the 5 minute figure to the support notes on search behavior. If customers keep asking, the next step is deleting only the cached pages that contain the removed event id.

summary: Prepared the check of the sixth tenant on the monthly layout by pulling the baseline numbers of the old layout and writing down what the night check must compare
body:
Prepared the comparison for the sixth tenant, 210 GB, which is on the monthly layout with 52 monthly indexes, using the traffic of the last 10 hours as the baseline window.

On the old layout the numbers from the same window are short range p95 of 91 ms and long range p95 of 314 ms. I saved the query set and the time window so the comparison can be run the same way for the next tenant, and so the numbers do not depend on which hour I look at.

I also wrote down what to read from the per shard timings: the slowest shard against the median, and the coordination cost of 52 indexes on a long range query. For the earlier tenants the spread was uneven, so this is the number I want to look at first.

Disk on the lowest node went down to 36.8 percent during the copy and is back at 38 percent after the cleanup of temporary segments. Nothing else is moving, so the floor was not touched.

The night check is queued. It compares the document counts of old and new indexes once more, and I will read the report tomorrow before I compare the latency numbers. Until then I make no claim about how the layout performs for this tenant.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why a customer sees search results from a deleted event: the delete reaches OpenSearch within one minute, but the cached page can live for 5 minutes
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer still saw an event in a search after deleting it.

The delete goes to Postgres first and then to the queue, and the worker removes the document from OpenSearch. This normally takes under one minute, and I checked the lag panel for the time of the report: it was 20 seconds.

The search API caches result pages in Redis with a TTL of 5 minutes. A page that was cached before the delete shows the event until it expires. A new search with a different query or page is correct at once.

I told Sam to ask the customer to wait 5 minutes, or to change the query. I did not suggest purging the cache by hand.

It would be possible to purge the cached pages of a tenant after a delete, but for large deletes that costs more than it helps. I wrote the answer into the support docs for Sam.

summary: Tried to replace the hand written query cache serialization with a faster library and rolled it back: the saving was 0.4 ms per hit and a date field changed type
body:
The search API serializes every cached result page with JSON before it writes to Redis and parses it on a hit. I wanted to see whether a faster library would cut the latency on cache hits.

I picked a library that compiles a serializer from a schema and wrote the schema for the result page. In a local benchmark with 200 real pages the parse time fell from 1.1 ms to 0.7 ms per page.

On staging with replayed traffic the p50 of a cache hit went from 6.2 ms to 5.8 ms. This is 0.4 ms, below the noise of the network round trip to Redis.

Then I found a problem. The date field of the events came back as a string where the old code gave a string too, but the faceted counts, which use big integers, were returned as numbers with a different type in one edge case. A test for the facet route failed on it. I could fix it with a custom type, but that adds code for a gain nobody will notice.

I also thought about the cost of a schema per route: five routes, each with its own file to keep in step with the response types. That is more upkeep than the gain justifies.

I reverted the branch and left a short note in the performance list: serialization is not the bottleneck of a cache hit, the round trip is. Next time look at pipelining the cache reads for the facet route, which makes three calls per request.

summary: Pipelined the three Redis reads of the facet route into one round trip; p50 on the route fell from 14.6 to 11.9 ms on staging and the result is the same
body:
The failed serialization test pointed me to the real cost: the facet route does three separate Redis reads per request, for the facet counts, the tenant settings and the result page.

I changed the route to send the three reads as one pipeline. The code is a small change in the cache module, since the key builder gives all three keys up front. If one read misses, the others are still used.

One point needed care. The settings read has a different TTL logic, with a refresh on read, and I kept that outside the pipeline so it does not change.

On staging with replayed traffic from yesterday, the p50 of the facet route went from 14.6 ms to 11.9 ms, and p95 from 41 to 36 ms. The hit and miss counts are the same as before.

I added a test that checks the result of the pipelined path against the three separate reads, including a case where one key is missing. All tests pass.

I deployed to production in the evening. The first hour shows the p50 at 12.3 ms and no new errors on the Redis client panel. The number of Redis commands per second did not change, but the number of round trips fell by about a third.

Next is the same for the suggest route, which has two reads. I will do it tomorrow if the numbers hold overnight.

summary: Night check for the sixth middle tenant is clean: document counts match on all 52 monthly indexes, and the facet route p50 holds at 12 ms after the pipeline change
body:
Read the night check for the sixth tenant. The document counts of the old index and the 52 monthly indexes match, with a difference of zero, and no search errors were logged for this tenant.

The old index stays for another day, as agreed with Mara for the 48 hours. Search for this tenant still reads from the old index, and nothing is switched over yet.

The facet route p50 after the pipeline change is 12.1 ms over the night and the morning, and p95 is 37 ms. The Redis client panel shows no new timeouts.

I will do the suggest route pipeline next, and then ask Mara about the seventh tenant, which is the first of the large ones.

summary: Looked at what a first large tenant needs for the monthly layout: the 520 GB tenant fits only with the node limit and no other move, so I proposed a staged copy
body:
Mara asked for a concrete plan for the first large tenant, the 520 GB one. I used the disk plan from last week and the real numbers after the node replacements.

With five new nodes the free space on the lowest is 38 percent. A double write of 520 GB adds about 104 GB per node if it spreads evenly, and the lowest node would go down to about 31 percent. The floor is 30 percent, so this fits, but with almost no room.

The risk is the spread. In earlier moves the allocator did not spread evenly during the copy, and the lowest node dropped about 1.5 points more than the even number. That would bring us below 30 percent.

So I propose to copy in stages instead of one go. The tenant has 61 months of data. Copy the oldest 30 months first, switch the reads for those months, delete the matching part of the old index, and then copy the newer 31 months. At the peak the double write is then about half.

There is one cost. The staged copy needs the read path to know which months are in which layout for a few days. The search API already routes by month range for the monthly indexes, so I checked that a mixed state works. On staging I built a test tenant with half of the months on each layout and ran the long range query set. The results were identical to the old layout in all 40 queries.

The delete of the old part is the step I like least, because it cannot be undone without a restore. I would keep a snapshot of the old index until the whole move is done and checked, which costs 520 GB in the snapshot bucket.

So the plan is: snapshot first, then stage one with 30 months, a night check, stage two, a night check, then the delete of the old index after 48 hours. Estimated total time is 3 days.

I wrote this up for Mara with the disk numbers at each stage. The decision is hers, and I did not start anything. I also noted that the seventh middle tenant could go before the large one, to use the quiet days.

summary: Bumped the Redis client pool idle timeout in the search API after seeing stale connections in the logs; no more ECONNRESET warnings in a morning of traffic.
body: The search API logged ECONNRESET warnings about every few minutes. The cause was an idle timeout of 300 seconds in the client, while the server side closes idle connections earlier. I set the client idle timeout to 120 seconds in src/cache/redis.ts and added a small test that checks the option is passed through. After deploying to staging I watched the logs for two hours and saw no new warnings. The production deploy is planned for tomorrow. I did not touch the pool maximum.

summary: Wrote the first part of the per-month shard layout plan for the search index: sizes per customer, the month sizes, and the number of shards that fit the nodes.
body:
The user asked for a written plan before any migration work starts. I pulled the index stats from OpenSearch with _cat/shards and summed them per customer and per month of the event time.

The current layout has one index per customer. The three large customers hold about 70 percent of the data, and their shards are far above the 50 GB range we aim for. The small customers have shards of a few hundred MB, which wastes heap on the nodes.

A monthly layout would give indexes of roughly 40 to 90 GB for the recent months. With 12 primary shards per monthly index the shards would be around 4 to 8 GB, which is fine.

The open problem is the customer filter. Every query then needs a filter on the customer id, and the large customers lose the isolation they have today. I listed two options: a routing key on the customer id, or a filtered alias per customer. Routing is cheaper at query time but makes the large customers hot on a single shard.

I also listed what the reindex job needs: it has to write to the monthly index by event time, and old months must become read only. The nightly job runs for about 50 minutes now and I expect it to be shorter.

The plan is a markdown file in docs/plans, still marked as draft. Next I want to measure query latency with routing on a copy of one large customer. I will ask Tobias about the disk headroom on the nodes before I write numbers on the cost.

summary: Fixed a slow Postgres query in the admin console's API key list by adding a composite index on (customer_id, revoked_at); the query went from 900 ms to 6 ms.
body:
Lena reported that the API key page in the admin console took almost a second to open for the larger customers. I ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the query from the keys route. It did a sequential scan on api_keys, which has about 400k rows because revoked keys are never deleted.

The query filters by customer_id and revoked_at is null, then orders by created_at. The only index was on customer_id alone, and the planner chose the scan for the big customers.

I wrote a migration that creates a partial index on (customer_id, created_at desc) where revoked_at is null. I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so the table is not locked. On the staging copy the query dropped from 900 ms to 6 ms.

I also checked the other queries that touch api_keys. The rate limiter lookup uses the key hash and has its own unique index, so it is not affected.

The index is 11 MB, which is nothing. The migration ran in production in about 20 seconds. I looked at the page again afterwards and it opens at once for the largest customer.

One leftover: the revoked keys could be archived. I wrote a note in the backlog but did not start it.

summary: Reviewed the schema registry branch: compatibility checks work, but the error text for a breaking change names no field, so I asked for that before merging.
body:
I reviewed the current state of the schema-registry branch with Mara. The registry stores each event type schema with a version and checks a new version against the last one when it is registered.

The checks for removed required fields and for changed types work. I ran the test suite and it passes, 64 tests. I also tried five real schema changes from our history by hand, and the registry rejected the two that were breaking and accepted the three that were not.

The weak point is the error message. When a change is rejected, the API returns only 'incompatible schema'. A person who registers a schema with forty fields has to guess what is wrong. I asked that the message names the field path and the kind of change, for example 'field payload.user.id changed type string to integer'.

Two smaller comments: the version number is read and then written without a lock, so two parallel registrations could get the same version. A unique constraint on (event_type, version) would make the second one fail cleanly. And the registry cache in the ingest worker has no TTL, so a new version is only seen after a restart.

Mara agreed on all three. She will do the message and the constraint first and the cache TTL in a separate change.

summary: Answered a support question from Sam: why a customer's dashboard showed a gap of two hours; the loader had paused during a deploy and the backlog was caught up later.
body:
Sam asked why a customer saw no events between two points in the dashboard, and then saw them appear later. I checked the loader logs for that window. The loader pod was replaced during a deploy and stopped consuming for about 25 minutes, and then worked off the backlog.

The events had the right event time, so they appeared in the right place once the backlog was done. The dashboard reads from the materialized view, which updates in batches, and that added more delay.

I wrote a short answer for Sam that she can send to the customer. It says that no events were lost and that the data is complete as of now. I also confirmed the count: events in the topic for the window match the rows in ClickHouse.

A possible improvement is a note on the dashboard when the loader lags. I put it on the backlog.

summary: Started the ingest batching branch work in the worker: events are now collected per partition and written in one round trip, which cut the write calls by about 8x in the first test.
body:
This is the first real step of ingest-batching after the design last week. Until now the worker wrote each event of a request to the store with its own call. At our batch sizes that is a lot of small calls.

I added a batcher in internal/worker/batcher.go. It collects events per partition and flushes when it has 500 events or when 50 ms have passed since the first event in the buffer, whichever comes first. The flush runs in the goroutine of the partition, so ordering within a partition stays the same.

I first tried a single shared buffer with a mutex. The profile showed contention on the lock at 8 workers, so I dropped it for the per-partition buffers.

The offset commit was the tricky part. An offset must only be committed after the whole batch is written. I commit the highest offset of a flushed batch and not before. On a failed write the batch is retried as a whole with the existing backoff, and the offsets stay uncommitted.

I wrote unit tests for the flush by size, the flush by time, and the failed write. All pass.

Then I ran the worker against the staging queue with a replay of one hour of real traffic. Write calls went from about 410k to 52k, which is roughly 8x fewer. CPU on the worker fell by a fifth. The p99 of the time from queue to store went up by about 30 ms because of the wait for a flush, which is acceptable for now.

Not done yet: the shutdown path must flush the buffers before the worker exits, and the batch size needs to be configurable per event type. I will do the shutdown next because it is a risk for lost events.

summary: Made the ingest worker flush its batches on shutdown and added a test with SIGTERM; without this a deploy would have dropped up to 50 ms of buffered events.
body:
After the batcher from this afternoon, the open question was the shutdown. On SIGTERM, ECS gives the container 30 seconds. The worker stopped the consumers but did not flush the buffers, so the events in them would have been read from the queue again after the restart, which is safe, but only if the offsets were not committed.

I checked that: offsets are committed only after a flush, so nothing would be lost. Still, duplicates after each deploy are not nice, so the worker now drains.

The shutdown order is now: stop fetching, flush all buffers, commit offsets, close the connections. I added a timeout of 20 seconds for the flush so that a stuck store cannot block the exit.

The test starts a worker with a fake store that records writes, sends 120 events, sends SIGTERM and checks that all 120 are written once and that the committed offset is the last one. I also ran it with a store that blocks, and the worker exits after the timeout and commits nothing.

I deployed it to staging and replaced the worker three times during a replay. The count of events in the store matched the queue each time, with no duplicates.

The config per event type is still open. I will leave it for tomorrow.

summary: Made the batch size and flush interval configurable per event type in the ingest worker, with defaults of 500 events and 50 ms.
body:
I added a section batching in the worker config file. Each event type can override max_events and max_wait. The defaults stay at 500 and 50 ms.

The config is loaded at start, and an unknown event type falls back to the defaults. I wrote a test for the override and one for the fallback. For the large 'pageview' type I set 1000 events, since it has the highest volume, and left everything else alone. The change is only on staging for now.

summary: Ingest batching now has a per-partition retry for failed bulk writes, and a poison event no longer fails a whole batch of 500; it goes to a dead-letter topic.
body:
Slot 9 continued the ingest-batching work in the worker. The earlier tests showed that a single bad event made the whole bulk write fail, so all 500 events of the batch were written again and the bad one failed again. In the first load test on staging this produced a loop of about 40 repeated writes per minute for one partition.

The new logic splits a failed batch in half and writes each half separately. It repeats this until the failing event is alone. That event is sent to a dead-letter topic named ingest.dead, with the error text and the partition in the headers. The rest of the batch is stored as normal.

The split costs at most nine extra writes for a batch of 500, because the batch is halved each time. I counted this in a unit test with one bad event at the start, in the middle and at the end of the batch. The write count was 10, 9 and 10 in these cases. A batch with no bad event still needs one write, so the normal path did not change.
