I added a cap of three split rounds per second per partition. Without the cap, a stream of broken events from one customer could hold the worker busy and let the queue lag grow. When the cap is hit, the worker writes the events one by one at a lower rate and logs a warning with the customer id.

While working on this I found that the old code used the same error type for a timeout and for a rejected event. A timeout must not send events to the dead-letter topic, because the events are fine. I split the error type in two, so only a schema or constraint error leads to the split. Timeouts keep the existing backoff with the three attempts of the client.

On staging I replayed an hour of the real stream and added 200 broken events by hand. All 200 ended up in ingest.dead, the other events were stored, and the queue lag stayed flat. The count in the store matched the count in the topic minus 200.

Still open: a small tool to replay events from the dead-letter topic after a fix, and an alert on its size. Mara will look at the tool next week. I will do the alert tomorrow, together with the dashboard panel for the split rounds.

summary: Fixed a flaky CSS build in the admin console's CI: the cache key ignored the lockfile, so old dependencies sometimes leaked into the build.
body:
Lena asked for help with a CI job that failed about once a day with a style that did not exist. I looked at the workflow file. The dependency cache key used only the OS name, so a cached node_modules from an older lockfile was sometimes restored.

I changed the key to include the hash of package-lock.json. The first run after that was a cache miss and took four minutes instead of one. The following runs were fast again.

I re-ran the job ten times on the branch and all passed. I told Lena. She will watch it for a few days before we close the issue.

summary: Added the audit export format check for CSV quoting: fields with commas and line breaks broke the file in a spreadsheet, so the writer now quotes them per RFC 4180.
body:
A test export for the audit-export branch opened wrongly in a spreadsheet. Some audit entries have a free-text reason that contains commas and line breaks, and the writer joined fields with plain commas.

I replaced the hand-made join with the csv writer from the standard library in internal/export/csv.go. It quotes fields as needed and doubles quote characters.

I added a test with five nasty values: a comma, a quote, a line break, a leading space and an empty value. The test reads the output back with the csv reader and compares the values.

I also exported 200k rows from staging and opened the file in two spreadsheet programs. The row count was right in both.

One thing remains: the export of unicode text. The file has no byte order mark, so one program guessed the wrong encoding. I will decide with Sam whether compliance people need the mark. For now it is off.

summary: Looked into Redis memory growth in the session store and found that sessions of logged-out users kept their keys for 30 days; set a TTL of 24 hours on logout.
body:
The Redis memory graph for the session store rose by about 1.5 GB over the last month. I scanned the keys with a sample of 10k from the sess: prefix and checked their TTLs.

Sessions of users who logged out kept the full 30 day TTL, because the logout handler only marked the session as ended and did not delete it. Over time that adds up.

I changed the handler in the admin console API to delete the key on logout. For sessions that expire on their own nothing changes.

For the existing keys I wrote a one-time script that sets the TTL to 24 hours on every session with the ended flag. It touched about 210k keys and freed around 900 MB. I ran it in batches of 1000 with a short pause so that Redis stays responsive.

I will look at the memory graph again in a week.

summary: Wrote the per-key rate limit lookup for the rate-limits branch with a Lua script in Redis, so check and increment happen in one call; tested at 5k requests per second.
body:
The rate-limits branch needs a limit per API key and not only per customer. The first version did a GET and then an INCR, which allows a burst to pass between the two calls.

I wrote a Lua script that does the sliding window in one call. It takes the key, the window in ms, the limit and the current time, removes old entries from a sorted set, counts, and adds the new entry only if the count is below the limit. It returns the count and the time until the next free slot.

The key naming follows what we have: rl:{customer}:{keyhash}. The braces put the customer in the hash tag, so the keys of one customer stay together if we ever use a cluster.

In the Fastify plugin I load the script with SCRIPT LOAD at start and call it with EVALSHA. If Redis answers NOSCRIPT after a restart, the plugin loads it again and retries once.

Tests: unit tests for the plugin with a real Redis in docker, covering the limit, the window moving on, two keys of one customer, and the NOSCRIPT case. All pass.

Then a load test with k6 at 5k requests per second over 200 keys. Added latency from the limiter was p50 0.4 ms and p99 1.8 ms. Redis CPU stayed under 15 percent.

The sorted set uses memory per request in the window. For a key with a limit of 1000 per minute that is up to 1000 entries. With 40 customers and a few keys each, that is small, but I will put a note on it in the design doc.

Open: the response headers with the remaining count, and how a customer sets a limit for a key in the admin console. Lena will need an API for that.

summary: Added X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers to the per-key limiter and a 429 body with the limit name; clients can now back off without guessing.
body:
On top of the Lua limiter from earlier I added response headers. Every response from a limited route carries X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset. A 429 also has Retry-After in seconds, rounded up.

The 429 body is JSON with the fields error, limit_name and retry_after_ms. The limit name tells whether the per-key or the per-customer limit was hit, which Sam said support needs.

I wrote tests for the header values at the start of the window, in the middle and at the limit. The remaining count never goes below zero.

I also updated the OpenAPI file so the public docs list the headers. Sam will check the wording.

Not done: the admin console API for setting the limits.

summary: Dug into why the reindex job fails on documents with a very long message field and added a truncate step at 32k characters; 41 documents had been skipped for weeks.
body:
The nightly reindex job reported 41 failed documents each night, and nobody had followed up because the count was stable. Today I looked at the errors. OpenSearch answered with 'immense term' style errors for the keyword subfield of the message field, which has a limit of 32766 bytes.

All 41 documents came from two customers who send stack traces as one string. They were in the old index, but the full text part never made it into the new index after each reindex, so they could not be found by search.

I checked the mapping. The message field is text with a keyword subfield with ignore_above unset. The simple fix is ignore_above 8191 on the subfield, so the long ones are not indexed as keywords but still as text.

I changed the mapping template and tested on a small test index. All 41 documents were indexed and found by a text search for a word in the stack trace.

The change applies to new indexes only, so it will be used at the next full reindex. This fits with the shard layout work, as the monthly indexes will be created from the same template.

I put the mapping change in the template file and added a test fixture with a 100k character message. I also changed the job to fail the run if more than 10 documents fail, so a stable error count does not hide again.

summary: Replied to Mara's question about why the ingest client retries three times: it was a guess in the first version, and the logs show a second attempt fixes nearly all failures.
body:
Mara asked in review why the ingest client in our SDK retries three times with backoff. I looked at the logs of the last month. Of the requests that failed on the first try, about 94 percent worked on the second. Only 0.3 percent needed a third, and almost none a fourth.

So three is a fine limit, and I will not change it. I did suggest adding jitter, as the backoff is fixed at 200, 400 and 800 ms, and clients that fail together retry together.

Mara will add jitter of up to 25 percent in her change.

summary: Tried a different JSON library in the ingest worker to save CPU and dropped it: it was only 3 percent faster and handled unknown fields differently.
body:
I tried a faster JSON decoder in the ingest worker, since decoding is the top item in the CPU profile. The benchmark on 100k real events showed 3 percent better throughput, much less than the vendor's claims.

Worse, two of our tests failed. The library keeps duplicate keys differently, and with unknown fields it behaves differently from the standard one, which the schema checks rely on.

I could have worked around that, but a gain of 3 percent is not worth the risk and the extra dependency. I reverted the branch and noted the result in the performance doc so nobody repeats it.

summary: Upgraded Redis from 7.0 to 7.2 on staging and ran the full test suite and a load test; no differences found, production is planned with Tobias next week.
body:
Tobias had prepared the Terraform change for the new Redis engine version, and I used staging to check the application against it.

I ran the whole API test suite, the rate limiter tests with the Lua script, and the session tests. All passed without changes.

Then I ran the k6 load test that I used for the limiter at 5k requests per second for 30 minutes. Latency and memory looked the same as on 7.0. I also checked the INFO output for new warnings and found none.

I read the release notes for changes that touch us. The Lua scripting engine has small changes, but our script uses only basic commands. The client library version we use supports the new version.

The plan for production: do it in the maintenance window with a snapshot taken before. Tobias will do the change and I will watch the error rate and the connection counts afterwards.

summary: Morning check of the dashboards after the batching deploy on staging: queue lag is flat and the write call count stays low; no duplicates in the store overnight.
body:
I checked the staging dashboards from the overnight replay with the batching worker. Consumer lag on the queue was flat, with a maximum of 1.2 seconds. Write calls stayed at the lower level from yesterday.

I counted events by id in the store for the night and found no duplicates. The batch flush times in the logs were mostly below 40 ms, which is in line with the 50 ms wait.

I see no reason to hold the branch back from a production trial for one partition group. I will prepare that after the review.

summary: Wrote the reindex job change for monthly search indexes: documents go to the index of their event month, and the run on staging took 31 minutes instead of 50.
body:
This is the next step of the shard layout plan: the reindex job must write to monthly indexes.

Until now the job read all events of one customer and wrote them to the one index of that customer, then switched an alias. For the new layout it reads by time range and writes to an index named events-YYYY-MM, which it creates from the template if it does not exist. The template has 12 primary shards, the routing partition size of 3 and the new ignore_above setting.

The code change is in jobs/reindex/index.ts. I split the work by month so that a failure in one month does not stop the rest. Each month is a unit with its own checkpoint in Postgres, so the job can resume.

The aliases changed too. There is now a read alias per customer with a filter on the customer id and the routing value, pointing at all monthly indexes. The search API does not need to know about the months.

I tested on the staging cluster with a copy of three customers: one large, one medium and one small. The run took 31 minutes against 50 for the old layout on the same data. I think the main reason is that the months are written in parallel, 4 at a time.

I compared document counts per customer between the old and the new indexes. They matched exactly. A sample of 500 searches from the log returned the same top 10 for 497; the other three differed in ties of equal score, which is normal when documents sit on other shards.

Open points: old months should become read only and be force merged after the last write. I wrote that as a follow-up. Also the number of indexes will be 36 or more per year, so I asked Tobias about the cluster state size.

The branch is not part of search-v2 anymore, as that branch ended some time ago. The change is in main behind a flag, which is off in production. The real migration has not started.

summary: Merged the first part of the audit export: a streaming endpoint that writes CSV in chunks, so a 5 million row export no longer needs the whole result in memory.
body:
The audit-export branch had an endpoint that loaded all rows of the requested period into memory and then built the file. For the largest customer, one year of audit entries is around 5 million rows, and the API process went over 2 GB in a test.

I changed it to use a Postgres cursor with batches of 5000 rows. The rows go through the CSV writer, which I fixed for quoting a few days ago, and then straight into the response stream. Memory stays flat at about 80 MB.

Backpressure matters here. When the client is slow, the stream pauses and the cursor is not read further. I used the pipeline function from node:stream/promises so errors and client disconnects close the cursor. I tested a disconnect in the middle by killing curl, and the cursor was closed and the connection went back to the pool.

One issue: a long cursor holds a transaction open, which blocks vacuum for old rows. I set the transaction to read only and added a statement timeout of 15 minutes. For the 5 million row case the export took about 6 minutes on staging.

I also added the row count in a trailer line, so that the customer can check completeness. The count is taken at the start from the same snapshot, so it matches the rows.

The tests: an export of 20k rows with the check of the first and last row, an export with a disconnect, and an export with a failing cursor in the middle, where the stream ends with an error and no trailer, so the file is recognised as incomplete.

I asked Mara to review the SQL, since the ordering needs an index on (customer_id, created_at, id). The index exists. The query plan on staging shows an index scan.

What is left: signing the file with a hash for compliance, and the schedule for recurring exports. I will start with the hash.

summary: Investigated a rise of the cache miss rate for the dashboard queries after a key naming change and fixed the key builder, which put the time range in unrounded; hit rate back to 82 percent.
body:
The Grafana panel for the query cache showed the hit rate for dashboard queries falling from about 80 percent to 41 percent after the release of two days ago.

I looked at the keys in Redis. The new key builder in the search API included the time range as exact milliseconds. Dashboards ask for 'last 24 hours', and the range moves each time, so almost every request produced a new key.

The old builder rounded the end of the range to the minute. When Lena's change moved the key code into a shared helper, the rounding was not carried over, and the tests did not notice, because they used fixed ranges.

I put the rounding back, now with a parameter per query type: one minute for dashboards, and no rounding for exact searches. I also added a test with a moving range that checks that two calls within the same minute get the same key.

After the deploy to production I watched the hit rate. It climbed within 20 minutes and settled at 82 percent, which is a bit above the earlier value, because the one minute rounding is applied to more query types now.

There was a side effect: with so many misses the cache had stored many useless keys. The memory of the cache instance had grown by 700 MB. Those keys have a TTL of 10 minutes, so they went away on their own. I did not have to clean anything.

To prevent a repeat I added a small metric for the number of distinct keys per query type per minute. If it grows without bounds, we can alert on it. The alert rule is not written yet.

I told Lena what happened. There was no blame, since the helper was a good idea, only the rounding was lost.

summary: Wrote the alert rule for cache key churn and tested it against the bad release data: it fires after 10 minutes, and stays quiet during the normal week.
body:
Following the cache hit rate problem, I wrote the alert rule in the alerts-as-code repository. It uses the metric for distinct keys per query type per minute.

The rule fires when the number of distinct dashboard keys per minute is more than three times its value of a day before, for 10 minutes. I used a ratio so that growth of customers does not trigger it.

I tested with promtool on the recorded data of the bad days: the rule fired about 10 minutes after the release. On a normal week it never fired.

The alert goes to the Slack channel, not to PagerDuty, as it is not an emergency. I added a short runbook entry that points at the key builder and the rounding setting.

The change is in review with Tobias.

summary: Finished the first full version of ingest batching on staging: per-partition buffers, flush on size or interval, and a dead-letter path, with duplicates checked over a 6 hour soak.
body:
Today's work closed the loop on the ingest batching branch. The worker now collects events per partition, flushes at 500 events or 50 ms, and writes in one bulk call. A poison event goes to the dead-letter topic instead of failing the batch.

I ran a soak on staging with the replayed event stream for 6 hours. Write calls stayed at about one eighth of the old count and queue lag was flat. I compared event ids in the store against the ids in the replay file and found no duplicates and no gaps.

One thing showed up in the soak. When a bulk write failed halfway, the per-partition retry resent the whole batch, and the store accepted the repeated events twice for a short moment before the dedupe key caught them. The dedupe held, but it made the write path noisier than I want. I changed the retry to resend only the events after the last acknowledged offset.

I added a test that fails the third write of a batch on purpose and checks that the retry resends only the rest. It passes in 40 runs in a row. The metrics got a new counter, ingest_batch_retry_events_total, so the resent count is visible in Grafana.

Not done yet: the batch size per event type still has only the defaults, and nobody has tuned them against the real traffic mix. I also still need to check the memory use of the buffers when a partition stalls. Next step is a load test with one stalled partition, then a review request to Tobias for the deploy settings.

summary: Added a Grafana panel for batch size and flush reason in the ingest worker, so size-triggered and timer-triggered flushes can be told apart.
body:
After the soak I wanted to see how the batches fill in practice. The worker now exports a histogram of batch sizes and a counter labelled by flush reason: size, interval or shutdown.

I added both to the ingest dashboard in Grafana as one panel. On staging with replayed traffic about 70 percent of flushes were by interval and the median batch was 120 events. That means the 500 default is rarely reached for most event types.

The high-volume types do hit the size limit. For those, a larger batch could save more calls, but I did not change anything yet. I want to see production-like traffic first.

The panel JSON is committed with the dashboards in the repo. I told Tobias where it is so he can look at it before the review.

summary: Load-tested ingest batching with one stalled partition: buffers stayed bounded after adding a per-partition cap, and healthy partitions kept their latency.
body:
I started the morning with the stalled partition test I had planned. I paused consumption on one of the partitions in staging and kept the replay running at normal rate.

The first result was bad. The buffer for the stalled partition grew without limit, and after about 4 minutes the worker memory had climbed by 600 MB. The other partitions were fine, but a long stall could have pushed the worker out of memory.

I added a cap per partition buffer, 5000 events by default. When the cap is reached the worker stops reading for that partition and lets the backpressure go back to the queue. The cap is a config value next to the batch size.

I ran the test again. Memory stayed flat, and the p99 write latency of the healthy partitions did not move. When I resumed the stalled partition, it drained its backlog in about 20 seconds.

I also checked the shutdown path with a full buffer. The flush on SIGTERM wrote all 5000 events within the grace period, so nothing is lost on a deploy.

One open point is the metric for a capped partition. Right now there is only a log line. I will add a gauge in the next session so an alert is possible.

I wrote the results in the PR description with the memory graphs. The review request goes to Tobias after the gauge is in.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why exports of large customers sometimes arrive in several files: the audit export splits at 1 million rows by design.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer got three CSV files for one audit export. I looked at the export code on the audit-export branch and at the docs.

The streaming writer rolls over to a new file at 1 million rows. This was chosen so that spreadsheets and the usual import tools can open each file. The file names carry a part number, like export-part-2.csv.

The docs did not say this anywhere. I wrote a short paragraph for Sam to put into the compliance export page, with the row limit and the naming of the parts. I also suggested a line in the email that tells the customer the export is ready.

summary: Wrote the first half of the schema registry change that makes breaking-change errors name the field, after the review asked for it; the compatibility checker now returns paths.
body:
The review of the schema registry branch last week had one open request: the error for a breaking change should say which field broke. I started on it this morning.

The compatibility checker compared two schema versions and returned only a boolean and a reason code. I changed it to return a list of findings, each with a JSON path, the kind of change and the old and new type. The kinds are field removed, type changed and required added.

The tricky part was nested objects and arrays. For arrays of objects the path uses a star, as in items.*.price, so the message stays stable when the array has many entries. I wrote 14 test cases for nesting, optional to required, and a widened number type.

The widened type was a question. Going from int to number is safe for readers, but the old rule flagged it as breaking. I looked at the event schemas of customers and found two that did this change in the past, with no issue. I kept the old rule and added a finding kind named widened, marked as a warning, so nothing changes in behavior but the message is clearer.

The HTTP error body now has a findings array. The text form reads like: breaking change at payload.user.id: type changed from string to integer. The CLI prints that text.

Tests pass locally. What is left is the CLI formatting for many findings, since a schema with 40 changes would print a wall of text. I plan to cap it at 10 and show a count. I also need to update the docs of the registry API.

summary: Looked into a slow reports query in Postgres for the admin console and fixed it with a partial index; the query went from 2.4 seconds to 40 ms.
body:
Lena reported that the usage report page in the admin console took several seconds to load for the two largest customers. I took the query from the slow query log and ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of the production data.

The plan showed a sequential scan over the usage_daily table, about 11 million rows, filtered by customer_id and a status column. The status filter kept only about 2 percent of the rows, which made an index on the status worthwhile.

I created a partial index on (customer_id, day) where status = 'billable'. I built it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so the table was not locked. The build took 3 minutes on the copy.

After that, the plan used an index scan and the query dropped from 2.4 seconds to 40 ms. I also checked that the other query that reads this table, the invoice export, does not get slower. Its plan did not change.

I looked at the vacuum statistics too, since the table has a lot of updates. Autovacuum was keeping up, with the dead tuple ratio under 3 percent, so no tuning was needed.

The migration file is in the PR. I will run it on production in a quiet hour and check the size of the index afterwards, which I expect to be around 150 MB.

summary: Wrote the Terraform change for Redis 7.2 on production and a rollback note; the rollout with Tobias is set for next week, starting with the cache cluster.
body:
The staging upgrade of Redis was clean, so I prepared the production change. The Terraform edit bumps the engine version for the cache cluster and the session cluster, and keeps the rate limiter cluster on 7.0 for the first round.

The order matters. The cache cluster is the safest one, because a lost key only means a cache miss. The session store holds logins, so a problem there logs users out. The rate limiter has the Lua script, which I want to test against 7.2 once more with the per-key limits.

I wrote a rollback note. A managed engine version cannot go down in place, so the rollback is to restore a snapshot taken before the change into a new cluster at 7.0 and switch the endpoint. I tested the snapshot restore on staging, which took 9 minutes for a small dataset. For production I estimate about 25 minutes, which is acceptable for the cache and not nice for the sessions.

Because of this I added a step: take a manual snapshot of the session cluster right before the change, and run the change in the lowest traffic hour.

I checked the client libraries as well. The Node client in the search API and the Go client in the workers both support 7.2 without flags. I did not find any use of removed commands by grepping for the deprecated ones.

The plan is in the infra repo as a short markdown file. Tobias will review it, and we will do the cache cluster first.

Open: the alert thresholds for memory were set for 7.0 behavior, and I want to compare the memory numbers on staging between the versions before the rollout.

summary: Added a gauge for capped partitions in the ingest worker and an alert rule; opened the ingest batching PR for review by Tobias with soak and stall test results.
body:
As planned yesterday, I added the missing metric. The worker now exports ingest_partition_capped, a gauge that is 1 while a partition buffer is at its cap and the worker has paused reading.

The alert rule fires when any partition stays capped for more than 2 minutes. I tested it on staging by pausing a partition, and it fired after 2 minutes and cleared after the resume. I wrote the rule in the alert rules repo, in code like the other rules.

Then I cleaned up the branch. I squashed three fixup commits, rewrote the README section about the batch settings, and listed all config keys with defaults: batch size, flush interval, partition cap and dead-letter topic name.

The PR description has four parts. First the idea and the 8x drop in write calls. Second the soak result with no duplicates. Third the stall test with the memory graphs before and after the cap. Fourth the open points.

The open points are honest ones. The defaults for the high-volume event types are not tuned. The dead-letter topic has no consumer yet, so poison events pile up with no one looking. And I did not test with a broker restart in the middle of a flush.

I asked Tobias to review the deploy parts: the new env vars in the Terraform task definition and the topic creation for the dead letters. I also asked Mara to look at the retry code, since she wrote the first worker.

Next I will write the dead-letter consumer as a small tool that prints and counts events by reason.

summary: Finished the finding cap in the schema registry CLI: it shows 10 findings and a count of the rest, and the docs for the registry API now describe the findings array.
body:
I finished the open points from this morning on the schema registry branch. The CLI prints at most 10 findings, then a line such as: and 30 more, use --all to show them.

The flag --all prints everything. I also added --json for scripts, which prints the findings array as it comes from the API.

Then the docs. The registry API page has a new section with an example of the error body and a table of the finding kinds: removed, type_changed, required_added and widened. Sam will read it for clarity tomorrow.

All tests pass, 22 in total for the checker and the CLI. I pushed the branch and asked for a second look at the review from last week, so the merge can happen.

summary: Investigated why cache hit rate for the search API drops every night at the same time and found the nightly reindex invalidates a key prefix too broadly.
body:
Mara pointed out that the cache hit rate graph for the search API has a dip every night, down from about 80 percent to 35 percent for around 40 minutes. I looked at the timing and it matches the reindex job.

The reindex job calls a function that deletes cache keys after it finishes writing an index, so that users do not see old results. The function deletes by the prefix search:v2:, which covers all customers. It does this once per index, and there are many indexes.

So every customer loses the whole cache several times during the run, even if their own index was not touched. That explains the long dip.

I changed the invalidation to use the customer id in the prefix, search:v2:{customer}:, and to run it once after the last index of that customer is done. The key naming was already per customer, so this needed no change in the key builder.

I tested on staging with the reindex job. The hit rate for customers not being reindexed stayed flat. For the customer being reindexed, it dropped once at the end, as expected.

I checked the scan cost too. The deletion uses SCAN with a match pattern and a count of 500, in small steps, so it does not block Redis. With the narrower prefix there are fewer keys to scan.

There is one more thing for later. The monthly indexes planned for the new shard layout will make more indexes per customer, so the invalidation must stay once per customer and not once per index. I left a comment in the code about this.

The change is merged to main and goes out with the next deploy. Tomorrow I will check the graph after the first night.

summary: Wrote the dead-letter inspector for the ingest worker: a small CLI that counts poison events by reason and prints samples, so the dead-letter topic is not a black hole.
body:
The ingest batching PR sends poison events to a dead-letter topic, but nobody was reading it. I wrote a small Go tool in the tools directory that reads the topic from the start and groups events by failure reason.

The output is a table with the reason, the count and the first seen offset. With the flag --sample 3 it prints three example payloads per reason, with the customer id kept and the values cut to 80 characters.

I ran it against staging after feeding a few bad events on purpose: invalid UTF-8, an oversized field and a missing type. It listed all three reasons with the right counts.

I did not build a replay function. Replaying needs a decision about what to fix first, and that depends on the real reasons we see in production. I noted this in the PR as a follow-up.

I added the tool to the runbook page for ingest, with the command line.

summary: Reviewed Lena's change to the admin console API key page: logic is fine, but the revoke button had no confirmation and the list did not refresh after revoking.
body:
Lena asked for a review of the API key page changes. I read the diff and ran the console locally against staging.

The new table with sorting by last used works well. The composite index from last week keeps the list fast, and I saw 7 ms for the query on a customer with 300 keys.

Two problems came up. First, the revoke button acts at once without a confirmation. A misclick would break a customer's integration, since a revoked key is rejected on the next request. I asked for a confirm dialog that names the key.

Second, after a revoke the list did not refresh, so the key still showed as active until a reload. The mutation did not invalidate the query cache entry for the list. This is a one-line fix with the query key, and I wrote the exact key in the comment.

I also noticed that the last used column shows the raw timestamp in UTC without a label. A short label or a tooltip would help, but it is a small point and I marked it as optional.

I approved with the two requests. Lena said she would fix them tonight, so I will look again tomorrow morning.

summary: Tried to speed up the reindex job by raising bulk size to 5000 documents, found it overloaded the search nodes, and went back to 1000 with a parallelism of 2.
body:
The monthly reindex run takes 31 minutes on staging, and I wanted to see if it could be shorter. The bulk size was 1000 documents, so I tried 5000 on staging.

The run got faster at first, down to about 24 minutes. But OpenSearch started to reject requests with 429 responses after around 10 minutes, and the job log showed many retries. The node heap use also reached 85 percent, which is higher than I like.

I tried 2500 as a middle step. It had the same pattern, with fewer rejections but still some. The gain was only about 3 minutes, and not worth the risk to the live search traffic, since staging has the same node types as production.

Then I went the other way and kept the bulk size at 1000 but raised the parallelism of the bulk writers from 1 to 2. That gave 26 minutes with no rejections and a heap peak of 62 percent.

I set parallelism 2 as the new default and left the bulk size alone. I wrote the three results in the job README so the next person does not repeat the test.

The larger bulk size is dropped as an idea. Parallelism 3 is untested and I want to wait until the shard layout plan is clearer, because the number of shards changes how the writes spread over the nodes.

The change is a config default and a short code change in the writer pool, in the main checkout.

summary: Checked the cache hit rate graph after the first night with the narrower reindex invalidation: the nightly dip is gone for customers outside the run.
body:
This is the follow-up check from the earlier session. The change to the invalidation prefix went out this afternoon, and the first reindex run with it happened at the usual hour.

I looked at the hit rate per customer in Grafana. The overall dip was down from 35 percent to about 70 percent at its lowest. Customers that were not in the run stayed at their normal 80 percent.

The customers being reindexed saw one drop at the end of their own index, and it recovered in about 6 minutes. That matches what I saw on staging.

I also checked Redis memory and the number of SCAN calls, and both were lower than on the nights before. No errors in the logs.

Nothing more to do here.

summary: Rebased the audit-export branch on main and fixed a conflict in the CSV writer; the part rollover at 1 million rows now has a test that crosses the limit.
body:
The audit export branch had fallen behind main after the CSV quoting fix and the streaming endpoint merge. I rebased it today.

There was one conflict in the CSV writer. Both sides changed the function that writes a row, one for quoting per RFC 4180 and one for counting rows for the rollover. I kept both, quoting first and then the count.

The rollover logic had no test that crossed the limit, because 1 million rows are slow to generate. I made the limit configurable and wrote a test with a limit of 50 rows that checks that part 2 starts with the header, that no row is split and that the part numbers are in the file names.

I ran the full suite and it passed. I also did a manual export of 2.5 million rows on staging and got three parts, with row counts of 1000000, 1000000 and 500000.

Next I want to look at the signed download links for the parts, since right now each part has its own link with a short expiry. A customer downloading three large files might see the link of the third part expire.

summary: Made the audit export download links valid for 6 hours and tied all parts to one export id, so large exports no longer lose the last part to an expired link.
body:
Following the note from the rebase, I looked at the download links of the audit export. Each part had a signed link with an expiry of 15 minutes, counted from the time the export finished.

For a customer on a slow connection, the third part could expire before the first two were done. Sam had seen one such complaint, which fits.

I changed it in two ways. The links now carry an export id and a signature, and the expiry is checked against the export, not against each part. The export lives for 6 hours after it finishes, and every link for its parts is valid for that time.

I also added an endpoint that returns the list of parts with fresh links, so the console page can offer a reload of the links without a new export. That avoids rerunning an export of millions of rows just for a link.

Security was something I checked on purpose. The signature covers the export id, the customer id and the expiry, so changing the id in the URL to look at another customer's export fails with 403. I wrote a test for that case.

The tests pass. The docs page needs a sentence about the 6 hours, and I passed that to Sam.

summary: Wrote the staging checklist for the Redis 7.2 production rollout with Tobias, including the memory comparison between 7.0 and 7.2 under the same load.
body:
Before the production change, I ran the same load test on staging against 7.0 and 7.2 and compared memory. The dataset was a copy of the production key distribution at about 20 percent of the size.

Memory use with 7.2 was about 2 percent lower for the cache data, which is within the noise. The latency of GET and SET at p99 was the same in both. The Lua script of the rate limiter ran at 5k requests per second on both versions with no difference.

Based on this I wrote a checklist for the rollout. It has the snapshot step, the order of clusters, the checks after each one (error rate, hit rate, connection count) and the point at which we stop and restore.

Tobias suggested doing the rate limiter cluster in a separate week, and I agreed. The checklist is in the infra repo and the first run is for the cache cluster only.

summary: Built the first version of the per-month shard sizing script for the search index plan, and the numbers show the largest month is about 3 times the median.
body:
The shard layout plan needs real numbers, so I wrote a script that asks OpenSearch for the document count and size per index and groups it by event month. It runs against a snapshot of the cluster statistics, not the live nodes, so it is safe to repeat.

The output is a table with the month, the number of documents, the size in GB and the share of the whole. I ran it on the production stats, taken from the cat API output that Tobias exported.

The results are interesting. The median month is about 140 GB. The largest month is about 420 GB, which is three times more. This comes from two large customers who sent a one-time import in that month.

That matters for the plan. If every month gets the same number of shards, the big month has shards that are far too large, and the target I had was 30 to 50 GB per shard. With 12 shards a month, the median month has shards of about 12 GB, which is small, and the big month has shards of 35 GB, which is fine.

So the choice of the shard count depends on whether we look at the median or the peak. I tried three options in the script: a fixed 12 shards, a fixed 6 shards, and a count derived from the month size.

The derived count gives 4 shards for the median and 9 for the peak month. It needs the size before the month index is created, which is not possible for the current month while it is still filling. So a rule for the current month is needed, for example to start with 6 and use the rollover after a size limit.

The fixed 12 shards are simple and are what the plan said so far. The cost is many small shards, and each shard has a fixed overhead in heap on the nodes. I computed the overhead as about 20 MB per shard in the cluster state, so 12 months of 12 shards is 144 shards, which is no problem.

I wrote the three options and the table into the plan document and marked the choice as open. I would like Tobias to check the node numbers before we decide.

The script is in the tools directory as shardsizes.ts with a short usage note.

summary: Fixed a bug in the Go ingest client where the backoff after a 429 started at the wrong value, so clients waited 10 ms instead of the Retry-After time.
body:
Mara noticed in the logs of a test client that after a 429 response it retried almost at once. I looked at the Go ingest client and found the cause.

The client has an exponential backoff with a base of 100 ms. The code read the Retry-After header, but it parsed the value as milliseconds, while the header is in seconds. A header with 2 gave a wait of 2 ms, and with the jitter it came out around 10 ms at most.

That is bad together with the new per-key limits, since a client that does not wait only gets more 429 responses and adds load. I wrote a failing test first, with a mock server that returns 429 and Retry-After: 2, and checks that the second request comes no earlier than 2 seconds later.

The fix parses the header as seconds, and also accepts the HTTP date form, since the spec allows both. If the header is missing or invalid, the client falls back to the exponential backoff. I capped the wait at 30 seconds, so a wrong header cannot stall a client for ever.

The number of attempts is still three, as before. I did not touch that, and the earlier look at the logs showed that the second attempt fixes nearly all failures.

I also checked the TypeScript client in the docs examples. It already used seconds, so it was fine.

I ran the tests, and the new one passes, plus the old 18. The change is released as a patch version of the client, and I added a line to the changelog. Sam will mention it in the next customer note.

One follow-up is open: the jitter is a full jitter, between 0 and the wait. For a Retry-After value, I think it is better to add jitter only on top of it. I made the change in this release, so the client waits at least as long as the server asked.

summary: Started the loader-retry work: the document loader now resumes a large file from the last committed chunk after a failure instead of starting from the beginning.
body:
The document loader for large files fails now and then, for example on a network error to storage in the middle of a 4 GB file. Today it starts again from byte zero, which can waste an hour. I started the loader-retry branch to fix that.

The design is simple. The loader reads the file in chunks of 64 MB, aligned on record boundaries, and after a chunk has been written to the queue it records a checkpoint in Postgres: the file id, the byte offset and a chunk counter. On a restart, the loader reads the checkpoint and seeks to that offset.

The table is called loader_checkpoints, with a unique key on the file id. I wrote the migration, and an upsert that updates the offset only if the new offset is larger, so a slow old worker cannot move it back.

Aligning on record boundaries was the part that took longest. NDJSON is easy, since a record is a line. For CSV, a quoted field can contain a line break, so I cannot just cut at a newline. The reader keeps the parser state, and a checkpoint is only written at a point where the parser is outside of a quoted field.

I tested with a generated NDJSON file of 2 GB, and killed the loader at random points 20 times. In each case the restart resumed, and the event count in the queue matched the file with no duplicates, because the checkpoint is written after the chunk is acknowledged. A crash between the acknowledgement and the checkpoint can duplicate one chunk. I accepted that for now, since the events have ids and the store dedupes on them.

The CSV tests are only partial. I had a case with a line break in a quoted field exactly at a chunk border, and the first version failed it by cutting inside the field. After the parser state fix it passes.

Still missing: the retry policy itself, which decides how often and how long to wait between attempts, and the cleanup of old checkpoints when a file is done. I plan to do the policy next, with a backoff and a limit of attempts per file.

The branch builds and the tests pass locally. No review requested yet.

summary: Added the retry policy to the document loader: five attempts with exponential backoff, a permanent failure state for bad files, and checkpoint cleanup when a file finishes.
body:
This continues the loader-retry branch from yesterday evening. The resume from a checkpoint worked, so now the loader needs a policy for when to try again.

I separated two kinds of errors. Transient ones, like a storage timeout or a connection reset, are retried. Permanent ones, like a malformed record or an unsupported encoding, mark the file as failed at once, since another attempt gives the same result.

For transient errors the loader waits 2 seconds, then 4, 8, 16 and 32, with jitter, for five attempts in total. The attempt counter lives in the checkpoint row, so a restart of the process does not give a file a fresh set of attempts.

A failed file gets a status and the last error text in the loader table, and the admin console already shows that status for imports. I checked that the text is readable there.

Cleanup is a delete of the checkpoint row when the file is complete. I also added a daily job that removes rows of files older than 30 days that never finished, so the table does not grow.

Tests cover a transient error that clears on the third try, one that never clears, and a permanent error. All pass.

summary: Replied to Sam about why a customer's search showed results from a deleted index: the cache served them for up to 10 minutes because the delete does not clear the key prefix.
body:
Sam forwarded a ticket. A customer deleted a set of events and still saw them in search for a while afterwards.

I checked the delete path in the search API. The events are removed from OpenSearch at once, but the query cache keeps the old result lists until their TTL, which is 10 minutes for search queries. So users can see removed events for that time.

The invalidation I changed this week works for the reindex job, but the delete endpoint does not call it. I opened a ticket to call the same per customer invalidation after a delete. I wrote to Sam that the effect is limited to 10 minutes, and gave a short text for the customer.

summary: Made the delete endpoint of the search API clear the customer's cache keys after removing events, so deleted events disappear from search results at once.
body:
This is the fix for the ticket from this morning. The delete endpoint now calls the invalidation function for the customer prefix after the OpenSearch delete returns.

I wrote a test that runs a search, deletes an event, runs the same search again and checks that the event is gone. Before the change, the test failed as the cache returned the old list.

The invalidation is done in the background, so the delete request does not wait for the SCAN. The response says accepted, and the cache clears within a second or so in my tests. That is fine for the user, because the next search after the delete is rarely so quick.

The test passes and the change is merged to main.

summary: Dropped an attempt to replace the hand-written NDJSON line splitter in the loader with a streaming parser library, because it was slower and hid the byte offsets that checkpoints need.
body:
I wanted to remove some of our own code in the loader, so I tried a streaming NDJSON parsing library in place of our line splitter on the loader-retry branch.

The first problem was speed. On a 2 GB test file the library took 94 seconds against 61 seconds for our splitter, since it decodes each record fully, and we only need the line boundaries at that stage.

The second problem was worse. The checkpoints need exact byte offsets for the end of each record. The library gives records, but the offsets it reports are character counts, which differ from bytes for multi-byte text. I could compute the bytes again, but then I would have written the splitter again, only more slowly.

I also found that it skips empty lines silently, and our counts of records per chunk must match the lines of the file, so I would need a workaround for that too.

I dropped the library and reverted the commit. I kept one thing from the experiment, a benchmark script for the splitter, which is now in the repo next to the loader. The splitter stays as it is.

summary: Prepared the loader-retry PR: end-to-end test with a flaky storage mock passes, and the PR lists the duplicate-chunk case and how the store dedupe covers it.
body:
I finished the branch work for the loader and wrote an end-to-end test. It uses a storage mock that fails randomly on about 10 percent of reads, with both timeouts and resets, and one that returns a permanently broken record.

The test loads a 500 MB file with the mock. The loader needed 7 restarts on average over 10 runs, and the final event count matched the file every time. The broken-record file ended in the failed state after the first attempt, as intended.

Then I looked at the duplicate chunk case again. If the process dies after the queue acknowledged a chunk and before the checkpoint is written, the next run sends that chunk again. I measured how often this happens in the test, and it was in 3 of 70 restarts. The duplicates were all dropped by the dedupe on the event id in the store, and the counts were right.

Still, I do not like to rely only on the dedupe. The window is short, but I considered writing the checkpoint in the same step as the acknowledgement. That is not possible, since the queue and Postgres are two systems. I wrote the reasoning in the PR so that the reviewer sees it was a choice.

The PR description has the design, the error classes, the retry numbers and the test results. I also added a note for the docs: the loader now resumes, so a customer does not need to upload a failed large file again.

I asked Mara for the review, since she knows the loader best, and Tobias for a look at the new table and the daily cleanup job.

Two small things are left for after the review: a metric for the number of resumes per day, and a line in the runbook about how to reset a checkpoint by hand if a file must start from the beginning.

summary: Merged the loader-retry PR after Mara's review: the checkpoint file now carries a format version so old checkpoints are discarded cleanly instead of crashing the loader.
body:
Mara reviewed the loader-retry PR this afternoon and found one real problem: a checkpoint written by the old loader build had no version field, and the new code panicked on it with 'unexpected end of JSON input'. I added a version field to the checkpoint and made the loader drop any checkpoint without a known version and restart that file from the beginning. A unit test covers an old-format file and a truncated file.

She also asked for the attempt count to show up in the log line, so each retry now logs the file id, the chunk number and the attempt. The duplicate-chunk explanation in the PR text was fine for her. The PR is merged and goes out with the next deploy. Still open is a metric for files in the permanent failure state, which I will add later this week.

summary: Added a counter and an alert for files that reach the permanent failure state in the document loader, so a bad customer file is noticed by us before the customer writes to support.
body:
The loader-retry change had no signal for files that give up after five attempts. I added a Prometheus counter, loader_files_failed_total, labelled by reason: bad_format, storage_error and too_many_attempts. A Grafana panel next to the existing loader panels shows the counter per hour.

The alert rule fires when more than 3 files fail permanently within an hour. I tested it on staging by feeding it 5 deliberately broken NDJSON files, and it fired after the evaluation window as expected. It does not page; it goes to the team channel only, since a bad file is not an incident.

I wrote a short note for Sam on what the three reasons mean and what to tell a customer in each case. The note is in the support docs draft.

The next step is to check the numbers after a few days of production traffic and see whether the threshold of 3 is too low.

summary: Morning review of the monthly shard plan for the search index: the sizing script shows one month at 3 times the median, so the plan needs a split rule for that month before anything is built.
body:
I started the day with the sizing numbers from the script I wrote two days ago. The plan is one index per event month instead of one per customer. The median month holds about 38 million documents, and the largest month holds about 115 million. That is the month of a big customer import.

A single index with the usual primary shard count would give shards of very different sizes. I looked at three options. The first is a fixed shard count for all months, which wastes space on small months. The second is a shard count that depends on the expected document count, set when the index is created. The third is a rollover inside the month once a size limit is reached.

The second option is the simplest to run, because the reindex job already knows the document count of a month before it writes. The third needs aliases per month and more logic in the search API. I wrote the second option into the plan: the count is the document total divided by a target of about 30 million per shard, rounded up, with a minimum of 1.

I checked what this gives for the 12 months in the sizing data: shard counts between 1 and 4. That is far fewer shards in total than today, which is good for the heap use on the search nodes.

One open question is queries that span many months. A search over a year now touches 12 indexes, each with a few shards. I want a measurement of that on staging before I commit. The search API already builds the index list from the time range, so the code change should be small.

I added a section on this to the plan document with the table of months and shard counts. Tobias should look at the node memory part. I also listed what must not change: the customer filter has to stay in every query, since customers share an index after this change. That is the main risk of the whole plan, so it gets a test of its own later.

Next is a staging test of the multi-month query latency.

summary: Wrote the first draft of the split rule for the oversized month in the monthly search index plan: a month above 2 times the median gets extra shards, sized from document count.
body:
After the morning review showed one month at about 3 times the median, I wrote a split rule into the shard sizing script. A month whose document count exceeds 2 times the median gets its shard count scaled up in proportion, rounded up, with a hard cap of 12 shards per month index.

I considered splitting the big month into two indexes by half-month. That would keep shard sizes even, but it makes every query over that month hit two indexes and complicates the delete path. I dropped that idea for the plan and kept one index with more shards.

The target I used is 30 to 40 GB per shard, which is what the current per-customer indexes look like on average. With that target the largest month comes out at 9 shards, and the median month at 3. The script now prints a table with month, document count, size estimate and chosen shard count, so the plan can be reviewed without reading code.

I ran it against the staging copy and against the production counts from the metrics. The two tables differ by less than 5 percent in the shard counts, so the staging data is a fair stand-in. One open point is that new months grow while they are current, so a month created at its start would be too small at its end. For now the rule uses the previous month's size as the estimate for the current one.

I wrote this down in the plan document as an open question for the review with Tobias. Next I want to see how the reindex job picks the shard count at creation time, because it has to call the same rule and not a copy of it.

summary: Reviewed the Redis 7.2 staging run with Tobias: memory use is 6 percent lower than on 7.0 under the same load, and the connection counts are the same.
body:
Tobias and I went through the staging run of Redis 7.2 that we prepared yesterday. The test used the same recorded load as the 7.0 baseline: the query cache traffic, the rate limiter counters and the session reads of the admin console.

Memory after 2 hours was 3.1 GB on 7.2 and 3.3 GB on 7.0, so about 6 percent lower. We think most of it comes from the smaller encoding of small hashes. Command latency was equal: p99 under 1.2 ms for both.

Connection counts stayed the same, at around 38 from the search API and 12 from the ingest side. We did not see any client library warnings. The Node client and the Go client both worked without changes.

We checked the persistence settings too, and the snapshot time was a little shorter on 7.2.

One point from the checklist is still open: the failover test. Tobias will run it on staging tomorrow, with a primary killed during load, and measure how long the clients need to reconnect.

The rollout stays set for next week, starting with the cache cluster. I updated the checklist with the measured numbers.

Nothing was surprising, which is what we wanted.

summary: Answered Lena's question about why the API key page showed a key as active for a minute after revoking it: the rate limiter caches key status for 60 seconds.
body:
Lena saw that a revoked key still worked for a short time in her tests and asked if the console was broken. It was not. The console writes the revoke to Postgres at once, but the ingest API and the search API read key status through a Redis cache with a TTL of 60 seconds.

So a revoked key can still be used for up to a minute. That is a deliberate tradeoff from the rate limiter work. I told her the console can show the state as 'revoking' in that minute, which is honest and needs no backend change.

I also noted that a hard revoke, which deletes the cache key, would be easy to add for the case of a leaked key. I put that in the backlog.

summary: Created the monthly search indexes from the reindex job with a computed shard count and checked on staging that document counts match the source for every month.
body:
Today I wrote the index creation part of the reindex job change. Before writing documents for a month, the job asks Postgres for the document count of that month and computes the shard count with the rule from the plan: count divided by 30 million, rounded up, minimum 1.

The index name is events-YYYY-MM, built from the event month. The job creates the index with explicit settings and mappings from the same template that the per-customer indexes use, so the field boosts of search v2 are unchanged. If the index already exists, the job checks that the settings match and fails with a clear message if not.

I ran it on staging for the last 12 months. The run took 33 minutes. After it, I compared the document count of every monthly index with the count in Postgres, grouped by month. All 12 matched exactly.

I then compared the counts per customer inside each index, using an aggregation on the customer field. Here one month was off by 214 documents. The cause was events with a timestamp in the future by a few hours, which the month rule put in the next month. The count query used the ingest time instead. I changed the count query to use the same event time as the writer, and a second run matched everywhere.

I added a test for events at the month boundary, in both directions: one second before midnight and one second after, in UTC.

A related point is the refresh interval. During the bulk load I set it to -1 and restore it to 5 seconds at the end. If the job dies in between, the index would stay without refresh. I added a cleanup step at the start of the job that resets the setting on any monthly index that has it at -1 and is not being written.

The alias handling is not done. The search API will need an alias or a list of indexes. For now it builds the list from the time range, as before. I left a note in the code for that.

The next piece is the switch of the search API to read the monthly indexes behind a flag, so staging can be compared with the old layout side by side.

summary: Wrote the first full pass of the Redis 7.2 rollback note and a pre-flight script for the cache cluster rollout, after the staging review showed no surprises.
body:
Tobias and I are going to roll Redis 7.2 out to the cache cluster first, so I spent the afternoon on the parts that make that safe. The rollback note from last week was only a list of steps. It now has the exact Terraform variable to change, the order of nodes, and the point after which a rollback needs a restore instead of a version switch.

I also wrote a pre-flight script that runs before the rollout starts. It checks the current version on every node, the replication state, the memory use against the limit, and the number of connected clients. It refuses to continue if any replica is behind by more than a few seconds, or if memory use is above 75 percent.

The memory check came from the staging review. Memory was 6 percent lower on 7.2, but the peak during the replica resync was still high. A node that starts the rollout close to its limit could hit trouble during the resync, so the 75 percent guard is deliberate.

I tested the script against staging in three states. In the healthy state it passed. With one replica stopped it failed with the message that names the node. With a memory limit lowered on purpose it failed with the memory message. All three results were what I wanted.

Then I looked at the clients. The ingest workers and the search API both use connection pools, and a node restart drops every connection on it. I checked that both reconnect without a restart of the service, by restarting a staging node while the load test ran. The search API recovered within 2 seconds. The ingest workers logged a burst of connection errors for about 4 seconds and then stopped.

Those 4 seconds are acceptable for the cache cluster. They would not be for the rate limiter counters, so the rate limiter cluster goes later and gets its own check. I added that to the note as a separate section.

The last thing was a Grafana dashboard with the metrics that Tobias and I want to watch during the rollout: client count, memory, hit rate, command latency and the error counters from the pools. I tested the panels against staging data from the load run. Tomorrow I will go through the note with Tobias and fix what he finds unclear.

summary: Fixed a bug in ingest batching where a flush timer kept firing for an empty partition buffer, creating zero-length writes that showed up as noise in the store logs.
body:
While reading the staging logs after the soak I saw lines in the store log about writes with 0 rows. They came from the ingest worker, about one per partition per flush interval, only for partitions that had no traffic.

The cause was in the buffer code. The timer for the flush interval was started when a buffer was created and re-armed after every flush, whether or not the buffer had events. The flush function did not check for an empty buffer, and sent a batch with no rows.

The writes were harmless, but they counted in the write call metric, which made the batching look less effective than it is. On staging, with 12 partitions and a 200 ms interval, it was around 60 empty calls per second.

The fix has two parts. The flush function returns at once if the buffer is empty. The timer is now started on the first event that arrives in an empty buffer and not re-armed after a flush, so an idle partition has no timer at all.

I wrote a test with a fake clock: an idle buffer produces no flush calls over 10 intervals, a single event produces exactly one flush after the interval, and an event arriving right at the interval boundary is not lost.

The second test was the one that mattered. With the old timer logic, an event arriving just as a flush started could wait for a full extra interval. With the new logic it gets its own timer. I checked this with 100000 random arrival times in the test, and the maximum wait was the interval.

On staging, the write call count dropped again after the deploy, from about 95 per second to 41 per second at the same traffic. The batch size panel shows the same sizes as before.

I added the fix to the open PR for Tobias, with a note on the change in the metric so nobody is confused by the new number. I also reran a short soak of 2 hours and checked for duplicates and gaps by event id. There were none.

What is left is the review by Tobias and the production rollout plan, which should start with one partition group.

summary: Tobias reviewed the ingest batching PR and asked for a drain on shutdown; implemented it so buffered events are flushed on SIGTERM within the ECS stop timeout.
body:
Tobias went through the batching PR and had three comments. The important one was about shutdown: when ECS stops a task, the worker gets SIGTERM, and events in the per-partition buffers could be lost if the process exits before a flush. Offsets are committed only after a successful flush, so nothing would be lost for good, but the events would be processed again, and that depends on the store dedupe.

I wanted a clean drain anyway. On SIGTERM the worker now stops reading from the queue, flushes all buffers, commits the offsets and then exits. There is a deadline of 25 seconds for the drain, since the ECS stop timeout is 30 seconds. If the deadline passes, the worker logs how many events were left in which partitions and exits.

I tested it locally with a kill during load. Without the change, a restart caused about 400 events to be read twice; with the change, none. I also tested with a stalled store, where the flush cannot finish. The worker waited for the deadline and then exited with the log line, as designed.

His second comment was about the name of the interval setting. It was called FLUSH_MS in one place and BATCH_INTERVAL in another. I made them one name, BATCH_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS, and kept the old name as a fallback for one release with a warning in the log.

The third was a question about the per-partition cap, since a cap that is too low could block healthy partitions under a burst. I explained that the cap applies per partition and that the stall test showed the others unaffected. He asked me to add the cap value to the startup log, which I did.

He also asked how the rollout would go. My proposal is the following:
- one worker task in production with batching on, for a day
- then a third of the tasks
- then all of them
At each step we look at queue lag, write call count and the dead-letter topic. The flag to turn batching off is a setting that needs a restart, but no deploy.

He agreed with that, and wanted the first step to be on a quiet day for the large customers. We will look at the traffic graph for that.

I pushed the changes and the PR is waiting for his second look. Then I updated the PR text with the drain behaviour and the test results.

summary: Investigated a slow Postgres vacuum on the audit log table, which had grown to 180 GB, and set per-table autovacuum thresholds so it runs more often in smaller steps.
body:
Tobias pointed out that a vacuum on the audit log table had been running for more than 9 hours the night before and overlapped with the morning traffic. I looked at it in the database.

The table has 180 GB and about 900 million rows, and it only grows by inserts, with a few updates when an entry is marked as exported by the audit export. The default autovacuum settings trigger on 20 percent of changed rows, which for this table means a vacuum only after many millions of changes. When it finally runs, it runs for hours.

Because the table is append-only, the real need is freezing and the visibility map, not removing dead rows. I checked n_dead_tup, which was low, at about 2 million, and the age of the oldest unfrozen transaction, which was getting closer to the freeze limit than I like.

I changed the settings for this table only:
- autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.01
- autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor 0.02
- autovacuum_freeze_max_age lowered a little
The insert scale factor makes the vacuum run after inserts as well, which is the feature of Postgres 16 that fits this case.

I tried it on a staging copy of the table, scaled to a smaller size, and the vacuum runs were short, about 10 minutes each, and happened every hour or so under the replayed insert rate.

I also checked the cost limit, since vacuum should not starve the reports queries of IO. I left the cost limit at the default and set a cost delay of 2 ms for this table. On staging the reports query p95 did not change during a vacuum.

I wrote the change as a migration file with the ALTER TABLE statements and a comment that explains why. I did not apply it to production yet, since Tobias wants to be there when it starts the first big vacuum run, which will take a while because it has to catch up.

One more thing: partitioning the audit log by month would make all this easier, and old partitions could be frozen and left alone. I noted the idea in the backlog, but it is bigger than this change, and the audit export branch reads from the table in a way that I would have to check first.

Next is to apply the change in production with Tobias tomorrow morning and watch the first run.

summary: Wrote the runbook draft for rolling back the search index from monthly to customer layout, with the flag switch and the checks before and after.
body:
Tobias is the owner of the rollback runbook for the new shard layout, but he asked me to write the first draft, since I know the search API side. I wrote it in the docs folder of the repo.

The key point is that the rollback needs the old per-customer indexes to still exist. So the plan is to keep them, read-only, for 14 days after the switch and delete them only after that. Until then, a rollback is a change of the SEARCH_LAYOUT setting and a restart of the search API.

The runbook has these steps:
- check that the per-customer indexes exist and have the expected document counts
- check how many documents were written to the monthly indexes since the switch, since these are missing from the old ones
- run the catch-up job that copies them back, with the count of documents per customer as a check
- switch the flag, restart, and watch error rate and latency for 15 minutes

The second point is the hard one. During the time of the new layout, new events go to the monthly indexes only, unless the reindex job writes to both. I wrote that the job should write to both during the 14 days, which doubles the write load of the nightly run. That is a cost, and I put it into the plan as an explicit item for Tobias to accept or change.

I also listed the cache: after the flag switch the cache keys of the search API stay valid, since they do not include the layout, and the results should be the same except for tie order. If that turns out to be wrong, the cache for the search API has to be cleared by prefix.

The draft is in a PR for Tobias. I marked two places as questions for him: the dual write cost and the length of the retention of the old indexes.

summary: Rebased the schema-registry branch and finished the compatibility checker output with field paths for nested arrays, after a bug where array items were reported as the parent field.
body:
After the CLI change of the last days, I tested the checker on the real schemas of our customers' event types, and found a flaw. When a breaking change was inside an array of objects, the finding named the array field instead of the item field. For example, a removed required field in items[] was reported as 'items', which does not help anybody to find the change.

The cause was in the path builder of the checker. It added the property name when it went into an object but did not add anything for the array items step. So the path stopped at the array. I changed it so the path has the form items[].sku, using the same notation as the docs for the registry API.

I went through the cases that need a path:
- a removed field inside an object inside an array
- a type change of an array item, from string to integer
- a field that became required in a nested object
- an enum value removed in an array of strings
For each one I wrote a test with the expected path. Two of them failed before the change and all of them pass now.

There was one more case I had not thought about: anyOf and oneOf. A change in one branch of a oneOf gets a path like payload.(oneOf 1).id in the new code. This is not pretty, but it tells you which branch. I looked at how other tools write it and kept a simple form.

The branch was behind main by about 30 commits, so I rebased. There was one conflict, in the CLI output code, where main had a change of the colour handling. I resolved it by keeping both. All tests passed after the rebase.

I ran the checker against the 140 schema versions in the staging registry, comparing every version with the previous one, and checked that the number of findings did not change compared with the old checker; only the paths changed. The count was the same, 212 findings, which is good.

Then I updated the docs example in the registry API page so the findings array shows a nested path. Sam will look at the wording tomorrow.

What is left in this topic is the check in the CI pipeline that runs the checker for pull requests that touch schemas. That is next.

summary: Added the schema compatibility check to CI for pull requests that touch schemas: it fails with the findings and their paths in the job log, and skips unrelated pull requests.
body:
The registry checker is only useful if it runs without anybody remembering to run it, so I wired it into CI today. The job runs on pull requests that change files under schemas/, and it skips for all others by a path filter, so it costs nothing on most pull requests.

The job gets the base version of each changed schema from the target branch, runs the checker between base and head, and prints the findings. A finding of the type breaking makes the job fail. A finding of the type warning is printed but does not fail the job.

There are two details I had to solve. First, new schema files have no base, and the checker should accept them. I made the job treat a missing base as a new schema and only validate that it is well formed. Second, deleted schemas. Deleting an event type that customers still send is breaking in practice. The job fails on this too, with the message that deletion needs an explicit approval label on the pull request.

I tested it with four throwaway pull requests on a fork of the repo:
- a harmless added optional field, which passed
- a removed required field in a nested array, which failed with the path items[].sku
- a new schema file, which passed
- a deleted schema, which failed, and passed after the label was added
The log output was readable. I limited it to the same 10 findings plus a count, like the CLI.

The run time is about 25 seconds, most of it for installing dependencies. I added the dependency cache of the CI system, and it dropped to 11 seconds.

Mara asked in the review of the earlier change whether the checker should also run on the schema registry service when a schema is registered. It does already, since the service uses the same library, so a breaking schema cannot be registered without the override flag. The CI job is only the early warning, before the merge.

I wrote a short section in the contributing docs about the job and the approval label, and linked it from the error message of the job.

One limitation: the job does not know about customers who use an old schema version. It only compares versions. A later step could look up which customers still send the old shape. I wrote that down as an idea but did not start it.

The branch is ready for review. Mara will have it tomorrow.

summary: Morning check after the first night with the audit log vacuum settings applied: runs took 8 to 14 minutes each and no run overlapped the morning traffic.
body:
Tobias and I applied the autovacuum settings for the audit log table yesterday evening, so I looked at the results this morning. The first run was the catch-up and took 3 hours 20 minutes, which is much shorter than the 9 hours of the old run, since it only had to freeze and set the visibility map for the part that was never done.

After that the runs happened about once an hour, between 8 and 14 minutes each. None of them ran into the morning traffic in a way that mattered. The reports query p95 was 38 ms, the same as on a normal day.

The table age, which I watch for the freeze limit, fell from 1.4 billion to about 200 million transactions. That removes the worry about a forced anti-wraparound vacuum.

I saw no lock waits in the log and no change in the replication lag. The disk use went up a little from the visibility map files, about 300 MB.

I added a Grafana panel for the table age and the last autovacuum time of the three biggest tables, so this is visible without a query. The panel has a line at the freeze limit.

summary: Went through the monthly index plan with Tobias and agreed that the reindex job gets its shard count from one shared function, so the plan and the job cannot drift apart.
body:
Tobias and I read the shard plan together this morning. He had two questions: what happens to a customer whose events all sit in one old month, and how the job decides the shard count when it creates an index.

The first case is fine. A month is sized by all customers together, so one customer in one month only matters if that month is large, and then the split rule already adds shards. The second question showed a real gap. The sizing script and the reindex job both had their own idea of the rule, and the job still used a fixed number on staging.

I moved the rule into one small module that takes a document count and returns a shard count. The script and the job now both call it, and a unit test covers the cases at the border: exactly 2 times the median, just above it, and the cap.
