Tobias also asked for a check that fails the job when a month index is created with a different shard count than the rule says. I added that as an assertion after index creation. It logs the expected and the actual value, and the job stops before it writes any documents.

I ran the job on staging again. All month indexes were created with the shard counts from the table, and the assertion stayed quiet. The run took 32 minutes, about the same as before. Next is the dual write test for production-like data.

summary: Wrote the rate-limits change that lets each API key carry its own limits, stored in Postgres and cached in Redis, with a fallback to the plan default when a key has none.
body:
This session worked on the per-key limits in the rate-limits branch. Until now the limits came from the plan of the customer, and every key of a customer shared the same numbers. Two customers asked for a lower limit on keys that are used by their test systems, so a runaway script cannot use the whole quota.

The data model is small: a table api_key_limits with the key id, the requests per minute, and the burst size, both nullable. A null means that the plan default applies. I wrote the migration and the repository functions. Postgres is the source of truth and Redis only holds a copy.

The lookup order in the limiter is now:
- the cached limits of the key, if present
- otherwise a read from Postgres, which is then cached with a TTL of 60 seconds
- otherwise the plan default
The cache key is rl:limits:{keyId}, following the naming scheme we agreed on for the limiter keys.

I had to decide what happens when the key has a limit higher than the plan. I decided that the lower of the two numbers wins, because a per-key limit is meant as a restriction. The admin console will say so in the form. If a customer wants more than their plan, that is a plan change, and a sales question.

The counters use the same sliding window as before, and I did not change that part. Only the limit that is compared with the counter comes from the new lookup.

The test cases I wrote are:
- no override, plan default applies
- override lower than plan, override applies
- override higher than plan, plan applies
- override with null burst, plan burst applies
- cache miss followed by a database read, and a second request that hits the cache
All of them pass. I also ran a benchmark of the limiter on a local setup, with 20000 requests per second over 500 keys, and the added latency from the lookup was below 0.1 ms at p99 for cache hits.

One thing I noticed is that a key with no override still causes a database read on every cache miss, and with a TTL of 60 seconds that means many reads for keys that never have an override. I added a negative cache entry, with the value none, and the same TTL, so that those keys cost one read per minute.

The API for setting limits and the console form are not done. Lena will need the endpoints, and I wrote the OpenAPI part for them so she can start. The endpoints are PUT and DELETE on /keys/{id}/limits.

Next is the endpoint code and the audit log entry for every change of a limit.

summary: Built the endpoints for per-key limits with audit log entries and validation, and handled the case where a limit is lowered below the current usage of a key.
body:
I continued the rate-limits work from this morning with the endpoints PUT /keys/{id}/limits and DELETE /keys/{id}/limits, and a GET that shows the effective limits of a key, including where each number comes from: key or plan.

Validation was the first part. Requests per minute must be an integer between 1 and the plan limit, burst must be between 1 and the plan burst, and at least one of the two must be given for a PUT. Errors have a code and a message that names the field, like the registry errors, so Lena can show them next to the input.

Authorization uses the existing check that the caller is an admin of the account that owns the key. I added a test that an admin of another account gets a 404 and not a 403, so we do not reveal which keys exist. That matches how the key listing already behaves.

Every change writes an audit log entry with the old and the new values, the actor, and the key id. The audit log is in Postgres, and the entry is written in the same transaction as the change of the limits. I tested a failure between the two writes by raising an error in the test, and checked that neither was stored.

After a change, the cache entry of the key is deleted, so that the new limit applies at once on the instance that handled the request, and within 60 seconds on the others. I thought about publishing the invalidation to all instances, but the delay is acceptable, and it adds a moving part. Noted for later.

The interesting case was lowering a limit while the key is in use. With a sliding window, the counter of the last minute may already be above the new limit. The key is then blocked until the window moves on, which can be up to a minute. I think that is the right behaviour, since the new limit is a limit on the last minute as well. I wrote that into the docs for the endpoint, with an example.

I ran the whole flow against staging with a script: set a limit of 10 per minute, send 30 requests, check that 10 pass and 20 get a 429 with a Retry-After header, delete the limit, and check that the plan default applies again after the cache TTL. It behaved as expected. The Retry-After value was within a second of the real wait, which is good, since the ingest client now uses that value after the fix of the other day.

The branch has 14 commits now. I opened a PR and asked Mara to review the Postgres part and the transaction handling. Lena has the OpenAPI file and the staging URL.

summary: Added a Postgres migration for per-key rate limits and a Redis cache path with explicit invalidation, so a changed limit is seen by the limiter right away instead of after the TTL.
body:
The per-key limits need a table and a way to reach the limiter quickly, and I worked on both today. The migration creates a table keyed by API key id with the limit per minute, the burst size, who changed it and when. A key without a row uses the plan default, so no data had to be backfilled for the existing keys.

For the cache I used a key per API key id with a TTL of 5 minutes. A cache miss reads the row from Postgres and stores the result, and a missing row is stored too, as an explicit marker for the default. Without that marker every request from a key with no custom limit would go to Postgres after each expiry.

The TTL alone was not good enough. When someone raises a limit for a customer who is being throttled, waiting up to 5 minutes is the wrong answer. So the endpoint that changes a limit now deletes the cache key right after the Postgres commit. I put the delete after the commit on purpose: deleting before it can let a concurrent request put the old value back.

There is still a small window where a request that read the old row before the commit writes it to the cache after the delete. To handle that I added a version number to the row and store it in the cached value. The limiter compares the version it has with the one in a short-lived marker key that the endpoint also sets.

I tested this with a script that changes a limit while 200 requests per second run against a staging key. The new limit applied within one request after the change in every one of 50 runs. A second test stopped Redis for 20 seconds, and the limiter fell back to reading Postgres with a small local cache, with no errors for the client.

The load on Postgres during that fallback was about 300 reads per second on a primary key lookup, which is nothing for it. I wrote the numbers into the PR description. What is left is the audit log entry for a limit that is lowered below current usage, which is the next piece.

summary: Replied to Sam's question on how long a customer's events stay searchable: the search index keeps all events for the plan's period, and the analytics store has its own retention.
body:
Sam asked for a clear answer for the docs and for a customer who wanted to know how long events stay searchable, and whether the dashboards and the search show the same period.

The answer has two parts, since two stores are involved.

Search: the OpenSearch index holds the events for the retention period of the customer's plan, which is 90 days, 1 year or 2 years depending on the plan. The nightly job deletes older documents. When the monthly layout comes, this becomes easier, since a whole month index is dropped at once, but the visible behaviour stays the same. The deletion happens at night, so an event can stay up to a day longer than the plan says.

Dashboards: these read from the analytics store, which has its own retention rules, and they are not the same as for search. The dashboards can show a longer period than search for plans with short search retention, since the analytics data is kept in a compressed form. Sam should check the exact numbers in the retention page of the docs, which are kept up to date by the people who changed it, instead of relying on my memory.

I also pointed out two cases where the two views differ:
- an event deleted through the delete endpoint disappears from search at once, but remains in the aggregates of the dashboards, since those are not recalculated
- an event that failed full text indexing, which goes to the dead-letter path, may be counted in the dashboards and not found by search

The second case is rare. In the last month it was 0.002 percent of events, and it is caused by documents with fields that break the mapping.

Sam asked if a customer can be told the second case can be repaired. It can, by replaying the dead-letter events after a mapping fix, and the new inspector for the dead-letter topic helps to see which events these are. But this is a manual job for us, not a customer feature.

I wrote a draft paragraph for the docs with the main sentence: search and dashboards each follow their own retention, and the numbers can differ by plan. I left the exact periods out of the paragraph and linked to the retention page, so that the paragraph does not become outdated.

Sam will edit the text and put it in the FAQ. I also suggested a small table with the plan names, which he liked.

summary: Dropped an attempt to give the admin console's key page live updates over server-sent events, because polling every 10 seconds was simpler and good enough.
body:
Lena asked whether the API key page could update live when a key is revoked or its limits change, instead of needing a reload. I tried server-sent events with a Fastify endpoint that publishes key changes from a Redis channel.

It worked in a quick prototype, but it needs a long-lived connection per open page, and the load balancer closes idle connections after 60 seconds, so I had to add keepalive messages and a reconnect logic with the last event id. That was already more code than the whole page.

I compared this with polling the key list every 10 seconds with an ETag. The ETag makes an unchanged response cost nearly nothing, and the page needs no new server code. Lena measured the effect on the client and saw no visible difference for users.

I removed the prototype branch and told Lena to use polling with the ETag. The ETag support is already in the key list endpoint, so only the client needs a change.

summary: Wrote the staging test for the dual write of the reindex job into both the monthly and the per-customer indexes, and found that deletes need to go to both as well.
body:
The rollback runbook for the new shard layout assumes that the reindex job writes to both layouts for 14 days after the switch. Today I implemented that on staging and tested it.

The job now has a setting, REINDEX_TARGETS, with the values customer, month or both. With both, every document goes to its monthly index and to the per-customer index. I did the writes in sequence, monthly first, and a failure in the second one fails the batch, so the batch is retried. Retries are safe, since the document id is the same in both and the writes are idempotent.

The run on staging with both targets took 52 minutes, against 33 for the monthly layout alone, and 50 for the old layout. So the dual write costs about what the old job cost, which is nice to know: the nightly window of the job is long enough for it.

The search nodes took the extra load without trouble. I watched the bulk rejections, and there were none with the bulk size of 1000 and parallelism 2, which is the setting from the other day.

Then I wrote the check for consistency. After the run, a script compares document counts per customer and month between both layouts and lists the differences. On the first run, there was a difference of 41 documents for one customer. They were events that had been deleted through the delete endpoint after the last run: the endpoint removed them from the customer index only, and in the monthly index they were still there.

That is a real finding. During the time of the dual write, the delete endpoint has to remove documents from both layouts, otherwise a rollback would bring deleted events back, which would be a data protection problem. The same applies the other way around after the switch.

I changed the delete endpoint to take the layout setting into account: with both, it uses a delete by query on both indexes, with the customer filter and the event ids, and it clears the cache keys of the customer as before. The count of deleted documents is the sum, and the audit log records both numbers.

A test now checks that after a delete in both mode, none of the layouts returns the event. It passes.

I added the point about deletes to the runbook, since it is easy to forget, and noted that the GDPR style deletion job of Mara's has the same problem. I wrote to Mara about it. She will look at that job tomorrow.

Still open: the cleanup of old per-customer indexes after the 14 days, which should be a separate command with a dry run, so that nobody deletes them by hand.

summary: Wrote the cleanup command for the old per-customer indexes with a dry run and a guard that refuses to run before the retention window has passed.
body:
Following the finding of this afternoon about the dual write, the last piece of the plan is the removal of the old per-customer indexes. I did not want that to be a manual job with curl, so I wrote a command in the ops scripts: search-indexes cleanup-legacy.

Without flags it does a dry run. It lists every per-customer index it would delete, with the size and document count, and the total size it would free. Only with --confirm does it delete anything.

There are three guards in the command:
- it reads the switch time from a setting document in the cluster and refuses to run if less than 14 days have passed, unless --force is given
- it checks that every customer index has a counterpart month coverage, meaning that the sum of documents of that customer in the monthly indexes is at least the count in the old index minus the deleted ones
- it refuses to delete an index that is still the target of an alias used by the search API

The second guard needed some thought. A strict equality would fail whenever events were deleted from only one side. I settled for a tolerance of zero extra documents in the old index: the old index may have fewer documents than the monthly ones, but not more.

I tested the command on staging with both layouts present. The dry run listed 186 indexes and 410 GB. With the switch time set to 3 days ago, it refused to run. With --force, and one index that I had filled with 5 extra documents, it refused only for that index and deleted the others after confirmation. That was the behaviour I wanted.

The command writes a line per deleted index to the log and to the audit log table, with the operator name.

I added the command and its guards to the runbook and asked Tobias to read it. Nothing of this runs in production yet, since the migration has not started.

summary: Checked the first day of the Redis timeouts change on the ingest side: error log lines on idle connections dropped to near zero and no rate limits were skipped.
body:
The settings for the Go Redis client, with the shorter dial timeout and the health check of idle connections, went out to the ingest service on staging earlier, and I looked at them tonight after a full day of traffic.

The error log lines about Redis commands fell from several hundred an hour, mostly from idle connections that were found dead when used, to 3 in the whole day. All three came from a deliberate restart of the staging Redis during a test by Tobias.

I also checked that the rate limiter did not skip any checks. The limiter has a counter for fail-open decisions, and it stayed at 0 outside of the restart. During the restart it counted 212 skipped checks over 4 seconds, which matches the failover test.

The pool size did not change, and the number of connections stayed at 12 on the ingest side. The health check adds a small number of PING commands, about 6 per second in total, which is not worth worrying about.

I will let the setting run on staging for two more days and then bring it to production with the Redis 7.2 rollout, so that the two changes are not mixed in one deploy.

summary: Wrote the staging check for per-key rate limits when a key is deleted: the Redis cache entry and the limiter counters are removed together, so a deleted key stops working at once.
body:
The per-key limits from earlier in the day left one gap: a deleted API key kept its cached limits in Redis until the TTL ran out. I added a delete hook that removes the limits entry and the counter keys in one pipeline call.

The staging test creates a key with a low limit, sends traffic until it is limited, deletes the key and checks that the next request gets 401 instead of 429. It failed the first time because the counter key used the old name format without the key id prefix. I fixed the key naming in one helper so the limiter and the delete hook build the names the same way.

The test now passes ten runs in a row. The audit log gets an entry for the delete with the limits the key had. Still open is a cleanup for counters of keys that were deleted before this change. Tomorrow I will write a small script for that and run it on staging first.

summary: Ran the cleanup script for orphaned rate limit counters on staging: it found 1,840 keys of deleted API keys and removed them without touching live keys.
body:
The script scans the Redis counter keys with SCAN in small batches and checks each key id against the Postgres table of API keys. Keys with no matching row are listed first in a dry run.

On staging the dry run listed 1,840 orphaned keys out of about 21,000. I checked a sample of 30 by hand and all belonged to keys deleted weeks ago. The real run took under a minute and did not change the command latency in Grafana.

I added a limit of 500 keys per second so the production run cannot load the cache cluster. Production will wait until Tobias confirms the window. The script is in the scripts folder with a short note on how to run it.

summary: Found why the monthly index plan gave the oversized month too few shards: the sizing used document count while the real cost was bytes, so the split rule now uses both.
body:
I went back to the split rule for the oversized month because the staging index for that month was slow on the heavy queries. The rule sized extra shards from the document count only. That month has fewer but much larger documents, because one customer sent events with big payload fields.

I pulled the numbers from the sizing script. The month had 2.6 times the median document count but 4.1 times the median size in bytes. With the old rule it got 5 shards, and the largest shard was 61 GB, well above our target of 30 GB.

The new rule takes the larger of two values: shards from document count and shards from bytes divided by the 30 GB target. For that month it gives 9 shards. For the normal months nothing changes, so the plan for them stays the same.

The shared shard count function that Tobias and I agreed on holds this logic, so I changed it there and the reindex job picks it up. I added unit tests with three cases: a normal month, a month heavy in count and a month heavy in bytes. All pass.

I also changed the sizing script to print both ratios per month, so the plan review shows why a month got its number. The output of the script now has a column for the limiting factor.

I rebuilt the oversized month on staging with 9 shards. The heavy query went from 2.9 seconds to 1.1 seconds at p95. Document counts match the source.

Open is the question of what happens when a month grows after the index is built. For now the plan says to reindex the month, but that needs a decision with Tobias. I wrote it down in the plan document as an open point.

summary: Answered Sam's question about why a customer's CSV import showed 3 fewer rows than the file: the loader skips blank lines and the file had three.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel because a customer counted 10,003 lines in the file and saw 10,000 events in the dashboard. I took the file from the support bucket and checked it.

Three lines were empty, two in the middle and one at the end. The NDJSON line splitter skips empty lines on purpose, and the loader reports them in the skipped counter of the import summary. The customer only looked at the dashboard, not at the summary.

I confirmed that the skipped counter showed 3 for this import. No events were lost.

Sam will tell the customer. I suggested that the import summary page in the admin console shows the skipped count in plain words, and Sam will ask Lena if that fits into her next change. I did not change any code for this.

summary: Reviewed the ingest batching flush settings under a replay of busy-hour traffic: a 200 ms flush interval and a 500 event batch size gave the best write rate for the store.
body:
Mara asked for numbers behind the flush settings of the batching branch, so I replayed a recorded busy hour against staging with four combinations.

The setup used the recorded stream at normal speed on three workers. I tried flush intervals of 100 and 200 ms and batch sizes of 250 and 500 events. For each run I looked at store write calls per second, the p99 of the time an event waits in the buffer and CPU of the workers.

With 100 ms and 250 events there were about 2,900 write calls per second and the store logs showed many small writes. With 200 ms and 500 events there were about 1,100 calls per second, the p99 wait was 210 ms and worker CPU dropped by around 9 percent.

The other two combinations were in between. Batch size 500 with 100 ms was nearly as good, but the timer fired often before the buffer filled, so it behaved like the small setting at low traffic.

A wait of 210 ms at p99 is fine for our dashboards, which refresh every 30 seconds. The customers only see the delay in the freshness of search results, and that stays well below one second.

I set 200 ms and 500 events as defaults in the config of the branch and left both values changeable through environment variables. I noted the numbers in the PR description.

One thing I noticed is that during the quiet part of the replay the buffers of rare event types waited the full 200 ms every time. That is expected, but I added a metric for the buffer wait per partition so we can see it on the dashboard.

Next step is to run the same replay with the shutdown drain active and kill one worker in the middle, to see that no events are lost.

summary: Killed an ingest worker during the batching replay and found 14 events missing; the drain flushed the buffer but the last offset commit happened before the flush finished.
body:
Following up on the replay of this afternoon, I ran the test where one of three workers gets SIGTERM in the middle of the busy hour. The check compares the event ids sent by the replay with the ids in the staging store.

In the first run 14 events were missing out of about 410,000. That is small, but for an ingest service any loss is a bug. The ECS stop timeout was not the cause, because the worker logged that it finished the drain 3 seconds after SIGTERM, well inside the limit.

The log order showed the problem. On shutdown the worker committed the queue offsets first and then flushed the buffers. If the store write of the last flush failed or the process was killed in between, the offsets were already committed and those events would not be read again.

In the test the store write itself did succeed, but the commit happened for offsets that included events still in a buffer of a second partition that was flushed later. The flush of that partition hit the shutdown deadline of the drain loop, which I had set to 2 seconds per partition.

I made two changes. The offset commit now happens after the flush of the partition, and only up to the highest offset that was written. The drain deadline is shared by all partitions instead of per partition, with a total of 20 seconds, and it logs the number of events left if it runs out.

I ran the test again five times. All five had zero missing events and the drain took between 1 and 4 seconds.

I also added a test with a store mock that fails the last write. In that case the worker now leaves the offset uncommitted, so the events are read again after restart. The duplicates are caught by the store dedupe.

I wrote the finding and the fix in the PR and asked Tobias to look at the shutdown part again. I also want a second look at the case where two partitions are assigned to one worker, since that is where the commit logic is most complex.

Still open: the rebalance case, when a partition moves to another worker while a buffer still has events. I will test that tomorrow.

summary: Checked the Redis 7.2 memory numbers on the cache cluster canary after the first evening: used memory is steady and there were no new connection errors.
body:
Tobias moved one node of the cache cluster to Redis 7.2 this afternoon as a canary. I looked at the dashboards at the end of the evening peak.

Used memory on the canary was 5 to 6 percent below the other nodes under similar key counts, which matches the staging run. Connection counts were the same as on the old nodes. The error rate of the cache client was zero on the canary and unchanged elsewhere.

I also checked the slow log of the canary. It had two entries over 10 ms, both from a KEYS call by a debug script, not from the services. I told Tobias about the script and he stopped it.

The rollback note stays as written. We will leave the canary for a full day and go on with the next node after that.

summary: Handled the rebalance case in ingest batching: when a partition is taken from a worker, its buffer is flushed and committed before the worker gives it up.
body:
Today's shutdown test left the rebalance open, so I took it now. When another worker joins, the group coordinator takes partitions away from running workers, and the worker had no hook for that. Its buffers for the lost partitions stayed in memory and were flushed later, after the new owner had already started reading from the old committed offset.

The effect was duplicates, not loss. In a test with a worker joining in the middle of the replay I saw about 260 events written twice. The store dedupe removed them, but it makes the store do needless work.

I added a revoke callback. It stops accepting new events for the revoked partitions, flushes their buffers, commits the offsets and then returns. The callback has the same shared deadline as the shutdown drain, so a slow store cannot block the rebalance for longer than the session timeout.

The second part was the assignment callback. After a partition is assigned, the worker creates an empty buffer for it and resets the flush timer. Before, the timer of a partition kept running from the earlier assignment, which gave one odd early flush.

I ran the join test three times and a leave test three times. Duplicates dropped to zero in all six runs, and the rebalance took 1 to 2 seconds longer than before, which is fine.

The unit tests got a fake group with scripted revoke and assign events. They check that no offset is committed beyond the flushed events and that a revoked partition receives no more writes.

I updated the PR description with the three cases that are now covered: shutdown, failed last write and rebalance. Mara will review tomorrow.

What is left is a long run of a full day on staging with random worker restarts, to see if some other path is hiding. I will start it tonight so the result is there in the morning.

summary: Morning result of the full-day batching run on staging with random worker restarts: 31 restarts, zero missing events and zero duplicates reaching the store.
body:
The run started last night and used the recorded traffic in a loop with a script that restarted a random worker every 15 to 40 minutes.

There were 31 restarts, mixed between SIGTERM and a hard kill. After the run I compared the ids from the replay with the store. With SIGTERM there were no missing events. With the hard kill the buffered events were not flushed, as expected, but the offsets were not committed either, so they were read again and written once by the dedupe.

The ingest metrics look normal. The wait metric per partition showed the long tail for rare event types, as I saw before.

I put the result into the PR and told Mara it is ready for review. I will wait for her comments before touching the branch again.

summary: Mara reviewed the ingest batching PR and asked for a cap on buffer memory; added a limit of 64 MB per worker that makes the buffers flush early instead of growing.
body:
Mara's main point in the review was that the buffers had no upper bound in bytes. With a few very large events, 500 events per batch could mean a lot of memory, and the ECS task limit would kill the worker.

I checked the largest events in the stream. Most are under 2 KB, but the large customers send some up to 256 KB. A batch of 500 of those would be 128 MB for one partition.

I added a byte counter per partition and a total counter per worker. A buffer flushes when it reaches the event count, the flush interval or a byte limit of 4 MB. If the total of all buffers passes 64 MB, the largest buffer is flushed first.

The tests got two new cases, one with large events that hit the per partition limit and one that fills many partitions to hit the total limit. Both passed on the second try, after I fixed an off by one in the byte counter after a flush.

I replayed the busy hour once more to see if the new limits change the write rate. The result was the same as before, about 1,100 calls per second, because normal events are small. A run with a synthetic stream of 200 KB events showed flushes of 20 events, as expected, and worker memory stayed under 300 MB.

Mara also asked for a metric for flushes by reason. I added a counter with the labels count, time, bytes and memory, and a panel for it on the ingest dashboard.

She approved after these changes with one small comment about a log message, which I fixed. The PR waits for the merge window tomorrow morning, when traffic is low.

summary: Replied to Lena about slow loading of the audit log page in the admin console: the query sorted by time without an index on the customer and time columns.
body:
Lena saw the audit log page take 6 to 8 seconds for one of the large customers. She asked if the frontend should paginate differently.

I ran EXPLAIN on the query. It filters by customer id and sorts by created time. Postgres used the index on created time alone and filtered the customer rows afterwards, which scanned a large part of the 180 GB table.

A composite index on customer id and created time descending fits the query. I tested it on a copy of the table in staging. The query dropped to about 40 ms.

The index will be built on production with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid locking writes. I wrote the migration and will run it in the quiet hours. The pagination in the frontend is fine as it is, so Lena does not need to change anything.

summary: Merged the ingest batching PR in the low traffic window and watched the first hour: write calls to the store dropped from about 2,800 to 1,200 per second.
body:
The merge went out at the start of the quiet window. Tobias did the deploy with a rolling replacement of the workers, one at a time, so I could watch the drain code run on real shutdowns.

Each of the old workers logged the drain and finished in 1 to 3 seconds. No errors from the offset commit, and the consumer lag stayed under a few hundred events during the whole rollout.

After all workers had been replaced I compared the store metrics with the hour before. Write calls dropped from about 2,800 to 1,200 per second. Worker CPU went down by around 8 percent, in line with staging. The p99 of the buffer wait was 190 ms.

The flush reason counter showed mostly count and time, with bytes rare and memory zero. That fits what I expected from the event sizes.

I checked the end to end freshness with a probe event every minute. The time until the event is searchable stayed under one second all hour.

I left a note for the on-call that the batching is new and where the dashboard panels are. If something goes wrong, the old behavior comes back by setting the batch size to 1 in the config, which I tested on staging.

Open is the cleanup of the config after a week without problems.

summary: Wrote the index build for the audit log customer and time index on production in steps, and found a long running transaction that blocked the concurrent build until it was ended.
body:
This morning I started the CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the audit log table that I prepared for Lena's slow page. I expected it to take 30 to 40 minutes, based on the copy in staging.

After 50 minutes it was still waiting. I looked at pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_progress_create_index. The build was in the phase waiting for old snapshots. A session had been open for almost 4 hours with a transaction in state idle in transaction.

The session came from a reporting script that one of the analysts had started from a notebook. It had read a table and never committed. A concurrent index build has to wait for all transactions that began before it, so it could not move on.

I asked in the team channel who owned the session. Mara found it was an old notebook and closed it. The build moved on within seconds and finished 22 minutes later.

The resulting index is valid, which I checked in pg_index. Then I ran the page query again for the large customer. It took 35 ms instead of 7 seconds.

The write latency on the table was normal during the build, and the vacuum did not have trouble either. I checked the autovacuum log from the settings of last week and the next run was done in 9 minutes.

The lesson is that long idle transactions are a risk for builds and for vacuum, since they hold back the cleanup of dead rows. I set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10 minutes for the reporting role. The application roles already had one.

I also added a line to the migration notes: before a concurrent index build, look for sessions that are idle in transaction. The query I used is in the note.

I told Lena that the page is fast now and she can test it on her side. She confirmed 200 ms for the whole page load.

One more check is the size of the new index, which is 11 GB. That is acceptable for the gain, but I noted it for the storage review.

There are two other tables with a similar pattern, the settings history and the key usage table. I will look at their slow queries next week and not change anything in a hurry.

summary: Dropped the idea of generating the shard count table for the search plan as a static file, because the shared function can be called by the plan document script directly.
body:
I had started to export the shard count per month into a static JSON file that the plan document and the reindex job would both read. After an hour I saw it brings the drift problem back: the file can get old, and then the plan and the job disagree again.

Tobias and I agreed last week that there is one shared function. The plan script can import it, so I removed the export step and the file.

The plan script now calls the function with the sizes of each month and prints the table. I ran it and it matches the numbers of the reindex job on staging for all months.

This was a short detour. The script needs a small README line, which I added.

summary: Looked at the Redis key naming of the cache layer with Tobias and agreed on a prefix scheme with the service name and a version, so a key set can be dropped by prefix.
body:
The delete bug of a few days ago showed that we cannot clear a set of keys cleanly because the names are inconsistent. Some start with the customer id, some with the feature name, and some have no prefix at all.

We listed the key families in use: search cache, rate limiter counters, key status, session store and a few small ones. For each we wrote the current pattern and the proposed one. The proposal is service, version, family and then the id, for example search:v1:cache:customer-id:hash.

The version part lets us change the format of a family without old keys being read by new code. The old keys then just expire by their TTL.

We did not change code today. The plan is to do it family by family, starting with the search cache, since it has the most keys. Tobias will write the SCAN based cleanup for old patterns so we do not leave junk.

summary: Changed the search cache keys to the new prefix scheme with a version and made the delete endpoint clear a customer's keys by the new prefix.
body:
First family of the key naming plan was the search cache. The new key is search:v1:cache:customer-id:query-hash.

The code change was small, because all keys are built in one function in the search API. I changed that function and the one place that reads keys for the delete endpoint. The delete used a list of known keys from last week. Now it can scan by the customer prefix.

I used SCAN with a count of 200 and delete in batches, so it does not block the server. On staging with 50,000 keys for one customer the delete took 1.4 seconds and the command latency of other clients did not change.

The old keys stay in Redis until their TTL ends, which is 10 minutes for most of them, so there is no migration needed. During that time the hit rate drops once, because the new keys start empty. I watched it on staging: the hit rate fell from 71 to 40 percent and was back at 70 after about 12 minutes.

I wrote tests for the key builder and for the delete by prefix with a customer that has similar ids, to make sure customer 12 does not delete customer 123. That case found a bug in my first version, where the prefix had no trailing colon. It is fixed now.

The change will go out with the next deploy outside the busy hours, since the hit rate dip hits latency a little. Next family is the rate limiter counters.

summary: Wrote the validation for per-key limits in the admin console API: a limit cannot be negative, zero means blocked, and the burst value must not be lower than the rate.
body:
Lena asked what the console should do with odd values in the per-key limit form, so I made the rules explicit on the API side first.

The rules are: rate and burst are integers, a rate of zero means the key is blocked and the console should show that as a warning, a negative value is rejected, and burst must be at least the rate per second. The upper bound is 100 times the plan default, to catch typing errors like an extra zero.

The error responses carry a field name and a short message in the same format as the other endpoints, so Lena can show them under the inputs.

I wrote tests for each rule and a test that a rejected change does not write an audit log entry. One test failed at first because the audit entry was written before the validation of the burst. I moved the validation to the start of the handler.

I also documented the rules in the API docs source so Sam can use them for the public text.

Lena will build the form this week against the staging endpoint. Open: what a customer sees when the limit is lower than the usage of the key, which is handled on the server but needs a text for the console.

summary: Moved the rate limiter counters to the new Redis key prefix scheme with a dual read period, so no key lost its count in the switch and no customer was limited early.
body:
The second family of the key naming plan was the rate limiter counters, which is more delicate than the cache, because a lost counter means a customer gets more requests than allowed for a short time, and a wrong one can block someone.

The counters are short windows of one second and one minute. The old keys are like rl:api-key-id:window. The new ones are ratelimit:v1:counter:api-key-id:window.

Because the windows are short, the simplest path is a switch with a short overlap. For the first two minutes the limiter writes to the new key and reads the sum of the new and the old key. After two minutes all old keys have expired, since the longest window is one minute, and the read of the old key can go.

I put the dual read behind a config flag with a timestamp for the end of the overlap, so I do not need a second deploy. The limiter code checks the flag on each call, which costs one extra GET only during the overlap.

On staging I ran a load test with three API keys, each at its limit, and switched in the middle. The counts of allowed requests per second stayed within 2 percent of the limit through the switch. Without the dual read, the same test let about 40 percent extra requests through for one second.

I wrote a test for the overlap logic with a fake clock. It covers the start, the middle and the end of the window and the case where a key exists only in the old format.

The per-key limit cache from last week also needed the new names. Its keys are ratelimit:v1:limits:api-key-id. The invalidation path builds the name from the same helper, so the change in one place was enough. I checked this by changing a limit on staging and watching the limiter pick it up in under a second.

The delete hook that I wrote earlier for the orphaned counters uses a helper too. I updated the cleanup script to know both name patterns so it can still clear old keys.

The rollout is planned for the quiet hours tonight. The rollback is to turn off the new write and read only the old key, which works as long as the old code is still in the build.

After the rollout I will check the rate of 429 responses and compare it with the same hour last week. A big difference would mean the switch changed behavior.

summary: Checked the night rollout of the rate limiter key change: 429 responses were within 3 percent of last week at the same hour and the old keys were gone after two minutes.
body:
The rollout ran at the start of the quiet window. The flag for the overlap ended after two minutes as planned, and the limiter was reading only the new keys after that.

I compared the 429 count for the hour of the rollout with the same hour a week ago. This week it was 1,184, and last week 1,150. That is a difference of 3 percent, which is inside the normal variation.

I scanned Redis for the old pattern rl:* an hour later and found 14 keys. All belonged to a client that sends with a very long window setting, a legacy plan with a 10 minute window. I had missed that plan. The keys expire on their own and the overlap logic would have been wrong for that plan for the first 10 minutes.

I looked at the logs for that customer. They were not limited wrongly, because their traffic is far below the limit, so nothing was visible. Still, I changed the overlap time from two minutes to the longest window in the plan table, and noted it in the code. Next time for another key family I will look at the plan table first.

The Redis memory used did not change, and the command rate on the limiter was up only 4 percent during the overlap.

The cleanup script now has a rule to delete any key of the old pattern that has no TTL, which I used once for a leftover key from a test. It found one and I removed it.

Next family are the sessions of the admin console. They are different, because a changed name would log users out. I will talk to Lena before touching them.

summary: Checked the schema-registry compatibility checker against the ten largest customer schemas and found two false breaking findings, both caused by reordered enum values.
body:
Ran the compatibility checker from the schema-registry branch against the current schemas of the ten largest customers, comparing each one with the version from three months ago. The goal was to see whether the checker would have flagged changes that customers actually shipped without trouble. It reported 31 findings in total, and 29 of them were real: removed fields, narrowed types and a required field added without a default.

Two findings were wrong. In both cases an enum had the same values in a different order, and the checker treated the list as positional, so it reported every value as changed. That would have blocked a harmless pull request in CI and annoyed whoever hit it first.

Fixed it in the enum comparison in checker/compare.ts by comparing the values as sets. I also kept a separate note for the case where a value is removed, because that stays a breaking change for readers of old events. Added three unit tests: reordered values, one value added and one value removed.

After the fix the same run gave 29 findings, all of them real, and the run took about 40 seconds for all ten customers. The paths in the output were correct for nested arrays, which was the bug from last week, so that fix holds on real data.

One open question is arrays of objects whose item schema changes shape, such as a string turning into an object. The checker reports it as a type change on the item path, which seems right, but I would like Mara to read two of those cases before we call the output final. Next step is to add the ten schemas as fixtures to the repo, with the customer names removed, so the CI check has real input to test against.

summary: Looked at a failing CI job for the schema compatibility check and found it compared against a stale base branch checkout, so it now fetches the base ref fresh.
body:
A pull request that only touched a comment in a schema file failed the new compatibility check with findings about fields it never changed.

The job compares the schema files of the pull request with the base branch. It used the checkout of the base from the cache of the CI runner, which was three days old. Other merged changes were seen as new differences.

I changed the job to fetch the base ref with depth 1 at the start and to compare against the fetched commit. I tested it on the failing pull request and on one that really breaks compatibility. The first passed and the second failed with the right path.

I added the commit id of the base to the job log so a finding can be traced to a state.

summary: Planned the move of console sessions to the new Redis key scheme with Lena: new sessions use the new prefix, old ones are read once and rewritten, so nobody gets logged out.
body:
The session store is the third family of the key naming plan and the one where a mistake is visible to every user, so Lena and I sat down before writing code.

The admin console keeps one key per session with a sliding TTL of 8 hours. The key is sess:session-id and the value is a small JSON with the user id, the customer and the csrf token. About 600 sessions are live at a time.

The new key will be console:v1:session:session-id. We discussed three options. The first was to just switch, which logs everybody out once. It would be easy, but a customer in the middle of an export would lose work, so we rejected it.

The second was a dual write for the whole TTL of 8 hours. This is safe but needs two code paths for a long time. The third is read through: a lookup tries the new key, and if it is missing it tries the old key, copies the value to the new key with the remaining TTL and deletes the old one. After 8 hours at the longest, no old keys remain, and the fallback path can be removed.

We chose the third option. The part that needs care is the TTL. We read the remaining TTL of the old key with PTTL and set it on the new key, so a session does not live longer than it should. If the PTTL returns a negative value, the key is gone or has no TTL, and we treat it as no session.

The second detail is the race of two requests of one session at the same moment, both finding only the old key. Both would copy the value, which is harmless, because the content is the same. The delete of the old key can fail on the second one with no effect. We decided not to add a lock.

Lena will write the change in the console server since she owns that code. I will review it and write the check script that counts keys of both patterns, so we can see the migration run down.

We also decided to put the end date of the fallback into the code as a comment and a log line that fires if the fallback is still used after 9 hours. That way it does not stay forever.

The test plan has four cases: a new session, an old session in the middle of its TTL, an old session near its end and a missing session. We will run them on staging with a real login, then by hand with a session created by the old version.

The rollout is planned for the next quiet window after the review. I wrote the plan into the shared notes so Tobias knows when the rollout happens and can watch the memory.

summary: Wrote the script that counts Redis keys per family and prefix version and prints a table, so the progress of the key naming migration can be seen at a glance.
body:
For the key naming work I needed a clear view of how many keys are in the old and in the new format. Until now I used ad hoc SCAN commands in a shell.

The script scans with a count of 500 per call and sleeps 10 ms between calls. It matches each key against a list of patterns, one for each family and version, and counts. Keys that match nothing are counted as unknown and the first 20 are printed as samples.

On staging the output showed search cache v1 with 48,000 keys, rate limiter v1 with 310, sessions in the old format with 41 and the new format with none yet, and 190 unknown keys. The unknown ones were mostly from a feature that stores small flags with names like flag.customer-id.

That family was not on our list. I added it to the list of families with the pattern and told Tobias. We will rename it in the last round, since it is tiny.

The script runs on one node with the replica read option so it does not load the primary. I measured the command rate during a run on staging and it stayed below 100 per second.

I also made it exit with a non zero code if the unknown count is above a threshold, for use in a check later.

I ran it on production with Tobias watching the cache latency. The scan took 4 minutes for about 1.9 million keys. The latency did not move. The result showed the same unknown family with 2,300 keys and a few hundred keys of a very old format from the search cache with no TTL. Those are leftovers from before last month, and I will look into where they come from before deleting anything.

summary: Traced the old search cache keys without a TTL to a code path in the reindex job that wrote warmup entries with no expiry, and added a TTL of one hour to it.
body:
The key count of this evening showed about 700 keys of the old search cache format that had no TTL. They would stay in Redis forever, so I wanted to know where they came from.

The key names had a warmup marker in them. I searched the code and found it in the reindex job. After a reindex, it runs the 200 most frequent queries per customer to fill the cache. That code used SET without an expiry, while the normal search path sets the TTL through a helper.

The warmup was added a year ago and nobody noticed, since the number of keys is small and each is replaced by the same key after the next reindex. When query popularity changes, the old ones stay.

I changed the warmup to use the same helper as the search path, so it gets the same TTL rules and the new prefix scheme. I added a test that checks that every key written by the warmup has a TTL greater than zero.

For the existing keys, I wrote a one time cleanup in the key script: with the option to delete keys of the old format that have a TTL of -1. A dry run listed 712 keys, I checked 20 by hand, and I ran the delete on staging first. After that, I ran it on production in batches of 100 with a short pause.

The memory used on the cache cluster went down by about 30 MB, which is small, but the point was to close the leak. A second scan after the cleanup showed zero keys without TTL in the search family.

I also looked at the other families for keys without a TTL. The flags family has none on purpose, they are meant to stay, and the sessions and counters all have one.

I noted the finding in the key naming document, with a rule: every new write path must go through a helper that sets a TTL, unless the family is listed as permanent. The next step is the session change that Lena is writing, which I will review once it is ready.

summary: Ran the Redis key family counter after the session key move and found 212 old-prefix session keys still without a TTL, so the session rewrite now sets one.
body:
The counter script from earlier tonight printed its first full table on the production Redis. Cache and limiter families were on the new prefix scheme, as expected. The session family showed 212 keys still on the old prefix, all without a TTL.

The cause was in the read-once-and-rewrite path from Lena's plan. It copied the value to the new key but did not copy the remaining lifetime, and the old key was left in place. The rewrite now sets the new key with the remaining TTL of the old one and deletes the old key in the same step.

I added a unit test with a session that has 20 minutes left and checked that the new key ends up with about 20 minutes. I ran the cleanup on staging first. The 212 old keys on production are left for tomorrow, when Lena can confirm that no active sessions are among them. The counter table goes into the weekly Redis check.

summary: Measured the search API latency by query type and found that wildcard queries on the message field cause most of the slow p99 tail, not the cache misses we suspected.
body:
After last week's latency complaints I split the search API timings by query type. I used the request logs of the last three days, about 1.9 million queries. Plain term queries have a p99 of 90 ms. Phrase queries are near 140 ms. Queries with a leading wildcard on the message field have a p99 of 1.1 seconds.

They are only 2 percent of the traffic, but they make up most of the slow tail in the overall p99. Cache hit rate for them is low, since customers type different patterns each time. So caching will not help much here.

Two options came out of it. The first is to reject leading wildcards on message in the v1 parser and return a hint to use phrase search. The second is to add a length limit and a timeout to those queries. I asked Lena whether the console search box produces them often. She said it does when users paste partial IDs.

For now I added a per-query timeout of 2 seconds for wildcard queries in the search API, with a clear error text. I also wrote down the top 20 slowest patterns for a talk with Sam about customer docs. The question of an ID-prefix field is left open. Next step is to check how much of this traffic comes from three customers.

summary: Wrote the staging test for the monthly index shard sizing with the oversized month and confirmed the combined document count and byte rule gives balanced shards.
body:
Since the split rule now uses both document count and bytes, I wrote a test that builds the plan from a copy of the staging index statistics. The copy includes the oversized month of the largest customer.

Before the change that month got 2 shards and each held about 41 GB. With the new rule it gets 5 shards of 16 to 18 GB. The small months keep 1 shard. The total number of shards for the plan is 12 more than before, which is still inside the limit Tobias set for the cluster.

I also tested an edge case: a month with many tiny documents and few bytes. It gets shards by count only up to a cap, so it does not explode. The cap is 4 shards and it is configurable.

The test runs in about 20 seconds and is part of CI now. The plan document script calls the same function, so the table in the document and the test cannot drift apart.

Open point: the rule uses the sizes of the last full month. A month that is still running can grow past its plan. I noted that as a question for the next planning session, with the idea of a rollover on size.

summary: Found that the per-key limit change path invalidated the Redis cache entry but not the limiter's local copy, so a lowered limit took up to 30 seconds to apply.
body:
A staging test that lowers a key's limit and sends traffic right away still saw the old limit for a short time. I traced it in the limiter middleware.

The middleware keeps a small in-process copy of each key's limit for 30 seconds to save Redis reads. The explicit invalidation from the earlier change cleared the Redis cache entry only. Each Fastify instance kept its own copy until it expired.

I looked at two fixes. One was to drop the local copy. That raised Redis reads by about 40 percent in a load test, which is too much. The other was to publish an invalidation message on a Redis channel when a limit changes. Each instance subscribes and clears its local entry.

I built the second one. The message carries the key id and a version number, so a late message cannot undo a newer limit. If the subscription connection drops, the instance clears all its local copies and resubscribes. That makes the failure case safe.

The test now shows the new limit applied in under 200 ms on three instances. The Redis read rate stays the same as before. I added a metric for the number of invalidation messages and a log line at reconnect.

Still to do: test deleting a key through the same channel, and write a short section in the rate limit docs about the delay.

summary: Cleared the 212 old session keys on production after Lena confirmed none belonged to active sessions, and the key counter table now shows only the new prefix.
body:
Lena checked the list of the 212 old-prefix session keys against the active console sessions. None of them were in use. They were left from the rewrite path that did not delete the old key.

I deleted them in batches of 50 with a short pause between batches, using SCAN and not a pattern delete over the whole keyspace. The whole run took about a minute. No errors, and Redis latency stayed flat in Grafana.

After that I ran the counter script again. All session keys are on the new prefix with a TTL. The cache and limiter families were clean already.

One old family remains, the warmup entries of the reindex job. They carry the one hour TTL now and will be gone by this evening. I will run the counter once more then and, if it is clean, close the key naming migration item.

summary: Reviewed the schema registry's handling of optional field removal and made it a warning for consumers on older versions instead of a hard break.
body:
The compatibility checker treated every removed field as breaking. For required fields that is right. For optional fields several customers remove them on purpose and nothing breaks for readers.

I went through the ten largest customer schemas again. In 14 of the 19 findings the field was optional. Those were all reports the customers saw as noise.

The change: removing an optional field is now a warning with the text 'optional field removed, readers of older versions get null'. Removing a required field, changing a type, or narrowing an enum remain errors. The enum order fix from last week is kept.

I added test cases for each rule and a case where a field changes from required to optional. That one is allowed and produces no finding.

Mara looked at the rule table and asked for a switch so strict customers can keep the hard error. I added a per-schema setting called strict_removal, default off. It is stored in the registry settings in Postgres and needs one migration, which I wrote and ran on staging.

Next step is the docs text for Sam, plus a look at how the CI comment shows warnings. Right now warnings and errors look alike in the PR comment.

summary: Looked into the audit log export design for large customers and chose cursor-based paging over time ranges, because offset paging got slow after 1 million rows.
body:
For the audit export I tested how the query behaves for the largest customer, who has about 6 million audit rows. With offset paging, page 1 takes 20 ms and page 400 with 5000 rows each takes over 3 seconds. The cost grows with the offset.

I tried keyset paging on the customer and time index that was built recently, with the id as a tie breaker. Every page takes about 25 ms, no matter the position. The EXPLAIN shows an index scan with no sort step.

The export format stays NDJSON with one line per entry. The export job writes in chunks of 10,000 rows to a file and then uploads it, so a failure in the middle can resume from the last cursor. The cursor is stored in the job row.

I also checked what happens when rows are written during the export. The job fixes an upper time bound when it starts. Rows after that are not part of the export. This gives a stable result and the compliance team can state it in the report.

Things left: the signing of the file with a checksum, the download link expiry, and a test with a job that is killed in the middle. I wrote these as tasks in the branch notes. Tobias asked about the bucket policy, and I will look at it with him tomorrow.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why the search API returns fewer results on page 50 than on page 1: results are capped at 10,000 per query by the index setting.
body:
Sam saw a customer who paged to the end and got an empty page long before the total count was reached. The cause is the index setting for the maximum result window, which is 10,000. Paging beyond that is refused by OpenSearch and the API returns an empty list.

The total count shown above the list is real, so it looks like results are missing. I told Sam that the customer should narrow the time range or use the export. A note in the docs would help.

I also opened a task to make the API return a clear message when the window is exceeded, instead of an empty page.

summary: Tested the loader retry backoff with a flaky object store stub and found the retries all fired at the same moment after a shared outage, so jitter was added.
body:
The loader for large files retries failed chunk uploads. I wrote a stub of the object store that fails for 20 seconds and then recovers, and ran 40 loader jobs against it at the same time.

The backoff doubled from 1 second up to 32 seconds. Since all jobs failed at the same second, they also retried at the same seconds. When the store came back, it saw bursts of 40 requests at once and the stub rejected some of them again. In the first run the load completed only after 6 rounds.

I added full jitter, so each wait is a random value between zero and the current backoff. With the same stub, the 40 jobs finished in 2 to 3 rounds, and the peak of simultaneous requests dropped from 40 to about 12.

I also set a limit of 8 attempts per chunk and a total time limit per file of 15 minutes. After that the job is marked failed with the last error text and the chunk offset, so an operator can resume.

A second finding came from the logs. A chunk that failed on the response, after the store had stored the data, was uploaded twice. The store keys chunks by file and index, so the second upload just overwrote the first. That is harmless, and I added a test to keep it so.

Still open are the metrics for the attempt counts and a dashboard panel. I will do these next, then run the loader on a 4 GB test file with the stub.

summary: Added loader metrics for attempts per chunk and failed files, and a Grafana panel that shows the retry rate by error type.
body:
After the jitter change I wanted to see retries on a dashboard. The loader now exports a counter of attempts by error type, a histogram of attempts per chunk, and a counter of failed files.

Error types are timeout, connection reset, 5xx from the store and other. I kept the label values to this list to keep the cardinality small. File names and customer ids are not labels.

The Grafana panel shows the rate per type and a stat for the share of chunks that needed more than one attempt. On the stub test it showed 100 percent during the outage and fell back to 0 within a minute after recovery.

I also added an alert rule in the alert code repo. It fires when more than 5 percent of chunks need a retry for 15 minutes. Tobias will review the rule, since it touches the shared alerts file.

Next is the run with the 4 GB file.

summary: Ran the loader on a 4 GB NDJSON file with the flaky store stub and it finished with 3 resumed chunks and no missing rows.
body:
I ran the large file test. The file has 21 million lines, 4 GB. The stub of the store failed randomly for 3 percent of the requests and had two longer outages of 20 seconds each.

The loader finished in 38 minutes. The metrics showed 412 retries in total, and 3 chunks needed more than 4 attempts. No chunk reached the limit of 8. The row count in the target was 21,000,000 exactly, and I checked the sum of the event ids against the source file with a small script.

Then I tested the resume. I killed the loader process at about 60 percent. The job row held the last committed chunk. After a restart it continued from there and did not read the first 60 percent again. The last chunk before the kill was uploaded a second time, which was harmless as before.

I found one small bug in this test. The progress counter after a resume started at zero and the console showed 0 percent for a while. The number of rows done is now loaded from the job row at startup.

Memory use of the loader stayed under 300 MB the whole time, since it reads in a stream. That was an earlier worry of Mara's.

What remains is the PR text, the docs for the failure case, and a review by Mara. I will also test a file with a bad line in the middle, to see how the error report looks. That case existed in the old loader and I do not want it to change by accident.

summary: Dropped an attempt to compress the Redis cache values with a library, since CPU use went up 15 percent and memory fell by only 6 percent.
body:
The cache cluster is at about 70 percent of its memory, and I wanted to see if compressing the search cache values would help. I tried a fast compression library on the values over 1 KB in the search API.

I tested on staging with a replay of one day of queries. The cached values are JSON result pages with an average size of 14 KB. I expected a ratio of 3 or better.

The real result was different. The values compress 3 to 1 on their own. But most of the cache memory is in many small keys, the metadata and counters, which are not compressed. The total memory dropped by 6 percent. The CPU of the search API instances went up by 15 percent, and p50 latency rose by 4 ms.

That is a bad trade. I also looked at the debugging cost, because values in the cache can no longer be read with redis-cli directly. Tobias said he uses that often during incidents.

So I dropped the change and removed the branch for it. A better path for memory is to shorten the TTL of the rarely used result pages and to look at the key sizes. I made a list of the 20 biggest key families and sent it to Tobias.

One useful result stays. The key family counter now also prints the average value size. It showed that one family, the facet counts, is 30 percent of the memory with a hit rate of 8 percent. That is the first thing to look at tomorrow.

summary: Shortened the TTL of the facet count cache keys from 6 hours to 30 minutes, since their hit rate was only 8 percent and they used 30 percent of cache memory.
body:
The facet counts family had a TTL of 6 hours. With a hit rate of 8 percent most entries expired without being read once. I changed the TTL to 30 minutes in the search API config.

I deployed it to the canary first. After an hour the facet family was 40 percent smaller on the canary. The hit rate was 7 percent, so users did not lose anything.

I will check the full cluster memory tomorrow morning, after the TTL change has gone through one full cycle.

summary: Wrote the draft of the cutover steps for the monthly search index, with the dual write period, a check of counts per customer and a rollback path at each step.
body:
I wrote the cutover plan as a document for the review with Tobias and Mara. It builds on the dual write of the reindex job and the cleanup command from last week.

Step 1 is the dual write on production for one week, with deletes going to both indexes. Step 2 is a count check per customer between the old and the monthly indexes, run every night. A difference of more than 0.1 percent stops the plan. Step 3 is a switch of the read path for 5 customers, chosen by Sam as the least critical, with a flag per customer.

Step 4 widens the flag in groups: 10, then 20, then all. After each group the plan waits one day and compares p99 latency and error rate. Step 5 stops the write to the old indexes. Step 6 is the cleanup with the dry run and the retention guard.

Every step has a rollback. Before step 5 the rollback is just the flag. After step 5 it needs a rebuild of the old indexes from the reindex job, which takes about 9 hours for the largest customers. I marked step 5 as the point of no easy return.

I added a section about load. Dual write raises the write load on the cluster by about 80 percent. Tobias has to confirm that the cluster has room, or we need to add a node for the time of the dual write.

Open questions: how the shard count for the running month is changed, and whether the nightly reindex window needs to move. I listed them at the end of the document. The review is planned for the next days.

summary: Confirmed the full cache cluster memory fell by 11 percent after the facet TTL change and the session key cleanup, with the hit rate unchanged.
body:
I looked at the cache cluster after two days. Used memory went from 70 percent to about 62 percent of maxmemory. The facet family dropped from 30 percent of the total to 14 percent.

The overall hit rate of the search cache stayed at 61 percent, within noise of before. The p99 of the search API did not change either. So the TTL change cost nothing that we can see.

The session cleanup and the warmup TTL together account for around 2 points of the drop. The rest is from the facet change.

I ran the key counter again and it shows no old prefix keys and no keys without a TTL in the cache or session families. The limiter counters are the only family with a few keys that have no TTL by design.

I closed the key naming item in the task list. The next memory topic is the key sizes of the result pages. There is no need to act on it now since we have room.

summary: Answered Lena's question on whether the console should show limit changes in the audit log: yes, and the limit change path now writes an entry with the old and new values.
body:
Lena asked whether changes to per-key limits appear in the audit log, because a customer admin asked who raised their limit. They did not. I added an audit entry in the limit update handler.

The entry has the key id, the actor, the old and new rate, the old and new burst, and the time. For a deleted key it records the last known limit. The write happens in the same Postgres transaction as the limit change, so one cannot exist without the other.

I tested it on staging with an update, a delete and a rejected invalid value. The rejected one writes nothing, as intended. Lena will add a filter for the event type to the audit page.

summary: Tested the Redis pub/sub invalidation for limits during a Redis failover on staging and found instances recovered their subscription within 4 seconds.
body:
I wanted to see the invalidation channel behave in a failover, since a lost subscription could leave stale limits. On staging I triggered a failover of the Redis primary while a script changed limits every second.

All three limiter instances saw the connection drop. Each cleared its local limit copies, as designed, and reconnected. The longest time without a subscription was 4 seconds. In that window the limiter read limits directly from Redis, so no stale value was used.

One problem showed up. Two instances logged the reconnect at error level every 500 ms during the failover, which would be noisy in production. I added a backoff of up to 5 seconds for the reconnect and logged only the first failure at error level.

After the failover the limit changes arrived again in under 200 ms. The invalidation message counter matched the number of changes sent by the script, apart from the 4 seconds in the window.

The PR is ready for review by Mara.

summary: Ran a Postgres vacuum review of the largest tables and found the audit log had 38 percent dead rows after a bulk cleanup, so a manual vacuum was scheduled.
body:
I checked the bloat of the biggest Postgres tables with the usual statistics query. Most tables are healthy. The audit log table has about 38 percent dead rows.

The cause is the cleanup of old entries for two customers last week. It deleted 4 million rows in one run. Autovacuum started but the table is large and the default cost limit made it slow. It had not finished after 5 days.

I ran a manual vacuum in a quiet period with a higher cost limit for the session. It took 26 minutes and the table size on disk did not change much, but the space is now reusable. The dead row share fell to 2 percent. Query times for the audit page went back to normal.

I also changed the autovacuum settings for this one table. The scale factor is lower and the cost limit higher. Tobias agreed. I did not use a full vacuum, since it takes a lock that we cannot afford.

summary: Reviewed the monthly index cutover plan with Tobias and Mara and agreed to add a node before the dual write week and to roll over the running month by size.
body:
The review of the cutover document took about an hour. Tobias confirmed that the 80 percent extra write load would push the cluster to over 85 percent disk use in the second half of the week. We agreed to add one data node before the dual write begins and to remove it after the cleanup, if the disk use allows.

Mara raised the question of the running month. We agreed on a rollover by size: when the index of the running month passes a limit of 50 GB per shard, a new shard set starts with an alias over both. The reads use the alias, so the API does not change.

We also discussed the nightly reindex window. It stays, but the job will skip the monthly index of the running month on the nights when the rollover happens.

Mara asked for a stricter stop rule in the count check. The rule is now a difference of more than 0.1 percent or more than 50 documents for any single customer. The smaller customers would otherwise hide a gap in the percent.

I updated the document with all of this and marked the first two steps as approved. Step 3 waits for the node. The remaining task is the rollover code, which I started.

summary: Built the size-based rollover for the running month index and tested it on staging, where a 50 GB per shard limit produced a clean second shard set behind one alias.
body:
I wrote the rollover check as part of the reindex job. Before each run it reads the shard sizes of the running month index. If any shard is over the limit, it creates a new index with the same mappings and a suffix, and moves the write alias to it. The read alias covers both.

On staging I set the limit to a low value so I could trigger it with the test data. The first run created the second index and moved the write alias. Documents written afterwards went into the new index. A search over the read alias returned documents from both with no duplicates.

I tested updates and deletes too. A document that lived in the first index and was updated after the rollover caused a problem. The update went to the new index and the old copy stayed. Searches then showed both. The fix is to write updates to the index where the document id already lives. The reindex job looks up the id on the read alias before it writes.

That lookup costs about 12 percent more time in the job on staging. I think it is acceptable, since it only applies to the month with two indexes.

The dual write also has to know about the rollover. I made the writer ask for the write alias each time and not cache the index name. A test covers this.

What remains is the count check, which must sum over both indexes of the month. I will extend it next. Then the rollover can go into the PR with the plan document.

summary: Extended the nightly count check to sum over both indexes of a month with a rollover, and it matched the source counts for all 40 staging customers.
body:
The count check compared the per-customer counts of the old index with the monthly index. With a rollover, a month can have two indexes, so I changed it to query the read alias and not the single index name.

I ran it on staging after the rollover test. All 40 customers matched. The stop rule of 0.1 percent or 50 documents was applied and none reached it.

I also made the check write its result to a table in Postgres, one row per customer and night. That gives a trend and a record for the cutover review.

summary: Added a second search node to staging and re-ran the monthly index load, which finished in 52 minutes with balanced shards and no rejected bulk requests.
body:
Following the review with Tobias and Mara, I added a third data node to the staging search cluster and re-ran the full load of the monthly indexes. The earlier staging run had needed 74 minutes and produced a few rejected bulk requests, so this was the first test of whether the extra node is enough.

The load finished in 52 minutes. No bulk request was rejected, and the queue of the write thread pool stayed below 40 at its peak.

Shard sizes after the load were between 21 and 27 GB for the normal months. The oversized month, with the largest customer's backfill, split into two shard sets behind one alias because of the size-based rollover from this morning.

I compared document counts per customer against the source tables. All 40 staging customers matched, including the two whose events are spread over the rollover boundary.

One thing I noticed is that the refresh interval of 1 second made the bulk load slower than it had to be. For the load I set it to 30 seconds and set it back afterwards. That should be part of the cutover steps, so I added a line to the draft.

Tobias will check the node sizing for production tomorrow. Mara wants the dual write week to start only after the production node is in and healthy for two days.

Next step is a test of the search API against the monthly layout with the real query set, to see whether the latency of wildcard queries changes when a query touches 12 shards instead of one.

summary: Wrote down the refresh interval handling for the bulk load in the cutover draft, with the exact settings calls for setting and restoring it.
body:
