summary: Wrote and ran a load test of the audit export runner with large customers' data on staging and found the manifest checksum step doubled the run time, so it now hashes while writing.
body:
The audit export scheduler is feature complete, so I ran a load test with data shaped like the three largest customers: 500,000 entries each, one export job per customer.

The first run took 11 minutes per job. A profile showed that the runner wrote the file, then read it back to compute the SHA-256 for the manifest. For a 600 MB file that is a second full pass over the disk and the network volume.

I changed the writer to feed every chunk into the hash while writing it to the bucket upload stream. The manifest checksum is then ready when the upload finishes. The same applies to the per-file checksums of split files.

After the change the time dropped to 6 minutes per job, and the memory of the runner stayed flat at about 180 MB.

I checked correctness in two ways:
- the checksum in the manifest equals sha256sum of the downloaded file for all 9 files
- an interrupted upload leaves no manifest entry

The second point needed a small change. The manifest entry is written only after the upload call returns successfully, and a failed upload removes the partial object.

I added a test with a fake bucket that fails the upload in the middle of a file. It confirms the job is marked failed and that the next run starts the file again from the beginning.

One issue is left. The 500,000 entry cap per run means large customers need several runs for the first export. That is intended, but the console does not say that the first export is partial. I told Lena, who will add a line below the form.

I did not touch the dashboards today.

summary: Wrote down a plan for how the ingest worker's batch size should adapt to queue lag, after batch writes showed smaller batches than configured at low traffic.
body:
Looking at the metrics of the ingest worker batch writes, I saw that at night the batches held 40 events on average, while the configured maximum is 500. The worker flushes on a timer of 200 ms, so at low traffic it writes small batches and makes many small database calls.

That is correct behaviour, but it costs more per event. The cost at night is not a problem today, because the load is low.

The opposite case is more interesting. When lag builds up, the worker should use full batches, and it does, since the batches fill before the timer fires. So the fixed settings work at both ends.

I wrote the options in the branch notes:
- keep the fixed timer, which is simple and works
- raise the timer at low lag, which saves little
- make the timer depend on lag, which adds a moving part

I recommend keeping the fixed timer. I will ask Mara, who owns the worker, to confirm tomorrow. No code change was made.

I also noted that the batch size metric has no label for event type, which makes it hard to see whether one type has small batches. Adding the label is cheap, so that is the next small step.

summary: Dropped two Postgres indexes on the audit table that the new composite index made redundant, after a check of the usage statistics.
body:
This follows the index added earlier today. The index usage statistics showed that the two older indexes on the audit table had zero scans since the new one went in, and their sizes together were 510 MB.

I checked every query that touches the table, including the export scheduler, the console list and the retention job. All of them filter by customer first, so the composite index covers them.

I dropped both indexes with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, kept the definitions in the migration file for a rollback, and watched the slow query log for an hour. Nothing new appeared, and write time on the table fell a little.

summary: Applied the volume resize on the two fullest search nodes and confirmed the cluster stayed green and shards did not move during the change.
body:
Tobias grew the volumes of the two nodes that were above 70 percent disk, and I followed along as the reviewer of the checklist step zero. We did one node at a time, with a pause to let the cluster settle.

Before each resize I checked that the cluster was green and that shard rebalancing was not running. After the file system grow, I checked the new size and the disk watermark settings.

The first node took 9 minutes and the second 11. The cluster stayed green the whole time, and search latency showed no change on the dashboard.

The two nodes now sit at 48 and 50 percent, so the dual write needs fit with room to spare. The step is marked done in the checklist.

One thing we noticed is that the Terraform value for the volume size was still the old one, so the next apply would have shrunk the plan. Tobias updated the value in code and ran a plan to confirm no changes are pending.

The next step is the dry run of the dual write on staging, which is planned for tomorrow.

summary: Ran the dual write dry run of the monthly search index on staging for three hours and found that bulk requests for old months were rejected until the month templates existed.
body:
I started the dry run of the dual write on staging with the replay of production traffic. The writer sends every indexing request to the old layout and to the monthly one.

The first 20 minutes showed bulk rejections on the monthly side. The errors were about missing indices for older months, because documents with old timestamps arrive in the replay, and the monthly index is created only when its month starts.

There are two ways to deal with that: auto-create the index on first write, or create all months ahead. I chose to create them ahead with a small script, since auto-create would give indices without the right settings if the template did not match. The template pattern is checked by a test, so a mismatch would be seen.

After the script created 26 monthly indices, the rejections stopped. The rest of the run went like this:
- 410,000 documents written to both layouts
- no rejections after the fix
- indexing latency up by 11 percent on the writer, within the limit of 20 percent in the plan

The count comparison script reported a difference of zero for all months except the current one, where it showed a pending difference of 6 documents, and the content sample found no mismatch.

I added the month creation script to the checklist as a step before the production start. It must run on the first day of each month as well. Tobias will add that to the cron jobs.

I did not start anything on production.

summary: Fixed a bug where the Redis session store in the admin console kept sessions of deleted users alive, by deleting the session keys when a user is removed.
body:
Sam reported that a former customer admin could still open the console after his account was removed. I reproduced it on staging: delete the user, keep the browser tab open, and the next request still worked.

The user delete in the console API removed the row in Postgres, but the session was a separate key in Redis and was checked only for existence and expiry. Nothing connected the two.

There are two parts to the fix. First, the delete now also removes the session keys of that user. To find them, I added a small set per user (sessions:user:<id>) that holds the session ids, which is updated on login and logout. Second, the session check now loads the user and rejects the request if the user is gone or disabled. That covers sessions that were created before the set existed.

The second part costs one extra Postgres read per request, so I put the user lookup behind a short cache of 30 seconds. That is a trade off: a removed user may still pass for up to 30 seconds. I think this is acceptable, and I wrote it in the code comment.

Tests added:
- delete user removes all of the user's sessions
- a session of a missing user gets 401
- the cache expires after the set time

I ran a one-off script on production to clean the existing sessions of users that no longer exist. It found 17 sessions and removed them. I will mention it to Lena since she owns the login flow.

summary: Reviewed Lena's change to the rate limit form in the console and asked that the default limit be shown as placeholder text for keys without a limit row.
body:
Lena's pull request follows the question of last week about keys with limit 0. It adds a limit section to the key page.

I tested it on staging. For a key with a limit row the numbers show up as expected. For a new key the field was empty and a save sent null, which the API treated as no limit row and kept the default. That works, but the user cannot see this.

I asked for the default to be shown as placeholder text, for example the number from the settings endpoint with a label saying default. Saving an empty field should keep the default.

There was also a small bug: the burst field accepted a value lower than the per-second limit, which the API rejects with a 422, but the form showed no message. I asked her to show the API message below the field.

The code was otherwise tidy, and the tests cover the validation. I approved after the two changes and she said she would update the pull request in the afternoon.

summary: Checked the bounded jitter of the loader backoff against a long throttle period on staging and confirmed the maximum wait stays under two minutes.
body:
After the rollout of the jittered backoff, Mara asked whether a long throttle period could stretch the waits too much. I replayed a ten minute throttle on staging with 2,000 files.

The backoff is exponential with full jitter and a cap of 90 seconds. The longest single wait seen was 88 seconds, and no file waited longer than 4 minutes in total over its attempts. All files finished after the throttle ended, and none exceeded the maximum of 8 attempts.

The attempt counts were mostly 1 to 3, with a long tail at 6. I wrote the numbers into the branch notes. No change was needed.

summary: Prepared the dual write of the monthly search index: wrote the dual writer behind a feature flag and tested it on staging, with nothing turned on in production yet.
body:
The checklist for the dual write week begins with a small canary, so today I prepared the first step and did not turn anything on for a real customer. The writer changes are in the indexing service. When the flag is on for a customer, every bulk request goes to the old layout first. If that succeeds, the same request goes to the monthly layout. A failure on the monthly side is logged and counted, but does not fail the request, so the customer would see no effect.

I chose this order on purpose: the old layout stays the source of truth until the end of the week, and the monthly one is allowed to lag. The flag is off for every customer, and the canary customer is picked but not enabled.

On staging I ran the month creation script and made the 26 monthly indices with the template settings. I checked one of them by hand for shard count, replicas and the mapping of the numeric field that had caused a mismatch in the earlier dry run. The mapping now matches the old layout.

Then I ran the dual writer on staging with the flag on for one test customer and replayed a sample of traffic:
- about 61,000 documents written to both layouts
- zero failed monthly writes
- indexing latency up by 9 percent for that test customer
- the count script showed a difference of zero for older months

I also ran the content sample of 200 documents, with no mismatch.

I wrote an alert on the counter of failed monthly writes, which pages only if it is above zero for ten minutes. For the canary it will be a warning and not a page.

The plan says to widen the flag to ten customers on the second day if the thresholds hold. The disk use on the staging nodes rose by 1 percent, as the plan predicted.

One small problem came up: the dashboard for indexing latency did not have a panel by layout, so I added one with the two layouts side by side. Tobias will check the panel tomorrow morning, and after that I will deploy the writer and turn the flag on for the single small customer.

summary: Wrote the second step of the monthly search index dual write check: a per-customer lag report showing how far the monthly layout trails the old one during bulk bursts.
body: The first part of the comparison compared document counts only at one moment, which hid short periods where the monthly layout was behind. This morning's step adds a lag report that samples both layouts every minute and records the difference per customer. The sampling reads the count per customer from each index through the existing search API client, so it needs no new credentials. Results go into a small Postgres table with the customer, the minute and both counts. On staging with the replayed event stream, the lag stayed at zero for most customers and reached about 1,800 documents for the largest customer during a bulk import. It cleared within two minutes after the import ended. The report prints the worst minute per customer and flags anything over 5,000 documents, which is the threshold from the dual write plan for stopping. I also found that the count for a customer with many deleted documents was off until the refresh interval passed, so the sampler now waits for a refresh before reading. Next is running it against the ten production customers during the evening peak and attaching the report to the checklist.

summary: Answered Mara's question on whether the Redis client should reconnect with a fixed delay or backoff: a short backoff with jitter, capped at two seconds.
body:
Mara was fixing reconnects in the search API Redis client and asked which strategy to use after a connection drop. I looked at what the client library offers and at the way the last Redis restart on staging behaved.

A fixed delay of 100 ms made all instances reconnect at the same moment, and the Redis log showed a burst of 60 new connections in one second. That matters because the pool limit is low and we do not want to hit it again.

I recommended a backoff that starts at 50 ms, doubles, adds random jitter, and stops growing at 2 seconds. Requests during the outage should fall back to the database path and not wait for the reconnect.

Mara will set that in the client options and test it with a restart of staging Redis.

summary: Prepared to widen the dual write of the monthly search index to ten customers, found a mapping conflict on the duration field in the shared template, and worked out a fix before touching the flag.
body:
The canary of yesterday held, so I planned to widen the flag to ten customers with Tobias watching the cluster. Before changing anything in production I replayed a sample of events from the ten customers against a staging copy of the monthly template, to see whether the shared mapping would reject anything the old per-customer layout accepted.

One customer did. A field called duration is a number for most customers, but this customer sends it as a string like "3.2s" in some events. The staging bulk call returned a mapper parsing exception for 212 of the sampled documents from that customer.

In the old layout this worked because the index was created per customer and the mapping came from the first documents. The monthly layout shares one mapping for all customers, so one customer's type decides for all.

There were three ways to deal with it:
- coerce the value in the indexer, which would change the stored data
- map the field as keyword in the template, which loses range queries on it
- store the string variant under a second field name

I chose the third. The indexer on staging now writes values that are not numbers to duration_raw and keeps duration for numbers only. The template has both fields. Queries that use range on duration keep working, and the customer's strings stay searchable.

Existing monthly indices cannot change a field type, but a new field can be added with a mapping update. I tried a put mapping call for duration_raw on the staging indices and it went through. The same call for the 26 production monthly indices is written into the plan, together with the template update, but I have not run it yet.

I also searched the old layout's mappings for other fields with mixed types between customers. There were two more candidates, status_code and size. Both are numbers for every customer today, so I left them and added both to a watch list, with a test that flags a new conflict.

The flag stays where it is for now. The widening to ten customers waits until the template change is in place and the replay of the sample shows a difference of zero. I wrote the duration finding into the search index notes, since it is a good example of what the shared mapping means for customers.

summary: Profiled the Postgres connection use of the search API and the console and cut idle connections from 140 to 60 by lowering the pool minimum, without any latency change.
body:
Postgres showed 140 connections most of the day, while the real concurrent queries were below 15. The limit is 200, and the audit export runner now needs its own connections too, so I looked at who holds them.

The breakdown by application name was:
- search API: 64
- console API: 48
- ingest workers: 20
- everything else: 8

Both the search API and the console API had a pool minimum of 8 per instance, and with 8 instances each that kept 64 and 48 connections open. Most of them were idle.

I lowered the minimum to 2 and kept the maximum at 10. Idle connections are closed after 30 seconds. I did this on staging first and ran the standard load test, which showed the same p50 and p99 as before, since connections are opened on demand and opening is fast inside the network.

On production I changed one service at a time and watched the connection count and query latency. After both changes the total settled at about 60 during the day, and 35 at night.

One issue came up on the console side. A health check opened a fresh connection on every call and did not close it properly when the check timed out, which slowly leaked connections. The count rose by about 1 per hour. I fixed the check to use the pool and added a timeout that releases the connection.

I also added the application name to the connection strings of the audit export runner and the loader, which were missing it. That makes the next look at the numbers easier.

There is now room for the export runner's pool of 6 and for the migrations tool. I wrote the numbers into the Postgres notes. No change was needed for pgbouncer, which we do not run; I am not sure we need it at this size.

summary: Ran the lag report on production for the ten dual write customers through the evening peak and found the monthly layout never trailed by more than 900 documents.
body: The lag report from this morning ran against production from late afternoon until the peak had passed. The ten customers in the dual write stayed within the threshold the whole time, and the worst minute was 900 documents behind for the largest one. That minute matched a bulk import of that customer, and the lag was gone two minutes later. One smaller customer showed a constant difference of 3 documents. I traced it to documents written to the old layout just before the writer flag was switched on for that customer, so it is not a live problem. I added a baseline offset option to the report so that such leftovers do not look like lag. The sampler itself added no measurable load to the search nodes, and the cluster stayed green. The result goes into the checklist as the evidence for the current step. Tomorrow we decide whether to widen the dual write to the next group of customers.

summary: Wrote a script that lists audit export jobs that missed their schedule, and found two jobs that skipped a run after the runner restarted during a deploy.
body:
After the load test of the export runner I wanted a way to see missed runs. I wrote a query and a small script that compares the expected run times from each job's interval with the recorded runs in the last week.

It found two jobs with one missed run each. Both were due while the runner restarted during a deploy, and the runner did not look back for runs that were due while it was down.

The fix is a catch up step at startup: for every job, if the last planned time is older than one interval, schedule a single run now. It is a single run on purpose, not one for every missed slot, so that a long outage does not make a storm of exports.

I added the step and tests for three cases: no miss, one miss and a long outage with many missed slots, which gives only one run. The manifest of a catch up run notes that it was late.

The two skipped runs were started by hand with the script and finished fine.

The script also became a check in the scheduler's alert: if a job is more than 1.5 intervals late, a warning is sent, not a page.

summary: Replaced the hand-written cache key builder in the search API with a small shared function and tests, after finding three variants of the same key format in the code.
body:
While fixing the suggest endpoint earlier in the week I saw that cache keys were built by string concatenation in several places. Today I counted them: 11 places and 3 slightly different formats, one with the customer id before the endpoint name and two with it after.

The mix did no harm yet, but it meant that a purge by customer pattern missed one family of keys. I found that with a scan of staging Redis: 2,300 keys of the family did not match the pattern for a customer purge.

I wrote one function, cacheKey(family, customerId, parts), that returns the format service:family:customer:hash, which is the convention from the Redis notes. The hash is over the sorted, normalised parts, and it ignores request ids, which was the cause of the low hit rate on suggest earlier.

The change touches 11 call sites. I converted them one by one and ran the full test suite after each, which found one place that relied on the old key for a test fixture.

Tests for the function cover:
- the same parts in a different order give the same key
- different customers give different keys
- a request id never changes the key
- keys stay under 200 characters

On deploy, old keys are not read anymore, so they expire by their TTL. The hit rate fell for about 20 minutes after the deploy and then returned to normal, at 88 percent overall.

I also changed the customer purge to use the new pattern and checked on staging that it removes every family.

There is one risk: a rollback would read no new keys and would rebuild the cache, which costs a short load on OpenSearch. I judged that acceptable.

summary: Checked the monthly index dual write at the end of the day with ten customers and found writes clean, with the duration_raw field in use for one customer.
body:
Evening check of the dual write with ten customers. The failed monthly write counter is at zero since the template fix, and the count script shows differences only in the current month, at most 9 documents pending.

The duration_raw field holds 640 documents so far, all from the one customer with string values. The content sample of 500 documents per customer found no mismatch for any of the ten.

Disk use rose by 2 percent in total, which is the plan's prediction for this share of customers. Indexing latency is 10 percent above the old layout.

The flag stays as it is overnight. Tobias will look at the node disks in the morning, and I will run the status status check again before widening.

summary: Prepared to widen the monthly search index dual write from ten to thirty customers, and fixed an oversized batch problem found while testing with the largest documents.
body:
The ten customer dual write had run clean through the evening, so I spent the last part of the day getting ready for the next widening to thirty customers. The writer reads the customer list from the flag config, so the widening needs no deploy. I prepared the new list but did not apply it yet.

While checking the customers on the new list, I looked at one with very large documents. In a dry run against a copy of its data, bulk requests went over the 10 MB request limit once documents for several months were grouped into one request. The writer groups documents per request by count, not by size, so this customer would have had rejected requests as soon as it was added.

I changed the writer to split a bulk request when its byte size passes 5 MB, and added a test with a batch of 300 documents of 40 KB each. The test passes. I also read the writer's failure log from the ten customer run to confirm that nothing there had been rejected for the same reason, and it was empty.

The document count comparison for the ten customers was run again and showed no differences. The lag report showed the longest lag at about 700 documents, which is in line with the earlier check.

Left for tomorrow: get the size split reviewed, since it is on the search-v2 branch and not yet reviewed, then apply the thirty customer list, watch the bulk error rate for a while, and look at the disk growth on the search nodes before deciding on the next widening.

summary: Checked disk growth on the search nodes overnight with thirty customers dual writing and found it matched the estimate of the plan, so the next widening can go ahead.
body:
The plan estimated that each dual written customer adds its index size once more on the nodes. I compared the disk graphs from last evening to this morning for all nodes.

Growth was 38 GB in total across the cluster. The estimate for thirty customers was 35 to 42 GB, so it fits. The fullest node is at 71 percent after the resize, well under the 80 percent stop threshold from the plan.

I also checked segment merges. Merge activity rose for about two hours after the widening and then returned to normal. No shard moved and the cluster stayed green all night.

The nightly reindex job runs on the old layout only for now. I confirmed it does not touch the monthly indices, so the two do not compete for disk. Making the reindex job aware of the monthly layout is a later task and is not planned before the dual write is complete.

Next step is to widen to all customers except the five largest, which will be done after the lunch check of the lag report.

summary: Planned the next widening of the monthly index dual write, fixed a template gap for old months on the ten customers already writing, and checked counts with the comparison script.
body:
After the lag report at the start of the session looked fine, I went through the list of customers that are next in line for the monthly index dual write. The flag stays at the customers who are already on it today. I only prepared the widening: I listed the roughly 35 customers that would come next, everyone except the five largest, and checked their oldest documents against the template pattern.

That check found the problem early. Two customers have documents with timestamps from before the first month template. The pattern started at a month that was too late for them, so their bulk requests would have been rejected. I added templates for the earlier months on staging and replayed a sample of old documents for those two customers. All of them were accepted. I wrote the template change into the plan so it goes in before the flag is widened.

I then ran the document count comparison for the customers already dual writing. Two customers showed differences of 12 and 31 documents. The cause was documents deleted in the old layout while the comparison ran. The delete path of the writer is not yet part of the dual write. I confirmed this by looking at the delete requests in the API log for those customers.

So deletes are not mirrored. This is a real gap and it blocks the widening. I wrote a ticket for it and started the change: the delete by query and the single delete both call the monthly writer behind the same flag. The single delete is done and tested. The delete by query needs the month list for the customer and is not done.

The content sample check of 200 documents per customer found no differences for the customers without deletes. Peak lag in the late morning was below 1,200 documents.

Next: finish the delete by query, run the comparison again, then apply the templates and widen the flag.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why the audit export file for a customer has fewer rows than the console shows: the console counts rows of all event types, the export only audit ones.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel why a customer's export showed 8,400 rows while the console list showed about 11,000.

I checked the export query and the console query. The console list merges audit entries with settings change entries for the same account. The export reads only the audit table. The settings changes are not part of the compliance export by design, which is stated in the first spec of the export.

I ran both counts for the customer for the same time range and got 8,412 and 10,975. The difference of 2,563 matched the number of settings entries exactly.

I gave Sam a short text for the docs and for the customer. Sam will add a sentence to the export docs page. No code change was made.

summary: Worked on the delete by query path of the monthly index dual write, with the month list per customer and tests, and planned the replay of deletes for the two customers with count differences.
body:
The single delete had been mirrored in the morning. The delete by query was the harder one, because it can touch several months and the writer needs to know which monthly indices exist for the customer.

I wrote a function that lists the monthly indices of a customer from the index aliases, with a short cache of 60 seconds in the search API. The delete by query now sends the same query to each of those indices. If one index fails, the old layout result still counts as the truth, and the failure goes to the writer's failure log with the query text.

Tests: a delete over three months, a delete where one month index is missing, and a delete where the monthly request times out. All three pass. I kept the version count check out, because deletes by query are rare.

On staging I created 500 documents over four months, deleted 120 by query, and compared both layouts. Counts matched and the content sample matched.

The branch is not deployed to production yet, and the flag is unchanged. The two customers who showed 12 and 31 documents of difference still show them in the count comparison. I looked at their extra documents and they look like deletes that were made before the delete mirroring existed. My plan is to replay their deletes from the API log after the deploy, and then re-run the comparison. The log of the last day should be enough, because the dual write only started recently for these customers, but I want to check that before relying on it.

Next: deploy the delete path with the flag unchanged, do the replay for the two customers, and widen to the five largest customers after the disk check.

summary: Looked at why Redis memory rose by 300 MB over two days and found the suggest cache keys had no TTL; added a TTL of one hour.
body:
The Redis memory graph showed a slow rise of about 300 MB since the suggest endpoint change from a few days ago. I listed the key prefixes with a scan on a replica and counted them by prefix.

The prefix of the new batch call cache for suggestions held about 1.1 million keys, and none had a TTL. The earlier per-field keys had one, but the new shared key function did not set it. This came from the key builder change, which only builds the key and left the TTL to the caller.

I set a TTL of one hour for these keys in the suggest handler and added a test that checks the TTL after a write. The existing keys without a TTL were given the same TTL with a short script, run in batches of 1,000 keys to keep the load low.

The memory graph should flatten over the next hours. I will look at it again in the evening.

summary: Prepared to widen the monthly index dual write to the five largest customers, checked disk headroom and found the largest customer needs a separate bulk concurrency limit.
body:
The disk check in the morning showed 74 percent on the fullest search node, still under the threshold of the plan. So I used the time to prepare the step for the five largest customers, which has not started yet. The plan is to go one customer at a time, with a pause of 20 minutes between them.

To see what to expect, I looked at the lag reports of the thirty customers that already dual write. During their bulk bursts the lag went up to about 2,000 documents and drained within a minute. The largest customers will be higher than that, but the numbers give a reasonable guess for the first three of the five.

The largest customer worries me more. Their ingest has up to 40 bulk requests in parallel, and with the dual write the cluster would receive twice as many. I looked at the write queue sizes of the nodes and saw that two of them have little room. A burst of that size could fill the queue and cause rejections with es_rejected_execution_exception.

So I started a concurrency limit for the monthly writer, drafted at 8 parallel requests per customer, with the rest waiting in an in-process queue. The writes of the old layout stay unlimited. I wrote a first version of it and a test with 40 parallel requests on staging. The queue holds the surplus and nothing is rejected there. The test only shows the logic, not the real load of the cluster.

I estimate that the lag of this customer would peak at a few thousand documents during their nightly import and drain in a few minutes. That would be under the plan's threshold of ten minutes, but it is a guess until I see a real night import.

Nothing was widened to the five largest customers today. To do: review the limit with Mara, write the concurrency limit into the plan as a proposed setting, and decide on the order of the five customers.

summary: Reviewed Mara's schema registry change that stores compatibility results, found a race when two versions are registered at once, and proposed a unique constraint.
body:
Mara asked for a review of the pull request that stores the result of each compatibility check in Postgres, so the console can show why a version was refused.

The code is clear and the tests cover the main cases: adding an optional field, removing a required field, changing a type. The earlier problem of an optional field reported as breaking is fixed.

One issue: when two clients register a new version of the same schema at the same time, both read the latest version number, both check against it, and both insert version n+1. In a test I wrote with two parallel requests, I got two rows with the same version number about once in five runs.

I proposed a unique constraint on the schema id and the version number, and to catch the conflict error and retry the check once against the new latest version. I added the test for this as a suggestion in the review. The migration for the constraint needs a check for existing duplicates first. I ran the check on a copy of the production data and found none.

Smaller points:
- the result column stores the full diff as JSON, which can become large, so I asked for a size limit of 64 KB with a note if it is cut.
- the console API returns the diff unsorted, so the order changes between calls. Sorting by field name makes it stable.
- one log line prints the whole schema, which can contain customer field names. I asked to log only the id.

Mara agreed on the constraint and the sorting. She wants to keep the full diff for now and look at sizes after a week. I accepted that, with the log line change.

I marked the review as changes requested.

summary: Checked the night import lag for the largest customer in the dual write plan ahead of time by replaying a copy of last night's import on staging, which stayed under six minutes.
body:
I did not want to wait for the real night import, so I replayed the bulk traffic of the previous night for the largest customer on staging. The traffic came from the writer's request log, with about 310,000 documents in 2,900 bulk requests.

Staging has fewer nodes than production, so I scaled the replay speed to 60 percent. With the concurrency limit of 8 the monthly writer trailed by 5,400 documents at the peak and caught up in five minutes and forty seconds.

I also tried a limit of 4 to see the effect. The lag grew to 21,000 documents and took 17 minutes to drain, which would break the ten minute threshold. A limit of 12 gave nearly the same result as 8, with more rejections on the write queue. So 8 stays.

The replay also showed that the in-process queue grows to about 900 requests at the peak, which means some memory in the search API pods. I measured about 70 MB more, which is fine.

Summary for the plan: limit 8 is right, and the real night import is still to be watched once. I will check the lag report tomorrow morning.

summary: Fixed the audit export runner so that a job interrupted by a deploy resumes from its last written part instead of starting again, and added a test for it.
body:
Last week's script that lists missed export jobs found two jobs that skipped a run after the runner restarted during a deploy. Today I looked at what happens to a job that is running when the runner stops.

The job state stays running, and the next start treats running jobs as stale after 30 minutes and marks them failed. With a large customer, an export takes about 25 minutes, so a restart late in the run costs most of the work, and the next scheduled run is then skipped because the failed job blocks it.

The change has three parts:
- the runner writes a checkpoint to Postgres after every finished part file, with the part number and the last row key.
- on start, jobs in the running state with an old heartbeat are picked up and continue from the checkpoint, not marked failed.
- the scheduler no longer skips a run because of an interrupted job, only because of a job with a live heartbeat.

The manifest is written only at the end, and lists all parts, so a resumed job produces the same manifest as an uninterrupted one. The checksum is computed while writing, so for the resumed part I store the running hash state is not possible. I chose to re-hash the already written parts by reading them back from the bucket, which costs a little time but is simple and correct.

Tests: kill the runner after part 3 of 6 and check that the second start writes parts 4 to 6 only, and that the manifest lists 6 parts with correct checksums. A second test kills during a part and checks that the half-written part is overwritten. Both pass.

On staging I ran the large customer export and killed the runner twice. The result had the same checksum as the uninterrupted export. The change is deployed to staging and waits for review.

summary: Watched the real night import of the largest customer in the monthly index dual write, saw the lag peak at 7,800 documents and drain in four minutes, and began the ordering fix.
body:
The lag report for the night showed the import of the largest customer between 02:10 and 02:50. The monthly writer trailed by 7,800 documents at the peak and caught up four minutes after the import ended. That fits the staging replay, which predicted about 5,400 at 60 percent speed, and it stays well below the ten minute threshold.

There were 11 bulk rejections in the whole night, all in the first minute of the import, and all were retried by the writer and accepted. No entries are in the failure log.

The count comparison this morning had zero differences for the four large customers already in the dual write. The content sample check had one difference: a document that was updated twice within a second, where the monthly layout had the older version. The writer sends updates in parallel for different months, but for the same document it should keep the order. I checked and found that the concurrency limit queue does not keep the order per document id.

I started the fix. The queue now routes requests by a hash of the customer and month, so that requests for the same month are handled in order. Parallelism across months stays. The code change is written, and the tests are still to do.

I did not widen the dual write to the fifth customer yet. The night looked good, but I want the ordering fix tested first, so that the new customer does not start with the known gap. The four customers already on keep running as they are.

Next: tests for the ordering, then a decision with the plan on when the fifth customer starts, when all customers are on and how long to observe before the read switch.

summary: Added tests for per-month ordering in the monthly writer queue, including two rapid updates of one document, and all pass.
body:
The ordering change from this morning needed tests before it could go out. I wrote three.

The first sends two updates for the same document in the same month within a few milliseconds and checks that the final version in the monthly index is the second one. Before the change it failed in about one run in four.

The second sends updates for documents in different months and checks that they run in parallel, by measuring that two slow mock requests finish in about the time of one.

The third fills the queue beyond the limit and checks that no request is lost and the order per month is kept.

All three pass over 50 runs. I will deploy the change after review.

summary: Slow reports query on Postgres traced to a missing composite index on (account_id, created_at); adding it cut the run from 9 seconds to 300 ms.
body:
The support queue had two complaints about the monthly report page loading slowly. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the reports query showed a sequential scan over the audit_log join, with about 4 million rows read for each account.

The query filters on account_id and a created_at range, but only separate single-column indexes existed. Postgres picked the one on created_at and filtered the rest.

I created the composite index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so writes were not blocked. The build took 6 minutes on the production replica first, and then on the primary.

After the index, the same query for the largest customer dropped from 9 seconds to 300 ms. The plan now uses an index scan with a bitmap heap on the date range.

I also checked that the write path was not hurt. Insert latency on the audit table stayed within noise, at about 1.2 ms median.

The migration file is in the main checkout under db/migrations. I did not drop the old created_at index yet, because two other queries might still use it. I will check pg_stat_user_indexes in a week and decide then.

The next step is to look at the other two report queries, which have a similar shape.

summary: Redis memory grew about 15 percent in a week; most of it was session keys with no clear prefix, so I wrote a key naming guide and renamed the worst offenders.
body:
Tobias pointed out on the Grafana board that Redis used memory had climbed from 2.6 GB to 3.0 GB over the week. I ran a SCAN with a sample of 50,000 keys and grouped them by prefix.

About 40 percent of the sample were session keys of the admin console. They were written as sess:<id> in some code paths and as session_<id> in others, so two sets existed side by side for the same users.

I wrote a short key naming guide in docs/redis-keys.md. The format is <area>:<entity>:<id>, for example cache:search:<hash> and rl:key:<apikey>.

The console now writes only sess:<id>. A one-off script removed the old session_ keys that had not been touched for a day.

Used memory dropped by about 280 MB after the cleanup. The query cache keys are named correctly already and I left them alone.

No user was logged out, because the script skipped keys with a TTL left under an hour only for the old name when the new one existed. I checked this with two test accounts.

Lena will review the console change tomorrow.

summary: Started the schema registry compatibility checker: it now rejects a new event schema version that removes a required field, with tests for six change types.
body:
Today's work on the schema-registry branch was the compatibility check that runs when someone registers a new version of an event schema. Until now the registry accepted anything that was valid JSON Schema.

I defined the rules in a small module, registry/compat.ts. A change is breaking if it removes a required field, changes a field type, narrows an enum, makes an optional field required, tightens a numeric limit, or adds a required field without a default.

Adding an optional field, widening an enum and loosening a limit are allowed. Each of the six breaking cases and three allowed cases has a test with a before and an after schema.

The first version of the type check failed on a field that changed from integer to number. That is a widening, and I treated it as breaking. I added an explicit rule that integer to number is allowed.

The registry API now answers 409 with a list of the violated rules, one entry per field path. This is easier to read than a single message, and Sam asked for exactly that for the docs.

I ran the checker against all 31 existing schema versions in staging. Two real histories came out as breaking: the click event lost a required field in an old version, and the session event changed a type.

Both are old and already live, so I added an allowlist file for them with a comment for each. I did not want to rewrite history.

The tests pass locally, 27 of them. CI has not run yet.

Not done: a dry-run endpoint so that producers can check a schema before they register it, and a setting for stricter or looser modes per event type.

The next session will add the dry-run endpoint, since the check is a pure function and it should be cheap.

summary: Dashboard timeouts for one large customer were caused by a materialized view that missed the hourly rollup; fixed the view definition and refilled 11 days of data.
body:
A support ticket said the traffic dashboard of one of our largest customers showed empty hours and sometimes timed out. I started with the dashboard query in ClickHouse and found it read the raw events for any range under 14 days.

The hourly rollup view should have served that range. The query planner in our code picks the view only when the rollup table has data for the whole range, and it had a gap.

The gap started 11 days ago. That was the day we changed the event schema for a new optional field, and the materialized view select list still used the old column order in an INSERT ... SELECT without names.

New rows therefore went into the wrong columns for that customer's event type and were dropped by a filter. Other customers were not affected because their event types do not have the field.

I fixed the view by naming all columns explicitly. I then dropped and recreated it, and refilled the rollup for the 11 days from the raw events.

The refill ran for 38 minutes for that one customer and used about 6 GB of memory on the node, so I ran it in daily chunks to keep it small.

After the refill I compared the rollup counts to the raw counts for each day. They match exactly for all 11 days.

The dashboard now loads in 700 ms for a 7 day range instead of timing out at 30 seconds.

I wrote a check that runs each night and compares rollup and raw counts for the last 3 days per customer. It posts to the team channel if the difference is above 0.1 percent.

I also added a line to the schema registry checklist: any new optional field needs a look at the materialized views that select from the table.

I told Sam what happened so that the answer to the customer is accurate. No data was lost, only the rollup was wrong.

summary: Tried the new Go HTTP client library for the ingest SDK sample code and dropped it after it failed to reuse connections; the standard client stays.
body:
I tried a third-party HTTP client for the Go sample in the public docs, because it promised easier retries and nicer timeouts. The goal was shorter example code.

In a load test of 200 concurrent senders it opened a new connection for almost every batch. The load balancer showed connection counts about 8 times higher than with the standard client.

I looked for a setting and found that the library creates a new transport unless one is passed in. Passing the shared transport fixed the count, but then the example was as long as the standard version.

So there was no gain. I removed the dependency and kept net/http with a small helper for backoff.

Nothing is changed in the docs. I left a note in the docs repo issue so nobody tries it again in a month.

summary: Postgres autovacuum fell behind on the events metadata table; tuned per-table settings and a manual vacuum freed 18 GB of bloat.
body:
An alert for disk use on the primary fired in the morning. Disk had grown by 20 GB in a week, which did not match the data growth.

I looked at pg_stat_user_tables and found the import_jobs table with 62 percent dead tuples. Autovacuum ran on it, but each run was cancelled by a lock from the nightly cleanup job.

The cleanup job deletes finished jobs older than 30 days in one large transaction. It held its lock long enough that autovacuum gave up every time.

I changed two things. The cleanup now deletes in batches of 5,000 rows with a commit between batches. The table also has its own autovacuum settings: scale factor 0.02 and a lower cost delay.

Then I ran a manual VACUUM (VERBOSE) in a quiet period. It took 14 minutes and removed about 31 million dead tuples.

The disk did not shrink on its own, because plain vacuum does not return space to the system. I used pg_repack on the table, which needs only a short lock at the end, and it freed 18 GB.

Tobias checked replica lag during the repack. It stayed under 2 seconds.

I added a Grafana panel for dead tuple ratio of the five largest tables, with an alert at 40 percent.

I checked the other tables. The audit log is append-only and fine. Accounts and settings are small.

Next I want to look at whether the cleanup job needs to run every night, or whether a weekly run is enough.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console change for the API key table; found a missing permission check on the revoke button and sent it back with two comments.
body:
Lena asked for a review of the pull request that adds a list of API keys with last-used times to the admin console.

The layout and the paging are good, and the table renders 500 keys without lag. The last-used value comes from the Redis rate limiter counters, which is a neat use of data we already have.

The revoke button is shown to every logged-in role, and the API behind it checked only that the user was logged in. A read-only support user could revoke a key by calling it directly.

I wrote a test that proves it and added it to the review as a failing case. Lena will add the role check in the Fastify route, and hide the button for roles without the right.

The second comment was small. The relative time text shows 'NaN minutes ago' for keys that were never used, so that case needs an explicit label.

I approved it conditionally. Nothing was merged.

summary: Planned the new search index shard layout by month: sized the data per month, compared shard counts, and wrote the plan with a migration order.
body:
Today I wrote the design note for moving the search index from one shard set per customer to one per month. The reason is that small customers have tiny indexes that waste shards, while a few large ones have shards that are too big.

I queried the index stats and listed the size per customer and per month for the last 14 months. The monthly total is between 90 and 130 GB of primary data.

With a target of 20 to 30 GB per shard, a month needs 4 to 6 shards. I propose 4 shards and a rollover rule that adds a fifth if a month passes 110 GB.

Searches for a customer then filter by a customer field and a date range. A routing value on the customer id keeps one customer on few shards of the month, so a query does not touch every shard.

The risk is a large customer who sends a lot in one month. That customer would load a small number of shards through the routing. I want to measure this with a test before we decide the routing is good enough.

The note also covers the reindex job. It must write to the monthly indexes and must stay idempotent. The nightly run reindexes only the current and the previous month.

The migration order I wrote is: create the new indexes next to the old ones, copy the oldest months first, and then switch reads by an alias. The newest months go last, together with the switch of writes.

I estimated the copy time at 9 hours for all months at the current rate of the reindex API, with throttling to protect search latency.

Open questions are the cost of the extra storage during the migration, which is about 1.3 times for some days, and the cache keys of the search API. The query cache uses the index name in its keys, so they must change with the alias.

Tobias will check the disk headroom on the data nodes. I will ask Mara whether the ingest side needs a change for the routing value.

The note is in docs/plans/search-shards-by-month.md. Nothing is started and no index is created.

summary: Added a dry-run endpoint to the schema registry that checks a new schema against the latest version without storing it, with a strict and a loose mode.
body:
This continues the compatibility checker from yesterday. Producers wanted to know before a deploy whether their new schema would be accepted, so I added POST /schemas/:type/check.

The endpoint reuses the same compat function and returns the violation list as the register call does. It returns 200 with an empty list when the schema is fine, and never writes.

The modes are strict and loose. Strict is the default and applies all six rules. Loose allows a type change between integer and number and an enum narrowing, as long as no data of that value exists.

The loose mode needed a query against ClickHouse to see if the removed enum value appears in the last 30 days. I limited it to a count with a short timeout, so a slow query cannot block the check.

If the query times out, the answer is strict. I decided that unsafe is worse than slow here.

I added 11 tests, including one for the timeout. The suite is at 38 tests and all pass in CI.

I wrote the endpoint into the OpenAPI file. Sam will add a short section to the docs with an example call.

Not done: a CLI wrapper for the check, which Mara asked for, and a hook in the deploy pipeline. Those come next.

summary: Cache hit rate of the search API fell to 58 percent after a key change; found the hash included a volatile request id and fixed it, bringing the rate back to 84 percent.
body:
Grafana showed the search query cache hit rate at 58 percent, down from about 85 percent. The drop began after the release two days ago, so I looked at the diff of that release first.

The release had a small change to the request logging. It added a request id to a context object that the cache key builder also read, to hash the normalized query.

So every request had a unique key. The only hits were from the clients that retried within one request, which explained why the rate was not zero.

I wrote a test that builds the key twice for the same query with different request ids and asserts the keys are equal. It failed as expected.

The fix is to build the key from an explicit list of fields: customer, query text, filters, sort, page and the index alias. Nothing from the logging context is used anymore.

I deployed it to staging and replayed one hour of production queries. The hit rate was 83 percent after the cache warmed up.

In production, the rate climbed to 84 percent within 25 minutes of the deploy. The p95 of the search API went from 310 ms to 190 ms.

The Redis memory use had grown a bit during the bad period, because of many unique keys with the same TTL. They expire by themselves, and I did not delete any by hand.

I checked the Redis memory after one TTL period. It is back to the earlier level, around 3.0 GB.

Two other cache users, the dashboard cache and the suggestions cache, build keys in their own code. I read both and they use explicit fields already.

I added a short rule to the contributing doc: keys are built from explicit fields only, never from a context object.

One more point for later. The plan for monthly shards will change the alias in the key. I put a note into the shard plan so that the key change is part of the switch.

Mara reviewed the fix and merged it. A follow-up is to add a hit rate alert at 70 percent, which I did not do yet.

summary: Added the Grafana alert for the search cache hit rate at 70 percent, sent to the on-call channel with a note on the first checks.
body:
As a follow-up to yesterday's cache key fix I added the alert. It fires when the hit rate stays below 70 percent for 20 minutes.

The rule is in the alert code repository with the other rules, not in the Grafana UI. The annotation lists the first checks: the last release diff, the key builder test and the Redis memory graph.

I tested it by lowering the threshold in staging until it fired. The message arrived in the on-call channel.

summary: Reindex job duration grew from 50 to 95 minutes; profiling showed the bulk requests were too small, and in staging a batch size of 2,000 documents brought the run to 62 minutes.
body:
Tobias noticed that the nightly reindex job takes longer each week. It ran 95 minutes last night, and a few weeks ago it was 50.

I first checked whether the data grew that much. It had grown by about 12 percent, which does not explain the difference.

The job sent bulk requests of 500 documents. The OpenSearch node stats showed a high rate of small bulk requests and the write queue was often full, with some 429 answers.

The job handled the 429 answers with a fixed one second wait. That adds up to a lot of idle time with thousands of requests.

I changed the batch size to 2,000 documents and capped the payload at 10 MB. The wait after a 429 now uses a backoff that starts at 200 ms and doubles up to 5 seconds.

I ran the job in staging with a copy of the data. The run took 62 minutes, and there were no 429 answers.

I also tried 5,000 documents. It was only 3 minutes faster and the node heap use rose, so I kept 2,000.

The schedule is a separate question. The job still starts at its current time, and I only looked at it and did not change it. I will think about whether it should move away from the heavy traffic of the evening, but that is for another change.

The change is in the main checkout, since search-v2 is about the parser and the boosts, not about this job. I opened a pull request.

For the shard plan, the monthly layout should reduce the data per run further, because only two months would need to be reindexed.

summary: Wrote the CLI wrapper for the schema check, so producers can run it in CI with one command and get a non-zero exit on a breaking change.
body:
Mara asked for a command line tool for the dry-run endpoint. I wrote it as a small Node script, nebula-schema check <type> <file>.

It reads the schema file, calls the check endpoint with the API token from an environment variable, and prints the violations as one line per field path.

The exit code is 0 for a clean check, 1 for violations and 2 for errors such as a network failure. CI can then tell a real break from a broken setup.

I added a --loose flag that maps to the loose mode. The default stays strict.

Tests use a local fake of the endpoint. There are 7 for the CLI, covering the three exit codes and the flag.

Still to do is the hook in the deploy pipeline, which Tobias and I will do together.

summary: Investigated a slow ingest consumer lag after a deploy; the workers were fine but one Redpanda partition got most of the traffic from a single large event type.
body:
The lag alert for the queue fired twice in the early morning. The total lag was never high, but one partition had a lag of 40,000 messages while the others were near zero.

I looked at the per-partition rates in Grafana. The queue is partitioned by event type, and one customer had started to send a very large number of page view events through a new integration.

That event type maps to one partition, and a single worker consumes it. The worker was at its limit of about 3,000 events per second.

I checked whether this was a bug in the worker or just load. A profile showed that the time goes into the JSON decoding and the write to the store, and nothing unusual.

The quick fix was to raise the number of consumers in the group for that partition. That does not help, since a partition has only one consumer per group.

So I looked at the work per message. The write to ClickHouse was done for each message in some paths, so the batch writes of the ingest-batching work matter here. That work is not merged yet.

I sent a note to the user with the numbers. The decision about the partition key is a larger topic. Splitting the queue by tenant was already ruled out before, so I will not suggest it again.

As a temporary measure the customer's integration was throttled to a lower rate by the rate limiter. The customer was told by Sam.

The lag cleared within 20 minutes after the throttle.

The next step is to finish the batch write path and measure again with this event type.

I also added a per-partition lag panel to the board, because only the total was shown before.

summary: Merged the batch write path for the ingest worker behind a flag; in staging it raised the throughput of the busiest partition from 3,000 to 9,500 events per second.
body:
The ingest-batching branch had a working batch writer, and today I finished the parts that were missing before a merge.

The writer collects events per type up to 1,000 events or 200 ms, whichever comes first, and writes them in one insert to ClickHouse. The earlier path wrote per message.

The missing parts were error handling and shutdown. If the insert fails, the whole batch is retried with a backoff, three times, and then goes to the dead letter topic. On shutdown the worker flushes the open batches before it commits the offsets.

I wrote a test for the shutdown case. It sends 500 events, stops the worker and checks that the 500 are in the store and the offsets are committed afterward.

A bug showed up in this test. The offset was committed for the batch before the flush finished in one path, so a crash at that moment would lose events. I moved the commit after the flush.

In staging I replayed the page view stream of the large customer. The busiest partition went from 3,000 to 9,500 events per second with one worker.

CPU use of the worker went down by about a third, since the decoding is the same and the number of network calls is much smaller.

The path is behind the flag INGEST_BATCH_WRITES and is off by default. I plan to turn it on for one worker first in production.

One open point is the duplicate risk: a retried batch may be partly written. The event ids are unique in the analytics table through the dedup of the engine, so this should be fine, but I want to test it with a forced failure.

summary: Tested duplicate handling of the batch writer with a forced insert failure; the retried batch left no duplicates after the merge of parts.
body:
Following the merge this morning I ran the duplicate test. A staging worker was set to fail the first insert after half of the rows were written, using a fault flag in the test build.

The batch was retried and written again in full. Right after, a count showed 500 extra rows.

After forcing a merge of the parts with OPTIMIZE ... FINAL on the test table, the count was exactly the sent number. So the dedup works, but only after merges, and queries in between can see duplicates.

Dashboards use the rollup views with a unique count on the event id, so they are not affected. I noted that raw count queries should use FINAL or a unique count.

summary: Turned on the batch writes in production for one ingest worker and watched for two hours; lag on the big partition dropped to zero and no events were lost.
body:
After yesterday's test I enabled INGEST_BATCH_WRITES on one of the four production workers, the one that consumes the page view partition.

Before the change I wrote down the counts from the ingest API and the store for a 30 minute window, so that I could compare afterward.

The lag on that partition fell from 12,000 messages to zero in 9 minutes. The worker CPU went from 85 percent to 41 percent.

I checked the insert sizes in ClickHouse. The average batch was 640 events, which means the 200 ms limit triggers more often than the 1,000 limit at this rate. That is fine for latency.

The query latency of the dashboards did not change. The number of parts in the table went down a little, since there are fewer and larger inserts.

After two hours I compared the counts again for a closed window. The API accepted 4,812,330 events and the store had the same number after the merge, with no gaps.

One warning appeared in the log: a flush on a quiet event type took the full 200 ms and wrote 3 events. This is expected, but it makes many tiny inserts for rare types. I may add a longer wait for types below a rate.

I left the flag on for that worker over the afternoon and the evening. Mara watches the dead letter topic, which is empty so far.

The next step is the other three workers tomorrow, if the numbers stay good.

I wrote the results in the branch notes, including the counts and the CPU graphs.

summary: Answered Sam's question about how long an API key keeps working after revoke: the rate limiter and the key cache can honor it for up to 60 seconds.
body:
Sam asked for the docs how fast a revoked API key stops working. I read the code to give an exact answer.

The ingest API checks keys against a Redis cache with a TTL of 60 seconds. A revoke deletes the key in Postgres at once, but the cache entry stays until its TTL ends.

So a revoked key can still be accepted for up to 60 seconds. The search API has the same cache with the same TTL.

I checked whether the revoke endpoint also deletes the cache entry. It does not. That is a small gap that I can close, and then the delay is a few hundred milliseconds in practice.

I opened a ticket for it and told Sam to write 'within one minute' in the docs until the fix is in.

summary: Rolled batch writes to all four ingest workers, then pulled the flush wait for rare event types up to one second after seeing thousands of tiny inserts.
body:
All night the one worker with batch writes ran without problems, so this evening I enabled the flag on the other three.

Before doing so I looked at the numbers of the first worker again. The dead letter topic was empty, and the counts matched.

After the rollout, total CPU of the ingest workers fell by about 30 percent. The write rate to ClickHouse in inserts per second fell from about 2,400 to 310.

Then I looked at the insert size distribution. About 60 percent of the inserts had fewer than 10 rows. They come from rare event types with a few events per second, and each waited for the 200 ms flush.

Small inserts are the thing batching should avoid, since each creates a part. The merge load of ClickHouse showed a small rise in background merges for those tables.

I added a per-type wait. Types with a rate under 20 events per second flush after 1 second, and others after 200 ms. The rate is measured over the last minute in the worker.

The change needed a small moving average class. I wrote it with tests for a rising and a falling rate.

With the new wait, inserts under 10 rows fell to 15 percent. The latency until an event is visible in the store grows to 1 second for the rare types, which is fine for analytics.

Search indexing is not affected by this, because that goes through another consumer.

One more check was the shutdown. I did a rolling restart of the workers and counted events in a closed window. There was no loss.

I also wrote the runbook entry: how to turn the flag off, what the dead letter topic means, and how to count events with FINAL.

The flag is still there but now defaults to on in the config. I will remove the flag in two weeks if nothing happens.

A remaining item is the load test with 3 times the normal rate, which I plan for next week.

summary: Added the pipeline hook for the schema check and ran into a broken CI cache; the hook now blocks merges that break a schema, and 3 repos use it.
body:
Together with Tobias I put the schema check into the deploy pipeline today. The idea is that a pull request which changes a schema file runs the CLI and fails on a breaking change.

The first step was a small CI template that other repos can include. It detects changed files under schemas/, runs nebula-schema check for each, and fails on exit code 1 or 2.

The first run failed with a strange error: the CLI could not be found, although it was installed in the previous step. The cause was a CI cache of node_modules that was keyed on the lock file of the wrong directory.

It restored an old copy without the CLI. Tobias fixed the cache key to use the lock file of the template, and the run passed.

Then I tested the failing case. A test pull request removed a required field. The check failed and printed the field path, as planned.

I also tested the allowlisted case with the two old histories. They pass as expected.

Three repos include the template now: the ingest SDK samples, the console and the importer. Each had one schema file only.

Some details came out in the work. The token used by CI has read-only rights for the check endpoint, so it cannot register schemas. I created it with that right only.

A CI run takes 9 seconds more when a schema changes, and nothing if not.

What is left: a registration step on merge to main, so that the registry gets the new version automatically. This needs a write token and a decision about who may register.

I asked the user, and the answer was to keep registering manual for now, with a command in the runbook. The risk of an automatic registration of a wrong version is higher than the gain.

I wrote the runbook section and a short guide for producers, and Sam will link it from the docs.

The branch is ready for a review by Mara, with 41 tests green.

summary: Fixed the revoke gap: revoking an API key now deletes its Redis cache entry, so a revoked key stops working at once instead of after up to 60 seconds.
body:
This is the follow-up from the question Sam asked two days ago. A revoked key stayed valid for the cache TTL of 60 seconds.

The revoke endpoint now deletes the key's entry in Redis after the Postgres update succeeds. The cache key follows the naming guide: auth:key:<hash>.

I thought about the order of the two steps. If the cache delete came first, a request in between could refill the cache from the old Postgres row. So Postgres is first, and the delete is second.

There is still a tiny window. A request that read the old row just before the update can write it back after the delete. I closed that by writing a short negative entry with a 5 second TTL when a key is revoked, and checking it before the cache.

The negative entry is a marker with name auth:revoked:<hash>. It stops a stale write from making the key valid again, and it expires by itself.

I wrote tests for four cases: revoke with a warm cache, revoke with a cold cache, a stale write after the revoke, and a key that was never revoked.

The stale write test uses a hook to pause a request between the read and the cache write. It was a bit awkward, but it shows the race well.

In staging I measured the time from the revoke call to the first rejected request. It was 40 ms on average and never above 120 ms.

The search API uses the same helper, so it gets the fix as well. I checked that its tests pass.

Redis load is not changed in any way I could see. One more delete and one set per revoke is nothing.

I deployed the change in the afternoon and revoked a test key in production. It was rejected on the next request.

I told Sam so that the docs can say that a revoked key stops working immediately, with at most a second of delay.

A separate note: the rate limiter counters for the revoked key stay in Redis until their TTL ends. They do no harm.

summary: Load test of the batch write path at three times the normal rate showed the ClickHouse inserts hold up; the first limit was the load generator, not the workers.
body:
I ran the load test I planned for the batch writes. The target was 3 times the normal peak, about 30,000 events per second over all event types, for 30 minutes.

The test used the staging environment with a copy of the production worker count of four. The load generator replays recorded production batches with the customer ids changed.

The first run reached only 18,000 events per second, and the workers were at 50 percent CPU. So the workers were not the limit. The generator itself was at 100 percent on one core, because of the JSON parsing of the recorded batches.

I changed the generator to parse once and reuse the payloads with new ids, and to run in 4 processes. The second run reached 30,000 events per second.

At this rate the workers ran at 78 percent CPU. Consumer lag stayed under 2,000 messages on all partitions, and it was zero within a minute after the run ended.

ClickHouse showed about 520 inserts per second and merges kept up. The part count of the busiest table peaked at 190 and went back down to 60. This is under the limit where inserts get slowed.

The p99 of the ingest API response stayed at 85 ms, because the API only puts the batch into the queue and does not wait for the store.

The dead letter topic got 0 messages. I checked the counts for a closed window after the merge, and they matched the sent number.

Then I tried a failure during the load. I stopped one worker for 2 minutes. The others did not take its partitions fast enough, since the rebalance took 40 seconds, and the lag of those partitions reached 60,000 messages.

After the worker came back, the lag was gone in 4 minutes. That is acceptable, but the rebalance time is something to note for the runbook.

I also looked at memory. The open batches per worker use about 120 MB at the peak, so memory is not a concern.

The results with graphs and settings are in the branch notes. I think the branch can be merged to main and the flag removed in two weeks, as planned.

What I did not test is a ClickHouse node failure under load. That needs Tobias and a plan, and I put it on the list for the next quarter.

summary: Added a compatibility mode setting per event type to the schema registry, so producers can choose backward, forward or none, with backward as the default.
body:
Until now the checker applied one rule to every event type, and two teams asked for a looser rule for their internal debug events. I added a compatibility column to the subjects table with a migration and a default of backward. The dry-run endpoint and the CLI wrapper now read the mode from the registry unless the caller passes the strict or loose flag.

The change touched three places: the migration, the checker in registry/compat.ts, and the API handler for PUT /subjects/:name/config. I wrote tests for each of the three modes against the six change types from last week. Forward mode took the longest, because adding a required field is fine there but removing one is not, which is the opposite of backward. Two of my first test expectations were wrong and I fixed them after rereading the rules.

I also added an audit log entry whenever someone changes the mode, since a loose mode on a busy event type is something we want to see later. The entry has the subject, the old mode, the new mode and the user. Mara reviewed the migration and asked for an index on the subject name, which was already there.

Open points: the CLI help text still talks about one rule only, and the docs page for the registry needs a section on the modes. I will ask Sam to review the wording once the text is written. Next step is the pipeline hook, which should pass the mode through so CI behaves like the API.

summary: Updated the schema registry CLI help and the docs draft so the three compatibility modes are explained with one example each.
body:
The CLI help still described a single rule, which would confuse anyone who set a subject to forward or none. I rewrote the help text and added a short table of what each mode allows. The docs draft got a new section with one example per mode, using the real order_created event.

I sent the draft to Sam for wording. Sam answered quickly with two changes: spell out what a required field is, and say plainly that none mode never blocks a merge. Both are in now.

The docs page is not published yet. It waits for the pipeline hook to pass the mode through.

summary: Redis memory on the session store dropped by about 9 percent after setting a TTL on admin console session keys that never expired.
body:
After the key naming cleanup of last week I looked at what was left in the session namespace. A scan of 20,000 keys showed that about a third had no TTL at all. They came from an older version of the console login that wrote the session without an expiry and never touched it again.

I wrote a small script that sets a 7 day TTL on keys without one, matching the current session lifetime. I ran it first on staging, then in production in batches of 500 keys with a short pause, watching the command latency in Grafana. Nothing moved.

Memory used went from 6.4 GB to 5.8 GB over the next hour. The fix for new sessions was already in place, so the leak should not come back.

I added a check to the weekly Redis report that counts keys without a TTL per prefix. Today it shows zero for sessions and a few hundred for an old feature flag prefix, which I will ask Lena about.

summary: Wrote the first part of the audit export for compliance: a streaming query that reads the audit log in pages and writes NDJSON, tested on 2 million rows.
body:
The audit export is for customers who must hand the audit log to their own auditors. The first part is the reader. A naive query with OFFSET got slower with each page, so I used keyset pagination on (created_at, id), which stays at about 40 ms per page of 5,000 rows.

The export writes NDJSON through a stream, so memory stays flat. I tested it on a copy of the audit table with 2 million rows. The run took 4 minutes and the process stayed under 150 MB.

One problem came up: rows inserted in the same millisecond with ids that are not in order could be skipped. I confirmed that ids come from a sequence, so ordering by the pair is stable, and I added a test with 500 rows at the same timestamp.

Also added the filter by account and by time range, because every export is for one customer. The account filter uses the existing index and the planner chose it on the first try.

Not done yet: the output goes to stdout only, there is no file upload to S3 and no signed link. There is also no check that the caller may export for that account. Both come next, the permission check first.

summary: Added the permission check and the S3 upload to the audit export, so an export is written to a per-account prefix and the user gets a signed link valid for 24 hours.
body:
Yesterday's reader only wrote to stdout. Today it became a job. The API creates a job record, a worker runs the reader and uploads the NDJSON to S3 in multipart parts, and the record holds the state and the object key.

The permission check requires the compliance role in the admin console and that the account matches the user's account. Support users cannot start an export for another account. I wrote tests for both cases and for a missing role.
