The signed link lasts 24 hours. Objects go under exports/<account_id>/ and a lifecycle rule deletes them after 7 days. I asked Tobias to add the rule to Terraform and he did it in the same hour.

The first test with a large account gave a 3.1 GB file in 11 minutes. The upload was not the bottleneck, the reader was. I left that alone for now.

Still open: failed jobs do not retry, and the console has no button yet. I will talk to Lena about the button next.

summary: Found the Redis connection count in the search API climbing after each deploy and traced it to config reloads that leave old pools open; I have a local reproduction and a plan for the fix.
body:
The search API showed more Redis connections after each deploy than it should have. It held about 30 connections after startup and about 70 after a few config reloads. The pool has a per-process maximum, but that did not stop the growth, so the extra connections must be coming from somewhere outside the pool limit.

I reproduced it locally by sending the reload signal ten times and watching CLIENT LIST. Each reload left 5 idle connections behind. Reading the reload code, I found the cause: it builds a new client from the new config and swaps it in, but nothing closes the old client, and a second reference to the old one in the health check keeps it alive.

The plan is to call quit on the old client once the new one is ready, and to keep a single reference to the active client, so the health check asks the holder instead of keeping its own copy. I wrote down the steps and started on the test. It will reload three times and check that the connection count stays the same. I have not changed the reload code yet.

I also want to put the pool size and a reload counter on the dashboard, so the next leak shows up quickly.

The ingest workers use another client library and do not reload config. I read through their startup code to be sure, and they are not affected. Next I will make the fix and try it in staging before it goes to production.

summary: Reviewed the loader retry design for large files and wrote down the rules: per-chunk retries with backoff, resumable offsets, and a hard stop after five attempts.
body:
The document loader fails on large files when a single request to the object store times out, and today the whole file starts again. Before writing code I wrote the design for the loader-retry branch and reviewed it with Mara.

The file is split into chunks of 8 MB. Each chunk is processed on its own and its result is recorded in a small state table with file id, chunk index and status. A failed chunk is retried with exponential backoff starting at 500 ms, doubling, with jitter, up to five attempts. After that the file is marked failed and the error of the last attempt is stored.

The resume rule is simple: when a file is picked up again, chunks marked done are skipped. This only works if chunk processing is idempotent. Mara pointed out that the NDJSON importer writes events with a deterministic id, so a repeated chunk just overwrites the same rows. The CSV path does not, and it generates ids on insert. That needs a change first.

We talked about what counts as retryable. Timeouts, connection resets and 5xx from the object store are retryable. A parse error is not, because retrying cannot fix it. A 403 is not either.

I also decided that the loader will report each retry as a metric with the reason as a label, so we can see whether one cause dominates.

The plan has four steps: the state table, the CSV id change, the retry loop, and metrics. I started with the state table and wrote the migration. It has a unique key on (file_id, chunk_index) so that two workers cannot record the same chunk twice.

Nothing is merged yet. The next session takes the CSV id change, since the retry loop depends on it.

summary: Made CSV imports idempotent by deriving row ids from file id and row number, so a repeated chunk overwrites instead of duplicating rows.
body:
The retry design needs chunks that can run twice with no harm. The NDJSON importer was already deterministic. The CSV importer generated a random id per row on insert, so a repeated chunk would double the rows.

I changed the CSV path to build the id from a hash of the file id and the row number. The insert is now an upsert on that id. I wrote a test that imports the same 10,000 row file twice and counts the rows, and it stays at 10,000.

One risk is old imports. Rows imported earlier have random ids, so a rerun of an old file would duplicate them. That only matters if someone reimports a file, and support does that rarely. I noted it for Sam in the docs.

The import of a 1 million row file got about 3 percent slower, because of the conflict check. I decided that is acceptable.

Next is the retry loop itself.

summary: Implemented the chunk retry loop in the document loader with backoff and jitter; a forced failure test shows a file with three failing chunks finishing on the second attempt.
body:
With the state table and idempotent CSV ids in place, I wrote the retry loop. Each chunk runs inside a function that classifies errors as retryable or permanent. Timeouts, resets and 5xx answers retry. Parse errors and 403 do not.

Backoff starts at 500 ms and doubles up to a limit of 30 seconds, with up to 20 percent random jitter. After five failed attempts the chunk and the file are marked failed, and the last error is stored in the state table.

For the test I wrapped the object store client in a fake that fails chosen chunks a set number of times. A file of 40 chunks with three chunks failing once finished with exactly three retries. A chunk that always fails stopped after five attempts and the file was marked failed with the right message.

A resume test also passed. I killed the worker halfway through a file and started it again, and it skipped the 18 chunks already done.

One detail needed care: the attempt counter must be stored before the wait, otherwise a crash during the wait resets the count. I fixed that.

The metrics are still missing. The change is on the branch and not merged, and I want the metrics in the same merge request.

summary: Added retry metrics to the document loader, with counters by reason and a gauge for chunks waiting in backoff, and a first panel in Grafana.
body:
The loader now exports loader_chunk_retries_total with a reason label: timeout, reset, server_error. A second counter tracks permanent failures, and a gauge shows how many chunks are waiting in backoff.

I kept the label set small on purpose. Using the file id as a label would blow up the series count, so it is only in the logs.

The Grafana panel shows retries per minute by reason and the failed files per hour. I did not add an alert yet. We have no baseline, and I want a week of data before picking a threshold.

summary: Cache hit rate of the search API sat at 84 percent, but a look at the keys showed that sorted filter lists were hashed in request order, so I normalized them.
body:
After the earlier fix for the volatile request id, the hit rate came back to 84 percent. I wanted to know whether it could go higher, so I sampled 5,000 cache keys and grouped them by query.

Many queries differed only in the order of the filter values, for example status=open,closed and status=closed,open. The console builds the filter list from a set of checkboxes, and the order depends on the click order. Each order produced a separate key.

I changed the key builder to sort the values of multi-value filters before hashing. I also lowercased the field names, which the parser already treats as equal. A unit test builds the key from six permutations and expects one result.

The key prefix stayed the same, so the old keys expire on their own TTL of ten minutes and there is no flush.

In production the hit rate went from 84 to 89 percent within an hour of the deploy. The p95 latency of the search API went from 310 to 270 ms.

I did not touch the TTL. A longer TTL would raise the hit rate more, but results would lag behind the index, and Lena said customers already notice when new events show up late.

Next I will look at the queries with a time range like last 24 hours, whose end time moves every second and defeats the cache. Rounding the end time to a minute is the likely fix, but I want the product side to agree first.

summary: Rounded the moving end time of relative time range searches to the minute, lifting the search cache hit rate from 89 to 93 percent after Lena agreed on the behavior.
body:
The remaining misses came from relative ranges such as last 24 hours. The console sends an end time with second precision, so every request makes a new key.

I asked Lena whether a result that is up to one minute behind is acceptable. She checked the console and said the dashboards already refresh once a minute, so users cannot tell. We agreed on rounding down to the minute for the cache key only. The query that goes to OpenSearch still uses the exact end time on a miss.

That last point matters. If the cached result were computed for the rounded time, it could miss events from the last seconds. So on a miss the query uses the rounded end time as well, and the response says which time it used. Mixing the two would give different answers for the same key.

I changed the key builder and the query builder together and added tests with times at 59.9 seconds and 00.0 seconds. Both give the same key and the same query.

Absolute ranges are untouched. Those are exact on purpose, because customers use them for exports and checks.

After the deploy, the hit rate reached 93 percent by the evening. The OpenSearch query rate dropped by about 15 percent. The load on the data nodes dropped a little, which helps the reindex job at night.

I added a line to the API docs draft about the one minute granularity for relative ranges. Sam will read it tomorrow.

One leftover: the alert for the hit rate is set at 70 percent. With the rate now at 93, the alert would only fire for a big drop. I think that is fine, but I will review it after a week.

summary: A slow Postgres query in the audit log listing came from sorting without a matching index; adding (account_id, created_at desc) cut it from 4 seconds to 20 ms.
body:
Support reported that the audit log page in the console took several seconds for large accounts. The slow query log showed a listing query with ORDER BY created_at DESC and a filter on account_id.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed an index scan on account_id followed by a sort of about 900,000 rows for the largest account. The existing index had only the account column.

I created a composite index on (account_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes were not blocked. The build took about 6 minutes on the 40 GB table.

Afterwards the same query used an index scan with no sort and ran in 20 ms. The older single column index is now redundant, but I left it for a week in case another query depends on it.

The audit export branch reads the same table with keyset pagination, and it benefits from the new index as well.

summary: Dropped the redundant single-column audit log index after checking pg_stat_user_indexes showed no scans on it for a week.
body:
I left the old account_id index for a week after adding the composite one. Today I checked the statistics. The scan counter had not moved since the new index was built, so no query was using it.

I also searched the code and the slow query log for queries that filter on account_id alone. The few that exist use the leading column of the composite index and the planner picks that.

I dropped the old index with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It freed 3.2 GB and made inserts a little cheaper.

The migration file for the drop is in the repo, so staging and production stay the same. I ran it on staging first and nothing changed in the query plans.

summary: Answered Sam about how long customers can search old events: raw analytics events stay for 13 months, and the search index follows its own rules.
body:
Sam asked what to tell a customer who wants to look up events from about 18 months ago. The answer has two parts, and I wrote it down for the support notes.

The analytics store keeps raw events for 13 months, and older data exists only as daily rollups. So dashboards can show counts for 18 months ago, but not single events.

The search index is separate. It keeps events according to the retention setting of the account, and for most accounts that is 12 months. A few large accounts have longer settings in their contract. I checked the settings table and found 3 such accounts.

So for this customer the answer depends on their account setting. I looked it up, and they have 12 months, so single events from 18 months ago are gone, and only daily counts remain.

Sam will add a short table to the support notes.

summary: Planned moving the Redis pool and search cache alerts into the alert rules repo as code, with a lint check that every rule has a runbook link.
body:
Two alerts were still only in the Grafana UI: the pool saturation alert for Redis and the search cache hit rate alert. If someone changed them by hand, nobody would know. I exported both and started writing them as rule files in the alert rules repo, as a draft that is not merged yet.

The pool alert is meant to fire when the connections in use stay above 80 percent of the maximum for five minutes. The pool maximum is still 10 and the batch import still opens one connection per worker, so I wrote the threshold as a fraction of the configured maximum instead of a fixed number. That way the rule does not need to change if the pool size is changed later. The cache alert is the 70 percent one from last week, copied as it is.

The repo has a lint step, and I added a check that every rule has a runbook annotation with a link. Both rules failed the check at first, because they had a text note and no link. I wrote two short runbook pages and linked them from the annotations, and the check passes locally now.

Next I want to have the rules reviewed, let the pipeline apply them, and compare them in Grafana with the old ones before deleting the UI copies. The old copies stay until then.

There are also 4 alerts in the UI from the old on-call setup. I listed them in an issue for later.

summary: Investigated why the reindex job slowed again at night and found it competes with the backup for disk I/O on the Postgres replica it reads from.
body:
The reindex job had gone down to 62 minutes after the batch size change, but in the last three nights it was back at 80 to 90 minutes. Nothing in the job had changed.

I compared the job log with the Grafana panels of the replica it reads from. The slow nights matched a spike in disk read latency on the replica, from about 2 ms to 15 ms. That spike lined up with the start of the nightly backup, which runs on the same replica.

I checked the schedule in the Terraform for the backup and in the cron for the job. The reindex starts at 00:30 and the backup window starts at 00:45, so they overlap for most of the run. When the job started earlier, the overlap was shorter, and that is probably why the fix looked good at first.

I considered three options: move the backup, move the job, or point the job at a different replica. Moving the backup is Tobias's area, and he prefers to keep it where it is because of other jobs. A second replica costs money. Moving the job after the window is free.

I wrote this down in the issue and proposed moving the job to the time after the backup ends, which takes about 45 minutes. I did not change the schedule yet, because I want Tobias to confirm the backup end time.

I also measured how much time the job spends reading. The reading part took 40 of the 85 minutes in a slow night, and 18 of 62 in a good one, so the disk is the cause and not the OpenSearch side.

Tobias answered in the evening that the backup usually ends before 01:30. That means starting the job at 01:00 would still overlap a little. I will test the later time for a few nights.

I left the schedule as it is for tonight and set a note in the issue with the plan and the numbers.

summary: Built the console button for audit exports with Lena: a compliance user can start an export, see its state, and download it when ready.
body:
Lena built the button and the status table in the admin console, and I worked with her on the API side. The API got two calls: one to list the export jobs of an account and one to get a fresh signed link for a finished job.

The list returns the state, the time range, the size and the time it was created. The state is one of queued, running, done and failed. The console polls every five seconds while any job is running and stops afterwards.

The second call matters because the signed link lasts 24 hours. Instead of storing the link, the API creates a new one on each request, as long as the object still exists. After 7 days the lifecycle rule deletes the file, and the API answers with a clear message that the export has expired.

We found a bug together. A user with the compliance role in one account could see the job list of another account by changing the id in the URL. The check was only on the create call. I added the same account check to both new calls and a test for each.

Lena also asked for a limit of one running export per account, because two large exports at once would slow down the audit table. I added that in the job creation, and it answers with a 409 and a message with the id of the running job.

The first real test in staging used a 600,000 row account. The export finished in 3 minutes and the download worked in the console.

Failed jobs still do not retry by themselves. For now the user can start a new one. I decided to wait and see how often they fail.

summary: Tried to speed up the audit export reader with parallel page fetches and rolled it back, because the order of rows broke and the gain was only 12 percent.
body:
The 3.1 GB export took 11 minutes and the reader was the bottleneck, so I tried to fetch several time slices at once and merge them.

The approach was to split the time range into four slices and read each in its own query, writing the parts to S3 as separate multipart parts in order. In a test on a copy of the table, the run went from 11 to 9.7 minutes, a gain of about 12 percent.

The cost was high. Auditors expect the file in time order, so the parts had to be joined in order, and that needed a buffer for slices that finished early. Memory grew from 150 MB to over 600 MB for the large account. A slice boundary in the middle of rows with the same timestamp also produced one duplicated row in a test, which I only found because I compared the row count.

The database side also suffered. Four parallel scans raised the load on the primary enough to show in the query latency of the console.

I decided the gain was not worth the risk and memory. The code is reverted and I kept the notes in the issue. The sequential reader stays, since 11 minutes for the biggest account is fine for a compliance export that runs rarely.

A cheaper improvement may be compressing the output. NDJSON of audit rows compresses well. I will try gzip on the stream next, which also cuts the upload time.

summary: Gzip on the audit export stream cut the largest file from 3.1 GB to 410 MB and the job time from 11 to 8 minutes.
body:
After yesterday's failed parallel attempt, I tried compressing the stream. The reader pipes the NDJSON through gzip before it goes to the multipart upload.

The largest account now exports as 410 MB instead of 3.1 GB. The job took 8 minutes instead of 11, since less data goes over the network. CPU on the worker went up a little but stayed under 40 percent.

The file name now ends in .ndjson.gz and the content type is set so browsers do not try to open it. I updated the console text and the docs draft, because auditors need to know to unzip it.

I added a test that downloads a small export, unzips it and checks the row count and the first and last row.

summary: Tested the reindex job at a later start time for the first night and saw the run drop back to 58 minutes with no disk read spike on the replica.
body:
Following the plan in the issue, I moved the reindex start for tonight's trial to a time after the backup normally ends. I did it with a one-off override in the cron config, not a permanent change.

The job ran for 58 minutes. The read part took 16 minutes, close to the good nights before. The disk read latency on the replica stayed at about 2 ms during the whole run, so there was no overlap with the backup.

One night is not enough to be sure, because the backup duration varies with the amount of changed data. I will keep the override for three more nights and look at the backup end time each morning.

I also checked that the later start does not hurt customers. Fresh data from the day appears in search through the live indexing path, and the nightly job only rebuilds the index. The job still finishes well before the morning traffic.

If the next nights look the same, I will make the new time permanent in the cron definition and close the issue.

summary: Rate limit counters in Redis were checked for key naming and TTL after a customer saw limits reset late; counter keys lacked an expiry on the window rollover path.
body:
A customer reported that after hitting their per-key limit, the limit seemed to stay active a few minutes longer than the window. I looked at the rate limiter in the rate-limits branch to find out why.

The limiter uses a counter key per API key and window. The key is created with INCR and then gets an expiry equal to the window. I read the code path for the rollover, when a request arrives exactly as the window changes. In that path the new counter was created with INCR, but the expiry call ran only when the counter value was 1 and the earlier call had returned. Under concurrency, two requests could both see a value above 1, and neither set the expiry.

I reproduced it with a small script of 200 concurrent requests at a window boundary. In 7 of 50 runs, a counter key was left with no TTL. Such a key keeps counting until something deletes it, and that is the late reset the customer saw.

The fix puts INCR and EXPIRE in one Lua script, so the two steps cannot be separated. The script sets the expiry only if the key has none, which is safe to run on every call. I checked that the cost is one round trip, the same as before.

I wrote a test that runs the concurrency script against a real Redis in CI. After the fix, 200 runs produced no key without a TTL.

Then I looked for damage that was already there. A scan of the counter prefix found 41 keys without a TTL. I set an expiry on them, matching the longest window, and the customer's key was one of them.

I also added a metric for counter keys found without TTL in the weekly report, like the one for sessions. It shows zero now.

The key naming follows the guide from last week: rl:{key_id}:{window}. I checked the others in the prefix and they all matched.

The change is in the rate-limits branch and has been reviewed by Mara. I will deploy it tomorrow morning when traffic is low, and write to the customer afterwards with a short explanation of what happened.

summary: Deployed the atomic counter script of the rate limiter and watched the first hours; no counters without TTL and the 429 rate matched the usual level.
body:
The Lua script change from yesterday went out this morning. I deployed to one search API process first and compared its 429 rate to the others for an hour. They were within noise of each other.

Then I rolled it to all processes. The Redis command latency did not change, and the script shows up in the slow log zero times.

After three hours I scanned the counter prefix again and found no key without a TTL. I wrote to the customer, explaining the cause and the fix, and told them that the late reset should not happen anymore.

I will check the prefix again tomorrow before I close the issue.

summary: Wrote the plan for per-key rate limit overrides: a settings table in Postgres, a cache in Redis with a short TTL, and a console view for support.
body:
Two large customers asked for higher limits than the plan defaults, and today support changes them by editing a config file and deploying. That is slow and Sam cannot do it alone. I wrote a plan for overrides stored in the database.

The storage is a table rate_limit_overrides with the key id, the limit, the window, who set it, a reason and an optional end time. The end time allows a temporary raise for a launch day. The audit log records every change, using the existing audit code.

The limiter should not query Postgres on each request. It reads overrides through a Redis cache with key rl:override:{key_id} and a TTL of 60 seconds. A missing override is cached as a marker, so keys without one do not cause a database read each time. A change in the console deletes the cache entry, in the same way as the fix for revoked keys, so changes apply at once.

I thought about what happens when Postgres is down. The limiter should fall back to the plan default and log it, and not reject traffic. I wrote that as a rule in the plan, and a test for it is in the list.

The console view is a table of keys with their effective limit and a form for support. Lena will build it. I wrote the API shape for her: list, set and remove calls, all with the compliance of the same account checks as the other admin calls.

Some questions remain. Should an override be allowed to go below the plan default? I think yes, for abuse cases, but it needs a clear label. Should there be a maximum? I suggested a hard cap of ten times the default unless a lead approves, and I will ask for the final word.

The order of work is: migration and table, the cached read in the limiter, the API calls, the console view, then the docs for support. I started with the migration, which is small, and it is merged to the branch.

I estimate about four days for everything, mostly the tests for the cache and fallback paths.

summary: Implemented the cached override lookup in the rate limiter, with a no-override marker and a fallback to plan defaults when Postgres fails.
body:
With the table in place, I wrote the lookup in the limiter. It first reads rl:override:{key_id} from Redis. If the value is a marker meaning none, it uses the plan default. If the key is missing, it reads Postgres, writes the result or the marker with a TTL of 60 seconds, and continues.

To avoid a burst of reads when a popular key's cache entry expires, I added a short in-process lock per key, so only one request reads the database and the others wait for it. Without this, a test with 100 concurrent requests made 100 database reads. With it, it made one.

The fallback was tested by making the database client throw. The limiter used the plan default, logged a warning with a counter and did not reject the request. I added a metric for fallbacks so we notice a long outage.

Expired overrides are ignored by the query, which compares the end time with now, so a temporary raise ends on its own. A test covers a raise that ended one second ago.

The next step is the API calls, and the cache delete on change that makes updates apply at once.

summary: Added the console view for per-key rate limit overrides, so support can see, set and remove an override and see when the cache will pick it up.
body:
Lena and I built the support view for the override table that the lookup code reads. The list shows API key prefix, account, the limit per minute, who set it and when. Support can add an override with a reason and an optional end time, and remove it again.

The save endpoint writes to Postgres first and then deletes the Redis cache entry for that key. Before this, a change would have shown up only after the short TTL of the override cache. Now it is usually live within a second, and the view still says that it can take up to the TTL if the delete fails.

I added validation: the override must be a positive integer and not above 20 times the plan default. Without that cap one typo could remove the protection for a whole account. Every change goes into the audit log with the old and new value.

Tests cover the three paths: no override with the marker cached, override present, and a delete of a key that was never cached. One test failed at first because the no-override marker stayed in the cache after a new override was added. The save path now deletes the marker as well, since it uses the same key.

What is left is the permission for the view. It is open to every admin now, and Sam asked that only the support role can change values. That is the next step.

summary: Limited the override view to the support role and added a read-only mode for other admins, after Sam asked who should be able to change limits.
body:
Followed up on the open point from the override view. Changing a limit affects what a customer can send, so it should not be open to every admin of the console.

The save and delete endpoints now check for the support role and return 403 otherwise. Other admins still see the list, but the buttons are hidden and a short note explains why. Lena did the frontend part, and I wrote the check in the Fastify route as a pre-handler that other routes can reuse.

I wrote tests for an admin without the role and for a support user. Both pass. The audit log entry now also holds the role of the user who made the change.

Sam tried it on staging with a test account and set an override for a test key. The 429 behavior changed within a second, as expected. Sam also asked for an end time to show as a countdown, which went on the list for later. Nothing else is open on this topic except docs for support.

summary: Checked the Postgres autovacuum settings on the audit log table after dead tuples piled up, and made the table vacuum more often than the default.
body:
The audit log table grew a lot of dead tuples since the export work started, because of updates to the export state rows. pg_stat_user_tables showed about 18 percent dead tuples, and autovacuum ran only every few hours.

The default scale factor of 0.2 is too high for a table of this size. I set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 for this table only, with a threshold of 5000. A global change was not needed, since the other tables look fine.

I ran a manual vacuum first and watched it. It took 6 minutes and the table size did not shrink, but the dead tuples went to zero. After the setting, I watched two autovacuum runs. Each took under a minute.

I also noted that the export state rows should live in their own small table. It would avoid updates on the big table. That is a separate change and I did not start it.

summary: Split the audit export state out of the audit log table into its own export_jobs table, which removes the updates that bloated the big table.
body:
Following the vacuum finding from earlier, I moved the export state into its own table. The audit log is append-only by design, and it should stay that way. State changes like queued, running, done and failed now go to export_jobs.

The table has id, account_id, requested_by, state, rows_written, file_key, error and timestamps. There is an index on (account_id, created_at desc) for the console list. The migration creates the table and copies the existing rows from the old state columns.

I changed the export worker to write progress to the new table. It updates rows_written every 10000 rows instead of every page. That cut the number of updates by a factor of ten.

The console list endpoint reads from export_jobs now. Lena checked the button and the state display, and nothing changed visibly. One old export was stuck in running state from a test, and the migration marked it as failed with a note.

I ran the migration on a copy of the production database first. It took 14 seconds. The down migration restores the columns, but I did not drop them yet. That will wait one release, so we can roll back.

Tests: 31 pass, and I added two for the copy of old rows. Next I will drop the old columns after a week.

summary: Added a cleanup job for finished audit exports: files and signed link records older than 30 days are removed from S3 and marked as expired.
body:
Exports were piling up in the per-account prefixes on S3. A signed link lasts 24 hours, but the files stayed forever. The compliance customers do not need them after a month, and they can start a new export at any time.

The cleanup job runs once per day. It reads export_jobs for done rows older than 30 days, deletes the object and sets the state to expired. If the delete fails, the row stays and the job tries again the next day. The job logs the count of deleted files and bytes.

I first thought about an S3 lifecycle rule, but the rule would leave the table out of sync. With the job, the console can say that an export has expired instead of showing a dead link.

I ran it on staging with 40 old test exports. All were removed and the console showed them as expired. The job needs s3:DeleteObject on the export prefix. I added that to the Terraform role and Tobias reviewed it.

Open: an alert if the job fails three days in a row.

summary: Wrote the plan for the new shard layout of the search index by month instead of by customer, with the reasons, sizes and a migration order.
body:
Spent the morning on a written plan for the search index. The index is sharded by customer now. The three largest customers have shards of 60 to 90 GB, while most have under 2 GB. Queries for the large ones are slow, and the small shards waste overhead.

The new layout has one index per month with 12 shards, and the customer id is a routing value and a filter. Old months become read-only and can be merged and compressed. Retention then means deleting whole indices instead of delete-by-query, which is expensive today.

I measured the current numbers from the cluster stats: about 640 shards in total, with an average of 3.5 GB. The new layout would have about 12 shards per month. Cross-month searches hit more indices, so a search over 13 months touches 13 indices. I expect this to be fine with the date filter, since most searches are for the last days.

Risks I wrote down:
- Routing by customer can make hot shards for the big customers.
- Queries without a date range now touch every index.
- The reindex job must write to the right monthly index.

Migration order: build the new indices in parallel, copy by month starting with the oldest, then switch reads behind a flag, then writes. Rollback is to switch the flag back as long as the old indices exist.

The plan is in the docs folder of the repo. I asked Mara and Tobias to review, especially the disk need during the copy, which needs about 1.6 times the current space.

No code was changed today. Next is a test of one month on a staging cluster.

summary: Tested the new monthly index layout on staging with one month of data and found that queries without a date filter were 3 times slower, so a default range is needed.
body:
Built a monthly index on the staging cluster, with 12 shards and routing by customer id, and copied one month of real data into it. The test set was 1,200 recorded queries from last week.

For queries with a date range inside the month, the median went from 140 ms to 95 ms. The p95 improved from 610 ms to 380 ms. That matches what we hoped for.

Queries without any date filter are a problem. With only one month loaded I simulated 13 indices by creating 12 empty ones, and the median went up to 420 ms. Much of that is the overhead of many small requests per shard, and the empty ones add some of it too.

Two options came out of this. One is to apply a default range of 30 days when the query has no date and tell the client in the response. The other is to refuse such queries. I prefer the default, but it changes behavior, so I wrote the question for Lena and Sam, since the console and docs show it.

I also looked at routing. The biggest customer has 40 percent of the events of the month, so its routed shards take most of the data. With 12 shards and routing, it lands on a few shards. I tried a routing partition size of 3, which spreads one customer over 3 shards, and the skew between shards dropped from 5x to 2x.

I will use the partition size 3 in the plan. The test cluster was cleaned up afterward. Next: the reindex job needs to know the monthly target.

summary: Made the reindex job write to monthly indices behind a flag, tested on staging; the old customer layout stays the default until the switch.
body:
The reindex job knew only the per-customer index name. I changed the target selection into one function that takes the event time and the layout flag. With the flag off, it behaves as before. With the flag on, it computes the index name like events-YYYY-MM from the event timestamp.

Events with a bad or missing timestamp used to land in the customer index without trouble. For monthly indices I send them to a catch-all index called events-undated and count them in a metric. In staging data this was 0.02 percent of the events.

The job creates a missing monthly index from a template with 12 shards, a routing partition size of 3 and the same mappings as today. I checked that the template and the mapping stay equal by a test that compares the two JSON files.

I ran the job on staging with the flag on for a full night of data. The run took 61 minutes, about the same as before. Bulk requests are now grouped by target index, and I saw that bulk size matters: with many targets each bulk got smaller. I raised the batch to collect 5000 per index before flushing, which brought back the throughput.

One bug: the first version created the index twice when two workers hit a new month at once. The second create returned a resource_already_exists error and failed the batch. I now treat that error as success.

Open: reads still use the customer layout, and the query side needs the same switch.

summary: Looked at Redis memory by key prefix after Tobias saw growth; the query cache holds about 60 percent, and one prefix has TTLs far longer than needed.
body:
Tobias saw the Redis memory graph rising slowly over three weeks. I sampled keys with SCAN and grouped them by prefix, using MEMORY USAGE on a sample of 20000 keys.

The query cache is about 60 percent of memory, rate limiter counters about 8 percent, sessions about 15 percent, and the rest is small things. One prefix, report:preview, had a TTL of 7 days, set long ago for a feature that now changes rarely, but the values are large, around 40 KB each.

I cut that TTL to 6 hours after checking with Lena that the console reloads the preview when it is missing. The reload costs one query to ClickHouse that takes under 300 ms.

I will watch the memory over the next days. If the trend stays flat, we do not need to resize the instance. I also added the per-prefix numbers to a short note in the runbook so the check is easy to repeat.

summary: Memory of Redis fell by 11 percent after the shorter report preview TTL and has stayed flat for a day, so no resize is needed for now.
body:
Looked at the Redis graphs again. Memory went from 5.4 GB to 4.8 GB in the day after the TTL change on the report preview keys and has been flat since.

The cache hit rate for those keys fell a little, from 71 to 66 percent, which is expected with a shorter TTL. The extra ClickHouse queries are not visible in the latency of the console.

I checked the other prefixes for the same pattern. Search cache keys have a TTL of 10 minutes, and rate limit counters follow the window. Session keys have a TTL now, since the change of last week.

I wrote down the numbers in the ticket Tobias opened and closed it. The instance stays at its size. I will check again in two weeks.

summary: Added a metric and an alert for chunks that hit the five-attempt limit in the document loader, so failed files no longer go unseen.
body:
The loader stops after five attempts on a chunk, as agreed in the design. Until now, that ended as a log line and a failed state of the file, and nobody looked unless a customer wrote to us.

I added a counter loader_chunks_abandoned_total with the reason as a label, and a panel that sits next to the retry panels. An alert fires if more than 3 chunks are abandoned within an hour. It goes to the normal channel, not the pager, because a customer can start the file again.

I also changed the failed file state to keep the offset of the last good chunk. A later restart then resumes from there instead of from zero. I tested it with a forced failure in chunk 7 of 20: the restart began at chunk 7 and finished the file.

The alert rule is in the rules repo with a runbook link, and the test that checks for links passes. Open: a way for support to restart a failed file from the console.

summary: Built a restart action for failed loader files in the admin API, which resumes from the stored offset, and tested it with a 2 GB file.
body:
Support had no way to restart a failed file. They asked engineers, which cost time on both sides. I added an endpoint POST /files/:id/restart that works only for files in the failed state.

The endpoint checks the account permission, sets the file to queued, resets the attempt counter of the failed chunk and puts the file back on the queue. The loader then reads the stored offset and continues. Rows are idempotent by file id and row number, so a chunk that was partly written is not duplicated.

Test with a 2 GB NDJSON file: I made chunk 40 of 100 fail with a forced error. The file failed after five attempts. After the restart, the loader started at chunk 40 and finished. The row count in ClickHouse matched the file, and a check for duplicates found none.

One case I did not like: a restart while the old worker still held a lease on the file. I added a lease check, and the endpoint returns 409 in that case with a message to wait a minute.

I also limited restarts to 3 per file per day. More than that points to a real problem in the file, and support should write to the customer.

Tests: 9 new, all pass. Lena will add the button to the console next week.

summary: Handled files that fail on the same row every time: the loader now records the bad row number and gives up on that chunk early instead of using all five attempts.
body:
Looking at the abandoned chunk metric, most failures were not transient. A malformed row, for example a broken JSON line, fails five times in a row with the same error, and the backoff wasted several minutes.

I split the errors into two classes. Transient: timeouts, 5xx from the store, connection resets. Permanent: parse errors and schema violations. Permanent errors skip the retry loop and fail the chunk at once, with the row number and the error text in the file record.

The backoff for transient errors is unchanged. I did not touch the jitter or the limit of five attempts.

To check the classification, I took 14 failed files from the last month in the logs. Eleven had parse errors on the first attempt and would have failed fast. Three had timeouts that did pass on a later attempt, which the old logic handled and the new one does too.

One edge case: a ClickHouse error for a too-long string field is a permanent error, but the message looked like a generic server error. I matched it by error code, not by text.

The file record now shows first_bad_row. Sam said this is what customers ask for, because they can fix the line and upload again. I added a line about it to the docs draft.

Tests: added a table of 12 error samples with their expected class. All pass.

summary: Answered Mara's question on why ingest workers keep a flush wait: it is one second for rare types and 50 ms for common ones, and the reason is insert size.
body:
Mara asked why the flush wait differs by event type in the batch writer, and whether it could be one value. I looked at the code and the numbers from the past weeks to give an answer.

Common event types fill a batch of 5000 rows in well under 50 ms, so the wait rarely matters for them. Rare types get a few events per second. With a short wait they produce tiny inserts, and ClickHouse makes a part for each insert, which led to the thousands of small inserts we saw before.

A single value would be either too slow for common types, where events would wait for nothing, or too fast for rare ones. The cost of a longer wait for rare types is a delay of up to one second before the event can be seen in dashboards, which the dashboards do not show anyway because they refresh every 30 seconds.

Mara agreed to keep it and asked to put the explanation into a comment next to the setting. I added it.

summary: Added a graceful shutdown to the batch writer so workers flush pending rows on deploy, after finding that a rolling deploy lost up to one second of rare events.
body:
While checking row counts after yesterday's batch write rollout, I compared the number of events accepted by the ingest API with the rows in ClickHouse for rare types. They differed by a few dozen during each deploy window.

The cause was the shutdown. On SIGTERM the worker stopped consuming and exited, and the in-memory batch of the last flush window was lost. The queue offset for those messages had not been committed yet, so in theory they should be read again. But the commit happened on a timer, and in one path the offset was committed before the flush finished.

I fixed two things. First, the commit of offsets now happens only after the insert has returned, in one place. Second, on SIGTERM the worker stops reading, flushes all open batches, commits and then exits. The ECS stop timeout is 30 seconds, and a flush takes under 2 seconds, so there is room.

To test this, I wrote an integration test that sends 10000 events of mixed types, sends SIGTERM in the middle and then checks that the count in ClickHouse equals the count sent. Before the fix it was off by 40 to 200 rows. After the fix, five runs in a row were exact.

Because the old path could commit early, there may be a few events missing from the last deploys. I searched for gaps with the sequence number that clients send in the batch header, and found 3 gaps in the last week for one customer, 17 events in total. The events are not recoverable from the queue anymore, since retention there is short. I wrote this down for Sam so support can tell the customer if they ask.

The fix goes out with the next deploy, and I will compare counts again after it.

summary: Deployed the graceful shutdown of the batch writer and compared event counts across a full rolling deploy: accepted and stored counts matched exactly.
body:
The shutdown fix went out in the afternoon deploy. Before it, I wrote a small script that reads the accepted count from the ingest API metrics and the stored count from ClickHouse for a time window.

The deploy replaced all four workers one by one, over about 6 minutes. Afterward the script showed 1,284,310 accepted and 1,284,310 stored in the window, with every event type matching.

I also watched the flush on shutdown in the logs. Each worker logged its final flush at between 0.4 and 1.1 seconds. No worker hit the stop timeout.

I will run the script after the next two deploys as well, and then drop it into the runbook as a check.

summary: Wrote the per-key rate limit docs for support, with how overrides work, how fast changes apply and when to use one, and added a section to the public docs.
body:
Sam asked for docs that answer the questions support gets about rate limits. I wrote two parts: an internal page for support and a short section in the public API docs.

The internal page explains the order: plan default first, then an override for the key if one exists. Changes made in the console apply within about a second, since the cache entry is deleted on save. If the delete fails, it applies after the short cache TTL, which is a minute. It also says how to read the console view and what the reason field is for.

It gives guidance on when to set an override. A temporary raise for a known import is fine with an end time. A permanent raise should go through the lead, because it usually means the customer should be on another plan.

The public section describes the 429 response, the Retry-After header and the headers that show the limit and the remaining count. I added an example of a client that waits for Retry-After and then continues, with jitter, since a plain sleep makes all clients return together.

Sam read both and asked for a table of the plan defaults. I added it to the internal page only. Lena will look at the public text for tone.

The docs build passes with no broken links.

summary: Moved the search read path to the monthly index layout behind a flag and compared results with the old layout on 5,000 recorded queries; 4,962 were identical.
body:
The reindex job already writes to monthly indices on staging, so I did the read side. The search API builds a list of index names from the date range of the query and uses the routing value for the customer. With the flag off, it uses the old per-customer index.

For queries with no date range, I used a default of 30 days, as proposed after the earlier test. The response has a field that tells the client the range that was applied, so nobody is surprised. Lena has seen the field and will show it in the console later.

To check correctness, I ran 5,000 recorded queries against both layouts on staging with the same data and compared the result ids and the order of the first 20 hits. 4,962 were identical.

Of the 38 differences, 31 were queries with no date range where the old layout searched everything and the new one only 30 days. That is the expected change. Five were ties in score where the order differed, which is not a problem. Two were real bugs: events with a missing timestamp, which live in events-undated, were not searched. I added that index to every query when the flag is on. After that fix, the two matched.

Latency on the same set: the median went from 150 to 102 ms, and the p95 from 690 to 410 ms.

The cache key of the search cache now includes the layout flag, so results do not mix when I switch it in tests. I also checked that the key normalization from earlier still works.

Nothing runs in production yet. Open: the copy of old months, which needs the disk space that Tobias is checking.

summary: Removed the old per-customer index fallback from the search-v2 query path in staging and found two filters that still assumed one index per customer, so both were fixed.
body:
The monthly layout work needed a check that the search API no longer depends on the customer index naming. I grepped the search API for the old index name builder and found it used in five places. Three were only in log messages and tests, and I changed those to use the new alias helper.

Two places were real problems. The saved search filter added a customer prefix to the index pattern, which would have returned nothing on monthly indices. The export of search results built its scroll request against a single customer index and would have failed for any range that crosses a month.

I changed both to use the customer filter inside the query instead of in the index name. Each customer now gets a term filter on account_id, and the index pattern comes from the date range. For the export I made the scroll run over the list of monthly indices for the range, one after the other, so a three month export reads three indices in order.

I ran the unit tests, which passed after I fixed two fixtures that had the old names. On staging with one month of data, a saved search and an export of 400,000 events both returned the same rows as the old layout. A range of two months with only one month loaded also worked, because missing indices are ignored.

One thing is left. Queries without a date filter still need the default range from the staging test of last week, and I did not touch that here. Next is a comparison of results on recorded queries, with the read path behind a flag.

summary: Added an alert for the audit export cleanup job failing three days in a row, with a runbook that tells on-call how to check the S3 permissions.
body:
The cleanup job for old exports had no alert. If the role lost its delete permission, files would pile up again without anyone seeing it.

The job now exports a gauge with the unix time of its last success. The alert fires if that is older than 3 days. I put the rule in the rules repo, and the test for runbook links passes.

The runbook says: check the job log for AccessDenied, check the role in Terraform for s3:DeleteObject on the export prefix, and run the job by hand once. It also says it is safe to run the job twice, since it only touches rows that are done and older than 30 days.

I tested the alert on staging by removing the permission from the role for an hour. The alert showed as pending, and the log had the error. I put the permission back and the next run succeeded.

summary: Investigated why the ingest API showed about 300 open Redis connections at peak and traced it to one rate limit path that seemed to create its own client, with a fix planned.
body:
I started by looking at where the Redis connections come from. The ingest API showed around 300 open connections at peak, far more than its pool size suggested, so something had to be opening clients outside the pool.

A code search turned up a helper in the rate limit check for the batch endpoint that appeared to create a new client whenever it was called with an options object. The normal path used the shared pool, but this one seemed to have its own client and never closed it, apart from the timeout on idle connections. I have not changed anything yet.

To confirm the suspicion I wrote a test that counts connections after 1000 calls. Against the current code it showed 1000 connections, one for each call, which matches the theory. I kept the test in a scratch file for now, since it is only useful once the helper uses the shared client.

The plan is small. Replace the helper's own client with the shared one and pass the options as arguments to the call. I expect a change of about 15 lines. I will try it on staging first with a load of about 3x normal and compare the connection count and the p95 of the rate limit check, which I expect to improve because no new handshake would be needed per call.

I also thought about a lint rule that flags a direct call to the client constructor outside the factory module, and about an alert on connections per service, using the connection metric we already have. Both go on the list after the main fix is understood.

I checked the search API and the console backend for the same pattern by reading the code, and did not find it there. I will check again with a metric before I close the topic.

summary: Investigated a slow reports query in Postgres, found a missing index on the settings join, and cut the query from 2.3 seconds to 90 ms after adding it.
body:
Lena reported that the reports page in the console felt slow for the largest accounts. I took the query from pg_stat_statements, which had a mean time of 2.3 seconds and ran about 4,000 times a day.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on report_settings joined on account_id and report_type. The table has 1.1 million rows, because every saved view creates a row. The planner was filtering nearly all of them away.

I considered rewriting the query, but the join is right. The table only lacked an index. I created an index on (account_id, report_type) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes were not blocked. It took 9 seconds.

After the index, the plan used an index scan and the query time fell to 90 ms in the same EXPLAIN on production. I checked the mean time again after a few hours and it was 85 ms.

I also looked at why the table is so large. Old saved views that nobody has opened for a year make up most of it. I did not delete anything, because the retention of saved views is a product question. I wrote a short note for the lead with the counts: 71 percent of rows have not been read in 12 months.

While there, I checked the other top queries by total time. The audit log listing is fine since the index change. A session lookup query is the third and runs fast, only called very often.

I added a note to the migration folder with the reason for the index and the before and after numbers. The report query itself is unchanged, so the rollback is to drop the index.

Next time the Postgres minor version comes up, I want to rerun this check, since planner changes already hit this query earlier.

summary: Reviewed the disk need for the monthly index copy with Tobias and decided to copy in three batches of four months, since the cluster has room for only 1.4 times the data.
body:
Tobias checked the free space of the search cluster for the plan. The copy needs the old and the new data at the same time. My estimate was 1.6 times the current size, and the cluster has room for about 1.4 times, so a full parallel copy does not fit.

We talked through the options. Adding nodes just for the migration costs money and takes a day or two to set up and shrink again. Copying in batches and deleting the old customer data of each month after a check would keep us under the limit, but deleting old data conflicts with the rollback plan, since the flag switch back would find holes.

We settled on a middle path. We copy the oldest months first, in three batches of four months. Old months are read-only, and they compress well after a force merge, so the new indices of old months are about 40 percent smaller than the old data of the same months. That frees up room for the next batch without deleting anything.

I estimated the numbers with the staging month: after a force merge to one segment per shard, the size went from 61 GB to 37 GB. For the oldest 12 months the saving is enough to fit the later ones under 1.4 times.

The rollback story stays the same for the recent months, which are not touched until the end. For old months, the old data stays until the flag has been on for a week.

I updated the plan document with the batch order and the size estimates. I also added a check before every batch that stops if the free disk is under 25 percent.

Tobias will add a disk alert for the search cluster at 75 percent used, which we do not have yet. Mara will review the copy script, which I started writing today as a skeleton with the batch loop, the force merge and the document count comparison between old and new.

The next step is a dry run of the first batch on staging.

summary: Planned the copy of the search index to the monthly layout with Tobias and prepared a dry run of the first batch of four months on a test index, without touching the live index.
body:
Sat down with Tobias this morning to plan the disk use of the monthly index copy. The cluster has room for only 1.4 times the data, so a single copy is not possible. We agreed to work in three batches of four months each, with the oldest four months first because that batch is the smallest.

After that I prepared the reindex job for a dry run. I added the monthly flag to the job configuration and kept it off in the shared settings, so the nightly run still uses the customer layout. I wrote a small script that takes a customer and a month and counts documents in both layouts, so the numbers can be compared later per customer and month.

I ran the script against the old layout alone to see the baseline counts and to check that it handles customers with no events in a month. It had a bug with empty months that returned an error instead of zero, and I fixed it.

I also estimated the disk use. Smaller segments in the monthly indices will probably add a few percent, so I used a margin of 5 percent in the plan. The cluster is at about 58 percent now. Tobias will set an alert at 80 percent so we notice early.

Next is a dry run of the first batch on a small test index, to measure the time before anything is copied for real. The old customer indices stay untouched. The plan for the second and third batches waits until we have the first timing and the first comparison.

summary: Found that the Redis key prefix for session data had no documented naming rule, wrote one, and renamed two odd prefixes in the console without losing sessions.
body:
While looking at Redis memory last week I noticed that keys of the admin console used three different styles: session:, sess_ and console-session. Nobody could say which code wrote which. I searched the console and the search API for every call that sets a key.

The result was that two prefixes came from old code paths. One of them was a leftover of the first console version and was only read, never written. The other was written by the password reset flow.

I wrote a short naming rule in the docs folder: service name, then purpose, then id, separated by colons, for example console:session:<id>. Each prefix also lists its TTL.

The renaming of the reset flow keys was done with a read-both, write-new step. For one day the code reads the new key first and then the old one. This avoids logging out users who have a session open.

I tested the flow on staging with 20 open sessions and none were lost. The old prefix keys will expire by themselves within their TTL of 24 hours. After that I will remove the fallback read.

The leftover prefix with only reads was removed from the code. A scan on staging found 1,200 keys of it, all with a TTL. Production has not been touched yet; the change goes out tomorrow.

summary: Looked at why the cache hit rate of the search API dropped to 62 percent and found the cache key included a request id header that changed on every call.
body:
Mara pointed out that the hit rate in Grafana had been falling for two weeks. I took a sample of 200 cache keys from Redis and compared them for the same query.

The keys for identical queries differed in the last part. A new middleware had added the request id to the normalized query object, and that object is hashed for the key. So each call made a new key and the cache only hit on retries from the same client.

I removed the id from the hashed part and added a test that builds the key for two requests with different headers and expects the same result.

On staging, replaying 10,000 recorded queries gave a hit rate of 81 percent, against 63 percent before the change.

The fix is small, but it shows that nobody looks at the key shape when middleware changes. I added a line to the review checklist for the search API.

The change is merged and goes out with the next deploy. I will check the hit rate after one day of production traffic.

summary: Deployed the fixed cache key of the search API and the hit rate rose from 62 to 79 percent within two hours, with p95 latency down by about a fifth.
body:
The deploy went out at lunch time. I watched the dashboard for the cache hit rate, the p95 latency and the Redis memory.

The hit rate began to climb after the first ten minutes, since the cache needs to fill with the new keys. After two hours it was stable at 79 percent. This is a little lower than the 81 percent from the replay, which fits, because real traffic has more unique queries.

The p95 latency of the search API went from 410 ms to 330 ms. The p99 changed less, from 1.2 seconds to 1.1 seconds, because the slowest queries are the uncached ones with wide date ranges.

Redis memory grew by 6 percent during the fill and then stopped. The old keys with the request id expire by TTL, so they will leave within the hour. I saw no growth beyond that.

The load on OpenSearch fell. The query rate on the cluster went down by about 17 percent. Tobias noticed it first, because the CPU graph of the data nodes dropped.

One side effect I checked was the per-customer cache isolation. The key still has the customer id as the first part, so one customer cannot get the result of another. A test covers that case.

I wrote the numbers into the ticket and closed it. If the hit rate falls again, the first thing to check is the shape of the keys.

Next I want to look at the TTL of the cached queries, which is 5 minutes for all of them. Dashboards that refresh each minute could use a longer one.

summary: Planned the second batch copy of the monthly search indices with Tobias and tested the resume of the reindex job on staging, so the batch can run at night with slower settings.
body:
The second batch covers four middle months and is about twice as large as the first. Before starting anything on the real cluster, I wanted to know how the job behaves when it is stopped and started again, because I expected to have to pause it at some point.

I ran the reindex job with the monthly flag against a small set of months on staging. The job stores its position per month, so it should resume where it stopped. I started it, stopped it after one minute and started it again. It continued at the right month and did not copy documents twice. I checked this by comparing the document counts of the monthly indices with the customer-layout indices after the second start, and they matched.

Then I looked at the load. The first batch ran in a quiet period and the data nodes were fine, but the second batch is twice as large, and the search API p95 is currently around 330 ms. I do not want customers to see it rise during the day. On staging I tried a smaller bulk size of 2,000 documents instead of 5,000, with a pause of 200 ms between bulks. This gave about 70 percent of the old speed. It is slower, but it should keep the merge load on the nodes smaller.

I talked with Tobias about the timing. He pointed out that the nightly reindex job and the backup both read a lot of data, so we should keep the copy away from both of them and pick a quiet part of the night. We agreed to run the second batch at night with the slower settings and to look at the merge load and the p95 of the search API during the first hour. The exact start time relative to the nightly jobs is still open, and we will settle it before the run.

The count check for the first batch is still fine, all four months match. I wrote the settings and the resume steps into the notes for the migration, so that anyone on call can pause the job if the latency rises. The job is not started yet. I will decide on the schedule later today.

summary: Reviewed Mara's batch writer change for ingest and asked for a fix, because a failed insert dropped the whole batch instead of only the bad rows.
body:
Mara asked me for a review of the change to the batch writer in the ingest worker. The goal is to write larger inserts for common event types.

The code itself is clean, and the tests cover the flush by size and the flush by time. The problem is in the error path. When the database rejects an insert because of one bad row, the writer logs the error and drops the whole batch.

I wrote a test for it with a batch of 100 rows and one row with a value that is too long. All 100 rows were lost, and only one log line was written. In production this would be a silent loss of data from one broken event.

I suggested that the writer split the batch in halves on error and try again, until the bad row is alone. That row goes to the dead letter topic with the error message. Mara agreed and said she had thought about it, but wanted to ship the simple version first.

I said that the simple version should not be shipped, since dropping data is the one thing the ingest path must not do. She changed the code in the afternoon, and I checked the new test.

With the split, the test now stores 99 rows and one row is in the dead letter topic. The extra inserts are at most log2 of the batch size, which is 7 for 100 rows.

I also asked for a metric on the number of rows sent to the dead letter topic. Without it nobody would see a rise.

The change is approved with these two points. Mara will merge it after the metric is added.

summary: Added a dead letter row counter metric to the batch writer and a Grafana panel, so rises in rejected events are visible.
body:
After the review I added the metric myself, since it was a small change. The counter is called ingest_dead_letter_rows_total and has a label for the event type.

I added a panel to the ingest dashboard that shows the rate per type for the last 24 hours. A second panel shows the share of dead letter rows against all stored rows.

I also wrote an alert that fires if the share is over 0.5 percent for ten minutes. In the test on staging the share was 0, so it should be quiet.

Mara merged the batch writer change with the metric.

summary: Answered Sam's question on how long a changed rate limit override takes to apply: up to 30 seconds because of the cache TTL, and immediately for removed overrides in the console view.
body:
Sam asked in the support channel how long a customer must wait after support changes an override, because a customer called twice about it.

The lookup in the rate limiter caches the override in Redis with a TTL of 30 seconds. So a change applies within 30 seconds at the latest. The console view shows the time when the cache will pick it up, and Sam had not seen that line.

For a removed override the console deletes the cache key at the same time, so the plan default is used on the next request. I tested this on staging with a key that had a low limit, and the next request after removal got through.

I suggested that Sam tell customers to wait one minute, which has a margin. I also added the answer to the support docs page for overrides.

summary: Looked into the slow vacuum of the events table in Postgres and found one long running transaction from a report job that kept dead tuples from being removed.
body:
Tobias saw that the vacuum of one large table ran for six hours and removed little. I looked at pg_stat_activity and found a transaction that had been open for 5 hours from the reports job.

The job opened a transaction, ran a long export and kept the transaction open while it wrote files. This holds the snapshot, so vacuum cannot remove rows that died after the start.

I changed the job to read in pages with short transactions and to close the transaction before writing files. I also set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10 minutes for the role the job uses, so it cannot happen again unseen.

After the change on staging the vacuum finished in 40 minutes for a copy of the table. I will check production tomorrow after the next run of the job.

summary: Planned the next index batches with Tobias and Mara and prepared the checks of the earlier batches, with nothing of the third batch started yet.
body:
I went through the plan for the monthly search index layout with Tobias and Mara. The first two batches are still the ones we are checking, and nothing of the third batch has been started.

Tobias and I looked at the disk first. Use is at 78 percent now. The third batch of four months is the newest and largest, with about 45 percent of all data. It would fit, but only 8 percent would be left after the copy, which is too tight for us. So we want to delete the old copy of the first batch before we plan the third run, and we agreed to do that only after the checks are signed off.

I wrote down what the third batch needs. The reindex job should be able to resume after a stop, so I read through its resume logic again and listed the cases I want to test on staging. I also drafted the slower bulk settings for the night run, with smaller bulks and a longer pause between them, so daytime traffic stays unaffected. In the earlier test runs the p95 of the search API stayed at 330 ms in the morning peak, and I want to keep that as the limit.

For the sign-off, I prepared a short list for Mara, who owns the queries. It has the 2,000 recorded queries with a date filter, the result lists for the old and the new layout, and the 6 queries whose lists differed. Five of them look like ties in the score, where the order of documents with equal scores changes. The sixth is a query with a boost on a field that is missing in one old document, and I put it into the notes. I asked Mara to look at all 6 today.

I will not delete anything until she has answered. We also agreed to keep the snapshot of the old indices until the whole checks are done.

summary: Investigated the Redis connection spikes at the top of each hour, traced them to the cache warmer opening a new pool per run, and planned a fix for the next session.
body:
The Redis connection graph showed a spike of about 120 connections at the start of each hour, lasting two minutes. I wanted to understand every source of connections, so I started with the spike times.

I matched them with the cron list. The cache warmer for the dashboard queries runs at the top of each hour. It creates a Redis client in the function that runs the job and never closes it.

Each run made a client with its own pool of 10 connections for each of the 12 job workers. The connections stayed open until the idle timeout of 2 minutes. This explains both the height and the length of the spike.

I sketched the change but did not make it yet: move the client creation to the start of the process and pass it to the workers, so the pool is shared with one limit for the whole warmer. To check the idea, I ran the warmer on staging three times with a local patch and watched the connection count. It stayed flat at 14, and the warm-up time was the same as before, about 90 seconds. I threw the patch away, because I want Mara to look at the design first and the change should go in a clean commit.

I also wrote down the plan for a test that counts the open connections before and after a job run and expects no growth, using the real Redis from the test compose file. It is not written yet.

I searched the rest of the code for the same pattern. Found one more place in the report preview service, but it is created once per process, so it is fine.

I wrote a short note in the ticket for Tobias, who had asked about the spikes in the infrastructure channel. It explains the cause and the plan, and lists the pool limits of the services, which add up to less than the limit of the Redis instance. The deploy is for the next days, after the review.

summary: Tried a different JSON library for the search API response to save CPU and dropped it, since the gain was 3 percent and it changed the output of floating point scores.
body:
The flame graph of the search API showed that about 14 percent of the CPU goes into JSON serialization. I tried a faster library as a drop-in for the response path.

On a benchmark with 5,000 recorded responses the new library was 2.1 times faster for the serialization step. But in the full request the gain was only 3 percent, because most time is spent waiting for OpenSearch and Redis.

There was also a problem. The library wrote some scores with a different number of digits, for example 12.300000190734863 instead of 12.3. Our contract tests for the public API compare the strings of a few fixtures, and four of them failed.

I could have changed the fixtures or set an option, but a change in the output of a public API for 3 percent of CPU is not worth the risk. Customers may compare responses byte by byte in their tests.

I reverted the branch and wrote the result into the notes of the performance ticket, with the numbers. If CPU becomes a problem, caching helps more, and the cache hit rate has just improved.

summary: Reviewed the six differing queries from the first two index batches with Mara and started on the missing boost default for older months in the monthly layout.
body:
Mara looked at the six queries this morning. She agreed that five are ties in the score and said that the order of equal scores was never promised in the docs. She did not sign off the batches yet, because the sixth query still needs an explanation.

The sixth seems to be caused by one old document with a missing boost field. In the customer layout the field was filled by a default in the mapping, and the monthly layout has no such default for older months. I wrote the default into a draft of the template for the monthly indices and have not applied it. I also listed which older months would need a partial reindex, so we know the size of the job before we run anything.

After the fix I want to rerun the 2,000 queries and compare the lists again, ignoring ties. Today I only ran the sixth query against a scratch index with the default set by hand, and it returned the same list as in the old layout. That is a hint, not a result.

The old copy of the first batch stays where it is for now. Once Mara has signed off the batches after the rerun, I will talk to Tobias about deleting it, ahead of the third batch.

summary: Planned how to free disk space for the third index batch, which does not fit in one run, and prepared a snapshot of the old indices for the first four months.
body:
Tobias took a snapshot of the old customer-layout indices for the first four months and checked that it could be listed in the repository. I did not delete anything yet. First I wanted to know exactly how much space the old data takes, and whether the snapshot was enough of a safety net.

Disk use is at 78 percent. I added up the size of the old indices per month and found that the first four months are the smallest part of the old data, so removing them later will free less than we hoped, probably only a few percent. The search API showed no errors while the snapshot was running, and latency stayed flat.

The third batch needs about 45 percent of the data size, so it still does not fit in one run. We decided to split it into two halves of two months each, and to remove the old copy of the second batch between the two halves, once Mara has confirmed that the counts match and that she no longer needs the old copy for comparing queries.

I wrote the plan with the order of the steps in the migration notes, including the check of the snapshot before every removal, and asked Mara to review it tomorrow.

summary: Added a Postgres index on the audit log for the actor and time columns after the console's audit view needed 4 seconds to open for large customers.
body:
Lena reported that the audit view in the admin console was slow for the biggest customers. The query filters by customer, actor and a time range, and sorts by time.

EXPLAIN showed a scan of the customer index and a sort of about 800,000 rows. The audit log had an index on customer and time but not on actor.

I created an index on (customer_id, actor_id, created_at desc) with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so writes were not blocked. It took 14 minutes on production and added 1.9 GB.

The query went from 4.1 seconds to 60 ms for the biggest customer. For queries without an actor, the old index is still used.

I also checked that the index does not slow the insert path: the insert time of the audit log rows stayed at the same level in the metrics.

Lena confirmed that the view opens at once now. I put the index into a migration file, so staging and the next environment get the same one.

summary: Ran the first half of the third index batch overnight with the slow settings; the first month finished with matching counts and the newest month is left for the next night.
body:
The job started at 22:00 with two months of the newest data, since these are the largest. I used the same bulk size of 2,000 and a pause of 200 ms as in the earlier batches.

After 2 hours and 20 minutes the first of the two months was copied, and I let the job stop at the month border, as planned. I did not want to run a month that big while nobody watches.
