The count check for the finished month matched for all customers. Two customers had a few documents that arrived in the old index during the copy, because ingest keeps writing. I ran the catch-up step for them, and the counts matched after that.

The cluster load was fine, and the latency of the search API showed no change during the night. Disk use is at 75 percent.

The remaining part is the newest month. It is the most active, so the catch-up step will matter more there. I will plan the final switch of the writes only after that copy is done and the full set of checks has passed, and not before.

I also wrote down the time of each step in the notes. They will be useful when the same copy needs to run for the production switch.

summary: Ingest API returned 503 for all writes since 08:40; the first look shows the load balancer marking every ingest node as down, while the nodes themselves answer normally.
body:
The on-call alert came at 08:44 with the message that the ingest success rate fell to 0 percent. I opened the dashboard for the ingest API and saw that every write failed with 503 from 08:40 on. Reads of the search API were fine, so the problem was limited to ingest.

First I looked at the load balancer. The target group for the ingest API showed all 9 nodes as unhealthy. This explained the 503, since the balancer had nothing to send requests to.

Then I checked the nodes. I logged into one of them and called the health endpoint from the node itself. It answered with 200 and the expected body. The CPU, memory and the queue connection of the node were normal. The worker logs showed no errors.

The nodes were healthy and the balancer thought they were not. That pointed at something between them. I checked the security groups and found no change in the last days. The deploy log showed no deploy since yesterday afternoon.

I started the incident channel and wrote the first message with the facts so far. I asked Tobias to join, since he knows the balancer setup best. Mara was told that no deploys should go out, and I paused the pipeline so that nobody pushed by mistake.

I also wrote to Sam, so that support could tell customers that the ingest was down and that we are working on it. The status page text said that writes fail and that searching still works.

While Tobias looked at the balancer, I checked the client side. Customers retry failed batches, and the retry traffic was visible as a rise of requests at the balancer, about 3 times the normal rate. All of them got 503 quickly, so the load on our side was low.

The queue was empty and growing nowhere, which means that no events were lost inside our system. Events that clients could not send stay with the clients, and most of our SDKs keep them in a buffer for some hours.

I wrote down the state at 09:00 in the channel: all targets unhealthy, nodes fine, no recent change found, retries rising. The next step is to compare what the health check sends with what the node answers.

summary: Compared the health check path of the balancer with a direct call and found the check fails at the TLS handshake, while plain calls to the same endpoint succeed.
body:
Tobias and I continued from the point that the nodes are fine and the balancer marks them down. He opened the target group settings and read them out. The health check uses HTTPS on the internal port, with the path /healthz, and expects a 200.

The balancer gives a reason code for each failed target. All 9 showed the same one: a failure of the connection, with no HTTP status. That means the check never got to the point of an answer.

I called the health endpoint from a jump host in the same network, once with plain HTTP on the debug port and once over HTTPS on the internal port with curl -v. The plain call returned 200. The HTTPS call stopped during the handshake.

The curl output showed the line that the certificate verification failed, but I did not read the detail at first, because the verbose output was long. I ran it again with only the error part, and it said that the certificate had a problem with its validity. I wanted to be sure, so I did not conclude yet.

I looked at the other internal services that use the same kind of certificate. The metrics endpoint of the workers uses the same internal authority. That endpoint failed in the same way from the jump host.

This explained why Grafana had gaps for the ingest nodes since 08:40 too. I had not looked at that, because the focus was on the traffic.

Tobias checked the time on the nodes, since a wrong clock could also make a certificate invalid. The clocks were in sync with the time service, with an offset of a few milliseconds.

So the failure was in the certificate itself, and I asked for the exact validity dates. I used openssl s_client against a node and printed the dates of the certificate.

I wrote to the channel that the failure is at the TLS handshake of the internal listener and that the next step is to read the validity of the certificate. I also said that nobody should restart the nodes, because a restart would not change a certificate problem and would lose the evidence in the memory of the processes.

Sam asked for an estimate for the customers. I said that I could not give one yet, but that we know where to look. She put this into the status page as a short update.

Mara used the time to check the SDK documents for the buffer limits, so we could tell customers how long they can wait without losing events. The default is 6 hours for the main SDKs and 1 hour for the older ones.

summary: The validity dates show the internal certificate of the ingest nodes expired at 08:39, one minute before the first 503; the renewal job is the next thing to check.
body:
The openssl output was clear. The certificate on the ingest nodes had a notAfter time of 08:39 this morning. The first 503 came at 08:40, when the next health check ran after the expiry.

The same certificate is used for the health check listener and for the metrics endpoint. This is why both failed together.

I told the channel that this is the cause of the failing checks. The nodes were healthy, but the balancer verifies the internal certificate and rejects an expired one.

Then the question was why it was not renewed. We have a renewal setup that should replace the certificate well before the end. I looked at the machine that runs the renewal and at the cron list.

I did not want to guess, so I looked at what the cron list contained. The renewal entry was not in the active list of the scheduler. I saw it only in the old definitions in the Terraform history, which means that it had existed before.

I did not look into the full story at this point. The job is to bring the writes back first. I asked Tobias whether we can issue a new certificate from the internal authority by hand and install it on the nodes without a deploy.

He said yes, the authority is still working, and he started to prepare the request. The plan was to issue one certificate for the ingest nodes, put it into the secret store and tell the nodes to reload it. The reload does not need a restart of the process.

I prepared the check for after the install: the health endpoint from the jump host over HTTPS, then the target group state, then the success rate.

While waiting I wrote the timeline so far into the incident document: 08:39 certificate expired, 08:40 first 503, 08:44 alert, 08:50 nodes shown healthy by direct call, 09:30 handshake failure found, 09:50 expiry time confirmed.

I also noted the question for later: how did the renewal stop without anyone seeing it. There was no alert on the age of the certificate, which is the second gap.

Sam reported that three customers had already written to support. She answered them with the status text and said that their data is safe if their SDK buffer is on.

The next entry will have the cause of the missing renewal and then the fix.

summary: Tobias issued a new certificate by hand and the first four nodes accepted the reload; the targets turned healthy one by one while I watched the success rate and the retry bursts.
body:
At 10:02 Tobias had the new certificate in the secret store. We reloaded the first node and I tested it over HTTPS from the jump host. The handshake worked and the health endpoint returned 200.

The balancer needs two good checks in a row before it marks a target as healthy, with an interval of 10 seconds. So after about 25 seconds the first target was back. We then reloaded the others in groups, first three nodes, then the remaining five, to keep an eye on the effects.

I watched the ingest dashboard. The success rate rose from 0 to about 45 percent when four nodes were healthy. Those four nodes took the whole load, including the retries of the clients, which were about 3 times the normal rate. CPU on them went to 70 percent, which was fine.

When all 9 nodes were healthy, the success rate went to 99.9 percent. The queue showed a large rise of messages for a short time, as the clients sent their buffers. The workers worked through them in about 12 minutes. I looked at the lag of the consumers and it fell to the normal value by 10:25.

I checked for lost events by comparing the accepted counts of the balancer with the stored counts in the analytics store for the hour after the recovery. They matched within the rate of normal duplicates, which the dedup step removes.

The events from the outage window are with the clients. Most SDKs sent them from their buffers. Sam asked the three customers who wrote to us and one of them with the old SDK had lost about 20 minutes, because of the 1 hour limit and a restart of their app. We told them clearly.

I wrote down the stop of the writes as 08:40 to 10:12, so 1 hour and 32 minutes. The first node was fine at 10:03, but a full recovery needed all targets.

The remaining work is to find out why the renewal did not run, to renew all other internal certificates and to add an alert. I also want a review of what else was turned off without being noticed. Mara offered to go through the cron list with me this afternoon.

I closed the incident channel state to monitoring and left the deploy pause on until the afternoon, so that the next deploy goes out only after the other certificates are checked.

summary: Watched the ingest targets turn healthy after the new certificate and tracked the success rate and client retry bursts until writes were back to normal.
body: Tobias reloaded the new certificate on the first four nodes, and I stayed on the dashboards while the rest followed. The load balancer marked each target healthy after two passed checks, so the pool refilled in steps of about a minute. Success rate of the ingest API went from 0 percent to 35 percent after the first four nodes. It reached 70 percent when eleven of sixteen nodes were in. At the last node it was back at the normal 99.9 percent. The first thing I wanted to know was whether the returning traffic would knock the fresh nodes over again. It did not, but it came close at one point. Clients had been retrying with backoff for more than an hour, and many of them were waiting at the same long interval. When the first nodes came back, those clients all arrived within a few seconds of each other. Requests per second on the four early nodes jumped to almost 4 times the usual peak. CPU on those nodes went to 88 percent and p99 latency reached 2.4 seconds for a short time. A few clients got 429 from the rate limiter in that burst, which is correct behaviour but still looked bad on the graph. As more nodes joined, the load spread out and latency came down within five minutes. I did not pause or throttle anything by hand, because every change would have slowed the recovery. Redpanda accepted the writes without trouble, and producer errors in the ingest metrics stayed at zero. The consumer lag was a different matter and started to climb, which I left for the next entry. I wrote down the timeline in the incident channel as I went: first node healthy at 10:06, all nodes healthy at 10:12. Mara asked whether we should have kept the deploys paused. We kept them paused, and I told her to leave them so until the certificate topic is fully closed. One thing was unclear: some customers showed fewer requests than usual even after 10:12. I checked three of them and saw their clients still in a long backoff, so they will come back by themselves. The two largest customers had already recovered, which I confirmed by their per-key request counters. Nothing in this session changed code or configuration beyond what Tobias did. The open points are the queue backlog, the count of events that were lost or kept on the client side, and what to say to customers. I also noted that the health check failures had been visible in the balancer metrics, but no alert was set on that signal in a useful way. That goes on the list for the postmortem. For now the service is up, and I will keep watching the success rate for another hour.

summary: Drained the Redpanda backlog after the ingest recovery by watching consumer lag per partition and raising the worker count temporarily, with lag back to normal in about 40 minutes.
body: Once the ingest nodes were back, the retry bursts from clients put about 1.9 million events into the queue within 20 minutes. Consumer lag on the high priority topic partitions rose to 310,000 messages on the busiest partition. I looked at lag per partition first, because the topic is partitioned by event type and the load was not even. The partitions for page view and click events carried most of the backlog. The partitions for rare types were already at zero. Workers were running at the normal count of 12, and CPU on them was at about 60 percent. The batch writer was the limit, as it flushes in 50 ms intervals for common types and the inserts are sized for normal load. I raised the worker count from 12 to 20 through Terraform variables and a plain apply, not a manual change in the console. The new tasks started within three minutes. Lag started to fall at about 9,000 messages per minute per busy partition. I kept an eye on Postgres at the same time, because the workers write there as well. Connection use rose from 140 to 210 of the 300 allowed, which was fine. Insert latency stayed under 30 ms at p95. Redis also took part, because the rate limiter counters grew while clients retried. I checked key counts and memory use, and both stayed well within their usual range. The memory use of Redis rose by about 4 percent and went back after the counters expired. I did not change any limits during the incident. At 11:20 the lag was below 20,000 on every partition, and by 11:30 it was zero. Then I scaled the workers back to 12 and watched for ten minutes to see that lag stayed at zero. It did. The ordering of events inside a partition was kept, so no customer should see events swapped for the same key. I wrote the numbers down for the postmortem: peak lag 310,000, drain time about 40 minutes with 20 workers. Mara pointed out that the worker count should become a variable we can raise quickly, and I added a short runbook line for it. Still open is a check of whether any events were rejected during the burst.

summary: Compared accepted and stored event counts for the outage window and found about 4,100 events missing that clients had dropped after exhausting their own retries; the rest arrived late but complete.
body: After the backlog was gone, I wanted to know what the outage cost in events. I started with the number of events the ingest API accepted per minute and compared it to the rows stored by the batch writer per minute. Between 08:40 and 10:12 the API accepted almost nothing, so the question was about the time after. From 10:12 to 11:30 accepted and stored counts matched to the event, which is the same check I did after the rolling deploy of the batch writer. That part is clean. The harder question is about events that never reached us. The ingest clients we ship in two SDKs keep a local buffer and retry with backoff for up to 60 minutes. After that they drop the batch and log a warning. Customers whose apps run on those SDKs lost whatever was still waiting after an hour. To estimate it, I took the normal event rate for each customer from the same hours on the days before. Then I subtracted what actually arrived in the window 08:40 to 11:30. The gap summed to about 4,100 events more than the usual noise, spread over 6 customers. Most of the 6 use the older SDK with the 60 minute limit. The newer SDK keeps events on disk and sent everything after the recovery. Two of the six are large customers, but their gap was small, under 1 percent of their daily volume. I did not trust the estimate fully, since traffic is never identical from day to day. So I also looked at the batch ids that clients put into the request headers. For three customers I could count batches that were retried more than 20 times and then never seen again. Those counts agreed with the estimate within about 10 percent. I wrote the list of the six customers and the sizes in a note for Sam. He will decide who gets a message and in which words. I suggested that the message states clearly which time window is affected. I also suggested that the older SDK users be told about the newer SDK and its disk buffer. Another point is the 60 minute limit itself. It looks too short for an outage like this one, and I opened an issue to discuss a longer default. No data was lost on our side after the queue accepted it. Searching the events from the late arrivals also worked, since the OpenSearch indexing follows the queue and the lag there had already cleared.

summary: Ran the last part of the third monthly index batch copy and verified document counts for all four months, which completes the copy to the new shard layout in staging order.
body: The overnight copy of the third batch stopped at 55 percent, and the rest was waiting for today. I did not want to run it while the ingest outage was being handled, since the cluster also takes the indexing load from the queue. With the backlog cleared, the cluster was calm enough by late morning. I started the second half of the batch with the same slow settings as before. These settings lower the copy rate to about 6,000 documents per second and give the merge threads room. The replica showed a merge load of 35 percent at the start and stayed below 50 percent. Search latency at p95 did not move outside its normal band of 180 to 230 ms. The copy took 2 hours and 10 minutes in total for the remaining part. When it finished, I checked document counts for each of the four months against the customer-layout indices. The counts were summed over all customers, since the new indices are by month and the old ones by customer. Three months matched exactly. The fourth was off by 12 documents, which I traced to events that were written during the copy to the old layout. A delta pass with a time filter fixed it and the counts matched. I also ran the 5,000 recorded queries against the new layout for these four months. 4,987 came back identical, and 13 differed in the order of results with equal scores. Equal scores have no defined order across shards, so I treated those as acceptable and marked them in the sheet Mara uses. The differences were all in queries without a sort field. I did not delete any old index, because the plan says to wait for Mara's sign-off first. Disk use is now at 74 percent with both layouts present. That is below the 80 percent line where I want to stop, but it leaves little room. The next step is the sign-off and then a snapshot before deleting the old copies of the first batches. The outage this morning cost two hours of this plan but did not change it. I wrote the delta pass command into the migration notes, so it can be reused for the next batches. The cutover of the write path is still a separate decision, and it has not started.

summary: Prepared the Redis minor version upgrade on staging, checked client compatibility and memory use after the restart, and wrote the steps for production with a rollback point.
body: The plan for the Redis minor upgrade has been open for a while, and today was a quiet slot for staging. I started by reading the release notes between our version and the target. There were no changes to commands we use, but one change to how the replica handles a full sync. That matters for us because the console sessions live in Redis and a long sync could slow them down. On staging I took a snapshot, then upgraded the replica first and the primary after a failover. The failover took 4 seconds, and the console sessions of the test users stayed valid. The ingest API client and the search API client both reconnected without errors in their logs. Then I ran the load script that mimics the rate limiter traffic, about 8,000 operations per second for 20 minutes. Latency at p99 was 1.1 ms before and 1.0 ms after the upgrade, so no change worth a note. Memory use for the same data set was 3 percent lower after the restart. I believe that comes from a change in the allocator, but I did not dig into it. Then I checked the connection pool of the ingest API against the new version. Its maximum is still 10 connections, and the batch import opens one connection for each worker, so the pool was close to full during the load script. It did not fail on staging, but I wrote down that the limit looks too tight for a real import and that it needs a closer look. The cache warmer reused its pool as expected. One problem showed up in the admin console. A health endpoint there calls an info command and parses one field whose format changed slightly. The parser threw on the new format, and the console showed the Redis status as unknown. Lena fixed the parser in a small change, and I redeployed staging. After that the status showed normally. I wrote the production steps as a list. First the replica, then a failover, then the old primary. Between the steps there is a check of the pool metrics and the session count. The rollback point is the snapshot taken just before, and the steps say how long a restore takes, about 12 minutes for our data size. I did not schedule the production upgrade today. The ingest outage of this morning means Tobias and I want a calmer week before we touch anything shared. I put it on the list for next week and asked Tobias to review the steps. Open items: the review, the date, the pool size question, and a test of the restore on staging, which I have not done yet.

summary: Tuned autovacuum for the events table in Postgres after last week's long transaction finding, and moved the report job to a read replica so it can no longer hold back cleanup.
body: Three days ago I found that a long running transaction from a report job kept dead tuples from being removed in the events table. Today I did the two changes that follow from it. The first was to move the report job to the read replica. The job only reads, so this is simple, but its connection string was set in several places. I changed it in the config of the job and in the Terraform variable, and then ran the job once by hand. It finished in 14 minutes, against 11 minutes on the primary. That is slower, but nobody waits for it. On a replica a long query can still conflict with replay of changes from the primary. So I set the replica to delay cancelling queries up to 15 minutes, with hot standby feedback left off. With feedback off, the primary can clean up while the report runs. The second change was autovacuum for the events table. The default scale factor of 20 percent means a vacuum starts only after tens of millions of changed rows. I set the factor to 1 percent for this table and raised the cost limit so each run finishes faster. Before the change the table had about 38 million dead tuples. I ran a manual vacuum first to bring it down, and it took 50 minutes. The vacuum did not hurt the ingest writers, whose insert latency stayed at 25 ms at p95. After it, dead tuples dropped to 1.2 million and the table size stopped growing. I will watch the number over the next days to see whether the new settings keep it low. There was one surprise. The audit log table has the same problem in a smaller form, and I applied the same per-table setting there. The outage this morning did make the writers a bit noisy in the logs. That did not change anything about the vacuum, though. I wrote the settings and the reason into the database notes in the repository. I also added a Grafana panel for dead tuples per table. It has a line at 10 million for a future alert, which I have not created yet. Mara wondered whether we should partition the events table instead. That is a larger topic, and the analytics events are in ClickHouse anyway. The Postgres events table is mostly for recent data and will stay that way. The open item is the alert, which I will add to the alert rules in code.

summary: Wrote customer guidance on how the ingest client should retry and buffer during an outage, answering Sam's request, and opened an issue to raise the old SDK's 60 minute drop limit.
body: Sam asked for text he can send to customers who saw failed writes this morning. He also wanted a standing section in the docs about what clients should do when the ingest API is down. I started with what the clients do today. The older SDK keeps events in memory and retries with exponential backoff up to 60 minutes. The newer SDK writes events to disk and retries with a cap of 5 minutes between attempts, without a time limit. Plain HTTP users have whatever they built themselves. From that I wrote three recommendations. First, buffer events locally, on disk if possible, and do not drop a batch until the buffer is full. Second, use backoff with jitter. This morning showed what happens without jitter, since many clients came back in the same few seconds. Third, treat 503 and 429 as retryable and all other 4xx responses as errors that need a fix. I added a short table of status codes and what each one means for a client. I also described the batch id header. If a client sends the same batch id twice, the ingest API deduplicates it, so a retry after an unclear failure is safe. That fact was not in the docs before, and I checked it in the code to be sure. The dedup window is 24 hours, which I wrote down too. For the customer message, I kept it short and factual. It says that writes failed from 08:40 to 10:12, and that events buffered by the client were accepted afterwards. It also says that clients with a buffer limit shorter than 90 minutes may have lost events. I left out the cause, because the postmortem is not written yet and Sam agreed to wait for it. For the six customers with a gap, Sam will send a personal note with the size of the gap. I gave him the numbers from the count comparison. In the docs I added the retry section to the ingest page and a link from the SDK pages. Then I opened an issue for the older SDK, to raise its drop limit from 60 minutes to 6 hours and to add jitter. Lena does not own that code, so I tagged Mara, who does. Sam reviewed the text and changed two sentences for tone. The docs build passed and the page is live. What remains is the SDK change, and the message after the postmortem is out.

summary: Added a compatibility check to the schema registry branch that rejects a field type change from integer to string, and fixed two cases where the check was too strict.
body: Work on the schema registry continued today in its own worktree. The registry stores the event schemas per type and version, and customers can propose a new version. Until now it accepted any valid JSON schema, which let a customer change a field from integer to string. Dashboards on ClickHouse then broke for that field, because the column type stayed the same. I wrote a compatibility check that compares a new version with the latest one. Adding an optional field is allowed. Removing a required field is not. Changing a type is not, except for the widening of integer to number. The check lives in a separate module, so the HTTP handler stays small. I wrote 28 unit tests for the module, including nested objects and arrays of objects. Two of them failed at first, and both pointed to real errors in my first version. The first was about a field that moved from required to optional, which I had flagged as a break. That change is safe for readers, so I allowed it. The second was an enum that gained a value. That is safe as well, but an enum that lost a value is a break, since old events still carry it. After those fixes all 28 tests passed. Then I ran the check against the real history of the registry. There are 214 version pairs for 37 event types in production. The check flagged 6 pairs as breaking. I looked at each one by hand. Four were genuine type changes that had been fixed by a migration of the data. Two were false alarms because of a nullable type written in two different ways. I added a normalisation step for the nullable forms and ran it again. Now 4 pairs are flagged, and I wrote them into the pull request as known history. The handler returns a 409 with a list of the breaking changes and the path of each field. I wrote that response format with Lena in mind, since the admin console will show it. She said she can show the list in a dialog next week. The registry has a flag to force a breaking change, for the rare case where support and the customer agree on it. I made the flag require an admin role and write an entry into the audit log. I did not merge today, because Mara wants to read the normalisation code first. The outage of the morning did not touch this branch. The next step after the review is a staging run with the customers' real proposals from the last month.

summary: Added alert rules in code for queue consumer lag and for load balancer unhealthy target counts, since neither signal paged anyone during this morning's incident.
body: This morning showed two gaps in our alerts. The load balancer marked all ingest nodes as down, and the first page came from the success rate rule, not from the target health. Also, the consumer lag climbed to 310,000 without any alert. Since our alert rules live in code, I added both in a branch of the main checkout and tested them locally. The first rule fires when the number of healthy targets of any ingest target group falls below 70 percent of the registered targets for 2 minutes. The second fires when the consumer lag of a partition stays above 50,000 messages for 10 minutes. I chose those numbers from the data of the last 30 days. The lag normally peaks below 8,000, so 50,000 gives room and still catches a real problem. The healthy target rule would have fired at 08:42 this morning, which is two minutes after the first 503. The existing success rate rule fired at 08:44 and paged the on-call person at 08:45. So the new rule is not much faster in this case, but it points to the cause more directly. I put the runbook link into both annotations. The runbooks are short. For the health rule, it says to compare the balancer check with a direct call to a node. For the lag rule, it says to look at lag per partition and consider raising the worker count. That is the same step I used earlier today, and I wrote down the Terraform variable for it. For testing, the rules have unit tests in our rule test format, with synthetic series. I wrote 6 cases and all passed. I also ran the rules against the recorded metrics of this morning with a replay. Both fired as expected. The lag rule fired at 09:50, which is late, because the lag only grew once the nodes came back. That is fine for what it is meant to catch. A lag alert cannot warn before the queue receives traffic. Tobias reviewed the change and asked to route the health rule to the on-call channel and the lag rule only to the team channel at first. I agree with that, since lag alone is not always urgent. After the merge, the pipeline loaded the rules, and I checked in the Prometheus UI that both were active and green. One thing I did not do is an alert on certificates, because Tobias is doing that one today. The next step is to look at the noise of the rules after a week.

summary: Tried a Grafana dashboard generator library for our dashboards in code and dropped it after it could not express our template variables and produced diffs of thousands of lines.
body: Our dashboards are JSON files that people edit in the Grafana UI and then export. The diffs are huge and hard to review. So I tried a library that generates the JSON from code, hoping to keep dashboards small and reviewable. I picked the ingest overview dashboard as the test, since it has 18 panels and is changed often. Setting up the library and writing the first 6 panels took about an hour. The result looked fine in the preview. Panels with plain queries worked well, and the code was about a tenth of the size of the JSON. The trouble started with template variables. Our dashboards use a variable for the environment and one for the customer, and the customer list is built by a query. The library supported only fixed lists for variables of that kind. I tried a workaround with raw JSON for that part of the file. It worked, but then the benefit was mostly gone for the variables, which are exactly the part that causes the diffs. Next I checked the output diff. When I regenerated the six panels and imported them over the exported version, Grafana changed ids and positions of every panel. The first import produced a diff of 3,400 lines against the existing file. That could be fixed by pinning ids, but the library has no option for it. I looked at the issue tracker of the library and found the same request open for a year. At that point I stopped. I considered writing a small wrapper to patch ids, but that means we maintain code around a tool that we adopted to save work. The cost is not worth it for 14 dashboards. What I did instead was smaller. I wrote a script that normalises exported dashboard JSON, sorting keys, removing ids that Grafana sets itself and dropping the version field. With the script in a pre-commit hook, diffs of an edited panel are now about 20 lines. I tested it on the ingest overview dashboard and on the search latency one. Both gave small diffs after an edit in the UI. I deleted the branch with the library experiment and wrote a note in the repository docs about why we did not use it. Mara and Lena both use the dashboards, so I asked them to try the hook. Lena found one case where the script reordered the annotations, and I fixed it. The hook is merged. The dashboards are still edited in the UI, and that is fine for now.

summary: Investigated the p95 latency of the search API after per-field boosts and found that queries with five or more boosted fields spend most of their time in query building, not in OpenSearch.
body: The p95 latency of the search API has been at 210 ms for a week, up from 170 ms before the boosts were turned on for all customers. I wanted to know whether the time goes to OpenSearch or to our own code. First I took the traces of 2,000 slow requests from the last day. In the spans, the OpenSearch call took a median of 95 ms, and that did not differ much from before. The rest, about 70 ms in the slowest group, was spent in the query parser and the builder of the final query body. Then I grouped the requests by the number of boosted fields. For requests with up to 3 boosted fields, the building time was 4 ms. With 5 or more, it was 38 ms at median and over 100 ms at p95. That looked wrong for what is just string handling. I profiled the builder with a recorded query of 7 boosted fields. The profile showed that for each field, the builder looked up the field settings of the customer by calling the settings function again. Each call built a new object from the cached settings and ran a validation of the whole field map. With 7 fields that happened 7 times, each over 7 fields. The cost grows with the square of the field count. I changed the builder to read the settings once per request and validate once. After that the building time for the 7 field query went from 41 ms to 3 ms in a local benchmark. I ran the full test suite and the 5,000 recorded queries against the changed code. All results were identical to the old code, since the change affects only how fast the same body is built. The outage of this morning did not touch search, because search reads from OpenSearch and the Redis cache, while only writes were down. I did notice that the cache hit rate dipped to 70 percent during the recovery, since the cache warmer waited for the queue. It was back at 79 percent by noon. I deployed the change to staging and compared the latency with production under a replay of the morning's queries. The p95 in staging was 168 ms against 212 ms in production. That matches the expected gain. I want one more look at the effect on the long tail before shipping. Mara will review the diff tomorrow, and I will deploy to production after that and watch the p95 for a day. A second idea is to cache the built query body per customer and query shape. I wrote it into the notes, but it is not needed once the quadratic part is gone. The remaining time in OpenSearch is the part the new shard layout should improve.

summary: Went through the crons and scheduled jobs switched off during the account migration and found that all are accounted for, with one disabled by intent, and wrote the list into the runbook.
body: The postmortem action I took first was to check every cron that the infrastructure migration turned off. The migration moved jobs and secrets into the new AWS accounts, and the certificate renewal was one that was never switched on again. I started from the Terraform state and the scheduler configuration in both the old and new accounts. The list has 41 scheduled jobs in the old account at the time of the migration. In the new accounts, 39 of them are enabled. That left two to explain. The first was a cleanup job for old export files that had been replaced by the audit export cleanup. Its schedule was disabled on purpose, and the commit message of that time says so. The second was a weekly job that rotated a test API key in the sandbox. It is off, and nobody missed it, but I did not find a decision. I asked Tobias, and he said it is not needed since the sandbox keys no longer expire. I deleted the job and its secret, with Tobias's agreement. Next I looked at the jobs that are enabled, to see whether they actually ran. For this I took the last run time from the scheduler for each job and compared it to the schedule. All 39 had run within their expected interval. Three of them had failures in the last month, and I checked those too. One was a flaky network call that succeeded on the next run. The other two were the audit export cleanup, which already has an alert. The nightly reindex job ran every night as well. Then I added a check for this class of problem. It is a small script that compares enabled jobs against a file in the repository listing the jobs we expect, and it fails if a job is missing or disabled without a note. It runs in the deploy pipeline for the infrastructure repository. I tested it by disabling a job on a copy of the state, and it failed with the job name. Last, I wrote the table of all jobs into the runbook, with owner, schedule and what breaks if it stops. For the certificate renewal, the owner is Tobias, and the new alert fires 14 days before an expiry. The table also has a column for how we notice a stop. For five jobs the answer was nobody would notice, and I marked them for a failure alert. Those will be done in the next days. The review of the postmortem will use this table as one of its inputs.

summary: Reviewed the Redis memory growth of the session store and found that expired console sessions were kept for seven days because of a TTL set in two places, so one is removed.
body:
Started from the memory graph of the Redis instance, which had grown by about 30 percent over a month while the number of active console users stayed flat. A scan of the key space by prefix showed that the session keys made up most of the growth. Many of them had a TTL of seven days, although the console is meant to log users out after 12 hours of inactivity.

The cause was in two places. The session middleware set the TTL at login, and a helper in the console backend set it again on every touch with a constant from an old config file. The second call won, so every session lived seven days after the last request. I removed the helper call and kept one TTL setting in the middleware, read from the config.

I wrote a small script that counts session keys by remaining TTL bucket, and ran it on staging before and after the change. Before, nearly all keys sat in the buckets above 100 hours. After a day of test traffic the keys were under 12 hours.

The production keys will not shrink by themselves quickly, so I did not touch them by hand. Old sessions will run out within seven days after the deploy. I asked Lena whether the console shows anything that depends on long sessions, and she confirmed that nothing does.

I also renamed nothing, since the key naming of the sessions is used by the logout endpoint. A note in the runbook now lists the key prefixes and who owns each.

The next step is to deploy this with the next console release and compare the memory graph after a week. If memory is still high then, the next suspect is the cache warmer keys with long TTLs. I left a ticket for that check with the script attached.

No user was logged out by the change on staging. The deploy is planned for tomorrow morning, outside the busy hours of the large customers.

summary: Fixed a slow Postgres query behind the console's API key list by adding a composite index, which took the page from 3.2 seconds to 40 milliseconds for the largest customer.
body:
Sam reported that the API key page of the admin console was very slow for one of the large customers, which has a few thousand keys. I took the query from the Fastify logs and ran it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of production data. It did a sequential scan over the keys table and sorted the result in memory, which took 3.2 seconds.

The query filters by account and a revoked flag and sorts by creation time. The existing index covered only the account column. I added a composite index on account, revoked flag and creation time, in descending order for the last column, and built it concurrently so writes were not blocked.

After the build, the plan used an index scan and no separate sort. The same query ran in 40 milliseconds. I also checked the query for a small customer, to be sure the planner did not choose worse for small tables, and it stayed at about 2 milliseconds.

The index adds some size to a small table, about 6 MB, which is no concern. Write speed on the table is not an issue either, since keys are created rarely. I added the migration file with the concurrent build and a comment about why it is outside of a transaction.

While in there I noticed the page loads all keys and does the paging in the browser. That is a larger change in the console, so I opened an issue for Lena instead of changing the API now. A paged endpoint would make the page fast for any size.

The migration ran on production in the early afternoon without locks. I checked the slow query log afterwards and the query no longer shows up. Sam will ask the customer to confirm that the page feels fast again.

Nothing is left on the index itself. The paging issue is open and has the numbers from this session. The next time such a report comes in, the first check is whether the query filters on more than one column.

summary: Tested the rate limiter on Redis after the connection spike findings and found that the counters use one round trip per request, so it is fine, but the Lua script lacks a timeout guard.
body:
After the connection spikes of the last days I wanted to be sure the rate limiter was not part of the problem. I read the limiter code in the search API and traced one request with the Redis monitor on staging. Each request makes a single call of a Lua script that increments the counter and sets the TTL, so there is one round trip and no extra connection.

The load test used 2,000 requests per second over 200 keys for ten minutes. The pool size stayed flat, and the p99 time of the script call was 1.4 milliseconds. The limiter is therefore not the cause of the spikes.

While reading the script I found that it sets the TTL only when the counter is created. If the key exists without a TTL, for example after a manual edit, it would live forever and block that API key for good. This has not happened, but it is a possible trap. I changed the script so it sets the TTL when the key has none.

I added a test for this case with a key written without a TTL. The test failed before the change and passes now. The other limiter tests pass as before.

I also looked at the client side. If Redis does not answer, the limiter waits for the default client timeout of five seconds, which is too long for a request path. I set a timeout of 100 milliseconds and made the limiter let the request through when Redis fails, and count these cases in a metric. This follows the earlier decision that a limiter outage should not become a customer outage.

The metric is called limiter_redis_errors_total and has a Grafana panel next to the other limiter panels. I did not add an alert, since a short burst is harmless. A longer burst will be visible on the panel, and an alert can follow if it turns out to matter.

The change is in review with Mara. The per-key limit work of the rate-limits branch is not touched by it, but the script change will need a merge there. I left a note on the branch.

summary: Went through the Postgres slow query log of the week and picked the three worst queries, two of which were fixed by an index and one by removing a repeated call in the console backend.
body:
I read the slow query log with pgBadger for the last seven days. Most entries came from three queries, and everything else was far below. I handled them in order of total time spent.

The first was the settings lookup by account, called on nearly every console request. It took only 8 milliseconds, but ran 400,000 times a day. The cause was a missing cache in one route handler, which loaded settings twice per request. I removed the second call and passed the loaded object on, which cut the calls by about half.

The second was a join between the audit log and the accounts table for the audit view. After last week's index on actor and time, the filter was fast, but the join still scanned accounts. An index on the account id column of the audit log fixed this. Time fell from 900 to 60 milliseconds on the copy.

The third was the weekly usage report, which now runs on the replica. It is slow by nature, because it aggregates all events of an account. I left it, since it no longer affects the primary and no user waits for it.

I ran both indexes on staging first and compared the plans. Then I built them concurrently on production. Index size together is about 1.1 GB, and the disk has enough room.

Afterwards I looked at unused indexes with the statistics view. There are four indexes that were never scanned in 90 days, but two of them back unique constraints. I did not drop anything and only listed the other two in the ticket, to check after the next quarterly report has run.

The pgBadger report is saved in the shared folder, and I wrote the three findings into the weekly notes. The next review of the log is in a week, and I will compare total time against this one.

Nothing is broken at the moment, so this is housekeeping. Still, the settings double call showed that the console backend has more places where objects are loaded twice.

summary: Reviewed the search API cache after the day's incident and found the warmer and the ingest outage did not interact, then wrote down three cache follow-ups with owners.
body:
This was a late session on the search API cache, after the morning outage had been handled and the team had moved on to cleanup. The question was whether the ingest outage had left any trace in the search cache, because writes failed for about ninety minutes and the cache could have served stale results for longer than usual. I started with the hit rate panel, which had been at 79 percent since the cache key fix of three days ago, and it showed no dip during the outage window.

Next I compared the cache TTLs with the length of the outage. Most search keys live for 60 seconds and a few dashboard keys for 5 minutes. No key could have outlived the gap in writes by more than 5 minutes, so customers saw at most slightly old results and nothing wrong. I also looked at the search API error rate for the same window and found it flat. The search path does not use the internal certificate that expired, so it was never affected.

The second thing I checked was the cache warmer. Last week I found that it opened a new Redis pool on every run. That fix is already deployed, and I confirmed it by reading the connection count at the top of the last four hours. The spike is gone and the count stays near 18 connections. During the outage the warmer ran normally and warmed keys for data that did not change, which is harmless but wasteful.

Then I looked at key naming, since I had the keys open anyway. The search keys use the prefix search:v2 followed by a hash, while the dashboard keys use a mix of dash: and dashboard: prefixes. I counted about 1,900 keys with the short prefix and about 6,400 with the long one. This is not a bug, but it makes the memory report by prefix misleading, because the same kind of data is split across two groups. I did not rename anything today, because a rename would drop the warm cache for the large customers in the middle of the afternoon peak.

I also sampled 200 keys to check that every key has a TTL. All of them did, which was the point of the check. One group, the per-account feature flag keys, has a TTL of 24 hours, which is longer than needed. A flag change by support takes up to a day to show up in the search API. Sam had not complained, but I think this is wrong and the TTL should be about 5 minutes.

I wrote down three follow-ups. First, unify the dashboard key prefix, to be done at night with a gentle warm-up so the cache refills before the morning. Second, shorten the TTL of the feature flag keys to 5 minutes and check that the Postgres load from the extra reads stays small, which I expect, since the table has fewer than 300 rows. Third, add the cache hit rate per key prefix to Grafana, so a drop like the one three days ago points to the cause faster. I gave the first and third to myself and the second to Mara, because it touches her flag service.

Nothing was changed in production in this session. The result is that the outage did not hurt the cache, and the small cleanups are listed for the coming days. The next step is the prefix panel in Grafana, which I will do tomorrow morning before the prefix change.

summary: Dropped an attempt to replace the Redis client library of the console backend after the new library handled reconnects differently and broke the session store in two tests.
body:
I wanted to try a newer Redis client for the console backend, because it promised smaller memory use and better pipeline support. The goal was to see if it could reduce the connection spikes we had seen in the last days. I made a branch of the main checkout and swapped the library in the session store and the cache helper.

The unit tests of the cache helper passed after small changes to the call signatures. The session store tests failed in two places. Both involve a connection that drops during a request.

The old library reconnects and replays the command once. The new one returns an error for the command that was in flight and reconnects only for the next one. In the session store this meant a user could see an error page when Redis restarted, where before they saw nothing.

I could have added our own replay logic, but that is code we would have to maintain, and it is the kind of thing the old library did for us. A smaller point was the memory use. In a test with 5,000 sessions the difference was under 2 percent, far from the promise.

With no gain in memory and a worse failure mode, I decided to drop the change. I deleted the branch and kept a short note in the wiki with what I tried and the two failing cases. Someone who looks at this again will know why.

The connection spikes remain a separate topic. The cause found earlier was the cache warmer opening a pool per run. The fix for that is in review, and it does not depend on any library.

I used the remaining time to read the release notes of the current library. A minor version has a fix for a leak in the pub/sub handling, which we do not use, so the upgrade is optional. I put the upgrade on the list for the next dependency round.

Nothing was merged, and nothing changed in production. The only outcome is the note.

summary: Wrote the draft of the compatibility rules for the schema registry branch, covering which field changes are allowed, which need a new version, and which are always rejected.
body:
The check from earlier today rejects a change from integer to string, but the rules around it were only in my head. I wrote them down as a document in the branch, so Mara and Sam can read and question them before we freeze the behavior.

There are three classes. Allowed changes are adding an optional field, adding an enum value at the end, and widening a number from 32 to 64 bits. These never break a consumer that reads the old schema.

Changes that need a new schema version are renaming a field, making an optional field required, and narrowing a type. The registry accepts them only under a new version number, and the old version stays readable for consumers that have not moved yet.

Always rejected changes are changing the type between unrelated kinds, such as integer to string or object to array, and removing a field that is used as a partition key. The partition key rule matters because the queue is partitioned by event type, and a change there would reorder events.

I added a table of examples for each rule with a real event type from our own schema, so the rules are easy to follow. For each one I wrote the result the check gives, and I confirmed all of them by running the check on the sample files.

Two cases are still open. One is changing a string to a string with a format, such as a date. The check treats this as a narrowing, but customers do it often. The other is a field that moves into a nested object. I did not decide these and marked them as open in the document.

I also thought about how customers see a rejection. The message now says the field and the rule, which is better than a general error. Sam will review the wording, since support will get the questions.

The next step is the review of the open cases with Mara, and then turning the document into tests, one test per rule.

summary: Answered Sam's question on why the ingest API sometimes accepts the same batch twice after a client retry, and explained that the dedupe window is ten minutes by batch id.
body:
Sam asked why a customer saw some events twice in the search after the morning's trouble. The customer's client had sent batches again after the 503 errors, and some of the first attempts had in fact been stored before the error reached the client.

I looked at how the ingest API handles this. Each batch can carry a batch id, and the API remembers the ids for ten minutes in Redis. A second batch with the same id in that time is accepted but not stored again. After ten minutes the memory is gone, and the batch is stored as new.

The customer's client sent its retries with growing waits, and some came after more than ten minutes. Those had the same batch ids, but the window had already passed. That explains the doubles.

I checked the numbers for this customer. Of the events sent again during the outage, about 300 were stored twice. The count is small compared to the volume, but dashboards that count events show a slight rise for that period.

There are three options. We can raise the window, which costs memory in Redis in proportion to the batch rate. We can leave the window and tell customers to send events with their own event ids, which the store can use to drop doubles. Or we can clean up the doubles for this customer by hand.

For now I suggested to Sam that she tells the customer about the event id field, since it solves the problem on their side without our change. I also offered a one-time cleanup query for the 300 events, and she will ask the customer if they want it.

I wrote a short section for the docs on the batch id window and the event id, with the ten minute number. The window is not changed, and I did not open a ticket to change it, since memory use is already a topic we watch.

summary: Reviewed the first part of the audit export branch and found that the export reads the whole audit log of an account into memory, so it needs a cursor before large customers can use it.
body:
Read through the first part of the audit export for compliance, which Mara and I had started. The export builds a file with all audit entries of an account in a chosen time range, in CSV or NDJSON. The structure is clean, with a job table, a worker and a download link that expires.

The problem is in the worker. It runs one query for the whole range and holds the result in memory before writing the file. For a small account this is fine. I tried it with the biggest account on a copy of the data, which has about 9 million entries for the last year, and the worker used 6 GB of memory before it was killed.

I changed the query to use a cursor that reads 5,000 rows at a time and writes each part to the file right away. With this the memory stays at about 80 MB, whatever the size. The 9 million entries took 4 minutes and the file was 1.3 GB before compression.

Compression is the next point. The worker now compresses while writing, and the file is 190 MB. That is easier to send to a customer, and the download link stays valid for the same time.

I also found that the time range filter used the created time column without the new index on actor and time, which does not help here. The existing index on time alone is enough, and the plan showed an index scan. I did not add another index.

I wrote two tests. One checks that a file from the cursor path has the same rows as the old path for a small account. The other checks that the file is complete when the job restarts in the middle, which needed a small change to write to a temporary name first and rename at the end.

Open points are the order of entries when two have the same time, which I settled with the id as a tie breaker, and what happens to a running export when an account is deleted. The second one I left as a note for Mara.

The export for the large account has been run only on the copy. Before it goes to production, Tobias has to confirm that the worker has enough disk for the temporary file. I asked him in the infrastructure channel.

The next step is the access check, so only account admins can create an export, and an audit entry for each export itself.

summary: Added the access check and a self-audit entry to the audit export, so only account admins can create exports and every export is recorded in the audit log.
body:
This continued the review of the audit export from the afternoon. The cursor change was done, and what was missing was who may start an export. I added the check in the route handler, using the same role helper as the rest of the console.

Only users with the admin role of the account can create an export. Support staff with the internal role can create one for any account, but only with a reason text, which is stored in the job. I made the reason required in the schema of the request, so a missing text gives a 400 with a clear message.

Each export now writes an audit entry of its own, with the actor, the account, the time range and the format. The entry is written when the job is created and not when the file is ready, so a failed job still leaves a trace. I thought about it and decided that trying to export is itself something that compliance wants to see.

A second entry is written when the file is downloaded, with the actor and the address the request came from. This took a small change to the download route, which had no access to the request context before.

I wrote tests for four cases: an admin of the same account, a normal user, an admin of another account and a support user with and without a reason. All four give the expected result. The test with the other account's admin was the one I worried about, and it returns a 404 instead of a 403, so the existence of the job is not revealed.

The download link is signed and expires after 24 hours. I checked the signature code and found that it did not include the account id, so a link could in theory be used with a changed path. I added the account id to the signed data, and a test now changes the path and expects a 403.

One point I left open is the retention of the export files. They are stored in an S3 bucket, and I set a lifecycle rule of seven days in Terraform. Tobias should read the change, since the buckets are in the new account setup.

The audit view in the console shows the new entry types, but with the raw type name. Lena will make labels for them. I wrote the list of the type names in the ticket.

The branch is ready for a second review. Mara will look at it tomorrow, and after that the first real export can be tried with a friendly customer.

summary: Looked at the loader for large files and found that a retry after a partial failure re-reads the file from the start, so the retry now resumes from the last committed chunk.
body:
Sam passed on a complaint from a customer who loads files of 20 GB or more. When the loader failed late in a file, the next attempt began again from the start and took as long as the first one. The customer had waited for hours in two attempts in a row.

I read the retry code in the loader branch. The loader splits the file into chunks of 50 MB and sends each to the ingest API. On any error that ends the run, the retry logic starts a new run with the same file, and nothing remembers which chunks were already stored.

I added a small table in Postgres, called load_progress, with the load id, the chunk number and a status. After a chunk is accepted, the loader writes its number in the same step as it moves on. A new run for the same load reads the table and skips chunks that are done.

Skipping needs an offset in the file. For NDJSON this is easy, since the loader keeps the byte offset per chunk. For CSV the header and quoted line breaks make it harder, so I store the offset of the start of a record, and the first chunk keeps the header for the parse.

There is a risk that a chunk was stored but the progress write failed. Then the chunk is sent again, and doubles could appear. The batch id of each chunk is made from the load id and the chunk number, so the ingest API dedupe handles it, as long as the retry comes within ten minutes. For longer gaps I added the event ids from the file when it has them.

I tested with a 2 GB file on staging. I killed the loader at 70 percent, started it again and watched. It skipped 28 chunks and sent the remaining 12, and the final count matched the file. The run took 4 minutes instead of 14.

I also tested a failure in the middle of a chunk. The partial chunk was sent again as a whole, and the ingest dedupe dropped the part that was already stored. The counts matched here as well.

Open points are the cleanup of old rows in load_progress, which I set to 30 days with a job, and the console display of progress, which Lena may want. I put both in the ticket.

The branch is ready for review by Mara. After her review it can go to the first customer with large files, with Sam as contact.

summary: Wrote the notes of the day for the team: what the ingest outage taught, which small changes shipped, and what is planned for the coming days on the search index and Redis.
body:
At the end of this long day I wrote a note for the team channel, so that everyone has the same picture. The main event was the ingest outage of the morning. Its cause was an expired internal certificate, and the fix and the follow-up actions are in the postmortem.

After the outage, the day went on with normal work. In short, the index copy to the new shard layout for the first four months is complete. The Redis minor version upgrade is prepared on staging and waits for a quiet time in production. Autovacuum is tuned, and the report job runs on the replica.

The alert rules for queue lag and for unhealthy load balancer targets are in code and in review. The crons that were switched off in the account migration are all accounted for, and the list is in the runbook. I asked Tobias to check the list again once a quarter.

Smaller items include the session TTL fix in the console backend, two Postgres indexes, the limiter script change, and the audit export and loader work on their branches. A few attempts did not work out. The Grafana generator library and the new Redis client were dropped, and the reasons are in the notes.

For the next days the plan is as follows. First, the tie breaker change in the search API and the first read switch on staging. Second, the Redis upgrade in production, with the rollback point from the steps. Third, the review of the postmortem actions, so that none is forgotten.

I also noted two risks. The old SDK drops events after 60 minutes of failed sends, and the 4,100 lost events of the outage came from that. Until the limit is raised, customers on the old SDK stay exposed to a longer outage.

The second risk is disk space on the search cluster while two layouts exist. Tobias knows the numbers, and the extra storage is planned for two weeks from now.

After the message I closed the open tabs on staging, left the nightly copy job scheduled and checked that the on-call channel gets the new alerts. Tomorrow starts with the postmortem review preparation.

summary: Wrote the production steps for the Redis minor upgrade after the staging run, with a rollback point and a check of the client pool settings before and after.
body:
The staging upgrade from this afternoon went cleanly, so tonight I turned the notes into a runbook page. The page starts with the preconditions: a fresh snapshot, no batch import running, and the on-call person told in the channel. Then come the steps in order. First the replica is upgraded and restarted. After that we check that it catches up and that the memory use is close to the value from before. Then we fail over and upgrade the old primary.

The pool settings needed their own section. The pool maximum is still 10 for the console backend and was raised only for the import job, so I listed which services open how many connections. During a failover every client reconnects at once, and I wanted to know that number before we do it. The sum is well below the limit of the server. I also noted that the search API cache client reconnects slowly, about two seconds, and that this is normal.

The rollback point is the snapshot plus the old package version, which Tobias confirmed is still in our repository. Rolling back means restoring the snapshot, so any session or rate limit counter written after the upgrade would be lost. That is acceptable for counters, which are rebuilt within a minute. For the session store it would log out the console users, and I wrote that into the page so nobody is surprised.

I added a short list of checks after the upgrade: the version string on both nodes, the hit rate of the query cache after ten minutes, the pool metric, and the error rate of the limiter. Each has the dashboard panel name next to it. I also wrote what a bad result looks like for each, for example a hit rate under 60 percent that does not recover.

Open points remain. I did not decide the time window yet. Tobias prefers early morning, and I would rather avoid the hour of the nightly jobs. Tomorrow I will ask him and put the final time into the page. The upgrade itself is not scheduled until the index copy is done and the incident follow-ups have settled.

summary: Went through the monthly shard copy plan for the search index and listed what must be checked before the first month is switched over, mainly counts, boosts and alias handling.
body:
After the copy to the new layout finished in staging order, I sat down and wrote a checklist for the switch. The migration itself has not started, and I wanted the list to exist before anyone is tired. The plan uses one index per month instead of one per customer. Searches then go through an alias that spans the months in the requested range.

The first check is document counts per month between the old and the new index, which we already did for four months. The second check is that the per-field boosts from search v2 give the same ranking. I took 200 real queries from the log, ran them against both layouts and compared the top ten. In 187 cases the order was identical. In the other 13 the difference came from ties in the score, where the shard that holds a document changes the tie breaking. That is harmless but I noted it for Sam, so support does not get surprised by a customer who sees a slightly different order.

The third check is the alias handling. A query that spans 14 months touches 14 indexes, and I want to know the cost. In staging a query over 14 months took about 30 percent longer than the same query on the old layout for a small customer. For a large customer it was faster, because the old shard was big. This confirms the reason for the plan, but it also means we should keep the default range of the console search short.

The fourth point is the nightly reindex job. It writes to one index per customer today. It has to learn the monthly names, and it must not run during the backup window. I wrote down that the job needs a dry run mode that prints which index each document would go to.

I also listed the rollback. As long as the old indexes are kept, switching the alias back is a single call. The old indexes can be removed only after a week without problems. The list is in the planning document, and I asked Mara to read it tomorrow.

summary: Checked how the console backend uses Redis TTLs and found four key groups with no expiry at all, which explains part of the slow memory growth.
body:
Following the session store finding of this afternoon, I scanned the keys of the console backend and the search API to see which have no TTL. I used a scan with a small count on a replica, so the primary saw no extra load. The scan took about twenty minutes and I sampled one in ten keys.

Four groups had no expiry. The first is the per-user preferences cache of the console, which is rebuilt from Postgres and should live a day. The second is the cached account settings, also easy to rebuild. The third is a set of old keys of the previous rate limiter counters, which the cron removal will take care of. The fourth is the search API suggestion cache, where a bug set the TTL only on the first write of a key and then replaced the value with a call that clears it.

Together the four groups held about 22 percent of the keys by count, though less by size. The suggestion cache was the largest part. I fixed that bug by setting the TTL in the same command as the write, and added a test that reads the TTL after two writes. The test failed before the fix and passes now.

For the preferences and the account settings I chose a TTL of one day, with a small random spread so that the keys of one customer do not all vanish together. I did not change the key names, because the naming proposal is a separate piece of work and I did not want to mix the two.

After deploying to staging I watched the memory for an hour. It grows more slowly, but the real effect will show only after a day. I wrote a Grafana panel that counts keys without a TTL from a daily job, so the problem cannot return quietly. The job runs at an off hour on the replica.

Tomorrow I will check the staging memory again and then ship the changes to production in two steps.

summary: Added a cursor to the audit export so large accounts are read in pages, and tested it against a copy of the largest customer's audit log with flat memory use.
body:
The review earlier found that the export read the whole audit log of an account into memory. Tonight I replaced that with a cursor on the Postgres side. The export now reads 5,000 rows per page, ordered by time and then by id, and remembers the last pair. The order by both columns matters, because many entries share the same timestamp to the second and a cursor on time alone would skip or repeat rows.

The new index on actor and time from this week helps the filter by actor but not this ordering, so I checked the plan for the export query. It uses the existing index on account and time and does not sort. That is what I wanted.

The writer streams each page into the output file and flushes it, so memory does not grow with the size. I tested it with a copy of the audit log of our largest customer on staging. That account has about 9 million entries. The old code needed more than 6 GB and was killed. The new code stayed around 180 MB for the whole run, which took about eleven minutes.

I checked the output two ways. The row count of the file matched a count query. I also compared a hash of the rows from the export with a hash computed in SQL over the same range, and they agreed. A second run during which I inserted new audit entries produced a file that stopped at the time the export started, which is the intended behaviour: the export is a snapshot by time, not by lock.

One case I fixed along the way is an export that is cancelled. The cursor job now checks a flag between pages and deletes the partial file. Before, it left the file in the bucket. I added a test for it.

The self-audit entry from earlier now also records the number of rows exported, which Sam asked for so that support can answer customers who want to know what left the system. It is written when the export ends, and a failed export writes an entry with the failure reason.

What is left: the export format for the compliance team still needs a field list approved, and the download link needs an expiry. I will ask Mara about the expiry tomorrow, because she built the link service.

summary: Made the loader resume from the last committed chunk and tested it by killing the process mid-file, which showed an off-by-one in the chunk offset that is fixed now.
body:
Earlier today I changed the loader so that a retry after a partial failure continues from the last committed chunk. Tonight I tested it properly instead of trusting the unit tests. I used a 2 GB NDJSON file and a script that kills the loader at random points.

The first runs exposed a bug. After a resume, the loader read the first line of the next chunk twice, because the stored offset pointed at the last byte of the committed chunk instead of the byte after it. The result was a duplicate event at each resume point. The dedupe by event id in the store hid it in most cases, but the counts of the import report were wrong by one for each resume. I fixed the offset and added a test with a file of lines of different lengths, since the bug was invisible when all lines had the same size.

After the fix I ran the kill script 40 times. Each run ended with the same number of events as the file has lines, and the report matched. The longest run had 7 resumes.

I also looked at the backoff. The loader waits one second, then two, then four, up to 60 seconds, with a random spread. For a store that is down for a few minutes this is fine. For a file with a bad line, resuming does not help, so I made the loader mark a chunk as failed after three attempts at the same offset and move the chunk to a rejected file with the line number. The import then continues with the rest. Before, one bad line stopped the whole import after many pointless retries.

The state of the import is stored in a small table in Postgres: file id, offset, chunk number and attempts. I added an index on the file id, though the table is tiny, to keep the lookup stable as it grows. Old rows are removed after seven days.

The report now shows how many chunks were resumed and how many lines were rejected. Sam will find this useful, since support often asks why an import has fewer events than the file. I wrote two sentences about it for the docs and sent them to Sam.

Next I want to test an import on staging with a store that is slow instead of down, because that is the case I have not seen yet.

summary: Reviewed the Redis query cache hit rate by customer and found that the three largest customers have hit rates under 50 percent because their cache keys include a timestamp.
body:
To end the day I looked at the hit rate of the query cache for each customer, which we had only as one global number. The global number looked fine at about 74 percent, but a global number hides what happens to the customers who matter most. I pulled it from the cache metrics with a label for the account.

The three largest customers had hit rates between 38 and 47 percent. The smaller ones were mostly above 80. This is the reverse of what we want, since the large customers send the most queries and their dashboards are the heaviest.

I looked at the keys of one large customer. The key includes the query text, the filters and the time range. The time range is given as an absolute timestamp with seconds, taken from the moment the dashboard was opened. Two users who open the same dashboard a few seconds apart ask for different ranges, so they never share a cache entry. Small customers mostly use fixed ranges like last month, which are rounded already.

The fix I propose is to round the end of a relative range to the minute, or to five minutes for ranges longer than a day, before the key is built. The result is then at most five minutes stale for a long range, which the dashboards can accept. I tried it on staging with a replay of one hour of real queries for the largest customer. The hit rate went from 41 to 79 percent, and the median latency of those queries fell accordingly.

There are two risks. The first is that a customer who watches the last few minutes live would see old data, so the rounding must not apply to ranges under an hour. The second is that rounding changes the keys, so the cache will be cold after the deploy, and the first minutes will put more load on the store. I will deploy it in a quiet hour.

I wrote the change as a small function with tests for the ranges, and I left it behind a flag, off by default. Tomorrow I will talk to Mara about the freshness limits and to Sam about whether the large customers should be told. After that we can turn the flag on for one customer first.

summary: Looked at the Redis key naming across the console and the search API and found three styles in use, with a proposal for one prefix scheme.
body:
The Redis upgrade preparation made me list the keys on staging by pattern. There are three naming styles: colon separated with the service first, such as search:cache:..., colon separated with the type first, such as session:..., and a few older keys with underscores from the first version of the rate limiter.

In total I counted 11 key families. The biggest by memory is the query cache of the search API, then the console sessions, then the rate limiter counters.
