The underscore keys belong to a counter that the rate limiter does not use anymore, but a cron still writes to it. That is 40 MB on staging, and on production probably the same order.

My proposal is service:purpose:id, for example search:cache:<hash>, console:session:<id>, ratelimit:key:<apikey>. It is mostly what we have, so only the older families have to move. A scan of the code shows 4 places that build keys by hand, and they should use one helper instead.

Changing key names is not free. A rename in the code makes the old keys unreachable, so the cache starts cold, and sessions would log users out. For the sessions I would not rename at all. For the cache, a cold start is acceptable at night, and the warmer exists. For the rate limiter, the counters are short lived and a rename costs nothing.

I wrote the proposal into the docs folder with the list of families, their TTLs and their owner. No code changed. I will ask Mara to look at it, since she wrote the first limiter keys. The old counter cron can be removed after she confirms it is unused.

summary: Went through the ingest worker batching branch after the outage: the batch size of 500 is fine, but a failed batch is written one event at a time and is slow.
body:
The ingest-batching branch groups events into larger writes to the store. Today's outage brought a lot of queued events to the workers, and I used the evening to look at how the branch behaves under a backlog like that.

I replayed a recorded stream of about 2 million events through the worker on staging, at 4 times the normal speed. With batches of 500 the worker reached 38,000 events per second per instance, against 21,000 on the main branch. CPU stayed at 70 percent, and memory was flat.

The weak point is the failure path. When a batch write fails, for instance because of one event that breaks a constraint, the code falls back to writing the events one at a time. With one bad event in a batch of 500, that makes 500 single writes. In my test, with 1 percent of batches containing a bad event, throughput fell to 29,000 events per second. With 10 percent it fell to 15,000, which is worse than main.

A better way is to split the failed batch in half and try each half, and repeat. A bad event is found after about 9 splits, and the good events go through in larger writes. I wrote it as a recursive function with a depth limit, and the bad events go to the dead letter topic, as before.

Results with the split: at 1 percent bad batches, 36,000 events per second, and at 10 percent, 31,000. The number of writes per bad event fell from 500 to about 17.

I added three tests: one bad event at the start, in the middle and at the end of a batch, and a batch that is all bad. The all-bad case ends with 500 events in the dead letter topic and no endless loop, because of the depth limit.

Open points:
- The constraint errors are the only ones that should split. A timeout of the store should retry the whole batch with a delay, otherwise the splitting makes load worse during a store problem. I handled this by checking the error class, but only for two classes so far.
- The metrics for splits and dead letters are not added yet.

Next I will add the metrics and then check the order of events within a partition, because the split changes the write order of a batch.

summary: Checked the order of events within a partition after the batch split change and found that the split keeps order, but the dead letter events come later.
body:
The question from last night was whether splitting a failed batch changes the order of events that the store sees. I wrote a test that sends 10,000 events with a sequence number per partition key, with 2 percent bad events mixed in.

The split writes the first half before the second half, so the good events keep their relative order. The bad events leave the stream and go to the dead letter topic. That means a bad event can appear in the dead letter topic after later good events were written. Nobody reads the order from the dead letter topic, so this is fine, but it should be said in the docs.

I also added the metrics: a counter for splits, a counter for events sent to the dead letter topic, and a histogram for the number of writes per batch. The names follow the ingest_worker prefix we use.

After that I ran the replay again on staging with the metrics on. The split counter matched the expected number from the test data, within 1 percent. The histogram shows that 97 percent of batches need exactly one write.

I wrote a short note for Sam on what the dead letter topic holds and how a customer can find out that an event went there. Today the answer is that support asks us, and that is not good. A console view is a later idea.

The branch is ready for Mara's review. I listed the tests and the replay results in the description.

summary: Mara reviewed the batching branch and asked for a limit on the dead letter rate; added a circuit that pauses the consumer when more than 20 percent of batches fail.
body:
Mara's review had two main points. First, if a deploy or a schema change makes most events bad, the worker would send millions of events to the dead letter topic in a few minutes. Second, the splitting would hammer the store with small writes in that case.

I added a simple guard. The worker counts failed batches over a sliding window of 200 batches. If more than 20 percent failed, the consumer pauses for 30 seconds and logs an error with the most common error class. After the pause it tries again, and the pause doubles up to 5 minutes.

A test feeds the worker a stream where every batch is bad. The consumer pauses after about 40 batches and the dead letter count stops growing. When the stream is fixed, the worker resumes within the next pause interval and the window clears.

The pause raises a question about the queue. While the consumer is paused, the lag grows, and the lag alert from the other day fires. I think that is right. The alert text now says to check the ingest_worker_paused gauge, which I added.

Mara also asked about the number 20. It is a guess from the test data, where real bad rates were below 1 percent. I made it a setting with that default, so it can be changed without a deploy of code.

She also noted that one log line printed the full event on a constraint failure. Events can hold customer data, so I changed it to print the event id and the error only.

The branch is approved with those changes. I will merge it to staging and let it run over the evening traffic.

summary: Merged the ingest batching branch to staging and watched the morning traffic: writes per second to the store dropped by about 70 percent with no change in lag.
body:
The branch has run on staging since the early morning, and the morning peak is the first real test with the traffic mirror. Staging receives a copy of about 25 percent of production events.

Writes per second to the store fell from about 4,800 to about 1,400 at the peak. Events per second are the same, so each write carries more events. The p95 of the write time went from 9 ms to 21 ms, which is expected for larger writes, and it is far below the limit that we set.

The consumer lag stayed under 2 seconds the whole time. CPU of the workers fell from 55 to 41 percent. Memory rose a little, by about 60 MB per instance, from the batch buffers.

I checked the new metrics. There were 3 splits in two hours and 3 events in the dead letter topic. I looked at them. All three had a timestamp field with a string that the schema does not allow, from the same customer and the same old SDK version. That is the kind of event that fell back to single writes before, so it fits.

The pause gauge stayed at zero. I also checked the order test again against staging data, and sequence numbers per key were in order for the whole window.

One issue came up. The batch buffer is flushed by size or by time, and the time limit is 200 ms. At night with low traffic, the events wait up to 200 ms before they are written. For ingest that does not matter, because the API has already answered the client. It only adds to the time until an event is searchable, and the search index is updated later anyway.

The plan is to leave it on staging for two days, and then roll it out to production one worker group at a time, beginning with the smallest. I wrote the rollout steps and the rollback, which is a setting for the batch size of 1, so no deploy is needed to go back.

Tobias will check the store disk and connection numbers after the first production group.

summary: Removed the old rate limiter counter cron after Mara confirmed nothing reads it, and moved the remaining limiter keys to the ratelimit prefix.
body:
Mara looked at the key naming proposal and confirmed that the underscore counter from the first limiter version is not read anywhere. She had replaced it before the admin console existed. I searched the code and the dashboards again to be sure, and found no reader.

I removed the cron that still wrote to it, and the code for the key. On staging I deleted the leftover keys with a scan and a batched delete, in groups of 1,000, so the server is not blocked. That freed about 40 MB.

The active limiter keys had two forms, with and without the service name. I added a key helper that builds ratelimit:key:<apikey>:<window>, and used it in the four places that built keys by hand. Counters are short, with windows of one minute, so the switch causes at most one minute of counts that restart. For customers near their limit that is a small gift, not a problem.

The Lua script uses the key as an argument, so it needed no change. I ran the limiter tests, and added one that checks that a key built by the helper matches the pattern in the docs.

The sessions and the cache keys are not changed, as agreed with the proposal. The cache helper is a later task, since it needs a cold start at night.

I updated the key family list in the docs with the new state. The change is on the rate-limits branch, as the limiter code is the topic there.

summary: Set a timeout guard in the rate limiter Lua script wrapper and tested it with a slow Redis response, so a stuck call now fails open after 50 milliseconds.
body:
Yesterday's test found that the Lua script of the limiter has no guard for time. If Redis answers slowly, each API request waits for it, and a slow Redis would slow the whole ingest path.

I added a timeout of 50 ms on the client call for the limiter. When it expires, the request is allowed and a counter named ratelimit_timeouts goes up. Failing open was the choice because a limiter problem should not reject paying customers. Mara agreed, with the condition that the counter has an alert.

To test it I used a proxy in front of the staging Redis that adds a delay. With 20 ms the limiter worked normally. With 80 ms every call timed out and every request was allowed, while the request latency rose by only 50 ms. When the delay was removed, the limiter went back to normal within a second.

The alert fires when more than 1 percent of limiter calls time out over 5 minutes, and goes to the on-call channel as a warning. It is in the alert rules repository.

One thing to keep in mind: during a fail-open period, limits are not enforced, so a customer could exceed their limit. The counters will undercount for that time. I wrote this in the runbook.

Next step is a load test with the real limit values for the largest API keys.

summary: Worked through the schema registry compatibility rules against the real event schemas of the five largest customers and found two fields that the draft rules would wrongly reject.
body:
Took the draft rules from yesterday and ran the compatibility check against the last 40 schema versions of the five largest customers. Most changes passed as expected. Two fields were rejected that should be allowed: an optional string that became required with a default, and a numeric field that widened from int32 to int64.

The first case is allowed by the rule table only if the default is stored in the registry, and the check did not read the default from the new version. That was a bug in the check, not in the rules. Fixed it in checker/compat.ts and added a test with the exact schema from the customer.

The widening case needed a rule change. Widening an integer is safe for all current consumers because the JSON payloads carry plain numbers. Added widening as an allowed change and kept narrowing as always rejected.

Also found that the check treats a renamed field as a delete plus an add. That is correct for the wire format, but the error message was confusing. Changed it to say that a rename is a breaking change and to list the old and new name.

Ran the full set again: 40 versions, 3 rejected, all three are real breaking changes that the customers did in fact fix by a new version. Left the rules document updated with the widening case.

Open: the check does not yet cover nested objects deeper than three levels. Wrote that down as the next step. Mara will review the rule table tomorrow.

summary: Looked at why the query cache keys of the three large customers include a timestamp and wrote a plan to round it to the minute, which should lift their hit rates.
body:
Followed up on the finding that the hit rate of the three largest customers is under 50 percent. The search API builds the cache key from the query text plus the time range, and the dashboards send a range ending at now in milliseconds. So no two requests share a key.

Checked 200 sampled keys from Redis. Over 90 percent of the keys differed only in the last three digits of the end time. Rounding the end of the range to the full minute would collapse them.

The cost is that a dashboard may show data up to a minute old. Asked in the team channel and Lena said the console refreshes every 30 seconds anyway, so one minute of rounding for ranges over an hour is acceptable. For ranges under an hour the rounding stays at 10 seconds.

Wrote the change in the key builder behind a flag per customer. It is not on yet. Added a test for the boundaries of the rounding.

Next step is to turn it on for one large customer and compare the hit rate for a day.

summary: Turned on the rounded cache keys for one large customer in staging replay and saw the hit rate move from 41 to 78 percent, with no wrong results in a diff of 5000 queries.
body:
Used the traffic replay in staging with a day of queries from the largest customer. First run with the old keys gave a hit rate of 41 percent. Second run with the rounded keys gave 78 percent.

To check correctness, compared the responses of 5000 queries between both runs. 4968 were identical. The other 32 differed in the last bucket of a time series, as expected from the rounding, and none of them in totals over the whole range.

Memory in Redis grew less than before, because fewer distinct keys are stored. The query cache keys had a TTL of 5 minutes and that stays as it is.

One surprise: a few queries use a relative range such as the last 15 minutes and a fixed bucket size of one minute. With rounding to 10 seconds these now align better with the buckets, which is a side benefit.

Plan is to enable the flag for that customer in production tomorrow morning and watch the hit rate and the p95 latency of the search API for a day.

summary: Reviewed the audit export branch end to end, ran it for the largest customer in staging, and fixed a wrong row count in the export footer and a slow ordering query.
body:
Did a full pass over the audit export branch now that the cursor and the access check are in. Created an export for a copy of the largest customer's audit log in staging: about 31 million rows.

The export finished in 19 minutes with flat memory. The footer of the file reported 30,998,200 rows, but a count in Postgres gave 31,004,512. The cause was that the cursor page boundary used created_at only, and rows with the same timestamp at a page edge were skipped. Changed the cursor to the pair created_at and id, and the footer then matched exactly.

The ordering query was slow for the first page of an old range. Looked at the plan: it used the index on account id and sorted the result. Added an index on (account_id, created_at, id) in a migration. The first page went from 4.1 seconds to 30 milliseconds.

Checked the file format with Sam, who needs it for the compliance requests of customers. She asked for ISO timestamps in UTC and a column for the actor type. Both were small changes and are done.

Tested a failed export by killing the process halfway. The export is marked failed, the partial file is deleted, and the self-audit entry says failed with the reason. A new export can start at once.

Also checked that the access check applies to downloads and not only to creation. It did not. A download link for an export of another account would have worked if one knew the id. Added the check and a test for it.

Remaining: the retention of finished export files, which are kept forever for now. Proposed seven days and wrote it into the branch notes. Mara will look at the migration in the morning.

summary: Checked the chunk resume of the loader against files of 2 to 20 GB and found that memory stays flat, but the checkpoint write per chunk costs 6 percent of the run time.
body:
Ran the loader with the new resume logic on three large files in staging: 2 GB, 8 GB and 20 GB of NDJSON. Each run was killed once at a random point and resumed.

All three runs ended with the same event counts as the source files. Memory stayed at about 300 MB in every case. The off-by-one fixed earlier did not show up again.

The checkpoint is written to Postgres after every chunk of 10,000 events. Measured that it costs 6 percent of the total time on the 20 GB file, mostly from round trips. Writing it every 5 chunks would cost about 1 percent, and a kill would then lose at most 50,000 events of work, which are re-read and deduplicated by the batch id.

Decided to make the interval a setting with a default of 5 chunks. Added the setting to the loader config and a test that kills the process between two checkpoints.

One more case: a source file that changes between the kill and the resume. The loader now stores the size and the first-chunk hash in the checkpoint and refuses to resume if they differ. It logs the reason and starts over only when told to.

The retry delay on temporary store errors stays at exponential backoff from 1 to 30 seconds. Nothing to change there.

Next step is to write the docs for support, so Sam can explain what happens when a customer's import is interrupted.

summary: Wrote the short support note for interrupted imports: what resumes by itself, what the customer sees, and when they need to upload the file again.
body:
Wrote a page for Sam in the support docs about the loader resume. It describes that an interrupted import continues from the last saved point, and that the progress shown in the console can step back a little after a resume.

It lists the cases where the customer must upload again: the file changed, or the import was older than seven days. The checkpoints are removed after seven days.

Added two example messages from the console with their meaning. Sam will test the page with a real ticket and tell me what is unclear.

summary: Checked the loader's checkpoint cost after the 6 percent finding and moved the write from every chunk to every eighth chunk, which cut the overhead to about 1 percent without losing the resume.
body:
The chunk resume of the loader worked, but the checkpoint write per chunk cost 6 percent of the run time, so today's work was about that cost. The checkpoint was a small Postgres update after each committed chunk, and on a 20 GB file that meant thousands of tiny writes. First I tried to batch the write with the chunk commit itself, but the two live in different transactions, so that was dropped after an hour.

The second try was to write the checkpoint only every eighth chunk. After a crash, the loader then re-reads up to seven chunks, and those are skipped by the dedupe on the chunk hash, so no event is stored twice. I ran it against files of 2, 8 and 20 GB and the overhead fell from 6 percent to about 1 percent.

I killed the process 40 times at random points in an 8 GB file and compared the final row count with a clean run. All 40 runs matched. The worst case re-read was 3.5 percent of the file, which is acceptable. The interval is a setting now, CHECKPOINT_EVERY, with 8 as the default, so support can lower it for a customer with very flaky uploads. Still open is a metric for the number of chunks re-read after a resume. I will add it next, and then ask Mara to review the branch.

summary: Reviewed Mara's rate-limit change for per-key burst limits and asked for the burst value to be read from the key settings, not from a constant.
body:
Reviewed the rate-limits branch. The change adds a burst allowance on top of the per-minute limit for an API key. The code works and the tests are clear.

My main comment is that the burst factor is a constant of 2 in limiter.ts. Customers with large batch jobs will want a different value, and support needs to change it without a deploy. Asked to store it with the key settings in Postgres and to cache it with the existing limit.

Second comment: the response header should show the burst remaining, otherwise clients cannot tell why they were limited. Mara agreed and will change both.

summary: Looked at the Postgres autovacuum on the audit log table, which had 18 percent dead rows, and tuned its scale factor so it runs more often on that table alone.
body:
The audit log table grew a lot with the export tests and the autovacuum was lagging. pg_stat_user_tables showed 18 percent dead rows and a last autovacuum from two days before.

The default scale factor of 0.2 is too high for a table of this size. Set autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 for this table only, in a migration, so other tables keep the defaults.

After a manual run the dead rows went to under 1 percent. Will check again in a few days that the autovacuum keeps up.

summary: Tried batching the schema registry lookups in the ingest worker and found the lookup is already cached per process, so the change gave nothing and was dropped.
body:
The idea was that the worker asks the schema registry once per event type and batch, which looked like many calls in a trace. Wrote a small change that collects the types of a batch and asks once.

Then measured it with the staging stream. The registry saw 12 requests per minute per worker before and 11 after. The existing in-process cache with a 60 second TTL already handles it. The calls in the trace were cache hits.

The change added code and gave no gain, so it was removed and the branch reset. Wrote a note in the registry docs that the worker cache exists, so nobody else tries this.

The time was not lost completely: found that the cache TTL is not configurable. Opened a small task for that.

summary: Enabled the rounded cache keys for the second and third large customers and wrote a short comparison, with hit rates at 71 and 69 percent after a day.
body:
After a calm day with the first customer, turned on the flag for the other two large customers. The numbers were taken after a full day.

Customer two went from 46 to 71 percent, customer three from 44 to 69 percent. The p95 of the search API fell for both, by 15 to 20 percent.

Checked the Redis memory: the query cache uses about 9 percent less than before, as fewer distinct keys are stored. The TTL of 5 minutes is the same.

One complaint from a customer came through Sam: a dashboard did not show an event from 40 seconds before. That is the rounding. Answered that dashboards can lag by up to a minute for long ranges and added a line to the docs.

Decided to turn the flag on for all customers next week, after one more look at the smaller ones, whose ranges are shorter and may gain less.

Wrote the numbers into the team notes.

summary: Extended the schema registry compatibility check to nested objects and arrays, found a performance problem with deep schemas, and fixed it with a memoized walk.
body:
The check did not look deeper than three levels. Removed that limit and made it walk objects and arrays recursively. Array item types are compared like fields.

On the test set the check was fast, but one customer has a schema with 14 levels and 900 fields, and the check took 11 seconds. The walk compared the same subtrees again and again, because the schema refers to shared definitions by reference.

Added memoization on the pair of definition ids. The same check now takes 80 ms.

Also added rules for arrays: changing the item type follows the rules of a field type change, and changing an array into a single value is always rejected. Wrote tests for both.

There is one case I am not sure about: a field that moves from the top level into a nested object. Technically it is a delete and an add. For now it is rejected, and the message points to the new version path. Will ask Mara if she wants a rename-with-move rule.

The full test suite is green. Updated the compatibility rules document with the nested cases.

summary: Asked by Sam why a customer sees different counts in the console and in the export, and traced it to the console using rounded cache keys while the export reads from Postgres.
body:
Sam brought a ticket where a customer compared the number of audit entries on the console page with the exported file, and they differed by 14.

First guess was the cache change of last week. But the audit log page does not use the query cache at all. It reads from Postgres directly.

The export started at 10:02 and the page was read at 10:07, so 14 entries came between them. The customer had saved the page count and compared it later. Nothing wrong with the data.

Checked all the same: counted the rows in Postgres for the account with the export's time range, and got exactly the export's footer count.

Answered Sam with that explanation and suggested to put the export start time in the file header, so a customer can see the cut-off. Added that to the audit export branch as a small change, with a line in the header.

No bug found, but the header will help the next ticket.

summary: Looked at Redis memory by key group after the TTL findings and set expiry on the four groups without one, which should stop the slow growth of used memory.
body:
Earlier I found four key groups without any expiry in the console backend. Today I counted them with a scan on the replica and sized them.

The groups are: console user preferences, saved search drafts, the export job status, and the import progress. Together they use about 1.4 GB, which is 11 percent of the memory.

For each group I checked with the code owners what a sensible lifetime is. Preferences are small and should stay, so they move to Postgres later and for now get 90 days, refreshed on read. Drafts get 30 days. Export job status gets 7 days, as the export files do. Import progress gets 7 days too, matching the loader checkpoints.

Wrote the change as a small helper that sets the TTL on every write, so a new key cannot be forgotten. Added a lint rule in the console backend that fails when a Redis set call has no TTL option.

For the keys already there, wrote a one-time script that sets the expiry by scanning with a low rate. Ran it in staging first: 2.1 million keys, 14 minutes, no impact on latency.

Ran it in production at a low rate in the afternoon. Watched the command latency in Grafana: no change. Used memory will fall over the next days as keys expire.

The lint rule found two more places with no TTL in tests, which are fine as tests. Added an exception for test files.

Next check is in a week, to see that the memory line is flat.

summary: Wrote the first version of the monthly shard layout check script for the search index, which compares document counts and boosts between old and new shards.
body:
The plan for the shard migration needs a check that can be run again and again. Wrote a script, scripts/shardcheck.ts, which takes a customer and a month.

For the old layout it asks the alias for the customer with a date filter. For the new one it asks the monthly index. It compares three things: the document count, the sum of a numeric field, and the top ten results of 20 stored queries.

The stored queries are taken from the real search log of the customer, with the boosts that search v2 applies. This is important, because a boost that works on one layout can behave differently if the term statistics differ between shards.

Tested it on a copy in the staging cluster, where I built a monthly index for one small customer by hand. Counts matched. The sum matched. Two of 20 queries had a different order of results at rank 8 and 9, with nearly equal scores.

The difference comes from the shard-local term statistics. Decided that a swap in rank between results with a score difference under 1 percent is not a failure. Added a tolerance to the script and print the cases so a person can look.

The script exits with a non-zero code on any other difference, so it can run in a pipeline.

Also added a mode that checks the alias: it makes sure the alias points to exactly one index per month and that no month is covered by two indices. That was a point from the list of checks made earlier.

Next step is to run it on a medium-sized customer and time it, as the stored queries could take long on large ones.

summary: Ran the shard check on a medium customer, found it takes 9 minutes because of the stored queries, and reduced it to 2 minutes with parallel requests and a size cap.
body:
Ran shardcheck on a medium customer with 14 months of data. It took 9 minutes, which is too long for a step that will run for every month.

Profiled it. Nearly all the time was in the stored queries, which ran one by one, and three of them were wide full text queries that fetched 100 hits each. The count and sum steps took seconds.

Changed two things. The queries now run with a concurrency of 4, which is safe for the staging cluster and will be set lower for production. And the result size is capped at 20, because the check only compares the top ten.

The run now takes 2 minutes. The results are the same as before: counts and sums equal, one rank swap within the tolerance.

While at it, I looked at what happens with a customer whose months are very uneven. One month had 40 times the documents of the next. The check works, but the monthly index for the big month is large, and a note in the plan says to look at the shard count per month index. Added the doc count per month to the output so the plan can use it.

Also fixed a bug with the month boundary. The old layout filter used less-or-equal on the end of the month and the new index uses less-than, so a document at midnight on the first day was counted twice in one test. Both now use half-open ranges.

Wrote the usage into the README of the scripts folder, with the arguments and the exit codes. Tobias will want to run it from the pipeline, so I described the environment variables for the cluster address.

Next: a dry run of the migration steps for one small customer in staging with the check at the end.

summary: Dry-ran the migration steps for one small customer in staging, from copy to alias switch, and found that the alias switch is not atomic in my first version.
body:
Did a dry run for a small customer in staging: create the monthly indices, copy the documents with reindex, run the check, switch the alias.

The copy worked. 11 months, about 3 million documents, 14 minutes in total. The check passed.

The alias switch was the problem. My first version removed the old alias and then added the new one in two calls. Between the calls, a search for the customer returned an error for about 200 ms. In a loop test with 50 requests per second, 9 requests failed.

The alias API has an actions endpoint that does both in one request, which is atomic. Changed the script to use it. The same loop test showed no failures.

Also thought about the rollback. The old index stays until the new one has been used for a week, so switching back is the same atomic call in the other direction. Wrote this as a step in the runbook.

A second finding: writes during the copy. New events keep coming in for the customer, and the reindex copies a snapshot. Events that arrive after the start would be missing in the monthly index. For the current month this matters. The plan is to dual write for the current month during the migration, and to run the check for older months only.

Wrote the dual write idea down for Tobias and Mara, as it touches the nightly reindex job and the ingest side. No code yet, the design needs a decision.

Updated the runbook with the atomic alias call, the rollback and the dual write question.

summary: Made the alias switch of the monthly shard migration atomic with a single alias update call, and re-ran the small customer dry run in staging with no gap in search results.
body:
The dry run of the last days showed that my first alias switch was not atomic: it removed the old alias and then added the new one in two calls. For a short moment a search for that customer returned nothing. Today I fixed this in the migration script.

The OpenSearch alias API accepts a list of actions in one request, and all of them are applied together. The script now sends the remove and the add action in one call, so a query sees either the old shards or the new ones. I also changed the order of the steps: copy, run the shard check, switch the alias, and keep the old index for a day.

To test it, I ran a loop of 20 searches per second against the staging alias for the small customer while the switch ran. Before the change the loop showed 3 empty answers in a run. After the change I did five runs and saw none, and the result counts were the same on both sides of the switch.

I also tested what happens when the call fails half way, by pointing the new alias at an index name that does not exist. OpenSearch rejected the whole request and the old alias stayed in place, which is the behavior we need. The script now logs both alias states before and after, so the person doing the migration can check them. One more finding: the write alias must be switched in the same request, otherwise new events from the ingest side would land in the old index for a short time. I added that action and a test for it. Next is a dry run for a medium customer with the shard check included, and a rollback step that points the alias back.

summary: Merged the registry nested-schema work to staging and watched the check run on 200 real schema updates over the afternoon without a false rejection.
body:
Deployed the schema registry branch to staging with the nested object and array support. The staging traffic includes schema updates from a replay of real customers.

Over the afternoon 200 updates came through. 186 were accepted, 14 rejected. I read all 14. Twelve were real breaking changes, such as a changed type or a removed required field. Two were a field moved into a nested object, which is the case I had doubts about.

Asked Mara. She said that moves are rare and the customers would rather be told to use a new version than have a silent change, so the rejection stays. The message text for it was improved to name the old and new path.

Latency of the check was 3 to 40 ms, with the deep schema at the high end.

No errors in the logs. The registry service memory is stable. The memoization cache is cleared per check, so it does not grow.

Next step is the documentation of the rules for customers, which Sam will edit, and then production.

summary: Turned the compatibility rules into a customer-facing doc page with a table of allowed, versioned and rejected changes and four worked examples.
body:
Took the rules document and wrote a version for customers. The first part is a table with three columns: allowed, needs a new version, always rejected. Each row is one kind of change, such as adding an optional field or widening an integer.

Then four examples, taken from real rejections with names removed. For each, what the customer sent, what the registry answered and what to do instead.

Kept the language plain, as Sam asked. Left out the internal details such as the memoization and the cache.

Sam will edit it tomorrow and add it to the public docs after a check of the error message texts against the page.

summary: Answered Tobias's question on whether the Redis minor upgrade can run before the shard work, and said yes, because the two do not share any step.
body:
Tobias asked whether the Redis minor upgrade should wait for the search index migration. The migration uses Redis only for the query cache, and the cache is flushed per customer at the alias switch anyway.

The upgrade steps from the staging run have a rollback point and a pool settings check. Neither touches the search cluster.

So the order does not matter. Suggested doing the upgrade first, in a quiet window, so that a cache problem is not confused with a migration problem later. Tobias agreed.

summary: Went through the on-call alerts of the last two weeks and found that 9 of 31 pages were the same noisy queue lag alert, so the threshold now needs a duration.
body:
Exported the pages from PagerDuty for the last two weeks and grouped them by alert name. There were 31 pages in total.

The largest group was the queue consumer lag alert, with 9 pages. All 9 resolved themselves within two minutes. The rule fires when the lag is over 10,000 for a single evaluation, and short bursts at the top of the hour trigger it.

Added a for-duration of 5 minutes to the rule in the alert code. A real stuck consumer will still page within 5 minutes, which is fine as the lag grows by thousands per minute.

The second group was the unhealthy target count of the load balancer, 4 pages, all during deploys. Added a mute for the deploy window by checking the deploy marker metric. Tobias should check that the marker is set by the pipeline for all services.

The remaining 18 pages were different alerts and mostly real. Left those as they are.

Wrote a summary table into the on-call notes with the before and after expected page counts. Expected is about 18 pages in two weeks instead of 31.

Checked the rule changes with promtool and the unit tests for the rules, all pass.

summary: Reviewed the rate-limits branch after Mara's update and approved it, with the burst value now in key settings and the remaining burst in the response header.
body:
Mara pushed the changes from my review. The burst factor is read from the key settings and cached together with the limit, so a change in the console takes effect within a minute.

The response header X-RateLimit-Burst-Remaining is set on every response, and on a 429 it is joined by a Retry-After value. Tested with a script that sends 300 requests in a burst: the header counted down correctly and the 429 came at the expected point.

The Lua script uses the timeout guard from earlier in the week, and the test with the slow Redis passes.

One small remark was left: the docs example still shows the old header list. Mara will update it. Approved the branch for staging.

summary: Ran the schema registry check against the ten next-largest customers' schemas and found one more rule that wrongly rejects a renamed optional field, now fixed.
body:
After the five largest customers last week, I took the next ten by event volume and ran the compatibility check over their full schema history. Nine passed without a single false rejection. The tenth had an optional field renamed with an alias, and the draft rule treated it as a removal plus an addition.

I changed the rule so that a rename with a declared alias counts as a versioned change, not a rejected one. The rule lives in the compatibility module of the registry, and I added a test with the real case, anonymized. The check still rejects a rename without an alias, which is what we want.

I re-ran all fifteen customers after the change. There were 412 schema updates in the history, and the result is the same as before for all but the one renamed field. The run took 38 seconds in total, so the memoized walk from the nested work holds up.

The doc page needs one more row in the table of versioned changes for the alias case. I wrote that down for tomorrow. Nothing else is open on the rules.

summary: Ran the schema registry check against the full set of schemas from the five largest customers' staging replay and found that the field-order check flagged harmless reorderings, now ignored.
body:
After the nested-schema work went to staging, I wanted one more pass over real data before the registry check is turned on for all customers. I took the schema update history of the five largest customers from the last two months, about 1,400 updates, and replayed them in order against the check. Most passed as expected, but 37 were rejected for a reason that did not match the compatibility rules in the doc page.

All 37 had the same cause. The customer's tooling regenerates the schema file on each release and the properties come out in a different order. My walk compared the property lists by position for objects inside arrays, so a pure reordering looked like a type change on two fields. The rules never say that order matters, and for JSON events it does not.

I changed the comparison to build a map by property name before comparing, for objects and for the item schemas of arrays. This also removed a small cost, because the old position-based compare did a second pass for deep schemas. The memoized walk from yesterday stays as it is, and I checked that the cache key still includes the schema version so a reordered copy is not treated as the same entry by mistake.

I added four test cases: a pure reorder, a reorder plus a real type change, a reorder inside a nested array item, and a reorder of required names. The last one needed care, because the required list is an array of strings and its order is also irrelevant, so I sort it before comparing. The tests pass, and the replay now shows zero false rejections across the 1,400 updates.

One real rejection remained in the replay and I looked at it by hand. It was a field that changed from string to integer, which the rules reject on purpose, so the check is right there. I noted it for Sam, since that customer may write in to ask.

Next I will run the same replay on the next ten customers by size, then ask Mara to look at the diff before the check becomes blocking. The branch is still the schema registry one and nothing was deployed from this session.

summary: Went through the replayed search queries of the large customers to find which ones still run without a time range, so the 90 day default window can be sized before it is specified.
body:
Before anyone writes the default window into the search API, I wanted to know how many real queries would be affected. I took a day of production search queries from the access log for the three large customers and counted the ones with no time range at all. It was 22 percent of the queries for the first customer, 9 percent for the second and 31 percent for the third.

For those queries I checked how old the hits on the first page were. For the third customer, 94 percent of the first-page hits were within 90 days, and for the other two it was above 97 percent. So a default of 90 days would change the first page for only a small share of queries. That is a good sign for the monthly shard layout too, because a window of 90 days touches at most four month shards instead of all of them.

The odd group was a set of about 600 queries per day from one integration of the third customer. They look for a single order number and always have no range, and the hits are often older than a year. With a plain default window these lookups would return nothing and the customer would think the data is gone. I wrote this down as a risk for the spec.

My suggestion is to keep the default at 90 days, but make it a per-customer setting and allow an explicit all option on every query. For queries that match one exact identifier field, the API could skip the window, since those are cheap anyway. I have not checked how the query parser marks exact fields, so I looked at the search-v2 parser and found that it already tags them, which makes this rule easy to add.

I put the numbers and the order number case into a short note for Mara. Next step is her view on the exact identifier exception, then the spec.

summary: Looked at why the search API p99 rose by 30 ms after the cache key change and found it comes from the cache miss path of a fourth customer, not from the rounding.
body:
The latency graph showed p99 for search up from about 210 ms to 240 ms since the rounded cache keys went live. I first suspected the rounding, since a coarser key might hit stale entries and trigger a refresh storm.

The refresh counters did not move. I split the p99 by customer and the rise comes entirely from one customer outside the three we changed. That customer sends long wildcard queries that never hit the cache, and their volume doubled last week after they enabled a new dashboard.

So the rounding is not at fault. The wildcard queries are slow in OpenSearch itself, about 600 ms each. I wrote the finding down and asked Mara whether the query parser of search-v2 can reject leading wildcards or cap them. No code change today.

summary: Replayed a day of production queries against the monthly shard layout in staging and found two query types that fan out to too many shards, with a fix proposed for one.
body:
The monthly layout splits each index by month, so a query without a time range must visit every month. I replayed 24 hours of real queries from three customers against a staging copy of the new layout to see how many shards each query touches.

Most queries carry a time range. 88 percent touch three shards or fewer, and latency was the same as with the customer layout. Two types are different: the queries with no time filter at all, and the ones with a range of more than a year.

For the first type the median is 14 shards touched and the latency is about 1.6 times higher. For the second type the number is 9 shards. Both are rare, together about 4 percent of the replay, but the large customers use them for audits.

I looked at what the console sends. The console search box sends no time range when the user leaves the field empty. That is a front end default, so I asked Lena whether the console could send the last 30 days by default, with a visible option for all time.

For the API queries without a range I suggest a default window in the search API, documented, with an explicit all option. That changes behavior, so I want Mara's view before any code. I wrote the numbers and the two options into the shard plan document.

Nothing was changed on staging beyond the copy. The migration itself still waits for the plan to be agreed.

summary: Wrote and tested a query-side shard pruning step for search-v2 so a time range maps to month shards, and measured a 35 percent drop in shards touched on the replay.
body:
The parser of search-v2 already extracts time ranges for the boosts. I reused that part to compute the list of month shards a query needs and to build the index pattern from it, so a range of two weeks goes to at most two shards.

The first version broke on ranges with an open end, like after a date with no upper bound. It produced an empty list and the search returned nothing. I changed it so an open end means up to the current month, and an open start means the oldest month that exists for the customer, which comes from a small cached list.

I added unit tests for 11 range shapes, including a range crossing a year boundary and a range in the future. One test showed an off-by-one at a month end when the time zone is not UTC, because I converted after the cut. The conversion happens first now.

Then I replayed the same day of queries as this afternoon. Total shards touched fell by 35 percent compared with querying all months. Queries with a range now cost the same as before the layout change.

Results were identical to the old layout in a diff of 4000 queries, apart from 6 where the order of equal-scored documents differed. I checked those six and they are ties, so they are not a problem, but I added a secondary sort on the document id to make it stable.

The queries without any range still touch all shards. That depends on the default window decision. The cache of the month list has a TTL of ten minutes, and I put it in a new Redis key group with the search prefix, as the key naming proposal asked.

Tomorrow I want Mara to look at the diff, and to decide about the default window.

summary: Mara agreed to a default window of 90 days for search queries without a time range, with an explicit all option, so the search API change is now specified.
body:
Mara and I talked through the default window over chat this morning. She prefers 90 days over 30, because several customers search for incidents within a quarter and a smaller window would surprise them.

The API will apply 90 days only when no range is given, and it will say so in the response in a field named window_applied. A request can set range to all to remove the limit. The console will show the applied window next to the search box.

We discussed whether this breaks existing integrations. Probably a few of them rely on all-time search. To be safe the change goes in as opt-in per customer first, with a flag in the account settings, and becomes the default after a notice of four weeks that Sam will write.

I updated the shard plan document with the decision and the flag. The code is next, in the search API, not in the parser. Lena got a note about the console field.

summary: Implemented the per-customer default window flag in the search API and tested it on staging with the three large customers' replayed queries.
body:
The flag is a boolean in the account settings table, named default_window, read through the same cached settings call as the other account flags, so it adds no query to the hot path. When it is set and a query has no range, the API adds a filter of the last 90 days.

The response now carries window_applied with the start and end of the window used, or null when none was applied. The all value of the range parameter bypasses the window.

I wrote 8 tests: flag on and off, range given, range all, a range that is invalid, and the cached settings after a change. All pass. Replaying a day of queries of the three large customers with the flag on, about 5 percent of their queries got a window, and those ran 40 percent faster at the median.

Two things remain. The console must show window_applied, which is Lena's part, and the docs need the new field and the all option. I opened a ticket for each.

summary: Checked the Redis minor upgrade steps with Tobias and found that the client library needs no change, so the upgrade is set for a quiet evening this week.
body:
Tobias had the runbook for the Redis minor upgrade ready, and I reviewed it from the application side. The risk is the client, since the console session store and the rate limiter both hold connections to it.

I read the release notes between our version and the target. There are no changes to the protocol and no removed commands that we use. I checked our usage by grepping for the commands in the console, the search API and the ingest limiter, and found only basic ones plus the Lua script of the limiter.

I ran the limiter script tests against a container with the target version, and they pass. Connections reconnect on a restart in about two seconds with the current pool settings, which are the 50 maximum from last week.

Tobias will do the upgrade on a replica first, then fail over. I asked him to watch the pool size metric during the failover.

summary: Built a small tool that lists stale month shards and empty aliases after the dry-run migrations, so cleanup of the staging cluster no longer depends on memory.
body:
After the dry runs for small customers the staging cluster had old copies, aliases pointing at nothing and a few shards with zero documents. I had cleaned them by hand twice, and that will not work for the real migration with 12 shards.

The tool is a script of about 120 lines in the migration folder. It reads all indices and aliases, groups them by customer, and prints what is stale: an index with no alias and no writes in 7 days, an alias with no index, and an index with zero documents.

First it only lists. A flag called apply deletes the aliases and indices, but only after an interactive confirmation that prints the exact list. I made deletion skip anything that has the name of a live alias target, and anything younger than a day.

I ran it on staging and it found 23 stale indices, about 41 GB. Two of them I would not have deleted by hand, because they looked current. They were the copies from the first dry run, from before the atomic alias switch, and had the old naming.

I deleted 21 and kept the two for a comparison with the new run. The script printed the freed space, and the cluster health went from yellow to green because of unassigned replicas of the stale indices.

I added the tool to the migration checklist as a step after each customer, and a second use before the final switch, to check nothing is left over.

One limit is that it cannot tell a stale index from one in use by a script outside the repo. For production I will run it in list mode only and look at the output.

summary: The Redis minor upgrade ran on the replica without trouble, and the failover caused one blip of 40 failed limiter calls that fail open as designed.
body:
Tobias upgraded the replica first, and I watched the dashboards. After the failover the pool size metric dipped and recovered in about 3 seconds.

The limiter logged 40 timeouts in that window. They hit the 50 millisecond guard and failed open, so no customer was blocked, and no requests were refused wrongly. The console session store showed no logouts.

After the failover the old primary was upgraded too. Memory use before and after was the same within one percent, and the hit rate of the query cache stayed in its normal band.

I wrote a short note in the upgrade ticket with the timeline. The runbook can say that a failover costs a few seconds of open limiter. Nothing else is needed.

summary: Investigated a slow reports query in Postgres that scans the audit log, and added a partial index that cut it from 4.2 seconds to 60 milliseconds.
body:
Sam relayed a complaint from a customer that the access report in the console takes several seconds. I found the query in the slow log: it filters the audit log by account and action type and a time range, then sorts by time.

The plan showed a sequential scan after a bitmap step on the account index. The table is large, and the action filter matches only a small part, about 3 percent, because the report asks only for exports and permission changes.

I tried a composite index on account, time with action in the include list. That helped a little, from 4.2 to 1.1 seconds. Then I tried a partial index on account and time, with a where clause on the three action types the report uses. The plan went to an index scan and the query took about 60 milliseconds.

The partial index is small, about 200 MB against 6 GB for the full composite one. That matters for the vacuum work I did last week on the same table.

I created it on staging first with the concurrent option and checked that the other audit queries did not change plans. Then I wrote the migration file. A risk is that a new action type is added to the report and the index will not cover it. I put a comment next to the report query and a test that checks the list of types matches the index definition.

Mara reviewed the migration and approved it. It runs in the next deploy window, and I will check the index size and the plan on production afterwards.

summary: Looked at the loader's retry delays for large file uploads and changed the backoff to start at 2 seconds with jitter, since synchronized retries hit the same minute.
body:
In the loader logs, retries of failed chunk uploads from several imports clustered at the same second, since all used a fixed delay of 5 seconds. When storage had a short problem, they all came back together.

I changed the delay to exponential backoff with a base of 2 seconds, a factor of 2, a cap of 60 seconds and random jitter of up to 25 percent. The maximum number of attempts stays at 6.

I tested with a fake storage that fails for 20 seconds. The old code issued all retries inside 3 seconds of the recovery, while the new one spread them across about 15 seconds. All chunks still arrived and the checkpoint was correct.

The config now takes the base and cap from settings, with the values above as defaults. I added a test for the jitter range with a seeded random source.

summary: Reviewed the day's pages and found the queue lag alert now fires 60 percent less after the duration was added, with one real incident still caught.
body:
The queue lag alert got a for-duration of 5 minutes last week. Looking at the pages since then, there were 4 instead of the usual 10 for the same span.

Of the 4, one was a real lag of 12 minutes during a deploy of the consumer, which the alert should catch. The other three lasted between 5 and 7 minutes and came from the batch import of one customer, a known pattern.

I considered a lower severity for the import pattern but did not make a rule for it. Distinguishing the import needs a label on the topic that does not exist, and adding one is more than the alert is worth.

I left the threshold as it is and noted the numbers in the alert ticket, which can be closed.

summary: Confirmed the Postgres audit log index is used on production after the deploy, with the report query at 55 milliseconds and the index at 190 MB.
body:
The migration ran in this morning's deploy window. I checked the plan of the report query on production with explain, and it uses the partial index.

The query takes about 55 ms for the account that complained, and about 80 ms for the largest account. The index size is 190 MB, matching staging.

I also checked that writes to the audit log did not slow down. Insert latency in the metrics is unchanged. I told Sam the report is fast now, so she can answer the customer.

summary: Worked on the audit export footer totals for exports over several chunks, found that the total was summed per chunk and rounded, and made it exact.
body:
A compliance customer compared the footer of an export with their own count and found the total off by 3 rows on an export of 2.1 million. I reproduced it on staging with a customer of a similar size.

The export writes chunks of 50000 rows in parallel. Each chunk reports its row count, and the footer sums them. The sum was right, but the count of the last chunk was taken before a final filter that removes rows marked as redacted after the query started.

So the chunk counted rows it had not written. The difference was small, but a footer that is wrong is a bad fault in a compliance export.

I changed the writer to count rows at the moment it writes them, and return that number. The footer sums the written counts. I also added a final check that reads the file back, counts lines, and compares with the footer; a mismatch fails the export with a clear message instead of delivering it.

The read back costs about 4 percent of the export time on a large file, which I think is fine for this kind of export. I made it a setting, on by default.

Tests: a unit test with redaction during the export, and an integration test with 3 chunks where one has all rows redacted. The second case exposed that an empty chunk produced a file with only a header. It is skipped now.

Then I re-ran the 2.1 million export. The footer matched the line count exactly, and the check passed. Total time went from 11 to 11.5 minutes.

I wrote to Sam what to tell the customer, and which exports in the last month may have been off. The log has the chunk counts, so I could list them: 7 exports, all with deviations of 5 rows or fewer.

summary: Sent Sam the list of 7 audit exports from the last month with small footer deviations, so the affected customers can be told.
body:
From the chunk count logs I built a table of the exports whose footer differed from the written rows. It has the customer, the export id, the footer count and the real count.

Seven exports are affected, from four customers. The largest deviation is 5 rows, the smallest 1. In all cases the footer was higher than the file.

I sent the table to Sam with a short text she can adapt. It says what happened, that the files themselves are complete and contain no wrong rows, and that new exports are checked against the footer.

I offered to regenerate the 7 exports. Sam will ask the customers if they want that.

summary: Answered Lena's question about how the console should show the applied search window, and suggested a small label with a link that sets the range to all.
body:
Lena asked how to present window_applied in the console. The field holds the start and end of the window or null.

My suggestion is a line under the search box that reads like last 90 days, shown only when the field is not null. Next to it a link, show all time, which repeats the search with range set to all. The link should not change the default for the next search.

I told her that the API returns the dates in UTC and the label should round to days, because the exact time of day means nothing to a user.

She will make a version for the staging console tomorrow. I will switch on the account flag for a test account so she has data.

summary: Found that a Redis key group for the month list cache had no TTL set by mistake in the new search code and fixed it before it reached staging.
body:
While looking at Redis memory by key group, I saw the new search month list key was written with a plain set call. The code in the shard pruning step used a helper that did not pass the TTL option.

The key per customer is small, but customers come and go, and without expiry it would grow like the four groups I fixed last week. Nothing was on production, only on my staging runs.

I changed the helper call to include the ten minute TTL, and added a test that reads the TTL of every key the search module writes. The test fails if any key has none.

I also searched the rest of the code for the same helper. One other use, a flag cache in the console, passes its TTL correctly.

summary: Wrote a rehearsal plan for the full 12-shard migration with timings from the dry runs and a rollback for each step, and Tobias reviewed the infrastructure side.
body:
The dry runs gave me real timings, so I wrote the rehearsal plan for the whole migration as a document with steps, expected durations and a rollback for each.

The steps per customer group are: create the month indices, copy documents, run the shard check, switch the alias, watch search for ten minutes and clean up. For a medium customer the copy took about 25 minutes, and the check two minutes. The large customers will take hours, so they run at night.

The rollback before the alias switch is to delete the new indices, which has no effect on search. After the switch the rollback is to point the alias back to the old index, which stays for 48 hours. The single alias call that is atomic works in both directions.

The main risk is disk space. The cluster needs room for both layouts at once. Tobias calculated that we have 38 percent free, and the largest group needs about 20 percent, so one group at a time is safe, and two at once is not.

Tobias also asked for a pause of the nightly reindex job during the copy, since both read a lot. I added a step to skip the reindex for a customer while their copy runs. I did not touch the job itself. It still starts at the same time as before, and we know it can run into the backup window, which is a separate question. I wrote down that the start time of the job may be changed, and that the plan should be checked again if it is.

We agreed on the order: small customers first, then medium, then the three large ones, each large one on a separate night. I added a stop rule: if search p99 rises by more than 20 percent during a copy, the copy pauses.

The document has an owner list for each step, and the on-call engineer gets a short version. We still need a decision on the date, which depends on the default window being live.

summary: Dropped an attempt to compress the audit export files on the fly with a streaming library, since it broke the resume of the export and saved little.
body:
I tried a streaming compression library for audit export files, hoping to reduce download size for large customers. The files are CSV with many repeated values, so I expected a good ratio.

The ratio was fine, around 6 to 1. The problem was resume. An export that fails in the middle restarts from the last finished chunk, and a stream that is compressed as one piece cannot be cut at a chunk border without writing a new stream per chunk.

Writing one stream per chunk works, but then the customer gets a file made of many concatenated streams, which a few tools cannot read. Two of the customer scripts I know of use such a tool.

The download is already compressed by the web server in transit, so the saving on the wire is the same. The only gain would be storage, which is small.

I dropped the change and removed the dependency from the branch. I wrote the reason in the export ticket so nobody tries it again without a plan for the resume.

summary: Ran the first full rehearsal of the migration plan on the staging cluster with three medium customers and fixed two problems in the copy script.
body:
I followed the rehearsal document step by step on staging for three medium customers, with the real timings in mind. The aim was to find faults in the plan, not to test speed.

The first problem came in the copy. The script used a scroll with a fixed keep-alive of one minute, and for the second customer a slow batch exceeded it, so the scroll expired and the copy stopped with a search context error. I raised the keep-alive to five minutes and made the script refresh it on each batch. It also now resumes from the last copied document id instead of from the start.

The second problem was in the shard check. For a customer with documents in the last hour, the count of the old index was higher than the new one, because new events kept arriving during the copy. The check treated this as a failure. I made the check compare documents up to the start time of the copy, and a separate step copies the documents after that time just before the switch.

With both fixes the three customers went through: copy, check, switch, watch, clean up. Search kept working throughout, and I replayed queries during each switch with no empty result.

Timings: 22, 27 and 31 minutes for the copy, and about 2 minutes for each check. The delta copy before the switch took under a minute each.

The stale shard tool found nothing after the cleanup step, which was the intended result. The cluster went back to green.

I updated the rehearsal document with the new keep-alive, the delta step and the changed check. Disk use on staging peaked at 31 percent above the baseline for one customer, which fits Tobias's estimate.

Still open: the rehearsal with a large customer, and the decision on the date. Mara wants to look at the delta step, because she is concerned about events that are updated and not only added. I think updates are handled, because the copy uses the document id, but I will add a test for it.

summary: Wrote the test for updated documents in the migration delta copy and confirmed that an update during the copy ends up in the new index once.
body:
Mara's question was whether an event updated during the copy could appear twice or with the old content. The documents keep their id, so a copy to the new index with that id overwrites.

I wrote a test that starts a copy of 5000 documents, updates 200 of them in the middle, runs the delta step and compares the new index to the old one.

All 5000 documents are present exactly once, and the 200 updated ones have the new content. The count and a hash of the content match.

summary: Rehearsed the migration for one large customer on staging with a copy of their real data, hit a disk watermark, and added a space check to the plan before each copy.
body:
I loaded a copy of the largest customer's index into staging last week, and today I ran the migration rehearsal on it. It is about 380 GB, so it shows what the production nights will look like.

The copy started well, at about 90 MB per second, and I expected around 70 minutes. After 40 minutes the cluster went to a red state for the new index. The cause was the disk watermark: staging nodes passed the high level, and OpenSearch stopped allocating shards to them.

The copy script did not notice, as it kept sending bulk requests that were rejected, and its retries kept going until I stopped it. That is a fault in the script, not only in the plan.

I made two changes. The script now reads the cluster allocation before each batch and pauses when any node is above 80 percent. It also treats a run of bulk rejections as a stop signal instead of retrying forever.

The second change is in the plan. A new first step estimates the space needed from the index size and compares it with the free space on every node, not on the cluster in total. For production, Tobias said the nodes are more evenly filled than on staging, but I want the check anyway.

After freeing space on staging, I deleted the partial new index and started again. This time the copy took 78 minutes and ended with no rejections. The shard check took about 6 minutes, with the parallel requests, and found the counts equal.

The delta step took 40 seconds because the staging replay of live events was small. Production will be larger. I measured the alias switch under replayed queries at about 200 queries per second, and saw no empty result and no error.

Search p99 during the copy rose by 9 percent on staging, below the stop rule of 20 percent. The production load will be higher, so I set the rule to pause the copy automatically and not rely on someone watching.

I updated the document with the disk check, the pause on allocation and the observed timings. A last point: the old index of this customer stays for 48 hours after the switch, so the peak disk use is the two layouts together. For the large customers the plan says one at a time, as before.

Next I will talk with Tobias about the night for the first large customer, and we will fix the date once the console shows the window label.

summary: Reviewed Lena's console change for the search window label, asked for the dates to be shown by the user's time zone, and approved the rest.
body:
Lena's change adds the line under the search box and the show all time link. I tried it on staging with the test account that has the default window flag on.

The label appears only when window_applied is set, and it disappears when the link is used. The link repeats the search with range set to all, as agreed, and does not change the default for the next search. That worked in my tests.

One thing I asked her to change: the label printed the dates in UTC, so a user in a time zone far from UTC saw a window that looked a day off. The label should convert to the browser time zone and round to days.

I also asked for the text to be put in the translation file, as the console does for the other labels. She had hard coded it in English.

A smaller point was the empty result state. When the window is applied and the search finds nothing, the empty message should suggest the show all time link, since the likely reason is that the events are older. She liked this and will add it.

I approved the pull request with these changes requested. The tests of the component pass. After the update, the docs ticket for the field and the all option is the last open item before the opt-in rollout can start.

I told Sam so she can plan the notice for customers.

summary: Re-ran the one-large-customer migration rehearsal on staging with the space check in place and it finished, with the copy taking 52 minutes instead of failing at the watermark.
body:
The rehearsal from earlier today stopped at a disk watermark, so this run used the new space check before each copy. The check compares the source shard size times 1.3 with the free space on the target nodes and stops the plan if it is short. On the first pass it stopped once, as intended, and the staging cluster got two extra data nodes for the test.

With the nodes added, the copy of the large customer's data ran through. It took 52 minutes for 410 GB, and the delta copy afterwards took 4 minutes. The document count in the old and new index matched exactly.

One thing came up in the check: the 1.3 factor is a guess. Actual use on the target peaked at 1.17 times the source during segment merges. I left the factor at 1.3 for safety and wrote the measured value into the plan.

Next is to time the cleanup of the old customer shards, which the plan has as the last step. The rollback for the copy step was also tried once by dropping the new month shards, and it took under a minute. Tobias will look at the node sizing for production tomorrow.

summary: Found that the console session keys in Redis were named in two different styles, wrote a rename plan with a dual-read period, and left the code change for tomorrow.
body:
While checking the key groups for TTLs after last week's finding, I listed all key prefixes in staging Redis. The session store uses sess:{id} while the older limiter code uses rl_{key}:count, and the new search code uses search:month:{customer}. Three styles in one instance make it hard to set alerts and to see memory by group.

I wrote a short naming rule: lowercase, colon separated, service first. The plan renames only the limiter keys, because the session keys are short lived and will change by themselves at the next release.

The limiter needs a dual-read period of one day, so counters are not reset by the rename. A reset would let clients burst for a minute, which is acceptable but not nice. The code reads the new key and falls back to the old one, and writes only the new one.

I did not change any code yet. Mara will look at the plan tomorrow, because the limiter is her area. I also added a line to the docs of the repo about the naming rule.

summary: Traced a rise in Postgres autovacuum time on the audit log table to a few very long transactions from the report job, and moved the job's reads to a snapshot with a shorter hold.
body:
Grafana showed autovacuum on the audit log table running 3 to 4 times longer than a month ago. The table is 61 GB now, which is part of it, but not the whole story. The dead tuple count stayed high after each run, which means vacuum could not remove rows.

I queried pg_stat_activity and found the cause: the nightly compliance report held a transaction open for about 40 minutes, because it read in a single cursor while it wrote files. Rows that changed during that time could not be cleaned.

I changed the job to read in chunks of 50,000 rows by id, each in its own short transaction. The output is the same, as the table is append only for the rows that matter. The test on staging with a copy of the data gave identical files by checksum.

The job now takes 9 minutes longer, which is fine at that hour. I did not touch the vacuum settings, because the settings were not the problem. I will check the dead tuple graph after tonight's run.

A second finding is that two old indexes on the table are unused according to the statistics. I did not drop them yet. I put them in the list for the next maintenance window, with the numbers.

summary: Added a jitter and a cap to the ingest client's reconnect delays in the Go SDK helper, after seeing that 300 clients reconnected in the same second after a deploy.
body:
After the deploy yesterday evening, the ingest API logs showed a spike of new connections within one second. About 300 test clients and some customer apps had reconnected at the same moment. The client helper used a fixed doubling delay with no randomness.

I changed the helper to use full jitter: the delay is random between zero and the current backoff. The cap is 30 seconds, and the first delay is 500 ms. I wrote a small simulation with 500 clients and a server restart, and the peak of connections per second fell from 500 to about 60.

A unit test checks that the delays stay within the bounds and that the cap holds. I did not test against the real load balancer, because the staging one has other limits.

The change needs a new SDK release, and customers update slowly. Sam will add a note to the changelog and the docs. The server side is not changed.

Open question: should the server send a retry-after header on 503? Mara thinks yes. I will write that up as a separate small task.

summary: Checked the dead tuple graph after last night's audit report run, and it dropped from 9 million to 1.2 million rows, so the short transaction fix works.
body:
The nightly report ran with the chunked reads this time. After the run, autovacuum finished in 11 minutes instead of 38. The dead tuple count on the audit log table fell to 1.2 million, from 9 million the night before.

The report itself took 49 minutes, ten more than before, which fits the plan. No lock waits showed up in the logs. I left the two unused indexes alone for now.

The graph is added to the Postgres dashboard so a return of the problem is visible.

summary: Wrote the production sizing for the migration to 12 month shards from the staging measurements, with disk needs of 1.2 TB extra during the copy and a note on the ordering of customers.
body:
Using the rehearsal numbers, I wrote a sizing page for the production migration. The copy needs about 1.2 TB of extra disk, because old and new indexes exist together until cleanup. The cluster has 1.9 TB free now, so there is room, but not for two shards at once.

The order is smallest customers first, so a problem shows up early with little data. The large customer goes last and alone, in a quiet hour. The staging time of 52 minutes for 410 GB gives a production estimate of about an hour, if the nodes are not busy.

The space check runs before each step and stops the plan if free space falls below 1.3 times the size. I also added a pause switch that Tobias can set, so the copy stops between steps without losing work.

Tobias will review the page tomorrow. If he agrees, the next step is to pick the night and tell Sam, so the customers get a short notice.

summary: Reviewed the loader-retry branch end to end, found that a failed chunk was retried with the old offset after a partial write, and fixed it with a test that kills the upload midway.
body:
Mara asked for a last look at loader-retry before it goes to staging. I read the diff and then ran the loader against a 3 GB NDJSON file with a proxy that cuts the connection at random points.

Most runs finished with the right row count. Two out of twenty ended with 1,800 extra rows. The cause was in the chunk logic: when a write failed after the server accepted part of the batch, the retry used the offset from before the chunk, so the accepted rows were sent twice.

The fix tracks the number of acknowledged rows per chunk and restarts from there. The server already returns that number in the response, but the loader ignored it on errors. When the response is lost, the loader asks for the status of the chunk before it sends again.
