I wrote a test with a fake server that accepts half a batch and then drops the connection. It failed before the fix and passes now. I also ran the proxy test 60 times, and all runs gave exact counts.

The backoff with jitter from last week is unchanged. One more thing I noticed is that the loader logs the full URL of the upload, which includes a signed token. I replaced it with the path only.

The branch is ready for staging, and I told Mara what was changed. I did not merge anything. The next step is a staging run with the customer-sized file of 12 GB.

summary: Ran the 12 GB loader test on staging and it finished in 31 minutes with exact counts after 14 injected connection drops.
body:
The staging run used the largest file we have from a customer, 12 GB of NDJSON with about 38 million events. The proxy dropped the connection 14 times during the upload, at random points.

The loader recovered each time. It asked for the status of the chunk, continued from the acknowledged row and went on. The final count in the table matched the file line count exactly. The whole run took 31 minutes, against about 27 minutes without drops.

Memory of the loader stayed under 400 MB. I watched it because the chunk status map grows with the file. It held at 18,000 entries, which is small.

One warning appeared in the logs about a slow status call of 6 seconds. It came from a staging node that was busy with the search rehearsal. I do not think it is a loader problem.

I wrote the result in the branch notes. What remains is the docs page for customers, which Sam will write, and the merge once Mara has approved.

summary: Answered Sam's question on what happens to a customer's upload if the loader is restarted midway, and explained that it resumes by chunk status for up to 24 hours.
body:
Sam asked for the support docs what happens when an upload stops because the loader restarts, for example during a deploy. I checked the code of the branch to give an exact answer.

The upload gets an id when it starts. The server keeps the chunk status for 24 hours. If the loader restarts, it can resume with the same id, and only unacknowledged rows are sent. After 24 hours the status is gone, and the upload starts from the beginning.

I also checked what the customer sees. The console shows the upload as running, and after a restart it shows paused until the loader resumes, which takes under a minute. There is no manual action needed.

One gap: if the customer's own client is stopped, the console shows running for 10 minutes before it changes to stalled. That is the existing timeout. I told Sam and suggested putting that in the docs, as it confuses people.

Sam will write the docs page tomorrow. I added a short summary of the answer to the branch notes.

summary: Merged the loader-retry branch after Mara's approval and a last green run of the 60 proxy tests, so the exact resume is now in the main line.
body:
Mara approved the branch this afternoon with one comment about a variable name, which I changed. The tests ran again in the pipeline and were green. I ran the proxy test another 60 times on the merged code, and all counts were exact.

The merge went into main and the pipeline deployed to staging. The production deploy is planned for the next regular release, not today, because of the migration work this week.

The branch notes are closed with the numbers of the 12 GB run. I removed the worktree of the branch.

Two follow-ups remain. The docs page from Sam, and a metric for the number of resumed uploads, so we can see how often it happens. I added the metric to the list for later.

summary: Looked at why the Redis memory graph climbs about 2 percent every day and found the month list cache growing with customers that were deleted, now cleaned by a daily sweep.
body:
The memory graph of the Redis primary shows a slow rise, and the last restart reset it. I grouped keys by prefix with a scan on the replica. Most groups are stable, but search:month:* has 14,000 keys for 40 customers, which is too many.

The keys belong to customer ids that no longer exist, left over from test accounts and two customers that left. The TTL fix from last week covers new keys, but these old ones were written before it, with a long TTL of 30 days that is refreshed on each read by a warm-up job.

The warm-up job read the customer list from an old snapshot file, so it kept refreshing keys of deleted customers. I changed it to read from Postgres. I also added a daily sweep that deletes month cache keys whose customer is not in the accounts table.

The first sweep removed 11,200 keys and about 600 MB. Memory dropped from 71 to 64 percent of the instance. I will watch the graph over the next days to see that the slope is gone.

The sweep is careful to use scan with small batches and a pause, so it does not block the primary. It ran in 40 seconds on staging.

summary: Dropped an attempt to batch the limiter's Redis calls with a pipeline per request, since it saved 0.2 ms and made the fail-open path harder to follow.
body:
I tried a pipeline for the two Redis calls the limiter makes per request, the counter increment and the expiry. In a local benchmark with 1,000 requests per second, the median time fell from 0.9 to 0.7 ms.

The cost was in the error handling. With a pipeline, a failure of one call needs its own branch to decide fail-open, and the tests for it grew to three times the size. For a gain of 0.2 ms, it does not pay.

I reverted the change and kept the benchmark script in the tools folder. The limiter stays as it is.

summary: Wrote the production-night runbook for the search index migration with the 12 shard steps, checks, pause rules and roles, and Tobias signed off on the infrastructure part.
body:
The sizing page and the rehearsals were turned into one runbook that can be followed at night without thinking. It lists the 12 shards in the agreed order, the command for each, and the check that must pass before the next one starts.

The checks for each step are the document count of old and new, a sample of 200 random documents compared by hash, and the search latency from the canary query that runs every minute. If the count differs by even one document, the step stops and the delta copy runs again. If it differs again, the rollback is to drop the new shard and keep the old alias.

The pause rules are: stop if the free disk falls below 1.3 times the next shard, if the canary p99 is over 400 ms for 3 minutes, or if the cluster health is not green. Tobias holds the pause switch, and I run the steps.

The large customer is step 12 and runs alone. The runbook has the estimated time of about an hour, and a rule that it does not start after 04:00, so a rollback is still possible before the morning traffic.

Tobias reviewed the infrastructure parts: the node sizing, the snapshot before the first step, and the alert silencing for the cluster during the run. He asked for a snapshot before each of the three largest customers, not only at the start. I added it, which costs about 10 minutes each.

What remains is choosing the night and telling Sam. I proposed the night after next. The nightly reindex runs late and overlaps with the backup window, which is a separate problem I want to look at, so I left the start time of the first step open until we know when the reindex ends. Tobias will confirm tomorrow.

summary: Ran the search index migration dry run on staging with the runbook's pause rules and found that the pause after shard 6 took longer than planned, so the runbook now has a check for it.
body:
Today's session was a timed walk through the production runbook on the staging cluster, with Tobias watching the infrastructure side. The goal was to check that the 12 shard steps, the checks after each step and the pause rules work as written, before they are used on the real night. Staging holds a scaled copy of three large customers, so the timings are smaller than production, but the order of steps is the same.

Shards 1 to 5 went as planned. Each copy finished inside its estimate, and the count check after each step matched the old index exactly. After shard 6 the runbook says to pause and wait until the search latency is back to normal, and this pause took 14 minutes instead of the 5 that the runbook assumed.

The cause was the query cache. After a shard moves, the cache keys for the month list are invalid, and the first queries all miss and go to the cluster at the same time. The p99 stayed high until the cache was warm again. Nothing was wrong with the migration itself, and no query failed.

The runbook now says to wait for the cache hit rate to climb above 80 percent, not for a fixed number of minutes. I added the Grafana panel for this rate to the runbook page with a link. The pause rule for a failed count check was also tested on purpose: I broke one count by hand, and the runbook stopped at the right step and gave the right rollback.

One step was unclear, the one that says who confirms the alias switch. Tobias and I agreed that he confirms it and the on-call person is told in the channel. Shards 7 to 12 were run without findings. The whole dry run took 3 hours and 10 minutes on staging. Next I want to run the rollback of shard 9 once, since that step has only been read, not run.

summary: Went through the 14 open alert rules that still point at the old AWS account names and fixed the labels, so pages show the right service and runbook link.
body:
Mara noticed a page last week where the runbook link led to a page that no longer exists. I listed all alert rules in the repo, since they are code now, and searched for the old account names and old wiki links.

Fourteen rules had old labels. Nine had a runbook link to the old wiki, three had a service label with the old account name, and two had both. This is left from the infrastructure migration, where the rules were moved but the labels were not checked.

I replaced the links with the current docs pages. For four rules there was no current page, so I wrote short runbook stubs with the first three checks and the owner. The service labels now use the names from the Terraform modules.

A test in the alert repo now fails if a rule has no runbook link or if the link does not match a known pattern. It found nothing else.

The change was reviewed by Tobias and deployed to Prometheus. I checked that the rules loaded without errors and that the alert list in Grafana shows the new labels.

The postmortem action to check everything a migration turned off is partly related. I added the finding to that action list, so the check includes labels and links, not only crons.

summary: Found a slow search API request path for customers with many saved queries, where each saved query was loaded with its own Postgres call, and replaced it with one query.
body:
The p99 of the saved queries endpoint was 800 ms for two customers, while the rest are under 100 ms. A trace showed one Postgres call per saved query, so a customer with 300 saved queries made 300 calls in sequence.

I changed the handler to load all saved queries of the account in one call, with the sharing settings joined. The result is grouped in memory. The response is the same, and I compared the JSON of both versions for the five largest accounts, with identical output.

On staging with a copy of the largest account, the time fell from 790 ms to 45 ms. The number of calls per request is one now, and I added an assertion in the test that counts calls, so the pattern does not come back.

I looked for the same pattern in the neighbours. The dashboards endpoint has a small version of it, with up to 10 calls, which is not worth changing now. I noted it.

The change is deployed to staging and goes out with the next release.

summary: Told Lena which of the saved query fields the console can rely on being present, after she asked while changing the list view.
body:
Lena asked whether the console can assume that the description and the last run time of a saved query are always set. I checked the schema and the handler. The description can be empty, and the last run time is null for queries never run.

I also checked the old data: about 12 percent of saved queries have an empty description, and 30 percent have no last run. The API returns null and not a missing field, in both cases.

I suggested she show a dash for both. She will do that, and I will add the nullable marks to the API docs, since they were missing.

summary: Updated the API docs for the saved queries endpoint with the nullable fields and the new faster response, and fixed an example that used a field name from the old version.
body:
After the answer to Lena, I opened the docs source for the saved queries endpoint. The field table did not mark description and last run time as nullable, so I added that, with a short sentence on when each is null.

While reading the examples, I found one that still used the field name query_text, which was renamed to query two versions ago. A customer following the example would have got an error. I fixed it and ran the example against staging to confirm it works.

I also checked the other examples on the page, and they are fine. The page has no mention of the number of saved queries per account, though there is a limit of 500 in the code. I added it to the limits section.

Sam will read the changes tomorrow, since they touch the support texts too.
